THE NEUROSCIENCE OF COGNITION

A Complete, Comprehensive, and Thorough Manuscript

Written for the beginner, the layperson, the learner, and the student.

Compiled for the konnectome repository, Certified_Neuroscientist corpus, of D. R. Dison, Founder, Artificial Intelligence University (AIU).

Date of compilation: August 10, 2026.


WHAT THIS BOOK IS

This is the manuscript built from the companion document THE_NEUROSCIENCE_OF_COGNITION_OUTLINE.txt, which sits beside this file in the same folder.

That outline has fifteen parts, eighty chapters, three hundred and thirty-two sections, and one thousand three hundred and twenty-five sub-sections.

This manuscript writes out every one of those line items.

Each line item was researched by web search before it was written, and the findings were then set down in the pages that follow.


WHAT THIS BOOK IS ABOUT

Cognition means the set of processes by which a nervous system acquires, represents, transforms, stores, retrieves, and acts upon information.

Neuroscience means the empirical and theoretical study of nervous systems at every scale, from the single ion channel up to the population of behaving organisms.

The neuroscience of cognition, therefore, is the research programme that seeks mechanistic explanations of mental capacities in terms of neural structure and neural dynamics.

The field is also called cognitive neuroscience, and the two names are used interchangeably throughout.

The organising idea of this book is a single sentence: cognition is what a nervous system does when it builds and uses internal models of a world it cannot touch directly.


HOW TO READ THIS BOOK

The book has four levels of heading.

• PART, of which there are fifteen.

• CHAPTER, of which there are eighty, numbered continuously from 1 to 80 across the whole work.

• SECTION, numbered as chapter-point-section, for example 12.3.

• SUB-SECTION, numbered as chapter-point-section-point-subsection, for example 12.3.4.

Each chapter carries one of three tags in its heading.

• (CORE) marks a chapter that states a cognitive capacity or the mechanism of one, and that a reader could not skip without leaving a hole in the account.

• (APPARATUS) marks a chapter that supplies method, mathematics, or biological substrate, and that exists to make the CORE chapters checkable.

• (CONTEXT) marks a chapter that situates the science historically, clinically, ethically, or comparatively.

Each chapter opens with a short statement of what it covers and closes with a passage headed WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED.

Chapters were written to stand alone.

That means an acronym or a technical term may be spelled out and defined more than once across the book, once in each chapter where it appears.

This is deliberate.

A reader who opens the book at chapter 43 should not have to hunt back to chapter 8 for a definition.


A NOTE ON HONESTY

Cognitive neuroscience is a young science with many open disputes.

Where a claim is genuinely contested in the field, this book says so and names both sides rather than presenting the dispute as settled.

Where a result is recent and not yet replicated, the text says that too.

Landmark studies are credited in the prose by author and year rather than in a bibliography, so that the reader can see where a claim comes from without leaving the sentence.

Nothing here should be read as the final word.

It should be read as an accurate report of where the field stood in 2026.


HOW THIS BOOK RELATES TO THE REST OF THE CORPUS

The konnectome corpus is organised into fifteen encapsulated layers of abstraction, running from the quark at Layer 1 to the species at Layer 15.

That corpus is substrate-first: it catalogues what the nervous system is made of, layer by layer.

This book is cognition-first: it catalogues what the nervous system does, capacity by capacity.

The two are meant to be read against each other, and chapter 80 sets out the correspondence between them in detail.


PART ONE. FOUNDATIONS: WHAT IS BEING EXPLAINED, AND WHAT WOULD COUNT AS AN EXPLANATION


CHAPTER 1. THE OBJECT OF STUDY: DEFINING COGNITION (CORE)

This chapter asks a question that sounds simple and is not: what exactly is the neuroscience of cognition trying to explain?

Before we can look for cognition in brain tissue, we have to say what would count as having found it.

We will build a working definition, test it against the awkward cases at its borders, examine the traditional list of mental faculties and the trouble that list is in, introduce the idea that has quietly become the field's central theoretical object - the internal model - and finally set out four criteria by which a completed neuroscience of cognition could be recognised.

The chapter matters because almost every dispute later in this book is, underneath, a dispute about definitions made here.

If you get the object of study wrong, every measurement you take afterwards is a measurement of something else.


1.1 The working definition and its boundaries

A definition in science is not a dictionary entry.

It is a decision about where to point the instruments.

This section offers a working definition of cognition, then immediately does the honest thing and shows you the places where the definition frays.


1.1.1 Cognition as information acquisition, representation, transformation, storage, retrieval, and use

The working definition used throughout this book is that cognition is the set of processes by which a nervous system acquires information, represents it, transforms it, stores it, retrieves it, and uses it to guide behaviour.

Each of those six verbs is doing real work.

Acquisition means getting information in, as when light striking the retina is converted into patterns of neural firing.

Representation means holding that information in some physical form that stands for something beyond itself - a pattern of activity that means "there is an edge here" rather than merely being an electrical event.

Transformation means changing the representation into a more useful one, as when edges are combined into shapes and shapes into a recognised face.

Storage and retrieval mean laying the information down so it survives the moment and can be brought back later, which is what we ordinarily call memory.

Use means that the information ends up making a difference to what the organism does, because a representation that can never influence behaviour is, from the outside, indistinguishable from no representation at all.

This framing descends from the information-processing approach that came to dominate psychology from the 1950s onward, in which the mind is treated as a system that takes in input, operates on it through internal stages, and issues an output.

The approach is powerful, and it is also a metaphor that borrows heavily from the digital computer, a point critics have pressed for decades and which we will return to.


1.1.2 The contested border with sensation, with reflex, and with emotion

Sensation is the raw transduction of physical energy into neural signals, and perception is what the brain makes of it, but the line between them is drawn differently by different researchers, and it moves as we learn more.

The retina is not a passive camera - it already performs contrast enhancement and motion detection before a single signal reaches the brain, so even "raw" sensation contains transformation, which was one of our six cognitive verbs.

Reflexes pose the opposite problem.

The knee-jerk reflex is usually excluded from cognition because it is fast, fixed, and runs through the spinal cord without cortical involvement, yet reflexes can be modulated by context and expectation, which means that even a reflex arc can be informed by a representation.

The border with emotion is the most contested of all.

The traditional picture separated a thinking brain from a feeling brain, with structures such as the amygdala assigned to emotion and the prefrontal cortex assigned to reason.

Luiz Pessoa, in The Cognitive-Emotional Brain (2013) and in his 2008 Nature Reviews Neuroscience paper, argues that this separation does not survive contact with the data, because the amygdala contributes heavily to attention and decision-making and complex behaviour arises from coalitions of networks that are neither purely affective nor purely cognitive.

Lisa Feldman Barrett goes further with the theory of constructed emotion, set out in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience in 2017, proposing that emotions are not hard-wired reactions but categorisations that the brain constructs predictively from interoceptive signals, past experience, and social context - which would make emotion a species of cognition rather than its opposite.

Both positions have serious critics, and the field has not settled the matter, so this book will treat the cognition-emotion boundary as unresolved rather than pretending otherwise.


1.1.3 The contested border with consciousness: cognition without awareness

It is tempting to define cognition as whatever happens in the mind that you can notice happening, but the evidence rules that out.

Blindsight is the standard demonstration.

Patients with damage to primary visual cortex report seeing nothing in part of their visual field, yet when forced to guess about a stimulus placed there they perform well above chance, apparently by way of surviving pathways through the superior colliculus and other subcortical routes.

Something in these patients is acquiring, representing, and using visual information, and by our working definition that is cognition, even though the person has no awareness of it.

Subliminal priming makes the same point in healthy volunteers - a word presented too briefly to be reported can still speed or slow the response to a related word that follows, which means its meaning was extracted.

Implicit learning is a third case, in which people come to respond correctly to a complex structured sequence while remaining unable to state any rule they have learned.

There is genuine methodological dispute here.

Critics have argued that many claimed demonstrations of unconscious processing rest on imperfect measures of awareness, so that a trace of conscious perception contaminates what is reported as unconscious, and that some findings arise from selecting participants or trials after the fact.

The defensible summary is that a great deal of cognition demonstrably proceeds without awareness, while the exact amount, and the exact criteria for calling any single instance unconscious, remain actively argued.


1.1.4 Why every boundary drawn here is a research decision rather than a fact of nature

Nothing in the brain is labelled.

There is no membrane, no molecule, and no anatomical seam that marks where sensation stops and cognition begins, or where cognition stops and emotion begins.

The boundaries in the preceding sub-sections were drawn by researchers for practical reasons - to make experiments tractable, to define what a journal counts as within scope, to decide which patients go to which clinic.

This is not a scandal, because every science carves its subject matter somewhere, and the carving is judged by whether it yields lawful, replicable findings rather than by whether it matches some pre-existing fact.

But it does carry an obligation, which is to hold the boundaries loosely and to notice when they start generating contradictions rather than resolving them.

When a field keeps finding that its categories do not map onto its mechanisms, the correct response is often to revise the categories, and that is precisely the situation described in the next section.


1.2 The classical faculty list and its fate

Psychology inherited a list of mental faculties, and cognitive neuroscience has spent thirty years discovering that the list does not divide the brain along its joints.

This section presents the list, explains why it survives despite its problems, and describes the inferential trap it sets.


1.2.1 Perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, action, emotion, self

The standard headings are perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, action, emotion, and self, and it is worth saying what each one is before criticising the list.

Perception is the construction of a usable description of the world from sensory signals.

Attention is the selection of some subset of available information for privileged processing, because the input vastly exceeds the capacity to process it.

Memory is the storage and retrieval of information across time, and it fractionates into working memory held over seconds, episodic memory for particular experienced events, and semantic memory for general facts.

Language is the system that maps sound or sign onto meaning and back again, with structure at the levels of sound, word, and sentence.

Reasoning covers inference, problem-solving, and decision-making, which is the selection among options according to their expected value.

Action covers the planning and execution of movement, including the control loops that correct movement while it is happening.

Emotion, as discussed, covers valenced states that prepare and bias the organism, and self covers the representation of the organism itself, its body, its history, and its standing among others.

These headings organise textbooks, funding calls, and this book, which is a fact about how research is administered as much as about how minds work.


1.2.2 Faculties as convenient labels rather than natural kinds

A natural kind is a category that carves nature at a real joint, so that its members share a deep underlying nature and support reliable generalisations - chemical elements are the standard example.

The question is whether "attention" or "working memory" is a natural kind of that sort, or merely a useful label for a family of loosely related phenomena.

The evidence increasingly favours the second reading.

What researchers keep finding is not one-to-one mappings between brain structures and cognitive functions but many-to-many mappings, in which a single region participates in many tasks and a single task recruits many regions.

Michael Anderson's neural reuse proposal, set out in After Phrenology (2014), argues that brain regions are routinely redeployed across quite different cognitive domains, which would explain the many-to-many pattern directly.

Cathy Price and Karl Friston argued as early as 2005 that the resolution may require revising the psychological categories themselves so that they can be integrated with neural ones, rather than assuming the inherited categories are correct and hunting for their locations.

There is a real dispute here about how radical the revision needs to be, with some philosophers and neuroscientists arguing for wholesale replacement of the cognitive ontology and others arguing for a pluralism in which several category schemes coexist because each is useful for different purposes.


1.2.3 The reverse-inference problem: reading a faculty off a brain activation

Reverse inference is reasoning backwards from observed brain activity to the cognitive process presumed to have caused it - for example, concluding that a task involves emotion because the amygdala lit up.

Russell Poldrack named and analysed the problem in a 2006 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, pointing out that this reasoning is not deductively valid.

The logical shape of the error is affirming the consequent - the fact that emotion activates the amygdala does not license the conclusion that amygdala activation implies emotion, because the amygdala does many other things.

The strength of any such inference depends on selectivity, meaning how exclusively the region in question is engaged by the process in question, and selectivity in the brain is generally low.

Poldrack's own position is not that reverse inference must be abandoned, but that it is a hypothesis-generating move whose confidence can be quantified, for instance using Bayesian reasoning over large databases of imaging results to ask how much the observed activation actually shifts the odds.

Others, including Marco Hutzler in a 2014 NeuroImage exchange, have defended reverse inference more strongly, arguing it is a legitimate form of abductive inference rather than a fallacy as such.

The practical lesson for a reader of neuroscience headlines is direct - a claim of the form "region X lit up, therefore the subject was experiencing Y" should be treated as a suggestion, not a result.


1.2.4 Ontologies of cognition: the Cognitive Atlas and its successors

An ontology, in this technical sense, is a formal, explicit catalogue of the entities in a domain and the relations among them, of the kind used to make databases interoperable.

The Cognitive Atlas, developed by Poldrack and colleagues at Stanford and described in a 2011 paper in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, is an attempt to build such a catalogue for cognitive neuroscience - a controlled vocabulary of mental processes such as working memory and cognitive control, together with the experimental tasks used to measure them, and explicit statements of which task is claimed to measure which process.

The point of separating tasks from processes is to make a hidden assumption visible, because the assumption that the Stroop task measures "cognitive control" is a theoretical claim that can be wrong, not a definition.

Related efforts include the Cognitive Paradigm Ontology for describing experimental designs, the NeuroQuery and Neurosynth platforms for automated meta-analysis over thousands of published imaging studies, and the Research Domain Criteria framework from the United States National Institute of Mental Health, which proposes dimensional constructs cutting across psychiatric diagnoses.

Poldrack and Tal Yarkoni set out the broader programme in a 2016 Annual Review of Psychology article, arguing that data-driven analysis of large corpora could eventually let the ontology be discovered rather than stipulated.

That promise remains largely unredeemed, and it is fair to say the ontology problem is currently better characterised than solved.


1.3 Cognition as model-building

If the faculty list is a poor guide to mechanism, the field needs a different organising idea.

The candidate that has gained the most ground is that nervous systems build and use internal models of the world.


1.3.1 The internal model as the field's central theoretical object

An internal model is a structure inside the organism whose states stand in a systematic correspondence with states of the world, such that operating on the model tells the organism something about the world.

The classical statement is Kenneth Craik's, in The Nature of Explanation (1943), where he proposed that an organism carrying a small-scale model of external reality can try out alternatives ahead of acting, and so react to future situations before they arise.

The appeal of the idea is that it explains the single most striking feature of cognition, which is decoupling - the ability to think about what is not present, whether that is next week, another country, or a situation that has never occurred.

An organism restricted to reacting to current stimulation cannot plan, and cannot be wrong in the interesting way that a mistaken belief is wrong.

The idea is elegant, and it should be said plainly that "the brain has an internal model" is close to unfalsifiable unless one specifies what the model represents, in what format, and how it is used - which is exactly the work the rest of this book will describe.


1.3.2 Generative models, forward models, and inverse models

These three terms are used constantly in the literature and are routinely confused, so it is worth pinning them down.

A generative model is a model of how the causes in the world produce the sensory data you receive, so it runs from hidden causes to observations, and perception becomes the problem of inverting it - given these observations, what causes most likely produced them?

A forward model, in motor control, predicts the sensory consequences of a motor command you are about to issue, which is what allows you to know where your arm will be before the slow feedback from your arm arrives.

An inverse model runs the other way, computing what motor command would be needed to achieve a desired outcome, which is the controller's problem rather than the predictor's.

Daniel Wolpert and Mitsuo Kawato's work in the 1990s established the pairing of forward and inverse models in cerebellar motor control, and the forward model neatly explains why you cannot tickle yourself - the predicted sensation from your own movement is subtracted from the actual sensation, leaving little to be surprised by.

The generative-model framing has been developed most aggressively by Karl Friston under the heading of predictive coding and the free-energy principle, laid out in a 2010 Nature Reviews Neuroscience article, in which forward connections in cortex carry prediction errors upward and backward connections carry predictions downward.

The free-energy principle is mathematically ambitious and has been criticised as being so general that it is difficult to test against any particular experiment, a criticism its proponents dispute, and readers should treat it as a promising and contested framework rather than an established result.


1.3.3 Prediction as the currency of cognition

If the brain runs a generative model, its main activity is prediction, and the useful signal is prediction error - the difference between what was expected and what arrived.

This idea has a strong empirical anchor in reward learning, where Wolfram Schultz and colleagues showed in the 1990s that midbrain dopamine neurons in monkeys fire not to reward as such, but to reward that was not predicted, and fall silent when an expected reward fails to appear.

That firing pattern matches the reward prediction error term in temporal-difference learning algorithms, which is one of the cleanest correspondences between a computational quantity and a measured neural signal anywhere in neuroscience.

Analogous mismatch responses appear in perception, such as the mismatch negativity, an electrical brain response to an unexpected sound in a regular sequence, first reported by Risto Näätänen and colleagues in 1978.

Prediction is economical for the same reason that video compression is economical - transmitting only what could not be anticipated costs far less than transmitting everything.

It is worth noting that not every researcher accepts that prediction error is the universal currency, and there are well-argued alternatives in which dopamine signals reflect other quantities, so the reward-prediction-error account, though strong, is not unchallenged.


1.3.4 Why model-building unifies perception, memory, and planning under one description

The practical virtue of the model-building framing is that it makes three apparently different faculties into three uses of one machine.

Perception becomes inference about the present - given current sensory data, what state of the world is most likely?

Memory becomes inference about the past, reconstructing a probable earlier state rather than replaying a stored recording, which fits the well-documented reconstructive and error-prone character of human recollection.

Planning becomes inference about the future, simulating the sensory consequences of actions not yet taken and choosing among them.

This is why the same brain structures keep appearing across these domains - the hippocampal system, long known for episodic memory, is also engaged when people imagine future events, a finding reported by Demis Hassabis, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues in 2007, who showed that patients with hippocampal amnesia were impaired at imagining novel experiences as well as at remembering past ones.

That result is exactly what the model-building account predicts and is difficult for a pure storage account of memory to explain.


1.4 What a completed neuroscience of cognition would look like

It is worth being explicit about the finish line, because a field that cannot say what success looks like cannot tell whether it is approaching it.

Four criteria are proposed here, in increasing order of difficulty, and the honest verdict is that the field currently satisfies the first partially and the others hardly at all.


1.4.1 The mapping criterion: every capacity assigned a mechanism

The first criterion is that every cognitive capacity should be assigned a mechanism, meaning a specified set of components and activities organised so as to produce the capacity.

This is not the same as assigning a capacity to a location, and the difference matters enormously - saying that face recognition happens in the fusiform gyrus is a fact about geography, while saying how a population of neurons transforms an image into an identity is a mechanism.

David Marr's framework, set out in Vision (1982), remains the standard way to organise this ambition, distinguishing the computational level, which states what problem is being solved and why, the algorithmic level, which states the representations and procedures used, and the implementation level, which states how those are realised in neural hardware.

Carl Craver and others in the new mechanist tradition treat incomplete descriptions at the upper levels as mechanism sketches - placeholders to be filled in - while Bradley Love and others argue that the algorithmic level is the genuine bridge and should not be treated as merely provisional.

The mapping criterion is where cognitive neuroscience has made most of its progress, and it remains far from met, largely for the ontology reasons given in section 1.2.


1.4.2 The prediction criterion: novel behaviour forecast from neural state

The second criterion is that from a measurement of neural state one should be able to forecast behaviour that has not yet occurred, including behaviour in situations never previously tested.

Decoding work has established the weaker version of this - patterns of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) activity, which measures blood-oxygen changes as a proxy for neural activity, can be classified to recover which of a known set of tasks or stimuli a person is engaged with, and graph-based neural networks now do this at high accuracy on the Human Connectome Project task battery.

Classifying among known alternatives is a much weaker achievement than forecasting genuinely novel behaviour, and the field should not conflate the two.

The strongest current examples come from simpler animals - connectome-constrained models of the fly visual system, published in Nature in 2024 by Janelia researchers, predicted neural responses in cells that had never been recorded, using connectivity plus a task objective alone.

That is a real instance of the prediction criterion being met in a restricted domain, and it is a reasonable template for what success would look like at larger scales.


1.4.3 The intervention criterion: capacities switched on and off at will

The third criterion is causal control, because a mechanism you understand is a mechanism you can operate.

Optogenetics, in which neurons are genetically modified to express light-sensitive proteins so that specific cells can be switched on or off with light, has given this criterion real teeth in rodents.

Susumu Tonegawa's laboratory used the technique to tag the hippocampal neurons active during fear learning and then reactivate them with light, causing mice to freeze in a context where nothing bad had happened, reported in Nature in 2012 by Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez and colleagues, and then to implant a false fear memory by pairing artificial reactivation of one context's engram with a shock delivered elsewhere, reported in Science in 2013.

In humans, the available tools are far blunter - transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which uses a magnetic pulse through the scalp to transiently disrupt or excite cortical tissue, can produce brief and reversible interference with a cognitive function, and deep brain stimulation delivers current through implanted electrodes in patients who need it clinically.

Theodore Berger, Robert Hampson and colleagues went further with a hippocampal memory prosthesis, using a nonlinear multi-input multi-output model to read out and then re-inject firing patterns, improving memory performance first in rats and monkeys and later, in a 2018 report, in human epilepsy patients with implanted electrodes.

These are genuine but narrow successes, and no one can currently switch a capacity such as language comprehension or planning on and off at will.


1.4.4 The construction criterion: capacities rebuilt in an artificial substrate

The fourth and hardest criterion is that a capacity should be rebuildable in a different physical substrate, on the principle that you do not understand a thing until you can make one.

The most complete attempts start small - the OpenWorm project has aimed since 2011 to simulate the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, an animal with exactly 302 neurons and a fully mapped wiring diagram, and after more than a decade it produces plausible locomotion but not the animal's full behavioural repertoire.

The obstacle is instructive - knowing the wiring is not knowing the dynamics, because the strengths, signs, and time courses of the connections are mostly unmeasured and must be guessed.

At the next scale up, the FlyWire reconstruction of the adult fruit fly brain, released in 2024 with over 127,000 neurons and roughly 50 million synapses, has already supported a leaky integrate-and-fire whole-brain model that correctly predicted which neurons drive feeding and grooming, with predictions confirmed by optogenetic experiment.

Large artificial neural networks present a different and awkward case, because systems trained on text now perform many tasks that were treated as diagnostic of human cognition, while plainly not being built the way brains are - which shows that passing a behavioural test is not by itself evidence of having rebuilt the mechanism.

The construction criterion therefore needs care in its statement - what would count is rebuilding a capacity by way of the mechanism the biological system actually uses, not merely matching its output.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognition is defined here as the acquisition, representation, transformation, storage, retrieval, and use of information by a nervous system, a definition that deliberately includes a great deal of processing that never reaches awareness, as blindsight, subliminal priming, and implicit learning all demonstrate.

Its borders with sensation, reflex, emotion, and consciousness are research decisions rather than facts of nature, and the border with emotion in particular is actively disputed, with Pessoa and Barrett arguing that no clean separation survives the evidence.

The inherited list of mental faculties organises the field but is probably not a list of natural kinds, since the brain yields many-to-many rather than one-to-one mappings between structures and functions, which is what makes reverse inference from an activation to a mental state unreliable and what motivates ontology projects such as the Cognitive Atlas.

The framing with the best current claim to unify the field is that nervous systems build internal generative models and trade in prediction error, which makes perception, memory, and planning three uses of one machine rather than three separate faculties - an elegant proposal whose most ambitious version, the free-energy principle, remains difficult to test.

Success would mean meeting four criteria - mapping capacities to mechanisms, forecasting novel behaviour from neural state, switching capacities on and off at will, and rebuilding them in another substrate - and at present the field meets the first partially, the second and third only in narrow and mostly non-human cases, and the fourth not at all.


CHAPTER 2. A HISTORY OF THE NEUROSCIENCE OF COGNITION (CONTEXT)

This chapter tells the story of how a question that began as philosophy became a laboratory science.

It follows one long argument across two and a half thousand years: where does thinking happen, and what is thinking made of.

You will meet the people who guessed wrong in interesting ways, the people who guessed right for bad reasons, and the instruments that eventually settled arguments no amount of debate could settle.

The history matters because the field's present shape is not inevitable - it is the residue of which questions were askable with the tools of each era.

Nearly every live controversy in modern cognitive neuroscience is a descendant of a dispute you will meet in these pages.


2.1 Before the brain: mind without mechanism

For most of recorded history, thinkers had opinions about the mind but no way to look inside a living head.

They reasoned from injury, from dissection of the dead, from analogy, and from theology.

The result was a set of theories that were sometimes strikingly close to the truth and sometimes wildly off, with no reliable way to tell which was which.


2.1.1 Cardiocentric and encephalocentric traditions in antiquity

The ancient argument had two camps: the cardiocentric camp, which placed thought and sensation in the heart, and the encephalocentric or cephalocentric camp, which placed them in the brain.

Aristotle, in the fourth century before the common era, was the great systematiser of the cardiocentric view - he held the heart to be the seat of sensation and intellect, and treated the brain as essentially a radiator whose job was to cool the hot blood.

The Hippocratic tradition took the other side, and the treatise On the Sacred Disease argues plainly that from the brain and from the brain only arise our pleasures, joys, laughter, and griefs.

Earlier still, Alcmaeon of Croton is credited with tracing sensory channels from the sense organs inward toward the brain, and in the Hellenistic period the Alexandrian anatomists Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies and located the hegemonikon - the commanding part of the soul - in the brain.

Galen, in the second century of the common era, argued forcefully for the brain on experimental grounds, including the observation that cutting particular nerves in a living animal abolishes particular functions such as the voice.

It is worth noticing that the cardiocentric view was not stupid: the heart visibly races with emotion, stops at death, and is warm, whereas the brain is cool, silent, and insensitive to being cut - the correct answer was genuinely counterintuitive.


2.1.2 Ventricular localisation in the medieval and Renaissance periods

When the anatomists of late antiquity opened the skull, the most conspicuous features they found were not the folds of grey matter but the ventricles - the fluid-filled cavities inside the brain.

Because the prevailing physiology held that function was carried by a subtle fluid called animal spirit, it seemed obvious that the mind lived in the chambers that held fluid rather than in the surrounding tissue.

Nemesius of Emesa, a bishop writing around the year 390, gave this idea its influential form, assigning perception to the front chambers, reasoning to the middle, and memory to the rear - a scheme usually called the cell doctrine or ventricular localisation, where cell here means chamber, not the biological cell.

Latin translations carried Nemesius to the medieval schoolmen, and Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century entrenched the three-chamber scheme in European learning, where it survived in printed diagrams into the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Andreas Vesalius, in De humani corporis fabrica of 1543, produced the most accurate brain illustrations then made and openly doubted the doctrine, pointing out that the ventricles of animals thought to lack reason look much like our own.

The cell doctrine is a useful cautionary tale: it was localisationist, it was specific, it made a map, and it was almost entirely wrong, because the mapmakers had mistaken the plumbing for the machinery.


2.1.3 Cartesian dualism and the interaction problem

Rene Descartes, writing in the mid seventeenth century, proposed substance dualism - the claim that mind and body are two different kinds of stuff, the mind being a thinking thing without spatial extension and the body an extended thing without thought.

In The Passions of the Soul of 1649 he nonetheless needed the two to touch somewhere, and he nominated the pineal gland, a small unpaired structure near the centre of the brain, as the point at which the soul could deflect the flow of animal spirits through the nerves.

Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia demolished this in correspondence beginning in May 1643, asking how a purely thinking substance, having no surface and no extension, could push anything at all, since Descartes' own physics had banished action at a distance in favour of contact and impact.

Descartes never gave her a satisfying answer, and Elisabeth eventually remarked that she found it easier to grant extension to the soul than to grant an unextended thing the power to move a body.

This is the interaction problem, and it is the reason dualism has largely been abandoned as a working scientific hypothesis: a theory that puts the mind outside the causal order cannot then explain how the mind causes an arm to rise.

Descartes still earns his place here, because his mechanical account of reflexes - a stimulus at the skin producing an automatic movement without any decision - was a genuine anticipation of how much of behaviour would later be explained.


2.1.4 British empiricism, associationism, and the seed of the learning rule

The British empiricists held that knowledge comes from experience through the senses rather than from innate ideas, and that complex thoughts are built from simple sensations glued together by association.

John Locke coined the phrase association of ideas as a chapter title in the fourth edition of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding in 1700, and David Hume in the following century set out three principles by which ideas attract one another: resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect.

David Hartley, in his Observations on Man of 1749, went further than his predecessors by proposing a physical substrate - vibrations in the nerves - so that repeated co-occurrence in experience would leave a lasting physical change.

Contiguity, the principle that things experienced together become linked, is the direct ancestor of the modern learning rule associated with Donald Hebb in 1949 and summarised in the slogan that cells that fire together wire together.

The lineage is real but should not be overstated: the empiricists had a principle without a mechanism, and it took two centuries of physiology to supply the synapse that the principle needed.


2.2 The localisation century

The nineteenth century is when the question shifted from whether the mind is in the brain to which part of the brain does what.

The tools were crude - skull shape, surgical destruction of tissue in animals, and the accidents that damaged human brains - but the question was finally empirical.

The century swung between two poles, localisation and holism, and the swinging has never entirely stopped.


2.2.1 Gall, Spurzheim, and phrenology as a wrong answer to a right question

Franz Joseph Gall, an anatomist working around the turn of the nineteenth century, proposed what he called organology: the mind is not a single faculty but a collection of independent faculties, each with its own organ in the cerebral cortex, and a well-exercised organ grows larger.

Gall identified roughly twenty-seven such organs, and his assistant Johann Gaspar Spurzheim expanded the list to about thirty-five and gave the doctrine the name phrenology, a name Gall himself disliked.

The fatal step was the inference from brain to skull - the claim that a large organ pushes out a bump on the overlying bone that can be read by the fingers of a trained examiner - which is false, because the inner and outer surfaces of the skull do not track the cortex in that way.

A commission of the Institut de France judged Gall's doctrine devoid of scientific value in 1808, and phrenology went on to a long disreputable career in popular culture and in the service of racial and criminal pseudoscience.

Yet two of Gall's premises survived and are now orthodoxy: that the cortex, not the ventricles, is the organ of mind, and that different regions of it do different things.

Gall and Spurzheim also differed in a way that still echoes, with Gall treating the faculties as innate and fixed and Spurzheim insisting that education could reshape them.


2.2.2 Flourens and the doctrine of mass action

Marie-Jean-Pierre Flourens set out to test Gall experimentally, using ablation - the controlled surgical removal of a piece of brain tissue followed by observation of what the animal can no longer do.

In work on pigeons and other vertebrates published in 1824 as Recherches experimentales sur les proprietes et les fonctions du systeme nerveux dans les animaux vertebres, he found clean localisation in the lower structures: destroy the cerebellum and the animal loses coordination and balance, destroy parts of the medulla and it stops breathing.

But in the cerebral hemispheres he found no such divisions - removing tissue anywhere in the hemispheres dulled perception, volition, and judgement in proportion to how much was taken, not according to where it was taken from.

He concluded that the hemispheres act as a unified whole in what he called a community of action, a position later labelled the aggregate field view, and its quantitative version is the doctrine of mass action.

Flourens was right about the method and about the lower structures, and wrong about the hemispheres for a reason that would recur throughout the history of the field: pigeons have very little cortex to divide up, and his behavioural tests were too coarse to detect the deficits that were there.

The lesson is that a null result from an insensitive measure is not evidence of absence, and much of the subsequent history is the story of measures becoming sensitive enough.


2.2.3 Broca in 1861 and Wernicke in 1874: language localised by lesion

In April 1861 Paul Broca examined a patient at the Bicetre hospital named Louis Victor Leborgne, who had lost speech more than twenty years earlier and could utter little more than the syllable tan, while apparently still understanding what was said to him.

Leborgne died within days, Broca performed the autopsy, and found a lesion in the posterior part of the left frontal lobe - the region now called Broca's area.

Broca went on to accumulate a further series of cases with damage in the same place and the same loss of fluent speech, and by 1865 he was arguing publicly that articulate language is a function of the left hemisphere in particular, not of the brain in general.

Carl Wernicke, a young German physician, described a second and different pattern in 1874: patients with damage to the posterior superior temporal region of the left hemisphere who spoke fluently but produced nonsense and could not understand what was said to them.

Two dissociable deficits with two different lesion sites is a far stronger argument than either alone, because it shows that the brain divides labour rather than simply having more or less of a single resource, and this logic of the double dissociation remains the backbone of neuropsychology.

Modern re-examinations complicate the tidy story - Leborgne's brain, imaged with magnetic resonance imaging by Dronkers and colleagues in 2007, showed damage extending well beyond the classical area and into underlying white matter, and many researchers now describe language as a distributed network rather than two centres joined by a cable.


2.2.4 Brodmann's cytoarchitectonics and the parcellation impulse

Korbinian Brodmann approached localisation from the microscope rather than from injury, using cytoarchitectonics - the study of how the cell bodies of neurons are sized, layered, and packed in a piece of tissue.

In his 1909 monograph he stained thin slices of cortex, looked for boundaries where the layering changed character, and produced a numbered map whose labels run from 1 to 52, though not every number is used in the human map.

The bet behind the map is a deep one and has held up well: a difference in the local wiring pattern signals a difference in the computation performed, so structure can be used to predict function before any function is measured.

Brodmann's numbers are still in daily use - area 17 is primary visual cortex, area 4 is primary motor cortex, areas 44 and 45 approximate Broca's region - which is a remarkable run for a hand-drawn map more than a century old.

The parcellation impulse continues with better data: the Human Connectome Project analysis by Glasser and colleagues in 2016 combined cortical thickness, myelin content, task activation, and connectivity to define 180 areas per hemisphere, 360 in total.

The impulse also has its critics, who point out that area boundaries vary between individuals, that some transitions are gradients rather than borders, and that a parcel is a convenience for analysis rather than a natural kind.


2.2.5 Lashley, equipotentiality, and the search for the engram

Karl Lashley spent three decades looking for the engram - the physical memory trace, the actual change in tissue that stores a learned habit.

His method was to train rats on mazes, remove varying amounts of cortex from varying locations, and test how much of the habit survived, and his results were reported in Brain Mechanisms and Intelligence in 1929.

He found that performance degraded with the amount of tissue removed and hardly at all with its location, which he formulated as two principles: mass action, that complex learning depends on the quantity of intact cortex, and equipotentiality, that within limits one region can take over the job of another.

In his 1950 address In Search of the Engram, Lashley wrote with some humour that his results made learning seem impossible, and concluded that the memory trace is not stored in any one place.

Modern work has partly overturned him and partly vindicated him: engram cells for specific memories have now been tagged and reactivated in mice, notably by Liu, Ramirez, Tonegawa and colleagues from 2012 onward, showing that particular sparse sets of neurons do carry particular memories.

But Lashley's deeper point survives - a maze habit is not one memory, it is a bundle of visual, spatial, tactile, and motor components stored in different systems, so no single cut could ever remove it cleanly.


2.3 The neuron and its signal

While the localisers argued about the map, a second line of work asked a different question: what is the brain actually made of, and what physically travels through it.

This line produced the two ideas on which all of modern neuroscience rests - that the brain is built of discrete cells, and that those cells communicate with electrical and chemical signals that can be measured and modelled.


2.3.1 The reticular theory against the neuron doctrine: Golgi and Cajal

Nervous tissue is nearly transparent and impossibly tangled, and before 1873 nobody could see a single nerve cell in its entirety.

Camillo Golgi solved this with what he called la reazione nera, the black reaction: hardening tissue in potassium dichromate and then immersing it in silver nitrate, which for reasons still not fully understood stains only a small random fraction of cells, but stains those completely and black.

Golgi, looking at his own preparations, concluded that the fine branches of nerve cells fuse into one continuous network - the reticular theory, from the Latin for little net - in which the nervous system is a single connected mesh rather than a population of individuals.

Santiago Ramon y Cajal took Golgi's method, improved it, applied it to young animals whose fibres are less densely packed, and reached the opposite conclusion: the branches come close but never fuse, so each neuron is a separate cell that contacts others across a gap.

This is the neuron doctrine, and Cajal added to it the law of dynamic polarisation, that signals travel in one direction, from the branching dendrites toward the cell body and out along the axon.

The two men shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1906 and used their Nobel lectures to contradict each other in public, Golgi defending the reticular theory to the last and Cajal defending independence.

Cajal was vindicated, decisively by electron microscopy in the 1950s, which showed the synaptic gap directly - though the story has a small twist, since electrical synapses, where cells really are continuous through channels called gap junctions, do exist and are common in some circuits.


2.3.2 Sherrington and the synapse

Charles Scott Sherrington coined the word synapse in 1897, in a revision he wrote for Michael Foster's Textbook of Physiology, to name the junction between one neuron and the next - the gap whose existence Cajal had inferred but nobody could yet see.

Naming it mattered, because it turned a hypothetical gap into a place where things happen, and Sherrington spent his career working out what happens there.

Studying spinal reflexes in animals, he showed that the junction imposes properties the nerve fibre itself does not have: a delay, a summation of inputs arriving close together in time, and above all inhibition.

Reciprocal innervation was his key demonstration - when a reflex excites a muscle it simultaneously inhibits that muscle's antagonist, so the limb can move at all, which means the nervous system must have a way of subtracting as well as adding.

In The Integrative Action of the Nervous System of 1906 he assembled this into a general picture in which the reflex is the elementary unit and the nervous system is fundamentally an integrator, combining many competing influences into one coherent output.

He shared the 1932 Nobel Prize with Edgar Adrian, and his insistence that inhibition is as fundamental as excitation is one of the most consequential ideas in the whole of neuroscience.


2.3.3 Adrian and the rate code

Edgar Douglas Adrian took advantage of a new technology, the thermionic vacuum tube amplifier, to make signals from a single nerve fibre large enough to record.

Working in the 1920s, he dissected a frog muscle preparation down until only one stretch receptor and one nerve fibre remained, then recorded what that single fibre did as he varied the stimulus.

The result was the foundation of sensory coding: the individual impulse is always the same size no matter how strong the stimulus, so intensity cannot be carried by amplitude - it is carried by how many impulses arrive per second.

This is the rate code, set out in his 1928 book The Basis of Sensation, and Adrian also documented adaptation, the tendency of a receptor to fire fast at the onset of a constant stimulus and then slow down, which is why you stop feeling your clothes.

Adrian is also the figure who began, around 1926, to describe nerve activity in the vocabulary of messages, signals, and codes - the beginning of the informational way of talking about the brain that now dominates the field.

The rate code is real but not the whole story, and there is an active and genuinely unsettled debate about temporal coding, in which the precise timing of individual spikes, and their timing relative to ongoing brain rhythms, carries information that a firing rate would discard.


2.3.4 Hodgkin and Huxley and the quantitative action potential

Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley wanted to know not just that a nerve impulse happens but exactly why, in the language of physics.

They worked on the giant axon of the squid, a nerve fibre up to a millimetre across, large enough to have wires threaded down its inside, and they used the voltage clamp, a feedback circuit that holds the membrane voltage at a chosen value and measures the current needed to hold it there.

By clamping at many voltages and by removing sodium from the bathing solution, they separated the total current into a fast inward sodium current and a slower outward potassium current, each with its own dependence on voltage and time.

In a series of five papers in the Journal of Physiology in 1952, culminating in a set of four coupled nonlinear differential equations, they showed that these two currents alone reproduce the action potential's shape, its threshold, its speed, and its refractory period, computed by hand on a mechanical calculator.

This was a turning point in kind, not merely in degree: for the first time a cognitive-relevant biological event was predicted quantitatively from physical principles, and the equations remain in use today as the backbone of computational neuroscience.

Hodgkin and Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel Prize with John Eccles, whose work on synaptic inhibition completed the picture at the junction.


2.4 The cognitive revolution

The physiologists had the cell and the signal, but psychology in the first half of the twentieth century had officially banned the very things the signals were supposed to be about.

The cognitive revolution is the story of how internal mental states became scientifically respectable again, and how a new machine supplied the vocabulary that made them so.


2.4.1 Behaviourism and its explanatory ceiling

Behaviourism, launched by John B. Watson's manifesto of 1913 and developed most rigorously by B. F. Skinner, held that psychology should confine itself to observable stimuli and observable responses and say nothing about unobservable inner states.

This was a disciplined response to a real problem: the introspective psychology it replaced relied on trained observers reporting their own conscious contents, and those reports could not be checked by anyone else.

Behaviourism delivered a great deal - the laws of classical and operant conditioning, schedules of reinforcement, and a body of experimental technique that is still used - and it should not be caricatured.

Its ceiling was reached where behaviour depends on structure that no history of reinforcement can supply, and the clearest case was language: Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that terms like stimulus and reinforcement, when stretched to cover speech, become empty relabelling, and that children produce and understand sentences they have never heard and have never been reinforced for.

Even inside the behaviourist tradition the ceiling was visible, as when Edward Tolman's rats in the 1930s and 1940s showed latent learning, navigating a maze efficiently on first reward after unrewarded wandering, which is hard to describe without saying they had acquired a map.

It should be said that the standard triumphal account is contested: behaviour analysts, including Kenneth MacCorquodale in 1970, argued that Chomsky attacked a caricature, and applied behaviour analysis remains a productive field.


2.4.2 Information theory, cybernetics, and the computer metaphor

The year 1948 supplied psychology with two new vocabularies at once.

Claude Shannon's A Mathematical Theory of Communication defined information quantitatively in bits, showed how to measure the capacity of a channel, and made it legitimate to ask how much information a person can transmit without ever asking what it feels like to do so.

Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics, published the same year, supplied feedback and control - the idea that a system with a goal, a measurement of its current state, and a loop between them behaves purposefully without anything mysterious being added.

Alan Turing's earlier work supplied the third piece: a machine defined purely by rules for manipulating symbols can compute anything computable, which means that a symbol-manipulating description of a process is a legitimate scientific description, independent of what the symbols are made of.

Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts had already, in 1943, shown that idealised all-or-none neurons wired together can implement logical operations, joining the physiology of Adrian's spikes to the logic of Turing's machines.

Out of these came the computer metaphor - the mind as an information-processing system with inputs, encoding, storage, retrieval, and outputs - which is best understood not as a claim that the brain is a digital computer but as a licence to describe internal states in a testable vocabulary.


2.4.3 Miller, Chomsky, Newell and Simon, and the recovery of internal states

The symposium on information theory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on the eleventh of September 1956 is the date most often given as the birthday of cognitive science, and George Miller himself named it as such.

Miller presented the material of The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, published in Psychological Review in 1956, showing that immediate memory holds roughly seven items regardless of how much information each item carries, and that people beat the limit by chunking - recoding several small items into one larger one.

The chunking result is the crucial move, because a limit that depends on how the material is internally organised cannot be described in terms of stimuli alone: the internal representation has become the measured variable.

Chomsky presented an early form of transformational generative grammar, arguing that the sentences a speaker can produce are the output of a finite system of rules operating on abstract structure, not a list of learned responses.

Allen Newell and Herbert Simon presented the Logic Theorist, a running computer program that proved theorems from Principia Mathematica by searching a space of possibilities with heuristics, and which therefore constituted an existence proof that goal-directed reasoning could be given a mechanical description.

The three presentations converged: a capacity limit, a rule system, and a working simulation, all describing what happens between stimulus and response, and all checkable.


2.4.4 The naming of cognitive neuroscience by Gazzaniga and Miller in the late 1970s

For two decades cognitive psychology and neuroscience ran largely in parallel, the first modelling the mind without reference to tissue and the second studying tissue without much reference to cognition.

The field that joins them was named, by the accounts of the participants, in the back of a New York taxi in the late 1970s, when Michael Gazzaniga and George Miller were travelling to a dinner at the Algonquin Hotel for scientists from Rockefeller and Cornell who were combining forces to study how the brain enables the mind.

The term cognitive neuroscience came out of that ride, and Gazzaniga and Miller began using it publicly in the following years, with sources variously dating the launch to 1976 or 1978.

A name is not a small thing here, because it defined a research programme with a specific demand: an explanation must be stated at both levels at once, in terms of the cognitive operation and in terms of the neural implementation.

The programme acquired its institutions steadily thereafter, including the journal Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience in 1989 and the Cognitive Neuroscience Society in 1994.


2.5 The instrument-driven expansions

The remainder of the story is largely a story of instruments.

Each new way of measuring or manipulating the brain opened a class of questions that had been unanswerable, and each also imposed its own characteristic distortions on what the field chose to ask.


2.5.1 Single-unit recording and the receptive field: Hubel and Wiesel

David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, working at Johns Hopkins and then Harvard from the late 1950s, pushed fine electrodes into the primary visual cortex of anaesthetised cats and recorded from one neuron at a time.

The organising concept is the receptive field: the region of the sensory world, and the kind of pattern within it, that makes a particular neuron change its firing rate.

Their famous accidental discovery came when a glass slide's edge, moving in the projector, produced a burst of firing from a cell that had ignored the spots they had been showing it - cortical cells wanted oriented edges, not dots.

They described simple cells, which respond to an edge of a particular orientation at a particular position and sum their inputs roughly linearly, and complex cells, which respond to the same orientation over a range of positions, and they proposed a hierarchy in which complex cells are built from simple ones.

They also mapped the organisation of the tissue, showing orientation columns and ocular dominance columns - vertical slabs of cortex in which all cells prefer a similar orientation or favour the same eye - in work published in 1962 and 1968.

Their deprivation experiments, closing one eye in a kitten during a limited critical period, showed that the columns are shaped by experience and that the damage is permanent if the period is missed, which gave developmental plasticity a rigorous experimental basis.

They shared the 1981 Nobel Prize with Roger Sperry, and their hierarchy of increasingly complex feature detectors is the direct ancestor of the convolutional neural networks of modern machine vision.


2.5.2 The patient literature: Henry Molaison, Phineas Gage, split-brain studies

Phineas Gage was a railway foreman who in 1848 survived an iron tamping rod driven up through his left cheek and out of the top of his skull, destroying much of the left prefrontal cortex.

His physician John Harlow reported that Gage's memory, speech, and movement were largely intact but his character was not, and the case became the founding demonstration that the frontal lobes are involved in social conduct and the regulation of behaviour - though it should be said plainly that the contemporary records are thin, that later retellings exaggerated the deterioration, and that Gage appears to have recovered substantially and worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile.

Henry Molaison underwent bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobes, including most of the hippocampus, at the hands of William Beecher Scoville in 1953, as a treatment for intractable epilepsy.

Brenda Milner's testing, first reported with Scoville in 1957, showed a devastating anterograde amnesia - an inability to form new lasting memories of facts and events - alongside intact perception, intact language, intact intelligence, and intact memory for the remote past.

The decisive finding came when Milner showed that Molaison improved day after day at mirror drawing while denying each morning that he had ever done it, which proved that memory is not one system: skill learning and conscious recollection are separable, and only the latter depends on the hippocampus.

The split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, from the early 1960s, examined patients whose corpus callosum - the great fibre bundle joining the hemispheres - had been cut to control epilepsy, and found that information presented to the right hemisphere alone could guide a left-hand response while the speaking left hemisphere denied having seen anything, and would confabulate a reason for the action.

Modern reappraisals, including work by Pinto and colleagues from 2017, argue that split-brain patients retain more unified perceptual awareness than the classic accounts implied, so the interpretation of these cases is still under active revision.


2.5.3 Positron emission tomography (PET) and then functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)

Positron emission tomography (PET) works by injecting a short-lived radioactive tracer, commonly water labelled with oxygen-15, and detecting the paired gamma rays emitted when the positrons annihilate, which yields a map of blood flow - a proxy for local neural activity.

Applied to cognition by Marcus Raichle, Steven Petersen, Michael Posner and colleagues in landmark papers of 1988 and 1989 on single-word processing, PET made it possible for the first time to watch a healthy human brain at work rather than inferring function from damage.

The method that displaced it was born from a discovery by Seiji Ogawa in 1990: haemoglobin's magnetic properties differ depending on whether it carries oxygen, so local changes in blood oxygenation alter the magnetic resonance signal without any injection at all.

This is the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) contrast, and in 1992 three groups - Kwong and colleagues, Ogawa and colleagues, and Bandettini and colleagues - independently demonstrated it in working human brains, launching functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

The consequences were enormous and mixed: fMRI is non-invasive, needs no radiation, and can be repeated on the same person, but it measures blood flow rather than spikes, with a resolution of a few millimetres and a few seconds, and it therefore reports the aggregate demand of hundreds of thousands of neurons.

The field also passed through a genuine methodological crisis, with Vul and colleagues in 2009 documenting implausibly high brain-behaviour correlations arising from non-independent analysis, Bennett and colleagues in 2009 famously finding apparent activation in a dead salmon when multiple comparisons went uncorrected, and Button and colleagues in 2013 showing chronic low statistical power - problems that have since driven preregistration, larger samples, and shared data.


2.5.4 Optogenetics, high-density silicon probes, and whole-brain imaging

Recording tells you what a neuron did while something happened; it cannot tell you whether that neuron caused it, and for that you need to intervene.

Optogenetics supplied the intervention: genes for light-sensitive ion channels borrowed from algae, notably channelrhodopsin-2, are introduced into a genetically defined population of neurons, after which a pulse of blue light through a fibre makes exactly those neurons fire, on a millisecond timescale.

The founding demonstration in neurons was published by Edward Boyden, Karl Deisseroth and colleagues in 2005, and inhibitory tools such as halorhodopsin followed, allowing a defined population to be silenced as well as driven.

Neuropixels probes, introduced by Jun and colleagues in 2017 and extended in later versions, are silicon shanks carrying hundreds of recording sites, so that a single insertion can isolate hundreds of individual neurons across several brain regions simultaneously.

In small transparent animals the ambition goes further still: light-sheet microscopy combined with genetically encoded calcium indicators has allowed whole-brain activity imaging at near-cellular resolution in larval zebrafish, as demonstrated by Ahrens, Keller and colleagues from 2013 onward.

Together these tools change the logic of the field from correlation to causal manipulation of identified cell types, which is the strongest form of evidence the discipline has yet had - though a standing caution applies, since a circuit that has been forced to fire artificially may not be doing what it does naturally.


2.5.5 Deep learning, large-scale datasets, and the foundation-model era

The most recent turn is that artificial neural networks stopped being merely a metaphor for the brain and became a tool for studying it.

Deep convolutional networks trained to recognise objects turned out, as Yamins, DiCarlo and colleagues reported in 2014, to predict the responses of neurons in monkey inferotemporal cortex better than any hand-designed model, which suggested that a system optimised for the same task arrives at similar internal representations.

At the same time the field acquired datasets on an industrial scale - the Allen Brain Observatory, the Human Connectome Project, the UK Biobank imaging arm with tens of thousands of scanned participants, and the electron-microscopy connectomes of the fruit fly and of a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex.

The current phase is the foundation model: a large network pretrained on enormous quantities of neural data and then adapted to specific questions, exemplified by the model of mouse visual cortex reported by Wang, Tolias and colleagues in Nature in 2025, which predicted responses to entirely new classes of stimuli and generalised to animals it had never recorded from.

Comparable efforts are underway for electroencephalography and magnetoencephalography and for functional imaging across thousands of participants and dozens of conditions.

The honest assessment is that this is genuinely powerful and genuinely unsettled: a model that predicts neural responses accurately has captured something real, but prediction is not the same as understanding, and the field is actively arguing about whether these systems explain the brain or merely mimic it in a way that is itself opaque.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The question of where thinking happens was answered slowly and against intuition, moving from the heart to the ventricles to the cortex, with each wrong answer failing for an instructive reason.

The nineteenth-century pendulum between strict localisation and holistic mass action never fully stopped, and the modern settlement - functionally specialised regions organised into distributed networks - inherits from both Broca and Flourens.

The neuron doctrine of Cajal, the synapse and inhibition of Sherrington, the rate code of Adrian, and the quantitative membrane model of Hodgkin and Huxley together supplied a physical account of the signal on which every later cognitive claim depends.

The cognitive revolution of 1956 restored internal states to science by supplying a testable vocabulary - information, rules, representations, programs - and Gazzaniga and Miller's naming of cognitive neuroscience in the late 1970s made it a requirement that explanations be given at both the cognitive and the neural level at once.

Above all, the history is instrument-driven: what the field could ask has always been set by what it could measure or manipulate, from the silver stain to the voltage clamp to the microelectrode to the scanner to optogenetics to the foundation model.

Every one of those instruments answered questions and also biased the field toward the questions it happened to be good at, which is a caution to carry into the chapters that follow.


CHAPTER 3. PHILOSOPHY OF MIND AND THE FORM OF EXPLANATION (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about what an explanation of the mind would have to look like before we could call it finished.

Neuroscience produces an enormous quantity of measurement, and measurement alone does not settle whether anything has been explained.

The questions in this chapter are old, but they are not idle - they decide what a laboratory result is allowed to mean.

You will meet the mind-body problem in a form that touches experimental design, the difference between reducing a theory and describing a mechanism, the vexed question of whether a pattern of neural firing genuinely represents anything, and a short catalogue of the ways good scientists talk themselves into thinking they have explained something when they have only redescribed it.

None of this requires prior training in philosophy or in neuroscience.

It does require patience with the idea that a well-run experiment can still leave the central question untouched.


3.1 The mind-body problem in a laboratory-relevant form

The mind-body problem is the question of how mental things - seeing red, feeling afraid, intending to stand up - relate to physical things such as neurons, ions and blood flow.

Stated that abstractly it sounds like a puzzle for armchairs.

Stated concretely it is a working scientist's problem, because the answer you assume determines what you think you are measuring when you point an instrument at a brain.

If mental states simply are brain states, then a brain measurement is a direct measurement of the mind.

If mental states are something else that merely correlates with brain states, then every scan is an indirect proxy, and the gap between proxy and target has to be argued for rather than assumed.

The four sub-sections below walk through the main positions and the price each one pays.


3.1.1 Substance dualism, property dualism, and their empirical costs

Substance dualism, associated above all with Rene Descartes in the seventeenth century, holds that there are two fundamentally different kinds of stuff in the world - physical substance, which occupies space, and mental substance, which does not.

Property dualism is the weaker cousin: there is only one kind of stuff, physical stuff, but it has two irreducibly different kinds of properties, physical ones such as mass and charge, and mental ones such as what an experience feels like from the inside.

The standard scientific objection to substance dualism is the causal closure of the physical, which is the principle that every physical event that has a cause at all has a sufficient physical cause.

If that principle holds, an immaterial mind pushing a neuron around would be an uncaused physical push, and would appear either as a violation of the conservation of energy or as a physical effect with no physical antecedent.

Defenders of dualism reply that conservation laws are stated for closed systems, and that assuming the brain is closed is assuming exactly what is in dispute; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on dualism sets out this exchange fairly, and it remains unresolved rather than won by either side.

The empirical cost is what matters for a laboratory: dualism makes no prediction that anyone has been able to test, and it converts every neural correlate of a mental state into a coincidence requiring separate explanation.

Property dualism escapes the energy objection but inherits a different one, epiphenomenalism, which is the awkward conclusion that mental properties are along for the ride and do no causal work at all.


3.1.2 Identity theory, functionalism, and multiple realisability

The identity theory, formulated by U. T. Place in 1956 and J. J. C. Smart in 1959, says that mental states are brain states in the same flat way that lightning is an electrical discharge - not correlated with it, not caused by it, but identical to it.

This is a strong and admirably testable thesis, and it is the implicit working assumption of a great deal of neuroscience.

Its most famous difficulty is multiple realisability, pressed by Hilary Putnam in 1967 and Jerry Fodor in 1974: if pain in a human is one neural configuration, in an octopus another, and in a hypothetical silicon creature a third, then pain cannot be identical to any single physical type.

Functionalism was the response - a mental state is defined not by what it is made of but by what it does, that is, by its causal role between inputs, other mental states, and outputs.

On this view a mousetrap is a useful analogy: what makes something a mousetrap is what it accomplishes, not whether it is made of wood or wire.

Functionalism is the reason cognitive scientists can talk about working memory without first settling which neurons implement it, and it is also, as Putnam himself later argued, vulnerable to the same multiple realisability point pushed one level up, since a functional role can itself be specified at many grains.


3.1.3 Eliminativism and the fate of folk-psychological terms

Folk psychology is the everyday framework in which we explain each other using beliefs, desires, hopes and intentions.

Eliminative materialism, argued most forcefully by Paul Churchland in his 1981 paper on eliminative materialism and the propositional attitudes and by Patricia Churchland in her 1986 book Neurophilosophy, holds that this framework is a theory, that it is a bad theory, and that a mature neuroscience will replace rather than vindicate it.

Churchland's case rests on the observations that folk psychology predicts poorly, that it is silent about mental illness, sleep, learning and memory, and that it has barely changed in millennia while every other folk theory has been overturned.

The precedent offered is phlogiston or caloric - terms that were not refined by chemistry but retired by it.

The main objections are that folk psychology is not obviously a predictive theory at all but a social practice, and that the position looks self-undermining, since to assert eliminativism is to express a belief while denying that beliefs exist.

Most working cognitive neuroscientists occupy a middle position without stating it: they keep the vocabulary of belief and attention while accepting that specific folk categories may be carved up or discarded, which is revision rather than elimination.


3.1.4 The explanatory gap and the hard problem

Joseph Levine coined the phrase explanatory gap in 1983 to name a specific dissatisfaction: even granting that pain is a certain neural process, nothing in the description of that process tells you why it should feel like anything at all.

Levine was careful, and his carefulness is often lost in retelling - he framed the gap as epistemic, a limit on what we can currently understand, not as proof that consciousness is non-physical.

David Chalmers sharpened it in 1995 into the distinction between the easy problems of consciousness, which concern functions such as discrimination, reportability and attentional control, and the hard problem, which is why the performance of those functions is accompanied by subjective experience.

Qualia is the term of art for the felt qualities of experience, the redness of red, and the hard problem is precisely the problem of qualia.

There is no consensus resolution.

One influential physicalist reply is illusionism, developed by Keith Frankish in 2016, which argues that we should explain not phenomenal consciousness but our unshakeable conviction that we have it - a position its critics regard as changing the subject and its defenders regard as the only honest option.

For a laboratory this matters practically: a theory of consciousness that predicts reports and neural signatures has addressed the easy problems, and whether it has touched the hard one is a separate question that should be asked out loud rather than assumed.


3.2 Reduction, emergence, and mechanism

Even setting consciousness aside, there is a question about how levels of description fit together.

Psychology speaks of memory, cellular neuroscience of receptor trafficking, and biophysics of ion flow.

Reduction is the claim that the higher-level story is, in some strict sense, the lower-level story retold.

Emergence is the claim that something at the higher level is not captured by the lower-level story.

Mechanism is a third option, now dominant in the philosophy of neuroscience, which sidesteps both by describing how organised parts produce a phenomenon.


3.2.1 Classical intertheoretic reduction and why it rarely fits neuroscience

The classical account comes from Ernest Nagel in 1961, and it treats reduction as a relation between theories: theory A reduces to theory B if the laws of A can be logically derived from the laws of B, given bridge laws linking the vocabulary of the two.

A bridge law is a statement connecting terms across theories, such as the claim that temperature in a gas is mean molecular kinetic energy.

The textbook success story is thermodynamics reducing to statistical mechanics, and it is worth noticing how atypical it is.

Neuroscience almost never supplies the required ingredients.
