Psychology has few strict laws to derive, its terms rarely map one-to-one onto neural terms, and bridge laws cannot be tested independently of the reduction they are supposed to enable - a problem Nagel himself flagged.

There is a dissenting position: James Bickle has defended what he calls ruthless reductionism, arguing that molecular and cellular neuroscience really does displace psychological explanation in cases such as memory consolidation, and this remains a live minority view rather than a refuted one.


3.2.2 The new mechanist account: entities, activities, and organisation

The new mechanism is the view set out by Peter Machamer, Lindley Darden and Carl Craver in their 2000 paper Thinking About Mechanisms, and it has become the default philosophy of much of biology and neuroscience.

Their definition is that mechanisms are entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes from start or set-up conditions to finish or termination conditions.

Entities are the things - a receptor, a vesicle, a cortical column.

Activities are what those things do - bind, release, oscillate - and the account insists on activities as genuine constituents rather than treating causation as a black box between states.

Organisation is the spatial and temporal arrangement that makes the difference between a heap of parts and a working system.

On this account an explanation is not a derivation from laws but an accurate description of the responsible mechanism, and the explanation can be incomplete in a principled way, with acknowledged gaps called mechanism sketches that later work fills in.

This fits neuroscience far better than Nagelian reduction, because it is what neuroscientists actually produce.


3.2.3 Weak and strong emergence

David Chalmers, in a widely cited 2006 discussion, drew the distinction that has organised the modern debate.

Weak emergence is when a high-level property is unexpected given the low-level facts, and cannot practically be derived except by running the system or simulating it - Mark Bedau's 1997 formulation makes incompressibility, the impossibility of a shortcut, the defining feature.

Traffic jams, flocking, and most of the interesting behaviour of large neural networks are weakly emergent in this sense, and nothing metaphysically alarming follows.

Strong emergence is the far more demanding claim that the high-level property has genuinely novel causal powers not fixed by the low-level facts at all.

Bedau's verdict on strong emergence is blunt and often quoted - that it is uncomfortably like magic - and Chalmers, who is sympathetic, concedes that consciousness is the only remotely plausible candidate.

The practical lesson for a neuroscientist is to notice which claim is being made, because papers frequently announce emergence in the harmless weak sense while borrowing the rhetorical weight of the strong one.


3.2.4 Downward causation and its critics

Downward causation is the idea that a higher-level property, such as a network state, can cause changes in its own lower-level constituents, such as individual neurons.

The central objection is Jaegwon Kim's causal exclusion argument, developed through the 1990s and 2000s: if every physical effect already has a sufficient physical cause at the lower level, and we are not permitting systematic overdetermination, then there is no causal work left for the higher-level property to do.

Defenders reply in several ways - by denying that causation must be exclusive, by arguing that higher-level causes are better because they are more stable across background variation, and by pointing to formal measures of causal emergence such as those developed by Erik Hoel and colleagues from 2013 onward, which attempt to show that a coarse-grained description can carry more information about a system's dynamics than the fine-grained one.

Critics of that formal work argue that it establishes a fact about descriptions and modelling, not about causal powers in the world.

The dispute is genuinely open, and honest practice is to say which sense of downward causation is meant - a claim about which model predicts better, or a claim about what is really doing the pushing.


3.3 Representation as a scientific posit

Neuroscience is saturated with representational language.

A neuron represents an edge, a place cell represents a location, a population code represents a decision variable.

This talk is so useful that it is easy to forget it is a theoretical commitment rather than an observation.

You never see a representation in a recording; you see spikes, and you infer that they stand for something.

This section asks what would license that inference, what fixes what a neural state represents, whether the whole idiom can be dispensed with, and whether it should be read as a literal claim or a convenient tool.


3.3.1 What licenses calling a neural state a representation

The sharpest formulation of the problem comes from William Ramsey in his 2007 book Reconstructing the Cognitive World, and is known as the job description challenge.

Ramsey's demand is simple: to call something a representation, you must show that being a representation is the job it performs in the system, not merely that an observer can read it as informative.

Mere correlation is not enough, because on that standard a tree ring represents a year and a rusted pipe represents humidity, and the term stops doing explanatory work.

The most widely accepted positive criterion is structural representation, sometimes called an S-representation, where a set of internal states stands in a relation-preserving mapping to a set of external states, and - crucially - the system itself exploits that mapping to guide behaviour.

The rodent hippocampal place-cell and grid-cell system, from John O'Keefe's discovery of place cells in 1971 to the grid cells reported by Edvard and May-Britt Moser's group in 2005, is the usual textbook case, because the internal structure mirrors spatial structure and the animal navigates by it.

Even here the field is not unanimous; a 2021 Synthese paper by Facchin argues that structural representations still fail Ramsey's challenge, so the criterion is contested rather than settled.


3.3.2 Content determination: causal, informational, teleosemantic accounts

Granting that some neural states are representations, a further question is what determines their content - what makes this pattern be about a vertical edge rather than about anything else it happens to correlate with.

Causal and informational theories, associated with Fred Dretske from 1981 and with Jerry Fodor, say that a state means whatever reliably causes it, or whatever it carries information about.

The standing objection is the disjunction problem: if a cat on a dark night also triggers the dog-detector, then strictly the state carries information about cats-or-dogs, and misrepresentation becomes impossible to define, which is fatal because getting things wrong is exactly what representations characteristically do.

Teleosemantics, developed by Ruth Millikan from 1984 and by Karen Neander, adds a historical ingredient: content is fixed by what the state was selected to indicate, by evolution or by learning, so a misfire is a failure to perform a function rather than a change of meaning.

Nicholas Shea's 2018 book Representation in Cognitive Science offers the leading contemporary synthesis, combining exploitable structural correspondence with a task-function account of what the system is supposed to be doing.

No account commands consensus, and it is fair to say the unifying programme that Dretske, Fodor and Millikan launched in the 1980s has not delivered the single theory it promised.


3.3.3 Anti-representationalism from dynamical systems theory

A minority tradition argues that the representational idiom is not merely hard to ground but unnecessary.

Timothy van Gelder's 1995 paper on the dynamical hypothesis used the Watt centrifugal governor - the eighteenth-century device that regulates steam engine speed by spinning weights - as its centrepiece, arguing that the governor solves a control problem beautifully while containing nothing that plays a representational role, since engine speed and arm angle are continuously and mutually coupled rather than one standing for the other.

Anthony Chemero's 2009 book Radical Embodied Cognitive Science develops this into a general programme, describing cognition in terms of agent-environment dynamics and drawing on James Gibson's ecological psychology, in which the environment offers affordances - opportunities for action perceived directly - rather than being reconstructed internally.

The strongest cases for this view are tightly coupled sensorimotor behaviours such as catching a fly ball or infant reaching, where a simple control law outperforms a model that computes trajectories.

The strongest cases against it are offline capacities such as planning a route, remembering an absent object, or imagining a counterfactual, where something inside must stand in for something not present.

The honest summary is that the dynamical critique has permanently raised the standard of evidence for representational claims without displacing them.


3.3.4 Representation talk as an instrument versus as a commitment

There is a third position that neither defends representation as a robust natural feature nor eliminates it.

Frances Egan, in work culminating in her 2025 book Deflating Mental Representation, argues for a deflationary view: the vehicles are real, the neural states genuinely exist and genuinely cause behaviour, but the assignment of everyday content to them is a pragmatic gloss reflecting our explanatory interests.

On Egan's account the scientifically essential part of a computational theory is its mathematical content - a function from input values to output values - and calling the input edge orientation is an interpretive convenience for connecting the theory to the organism's ecological setting.

This is realist about mechanism and anti-realist about meaning, and it dissolves the content-determination disputes of the previous sub-section by denying they need an answer.

For a working scientist the practical question is one of bookkeeping: when you say a population represents reward prediction error, are you claiming a discovered fact about the brain, or summarising a fit between your model's variable and your recorded signal?

Both are legitimate, and confusion between them is a major source of overclaiming.


3.4 Explanatory virtues and vices in the field

The final section is a catalogue of failure modes.

These are not the errors of bad scientists; they are the errors that competent, careful people make because the errors are structurally easy to make and hard to see from the inside.

Each one has an antidote, and the antidotes are the practical residue of everything above.


3.4.1 Description mistaken for explanation

The most common vice in cognitive neuroscience is to report where and when something happens and to call that why it happens.

A statement that region X activates during task Y is a description; it becomes an explanation only when it tells you what X does such that Y is possible.

David Kaplan and Carl Craver made this precise in 2011 with the model-to-mechanism-mapping constraint, usually abbreviated 3M, which requires that variables and relations in an explanatory model correspond to identifiable components and causal dependencies in the mechanism producing the phenomenon.

By that standard a curve-fit that predicts a firing rate perfectly is a phenomenal model - it saves the data without saying what produces it.

The 3M requirement is itself disputed; Lauren Ross and others have argued that dynamical and mathematical models can explain without decomposing into parts, and that mechanists set the bar in a way that disqualifies legitimate science.

The safe practice, whichever side you take, is to state plainly which kind of model you have built.


3.4.2 The homunculus and how to discharge it

The homunculus fallacy is explaining a capacity by positing an inner agent that already has it - the little person in the head who watches the visual image, who then needs eyes of their own, and so on without end.

The problem is not that the posit is silly but that it is an infinite regress dressed as progress.

Daniel Dennett's solution, developed from the 1970s and known as homuncular functionalism, is to allow homunculi provided each one is stupider than the system it helps constitute, so that the hierarchy terminates in components so simple they can be built from mechanism - in his phrase, parts with only hemi-semi-demi-proto-quasi-pseudo intentionality.

That is what discharging the homunculus means: the debt is paid when the last level requires no intelligence at all.

Maxwell Bennett and Peter Hacker, in their 2003 book Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience, press a related but stronger complaint they call the mereological fallacy, which is ascribing to a part what only makes sense of the whole - brains do not decide, believe or see; animals do.

Dennett's reply is that this attribution is precisely the enabling move that lets us build whole persons out of mechanical parts, and the exchange is a standing disagreement rather than a settled point.

The practical test is simple and worth applying to your own writing: if you delete the mental verb from a sentence about a brain area, does an actual mechanism remain?


3.4.3 Circularity in cognitive ontologies

A cognitive ontology is the catalogue of mental categories a field uses - attention, working memory, inhibition, salience.

Russell Poldrack and Tal Yarkoni, in a 2016 Annual Review article, described the circularity that threatens it: tasks are designed to measure a construct, the construct is validated by the tasks, and neither is independently anchored.

Reverse inference is the specific inferential move at risk, meaning the step from an observed pattern of activation back to the mental process supposedly responsible - a step that is only valid if the region is fairly selective for that process, which is rarely established.

Poldrack's 2006 analysis showed how weak such inferences are when the base rates of activation across tasks are taken into account.

The remedies now in use are large-scale meta-analytic databases such as BrainMap and Neurosynth, formal task and construct ontologies such as the Cognitive Atlas and the Cognitive Paradigm Ontology, and decoding approaches that require agreement between forward and reverse inference before crediting a mapping.

The deeper worry survives the remedies: if the categories themselves are inherited from folk psychology, better statistics will only give us precise estimates of the wrong things.


3.4.4 Neuroessentialism and seductive-detail effects

Neuroessentialism is the tendency to treat a brain-level description as the real explanation and the psychological or social description as a mere appearance - to hear it is your amygdala as more fundamental than you were frightened, when the two are descriptions of one event at different grains.

There is experimental evidence that this bias is easy to induce.

Deena Weisberg, Frank Keil and colleagues reported in 2008 that adding logically irrelevant neuroscience information to a psychological explanation made non-experts rate bad explanations as better, an effect since named the seductive allure of neuroscience explanations.

A related claim by David McCabe and Alan Castel in 2008, that brain images specifically drive the effect, has largely failed to replicate.

The verbal effect itself has held up better - Diego Fernandez-Duque and colleagues reproduced it in 2015 using the original materials and found no additional contribution from images, and a 2024 replication in Royal Society Open Science recovered it in classroom and online samples.

The finding is a warning aimed inward as much as outward, because the people most fluent in neuroscientific vocabulary are also the people best equipped to produce explanations that sound mechanistic while being empty.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The choice between dualism, identity theory, functionalism and eliminativism is not decorative, because it fixes whether a brain measurement is a measurement of the mind or a proxy for it, and each option carries an empirical cost that should be stated rather than hidden.

Classical Nagelian reduction almost never applies to neuroscience, and the working alternative is mechanistic explanation in the sense of Machamer, Darden and Craver - entities and activities organised so as to produce a phenomenon - with weak emergence being common and harmless while strong emergence and downward causation remain contested and unproven.

Calling a neural state a representation is a commitment that must be earned, by showing the system exploits a structural correspondence rather than merely that an observer can read information off it, and the competing content theories, the dynamical critique, and Egan's deflationary alternative all remain in play.

The explanatory vices - description passed off as explanation, undischarged homunculi, circular cognitive ontologies, and the demonstrated seductive pull of neural detail - are the practical reason the philosophy matters.

The rest of this book should be read with one question held ready for every finding: has a mechanism been described, or has a location been reported?


CHAPTER 4. LEVELS OF ANALYSIS (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about the tools you use to decide what kind of answer you are looking for.

A brain can be described as a bag of chemicals, as a network of cells, as a machine running procedures, or as a person doing something for a reason, and all four descriptions can be true at the same time about the same event.

The apparatus in this chapter - Marr's three levels, the ladder of spatial and temporal scales, the konnectome fifteen-layer scheme, and the inside-out versus outside-in framing - exists to keep those descriptions from being confused with one another.

This matters because most sterile arguments in the science of cognition are not disagreements about facts.

They are two people answering different questions and each accusing the other of getting it wrong.

By the end of the chapter you should be able to hear a claim about the brain and say, immediately, which level it lives on and what would count as evidence for or against it at that level.


4.1 Marr's three levels

David Marr was a British neuroscientist and computer scientist who died of leukaemia in 1980 at the age of thirty-five, and whose book Vision, published posthumously in 1982, set the terms of this discussion for the next forty years.

Marr's central proposal is that any information-processing system - a cash register, a pocket calculator, an eye, a brain - must be understood at three separate levels, and that an explanation at one level does not automatically deliver an explanation at another.

The word he used was levels of analysis, not levels of nature.

That distinction is important: Marr was not claiming that the brain is built in three physical storeys, but that there are three different sorts of question you can ask about it, and that a complete understanding requires answering all three.

An information-processing system, in Marr's sense, is any device that takes in some representation of the world, transforms it, and puts out another representation that is useful for something.


4.1.1 Computational: what problem is solved and why

The computational level asks what the system is doing and why it is worth doing.

It is a specification of the input-output mapping - what goes in, what comes out, and what constraint from the world makes that particular mapping the right one.

Marr's own illustration was a cash register: at the computational level a cash register performs addition, and it performs addition because addition has the properties we want from a fair total, such as the order of items not mattering.

Applied to vision, the computational-level question is not how the retina wires up but why recovering three-dimensional shape from a flat, ambiguous, noisy image is even possible, and what regularities of the physical world make it possible.

Note the presence of the word why.

The computational level is the only one of the three where the environment enters the explanation, which is why William Bechtel and Oron Shagrir, writing in Topics in Cognitive Science in 2015, argued that this level makes a contribution the others cannot make: it is where the mechanism is related to the world it evolved to cope with.


4.1.2 Algorithmic and representational: by what procedure and over what formats

The algorithmic and representational level asks how the problem is actually solved, step by step, and in what format the information is held while it is being worked on.

Addition is one problem, but Arabic numerals, Roman numerals, tally marks, and binary are different representations of number, and each supports different procedures with different costs.

Anyone who has tried to multiply in Roman numerals has felt the point directly: the representation you choose determines which algorithms are cheap and which are agonising.

For the brain, this level covers questions such as whether a memory is stored as a pattern across many cells or as a change in a single cell, and whether a decision is made by accumulating evidence until a threshold is crossed or by comparing two quantities in one shot.

Bradley Love argued in 2015, in the same journal issue, that the algorithmic level is the natural bridge between the other two, because it is the only level stated in terms concrete enough to be tested against neural data and abstract enough to still be about the problem being solved.


4.1.3 Implementational: in what physical substrate

The implementational level asks what the thing is made of and how the physical stuff carries out the algorithm.

For a calculator this is silicon, transistors, and voltages; for a brain it is membranes, ion channels, neurotransmitters, cells, and the wiring between them.

Most of what is loosely called neuroscience in the public mind lives here, and the great instrument-driven programmes of the last two decades - connectomics, which is the reconstruction of complete wiring diagrams, and large-scale electrode recording - are implementational-level enterprises.

Marr's warning was that implementation on its own does not explain, and the sharpest modern restatement of that warning is a 2017 paper by Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording in PLOS Computational Biology titled Could a Neuroscientist Understand a Microprocessor.

They took a simulated MOS 6502 microprocessor, the chip inside the Apple I and the Atari games console, where the complete wiring diagram and every transistor state are known perfectly, and applied standard neuroscience analyses to it: lesions, tuning curves, correlations, dimensionality reduction.

The methods produced plausible-looking results and did not recover how the chip works, which is a hard demonstration that having all the implementational data is not the same as having an explanation.


4.1.4 The independence claim and its limits

Marr's strongest and most contested claim was that the levels are, to a large degree, independent: you can understand the algorithm without knowing the hardware, and the same algorithm could run on very different hardware.

The technical name for that possibility is multiple realizability, meaning that one higher-level description can be realised by more than one lower-level arrangement.

The independence claim has been under sustained attack from two directions.

Tomaso Poggio, who worked with Marr, has himself argued that treating the levels as independent was a mistake, because the hardware constrains which algorithms are plausible and the learning process constrains which representations arise at all.

Bechtel and Shagrir take a softer line, defending each level as making a non-redundant contribution while denying that any of them can be pursued in isolation, since implementation details routinely rule out otherwise attractive algorithms.

The argument is genuinely live rather than settled: a 2024 formal debate circulated from Jonathan Pillow's laboratory at Princeton was staged on the explicit motion that Marr's three levels are not a useful framework for neuroscience, with credible researchers on both sides.

The honest position for a beginner is that the three levels are an excellent set of questions and a poor description of how research actually proceeds, because in practice findings at one level constantly reshape hypotheses at the others.


4.2 Spatial and temporal scales

Marr's levels are about kinds of question.

Scales are about size and duration, and they are a different axis entirely, which is why confusing the two produces so much muddle.

The nervous system spans something like fifteen orders of magnitude in space and at least as many in time, and Patricia Churchland and Terrence Sejnowski made this vivid in a 1988 paper in Science, Perspectives on Cognitive Neuroscience, with a now-classic diagram plotting structural levels from the synapse up to the whole brain against the spatial scale at which each can be identified.

An order of magnitude is a factor of ten, so fifteen orders of magnitude is the difference between one and a thousand million million.


4.2.1 Molecule, synapse, neuron, microcircuit, area, system, whole brain, organism, group

Walking up the spatial ladder gives a rough sense of what each rung contains and what it explains.

A molecule such as a neurotransmitter or an ion channel protein sits at the nanometre scale, a billionth of a metre, and explains how a signal is chemically encoded or how a membrane is made permeable.

A synapse, the junction where one neuron passes a signal to another, is a fraction of a micrometre across, a millionth of a metre, and explains how strength and therefore learning is stored between two cells.

A neuron with its branches may span from tens of micrometres to, in the case of a motor neuron running to the foot, a full metre, and it explains how many inputs are integrated into a single decision to fire.

A microcircuit is a small, repeating pattern of a few cell types wired in a stereotyped way, spanning tens to hundreds of micrometres, and it explains generic operations such as lateral inhibition, in which an active cell suppresses its neighbours to sharpen contrast.

A brain area or region is a millimetre-to-centimetre block of tissue with a distinct connectional signature, and it explains why damage in one place costs one specific capacity.

A system, such as the visual system or the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that runs the stress response, is a chain of areas considered as a functional whole.

Above that sit the whole brain, the behaving organism, and finally the group, because a great deal of human cognition is only intelligible as something two or more brains do together.


4.2.2 Millisecond, second, minute, day, year, lifespan, evolutionary time

The temporal ladder is just as long, and each rung hosts different mechanisms.

At the millisecond, a thousandth of a second, an action potential fires and a synapse releases transmitter; this is the timescale of the elementary signalling event.

At tens to hundreds of milliseconds, oscillations organise activity into rhythms and a perceptual decision is made.

At seconds, working memory holds a phone number and the blood-oxygen response that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures rises and falls.

At minutes to hours, proteins are synthesised and a fragile new memory is consolidated into a more durable form.

At days to years, synapses are structurally rebuilt, skills become automatic, and the developing brain prunes connections it does not use.

Across a lifespan, myelination of the frontal lobes continues into the twenties and decline sets in decades later.

Across evolutionary time, measured in millions of years, the architecture itself is selected, which is why Poggio treats evolution as a level in its own right.


4.2.3 Scale mismatch between measurement and mechanism

Here is the practical problem that this ladder exposes: our instruments are almost never matched to the scale of the mechanism we care about.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) does not measure neural activity at all; it measures the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, a slow change in local blood oxygenation triggered indirectly by neural activity through a process called neurovascular coupling.

A single fMRI voxel, the small cube that is the image's unit of measurement, typically contains on the order of a million neurons, and the haemodynamic response it tracks unfolds over several seconds while the spiking it is meant to reflect happens in milliseconds.

So fMRI is roughly six orders of magnitude too coarse in space and three too coarse in time for the events that most cellular theories are about.

The mirror-image problem afflicts single-unit recording, which gives exquisite millisecond resolution from a handful of cells out of tens of billions, and therefore cannot see a distributed pattern even in principle.

Every method sits in some box on the Churchland and Sejnowski plot, no method covers the whole space, and a very large fraction of published disagreement is really two techniques looking at different boxes.


4.2.4 Cross-scale bridging laws and their scarcity

A bridging law would be a principled statement connecting a description at one scale to a description at another, of the sort that statistical mechanics provides when it derives temperature, a bulk property, from the average kinetic energy of molecules.

Neuroscience has very few of these, and the absence is the field's central structural weakness rather than a temporary gap in the data.

John Krakauer and colleagues made this case forcefully in Neuron in 2017, in a paper titled Neuroscience Needs Behavior: Correcting a Reductionist Bias, arguing that the field has accumulated an enormous stock of descriptions and remarkably few explanations, because measuring ever more of the implementation does not by itself tell you what the implementation is for.

Some partial bridges do exist: the Hodgkin-Huxley equations of 1952 connect ion channel conductances to the shape of an action potential, and mean-field models connect population firing rates to large-scale imaging signals with mixed success.

What is largely missing is any comparable derivation of a psychological quantity from a cellular one, and claims that such a derivation has been achieved should be examined very carefully.

Say plainly what is and is not known: we can often show that a molecule matters for a behaviour, and we can rarely show how the behaviour follows from the molecule.


4.3 Alternative level schemes

Marr's is not the only scheme, and the alternatives are not merely rival brandings.

Each one is a bet about which distinctions will pay off, and the bets differ.


4.3.1 Poggio's addition of learning and evolution to Marr

Tomaso Poggio, a computational neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who collaborated with Marr in the 1970s, revisited the framework in a 2012 paper in the journal Perception titled The Levels of Understanding Framework, Revised.

His central move was to add levels above the computational one: learning, which is change within a single organism over its lifetime through neural plasticity, and evolution, which is change across a species through natural selection.

The motivation is straightforward once stated.

For hard problems such as recognising an object, nobody has ever written down a satisfying computational-level specification, and yet brains and modern learning systems solve the problem anyway, which suggests that the real explanation is not a clever hand-specified algorithm but the process that produced one.

Poggio's revised scheme runs to roughly seven levels, adding wetware, hardware, and circuits below as well, and it explicitly rejects Marr's independence claim on the grounds that learning determines which representations and algorithms appear at all.


4.3.2 The konnectome fifteen-layer scheme and its address system

The konnectome framework, within which this book sits, uses a fifteen-layer scheme that is a levels-of-nature ladder rather than a levels-of-question ladder, and the two should not be mixed up.

Its layers run from Layer 1, the subatomic, through Layer 2 atomic, Layer 3 ionic and simple molecular, Layer 4 macromolecular, Layer 5 subcellular and organellar, Layer 6 cellular, Layer 7 synaptic and junctional, Layer 8 microcircuit, Layer 9 brain regions and pathways, Layer 10 neural and neuroendocrine systems, Layer 11 the whole nervous and endocrine system, Layer 12 organism and behaviour, Layer 13 dyad and small group, Layer 14 community and society, to Layer 15 the evolutionary and species layer.

Two design commitments give the scheme its content.

The first is encapsulation: each layer has its own components, its own governing laws, and its own vocabulary, and ordinarily talks only to the layer directly above and the layer directly below, so that a claim jumping several layers in one step is treated as an extraordinary claim requiring an explicit mechanism.

The second is the address system, in which identity at a layer is given by interfaces rather than by internal composition; the framework's slogan is that a brain region is defined by what it receives and to whom it sends, so that a named white matter tract, such as the fornix or the corticospinal tract, is read as an interface with a defined origin, destination, cargo, and format, in the way a wall socket is an interface between a power station and a lamp.

Layer 7, the synaptic layer, is singled out as the framework's one relation layer, because a synapse is built from parts owned by two different cells and its strength therefore belongs to the relationship rather than to either cell.

The framework also admits seven documented exceptions to the adjacency rule, called Layer-Skipping Channels, in which a signal crosses non-adjacent layers without being re-encoded on the way; the steroid hormone channel is the clearest case, since cortisol is fat-soluble enough to cross the blood-brain barrier and act directly on receptors inside neurons.

The stated logic of these exceptions is economic: layer-by-layer relay is what you pay for when a message needs a specific address, and you refuse to pay it when the message is a broadcast to everybody.

The reader should hold this scheme as a working framework proposed by this corpus rather than as a consensus position of neuroscience, and should judge it by whether the layer boundaries earn their keep in the chapters that follow.


4.3.3 Multi-level mechanistic models in the new mechanist tradition

A third scheme comes from philosophers of science working in what is called the new mechanist tradition, notably Carl Craver and William Bechtel.

Their proposal is that explanation in neuroscience is not the discovery of laws at all but the description of mechanisms, where a mechanism is a set of components, their activities, and the organisation by which they together produce some phenomenon.

Levels, on this view, are levels of composition rather than levels of abstraction: a level appears whenever you decompose a whole into organised parts, so the parts of a mechanism sit one level down from the mechanism itself, and the resulting hierarchy is local to that mechanism rather than global to the universe.

Craver's key methodological contribution is the notion of interlevel experiments, in which you intervene at one level and detect at another - blocking a receptor molecule and measuring a rat's spatial memory, for example - and he argues that spatial memory research is the field's best example of a genuinely multilevel mechanistic sketch, running from molecules through cells and regions to a navigating animal.

The word sketch is deliberate and load-bearing, because a sketch has gaps in it that are filled by black boxes, and Craver's honesty about how many boxes remain black is part of why the tradition is worth taking seriously.


4.3.4 Choosing a level as a strategic rather than metaphysical act

The practical upshot of all this is that choosing a level is a decision about research strategy, not a discovery about the furniture of the universe.

Nobody is obliged to believe that reality comes pre-cut into layers in order to find it useful to hold most variables fixed and study one grain size at a time.

The right question when picking a level is therefore not which level is real but which level makes the phenomenon you care about tractable, and which one your instruments can actually reach.

A good rule of thumb is to choose the coarsest level at which the phenomenon still has a describable structure, and then push one level down for mechanism and one level up for function.

The failure mode to avoid is level chauvinism in either direction: the belief that only molecules are real, or the belief that molecules are irrelevant because psychology has its own vocabulary.


4.4 Inside-out versus outside-in framing

The last piece of apparatus is not a ladder at all.

It is a question about which end of the brain you treat as the starting point, and it changes what your experiments can possibly discover.


4.4.1 The stimulus-response framing and its inherited assumptions

The dominant experimental framing in neuroscience is outside-in: present a stimulus, record a response, and infer what happened in between.

This is inherited fairly directly from the reflex arc of the nineteenth century and from behaviourism, and it carries assumptions that are rarely stated aloud.

It assumes that the brain is essentially idle until the world pokes it, that perception and action are separate processes with cognition sandwiched between them, and that the categories the experimenter chose - a face, a tone, a reward - correspond to categories the brain itself uses.

György Buzsáki's criticism of that last assumption is that it smuggles a human observer into the explanation, because a neural change in response to a stimulus does not by itself represent anything to the brain; somebody outside has to notice the correlation and declare it meaningful.

There is a further practical cost, which Buzsáki has argued in work including a 2021 Current Biology essay, If the Brain Is the Answer, What Was the Question: decades of stimulus-response experiments have not produced consensus on what neural oscillations are for, and he attributes this partly to the framing itself.


4.4.2 Buzsaki's inside-out alternative: brain-initiated activity grounded by action

Buzsáki's alternative, set out at length in his 2019 book The Brain from Inside Out, reverses the direction of explanation.

On his account the brain is a self-organised system that is always active, generating a huge repertoire of internal activity patterns before and independently of any stimulus, and the job of experience is not to write patterns in but to assign meaning to patterns that already exist.

The assignment is done by action: when a spontaneously occurring neural trajectory happens to coincide with an action that turns out useful, that trajectory acquires meaning, and until then it is, in his phrase, gibberish.

This is why he insists that action is the source of grounding, and why an animal that is moved passively through an environment learns very differently from one that moves itself.

The proposal has a strong flavour of an idea from robotics and philosophy called embodied cognition, and Buzsáki's version is unusual in being tied to concrete hippocampal physiology, in particular the finding that the same neural machinery that maps physical space is reused for memory and imagined trajectories.

It is fair to say that the inside-out programme is at present a compelling reframing with strong supporting phenomena rather than a fully tested theory, and its critics have argued, for example in a 2020 commentary titled Against the Epistemological Primacy of the Hardware, that it overcorrects by demoting the role of the external world.


4.4.3 Spontaneous activity as signal rather than noise

The empirical anchor of the inside-out view is the status of spontaneous activity, meaning the activity a brain produces when nothing in particular is being presented to it.

For most of the twentieth century this was treated as noise and averaged away across trials, which is exactly what you do to something you believe carries no information.

Amos Arieli, Alexander Grinvald and colleagues undermined that assumption in a 1996 paper in Science, using real-time optical imaging of cat visual cortex together with electrode recording to show that the notorious trial-to-trial variability of evoked responses is largely not random at all.

Their result was that a single-trial response could be predicted, to a good approximation, as the linear sum of a deterministic evoked response and the ongoing activity that happened to be present just before the stimulus arrived.

In other words the noise was the brain's current state, and averaging it away was throwing out the one variable that explained the variability.

The finding scales up: resting-state fMRI, developed from work by Bharat Biswal in 1995 and made central by Marcus Raichle and Michael Fox in the 2000s, showed that a brain doing nothing displays highly structured, reproducible correlated activity across distributed networks, and that this ongoing activity consumes the great majority of the brain's energy budget while task-evoked increases add only a small fraction on top.

The interpretation of resting-state networks remains contested - how much of the signal reflects neural coordination as against breathing, heart rate, and head motion is an active methodological dispute - but the basic claim that spontaneous activity is structured and consequential is now well supported.


4.4.4 Consequences for experimental design

Taking the inside-out view seriously changes what you do in the laboratory, and this is where the framing stops being philosophy and starts costing money.

First, you stop averaging across trials as a reflex and start measuring the pre-stimulus state, so that variability can be explained rather than discarded.

Second, you prefer self-generated behaviour to imposed stimulation, because if grounding comes from action then a passively stimulated animal is missing the ingredient that makes the activity mean anything.

Third, you treat the brain's own activity as the independent variable where you can, which in practice means causal tools: optogenetics, in which light-sensitive proteins are inserted into neurons so that specific cells can be switched on or off with light, and closed-loop designs that trigger a manipulation on the basis of an ongoing internal pattern such as a hippocampal sharp-wave ripple.

Fourth, you let the animal's own behavioural repertoire, rather than your task categories, carve up the data, which is the motivation behind the recent growth of markerless pose-tracking tools such as DeepLabCut, introduced by Alexander Mathis and colleagues in 2018, and behavioural segmentation methods that discover an animal's natural movement syllables.

None of this makes the outside-in experiment worthless; carefully controlled stimulus-response work remains the cleanest way to establish many facts, and the sensible reading is that the two framings ask different questions and should be run against each other rather than one replacing the other.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Marr's three levels - computational, algorithmic and representational, and implementational - are three different questions about the same system, and answering one does not answer the others, a point made concrete by Jonas and Kording's demonstration that complete implementational data about a microprocessor did not yield an understanding of it.

The independence of those levels, which Marr asserted, is disputed, with Poggio, Bechtel and Shagrir all arguing that findings at one level constrain hypotheses at the others, so the levels are best treated as a checklist of questions rather than a description of how research proceeds.

Levels of analysis are a different axis from spatial and temporal scales, and the nervous system spans roughly fifteen orders of magnitude on each, with the consequence that almost every instrument is badly matched to the mechanism it is used to study and that genuine bridging laws across scales remain scarce.

Alternative schemes make different bets: Poggio adds learning and evolution above the computational level, the new mechanists replace levels of abstraction with levels of composition inside a particular mechanism, and this corpus's fifteen-layer scheme organises nature itself into encapsulated layers identified by their interfaces, with seven documented exceptions where signals skip layers.

Choosing among these is a strategic act rather than a metaphysical discovery, and the working rule is to pick the coarsest level at which the phenomenon still has structure, then look one level down for mechanism and one level up for function.

Finally, the outside-in stimulus-response framing that still organises most experiments carries unstated assumptions that Buzsáki's inside-out alternative rejects, and the evidence that spontaneous activity is structured signal rather than noise, running from Arieli and colleagues in 1996 through the resting-state imaging literature, is strong enough that experimental design has begun to change in response.


CHAPTER 5. THE CONCEPTUAL VOCABULARY OF THE FIELD (APPARATUS)

Every field has a set of words that its practitioners use so often that they stop noticing them.

In the neuroscience of cognition those words are information, code, computation, dynamics, mechanism, and cause.

This chapter takes each of those words apart, says what it means precisely, says where the precise meaning came from, and says where the word gets used loosely in ways that can mislead you.

This matters because a great deal of apparent disagreement in the field is really disagreement about vocabulary - two researchers who both say the hippocampus "encodes" place can mean very different things and can be arguing past one another.

By the end you should be able to read a paper abstract and know which of these claims the authors are actually making, and how much evidence a claim of that kind would need.

Think of this chapter as the toolbox rather than the building.


5.1 Information, code, and channel

The word information in neuroscience almost always traces back to one mathematical source: the theory of communication published by Claude Shannon in 1948 while he worked at Bell Telephone Laboratories.

Shannon was not interested in meaning at all.

He was interested in a narrow engineering question - if you must send a message down a noisy wire, how many distinguishable messages can get through per second, and how should you code them.

That narrow question turned out to give neuroscience a precise, measurable notion of "carrying information," and also a persistent temptation to read more into the word than the mathematics licenses.


5.1.1 Shannon information, entropy, and mutual information

Entropy, in Shannon's sense, is a measure of uncertainty - how surprised you should expect to be by the next thing a source produces, measured in bits, where one bit is the uncertainty of one fair coin flip.

A source that always produces the same symbol has zero entropy, because you learn nothing when you observe it; a source that produces eight equally likely symbols has three bits of entropy, because it takes three yes-or-no questions to pin down which one occurred.

Mutual information is the quantity that matters most for neuroscience: it is the amount by which your uncertainty about one variable drops once you observe another.

Formally, the mutual information between a stimulus and a neural response equals the entropy of the response minus the average entropy of the response once the stimulus is known - it is the part of the response variability that tracks the stimulus rather than noise.

Two properties make it attractive: it is measured in bits, so responses in different brain areas and different species can be compared on one scale, and it captures any statistical dependence, linear or non-linear, rather than only the straight-line relationships that a correlation coefficient would catch.

The practical difficulty is that estimating mutual information well requires a great deal of data, because you are estimating a whole probability distribution rather than a single number, and small samples produce a systematic upward bias - this is why the literature is full of correction methods and why single-cell information estimates from short recordings should be read with caution.


5.1.2 What it means to say a neuron carries information about a variable

The strict meaning is disappointingly modest: a neuron carries information about a variable if, and only if, knowing the neuron's response reduces your uncertainty about that variable.

That is a statistical statement about a relationship between two measured quantities, and nothing more.

It does not say the information is used, it does not say the rest of the brain can get at it, and it does not say the neuron is "about" that variable in any richer sense.

A concrete example makes the modesty clear: a neuron in primary visual cortex whose firing rate rises with the contrast of a bar carries information about contrast, but the very same firing rate also carries information about the time of day, the animal's arousal, and the amount of anaesthetic in its blood, because all of those also shift firing rates.

Which of these we call "the" encoded variable is a decision made by the experimenter about what was varied in the experiment, not a fact discovered about the neuron.

This is why careful writers distinguish information that is present in a signal from information that is available to a downstream reader - a distinction that the mathematics itself does not make.


5.1.3 Encoding versus decoding, and the observer's role

An encoding model runs forwards: it takes the stimulus or the behaviour and predicts the neural response, answering the question "what does this brain area respond to."

A decoding model runs backwards: it takes the neural response and reconstructs the stimulus or the behaviour, answering the question "what could an observer read out of this activity."

The two are not interchangeable, and the asymmetry is where the trouble lives.

Romain Brette, in a much-discussed 2019 target article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences titled "Is coding a relevant metaphor for the brain?", pressed the point that a successful decoder demonstrates something about the experimenter, not necessarily about the animal.

The experimenter knows the stimulus, has thousands of trials, can apply arbitrary mathematics offline, and can use recordings from cells that are not anatomically connected to anything downstream - the brain has none of those advantages and never gets to see the external variable it is supposedly decoding towards.

Brette's own conclusion, that the coding metaphor should largely be replaced by talk of internal sensorimotor models, remains a minority position and was contested by many of the commentators published alongside him; the weaker version of his point, that decoding accuracy is an upper bound on what the brain could be doing rather than a measurement of what it does do, is now fairly widely accepted.

The practical upshot for a reader is a habit of mind - when a paper reports that a classifier decoded a category from cortical activity at eighty percent accuracy, ask whether anything in the paper shows that the animal's own downstream circuits perform, or could perform, the same read-out.


5.1.4 The efficient coding hypothesis

The efficient coding hypothesis is the proposal that sensory systems are built to represent natural signals using as few resources as possible - fewest spikes, least metabolic energy, least redundancy.

It was stated by Fred Attneave in 1954 in terms of visual perception and given its influential form by Horace Barlow in 1961 as redundancy reduction: because natural images and natural sounds are highly predictable, with neighbouring pixels and neighbouring moments strongly correlated, an efficient sensory system should strip out the predictable part and transmit mainly what is new.

The most-cited empirical support came from Simon Laughlin in 1981, who measured the distribution of contrasts in the natural environment of the blowfly and then measured the input-output curve of its large monopolar cells - second-order neurons in the fly's eye - and found that the neuron's response curve matched the cumulative distribution of natural contrasts, which is exactly the shape that maximises the information transmitted by a channel with a limited output range.

The hypothesis has been genuinely productive: it predicts centre-surround receptive fields in the retina, the shift of retinal filtering from band-pass in bright light to low-pass in dim light, and much of the structure of oriented filters in primary visual cortex.

It is also contested at the edges.

Later reanalyses of the blowfly data, including work associated with Il Memming Park and Jonathan Pillow on Bayesian efficient coding, argue that the fly's response curve fits a code minimising a decoding error criterion at least as well as it fits pure information maximisation - which matters, because it shows that "efficient" is not one hypothesis but a family of hypotheses that differ in what is being made efficient.

The honest summary is that the principle is elegant and has real predictive successes in early sensory systems, and that its explanatory grip weakens the further you move from the sensory periphery towards cortex, where what counts as the relevant cost and the relevant task both become much harder to specify.


5.2 Computation

To say the brain computes is to make a claim, but it is not obvious which claim.

The word carries at least three distinct senses in the literature - a mathematical sense, an engineering sense, and a metaphysical sense - and arguments between researchers frequently turn out to be arguments between senses.

This section separates them and then asks what would make a computational claim about the brain substantive rather than empty.


5.2.1 Digital, analogue, and hybrid senses of computation

Digital computation is the manipulation of strings of discrete symbols - digits - according to rules defined over those digits, which is what a laptop does.

Analogue computation is the manipulation of continuously varying quantities, such as voltages in an old electronic differential analyser, where the quantity itself stands in for the modelled variable.

The brain fits neither template cleanly, and Gualtiero Piccinini, a philosopher, together with the biophysicist Sonya Bahar, argued in a 2013 paper in Cognitive Science that neural computation is therefore sui generis - a category of its own.

Their reasoning is concrete: a spike is a discrete, all-or-nothing event, so neural signals are not continuous, but a firing rate is a graded quantity built out of those discrete events and carrying no digit-by-digit syntax, so neural signals are not strings of digits either.

The practical importance of this is that arguments which assume the brain must be one or the other - "the brain cannot be a computer because neurons are analogue," or "the brain is just a digital machine made of meat" - are both attacking a template the brain does not fit.


5.2.2 Neural computation as transformation of population state

Contemporary systems neuroscience has largely settled on a working sense of computation that sidesteps the digital-analogue question entirely: a computation is a transformation of the joint activity state of a population of neurons over time.

The unit of analysis is not the single cell but the population vector - a list of the firing rates of all recorded neurons at one instant, which can be thought of as one point in a space with as many dimensions as there are neurons.

On this view, a brain area performs a computation when its recurrent connectivity reliably carries one region of that space to another, and the "answer" is the location the population arrives at.

Krishna Shenoy and Saurabh Vyas and colleagues set out this framework in a 2020 Annual Review of Neuroscience article, "Computation Through Neural Population Dynamics," building on a decade of work in motor cortex.

The advantage of this framing is that it is directly measurable with modern large-scale recording, and that it explains phenomena single-neuron tuning curves handled badly - most famously, that individual motor cortex neurons have messy, inconsistent tuning while the population trajectory during reaching is smooth, rotational, and highly reproducible.


5.2.3 The trivialisation objection: is everything computing

The sharpest philosophical challenge to computational neuroscience is that the notion of computation, if left unconstrained, applies to everything and therefore explains nothing.

Hilary Putnam argued in 1988, and John Searle pressed the point in 1992, that any sufficiently complex physical system can be mapped onto the state transitions of an arbitrary finite automaton if you are permitted to choose the mapping freely - Searle's memorable formulation being that on such a reading the wall behind him is implementing a word-processing program.

If that is right, then saying "the brain is a computer" says no more than saying the brain is a physical object, and this position, in its general form, is called pancomputationalism.

The objection is not merely a philosopher's game, because it identifies a real methodological hazard - a modeller who fits any input-output mapping to neural data and calls the fit a computation has not thereby explained anything.

The standard reply is that computation must be tied to the actual causal organisation of the system rather than to a freely chosen mapping, which is what the next sub-section unpacks.


5.2.4 Criteria for a substantive computational claim

Piccinini's mechanistic account, developed across several papers and consolidated in his 2020 book Neurocognitive Mechanisms, holds that a physical system computes when it is a mechanism whose function is to manipulate vehicles - physical states such as spike trains - according to a rule defined over those vehicles and sensitive only to differences between them, not to what the vehicles are made of.

The key phrase is "whose function is": on this account computation is not in the eye of the observer, because whether manipulating those vehicles is what the mechanism is there to do is a fact about the system's causal organisation and its evolutionary or developmental history.

Three practical tests follow, and they are worth carrying into any paper you read.

• Is the proposed computation realised by identifiable parts with identifiable causal roles, or is it only a curve fitted to the output.

• Does the proposal predict what happens under perturbation - if you silence this population, the model says the trajectory should fail in this specific way, and it does.

• Does the proposal rule anything out, or would it have accommodated the opposite result equally well.

David Marr's 1982 three-level scheme - the computational level asking what problem is being solved and why, the algorithmic level asking what representations and procedures solve it, and the implementational level asking how neural hardware realises the procedure - remains the standard way of keeping these questions apart.

Marr's framework is not uncontested, and recent critiques argue that its assumptions of a priori specifiable goals and of substrate-independent realisation both fail for biological systems; its defenders reply that the levels remain useful as a division of labour even if they are not cleanly separable in nature.


5.3 Dynamics

Dynamics is the study of how a system changes over time, and it supplies the geometrical vocabulary - state space, trajectory, attractor, bifurcation - that has become the common language of systems neuroscience.

The appeal of this vocabulary is that it describes what a network does without first committing to what the network represents, which makes it a useful common ground between researchers who disagree about coding.


5.3.1 State space, trajectory, fixed point, limit cycle, chaos

A state space is the set of all possible states a system can be in, with one axis per variable - for a population of one hundred recorded neurons, a hundred-dimensional space in which each axis is one neuron's firing rate, and the whole population at one instant is a single point.

A trajectory is the path that point traces out as time passes, and the rules of the network determine, from any starting point, where the trajectory goes next.

A fixed point is a state that maps to itself - once there, the system stays put; it is stable, and then called an attractor, if nearby trajectories fall into it, and unstable if nearby trajectories flee.

A limit cycle is a closed loop that trajectories settle onto, producing self-sustaining rhythmic activity - the natural formal description of a central pattern generator such as the circuit that drives locomotion or breathing.

Chaos is bounded, deterministic behaviour in which trajectories starting arbitrarily close together diverge exponentially, so the system is perfectly rule-governed and yet unpredictable in practice beyond a short horizon.

Chaotic dynamics appear routinely in models of balanced cortical networks and are one proposed source of trial-to-trial variability in cortex, but demonstrating chaos in real neural data as opposed to noise remains genuinely difficult and is not settled.


5.3.2 Attractors as memory and as decision

The attractor concept gives a mechanism for two cognitive functions at once, which is why it has been so influential.

For memory, a discrete point attractor lets a network hold a state after the input that caused it has gone - the network is pushed into a basin and stays there, which is the standard account of persistent delay-period firing in prefrontal cortex during working memory, an account developed formally by Xiao-Jing Wang and colleagues from the late 1990s.

For decision, a network with two stable fixed points and mutual inhibition between the populations that lead to them will, given noisy evidence, be driven into one basin or the other and stay - so the same machinery that stores also commits.

Continuous attractors, where the stable states form a connected line, ring, or surface rather than isolated points, handle graded quantities: a ring attractor can hold any heading direction, and a line attractor can hold any value of an accumulating variable.

The evidence here has become unusually strong for a theoretical construct.

Johannes Seelig and Vivek Jayaraman reported in 2015 and 2017 that the ellipsoid body of the fruit fly holds a single localised bump of activity that tracks the animal's heading, persists in darkness, and slides as the fly turns - the signature behaviour of a ring attractor in an anatomically ring-shaped circuit.

Richard Gardner, Edvard Moser, May-Britt Moser and colleagues, publishing in Nature in 2022, applied topological analysis to simultaneously recorded grid cells in rat medial entorhinal cortex and showed that the population activity lies on a torus - a doughnut surface - exactly as continuous attractor models of grid cells had predicted, and that it does so during sleep as well as during navigation, which is hard to explain if the structure were merely inherited from the animal's movement.

Line attractor structure has also been reported in mouse hypothalamus, where Ann Kennedy, David Anderson and colleagues found in 2020 a slowly evolving population variable tracking aggressive arousal, with later work adding causal manipulation.


5.3.3 Bifurcation and state transition

A bifurcation is a qualitative change in a system's behaviour produced by a smooth change in a parameter - the parameter moves a little further and a fixed point vanishes, or splits, or loses stability, and the system's whole repertoire changes.

This is the formal reason that neurons have thresholds: as injected current rises, the neuron's resting fixed point is destroyed or destabilised, and the system leaves rest for a limit cycle, which is spiking.

Eugene Izhikevich's 2007 book Dynamical Systems in Neuroscience classified neurons by which bifurcation does this, and the classification has real experimental consequences.

Type I excitability arises from a saddle-node on invariant circle bifurcation and allows arbitrarily low firing rates just above threshold, so the firing-rate-versus-current curve rises continuously from zero; type II excitability arises from an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation and starts abruptly at a non-zero rate, so the curve jumps.

That difference is not cosmetic - it determines whether a neuron behaves as an integrator, summing inputs, or as a resonator, responding preferentially to inputs at a particular frequency, and therefore what kind of network computation it can participate in.

Bifurcations are also the natural language for abrupt state transitions at larger scales, including the transition from waking to anaesthesia and the onset of a seizure, though whether particular clinical transitions are true bifurcations with detectable early-warning signals remains an active and unresolved research question.


5.3.4 Timescale hierarchies across cortex

Different cortical areas do not merely process different content; they operate at systematically different speeds.

John Murray, Xiao-Jing Wang and colleagues showed in a 2014 Nature Neuroscience paper that the intrinsic timescale of a cortical area - estimated from how quickly the autocorrelation of its spontaneous spike counts decays, that is, how long the area's activity keeps predicting itself - increases progressively from sensory areas such as middle temporal visual area, at tens of milliseconds, up through parietal and then prefrontal areas, at hundreds of milliseconds or more.

The same ordering appears in a complementary human measure: Uri Hasson and colleagues, from 2008 onwards, used temporal receptive windows, measured by scrambling films or narratives at different grain sizes and asking which areas still responded reliably, and found early visual and auditory areas tracking events over a second or less while areas such as the angular gyrus and medial prefrontal cortex required coherent structure over tens of seconds.

The convergence of an electrophysiological measure in monkeys with an imaging measure in humans, and subsequent replication of the timescale gradient in mice and in single-neuron data across all three species, makes this one of the better-supported organisational principles in cortex.

Its functional interpretation is that a hierarchy of timescales lets the brain hold fast-changing sensory detail and slow-changing context simultaneously, each at the level where it is needed - though the causal direction, whether the gradient produces the functional hierarchy or reflects it, is not established, and the underlying gradients of recurrent connection strength and receptor expression that are proposed to generate it are still being mapped.


5.4 Mechanism, causation, and necessity

The final piece of the vocabulary concerns evidence.

Cognitive neuroscience is, for the most part, an observational science that periodically gets to intervene, and the words used to report interventions - necessary, sufficient, required, drives, causes - carry logical commitments that are often stronger than the data supports.


5.4.1 Necessity, sufficiency, and modulation as distinct causal claims

Three claims are routinely run together and should not be.

• Necessity: without this component the function fails, which is what a lesion or a silencing experiment tests.

• Sufficiency: activating this component produces the function on its own, which is what a stimulation or optogenetic activation experiment tests - optogenetics being the technique of inserting light-sensitive ion channel genes into chosen neurons so that light can switch them on or off within milliseconds.

• Modulation: this component changes the strength, speed, or reliability of a function without being required for it or able to produce it alone.

These come apart in ordinary cases: the power supply is necessary for a radio to play music but tells you nothing about how tuning works, and stimulating a motor pathway can produce a movement without that pathway being the structure that normally selects the movement.

A useful refinement comes from Steffen Wolff and Bence Ölveczky, who distinguish instructive roles, where a region supplies the specific content of a behaviour, from permissive roles, where a region supplies background activity that other regions need in order to function - both show up as "necessary" in a silencing experiment while meaning entirely different things.

There is a live methodological argument here, articulated among others by Yarden Katz and by commentators in The Transmitter, that necessity-and-sufficiency language borrowed from molecular genetics is a poor fit for highly interconnected systems where behaviour emerges from many interacting parts, and that the field would do better to report graded causal contributions.


5.4.2 Correlation, perturbation, and the ladder of causal evidence

Judea Pearl's ladder of causation gives a clean way to rank evidence: the first rung is association, seeing what goes with what; the second is intervention, doing something and observing the effect; the third is counterfactual reasoning, asking what would have happened to this particular case had things gone otherwise.

Most neuroimaging, including nearly all functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), lives on the first rung - it shows that activity in an area covaries with a task, which is compatible with the area causing the behaviour, being caused by it, or both being driven by something else.

The second rung is reached by lesions, by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which uses a rapidly changing magnetic field to transiently disrupt a patch of cortex through the intact skull, by pharmacological inactivation, and by optogenetics.

But climbing the ladder does not settle interpretation, because perturbing one node of a densely recurrent network changes the network, not just the node.

Constance Holgado Pisco and colleagues, and separately the review by Wolff and Ölveczky in Current Opinion in Neurobiology, emphasise that acute perturbations push the system into states it never visits naturally, so the observed deficit may reveal how the perturbed network behaves rather than what the intact region did.

The century-old term for this is diaschisis, coined by Constantin von Monakow in 1914 - damage in one place depresses function in distant, connected, undamaged places - and modern whole-brain imaging after focal optogenetic silencing confirms that the effects propagate widely.

The practical conclusion is that convergence matters more than any single method: a claim supported by correlation, by loss-of-function, by gain-of-function, and by a model that predicted the specific pattern of failure is worth far more than four times a claim supported by one of them.


5.4.3 Degeneracy: many mechanisms for one function

Degeneracy is the property of a system in which structurally different components can produce the same output.

Gerald Edelman and Joseph Gally set out the concept for biology in a 2001 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and were careful to separate it from redundancy: redundancy means duplicate identical parts, as in two copies of the same circuit, whereas degeneracy means different parts arriving at the same functional result.

The most rigorous demonstration comes from Eve Marder's laboratory working on the stomatogastric ganglion of the crab - a circuit of about thirty neurons that generates the rhythm of the stomach, small enough to be fully characterised.

Marder, together with Astrid Prinz and Dirk Bucher, showed in 2004 that many widely different combinations of synaptic strengths and ion channel densities produce essentially indistinguishable rhythmic output, and measurements across individual animals found ion channel messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) expression varying several-fold between animals whose circuits behaved almost identically.

The consequence for cognitive neuroscience is uncomfortable and important: if the same function can be built many ways, then averaging across subjects can describe a mechanism that no individual actually uses, and a model that reproduces the observed behaviour is not thereby shown to be the model the brain implements.

Degeneracy also cuts the other way as a positive claim - it is a plausible explanation for why nervous systems tolerate enormous genetic, developmental, and environmental variation and still work.


5.4.4 Robustness, redundancy, and compensation after damage

Robustness is the maintenance of function despite perturbation, and degeneracy is one of its main sources - the others being redundancy proper and active homeostatic regulation.

At the cellular level, homeostatic mechanisms continuously adjust ion channel expression to hold a neuron's activity near a target level, so a deficit in one conductance is offset by changes in others; Marder's group and others have shown that this regulation can restore rhythmic output after the circuit has been silenced for hours or days.

At the systems level, recovery after stroke or surgery involves a mixture of resolution of diaschisis in the first weeks, reorganisation within surviving perilesional tissue, and recruitment of homologous regions in the other hemisphere, with the relative contribution of each still debated and probably dependent on lesion size and age at injury.

Age matters enormously: children who undergo hemispherectomy, the surgical removal or disconnection of an entire cerebral hemisphere for intractable epilepsy, can recover fluent language when the operation happens early, whereas equivalent adult damage is typically permanent - though the recovery is not free, and the crowding hypothesis holds that language squeezed into a remaining hemisphere displaces its usual visuospatial functions, a proposal with mixed empirical support.

For the reader of this book, compensation is chiefly a warning about inference: the behaviour of a damaged brain some months after injury reflects the reorganised system, so what a patient can no longer do tells you about the current configuration and only indirectly about what the missing tissue originally contributed.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Information in this field means Shannon's mutual information - a measurable reduction in uncertainty, which establishes a statistical relationship and by itself establishes nothing about use, meaning, or availability to the rest of the brain, so a successful decoder demonstrates a capacity of the experimenter before it demonstrates one of the animal.

Computation in contemporary systems neuroscience means the lawful transformation of population states, a formulation that avoids the sterile digital-versus-analogue dispute, and it escapes the pancomputationalist charge of triviality only when the proposed computation is tied to identifiable parts, predicts the effects of perturbation, and could have been wrong.

The dynamical vocabulary of state space, attractor, and bifurcation has moved from metaphor to measurement, with the fly's ring attractor for heading and the toroidal geometry of rat grid cell activity standing as the strongest confirmations, and with the intrinsic timescale gradient from sensory to prefrontal cortex now replicated across imaging and electrophysiology in several species.

Causal claims come in at least three distinct grades - necessity, sufficiency, and modulation - and none of them can be read off correlational imaging, while even intervention is complicated by the fact that perturbing a recurrent network changes the whole network.

Finally, degeneracy means that one function can be built many ways, so a model that reproduces behaviour has not thereby been shown to be the brain's model, and a recovered patient reveals a reorganised system rather than the original one.


PART TWO. THE SUBSTRATE: THE NEUROBIOLOGY THAT COGNITION IS MADE OF


CHAPTER 6. CELLS: NEURONS AND GLIA (APPARATUS)


Cognition is not made of ideas.

It is made of cells, and of the electrical and chemical traffic between them.

This chapter opens the box at the smallest level that still matters for thought - the individual cell - and asks what a neuron actually does, how neurons differ from one another, and what the other half of the brain's cell population, the glia, contributes.

The chapter matters because every claim made later in this book about memory, attention, language, or decision-making must eventually be paid for in cellular currency.

It matters just as much because the cellular level is not sufficient on its own.

Some cognitive capacities live comfortably in the properties of single cells; many do not, and pretending otherwise has cost the field decades.

So the chapter ends honestly, with what cells explain and what they do not.


6.1 The neuron as a computational element

A neuron is a cell that has specialised in handling information.

Other cells in the body also have electrically excitable membranes - heart muscle, for example - but the neuron is unusual in combining excitability with an elaborate branching shape and thousands of specific contacts onto other neurons.

The useful way to think about a neuron is as a device that takes in many signals, weighs them, combines them across space and time, and emits a much simpler output: a train of electrical pulses.

The word computation here means nothing mystical.

It means only that the relationship between input and output is a systematic transformation, and that the transformation can be described.


6.1.1 Soma, dendrite, axon, terminal, and the polarity of signalling

A typical neuron has four functional parts.

The soma is the cell body, the bulge that holds the nucleus and most of the machinery for keeping the cell alive.

The dendrites are branching processes that spread out from the soma and receive incoming signals from other neurons; a single cortical pyramidal neuron may carry several thousand input contacts on its dendrites.

The axon is a single long process that leaves the soma and carries the neuron's output away, sometimes only a fraction of a millimetre, sometimes the better part of a metre in the case of a motor neuron running from the spinal cord to the foot.

The axon ends in terminals, small swellings that release chemical messengers onto the next cell.

This arrangement gives the neuron polarity - a built-in direction of flow, from dendrite to soma to axon to terminal.
