Polarity is not a passive fact of geometry; it is actively established during development, and the current understanding, reviewed in Development in 2015 by Takano, Xu and colleagues and refined since, is that a positive feedback signal stabilises one growing process as the axon while a negative feedback signal spreading back from that nascent axon suppresses the others so that only one axon forms.

The reason polarity matters for cognition is that it makes the brain a directed network rather than an undirected one, and a directed network can implement sequences, hierarchies and loops - which an undirected one cannot.


6.1.2 Excitable membrane, ion channels, resting potential, action potential

The neuron's outer membrane is studded with ion channels - protein pores that let specific charged atoms, chiefly sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride, cross the membrane.

Because pumps in the membrane keep potassium concentrated inside and sodium concentrated outside, and because the resting membrane leaks potassium more readily than sodium, the inside of a resting neuron sits at roughly seventy millivolts negative relative to the outside; this is the resting potential.

If inputs push that voltage up past a threshold of around fifty-five millivolts negative, voltage-gated sodium channels snap open, sodium floods in, and the voltage swings sharply positive before potassium channels open and drag it back down.

That stereotyped one-millisecond spike is the action potential, and it is the brain's fundamental unit of long-distance signalling.

The quantitative account of this process was given by Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley in a series of 1952 papers on the squid giant axon, work that won them a share of the 1963 Nobel Prize and that remains the template for essentially every biophysical neuron model in use today.

The critical feature for cognition is that the action potential is all-or-none and regenerating: it does not fade with distance, so a neuron can send an undegraded signal across the brain, and its meaning must therefore be carried in when spikes occur and how many, not in how big they are.


6.1.3 Cable properties, electrotonic length, and passive filtering

Before a signal reaches the axon it has to travel through the dendrites, and dendrites are leaky.

A dendrite behaves rather like an undersea telegraph cable with poor insulation - hence cable theory, the mathematical treatment of how voltage spreads along such a structure, developed for neurons principally by Wilfrid Rall from the late 1950s onward and extended in his influential 1962 analysis showing that a branching dendritic tree can under certain conditions be collapsed into a single equivalent cylinder.

The key quantity is the length constant, written with the Greek letter lambda, which is the distance over which a steady voltage signal decays to about thirty-seven percent of its starting size.

Electrotonic length is the physical length of a dendrite expressed in units of lambda; it tells you how electrically distant a synapse is from the soma, which can differ wildly from how far away it looks under a microscope.

Cable structure also acts as a low-pass filter, meaning it passes slow voltage changes fairly faithfully while smearing out and shrinking fast ones, so a brief sharp synaptic event on a distal dendrite arrives at the soma as a small slow bump.

The cognitive consequence is that where an input lands on a cell is itself a form of weighting, applied before any learning-related change in synaptic strength is considered.


6.1.4 Axonal conduction, myelination, and conduction delay as a computed quantity

An unmyelinated axon conducts an action potential by regenerating it continuously along its length, which is reliable but slow, on the order of one metre per second.

Myelin is a fatty insulating wrap, laid down by oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nerves, that covers the axon in segments called internodes separated by short bare gaps called nodes of Ranvier.

Because current can only cross the membrane at the nodes, the impulse effectively jumps from node to node - saltatory conduction - raising speed to as much as a hundred metres per second while using far less energy.

The point that has changed most in the last fifteen years is that conduction delay is no longer treated as a fixed anatomical accident.

Reviews such as Pajevic, Basser and Fields in Neuroscience in 2014 argue that adjusting myelin thickness or internode length tunes arrival times, and that this matters because a delay of only a few milliseconds can flip two coupled oscillators in the gamma range from constructive to destructive interference.

Arancibia-Carcamo and colleagues, writing in eLife in 2017, showed that node of Ranvier length varies systematically and is itself a plausible regulator of conduction speed - and a metabolically cheaper one to change than the myelin sheath.

The upshot is that when a signal arrives may be as much a computed quantity as whether it arrives at all.


6.2 Neuronal diversity

There is no such thing as the neuron, in the way there is such a thing as the transistor.

The human brain contains on the order of eighty-six billion neurons falling into a very large number of distinct types that differ in shape, in which ion channels they express, in which neurotransmitter they release, in where they send their axons, and in which genes they switch on.

This section surveys the main divisions and then asks why the catalogue matters rather than being mere stamp-collecting.


6.2.1 Excitatory principal cells: pyramidal, stellate, granule

Excitatory neurons release glutamate, the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, and make up roughly eighty percent of cortical neurons.

The pyramidal cell is the archetype: a triangular soma, a long apical dendrite that climbs toward the cortical surface, several basal dendrites spreading sideways, and an axon that typically leaves the local area entirely to reach other cortical regions or subcortical targets.

That two-ended dendritic architecture is functionally important, because the apical tuft tends to receive feedback and contextual input from higher areas while the basal dendrites receive feedforward sensory drive, so a single pyramidal cell is positioned to compare bottom-up evidence against top-down expectation.

Spiny stellate cells are the other main excitatory type in cortex, concentrated in layer four of primary sensory areas; they lack an apical dendrite, keep their dendrites within their own layer, and serve as the principal recipients of incoming signals from the thalamus, distributing that input vertically to other layers.

Granule cells are small densely packed excitatory neurons found in the cerebellum, the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and the olfactory bulb; the cerebellar granule cells alone outnumber all other neurons in the brain combined, and their thin parallel fibres provide the enormous fan-out of inputs onto Purkinje cells that classical cerebellar learning theories depend on.

The broad rule is that pyramidal cells export information between regions, stellate cells import it into a region, and granule cells expand a signal into a high-dimensional code that is easier to separate.


6.2.2 Inhibitory interneuron classes: parvalbumin, somatostatin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and others

Inhibitory neurons release gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which pushes target cells away from threshold, and they make up the remaining fifteen to twenty percent of cortical neurons.

Most are interneurons - cells whose axons stay local rather than projecting to distant regions - and they are conventionally sorted into three largely non-overlapping classes named after marker proteins they express.

Parvalbumin (PV) cells are fast-spiking and target the soma and proximal dendrites of pyramidal cells, which puts them in a position to veto output directly and to pace fast gamma-band rhythms.

Somatostatin (SST) cells instead target distal dendrites, where they gate the top-down and contextual input arriving on the apical tuft rather than blocking output wholesale; the Martinotti cell is the best-known example.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) cells are the odd ones out, because they synapse mainly onto other interneurons, especially SST cells, so activating them removes inhibition from pyramidal dendrites - a disinhibitory circuit, described by Pi, Kepecs and colleagues in Nature in 2013, that appears to be how arousal, reward signals and motor activity open a cortical area to new input.

Beyond these three there are further classes, including neurogliaform cells that release GABA diffusely into the surrounding tissue rather than at a single point, and chandelier cells that target the axon initial segment itself, the precise spot where the action potential is born.

One caution worth stating plainly: the neat three-class scheme is a useful simplification, and the disinhibition story is elegant, but recent work - for example Sachdev, Ferrari and colleagues in Neuron in 2023 - has found that VIP-driven disinhibition does not straightforwardly account for attentional modulation in visual cortex, so the mapping from cell class to cognitive function should be held loosely.


6.2.3 Transcriptomic cell-type censuses and the Brain Initiative Cell Census Network

For most of the twentieth century cell types were defined by shape under a microscope and by electrical behaviour under an electrode, both of which are laborious and somewhat subjective.

Single-cell ribonucleic acid sequencing (single-cell RNA sequencing) changed this by reading out which genes an individual cell is expressing, giving a high-dimensional fingerprint that can be clustered automatically.

The Brain Initiative Cell Census Network (BICCN), funded by the United States National Institutes of Health, applied this at scale, and in October 2023 published a package of papers in Science including a first draft brain-wide cell atlas of the adult human brain that identified more than three thousand transcriptomically distinct cell types and showed that diversity is distributed very unevenly across brain regions.

A parallel technique, Patch-seq, records a cell's electrical behaviour and recovers its shape and then sequences its RNA from the same cell, which is what allows the gene-expression clusters to be tied back to the older morphological and physiological categories; Scala, Tolias and colleagues used this in Nature in 2020 to characterise the phenotypic variation of transcriptomic types in mouse motor cortex.

The successor programme, the Brain Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN), is extending the work toward a complete human and non-human primate reference.

Two honest caveats: a transcriptomic cluster is a statistical grouping, not a proven functional kind, and the number of types you find depends on how finely you choose to cut the data, which is why headline counts should be read as orders of magnitude rather than exact tallies.


6.2.4 Why cell type constrains the circuit hypotheses that are available

The reason a catalogue of cell types is not stamp-collecting is that it eliminates hypotheses.

If you propose that a cortical area implements a particular computation, and that computation requires an excitatory cell to inhibit its neighbours directly, the census tells you no such cell exists there - the inhibition must be routed through an interneuron, which adds a synaptic delay and a nonlinearity that your model has to account for.

Cell type also fixes wiring: work from the MICrONS consortium and collaborators, published in Nature in 2025, integrated Patch-seq with electron-microscope reconstructions and found that predicted somatostatin transcriptomic subtypes differ systematically in which targets they contact and how many synapses they make onto each, meaning that the type label carries real connectivity information.

Cell type further constrains dynamics, because the ion channel genes a cell expresses determine its firing pattern, and combined statistical-biophysical modelling has begun to predict physiology from expression directly.

Put simply, the cell-type census turns circuit modelling from free invention into a constrained search, and constrained searches are the only ones that converge.


6.3 Glia as participants in cognition

Glia are the non-neuronal cells of the nervous system, and for a century they were regarded as glue and scaffolding - the word glia is Greek for glue.

Careful counting by Suzana Herculano-Houzel and colleagues has since established that glia and neurons are present in the human brain in roughly equal overall numbers, correcting a widely repeated claim of a ten-to-one glial majority.

More importantly, each of the three main glial classes has turned out to do something that bears directly on information processing rather than merely on housekeeping.


6.3.1 Astrocytes, calcium signalling, and the tripartite synapse

Astrocytes are star-shaped cells whose fine processes wrap around synapses, with a single human astrocyte contacting on the order of a hundred thousand of them.

They do not fire action potentials, but they do signal, using waves of calcium ions inside their processes that can be triggered by the neurotransmitters spilling out of nearby synapses.

The tripartite synapse hypothesis, associated with Alfonso Araque, Philip Haydon and colleagues from the late 1990s, holds that the synapse is properly a three-part structure - presynaptic terminal, postsynaptic membrane, and enveloping astrocyte process - and that calcium-triggered release of gliotransmitters such as glutamate and adenosine triphosphate from the astrocyte feeds back to modulate synaptic strength.

This is one of the genuinely contested claims in cellular neuroscience and should be presented as such: critics have argued that the calcium-dependent release mechanisms invoked are not clearly demonstrated in mature astrocytes under physiological conditions, and that much of the supporting evidence came from bulk dye-loading and pharmacological manipulations that are not cell-specific.

What is not in dispute is that astrocytes take up glutamate and potassium from the synaptic cleft, supply neurons with metabolic substrate, and are structurally positioned to influence transmission; what is disputed is whether they actively release signalling molecules to shape plasticity, and a 2025 review in this area concludes that better tools for specific manipulation are still the limiting factor.


6.3.2 Oligodendrocytes, adaptive myelination, and learning

Oligodendrocytes are the cells that produce myelin in the brain and spinal cord, each one wrapping segments of up to fifty different axons.

The traditional picture had myelination as a developmental programme that finished in early adulthood and then stopped, which would make it irrelevant to learning.

Two papers in Science in 2014 overturned that.

Gibson, Monje and colleagues used optogenetics - a technique that makes neurons fire in response to light by giving them a light-sensitive ion channel - to drive premotor cortex at twenty hertz in mice, and found rapid proliferation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells and new myelin specifically within the stimulated circuit.

McKenzie, Richardson and colleagues, in the same year, trained mice on a running wheel with irregularly spaced rungs and showed that mice genetically blocked from making new oligodendrocytes - through deletion of the gene for myelin regulatory factor - could not consolidate the skill, establishing that new myelin is required for motor learning and not merely a by-product of it.

This is now called adaptive myelination, and it gives learning a second substrate alongside synaptic change: experience can alter not only how strongly signals are weighted but how fast they arrive.

The open question is how far it generalises beyond motor learning, and how the system decides which axons to myelinate.


6.3.3 Microglia and activity-dependent synaptic pruning

Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells, derived not from neural tissue but from early embryonic macrophages, and they continuously extend and retract processes that survey the surrounding tissue.

Their role in cognition comes from pruning: the developing brain overproduces synapses and then removes the ones that are not carrying useful traffic, and microglia are the cells that do the removing.

Stevens, Barres and colleagues showed in 2007 that components of the complement cascade - an ancient immune system for tagging targets for destruction - are repurposed in the brain, with the proteins C1q and C3 marking weak synapses in the developing visual pathway.

Schafer, Stevens and colleagues, in Neuron in 2012, then demonstrated that microglia engulf these tagged synapses through the complement receptor CR3, and that the process is activity-dependent, with less active inputs preferentially eliminated; mice lacking C3 or CR3 show incomplete pruning.

Paolicelli and colleagues in 2011 independently reported that impairing microglial function delays the maturation of hippocampal circuits.

The same machinery appears to be reactivated pathologically in adulthood - Hong, Stevens and colleagues reported in Science in 2016 that complement and microglia drive early synapse loss in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease - which is one of the clearest cases in this book of a developmental mechanism becoming a disease mechanism.


6.3.4 The glymphatic system, sleep, and clearance

The brain has no conventional lymphatic vessels, so the question of how it disposes of metabolic waste was long unsettled.

The glymphatic hypothesis, proposed by Maiken Nedergaard and colleagues in 2012 and 2013, holds that cerebrospinal fluid is driven into the brain along the outsides of arteries, exchanges with the fluid between cells through astrocytic water channels called aquaporin-4, and carries waste out along veins - the g in glymphatic marking the glial dependence.

Xie and colleagues, in Science in 2013, reported that the space between cells expands substantially during natural sleep and anaesthesia and that clearance of amyloid-beta, the protein that aggregates in Alzheimer's disease, roughly doubles, which supplied an attractive functional reason for sleep.

This is an actively contested area and must be reported as such.

Miao and colleagues in 2024 used a different measurement approach and reported that clearance is in fact reduced during sleep and anaesthesia, the opposite of the original finding, and earlier work from 2018 had similarly found faster drainage in awake active mice.

Nedergaard has publicly and sharply disputed the methodology of the 2024 study, and the disagreement centres on whether the tracer techniques used measure bulk fluid flow or simple diffusion.

The prudent summary for a reader in 2026 is that solute clearance from the brain is real and that astrocytes participate in it, that its dependence on sleep state is genuinely unresolved, and that anyone presenting the sleep-clears-your-brain story as settled fact is going beyond the evidence.


6.4 What the cellular level does and does not explain

Having laid out the apparatus, it is worth being explicit about its explanatory reach.

The temptation in a field with powerful cellular tools is to assume that every cognitive phenomenon must have a cellular explanation waiting to be found, and that assumption is not safe.


6.4.1 Capacities plausibly reducible to single-cell properties

Some things really are properties of individual cells.

Feature selectivity is the clearest case: Hubel and Wiesel's recordings from cat visual cortex in the late 1950s and 1960s showed single neurons that respond to an edge at a particular orientation, and no population-level story is needed to state that fact.

Coincidence detection is another: a cell with a short membrane time constant fires only when inputs arrive nearly simultaneously, which is a single-cell computation that underlies sound localisation in the auditory brainstem.

The reach of the single cell is greater than was long assumed.

Gidon and colleagues, in Science in 2020, recorded from dendrites of human layer two and three pyramidal neurons and found calcium-mediated dendritic action potentials that are graded rather than all-or-none, and whose amplitude decreases as stimulus strength rises - a non-monotonic response that lets a single dendrite compute the exclusive-or function, a classification problem that textbook accounts had said requires a multi-layer network.

At the far end, Quian Quiroga, Fried, Koch and colleagues reported in Nature in 2005 single neurons in the human medial temporal lobe that responded to a particular person across photographs, drawings and even the written name - the so-called concept cells, most famously a Jennifer Aniston cell.

Even here caution is needed: such a cell is sampled from a population, and the fact that one recorded neuron responds invariantly does not establish that the concept is stored in that neuron rather than distributed across thousands the electrode never touched.


6.4.2 Capacities requiring population-level description

Many capacities have no sensible single-cell statement at all.

Working memory, decision formation, and motor preparation are described far better as trajectories - the coordinated pattern of activity across a whole population evolving through time - than as the behaviour of any member of it.

The empirical finding that made this tractable is that recordings from thousands of neurons typically vary along only a handful of dimensions, so the population activity lies on a low-dimensional surface within the vast space of possible firing patterns; that surface is called a neural manifold and its coordinates are called latent dynamics.

Gallego, Miller and colleagues developed this framing in Neuron in 2017 and 2020, and the practical consequence is that two neurons with entirely different individual tuning can be doing the same job in the population, while the population trajectory stays stable across days even as individual cells drift.

The strict claim to make is not that single neurons are unimportant but that the correct explanatory variable for these capacities is a collective one, and no amount of finer single-cell measurement will produce it by itself.

There is a live methodological dispute here too, over whether low-dimensional structure reflects genuine constraints in the circuit or is partly an artefact of the limited variety of tasks animals are given in the laboratory.


6.4.3 The multiscale gap and current attempts to close it

The gap between a millisecond spike in a cubic micrometre and a decision made over seconds by a whole brain spans roughly six orders of magnitude in space and time, and no single framework currently crosses it.

David Marr's response, set out in Vision in 1982, was to insist on three separate levels of explanation - the computational level, which states what problem is being solved and why, the algorithmic level, which states the representation and procedure used, and the implementational level, which states how neurons do it - and his warning was blunt: trying to understand perception by understanding neurons is like trying to understand a bird's flight by studying only feathers.

John Krakauer and colleagues renewed the argument in Neuron in 2017 in a paper titled Neuroscience Needs Behavior, arguing that the field's method-driven turn had produced many descriptions and few explanations, and that a well-characterised behaviour has to define the problem before neural data can answer it.

Current attempts to close the gap fall into three families: large-scale biophysical simulation, which builds detailed circuits from measured cell types and hopes emergent function appears; recurrent neural network modelling, which trains an artificial network on the task and then compares its internal dynamics to recorded neural manifolds; and multilevel causal modelling, which tries to state formally what it would mean for a neural variable to cause a cognitive one, as in the framework put forward by Weichwald and colleagues and in Bein and Love's 2023 multilevel account of hippocampal function.

None of these is yet a solution, and it is worth saying so.

The honest position for the rest of this book is that cellular facts constrain cognitive theories without determining them, and that a good explanation of a cognitive capacity will normally name the level it lives at.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The neuron is a polarised device whose dendrites weigh inputs, whose membrane biophysics converts that weighting into all-or-none spikes, and whose axonal conduction delay is itself an adjustable quantity rather than a fixed one.

Neurons come in a very large number of types - excitatory pyramidal, stellate and granule cells, and inhibitory interneuron classes marked by parvalbumin, somatostatin and vasoactive intestinal peptide - and the transcriptomic censuses of the Brain Initiative Cell Census Network matter because knowing which cells exist eliminates circuit hypotheses that would otherwise be free to be invented.

Glia are participants and not scaffolding: oligodendrocytes remyelinate in response to learning, and microglia prune synapses using repurposed complement proteins, both on solid evidence, while the tripartite synapse and the sleep-dependence of glymphatic clearance remain genuinely disputed and were reported here as disputed.

Single cells can do more than was long believed, up to computing an exclusive-or in one human dendrite, yet working memory, decision formation and motor preparation are properly described as low-dimensional trajectories across populations.

The gap between the spike and the thought is not closed, and the working rule adopted here is that cellular facts constrain cognitive theories without determining them.


CHAPTER 7. SYNAPSES, TRANSMITTERS, AND RECEPTORS (APPARATUS)

A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes a signal to another.

There are roughly a hundred trillion of them in a human brain, and almost everything we call thinking happens because of what they do.

This chapter takes the synapse apart and shows you the pieces: the packets of chemical that get released, the receptors that catch them, the direct electrical bridges that bypass chemistry altogether, and the way a synapse changes its own strength from one millisecond to the next.

It matters because nearly every theory of learning in this book, and nearly every psychiatric drug in a pharmacy, is a claim about synapses.

It also matters because the most popular picture of memory - a single number stored at each synapse, like a weight in an artificial neural network - is an approximation, and this chapter shows you exactly where it starts to leak.


7.1 Chemical transmission

Most synapses in the mammalian brain are chemical.

The sending neuron, called the presynaptic neuron, does not pass electricity directly to the receiving neuron, called the postsynaptic neuron.

Instead it squirts a small dose of a chemical messenger, called a neurotransmitter, across a gap about twenty billionths of a metre wide, and the receiving cell detects that chemical with proteins called receptors.

This seems like a wasteful design - it is slower than a wire and it costs energy - but it buys something a wire cannot give: every step in the chain is adjustable, which is what makes a brain able to learn.


7.1.1 Vesicle release, quantal content, and release probability

Neurotransmitter is not released as a continuous stream; it is packaged in tiny membrane bubbles called vesicles, each holding a few thousand molecules.

Bernard Katz and José del Castillo showed in 1954, working at the frog neuromuscular junction, that the postsynaptic response comes in whole-number multiples of a fixed small unit, exactly as you would expect if transmitter were released in discrete packets.

Their description is still the working model, usually written as three numbers: N, the number of release sites available; p, the probability that any one site actually releases when an action potential arrives; and q, the size of the response to one packet - so the average number of packets released, called the quantal content, is roughly N multiplied by p.

The crucial and slightly shocking fact is that p is often low, in many central synapses somewhere between about 0.1 and 0.5, meaning a single cortical synapse frequently fails to transmit at all.

Reliability, in the brain, is bought by having many synapses rather than by making any one of them dependable.

Katz shared the 1970 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this line of work, and a 2017 review in Physiological Reviews by Neher and colleagues shows the quantal framework being refined rather than replaced, with attention now on the docking sites where vesicles wait.


7.1.2 Ionotropic and metabotropic receptors

Receptors on the receiving side come in two fundamentally different designs, and the difference sets the timescale of everything downstream.

An ionotropic receptor is itself a pore through the membrane: the transmitter binds, the pore opens, charged particles called ions flow, and the electrical state of the cell changes within a millisecond or so.

A metabotropic receptor has no pore; it is coupled to an internal messenger system called a G protein - a protein that, once switched on, triggers a chain of chemical reactions inside the cell - so its effects take tens to hundreds of milliseconds and can last far longer.

The alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor are ionotropic; the metabotropic glutamate receptors and the gamma-aminobutyric acid type B (GABA-B) receptor are metabotropic.

The practical consequence is a division of labour: ionotropic receptors carry the fast message, metabotropic receptors set the terms on which the fast message is interpreted.


7.1.3 Excitation and inhibition: glutamate and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)

Roughly eighty percent of cortical synapses use glutamate, the main excitatory transmitter, which makes the receiving cell more likely to fire.

Most of the rest use gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory transmitter, which makes the receiving cell less likely to fire, usually by opening a channel to chloride ions.

Glutamate acts on the fast AMPA receptor, on the NMDA receptor - which is unusual because it needs both glutamate and a depolarised membrane at the same time, making it a coincidence detector and the workhorse of learning - and on slower metabotropic glutamate receptors.

GABA acts on the ionotropic GABA type A (GABA-A) receptor, the target of benzodiazepine tranquillisers, alcohol, and many general anaesthetics, and on the metabotropic GABA-B receptor, which produces a long, slow damping of the cell.

It is worth being precise about a common confusion: a transmitter is not intrinsically excitatory or inhibitory - the receptor decides.

Early in development, and in some adult conditions, GABA is actually excitatory, because the chloride gradient inside immature neurons runs the other way.


7.1.4 Excitation-inhibition balance as a systems-level constraint

Because excitation is self-amplifying, a cortex without inhibition runs away into seizure within seconds, which is what a convulsion is.

Cortical circuits therefore sit in a regime that theorists call balanced: excitatory and inhibitory currents into a neuron are large, opposed, and roughly cancelling, so that the cell's firing is driven by the moment-to-moment fluctuations in the difference rather than by a steady push.

This is not a housekeeping detail; it determines how much information a population can encode, how fast it responds, and whether it sits near the critical point where activity neither dies out nor explodes, a link examined in a 2024 review by Zhang and colleagues.

Rubenstein and Merzenich proposed in 2003 that autism might reflect an increased ratio of excitation to inhibition in key circuits, a paper now cited thousands of times and extended to schizophrenia and epilepsy.

Here honesty is required: the excitation-inhibition ratio hypothesis is influential but contested.

Critics point out that the ratio is measured very differently across studies - patch-clamp recordings, magnetic resonance spectroscopy of glutamate and GABA levels, the slope of the electroencephalogram spectrum - that these measures correlate poorly with one another, and that a shift in the ratio may be a compensatory consequence of a disorder rather than its cause.

Treat it as a productive framework, not an established mechanism.


7.2 Electrical transmission and non-synaptic signalling

Chemical synapses are the main event but not the only channel.

Neurons also talk through direct electrical bridges, through transmitter that drifts free in the extracellular fluid, and through the raw electric fields their own activity generates.

These routes are slower to be accepted in textbooks because they are harder to measure, and their functional weight is still argued over.


7.2.1 Gap junctions and interneuron synchrony

A gap junction is a physical pore linking the interiors of two cells, formed by two half-channels called connexons meeting across the membranes.

Current passes through directly and almost instantly, in both directions, with no transmitter and no delay - an electrical synapse.

In the cortex and hippocampus these are built mainly from the protein connexin36 and are found overwhelmingly between inhibitory interneurons, and strikingly they connect interneurons of the same class - fast-spiking cells to other fast-spiking cells, low-threshold-spiking cells to their own kind - and only rarely across classes.

Galarreta and Hestrin, and independently Gibson, Beierlein, and Connors, both reported this in 1999, and the functional payoff is synchrony: coupled interneurons fire together, and an inhibitory network firing together is what imposes rhythm on the excitatory cells it controls.

Mice lacking connexin36 lose this coupling and show disrupted gamma-band oscillations, which is about as direct a causal test as the field offers.


7.2.2 Volume transmission and extrasynaptic receptors

Not all transmitter is caught by the synapse that released it.

Some escapes, some is released from swellings on axons that have no synapse at all, and it then diffuses through the fluid-filled space between cells to reach receptors far from any release site.

Agnati and Fuxe named this volume transmission in 1986, and it is now thought to be the dominant mode for the monoamines - dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline - whose fibres release from asynaptic varicosities and bathe large territories.

GABA does it too: a persistent low concentration of GABA in the extracellular space continuously activates high-affinity extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors, producing a standing leak current called tonic inhibition that sets a neuron's overall gain rather than delivering a message.

The conceptual upgrade is significant - the brain is not only a wiring diagram but also a chemical medium, and a drug that changes an ambient concentration can change computation without touching a single connection.


7.2.3 Ephaptic coupling and field effects

Every active neuron creates an electric field in the tissue around it, and that field falls across the membranes of neighbouring cells whether they are connected to it or not.

Influence by field alone, with no synapse and no gap junction, is called ephaptic coupling.

Anastassiou, Perin, Markram, and Koch showed in 2011, in rat hippocampal slices, that fields of only one to a few millivolts per millimetre - within the range the brain generates naturally - reliably shift spike timing by one to a few milliseconds, with the effect depending on the cell's shape and its orientation to the field.

Fröhlich and McCormick reported in 2010 that weak fields matching ongoing slow oscillations could entrain and amplify those oscillations, suggesting a positive feedback loop between population activity and the field it creates.

The disagreement is about magnitude, not existence: nobody doubts the effect is real, and few claim it dominates, so the live question is whether a one-millisecond timing nudge matters in a system where spike timing is used as a code.


7.3 Short-term synaptic dynamics

A synapse's strength is not a constant even over the span of a single second.

Send two spikes in quick succession and the second response may be much larger than the first, or much smaller, depending on the synapse.

These changes last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds and then vanish, which is why they are called short-term, and they turn each synapse into a small dynamical device rather than a fixed multiplier.


7.3.1 Facilitation and depression

Short-term facilitation is an increase in response to closely spaced spikes, caused mainly by residual calcium: calcium ions that entered the terminal on the first spike have not yet been cleared, so the second spike releases more.

Short-term depression is the opposite, a decrease, caused largely by depletion - the readily releasable pool of vesicles has been partly emptied and needs time to refill, with receptor desensitisation contributing as well.

Which one a synapse shows is largely predicted by its initial release probability: a synapse with high p spends its vesicles fast and depresses, a synapse with low p has little to deplete and facilitates.

Tsodyks and Markram formalised this in 1997 with a compact model of vesicle depletion and calcium-dependent facilitation that is still the standard workhorse in network simulations, and Zucker and Regehr's 2002 review remains the reference account of the underlying mechanisms.

A vivid illustration: the same cortical pyramidal cell can depress onto one target interneuron and facilitate onto another, so a single spike train is transformed differently for each recipient.


7.3.2 Synaptic filtering as temporal computation

If a synapse's gain depends on recent firing rate, then the synapse is a filter, and Abbott and Regehr made this argument explicitly in their 2004 Nature paper "Synaptic computation".

A depressing synapse transmits the first spikes of a burst strongly and then fades, so it passes low rates and changes in rate while suppressing sustained high rates: functionally a low-pass filter and a change detector.

A facilitating synapse does the reverse, staying quiet at low rates and coming alive during bursts, so it acts as a high-pass or band-pass filter that reports bursts specifically.

This gives a mechanistic answer to a real puzzle - how a network detects that something has changed rather than merely that something is present - and it does so without any dedicated circuitry, using only the physics of vesicle supply.

Depression also implements automatic gain control: because the depressed steady-state response scales roughly with the inverse of the input rate, a synapse can signal relative change across a wide range of absolute rates.


7.3.3 Short-term plasticity as a substrate for activity-silent working memory

Working memory - holding a phone number in mind for ten seconds - was long assumed to require neurons to keep firing continuously, a pattern called persistent activity, first recorded in monkey prefrontal cortex by Fuster and Alexander in 1971.

Mongillo, Barak, and Tsodyks proposed in Science in 2008 that this is not necessary: residual calcium in the terminals of the relevant synapses could hold the item as a facilitated pattern of connections, invisible in the spike record, and be refreshed by occasional bursts.

This is the activity-silent hypothesis, and it is elegant, cheap in energy, and testable in principle - Wolff and colleagues in 2017 used a pulse of transcranial magnetic stimulation to "ping" human cortex and read out information that was not visible in ongoing activity, which is the kind of evidence the theory predicts.

But the case is not closed, and the dispute is sharp: Barbosa and colleagues in 2020 argued the two mechanisms interact, with silent synaptic traces producing the serial biases seen in behaviour while attractor activity carries the current item, and a 2024 Nature paper by Lundqvist and colleagues reported that memoranda are held by intermittent, cue-specific spiking rather than by silence.

The fair summary as of 2026 is that short-term plasticity almost certainly contributes something to working memory, and that the strong claim - storage with no spiking at all - is not established.


7.4 The synapse as the unit of storage

The founding assumption of most theories of memory is that experience is stored by changing synapses.

This section states that assumption carefully, then shows where it is incomplete.

Both halves matter: the assumption is enormously productive and largely correct, and taking it too literally has misled people about what a memory physically is.


7.4.1 Synaptic weight as the classical memory variable

Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 that when one cell repeatedly helps fire another, some growth process strengthens the connection between them - the idea compressed into the slogan that cells that fire together wire together.

Bliss and Lømo supplied the physiological demonstration in 1973, showing in the anaesthetised rabbit that a brief high-frequency burst to the perforant path produced a lasting increase in the response of dentate gyrus cells, a phenomenon named long-term potentiation (LTP), with its mirror image, long-term depression (LTD), characterised later.

From this comes the weight metaphor: each synapse holds one number, the weight, and learning is the adjustment of those numbers - the abstraction that artificial neural networks inherited and that made modern machine learning possible.

The metaphor earns its keep because it is mechanistically grounded: the main currency of LTP expression is the number of AMPA receptors inserted into the postsynaptic membrane, which really is close to a single scalar quantity.


7.4.2 Limits of the weight metaphor: intrinsic excitability, structural change, molecular state

The first leak is that neurons also change themselves, not just their connections.

Intrinsic plasticity - a shift in the density or properties of a cell's own ion channels, altering how readily it fires - accompanies learning, and work on memory engrams (the specific set of neurons that carry a given memory) shows that cells with momentarily high excitability are preferentially recruited into the engram, so excitability is not a side effect but part of the allocation mechanism.

The second leak is that plasticity is structural: dendritic spines, the small protrusions carrying most excitatory synapses, grow, enlarge, and disappear, so learning changes which synapses exist rather than only how strong they are, and spine volume tracks strength closely enough that the "weight" is partly a geometry.

The third leak is molecular and the most awkward: a synapse's behaviour depends on its internal biochemical state - kinase activity, receptor phosphorylation, local messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) waiting to be translated - so two synapses of identical current strength can respond to identical future input in different ways.

The honest conclusion is that a synapse is a small stateful machine of which strength is one readout, and models that store one number per synapse are approximating a system with several hidden variables.


7.4.3 Synaptic tagging and capture

There is a puzzle in making memory last: converting early, short-lived potentiation into late, protein-synthesis-dependent potentiation requires new proteins, but proteins made in the cell body would reach every synapse, so how does only the right synapse get strengthened?

Frey and Morris answered this in Nature in 1997 with the synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis: activity sets a local, short-lived molecular "tag" at the stimulated synapse, and plasticity-related proteins produced cell-wide are captured only where a tag is waiting.

The elegant prediction, which they confirmed, is that a weak stimulation too feeble to produce lasting potentiation on its own becomes lasting if a strong stimulation occurs at another synapse of the same neuron within about an hour, because the weak input's tag captures proteins the strong input paid for.

The behavioural version followed: Moncada and Viola in 2007 and Wang, Redondo, and Morris in 2010 showed that a weak, normally forgettable learning experience in rats becomes a durable memory if a novel event occurs nearby in time, which is a mechanism for why emotionally salient moments preserve the mundane details around them.

The identity of the tag itself remains unresolved - candidates include calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and actin cytoskeleton reorganisation - and this is a genuine open question rather than a detail.


7.4.4 Cascade and metaplastic models of long-lived memory

There is a hard arithmetic problem underneath all of this, sometimes called the stability-plasticity dilemma: if synapses change readily enough to record today's experience, tomorrow's experience overwrites today's, and memory capacity in simple models collapses to a disappointingly small number of recent items.

Metaplasticity is the proposed escape - plasticity about plasticity, meaning a change that does not alter a synapse's current strength but alters how easily that strength can be changed in future, a concept named by Abraham and Bear in 1996.

Fusi, Drew, and Abbott built this into the cascade model in Neuron in 2005: each synapse has a chain of internal states at the same two strength values but with progressively lower probability of switching, so a repeatedly confirmed synapse sinks deeper into the cascade and becomes increasingly hard to overwrite, while a fresh synapse stays labile.

The result is a memory trace that decays roughly as one over elapsed time rather than exponentially, which means the model holds both a large number of recent memories and a thin tail of very old ones - closer to how human forgetting actually behaves.

Benna and Fusi extended this in 2016 with a model of interacting internal variables at multiple timescales that pushes capacity close to the theoretical bound.

The important lesson is conceptual rather than technical: the extra hidden state inside a synapse, which the weight metaphor discards as biological clutter, may be precisely what makes long-term memory possible.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Chemical transmission is quantal, probabilistic, and unreliable at the single synapse, so the brain buys reliability through numbers, and the release probability that makes a synapse unreliable is the same parameter that determines whether it facilitates or depresses.

Fast ionotropic receptors carry the message while slow metabotropic receptors set the terms of its interpretation, and cortical circuits survive only because excitation and inhibition are held in a large, opposed, near-cancelling balance - a framework whose extension to autism and schizophrenia remains influential but genuinely contested.

Chemistry is not the only channel: connexin36 gap junctions synchronise interneuron networks and thereby impose rhythm, volume transmission lets monoamines and ambient GABA set gain across whole territories, and ephaptic field effects nudge spike timing by real if modest amounts.

Short-term plasticity makes each synapse a temporal filter, giving networks change detection and gain control for free, and possibly a substrate for holding information without spiking - though the strong activity-silent claim is not settled.

The synapse is the unit of storage, but it is a stateful machine rather than a single number, and its hidden internal state - the tag of Frey and Morris, the cascade depth of Fusi, Drew, and Abbott - is what allows a memory to be both easy to write and hard to erase.


CHAPTER 8. NEUROMODULATION AND GLOBAL STATE (APPARATUS)


Most descriptions of the brain stop at the wiring diagram - which neuron connects to which, and how strongly.

This chapter is about the other half of the story: the chemical systems that change what that wiring does from moment to moment.

A neuromodulator is a chemical messenger that does not simply pass a message from one neuron to the next, but instead adjusts how a whole population of neurons behaves - their excitability, their sensitivity, their willingness to change.

The same circuit, bathed in different modulators, computes different things.

This matters because cognition is not a fixed function.

You are a different information processor when alert than when drowsy, when hungry than when fed, when frightened than when safe, and the difference is not in your wiring but in the chemistry running through it.


8.1 The broadcast systems

The systems in this section share a striking anatomical design.

Each begins in a small cluster of cells - often only tens of thousands of neurons, sometimes fewer - buried deep in the brainstem or the base of the forebrain.

Each then sends axons, the long output fibres of neurons, out across enormous swathes of the brain, so that one small nucleus can influence the cortex, the hippocampus, the thalamus, and the spinal cord at once.

This is why they are called broadcast systems: the ratio of senders to receivers is extreme, so the signal cannot be very detailed, but it can be very widespread.

A useful mental image is a lighting rig rather than a telephone line.

The telephone line carries specific content to a specific address.

The lighting rig changes the conditions under which everything else in the room is seen.


8.1.1 Dopamine from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra

Dopamine is manufactured by two neighbouring midbrain cell groups: the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which sits near the midline, and the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), which sits just lateral to it.

The substantia nigra, Latin for black substance, is named for its dark pigmentation, and it is the loss of these cells that produces the movement symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Broadly, VTA dopamine cells project to the ventral striatum, the amygdala, the hippocampus, and the frontal cortex, and are associated with reward, motivation, and learning, while SNc cells project to the dorsal striatum and are associated with the initiation and vigour of movement.

That tidy split is now known to be too tidy.

Work using transcriptomics, the measurement of which genes a cell is expressing, and intersectional genetics, which lets researchers target cells by combinations of markers, has shown that dopamine neurons come in many molecularly distinct subtypes with different projections and different task-related firing patterns.

A substantial minority of these cells release glutamate, the brain's main excitatory transmitter, or gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), its main inhibitory transmitter, alongside or instead of dopamine, so even the label dopamine neuron is an approximation.


8.1.2 Noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus

Noradrenaline, also called norepinephrine, is supplied to the forebrain almost entirely by a single nucleus, the locus coeruleus (LC), whose name means blue spot - again a pigmentation.

It is astonishingly small: on the order of fifteen thousand neurons per side in the human brain, yet its axons reach nearly the whole cortex, the cerebellum, the hippocampus, the amygdala, and the spinal cord.

Locus coeruleus neurons fire in two distinguishable ways: phasic bursts, meaning brief high-frequency volleys locked to a specific event, and tonic activity, meaning a sustained background rate.

The nucleus receives strong input from the anterior cingulate cortex and the orbitofrontal cortex, two frontal regions associated with tracking how well the current task is going, which gives it a plausible route by which the value of what you are doing can influence how alert you are.

Because noradrenaline also drives the pupil, LC activity leaves a measurable trace in the eye, a point taken up in section 8.4.


8.1.3 Acetylcholine from the basal forebrain and brainstem

Acetylcholine was the first neurotransmitter ever identified, by Otto Loewi in the 1920s, and in the brain it arrives from two main sources.

The basal forebrain, a set of nuclei beneath the front of the brain including the nucleus basalis of Meynert, supplies acetylcholine to the cortex, the hippocampus, and the amygdala.

A separate brainstem group, the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, supplies the thalamus and other subcortical targets and is heavily involved in the sleep-wake cycle.

Functionally, cortical acetylcholine tends to strengthen incoming sensory signals from the thalamus while damping the internal, feedback connections that carry the brain's own expectations - in other words, it tilts the balance toward listening to the world rather than to one's model of it.

The basal forebrain cholinergic cells are among the earliest and most severely affected in Alzheimer's disease, which is why the mainstay symptomatic drugs, the cholinesterase inhibitors, work by slowing the breakdown of acetylcholine.


8.1.4 Serotonin from the raphe nuclei

Serotonin, chemically 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), comes from the raphe nuclei, a string of cell groups running along the midline of the brainstem.

The dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) is the principal source for the forebrain, and its projections are, if anything, even more diffuse than those of the locus coeruleus.

Serotonin is unusual in the sheer number of receptor types it acts on - at least fourteen are recognised, spread across seven families - which is one reason its functional description is so much messier than dopamine's.

Different receptors on different cells can make the same released molecule excitatory in one place and inhibitory in another, so asking what serotonin does without specifying where and through which receptor is close to meaningless.

Most of the body's serotonin is not in the brain at all but in the gut, and the brain manufactures its own, which is why dietary claims about serotonin should be treated with caution.


8.1.5 Histamine, orexin, and the wake-promoting systems

Histamine in the brain comes from the tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus, and it is strongly wake-promoting.

The everyday proof is the sedating effect of older antihistamine drugs, which cross into the brain and block histamine receptors there.

Orexin, also called hypocretin, is a pair of neuropeptides - short protein-like signalling molecules - discovered independently by two teams in 1998, one led by Takeshi Sakurai and one by Luis de Lecea.

Orexin neurons live in the lateral hypothalamus and excite the other arousal systems, including the histaminergic tuberomammillary nucleus, the locus coeruleus, and the raphe, acting less like an arousal system in their own right and more like a stabiliser that holds the wake state together.

The clinical demonstration is narcolepsy type 1, in which orexin-producing neurons are lost, most likely through an autoimmune attack; patients show very low or undetectable orexin in the cerebrospinal fluid and suffer both excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion.

Orexin receptor drugs now run in both directions clinically, with antagonists licensed for insomnia and agonists in trials for narcolepsy.


8.2 Computational readings of the modulators

The anatomy tells you where these chemicals go.

It does not tell you what they mean.

Over the past three decades a distinct research programme has tried to assign each modulator a computational role - a specific quantity it might represent in an algorithm the brain is running.

These accounts are the most intellectually satisfying part of the field and also the part most in flux, so each sub-section below says both what the theory claims and where it is contested.


8.2.1 Dopamine as reward prediction error and as incentive salience

The dominant computational account is the reward prediction error hypothesis, set out by Wolfram Schultz, Peter Dayan, and P. Read Montague in Science in 1997.

A reward prediction error is the difference between the reward you got and the reward you expected: positive when things go better than predicted, zero when they match, negative when they go worse.

Schultz's recordings in monkeys fit this remarkably well - dopamine cells burst to an unexpected reward, shift their burst to the cue once the cue reliably predicts the reward, and fall silent below baseline at the exact moment an expected reward fails to arrive.

This quantity is precisely the teaching signal used in temporal-difference reinforcement learning, an algorithm developed in computer science by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto, which made dopamine the strongest bridge yet built between neuroscience and machine learning.

The main rival account comes from Kent Berridge, who argues that dopamine does not carry pleasure or learning so much as wanting - the attribution of incentive salience, meaning the property that makes a stimulus grab attention and get pursued.

His evidence is that rats with dopamine depleted still show normal facial liking reactions to sweet tastes but will not work to obtain them, dissociating wanting from liking.

The honest summary is that these are not fully reconciled: the prediction-error account explains the moment-to-moment firing beautifully, the incentive-salience account explains the motivational consequences better, and much current work treats dopamine as carrying several signals in parallel across anatomically distinct subpopulations rather than one.


8.2.2 Noradrenaline as unexpected uncertainty, gain, and network reset

Three overlapping proposals compete here, and they are more complementary than contradictory.

Angela Yu and Peter Dayan, in an influential 2005 paper, proposed that noradrenaline signals unexpected uncertainty - the surprise that arises when the whole situation has silently changed, so that your entire model, not just one prediction, is suspect.

Gary Aston-Jones and Jonathan Cohen, also in 2005, proposed the adaptive gain theory: noradrenaline sets the gain of neurons, meaning the steepness of the function relating their input to their output, so that high gain makes a neuron respond sharply and decisively to its input and low gain makes it respond sluggishly and indiscriminately.

In their scheme, phasic locus coeruleus bursts sharpen processing and support exploitation of the current task, while a high tonic rate loosens behaviour and favours abandoning the task to explore alternatives.

Sebastien Bouret and Susan Sara, in the same year, offered network reset: a locus coeruleus burst interrupts ongoing cortical assemblies and permits a rapid reorganisation into a new functional configuration, which is a good description of what happens when something unexpected makes you drop what you were doing.

These accounts are best read as different descriptions of one underlying operation - a global, fast, non-specific signal that says the current settings may no longer be right.


8.2.3 Acetylcholine as expected uncertainty and as the encoding-retrieval switch

The same Yu and Dayan 2005 framework assigns acetylcholine the complementary quantity: expected uncertainty, the known unreliability of a cue within a situation you otherwise understand.

If a traffic light is normally right but occasionally faulty, that is expected uncertainty; if the whole road layout has been changed overnight, that is unexpected uncertainty.

The prescription follows naturally: when your predictions are known to be unreliable, weight sensory evidence more and prior expectation less, which is exactly the cortical effect described in section 8.1.3.

A second and largely independent proposal comes from Michael Hasselmo, who argued that acetylcholine acts as a switch between encoding and retrieval in the hippocampus.

High acetylcholine suppresses the recurrent, internal connections that would replay stored patterns while favouring plasticity on incoming pathways, which biases the system toward laying down new memories; low acetylcholine, as in slow-wave sleep, releases those recurrent connections and favours replaying and consolidating what is already stored.

Direct tests have generally supported the scheme, though experiments such as Douchamps, Jeewajee, Blundell, Burgess and Lever's 2013 work in the Journal of Neuroscience indicate that acetylcholine operates alongside, not instead of, a faster scheduling mechanism tied to the phase of the hippocampal theta rhythm.


8.2.4 Serotonin as patience, aversive prediction, and behavioural flexibility

The oldest computational proposal, associated with Nathaniel Daw, Sham Kakade, and Peter Dayan in 2002, cast serotonin as dopamine's opponent - a signal for aversive prediction and behavioural inhibition.

That symmetry is elegant, and it is weakly supported.

When researchers looked directly for the predicted signature, namely a serotonin response to the omission of an expected reward, they did not reliably find it.

The account with the strongest direct causal evidence instead concerns patience.

Katsuhiko Miyazaki, Kayoko Miyazaki, and Kenji Doya recorded dorsal raphe serotonin neurons firing specifically while animals waited for a delayed reward, and in 2014 showed with optogenetics - a technique that uses light to switch genetically targeted neurons on or off - that activating these neurons made mice wait longer for future rewards.

Their 2018 follow-up in Nature Communications refined this: the patience-enhancing effect was largest when reward was probable and its timing uncertain, which they modelled as serotonin raising the animal's subjective confidence that the reward will eventually arrive.

Separately, serotonin depletion in humans and animals impairs reversal learning, the ability to abandon a previously correct response when the rules change, which is the main evidence for a role in behavioural flexibility.


8.3 Neuropeptides and hormones in cognition

The systems in section 8.1 act on a timescale of milliseconds to seconds.

The signals in this section act over minutes, hours, days, and years, and many of them originate outside the brain entirely, in the adrenal glands, the gonads, the pancreas, the fat tissue, or the stomach.

They are a standing reminder that the brain is an organ in a body, not a computer in a case.


8.3.1 Oxytocin and vasopressin in social cognition

Oxytocin and vasopressin are closely related nine-amino-acid peptides made in the hypothalamus, differing from each other at only two positions, which is why they cross-react at each other's receptors.

In animals the evidence for a social role is strong and mechanistic: the classic comparison, from Thomas Insel, Larry Young and colleagues, is between the monogamous prairie vole and the promiscuous montane vole, which differ in where their brains express oxytocin and vasopressin receptors.

Human work has leaned heavily on intranasal administration, spraying the peptide into the nose in the hope that some reaches the brain, and this literature is genuinely troubled.

Early single studies reporting increased trust, generosity, and emotion recognition have often failed to replicate, effect sizes have shrunk as sample sizes have grown, and it remains disputed how much intranasally delivered peptide reaches the brain at all, as against acting peripherally or through vagal stimulation.

Clinical trials of oxytocin for social difficulties in autism have produced mixed and largely disappointing results, and current work is focused on whether dosing schedule and duration explain the inconsistency rather than on assuming a robust effect exists.

This is a case where the animal biology is solid and the human pharmacology is not, and those two things should not be quietly merged.


8.3.2 Corticosteroids, the stress axis, and memory

The main stress pathway is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: the hypothalamus signals the pituitary gland, which signals the adrenal glands, which release glucocorticoids - cortisol in humans, corticosterone in rodents.

Cortisol crosses into the brain and acts on receptors that are unusually dense in the hippocampus, the structure most central to episodic memory.

The dose-response relationship is an inverted U: moderate levels support synaptic plasticity and memory, while both too little and too much impair it.

Crucially, the direction of the effect depends on which memory process is being tested and when - glucocorticoids enhance the consolidation of new memories, especially emotionally arousing ones, while simultaneously impairing the retrieval of memories already stored.

This single fact explains a familiar experience: a frightening event is burned in vividly, yet under exam stress you cannot retrieve what you certainly know.

Chronic elevation is a different matter again, and is associated with hippocampal atrophy and cognitive impairment rather than with any enhancement.


8.3.3 Sex hormones and cognitive variation

Oestradiol, the principal oestrogen, and testosterone act on receptors found throughout the brain, including the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, and in rodents oestradiol demonstrably increases dendritic spine density in the hippocampus, meaning more sites for synapses.

The human cognitive literature is far weaker than the cellular literature.

Studies across the menstrual cycle have reported that higher oestradiol goes with better verbal fluency and verbal memory and, in some studies, poorer mental rotation, giving rise to the widely repeated claim of a verbal-spatial trade-off.

That claim should be treated cautiously: effect sizes are small, samples have often been small, hormone measurement is frequently indirect, and more recent work suggests oestradiol changes navigation strategy and flexibility rather than raw spatial ability.

The safest statement supported by the evidence is that sex hormones modulate the cognitive system measurably at the cellular level and modestly and inconsistently at the behavioural level, and that popular accounts overstate the behavioural findings considerably.


8.3.4 Metabolic signals: insulin, leptin, ghrelin

Three hormones report the body's energy state to the brain: insulin from the pancreas, rising after a meal; leptin from fat tissue, reporting long-term energy stores; and ghrelin from the stomach, rising before a meal when you are hungry.

All three have receptors in the hippocampus, and none of them is purely about appetite.

Ghrelin receptors are densely expressed in the dentate gyrus and the CA1 to CA3 fields of the hippocampus, and ghrelin signalling promotes hippocampal-dependent spatial and episodic memory - which makes adaptive sense, since a hungry animal needs to remember exactly where food was found.

Insulin delivered into the brain enhances performance on memory tasks, and impaired brain insulin signalling, sometimes called brain insulin resistance, is now a serious line of investigation in Alzheimer's disease.

Leptin promotes neurite outgrowth and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus and cortex, and diet-induced obesity in rodents blunts the transport of both leptin and ghrelin into the brain, with measurable cognitive cost.

The mechanistic story here is well founded in animals; the translation to human dietary advice is not yet secure and should not be overclaimed.


8.4 State as a cognitive variable

The final section draws the practical moral.

If the systems above are real, then any account of cognition that specifies only a network and its weights is incomplete, because the same network in a different state is a different computation.

State is not noise around the signal.

It is a variable in its own right, and one that can be measured.


8.4.1 Arousal, pupil-linked gain, and the Yerkes-Dodson relation

The Yerkes-Dodson relation, first proposed by Robert Yerkes and John Dodson in 1908 from experiments on mice, holds that performance is an inverted-U function of arousal: too little and you are disengaged, too much and you are disorganised, with a peak in between.

The original experiments were narrow, the law was generalised far beyond them, and for much of the twentieth century it functioned more as a slogan than as a finding.

What has revived it is a mechanism and a measurement.

The mechanism is Aston-Jones and Cohen's adaptive gain theory from 8.2.2, in which the peak corresponds to the gain setting at which neurons discriminate their inputs best.

The measurement is pupillometry: pupil diameter, recorded with an eye tracker under constant lighting, tracks noradrenergic and cholinergic arousal closely enough to serve as a non-invasive proxy, and both baseline diameter and event-locked dilation can be read out continuously during a task.

Studies using this method have found that apparently linear relationships between pupil size and performance turn into clean inverted U-shapes once time-on-task effects are controlled, and recent work combining human imaging with direct manipulation of locus coeruleus neurons in animals has begun to establish the link causally rather than by correlation.

One caution: pupil size reflects several modulators, not noradrenaline alone, so it should be read as an index of arousal broadly rather than as a locus coeruleus meter.


8.4.2 Brain state transitions during sleep, quiet waking, and active engagement

Cortical state can be read from the electroencephalogram (EEG), which records voltage fluctuations from the scalp, or from intracellular recordings of a single neuron's membrane potential.

Two broad regimes recur.

The synchronised state, seen in slow-wave sleep, under anaesthesia, and during drowsy quiet waking, shows large low-frequency fluctuations in which whole populations rise and fall together between up states of activity and down states of near silence.

The desynchronised state, seen in active waking and in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, shows those slow fluctuations suppressed, membrane potentials depolarised and steadier, spiking less correlated across neurons, and sensory responses enhanced and more reliable.

The critical modern finding, from work in awake mice by groups including those of David McCormick, Jessica Cardin, and Matteo Carandini, is that these are not two discrete conditions but a continuum traversed continuously during waking, with switches occurring on a timescale of one to two seconds and tracked in real time by pupil diameter, and with locomotion reliably pushing the cortex toward the desynchronised end.

The neuromodulators are the drivers: basal forebrain stimulation alone is sufficient to desynchronise the cortex.


8.4.3 Neuromodulatory tone and the exploration-exploitation setting

Every learning agent faces the exploration-exploitation dilemma: take the option currently believed best, or try something else in case it is better.

Human work, notably by Robert Wilson, Jonathan Cohen and colleagues, distinguishes two solutions - directed exploration, in which choices are deliberately steered toward informative options, and random exploration, in which added decision noise produces exploration by accident.

The tidy hypothesis maps tonic locus coeruleus activity onto random exploration, since raising decision noise is close to lowering gain, and there is supporting evidence that increased tonic locus coeruleus firing increases exploration in a way best modelled as added noise.

Tonic dopamine has been proposed to set the opposite lever, with higher tonic levels favouring exploitation, though mice with elevated striatal dopamine from dopamine-transporter knockdown show more random exploration, which complicates the simple story.

Human pharmacological tests have been mixed: several studies using atomoxetine, a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, have failed to find the predicted change in random exploration, and recent work attempting to separate dopamine and noradrenaline contributions has produced inconsistent results across studies.

The framework is attractive and the mapping is not established - this is a live question, not a settled result, and it should be presented as such.


8.4.4 Why fixed-architecture models fail without a state term

Everything in this chapter converges on a single design point.

A model that specifies only units and weights implicitly assumes one operating regime, and the biology plainly runs many.

Eve Marder's work on the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion, a small and completely mapped circuit of roughly thirty neurons, is the sharpest demonstration: the same fixed anatomical connectivity produces entirely different rhythmic outputs under different neuromodulators, so knowing the wiring diagram does not tell you the behaviour.

Marder's group also established degeneracy in these circuits - very different combinations of underlying parameters can produce the same output - with the consequence that a fixed modulation rule is not robust, and state-dependent modulation is required instead.

The lesson has begun to travel into artificial systems, where adding a global gain parameter that mimics arousal to a recurrent network produces a phase transition between a low-gain regime dominated by internally generated dynamics and memory retrieval and a high-gain regime dominated by incoming sensory input.

That is, in miniature, the difference between sleeping and being awake, produced by one scalar rather than by rewiring.

The practical implication for anyone building or interpreting a model of cognition is blunt: if your architecture has no state term, you have modelled a single slice of one organism at one moment, and you should not expect it to generalise across the others.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

A handful of tiny nuclei - the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra for dopamine, the locus coeruleus for noradrenaline, the basal forebrain and brainstem for acetylcholine, the raphe for serotonin, the hypothalamus for histamine and orexin - broadcast chemical signals across the whole brain and set the conditions under which every local circuit operates.

Each has a candidate computational meaning, and these vary sharply in how well they are supported: dopamine as reward prediction error is strong but incomplete without the incentive-salience account, noradrenaline as gain and unexpected uncertainty is well motivated, acetylcholine as expected uncertainty and as an encoding-retrieval switch is supported but operates alongside other mechanisms, and serotonin's best-evidenced role is patience rather than the elegant but weakly supported opponency with dopamine.

Slower peptide and hormone signals from the adrenals, gonads, pancreas, fat, and stomach also shape cognition, with the glucocorticoid dissociation - enhanced consolidation, impaired retrieval - being the clearest and most useful single result, and the human intranasal oxytocin literature being the clearest cautionary tale.

Global state is measurable, most conveniently through pupil diameter, and it fluctuates continuously during ordinary waking on a timescale of seconds, carrying cortical dynamics between synchronised and desynchronised regimes.

Because the same anatomy computes different functions under different modulatory conditions, as Marder's stomatogastric work shows directly, any model of cognition that fixes an architecture without a state variable has described one operating point and mistaken it for the machine.


CHAPTER 9. PLASTICITY: HOW THE SUBSTRATE CHANGES (CORE)


A brain that could not change would be a brain that could not learn.

This chapter is about plasticity - the family of processes by which the physical brain modifies itself in response to experience, so that what happened yesterday changes how it responds today.

We begin with the oldest and best supported idea in the field, that connections between neurons strengthen when the neurons are active together, and we follow that idea from a psychologist's 1949 guess to the molecular machinery that turns out to implement it.

We then confront the problem that this idea, taken alone, is unstable: a rule that says strong connections get stronger will run away, so the brain must also possess brakes, and we examine what those brakes are.

Next we look past the synapse, because the brain also changes by growing and pruning physical structures, by wrapping axons in insulation, and by chemically marking its own genes.

Finally we reach the hardest unsolved problem in the whole area - how a single synapse, buried deep in a network of billions, could possibly know whether it helped or hurt the animal's performance minutes later.


9.1 Hebbian and correlational plasticity

The founding intuition of learning neuroscience is correlational: the brain notices what goes with what, and it records that noticing by changing the strength of the connections between cells.

A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes a signal to another, and synaptic strength (also called synaptic weight or efficacy) is how much effect a signal arriving at that junction has on the receiving cell.

Correlational plasticity means that the strength of a synapse is adjusted according to the statistical relationship between the activity of the sending cell and the activity of the receiving cell.

This section traces that principle from its verbal statement, through its experimental demonstration, to the molecule that makes it possible.


9.1.1 The Hebb postulate and its formalisations

In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald O. Hebb published The Organization of Behavior, containing a sentence that has shaped the field ever since: when an axon of cell A is near enough to excite cell B and repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing it, some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells such that A's efficiency, as one of the cells firing B, is increased.

An axon is the long output fibre of a neuron, so Hebb was proposing that a connection which repeatedly helps to cause firing gets physically reinforced - a claim later compressed into the slogan that neurons which fire together wire together.

Note what Hebb actually required, because the slogan loses it: cell A must take part in firing cell B, which is a causal claim, not a merely correlational one.

Formalised mathematically, the simplest Hebbian rule says that the change in the weight between two cells is proportional to the product of the sending cell's activity and the receiving cell's activity, scaled by a learning rate - a small constant controlling how fast weights move.

The rule is local, meaning each synapse can compute its own update from signals physically available at that synapse, which is precisely why it is biologically attractive, and it is unstable in its raw form, because a product-based rule with no ceiling grows without bound - a problem that motivates all of section 9.2.


9.1.2 Long-term potentiation and long-term depression

Hebb's postulate remained a conjecture for a quarter of a century, until Timothy Bliss and Terje Lomo, working in Per Andersen's laboratory in Oslo and publishing in 1973, delivered the experimental demonstration.
