Stimulating the perforant path - a bundle of fibres carrying signals into the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure critical for forming new memories - at high frequency in anaesthetised rabbits, they found that the synaptic response in the dentate gyrus remained enlarged for hours afterwards, a phenomenon named long-term potentiation (LTP).

Bliss and Lomo saw the implication immediately, writing that they had found synapses whose efficiency was influenced by activity that may have occurred several hours previously, a time scale long enough to be potentially useful for information storage.

Its mirror image, long-term depression (LTD), a lasting weakening of synaptic strength typically produced by prolonged low-frequency stimulation, was described in the hippocampus by Alger and Teyler in 1976 and characterised in detail through the 1980s and 1990s.

Both are input-specific, meaning the change is confined to the synapses that were actually stimulated rather than spreading across the whole cell, which is essential if synapses are to store distinct pieces of information.

The half-century since has, on balance, supported the LTP-and-memory hypothesis, but with an important caveat that honest reviews state plainly: LTP is a laboratory phenomenon induced by artificial stimulation, and demonstrating that the same process, in the same synapses, stores a particular natural memory remains a much harder standard of proof than showing a correlation.


9.1.3 N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor dependence and the coincidence detector

Hebb's rule requires that something in the cell be able to detect the conjunction of two events - a signal arriving and the receiving cell being active - and the brain's solution is a receptor protein.

The N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor is one class of receptor for glutamate, the brain's principal excitatory neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger released at synapses).

The NMDA receptor is peculiar because it is doubly gated: it needs glutamate to bind, which reports that the sending cell fired, and it also needs the receiving cell's membrane to be depolarised - shifted toward a more positive voltage - because at resting voltage a magnesium ion sits in the channel pore and physically plugs it.

Depolarisation expels the magnesium, and only when both conditions hold at once does the channel open and admit calcium, an ion that acts as a chemical trigger for the enzyme cascades that install LTP.

This makes the NMDA receptor a molecular coincidence detector, and it is the most satisfying case in neuroscience of a theoretical requirement being met by an identified molecule - Hebb described the logic in 1949, and the protein implementing it was characterised decades later.

Blocking NMDA receptors pharmacologically blocks the induction of most forms of LTP and impairs many kinds of learning, which is the central line of evidence tying the molecule to memory.


9.1.4 Spike-timing-dependent plasticity and causal asymmetry

Hebb's phrase takes part in firing implies an order in time, and experiments in the 1990s were able to test that implication directly by controlling the timing of individual spikes.

Henry Markram and colleagues in 1997, working on neocortical pyramidal cells, and Guo-qiang Bi and Mu-ming Poo in 1998, working on cultured hippocampal neurons, paired presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes at millisecond precision and found a strikingly asymmetric result.

If the sending cell spiked shortly before the receiving cell - the causally consistent order, since the input could have contributed to the output - the synapse strengthened, and if the order was reversed, the same synapse weakened, with the effect falling off over roughly a few tens of milliseconds on each side.

This is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), and its appeal is that it appears to make synapses sensitive to causal direction rather than mere co-occurrence, which is exactly what a system trying to learn what predicts what would want.

The interpretation is not unanimous, however: an analysis by Bono, Clopath and colleagues published in Cerebral Cortex in 2023 argued that under realistic firing conditions STDP rewards synchrony rather than causality, and a competing view represented by Shouval, Wang and Wittenberg treats STDP as an epiphenomenon of more fundamental calcium-dependent rules rather than a learning rule in its own right.

The honest summary is that the timing asymmetry is a solid experimental fact, and its status as the brain's learning rule is contested.


9.2 Constraints that make plasticity stable

Purely Hebbian learning has a fatal arithmetic property: strengthening the connections between cells that fire together makes them more likely to fire together, which strengthens the connections further.

Left unchecked this positive feedback drives every synapse to its maximum and every neuron into runaway excitation, and it also erases the differences between synapses, which is the very thing the information was stored in.

Real brains do not do this, so there must be stabilising mechanisms operating alongside Hebbian ones, generally slower and more global.

This section covers four of them, moving from adjustments to synaptic strength, to adjustments to the neuron's own responsiveness, to adjustments to the rules of plasticity themselves, and finally to the unsolved computational dilemma that sits underneath all of it.


9.2.1 Homeostatic synaptic scaling

Homeostasis means keeping an internal variable near a set point, and in the 1990s Gina Turrigiano and colleagues showed that neurons do this for their own average firing rate.

If cultured cortical neurons are silenced for a day or two, they respond by strengthening all of their excitatory synapses, and if they are chronically over-excited, they weaken them all, pulling activity back toward a target level.

Crucially the adjustment was reported to be multiplicative, meaning every synapse is multiplied by the same factor rather than having a fixed amount added, which preserves the ratios between synapses and so preserves the information Hebbian learning stored in those ratios - an elegant division of labour in which a fast specific process writes and a slow global process stabilises.

One striking mechanistic finding is that the signal is partly glial rather than neuronal: Stellwagen and Malenka reported in Nature in 2006 that tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), an immune signalling molecule released by glia, the non-neuronal support cells of the brain, mediates scaling, though later work by Steinmetz and Turrigiano in 2010 recast TNF-alpha as permissive - required to keep synapses capable of scaling - rather than as the instructive signal itself.

The multiplicative claim has also been softened by later evidence: population-level scaling can look multiplicative while individual synapses scale by variable amounts, so the clean preservation-of-ratios story is an approximation rather than a law.


9.2.2 Intrinsic excitability regulation

A neuron's responsiveness is not determined only by its incoming synapses but also by its own membrane, specifically by which voltage-gated ion channels - proteins that open and close with voltage and carry the currents underlying the spike - it expresses and in what numbers.

Neurons regulate these channel populations in an activity-dependent way, so that a cell driven too hard will, over hours to days, reduce excitability by adjusting sodium, potassium or hyperpolarisation-activated currents, and a chronically quiet cell will do the reverse.

The axon initial segment, the short stretch of axon just past the cell body where the spike is actually initiated, can itself change length and position, shifting how much input is required to fire.

Different currents are also functionally coupled, so that a fall in one triggers a compensating rise in another, which stabilises output without requiring the cell to monitor every channel separately.

Intrinsic plasticity is not purely homeostatic, however: persistent, input-specific changes in excitability accompany learning, which means the neuron's own membrane is a second storage medium alongside the synapse - a point often neglected in synapse-centric accounts.


9.2.3 Metaplasticity and the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro sliding threshold

Metaplasticity is the plasticity of plasticity - a change not in synaptic strength itself but in how easily synaptic strength can subsequently be changed, a term popularised by Wickliffe Abraham and Mark Bear in the mid-1990s.

Its most influential formalisation came earlier, in the 1982 theory of Elie Bienenstock, Leon Cooper and Paul Munro, known as BCM theory, developed to explain how neurons in visual cortex acquire selective responses depending on the visual environment they grow up in.

BCM posits a modification threshold: postsynaptic activity above the threshold produces strengthening, activity below it produces weakening, and, crucially, the threshold itself slides according to the recent average activity of the cell.

The consequence is self-stabilising in a way plain Hebbian rules are not - after a period of high activity the threshold rises, making further potentiation harder and depression easier, and after a quiet period the threshold falls and potentiation becomes easy again.

BCM was proposed as theory and subsequently earned experimental support, most directly through the discovery of homosynaptic LTD and through demonstrations that prior activity shifts the LTP-versus-LTD crossover point, which is a genuine case of a computational model predicting a biological phenomenon before it was observed.


9.2.4 The stability-plasticity dilemma and catastrophic forgetting

The stability-plasticity dilemma names the underlying tension: a system rigid enough to protect old knowledge cannot readily absorb new knowledge, and a system flexible enough to absorb new knowledge will overwrite the old.

In artificial neural networks the failure mode is stark and has a name - catastrophic forgetting, in which training a network on a second task drives the weights to a solution for that task and destroys performance on the first, often almost completely.

Brains clearly do better, though not perfectly, and the mechanisms discussed above are part of why: synapses appear to have multiple states with different lifetimes, consolidation moves memories between structures over time, and neuromodulators gate when plasticity is permitted at all.

The machine learning field has attacked the problem with regularisation terms that penalise moving weights deemed important to old tasks, with replay of stored or generated old examples - a strategy with a biological echo in hippocampal replay during sleep - and with architectural separation of tasks into distinct parts of the network.

Work through 2024 and 2025 has shifted from treating the goal as merely preventing forgetting to treating stability and plasticity as two objectives to be traded off explicitly, including analyses suggesting different network components carry the two roles, and the problem remains open in both fields, which is a fair signal that it is deep rather than merely technical.


9.3 Beyond the synapse

It is tempting to identify plasticity with changes in synaptic weight, because that is where the theory is best developed, but the brain is not a fixed graph with adjustable edge weights.

The edges themselves appear and disappear, new nodes are added in at least one region, the transmission delays along the wires are tunable, and the readout of the genome inside each cell is chemically annotated by experience.

This section takes these four in turn, and the honest theme running through it is that these mechanisms are better established as phenomena than as explanations - we know they happen, and we understand less well what they compute.


9.3.1 Structural plasticity: spine turnover, axonal sprouting

A dendritic spine is a tiny protrusion from a neuron's receiving branches, and it is the postsynaptic partner of most excitatory synapses in the cortex, so spines can be counted and tracked as a physical proxy for synapses.

Two-photon microscopy, a technique that images fluorescently labelled structures hundreds of micrometres deep in living tissue, allows the same spines on the same dendrite in a living mouse to be revisited day after day, and what it reveals is constant turnover - spines appear and vanish continuously, with small spines much more volatile than large ones, and reported turnover in hippocampus reaching roughly 40 percent over four days in chronic super-resolution imaging by Pfeiffer, Nagerl and colleagues in 2018.

Learning biases this turnover: new spines form near the sites of activity during training, they cluster together on the same dendritic branches, and spines gained during learning that survive predict retention of the skill.

Work by Frank, Fu and colleagues published in Nature Communications in 2018 reported that the rate of spine turnover before learning predicts subsequent learning performance, and that genetically increasing turnover increased both learning and spine clustering, which supports a hotspot account in which volatile regions of dendrite are where new memories get written.

At the coarser scale of whole axons, sprouting - the growth of new axonal branches and connections - is limited in the healthy adult brain but is triggered by injury, and S. Thomas Carmichael's work on rodent stroke describes a stereotyped time course in which sprouting is triggered within one to three days, established over one to two weeks, and yields new connection patterns by around four weeks, with recovery of function tracking the reorganisation of cortical maps in surviving tissue around the lesion.


9.3.2 Adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus and its disputed role

Neurogenesis is the birth of new neurons, and in most of the adult mammalian brain it does not occur, but the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus is a well documented exception in rodents, where new granule cells are generated throughout life, pass through a period of heightened excitability and plasticity, and are then either integrated or eliminated.

The computational proposal, developed in modelling work and supported by rodent behavioural experiments, is pattern separation - making similar experiences into distinguishable memory traces so they do not interfere, with the young hyperexcitable cells providing a supply of fresh, initially unassigned coding capacity.

Whether adults humans do this at all has been one of the most public disputes in modern neuroscience: in 2018 Sorrells, Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues reported in Nature that markers of new neurons fall to undetectable levels in the human hippocampus by adulthood, while Boldrini, Mann and colleagues reported in Cell Stem Cell that same year that immature neurons persist at all ages examined up to 79 years.

Much of the disagreement is methodological rather than conceptual, turning on how quickly tissue was collected after death, how it was fixed, and whether the antibody markers used, especially doublecortin, are specific to genuinely new neurons in human tissue.

The balance of evidence shifted in 2025, when Marta Paterlini, Jonas Frisen and colleagues at the Karolinska Institute published in Science an analysis combining single-nucleus RNA sequencing of over three hundred thousand hippocampal nuclei spanning ages zero to 78 with staining for the proliferation marker Ki67, using a machine learning classifier trained on unambiguous childhood tissue, and reported dividing neural progenitors in adult dentate gyrus - with the important qualification that the numbers varied enormously between individuals, some adults having many and others almost none.

The current state is therefore that adult human hippocampal neurogenesis is now better supported than it was, that its magnitude is small and highly variable, and that its functional contribution to human cognition remains genuinely unestablished rather than merely unmeasured.


9.3.3 Myelin plasticity and the timing of learning

Myelin is the fatty insulating sheath wrapped around many axons by oligodendrocytes, a class of glial cell, and its function is to speed conduction by forcing the electrical signal to jump between the gaps in the sheath, called nodes of Ranvier.

Myelin was long assumed to be laid down during development and thereafter static, but it is now clear that new oligodendrocytes continue to be generated in adulthood from oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and that this generation is driven by neural activity.

The decisive experiment was reported by McKenzie, Richardson and colleagues in Science in 2014: genetically preventing the production of new oligodendrocytes in adult mice, while leaving existing myelin untouched, left the animals unable to master a complex running wheel with irregularly spaced rungs, showing that new myelin is required for motor skill learning and not merely correlated with it.

The proposed computational role is control of timing - since conduction velocity depends on myelination, adjusting myelin adjusts the arrival times of signals, and in a system where plasticity itself is timing-dependent at the millisecond scale, control over delays is control over what gets learned.

This is an elegant idea with real experimental support for the necessity claim, and considerably weaker direct evidence that the brain tunes specific delays to specific computational ends, so it should be held as a promising hypothesis rather than an established mechanism.


9.3.4 Epigenetic and transcriptional memory

Epigenetics refers to chemical modifications to deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and to the histone proteins it is wound around, which change how readily genes are transcribed without altering the genetic sequence itself.

Two modifications dominate the memory literature: DNA methylation, the attachment of methyl groups to DNA, which generally suppresses transcription, and histone acetylation, which loosens the packing of chromatin and generally promotes it, and which is reversed by enzymes called histone deacetylases.

Learning produces rapid and specific changes in both marks in the hippocampus and amygdala, and interfering with the enzymes that write or erase them impairs the consolidation of new memories - inhibiting histone deacetylases, for instance, tends to enhance memory formation in rodents, which is one of the more robust findings in the area.

The functional logic is that lasting synaptic change requires new proteins, new proteins require transcription, and epigenetic marks are the cell's way of holding a gene in a more or less readable state over long periods, which makes them a candidate substrate for memory persistence beyond the lifetime of any individual protein.

Recent work has become considerably more precise, including cell-type-specific and locus-specific epigenetic editing in memory-bearing engram cells - the sparse populations of neurons reactivated during recall - reported in Nature Genetics in 2025, which moves the field from correlation toward causal manipulation of a specific mark at a specific gene in a specific cell.


9.4 Credit assignment, the field's hardest substrate problem

Suppose an animal takes an action and, two seconds later, receives a reward.

Somewhere in its brain, a particular synapse, one among perhaps a hundred trillion, made a small contribution to that action.

The credit assignment problem is the question of how that synapse could possibly know this - how a purely local device, with access only to the signals physically reaching it, can determine its contribution to a global outcome that occurred elsewhere in the network and later in time.

Every learning system, biological or artificial, must solve some version of this, and the reason it dominates contemporary theoretical neuroscience is that the machine learning solution is spectacularly effective and manifestly not what brains do.


9.4.1 The spatial credit assignment problem in deep hierarchies

Spatial credit assignment is the problem of distributing responsibility across the layers of a deep network - the cortex is hierarchically organised, with early sensory areas feeding later association areas, and a synapse in an early area affects behaviour only through a long chain of intervening cells.

Artificial networks solve this with backpropagation, an algorithm that computes exactly how much each weight contributed to the output error by applying the chain rule of calculus backward through the network.

Backpropagation is implausible as biology for several specific reasons: it requires the backward pass to use the transpose of the forward weights, meaning each synapse would need to know the strength of a different synapse elsewhere - the weight transport problem; it requires separate forward and backward phases with distinct signal types; and it requires error signals that propagate without themselves causing the neurons to fire.

The most influential biological proposal, set out by Blake Richards and Timothy Lillicrap in a 2019 review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology, exploits the anatomy of cortical pyramidal neurons, which have two largely separate dendritic compartments - basal dendrites near the cell body receiving bottom-up input, and distal apical dendrites receiving top-down feedback from higher areas.

Because these compartments are electrically distinct and the apical compartment has its own nonlinear spiking properties, a single neuron can in principle keep feedforward information and feedback teaching signals separate while combining them locally at the synapse, which is a genuinely attractive answer to the objection that credit signals would be indistinguishable from ordinary input.


9.4.2 The temporal credit assignment problem across delays

The temporal version of the problem is arguably worse: the reward arrives seconds after the relevant activity, but the biochemical signatures of that activity - calcium transients, receptor states - last milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.

Something must bridge the gap, holding a record of what just happened until the outcome is known, and doing so at each synapse independently.

In reinforcement learning theory the standard device is the eligibility trace, a decaying tag left at a synapse marking it as recently active and therefore eligible for later modification, an idea introduced by A. Harry Klopf and developed extensively by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto.

Biology supplies a striking existence proof at behavioural timescales: Katie Bittner, Aaron Milstein, Jeffrey Magee and colleagues reported in Science in 2017 that hippocampal CA1 neurons form place fields - selective responses to a particular location - through behavioural timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), in which a large dendritic plateau potential potentiates inputs that were active during a window of several seconds before and after it.

This is not Hebbian in the classical sense, because it requires neither millisecond coincidence nor repetition - a single plateau can install a place field in one trial - and it directly demonstrates that synapses can carry a memory of their own recent activity across seconds.


9.4.3 Biologically plausible alternatives to backpropagation: feedback alignment, target propagation, predictive coding schemes, burst-dependent plasticity

Feedback alignment, introduced by Lillicrap, Cownden, Tweed and Akerman in 2016, made the surprising discovery that the backward weights need not be the transpose of the forward weights at all - fixed random feedback weights suffice, because the forward weights gradually align themselves with the random feedback, dissolving the weight transport objection.

Its limitation is scale: feedback alignment degrades badly on deep convolutional networks and large datasets, which weakens the claim that it is sufficient for brain-scale learning even if it is biologically permissible.

Target propagation, developed by Yoshua Bengio and colleagues, replaces error gradients with targets - each layer is told what its output should have been, computed via approximate inverse mappings learned for each layer - which avoids propagating derivatives but requires each layer to send two kinds of signal and can be unstable to train.

Predictive coding, associated with Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard and with Karl Friston, proposes that the cortex continuously generates top-down predictions and transmits only the prediction errors upward, and there are formal results, including work by Whittington and Bogacz and subsequent analyses in PLOS One in 2022, showing that predictive coding networks can approximate or under certain conditions equal backpropagation, which is why the scheme attracts so much attention.

Burst-dependent plasticity, proposed by Payeur, Guerguiev, Zenke, Richards and Naud in Nature Neuroscience in 2021, offers a mechanistically concrete option in which a neuron multiplexes two signals on one axon - its firing rate carries feedforward information while its bursts, short high-frequency clusters of spikes triggered by apical dendritic input, carry the teaching signal, with plasticity keyed to burst rate.

None of these is established as what the brain does, and their intellectual value is chiefly negative and clarifying: they demonstrate that the standard objections to gradient-based learning in brains are not decisive, which removes an argument without supplying an answer.


9.4.4 Three-factor rules and neuromodulated eligibility traces

The most widely accepted partial answer is the three-factor learning rule, reviewed authoritatively by Nicolas Fremaux and Wulfram Gerstner in 2016 and by Gerstner and colleagues in 2018.

The first two factors are the classical Hebbian pair, presynaptic and postsynaptic activity, whose coincidence sets an eligibility trace at the synapse - a transient chemical tag that decays over seconds and by itself produces no lasting change.

The third factor is a broadcast neuromodulatory signal - a phasic burst of dopamine, noradrenaline, acetylcholine or serotonin, released diffusely by small nuclei whose axons blanket wide regions of cortex - which converts eligible synapses into permanently changed ones.

Dopamine is the best studied case, because midbrain dopamine neurons fire in a pattern closely matching the reward prediction error of reinforcement learning theory, so a rule of the form change equals eligibility multiplied by dopamine implements something close to a well understood learning algorithm using only signals a synapse actually has.

The scheme's strength is that it solves temporal credit assignment plausibly and has direct experimental support, including demonstrations that plasticity can be gated by neuromodulators delivered seconds after the pairing, and its weakness is that a signal broadcast to millions of synapses at once carries almost no spatial information, so three-factor rules address when to learn far better than they address which synapse deserves the credit.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Hebb's 1949 conjecture that co-active neurons strengthen their connection was vindicated experimentally by Bliss and Lomo's 1973 discovery of long-term potentiation and mechanistically by the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor, whose magnesium block makes it a genuine molecular coincidence detector.

Correlational learning alone is unstable, so the brain layers stabilising processes over it - homeostatic synaptic scaling, regulation of intrinsic excitability, and the sliding modification threshold of Bienenstock, Cooper and Munro - and the underlying stability-plasticity dilemma remains unsolved in both neuroscience and machine learning.

Plasticity is not confined to synaptic weights: spines turn over continuously and cluster where learning occurs, axons sprout after injury, activity-dependent myelination is required for motor learning, and epigenetic marks provide a long-lived transcriptional substrate.

Adult hippocampal neurogenesis in humans was genuinely disputed for a decade, and the 2025 Karolinska work identifying proliferating progenitors has strengthened the case for its existence without settling what, if anything, it contributes to human cognition.

Credit assignment is the field's deepest open problem, and the current landscape consists of an implausible but effective algorithm in backpropagation, a set of plausible alternatives that are not yet demonstrated in brains, and one partial biological answer - neuromodulated eligibility traces - that handles timing well and specificity poorly.


CHAPTER 10. THE SINGLE NEURON AS A COMPUTER (APPARATUS)

For most of the twentieth century the nerve cell was treated as a simple adding machine, a device that summed its inputs and fired when the total crossed a line.

This chapter takes that picture apart.

A neuron is a branched, leaky, chemically active object whose branches can make decisions of their own, whose output is a pattern in time and not just a number, and whose behaviour can be written down in mathematics of several different grades of realism.

Understanding the cell as an apparatus matters because every claim later in this book about memory, attention, or decision rests on assumptions about what one cell can and cannot do.

If a single cell can already perform an operation that engineers once thought required a whole network, then our accounting of how much circuitry cognition needs has to change.

The chapter also asks the harder question at the end - whether the single cell is even the right unit to be counting.


10.1 Dendritic computation

Dendrites are the branching input structures of a neuron, the tree-like processes that receive contacts from other cells.

The word comes from the Greek dendron, meaning tree.

For decades dendrites were treated as passive wiring, mere cables carrying signals inward to the cell body.

That view is now known to be wrong in an interesting way - the cable does arithmetic on the way.

This section builds the story from the passive idealisation outward to the modern view of the dendritic tree as a layered computing device.


10.1.1 Passive integration and the point-neuron idealisation

The simplest possible model treats the whole cell as a single electrical point, with no spatial extent - this is the point-neuron idealisation, and it assumes the cell is isopotential, meaning the voltage is the same everywhere inside it.

Real dendrites are not isopotential, and the mathematics that describes them is cable theory, borrowed from nineteenth-century work on undersea telegraph cables and adapted to neurons by Wilfrid Rall from the late 1950s onward.

Cable theory gives a quantity called the length constant, written with the Greek letter lambda, which is the distance over which a steady voltage signal decays to about thirty-seven percent of its starting size as it spreads along the process.

The practical consequence is that a synapse - the junction where one neuron passes signal to another - placed far out on a distal branch delivers a much smaller voltage at the cell body than an identical synapse placed nearby, so location itself is a variable in the computation.

Rall also showed that under particular geometric conditions a whole branching tree can be collapsed into a single equivalent cylinder, which was the first mathematically honest way to keep some dendritic structure without simulating every twig.

The point neuron survives because it is cheap and often good enough for network-scale work, but it is an approximation that discards real computational machinery, and knowing what it discards is the point of the rest of this section.


10.1.2 Active dendritic conductances and dendritic spikes

Dendritic membranes are studded with voltage-gated ion channels - protein pores that open or close depending on the local voltage - which means the dendrite can amplify and regenerate signals rather than merely leaking them away.

The result is the dendritic spike, a locally generated electrical event confined to a branch or region of the tree, and there are several kinds, driven by sodium ions, by calcium ions, or by the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, a glutamate receptor that conducts current only when the cell is already somewhat depolarised and therefore acts as a built-in coincidence detector.

Because a dendritic spike is triggered when enough nearby synapses fire together, the branch effectively applies a threshold to its own local input, which is a nonlinear operation - the output is not simply proportional to the sum of inputs.

A striking recent result is from Gidon and colleagues, working with Larkum, published in Science in 2020, who recorded from human layer 2 and 3 cortical pyramidal neurons and found a previously undescribed class of calcium-mediated dendritic action potentials, abbreviated dCaAP.

These events were graded rather than all-or-none, and unusually their amplitude was largest for threshold-level input and became smaller for stronger input, which allowed a single dendrite to implement an exclusive-or (XOR) operation - respond to input X alone or input Y alone, but not to both together.

That matters because XOR is the textbook example of a computation that a single-layer artificial network cannot perform, so a result of this kind, if it generalises, moves a whole layer of computation inside one cell.

The finding is recent and was obtained in tissue resected from epilepsy surgery patients, so its generality across cell types, species, and behaving conditions is still being worked out - treat it as important and real but not yet fully settled in scope.


10.1.3 The two-layer and deep-network views of a pyramidal cell

If each dendritic branch thresholds its own inputs and the cell body then thresholds the sum of the branches, the cell is formally a two-layer network, and this is exactly the claim Poirazi, Brannon and Mel made in Neuron in 2003 in a paper titled Pyramidal Neuron as Two-Layer Neural Network.

They ran a detailed compartmental simulation of a hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cell, drove it with dozens of scattered synaptic inputs, and found the firing rate was well predicted by a formula in which independent sigmoidal subunits - saturating S-shaped functions, one per dendritic domain - feed a single summing output unit.

Roughly two decades later Beniaguev, Segev and London, in Neuron in 2021, pushed the same question with machine learning, training artificial deep networks to reproduce the millisecond-resolution input-output behaviour of a biophysically detailed layer 5 cortical pyramidal cell.

They found that five to eight layers of a temporally convolutional network were needed to match the real cell's behaviour, which is a quantitative statement of how much computation one neuron does.

The most informative part of that study is a control - when NMDA receptors were removed from the simulated cell, a single hidden layer sufficed, showing that most of the extra depth comes from NMDA-dependent dendritic nonlinearity rather than from branching geometry alone.

It is worth being careful about what these results claim - the depth figure describes a simulated cell, and it measures how hard the cell's input-output map is to imitate, not that the brain uses the cell that way in any given task.


10.1.4 Apical dendrites, feedback, and the coincidence of top-down and bottom-up input

Cortical pyramidal cells have two structurally and functionally distinct input regions - the basal dendrites near the cell body, which receive mostly local and feedforward input, and the apical tuft, a spray of branches far above in the upper cortical layers, which receives mostly long-range feedback from other cortical areas and from the thalamus.

Larkum and colleagues showed in 1999 that these two zones can talk to each other through a mechanism now called backpropagation-activated calcium spike firing, abbreviated BAC firing.

The mechanism works like this - a sodium spike initiated near the cell body travels backwards up the apical trunk, and if it arrives while the distal tuft is also receiving synaptic input, the two together trigger a calcium spike in the tuft, which floods back down and makes the cell fire a burst rather than a single spike.

Functionally this is a coincidence detector across cortical layers - the cell fires weakly for bottom-up sensory drive alone, and fires hard only when bottom-up drive and top-down feedback arrive together.

This is a theoretically attractive bridge to cognition, because attention, expectation, and conscious report have all been proposed to work through exactly such top-down and bottom-up matching, a view Larkum has developed as a dendritic integration theory of cortex.

Be honest about the evidential status - the cellular mechanism is solidly established in rodent slices and in vivo, but the leap from BAC firing to consciousness or attention is a hypothesis with suggestive support, not a demonstrated fact, and critics reasonably point out that many things modulate bursting.


10.2 Spiking and coding at the cell level

Having decided what a neuron computes, we now ask how it says the answer.

The output of a neuron is a train of action potentials - brief, stereotyped electrical pulses, all essentially the same size, so the information cannot be in their amplitude.

It has to be in how many there are, when they occur, how they are grouped, and how they change over time.

This section walks through the candidate codes and the evidence for each.


10.2.1 Rate codes, temporal codes, latency codes, phase codes

A rate code holds that information lives in the number of spikes per unit time, an idea traceable to Edgar Adrian's work in the 1920s showing that stretching a muscle harder made its sensory nerve fire faster.

A temporal code holds that the precise timing of individual spikes, relative to some reference, carries information beyond what the rate carries.

A latency code is a specific temporal scheme in which the information is in how quickly the first spike arrives after a stimulus - a bright edge produces an earlier first spike than a dim one - and latency coding has been described in retinal ganglion cells and in auditory pathways, where it has the virtue of being fast, since a decision can be made before a rate has time to accumulate.

A phase code, more fully a phase-of-firing code, uses the timing of spikes relative to an ongoing network oscillation, and the classic example is hippocampal phase precession, described by O'Keefe and Recce in 1993, in which a place cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the roughly five to twelve hertz theta rhythm as the animal moves through the cell's preferred location.

Phase precession is the cleanest existing demonstration that rate and timing can carry different information in the same spike train at the same time - the rate says how close you are to the field centre, the phase says where within it you are.

The honest summary is that this is not a competition with a winner; different systems and timescales use different mixtures, and much current work is about how to read the mixtures rather than which one is correct.


10.2.2 Bursting as a distinct signalling channel

A burst is a tight cluster of spikes separated by very short intervals, followed by a longer silence.

Lisman argued in Trends in Neurosciences in 1997, in an article titled Bursts as a unit of neural information, that bursts matter because individual synapses are unreliable - a single spike often fails to release any neurotransmitter at all - whereas a rapid volley greatly raises the chance that the receiving cell hears something.

On that account a burst is not just a fast rate, it is a message flagged as important.

Naud and Sprekeler, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2018, developed this into a multiplexing proposal - because a population can independently vary its overall event rate and the fraction of those events that are bursts, one cell population can carry two separate information streams at once with little cross-talk.

This dovetails neatly with the dendritic story of section 10.1.4, since bursting in pyramidal cells is often triggered by apical, feedback-driven calcium spikes, giving a physical implementation in which the single-spike channel carries bottom-up information and the burst channel carries top-down information.

The theory is elegant and biophysically grounded, but the direct evidence that downstream circuits actually decode these two channels separately during behaviour is still thin, and that gap should be kept in view.


10.2.3 Adaptation and the encoding of change

Spike-frequency adaptation is the very common phenomenon in which a neuron given a constant, unchanging input fires rapidly at first and then slows down, usually because slow potassium currents or calcium-activated currents build up and oppose further firing.

The functional reading is that neurons are built to report change rather than steady state, which is efficient - a signal that never varies carries no new information, so spending spikes on it wastes energy.

Adaptation also implements a kind of automatic gain control, letting a cell with a limited firing range remain sensitive across the enormous range of intensities the world actually delivers, which connects to the broader efficient-coding tradition running from Attneave in 1954 and Barlow in 1961.

Adaptation has subtler effects too - modelling work shows that an adaptation current changes not just the average rate but the cell's effective threshold, its gain, and the variability of its spiking, reducing interval variability at low rates while increasing it at high rates.

This means adaptation is not a nuisance to be subtracted off before analysing a code; it is part of the code.


10.2.4 Noise, variability, and the Poisson idealisation

Present the same stimulus to the same cortical neuron many times and you get a different spike train each time, and this trial-to-trial variability is large.

The standard summary measure is the Fano factor, the variance of the spike count divided by its mean, which equals one for a Poisson process - a process in which each spike occurs independently and unpredictably at some instantaneous rate.

Cortical neurons often show Fano factors near or somewhat above one, which is why the Poisson idealisation became the default working assumption in computational neuroscience.

There is a real and long-running dispute here, opened by Softky and Koch in the Journal of Neuroscience in 1993, who argued that highly irregular cortical firing is inconsistent with a cell that integrates thousands of small inputs, since averaging that many inputs should produce regular output - so, they concluded, cortical cells must be doing something more like coincidence detection.

Shadlen and Newsome replied through the 1990s that a balance of excitation and inhibition can keep the membrane voltage fluctuating near threshold and reproduce irregular firing in an ordinary integrator, and that variability may simply be a tolerable cost of a rate code.

Later work complicated both positions - Churchland, Goris and others in the 2010s showed that variability is not fixed but drops sharply at stimulus onset and is partly explained by slow fluctuations in the animal's internal state rather than by genuinely random spike generation.

The current position is that Poisson is a convenient null model rather than a mechanism, that much apparent noise is shared across neurons and therefore is not noise in the useful sense, and that treating variability as structured signal has been more productive than treating it as randomness.


10.3 Formal single-neuron models

Everything above is descriptive.

To do real work, a neuroscientist writes the cell down as equations, and there is a ladder of models from very abstract to very detailed.

Choosing a rung is a genuine scientific decision, because a more detailed model is not automatically a better model - it may be unfittable, unrunnable, or uninterpretable.

This section climbs the ladder and then examines the trap waiting at the top.


10.3.1 Integrate-and-fire and its generalisations

The leaky integrate-and-fire model, whose ancestry runs back to Louis Lapicque in 1907, treats the cell as a leaky capacitor - input current charges a voltage, the voltage leaks away toward rest, and when it crosses a threshold you declare a spike, reset the voltage, and carry on.

It does not model the spike itself, it merely records that one happened, which is the source of both its speed and its limits.

Generalisations add the missing physiology piece by piece - the exponential integrate-and-fire model adds a sharp exponential term that reproduces the runaway upswing at spike initiation, and the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model, introduced by Brette and Gerstner in the Journal of Neurophysiology in 2005, adds a second variable representing adaptation.

That two-variable model is remarkably capable for its size - Brette and Gerstner reported it correctly predicting the timing of about ninety-six percent of spikes to within two milliseconds when matched against a detailed conductance-based model driven by noisy synaptic input, and it also reproduces the qualitatively different firing patterns real cells show, such as regular spiking, bursting, and adapting.

The international quantitative single-neuron modelling competition, run from 2007 onward by Gerstner, Jolivet and colleagues, tested such models against real recordings and found that well-fitted generalised integrate-and-fire models beat far more elaborate models at predicting actual spike times.

That result is the strongest available argument that for many purposes the cheap model is not merely cheap - it is the right tool.


10.3.2 Hodgkin-Huxley and reduced conductance models

The foundational biophysical model is that of Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley, published in 1952 from experiments on the giant axon of the squid, work that won them the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963.

Their model represents the membrane as an electrical circuit with a capacitance and several parallel conductances - one for sodium, one for potassium, one leak - and crucially makes each conductance depend on voltage through gating variables that follow their own differential equations, giving four coupled equations in total.

The achievement is that the action potential is not put in by hand as it is in integrate-and-fire; it falls out of the equations as a consequence of sodium channels opening fast and potassium channels opening slowly.

Four dimensions is hard to reason about, so reduced models exist - FitzHugh in 1961 and Nagumo in 1962 collapsed the system to two variables, one fast for excitation and one slow for recovery, and Morris and Lecar in 1981 produced a two-variable calcium-and-potassium model of the barnacle muscle fibre.

The two-variable versions can be drawn as a phase plane, a two-dimensional picture of the system's state, which is why they became the standard teaching tool for concepts such as excitability, thresholds, and the different classes of neuronal onset dynamics later systematised by Izhikevich.

The general lesson is that reduction is not simply loss - moving from four dimensions to two turned a simulation into something you could understand by looking at it.


10.3.3 Multicompartment biophysical models

A multicompartment model chops the neuron's anatomy into many small pieces, treats each piece as electrically uniform with its own Hodgkin-Huxley-style channels, and couples neighbouring pieces with resistors representing the cytoplasm, which is Rall's cable theory implemented numerically.

This is the level at which the dendritic phenomena of section 10.1 can actually be studied, since you cannot have a dendritic spike in a model that has no dendrite, and it is the level used by Poirazi and Mel and by Beniaguev and colleagues.

Models of this kind are built from real reconstructed morphologies, traced from filled and imaged cells, and are usually run in dedicated simulators such as NEURON, developed by Hines and Carnevale, or GENESIS.

The largest programme of this sort has been the Blue Brain Project at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, led by Henry Markram from 2005, which built detailed multicompartment reconstructions of a rat somatosensory cortical microcircuit, published in Cell in 2015 with roughly thirty-one thousand neurons and around thirty-seven million synapses.

Blue Brain and its successor the Human Brain Project have been genuinely controversial - critics, including hundreds of European neuroscientists who signed an open letter in 2014, argued that extreme biophysical detail without a governing theory does not by itself explain anything, while defenders argue that a detailed reconstruction is a testable object that predicts phenomena nobody put in.

The methodological point for a reader is simple - detail buys realism and costs both computation and interpretability, and the exchange rate is not always favourable.


10.3.4 Fitting neuron models to data and the identifiability problem

Once a model has many parameters - maximal conductances for a dozen channel types, kinetic constants, geometric details - the question becomes whether recorded data can pin those parameters down, and the usual answer is no.

This is the identifiability problem, and its most influential demonstration comes from Eve Marder's laboratory - Prinz, Bucher and Marder, in Nature Neuroscience in 2004, simulated more than twenty million versions of a three-cell model of the pyloric circuit of the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion and found that essentially indistinguishable output arose from widely different sets of conductances and synaptic strengths.

The phrase for this is degeneracy - many different mechanisms produce the same behaviour - and it is not just a modelling artefact, since Marder's group also showed that individual animals of the same species have measurably different channel expression levels while producing the same rhythm.

There are two consequences, one discouraging and one liberating.

The discouraging one is that a model which reproduces your data does not thereby establish that the real cell uses those parameter values, so any single hand-tuned fit should be distrusted.

The liberating one is that degeneracy is a biological feature, giving nervous systems robustness and room to compensate for perturbation, temperature change, and damage, and later work from Marder's group extending to energy efficiency found that even demanding metabolic economy alongside correct output leaves substantial degeneracy intact.

Modern practice reflects this - rather than reporting one best fit, researchers now characterise whole populations of acceptable models, increasingly using simulation-based inference methods such as those Gonçalves, Macke and colleagues published in eLife in 2020, which return a probability distribution over parameters rather than a single answer.


10.4 What single-neuron computation buys the cognitive account

The chapter has so far been about cells.

This last section asks what any of it purchases for the study of thought, and where the cell-level story runs out.


10.4.1 Concept cells and sparse selectivity

Sparse coding means that any given item is represented by the activity of a very small fraction of the available neurons, as opposed to a dense code where most cells participate a little in everything.

The most vivid evidence in humans comes from Quian Quiroga, Reddy, Kreiman, Koch and Fried, in Nature in 2005, who recorded single neurons in the medial temporal lobe of epilepsy patients implanted with electrodes for surgical planning - a rare opportunity to hear individual human neurons while the person looks at pictures and reads words.

They found cells that responded to one person or place across radically different images, and even to the written and spoken name, the famous example being a cell that fired for photographs of the actress Jennifer Aniston but not for dozens of other people and objects.

Quian Quiroga renamed these concept cells and argued in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2012 that they are building blocks of declarative memory, encoding abstract identity rather than sensory appearance, which is exactly what an episodic memory system needs in order to link arbitrary items together.

The crucial interpretive caution, which Quian Quiroga himself insists on, is that these are not grandmother cells in the strong sense of one cell per concept - the electrode samples a tiny sliver of a very large structure, so a cell that responds to one of the hundred pictures you happened to show may respond to thousands of things you did not show, and the code is best described as sparse and distributed rather than singular.


10.4.2 Mixed selectivity and high-dimensional coding

Mixed selectivity is nearly the opposite intuition - many cortical neurons, especially in prefrontal cortex, do not have a clean preferred variable at all but respond to messy nonlinear combinations of several task variables at once.

Rigotti, Barak, Warden, Wang, Daw, Miller and Fusi, in Nature in 2013, analysed prefrontal recordings from monkeys performing an object sequence memory task and argued that this apparent messiness is the point.

Nonlinear mixed selectivity raises the dimensionality of the population representation, which means a simple downstream readout neuron drawing a single linear boundary can implement a far larger repertoire of input-output functions than it could if each cell coded one clean variable.

Their most persuasive evidence was behavioural - measured dimensionality collapsed on trials where the animal made an error, tying the geometric property directly to whether the animal got the task right.

Note the tension with the previous sub-section, which is real and instructive - the medial temporal lobe looks sparse and abstract, prefrontal cortex looks mixed and high-dimensional, and the field's working reconciliation is that different regions adopt different codes suited to different jobs, memory storage favouring separability and flexible control favouring dimensionality.


10.4.3 The single-neuron doctrine against the population doctrine

The neuron doctrine, credited to Santiago Ramón y Cajal in the 1890s and named by Waldeyer, holds that the neuron is the anatomical and functional unit of the nervous system, and for a century experimental practice followed it by recording one cell at a time and asking what that cell codes.

Rafael Yuste, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2015, argued that this has become a limitation - once you can record hundreds or thousands of cells simultaneously you see that ensembles have emergent properties, such as coordinated states and attractor dynamics, that are simply invisible in any single cell.

Saxena and Cunningham formalised the alternative as the population doctrine in 2019, and Ebitz and Hayden set out its commitments in Neuron in 2021 - the analytic unit is the population state, a point in a space with one dimension per neuron, and the object of study is the low-dimensional neural manifold, the much smaller surface within that space that activity actually occupies.

On this view a single neuron's tuning is close to meaningless, an arbitrary projection of the real variable, which explains why mixed selectivity looked like noise for so long.

The argument against pushing this too far is that populations are made of cells, that dendritic nonlinearity determines what a population can compute, and that concept cells show at least some single units carry interpretable, behaviourally relevant content.

The most defensible position, and the one this book takes, is that these are complementary levels rather than rivals - the cell is the mechanism, the population is the variable, and an explanation of cognition needs both, with a live open question being how much of the brain's computation happens inside cells versus between them.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The single neuron is not a point summing device; its dendrites carry active conductances, generate local spikes, and threshold their inputs regionally, making the cell at minimum a two-layer network and, by the deep-network estimates of Beniaguev, Segev and London in 2021, considerably more than that, with NMDA receptors supplying most of the extra computational depth.

The cell's output is not a single number but a structured signal in time, in which rate, precise timing, phase relative to ongoing rhythms, and burst versus single spike can carry distinguishable information, while trial-to-trial variability turns out to be largely structured rather than random.

Formal models of the neuron form a ladder from integrate-and-fire to full multicompartment biophysics, and the competition results show that the cheap models often predict real spike times better, so detail is a cost to be justified rather than a virtue in itself.

Marder's degeneracy results establish that many different parameter sets produce identical behaviour, which means fitted parameters are rarely identifiable and that model populations, not single fits, are the honest output of the modelling enterprise.

Finally, what single-cell computation buys the cognitive account is real but bounded - sparse concept cells and high-dimensional mixed selectivity are both genuine, they point in different directions, and the field's centre of gravity has moved from the neuron doctrine toward a population doctrine without ever showing that the cell stopped mattering.


CHAPTER 11. CORTICAL ARCHITECTURE (APPARATUS)

The cerebral cortex is the thin, folded sheet of tissue on the outside of the brain, roughly the thickness of a stack of a few coins, and it is where most of what we call thinking happens.

This chapter is about the architecture of that sheet: how it is layered, how those layers wire to each other and to the rest of the brain, and whether the sheet is built from repeating modules.

It matters because almost every claim in cognitive neuroscience eventually rests on an assumption about this wiring.

If you believe that expectation flows downward and surprise flows upward, you are making a claim about which cortical layer sends which axon where.

The chapter also tries to be honest about a hard fact: some of the most beautiful ideas in this field, such as the cortical column and the single canonical circuit, are far less settled than textbooks imply.


11.1 The laminar plan

Cut the cortex at right angles to its surface, stain it, and you see bands.

Those bands are the layers, or laminae, and they are not decorative: cells in different layers receive different inputs and send their axons to different destinations.

Neocortex, the evolutionarily newer cortex that covers most of the human brain, is conventionally described as having six layers, numbered from the surface inward.

The single most useful idea in this section is that a neuron's layer is a strong predictor of what that neuron is for.


11.1.1 Six layers and their canonical input, output, and association roles

Layer 1 is nearly cell-free and consists mostly of the dendrites (the branching input arms of neurons) of cells whose bodies sit deeper, plus incoming feedback and modulatory axons.

Layer 4 is the classic input layer: it is the main recipient of axons from the thalamus, the deep relay structure that funnels sensory information to cortex, and in heavily sensory areas it is dense with small, round granule cells, which is why such cortex is called granular.

Layers 2 and 3, usually grouped as layer 2/3 because the boundary between them is indistinct, are the association layers: their pyramidal cells (large excitatory neurons shaped like a pyramid with one long apical dendrite reaching toward the surface) project mainly to other cortical areas.

Layers 5 and 6 are the output layers, sending axons out of the cortex entirely - layer 5 to the striatum, superior colliculus, pons, brainstem and spinal cord, layer 6 chiefly back to the thalamus.

The textbook flow is therefore thalamus to layer 4, layer 4 to layer 2/3, layer 2/3 to layers 5 and 6, with layer 2/3 also exporting to the next cortical area.

Recent work complicates this tidy story: some authors, including Yasushi Miyashita in a 2022 review of primate cortex, argue that layers 5 and 6 form a second, parallel input-output pair rather than merely sitting at the end of a chain, and that recall in association cortex begins in the deep layers and feeds backward into layer 2/3.


11.1.2 Feedforward, feedback, and lateral connections defined laminarly

The key insight, made systematic by Daniel Felleman and David Van Essen in 1991, is that the direction of a connection between two cortical areas can be read off from its layers.

They surveyed hundreds of anatomical tracing studies in the macaque monkey and classified each pathway by where it started and where it ended.

Feedforward connections arise from the superficial layers, mostly layer 2/3, and terminate densely in layer 4 of the receiving area.

Feedback connections arise from the deep layers, 5 and 6, and avoid layer 4, terminating instead in layer 1 and layer 6.

Lateral connections, between areas of comparable rank, spread across layers without a strong preference.

Using only these laminar signatures, Felleman and Van Essen ranked 32 visual areas into about ten hierarchical levels, and that diagram has shaped the field ever since.

Later work by Henry Kennedy, Kenneth Knoblauch and colleagues refined the rule into a quantitative one, the fraction of labelled supragranular neurons, which yields a continuous rather than a stepwise hierarchy and emphasises that forward and backward pathways run as a paired counterstream rather than a simple ladder.


11.1.3 Layer 5 and layer 6 corticofugal outputs

Corticofugal simply means fleeing the cortex: axons that leave the cortical sheet for subcortical targets.

Layer 5 contains two broad classes of pyramidal cell that behave very differently.

Intratelencephalic (IT) cells stay within the forebrain, projecting across cortical areas, across the midline to the other hemisphere, and to the striatum.

Pyramidal tract (PT) cells, sitting deeper in layer 5, are the true exports: they send axons to the thalamus, superior colliculus, pons, brainstem and spinal cord, and they carry cortex's commands to the body.

The wiring between them is asymmetric, with IT cells contacting PT cells far more often than the reverse, which suggests a local hierarchy inside layer 5 itself.

Layer 6 is more specialised: its corticothalamic cells project back to the thalamic nuclei that fed the area in the first place, providing modulatory rather than driving input, and they also excite layer 5a while suppressing layer 4, so layer 6 acts as a gain control on the area's own input.

A useful contrast, developed by Murray Sherman and Ray Guillery, is that layer 6 modulates first-order thalamus while layer 5 drives higher-order thalamic nuclei, effectively routing cortical output through the thalamus and back into cortex elsewhere.


11.1.4 Laminar predictive coding proposals

Predictive coding is the theory that the brain continually generates predictions about incoming signals and transmits only the mismatch, the prediction error, upward.

Andre Bastos, Karl Friston and colleagues, writing in Neuron in 2012, mapped this scheme directly onto the laminar plan: superficial pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 encode prediction errors and send them forward, while deep pyramidal cells in layers 5 and 6 encode predictions and send them back.

The mapping is attractive because it needs no new anatomy - it reuses the Felleman and Van Essen laminar rule and adds a computational interpretation.

It also makes a rhythmic prediction: forward, error-carrying traffic should be carried by fast gamma-band oscillations in superficial layers, backward, prediction-carrying traffic by slower alpha and beta rhythms in deep layers, and Bastos and colleagues reported exactly this pattern in macaque cortex in 2015.

Human evidence arrived more recently: a 7 tesla laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study published in Current Biology in 2024 found that expected visual events were decodable across deep, middle and superficial layers of primary visual cortex, whereas unexpected events were robustly decodable only in superficial layers.

Caution is warranted, however: laminar fMRI suffers from a superficial bias, because draining veins near the cortical surface inflate the signal there, and critics note that many predictive coding results are also compatible with simpler adaptation or attention accounts.


11.2 Columns, maps, and modules

If layers describe the cortex's depth, columns and maps describe its surface.

The claim at issue is that the cortex is not a smooth sheet of undifferentiated tissue but a tiling of repeating vertical units, each processing one patch of the sensory world.

That claim has enormous intuitive appeal and a genuinely mixed evidential record, which this section takes seriously.


11.2.1 Orientation columns, ocular dominance, barrels

Vernon Mountcastle discovered in 1955 to 1957, recording in cat and monkey somatosensory cortex, that as an electrode passed straight down through the cortex it encountered cells responding to the same body part and the same kind of touch, while a slanted penetration crossed abruptly into different preferences.

David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel found the same vertical consistency in visual cortex from 1959 onward: cells in a vertical penetration shared a preferred edge orientation, and preference rotated smoothly as the electrode moved sideways, producing orientation columns.

They also described ocular dominance columns, alternating stripes about half a millimetre wide in which cells respond more strongly to the left or the right eye, visible anatomically as banded terminations of thalamic axons in layer 4.

Thomas Woolsey and Hendrik Van der Loos, in 1970, described the clearest module of all: in layer 4 of mouse somatosensory cortex, cells cluster into discrete barrels, one barrel per facial whisker, so the animal's whisker pad is stamped into the tissue as a visible map.

The barrel is the strongest case for a genuine anatomical module because you can see it in a stained section without recording a single neuron.


11.2.2 Topographic maps and their computational rationale

A topographic map is an arrangement in which neighbouring points in the world are represented by neighbouring points in cortex.

The three classic examples are retinotopy in vision, where the retina is mapped onto visual cortex, tonotopy in hearing, where sound frequency is laid out along auditory cortex, and somatotopy in touch, where the body surface is laid out along the postcentral gyrus.

These maps are systematically distorted rather than faithful: the fovea, the high-resolution centre of the retina, and the fingertips and lips occupy grossly disproportionate cortical territory, because cortical area is allocated by receptor density and behavioural importance, not by physical size.

The standard computational rationale is wiring economy: neurons that must interact frequently, such as those comparing nearby points in an image, are placed close together, which shortens axons, saves metabolic energy and reduces conduction delay.

Christopher Cherniak, Dmitri Chklovskii and Alexei Koulakov developed this into quantitative wire-length minimisation arguments in the 1990s and 2000s, showing that observed map layouts and even ocular dominance stripe patterns are close to what minimal-wiring optimisation predicts.

The rationale is persuasive but not a proof of purpose: a map can arise as a by-product of how axons find their targets during development and still be metabolically convenient afterwards.


11.2.3 The column as a disputed unit

Fifty years after Mountcastle's discovery, Jonathan Horton and Daniel Adams published a review in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, in 2005, provocatively titled to make the point that the column may be a structure without a function.

Their objections were concrete.

The word column is used for at least half a dozen different things, from a 30-micrometre minicolumn to a millimetre-wide hypercolumn, so agreement about the column often conceals disagreement about what is being claimed.

Ocular dominance columns are absent in many primate species and even in some individual squirrel monkeys with otherwise normal vision, which is awkward for the claim that they are computationally necessary.

The underlying uniformity claim also came under fire: Alan Rockel, Roger Hiorns and Thomas Powell reported in 1980 that a vertical strip of cortex contains about 110 neurons in every area and species examined, and Mountcastle leaned on this in his 1997 synthesis, but later reanalyses, notably by Christine Collins and colleagues in 2010 and by Suzana Herculano-Houzel and colleagues, found the sampling arbitrary and the constancy not reproducible.

The fair summary is that vertical functional clustering is real and repeatedly observed, but the strong claim that the cortex is built from a single kind of repeating computational module remains unproven and is rejected by many anatomists.


11.2.4 Cortical areas, gradients, and the parcellation problem

An area, as opposed to a column, is a patch of cortex distinguished by its cell architecture, its connections, its function and its map, and Korbinian Brodmann's 1909 numbering of about 52 such patches is still in daily use.

The parcellation problem is the difficulty of drawing the boundaries objectively, because different criteria do not always agree and human brains differ individually.

The most influential modern attempt is by Matthew Glasser and colleagues in Nature in 2016, who used multi-modal magnetic resonance imaging from the Human Connectome Project, combining myelin content, cortical thickness, task activation and resting connectivity in 210 adults, and delineated 180 areas per hemisphere, 97 of them newly described.

A live dispute is whether areas are the right unit at all: boundaries in some regions are sharp, but elsewhere properties change smoothly, and gradient-based descriptions argue that a continuous coordinate system fits the data better than a mosaic of discrete tiles.

The pragmatic position now common in the field is that both are needed, with discrete areas where transitions are abrupt and gradients where they are not.


11.3 The canonical microcircuit

Having described layers and columns, we now ask what the local circuit inside a patch of cortex actually computes.

The canonical microcircuit is the proposal that a single stereotyped wiring diagram, repeated everywhere, is doing the work, with only the inputs and outputs differing between areas.

This is one of the most consequential ideas in systems neuroscience because it licenses generalising from a mouse whisker circuit to human reasoning.


11.3.1 The canonical circuit hypothesis and its evidence

Rodney Douglas, Kevan Martin and David Whitteridge proposed the canonical microcircuit in 1989, based on intracellular recordings and anatomy in cat visual cortex, and Douglas and Martin restated and extended it in a widely cited 2004 review.

Their central observations were that thalamic input accounts for only a small minority of the synapses onto layer 4 cells, often cited as under ten percent, that the overwhelming majority of synapses in cortex come from other cortical neurons, and that excitation and inhibition are tightly yoked so the circuit does not run away.

The supporting evidence is genuinely broad: the layer 4 to layer 2/3 to layer 5 excitatory motif has been confirmed with paired recordings and with optogenetics, the technique of making neurons controllable by light, in visual, somatosensory and auditory cortex of several species.

The evidence against universality is equally real: motor and prefrontal cortex are agranular or dysgranular, meaning they have little or no layer 4, so the canonical diagram cannot be applied there unmodified, and the connection probabilities that define the circuit vary substantially between areas.

The honest verdict is that the canonical circuit is a good first approximation and a productive scaffold, not a law.


11.3.2 Interneuron motifs and disinhibition

Interneurons are local inhibitory cells, using the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and although they make up only about twenty percent of cortical neurons they largely determine what the excitatory cells do.

Three genetically defined types account for most of them: parvalbumin (PV) cells, which target the cell body and axon of pyramidal cells and impose fast, powerful control on whether a spike is emitted; somatostatin (SST) cells, which target distant dendrites and gate which inputs a cell listens to; and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) cells, which are small, superficial, and preferentially inhibit SST cells.

That last connection produces the disinhibitory motif: when VIP cells fire they silence SST cells, which lifts inhibition from pyramidal dendrites and lets those cells respond more strongly.

The motif matters behaviourally because VIP cells are driven by locomotion, arousal, reward signals and top-down input from other cortical areas, so it provides a concrete mechanism by which attention or context can amplify a local circuit's output rather than adding to it directly, a finding developed by groups including those of Massimo Scanziani, Adam Kepecs, Hillel Adesnik and Christopher Moore from around 2013 onward.

Modelling work, for example by Hahn and colleagues in eLife in 2022, shows these mutually inhibitory motifs can act as switches, flipping a microcircuit between an SST-dominated inhibited state and a disinhibited state.


11.3.3 Recurrence and amplification

Recurrence means that cortical neurons mostly talk to each other rather than to their inputs, and it is the numerically dominant fact about cortical wiring.

Douglas, Christof Koch, Martin and colleagues showed in Science in 1995 that weak thalamic drive is amplified by this local excitatory feedback, so the cortex behaves like an amplifier whose gain is set by the network rather than by any single synapse.

The engineering problem is stability, since strong positive feedback invites runaway excitation and seizure, and the standard solution is balanced amplification, in which inhibition tracks excitation closely enough to keep firing proportional to stimulus strength; Mark Goldman and Brendan Murphy formalised this in 2009, and evidence for balanced amplification in primate cortex was reported by Sanzeni, Histed and colleagues in Neuron in 2023.

Recurrence also buys memory: if a subnetwork excites itself strongly enough, its activity can outlast the stimulus, which is the standard attractor account of persistent delay activity in prefrontal cortex during working memory, developed by Xiao-Jing Wang and others.

This is disputed at the level of individual trials, since some researchers argue that apparently persistent activity is really sequential or bursty when examined trial by trial rather than averaged.


11.3.4 Uniformity versus specialisation across cortex

Kenneth Harris and Gordon Shepherd, in Nature Neuroscience in 2015, framed the tension well with the phrase themes and variations: the cell classes, their gene expression, their intrinsic electrical properties and their broad wiring logic are strikingly similar across areas and species, while the quantitative details differ systematically.

Evidence for uniformity includes the near-identical repertoire of excitatory and inhibitory cell types found across cortical areas in large single-cell transcriptomic surveys from the Allen Institute, and the fact that developing cortex can be rewired: Mriganka Sur's experiments in ferrets in the late 1980s and 1990s routed retinal input into auditory cortex, which then developed orientation-selective cells and visual maps.

Evidence for specialisation includes the loss of layer 4 in motor and prefrontal cortex, the marked expansion of layer 2/3 and of the supragranular to infragranular ratio in primate association cortex, and the finding by human cortical circuit studies, such as the 2023 Science report of directed and largely acyclic connectivity in human layer 2 to 3, that human microcircuits are not simply scaled mouse microcircuits.

The reasonable synthesis is that cortex uses one basic recipe with area-specific parameter settings, and that debates about uniformity are usually really debates about how large a parameter change has to be before it counts as a different circuit.


11.4 Hierarchy and gradients

The final section moves up in scale, from the local circuit to the organisation of the whole sheet.

Two related claims are at stake: that cortical areas can be ordered into a hierarchy, and that the ordering is not a discrete ladder but a smooth gradient along which many properties change together.


11.4.1 Anatomical hierarchy from laminar connection patterns

The hierarchy of section 11.1.2 is built purely from anatomy: an area is higher than another if its input from that area arrives in layer 4 and its output to it avoids layer 4.

Felleman and Van Essen's 1991 ranking of the macaque visual system was the landmark, but it produced many ties and some inconsistencies, and the hierarchy it yields is not unique.

The quantitative successor, the fraction of supragranular labelled neurons developed by Kennedy, Knoblauch, Nikola Markov and colleagues from around 2014, assigns each area a continuous hierarchical distance instead of an integer level, and reveals that the cortical network is much denser than earlier tracing suggested, with roughly two thirds of possible area-to-area connections actually present.

That density matters conceptually: a hierarchy embedded in a nearly fully connected graph is a set of biases in a heterarchy, not a chain of command.


11.4.2 The sensory-to-association gradient

Helen Barbas's structural model, developed from the 1980s onward, proposes that the laminar pattern of a connection is predicted simply by the difference in cytoarchitecture, the layered cell structure, between the two areas.

Cortex ranges from agranular, lacking layer 4, through dysgranular, with a poorly formed layer 4, to granular, with a well-defined layer 4; connections from a less laminated area to a more laminated one terminate in the superficial layers, and connections in the reverse direction terminate in layer 4.

Marsel Mesulam's parallel scheme, articulated in 1998, arranges cortex from primary sensory through unimodal association, to heteromodal association, then paralimbic and limbic cortex, with information becoming progressively less tied to any single sense as one moves along it.

Barbas's model has the advantage that it predicts connection patterns from a single measurable variable, and it has recently been extended to thalamocortical connections in work published in 2025, though critics point out that it is descriptive rather than mechanistic and that its predictions and the Felleman and Van Essen hierarchy sometimes disagree.


11.4.3 Timescale, myelination, and receptor gradients

The striking modern finding is that many independent measurements vary together along the same sensory-to-association axis.
