John Murray, Xiao-Jing Wang and colleagues showed in Nature Neuroscience in 2014 that intrinsic timescale, how long a neuron's activity remains autocorrelated, increases systematically from sensory to association cortex, so early visual neurons forget within a fraction of a second while prefrontal neurons hold information for seconds.

Joshua Burt, Murray and colleagues showed in 2018 that the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted magnetic resonance signal, a non-invasive proxy for myelin content, decreases along the same axis, and that this myelin map correlates with gene expression, with dendritic spine counts on pyramidal cells, and with receptor densities.

The mechanistic story that ties these together is that association cortex has more excitatory synapses per neuron and more of the slow N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor relative to fast receptors, which lengthens integration time, and Burt and colleagues built large-scale models in which this single hierarchical parameter reproduces observed dynamics.

A caveat worth stating plainly is that T1-weighted over T2-weighted ratio is an indirect proxy and is influenced by iron and by cortical thickness as well as myelin, so it should be read as a hierarchy marker rather than a myelin measurement.


11.4.4 The principal gradient and the position of the default mode network

Daniel Margulies and colleagues, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2016, applied a dimensionality-reduction technique called diffusion embedding to resting-state functional connectivity and asked what single axis explains the most variance in how cortical regions connect.

The answer, now called the principal gradient, runs from primary sensory and motor cortex at one end to the default mode network (DMN) at the other, the DMN being the set of midline and lateral parietal and temporal regions that are most active when a person is not engaged in an external task.

Their striking geometric observation was that DMN regions sit at the maximum geodesic distance, measured along the cortical surface, from all primary sensory and motor landmarks, and are roughly equidistant from each of them.

The interpretation offered is functional: by being maximally removed from any single sensory input, the DMN can process information detached from immediate perception, which fits its association with memory, imagination, mentalising and self-referential thought.

Two honest qualifications: gradients are statistical decompositions of correlation data, so the first component is guaranteed to exist and its interpretation is not, and the relationship between the principal gradient and the anatomical hierarchies of the preceding sub-sections is a correlation rather than a demonstration that they are the same thing.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The cortex is a layered sheet in which a neuron's layer predicts its job: layer 4 receives, layer 2/3 associates and exports forward, layers 5 and 6 export downward and backward.

That laminar rule, formalised by Felleman and Van Essen in 1991 and quantified by Kennedy and colleagues, is what makes it possible to read a hierarchy off pure anatomy, and it is what predictive coding accounts such as Bastos and colleagues in 2012 reinterpret computationally, with the first strong human laminar evidence appearing only in 2024.

Vertical functional clustering is real and visible in barrels and orientation columns, but the strong claim that cortex is built from a single repeating column has been seriously challenged since Horton and Adams in 2005 and should not be treated as settled.

The canonical microcircuit is a productive first approximation whose value lies in recurrence and in tightly balanced inhibition, with interneuron motifs such as vasoactive intestinal peptide cells disinhibiting pyramidal dendrites supplying a mechanism for top-down modulation.

At the largest scale, timescale, myelin proxy, receptor density, cytoarchitecture and resting connectivity all vary along a single sensory-to-association axis whose far end is the default mode network, which is the strongest available evidence that the cortex's local wiring and its global organisation are two views of the same design.


CHAPTER 12. THE SUBCORTICAL ENGINES OF COGNITION (APPARATUS)


It is tempting to think that thinking happens in the cortex, the wrinkled outer sheet of the brain, and that everything underneath it is plumbing.

That picture is wrong, and this chapter is about why.

Beneath the cortex sit several large, highly organised structures - the thalamus, the basal ganglia, the cerebellum, the medial temporal lobe and amygdala, and the brainstem and hypothalamus - and each of them does computational work that cognition cannot do without.

They decide what reaches awareness, which action is released and which is held back, what is predicted next, what is remembered, how alert you are, and what you want in the first place.

The aim here is apparatus: to say what each engine is made of, what it computes, and what breaks when it fails.

By the end you should be able to read a sentence like "the mediodorsal thalamus supports prefrontal working memory" and know exactly what is being claimed.


12.1 The thalamus

The thalamus is a pair of egg-shaped masses of grey matter sitting near the centre of the brain, one in each hemisphere, roughly the size of a walnut half each.

Grey matter means tissue dense in nerve cell bodies, as opposed to white matter, which is mostly the insulated fibres that carry signals between them.

Almost everything that reaches the cortex from the body or from the outside world passes through the thalamus first, with the notable exception of smell.

The old textbook description called it a relay station, as though it were a telephone exchange that simply forwarded calls.

That description has been steadily dismantled since the 1990s, most forcefully by S. Murray Sherman and Ray Guillery, whose 2007 review carried the blunt title "The thalamus is more than just a relay".

The thalamus is better understood as a set of controlled gates, where a gate can be opened, narrowed, or shut according to what the rest of the brain is doing.

Anatomically the thalamus is divided into nuclei - clusters of neurons with shared connections and a shared job.

Each nucleus talks to a particular patch or patches of cortex, and receives a return projection from that same cortex, so the traffic is two-way and, in raw fibre count, the descending traffic from cortex to thalamus outnumbers the ascending traffic several times over.

That asymmetry is the single most important anatomical fact in this section: the cortex spends more wiring telling the thalamus what to do than the thalamus spends telling the cortex what is out there.


12.1.1 First-order and higher-order relays

Sherman and Guillery's central distinction is between first-order and higher-order thalamic nuclei.

A first-order nucleus receives its main driving input from outside the cortex - the lateral geniculate nucleus, for instance, receives its driving input from the retina and passes it to primary visual cortex, and so carries genuinely new sensory information into the cortical system for the first time.

A higher-order nucleus receives its main driving input from layer 5 of the cortex itself, and sends its output to another patch of cortex, forming a trans-thalamic route by which one cortical area speaks to another through the thalamus rather than by direct cortex-to-cortex fibres.

The distinction rests on separating driver inputs, which are few, large, powerful synapses that dictate what the target cell fires, from modulator inputs, which are numerous, small, and adjust the gain rather than the message.

Sherman and Guillery further noted that many of these driving axons are branches of fibres that also descend to motor structures, so what the thalamus forwards to cortex is often a copy of a motor instruction already issued - an efference copy, in the technical term, meaning an internal duplicate of an outgoing command.

If that is right, then a large part of what the cortex receives is not a report of the world but a report of what the brain has just decided to do about it, which is a substantially different claim about the architecture of cognition.

The driver-modulator framework is widely used but not universally accepted in its strong form, and the extent to which trans-thalamic routes carry information that direct cortico-cortical fibres do not is still an open empirical question.


12.1.2 The pulvinar and attentional routing

The pulvinar is the largest thalamic nucleus in humans and among the most expanded in primates relative to other mammals, and it is a higher-order nucleus by the definition just given, connected chiefly to visual and parietal cortex rather than to the eye.

The landmark demonstration of its function came from Yuri Saalmann, Mark Pinsk, Liang Wang, Xin Li and Sabine Kastner, reporting in Science in 2012 that in monkeys attending to one of two visual locations the pulvinar synchronised the activity of the two cortical areas that needed to exchange information.

Synchronisation here means that the rhythmic fluctuations in excitability of the two cortical populations were aligned in time, so that messages from one arrived when the other was most receptive - the neural equivalent of two people agreeing when to speak and when to listen.

Crucially the direction of influence ran from pulvinar to cortex, not merely the reverse, which is what licenses the word "regulates" rather than "reflects".

The functional summary is that the pulvinar does not itself see; it decides which cortical conversation gets bandwidth.

Damage to the human pulvinar is associated with neglect-like deficits, in which patients under-attend to the side of space opposite the lesion despite intact eyes and intact primary visual cortex.


12.1.3 The mediodorsal nucleus and prefrontal function

The mediodorsal nucleus is the thalamic partner of the prefrontal cortex, the front-most cortical region most associated with planning, rule-following, and the deliberate control of behaviour.

Their connection is reciprocal and dense, and the functional consequence is that damage to the mediodorsal nucleus produces deficits that look prefrontal: impaired working memory, meaning the ability to hold and manipulate information over seconds, and behavioural inflexibility, meaning difficulty abandoning a rule that has stopped paying off.

The interaction is demonstrably two-way; inactivating prefrontal cortex weakens working-memory-related signals in the mediodorsal nucleus, and inactivating the mediodorsal nucleus weakens those same signals in prefrontal cortex.

The most interesting modern proposal comes from work by Michael Halassa, Sébastien Parnaudeau and colleagues, who argue that the mediodorsal nucleus does not itself store the contents of working memory but sustains and amplifies the cortical representation of the current task rule, which is why its loss shows up most sharply when the cue is weak or ambiguous and when the animal must switch contexts rapidly.

That is a genuinely different job description from "relay": it makes the thalamus a maintainer of context rather than a carrier of content.

Restricted mediodorsal lesions in humans, which are rare, produce executive control deficits consistent with this account, and abnormalities in this circuit are among the more replicated findings in schizophrenia research.


12.1.4 The thalamic reticular nucleus as a gate

The thalamic reticular nucleus is a thin shell of inhibitory neurons wrapped around the outside of the thalamus like a net.

Inhibitory means its neurons release gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that reduces the firing of its targets, so this structure's only job is to turn other thalamic neurons down.

It is unusual in that it receives copies of both the ascending traffic from thalamus to cortex and the descending traffic from cortex to thalamus, but sends its own output only back into the thalamus - it listens to the conversation and can silence parts of it, without speaking to the cortex directly.

Francis Crick, in 1984, proposed the searchlight hypothesis: that this nucleus implements an internal attentional spotlight by selectively suppressing the thalamic channels that are not currently relevant, so that the surviving channel is effectively amplified by contrast.

Subsequent recordings have supported the core of the idea, showing that reticular neurons are modulated by attention and by conditioning, and recent work has refined it by identifying distinct inhibitory inputs, including one from the external globus pallidus and inhibitory connections within the nucleus itself, which appear to control the searchlight's overall intensity and its focus somewhat separately.

The same nucleus generates the sleep spindles of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep and is centrally implicated in absence seizures, which is a useful reminder that the machinery of attention and the machinery of consciousness-level state are not separable pieces of hardware.


12.2 The basal ganglia

The basal ganglia are a group of interconnected nuclei buried deep in each hemisphere: the striatum, which comprises the caudate nucleus and putamen and, ventrally, the nucleus accumbens; the globus pallidus, divided into internal and external segments; the subthalamic nucleus; and the substantia nigra, itself divided into a compact part that makes dopamine and a reticular part that is an output structure.

Their most famous clinical associations are movement disorders - Parkinson's disease, in which the dopamine-producing cells of the substantia nigra die and movement becomes slow and hard to initiate, and Huntington's disease, in which striatal neurons die and movement becomes excessive and involuntary.

But the same machinery that releases or withholds a movement also releases or withholds a thought, and that is why the basal ganglia belong in a book about cognition.

The defining feature of the basal ganglia output is that it is tonically inhibitory: the output nuclei fire constantly, holding the thalamus and therefore the cortex under a permanent brake.

Behaviour is produced not by pushing but by releasing the brake selectively - by disinhibition, meaning the inhibition of an inhibitor, which nets out as permission.


12.2.1 Direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways

Three routes run through the basal ganglia from cortex to output.

• The direct pathway runs from cortex to striatal neurons carrying the D1 dopamine receptor, then straight to the output nuclei, which it inhibits; because the output nuclei were themselves inhibiting the thalamus, inhibiting them releases the thalamus, so the direct pathway is conventionally the "go" route.

• The indirect pathway runs from cortex to striatal neurons carrying the D2 dopamine receptor, then to the external globus pallidus, then to the subthalamic nucleus, and only then to the output nuclei, which it excites; the net effect is more braking, so this is conventionally the "no-go" route.

• The hyperdirect pathway, described in detail by Atsushi Nambu and colleagues in the early 2000s, runs from cortex straight to the subthalamic nucleus, bypassing the striatum entirely; because it is short it arrives first, and it broadly excites the output nuclei, so its effect is a rapid global brake.

A natural reading of the three is temporal: the hyperdirect pathway stops everything, the direct pathway then releases the one action selected, and the indirect pathway suppresses the competitors.

The hyperdirect route is the anatomical basis of the widely studied stopping network involving the right inferior frontal gyrus and the pre-supplementary motor area, which is engaged when a person cancels an action already under way.

The simple go/no-go opposition is, however, contested.

Simultaneous recordings show both pathways active together at movement onset rather than in opposition, and a 2023 study in eLife by Cui and colleagues reported that direct-pathway activation scaled behaviour roughly linearly while indirect-pathway activation had a non-linear, inverted-U effect depending on network state, leading the authors to propose a centre-surround-context model instead.

The honest summary for a learner is that the anatomy of the three pathways is solid and the strict go/no-go interpretation of them is a useful first approximation that the field is actively revising.


12.2.2 Parallel cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops: motor, oculomotor, associative, limbic

Garrett Alexander, Mahlon DeLong and Peter Strick, in a 1986 review in Annual Review of Neuroscience, established the organising principle that the basal ganglia are not one circuit but several structurally identical circuits running side by side.

Each loop starts in a particular region of cortex, projects to a particular territory of striatum, passes through pallidum and thalamus, and returns to approximately the region of cortex where it started - a closed loop.

The loops are conventionally named for their cortical origin: a motor loop from motor and premotor cortex through the putamen; an oculomotor loop from the frontal eye fields and supplementary eye fields through the body of the caudate; an associative or prefrontal loop from dorsolateral prefrontal cortex through the head of the caudate; and a limbic loop from orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex through the nucleus accumbens.

The theoretical payoff is large: if the circuitry is the same in each loop, then whatever computation the basal ganglia perform on movement, they perform the same computation on eye position, on abstract rules, and on motivation.

That is the strongest single argument that action selection and thought selection are the same operation applied to different content.

The strict parallel-and-segregated picture has been qualified since; human diffusion imaging and primate tracing both show substantial overlap and cross-talk between loops, and spiralling striato-nigro-striatal connections allow information to migrate from limbic toward motor territories, which is one leading account of how a motivated choice becomes an entrenched habit and, in addiction, a compulsion.


12.2.3 Action selection, gating of working memory, and habit formation

The most durable functional theory of the basal ganglia is that they solve the selection problem: many candidate actions compete, only one can have the motor apparatus, and the tonic brake plus selective disinhibition is a clean mechanism for choosing one and suppressing the rest.

Randall O'Reilly and Michael Frank extended this idea to thought in their prefrontal-basal-ganglia working memory model, developed from 2001 onward, proposing that the same disinhibitory gate that releases a movement also decides when a prefrontal working memory is allowed to be updated.

The problem this solves is real and specific: a memory system needs to be robust against distraction, which argues for a closed gate, but also needs to be updated the instant something important happens, which argues for an open one, and a learned gate resolves the conflict by opening only for inputs that experience has marked as worth storing.

Separately, Henry Yin and Barbara Knowlton, in a 2006 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, established the distinction between goal-directed action, which depends on the dorsomedial striatum (the caudate in primates) and remains sensitive to whether the outcome is still wanted, and habit, which depends on the dorsolateral striatum (the putamen) and continues to be performed even when the outcome has been devalued.

The evidence is a double dissociation in rodents: lesioning the dorsolateral striatum keeps overtrained behaviour goal-directed, while lesioning the dorsomedial striatum pushes behaviour into habit prematurely.

Habit, on this account, is not a weaker form of intention but a different circuit taking over, which is why habits survive a change of mind.


12.2.4 Dopaminergic learning within the striatum

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter released into the striatum by neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta and the neighbouring ventral tegmental area.

Wolfram Schultz and colleagues, in a body of work through the 1990s culminating in the influential 1997 paper with Peter Dayan and Read Montague, showed that these neurons do not signal reward as such but reward prediction error - the difference between the reward received and the reward expected.

The signature is precise: a burst of firing to an unexpected reward, no change to a fully predicted one, and a dip below baseline when an expected reward fails to arrive, and the burst migrates backwards in time from the reward to the earliest cue that predicts it.

This maps directly onto the temporal-difference learning rule of computational reinforcement learning, which is one of the cleanest correspondences between a theory and a cell type in all of neuroscience.

The mechanism by which the signal changes behaviour is a three-factor plasticity rule: a corticostriatal synapse is strengthened or weakened depending on presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity, and the level of dopamine at that moment, so dopamine acts as a global "that worked" or "that did not" stamp on whatever synapses were just active.

Because the D1 receptors of the direct pathway and the D2 receptors of the indirect pathway respond to dopamine in opposite directions, a burst tends to strengthen the go route while a dip tends to strengthen the no-go route, giving the system separate machinery for learning from success and from failure - a prediction Frank and colleagues tested in Parkinson's patients on and off medication, finding the expected shift between learning from positive and negative feedback.

More recent work has complicated the single-signal picture, showing regional heterogeneity in dopamine signals, including novelty and salience responses that are not prediction errors, so reward prediction error is best described as the dominant but not the only thing dopamine neurons report.


12.3 The cerebellum

The cerebellum, Latin for "little brain", sits beneath the back of the cerebral hemispheres.

It occupies about a tenth of the brain's volume but contains roughly four fifths of its neurons, an imbalance produced by the enormous number of tiny granule cells packed into its cortex.

For most of the twentieth century it was regarded as purely a motor organ, on the reasonable grounds that damaging it makes movement clumsy and inaccurate - ataxia, meaning uncoordinated movement, with dysmetria, meaning movements that overshoot or undershoot their target.

The modern view is that the cerebellum performs one operation, and that this operation is applied to motor and non-motor material alike depending on which cortical area a given cerebellar region is looped with.


12.3.1 The uniform cerebellar microcircuit and supervised learning

The cerebellar cortex is startlingly uniform: the same small cast of cell types repeats in the same arrangement everywhere, which is what makes a single computational description plausible.

Input arrives by two routes.

• Mossy fibres, carrying information from the spinal cord, brainstem, and via the pontine nuclei from the entire cerebral cortex, synapse onto granule cells, which are extremely numerous and each sample only a handful of mossy fibres; their axons rise and split into parallel fibres that run for millimetres across the sheet, contacting hundreds of thousands of Purkinje cells.

• Climbing fibres, arising exclusively from the inferior olive in the brainstem, wrap around a single Purkinje cell each with an overwhelmingly powerful synapse, and fire rarely, at about one spike per second.

The Purkinje cell is the sole output of the cerebellar cortex and is inhibitory, projecting to the deep cerebellar nuclei which in turn project out to thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord.

David Marr in 1969, James Albus in 1971, and Masao Ito from 1970 independently proposed that this is a supervised learning machine: the granule cell layer expands the input into a very high-dimensional, sparse code in which almost any two situations are distinguishable, and the climbing fibre delivers a teaching signal that adjusts the strength of the parallel fibre synapses that were active just before it fired.

Ito's laboratory subsequently found the predicted plasticity experimentally in the form of long-term depression, a lasting weakening of parallel fibre synapses when they are co-activated with the climbing fibre, and optogenetic work in the 2010s and 2020s has confirmed that climbing fibre activity is both necessary and sufficient as an instructive signal for cerebellar learning.

Marr, Albus and Ito differed in important respects - Marr predicted strengthening where Albus and Ito predicted weakening, and they disagreed about whether the climbing fibre carries a teacher or an error - and the field's fiftieth-anniversary reviews around 2020 concluded that the framework is essentially correct while the single-plasticity-site version is too simple, since plasticity is now known to occur at many cerebellar synapses at once.


12.3.2 Internal models and forward prediction

An internal model is a neural circuit that mimics some part of the world well enough to predict its behaviour.

A forward model in particular takes a copy of a command you have just issued and predicts what the consequence will be, before the sensory feedback arrives.

This is not a luxury: sensory feedback takes on the order of a hundred milliseconds to return, and any controller relying on feedback alone at that delay oscillates and becomes unstable, which is precisely what cerebellar tremor looks like.

Daniel Wolpert, Chris Miall and Masao Ito, in an influential 1998 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences and subsequent work, argued that the cerebellum is where such models are learned and stored, and that the climbing fibre error signal is exactly the training signal a forward model requires.

The generalisation to cognition is straightforward on this account: if the cerebellum can learn to predict the consequence of an arm movement, the identical circuit fed by prefrontal or temporal cortex can learn to predict the next word in a sentence or the next move of a social partner.

Evidence for the cognitive extension includes cerebellar activation when a semantic expectation is violated, reported by Moberget, Ivry and colleagues in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2014, and 2025 work in ataxia patients showing degraded responses to high-level cognitive violations of expectation.

The theory is elegant and its motor version is well supported; its cognitive version is plausible, actively researched, and not yet settled.


12.3.3 The cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome

The decisive clinical evidence that the cerebellum is not merely motor came from Jeremy Schmahmann and Janet Sherman, who described twenty patients with focal cerebellar damage in Brain in 1998.

They found a consistent pattern that they named the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, with four components: impaired executive function, meaning planning, set-shifting, verbal fluency and working memory; impaired visuospatial cognition; personality change with flattened affect or disinhibited behaviour; and language disturbance including agrammatism and abnormal prosody, the melody and stress of speech.

Damage to the posterior lobe and the vermis, the midline strip, produced the syndrome, while damage to the anterior lobe produced mainly motor signs, giving a topographic dissociation within the cerebellum itself.

Schmahmann's interpretation, published the same year as the dysmetria of thought hypothesis, is that the cerebellum applies one operation - keeping a process on target around a set point - to whatever it is connected to, so that damage produces overshoot and inconsistency in thought and emotion just as it does in reaching.

The syndrome is now well replicated; a 2019 meta-analysis confirmed the executive and language findings robustly, with visuospatial and affective findings more variable, and Hoche, Guell, Vangel, Sherman and Schmahmann published a dedicated bedside scale for it in Brain in 2018.

In children, resection of a posterior fossa tumour can produce a severe transient form including complete mutism, which is a striking demonstration that a structure long called motor is required for speaking at all.


12.3.4 Cerebellar contributions to language, timing, and social cognition

Timing is the oldest non-motor claim: Richard Ivry and Steven Keele reported in 1988 that patients with cerebellar lesions were impaired at judging the duration of tones as well as at producing timed taps, arguing for a cerebellar clock operating in the sub-second range.

The claim has been refined rather than overturned; Spencer and Ivry's later work distinguishes event timing, in which each interval is explicitly represented and which is cerebellum-dependent, from emergent timing, which arises from the dynamics of a continuous movement and which is not, and cerebellar patients are selectively impaired on the former.

For language, functional imaging consistently implicates the right cerebellar hemisphere - crossed, because cerebellar connections to cortex are contralateral - in verb generation, verbal fluency, and prediction of upcoming words, consistent with the forward-model account.

For social cognition, Frank Van Overwalle and colleagues meta-analysed over 350 functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies in NeuroImage in 2013, finding reliable cerebellar involvement in both understanding others' actions and inferring others' beliefs and traits, with the posterior region Crus II most strongly implicated in abstract mentalising; a 2020 consensus paper by Van Overwalle and many co-authors summarises the state of the field.

Two cautions belong here.

The cerebellum's social and linguistic activations may reflect domain-general sequencing and executive support rather than anything socially specific, a possibility Van Overwalle himself raises, and the effect sizes of cerebellar cognitive deficits are generally modest compared with cortical lesions of similar volume, which is consistent with a modulatory rather than a constitutive role.


12.4 The medial temporal lobe and the amygdala

The medial temporal lobe is the inner surface of the temporal lobe, containing the hippocampus and the cortical regions immediately surrounding it, together with the amygdala at its front end.

Its importance to cognition was established by a single patient, Henry Molaison, known during his life as H.M., whose medial temporal lobes were removed bilaterally in 1953 to control epilepsy and who was thereafter unable to form new conscious memories while retaining intelligence, language, and the ability to learn motor skills he could not remember practising - documented by William Scoville and Brenda Milner in 1957.

That dissociation is the founding evidence that memory is not one faculty.


12.4.1 Hippocampal subfields and the trisynaptic circuit

The hippocampus is a curved structure, named for its resemblance to a seahorse, divided into subfields: the dentate gyrus and the cornu ammonis fields CA3 and CA1, with CA2 between them, and the subiculum at the exit.

The classical trisynaptic circuit is three synapses in series: entorhinal cortex to dentate gyrus via the perforant path; dentate gyrus to CA3 via the mossy fibres; CA3 to CA1 via the Schaffer collaterals, with CA1 then projecting to subiculum and back to entorhinal cortex.

Each stage has a proposed computation.

• The dentate gyrus receives a large input and projects sparsely and powerfully to CA3, which is thought to implement pattern separation - making similar inputs into dissimilar representations, so that today's parking spot does not overwrite yesterday's.

• CA3 is unusual in that its neurons synapse heavily onto each other, forming a recurrent or auto-associative network, which is thought to implement pattern completion - retrieving a whole memory from a fragmentary cue.

• CA1 compares the CA3 output with the direct entorhinal input and functions as a comparator and as the main output stage, and human imaging finds it biased toward completion rather than separation.

Human high-resolution fMRI supports the separation/completion division of labour, with Bakker, Kirwan, Miller and Stark reporting the key demonstration in Science in 2008, though the mapping is not perfectly clean: recent work suggests the dentate gyrus and proximal CA3 act together as a separating unit while distal CA3 does the completing.

Long-term potentiation, the lasting strengthening of a synapse after high-frequency use, was first demonstrated in this circuit by Terje Lømo and Tim Bliss in 1973, and remains the leading cellular candidate for how memories are stored.


12.4.2 Entorhinal, perirhinal, and parahippocampal cortices

The hippocampus does not talk to the neocortex directly; nearly everything passes through the entorhinal cortex, which is fed in turn by the perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices.

The division of labour is broadly by content: the perirhinal cortex handles information about objects - what a thing is - and feeds the lateral entorhinal cortex, while the parahippocampal cortex handles spatial and contextual information - where you are - and feeds the medial entorhinal cortex.

This anatomy underwrites the dual-process account of recognition memory, in which perirhinal cortex supports familiarity, the sense that something has been encountered before without any accompanying detail, and the hippocampal system supports recollection, the retrieval of the episode itself.

The medial entorhinal cortex contains grid cells, discovered by Torkel Hafting, Marianne Fyhn, Sturla Molden, May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser in 2005, which fire whenever the animal occupies any vertex of a regular triangular lattice tiling the environment, and whose spacing increases systematically from the dorsal to the ventral end of the structure.

Grid cells, together with the place cells John O'Keefe discovered in the hippocampus in 1971, earned O'Keefe and the Mosers the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and they are the clearest evidence that the brain constructs a metric coordinate system rather than merely a list of landmarks.

Entorhinal cortex is also where the tau pathology of Alzheimer's disease first appears, which is why disorientation and loss of recent memory are the earliest symptoms.


12.4.3 The amygdala nuclei and valence processing

The amygdala is an almond-shaped cluster of about thirteen nuclei sitting just in front of the hippocampus, and its nuclei have quite different jobs.

The basolateral complex is cortex-like in its cell types and connections; it receives detailed sensory and cortical input and is where stimulus-value associations are formed, which is why lesioning it abolishes the learning of fear to a tone paired with shock.

The central nucleus is striatum-like and functions as the output stage, projecting to the hypothalamus and brainstem to produce the components of an emotional response - freezing via the periaqueductal grey, blood pressure changes via the medulla, stress hormone release via the hypothalamus - a circuit dissection worked out largely by Joseph LeDoux and colleagues from the 1980s onward.

Valence, meaning whether something is good or bad, is represented within the basolateral amygdala by largely non-overlapping populations of neurons that are anatomically intermingled but project to different targets: work from Kay Tye's laboratory and others has shown that positive-valence cells project preferentially to the nucleus accumbens and negative-valence cells to the central amygdala, and that optogenetically driving one population or the other produces approach or avoidance respectively.

The amygdala is not a fear centre, a description the field has largely abandoned; it responds to appetitive stimuli, to novelty, and to ambiguity, and LeDoux has argued forcefully that it produces defensive responses rather than the conscious feeling of fear, which he attributes to cortical circuits - a position not universally shared, with Lisa Feldman Barrett arguing for a still more distributed and constructed account of emotion and other researchers defending a more direct amygdala contribution to feeling.

Patient S.M., who has bilateral amygdala calcification from Urbach-Wiethe disease, shows the strongest human evidence: she fails to recognise fear in faces and reports no fear of snakes or haunted houses, yet panics when inhaling carbon dioxide, which shows that at least one route to felt fear bypasses the amygdala entirely.


12.4.4 The extended hippocampal system and the Papez circuit

James Papez proposed in 1937 a closed circuit running from hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus, then by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nuclei, then to the cingulate cortex, and back to the hippocampus.

He proposed it as the substrate of emotion, which turned out to be largely wrong; the circuit's real business is memory.

John Aggleton and Malcolm Brown, in a 1999 Behavioral and Brain Sciences paper, reinterpreted it as the extended hippocampal system and argued that this whole loop, not the hippocampus alone, supports recollection, while familiarity depends on the separate perirhinal-and-mediodorsal-thalamus route.

The clinical evidence is Korsakoff's syndrome, a dense amnesia caused by thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholism, in which the damage is not hippocampal at all but falls on the mammillary bodies and anterior and mediodorsal thalamus - a finding that is difficult to explain unless these structures are functionally part of the memory system rather than incidental to it.

Rodent work confirms it directly: Aggleton's group showed in eLife in 2013 that cutting the mammillothalamic tract impairs memory as severely as removing the mammillary bodies, isolating the critical link.

The strictly serial version of Papez's loop is now questioned - a 2022 review argued explicitly that it is time to retire the serial circuit in favour of parallel interacting pathways - but the involvement of these diencephalic structures in episodic memory is not in doubt.


12.5 The brainstem and hypothalamus

The structures in this final section are the smallest and the oldest, and they are the ones that determine whether the rest of the machinery runs at all.

The brainstem is the stalk connecting the brain to the spinal cord; the hypothalamus is a small region beneath the thalamus that regulates the body's internal state.

Neither is usually described as cognitive, and both set the conditions under which cognition occurs.


12.5.1 Ascending arousal systems

A set of small nuclei in the brainstem and basal forebrain send diffuse projections upward to almost the entire brain, each releasing a single neuromodulator - a chemical that does not carry a specific message but changes how the receiving circuits behave.

• The locus coeruleus, a tiny bilateral nucleus in the pons of about fifteen thousand neurons per side in humans, supplies essentially all the noradrenaline of the forebrain; it fires fastest during alert wakefulness and falls silent during rapid-eye-movement sleep, and Gary Aston-Jones and Jonathan Cohen's 2005 adaptive gain theory proposes that its tonic firing rate trades off exploitation of the current task against exploration of alternatives.

• The dorsal and median raphe nuclei supply serotonin, implicated in mood, patience, and the willingness to wait for delayed reward.

• The basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei supply acetylcholine to cortex and hippocampus, and are required for the encoding of new memories and for sustained attention; their degeneration is a feature of Alzheimer's disease and the rationale for cholinesterase-inhibitor drugs.

• The ventral tegmental area supplies dopamine to prefrontal and limbic targets, as discussed above.

The nineteenth-century and mid-twentieth-century notion of a diffuse ascending reticular activating system, following Moruzzi and Magoun's 1949 demonstration that stimulating the brainstem reticular formation woke a sleeping animal, has been substantially revised: Clifford Saper and colleagues have shown that arousal depends on specific identifiable cell groups, chiefly the parabrachial nucleus and basal forebrain rather than an undifferentiated reticular core, and that the classical dorsal route through non-specific thalamus is less critical than the ventral route.

The practical significance is that these small nuclei are the reason attention, memory and mood are chemically manipulable at all.


12.5.2 Superior colliculus and orienting

The superior colliculus is a layered structure on the roof of the midbrain, present in essentially all vertebrates, where it is the principal visual centre in animals without a large cortex.

Its superficial layers are visual; its intermediate and deep layers contain a map of space in which visual, auditory and somatosensory inputs are aligned, so a location is represented the same way whichever sense reported it.

Its output drives saccades, the rapid eye movements by which gaze jumps from one point to another, and head and body orienting, and it does so through a topographic code in which the site of activity specifies the direction and size of the movement.

It is best understood as a priority map: a representation of where in space is currently worth attending to, combining physical salience with behavioural relevance.

Crucially, its activity is tied to covert attention - attending to a location without looking at it - as well as to overt movement; Richard Krauzlis and colleagues showed that reversibly inactivating the superior colliculus impairs attentional selection even when no eye movement is made, and a 2018 comparison by Krauzlis's group found that the superior colliculus and the frontal eye fields contribute in dissociable ways.

The superior colliculus also supports blindsight, the ability of patients with destroyed primary visual cortex to respond above chance to stimuli they report not seeing, which is direct evidence that a subcortical structure can guide behaviour without conscious vision.


12.5.3 Periaqueductal grey and defensive states

The periaqueductal grey is a column of neurons surrounding the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain, and it is the final common path for defensive behaviour and for the brain's own pain-suppression system.

It is organised into longitudinal columns with distinct functions: the ventrolateral column produces freezing and quiescence, the lateral and dorsolateral columns produce flight and active defence, and stimulating them in humans during neurosurgery produces intense unprovoked feelings of terror or impending doom.

The organising concept is predatory imminence, a framework from Robert and Caroline Fanselow's work in which defence is not one response but a graded series - pre-encounter wariness, post-encounter freezing, and circa-strike flight or fight - selected by how close the threat is, and mapping onto anxiety, fear and panic respectively.

Dean Mobbs and colleagues demonstrated the human version in Science in 2007 using a virtual predator in the scanner: as the threat approached, activity shifted from ventromedial prefrontal cortex to the periaqueductal grey, and the degree of that shift predicted how badly the subject performed.

Recent optogenetic work has refined the strict column-to-behaviour mapping, finding genetically defined subpopulations that cut across columns, so the columnar scheme is a good approximation rather than a strict rule.

The cognitive relevance is direct: when the periaqueductal grey takes over, deliberative prefrontal control is demonstrably reduced, which is a mechanistic account of why people think badly under acute threat.


12.5.4 Hypothalamic drives as the boundary condition on cognition

The hypothalamus weighs about four grams and regulates feeding, drinking, temperature, sleep, circadian timing, reproduction, aggression, and the hormonal stress response, mostly through small nuclei with dedicated jobs and through control of the pituitary gland.

Its relevance to cognition is that it sets the value of everything: a cue predicting food is worth attending to when hungry and not when sated, and the hypothalamus is where that state is computed.

The clearest modern example is the agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons of the arcuate nucleus, which are activated by energy deficit and whose artificial activation in a sated mouse produces immediate voracious eating, and whose silencing in a starving mouse stops it.

These neurons are not simple homeostatic sensors: they fall silent within seconds of the animal merely seeing food, long before any calorie is absorbed, which has led to an allostatic reinterpretation in which they predict and pre-empt energy demand rather than merely reporting current deficit - allostasis meaning stability achieved through anticipatory change rather than through correction after the fact.

They also project into motivational circuitry and modulate dopamine release in the striatum, which is the concrete mechanism by which a bodily state reaches into the machinery of choice described earlier in this chapter.

The general principle is that cognition does not float free of the body; the hypothalamus supplies the objective function, and the cortical machinery is in the business of satisfying it.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The subcortical structures are not support staff for the cortex; each performs a distinct computation that cognition requires, and in several cases the cortex cannot do the job without them.

The thalamus is a controlled gate rather than a relay, with the pulvinar routing bandwidth between cortical areas, the mediodorsal nucleus sustaining prefrontal task context, and the reticular nucleus implementing selective suppression.

The basal ganglia solve selection by holding a tonic brake and releasing it selectively, and because the same circuit is repeated in parallel loops, the selection of an action, a saccade, a rule and a motive are the same operation on different content, tuned by dopaminergic prediction errors.

The cerebellum runs one uniform supervised-learning microcircuit that builds forward models, and the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome is the clinical proof that it applies that operation to thought and affect as well as to movement.

The medial temporal lobe supplies pattern separation and completion for episodic memory through an extended circuit that includes diencephalic structures, and the amygdala assigns valence through intermingled but separately projecting populations.

The brainstem and hypothalamus set arousal, orienting, defensive state and drive, which means they determine the conditions under which any of the above operates and supply the values that cognition exists to serve.


CHAPTER 13. THE CONNECTOME AND LARGE-SCALE ORGANISATION (APPARATUS)


A brain is not a bag of neurons.

It is a wiring diagram, and the pattern of the wiring is a large part of what the brain does.

The word connectome means the complete map of connections in a nervous system, in the same way that the word genome means the complete sequence of an organism's deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecule that carries hereditary instructions.

This chapter explains how such maps are made, at what scales, what they show about the highways of the human brain, which large-scale networks emerge from them, and which organising principles those networks obey.

It also explains, honestly, where the methods fail - because a map you cannot trust is worse than no map at all.

This is an apparatus chapter: its job is to give you the instruments and vocabulary that later chapters about memory, attention, and language will lean on.


13.1 Levels of connectomics

Connectomics is not one enterprise but three, working at three different magnifications.

At the finest scale you can trace every individual synapse, which is the microscopic junction where one neuron passes a chemical or electrical signal to another.

At an intermediate scale you can trace bundles of axons - an axon is the long output fibre of a neuron - running between named brain regions.

At the coarsest scale you can estimate, in a living human being inside a scanner, which large regions are connected to which.

Each scale answers different questions, and each buys its coverage with a loss of resolution.

A rule worth carrying through the chapter: the more of a brain you can see, the less of its detail you can see, and the human brain is currently visible only at the coarsest of the three scales.


13.1.1 Synaptic-resolution reconstruction: Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, the MICrONS cubic-millimetre volume

Synaptic-resolution connectomics means slicing tissue into sections thinner than a wavelength of light, imaging them with an electron microscope, and then reconstructing every neuron and every synapse in three dimensions.

The founding achievement is the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, whose nervous system John White, Eileen Southgate, Nichol Thomson and Sydney Brenner reconstructed by hand and published in 1986: 302 neurons in the hermaphrodite and roughly 7,000 chemical and electrical connections between them.

That work took more than a decade, and it stood almost alone for thirty years, until Steven Cook and colleagues published complete connectomes of both sexes in Nature in 2019, adding the 385-neuron male and quantifying connection strengths from sensory input all the way to muscle output.

The scale jumped enormously in October 2024, when the FlyWire consortium published in Nature a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit fly brain - 139,255 neurons and roughly 50 million chemical synapses - with companion work by Philipp Schlegel and colleagues annotating over 8,000 cell types, of which about 4,581 had never been described before.

This matters because the fly is the first animal that can walk, see, and learn whose whole brain has been mapped synapse by synapse.

For mammals, the current landmark is the MICrONS project, published across a set of Nature papers in April 2025, which reconstructed roughly one cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex: about 200,000 cells, some 84,000 neurons, and around 524 million synapses, in tissue where the activity of about 75,000 of those neurons had first been recorded in the awake animal.

That last point is the important one - MICrONS is a functional connectome, meaning the researchers knew what many of the neurons did before they cut the tissue, and could therefore ask whether wiring predicts function.

It does: neurons with similar visual response preferences connect to each other preferentially, a "like-to-like" rule that holds within and across cortical areas.

Keep the scale in view, though - one cubic millimetre is roughly a five-hundred-thousandth of a mouse brain, and a whole human brain at this resolution remains far out of reach.


13.1.2 Mesoscale tracer connectomes in mouse and macaque

The mesoscale sits between single synapses and whole lobes: it asks which region projects to which region, and how strongly.

The classic method is anatomical tracing, in which a substance is injected into one brain region and then transported along axons, so that after some days the researcher can see where the fibres from that region terminate.

Seung Wook Oh and colleagues used this approach at industrial scale for the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, published in Nature in 2014, injecting a virus that makes neurons produce a green fluorescent protein and then imaging the whole brain with automated serial two-photon tomography, yielding a directed, weighted map across nearly 300 mouse brain structures.

For the monkey, no single laboratory did the equivalent; instead the CoCoMac database (Collation of Connectivity data on the Macaque brain) aggregated results from several hundred published tracer studies into a common atlas, and later systematic retrograde-tracing campaigns by Henry Kennedy, Kenneth Knoblauch and colleagues added quantitative connection weights.

Two robust facts came out of this work: cortico-cortical connection strengths span roughly five orders of magnitude, and the cortex is far denser than earlier qualitative maps suggested, with a substantial fraction of all possible area-to-area connections actually present.

Mesoscale tracer data are the gold standard against which human imaging methods are validated, because the tracer follows real axons and knows which direction they run.


13.1.3 Macroscale human connectomes from diffusion imaging

In a living human being you cannot inject tracers, so the field relies on diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (diffusion MRI), a scanning method that measures how water molecules drift within tissue.

Water diffuses more freely along the length of an axon bundle than across it, because the fatty myelin sheaths that insulate axons act as barriers, so the direction of easiest diffusion in each small volume of tissue indicates the local fibre orientation.

Tractography is the computational step that stitches those local orientations into long streamlines, which are then interpreted as white matter pathways.

The Human Connectome Project, launched by the United States National Institutes of Health in 2010 and led by groups at Washington University, the University of Minnesota and the University of Oxford, scanned around 1,200 healthy young adults with purpose-built high-gradient scanners and released the data publicly, which made macroscale connectomics a mass discipline.

The output is typically a connectivity matrix: a grid in which every row and column is a brain region and each cell holds an estimate of how strongly those two regions are connected.

Be clear about what that number is, though - it is a count of reconstructed streamlines, not a count of axons, and it carries no information about direction of signal flow.


13.1.4 Functional and effective connectomes

Structural connectivity is about wires; functional connectivity is about correlation.

Functional connectivity is defined as the statistical dependence between the activity time courses of two brain regions, most often measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, an indirect index of local neural activity carried by changes in blood flow and oxygenation.

Two regions can be functionally connected without being directly wired together, because a third region may drive them both, so functional connectivity is a description of coordination rather than a claim about anatomy.

Effective connectivity goes further and tries to estimate directed causal influence - who is driving whom - most prominently through dynamic causal modelling (DCM), introduced by Karl Friston, Lee Harrison and Will Penny in 2003 and extended to resting-state data as spectral DCM around 2014.

The price of that ambition is that effective connectivity is model-based: you must specify a candidate architecture, and the method tells you which of your candidates fits best, not what the truth is.

A practical caution: functional connectivity estimates are strongly contaminated by head motion and by physiological noise from breathing and heartbeat, a problem documented forcefully by Jonathan Power and colleagues in 2012, and much of the methods literature since then has been a running argument about how to clean the data without scrubbing away the signal.


13.2 Major white matter tracts

White matter is the tissue made of myelinated axons, so called because myelin is pale; grey matter, by contrast, is where the cell bodies and synapses sit.

If grey matter is where computation happens, white matter is the cabling that lets distant computations talk.

The tracts below are the ones a beginner needs by name, because damage to them produces recognisable and instructive deficits.

Two naming conventions help: a fasciculus is simply a bundle, and association tracts link regions within one hemisphere while commissural tracts cross between hemispheres.


13.2.1 Arcuate, superior longitudinal, inferior fronto-occipital, uncinate

The arcuate fasciculus arches from the temporal lobe up and around into the frontal lobe, and in the classical model it links the posterior language comprehension region (Wernicke's area) to the anterior speech production region (Broca's area).

It belongs to the dorsal language stream, the route thought to map sound onto articulation, and its most cited clinical association is with the ability to repeat spoken words.

The superior longitudinal fasciculus is the larger frontoparietal system of which the arcuate is often treated as a component, and it is usually divided into three branches, with the third branch (SLF III) linked to speech perception and articulation and the upper branches linked to spatial attention - the right-hemisphere SLF is repeatedly implicated in hemispatial neglect, the syndrome in which a patient ignores one side of space.

The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus is the long ventral pathway running from occipital and posterior temporal cortex to the frontal lobe, and it is widely regarded as the backbone of semantic processing, meaning the retrieval of word and object meaning; intraoperative electrical stimulation of it during awake brain surgery, work associated with Hugues Duffau, reliably produces semantic errors.

Note a genuine dispute here: some anatomists question whether the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus exists as a distinct tract in monkeys, and a 2025 review in Brain treats its phylogenetic status as unresolved even while accepting its functional importance in humans.

The uncinate fasciculus is a hook-shaped bundle joining the anterior temporal lobe to orbital and inferior frontal cortex, and it is associated with proper-name retrieval, semantic association, and the emotional-evaluative side of memory.


13.2.2 Cingulum, fornix, corpus callosum

The cingulum bundle runs like a near-complete ring above the corpus callosum, from orbital frontal cortex backward along the cingulate gyrus and then down into the temporal lobe, linking frontal, parietal, and medial temporal sites and threading subcortical inputs into that circuit.

John Aggleton and colleagues, in a 2018 review, argued that the cingulum is better understood as several parallel subsystems than as one cable, which is why its damage has been reported in conditions as different as depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Alzheimer's disease.

The fornix is the principal output pathway of the hippocampus, the seahorse-shaped structure critical for forming new episodic memories, carrying its fibres forward to the mammillary bodies and the anterior thalamic nuclei; fornix damage produces amnesia, and thinning of the fornix is among the earliest structural markers of memory decline in ageing.

The corpus callosum is the largest fibre tract in the human brain, roughly 200 million axons linking the two cerebral hemispheres, with the anterior portion (the genu) joining prefrontal regions and the posterior portion (the splenium) joining visual and parietal regions.

Its function was made vivid by the split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga in the 1960s, in which patients whose callosum had been cut to control epilepsy could name an object shown to the right visual field but not one shown to the left, because the left hemisphere, which speaks, no longer received the right hemisphere's input.


13.2.3 Tract-function mapping and disconnection syndromes

A disconnection syndrome is a deficit caused not by destroying a processing region but by cutting the pathway between two intact regions.

Norman Geschwind revived and systematised this idea in his 1965 paper "Disconnexion Syndromes in Animals and Man", building on nineteenth-century work by Carl Wernicke, Joseph Jules Dejerine, and Hugo Liepmann.

The textbook example is pure alexia, or alexia without agraphia, described by Dejerine in 1892: a patient can write a sentence and then cannot read what they have written, because a lesion has destroyed left visual cortex and also cut the splenium, so visual word information from the intact right hemisphere can no longer reach left-hemisphere language areas.

Conduction aphasia, in which comprehension and fluent speech are preserved but repetition fails, was Geschwind's proposed arcuate-fasciculus disconnection, and modern connectome-based lesion-symptom mapping supports a dorsal-stream account, although the specific claim that the arcuate alone is responsible is contested, with cortical damage around the temporoparietal region (area Spt) also carrying predictive weight.

The modern generalisation of the idea is lesion network mapping, developed by Michael Fox and colleagues from around 2015, which takes a lesion location, looks up which regions that location is normally connected to in a healthy reference connectome, and asks whether symptoms track the network rather than the site - an approach that has explained why anatomically scattered lesions can produce the same syndrome.


13.2.4 Tractography's known failure modes

Tractography does not see axons; it sees the orientation of water diffusion and infers axons, and the inference breaks in specific, well-catalogued ways.

The central problem is crossing fibres: within a single imaging voxel, typically a cube of one to two millimetres holding hundreds of thousands of axons, several bundles may cross, kiss, or fan out, and the measured diffusion pattern cannot uniquely distinguish these cases.

The consequence is false positives - streamlines that connect regions with no real anatomical link - and the most important demonstration is Klaus Maier-Hein and colleagues in Nature Communications in 2017, an open challenge in which twenty independent research groups submitted 96 tractography pipelines run on the same simulated phantom brain, and the reconstructions contained substantially more invalid than valid bundles, with many of the same false bundles recurring across groups.

There is a second, quieter bias: streamlines preferentially terminate on gyral crowns rather than sulcal walls, and long or highly curved pathways are systematically under-recovered, so false negatives cluster where the anatomy is hardest.

Directionality is simply absent - diffusion cannot tell whether a pathway carries signals from region A to region B or the reverse - so any directed claim from diffusion data is an assumption imported from animal tracer work.

None of this makes tractography useless; it means results should be treated as hypotheses about connectivity, with validation from tracer studies, dissection, or clinical stimulation where possible, and the field's own consensus statements now say as much.


13.3 Canonical resting-state networks

In 1995 Bharat Biswal noticed something that at first looked like an artefact: when a person lies in a scanner doing nothing, the slow fluctuations in the BOLD signal in left motor cortex are strongly correlated with those in right motor cortex.

That observation founded resting-state functional connectivity, and it turned out that the whole cortex partitions into a modest number of such correlated systems, which are reproducible across people, present during sleep and under anaesthesia, and broadly aligned with the systems that task experiments engage.

The most widely used parcellation is that of Thomas Yeo, Fenna Krienen and colleagues, published in 2011 from 1,000 scanned subjects, which offers a coarse seven-network and a finer seventeen-network solution; the Schaefer parcellation of 2018 subdivides these into a few hundred labelled parcels for practical analysis.

Two cautions before the list: these networks are statistical summaries rather than anatomical objects with sharp edges, and their names were assigned by researchers from the tasks that happened to engage them, so a name is a hypothesis, not a definition.


13.3.1 Default mode, frontoparietal control, dorsal and ventral attention, salience

The default mode network, named by Marcus Raichle and colleagues in 2001, comprises medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate and precuneus, and lateral parietal and medial temporal regions, and it is distinctive because it is more active at rest than during demanding external tasks.

Its positive function is now reasonably well established as internally directed cognition: remembering the past, imagining the future, thinking about other minds, and self-referential thought, and Randy Buckner and Daniel Schacter's work tied it closely to episodic memory and prospection.

The frontoparietal control network, sometimes called the central executive network, spans lateral prefrontal cortex and lateral parietal cortex and is engaged when a task requires holding a goal in mind and adjusting behaviour to it; Nicolas Dosenbach and colleagues distinguished it from a more tonically active cingulo-opercular system that maintains task set over longer periods.

The dorsal attention network, centred on the frontal eye fields and the intraparietal sulcus, supports voluntary, goal-driven orienting of attention - deciding where to look.

The ventral attention network, biased to the right hemisphere and involving the temporoparietal junction and ventral frontal cortex, supports stimulus-driven reorienting when something unexpected occurs, a dorsal-ventral distinction articulated by Maurizio Corbetta and Gordon Shulman in 2002.

The salience network, described by William Seeley, Vinod Menon and colleagues in 2007, is anchored in the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and detects behaviourally relevant events, whether they are external stimuli, bodily states, or errors.

Terminology warning: the Yeo parcellation merges salience and ventral attention into a single "salience/ventral attention" system, so different papers may use these labels for overlapping tissue.


13.3.2 Somatomotor, visual, auditory, limbic

The somatomotor network covers primary motor and primary somatosensory cortex along the central sulcus and is the system whose left-right correlation Biswal first observed; in finer parcellations it splits into a body-and-limb portion and a separate face-and-mouth portion.

The visual network occupies occipital cortex and typically separates into a central-field system near the occipital pole and a peripheral-field system further forward, reflecting the retinotopic organisation of visual cortex, meaning that neighbouring points on the retina map to neighbouring points on the cortex.

The auditory system, centred on the superior temporal plane including Heschl's gyrus, appears as a distinct network in higher-dimensional solutions but is often absorbed into the somatomotor network in the coarse seven-network parcellation, which is a good illustration of how parcellation resolution changes the answer.

The limbic network in these parcellations covers orbitofrontal cortex and the temporal pole and is associated with emotion, reward valuation, and semantic memory - but it should be treated with particular caution, because those regions suffer severe signal loss in fMRI due to magnetic susceptibility artefact near the air-filled sinuses, so a low-quality signal can masquerade as a coherent network.


13.3.3 Network interaction and the triple-network model

Vinod Menon's triple-network model, set out in 2010 and 2011, proposes that much of cognition and much of psychiatric dysfunction can be understood through the interplay of three systems: the default mode network, the frontoparietal central executive network, and the salience network.

The specific claim is that the salience network, and particularly the anterior insula, acts as a switch: on detecting a behaviourally significant event it disengages the default mode network and engages the frontoparietal network, shifting the brain from internal to external processing.

The model has real evidential support, including causal-direction evidence from intracranial electroencephalography, where electrodes are placed directly on the brain of epilepsy patients; Saurabh Das and Menon reported in eLife in 2024 that directed information flow runs consistently from anterior insula to both the default mode and frontoparietal networks across multiple independent datasets.

It is nonetheless an elegant model that is easy to over-apply, and that is the honest verdict: a three-network framework has been invoked for autism, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, and dementia alike, and critics point out that a theory which explains every disorder discriminates between none of them.

The related and once-popular claim that the default mode network is strictly anticorrelated with task-positive networks is also weaker than it looked, because a common preprocessing step called global signal regression can manufacture negative correlations, a problem raised by Kevin Murphy and colleagues in 2009 and still not fully settled.


13.3.4 Individual-specific network topography and precision imaging

Group-average network maps blur across people, and the blur is not noise.

Precision functional mapping, exemplified by Evan Gordon, Timothy Laumann and colleagues in Neuron in 2017 - the Midnight Scan Club dataset, in which ten adults each contributed roughly five hours of resting-state scanning plus task and structural imaging - showed that each person's network borders sit in idiosyncratic places, and that these individual differences are stable across sessions and cannot be explained by head motion, registration error, or anatomical differences alone.

Some individuals possess network features simply absent from the group average, including small isolated patches of default mode or control network in unusual locations, which Rodrigo Braga and Randy Buckner also demonstrated in 2017 by showing that what looks like one default mode network in group data resolves into two interdigitated networks within a single well-sampled individual.

The practical consequence is substantial: if a group atlas places a boundary in the wrong place for a given person, then measurements taken with that atlas mix signals from two different systems, which inflates apparent individual differences in connectivity strength when the real difference is in topography.

Precision imaging has since been extended to clinical questions and to infants, and Charles Lynch, Conor Liston and colleagues used dense longitudinal sampling from 2024 onward to track a salience-network expansion associated with depression, which is the kind of finding that group-average imaging could not have produced.

The cost is scanning time - hours per person rather than ten minutes - and that trade-off between many subjects and deep sampling is now one of the live methodological arguments in the field.


13.4 Network architecture principles

Once you have a connectome as a matrix, you can analyse it with graph theory, the branch of mathematics that treats a system as nodes joined by edges.

Here a node is a brain region and an edge is a connection, and a handful of graph measures turn out to describe brains across species and scales with striking consistency.

The value of this framing is that it makes structural claims testable and comparable: you can ask whether a schizophrenia connectome and a healthy connectome differ in the same measurable way that a random network differs from a lattice.

The danger is that graph measures are seductive numbers that can be computed on any matrix, including a bad one, so every result in this section inherits the measurement caveats of section 13.2.4.


13.4.1 Small-world organisation, hubs, and the rich club

A small-world network, in the sense defined by Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz in 1998, is one that combines dense local clustering, meaning your neighbours tend to be connected to each other, with short path lengths, meaning any node can be reached from any other in few steps.

Brains show this signature at every scale examined, from the worm to the human cortex, and Ed Bullmore and Olaf Sporns made the case in a 2009 review that small-worldness reconciles two demands: local specialisation and global communication.

Short paths are achieved by hubs, which are regions with unusually many connections; in the human cortex these include the precuneus, posterior cingulate, superior frontal and superior parietal cortex, and the insula.

Martijn van den Heuvel and Olaf Sporns showed in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2011 that these hubs are not merely numerous in connections but are preferentially connected to each other, forming what network science calls a rich club - a densely interlinked core through which a large fraction of all shortest paths must pass.

Rich-club connections are long, and long axons are metabolically expensive, so this arrangement is a deliberate-looking splurge, which is exactly why hub damage is so damaging: Nicolas Crossley and colleagues reported in Brain in 2014 that lesions in a wide range of brain disorders fall on hub regions far more often than chance would predict.

One caveat that the field has taken seriously: Mark Hilgetag and Alexandros Goulas argued in 2016 that "small world" is a weak descriptor because almost any moderately dense network satisfies it, so the label alone should not be treated as an explanation.


13.4.2 Modularity, integration, and segregation

A module, in network terms, is a group of nodes more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the network, and brain networks are strongly modular, with the modules corresponding closely to the resting-state systems of section 13.3.

Segregation is the degree to which processing is confined within modules, and integration is the degree to which information is combined across them; the two pull against each other, and cognition appears to require balancing them rather than maximising either.

Jessica Cohen and Mark D'Esposito demonstrated this directly in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2016: a task drawing on a single system, finger-sequence tapping, increased modularity and segregation, whereas a working-memory task requiring coordination across systems, the n-back, decreased modularity and increased global integration - and, importantly, individual differences in that reconfiguration predicted individual differences in performance.

Related work by Danielle Bassett and colleagues on flexibility, meaning how often a region changes module membership over time, found that flexibility during motor learning predicted how quickly a person learned.

The claim is therefore not that a more modular brain is a better brain, but that a brain able to move fluidly between segregated and integrated configurations is a more capable one, and there is reasonable evidence that this capacity declines with age and in several clinical conditions.


13.4.3 Wiring cost against communication efficiency

Axons cost something to build, something to maintain, and something to run, and the brain consumes roughly twenty per cent of the body's energy budget for about two per cent of its mass.

A purely cost-minimising brain would connect only near neighbours, producing a lattice with long communication paths; a purely efficiency-maximising brain would connect everything to everything, at a volume and metabolic price no skull could pay.

Ed Bullmore and Olaf Sporns set out the resolution in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2012 under the heading of the economy of brain network organisation: real connectomes sit near a negotiated optimum, mostly wired short, but paying a deliberate premium for a minority of long-range connections that buy disproportionate gains in integration.

The evidence is that generative models which score candidate networks on a trade-off between wiring cost and topological value reproduce many real connectome features, work developed by Richard Betzel, Bullmore and colleagues from 2016 onward.

Two honest limits: these models reproduce summary statistics far better than they reproduce the specific placement of individual connections, and cost is usually operationalised as Euclidean distance between region centroids, which is a crude proxy for the true metabolic and volumetric cost of an axon.

The framing is nonetheless useful because it converts an anatomical description into a prediction - if wiring is near-optimal, then a deviation from optimality is a finding requiring explanation, whether developmental, evolutionary, or pathological.


13.4.4 Controllability and the network-control framing of cognition

Network control theory asks a different question of a connectome: given this wiring, how hard is it to push the system from one state to another by injecting energy at a particular node?

Shi Gu, Fabio Pasqualetti, Danielle Bassett and colleagues applied this to human structural connectomes in Nature Communications in 2015, defining average controllability as a region's capacity to steer the brain into many easily reachable states with little energy, and modal controllability as its capacity to push the brain into hard-to-reach states.

They reported that densely connected hub regions tend to score high on average controllability, while weakly connected regions, often in frontoparietal cortex, score high on modal controllability, and they interpreted this as an anatomical substrate for cognitive control.

The framing has been extended to development, to individual differences in cognitive flexibility, and to predicting the effects of brain stimulation, which is where it would be most valuable if it holds.

It should, however, be labelled clearly as promising and disputed: Tommy Tu, Emmanuel Stamatakis and colleagues published a critique in 2018 arguing that controllability metrics computed on structural connectomes are highly sensitive to preprocessing choices and can be closely approximated by simple node degree, and further commentaries have questioned whether the linear time-invariant dynamics assumed by the model bear any resemblance to real neural dynamics.

This is a good example of the pattern this chapter keeps returning to - an elegant mathematics laid over a measurement whose reliability is the actual bottleneck.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Connectomics operates at three scales, and they trade coverage against resolution: complete synapse-level maps exist for the worm and the fruit fly and for one cubic millimetre of mouse cortex, mesoscale tracer maps exist for mouse and macaque, and the human is currently reachable only at the coarse macroscale of diffusion imaging.

Human structural connectomes derived from tractography are hypotheses rather than anatomy, because diffusion imaging cannot resolve crossing fibres, cannot recover direction of signal flow, and produces more invalid than valid bundles under controlled test conditions.

Named white matter tracts carry real functional weight, and the disconnection syndromes - pure alexia, conduction aphasia, the split-brain findings - remain the clearest demonstration that cognition depends on communication between regions and not only on the regions themselves.

Resting-state functional connectivity partitions the cortex into a reproducible set of large-scale networks, and the useful modern refinement is that their borders are individual-specific and require hours of scanning per person to locate accurately.
