Across species and scales, connectomes share a small-world, modular, hub-dominated, rich-club architecture that sits near an economical compromise between wiring cost and communication efficiency.

The organising theories built on top of that architecture, including the triple-network model and network controllability, are attractive and partially supported, and each is currently limited more by the reliability of the underlying measurement than by the mathematics.


CHAPTER 14. ENERGY, BLOOD, AND THE PHYSICAL COST OF THINKING (APPARATUS)


Thinking is not free.

Every thought you have is paid for in sugar and oxygen, delivered by blood, burned by cells, and accounted for down to the individual electrical pulse.

This chapter is about that bill - who pays it, what the biggest line items are, and how the brain's tight energy budget shapes the way it represents the world.

It also matters for a practical reason: the most common way we look at the living human brain, functional magnetic resonance imaging, does not measure thought at all.

It measures blood.

Understanding the energy story is therefore not a side topic - it is the instruction manual for reading almost every brain image you will ever see.


14.1 Neuroenergetics

Neuroenergetics is the study of how the brain obtains, spends, and budgets energy.

The universal energy currency of a cell is adenosine triphosphate (ATP), a small molecule that stores chemical energy and releases it when one of its phosphate groups is broken off.

Almost everything in this section is ultimately a statement about how many molecules of ATP a given brain process consumes.

The reason to care is that the brain is an unusually expensive organ, and expensive organs are under strong evolutionary pressure to be efficient.


14.1.1 Glucose and oxygen budgets of the human brain

The adult human brain is roughly 2 percent of body weight but consumes about 20 percent of the body's oxygen and a comparable share of its glucose - a sugar carried in the blood that is the brain's near-exclusive fuel.

In everyday units that is on the order of 20 watts of continuous power, about the draw of a dim light bulb, running every second of your life whether you are solving equations or asleep.

Unlike muscle, the brain stores essentially no fuel of its own, which is why interrupting blood supply for even seconds produces unconsciousness and why low blood sugar produces confusion so quickly.

The brain can burn ketone bodies - alternative fuels made by the liver from fat during starvation or a very low-carbohydrate diet - and the infant brain uses them heavily, but glucose remains the default.

There is also a live argument, opened by Pellerin and Magistretti in 1994 with the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, over whether neurons take up glucose directly or receive lactate handed to them by astrocytes, a class of star-shaped support cell.

That hypothesis is elegant and has been debated for three decades without full resolution; the honest summary is that lactate certainly moves between cell types and matters, but the claim that it is the main fuel for active neurons is still contested.


14.1.2 Cost of spikes, of synaptic transmission, and of maintenance

The landmark accounting is Attwell and Laughlin's 2001 energy budget for grey matter, which asked, process by process, where the ATP goes.

Their estimate assigned roughly 47 percent to action potentials - the brief electrical pulses, also called spikes, that neurons use to signal - about 34 percent to the postsynaptic effects of the neurotransmitter glutamate, around 13 percent to maintaining the resting voltage across cell membranes, and a few percent to packaging and recycling transmitter.

The dominant physical cost in all of these is the sodium-potassium pump, a protein that pushes ions back across the membrane after they have flowed down their gradients, restoring the battery that every electrical signal drains.

Harris, Jolivet and Attwell revised the numbers in 2012, noting that mammalian action potentials are cheaper than the squid-axon figures originally assumed because the sodium and potassium currents overlap less, which shifts more of the burden onto synapses.

The headline conclusion survives the revision: the great majority of the brain's energy - on the order of three quarters in grey matter - is spent on signalling and computation rather than on mere cellular housekeeping.

That is the fact that licenses everything else in this chapter, because it means energy measurements carry information about information processing.


14.1.3 Energy as a design constraint favouring sparse coding

If spikes cost money, then a code that uses fewer spikes to carry the same message is cheaper, and evolution should prefer it.

This is the argument Levy and Baxter made in 1996 in a paper titled Energy Efficient Neural Codes, deriving that for a given amount of information there is an optimal, and surprisingly low, average firing rate.

Sparse coding - a representation in which any given stimulus is signalled by a small minority of active neurons rather than by a broad pattern across many - falls out of this reasoning naturally.

Lennie pushed the arithmetic to its uncomfortable conclusion in 2003 in The Cost of Cortical Computation: given the measured energy supply of human cortex, only something like a few percent of cortical neurons can be substantially active at any moment, since the brain simply could not afford to feed more.

Sparse firing is also independently observed in cortex, so here theory and measurement point the same way, which is rarer in neuroscience than one might hope.

The caveat worth stating is that energy efficiency is one pressure among several - speed, robustness to noise, and ease of learning also shape codes - so sparseness should be read as strongly favoured rather than as the sole explanation.


14.1.4 Baseline activity and the small cost of task-evoked change

The most counterintuitive fact in neuroenergetics is how little of the brain's spending is caused by what you are doing.

Marcus Raichle, summarising decades of imaging work in a 2006 Science piece and a 2010 Scientific American article both titled around the phrase the brain's dark energy, pointed out that performing a demanding task typically raises the local energy consumption of the involved region by under 5 percent above its ongoing baseline.

The other 95 percent is intrinsic activity: the brain talking to itself, maintained continuously, in organised patterns such as the default mode network, a set of midline and parietal regions that is more active during rest than during outward-directed tasks.

This reframes the brain from a stimulus-response device that switches on when needed into a system that is always running a model of the world, with tasks producing only small perturbations of it.

It also carries a methodological sting: because the task-evoked change is tiny, brain imaging works almost entirely by subtracting one condition from another, and the pictures you see are difference maps, not maps of activity.

Rest is not a neutral zero point but a rich condition in its own right, which is why what counts as a proper control condition is a live and sometimes fraught question in experimental design.


14.2 Neurovascular coupling

Neurovascular coupling is the mechanism by which local increases in neural activity produce local increases in blood flow within a second or two.

It is the reason non-invasive functional imaging is possible at all: we cannot see spikes through the skull, but we can see blood.

This section covers the machinery, the signal it generates, the delay it imposes, and the ways it fails.


14.2.1 The neurovascular unit

The neurovascular unit is the local team of cells that jointly translate neural activity into a blood-flow response.

Its members, as set out in Costantino Iadecola's 2017 Neuron review, are neurons, inhibitory interneurons, astrocytes, the endothelial cells lining blood vessels, smooth muscle cells on arterioles, pericytes wrapped around capillaries, and the surrounding extracellular matrix and immune cells.

Astrocytes are pivotal because their end-feet physically envelop blood vessels while their other processes sit at synapses, giving them a position from which to sense activity and signal to the vasculature.

The same assembly also builds the blood-brain barrier, the tight seal that controls what passes from blood into brain tissue.

There is genuine disagreement about which cell type does the dilating: capillary pericytes, arteriolar smooth muscle, and astrocytes have each been argued to lead, and evidence exists that the first response can begin at capillaries and propagate upstream.

Treat the neurovascular unit as a well-established anatomical fact and its internal division of labour as an active research question.


14.2.2 The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal and what it indexes

Haemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in red blood cells, has different magnetic properties depending on whether it is carrying oxygen: oxygenated haemoglobin is diamagnetic and magnetically quiet, while deoxygenated haemoglobin is paramagnetic and distorts the local magnetic field, weakening the magnetic resonance signal.

Seiji Ogawa and colleagues exploited this in 1990 to create blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) contrast, which is the basis of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

The physiological trick, first documented by Fox and Raichle in 1986, is that when a region activates, blood flow increases far more than oxygen consumption does - in their measurements roughly a 29 percent flow increase against about a 5 percent rise in oxygen use.

The result is paradoxical and worth stating slowly: active tissue ends up with proportionally less deoxygenated haemoglobin than resting tissue, so the magnetic resonance signal goes up rather than down.

As to what BOLD indexes, the pivotal experiment is Logothetis and colleagues in 2001, who recorded electrical activity and BOLD simultaneously in monkey visual cortex and found that BOLD tracked local field potentials - the summed synaptic and dendritic currents in a neighbourhood - better than it tracked the output spikes of neurons.

The practical reading is that BOLD is closer to a measure of input and local processing than of output firing, which means a region can appear active in an image while its neurons are being inhibited, since inhibition itself costs energy.


14.2.3 Haemodynamic lag and its consequences for inference

Blood is slow.

After a brief burst of neural activity the BOLD response rises over a couple of seconds, peaks around 4 to 6 seconds later, and then falls back with a mild undershoot, a shape known as the haemodynamic response function.

This means fMRI has excellent spatial resolution, on the order of millimetres, and poor temporal resolution, and no amount of faster scanning fixes it because the limit is in the physiology rather than in the machine.

Analysts recover timing by deconvolution - mathematically undoing the smearing by assuming a response shape - but the answer depends on the assumed shape, so the procedure adds a modelling commitment rather than removing one.

The sharpest problem for cognitive inference is that the lag varies by brain region, by individual, by age, and by vascular health, so an apparent difference in when two regions responded can be a difference in their plumbing rather than in their computation.

This is precisely why claims that region A drove region B, drawn from fMRI timing alone, deserve scepticism, and why converging evidence from electroencephalography or magnetoencephalography, which read electrical and magnetic fields directly with millisecond precision, is so valuable.


14.2.4 Neurovascular decoupling in disease and ageing

Neurovascular coupling degrades with age and with disease, a condition usually called neurovascular decoupling or uncoupling.

It is documented in hypertension, in small vessel disease, in diabetes, and prominently in Alzheimer's disease, where amyloid pathology and vascular dysfunction appear to reinforce each other; a 2022 review in Brain surveys the mechanisms in detail.

Pericyte loss is one candidate driver, and experiments that ablate cortical pericytes produce rapid uncoupling, which is about as direct a causal demonstration as this field offers.

There is growing interest in decoupling as an early marker rather than a late consequence, with work published as recently as 2026 examining whether it predicts subsequent cognitive decline.

For the reader of imaging studies the implication is blunt: if a study reports weaker activation in older or patient groups, a reduced vascular response is a serious rival explanation to reduced neural activity, and careful studies control for it by measuring cerebrovascular reactivity separately.


14.3 Metabolic constraint as an explanatory resource

The preceding sections treated energy as a constraint the brain must live within.

This section asks a stronger question: how much of cognition can be explained by that constraint?

The answer ranges from firmly established in sensory coding to genuinely unsettled in the psychology of effort.


14.3.1 Efficient coding derived from energy budgets

The efficient coding hypothesis, proposed by Horace Barlow in 1961, holds that sensory systems are built to represent the natural world using as few resources as possible by removing redundancy - the predictable, repetitive structure that natural signals are full of.

Barlow's original argument was about information; the energy budget work of the 1990s and 2000s gave it a physical price tag, letting predictions be derived rather than asserted.

Simon Laughlin and colleagues made this concrete in a 1998 Nature Neuroscience paper on the metabolic cost of neural information, measuring in the blowfly retina how many ATP molecules are consumed per bit transmitted, and finding the cost per bit rises steeply as a cell is pushed to higher information rates.

That non-linearity has a clean consequence: it is cheaper to spread a given amount of information across many slow, quiet neurons than to extract it from a few fast, busy ones, which explains why sensory pathways fan out into large populations.

This is one of the better success stories in theoretical neuroscience, because a physical measurement in an insect eye yielded a principle that holds up in mammalian cortex.


14.3.2 Effort, cost of control, and metabolic accounts of it

Mental effort feels costly, we avoid it, and we experience fatigue - but what exactly is being spent?

The simple metabolic story, that concentration burns glucose which must be replenished, was popular in the 2000s under the banner of ego depletion, and it is in serious trouble: the arithmetic never worked, since Section 14.1.4 tells us task-evoked energy changes are only a few percent of a baseline the body sustains easily, and a 23-laboratory preregistered replication by Hagger, Chatzisarantis and colleagues in 2016, with over 2,000 participants, found an effect indistinguishable from zero.

The leading alternatives are computational and economic rather than metabolic.

Shenhav, Botvinick and Cohen's expected value of control framework, introduced in 2013 and extended in a 2017 review, treats the brain as deciding how much control to allocate by weighing expected reward against effort cost and the likelihood that control will help, with the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex doing the arithmetic.

Kurzban and colleagues argued in 2013 that the cost is an opportunity cost: effort feels bad not because a tank is emptying but because the circuits in use could be doing something more valuable, and fatigue is the signal telling you to reconsider.

There is a partial reconciliation on offer - Wiehler and Pessiglione reported in 2022 that sustained hard cognitive work is associated with accumulation of glutamate in lateral prefrontal cortex, a genuinely metabolic mechanism - but that single finding is not yet replicated widely enough to settle the question, and it should be read as promising rather than established.


14.3.3 Sleep, clearance, and the restorative hypothesis

Sleep costs an animal a third of its life and leaves it defenceless, so whatever it buys must be substantial, and energy and waste are the two leading candidates.

The energetic version was sharpened by Tononi and Cirelli's synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, first published in 2003 and developed in 2006 and 2014, which proposes that learning during waking strengthens synapses on net, that stronger synapses cost more energy and space, and that the slow waves of deep sleep downscale them back to a sustainable baseline while preserving relative differences.

The waste-clearance version comes from Xie, Nedergaard and colleagues in 2013, who reported that in sleeping mice the space between brain cells expands and cerebrospinal fluid washes through it far more effectively, clearing solutes including amyloid beta, the protein that aggregates in Alzheimer's disease - a system Nedergaard's group named glymphatic, from glia plus lymphatic.

This is currently one of the most contested claims in the field: work published in 2024 using tracers injected into brain tissue rather than into cerebrospinal fluid reported that clearance slows rather than speeds during sleep and anaesthesia, and Nedergaard has publicly disputed the methodology.

Meanwhile human studies continue to find supporting evidence, including a 2024 to 2026 line of work reporting that a night of normal sleep raises morning blood levels of amyloid beta and tau relative to sleep deprivation, consistent with clearance from brain to blood.

The fair summary for a newcomer is that sleep clearly does something restorative, that both the synaptic-downscaling and the fluid-clearance accounts have real evidence, that they are not mutually exclusive, and that the specific glymphatic mechanism is actively disputed as of 2026.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The brain runs on about 20 watts and takes roughly a fifth of the body's oxygen and glucose despite being a fiftieth of its mass, and by the accounting of Attwell and Laughlin most of that goes to signalling rather than housekeeping.

Because spikes are expensive, sparse and efficient codes are not merely tidy but affordable, a line of reasoning running from Barlow through Levy and Baxter to Lennie and grounded in direct measurement by Laughlin.

Task-evoked energy changes are only a few percent above a large, organised, intrinsic baseline, which means functional imaging necessarily works by subtraction and that the resting brain is a subject in its own right.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging measures blood oxygenation, not neural firing; it tracks local field potentials better than spikes, lags neural events by several seconds, and its lag varies with age and vascular health, so timing-based and group-difference claims need independent support.

Metabolic constraint explains sensory coding well, explains mental effort poorly - the glucose-depletion account of willpower failed a large preregistered replication - and offers two competing but compatible accounts of what sleep restores, one of which, the glymphatic system, remains genuinely disputed.


CHAPTER 15. RHYTHMS, OSCILLATIONS, AND NEURAL TIMING (CORE)

Put an electrode near a living brain and you do not find silence between the spikes.

You find waves - voltage rising and falling in repeating cycles, some slow enough to count on a clock, some fast enough that hundreds pass in a second.

This chapter is about those waves: where they come from, how they coordinate distant patches of tissue, what work they may do for thought and memory, and how confident we are allowed to be that they do any work at all.

The topic matters because timing is the one resource the brain has that a list of connections does not capture.

Two neurons wired identically can mean entirely different things depending on when they fire relative to each other and relative to the ongoing rhythm around them.

But the field is also full of elegant theories resting on thin evidence, so this chapter will be careful to separate what is measured from what is merely proposed.

15.1 The oscillatory bands and their generators

An oscillation, in this context, means a roughly repeating fluctuation in the electrical activity of a population of neurons.

We usually see it in one of three signals: the electroencephalogram (EEG), which records voltage from the scalp; the local field potential (LFP), which records voltage from an electrode inside the tissue; or magnetoencephalography (MEG), which records the tiny magnetic fields those currents produce.

Crucially, these signals mostly reflect synaptic currents in the dendrites of many neurons at once, not the spikes themselves - so an oscillation is a population phenomenon, a chorus rather than a soloist.

The tradition is to divide these fluctuations into frequency bands, and the tradition is partly arbitrary: the boundaries were set by early human EEG work and have been inherited ever since rather than derived from biology.

Each band, however, does tend to be produced by identifiable circuits, and that is what makes the taxonomy worth keeping.

15.1.1 Delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, and high-frequency broadband

The conventional bands are delta (roughly below 4 hertz, where one hertz means one cycle per second), theta (roughly 4 to 8 hertz), alpha (roughly 8 to 12 hertz), beta (roughly 12 to 30 hertz), and gamma (roughly 30 to 80 hertz), with an additional high-gamma or high-frequency range above about 80 hertz.

Delta dominates deep non-rapid-eye-movement sleep and is generated largely by cortical networks alternating between an active up state and a near-silent down state.

Theta is the signature rhythm of the rodent hippocampus during running and of human medial temporal lobe during navigation and memory, though human theta is often slower than rodent theta, which is a live complication rather than a settled fact.

Alpha was the first human brain rhythm ever described, by Hans Berger in the 1920s, and it is strongest over the back of the head when the eyes are closed.

Beta is prominent over sensorimotor cortex and drops sharply just before and during movement, while gamma is a local rhythm generated by the interplay of excitatory and inhibitory cells, discussed in the next sub-section.

The highest range deserves special caution, and it gets a fuller treatment in section 15.4.2: much of what is called high-gamma is not a rhythm at all.

15.1.2 Interneuron-driven gamma and the pyramidal-interneuron network model

Gamma is the best-understood rhythm in the brain, mechanistically, because it can be produced in a slice of tissue on a laboratory bench and modelled with a handful of equations.

The central player is a class of inhibitory interneuron - a small local neuron that releases the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and thereby suppresses its targets - called the fast-spiking, parvalbumin-expressing basket cell, which wraps its terminals around the cell body of excitatory pyramidal neurons.

Two mechanisms are standardly distinguished: interneuron network gamma (ING), in which mutually inhibiting interneurons synchronise each other into a rhythm on their own, and pyramidal-interneuron network gamma (PING), in which pyramidal cells excite interneurons, the interneurons silence the pyramidal cells for a few milliseconds, inhibition decays, and the cycle repeats.

The decisive evidence came in 2009, when two groups using optogenetics - a technique in which light-sensitive proteins are inserted into a defined cell type so that light can switch those cells on or off - showed that driving parvalbumin interneurons rhythmically produced gamma in mouse cortex, and suppressing them abolished it (Cardin and colleagues, 2009; Sohal and colleagues, 2009).

Current reviews hold that PING predominates in neocortex while both mechanisms operate in hippocampus, and recent work in medial entorhinal cortex suggests the circuit can slide between ING and PING regimes as excitatory drive changes.

15.1.3 Hippocampal theta and the septal pacemaker

The hippocampal theta rhythm is the most studied oscillation in behavioural neuroscience, because in a running rat it is enormous, regular, and tightly tied to movement and memory.

Its pacemaker is generally located in the medial septum and diagonal band, a small structure at the base of the forebrain whose GABAergic neurons fire in rhythmic bursts and impose that rhythm on hippocampal interneurons; lesion or inactivate the medial septum and hippocampal theta collapses.

A 2022 study by Hangya and colleagues in Cell Reports described the septal pacemaker cells as achieving their synchrony through a mechanism analogous to Huygens synchronisation, the classic physics case of two pendulum clocks on a shared beam falling into step.

Two varieties of theta are distinguished pharmacologically: type 1, which accompanies voluntary movement and survives the drug atropine (which blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors), and type 2, which accompanies immobility, arousal, and fear, and is abolished by atropine, implying it depends on cholinergic input.

That double dissociation is old, robust, and a useful reminder that a single frequency band can be produced by more than one circuit doing more than one job.

15.1.4 Sleep spindles, slow oscillations, and sharp-wave ripples

Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep contains three distinctive events that are widely believed to serve memory consolidation - the process by which a fresh, fragile memory is stabilised and gradually made independent of the hippocampus.

The cortical slow oscillation, at roughly 0.5 to 1 hertz, is a global alternation between depolarised up states and hyperpolarised down states that sets the timing frame for everything else.

Sleep spindles are brief bursts at roughly 8 to 16 hertz generated by the interaction between the thalamic reticular nucleus, a shell of inhibitory neurons surrounding the thalamus, and thalamocortical relay cells.

Sharp-wave ripples are very brief, very fast events at roughly 80 to 200 hertz arising in hippocampal area CA1, during which the neural sequences experienced while awake are replayed in compressed form.

The influential model is a nesting hierarchy: slow oscillation up states carry spindles, and spindle troughs carry ripples, so that hippocampal replay arrives at cortex exactly when cortex is receptive - a proposal set out in detail by Ngo, Staresina and colleagues in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2024, with supporting human intracranial recordings showing stepwise increases in firing and cross-regional interaction along that sequence.

Honesty requires noting that a 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis of slow-oscillation-spindle coupling and memory found the evidence for the behavioural link weaker and more heterogeneous than the enthusiasm of the field would suggest, so the mechanism is better described as strongly indicated than as proven.

15.2 Cross-frequency and cross-area coordination

If rhythms did nothing but repeat locally, they would be a curiosity.

The reason they attract theoretical attention is that they appear to organise relations - between fast and slow rhythms in one place, and between distant places in the brain.

This section covers four such proposals, each of which is empirically well documented as a correlation and each of which is contested as a mechanism.

15.2.1 Phase-amplitude coupling

Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) means that the strength, or amplitude, of a fast rhythm rises and falls systematically with the phase, or position within the cycle, of a slower rhythm.

The canonical example is theta-gamma coupling in the hippocampus, where gamma bursts occur preferentially at a particular part of the theta cycle, first quantified in human cortex by Canolty and colleagues in 2006 using a mean vector length measure, and later by Tort and colleagues in 2008 using an entropy-based modulation index.

The intuitive reading is appealing: the slow rhythm carves time into slots and the fast rhythm fills each slot with content.

The methodological warnings are serious and should be taken to heart by any beginner reading a PAC paper.

A signal that is rhythmic but not sinusoidal - a sawtooth, or a wave with a sharp trough - will produce apparent phase-amplitude coupling as a pure artefact of the filtering, because the sharp edge injects energy into high frequencies at a fixed phase, a point made forcefully by Cole and Voytek in their 2017 review on waveform shape.

Increases in high-frequency power alone can also inflate some PAC measures, so a difference in coupling between two conditions may simply be a difference in broadband power, and no measure currently distinguishes true coupling from waveform artefact automatically.

15.2.2 Communication through coherence and its critiques

Communication through coherence (CTC), proposed by Pascal Fries in 2005 and elaborated in 2015, is the most influential functional theory of brain rhythms.

The claim is that two neural populations exchange information effectively only when their rhythms are phase-locked with the right lag, so that spikes from the sender arrive at the receiver during the receiver's window of high excitability rather than during its inhibitory trough; attention, on this account, works by adjusting which sender gets a well-timed window.

The correlational evidence is substantial: attended stimuli produce stronger gamma coherence between visual areas V1 and V4, and the strength of that coherence tracks behavioural performance.

The major critique reverses the arrow of causation.

Schneider, Broggini and colleagues, in Neuron in 2021, showed with a synaptic and source-mixing model that inter-areal coherence can arise as a by-product of connectivity and of the sender's power spectrum, with no oscillator coupling and no phase-locking between sending and receiving spikes - what they termed coherence through communication.

A 2023 modelling study by Yang and colleagues, published in PLOS Computational Biology in 2024, similarly found the scope of genuine CTC-style attentional selection to be narrower than the theory's broad statement implies.

The honest summary is that coherence is real, that it tracks cognition, and that whether it is a cause or a consequence of communication remains genuinely unresolved.

15.2.3 Travelling waves across cortex

Oscillations are often drawn as if the whole cortex went up and down together, but with dense electrode grids it becomes clear that the phase of an oscillation shifts smoothly across space, so the rhythm is better described as a wave sweeping across tissue.

Zhang, Watrous, Patel and Jacobs, in Neuron in 2018, recorded from human patients with implanted electrodes and showed that theta and alpha oscillations are travelling waves in human neocortex, generally moving from posterior toward anterior regions.

A companion review by Muller, Chavane, Reynolds and Sejnowski in Nature Reviews Neuroscience the same year laid out the network mechanisms - principally the graded conduction delays of horizontal cortical fibres - that make such propagation expected rather than surprising.

Function has since been probed directly: Davis and colleagues, in Nature in 2020, found that spontaneous travelling waves in behaving primates predicted whether a faint stimulus would be detected, and Mohan, Zhang, Ermentrout and Jacobs, in Nature Human Behaviour in 2024, reported that wave direction reversed between memory encoding and retrieval, with posterior-to-anterior waves during encoding and the reverse during retrieval.

Travelling waves are one of the healthier areas of this literature, in that the phenomenon is robust and the proposed mechanism is ordinary physics.

15.2.4 Feedforward gamma and feedback alpha-beta channels

The cortex is hierarchically organised, and the anatomy distinguishes feedforward projections, which originate in superficial layers and carry sensory detail up the hierarchy, from feedback projections, which originate in deep layers and carry expectation and context back down.

Two 2014 and 2015 papers proposed that these two anatomical streams use different frequencies: van Kerkoerle and colleagues, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2014, and Bastos and colleagues, in Neuron in 2015.

The evidence lines up: gamma synchronisation is strongest in superficial layers and alpha-beta synchronisation strongest in infragranular layers, directed-influence analysis using Granger causality shows feedforward influence carried by gamma and feedback influence by alpha-beta, and electrically stimulating V1 drives gamma in V4 while stimulating V4 drives alpha-beta in V1.

The scheme has been extended to auditory cortex, where feedforward signalling again uses gamma while feedback uses lower frequencies, suggesting a general cortical principle rather than a visual quirk.

This idea meshes naturally with predictive processing accounts, in which the brain continually predicts its input and passes only the errors upward, and it is one of the few oscillation theories with converging anatomical, correlational, and stimulation-based support.

15.3 Oscillations as cognitive mechanism

Having covered where rhythms come from and how they align across frequency and space, we now turn to the claims that they do specific cognitive jobs.

Read this section with the previous caveats active: each proposal below is well specified and well liked, and each rests on evidence that is strong in animals and thinner in humans.

15.3.1 Theta-gamma coding of item sequences

The theta-gamma neural code, argued at length by John Lisman and Ole Jensen in Neuron in 2013 and building on Lisman and Idiart's 1995 model, proposes that each gamma cycle holds one item and each theta cycle holds the whole ordered list.

The attraction is that it derives the famous limit on short-term memory from anatomy rather than stipulating it: if about seven gamma cycles fit inside one theta cycle, then about seven items fit in memory.

Direct support comes from the rodent hippocampus, where different locations are represented in different gamma subcycles of a single theta cycle, and from human work by Heusser and colleagues in 2016, who found that hippocampal theta-gamma coupling predicted memory for the temporal order of items.

There is also a causal hint: Vosskuhl, Huster and Herrmann reported in 2015 that slowing individual theta frequency with electrical stimulation increased short-term memory span, exactly as the model predicts, though this is a single small finding and should not be treated as settled.

The theory is elegant, it makes quantitative predictions, and it is not yet decisively confirmed in humans - all three of those things are true at once.

15.3.2 Alpha as functional inhibition in attention

The gating-by-inhibition account, set out by Ole Jensen and Ali Mazaheri in 2010, holds that alpha is not idling but active suppression: alpha power rises over cortical regions processing irrelevant information, blocking it from propagating.

The core observation is clean and replicable - attend to the left side of space and alpha power rises over the left hemisphere, which handles the ignored right side, and falls over the right hemisphere.

Refinements matter here.

Wöstmann and colleagues, in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2019, presented evidence that alpha lateralisation implements distractor suppression independently of target selection, which supports the inhibitory reading.

But Foster and Awh, reviewing the question in 2019, argued that alpha does not straightforwardly index inhibition, noting among other things that the spatial pattern of alpha decoded from the scalp tracks the attended location rather than the suppressed one - so alpha may be a marker of a spatial priority map rather than a suppression signal as such.

Treat the inhibition story as the leading interpretation, not the only one.

15.3.3 Beta and the maintenance of the current cognitive set

Andreas Engel and Pascal Fries proposed in 2010 that beta-band activity signals the status quo: beta is high when the current motor or cognitive state is to be maintained, and drops when a change is required, which fits the sharp beta drop before voluntary movement.

That framing has since been substantially revised in two ways.

First, what looks like a sustained beta oscillation in trial-averaged data is usually, on single trials, a set of brief beta bursts lasting only a few cycles - a methodological correction pressed by Mikael Lundqvist, Earl Miller and colleagues, and summarised in their 2024 Trends in Cognitive Sciences article Beta: bursts of cognition.

Second, the function looks less like passive holding and more like active control: in prefrontal working memory recordings, beta bursts and gamma bursts alternate, with gamma carrying the encoded content and beta apparently gating when that content is read out or cleared.

Spitzer and Haegens argued in eNeuro in 2017 that beta synchronisation is content-specific and can reactivate, rather than merely preserve, an endogenous cognitive set.

The through-line across all these versions is that beta is associated with control over content rather than with the content itself.

15.3.4 Phase coding, spike timing, and temporal reference frames

Phase coding means that information is carried by when a neuron fires within an ongoing cycle, not merely by how often it fires.

The founding demonstration is theta phase precession, reported by John O'Keefe and Michael Recce in 1993: as a rat crosses the firing field of a hippocampal place cell, the cell's spikes occur at progressively earlier phases of each successive theta cycle.

The consequence is that phase carries positional information that firing rate alone does not - rate tells you the animal is somewhere in the field, phase tells you where in the field - and Skaggs, McNaughton and colleagues showed in 1996 that across a population this compresses behavioural sequences lasting seconds into spike sequences lasting a theta cycle, which is short enough for spike-timing-dependent synaptic plasticity to act on.

The general principle is that an oscillation supplies a temporal reference frame, a shared clock against which individual spike times become meaningful, and without such a reference a spike five milliseconds early is indistinguishable from noise.

Huxter, Burgess and O'Keefe showed in Nature in 2003 that rate and phase can be varied independently in the same cell, which is the strongest single argument that phase is a genuinely separate coding channel rather than a side effect of rate.

15.4 The status of the oscillation as an explanation

This final section steps back and asks the uncomfortable question.

Rhythms are undeniably present and undeniably correlated with cognition, but presence and correlation are cheap, and a good deal of what is confidently written about oscillations outruns what has been shown.

15.4.1 Epiphenomenon or mechanism

An epiphenomenon is a by-product that accompanies a process without contributing to it, the way engine noise accompanies driving.

The sceptical case is that the LFP and EEG are summed synaptic currents, that rhythmicity in such a sum can arise from ordinary network properties without serving any computational role, and that showing an oscillation correlates with attention proves nothing about whether the oscillation does anything.

The case in favour points to evidence that the electric fields themselves feed back on neurons through ephaptic coupling - direct field effects on membrane potential that bypass synapses - and to rhythmic optogenetic experiments, such as work in ferret thalamocortical circuits published in 2024 showing that driving theta in higher-order visual thalamus improved sustained attention performance while driving alpha did not.

A useful reframing came from Doelling, Assaneo and colleagues in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2024, who argue that the debate conflates measurements with processes: the field potential is a measurement and may well be inert, while the underlying oscillatory process in the network may be entirely causal, and the two questions should be asked separately.

The current position of the field is genuinely divided, and any source that presents it as resolved in either direction is overstating.

15.4.2 Aperiodic broadband activity and the exponent as a separate signal

Every neural power spectrum contains, besides any peaks, a background that falls off with frequency in an approximately one-over-f pattern - more power at low frequencies, less at high, with no preferred cycle length.

This aperiodic component was long treated as noise to be subtracted or ignored, and that treatment produced a serious hidden error: if the background shifts, the power measured in a band shifts with it, so an apparent change in alpha power may be no change in the alpha rhythm at all.

Donoghue and colleagues, in Nature Neuroscience in 2020, introduced a parameterisation method, originally named fitting oscillations and one-over-f (FOOOF) and now generally called specparam, that separates a spectrum into aperiodic background plus genuine periodic peaks, and showed that some previously reported age-related declines in alpha are better explained as a flattening of the aperiodic exponent.

The exponent - the steepness of that falloff - is itself informative: steeper spectra are associated with greater inhibitory influence, flatter spectra with greater excitatory influence, so the exponent is used as an indirect index of excitation-inhibition balance, with reported changes across sleep and wakefulness, anaesthesia, aging, and Parkinsonian subthalamic recordings.

Two cautions.

The excitation-inhibition interpretation is an inference from modelling and pharmacology rather than a direct measurement, and a 2025 report linked some apparently cortical one-over-f age effects to cardiac contamination of the recording, so the measure is promising rather than clean.

Related to this, high-gamma above about 80 hertz is largely not an oscillation: Ray and Maunsell showed in PLOS Biology in 2011 that high-gamma and true gamma have different origins in macaque visual cortex, and that broadband high-gamma tracks local spiking, making it a useful proxy for firing rate rather than evidence of a rhythm.

15.4.3 Criticality, scale-free dynamics, and the critical brain hypothesis

The critical brain hypothesis holds that neural networks sit near a phase transition between quiescent and runaway activity, the point at which, in physical systems, information transmission and dynamic range are maximised.

The founding observation is Beggs and Plenz's 2003 discovery of neuronal avalanches in cortical slice cultures: cascades of activity whose sizes and durations follow power-law distributions with exponents matching a critical branching process, in which each active unit activates on average exactly one successor.

Scale-free means there is no characteristic size - avalanches of every magnitude occur in fixed proportion - and this signature has since been reported in awake primates, in human MEG, and in fMRI.

The criticisms are substantive rather than cosmetic.

Dehghani and colleagues found that avalanche sizes taken from actual spiking data in awake humans and monkeys did not show clean power-law scaling, even though simultaneously recorded LFPs did, which suggests the signature may be partly a property of the coarser measurement.

More broadly, power laws can be generated by many non-critical mechanisms, and subsampling a network can manufacture apparent scaling, so a fitted exponent is weak evidence on its own; the hypothesis remains attractive, unusually well specified for a brain-scale theory, and unproven.

15.4.4 Interventional evidence from rhythmic stimulation

The strongest way to test whether a rhythm matters is to impose one and see what happens to behaviour.

Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) applies a weak oscillating current through scalp electrodes, nudging membrane potentials up and down in time with the applied frequency, and numerous studies report frequency-specific behavioural effects.

Three limitations deserve emphasis for a beginner reading this literature.

First, the electrical artefact produced by tACS is far larger than the brain signal, so demonstrating entrainment in a simultaneously recorded EEG is technically very hard and often simply not done.

Second, the induced membrane fluctuation is subthreshold and largely stops when the current stops, so any lasting effect must be explained by plasticity - Wischnewski and colleagues in 2019 provided evidence that tACS after-effects depend on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-mediated plasticity - rather than by continuing entrainment.

Third, and most damaging, scalp currents also stimulate peripheral nerves in the skin and retina, and work by Asamoah, Khatoun and Mc Laughlin in 2019 showed that at least some classic tACS effects can be reproduced by stimulating peripheral nerves alone, which means transcranial does not automatically mean cortical.

Sensory entrainment offers a parallel cautionary tale: 40 hertz light and sound stimulation, the gamma entrainment using sensory stimuli (GENUS) protocol developed in Li-Huei Tsai's laboratory, reduced amyloid pathology in mouse models and produced encouraging early clinical signals in mild Alzheimer's disease, but a 2023 Nature Neuroscience study by Soula and colleagues reported that 40 hertz light did not robustly entrain native gamma oscillations in Alzheimer's model mice, and the clinical picture beyond small pilot and open-label extension studies remains unsettled.

Interventional work is the right instrument for this question; it has simply not yet delivered as clean an answer as the field would like.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Brain rhythms are real, are produced by identifiable circuits - parvalbumin basket cells for gamma, the medial septum for hippocampal theta, thalamic reticular circuits for spindles - and are not merely a smear of averaged noise.

They coordinate activity across frequency, through phase-amplitude coupling, and across space, through travelling waves and through the feedforward-gamma, feedback-alpha-beta division of the cortical hierarchy, which currently has the best-converged evidence of any functional oscillation theory.

The leading cognitive proposals - the theta-gamma code for item sequences, alpha as functional inhibition, beta bursts as control over cognitive content, and phase coding as demonstrated by theta phase precession - are well specified and supported by strong animal data, but each has a live and reasonable challenger in the human literature.

The causal status of oscillations is unresolved, and the most useful move available is Doelling and colleagues' distinction between the measured field potential, which may be inert, and the underlying network process, which may not be.

Two methodological lessons should outlast every specific theory in this chapter: much of what was once called high-gamma is broadband spiking rather than a rhythm, and band power cannot be interpreted at all without first separating the aperiodic background from the genuine periodic peak.


PART THREE. METHODS: HOW CLAIMS ABOUT COGNITION ARE MADE CHECKABLE


CHAPTER 16. BEHAVIOUR, PSYCHOPHYSICS, AND TASK DESIGN (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about the humblest and most important instrument in all of cognitive neuroscience - the task.

A task is a controlled situation that a person or an animal is placed in, together with a rule for what counts as a correct response.

Everything else in the field, every brain scan and every electrode recording, is interpreted by reference to what the participant was doing at the time.

If the task is badly designed, no amount of expensive neural measurement can rescue the conclusion.

So this chapter treats behaviour as an apparatus in its own right - something with a calibration, a resolution, a noise floor, and known failure modes.

We will move from the logic of behavioural measurement, through the mathematics of classical psychophysics, through the standard laboratory paradigms you will meet again and again, and finally out to the newer world of naturalistic and free behaviour.


16.1 Behaviour as the primary measurement

Behaviour is the only part of cognition that is directly observable.

Thoughts are not observable; button presses, eye movements, spoken words, and reaction times are.

Every claim about what a brain region "does" is ultimately a claim about a correlation between neural activity and some observable behaviour, so the quality of the behavioural measurement sets a hard ceiling on the quality of the neural claim.


16.1.1 Why no neural claim is interpretable without a behavioural anchor

Suppose a study reports that a patch of cortex "lights up" during a task.

That statement is empty until you know exactly what the participant was doing, what the comparison condition was, and whether performance actually differed between the two.

Krakauer, Ghazanfar, Gomez-Marin, MacIver and Poeppel made this argument forcefully in a 2017 paper in the journal Neuron titled Neuroscience Needs Behavior: Correcting a Reductionist Bias, arguing that modern tools for manipulating neural circuits - genetic targeting and optogenetics, the use of light to switch specific neurons on or off - have outrun the careful decomposition of the behaviour those circuits supposedly produce.

Their point is that if you silence a brain region and the animal stops doing something, you have learned very little unless you already have a precise theory of what that something is and what sub-processes it decomposes into.

The behavioural anchor is not a formality that precedes the interesting neural work; it is the thing that gives the neural work any meaning at all.


16.1.2 Accuracy, reaction time, and their joint modelling

The two workhorse measures of behaviour are accuracy - the proportion of responses that are correct - and reaction time, also called response time (RT), the interval between the appearance of a stimulus and the participant's response.

These two measures are not independent, and treating them separately creates a well known trap called the speed-accuracy tradeoff: a participant who slows down will usually become more accurate, so an apparent "improvement" in accuracy may be nothing more than a change in how cautious the participant chose to be.

The standard modern solution is to model the two jointly using an evidence accumulation model, the best known of which is the drift diffusion model (DDM) developed by Roger Ratcliff from 1978 onwards.

The DDM imagines that on each trial noisy evidence accumulates over time from a starting point until it hits one of two decision boundaries, and it fits the whole joint distribution of choices and response times - including the shape of the RT distribution for correct and for error responses - with a small number of interpretable parameters.

Those parameters separate the things that a raw accuracy score confounds: drift rate is the quality of the evidence, boundary separation is the participant's caution, non-decision time is the time spent on perception and motor execution that has nothing to do with deciding, and the starting point captures prior bias toward one response.

This decomposition matters clinically and developmentally, because a group difference in raw accuracy that looks like "worse perception" often turns out, under the model, to be a difference in caution or in motor speed instead.


16.1.3 The task as an operational definition of a construct

A construct is an unobservable theoretical entity such as attention, working memory, or inhibitory control.

Because constructs cannot be measured directly, researchers define them operationally - that is, they say that the construct is whatever the task measures.

When a paper says "we measured inhibitory control", what it actually did was measure the difference in reaction time between two conditions of, say, the Stroop task, and then assert that this difference indexes inhibition.

That assertion is a theoretical commitment, not a measurement, and it is where a great deal of confusion in the literature enters.

The honest reading of any behavioural result is therefore literal: the finding is about the task, and its extension to the construct is an inference that must be argued for.


16.1.4 Task impurity and the construct validity problem

Task impurity is the problem that no task measures one thing.

Any test of executive function - the family of processes that control and coordinate simpler ones - must embed that executive process inside some concrete activity involving perception, motor response, language, and motivation, so the score inevitably contains systematic variance from processes other than the one of interest.

Miyake and colleagues, in an influential year 2000 paper in Cognitive Psychology, addressed this by having participants perform several superficially different tasks that all tap the same putative ability, then using latent variable analysis - a statistical method that extracts only the variance shared across tasks - to isolate the common component.

Their unity and diversity framework proposed three separable but correlated executive functions: shifting between tasks, updating the contents of working memory, and inhibiting prevailing responses.

That framework is now one of the most cited models in the field, but it is genuinely contested: reanalyses published in the 2020s have argued that a substantial part of what the latent factors capture is task-specific variance rather than a general executive ability, and the inhibition factor in particular has repeatedly failed to emerge as a distinct construct in replication attempts.

Construct validity - the question of whether a measure really measures the thing it claims to - remains an open and active problem rather than a settled one.


16.2 Classical psychophysics

Psychophysics is the branch of experimental psychology, founded by Gustav Fechner in the nineteenth century, that measures the quantitative relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.

It is the oldest rigorous measurement tradition in psychology, and it supplies the mathematical machinery that most modern cognitive tasks still borrow.

Its central achievement is turning subjective report into a number with error bars.


16.2.1 Thresholds, psychometric functions, and adaptive staircases

A threshold is the stimulus intensity at which performance reaches some defined level - for example, the contrast at which an observer detects a faint patch on 75 percent of trials.

Plotting performance against stimulus intensity produces a psychometric function, an S-shaped curve whose position along the intensity axis gives the threshold and whose steepness gives the observer's sensitivity to small changes.

Measuring the whole curve by presenting many intensities equally often is wasteful, because trials far above or far below threshold are uninformative, so experimenters use adaptive procedures that concentrate trials near the threshold.

The simplest is the staircase, in which the stimulus is made harder after a correct response and easier after an error; the more efficient are Bayesian methods such as QUEST, introduced by Watson and Pelli in 1983, which maintains a running probability distribution over the likely threshold and places each new trial at its current best estimate.

Later generalisations - the Psi method of Kontsevich and Tyler in 1999, and Watson's QUEST+ in 2017 - estimate the slope as well as the threshold by choosing each stimulus to minimise the expected uncertainty of the posterior distribution.

One practical caution is well documented: a single staircase targeting one point on the curve gives biased slope estimates, so researchers interleave several staircases or use the Bayesian methods that estimate both parameters at once.


16.2.2 Signal detection theory: sensitivity and criterion

Signal detection theory (SDT) is the framework, given its definitive treatment by Green and Swets in 1966, that separates how well an observer can tell signal from noise from how willing that observer is to say "yes".

It assumes that both noise alone and signal-plus-noise produce internal evidence values drawn from overlapping distributions, and that the observer says "yes" whenever the evidence exceeds some internal criterion.

Two numbers follow: d prime, written d', is the distance between the two distributions in units of their standard deviation and indexes sensitivity; the criterion, often written c, indexes bias.

This distinction dissolves a classic confusion, because a person who reports seeing the stimulus more often may be either more sensitive or merely more liberal, and only SDT tells the two apart.

Practically, computing d' requires the hit rate - saying yes when the signal was present - and the false alarm rate - saying yes when it was absent - and a study that reports only accuracy has thrown away the information needed to separate sensitivity from bias.


16.2.3 Receiver operating characteristic analysis and confidence

If you ask an observer to hold different criteria - by changing the payoff, or by collecting confidence ratings - you can sweep out a whole curve of hit rate against false alarm rate, called the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.

The area under that curve is a measure of sensitivity that does not depend on where any single criterion was set, which makes it robust when bias differs across people or conditions.

The same machinery can be turned on confidence itself, giving what is called Type 2 analysis: instead of asking how well the observer discriminates signal from noise, you ask how well the observer's confidence discriminates their own correct responses from their own errors.

Maniscalco and Lau, in 2012, introduced meta-d', a measure defined as the first-order sensitivity that would have been required to produce the observed pattern of confidence ratings, and the ratio of meta-d' to d' gives metacognitive efficiency - how much of the available evidence a person actually uses when judging their own performance.

The approach is elegant and widely adopted, but it is not uncontested; papers appearing from 2022 onward have argued that its assumptions about how confidence is generated can distort the estimates, so meta-d' should be read as a model-dependent index rather than a direct readout of self-knowledge.


16.2.4 Weber, Fechner, and Stevens laws

Ernst Weber observed in the 1830s that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus - the just noticeable difference - is a roughly constant proportion of the baseline stimulus, so a weight must be increased by a fixed fraction, not a fixed number of grams, before the change is felt.

Fechner, in 1860, built on this to propose that sensation grows as the logarithm of stimulus intensity, which yields the familiar result that each further doubling of physical intensity buys a smaller and smaller increment of felt magnitude.

Stanley Smith Stevens challenged this in 1957 with the power law, in which sensation is proportional to intensity raised to an exponent that differs by modality - roughly 0.33 for brightness, near 1.0 for line length, and above 3.0 for electric shock, which is why shock feels like it escalates so violently.

The two laws are not merely alternative curve fits; they rest on different methods, Fechner's on accumulating just noticeable differences and Stevens's on asking observers to assign numbers directly to sensations, and the field has never fully resolved which method measures sensation and which measures the observer's use of numbers.

Commentaries continue into the 2020s - Algom's 2021 paper describes the very phrase "Weber-Fechner law" as a persistent misnomer, since Weber's empirical regularity does not by itself entail Fechner's logarithmic conclusion - and proposals for a unified law with an exponent lying between the two positions remain under discussion.


16.3 Canonical laboratory paradigms

Over roughly seventy years the field has converged on a modest number of tasks that recur in thousands of studies.

Learning them is not memorisation for its own sake; each was designed to isolate one specific inference, and knowing what that inference is tells you what the resulting neural data can and cannot support.


16.3.1 Attention: Posner cueing, visual search, attentional blink, change blindness

The Posner cueing task, devised by Michael Posner in 1980, asks participants to keep their eyes fixed on a central point while a cue - an arrow at the centre or a flash at the periphery - indicates where a target is likely to appear; responses are faster at cued locations and slower at uncued ones, which demonstrates that attention can move covertly, without the eyes moving at all.

Visual search, developed extensively by Anne Treisman and later by Jeremy Wolfe, measures how reaction time changes as the number of distracting items increases: some targets "pop out" with a flat search slope, implying parallel processing, while others require a slow item-by-item scan, implying serial deployment of attention.

The attentional blink, reported by Raymond, Shapiro and Arnell in 1992, uses rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP), a stream of items shown one after another in the same place, and shows that when two targets appear within about half a second of each other the second is frequently missed - evidence that attention has a refractory period in time as well as a location in space.

Change blindness, studied by Rensink, O'Regan and Clark in 1997 and by Simons and Levin, shows that large changes to a scene go unnoticed if the change coincides with a flicker, a blank frame, or an eye movement, which undermines the intuition that we hold a rich and complete internal picture of the world.

Together these four paradigms make the same underlying point from four directions: perception is selective, and what is not attended is very largely not seen.


16.3.2 Memory: free recall, recognition, paired associates, n-back, delayed match to sample

Free recall asks participants to study a list and then produce as many items as they can in any order, and it reveals the serial position curve - better memory for the first items, called primacy, and for the last items, called recency - which was one of the earliest pieces of evidence for separable memory stores.

Recognition presents items and asks whether each was studied, which is easier than recall and is the natural setting for signal detection analysis, because it yields hits and false alarms directly.

Paired associate learning, a paradigm going back to Hermann Ebbinghaus's self-experiments in the 1880s, requires learning arbitrary links between two items and then producing the second when given the first, and it isolates the formation of new associations rather than the strengthening of existing ones.

The n-back task presents a stream of items and asks whether the current one matches the item n positions earlier, with n typically between 1 and 3 and a 0-back condition serving as a control that requires vigilance but no memory updating; it is enormously popular in neuroimaging because it produces a clean parametric load manipulation.

Delayed match to sample shows a sample stimulus, imposes a blank delay, then asks whether a probe matches, and because it works in monkeys and rodents as well as humans it has been the main bridge between human working memory research and single-neuron recording; a BrainMap meta-analysis of 42 imaging studies found convergence in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and posterior parietal cortex.

A caution worth carrying forward is that n-back correlates only modestly with complex span tasks that are also called working memory measures, so the two are not interchangeable, and studies using one should not be read as straightforwardly confirming studies using the other.


16.3.3 Control: Stroop, flanker, go and no-go, stop signal, task switching

The Stroop task, published by John Ridley Stroop in 1935, asks participants to name the ink colour of a colour word, and responses are slower when word and ink conflict - for example the word RED printed in blue - which demonstrates that a highly practised process, reading, intrudes on a weaker one and must be suppressed.

The Eriksen flanker task, from 1974, surrounds a central target arrow with flanking arrows pointing either the same way or the opposite way, and the reaction time cost for incongruent flankers indexes the failure to restrict processing to the relevant location.

Go and no-go tasks require a response to frequent go stimuli and withholding on rare no-go stimuli, measuring the ability to refrain from an action that has already been prepared.

The stop signal task goes further: participants begin a response and are occasionally told to abort it, and by varying the delay of the stop signal one can estimate the stop signal reaction time (SSRT), a latent quantity that estimates how long the internal stopping process takes even though it produces no observable response.

Task switching alternates between two rules and measures the switch cost, the extra time and error incurred on trials where the rule changed, which indexes the reconfiguration of a task set.

These tasks share a serious and now well documented weakness: Hedge, Powell and Sumner, in a 2018 paper in Behavior Research Methods, tested the test-retest reliability of seven such tasks including flanker, Stroop, stop signal, go and no-go, and Posner cueing, and found reliabilities ranging from near zero to 0.82, mostly at the low end.

They named this the reliability paradox - a task can produce a rock-solid group-level effect precisely because everyone shows it to nearly the same degree, and that low between-person variance is exactly what makes the task useless for correlating with individual differences such as clinical status or brain structure.

The finding does not invalidate the experimental literature, but it does mean that any study correlating a Stroop or flanker score with anything else should be read with real caution, and work published since 2023 has focused on recalibrating these tasks to increase between-person variance.


16.3.4 Decision: random dot motion, two-armed bandit, intertemporal choice, gambling tasks

The random dot motion task presents a cloud of moving dots in which some fixed percentage - the coherence - move in a common direction while the rest move randomly, and the observer reports the overall direction; coherence provides a continuous difficulty knob, which is why the task, used by William Newsome, Michael Shadlen and colleagues from the late 1980s onward, became the setting in which evidence accumulation was first observed directly in single neurons of the macaque parietal cortex.

The two-armed bandit presents repeated choices between options with unknown reward probabilities and thereby operationalises the explore-exploit dilemma - whether to take the option currently believed best or to sample an alternative for information - and it distinguishes directed exploration, where choices are deliberately biased toward informative options, from random exploration produced by decision noise.

Intertemporal choice offers a smaller reward sooner against a larger reward later, and fitting the pattern of choices yields a discount rate that quantifies how steeply a person devalues delayed outcomes; steep discounting is reliably associated with addiction and other impulsive behaviours, though the direction of causation is unsettled.

The Iowa Gambling Task, introduced by Bechara, Damasio, Damasio and Anderson in 1994, has participants draw from four decks, two of which yield large immediate gains but larger occasional losses, and was designed as a test of Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis, the claim that bodily emotional signals guide advantageous choice.

The task is formally a four-armed bandit, and later computational reanalyses have argued that much of the performance it measures reflects ordinary reinforcement learning and exploration rather than emotional guidance specifically, so the original interpretation is disputed even though the task remains in wide clinical use.


16.4 Beyond the trial-based task

The trial-based task buys precision at the cost of realism.

Real cognition is continuous, self-paced, and embedded in a world that does not reset between trials, and a growing body of work argues that some phenomena simply do not appear under the strobe light of trial structure.

This section covers the methods built to study behaviour in that continuous regime.


16.4.1 Naturalistic viewing, narrative listening, and free behaviour

In a naturalistic paradigm, participants watch a film or listen to a spoken story while being scanned, with no task beyond attending.

The methodological breakthrough that made this analysable was intersubject correlation (ISC), introduced by Uri Hasson and colleagues in 2004, which sidesteps the absence of a stimulus model by correlating the time course of activity at each location in one participant's brain with the same location in another's; anything reliably driven by the stimulus will synchronise across people, and idiosyncratic noise will not.

ISC revealed a hierarchy of timescales, with early sensory areas tracking fast moment-to-moment changes and higher association areas integrating over tens of seconds of narrative context.

The practical advantages are considerable, especially with children and clinical groups: films hold attention, reduce head motion, and require no instruction.

The cost is interpretive - a film is what has been called a cognitive kitchen sink, engaging everything at once, so isolating a single process from it requires careful modelling of the stimulus after the fact rather than control of it beforehand.


16.4.2 Markerless pose tracking and computational ethology

Computational ethology is the effort to measure natural behaviour automatically and at scale, rather than having a human observer score video by hand.

Its enabling technology is markerless pose estimation: deep neural networks trained on a modest number of hand-labelled video frames that then locate body parts in every subsequent frame without any physical markers on the animal.

DeepLabCut, released by Mathis and colleagues in 2018, made this practical by adapting a human pose estimation network so that a few hundred labelled frames suffice to reach human-level labelling accuracy, and it has been applied to mice, flies, horses, cheetahs, and human infants.

SLEAP, from Pereira and colleagues in 2022, extended the approach to multiple interacting animals, which is the harder problem because identities must be maintained through occlusion - a requirement for any study of social behaviour.

Downstream methods then take the resulting pose time series and segment continuous movement into discrete recurring modules, an approach exemplified by Motion Sequencing (MoSeq) from the Datta laboratory, which identifies sub-second behavioural syllables and the grammar governing how they are strung together.

The promise is that behaviour can finally be described with the same resolution and objectivity as neural activity; the caveat is that a statistically discovered syllable is not automatically a meaningful behavioural unit, and validating that it is remains the hard part.


16.4.3 Ecological validity against experimental control

Ecological validity is the degree to which a laboratory situation resembles, and generalises to, the circumstances of real life.

Experimental control is the ability to hold everything constant except one manipulated variable so that a causal inference is licensed.

These two virtues genuinely trade off, and the field disagrees about the exchange rate: the classical position is that without control you cannot attribute an effect to any cause, while critics reply that models built under tight control often fail to explain variance outside the exact conditions of the manipulation.

A 2021 paper by Nastase, Goldstein and Hasson, titled Keep it real, argues explicitly for rethinking the primacy of experimental control, on the grounds that stripped-down stimuli may engage systems in ways unrepresentative of their normal operation.

The pragmatic resolution now emerging is a division of labour rather than a winner: controlled tasks establish mechanism, naturalistic paradigms test whether the mechanism survives contact with real input, and virtual reality and mobile recording sit between them by allowing a rich environment that is nonetheless fully specified and repeatable.


16.4.4 Eye tracking, pupillometry, and other peripheral measures

Eye tracking records where the gaze is directed, typically by imaging the reflection of infrared light from the cornea, and it supplies a continuous readout of attentional selection during free viewing where there are no button presses to score.

Pupillometry measures the diameter of the pupil, which changes not only with light level but with mental effort, surprise, and arousal, giving a cheap non-invasive index of internal state.

The physiological basis is reasonably well understood: cognitively driven dilation is thought to arise largely through the locus coeruleus - noradrenaline system, a small brainstem nucleus that projects noradrenaline throughout the brain and modulates arousal and neural gain, and whose activity inhibits the parasympathetic pathway that constricts the pupil.

That said, the mapping is not one-to-one - pupil size is influenced by luminance, by accommodation, and by other neuromodulatory systems - so pupil diameter is best treated as a correlate of arousal rather than a direct measurement of locus coeruleus firing, and careful studies control luminance explicitly.

Other peripheral measures round out the picture: blink rate has been proposed as an index of dopaminergic tone, though the evidence is mixed; skin conductance tracks sympathetic arousal; and heart rate variability indexes autonomic balance.

Their shared virtue is that they report on internal state continuously and without requiring the participant to do anything, which makes them the natural partner for the naturalistic paradigms of the preceding sub-sections.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Behaviour is the primary measurement in cognitive neuroscience, and the interpretability of any neural result is capped by the quality of the task that produced it.

Accuracy and reaction time must be modelled jointly, because the speed-accuracy tradeoff means either one alone can mislead, and evidence accumulation models such as Ratcliff's drift diffusion model separate evidence quality from caution and from motor speed.

Classical psychophysics supplies the tools that make subjective report quantitative - psychometric functions and adaptive threshold procedures, and signal detection theory's separation of sensitivity from decision criterion - and these tools remain indispensable rather than historical.

The canonical paradigms of attention, memory, control, and decision each isolate a specific inference, but two structural problems limit them: task impurity means no task measures one construct cleanly, and the reliability paradox documented by Hedge and colleagues in 2018 means the most robust group-level tasks are often the worst measures of individual differences.

Naturalistic paradigms, intersubject correlation, markerless pose tracking, and peripheral measures such as pupillometry extend measurement into continuous free behaviour, at the price of the tight control that licensed causal inference in the first place.

The mature position is not to choose between control and realism but to require that a mechanism established under control also survives being tested in the wild.


CHAPTER 17. RECORDING NEURONS AND POPULATIONS (APPARATUS)

Every claim in this book about what a neuron or a population of neurons is doing rests on a physical measurement made by a physical instrument.

This chapter is about those instruments.

It explains how electrical activity is picked up from single cells and from crowds of cells, how light can be used instead of wire, and what the slow smeared signal called the local field potential actually is.

It also explains, at the end, what these methods cannot do, because a method's blind spots shape the theories built on top of it just as much as its strengths do.

If you understand the apparatus, you can read a neuroscience paper and ask the right question, which is not only what did they find but what could they have found.


17.1 Electrophysiology at cellular resolution

Electrophysiology means measuring the electrical activity of living cells.

Neurons work by moving charged particles called ions across their outer membrane, and this movement makes voltages that an electrode - a fine conductor placed in or near the tissue - can pick up.

The methods in this section all aim at cellular resolution, meaning the measurement can be attributed to an identified individual cell rather than to a vague neighbourhood.

They differ in how invasive they are, how long they last, and how many cells they capture at once, and those three properties trade off against each other constantly.


17.1.1 Sharp electrodes, patch clamp, and in vivo whole-cell recording

The oldest cellular method is the sharp electrode, a glass pipette pulled to a very fine tip and pushed through the neuron's membrane so that its interior voltage can be read directly.

It works, but the puncture leaks, the cell is injured, and recordings are often short.

Patch clamp, developed by Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann in the late 1970s and honoured with the 1991 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, replaced puncture with suction: a blunt pipette is pressed against the membrane and gentle suction forms a very high resistance seal, so that the tiny currents through even a single ion channel - a protein pore that lets specific ions cross the membrane - can be resolved.

In the whole-cell configuration the patch of membrane under the pipette is then ruptured, giving low-noise access to the whole cell's voltage and current while also allowing the experimenter to dialyse chemicals into it.

Doing this in a living animal rather than a slice of tissue was systematised by Troy Margrie and colleagues in 2002, who showed that a pipette advanced blindly through the intact brain, without seeing the target cell, could obtain stable whole-cell recordings from neurons hundreds to thousands of micrometres deep, including in awake head-fixed animals.

Later variants use two-photon microscopy to aim the pipette at a genetically labelled cell, and robotic systems now automate the seal-hunting steps, but the cost of the family remains the same: exquisite detail from one or a few cells at a time, for tens of minutes at best.


17.1.2 Extracellular single-unit and multi-unit recording

Extracellular recording leaves the membrane intact and simply listens from outside, picking up the brief voltage transient that an action potential - the all-or-none electrical pulse a neuron fires - creates in the fluid around the cell.

Because the signal falls off steeply with distance, an electrode only hears cells within roughly a hundred micrometres, and the waveform it records is a distorted, low-amplitude shadow of the intracellular event.
