When the activity of one identified cell can be isolated, the result is called a single unit; when several nearby cells contribute an inseparable hash of spikes, it is called multi-unit activity.

This is the method behind most of the classical findings of systems neuroscience, including David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's orientation-selective cells in cat visual cortex in the late 1950s and 1960s and John O'Keefe's hippocampal place cells in 1971.

Its great virtues are that it is stable for hours, works in behaving animals, and preserves millisecond timing; its great limitation is that it tells you almost nothing about the cell's identity, shape, or internal state.


17.1.3 Spike sorting and its uncertainties

Spike sorting is the computational step that takes the raw extracellular voltage trace and decides which detected spikes came from which neuron, usually by clustering spikes according to their waveform shape and their pattern across nearby recording sites.

It is an inference, not a measurement, and this is easy to forget when a paper reports a tidy number of neurons.

Two errors haunt it: over-merging, where two cells with similar waveforms are treated as one, and over-splitting, where one bursting cell whose spike shrinks during a burst is treated as two.

Modern algorithms such as Kilosort, developed by Marius Pachitariu and colleagues and now in its fourth version, published in Nature Methods in 2024, fit a template model to the whole recording and perform far better than manual clustering, with the reported trade-off that Kilosort4 raises recall - it recovers more of the true spikes - at some cost in precision, meaning more false positives.

Validation is genuinely hard because true answers are scarce, so the field relies on simulated data and on rare paired recordings where a cell is patched and recorded extracellularly at the same time; community benchmarks such as SpikeForest, published by Jeremy Magland and colleagues in eLife in 2020, and the SpikeInterface framework of Alessio Buccino and colleagues in 2020, exist precisely because different sorters give different answers on the same data.

The honest position is that unit counts and single-neuron tuning curves carry a sorting-dependent error bar that is rarely quoted.


17.1.4 High-density silicon probes and the Neuropixels generation

For decades an experiment meant a handful of wires and a handful of cells; silicon microfabrication changed the scale by putting hundreds of recording sites on a single shank thinner than a human hair.

The Neuropixels probe, introduced by James Jun, Nicholas Steinmetz, Timothy Harris and colleagues in Nature in 2017, put 960 sites along a 10 millimetre shank with the amplifiers and digitiser built into the same piece of silicon, so that hundreds of neurons across several brain regions could be recorded at once from one insertion.

Neuropixels 2.0, reported by Steinmetz and colleagues in Science in 2021, shrank the hardware for chronic implantation in small freely moving mammals, offered more than 5000 sites, and paired the hardware with software that corrects for the brain drifting relative to the probe, allowing the same neurons to be followed for more than two months.

Denser successors continue to appear, with a 2025 Neuron report from the Neuropixels group showing that ultra-high site density improves both the detection of spikes and the confidence with which they are assigned to cells.

Two consequences matter for cognition research: brain-wide simultaneous recording is now routine enough that population-level claims can be tested directly rather than stitched together across animals, and dense sites reduce, though they do not eliminate, the sorting ambiguity described above, because a spike seen on many sites carries a spatial fingerprint as well as a shape.


17.2 Optical recording

Optical methods swap the electrode for a microscope, using molecules that change their fluorescence when a neuron is active.

The immediate gain is identity: you see where each signal comes from, you can label a genetically defined cell type, and you can return to the same cells tomorrow.

The immediate loss is time and directness, since most optical reporters track a chemical proxy for electrical activity rather than the voltage itself, and cameras are slower than amplifiers.

The rest of this section walks through the main optical families and what each one buys and costs.


17.2.1 Genetically encoded calcium indicators and two-photon imaging

When a neuron fires, voltage-gated calcium channels open and the concentration of calcium ions inside the cell rises sharply, so calcium is a usable stand-in for spiking.

A genetically encoded calcium indicator (GECI) is a fluorescent protein engineered so that binding calcium changes how brightly it glows, and because it is encoded in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) it can be delivered by a virus or bred into an animal and restricted to chosen cell types.

The GCaMP family, developed by Junichi Nakai and colleagues from 2001 and refined through GCaMP6 by Tsai-Wen Chen, Loren Looger, Karel Svoboda and colleagues in Nature in 2013, made single action potentials detectable in favourable conditions; the jGCaMP8 series from Janelia in 2023 cut the rise time substantially, so fast spike trains are better resolved.

These indicators are usually read with two-photon microscopy, in which two low-energy infrared photons must arrive at a molecule almost simultaneously to excite it, which confines excitation to a tiny focal volume and allows imaging several hundred micrometres deep in scattering brain tissue with little out-of-focus damage.

The unavoidable caveat is that calcium is slower than voltage: the fluorescence signal rises in milliseconds but decays over hundreds of milliseconds, so spike times must be inferred by deconvolution, sub-threshold activity is invisible, and low firing rates are easily missed.


17.2.2 Voltage indicators and their speed-sensitivity trade-off

A genetically encoded voltage indicator (GEVI) reports membrane voltage directly, removing the calcium middleman and in principle giving access to both spikes and the sub-threshold fluctuations that calcium hides.

The difficulty is physical rather than merely technical.

A voltage indicator must sit in the thin plasma membrane, so there are far fewer molecules to emit light than for a calcium sensor that fills the whole cell body, and resolving an action potential requires sampling at roughly a kilohertz, which leaves very little time per frame to collect photons.

This is the photon budget problem, and it forces designers to trade among brightness, speed, voltage sensitivity, and photostability - resistance to bleaching under the intense light needed for fast imaging.

Progress is real: rhodopsin-based and fluorescent-protein-based sensors now record spikes in awake animals, and 2025 reports describe indicators engineered specifically for photostability to allow long recordings, with two-photon voltage imaging remaining an active and difficult frontier.

For now, voltage imaging is best treated as a powerful specialist tool for small numbers of cells rather than a routine replacement for calcium imaging.


17.2.3 Miniature head-mounted microscopes in freely moving animals

Two-photon microscopes are heavy tabletop instruments, which historically meant the animal's head had to be fixed in place, ruling out the natural behaviours that most interest a student of cognition.

The miniature microscope, or miniscope, introduced by Kunal Ghosh, Mark Schnitzer and colleagues in Nature Methods in 2011, solved this by integrating a light source, lens, and image sensor into a device light enough to be carried on a mouse's head.

The bargain is explicit: miniscopes use one-photon illumination, so they give up the optical sectioning of two-photon microscopy and accept a blurrier image with more background from out-of-focus cells, in exchange for a freely moving animal.

Combined with an implanted gradient-index lens they can reach deep structures such as the hippocampus, and open-source designs such as the UCLA Miniscope and the widefield mesoscale version reported by Mathew Rynes and colleagues in Nature Methods in 2021 have made the approach widely available.

Much of what is now known about how hippocampal maps and amygdala fear representations change across days in behaving mice comes from this instrument.


17.2.4 Light-sheet and whole-brain imaging in transparent preparations

Some animals are small and transparent enough that the entire brain can be imaged at once, and the larval zebrafish, with roughly 100,000 neurons, is the standard example.

Light-sheet microscopy illuminates the specimen with a thin sheet of light from the side and photographs the illuminated plane from above, so only the plane being imaged is exposed, which makes volume scanning fast and gentle.

Misha Ahrens, Philipp Keller and colleagues, in Nature Methods in 2013, used this to record calcium activity from more than 80 per cent of the neurons in the larval zebrafish brain at single-cell resolution, covering the whole volume in about 1.3 seconds.

This is the closest existing approach to observing an entire vertebrate brain in action, and it has been extended to behaving and even virtual-reality-navigating fish.

Its limits are as clear as its power: the preparation must be transparent and usually immobilised, the sampling rate of roughly one brain volume per second is far slower than neural computation, and generalising from a larval fish to a mammal is a real inferential leap.


17.3 The local field potential and its relatives

Not every useful signal is a spike.

If you low-pass filter an extracellular recording, discarding the fast transients, you are left with a slow undulating voltage called the local field potential, which reflects the pooled activity of many cells and many synapses around the electrode.

Its relatives are electrocorticography, recorded from the brain's surface, and electroencephalography, recorded from the scalp, which are the same physics viewed from further away and through more tissue.

Understanding what these signals are made of determines what may legitimately be concluded from them.


17.3.1 Physical origin of the local field potential

The local field potential (LFP) is the low-frequency part of the extracellular voltage, conventionally below about 300 hertz, and its ultimate source is transmembrane ionic current, meaning charge crossing neuronal membranes.

In the influential 2012 review by György Buzsáki, Costas Anastassiou and Christof Koch in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, the largest contributor is synaptic current - current flowing where one neuron's terminals act on another's dendrites - but sodium and calcium spikes, currents through voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels, and intrinsic membrane oscillations all shape the field as well.

Geometry matters enormously: cortical pyramidal cells are elongated and aligned in parallel, so their currents add up into an open field that is measurable, whereas symmetric star-shaped cells largely cancel their own contributions and are nearly invisible.

Two important consequences follow.

First, the LFP is not simply local, because volume conduction spreads voltages through the tissue and a signal recorded at one site may originate hundreds of micrometres away or further.

Second, an LFP oscillation cannot be assumed to mean that the neurons near the electrode are firing, since strong synaptic input onto silent cells also produces a large field.


17.3.2 Current source density analysis

Current source density (CSD) analysis is the standard remedy for volume conduction, and it works by taking the second spatial derivative of the voltage measured at a row of evenly spaced contacts, which converts a smeared potential into an estimate of where current actually enters and leaves cells.

A sink is a location where current flows into neurons, typically indicating excitatory synaptic input, and a source is where it flows back out.

The method was developed for cortex and systematised by Ulla Mitzdorf, whose 1985 review remains the standard reference and whose visual cortex work with Wolf Singer in the late 1970s established the interpretive conventions still used.

Its assumptions should be stated because they are frequently violated: it presumes that activity is uniform in the plane perpendicular to the electrode and that extracellular conductivity is constant, and where either fails the estimated sinks are distorted.

Inverse CSD methods, developed by Klas Pettersen, Gaute Einevoll and colleagues from 2006, relax some of these assumptions by fitting an explicit forward model of the tissue instead of differentiating blindly.


17.3.3 Laminar recording and depth profiles

The cerebral cortex is built in six layers that differ in what they receive and where they send, with layer 4 the principal recipient of input from the thalamus, the deep relay station that feeds sensory signals to cortex, and layers 2 and 3 sending output to other cortical areas while layers 5 and 6 project subcortically.

A laminar probe is a single shank carrying many contacts spaced along its length, inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface so that all layers are sampled at once, which makes it possible to ask which layer a signal starts in.

The classic use is to identify the earliest current sink after a sensory stimulus, which marks the feedforward input layer and thereby anchors the depth coordinate of the whole recording, letting sources above and below it be assigned to superficial and deep layers.

This is how the field distinguishes feedforward from feedback processing empirically rather than by assumption, and Neuropixels probes have sharpened it further, as in the 2024 work of Xiaomo Chen, Marc Mancarella and colleagues on high-resolution laminar identification in macaque primary visual cortex.

Layer assignment from physiology alone is still an estimate, and careful studies confirm it against histology - the anatomical examination of stained tissue after the experiment.


17.4 What recording can and cannot show

The preceding sections describe increasingly powerful instruments.

This section is the counterweight, because the growth in the number of neurons recorded has not removed the fundamental interpretive problems, and in some cases has hidden them behind larger numbers.

Each sub-section names one limitation that should be held in mind whenever a result in this book is described as measured.


17.4.1 Sampling bias toward large and active cells

An extracellular electrode hears large cells more easily than small ones, because a bigger cell body and thicker processes drive a bigger extracellular current, and it hears frequently firing cells more easily than rare ones, because a cell that fires a handful of spikes in an hour will never form a cluster that spike sorting can recognise.

The consequence is that the recorded sample is not a random sample of the population, and inhibitory interneurons, granule cells, and very sparsely firing cells are systematically under-represented.

Shy Shoham, Daniel O'Connor and Ronen Segev raised this squarely in the Journal of Comparative Physiology A in 2006, asking whether neuroscience has a dark matter problem, by analogy with the astronomical matter that cannot be seen directly, and arguing that many brain areas are far more sparsely active than electrode studies suggest.

Optical imaging has a partly complementary bias, since it can see silent cells that express the indicator but is biased by expression level, depth, and the difficulty of detecting low firing rates in a slow calcium signal.

A 2021 eLife study by Joshua Siegle, Peter Ledochowitsch and colleagues at the Allen Institute compared the two methods on matched populations in mouse visual cortex and found systematic differences in the apparent tuning of neurons, differences that could be largely reconciled once selection and detection biases were modelled - a useful demonstration that the instrument leaves fingerprints on the result.


17.4.2 Chronic stability and cellular drift

Following the same neuron across days is harder than it sounds, for two quite different reasons that are easy to confuse.

The first is mechanical and biological: the brain moves relative to the implant, tissue reacts to the foreign body, and waveforms change, so the cell you call number 47 today may not be the cell you called number 47 last week.

Hardware and software improvements have made real progress here, and Neuropixels 2.0 with automatic drift correction demonstrated tracking of the same units for more than two months.

The second reason is not an artefact at all.

Representational drift is the finding that the mapping between stimulus and neural response itself changes over days even when behaviour and stimulus are constant, reported in mouse visual cortex by Daniel Deitch, Alon Rubin and Yaniv Ziv in Current Biology in 2021 and by Carl Schoonover, Sarah Fink and colleagues in piriform cortex in Nature in 2021, and observed in hippocampal place codes over weeks.

Whether drift reflects ongoing memory storage and synaptic turnover, or whether some of it remains measurement instability, is still argued in the literature, and interestingly the amount of drift depends on the stimulus, with responses to simple gratings staying far more stable than responses to natural movies.


17.4.3 Correlation without causation at the population level

A neuron whose firing predicts a decision may be causing the decision, may be reporting it after the fact, or may be driven by the same upstream input that causes it.

Recording alone cannot distinguish these, and the problem worsens rather than improves with population recordings, because in a large simultaneously recorded population many patterns will correlate with behaviour by construction.

The standard remedy is perturbation: change the activity and see whether behaviour changes, using microstimulation, as in the classic experiments of Chieko Salzman, Kenneth Britten and William Newsome, published in Nature in 1990, in which stimulating motion-selective cells in the macaque middle temporal area (MT), a region specialised for visual motion, biased the animal's perceptual judgement in the predicted direction, or using optogenetics, in which light-sensitive proteins are expressed in chosen cells so light can turn them on or off.

Perturbation carries its own interpretive traps.

Broad optogenetic stimulation drives many neurons at once and in unnatural synchrony, so a behavioural effect need not implicate the specific pattern that was correlated with behaviour, and conversely a null result can mean either that the correlated activity was epiphenomenal or that the circuit compensated, a point pressed by Steffen Wolff and Bence Ölveczky in their 2018 review of the promise and perils of causal circuit manipulations.

Two-photon holographic optogenetics, which can address chosen individual neurons with cellular precision, is the current attempt to make perturbations specific enough to license causal claims, and it is still an emerging method rather than a settled one.


17.4.4 Species and preparation constraints on generalisation

Almost everything in the preceding sections is done in mice, rats, macaques, zebrafish, flies, and slices of tissue, because the methods are invasive.

Human single-neuron data exist, but only from patients undergoing clinical procedures such as epilepsy monitoring with implanted depth electrodes, which means small samples, atypical brains, and electrode placements chosen by clinical need rather than scientific question - the work of Itzhak Fried, Rodrigo Quian Quiroga and colleagues on human medial temporal lobe neurons is the leading example.

Preparation matters too, since anaesthesia changes cortical dynamics substantially, head fixation constrains behaviour, and a brain slice has lost most of its long-range inputs.

None of this makes animal work invalid, and homologies across mammals are often strong, but the inference from a head-fixed anaesthetised mouse to a human deliberating over a choice is a chain with several weak links that should be named rather than skipped.

The practical rule is to ask, of any finding, which species, which preparation, which behavioural state, and to treat convergence across those conditions as the real evidence.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Claims about neurons rest on instruments, and each instrument has a characteristic bargain: patch clamp buys detail at the cost of yield and duration, extracellular arrays buy yield and stability at the cost of cellular identity, calcium imaging buys identity and cell-type specificity at the cost of temporal precision, and voltage imaging buys directness at the cost of a punishing photon budget.

High-density probes such as Neuropixels and whole-brain light-sheet imaging have raised the number of simultaneously recorded neurons by orders of magnitude since 2013, which makes population-level claims directly testable for the first time.

The local field potential is a real and useful signal, but it is a pooled, geometry-dependent, volume-conducted quantity, and only analyses such as current source density on laminar probes can localise its sources with any confidence.

Larger recordings have not solved the interpretive problems: spike sorting remains an inference with an unquoted error bar, sampling is biased toward large and active cells, the same cell is hard to hold across days and its tuning may genuinely drift, and correlation with behaviour still requires perturbation before it can be called causation.

Read every result in the chapters that follow with the apparatus in mind, and ask not only what was found but what the instrument was capable of finding.


CHAPTER 18. NON-INVASIVE ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY IN HUMANS (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about the two instruments that let us watch the living human brain work on the brain's own timescale, without opening the skull.

Those instruments are electroencephalography (EEG), which records tiny voltages on the scalp, and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which records the almost unimaginably faint magnetic fields those same currents produce.

Both are millisecond-accurate, and that matters, because cognition happens in milliseconds - a word is recognised, a conflict is detected, an error is registered, all inside a few tenths of a second.

The chapter explains what physically generates the signal, how the signal is referenced and cleaned, how it is carved into named components and rhythms, and how researchers try, with limited success, to say where inside the head it came from.

The honest theme running through the chapter is that these methods buy exquisite timing at the price of poor spatial certainty, and that every step from scalp voltage to claim about cognition adds assumptions that must be stated out loud.


18.1 Electroencephalography

Electroencephalography (EEG) is the recording of the brain's electrical activity from electrodes placed on the scalp.

Hans Berger, a psychiatrist working in Jena, Germany, published the first human scalp recordings in 1929, and described the rhythm at roughly eight to thirteen cycles per second that appears when a relaxed person closes their eyes - what we now call the alpha rhythm.

A century later the apparatus is far better but the principle is identical: a difference in voltage between two points on the head, sampled hundreds or thousands of times per second, amplified, and stored.

EEG is cheap relative to every other functional brain method, it is portable, it is tolerant of participants who are children or patients, and it is the only method that can be run for hours in a hospital ward or overnight in a sleep laboratory.

Its weaknesses are equally structural, and the rest of this section works through them.


18.1.1 Physical basis: synchronous postsynaptic currents in aligned pyramidal cells

What the scalp electrode picks up is not the action potential - the brief all-or-nothing electrical spike a neuron fires down its axon - but the postsynaptic potential, the slower voltage change produced in a neuron's dendrites (its receiving branches) when a synapse acts on it.

Postsynaptic potentials last tens of milliseconds rather than one or two, so they overlap in time and can add up, whereas action potentials are too brief and too unsynchronised to sum appreciably at a distance.

The cells that dominate the EEG are the cortical pyramidal cells, large excitatory neurons whose long apical dendrite runs perpendicular to the cortical surface, so that a whole population of them is geometrically aligned like a field of parallel batteries.

When thousands of these aligned cells receive synaptic input at the same instant, current flows into the dendrite at one depth and out at another, creating a current dipole (a paired current source and sink, describable as a small arrow with a direction and a strength), and at distances more than a few times the diameter of the active patch the summed activity behaves as a single dipole.

Three conditions are therefore required for a scalp-visible EEG signal - the cells must be many, they must be geometrically aligned so their dipoles point the same way rather than cancelling, and they must be active in near synchrony - which is why deep, radially disorganised nuclei contribute almost nothing to the surface record.

A practical consequence worth stating plainly: an increase in EEG amplitude does not straightforwardly mean more neural activity, because it can equally mean the same amount of activity that has become more synchronous.


18.1.2 Montages, references, and volume conduction

Voltage is never absolute; it is always a difference between two points, so every EEG channel is a comparison between an active electrode and some reference, and the arrangement of those comparisons is called a montage.

Common choices are a single physical reference such as the nose, mastoid or linked earlobes; a bipolar montage in which each channel is the difference between two neighbouring electrodes; the common average reference, which subtracts the mean of all electrodes; and the surface Laplacian, which subtracts a weighted average of an electrode's immediate neighbours.

The reference is not a neutral bookkeeping decision - it changes the apparent size, sign, and scalp location of every effect, because no point on a head is truly at zero potential, and a reference sitting near active tissue injects that tissue's activity, with opposite sign, into every channel.

The deeper problem is volume conduction, the fact that the head is a conductor, so current from one small cortical patch spreads through brain, cerebrospinal fluid, skull and scalp and reaches many electrodes at once, smearing a compact source over a broad region of the scalp.

Volume conduction is instantaneous, which is why it is so dangerous for connectivity analyses: two electrodes can appear perfectly correlated simply because they are both seeing the same single source, with no communication between two brain regions involved at all.

The surface Laplacian, which is a spatial second derivative and therefore emphasises what is locally sharp, is one standard countermeasure because it is reference-free and sharpens the topography, at the cost of discarding genuinely broad sources; the Reference Electrode Standardization Technique (REST) is another, estimating a theoretical infinity reference using a model of how the head conducts.

There is no consensus best choice, and the defensible practice is to state the reference, justify it, and where a result might hinge on it, show that it survives an alternative.


18.1.3 Artefact sources and correction

An artefact is any recorded voltage that did not come from the brain, and in EEG the artefacts are often far larger than the signal of interest.

The eye is the worst offender, because the eyeball is itself a standing dipole - positive at the cornea, negative at the retina - so every blink and every saccade sweeps a large voltage across the frontal electrodes, typically tens or hundreds of microvolts against an event-related signal of a few microvolts.

Muscle activity from the jaw, neck and scalp, recorded as electromyography (EMG), contaminates chiefly the higher frequencies and is a notorious source of spurious gamma-band findings; the heartbeat, sweating, electrode movement, cable movement, and mains electrical interference at fifty or sixty cycles per second complete the usual list.

Correction rather than mere rejection is now standard, and the workhorse is independent component analysis (ICA), a blind source separation technique that decomposes the multi-channel recording into maximally statistically independent components, some of which have the unmistakable topography and time course of blinks, lateral eye movements, or a single noisy electrode, and can be subtracted.

Regression-based correction, which estimates how much of a frontal electrode's signal is predicted by a simultaneously recorded electrooculogram (EOG, an electrode placed near the eye) and removes that fraction, is older, simpler, and still effective for blinks; Artefact Subspace Reconstruction (ASR) learns a statistical model of clean calibration data and attenuates transient high-amplitude bursts, which is what makes it popular for recordings made while people move.

Every correction method removes some brain signal along with the artefact, and ICA in particular depends on a human or an automatic classifier deciding which components are junk, so artefact handling is a documented analytic choice and not a neutral cleaning step.


18.1.4 High-density and mobile electroencephalography

Standard clinical EEG uses about nineteen to thirty-two electrodes placed by the international 10-20 system, a scheme that names positions by proportional distances between skull landmarks so that recordings are comparable across differently sized heads.

High-density EEG means sixty-four, one hundred and twenty-eight, or two hundred and fifty-six channels, and the point is not prettier maps but better spatial sampling for source analysis, since a sparse array cannot represent the spatial detail that the inverse methods of section 18.4 need.

The historic cost of high density was preparation time, because each electrode needed conductive gel and skin abrasion; dry electrodes, which contact the scalp mechanically without gel, have narrowed that gap - Fiedler and colleagues reported in 2021 a two-hundred-and-fifty-six-channel dry cap achieving eighty-four per cent channel reliability with a sixty-nine per cent reduction in preparation time, and resting alpha and pattern-reversal visual evoked responses that matched a gel system on most measures, though with a higher proportion of bad channels.

Mobile EEG carries the same idea further: battery-powered amplifiers, wireless transmission and lightweight caps allow recording while a person walks, cycles, converses, or moves through a real environment, an approach usually called mobile brain and body imaging.

The honest caveat is that mobility multiplies exactly the artefacts of section 18.1.3, so mobile findings should be read with attention to how motion and muscle contamination were controlled, and the field's best practice is to record motion explicitly, with accelerometers or motion capture, so that it can be modelled rather than hoped away.


18.2 Magnetoencephalography

Magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures the magnetic fields produced by the very same neural currents that produce the EEG.

Any electric current generates a magnetic field circling around it, so the two methods are two views of one physical event rather than two different phenomena.

David Cohen at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology made the first magnetic recording of the human alpha rhythm in 1968 using a copper induction coil in a shielded room, and in 1972 repeated it with a vastly more sensitive superconducting detector, which is the point at which MEG became a practical method.

The fields involved are around one hundred femtotesla, that is one hundred quadrillionths of a tesla, which is roughly a billion times weaker than the Earth's magnetic field - a fact that dictates almost everything about how MEG systems are built.


18.2.1 Physical basis and tangential-source sensitivity

MEG is generated principally by the intracellular current flowing lengthwise inside the dendrites of synchronously active pyramidal cells, whereas EEG reflects the associated extracellular return currents; both arise from the same postsynaptic events.

The direction of the magnetic field around a current follows the right-hand rule, which produces a strong geometric asymmetry: a current flowing tangentially, that is parallel to the scalp surface, wraps its field so that the field exits the head and can be detected outside it.

A current flowing radially, straight out towards the scalp, produces a field that in an idealised spherical head closes entirely inside the head and is invisible from outside, so MEG is largely blind to radial sources.

Because cortex is folded, this maps onto anatomy: neurons in the walls of the sulci - the infoldings - are oriented tangentially and are seen well by MEG, whereas neurons at the crowns of the gyri are oriented radially and are seen poorly.

EEG has no such blind spot, which is the main reason the two methods are complementary rather than redundant, and why combined EEG-MEG recording measurably improves source estimates.

A second geometric advantage of MEG is that magnetic fields are barely distorted by the skull, because the skull's magnetic permeability is essentially that of free space, whereas its low electrical conductivity smears the EEG badly.


18.2.2 Superconducting quantum interference device and optically pumped magnetometer systems

The classical MEG sensor is the superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), a superconducting loop interrupted by weak links whose output changes measurably in response to fractions of a single quantum of magnetic flux, making it one of the most sensitive detectors of any physical quantity ever built.

SQUIDs must be held near four kelvin, about minus two hundred and sixty-nine degrees Celsius, so they sit in a helmet-shaped vessel of liquid helium with a vacuum gap for thermal insulation, which fixes them in a rigid one-size helmet several centimetres from the scalp and requires costly periodic helium refills.

Whole-head SQUID systems use hundreds of channels arranged as magnetometers or as gradiometers - paired coils wired in opposition, so that a distant uniform disturbance affects both equally and cancels while a nearby brain source does not - and they sit inside a magnetically shielded room built of layered mu-metal and aluminium.

The newer alternative is the optically pumped magnetometer (OPM), a small cell of alkali vapour, typically rubidium, in which a laser polarises the atoms and the transmitted light reports how an external magnetic field disturbs them.

OPMs run at or near room temperature, so they can be mounted in a helmet or cap millimetres from the scalp, and because magnetic field strength falls sharply with distance this proximity yields substantially larger signals - reported gains of several-fold in amplitude, with recent comparison studies finding signal-to-noise improvements of the order of forty per cent over conventional MEG and considerably more over EEG.

Because the sensor array moves with the head, OPM-MEG tolerates movement provided the background field is actively nulled by surrounding coils, which opens MEG to children, to patients who cannot hold still, and to naturalistic tasks; the trade-offs are a smaller dynamic range and bandwidth than SQUIDs, dependence on very good field control, and a technology still maturing, so claims of wholesale replacement should be treated as forecast rather than fact.


18.2.3 Advantages and limits relative to electroencephalography

MEG's advantages are real but narrower than enthusiasts sometimes suggest: it is reference-free, since a magnetic field is measured absolutely rather than as a difference between two points, which removes the entire class of problems described in section 18.1.2.

Its fields pass through skull and scalp with little distortion, so its forward model is simpler and less dependent on uncertain tissue conductivities, and its source estimates for superficial tangential sources are correspondingly more trustworthy.

Against this, MEG is blind to radial sources, falls off more steeply with depth so that deep structures such as the hippocampus and brainstem are hard to see, costs on the order of a million pounds or more for a SQUID installation, and cannot be moved or run at the bedside.

Both methods share the fundamental limitation - the inverse problem of section 18.4.3 - so MEG's better forward model improves the situation but does not solve it, and typical localisation accuracy is measured in millimetres to centimetres depending heavily on signal-to-noise ratio and source depth.

The fair summary is that EEG and MEG have the same temporal resolution and the same underlying generators, that MEG has better and cleaner spatial information for a subset of sources, and that EEG has incomparably better accessibility, which is why EEG remains the dominant method by volume of research.


18.3 Event-related potentials and fields

An event-related potential (ERP) is the portion of the EEG that is reliably time-locked to a particular event, such as a stimulus or a response; the magnetic equivalent recorded with MEG is called an event-related field (ERF).

The problem this solves is one of scale: the response to a single word or a single flash may be a microvolt or two, buried in ongoing EEG of tens of microvolts, so it cannot be seen in a single trial.

The solution is repetition and averaging, and the entire enterprise of cognitive electrophysiology - the discovery of components that index attention, memory, language and error monitoring - rests on that one manoeuvre, along with the assumptions it quietly carries.


18.3.1 Averaging logic and its assumptions

The classical logic is additive: the recorded signal on each trial is assumed to be a fixed, stereotyped response plus ongoing background EEG that is random with respect to the event.

If the background is random then averaging many trials makes it tend towards zero while the fixed response survives, and the signal-to-noise ratio improves in proportion to the square root of the number of trials - so quadrupling the trials only doubles the clarity, which is why ERP experiments need dozens or hundreds of repetitions.

Three assumptions are doing the work here, and each can fail: that the response is the same on every trial, that it occurs at the same latency on every trial, and that the background is genuinely unrelated to the event.

Latency jitter - trial-to-trial variation in when a component peaks - is the most consequential failure, because it flattens and widens the average, and can both hide a real amplitude difference and manufacture an apparent one when two conditions differ in how variable their timing is.

Remedies exist, including single-trial estimation by regression, wavelet-based denoising, and Residue Iteration Decomposition (RIDE), which separates components by their differing time-locking before recombining them, but none is assumption-free.

A further complication is that in fast experiments the responses to successive events overlap in time, which is why regression-based deconvolution approaches, modelling all events in one additive design, have gained ground over simple condition averaging.


18.3.2 Sensory components: C1, P1, N1, mismatch negativity

Components are named by polarity and approximate latency, so P1 means the first substantial positive peak and N1 the first substantial negative one, a convention that is convenient and, as section 18.3.4 argues, misleading.

The C1 is the earliest visual response, beginning around fifty to sixty milliseconds and peaking near eighty to one hundred milliseconds, and it is unusual in being named for its variable polarity - it inverts sign between upper and lower visual field stimulation, which was long taken as a signature of generation in primary visual cortex (V1) because of the way V1 folds around the calcarine sulcus; that inference has been directly challenged, with Ales and colleagues arguing in 2010 that areas V2 and V3 also show polarity inversion, so the reversal alone does not diagnose a V1 source.

The visual P1 peaks around one hundred to one hundred and thirty milliseconds over lateral occipital sites and is reliably enhanced by spatial attention, and the visual N1 follows in roughly the one hundred and forty to two hundred millisecond range.

The auditory N1 peaks near one hundred milliseconds at frontocentral sites, is generated substantially in supratemporal auditory cortex, and scales with the physical properties of a sound and with its novelty after silence.

The mismatch negativity (MMN), described by Risto Näätänen and colleagues in 1978, is the negative deflection elicited between roughly one hundred and fifty and two hundred and fifty milliseconds by a sound that violates a regularity established by preceding sounds, and it is important because it occurs without attention and even in sleep or coma, making it a rare index of automatic prediction; work in cats by Pincze and colleagues and human topographic studies place its generators in secondary auditory cortex, separable from the N1, though whether MMN is a genuinely distinct memory-comparison process or an expression of adaptation in the N1 generators remains actively debated, and both readings still have advocates.


18.3.3 Cognitive components: N2pc, P300, N400, P600, error-related negativity, contingent negative variation

The N2pc, identified by Luck and Hillyard in 1994, is a negativity around two hundred to three hundred milliseconds at posterior electrodes contralateral to an attended item - the "pc" stands for posterior contralateral - and it is valued because it isolates the moment attention is deployed to a location in a visual search array.

The P300, first reported by Sutton and colleagues in 1965, is a large positivity from about three hundred milliseconds onwards elicited by rare, task-relevant events; Polich's 2007 synthesis distinguishes a frontally distributed P3a, associated with involuntary orienting to novelty, from a parietal P3b, associated with the updating of a task-relevant model, and the P300's stability makes it the standard signal in clinical testing and in brain-computer interface spellers.

The N400, discovered by Kutas and Hillyard in 1980, is a centroparietal negativity peaking near four hundred milliseconds that grows larger the harder a word is to integrate with its context, and its correct characterisation is not "semantic anomaly detector" but graded sensitivity to semantic fit and predictability.

The P600 is a later positivity, roughly five hundred to eight hundred milliseconds, originally reported by Osterhout and Holcomb in 1992 in response to syntactic violations; its interpretation is genuinely contested, with a syntactic-reanalysis account competing against accounts casting it as a domain-general reanalysis or conflict-monitoring response, since it is also elicited by semantic implausibility, spelling errors and pragmatic oddity.

The error-related negativity (ERN, also called the Ne) is a sharp frontocentral negativity peaking within about one hundred milliseconds after an incorrect response, reported by Falkenstein and colleagues in 1991 and independently by Gehring and colleagues in 1993, generally localised to anterior cingulate cortex, and notable because it appears before the person is consciously aware of the error - whether it reflects error detection, response conflict, or reinforcement-learning signalling is still argued.

The contingent negative variation (CNV), described by W. Grey Walter and colleagues in Nature in 1964, is a slow negative drift over frontal and central sites during the interval between a warning signal and an imperative signal requiring a response, and it was the first demonstration that scalp electrophysiology could index something purely internal - expectancy and preparation rather than a reaction to a stimulus.


18.3.4 Component identity as a theoretical rather than empirical matter

The naming convention hides a serious conceptual problem: a peak in an averaged waveform is not a thing, it is the summed projection of an unknown number of overlapping generators onto a scalp electrode, and two experiments that both report an "N2" may be measuring quite different underlying processes.

Conversely, one process may produce no visible peak at all if it is cancelled by an opposite-polarity neighbour, so the absence of a bump is not the absence of a process.

This is why careful practitioners define a component functionally rather than morphologically - as scalp activity generated by a particular neural process, identified by the experimental manipulation it responds to - and why Luck and Kappenman, in their 2011 Oxford Handbook of Event-Related Potential Components, treat component identity as a matter of accumulated theoretical argument rather than something readable off a waveform.

The practical tool that follows from this position is the difference wave: subtracting the waveform of one condition from another cancels everything the two conditions share and isolates the process that differs, which is precisely how the N2pc and the MMN are properly measured.

The methodological moral is that measurement choices - electrode, time window, baseline, reference, and whether a difference wave was used - are part of the definition of the component, which is why open, standardised resources such as the ERP CORE released by Kappenman and colleagues in 2021, which provides validated paradigms and data for seven components, matter for making these claims checkable.


18.4 Time-frequency and source analysis

Averaging into an ERP throws away a great deal, because it keeps only what is phase-locked to the event and discards the changes in ongoing rhythmic activity that are not.

Time-frequency analysis recovers that discarded material by asking, for each moment and each frequency band, how much oscillatory power there is and how consistent its phase is.

Source analysis then asks the harder question of where in the head the measured scalp pattern came from, and this section explains why that question can never be answered from the data alone.


18.4.1 Wavelet, multitaper, and Hilbert methods

All time-frequency methods confront the same trade-off, which is a mathematical fact rather than an engineering limitation: the more precisely you localise an event in time, the less precisely you can specify its frequency, and vice versa.

The short-time Fourier transform slides a fixed window along the signal and takes the frequency spectrum within each window, which gives the same time and frequency resolution at all frequencies.

Complex Morlet wavelet convolution instead uses a wave packet whose length is scaled to the frequency it is measuring - short packets for fast rhythms, long ones for slow - which gives better temporal precision at high frequencies and better frequency precision at low ones, and is usually the sensible default for cognitive data; Cohen's 2019 paper on defining Morlet wavelets makes the point that the parameter controlling this trade-off must be reported, because it silently determines what the result looks like.

The filter-Hilbert method band-pass filters the signal and then applies the Hilbert transform, which returns an instantaneous amplitude and an instantaneous phase at each time point, and it is attractive when a precise, custom-shaped frequency band is wanted.

Multitaper methods, developed by Thomson and imported into neuroscience notably by Mitra and Pesaran, apply several orthogonal taper functions to the same data segment and average the resulting spectra, which reduces variance at the price of deliberately smoothing over frequency, and this makes them the standard choice for broadband, high-frequency signals such as gamma.

The reassuring finding is that with careful parameter choice wavelet convolution, filter-Hilbert and short-time Fourier approaches give near-identical answers, so the choice of method matters much less than the choice of parameters and the honesty with which they are reported.


18.4.2 Evoked against induced responses, and inter-trial phase coherence

An evoked response is one whose phase is reset by the event, so it occurs at the same phase on every trial and survives averaging; an induced response is one whose power changes reliably after the event but whose phase varies from trial to trial, so it cancels in the average and is invisible in a conventional ERP.

The distinction was made vivid by Tallon-Baudry and colleagues in 1996, who showed that human visual gamma-band activity around forty cycles per second has both a phase-locked early component and a later non-phase-locked component with different stimulus specificity, which meant that a whole class of cortical response had been silently discarded by decades of ERP averaging.

The way to recover induced activity is to compute power on each single trial first and then average the power, since power is insensitive to phase, whereas averaging first and computing power afterwards keeps only the evoked part.

Inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), also called inter-trial coherence or the phase-locking value and attributed to Tallon-Baudry and colleagues in 1996, measures phase consistency directly: it ranges from zero, meaning phase is uniformly scattered across trials, to one, meaning every trial has identical phase at that time and frequency, and it does so ignoring amplitude entirely.

The important caveat, argued by van Diepen and Mazaheri in 2018, is that ITPC is not a clean index of phase resetting, because an additive evoked response or a change in power can raise measured ITPC without any change in the phase of ongoing activity - so a rise in ITPC is compatible with phase reset but does not demonstrate it, and this distinction has been at the centre of a long-running and still unresolved dispute about whether evoked potentials are generated by phase resetting of ongoing oscillations or by an additive response superimposed on them.


18.4.3 The inverse problem and source localisation: minimum norm, beamforming, dipole fitting

Computing the scalp pattern produced by a known source is the forward problem and has a unique answer; going the other way, from the scalp pattern to the sources, is the inverse problem, and Helmholtz showed in the nineteenth century that it has no unique solution.

The reason is arithmetic as much as physics: there are perhaps sixty-four or three hundred sensors and many thousands of candidate source locations, so infinitely many source configurations produce exactly the same measurements, and no amount of better data removes that fact.

Every source localisation method therefore works by adding an assumption strong enough to pick one solution out of the infinite set, and the honest way to read any source map is to ask what assumption produced it.

Equivalent current dipole fitting assumes there are only a small number of point sources, and fits their positions, orientations and strengths; it is well suited to early sensory responses and to epileptic spikes, and poorly suited to distributed cognitive activity, and it requires the researcher to decide in advance how many dipoles there are.

Minimum norm estimation assumes a distributed source spread over the cortical surface and selects, among all solutions fitting the data, the one with the smallest total activity; it is biased towards superficial sources, a bias that depth-weighted variants and standardised versions such as low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (LORETA) and its exact and standardised descendants attempt to correct at the cost of a blurry, low-resolution image.

Beamforming, of which the linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) filter is the standard form, takes a different route by building for each candidate location a spatial filter that passes activity from that location and suppresses everything else, using the data's own covariance; it gives good spatial precision at high signal-to-noise ratio, but it fails characteristically when two sources are strongly correlated, because the filter treats them as one and cancels them.

Comparative work bears this out rather than crowning a winner - standardised and exact LORETA variants tend to perform better at poor signal-to-noise ratio while beamformers overtake them when the signal is strong - and a 2026 benchmark by the invertmeeg project comparing over a hundred inverse solvers across ten algorithmic families found no single method dominant, which is the fairest possible statement of the field's position.


18.4.4 Head models, forward models, and individual anatomy

The forward model, sometimes called the lead field or gain matrix, states how a unit source at each candidate brain location would appear at each sensor, and every inverse method is only as good as this model.

Building it requires a volume conductor model of the head, that is a geometric description of the tissue layers and their electrical conductivities, and the crude version is a set of concentric spheres representing brain, skull and scalp - fast, analytic, and wrong wherever the head is not spherical, which is most places.

Realistic models are built from a person's own structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan by segmenting tissues, and are solved either by the boundary element method (BEM), which represents each tissue boundary as a mesh and assumes each compartment is uniform, or the finite element method (FEM), which fills the whole volume with small elements and can therefore represent anisotropy - direction-dependent conductivity, which white matter genuinely has because current flows more easily along fibre tracts than across them.

The dominant uncertainty in EEG forward modelling is the skull, whose conductivity is low, individually variable, and difficult to measure, and sensitivity analyses have repeatedly shown that this uncertainty alone can shift estimated source locations by clinically meaningful distances - which is a large part of why MEG, whose fields the skull barely perturbs, has the easier forward problem.

Practical accuracy also depends on unglamorous details: the true positions of the electrodes must be digitised rather than assumed, and the participant's head must be co-registered with the MRI scan using fiducial landmarks, and errors of a few millimetres in either propagate straight into the source estimate.

Where an individual MRI scan is unavailable, a standard template head such as the New York Head published by Huang and colleagues in 2016 is used and is better than a sphere, but a template imposes someone else's anatomy on the analysis and the resulting localisation should be reported with correspondingly wider error bars.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

EEG and MEG measure the same physical event - synchronous postsynaptic currents in geometrically aligned cortical pyramidal cells - from two different angles, EEG through the volume-conducted voltage on the scalp and MEG through the magnetic field, which makes MEG blind to radial sources and EEG hostage to its choice of reference.

Both deliver millisecond temporal resolution, and this is their real and unmatched contribution, since it is what allows the sequence of cognitive operations to be timed rather than merely located.

The event-related potential is not a raw observation but the product of an averaging procedure whose assumptions - stereotypy, latency stability, and event-independent background noise - can and do fail, and a named component is a theoretical claim about a generating process rather than a bump that speaks for itself.

Time-frequency analysis recovers the induced, non-phase-locked activity that averaging deliberately discards, but measures such as inter-trial phase coherence do not by themselves settle whether an evoked response reflects phase resetting or an additive signal, a question still open in the literature.

Source localisation is a mathematically insoluble inverse problem made tractable only by added assumptions and by a forward model that depends on individual anatomy and on poorly known skull conductivity, so every source map should be read as a claim conditioned on those assumptions rather than as a photograph of where the activity was.


CHAPTER 19. INTRACRANIAL HUMAN NEUROSCIENCE (APPARATUS)

Almost everything we know about the living human brain is measured from outside the head, through skull and scalp, which blur and slow the signal.

Intracranial human neuroscience is the exception: electrodes placed inside the skull, resting on or inside the brain tissue itself.

Those recordings are not made for science.

They are made because a person with epilepsy that will not respond to drugs needs surgeons to find the patch of brain where their seizures begin, and the only way to find it reliably is to listen from the inside.

This chapter explains how that clinical necessity became the most precise window cognitive neuroscience has onto the human brain, what the window shows that no other method shows, and why what you see through it must be read with care.

19.1 The clinical setting

Intracranial recording exists inside a hospital workflow, not a laboratory one.

Understanding that workflow is the first step to understanding what the data can and cannot say, because every electrode position, every recording duration, and every stimulation decision is set by a clinical question rather than a scientific one.

19.1.1 Epilepsy surgery evaluation as the enabling context

Roughly a third of people with epilepsy (a condition of recurrent seizures, which are bursts of abnormally synchronised electrical activity in the brain) do not become seizure-free on medication; this is called drug-resistant or refractory epilepsy.

For some of them, surgery to remove the small region where seizures start - the epileptogenic zone - can stop the seizures altogether.

When non-invasive tests such as scalp electroencephalography (EEG, the recording of brain electrical activity from the scalp) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI, a scan that maps brain anatomy using magnetic fields) do not agree or do not localise the seizure origin, the team implants electrodes and monitors the patient on a ward for days to weeks, waiting for spontaneous seizures to occur.

That waiting period - the patient awake, alert, wired up, and with nothing much to do - is the enabling context for research.

Between clinical duties, patients who consent can perform cognitive tasks while their implanted electrodes record, and this arrangement, not any purpose-built research programme, is the source of nearly all human intracranial cognitive data.

19.1.2 Electrocorticographic grids and stereotactic depth electrodes

There are two main hardware families.

Electrocorticography (ECoG) uses subdural grids and strips: flat sheets of silicone with embedded platinum contacts, laid directly on the cortical surface after a craniotomy (surgical opening of the skull), typically with contacts spaced about one centimetre apart, though high-density arrays go finer.

Stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) instead threads thin rigid needles - depth electrodes, each carrying eight to eighteen ring contacts along its shaft - through small burr holes along computer-planned trajectories, so that they sample tissue at whatever depth the trajectory crosses.

Grids give dense, continuous coverage of an exposed cortical surface but cannot reach buried structures such as the hippocampus (a curled structure deep in the temporal lobe, central to forming new memories) or the insula.

SEEG gives sparse, scattered coverage but reaches deep and sulcal tissue, samples both hemispheres in one implant, and carries a lower complication rate; over the past fifteen years it has become the dominant method in most North American and European centres, having long been standard in the French school where it originated with Talairach and Bancaud.

19.1.3 Ethical framing of research in patients

These participants are patients first, and they are vulnerable in specific, nameable ways.

The central worry is therapeutic misconception - the patient believing that the research task is part of their treatment, or that refusing it might affect the care they receive from the same doctors who are asking.

A second worry is the conflict of interest created when the treating neurosurgeon or neurologist is also the investigator who wants the data.

Interview work by Feinsinger, Pouratian and colleagues, and related analyses published in AJOB Neuroscience in 2021, found that investigators broadly agree on two commitments - never let research compromise clinical care, and make voluntariness genuinely real - but disagree substantially on the practical details, such as who should approach the patient and when.

The Neuroethics Division of the United States National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative has treated this as an open problem rather than a solved one, which is an honest description of where the field stands.

19.1.4 Sampling constrained by clinical need

No investigator chooses where the electrodes go.

The surgical team places them where it believes the seizures start and where the surrounding tissue must be checked before anything is removed, which means coverage is dictated by pathology.

The practical consequences are severe: temporal lobes are heavily sampled because temporal lobe epilepsy is common, occipital and parietal cortex much less so; most implants are unilateral; and two patients almost never have the same electrode set, so group analysis usually means pooling scattered, non-overlapping samples rather than averaging matched ones.

Studies therefore accumulate coverage patient by patient over years, and a claim about a region is only as strong as the number of independent patients who happened, for clinical reasons, to have an electrode there.

19.2 What intracranial recording adds

The case for intracranial work is not that it is fashionable but that it resolves things other methods physically cannot.

19.2.1 High-frequency broadband as a proxy for local population firing

When a patch of cortex becomes active, its recorded voltage spectrum shows a power increase spread across high frequencies, conventionally summarised as the 70 to 170 hertz range and often called high gamma.

Kai Miller and colleagues argued in a series of papers around 2009 and 2010 that this is not an oscillation (a rhythm at a particular frequency) at all, but a broadband, non-rhythmic power shift across the whole spectrum, and that it tracks the mean firing rate of the neurons under the electrode.

Supratim Ray and John Maunsell, recording in macaque monkeys in 2008 and afterwards, showed the same tight coupling between high gamma power and average spiking, giving the interpretation a direct animal-model anchor.

This matters enormously in practice: it means a surface electrode, which cannot see individual spikes, nonetheless yields a fast, spatially local index of how hard the local population is working, and one that shows sharp functional selectivity - a face-responsive site lights up for faces and not for houses.

The proxy is not exact, however.

Work by Leszczynski, Schroeder and colleagues published in Science Advances in 2020 reported conditions under which broadband high-frequency activity and actual neuronal firing dissociate, with part of the high-frequency signal reflecting dendritic and synaptic currents rather than output spikes; the honest position is that high gamma is an excellent but imperfect and still-debated stand-in for population firing.

19.2.2 Millisecond timing with anatomical precision

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, which infers activity from changes in blood oxygenation) has good spatial resolution but its signal unfolds over seconds, far slower than thought.

Scalp EEG and magnetoencephalography have millisecond timing but their signals are smeared by the skull and are hard to attribute to a specific gyrus.

Intracranial recording is the only human method that has both at once: sampling at kilohertz rates from a contact whose location is known to within a few millimetres on the patient's own MRI.

This is what allows questions of order to be settled empirically - whether frontal activity precedes or follows temporal activity in a given task, how long after a word appears its meaning is registered, whether two regions that both respond are responding simultaneously or in sequence.

19.2.3 Single-neuron recording in humans and concept cells

A small number of centres, following Itzhak Fried's development of hybrid depth electrodes carrying fine microwires at their tips, can record the spikes of individual human neurons.

The most celebrated result came from Rodrigo Quian Quiroga, Leila Reddy, Gabriel Kreiman, Christof Koch and Fried, published in Nature in 2005: neurons in the medial temporal lobe that fired to one particular person or place across wildly different images, and even to that person's written name or spoken name, but not to others.

The press called these Jennifer Aniston neurons, after one memorable example; the field calls them concept cells, because what they appear to encode is an invariant identity rather than any particular visual appearance.

Quian Quiroga's 2012 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience proposed them as building blocks of declarative memory - the memory for facts and events you can consciously report.

The interpretation remains contested in its details: a 2024 report in Cell Reports found human medial temporal lobe responses surprisingly insensitive to context, and other work finds the same neurons shifting their representations between spatial and memory tasks, so how rigidly the coding should be described as a single stable concept is still an open question twenty years on.

19.2.4 Long-duration recording across natural behaviour and sleep

Because patients are implanted for days or weeks, intracranial work can record continuously through eating, conversation, boredom, and full nights of sleep - regimes no scanner session can reach.

This has been decisive for sleep and memory research, where human recordings have documented sharp-wave ripples, brief high-frequency bursts in the hippocampus long studied in rodents, and shown them nested inside sleep spindles which are in turn nested inside slow oscillations, a coordination described in detail by Bernhard Staresina and colleagues in Nature Neuroscience in 2023.

Ripple-linked reactivation of task-related activity during non-rapid-eye-movement sleep has been reported to predict later memory, supporting the consolidation account in humans rather than only in rodents.

Long recordings also license genuinely naturalistic questions: a 2024 Nature Communications study recorded hippocampal ripples for up to fifteen days alongside experience sampling and found ripple rates fluctuating with the daily cycle and tracking spontaneous, self-generated thought.

19.3 Direct electrical stimulation

Recording tells you what co-occurs with a behaviour.

Passing current through the same electrodes tells you what happens when you perturb the tissue, which is a different and stronger kind of evidence.

19.3.1 Functional mapping before resection

Before removing tissue, the team must know what that tissue does for this particular patient, because functional anatomy varies between individuals.

Stimulation mapping delivers brief trains of current through pairs of contacts while the awake patient speaks, names pictures, moves, or counts, and the team notes what breaks.

Wilder Penfield pioneered the method during awake epilepsy surgery in the 1930s through 1950s, producing the famous sensory and motor maps of the cortical strip; George Ojemann standardised a bipolar short-pulse protocol in the 1970s and reported that language sites were scattered across frontal, temporal and parietal cortex with striking variability from person to person.

That variability is precisely why the mapping cannot be replaced by an atlas, and it is also a substantive scientific finding about how individual human brains are organised.

19.3.2 Causal inference from stimulation-induced deficits and percepts

Stimulation produces two kinds of informative result: it can subtract a function, as when current to a language site arrests speech mid-word, or it can add an experience, as when current to visual cortex produces a phosphene, a spot or streak of light.

A clean example is Josef Parvizi, Vinitha Rangarajan, Kalanit Grill-Spector and colleagues in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2012, who first used high-resolution fMRI to find face-selective patches in a patient's fusiform gyrus, then stimulated exactly those patches and had the patient report that the faces of people in the room became metamorphosed and distorted, while non-face objects were unaffected.

That sequence - localise with correlation, then perturb and observe a matched, specific change - is about as close to a causal experiment as human cognitive neuroscience gets.

The inference has limits worth stating: current spreads beyond the intended tissue, it also travels along fibre tracts to distant sites, and a deficit produced by disrupting a region does not prove that the region performs the function rather than merely being necessary to some network that does.

19.3.3 Cortico-cortical evoked potentials and effective connectivity

Instead of a train of pulses, one can deliver single pulses and average the responses recorded at every other electrode.

Riki Matsumoto and colleagues, in Brain in 2004 and later papers, named the resulting averaged responses cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) and used them to trace connections between cortical regions in the living human brain.

A negative deflection arriving roughly ten to fifty milliseconds after the pulse, called the N1, is read as evidence of a relatively direct connection from the stimulated site to the recording site.

This gives effective connectivity - a directed, causally probed measure of influence - as opposed to the merely correlational functional connectivity offered by resting-state fMRI, and unlike diffusion MRI tractography it reports whether a pathway actually conducts rather than only whether fibres appear to run between the regions.

Reviews of large series report the procedure to be generally safe, and combined CCEP-and-tractography approaches, sometimes called dynamic tractography, now attempt to put timing onto anatomical pathways.

19.3.4 Closed-loop stimulation for memory enhancement

The most ambitious use of stimulation is to improve cognition rather than to map it.

Under the United States Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Restoring Active Memory (RAM) programme, Michael Kahana's group at the University of Pennsylvania built classifiers that decode, from ongoing intracranial activity, whether the brain is currently in a good or a poor state for encoding a word into memory.

Youssef Ezzyat, Paul Wanda and colleagues reported in Nature Communications in 2018 that stimulating lateral temporal cortex only during predicted poor-encoding states improved later recall by around fifteen to eighteen per cent relative to unstimulated trials, whereas stimulating during good states did not help and could hurt.

The closed-loop logic - decode state, then intervene contingently - is the key idea, and it doubles as a strong test of the theory, since the classifier's success is itself evidence that the decoded neural states are real and behaviourally meaningful.

Caution is warranted: effects are within-session and modest, samples are small and heterogeneous, target selection matters a great deal, and no such system is yet an approved clinical treatment for memory impairment.

19.4 Interpretive cautions

Intracranial data have unusual authority, which makes their limitations unusually easy to forget.

19.4.1 The pathological brain as the sample

Every participant has severe drug-resistant epilepsy, has taken anticonvulsant medication for years, and may have structural lesions, hippocampal sclerosis, or reorganised function as a consequence.

Tissue near the seizure focus may behave abnormally even between seizures, which is why careful studies exclude channels showing interictal epileptiform discharges (brief abnormal spikes between seizures) and often exclude the seizure-onset zone entirely.

Recordings can also be contaminated by the aftermath of a recent seizure or by medication tapering, both of which are routine on the monitoring ward.

None of this invalidates the data, but it means the sample is not a random draw from humanity and the analysis pipeline has to do explicit work to argue that a given effect is not a product of the disease.

19.4.2 Spatial coverage bias

Coverage follows clinical suspicion, so the human intracranial map of the brain is densest exactly where epilepsy is commonest.

Medial and lateral temporal cortex is well covered; large parts of parietal, occipital and medial prefrontal cortex are sparsely covered; deep structures were nearly invisible before SEEG became widespread.

Because contacts are also confined to one hemisphere in many patients, questions about hemispheric asymmetry are systematically harder to answer than questions about a single region.

The field's response has been to pool across patients and across institutions, and shared archives such as the DARPA RAM datasets and public iEEG repositories have made that pooling possible, but pooled coverage is still not designed coverage.

19.4.3 Generalisation to healthy populations

The strongest defence of intracranial findings is convergence: when a result also appears in fMRI, in magnetoencephalography, in lesion patients, or in animal recordings, the epilepsy sample stops being the load-bearing assumption.

Concept cells, high gamma selectivity in face and language regions, and hippocampal ripples all have such external support, which is why they are treated as facts about human brains rather than facts about epileptic brains.

Where no convergent evidence exists, the honest statement is narrower - that the effect has been observed in drug-resistant epilepsy patients under clinical monitoring conditions - and readers should notice when authors quietly drop that qualifier.

The best current practice is to report how many patients, and how many independent electrodes, actually contributed to each claim, because a striking effect in two patients and a robust effect in forty are not the same kind of evidence.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Human intracranial recording is a by-product of epilepsy surgery, and that origin sets both its extraordinary power and its systematic limits.

Its power is real and specific: millisecond timing tied to millimetre anatomy, a broadband high-frequency signal that serves as a good if imperfect proxy for local population firing, single-neuron recordings that revealed invariant concept cells, and continuous recording across sleep and natural behaviour.

Direct electrical stimulation upgrades the evidence from correlational to causal, whether by arresting speech, distorting face perception, tracing effective connectivity with cortico-cortical evoked potentials, or improving recall through closed-loop intervention.

The limits are equally real: the sample is a diseased brain, coverage is dictated by pathology rather than by hypothesis, and the participants are patients whose consent must be protected against therapeutic misconception.

The discipline the chapter asks for is simple - state how many patients and electrodes support a claim, and prefer claims that converge with independent methods.


CHAPTER 20. HAEMODYNAMIC AND METABOLIC IMAGING (APPARATUS)


This chapter is about the family of methods that watch the living human brain by watching its blood and its chemistry.

None of them see a neuron fire.

Every one of them sees something downstream of firing - blood flow, blood oxygenation, glucose or oxygen use, the binding of a drug-like molecule to a receptor - and then reasons backwards to the neural activity that presumably caused it.

That backwards step is where the power of these methods lives, and it is also where every serious objection to them lives.

Understanding the apparatus is therefore not a technical detour from the science of cognition; it is the only way to know how much weight a coloured blob on a brain picture can carry.

The chapter walks through the physics, then the experimental design and statistics, then the sister methods, and finishes with four interpretive problems that no amount of better hardware has yet dissolved.


20.1 Functional magnetic resonance imaging


Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is the workhorse of human cognitive neuroscience.

It uses a large magnet and radio waves to make pictures of the inside of the head, and it repeats those pictures fast enough - typically once every half-second to two seconds - to track changes over the course of a task.

It is non-invasive, it involves no radiation, and it can be repeated in the same person many times, which is why it displaced almost everything else within a decade of its invention in the early 1990s.

This section explains where the signal actually comes from.


20.1.1 Nuclear magnetic resonance basics and image formation

Magnetic resonance imaging rests on nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), a physical effect discovered in the 1940s.

The hydrogen nucleus - a single proton, and the brain is mostly water, so there are vast numbers of them - behaves like a tiny spinning magnet, and when placed in a strong magnetic field a slight majority of these tiny magnets line up with the field.

A radiofrequency pulse at exactly the right frequency tips them out of alignment; as they relax back, they emit a faint radio signal that the scanner's coils detect.

To turn that signal into a picture, the scanner adds gradient coils, which make the magnetic field strength vary smoothly across space, so that protons in different places resonate at slightly different frequencies and phases - position is thereby encoded into the frequency and phase of the returning signal, and a mathematical operation called the Fourier transform unscrambles it into an image.

Two relaxation constants matter for what follows: T1, the rate at which the tipped magnetisation realigns with the main field, which gives beautiful anatomical images, and T2 and its cousin T2-star, the rate at which the signal fades because protons fall out of step with each other, which is what functional imaging exploits.


20.1.2 The blood-oxygen-level-dependent contrast mechanism

In 1990 Seiji Ogawa and colleagues at AT&T Bell Laboratories, imaging rat brains at 7 tesla, noticed dark lines tracing the blood vessels in gradient-echo images that were absent in spin-echo images.

The explanation is a piece of chemistry: haemoglobin carrying oxygen (oxyhaemoglobin) is essentially non-magnetic, while haemoglobin that has given up its oxygen (deoxyhaemoglobin) is paramagnetic, meaning it distorts the local magnetic field and makes nearby protons fall out of step faster, shortening T2-star and darkening the image.
