Deoxyhaemoglobin is therefore a contrast agent the body supplies for free, and blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) imaging is the measurement of its changing concentration.

The counter-intuitive part is the sign of the effect: when a patch of cortex becomes more active it consumes more oxygen, but the local blood supply over-responds, delivering far more oxygenated blood than the tissue extracts, so the proportion of deoxyhaemoglobin falls and the signal gets brighter.

Human application followed rapidly in 1992, in independent reports from Ogawa's group, from Kenneth Kwong and colleagues at Massachusetts General Hospital, and from Peter Bandettini and colleagues in Milwaukee.

The signal is thus at least three steps removed from neural firing - neural activity, then a vascular response, then an oxygenation change, then a magnetic effect - and Nikos Logothetis and colleagues, recording electrodes and BOLD simultaneously in monkey visual cortex (Nature, 2001), found that BOLD tracked local field potentials better than it tracked spiking output, suggesting it reflects a region's synaptic input and internal processing more than the messages it sends onward.


20.1.3 Echo-planar imaging, field strength, and multiband acquisition

Ordinary MRI takes minutes per image, which is useless for tracking thought.

Echo-planar imaging (EPI), devised by Peter Mansfield in the 1970s, collects an entire two-dimensional slice from a single radiofrequency excitation by rapidly oscillating the gradients, bringing acquisition down to tens of milliseconds per slice - it is the technique that made fMRI practical, and Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for magnetic resonance imaging work.

Field strength matters because both the raw signal-to-noise ratio (the size of the wanted signal relative to random fluctuation) and the BOLD effect itself grow with field strength: 1.5 tesla was standard in the 1990s, 3 tesla is now routine, 7 tesla scanners are widely available for research, and human scanners at 10.5 and 11.7 tesla exist at a handful of sites.

Higher fields also worsen certain problems - image distortion and signal loss near air-filled sinuses, and greater deposition of radiofrequency energy in tissue - so the gain is real but not free.

Multiband imaging, also called simultaneous multi-slice, excites several slices at once with a composite radiofrequency pulse and then separates them using the differing sensitivity profiles of multiple receiver coils; the Human Connectome Project used a multiband factor of 8 at 3 tesla to reach a repetition time of 0.72 seconds with 2 millimetre voxels.

The cost is so-called g-factor noise from the separation step, and a 2022 critique in Aperture Neuro by Risk and Zhu argued that aggressive multiband factors can degrade data quality in ways not always appreciated by users, so the field's advice is now to accelerate, but with caution.


20.1.4 Laminar and columnar imaging at ultra-high field

Cerebral cortex is layered, roughly six layers thick over about two to four millimetres, and the layers have different jobs: incoming sensory information from the thalamus arrives mainly in the middle layers, while feedback from higher areas arrives mainly in the superficial and deep layers.

At 7 tesla and above it becomes possible to acquire voxels well under a millimetre, enough to sample different cortical depths separately, and this laminar fMRI promises something genuinely new - the ability to tell feedforward from feedback traffic in a living human brain, which ordinary fMRI cannot do at all.

Work of this kind has, for example, imaged ocular dominance columns - the alternating stripes in primary visual cortex that prefer the left or the right eye - across depth, reporting that the monocular response is strongest at middle and deep depths while the effect of spatial attention appears near the outer, pial surface.

The severe technical obstacle is that ordinary gradient-echo BOLD is dominated by large draining veins running perpendicular to the cortical surface, which smear signal from deep layers up towards the surface; alternatives such as spin-echo BOLD and vascular space occupancy (VASO), which measures blood volume rather than oxygenation, are more specific to small vessels but have much less signal, and benchmarking studies comparing these sequences continue.

Laminar fMRI is currently a method of great elegance whose findings should be treated as promising rather than settled, because the depth-dependent vascular corrections it depends on are themselves still under active dispute.


20.2 Design and modelling


A scanner produces a very long, very noisy number series for each of a hundred thousand or more voxels.

Turning that into a claim about cognition requires a designed experiment and an explicit statistical model.

The choices made here determine what a study can possibly find, and they are made before a single participant is scanned.


20.2.1 Blocked, event-related, and mixed designs

In a blocked design, one condition is presented continuously for a stretch of perhaps twenty or thirty seconds, then another - faces for half a minute, then houses for half a minute - which produces large, easily detected signal differences because the haemodynamic responses to successive events pile up on each other.

Its weakness is that participants can anticipate what is coming, strategies can drift across a block, and events of different types cannot be sorted after the fact.

In an event-related design, individual trials are presented in a mixed and often randomised order with variable gaps between them, which allows trials to be sorted retrospectively - remembered versus forgotten items, correct versus error trials - at the price of considerably less statistical power.

Mixed designs, sometimes called mixed blocked and event-related designs, interleave the two so that a slowly varying sustained component (a task state, such as being on alert) can be separated from transient item-by-item responses, an approach developed in the early 2000s by Randy Buckner, Steven Petersen, and colleagues.

The general rule, worked out in the efficiency analyses of Rik Henson and others, is that blocked designs maximise detection power while event-related designs with jittered timing maximise the ability to estimate the shape of the response, and you cannot have both at once.


20.2.2 The general linear model and the haemodynamic response function

Almost all task fMRI is analysed with the general linear model (GLM), a statistical framework that expresses the measured time course in each voxel as a weighted sum of predicted time courses plus noise, and then asks whether each weight differs reliably from zero.

Building a predicted time course requires knowing what the blood response to a brief burst of neural activity looks like: this is the haemodynamic response function (HRF), which typically rises after a lag of one to two seconds, peaks around five seconds after the event, and then falls to a prolonged undershoot lasting ten to twenty seconds.

The canonical HRF used in Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM), formalised by Karl Friston, Keith Worsley and colleagues in the mid-1990s, is a difference of two gamma functions - one for the peak and one for the undershoot.

The predicted response is obtained by convolution, a mathematical smearing operation that replaces each modelled event with a copy of the HRF and adds up the overlaps; the underlying assumption is linearity, that responses to closely spaced events simply add, which is a good approximation but demonstrably breaks down for events less than about two seconds apart.

Because the true HRF varies between people, between brain regions, and with age and disease, analysts often add temporal and dispersion derivatives, or use a flexible basis set, to absorb shifts in timing and width; Lindquist and colleagues (2009) showed that getting the HRF shape wrong can produce both loss of sensitivity and outright bias in estimated activation.


20.2.3 Preprocessing: motion correction, registration, distortion correction, smoothing

Before modelling, the raw images pass through a pipeline of corrections, each addressing a specific way in which the data fail to match the assumptions of the analysis.

Motion correction, also called realignment, uses rigid-body transformation - three translations and three rotations, since the skull does not bend - to align every volume in the run to a reference volume, so that a given voxel refers to the same piece of brain throughout.

Registration, or spatial normalisation, warps each person's brain onto a common template, most often one of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) templates, so that coordinates can be compared and averaged across people; this step is what allows a paper to report an activation at a triplet of coordinates.

Distortion correction addresses the fact that EPI images are geometrically stretched and compressed near air-tissue boundaries such as the sinuses and ear canals, and is done either by acquiring a field map that measures the magnetic field directly, or by acquiring images with opposite phase-encoding directions and combining them, the approach implemented in the widely used topup tool.

Spatial smoothing deliberately blurs the images with a Gaussian kernel, usually four to eight millimetres wide at half its height, which sounds destructive but improves signal-to-noise for spatially extended effects and makes the statistical assumptions of random field theory hold better - though it also blurs away exactly the fine-grained patterns that multivariate analyses depend on, so smoothing is often skipped for those.

Standardised pipelines such as fMRIPrep, released by Oscar Esteban and colleagues in 2019, now package these steps so that different laboratories at least preprocess data the same way, a direct response to evidence that analytic choices alone can change a study's conclusions.


20.2.4 Physiological noise, respiration, and vascular confounds

A great deal of what fluctuates in an fMRI time series has nothing to do with cognition.

The heartbeat pushes cerebrospinal fluid and pulses arteries at around one hertz; breathing moves the chest, which shifts the magnetic field around the head, and changes the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood, a potent dilator of blood vessels that can produce brain-wide signal swings after a single deep breath.

Correction methods include RETROICOR, introduced by Gary Glover and colleagues in 2000, which models cardiac and respiratory cycles using externally recorded pulse and breathing traces, and data-driven methods such as CompCor, which extract nuisance signals from white matter and ventricles where no meaningful BOLD response should occur.

Head motion is the most damaging confound of all, and Jonathan Power and colleagues (2012) showed that even sub-millimetre movements systematically distort functional connectivity estimates - producing, for instance, apparently weaker long-range connections - which was troubling because children, older adults, and patients move more than healthy young controls, so a group difference in motion can masquerade as a group difference in brain organisation.

Their proposed remedy, censoring or scrubbing frames whose framewise displacement exceeds a threshold such as 0.5 millimetres, together with the complementary measure DVARS (the frame-to-frame change in image intensity), is now standard, though the best combination of nuisance regression, scrubbing, and global signal removal remains genuinely contested, with different groups defending different pipelines.

Finally there is a vascular confound that no regression removes: BOLD is weighted towards veins, including large draining veins that may lie millimetres downstream of the active tissue, so the brightest voxel is not necessarily the most active tissue.


20.3 Other haemodynamic and metabolic methods


fMRI is not the only way to watch the brain's housekeeping.

The alternatives are generally worse than fMRI on some axis - resolution, convenience, cost - and better on another, usually the ability to measure a specific chemical quantity rather than an uncalibrated ratio.


20.3.1 Positron emission tomography and receptor mapping

Positron emission tomography (PET) works by injecting a molecule labelled with a radioactive isotope that decays by emitting a positron, the antimatter counterpart of the electron; the positron annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two gamma rays that fly off in opposite directions and are caught by a ring of detectors, allowing the line of origin to be reconstructed.

Before fMRI existed, PET with oxygen-15-labelled water measured regional cerebral blood flow and produced the founding studies of human cognitive neuroimaging in the 1980s by Marcus Raichle, Steven Petersen, Michael Posner and colleagues at Washington University; fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) similarly maps glucose consumption and remains central in clinical neurology.

PET's enduring advantage is molecular specificity, because the tracer can be designed to bind a chosen target: carbon-11 raclopride binds dopamine D2-like receptors, and because it competes with the brain's own dopamine, a drop in its binding after a task or a drug is read as a rise in released dopamine - a measurement fMRI simply cannot make.

Other ligands map serotonin receptors, opioid receptors, and, in dementia research, amyloid and tau deposits, which is how the modern biomarker-based definition of Alzheimer's disease became possible.

The costs are severe: ionising radiation limits how often a person can be scanned, spatial resolution is coarser than fMRI at roughly four to six millimetres, temporal resolution is minutes rather than seconds, and carbon-11 tracers have a twenty-minute half-life that requires a cyclotron on site.


20.3.2 Functional near-infrared spectroscopy and its portability

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) shines near-infrared light into the head from sources on the scalp and measures how much emerges at nearby detectors.

Biological tissue is relatively transparent in this band, but oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin absorb different wavelengths differently, so with two or more wavelengths one can estimate changes in both separately - an advantage over BOLD, which conflates flow, volume, and oxygenation into one number.

Its decisive practical virtue is portability and tolerance of movement: fNIRS can be used on newborn infants, on people walking, on two people talking to each other face to face, and increasingly in wearable form, which opens experiments that a scanner bore forbids.

Its decisive limitation is depth, since usable light penetrates only about fifteen to twenty millimetres past the scalp, restricting measurement to the outer cortical surface and excluding the hippocampus, the basal ganglia, and everything else deep; spatial resolution is also coarse, on the order of a centimetre.

A further pitfall, documented repeatedly since around 2016, is contamination by blood flow in the scalp and skull itself, which is why current best practice requires short-separation channels that sample the superficial layer so it can be regressed out.


20.3.3 Arterial spin labelling and quantitative perfusion

Arterial spin labelling (ASL) turns the blood itself into a tracer without injecting anything: a radiofrequency pulse applied at the neck magnetically labels water protons in arterial blood, and after a delay allowing that blood to reach the brain, an image is taken and subtracted from an unlabelled control image, leaving only the contribution of newly arrived blood.

The result is a quantitative map of cerebral blood flow in physical units, millilitres of blood per hundred grams of tissue per minute, which is its central advantage over BOLD - BOLD gives only a percentage change relative to an arbitrary baseline, so it cannot answer whether one group's brain is globally more or less perfused than another's.

That property makes ASL valuable for comparing patients with controls, for tracking slow drug effects, and for studying conditions where the baseline itself is the question, such as ageing, hypertension, or early Alzheimer's disease.

Its weaknesses are low signal - the labelled blood contributes only about one percent of the image intensity, so many repetitions are needed - and consequently poorer temporal and spatial resolution than BOLD, though pseudo-continuous labelling and background suppression, standardised in a widely adopted consensus paper by Alsop and colleagues in 2015, have improved it substantially.


20.3.4 Magnetic resonance spectroscopy for neurotransmitter concentration

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) uses the same scanner but discards the image, instead measuring the spectrum of resonance frequencies within a single defined box of tissue, typically a couple of centimetres on a side.

Because a hydrogen nucleus resonates at a frequency very slightly shifted by the molecule it sits in - an effect called chemical shift - the spectrum contains separate peaks for different metabolites, including N-acetylaspartate (a marker of neuronal integrity), creatine, choline, glutamate, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the brain's main inhibitory transmitter.

GABA is hard to see because its peaks are buried under the far larger creatine peak, so specialised editing sequences are used, most commonly MEGA-PRESS, which acquires two interleaved conditions and subtracts them so that only the edited GABA signal survives.

MRS has supported an influential line of cognitive work relating resting GABA or glutamate concentrations in a region to individual differences in perception, learning, and plasticity.

The cautions are serious and widely acknowledged: the measurement is an average over a large voxel containing many cell types, it cannot distinguish transmitter held in vesicles from the metabolic pool, the signal-to-noise ratio is low, the GABA measurement is usually reported as GABA-plus because it includes contaminating macromolecules, and reproducibility across scanners and sites has been shown to be imperfect, which is why consensus reporting standards were issued by the MRS community from 2019 onwards.


20.4 Persistent interpretive problems


The four problems in this section are not bugs awaiting a patch.

They are structural features of measuring cognition through blood, and each has generated a literature of its own.


20.4.1 Spatial resolution against the scale of the underlying circuit

A typical fMRI voxel of three by three by three millimetres contains on the order of several hundred thousand to a million neurons and several kilometres of dendrite and axon.

Within that volume there may be excitatory and inhibitory populations doing opposite things, and cells with opposite tuning preferences - the voxel reports one number for all of them, so activity that cancels out is invisible, and a region can be genuinely busy while appearing quiet.

The vasculature imposes its own floor: the BOLD point spread function, the blur inherent in the vascular response even with a perfect scanner, is on the order of two to four millimetres for standard gradient-echo imaging at 3 tesla, better at higher field and with spin-echo methods, but never as fine as the cortical column.

Two developments have partly outflanked the problem: multivariate pattern analysis, introduced to fMRI by Jim Haxby and colleagues in 2001 and Kamitani and Tong in 2005, extracts information from the pattern across many voxels even when no single voxel differs, apparently reading out subvoxel structure through fine-grained sampling biases; and laminar imaging at ultra-high field, discussed earlier.

Both are real advances, and neither changes the basic fact that the measured unit is a vascular territory, not a circuit.


20.4.2 Temporal resolution against the speed of cognition

The neural events underlying a perceptual decision unfold over tens to a few hundred milliseconds; the haemodynamic response takes about five seconds to peak and twenty or more to resolve.

fMRI therefore acts as a low-pass filter, smearing a fast sequence of events into a single slow bump, so that two processes occurring two hundred milliseconds apart produce almost identical measured responses.

Sampling faster does not fix this, because the limit is in the biology and not the scanner - reducing the repetition time to half a second with multiband gives more samples of the same slow curve, which does help with noise modelling and with detecting small timing shifts.

Some ordering information can be recovered, since relative onset differences of a few hundred milliseconds between regions have been resolved under favourable conditions, but such inferences are fragile because the vascular lag itself differs between regions and between people by a comparable amount.

This is the standing argument for combining fMRI with electroencephalography (EEG) or magnetoencephalography (MEG), which have millisecond resolution but poor spatial localisation - the two families of method fail in complementary directions.


20.4.3 Subtraction logic and pure insertion

The dominant experimental logic in imaging is subtraction, inherited from the Dutch physiologist Franciscus Donders, who in 1868 timed reactions in tasks differing by one supposed mental step and attributed the extra time to that step.

Applied to imaging, one contrasts a task with a control condition intended to differ in exactly one component, and attributes the difference in activation to that component.

The logic depends on the assumption of pure insertion: that adding a mental component leaves all the others unchanged.

Karl Friston, Cathy Price and colleagues, in a 1996 paper bluntly titled The Trouble with Cognitive Subtraction, argued that this assumption is generally false for neural implementation, because adding a component can change how the existing components are carried out - the interaction, not the insertion, is what you have measured.

Their recommended remedies are factorial designs, which manipulate two factors at once and test explicitly for interactions rather than assuming they are absent, and parametric designs, which vary one quantity continuously - difficulty, memory load, stimulus contrast - and look for a graded response, avoiding the need for a matched control condition altogether.


20.4.4 Reverse inference and the base-rate problem

Forward inference is what imaging experiments actually license: given this task, this region activated.

Reverse inference runs the other way - given that this region activated, that mental process was engaged - and Russell Poldrack (2006) pointed out that as a piece of deduction this is simply the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

His formal argument is Bayesian and turns on base rates: the probability that a cognitive process was engaged given activation depends not only on how reliably that process activates the region, but on how often that region activates across all other tasks, and on how common the process is to begin with.

Poldrack's worked example used the amygdala and fear, and his analysis of the BrainMap database found the amygdala active in a substantial fraction of studies having nothing to do with fear, so its activation is weak evidence for fear; the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex are worse still, activating in a large share of all imaging experiments and therefore carrying almost no diagnostic weight on their own.

The response has not been to abandon reverse inference but to quantify it: large-scale automated meta-analysis, notably the Neurosynth framework introduced by Tal Yarkoni and colleagues in 2011 and its successor NeuroQuery, estimates the required base rates from thousands of published studies, and multivariate decoding shifts the claim from a single region to a whole-brain pattern, which can be far more selective.

Some philosophers and neuroscientists, including Machery and Hutzler, have argued that reverse inference is not inherently fallacious but is ordinary abductive reasoning whose strength depends on the evidence marshalled, and this remains a live methodological dispute rather than a closed question.

The practical lesson for a reader of any imaging paper is to distrust any sentence of the form the participants must have been feeling X because region Y lit up, unless the authors show the base rates.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Haemodynamic and metabolic imaging never measures neural activity directly; it measures blood and chemistry, and every inference back to cognition passes through neurovascular coupling, which Logothetis and colleagues showed tracks synaptic input more closely than spiking output.

The BOLD signal exists because deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic and because blood flow over-supplies oxygen to active tissue, a chain that limits spatial resolution to a vascular territory of a few millimetres and temporal resolution to the several-second timescale of the haemodynamic response.

What a study can find is fixed in advance by its design and its statistical model, and by a preprocessing pipeline whose choices - motion censoring in particular, after Power and colleagues in 2012 - can create or destroy apparent group differences.

The sister methods trade convenience for specificity: positron emission tomography identifies particular molecules, arterial spin labelling gives absolute perfusion, magnetic resonance spectroscopy gives metabolite concentrations, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy gives portability at the cost of depth.

Two logical problems survive all technical improvement - the falsity of pure insertion in subtraction designs, exposed by Friston and Price in 1996, and the base-rate weakness of reverse inference, exposed by Poldrack in 2006 - and both are managed by better design and explicit quantification rather than solved.


CHAPTER 21. STRUCTURAL AND CONNECTIONAL IMAGING (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about the machines and the mathematics that let us look at the shape and the wiring of a living human brain without opening the skull.

It covers structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which is a scanning method that uses a strong magnet and radio waves to make pictures of soft tissue, and it covers diffusion imaging, which infers the direction of nerve fibre bundles from the way water molecules drift inside them.

It matters because almost every claim in this book about where a cognitive function lives, or about how two brain regions talk to each other, ultimately rests on one of these measurements.

The apparatus is not neutral.

Each method has a characteristic way of being wrong, and a reader who does not know those failure modes cannot tell a real finding from an artefact of the pipeline.

So this chapter explains what the pictures actually measure, and where they stop being trustworthy.


21.1 Structural magnetic resonance imaging

Structural MRI produces a still photograph of the brain's anatomy rather than a movie of its activity.

The scanner does not measure brain tissue directly.

It measures hydrogen nuclei, mostly in water and fat, which behave like tiny spinning magnets and can be tipped over by a radio pulse and then listened to as they settle back.

Different tissues settle back at different speeds, and those speed differences are what produce the light-and-dark contrast that a neuroanatomist reads as grey matter, white matter, or fluid.

The workhorse image is the T1-weighted scan, so called because it is timed to emphasise a relaxation constant called T1.

In a T1-weighted image, white matter appears bright, grey matter appears mid-grey, and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid cushioning the brain, appears dark.

A typical research T1-weighted scan takes five to ten minutes and resolves detail down to about one millimetre, which is roughly the thickness of a fingernail.


21.1.1 Tissue contrast, segmentation, and surface reconstruction

Segmentation is the step in which software assigns every three-dimensional picture element, called a voxel, to a tissue class: grey matter, white matter, or cerebrospinal fluid.

Surface reconstruction goes further.

It fits a continuous, folded sheet through the boundary between white and grey matter, and a second sheet through the outer edge of grey matter where it meets fluid, so that the cortex - the crumpled outer rind of the brain - is represented as a surface rather than a stack of blocks.

The landmark implementation is the FreeSurfer pipeline described by Dale, Fischl and Sereno in two companion papers in NeuroImage in 1999: the first covering segmentation and surface reconstruction, the second covering inflation, flattening, and a surface-based coordinate system.

The pipeline is a chain of unglamorous corrections before the interesting part: correcting for the scanner's uneven sensitivity across space, stripping away skull and scalp, separating white matter, tessellating the boundary into a mesh of triangles, then inflating that mesh like a balloon so that tissue buried deep in a fold becomes visible.

The chain is also the pipeline's weakness.

An error in skull-stripping or bias correction propagates silently into every downstream measurement, which is why careful laboratories still inspect reconstructions by eye.


21.1.2 Voxel-based and surface-based morphometry

Morphometry means the measurement of shape and size.

Voxel-based morphometry (VBM), set out by Ashburner and Friston in NeuroImage in 2000, warps every participant's brain into a common template space, segments out grey matter, blurs the result slightly, and then runs a statistical test at every voxel to ask whether groups differ.

Its appeal is that it is automatic and makes no prior commitment about where a difference should be.

Its central criticism, pressed sharply by Bookstein in 2001 in a paper arguing that VBM should not be used with imperfectly registered images, is that the warping step and the voxel-wise testing step interact badly: wherever the alignment algorithm fails, the resulting statistic reports a registration failure rather than a biological difference.

Surface-based morphometry (SBM) instead aligns brains along the cortical surface, matching fold to fold, which respects the fact that two points can be millimetres apart in space yet centimetres apart along the cortical sheet.

Neither is simply better.

VBM covers the whole brain including deep structures that have no surface; SBM aligns cortex far more faithfully but says nothing about the thalamus or the cerebellum.


21.1.3 Cortical thickness, surface area, and gyrification as separable measures

Once a surface model exists, three distinct quantities can be measured: cortical thickness, which is the distance between the inner and outer surfaces and runs roughly one to four millimetres; surface area, which is how much sheet there is; and gyrification, which is how tightly that sheet is folded.

Grey matter volume is close to the product of thickness and area, and this is why volume is a treacherous summary - a volume difference could come from either factor, or from both pulling in opposite directions.

Panizzon and colleagues, writing in Cerebral Cortex in 2009 using a large twin sample, reported that cortical thickness and cortical surface area are essentially genetically uncorrelated, meaning the genes that influence one are largely not the genes that influence the other.

That finding is load-bearing for the rest of the field.

It implies thickness and area are separate developmental traits, that volume conflates at least two sets of genetic influences, and that studies should report thickness and area separately rather than collapsing them.

Gyrification, usually quantified as a gyrification index comparing the true folded surface to a smooth outer hull, tracks yet another process - the mechanical and developmental expansion of the sheet - and it changes on a different timescale across the lifespan than thickness does.


21.1.4 Quantitative mapping of myelin and iron

A standard T1-weighted image gives arbitrary intensity units: the number in a voxel has no meaning outside that particular scan on that particular day.

Quantitative mapping tries to recover physical quantities instead.

Glasser and Van Essen, in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2011, popularised dividing a T1-weighted image by a T2-weighted image of the same brain, because the division cancels much of the scanner's spatial bias and leaves a map that tracks myelin, the fatty insulating sheath wrapped around nerve fibres that speeds up signalling.

That T1w/T2w ratio is best described as semi-quantitative, and its validity as a myelin marker remains genuinely debated: it is not derived from a physical signal equation and is not a direct estimate of any single tissue property, so newer work compares it against properly fitted maps of the relaxation rates R1 and R2-star, which correlate strongly with it but are less contaminated by systematic error.

Iron is mapped by different means.

Because iron distorts the local magnetic field, techniques such as quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and R2-star mapping pick it out, and they show heavy iron loading in the basal ganglia - the deep grey structures involved in movement and habit - which increases with age.

The practical payoff of quantitative mapping is comparability: values expressed in physical units can be compared across scanners, sites, and years in a way that arbitrary intensities cannot.


21.2 Diffusion imaging

Diffusion imaging exploits a fact of physics rather than anatomy: water molecules at body temperature jiggle randomly, a process called Brownian motion, and in a few tenths of a second an unconstrained molecule wanders a few thousandths of a millimetre.

Inside a bundle of nerve fibres, that wandering is not free.

Cell membranes and myelin sheaths block sideways movement while permitting movement along the fibre, so the diffusion becomes directional, or anisotropic.

The scanner senses this by applying magnetic field gradients that label molecules by position; molecules that have moved lose signal.

Repeat the measurement along many directions and the pattern of signal loss reveals the local fibre orientation.

Nothing here images an axon.

The measurement is of water displacement averaged over a voxel containing perhaps hundreds of thousands of axons, and every interpretation must respect that gap in scale.


21.2.1 Diffusion tensor imaging and its scalar measures

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), introduced by Basser, Mattiello and Le Bihan in 1994, models the diffusion in each voxel as an ellipsoid described by a three-by-three symmetric matrix called a tensor - in plain terms, a stretched ball whose long axis points along the dominant fibre direction.

From that ellipsoid come the scalar summaries that fill the literature: mean diffusivity (MD), the overall rate of water movement; fractional anisotropy (FA), a number between zero and one describing how elongated the ellipsoid is; and axial and radial diffusivity, the rates along and across the main axis.

These numbers are routinely reported as measures of white matter integrity, and that phrase is where the trouble starts.

FA falls when fibres cross, when a bundle becomes less coherent, when myelin thins, when axons are lost, when partial volume with cerebrospinal fluid creeps in, and when a participant moves - all of which look identical in the output.

A 2022 review in NeuroImage on the pitfalls of FA, axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity as microstructural biomarkers makes the current consensus explicit: many diffusion specialists now avoid drawing strong reverse inferences about microstructure from these scalars used in isolation.


21.2.2 High angular resolution methods and crossing fibres

A single ellipsoid can point in only one direction, which is fatal wherever two or more fibre populations pass through the same voxel.

That situation is not rare.

Estimates from constrained spherical deconvolution studies, notably by Jeurissen and colleagues in Human Brain Mapping in 2013, put the proportion of white matter voxels containing crossing, kissing, or fanning fibres at roughly ninety percent.

High angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) is the family of acquisitions that samples many more directions, often sixty or more, and often at several diffusion strengths, so that a richer orientation model can be fitted.

Constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD), developed by Tournier and colleagues, treats the measured signal as the smearing of an underlying orientation distribution by a standard single-fibre response, and mathematically undoes that smearing to recover multiple peaks.

Multi-tissue CSD, described by Jeurissen and colleagues in NeuroImage in 2014, extends this by modelling grey matter and cerebrospinal fluid alongside white matter, which sharply reduces spurious orientations at tissue boundaries.


21.2.3 Deterministic and probabilistic tractography

Tractography is the procedure of stepping through the orientation field to draw streamlines, which are computer-generated curves intended to follow fibre bundles.

Deterministic tractography, of which the FACT algorithm is the classic example, takes the single most likely orientation at each step, producing clean, reproducible, visually convincing bundles.

Probabilistic tractography instead samples repeatedly from the uncertainty in orientation at each step, generating a fuzzy cloud of possible paths and, with it, an honest picture of how confident the data permit us to be.

The trade is stark and well documented, for example by Smith and colleagues in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine in 2020: deterministic methods buy specificity by discarding real connections, probabilistic methods buy sensitivity by inventing false ones.

Two refinements from Smith and colleagues attempt to split the difference.

Anatomically constrained tractography (ACT), published in NeuroImage in 2012, uses the tissue segmentation to reject biologically absurd streamlines such as those ending in cerebrospinal fluid, and spherical-deconvolution informed filtering of tractograms (SIFT) prunes a tractogram until the density of streamlines matches the underlying diffusion signal, so that streamline counts become a defensible proxy for connection strength.


21.2.4 Validation against tracer anatomy and known failure modes

The gold standard against which tractography must be judged is chemical tract tracing: injecting a substance into one region of an animal brain, letting it travel along axons, then sectioning the brain and looking.

It is definitive and it kills the animal, so it cannot be done in humans.

Thomas and colleagues, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2014, compared tractography in a macaque against tracer injections in the same animal and reached a blunt conclusion: accuracy is fundamentally limited regardless of how much data are acquired, because the diffusion signal simply does not contain the information needed to disambiguate certain configurations.

The open tractography challenge reported by Maier-Hein and colleagues in Nature Communications in 2017 sharpened this: across dozens of submitted pipelines, most reconstructed the majority of real bundles but also produced large numbers of invalid ones, and the methods that found the most true connections also found the most false ones.

The characteristic failure modes are now catalogued: streamlines jump between bundles that touch tangentially, long-range connections are systematically under-detected relative to short-range ones, sharp turns such as the fan of fibres entering the cortex are truncated, and streamline counts are biased by bundle length and curvature rather than by anatomical strength.

The reasonable position is therefore neither dismissal nor credulity: tractography is trustworthy for large, well-separated, previously described bundles, and untrustworthy as a discovery instrument for novel fine-grained connections.


21.3 Structure-function relations

Anatomy constrains function but does not determine it, and this section covers three ways researchers have tried to make that relationship quantitative.

The recurring question is whether a structural measurement predicts anything about behaviour or physiology that we did not already know, and the honest answer is usually partly, in aggregate, with wide individual variation.


21.3.1 Structural covariance networks

Structural covariance is a statistical rather than an anatomical relationship: it asks whether people who have a thicker cortex in one region also tend to have a thicker cortex in another, across a sample of individuals.

Regions that covary form structural covariance networks, and as Alexander-Bloch, Giedd and Bullmore reviewed in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2013, these networks are reproducible across samples and across species, and they partially resemble both the anatomical connections and the functional networks measured by other means.

They also resemble the spatial patterns of tissue loss seen in neurodegenerative diseases, which is one reason the field takes them seriously.

The interpretation is genuinely unresolved.

Candidate explanations include shared genetic influence, coordinated maturational timing between regions, and mutually reinforcing plasticity in regions that are used together, and current data do not decisively separate them.

A structural covariance network is a property of a population, not of any individual, and it should never be described as that person's brain network.


21.3.2 Predicting function from structural connectivity

Honey and colleagues, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2009, tested directly whether the pattern of anatomical connections predicts the pattern of correlated spontaneous activity measured at rest with functional MRI.

The answer was a qualified yes: where a strong structural connection exists, a strong functional correlation almost always follows, but the converse fails badly - many strong functional correlations join regions with no direct anatomical link, mediated instead by indirect multi-step paths.

Their computational model reproduced this by simulating neural activity on the measured anatomical skeleton, showing that indirect connections and the sheer physical distance between regions account for a substantial share of the otherwise unexplained variance.

Later work, including analytic communication models such as those of Goni and colleagues in the same journal in 2014, improved the prediction by allowing signals to travel via search-information or diffusion-like routes rather than only along shortest paths.

The standing conclusion is that structure sets the boundaries within which functional patterns fluctuate, and that a one-to-one mapping between the two was never a realistic expectation.


21.3.3 Structural change with learning and experience

Maguire and colleagues reported in 2000 that licensed London taxi drivers, who must memorise an enormous street network, had larger posterior hippocampi than controls, with size scaling with years of driving - suggestive but cross-sectional, and therefore unable to exclude the possibility that people with such hippocampi become taxi drivers.

Draganski and colleagues closed part of that gap in Nature in 2004 with a randomised training design: adults who learned a three-ball juggling cascade over three months showed grey matter expansion in mid-temporal visual motion areas and parietal cortex, and the expansion partly regressed after training stopped.

Their follow-up work reported changes detectable after roughly a week of practice, and Driemeyer and colleagues revisited the effect in PLOS ONE in 2008, finding that change appeared early and did not scale simply with how well people learned to juggle.

The caution is that all of this rests on voxel-based morphometry, which is sensitive to registration error, and the biological substrate of a grey matter signal change over weeks is not established - candidate mechanisms include synapse formation, glial proliferation, dendritic growth, and vascular change, and MRI cannot currently distinguish them.

The claim that learning changes brain structure is well supported; the claim that a particular percentage change equals a particular number of new synapses is not.


21.4 Atlases and reference frames

An atlas is a shared coordinate system plus a set of labels, and without one no two laboratories could say they were talking about the same piece of brain.

The difficulty is that no two brains have the same shape, so every atlas embodies a compromise between fidelity to the individual and comparability across individuals.


21.4.1 Talairach and Montreal Neurological Institute spaces

The Talairach and Tournoux atlas of 1988 defined a coordinate frame anchored on two landmarks, the anterior and posterior commissures, which are fibre bundles crossing the midline.

Its labels came from post-mortem sectioning of the brain of a single elderly French woman.

Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space replaced it with averages: first MNI305, built by aligning 305 scanned brains to a Talairach-like frame, then the ICBM152 templates built from 152 brains, in linear and later nonlinear versions such as the widely used ICBM152 2009 series.

The two frames are not interchangeable.

Lancaster and colleagues, in Human Brain Mapping in 2007, showed that MNI-fitted brains are consistently larger and tipped slightly nose-down relative to Talairach-fitted brains, with coordinate disparity approaching or exceeding a centimetre in anterior regions, and derived a corrective transform reducing the mismatch to one or two millimetres.

The practical rule is that a published coordinate is meaningless without a stated space, and that mixing spaces silently is one of the commonest avoidable errors in the literature.


21.4.2 Multimodal parcellations and the Human Connectome Project atlas

Parcellation means dividing the cortex into discrete areas.

Earlier parcellations relied on a single criterion, most famously Brodmann's 1909 map based on cell architecture seen under a microscope in a small number of post-mortem brains.

Glasser, Van Essen and colleagues, in Nature in 2016, produced the Human Connectome Project multimodal parcellation (HCP-MMP1.0) by requiring agreement across several independent measurements - myelin content from the T1w/T2w ratio, cortical thickness, task-driven activation, resting-state functional connectivity, and topographic maps - in 210 healthy young adults.

The result is 180 areas per hemisphere, 360 in total, of which 97 had not previously been described and 83 corresponded to areas reported earlier by microscopy or specialised methods.

A crucial enabling step was multimodal surface matching, an alignment algorithm that registers individuals using functional and myelin features rather than folds alone, because folding patterns and functional boundaries do not reliably coincide.

The atlas is now a common currency in the field, but it is a group-average product built from young healthy adults, and its transfer to children, older adults, and clinical populations is an active question rather than a settled one.


21.4.3 Allen human and mouse brain atlases and gene expression maps

The Allen Institute for Brain Science built atlases that add a dimension the MRI-based ones lack: which genes are switched on where.

The Allen Human Brain Atlas, described by Hawrylycz and colleagues in Nature in 2012, used microarray measurement - a technique that quantifies the activity of thousands of genes at once - on roughly 3,700 tissue samples taken from six donor brains, covering more than 20,000 genes, with each sample tied to a location in MRI-derived stereotactic space.

Six donors is a small number, sampling was mostly left-hemisphere, and processing choices materially affect results, which is why the abagen toolbox described by Markello and colleagues in eLife in 2021 exists to standardise the workflow and make imaging-transcriptomics analyses reproducible.

On the mouse side, the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas provides genome-wide expression by in situ hybridisation, a staining method that shows gene activity directly in tissue sections, and the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas provides a systematically injected, tracer-based mesoscale wiring diagram of the whole mouse brain - the ground truth that human tractography can only approximate.

The payoff of joining these to imaging is that a cortical map of, say, myelin or thickness can be tested against the expression pattern of specific genes, which turns a descriptive map into a mechanistic hypothesis.


21.4.4 Individual against group reference frames

Group averaging is a bargain: it suppresses noise and permits population inference, at the cost of blurring away anything that sits in a slightly different place in each person.

Gordon, Laumann and colleagues, in Neuron in 2017, made the cost visible with the Midnight Scan Club dataset, in which ten individuals each received about five hours of resting-state scanning plus hours of task and structural imaging - enough data to map each brain on its own terms.

Individual maps proved reliably more detailed than the group average, and some features present in every individual were absent from the average because their location varied from person to person, a phenomenon since termed precision functional mapping.

The corollary is that a small effect at the group level can be a large effect in each individual that has merely been smeared across a wider area, and this ambiguity cannot be resolved by increasing the number of participants.

The two reference frames answer different questions: the group frame asks what is true of people in general, while the individual frame asks what is true of this brain, and clinical applications such as surgical planning or targeted stimulation need the second.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Structural magnetic resonance imaging measures water in tissue, not tissue itself, and every anatomical quantity reported in the literature is the output of a long automated pipeline whose early errors propagate silently into the final number.

Cortical thickness, surface area, and gyrification are separable measures with largely distinct genetic influences, following Panizzon and colleagues in 2009, so grey matter volume is a conflation that should be decomposed rather than reported alone.

Diffusion imaging infers fibre orientation from constrained water movement, and because crossing configurations occupy roughly ninety percent of white matter voxels, single-tensor measures such as fractional anisotropy cannot be read as direct indices of white matter integrity.

Tractography validated against tracer injections, in Thomas and colleagues in 2014 and the Maier-Hein challenge of 2017, is dependable for large known bundles and unreliable as a discovery tool, because sensitivity and specificity trade against each other in every algorithm.

Structure constrains function without determining it: Honey and colleagues in 2009 showed that direct anatomical connections almost always produce functional coupling while strong functional coupling frequently occurs without any direct link.

Atlases are indispensable but not neutral, since Talairach and Montreal Neurological Institute spaces differ by up to a centimetre in places, and group-average reference frames systematically erase individual features that precision mapping recovers.


CHAPTER 22. CAUSAL MANIPULATION (APPARATUS)


Watching the brain while somebody thinks tells you what happens alongside the thinking, not what makes the thinking happen.

To get from alongside to because, you have to change something in the brain and see whether the behaviour changes with it.

This chapter is about the apparatus of that change: damage that nature or surgery inflicts, magnetic and electrical and ultrasonic fields applied through the scalp, implanted electrodes, and genetically targeted switches that let light or a drug turn a named population of cells on or off.

It matters because almost every strong claim in cognitive neuroscience - that this region is for that function - is ultimately a causal claim, and causal claims are only as good as the manipulation that supports them.

The chapter also spends real time on the ways a manipulation can mislead you, because the honest history of this field is a history of clean-looking interventions with messy consequences.


22.1 Lesion methods in humans

A lesion is an area of damaged or destroyed brain tissue - from stroke, tumour, infection, head injury, or surgery.

Lesion work is the oldest causal method in neuroscience and still the only one that tells you what happens when a piece of human cortex is genuinely, permanently gone.

Its great weakness is that the experimenter does not choose where the damage falls; the vasculature and the accident do.

That single fact - damage is not randomly assigned - shapes every methodological refinement in this section.


22.1.1 The single-case tradition and dissociation logic

The classical move is to find one patient who fails task A while performing task B normally, which is a single dissociation, and then to find another patient with the reverse profile, which together make a double dissociation.

The inference is that the two tasks draw on at least partly separable machinery, since one can be broken while the other is spared and vice versa; Tim Shallice set out the full logic and its assumptions in his 1988 book From Neuropsychology to Mental Structure, and Alfonso Caramazza argued forcefully in the 1980s that averaging across patients can destroy exactly the information a single case carries.

The classic worked example is the patient known as H.M., whose medial temporal lobes were removed surgically in 1953 by William Scoville: he could no longer form new conscious memories for facts and events, yet he could learn new motor skills, which pulls those two kinds of memory apart.

The logic has real critics.

Connectionist modellers, notably Martha Farah and James McClelland in the early 1990s, showed that a single undivided network with no separable parts can produce double dissociations when damaged in different ways, so a double dissociation demonstrates that two abilities can come apart but does not by itself prove that the brain contains two tidy modules.

A second worry is statistical: single cases are single, and a growing methodological literature argues that adequately powered simple dissociations across groups can sometimes be more informative than a rare double dissociation in one person.


22.1.2 Group lesion studies and voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping

The group approach pools many patients with varied damage and asks, at every point in the brain, whether the patients damaged there perform worse than the patients spared there.

Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping (VLSM) does exactly this, one voxel at a time - a voxel being a small three-dimensional cube of brain, the imaging equivalent of a pixel.

The method was introduced by Elizabeth Bates, Stephen Wilson, Ayse Pinar Saygin, Frederic Dick, Martin Sereno, Robert Knight and Nina Dronkers in Nature Neuroscience in 2003, using 101 patients with left-hemisphere damage and measures of speech fluency and auditory comprehension, and it recovered the expected front-versus-back contrast in language without anyone having to sort patients into diagnostic boxes first.

The crucial advantage over the single case is that behaviour is treated as a continuous score rather than a pass or fail, so mild impairments count.

The crucial limitation is that strokes follow arteries, so certain voxels are damaged together far more often than chance would predict, and the statistics can therefore assign blame to a voxel that was merely a bystander travelling with the guilty one.

Later work has attacked this with permutation-based correction for multiple comparisons and with multivariate methods that consider the whole lesion pattern at once rather than voxel by voxel.


22.1.3 Lesion network mapping and symptom localisation to networks

Some symptoms refuse to localise: patients with the same syndrome have lesions scattered in places that barely overlap, so no single voxel is implicated.

Lesion network mapping, introduced by Aaron Boes, Michael Fox and colleagues in Brain in 2015, handles this by asking not where the lesions are but what they were connected to.

Each lesion is placed on a reference brain and its functional connectivity is looked up in a normative connectome - a large database of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans from healthy people, describing which regions' activity fluctuates together.

Lesions that look unrelated in space often turn out to be connected to one common circuit, and that circuit is proposed as the localisation of the symptom; the approach has now been applied to dozens of symptoms including hallucinations, tics, blindsight, and pathological laughing and crying.

The method is popular and contested.

It uses connectivity from other, healthy brains rather than from the patient, and a 2025 Nature Neuroscience paper by several groups examined its methodological foundations directly, probing how much of the result depends on the choice of connectome, on lesion size, and on the spatial smoothness of connectivity maps rather than on the patient's symptom - so the technique should be read as a hypothesis generator whose assumptions are still under active audit.


22.1.4 Plasticity and reorganisation as confounds on inference

A lesion study measures the brain after it has had time to react to its own injury, and that reaction is not nothing.

In the days after a stroke, remote but connected regions become hypoactive even though they are structurally intact, a phenomenon called diaschisis, described by Constantin von Monakow early in the twentieth century; over months, spared tissue can take over some of the lost function.

This cuts two ways for inference.

Acute deficits may overstate the role of the damaged region because they include the temporary silencing of healthy partners, while chronic performance may understate it because the system has already routed around the hole.

The most striking demonstrations come from slow-growing tumours and from childhood injury, where patients can retain near-normal language despite damage that would be devastating if inflicted suddenly - which tells you the deficit you measure is a joint product of the lesion and of the time the brain had to adapt to it.


22.2 Non-invasive stimulation

Non-invasive stimulation lets the experimenter, rather than the accident, choose where and when to perturb, and lets the same person serve as their own control.

The price is that the perturbation is weaker, shallower, and less anatomically precise than a lesion, and its physiological meaning is often uncertain.


22.2.1 Transcranial magnetic stimulation: single-pulse, paired-pulse, repetitive, theta burst

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) passes a brief, very strong current through a coil held against the scalp, producing a changing magnetic field that passes freely through skull and induces an electric current in the cortex underneath, depolarising neurons directly; the method in its modern form was demonstrated by Anthony Barker and colleagues in Sheffield in 1985.

A single pulse over motor cortex makes a muscle twitch, and the size of that twitch, the motor evoked potential, is the field's standard readout of cortical excitability.

Paired-pulse protocols deliver a weak conditioning pulse followed milliseconds later by a test pulse, and the resulting suppression or enhancement is used to index inhibitory and excitatory circuits - short-interval intracortical inhibition at intervals of a few milliseconds is generally attributed to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the brain's main inhibitory chemical messenger.

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) delivers trains of pulses and produces effects that outlast the train, with low frequencies around one hertz tending to depress excitability and higher frequencies around ten to twenty hertz tending to raise it, though this rule of thumb is much less reliable than its popularity suggests.

Theta burst stimulation (TBS), introduced by Ying-Zu Huang, John Rothwell and colleagues in Neuron in 2005, packs bursts of three pulses at fifty hertz repeated five times a second: given continuously for forty seconds, six hundred pulses in all, it suppresses excitability, while the same six hundred pulses given intermittently in two-second trains every ten seconds enhance it, with effects lasting on the order of tens of minutes.

TBS is thought to engage synaptic plasticity resembling long-term potentiation and long-term depression, and its intermittent form is now approved for treating depression, but the individual variability is substantial and several replication attempts have found the group-level direction does not hold in a large fraction of individuals.


22.2.2 Virtual lesions, chronometry, and state dependence

The phrase virtual lesion, popularised by Vincent Walsh and Alan Cowey, captures the appeal of TMS: it can disrupt a region briefly and reversibly, giving something like a lesion that lasts a fraction of a second in a healthy volunteer.

Because the disruption is brief, you can move it in time and ask when a region is needed, not merely whether - this is chronometry, and it produces claims of the form that stimulation of a given visual area impairs performance only in a window roughly one hundred milliseconds after the stimulus.

Chronometry is arguably TMS's single strongest contribution, because no other human method delivers timing information about necessity.

The virtual lesion metaphor, though, is known to be too simple.

Juha Silvanto, Neil Muggleton, Alan Cowey and Vincent Walsh showed in 2007 that if you first adapt a population of neurons, TMS preferentially affects the less active population and can facilitate rather than impair perception - so the effect of a pulse depends on the state the cortex is in when it arrives.

The practical consequence is that a null result may mean the region is not needed, or merely that the brain state at that moment made the pulse ineffective.


22.2.3 Transcranial direct and alternating current stimulation

Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) passes a weak constant current, typically one to two milliamps, between scalp electrodes.

It does not make neurons fire; it shifts membrane potentials slightly, making cells modestly more or less likely to fire, with the anode (positive electrode) usually associated with increased excitability and the cathode with decreased, following Michael Nitsche and Walter Paulus's motor-cortex work from 2000.

Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) instead applies an oscillating current at a chosen frequency, on the theory that it entrains endogenous brain rhythms by nudging populations toward a preferred phase.

This is the most contested area in the chapter.

Jared Horvath and colleagues published systematic reviews in 2015 arguing that single-session tDCS produces little reliable neurophysiological effect beyond motor evoked potential changes, and little reliable cognitive effect in healthy people; defenders including Marom Bikson and colleagues replied that these reviews lumped together incompatible doses, durations and montages, so a null average says little.

The picture has not fully resolved: a 2024 meta-analysis of 134 tACS working-memory interventions found an overall effect size of about g equals 0.08 that fell to zero once publication bias was corrected, while other umbrella reviews report modest but real clinical benefits for depression, and modelling work confirms that only a fraction of the applied current reaches cortex at all.


22.2.4 Transcranial focused ultrasound and deep targeting

Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) at low intensity focuses acoustic pressure waves through the skull onto a small volume of brain, and unlike magnetic or electrical stimulation it can be aimed at deep structures without affecting the tissue above them.

Spatial resolution is on the order of a few millimetres, and targets already reported in humans include the thalamus, the amygdala and the nucleus accumbens.

The presumed mechanism is mechanical rather than electrical: pressure waves deform the membrane and open mechanosensitive ion channels, with the direction of the effect - excitation or suppression - depending heavily on parameters such as duty cycle and pulse repetition frequency, which is both the technique's flexibility and its interpretive headache.

Hardware has advanced quickly, with a 2025 Nature Communications report describing a 256-element helmet array operating near 555 kilohertz with individualised planning and simultaneous fMRI monitoring.

Two cautions are standard and worth stating: ultrasound can produce an audible auditory artefact that itself changes brain activity, so sham conditions must control for sound, and the long-term safety envelope in humans is still being mapped.


22.3 Invasive and molecular manipulation

Once you are willing to open the skull or alter the genome, precision improves enormously.

In humans that willingness is limited to clinical need; in animals it is limited only by technique, which is why the sharpest causal claims in neuroscience come from mice and the least generalisable ones come from mice.


22.3.1 Deep brain stimulation and responsive neurostimulation

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) implants electrodes in a deep target - most commonly the subthalamic nucleus or the internal globus pallidus for Parkinson's disease - and delivers continuous high-frequency pulses, typically around 130 hertz, from an implanted pulse generator.

It is a genuinely effective treatment for Parkinson's disease, essential tremor and dystonia, and it is a rare case where the manipulation is reversible: turn the stimulator off and the tremor returns.

Its mechanism remains debated, and reviews such as Cameron McIntyre and colleagues' work in the Journal of Neurophysiology conclude that no single account suffices - high-frequency stimulation appears to combine local effects on cell bodies and axons, disruption of pathological oscillatory synchrony in the beta band, network-wide antidromic effects, and neurochemical changes.

Responsive neurostimulation is the closed-loop cousin: the NeuroPace RNS System records continuously from one or two seizure foci and stimulates only when it detects the electrographic pattern that precedes that patient's seizures.

Long-term multicentre follow-up has reported median seizure reductions in the region of seventy-five percent at nine years, and because the device also stores years of intracranial recordings it has become an unexpected scientific instrument in its own right.

For cognition, the scientific value of these devices is that they permit within-patient on-versus-off comparisons in a human being, though patients are never neurologically typical and the samples are small.


22.3.2 Optogenetics: excitation, inhibition, and temporal precision

Optogenetics introduces a light-sensitive protein from microbes into chosen neurons, so that a pulse of light of the right colour changes their electrical state within milliseconds.

The workhorse for excitation is channelrhodopsin-2, a blue-light-gated cation channel; Ed Boyden, Feng Zhang, Ernst Bamberg, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth reported millisecond-precision optical control of neuronal spiking in Nature Neuroscience in 2005.

For silencing, halorhodopsin from Natronomonas pharaonis pumps chloride into the cell on yellow light, hyperpolarising it, and later anion-conducting channelrhodopsins improved silencing efficiency.

Two properties make optogenetics the reference standard for causal circuit work: cell-type specificity, because the opsin gene can be placed under a promoter active only in, say, parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons, and projection specificity, because you can illuminate the axon terminals in one target region and affect only the cells that project there.

The limitations are real and often understated: viral expression is uneven, light scatters and heats tissue, driving a population synchronously is physiologically unnatural, and prolonged chloride loading during silencing can paradoxically excite some cells.


22.3.3 Chemogenetics and designer receptors

Chemogenetics uses an engineered receptor that ignores everything in the body and responds only to an otherwise inert drug.

The dominant family is DREADDs - designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs - developed by Bryan Roth and colleagues from mutated muscarinic receptors, with hM3Dq raising excitability and hM4Di lowering it, classically activated by clozapine-N-oxide (CNO).

The trade-off against optogenetics is time: chemogenetic effects take minutes to arrive and last hours, which suits questions about sustained states such as hunger or anxiety but cannot address millisecond timing, and it requires no implanted fibre.

The field absorbed a serious blow in 2017 when Juan Gomez, Michael Michaelides and colleagues showed in Science that CNO barely crosses the blood-brain barrier and has low affinity for the DREADD; what actually reaches and activates the receptor is clozapine, formed by back-metabolism of CNO, and clozapine is an antipsychotic with many endogenous targets of its own.

The practical response has been to use very low doses of clozapine directly or newer agonists, and - crucially - to run the control in which the drug is given to animals that do not express the receptor at all, a control that many pre-2017 papers omitted.


22.3.4 Pharmacological challenge in humans and animals

A pharmacological challenge gives a drug that raises or lowers the activity of a particular neurotransmitter system and measures the cognitive consequence.

Familiar examples include scopolamine, which blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and impairs memory encoding; ketamine, which blocks the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor and produces working-memory and perceptual disturbances used as a model of psychosis; and levodopa or dopamine agonists, which shift reinforcement learning and can bias people toward learning from rewards over punishments.

The great advantage is that this is one of the very few ways to manipulate a specific chemical system in a healthy human being.

The great disadvantage is that the manipulation is anatomically indiscriminate - the drug reaches every receptor of that class in the brain and body.

A further complication that recurs across this literature is the inverted-U: dopaminergic drugs frequently help people who start low on a measure and impair people who start high, as in Roshan Cools's work on working memory, so a group-average null can conceal two real and opposite effects.


22.4 The logic of causal claims

Apparatus is only half the story.

The other half is knowing exactly what conclusion a given manipulation licenses, and this section is about the inferential rules rather than the machines.


22.4.1 Necessity and sufficiency tests and what each licenses

Removing or silencing a region tests necessity: if the behaviour disappears, that region was needed for it, under these conditions, in this task.

Activating a region tests sufficiency: if stimulation alone produces the behaviour or percept, the region's activity can drive it, as in Bill Newsome and Chris Salzman's 1990 microstimulation of motion-sensitive area MT in monkeys, which shifted the animals' motion judgements in the direction preferred by the stimulated column.

Neither test alone establishes that a region does the job in normal life.

Necessity is compatible with a region being a mere relay or a supplier of a general resource like arousal, and sufficiency is compatible with the stimulation entering the pathway at an unnatural point and driving downstream machinery that would ordinarily be driven by something else.

Several critical commentaries, including work by Ron Yizhar and colleagues and a pointed 2018 essay by Ralf Stanewsky and co-authors on misapplied logic in biology, note that the words necessary and sufficient are used far more loosely in neuroscience than in logic, and are almost always implicitly qualified by task, timescale and background condition.


22.4.2 Compensation, off-target effects, and network-wide consequences

Steven Wolff and Bence Olveczky argued in 2018 that in a distributed system the observable effect of silencing one node reflects both the node's normal contribution and the rest of the network's reaction to losing it.

Their most useful illustration is developmental compensation: silence a circuit from birth and behaviour may look normal, not because the circuit was irrelevant but because something else grew into the role, which is why acute, reversible manipulations are generally more interpretable than chronic ones.

The mirror-image error is also common: silencing region A can suppress activity in region B through disfacilitation, so the behavioural change may be caused by the intact region B falling silent rather than by the loss of A itself.

Off-target effects compound this - viral spread beyond the intended region, current spread beyond the intended electrode, drug action at receptors you did not intend, and in TMS the loud click and the scalp twitch, which are salient sensory events that must be matched in a sham condition.

The general lesson is that a manipulation delivers its effect to a network, and the behavioural readout is at the end of that network, not at the site of the intervention.


22.4.3 Perturbation strength against physiological plausibility

There is an unavoidable tension between making a manipulation big enough to produce a measurable effect and keeping it small enough to resemble anything the brain does naturally.

Optogenetically driving ten thousand neurons in perfect synchrony at twenty hertz produces a clear result and a pattern of activity that no natural circuit ever generates, and the downstream consequences may say more about how the target responds to an artificial barrage than about how it processes real input.

Weak, physiologically scaled perturbations are more faithful but risk being swallowed by the system's own variability, which is precisely the diagnosis some offer for the inconsistency of tDCS results.

The most respected recent designs try to escape the dilemma with precision rather than power: two-photon holographic optogenetics, developed in laboratories including those of Hillel Adesnik and Rafael Yuste, can stimulate a chosen handful of individually identified neurons, and such experiments have shown that activating on the order of tens of cells can bias an animal's behavioural report.

That is the current frontier - the smallest intervention that still moves behaviour is usually the most informative one.


22.4.4 Combining perturbation with recording

The strongest designs perturb and record at the same time, so you can see not only that behaviour changed but what the intervention did to the rest of the system.

In humans, concurrent TMS with electroencephalography (EEG) measures the TMS-evoked potential, the wave that propagates from the stimulated site through connected cortex, and TMS combined with fMRI shows which distant regions the pulse reaches - this is also the standard proof of target engagement, evidence that the intervention actually affected the intended tissue rather than nothing at all.

Combined TMS-EEG-fMRI work has shown that the same pulse produces different network consequences depending on the pre-pulse alpha rhythm, tying the state dependence of section 22.2.2 to measurable brain state.

In animals, optogenetic fMRI, introduced by Jin Hyung Lee, Karl Deisseroth and colleagues in Nature in 2010, drove excitatory neurons in one cortical region and imaged the whole-brain haemodynamic response, which also served as a calibration of what the fMRI signal reflects.

Perturbation plus dense electrophysiology now supports causal connectivity estimates that neither method yields alone, and the combination also provides the honest negative control: if you perturb, see the expected physiological change, and behaviour still does not move, you have learned something real about that region's dispensability.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Correlational imaging cannot by itself support claims that a brain region does a cognitive job; only manipulation can, which is why lesions, stimulation and molecular switches carry the causal weight in this field.

Each method trades away something: human lesions are permanent and unrandomised and contaminated by plasticity, TMS is precise in time but shallow and state dependent, transcranial electrical stimulation is cheap and popular but its effect sizes remain seriously disputed, and optogenetics and chemogenetics buy exquisite specificity at the cost of species and, in the case of clozapine-N-oxide, of a pharmacological assumption that turned out to be wrong.

Necessity and sufficiency are different tests licensing different conclusions, and both are always relative to a task, a timescale and a background state rather than absolute.

Because the brain is a network that reacts to being perturbed, the measured behavioural change reflects both the intervention and the system's compensation for it, so acute and reversible manipulations are more interpretable than chronic ones.

The best current practice is to perturb and record simultaneously, to demonstrate target engagement rather than assume it, and to use the smallest perturbation that still moves behaviour.


CHAPTER 23. NATURALISTIC, LONGITUDINAL, AND LARGE-SCALE APPROACHES (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about four changes in how brain science gathers evidence, all of which happened in roughly the last twenty years.

The first is naturalistic measurement - letting people watch films and listen to stories in the scanner instead of pressing buttons in response to flashing shapes.

The second is precision and longitudinal measurement - scanning a few people many, many times rather than many people once.

The third is population-scale measurement - assembling tens of thousands of brains so that small, real effects can be told apart from noise.

The fourth is the unglamorous plumbing that makes the other three checkable: file-format standards, public archives, containerised analysis pipelines, and rules for protecting the privacy of the people whose brains are in the dataset.

These are not side issues.

A great deal of what the earlier chapters of this book could honestly claim depends on whether the apparatus described here was in place when the claim was made.


23.1 Naturalistic neuroscience

For most of the history of experimental psychology, the price of control was artificiality.

To know exactly what caused a brain response, you had to strip the stimulus down to something you could describe completely - a bar of light, a single word, a tone.

The trouble is that nothing in ordinary life looks like that, and a brain doing something it never normally does may not reveal how it works when it is doing what it normally does.

Naturalistic neuroscience is the attempt to have both things: rich, lifelike stimulation, plus analysis methods clever enough to extract structure from it.
