The name traces back to a shift in vision research from artificial gratings to complex natural images, and it has since spread to hearing, language, memory, and social cognition.

The central methodological trick is this - if you cannot fully specify the stimulus, use the responses of other people, or a computational model of the stimulus, as your yardstick instead.


23.1.1 Film, narrative, and free-listening paradigms

In a film paradigm, a participant simply watches a movie inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner - a machine that tracks blood-oxygen changes as an indirect index of neural activity - while the scanner records the whole brain every second or two.

Narrative paradigms do the same with spoken stories, and free-listening paradigms with music, and none of them require the participant to perform a task at all.

Public resources have made this a shared enterprise rather than a set of one-off experiments: the studyforrest project released extensive fMRI and magnetoencephalography recordings of people experiencing the film Forrest Gump, and the Narratives collection released by Nastase and colleagues in 2021 aggregates 345 participants, 891 functional scans, and 27 spoken stories totalling roughly 4.6 hours of unique audio with time-stamped word and phoneme transcripts.

Naturalistic stimuli are unusually well suited to populations that struggle with instructions - developmental researchers have found that movie-watching data can reveal brain-behaviour relationships in children more readily than either resting-state scanning or conventional tasks, which matters because a bored, fidgeting six-year-old produces mostly motion artefact.

The costs are real and are often understated: film and audio editing are specialist crafts, presenting the same stimulus identically across scanner sites is genuinely hard, and a 2024 preprint by researchers examining between-movie variability argued that findings from one film often generalise poorly to another - meaning that a "naturalistic" result may be a result about that particular movie.


23.1.2 Inter-subject correlation and inter-subject functional connectivity

Inter-subject correlation (ISC) was introduced by Uri Hasson and colleagues in 2004 and is the founding analysis method of the field.

The idea is disarmingly simple - take the time course of activity in one brain region in person A, take the same region's time course in person B while they watched the same film, and correlate them.

Because the participants share nothing except the stimulus, any reliable correlation must be stimulus-driven, which gives you a model-free way of asking where in the brain the film is being processed, without having to specify in advance what "the film" consists of.

Hasson's original result showed extensive synchronisation across viewers, strongest in visual and auditory cortex but extending well into higher-order regions, and ISC has since become the standard way of measuring how much usable signal a naturalistic dataset contains.

Inter-subject functional connectivity extends the logic to pairs of regions - it correlates region X in person A with region Y in person B, so that only stimulus-locked coupling survives and the person's own idiosyncratic internal fluctuations and head-motion artefacts cancel out.

An important qualification is that ISC magnitude depends heavily on how the stimulus was constructed: professionally edited films drive markedly higher synchrony than unedited real-life footage, and narratively coherent material drives higher synchrony than scrambled material, so ISC is measuring the stimulus's grip on the viewer as much as it is measuring the viewer.


23.1.3 Encoding models over rich natural stimuli

An encoding model runs the explanation in the forward direction - it takes a description of the stimulus, passes it through a set of features, and predicts the measured brain response, then is scored on how well it predicts data it was never fitted to.

The voxelwise encoding model framework developed in Jack Gallant's laboratory does this separately for every voxel (a three-dimensional pixel of brain, typically a couple of millimetres on a side), so that each voxel ends up with its own fitted description of what it responds to.

The landmark application is Huth, de Heer, Griffiths, Theunissen, and Gallant's 2016 Nature paper, in which participants listened to hours of narrative stories and the fitted models were used to draw a continuous semantic map across the cortical surface - showing that words about people, places, numbers, and actions are represented in distinct but smoothly graded patches, and that these patches sit in broadly similar locations across individuals.

The critical discipline here is out-of-sample prediction: the model must predict responses to stimuli held back from fitting, which is a far harder test than reporting that some region was significantly active.

Since the mid-2010s the feature spaces have increasingly been taken from deep neural networks and large language models, which raises an unresolved interpretive question the field openly argues about - a model that predicts brain responses well may or may not be telling you anything about the brain's actual computations, and prediction accuracy alone does not settle it.


23.1.4 Hyperscanning and two-brain paradigms

Hyperscanning means recording two or more brains at the same time while the people interact, using electroencephalography (EEG, scalp electrodes measuring electrical activity), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS, optical measurement of blood oxygenation through the skull), or linked fMRI scanners.

The motivation is that conversation, cooperation, teaching, and joint attention are things that happen between people, and a single-brain experiment with a confederate on a video screen may not capture them.

The measured quantity is usually inter-brain synchrony - the temporal alignment of neural activity across the two participants - and studies report that it rises during cooperation, joint attention, and successful communication.

This literature has grown very fast, with scientometric reviews in 2024 charting two decades of output, and systematic reviews now applying it to autism and to stress and mood disorders.

It also has a serious methodological problem that its own practitioners have documented: a 2024 analysis in Imaging Neuroscience showed that arbitrary analysis choices in EEG hyperscanning substantially skew synchrony estimates, and there is continuing disagreement about how much inter-brain synchrony reflects genuine neural coupling as opposed to the two people simply seeing and hearing the same things and moving in similar ways.

The honest summary is that hyperscanning is an elegant idea with a real and growing dataset behind it, and a control problem that is not yet solved.


23.2 Precision and longitudinal designs

The standard cognitive-neuroscience experiment scans perhaps twenty to forty people for perhaps half an hour each, then averages across them.

Two different objections to that design emerged in the 2010s, pointing in opposite directions.

One says the sample is too small for reliable individual-difference claims, and the fix is tens of thousands of people.

The other says the averaging destroys the very thing you want to see, and the fix is to scan a handful of people for ten hours each.

Both objections turn out to be correct about different questions, and this section is about the second one.


23.2.1 Densely sampled individuals and the precision-imaging movement

Precision imaging means scanning one person repeatedly until their individual brain organisation can be measured with the confidence normally reserved for group averages.

The MyConnectome project, in which Russell Poldrack scanned himself across 104 sessions over 18 months alongside gene-expression, metabolomic, and psychological measures, was published in Nature Communications in 2015 and showed that functional connectivity changes systematically over days to months and tracks bodily and psychological state.

The Midnight Scan Club, reported by Evan Gordon, Timothy Laumann and colleagues in Neuron in 2017, scanned ten healthy adults for roughly five hours of rest and six hours of task each, and its central finding was that functional network boundaries are stable within a person but differ meaningfully between people - so-called network variants that a group average simply smears away.

The practical payoff is clinical as well as scientific: individually mapped networks are now used to target brain-stimulation treatment, because the group-average location of a network can be a centimetre or more off in a given patient.

The cost is obvious - a design with ten participants cannot support claims about population variation, so precision imaging and population-scale imaging answer complementary questions and neither replaces the other.


23.2.2 Test-retest reliability of cognitive-neuroscience measures

Reliability is the question of whether the same measurement, repeated on the same unchanged person, gives the same number, and it is usually quantified with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which runs from 0 for pure noise to 1 for perfect repeatability.

Maxwell Elliott, Ahmad Hariri, Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi and colleagues published a bracing answer in Psychological Science in 2020: a meta-analysis of 90 experiments totalling 1,008 participants found a mean ICC of about 0.40 for task-fMRI activation measures, and their own new data from the Human Connectome Project and the Dunedin longitudinal study gave ICCs between roughly 0.07 and 0.49 across eleven common tasks.

Values in that range are conventionally described as poor to fair, and the authors drew the blunt conclusion that common task-fMRI measures are not currently fit for biomarker discovery or individual-differences research.

The reason this is so damaging is arithmetical rather than rhetorical - an unreliable measure caps the correlation it can possibly show with anything else, so an entire literature correlating single-session task activation with personality, symptoms, or genotype was working with a ceiling far below the effect sizes it was reporting.

Part of the fix is more data per person, which is precisely the precision-imaging argument, and part of it is designing tasks for reliable individual differences rather than for large group-average effects, since those two goals actually pull against each other.


23.2.3 Within-person change against between-person difference

It is tempting to assume that a pattern found across people also holds inside a person - that if anxious people on average have smaller hippocampi, then a person becoming more anxious will show hippocampal shrinkage.

That assumption is called ergodicity, and it holds only under conditions that human psychology almost never meets: that people are structurally alike and that the process does not change over time.

Peter Molenaar formalised the point in 2004, and Aaron Fisher, John Medaglia and Bertus Jeronimus tested it empirically in 2018, reporting that the variability of correlations computed within individuals was typically several times larger than the corresponding between-person estimates - meaning group-level structure routinely fails to describe any particular person.

The methodological consequence is direct: if your question is about change within a person, such as whether treatment works or whether a skill is being learned, only a design that measures the same person repeatedly can answer it, and no amount of cross-sectional sample size substitutes.

This is why longitudinal and intensive-repeated-measures designs are not merely a nicer version of cross-sectional ones, and it is a good part of why the study designs described in section 23.3 went to enormous expense to follow the same people for years.


23.2.4 Ecological momentary assessment and wearable measurement

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) means prompting people, usually by smartphone, to report their state at moments during ordinary life, rather than asking them to remember a month afterwards in a clinic.

It exists because retrospective recall is systematically distorted - people reconstruct how they felt from how they feel now and from what they believe about themselves - and because a single laboratory visit samples one arbitrary point in a fluctuating process.

Wearables extend the same logic to signals people cannot report at all: accelerometry for movement and sleep, photoplethysmography for heart rate and heart-rate variability, and passively logged phone use, in a package often called digital phenotyping.

The main practical constraints are compliance and interpretation - a 2025 study of 108 older adults combining EMA with continuous wearable sensing reported about 67 percent adherence to prompts, which is typical, and a 2026 scoping review found the field still young, with heart-rate variability the most common physiological measure and much of the work concentrated on chronic stress.

For cognition specifically, the pairing that matters is EMA plus repeated laboratory or imaging measurement, because it lets an investigator ask whether the brain measure tracks the person's actual daily fluctuation rather than their average.


23.3 Population-scale resources

The four resources in this section share a design philosophy that broke with previous practice.

Instead of one laboratory collecting data to answer its own question and then archiving it, a consortium collects standardised data with no single hypothesis in mind and releases it to everyone.

This changes what kind of claim is possible - it makes small effects detectable and it makes independent replication a matter of downloading a file.

It also concentrates enormous influence in a few protocols, so that idiosyncrasies of a given study's scanner settings or cognitive battery propagate through hundreds of papers.


23.3.1 Human Connectome Project

The Human Connectome Project (HCP), led from Washington University in St Louis and the University of Minnesota with David Van Essen and Kamil Ugurbil among its principal figures, scanned roughly 1,200 healthy young adults with structural, diffusion, resting-state and task fMRI, plus extensive behavioural testing.

Its lasting contribution was as much technical as empirical - it developed faster imaging sequences, higher spatial resolution, surface-based rather than volume-based analysis, and a shared processing pipeline, and it set a standard for how such data should be released.

The design deliberately included many twin and sibling pairs, which lets investigators separate heritable from environmental contributions to brain organisation.

The programme was subsequently extended across the lifespan: the Lifespan HCP in Aging is recruiting more than 1,200 adults aged 36 to over 100 across four sites using matched Siemens Prisma 3-tesla scanners with centralised quality control, with a subset returning for longitudinal follow-up, and parallel projects cover development and infancy.


23.3.2 UK Biobank imaging

UK Biobank is a prospective epidemiological cohort of half a million British adults recruited from 2006 onward with genetics, blood biochemistry, and linked health records, and in 2014 it began re-inviting participants for an imaging visit with the target of 100,000 scanned.

The brain protocol, described by Karla Miller and colleagues in Nature Neuroscience in 2016, packs six modalities - T1-weighted and T2-FLAIR structural imaging, susceptibility-weighted imaging, diffusion imaging, resting-state fMRI and task fMRI - into about 35 minutes, alongside cardiac and abdominal imaging on the same visit.

Fidel Alfaro-Almagro and colleagues published the automated processing and quality-control pipeline in NeuroImage in 2017, which converts raw scans into thousands of image-derived phenotypes - single summary numbers such as the volume of a structure or the connectivity between two networks - that researchers analyse without touching the images.

The scientific value comes from the linkage: because imaging sits alongside genotypes and years of subsequent health outcomes, one can ask genuinely prospective questions about who later develops dementia or stroke.

Its main limitation is well documented and should be stated plainly - the cohort is healthier, wealthier, more educated and overwhelmingly more White than the United Kingdom population, so prevalence estimates from it are not representative even though within-cohort associations may be informative.


23.3.3 Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study

The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is the largest long-term study of brain development and child health in the United States, funded by the National Institutes of Health and coordinated across 21 active research sites.

It enrolled 11,880 children aged 9 to 10 years at baseline together with their parents or guardians, and is following them for at least ten years with annual in-person assessments and semi-annual telephone check-ins.

Each wave collects structural, diffusion, resting-state and task fMRI along with neurocognitive testing, mental-health assessment, physical measures, substance-use reporting, and detailed characterisation of family, school and neighbourhood environment.

Its purpose is to observe development as it happens, so that when an adolescent outcome such as substance use or the onset of a psychiatric condition occurs, the investigators already possess the preceding years of measurement rather than having to reconstruct them.

ABCD also became the empirical basis for one of the field's most important self-corrections, discussed next.


23.3.4 Enhancing Neuro Imaging Genetics through Meta Analysis and other consortia

Enhancing Neuro Imaging Genetics through Meta Analysis (ENIGMA), launched in December 2009 and led by Paul Thompson, took a different route to scale: rather than collecting new data, it federates existing studies.

Participating sites run an identical analysis script on their own data locally and share only the resulting summary statistics, which are then meta-analysed centrally - a design that sidesteps many of the legal and ethical barriers to moving individual-level brain data across national borders.

By the time of Thompson and colleagues' 2020 overview the consortium spanned more than 1,400 scientists in 43 countries and over 70 institutions, organised into working groups on schizophrenia, major depression, bipolar disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, epilepsy and many other conditions.

Its characteristic output is a well-powered, replicated map of where a disorder's brain differences actually lie, which repeatedly turned out to involve much smaller effects than the small single-site studies that preceded it had reported.

That theme was made general by Scott Marek, Nico Dosenbach and colleagues in Nature in 2022, who used ABCD, HCP and UK Biobank data to show that brain-wide association studies linking imaging measures to behavioural traits have effect sizes so small that reproducible results generally require samples in the thousands, and that at typical sample sizes such studies produce inflated effects and failed replications - while noting that within-person, lesion and intervention designs have much larger effects and do not need such numbers.


23.4 Data sharing and standards

None of the above is checkable unless other people can obtain the data, understand its layout, and rerun the analysis.

That requirement produced a body of infrastructure work that rarely appears in textbooks but determines whether a published result can be audited.

The four sub-sections here move from how data is organised, to where it is stored, to how it is processed, to what must be removed before it is shared at all.


23.4.1 Brain Imaging Data Structure and neurodata standards

The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), introduced by Krzysztof Gorgolewski and colleagues in Scientific Data in 2016, is a specification for how to name files and folders in a brain-imaging dataset and what metadata must accompany them.

It is deliberately unambitious in design - it uses ordinary directories, standard image formats, and plain-text metadata files - and that is why it succeeded where more elaborate proposals did not, because a laboratory can adopt it in an afternoon.

Its practical effect is that software can now find the anatomical scan, the task runs, the timing files and the acquisition parameters without a human explaining the layout, which is the precondition for automated pipelines.

BIDS has been extended by community proposals to magnetoencephalography, electroencephalography, intracranial electroencephalography, positron emission tomography, microscopy and more.

The parallel standard for cellular neurophysiology is Neurodata Without Borders (NWB), which handles spike trains, intracellular recordings and calcium imaging with rich embedded metadata, and the two standards are complementary rather than competing - archives commonly require BIDS for imaging and NWB for electrophysiology.


23.4.2 OpenNeuro, DANDI, and public repositories

OpenNeuro is a public archive, funded in part by the United States BRAIN Initiative, that accepts BIDS-formatted datasets across imaging modalities and shares them under the FAIR principles - findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

As described in its 2022 eLife paper it hosts well over 600 datasets from more than 20,000 participants across multiple species and measurement types, and its validator rejects non-conforming uploads, which enforces the standard at the point of deposit.

DANDI, the Distributed Archives for Neurophysiology Data Integration, launched in 2020 with BRAIN Initiative and Simons Foundation funding, is the corresponding archive for neurophysiology, requiring NWB format for cellular data and BIDS for imaging, storing on cloud infrastructure with versioned datasets, persistent digital object identifiers, and a command-line client for programmatic download.

Both archives make data available without registration or a data use agreement, which distinguishes them from the controlled-access model used by UK Biobank, ABCD and much of HCP, where identifiable or sensitive data requires an approved application.

Neither model is simply better - open access maximises reuse and audit, controlled access permits sharing of richer and more sensitive information, and most large projects now run a two-tier arrangement combining them.


23.4.3 Reproducible pipelines and containerisation

Reprocessing someone else's dataset used to fail for a mundane reason: the original analysis depended on particular versions of a dozen software packages, and those versions no longer existed on your machine.

Containerisation solves this by packaging the entire software environment - operating-system libraries, analysis tools, and their exact versions - into a single immutable image, usually built with Docker and run on shared academic clusters with Apptainer, formerly Singularity, which does not require administrative privileges.

BIDS Apps, described by Gorgolewski and colleagues in 2017, combine that idea with the BIDS layout: a container that takes a BIDS dataset as input and exposes a common command-line interface, so different tools from different laboratories are invoked the same way.

The most widely used example is fMRIPrep, published by Oscar Esteban and colleagues in Nature Methods in 2019, which performs a robust, well-tested standard preprocessing of functional MRI data and emits a visual report for quality control, replacing hundreds of idiosyncratic in-house scripts.

The remaining honest caveat is that reproducibility of this kind guarantees you get the same numbers from the same data - it does not guarantee the analysis was the right one, and the multiverse literature has repeatedly shown that defensible alternative pipelines applied to one dataset can yield materially different conclusions.


23.4.4 Privacy and de-identification of brain data

A brain scan is not anonymous by default, because a high-resolution structural magnetic resonance image contains the participant's face.

Christopher Schwarz and colleagues demonstrated in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019 that commercial face-recognition software could match rendered faces from research MRI scans to ordinary photographs of the same people at high accuracy, and follow-up work has put successful matching in the region of 80 percent and higher depending on sequence.

The standard countermeasure is defacing - automatically removing or blurring the face and often the ears from the image before sharing - and a refinement is refacing, in which a synthetic face is substituted, as implemented in tools such as mri_reface and deployed at scale in the fourth phase of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

There is a genuine trade-off here that the field is still negotiating: aggressive defacing can clip brain tissue and shift automated volume estimates, and studies have shown measurable effects of de-identification procedures on structural measures, particularly in children, so privacy protection is not free of scientific cost.

Beyond faces, brain data raises harder problems - functional connectivity patterns are individually distinctive enough to act as fingerprints, genetic data attached to imaging cohorts is inherently re-identifiable through relatives, and jurisdictions differ in whether brain data counts as a special category requiring extra protection.

The practical upshot for a reader is that open sharing of brain data is not a solved administrative matter but an active balance between the scientific value of reuse and a duty of care to the people who volunteered.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Naturalistic paradigms let cognition be studied under lifelike conditions, and inter-subject correlation and voxelwise encoding models supply the analytical rigour that rich stimuli would otherwise lack - though generalisation across films, and the interpretation of model-to-brain fit, remain open problems.

Precision imaging of densely sampled individuals, exemplified by MyConnectome and the Midnight Scan Club, revealed stable individual network organisation that group averaging destroys, and it responds to the reliability crisis that Elliott and colleagues documented in 2020 when they found mean intraclass correlations near 0.40 for common task-fMRI measures.

Because human psychological processes are generally non-ergodic, questions about change within a person require repeated measurement of that person, and no cross-sectional sample size substitutes.

At the other end of the scale, HCP, UK Biobank, ABCD and ENIGMA made small effects detectable, and Marek and colleagues used exactly those resources to show in 2022 that reproducible brain-wide association studies need thousands of participants.

Finally, all of this rests on infrastructure - BIDS and NWB for organisation, OpenNeuro and DANDI for storage, containerised BIDS Apps such as fMRIPrep for processing, and defacing for privacy - which is what converts a published claim from an assertion into something a stranger can check.


PART FOUR. ANALYSIS AND THEORY: TURNING MEASUREMENT INTO UNDERSTANDING


CHAPTER 24. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN AND STATISTICAL INFERENCE (APPARATUS)

A brain scanner does not tell you anything on its own.

It produces numbers, and numbers only become knowledge when they are collected under a design that can distinguish one explanation from another, and then analysed with a method that can tell a real effect from a lucky accident.

This chapter is about that apparatus - the logic of designing an experiment, the competing frameworks for drawing a conclusion from data, the special difficulty of testing hundreds of thousands of brain locations at once, and the sobering recent evidence about how much data you actually need.

It matters because the last fifteen years have shown that a great many published brain findings were not wrong in their measurement but wrong in their inference.

If you understand this chapter, you will be able to read a neuroscience paper and ask the questions that decide whether to believe it.


24.1 Design logic

Design logic is the part of an experiment that happens before any data exist.

It is the arrangement of conditions, participants, and orderings that determines which explanations your eventual numbers will be able to rule out.

A brilliant analysis cannot rescue a design that confounded the thing you care about with something else, because the information needed to separate them was never collected.


24.1.1 Factorial designs, interactions, and what they license

A factorial design crosses two or more factors (an experimental variable that the researcher manipulates, such as whether a word is familiar or novel) so that every combination of levels is tested.

The payoff is that a factorial design estimates not only the main effect of each factor on its own, but also the interaction - a change in the effect of one factor depending on the level of another, or more compactly, a change in a change.

Interactions are the workhorse of cognitive neuroscience because they license a stronger claim than a simple difference does: if brain region R responds more to hard than easy trials only when attention is directed toward the stimulus, then R is not simply tracking difficulty, and a whole family of low-level explanations is excluded.

Interactions also carry the logic of additive factors reasoning, which runs the other way: if two manipulations do not interact, that is evidence they act on separable processing stages, whereas if they do interact, the stages are likely shared or modulatory.

The caution, and it is a serious one, is that an interaction on a measured signal does not automatically mean an interaction in the underlying process, because the mapping from neural activity to a measured signal such as the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response is nonlinear, and a nonlinear measurement can manufacture an interaction out of purely additive causes.


24.1.2 Single and double dissociation

A single dissociation is the observation that some factor - a lesion, a drug, a manipulation - impairs performance on task A while leaving task B intact.

That pattern is suggestive but weak on its own, because task A might simply be harder, so that any general reduction in capacity shows up there first.

The remedy, formalised by Hans-Lukas Teuber in 1955 and developed at length by Tim Shallice and others in cognitive neuropsychology, is the double dissociation: one patient or manipulation impairs A but not B, and a second impairs B but not A.

Because the two patterns are mirror images, no single difficulty axis can explain both, and the inference to some degree of functional independence between the two abilities becomes much harder to dismiss.

The classic caveat comes from connectionist modelling: David Plaut and colleagues showed in the 1990s that damage at different points in a single distributed network with no separate modules can nevertheless produce a double dissociation, so the pattern licenses a claim about separable processing resources rather than a claim about anatomically discrete boxes.

There is also a live methodological argument that the field over-privileged double dissociations, since a well-powered simple dissociation carries considerable information and the demand for the double pattern discards usable evidence.


24.1.3 Within-subject and between-subject designs

In a within-subject design each participant experiences every condition, so each person serves as their own comparison.

That is enormously efficient, because the largest source of noise in most brain and behaviour data is the difference between one person and another, and a within-subject comparison subtracts that variability out.

In a between-subject design different people receive different conditions, which is unavoidable when the manipulation changes the participant permanently - you cannot un-teach a strategy, un-reveal a deception, or un-assign someone to a patient group.

The trade is statistical power: a between-subject test of the same effect typically needs many times as many participants to reach the same sensitivity, which is one reason group-difference studies in psychiatry and development have historically been so underpowered.

A further asymmetry, developed in section 24.4, is that the design features which make a within-subject effect large and robust are not the features that make a measure good at ranking individuals.


24.1.4 Counterbalancing, randomisation, and blinding

Counterbalancing means arranging the order of conditions across participants so that any effect of order - practice, fatigue, boredom, scanner drift - is spread evenly across conditions rather than piling onto one of them.

Randomisation means assigning participants or trials to conditions by a chance process, which protects against both the confounds you thought of and, crucially, the ones you did not, because in expectation it balances every unmeasured variable at once.

Blinding means keeping the participant, and where possible the experimenter and the person scoring the data, ignorant of which condition is in play, because expectations leak into behaviour and into subjective coding in ways that are invisible to the people doing it.

The strongest form is the double-blind design, in which neither participant nor experimenter knows the assignment until the analysis is locked.

Preregistration - publicly recording the hypothesis and the analysis plan before the data are seen - functions as a kind of blinding of the analyst against the data, and it is the single cheapest reform available to a neuroscience laboratory.


24.2 Inference frameworks

An inference framework is the set of rules that converts data into a statement about the world.

There is more than one such framework in use, they answer different questions, and much confusion in the literature comes from reading the answer to one question as though it were the answer to another.


24.2.1 Null hypothesis significance testing and its discontents

Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) works by assuming there is no effect, computing how surprising the observed data would be under that assumption, and reporting that surprise as a p-value.

The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed, given that the null hypothesis is true - and it is emphatically not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, a misreading that has been documented in survey after survey of working scientists since at least the 1980s.

In 2016 the American Statistical Association took the unusual step of issuing a formal statement, authored by Ronald Wasserstein and Nicole Lazar, spelling out what p-values can and cannot do, prompted by how far routine practice had drifted from the mathematics.

The specific complaints are the arbitrariness of the 0.05 threshold, the collapse of a continuous measure of evidence into a yes-or-no verdict, the resulting publication bias toward significant findings, and the fact that a non-significant result is treated as evidence of absence when it is usually just absence of evidence.

None of this makes p-values useless, and the honest position is that NHST is a reasonable error-control device that has been widely misused as an evidence measure.


24.2.2 Effect size, confidence intervals, and estimation

An effect size is a number expressing how big an effect is, in units that do not depend on how many participants you tested - for example Cohen's d, the difference between two condition means divided by the pooled standard deviation.

A confidence interval is a range computed so that, over many hypothetical repetitions of the experiment, a stated proportion of such intervals (usually 95 percent) would contain the true value.

The estimation approach argues that the scientifically interesting question is almost never whether an effect is exactly zero, which it rarely is, but how large it is and how precisely we know it - so report the interval and let its width speak.

This reframing has a practical bite in neuroscience, because an effect can be highly significant and simultaneously so small as to be useless for prediction, and a p-value alone hides that distinction while an interval displays it.

Estimation also makes underpowered literatures legible: when studies are small, the significant results that survive publication are systematically inflated, an artefact known as the winner's curse.


24.2.3 Bayesian inference and the Bayes factor

Bayesian inference treats probability as a degree of belief, starting from a prior distribution over possible values, updating it with the data through Bayes's theorem, and ending with a posterior distribution that directly answers the question researchers actually want answered.

The Bayes factor is the specific tool for comparing hypotheses: it is the ratio of how well one model predicted the observed data to how well a rival model predicted it, and a Bayes factor of 10 in favour of an effect means the data were ten times more probable under the effect model than under the null.

Its most valuable property for neuroscience is symmetry - it can supply positive evidence for the absence of an effect, whereas a non-significant p-value cannot, a point argued for the field by Zoltan Dienes and by Eric-Jan Wagenmakers and colleagues, and set out for neuroscientists in Nature Neuroscience in 2020 by Keysers, Gazzola and Wagenmakers.

Bayes factors also stop the clock problem: because they do not depend on the sampling intention, you may monitor evidence as data accumulate and stop when it is decisive, which is forbidden under strict NHST.

The standing objection, and it is a fair one, is that the Bayes factor depends on the prior chosen for the alternative hypothesis, so the default priors developed from Harold Jeffreys's work and popularised by Wagenmakers and colleagues are conventions rather than facts, and a conclusion that flips under a reasonable change of prior should be reported as such.


24.2.4 Mixed-effects and hierarchical models

A mixed-effects model, also called a hierarchical or multilevel model, separates the effects you want to generalise about (fixed effects, such as the difference between two conditions) from the units you sampled and wish to generalise across (random effects, such as participants and stimulus items).

The gain over older approaches is that it respects the nested structure of the data - trials inside participants, participants inside sites - instead of averaging it away, and it can handle participants and items as crossed random factors simultaneously, which the traditional analysis of variance could not do cleanly.

Dale Barr and colleagues argued in 2013, in a paper widely known by its slogan "keep it maximal", that for confirmatory hypothesis testing the random effects structure should include random slopes for every within-unit factor justified by the design, because omitting them inflates false positives.

That advice has been tempered since: maximal models frequently fail to converge, and work by Douglas Bates, Reinhold Kliegl and colleagues on parsimonious mixed models showed that overly complex random structures can cost power, so current practice is to fit the maximal structure justified by the design and reduce it in a principled, pre-specified way when it will not estimate.

Hierarchical models also enable partial pooling, in which noisy estimates from individual participants are shrunk toward the group mean in proportion to their uncertainty - a principled middle path between analysing everyone separately and pretending everyone is identical.


24.3 The multiple comparisons problem in brain data

A typical functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) analysis tests every voxel (a three-dimensional picture element, the smallest unit of a brain image) separately, which means running on the order of one hundred thousand statistical tests at once.

At a 5 percent threshold, pure chance would hand you thousands of significant voxels in a brain with no signal at all, which is the point made memorably by Craig Bennett and colleagues in 2009 when they found significant task-related activation in a dead Atlantic salmon.

Everything in this section is machinery for controlling that flood without discarding the real effects along with it.


24.3.1 Family-wise error and false discovery rate

The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making at least one false positive anywhere in the whole set of tests, and controlling it means the entire map is trustworthy as a map.

The simplest FWER method is the Bonferroni correction, which divides the threshold by the number of tests - correct but crushingly conservative in brain data, because neighbouring voxels are highly correlated and so the tests are nowhere near independent.

The false discovery rate (FDR), introduced by Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg in 1995 and brought to neuroimaging by Christopher Genovese, Nicole Lazar and Thomas Nichols in 2002, controls a different quantity: the expected proportion of false positives among the voxels you declared significant.

That is a weaker guarantee and therefore a more powerful procedure - with FDR set at 5 percent you accept that roughly one in twenty of your surviving voxels is noise, in exchange for detecting far more of the real ones.

Which to use is a scientific judgement rather than a statistical one: FWER when a single false blob would change the conclusion, FDR when you are generating a set of candidate regions to follow up.


24.3.2 Cluster-based permutation testing and its assumptions

Cluster-based methods exploit the fact that genuine effects are usually spatially or temporally extended, so instead of asking whether any single voxel or time point is extreme, they ask whether any contiguous cluster of supra-threshold points is larger than chance would produce.

The permutation version, formalised for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) by Eric Maris and Robert Oostenveld in 2007, builds the null distribution empirically by repeatedly shuffling the condition labels, recomputing the largest cluster each time, and comparing the real largest cluster against that distribution.

Because the null distribution is generated from the data themselves, this controls the family-wise error rate without assuming a particular shape for the noise, which is why Anders Eklund, Thomas Nichols and Hans Knutsson found in their 2016 PNAS study - three million random group analyses on resting-state data - that permutation gave nominal error rates while the parametric cluster inference in standard software packages did not.

The assumption people forget is about interpretation rather than validity: a significant cluster licenses the claim that there is some effect somewhere within it, and does not license claims about the cluster's boundaries, its peak location, or the onset time of the effect.

Guillaume Rousselet's 2025 simulation work in the European Journal of Neuroscience quantified exactly this for MEG and EEG onset estimation, showing that cluster-derived onsets are systematically biased late, so the honest summary is that the test is a good detector and a poor localiser.


24.3.3 Random field theory

Random field theory (RFT) is the parametric alternative, developed for brain imaging principally by Keith Worsley, Karl Friston and colleagues in the early 1990s.

It treats the statistical map as a smooth continuous random field rather than a pile of independent tests, and uses a result from geometry - the expected Euler characteristic, which at high thresholds is essentially the expected number of separate blobs surviving in a pure noise image - to derive the threshold at which blobs become surprising.

To do this it needs to know the effective resolution of the data, expressed in resels (resolution elements, defined by the full width at half maximum of the image smoothness), so that a smoother map is correctly treated as containing fewer independent tests.

Its great virtue is speed and a closed-form answer, and it remains the default in software such as Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM).

Its vulnerability is that it assumes the spatial autocorrelation of the noise has a roughly Gaussian shape, and Eklund and colleagues showed in 2016 that real fMRI noise has heavier spatial tails than that, which is the technical reason parametric cluster-extent inference was liberal - the field's response has been to raise cluster-forming thresholds and, increasingly, to prefer permutation.


24.3.4 Circular analysis and double dipping

Circular analysis, or double dipping, is using the same data twice - once to select what to look at, and again to test it - so that the selection guarantees the result.

Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, W. Kyle Simmons, Patrick Bellgowan and Chris Baker set this out in Nature Neuroscience in 2009, showing with simulation that a region of interest defined by the very contrast you then test will show that contrast even in pure noise, and that even sophisticated mapping procedures do not immunise you.

Their survey of fMRI papers published in 2008 in Nature, Science, Nature Neuroscience, Neuron and the Journal of Neuroscience found that 42 percent of 134 papers contained at least one non-independent selective analysis.

The same year, Ed Vul and colleagues made a related argument about implausibly high brain-behaviour correlations in social neuroscience, in a paper originally titled "Voodoo correlations in social neuroscience", where selecting the most correlated voxels and then reporting their correlation inflates the number badly.

The fixes are simple and now standard: define regions of interest from independent data or from anatomy, use cross-validation so that selection and testing happen on separate partitions, or preregister the region before looking.


24.4 Reliability, power, and generalisation

The previous sections concern whether a single result is a false positive.

This section concerns three deeper questions - whether the study could have detected a true effect at all, whether the measure is stable enough to rank individuals, and whether the finding extends beyond the exact stimuli, task, and people tested.

These are where the last decade of methodological reckoning has hit hardest.


24.4.1 Statistical power in small-sample neuroimaging

Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect an effect of a given size if that effect is real.

Katherine Button, John Ioannidis and colleagues estimated in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2013 that the median power of studies in the neurosciences lies somewhere around 8 to 31 percent, meaning most experiments were more likely to miss a true effect than to find it.

The under-appreciated consequence they emphasised is that low power does not merely cause misses - it also lowers the positive predictive value, so that a statistically significant result from an underpowered literature is less likely to be true, and its effect size is systematically overestimated.

A reanalysis by Camilla Nord and colleagues in 2017 using mixture modelling argued that neuroscience power is not uniformly low but bimodal, with a subset of well-powered studies alongside a large underpowered mass, which softens the headline without changing the prescription.

The historical driver in imaging was cost: scanner time is expensive, twenty participants was a convention, and the convention long outlived any statistical justification for it.


24.4.2 Brain-wide association studies and the sample-size lesson

A brain-wide association study correlates a brain measure across the whole brain with an individual trait such as cognitive ability or a psychiatric symptom.

Scott Marek, Brenden Tervo-Clemmens, Nico Dosenbach and colleagues published the decisive analysis in Nature in 2022, pooling roughly fifty thousand individuals from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, the Human Connectome Project and the UK Biobank.

Their finding was that the true brain-behaviour correlations at this scale are small - on the order of r equal to 0.01 in the tail and rarely above 0.16 - and that at typical sample sizes of a few dozen the significant results are dominated by inflated, sign-flipping, irreproducible effects.

The practical conclusion was that reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of participants, not dozens, which effectively ended a genre of small single-laboratory individual-differences imaging.

The paper drew substantive pushback - critics including Tamas Spisak, Ulrike Basten and others argued that multivariate methods, better task designs, more reliable measures, and aggregation across sessions can recover larger and more stable effects at smaller samples, so the fair statement is that the sample-size requirement is real but is a function of measurement quality rather than a fixed law.


24.4.3 Test-retest reliability against between-subject sensitivity

Test-retest reliability is the degree to which a measure gives the same value for the same person on two occasions, usually quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), where values below about 0.4 are conventionally called poor.

Maxwell Elliott, Ahmad Hariri, Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi and colleagues reported in Psychological Science in 2020 a meta-analysis of 90 task-fMRI experiments plus new data, finding a mean ICC of about 0.40 - too low to support the individual-differences and biomarker research that task-fMRI was being used for.

The underlying explanation is the reliability paradox, articulated for cognitive tasks by Craig Hedge, Georgina Powell and Petroc Sumner in 2018: experimental tasks are optimised to produce a large, uniform effect in everyone, which means they are deliberately engineered to minimise between-person variance - and between-person variance is precisely the signal an individual-differences study needs.

So the Stroop task is one of the most robust effects in psychology and simultaneously a poor instrument for ranking people, with reliability comparable to the task-fMRI average.

The consequence follows directly: unreliable measures attenuate correlations and group differences, so a study can fail not because the biology is absent but because the ruler is blunt - and the remedies are longer runs, more trials, aggregation across sessions, hierarchical models that separate measurement error from true individual variation, and tasks designed for variance rather than for uniformity.


24.4.4 Generalisation across stimuli, tasks, samples, and populations

Tal Yarkoni's paper "The generalizability crisis", published in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2022, argues that the field's verbal hypotheses are vastly broader than the statistical models used to test them.

His central technical point is that psychologists routinely treat participants as a random effect - acknowledging that they wish to generalise beyond the specific people tested - while treating stimuli, tasks, experimenters and testing sites as fixed, which formally restricts the conclusion to those exact stimuli in that exact laboratory.

Treating stimuli as random, an argument first made by Herbert Clark in 1973 in his "language-as-fixed-effect fallacy" paper, typically shrinks effective sample sizes and widens confidence intervals dramatically, which is why the practice was resisted for decades and why modern mixed-effects models make it feasible.

There is a separate and equally important generalisation problem in who is sampled: Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan showed in 2010 that behavioural science overwhelmingly draws on Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic (WEIRD) samples, which are unrepresentative outliers on many measures, and neuroimaging cohorts remain skewed further still by who can lie still in a scanner and who lives near a research hospital.

The constructive responses now in use are many-analyst and many-laboratory projects, multiverse analyses that report a finding across the whole space of defensible analysis choices, stimulus sampling with random effects, and explicit out-of-sample or out-of-site validation before a result is called general.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Design decides what can be inferred: factorial interactions and double dissociations license claims that simple comparisons cannot, and within-subject designs buy sensitivity that between-subject designs must pay for in participants.

Inference is plural - null hypothesis significance testing controls error rates but is widely misread as an evidence measure, estimation reports magnitude and precision, Bayes factors can supply positive evidence for absence, and hierarchical models let you generalise across the units you actually sampled.

Brain data multiply the testing problem by a hundred thousand, and the corrections that answer it come with fine print: false discovery rate trades a weaker guarantee for power, permutation clustering detects effects reliably but localises them poorly, and random field theory was shown by Eklund and colleagues in 2016 to rest on a smoothness assumption real data violate.

Circular analysis remains the most avoidable error in the field, and Kriegeskorte and colleagues found it in 42 percent of a 2008 sample of high-profile fMRI papers.

Finally, the power, reliability and generalisation literature - Button and colleagues in 2013, Elliott and colleagues in 2020, Marek and Tervo-Clemmens and colleagues in 2022, Yarkoni in 2022 - converges on one lesson: small samples, blunt measures, and narrow stimulus sets produced a generation of findings that were statistically significant and scientifically unreliable, and the fix is larger samples, better measurement, and analyses fixed in advance.


CHAPTER 25. DECODING, ENCODING, AND REPRESENTATIONAL ANALYSIS (APPARATUS)

This chapter is about the mathematical machinery that turns raw brain measurements into claims about what the brain represents.

For most of the history of brain imaging, the standard question was crude - which single spot lights up more in condition A than in condition B.

The methods in this chapter ask a better question - what information is carried by the pattern of activity across many measurement points at once, and can we read that information back out.

Three families of method dominate: decoding, which reads a mental state out of a pattern; encoding, which predicts a pattern from a description of the stimulus; and representational similarity analysis, which compares the geometry of one representation to another.

This matters because these tools are what let cognitive neuroscience make specific, falsifiable claims about mental content instead of vague claims about brain regions being involved.

It also matters because these same tools have produced the first genuine, if limited, mind-reading demonstrations, which raises questions this chapter ends on.


25.1 Multivariate pattern analysis

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) is the family of methods that treats the pattern of activity across many voxels - a voxel being a small three-dimensional cube of brain tissue, the basic picture element of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) - as a single object to be analysed jointly, rather than analysing each voxel on its own.

The founding demonstration is Haxby and colleagues in 2001, who showed that the identity of an object category a person was viewing could be read out from the distributed pattern of response in ventral temporal cortex, including from voxels that were not the ones responding most strongly.

The influential review that named and popularised the approach was Norman, Polyn, Detre and Haxby in 2006, titled Beyond Mind-Reading.

The core insight is statistical: information that is invisible when you average across voxels can be plainly present in the fine-grained pattern, because averaging destroys exactly the differences that carry the code.


25.1.1 Classification of cognitive states from distributed patterns

The standard recipe is to train a classifier - a machine learning algorithm that learns a boundary separating two or more classes of input - on brain patterns labelled by condition, then test it on patterns it has never seen.

A common choice is the support vector machine, an algorithm that finds the separating boundary with the widest possible margin between the classes.

Testing must be done on held-out data, using cross-validation - repeatedly training on most of the data and testing on the part left out - because a flexible classifier can memorise noise and report high accuracy on the data it was trained on.

The result is an accuracy figure compared against chance, and this has been used to decode viewed object category, attended location, working memory contents, intended action, and even which of two remembered items a person is currently rehearsing.


25.1.2 Cross-classification and generalisation tests of abstraction

A classifier that works only within the exact condition it was trained on may be picking up something superficial.

Cross-classification, sometimes called cross-decoding, trains on one condition and tests on a different one - for example, train on pictures of animals versus tools, then test on the spoken words for animals versus tools.

If the classifier still succeeds, the underlying code must be abstract enough to be shared across the two formats, which is a far stronger claim than plain within-condition decoding.

Kaplan, Man and Greening laid out this logic explicitly in 2015 as a way of characterising abstraction in neural representations.

Bernardi and colleagues extended the idea in 2020, in a study of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, defining abstraction operationally by the ability of a decoder to generalise to condition combinations it was never trained on, and showing that this requires a particular geometry of the neural population - roughly, that the relevant variable is coded along a consistent direction regardless of the other variables.


25.1.3 Searchlight and whole-brain mapping

Early MVPA required you to pick a region of interest in advance, which biases the result toward wherever you already suspected the answer would be.

Kriegeskorte, Goebel and Bandettini solved this in 2006 with the searchlight, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS).

The method slides a small sphere - typically a few millimetres in radius - through the whole brain, runs the full multivariate classification using only the voxels inside the sphere, and writes the resulting accuracy back to the sphere's centre.

The output is an information map: a whole-brain picture of where the local pattern carries information about the experimental variable, rather than where the average signal is large.

The caveat, well documented since, is that searchlight maps are blurred and their spatial precision is limited by the searchlight radius, so a hot spot indicates a neighbourhood, not a pinpoint.


25.1.4 What decoding accuracy does and does not tell us about use

This is the sharpest live dispute in the area, and it should not be presented as settled.

Ritchie, Kaplan and Klein, writing in the British Journal for the Philosophy of Science in 2019, attacked what they called the decoder's dictum - the assumption that if information can be decoded from a pattern, that pattern therefore represents that information.

Their point is that a decoder is an external observer with privileged access to the whole pattern and to labelled training data, whereas downstream brain regions have neither; information a machine can extract may be information no neuron actually reads.

There is also a nuisance problem: decoding can succeed on incidental correlates such as differences in eye movements, arousal, head motion, or blood vessel geometry rather than on the cognitive variable of interest.

The constructive reply, argued by Kriegeskorte and others and developed by Hebart, Baker and colleagues, is that decoding is best treated not as a direct readout of representation but as a tool for testing specific cognitive theories, where the theories predict a pattern of successes and failures across conditions rather than a single high number.

A practical consequence follows: raw decoding accuracy is nearly meaningless on its own, and what carries the inference is the contrast between conditions, regions, or generalisation tests.


25.2 Encoding models

An encoding model runs the arrow the other way.

Instead of predicting the stimulus from the brain, it predicts the brain response from a quantitative description of the stimulus.

The review that set out the framework and its relation to decoding is Naselaris, Kay, Nishimoto and Gallant in 2011, in the journal NeuroImage, which made the important point that a fitted encoding model can be inverted to produce a decoder, so encoding is in a sense the more fundamental object.

The landmark empirical demonstration is Kay, Naselaris, Prenger and Gallant in 2008 in Nature, who built a model of early visual cortex from Gabor wavelet features - simple oriented, spatially localised edge detectors - and used it to identify which natural image a person had seen out of a set of many thousands of candidates none of which had been used in training.


25.2.1 Feature spaces, voxel-wise models, and predictive accuracy

A feature space is a numerical description of the stimulus: for images, edge orientations and spatial frequencies; for speech, phonemes, syntactic categories, or word meaning vectors.

In a voxel-wise encoding model, a separate regression is fitted for every single voxel, giving each voxel its own set of weights over the features and thus its own tuning profile.

Because feature spaces are large and fMRI data are noisy, the fitting almost always uses ridge regression - a form of regression that penalises large weights, trading a little bias for a large reduction in variance and so preventing overfitting.

The verdict on a model is its prediction accuracy on a separate held-out stimulus set, usually the correlation between predicted and observed responses, and this is a strong test because a model that merely describes the training data will fail it.


25.2.2 Banded ridge regression and variance partitioning

A serious problem arises when you want to compare several feature spaces at once, because natural stimuli make features correlated - word meaning correlates with word frequency, and both correlate with the acoustics.

Banded ridge regression, developed in the Gallant laboratory and described in detail by Dupré la Tour, Eickenberg, Nunez-Elizalde and Gallant in 2022, fits a separate regularisation strength for each feature space rather than one shared strength.

This has an implicit feature-space selection effect: a feature space that is not predictive, or that is redundant given the others, gets penalised heavily and effectively drops out, which both improves generalisation and disentangles the correlated spaces.

Variance partitioning then splits the explained variance into the part unique to each feature space and the part they share, so you can say honestly that a region is explained by semantics over and above acoustics, rather than merely that a semantic model fits.


25.2.3 Semantic maps and continuous stimulus spaces

Huth, de Heer, Griffiths, Theunissen and Gallant, in Nature in 2016, played hours of natural spoken narrative to listeners in the scanner and fitted voxel-wise models using a word-meaning feature space derived from word co-occurrence statistics.

The result was a semantic map: broad, smooth, and largely symmetrical across the two hemispheres, covering much more cortex than classical language models had assumed, with different patches of cortex preferentially tuned to different meaning domains such as people, places, numbers, or bodily sensations.

The key methodological virtue is the use of a continuous stimulus space - real, uncontrolled narrative rather than a handful of discrete conditions - which gives enough coverage to fit a genuinely predictive model.

The maps proved reasonably consistent across individuals in group structure while differing in detail, and the naturalistic-stimulus approach has since become standard for language and vision alike.


25.2.4 Model comparison as the real inferential move

The single number giving a model's prediction accuracy tells you little, because accuracy is capped by the noise in the measurement and by how much of the stimulus space the experiment sampled.

The inference that carries weight is comparative: fit two or more models that embody rival hypotheses on the same data, and ask which predicts held-out responses better.

Naselaris and colleagues made this the centre of their 2011 framework, and it is why encoding modelling is closer to normal hypothesis testing than decoding usually is.

A necessary honesty here is the noise ceiling - an estimate of the best prediction any model could achieve given the reliability of the data - because a model explaining thirty percent of variance may be near-perfect or badly wrong depending on where that ceiling sits.


25.3 Representational similarity analysis

Representational similarity analysis (RSA), introduced by Kriegeskorte, Mur and Bandettini in 2008, sidesteps the problem that brain data, behavioural data, and computer models all live in incompatible spaces with different numbers of dimensions and no correspondence between them.

Its move is to throw away the raw activity values and keep only the relationships among them.


25.3.1 The representational dissimilarity matrix as a common currency

For a set of stimuli, you measure the response pattern to each one, then compute how dissimilar every pattern is from every other, usually with correlation distance or a Euclidean-type distance.

Arranging those numbers gives a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM) - a square table with one row and one column per stimulus, and the dissimilarity in each cell.

The RDM describes the geometry of the representation: which things the region treats as similar and which it separates.

Crucially, an RDM for a brain region, for a behavioural similarity judgement, and for a layer of an artificial neural network are all the same size and the same kind of object, so they can be compared directly.


25.3.2 Comparing brains, behaviour, and models in one space

The comparison is done by correlating one RDM with another, typically with a rank correlation such as Spearman's, which assumes only that the ordering of dissimilarities matches, not their exact values.

This is what allows a question like: does the geometry of monkey inferior temporal cortex match the geometry of human inferior temporal cortex, or does a deep network's layer geometry match a brain area's.

Kriegeskorte, Mur and colleagues in 2008 used exactly this to show a striking correspondence between human and monkey object representations, with the same broad animate versus inanimate division in both species.

Since then RSA has become the standard bridge between neuroscience and machine learning, and much of the current work comparing large neural network models to human brains is RSA at its core.


25.3.3 Second-order isomorphism and its assumptions

The formal name for what RSA exploits is second-order isomorphism, a term from Shepard and Chipman in 1970.

First-order isomorphism would require that the representation resemble the thing represented - that the neural code for a circle be circular; second-order isomorphism requires only that the relations among representations mirror the relations among the things represented.

The assumption being made is therefore substantive rather than trivial: it presumes that what matters about a representation is its distance structure and nothing else, so any rotation or rescaling of the underlying space is treated as irrelevant.

That assumption is defensible if downstream readout is linear and unbiased, but it is an assumption, and it discards information about which specific units carry what - the price of the method's generality.


25.3.4 Extensions: weighted, kernel, and temporal generalisation methods

Ordinary distance estimates are biased upward by noise, so two patterns look different even when they are identical in truth; Walther, Nili, Ejaz, Alink, Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen in 2016 showed that the cross-validated Mahalanobis or crossnobis distance - which whitens out correlated noise across voxels and cross-validates the distance estimate - is unbiased and has a meaningful zero point, so a distance of zero really means no difference.

Nili and colleagues in 2014 published the RSA toolbox and the associated inference procedures, and Schütt, Kipnis, Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte in 2023, in eLife, set out a fuller statistical framework for inference on representational geometries, including how to compare models against the noise ceiling.

Weighted and component-based variants allow a brain RDM to be fitted as a weighted mixture of several model RDMs rather than compared to each in isolation, and kernel formulations connect RSA to the wider machine-learning literature on similarity kernels.

The temporal generalisation method of King and Dehaene in 2014 applies the same relational logic across time: a classifier is trained at each moment after stimulus onset and tested at every other moment, producing a matrix whose shape diagnoses the underlying dynamics.

A square block of generalisation indicates a stable code held over time, as in maintenance; a narrow diagonal indicates a code that changes moment to moment as processing passes through successive stages - a genuinely informative distinction that no single-time-point analysis can make.


25.4 Reconstruction and generative decoding

Classification asks which of a fixed list of options a person is experiencing.

Reconstruction is more ambitious: produce the experience itself, as an image or a sentence, without a candidate list.


25.4.1 Stimulus reconstruction from brain activity

Early reconstructions from Gallant's group were blurry but genuinely open-ended, built by inverting encoding models rather than by choosing among stored options.

The field jumped sharply with generative image models: Takagi and Nishimoto, presented at the 2023 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), mapped fMRI responses onto the latent space of Stable Diffusion - a latent diffusion model, meaning a generative system that produces images by iteratively removing noise in a compressed representation - and produced reconstructions that were recognisably the viewed scene.

Ozcelik and VanRullen reported a related latent-diffusion approach in Scientific Reports in 2023, and MindEye2, from Scotti and colleagues in 2024, showed the approach could be adapted to a new person with about one hour of their data by first learning a shared subject model.

The honest caveat is that these results lean heavily on the generative model's prior knowledge about what natural images look like, so a plausible-looking reconstruction is partly the brain data and partly the model filling in; they also rely on very large per-person datasets such as the Natural Scenes Dataset, and none of it works on a person who has not spent many hours in a scanner.


25.4.2 Semantic decoding of continuous language

Tang, LeBel, Jain and Huth, in Nature Neuroscience in 2023, built a decoder that produced continuous intelligible word sequences from fMRI while a person listened to stories.

The system combined a voxel-wise encoding model of semantic representation with a language model that proposed candidate continuations, scoring each candidate by how well the encoding model predicted the observed brain response.

Output recovered the gist rather than the exact words, and it worked not only for heard speech but for imagined speech and for silent film, indicating that the decoded representation is semantic rather than acoustic or lexical.

Because fMRI measures blood flow, which is slow, the decoder operates on meaning accumulated over seconds - it cannot track speech word by word.

The authors also tested resistance deliberately: decoding failed when a person silently counted, named animals, or attended to a different story, and a decoder trained on one person did not transfer to another.


25.4.3 Mental imagery and dream decoding

Horikawa, Tamaki, Miyawaki and Kamitani, in Science in 2013, woke sleeping volunteers repeatedly during the sleep-onset period, recorded their verbal dream reports, and trained classifiers on brain activity evoked by ordinary waking images.

Those waking-trained classifiers predicted the categories of objects the sleepers reported dreaming about at above-chance accuracy, which is strong evidence that dream imagery recruits the same visual representations as perception.

Horikawa and Kamitani followed this in 2017 with a deep neural network feature analysis showing that dreamed objects are represented hierarchically in much the way seen objects are, with lower visual areas matching lower network layers.

The strong methodological point is that generalisation from perception to imagery to dreaming, using a classifier trained only on perception, is a cross-classification test of exactly the kind described in section 25.1.2, and it is far more informative than any within-condition accuracy could be.

The limitations should be stated plainly: the reports are subjective, the categories are coarse, and the sleep-onset period is not the same state as full rapid eye movement sleep dreaming.


25.4.4 Ethical limits on mind reading

The technical facts constrain the ethics, so it is worth being precise: current decoders require the person's sustained cooperation across many hours of training, are person-specific, and can be defeated by simple mental countermeasures - Tang and colleagues demonstrated this themselves and framed mental privacy as an active concern rather than a distant one.

That said, the trajectory is toward less data and better transfer, and legal frameworks have begun moving ahead of the technology.

Chile amended its constitution in 2021 to protect brain activity and mental privacy, the first country to do so, and its Supreme Court ruled in 2023 in a case concerning a consumer neurotechnology device; a 2026 Stanford Law analysis noted that inferred mental data still sits in a grey zone even under that law.

In November 2025 the General Conference of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) adopted the first global standard on the ethics of neurotechnology, agreed by its member states, building on its International Bioethics Committee report of 2022.

Much of the debate traces to the neurorights framework of Yuste and the Morningside Group, which proposed rights to mental privacy, personal identity, free will, fair access to enhancement, and protection from algorithmic bias.

There is genuine disagreement here: some ethicists argue existing data-protection and human-rights law already covers brain data and that new categories risk confusion, while others hold that brain data is different in kind because it can reveal content a person never chose to express - and this dispute is not resolved.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Distributed patterns of brain activity carry information that region-average analyses destroy, and multivariate pattern analysis, from Haxby in 2001 onward, is what recovers it.

Decoding success by itself is weak evidence about what the brain represents or uses, as Ritchie, Kaplan and Klein argued in 2019; the inferential weight lies in comparisons - across conditions, across generalisation tests, and across rival models.

Encoding models invert the question, predicting brain responses from stimulus features, and with tools like banded ridge regression and variance partitioning they support the cleanest form of model comparison available in the field.

Representational similarity analysis provides a common currency, the representational dissimilarity matrix, in which brains, behaviour, species, and artificial networks can be compared, at the cost of assuming that only the distance structure matters.

Reconstruction methods now produce recognisable images and gist-level sentences from brain data, but they depend on very large per-person datasets, sustained cooperation, and strong generative priors.

Those constraints are real today and are the reason mind reading remains limited - but law and international standards, from Chile in 2021 to UNESCO in 2025, are already being written on the assumption that they will loosen.


CHAPTER 26. POPULATION DYNAMICS AND NEURAL GEOMETRY (CORE)

For most of the twentieth century, the standard way to study the brain was to record one neuron at a time and ask what that neuron responded to.

Modern electrode arrays and imaging methods record hundreds or thousands of neurons at once, and that change in what we can measure has forced a change in how we think.

This chapter is about that shift: from asking what a single cell means to asking what shape the whole population's activity traces out, and how that shape changes over time.

The core idea is that the joint activity of many neurons can be treated as a point moving through a high-dimensional space, and that the path of that point - its geometry and its dynamics - is where computation actually lives.

This matters because it is currently the most productive bridge between recorded spikes and cognitive function, and because it underwrites practical technology such as brain-computer interfaces.

It also matters because the framework has real critics, and a beginner should learn the objections at the same time as the claims.


26.1 From single neurons to population state

Start with the basic move.

Suppose you record one hundred neurons.

At each moment in time you can write down one hundred firing rates - how many spikes per second each cell is producing.

That list of one hundred numbers is a single point in a space with one hundred dimensions, one axis per neuron.

This is called the neural state, and the space is called the neural state space.

As the animal thinks, perceives, or moves, the firing rates change, so the point moves.

It draws a trajectory - a path through the state space over time.

The whole population approach consists of taking that trajectory seriously as the object of study, rather than treating each neuron's tuning as the object of study.

The practical problem is that a one-hundred-dimensional path cannot be drawn or intuited, so most of this section is about honest ways to compress it.


26.1.1 The population vector and its history

The first influential population-level idea came from Apostolos Georgopoulos and colleagues, whose 1986 paper in Science with Andrew Schwartz and Ronald Kettner is the landmark reference.

They recorded from primary motor cortex in monkeys reaching in different directions and found that individual neurons were only broadly tuned - each cell fired somewhat for a wide range of directions, so no single cell could specify the reach precisely.

Their solution was the population vector: represent each cell as an arrow pointing in its preferred direction, scale each arrow by how hard that cell is firing right now, and add all the arrows together.
