The sum pointed in the direction the arm actually moved, far more precisely than any one neuron could.

This was a genuine conceptual advance and it seeded decades of brain-computer interface decoding work.

It also drew criticism: some argued the population vector was partly an artefact of how preferred directions happened to be distributed across the sampled cells, and that its apparent accuracy did not prove the brain reads out a vector sum.

That debate - coding versus epiphenomenon - was never fully closed, and it is the ancestor of the dynamics-versus-representation dispute later in this chapter.


26.1.2 Dimensionality reduction: principal components, factor analysis, demixed methods

Dimensionality reduction means finding a small number of composite variables that capture most of what the full population is doing.

Each composite variable is a weighted mixture of many neurons' firing rates.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is the workhorse.

It finds the directions in state space along which activity varies the most, ordered from most to least variance, and lets you keep the top few.

PCA is agnostic about the task: it does not know which variance comes from the stimulus, which from the animal's decision, and which from movement.

That is its main weakness in cognitive work.

Factor analysis is a close relative that explicitly separates shared variability - fluctuations common to many neurons, presumed to reflect network state - from private noise in each neuron, which makes it better suited to spiking data.

Demixed principal component analysis (dPCA), published in the journal eLife in 2016 by Dmitry Kobak, Wieland Brendel, Christian Machens and colleagues, was designed to fix PCA's agnosticism.

It decomposes population activity into components that each depend on a single task parameter - one component carrying stimulus information, another carrying decision, another carrying time - while still capturing most of the variance.

The result is a small set of components a human can actually interpret.


26.1.3 Latent variable models and state-space inference

A latent variable is something you cannot measure directly but infer from what you can measure.

Here, the latent variables are the hypothesised low-dimensional signals driving the recorded spikes.

Gaussian process factor analysis (GPFA), published by Byron Yu and colleagues in the Journal of Neurophysiology in 2009, was an important step because it worked on single trials rather than requiring averages over many repeats.

It smooths and reduces dimensions in one statistical step, so the extracted trajectory is not distorted by choosing a smoothing width first and a projection second.

Single-trial capability matters enormously, because averaging across trials destroys exactly the trial-to-trial variation that might carry the animal's actual decision or its lapse of attention.

State-space models go further by assuming the latent variables evolve according to some rule - a dynamical equation - and fitting that rule alongside the trajectory.

Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems (LFADS), published in Nature Methods in 2018 by Chethan Pandarinath and colleagues, uses a sequential autoencoder - a neural network trained to compress and reconstruct the spike trains - to infer per-trial initial conditions, low-dimensional temporal factors, and inferred external inputs.

It substantially improved single-trial decoding relative to earlier smoothing methods.


26.1.4 Nonlinear embedding and geometric deep learning approaches

PCA, factor analysis and dPCA are all linear: they take weighted sums of neurons.

If the true structure is curved - a ring, a sphere, a torus - a linear method will need extra dimensions to describe something that is intrinsically simple.

Nonlinear embedding methods try to recover curved structure directly. t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) are the two most common, and they produce striking pictures by preserving which points are near which other points.

Their weakness is interpretability and stability: the axes mean nothing, distances between distant clusters are unreliable, and the picture can change with parameter settings.

Treat them as visualisation, not as measurement.

CEBRA, published in Nature in 2023 by Steffen Schneider, Jin Hwa Lee and Mackenzie Mathis, addresses this by using contrastive learning - training a network to pull together neural states that share a behavioural label or occur close in time and push apart those that do not.

The claimed advantage is consistency: embeddings that match across sessions, animals and even recording modalities.

MARBLE, published in Nature Methods in 2025 by Adam Gosztolai and colleagues, takes a geometric deep learning approach, learning from the local flow fields on the manifold itself, which allows dynamics to be compared across conditions and animals without assuming a shared coordinate system.


26.2 The neural manifold

The word manifold comes from mathematics and simply means a surface that is locally flat but may be globally curved - the Earth's surface is a two-dimensional manifold sitting in three-dimensional space.

Applied to the brain, the neural manifold is the subset of the full state space that the population actually visits.

If you record one hundred neurons but their activity only ever lands on a curved ten-dimensional surface, that surface is the manifold.


26.2.1 Definition, intrinsic and extrinsic constraints, and evidence across species

Juan Gallego, Matthew Perich, Sara Solla and Lee Miller set out the modern formulation in Neuron in 2017: the manifold is the set of collective states available to a population given the constraints on the circuit.

Those constraints come in two kinds.

Intrinsic constraints come from inside - the wiring, which neurons connect to which, and with what sign and strength.

Extrinsic constraints come from outside - the limited range of stimuli and behaviours the animal actually produces during the experiment.

The minimum number of coordinates needed to specify a position on the manifold is its intrinsic dimension.

The number of recorded neurons is the embedding dimension.

The claim is that intrinsic dimension is far smaller than embedding dimension.

Evidence for low-dimensional structure has been reported very broadly: in monkey motor and premotor cortex, in rodent hippocampus, in fly central complex, in zebrafish, and in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, which has only 302 neurons.

That range across animal phyla is the strongest argument that the phenomenon is not an artefact of one preparation.


26.2.2 Low dimensionality as a signature of computation

Why would low dimensionality be meaningful rather than merely convenient?

The argument is that a recurrent circuit that computes something must constrain its own activity, and constraint shows up as reduced dimensionality.

If activity were genuinely unconstrained, every neuron would be free to do anything and the trajectory would fill the whole space.

Instead it lies on a surface, and the shape of that surface is a fingerprint of the connectivity that produced it.

A second argument is decodability.

If the useful information lives in a few dimensions, a downstream neuron can read it out with a simple weighted sum, which is exactly what a neuron does.

Low dimensionality thus makes biological readout plausible.

The honest caveat is that low dimensionality is necessary but not sufficient evidence for computation.

Many uninteresting things - a shared arousal signal, correlated noise, a slow drift - also produce low-dimensional structure.


26.2.3 Manifold stability across time, learning, and brain-computer interface training

The most persuasive evidence that manifolds are real, rather than statistical descriptions, comes from experiments that manipulate or track them.

Patrick Sadtler and colleagues, in Nature in 2014, gave monkeys a brain-computer interface controlling a cursor, then changed the mapping from neural activity to cursor motion.

When the new mapping demanded activity patterns that still lay within the existing manifold - a within-manifold perturbation - monkeys adapted within minutes.

When it demanded patterns outside the manifold - an outside-manifold perturbation - they largely could not adapt in a session, and only made progress over days.

That is a strong result, because it shows the manifold constrains what an animal can learn quickly, which is what you would expect if it reflects fixed connectivity rather than a description of behaviour.

Gallego, Perich and colleagues, in Nature Neuroscience in 2020, recorded from monkey motor, premotor and somatosensory cortex across up to two years.

Individual recorded neurons came and went, and decoders built on raw neural activity degraded badly, but after aligning the latent dimensions across sessions the low-dimensional dynamics were stable and decoding held up for the whole period.

This has a direct clinical payoff: a brain-computer interface anchored to latent dynamics rather than to particular units should need far less recalibration.


26.2.4 Critiques: dimensionality as an artefact of task and sampling

The field's most serious internal criticism is that measured dimensionality reflects the experiment as much as the brain.

Peiran Gao and Surya Ganguli argued this explicitly in Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2015 and in a subsequent theoretical treatment: if you only vary a few task parameters, you can only observe a few dimensions of variance, so simple tasks manufacture low-dimensional data regardless of the underlying circuit.

The empirical counterweight came from Carsen Stringer, Marius Pachitariu, Kenneth Harris and colleagues in Nature in 2019.

Recording roughly ten thousand mouse visual cortex neurons responding to thousands of natural images, they found the response was high-dimensional, with principal component variance falling as a power law - the nth component's variance scaling roughly as one over n - with no clear cut-off dimension.

That finding itself is now contested.

A 2025 reanalysis in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences argued that the cross-validated PCA estimator used was biased, that the true spectrum is better described as a broken power law with a steeper second slope, and that visual cortical representations are consequently lower-dimensional than Stringer and colleagues claimed.

The state of play is therefore genuinely unsettled.

Motor and navigational systems performing constrained tasks look convincingly low-dimensional; sensory cortex under rich naturalistic stimulation may not be; and the measured number depends on the estimator, the stimulus set, and the number of neurons recorded.

A beginner should read any stated dimensionality as a property of a measurement, not a constant of a brain area.


26.3 Dynamical systems accounts of cognition

A dynamical system is any system whose current state determines how the state will change next.

Written informally: the rate of change of the state is some function of the state, plus whatever inputs arrive.

The dynamical systems view of cortex says that neural populations are exactly this - the population state evolves according to internal rules set by connectivity, and inputs nudge the trajectory rather than dictating it moment by moment.

This reframes the explanatory question.

Instead of asking what a neuron codes for, you ask what the flow field looks like: where does the state get pulled, where does it get pushed, and what does the resulting path accomplish?


26.3.1 Fixed points, line attractors, ring attractors

A fixed point is a state where the flow is zero - if the system arrives there and nothing disturbs it, it stays.

A stable fixed point, or point attractor, pulls nearby states towards it, which is a natural mechanism for holding one discrete choice or one memorised item.

A line attractor is a continuous line of fixed points.

The state can sit anywhere along the line and stay put, so the line stores a continuous quantity.

The classic biological example is the oculomotor neural integrator in the brainstem, which holds eye position steady after a saccade by integrating velocity commands - a mechanism analysed by Sebastian Seung in the 1990s.

A ring attractor is a closed loop of fixed points, appropriate for storing a circular variable such as heading direction, where 359 degrees must connect back to 0.

The strongest confirmation of a ring attractor in a real brain came from the fruit fly.

Johannes Seelig and Vivek Jayaraman showed in 2015 that a bump of activity in the ellipsoid body tracks the fly's heading, and Sung Soo Kim, Jayaraman and colleagues, in Science in 2017, demonstrated the ring attractor signatures directly - a single persistent bump, angular velocity integration, and recovery of a single bump after perturbation.

Later connectome work traced the excitatory compass neurons and the inhibitory neurons that between them implement local excitation and broad inhibition.

This is one of the few places in neuroscience where a theoretical computational motif proposed decades earlier was later confirmed at the level of identified cells and wiring.


26.3.2 Rotational dynamics and dynamical motifs in motor and premotor cortex

Mark Churchland, John Cunningham, Krishna Shenoy and colleagues reported in Nature in 2012 that population activity in monkey motor cortex during reaching contains a strong rotational component - the trajectory sweeps around in a plane, at similar phase across many different reaches.

They found it using jPCA, a method that searches for the two-dimensional projection in which the dynamics are maximally rotational.

The interpretation offered was that rotation acts as an oscillatory basis - a set of rhythmic building blocks from which the required muscle activity patterns can be constructed - rather than as a code for reach direction.

The result was influential precisely because rotation is hard to explain with tuning-curve thinking, and easy to explain with a dynamical system.

It has also attracted sustained challenge.

One line of criticism holds that sequence-like responses across neurons, with no true rotation in the underlying circuit, can produce apparent rotational structure in jPCA. Another, from work published in eLife in 2021, shows that rotational dynamics are equally consistent with motor cortex acting as a feedback controller responding to sensory error, which is a different mechanistic story with the same signature.

Rotation is thus a robust empirical observation whose mechanistic interpretation remains open.


26.3.3 Recurrent network models trained on cognitive tasks

A recurrent neural network (RNN) is an artificial network whose units feed back onto each other, so it has internal state and its own dynamics.

Training one on a task the animal performed, then dissecting it, has become a standard theoretical method.

The founding example is Valerio Mante, David Sussillo, Krishna Shenoy and William Newsome in Nature in 2013.

Monkeys judged either the motion or the colour of a stimulus depending on a context cue.

The expected answer was early selection - gating out irrelevant input at the sensory stage - but the prefrontal data showed both features present in both contexts.

The trained RNN revealed the alternative: selection and integration are one process.

The network has a line attractor along which evidence accumulates, and context rotates the relevant input onto that line while the irrelevant input is projected into directions that do not accumulate.

Nothing is gated out; it simply fails to move the state along the axis that matters.

The obvious caution is that an RNN is a hypothesis generator, not evidence.

Different networks trained on the same task can reach different solutions, and the fact that one artificial network matches the data does not prove the brain uses that solution.


26.3.4 Dynamics as an alternative to representation talk

The strong version of the dynamical view says we should stop describing neurons as representing variables and describe circuits as machines that transform state.

Empirical support comes from work such as the 2016 PLOS Computational Biology study by Jonathan Michaels, Benjamin Dann and Hansjorg Scherberger, which found that reaching activity was better explained as a dynamical system than as representational tuning - and, importantly, that a dynamical model naturally produces the apparent tuning curves that representational accounts take as their primary evidence.

Philosophically, David Barack and John Krakauer have pressed the point that a neural representation is not the same thing as a mental representation, and that talk of neurons holding symbols invites the question of who reads them.

The counter-argument is that representation talk is not merely decorative.

If activity reliably carries information about a variable, is used downstream, and can be manipulated to change behaviour, calling that a representation is a legitimate and useful description.

A reasonable reading, and the one taken here, is that these are two levels of description rather than two competing facts.

Dynamics tells you the mechanism; representation tells you what the mechanism is for.

The dispute becomes substantive only when a representational claim smuggles in an unexamined reader.


26.4 The geometry of abstraction

The previous sections concerned how the state moves.

This section concerns how the states are arranged - the shape formed by the set of conditions, independent of time.

Geometry in this sense is about relative positions: which conditions are close, which are far, and whether the differences between conditions line up in parallel.

Those arrangements turn out to determine what a downstream neuron can and cannot learn.


26.4.1 Mixed selectivity and dimensionality expansion

Mixed selectivity means a neuron responds to a combination of task variables rather than to one.

Nonlinear mixed selectivity is stronger: the neuron's response to a combination is not the sum of its responses to the parts.

Mattia Rigotti, Stefano Fusi, Earl Miller and colleagues argued in Nature in 2013 that this apparently messy, disordered tuning in prefrontal cortex is computationally essential.

Diverse nonlinear mixing spreads the conditions out into a high-dimensional arrangement.

The payoff is that in a high-dimensional arrangement, a simple linear readout - a weighted sum with a threshold, which is what a downstream neuron can compute - can implement far more input-output functions, including combinations that are impossible to separate linearly in a low-dimensional layout.

Rigotti and colleagues also reported that when animals made errors, the dimensionality of the neural representation had dropped before the error, which links the geometric property to behaviour rather than leaving it a purely theoretical virtue.

Note the tension with section 26.2: mixed selectivity says high dimensionality is good, the manifold literature says activity is low-dimensional.

Both can hold, because they concern different things - the arrangement of task conditions can be expanded while the moment-to-moment trajectory remains constrained - but the tension is real and is a live topic.


26.4.2 Abstract format, cross-condition generalisation, and the parallelism score

Silvia Bernardi, Marcus Benna, Mattia Rigotti, Jerome Munuera, Stefano Fusi and colleagues, in Cell in 2020, gave abstraction an operational definition: a variable is represented abstractly if a decoder trained on some conditions still works on conditions it never saw.

They measured this with cross-condition generalisation performance (CCGP): train a linear decoder on a subset of conditions, test it on held-out ones, and see whether it transfers.

High CCGP means the code has a format that supports generalisation, not merely discriminability.

Their second measure is the parallelism score (PS), which asks whether the coding direction for a variable - the vector in state space that separates its two values - points the same way across different contexts.

Parallel coding directions are exactly what allows a single readout to work everywhere.

They found abstract, generalisable formats for multiple variables in both monkey hippocampus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and notably found them alongside high-dimensional mixed selectivity rather than instead of it.

The geometry that supports this is roughly that of a low-dimensional grid or parallelogram embedded in a high-dimensional space - structured enough to generalise, expanded enough to remain flexible.


26.4.3 Compositionality and the reuse of coding directions

Compositionality means building new things by combining reusable parts.

In geometric terms it means the same coding direction is reused, so that a state can be understood as a sum of independent contributions - this stimulus, plus this context, plus this rule.

Laura Driscoll, Krishna Shenoy and David Sussillo, in Nature Neuroscience in 2024, made the dynamical version of this argument.

Training recurrent networks on many tasks at once, they found the networks assembled solutions from shared dynamical motifs - attractors, decision boundaries, rotations - and reused the same motif across tasks.

Tasks needing memory of a continuous circular variable reused the same ring attractor.

Their proposal is that the dynamical motif is a natural intermediate unit of computation, sitting between the single neuron and the whole network, in much the way a subroutine sits between an instruction and a program.

On the biological side, recent macaque work published in 2025 reported that spatial working memory was encoded in a common low-dimensional subspace conserved across two different tasks, while task identity occupied an orthogonal subspace - a compositional architecture in which the memory code can be reused because context is carried separately.

Increases in the parallelism of coding directions during successful generalisation have been reported as a signature of this reuse.

The framework is attractive and gaining evidence, but it is young, and how far genuine compositionality extends beyond carefully designed laboratory task sets is not yet established.


26.4.4 Subspace separation for input, memory, and output

A subspace is a set of directions within the state space.

Two subspaces are orthogonal when activity in one produces no change along the other - the geometric equivalent of two signals not interfering.

Matthew Kaufman, Mark Churchland, Krishna Shenoy and colleagues reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2014 that motor cortex uses this trick to prepare movements without making them.

Preparatory activity lies in an output-null subspace, which the muscles do not read out, and movement begins when activity moves into the output-potent subspace.

This solves a real problem elegantly.

A monkey can plan a reach for a second without twitching, not because the planning signal is weak, but because it points in a direction the readout ignores.

The same principle recurs in cognition.

Elizabeth Buschman's group and others have shown that rotating a sensory representation into a different subspace when it becomes a memory reduces interference between incoming stimuli and stored ones, so a new input does not overwrite what is being held.

Related work has described communication subspaces between areas: one region's activity is only transmitted to another along particular directions, so a source area can compute internally without broadcasting everything it does.

Together these results suggest a general design principle - the brain routes and gates information by geometry, choosing which directions in state space are visible to which readout, rather than by switching connections on and off.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Recording many neurons at once shifts the unit of analysis from the single cell to the population state, a point moving through a high-dimensional space, and the tools of this chapter - principal component analysis, demixed principal component analysis, Gaussian process factor analysis, latent dynamical models, and nonlinear embeddings - exist to make that motion visible without distorting it.

Population activity is generally confined to a lower-dimensional neural manifold set by intrinsic connectivity and extrinsic task demands, and the strongest evidence that this manifold is real rather than descriptive comes from Sadtler and colleagues in 2014, where perturbations outside the manifold could not be learned quickly, and from Gallego and colleagues in 2020, where latent dynamics stayed stable for two years while individual neurons turned over.

Measured dimensionality is nonetheless partly a property of the experiment, as Gao and Ganguli argued, and the Stringer 2019 finding of high-dimensional visual cortical responses together with its 2025 reanalysis shows the question is genuinely open rather than settled.

The dynamical systems account explains cognition through fixed points, line attractors and ring attractors - the fly heading circuit being the clearest confirmed case - and through trained recurrent networks such as the Mante 2013 model, which recast contextual selection as rotation of inputs relative to an integrating axis rather than as early gating.

The geometric account adds that the arrangement of conditions matters as much as the trajectory: nonlinear mixed selectivity expands dimensionality so linear readouts can do more, while parallel coding directions measured by cross-condition generalisation performance and the parallelism score give abstraction and compositional reuse a concrete, testable form.

Underlying all of it is one design principle worth carrying forward - the brain appears to route, store and withhold information by choosing directions in state space, so that what a downstream population sees depends on geometry rather than on switching connections on and off.


CHAPTER 27. CONNECTIVITY AND NETWORK ANALYSIS (APPARATUS)

The brain is not a bag of independent parts.

Whatever a region does, it does in conversation with other regions, and the tools in this chapter are the ones neuroscientists use to describe that conversation quantitatively.

This chapter is about apparatus - the measures, models, and statistics that turn raw recordings into statements about how brain areas are wired together and how they influence one another.

It matters because almost every modern claim about "brain networks" rests on a chain of analytic choices, and a reader who cannot see those choices cannot judge the claim.

We will move from the basic kinds of connectivity, through the graph mathematics used to describe them, into time-varying and higher-order methods, and finally into the statistics that decide what counts as a real finding.

Along the way, we will be honest about which parts of this apparatus are solid and which are still contested.


27.1 Kinds of connectivity

The word "connectivity" in neuroscience does not name one thing.

It names at least three quite different ideas, which are measured by different instruments, mean different things, and are routinely confused with one another in popular writing and sometimes in the literature itself.

Karl Friston's 2011 review in the journal Brain Connectivity is the standard reference that sorts them out.

The distinctions below are the single most useful thing a newcomer can carry away from this chapter.


27.1.1 Structural, functional, and effective connectivity distinguished

Structural connectivity is physical wiring - the actual axons, the cables, the anatomical tracts that run between one region and another.

Functional connectivity is a purely statistical statement: it says that the activity in region A and the activity in region B rise and fall together over time, without claiming any cause and without claiming any direct anatomical link.

Effective connectivity is the strongest claim of the three: it says region A exerts a causal influence on region B, with a direction and a sign, and it can only be estimated by fitting a model that says how the influence would work.

The three can come apart badly, and this is not a technicality.

Two regions with no direct axonal connection can show strong functional connectivity simply because a third region drives them both, a situation called common input or confounding.

Friston's framing is that structural connectivity constrains which effective connections are even plausible, so anatomy should discipline the models we fit rather than be ignored by them.


27.1.2 Correlation, coherence, and phase-based measures

The simplest functional connectivity measure is the Pearson correlation coefficient between two time series - a number between minus one and one saying how tightly the two signals move together.

Correlation is the workhorse of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that measures blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal as a slow, indirect proxy for neural activity.

For electrophysiology - electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical fields at the scalp, and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which records the associated magnetic fields - researchers usually prefer frequency-resolved measures.

Coherence is essentially correlation computed separately at each frequency, so it can reveal that two regions are locked together in the alpha band (roughly eight to twelve cycles per second) while being unrelated at other frequencies.

Phase-based measures go further and ask only whether the timing relationship between two oscillations is stable, ignoring how large the signals are; the phase locking value (PLV) is the best-known example.

There is a serious artefact lurking here called volume conduction, the fact that a single electrical source inside the head spreads instantly to many sensors, creating apparent connectivity where none exists.

Two influential fixes exist: Nolte and colleagues (2004) proposed using only the imaginary part of coherency, and Stam and colleagues (2007) proposed the phase lag index (PLI); both work by discarding zero-lag relationships, on the reasoning that instantaneous field spread cannot produce a genuine time lag.

The cost of these fixes is real - they also throw away any genuine zero-lag synchrony, which almost certainly exists in the brain - so they buy specificity at the price of sensitivity.


27.1.3 Granger causality, transfer entropy, and their assumptions

Granger causality, imported into neuroscience from economics, asks a prediction question: does knowing the past of signal A help predict the future of signal B beyond what B's own past already tells you?

Transfer entropy is the information-theoretic cousin of the same idea, measuring in bits how much uncertainty about B's future is removed by knowing A's past; Barnett, Barrett and Seth (2009) proved that for Gaussian variables the two measures are formally equivalent.

Neither measure detects causation in the philosophical sense - both detect directed predictability, which is a weaker and more fragile thing.

Applied to fMRI, they have been sharply criticised, chiefly because the haemodynamic response function (HRF), the slow blood-flow smear that converts neural activity into BOLD signal, differs from region to region and can invert the apparent time order of events.

The field has not fully settled this dispute.

Some work, including Seth, Chorley and Barnett (2013), reports that Granger inferences are surprisingly robust to variation in the haemodynamic response, including its time to peak, while showing that severe downsampling and measurement noise can still produce wrong answers; the underlying mathematical question of whether the haemodynamic response function has the minimum-phase property that would guarantee safety has remained contentious into the 2020s.

The practical summary is that these methods are reasonably at home in EEG, MEG, and direct neural recordings where sampling is fast, and are treated with suspicion in fMRI where neural events unfold in milliseconds but the measurement is sampled in seconds.


27.1.4 Dynamic causal modelling and generative connectivity

Dynamic causal modelling (DCM), introduced by Friston, Harrison and Penny in 2003, takes an entirely different route to effective connectivity.

Instead of testing predictability between measured signals, DCM builds a generative model - an explicit forward simulation that says how hidden neural populations interact and how that hidden activity would produce the signal you actually recorded.

The analyst then uses Bayesian inference, a statistical procedure that updates beliefs about parameters given data, to estimate the strength and direction of connections and to compare competing model architectures.

Because the measurement process, including the haemodynamic response, is written explicitly into the model, DCM confronts the problem that damages Granger causality in fMRI rather than ignoring it.

Spectral DCM, now the most widely used variant for resting-state fMRI, fits the cross-spectral density of the data rather than the raw time series, which makes it computationally efficient for data with no task events.

The trade-off is stark and worth stating plainly: DCM's answers are only as good as the model space the analyst chose to consider, and it cannot discover a connection between regions the analyst declined to include.


27.2 Graph-theoretic description

Once you have a matrix of connections between brain regions, you can treat the brain as a graph - a mathematical object made of nodes joined by edges - and apply a large body of existing network mathematics.

This move, popularised for neuroscience by Bullmore and Sporns in their 2009 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, is what created the field now called network neuroscience or connectomics.

It is powerful because it gives precise vocabulary to vague intuitions about integration and segregation.

It is dangerous because the mathematics runs perfectly well on a badly constructed graph and will hand you confident numbers either way.


27.2.1 Nodes, edges, and the definitional choices that dominate results

Before any graph measure can be computed, someone must decide what a node is and what counts as an edge, and these two decisions frequently matter more than the findings reported downstream.

Nodes usually come from a parcellation, a scheme that divides the brain into a set of regions using anatomical landmarks, functional boundaries, or clustering of imaging data - and there is no agreed standard, with common schemes ranging from a few dozen regions to a thousand.

Zalesky and colleagues (2010), in a paper pointedly titled "Whole-brain anatomical networks: does the choice of nodes matter?", showed that the answer is yes: network properties change systematically with the number and size of regions.

Later work, including Bryce and colleagues (2021), found that parcellation choice meaningfully shifts estimates of individual differences in resting-state functional connectivity, though other groups have argued the effect is modest for some questions - so the size of the problem is itself somewhat disputed.

Edges require a second decision, namely thresholding: keeping only connections above some strength, since a raw correlation matrix is fully connected and most of those connections are noise.

Different thresholds give different densities, and because most graph measures depend on density, comparing two groups at a fixed threshold when they differ in overall connectivity strength can manufacture a difference out of nothing.


27.2.2 Degree, strength, centrality, hubs, and clubs

Degree is the simplest node measure - the number of edges attached to a node - and in weighted networks its analogue is strength, the sum of edge weights.

Centrality measures try to capture importance in a more subtle way; betweenness centrality counts the fraction of shortest paths in the whole network that pass through a given node, so a node with high betweenness sits on many routes and its removal would be costly.

A hub is a node that scores highly on such measures, and human imaging consistently identifies hubs in the precuneus, posterior parietal cortex, superior frontal cortex, insula, and thalamus.

The participation coefficient measures how widely a node spreads its connections across different modules, and it distinguishes a connector hub, which links separate subsystems, from a provincial hub, which is merely popular within its own neighbourhood.

Van den Heuvel and Sporns (2011) showed that human brain hubs are more densely interconnected with one another than chance would predict, a configuration borrowed from network science and called a rich club.

The rich club is attractive because it suggests a high-capacity backbone for integrating information across specialised systems, but it is also disproportionately expensive metabolically and disproportionately implicated in disorders, which is part of why it has attracted so much attention.


27.2.3 Paths, diffusion, navigation, and communication models

A path length is the number of steps between two nodes, and the classic claim that the brain is a small-world network - highly clustered locally yet with short paths globally - rests on this measure.

But short path length only matters if signals actually travel along shortest paths, and that assumption is biologically implausible, because a neuron would need global knowledge of the entire connectome to route a signal optimally.

This objection, pressed by Avena-Koenigsberger, Misic and Sporns and reviewed in their 2018 Nature Reviews Neuroscience article on communication dynamics, spurred a family of alternative communication models.

Diffusion models sit at the opposite extreme, assuming signals spread as random walks with no knowledge of the network at all, and intermediate models such as search information and k-shortest-path ensembles occupy the space between.

Navigation, developed by Seguin, van den Heuvel and Zalesky (2018), is a particularly appealing middle case: each node simply forwards the signal to whichever neighbour is physically closest to the target, using only local geometric information, and this greedy strategy turns out to be strikingly efficient on real connectomes.

Which communication model the brain actually uses is unresolved, and the honest position is that the choice of model is currently an assumption imposed by the analyst rather than a fact established by data.


27.2.4 Modularity, community detection, and null models

A module or community is a set of nodes more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the network, and finding modules is how researchers recover systems like the default mode network from raw data.

The dominant approach is modularity maximisation, introduced in network science by Newman and Girvan, which scores a proposed partition by comparing observed within-module connection density against what a null model would predict.

A null model is a randomised version of the network that preserves some features - most often each node's degree, in what is called the configuration model - and destroys the rest, so it tells you what "more connected than chance" actually means.

The search for the best partition is computationally hard, so heuristics are used; the Louvain algorithm has been standard for years, and the Leiden algorithm of Traag, Waltman and van Eck (2019) improved on it by guaranteeing that the communities it returns are internally connected.

Modularity maximisation suffers a known flaw called the resolution limit, described by Fortunato and Barthelemy (2007), whereby small genuine modules get absorbed into larger ones because the null model term depends on the size of the whole network.

Two practical consequences follow: the number of modules you find is partly a property of your resolution parameter rather than of the brain, and because these algorithms are stochastic, responsible practice runs them many times and reports a consensus partition rather than a single lucky answer.


27.3 Time-varying and higher-order structure

Everything so far treats connectivity as a fixed quantity, one number per pair of regions for an entire scan.

That is obviously an idealisation, because cognition changes on the scale of seconds while a resting-state scan lasts many minutes.

The methods in this section try to recover structure that a single static matrix throws away - change over time, and interactions involving more than two regions at once.

They are the most active and the least settled part of the apparatus.


27.3.1 Dynamic functional connectivity and brain states

Dynamic functional connectivity is the attempt to show that the pattern of coupling between regions reorganises over the course of a scan, typically by computing correlations within a sliding window - a short segment of time that is stepped forward across the recording.

Cluster the resulting sequence of matrices and you obtain a small number of recurring configurations, usually called brain states, each occupying some fraction of the scan.

The approach is genuinely contested, and this is one of the disputes a beginner should know about rather than be shielded from.

The core objection, pressed by Hindriks and colleagues (2016), Laumann and colleagues (2017), and Liegeois and colleagues (2017), is that a stationary process - one whose statistics never actually change - will still produce fluctuating windowed correlations purely by sampling noise, so apparent dynamics require a proper null model before they can be believed.

Laumann's group further argued that much of the observed variability tracks head motion and fluctuating arousal, including drowsiness, rather than cognitive state changes.

The window length is a further arbitrary choice: too short and estimates are noisy, too long and real fast transitions are smeared away.

The current defensible position is that time-varying structure exists but that any specific claim about brain states needs an explicit null model and careful control of motion and arousal.


27.3.2 Hidden Markov and switching models

A hidden Markov model (HMM) is a statistical model that assumes the data are generated by a system occupying one of a small number of unobserved states at each moment, with fixed probabilities of switching between them.

Applied to neuroimaging by Baker and colleagues (2014) and developed extensively by Vidaurre and colleagues from 2016 onward, HMMs offer a principled alternative to sliding windows because they infer state boundaries from the data rather than imposing a fixed window.

Applied to MEG, this approach revealed recurring network states lasting on the order of a hundred milliseconds - far faster than sliding-window fMRI could ever resolve - that nonetheless resemble the familiar resting-state networks.

Vidaurre and colleagues (2017) also reported that transitions between these states are hierarchically organised, with the brain cycling within one metastate for a period before switching to another, and that an individual's tendency to occupy one metastate relates to behavioural and demographic measures.

The assumptions remain strong: the number of states must be chosen by the analyst, and the Markov assumption - that the next state depends only on the current one - is a simplification whose adequacy is not guaranteed.


27.3.3 Edge-centric and hypergraph methods

Edge-centric analysis, introduced by Faskowitz, Esfahlani, Sporns and Betzel in Nature Neuroscience in 2020, inverts the usual perspective by treating connections rather than regions as the primary objects.

The trick is the edge time series: instead of collapsing two regions' signals into one correlation, you multiply the two standardised signals at each time point, yielding a running record of moment-to-moment co-fluctuation that can then be clustered into edge communities.

Because a region participates in many edges, this naturally produces overlapping communities, which is closer to biological reality than forcing each region into exactly one module.

The method drew a pointed critique from Novelli and Razi (2022) in Nature Communications, who showed mathematically that many published edge-centric findings follow directly from ordinary static node correlations and therefore reveal nothing new unless tested against a null that preserves those correlations.

Hypergraph and simplicial-complex methods attack a related limitation from another angle: an ordinary graph edge can only join two nodes, whereas a hyperedge can join three or more, allowing genuinely higher-order interactions among triplets of regions to be represented.

These higher-order approaches remain early-stage, with the field still debating which multivariate information measures are trustworthy and how to correct for the explosion in the number of possible interactions.


27.3.4 Network control theory applied to cognitive state transitions

Network control theory imports engineering mathematics that asks how much input energy is needed to steer a system from one state to another given its wiring.

Gu and colleagues (2015) made the first large-scale application to human structural connectomes, defining average controllability as a region's capacity to push the brain toward nearby, easily reached states, and modal controllability as its capacity to push toward distant, hard-to-reach states.

They reported that hubs of average controllability fall preferentially in the default mode system while hubs of modal controllability fall in cognitive control systems, an appealing correspondence between abstract mathematics and known functional anatomy.

The framework was challenged directly by Tu and colleagues (2018), who disputed both the claim that brain networks are controllable from single regions and the claim that real connectomes have distinctive controllability profiles relative to random networks; Gu's group replied defending their methods, and the exchange has not produced consensus.

The deeper worry is that the model is linear while neural dynamics are not, and that driving a whole brain from one node is not a real experimental manoeuvre - so the theory is elegant and mathematically sharp, but its empirical grounding remains thin, and both things should be said together.


27.4 Statistical connectomics

A whole-brain connectivity matrix with two hundred regions contains nearly twenty thousand distinct connections.

Testing all of them naively guarantees a great many false positives, and this is before considering that motion, breathing, and heartbeat all leave structured traces in the data.

This section covers the statistical machinery that separates a connectomic finding from a connectomic mirage.

It is the least glamorous part of the apparatus and the part most responsible for whether the literature is trustworthy.


27.4.1 Network-based statistics

The network-based statistic (NBS), introduced by Zalesky, Fornito and Bullmore in 2010, exploits a simple insight: real effects on connectivity are rarely scattered at random across the matrix, but tend to cluster into connected subnetworks.

The procedure sets a preliminary threshold on the test statistic at every edge, finds connected components among the surviving edges, and then uses permutation testing - repeatedly shuffling group labels to build an empirical distribution of the largest component expected by chance - to assign a corrected significance value to each component.

This buys substantial statistical power over testing edges one at a time, provided the effect really is clustered.

The price is that inference is at the level of the whole component, not individual connections: you may conclude that a subnetwork is affected without being licensed to say which specific edge within it is.

The method also depends on an arbitrary cluster-forming threshold, which motivated the threshold-free variant of Baggio and colleagues (2018) that adapts threshold-free cluster enhancement to networks.


27.4.2 Multiple comparison over edges

The alternative to component-level inference is to test every edge and correct for the number of tests performed.

Controlling the family-wise error rate, the probability of making even one false positive anywhere, is the strictest approach, and it is usually implemented by permutation rather than by the crude Bonferroni correction, which is badly conservative when edges are correlated with one another.

Controlling the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of declared findings that are false, is more permissive and more common in connectomics, following the procedure of Benjamini and Hochberg.

The choice is a genuine trade-off rather than a matter of correctness: family-wise control protects you from a single embarrassing false claim, while false discovery control accepts a known fraction of errors in exchange for finding weaker true effects.

Crucially, the correction must account for every analysis actually run, including the different thresholds, parcellations, and connectivity measures that were tried and discarded - and failure to do this, sometimes called analytic flexibility or the garden of forking paths, is a major undeclared source of false positives in this literature.


27.4.3 Confound structure: motion, physiology, and sampling

Head motion is the most notorious confound in functional connectivity, and Power and colleagues (2012) showed its signature is not random noise but a systematic distortion: motion inflates apparent connectivity between nearby regions and reduces it between distant ones.

This is destructive because motion correlates with the very variables researchers study - children, older adults, and clinical groups all move more - so an uncorrected motion artefact can perfectly mimic a group difference in network organisation.

Physiological signals compound the problem, since cardiac pulsation and respiration produce structured fluctuations in the BOLD signal that are not neural in origin but are rhythmic and therefore look like connectivity.

Standard countermeasures include censoring or scrubbing high-motion time points, regressing out estimated motion parameters and their derivatives, and removing signals from white matter and cerebrospinal fluid where neural activity should be minimal.

None of these fully solves the problem, and there is a lasting disagreement about global signal regression - removing the average signal across the whole brain - which suppresses motion and physiological artefact effectively but mathematically forces some correlations to become negative, complicating interpretation of anticorrelated networks.

Sampling is a quieter confound: short scans give unreliable individual estimates, and work in the precision-imaging tradition indicates that stable individual connectomes require far more data per person than the five or ten minutes that were conventional for years.


27.4.4 Reproducibility of connectomic findings

The reproducibility question came to a head with Marek and colleagues (2022) in Nature, who analysed brain-wide association studies using several large datasets containing thousands of participants.

Their conclusion was blunt: associations between individual differences in brain connectivity and behavioural or cognitive traits are typically very small, and studies with the sample sizes traditionally used - a few dozen participants - are so underpowered that their published effects are largely inflated or spurious.

Reliably detecting such effects, they argued, requires samples in the thousands, which reframes connectomics as a science that needs consortium-scale data rather than single-laboratory studies.

The paper prompted vigorous rebuttal as well as agreement; several groups responded that better measurement - longer scans, better denoising, multivariate rather than single-edge analysis, and outcome measures with higher reliability - can raise effect sizes substantially, so that the required sample size is a function of measurement quality and not a fixed law.

Both camps agree on the underlying diagnostic even where they differ on the remedy: much of the pre-2020 connectomics literature was underpowered, and the field's response has been a turn toward large open datasets, preregistration of analysis plans, and explicit reporting of the analytic choices described throughout this chapter.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Connectivity is three separate ideas - anatomical wiring, statistical co-variation, and modelled causal influence - and confusing them is the commonest error in reading this literature.

Every measure in the apparatus, from correlation and phase locking through Granger causality and dynamic causal modelling, carries assumptions that can be stated plainly and that determine when the measure is trustworthy.

Graph-theoretic description gives precise language for hubs, modules, and paths, but its outputs are hostage to upstream choices about parcellation, thresholding, null models, and the assumed model of how signals travel.

Time-varying and higher-order methods, including sliding-window dynamics, hidden Markov models, edge-centric analysis, and network control theory, are the field's growing edge and are also where the sharpest published disagreements currently sit.

Finally, the statistical layer is not an afterthought: motion and physiological confounds, edge-wise multiple comparison, and the small true effect sizes documented by Marek and colleagues in 2022 together mean that a connectomic result is only as credible as the null model, the sample size, and the analytic transparency behind it.


CHAPTER 28. COMPUTATIONAL FRAMEWORKS FOR COGNITION (CORE)

This chapter is about the mathematical languages neuroscientists use to say what the brain is doing, as opposed to merely describing what it looks like or when it lights up.

A recording tells you that a neuron fired; a computational framework tells you what that firing might be for.

We will work through five such languages: Bayesian inference and predictive processing, reinforcement learning, attractor and network dynamics, normative or rational analysis, and the symbolic and hybrid tradition.

Each one is a genuine scientific achievement, and each one has places where it is oversold.

The chapter matters because measurement without theory accumulates facts without producing understanding, and because the same theories now drive artificial intelligence systems, which makes getting them right a practical matter as well as a scientific one.

A word on terminology before we begin: a computational framework here means a set of mathematical assumptions about what problem the brain is solving and what quantities it must represent to solve it.


28.1 The Bayesian brain and predictive processing

The Bayesian brain idea starts from a simple observation about the situation the brain is in.

The brain never receives the world directly.

It receives signals from sensors that are noisy, ambiguous, and incomplete - a pattern of light on the retina is consistent with infinitely many three-dimensional scenes, and the same is true for sounds, touches, and smells.

The brain's job, on this view, is inference: working backwards from ambiguous effects to probable causes.

Bayesian statistics is the mathematics of exactly that problem, which is why it became the dominant normative framework in perceptual science over the last thirty years.

Predictive processing is the family of proposals about how neural circuits might actually carry out such inference.


28.1.1 Bayes rule as a normative standard for inference under uncertainty

Bayes rule, named for the eighteenth-century English clergyman Thomas Bayes, states how a rational agent should update its beliefs when new evidence arrives.

In words: the probability of a hypothesis given the data is proportional to the probability of the data given the hypothesis, multiplied by the prior probability of the hypothesis.

The word normative here means prescriptive rather than descriptive - Bayes rule says what an ideal reasoner ought to do, not what any particular brain does do.

This distinction is load-bearing for the rest of the chapter, because showing that behaviour matches a Bayesian prediction does not by itself show that the brain contains anything resembling Bayes rule.

The theorem is a mathematical fact, not an empirical claim; the empirical claim is that nervous systems approximate it, and that claim can be tested and can fail.


28.1.2 Priors, likelihoods, precision, and cue combination

A prior is what you believed before the current evidence arrived - for instance, the visual system's built-in assumption that light usually comes from above, which is why a photograph of craters turns into a photograph of domes when you flip it upside down.

A likelihood is how probable the current sensory evidence would be under each candidate hypothesis.

Precision is the inverse of variance, meaning simply how reliable a signal is: a precise signal is one you can trust, an imprecise one is noisy and should be discounted.

The cleanest evidence that human beings weight signals by precision comes from cue combination experiments, most famously Marc Ernst and Martin Banks in Nature in 2002, who had people judge the height of a ridge using vision, touch, or both.

When the two senses were combined, the perceived height was very close to the maximum likelihood estimate - each sense contributed in proportion to its reliability, and combining them produced a judgement more precise than either alone.

When Ernst and Banks degraded the visual signal by adding noise, the weighting shifted towards touch in the way the theory predicts, which is the crucial control, because it shows the weights are computed rather than fixed.


28.1.3 Predictive coding: prediction, prediction error, and hierarchical message passing

Predictive coding is a specific proposal for the circuitry, given its influential modern form by Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard in Nature Neuroscience in 1999, working on the visual cortex.

The proposal is that each level of a cortical hierarchy sends predictions downward about what the level below should be seeing, and the level below sends upward only the residual - the part of its activity that the prediction failed to explain.

That residual is the prediction error, and the term message passing means that computation proceeds by these two streams of signals travelling in opposite directions until the whole hierarchy settles into a consistent interpretation.

The appeal is efficiency and elegance: if the prediction is good, almost nothing needs to be transmitted, and Rao and Ballard showed that a network trained this way developed receptive field properties resembling those of real visual neurons, including end-stopping, where a cell responds to a short bar but not a long one.

Precision from the previous sub-section enters here as a gain control: prediction errors that are judged reliable are amplified, and attention has been proposed to be exactly this precision-weighting operation.

It is worth being clear that predictive coding is a hypothesis about cortical microcircuitry which remains under active test, not an established anatomical fact.


28.1.4 The free energy principle and active inference

Karl Friston's free energy principle attempts to derive predictive coding, and much else, from a single starting point.

The principle states that any system that persists over time must act so as to minimise a quantity called variational free energy, which is an upper bound on surprise - roughly, on how unexpected the system's sensory states are given its model of the world.

Friston's mathematical contribution, developed in a series of papers from around 2005 onward, was to show that the error term in the Rao and Ballard scheme can be identified with the variational free energy of variational inference, a standard technique in statistics for approximating hard probability calculations.

Active inference is the extension to action: instead of only changing your beliefs to fit the world, you can change the world to fit your beliefs, so perception and action become two routes to the same minimisation.

This is genuinely unifying, because it puts perception, learning, and motor control under one objective function rather than three unrelated ones.

The theory is elegant, and its scope is remarkable; whether that scope is a strength or a symptom is the subject of the next sub-section.


28.1.5 Empirical status: successes, unfalsifiability worries, and open tests

On the credit side, predictive processing has organised a large body of findings, particularly the mismatch negativity - an electroencephalography (EEG, the recording of electrical activity from the scalp) response elicited when a repeated sound is followed by a deviant one - and repetition suppression, the reduction in neural response to a repeated stimulus.

On the debit side, several of these findings have alternative explanations, and careful work has tried to separate genuine prediction error from simple neural fatigue; Ryszard Auksztulewicz and Karl Friston reviewed the contextual determinants of repetition suppression in 2016, and studies such as Amanda Robinson and colleagues in eLife in 2018 report that prediction error and repetition suppression have dissociable effects on neural representations, which complicates the simplest predictive-coding story.

The sharper dispute concerns the free energy principle itself.

Critics, including commentators writing in Entropy in 2021, argue that the principle is unfalsifiable, because almost any behaviour can be redescribed after the fact as free energy minimisation, and because Friston himself has stated that it is a mathematical principle rather than an empirically testable hypothesis.

Defenders reply that the principle is meant as a framework that generates falsifiable process models, and that those specific models, not the principle, are what should be tested.

The honest summary is that predictive coding as a circuit hypothesis is testable and partially supported, while the free energy principle as a general law occupies contested ground between mathematics and empirical science - and you should be suspicious of any presentation that blurs the two.


28.2 Reinforcement learning as brain theory

Reinforcement learning (RL) is the branch of machine learning concerned with an agent that acts in an environment and receives rewards, and must learn which actions produce reward over the long run.

Its relationship with neuroscience is unusually close and unusually two-way: the algorithms were partly inspired by animal learning theory, and then turned out to describe the activity of real neurons with startling accuracy.

Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto's textbook, first published in 1998 and substantially revised in 2018, is the standard reference and is explicit about these biological roots.

This section works from the formal setup outward to the neural evidence.


28.2.1 Markov decision processes, value, and policy

A Markov decision process (MDP) is the standard formalism: a set of states the world can be in, a set of actions the agent can take, a rule giving the probability of moving to a new state given the current state and action, and a reward function.

The word Markov means that the future depends only on the present state, not on the history of how you got there - an assumption that is often false in practice and is one of the framework's main simplifications.

A policy is the agent's rule for choosing actions in each state; it can be deterministic or probabilistic.

A value is the expected total future reward from a state, or from a state-action pair, usually with future rewards discounted so that sooner is worth more than later.

Almost every idea in the rest of this section is a claim about how a brain might compute or store one of these two quantities, value and policy.


28.2.2 Temporal difference learning and the dopamine reward prediction error hypothesis

Temporal difference (TD) learning, developed by Sutton in 1988, updates value estimates using the discrepancy between what you predicted and what you got plus what you now predict - the temporal difference error.

The landmark neuroscience result is Wolfram Schultz, Peter Dayan, and P. Read Montague in Science in 1997, who showed that midbrain dopamine neurons in monkeys behave like this error signal.

The pattern is precise and characteristic: an unexpected reward produces a burst of firing; once a cue reliably predicts the reward, the burst moves to the cue and the reward itself elicits nothing; and if a predicted reward is withheld, firing dips below baseline at exactly the expected time.

That third case is the strongest evidence, because a dip in the absence of any stimulus is hard to explain as a simple response to reward and easy to explain as a negative prediction error.

The hypothesis is not unchallenged: dopamine signals also track movement initiation, novelty, and salience, and researchers including Joshua Berke have argued that a single reward-prediction-error account is too narrow for a system that plainly does more than one job.

The fair position is that reward prediction error is a well-supported and quantitatively successful description of a large part of phasic dopamine signalling, not a complete theory of dopamine.


28.2.3 Model-free and model-based control and their arbitration

Model-free learning stores the cached value of actions from direct experience and does not represent the structure of the world; model-based learning holds an internal model of how actions lead to states and plans by simulating consequences.

Nathaniel Daw, Yael Niv, and Peter Dayan in Nature Neuroscience in 2005 mapped this computational distinction onto the older psychological distinction between habit and goal-directed action, and proposed that the brain arbitrates between the two systems by trusting whichever is more confident in its own estimate at that moment.

Daw and colleagues in Neuron in 2011 introduced the two-step task to separate the systems behaviourally: participants choose at a first stage, which leads with high probability to one second-stage state and with low probability to the other, so that a rare transition followed by reward discriminates the two strategies, because a purely model-free learner repeats the rewarded first-stage choice while a model-based learner switches.

Sang Wan Lee, Shinsuke Shimojo, and John O'Doherty in Neuron in 2014 reported that regions of inferior lateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortex track the reliability of each system, consistent with an arbitration mechanism.

There is real methodological dispute here: Thomas Akam and colleagues argued in 2015 that certain model-free strategies can mimic the model-based signature in the two-step task, so the task is less diagnostic than first hoped, and later work has proposed modified designs in response.


28.2.4 Actor-critic architectures mapped onto basal ganglia circuits

An actor-critic architecture splits the problem in two: the critic learns values and computes the prediction error, and the actor learns the policy using that error as its teaching signal.

The standard mapping proposes that the critic corresponds roughly to ventral striatum together with midbrain dopamine neurons, and the actor to dorsal striatum, with dopamine broadcasting the error to both.

Within the striatum, projection neurons expressing D1-type dopamine receptors form the direct pathway and those expressing D2-type receptors form the indirect pathway, and because the direct route contains two inhibitory synapses in series it has a net excitatory effect on thalamus and cortex, while the indirect route opposes it.

Michael Frank and colleagues built this asymmetry into influential models in which dopamine bursts strengthen the go pathway and dopamine dips strengthen the no-go pathway, which offers a natural account of why Parkinson's disease, a disorder of dopamine loss, impairs learning from positive outcomes more than from negative ones.

The mapping is a good working hypothesis rather than a settled fact - the two pathways are more intertwined anatomically than the tidy diagram suggests, and alternative framings, such as the believer-skeptic account of Jamie Bogacz-adjacent modelling work published in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2016, treat the indirect pathway as signalling evidence against an action rather than simply suppressing it.


28.2.5 Distributional reinforcement learning and its neural evidence

Classical TD learning tracks a single number, the expected value, and thereby throws away everything about the shape of the reward distribution.

Distributional reinforcement learning, developed at DeepMind by Marc Bellemare, Will Dabney, and Rémi Munos from 2017, instead learns the whole distribution of possible returns, and it improved performance on benchmark tasks substantially.

Will Dabney, Zeb Kurth-Nelson, Naoshige Uchida and colleagues, publishing in Nature in January 2020, then tested whether the brain does the same, and found that individual mouse dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area differ systematically in how asymmetrically they respond to positive and negative errors.

That asymmetry is the key prediction: a population of neurons with different optimism levels collectively encodes an expectile code, meaning a set of points that together pin down a distribution rather than a single mean.

Adam Lowet, Uchida and colleagues extended the finding, and work published in Nature Neuroscience in 2023 reported analogous distributional signatures in prefrontal cortex, so the idea now has support from more than one laboratory and more than one region.

It is a genuinely rare case of an artificial intelligence advance predicting a specific, previously unnoticed feature of real neural data.


28.2.6 Hierarchical reinforcement learning, options, and subgoals

Flat reinforcement learning scales badly, because searching for a reward that is a thousand actions away is hopeless if you only reason one action at a time.

Hierarchical reinforcement learning addresses this with temporally extended actions, formalised as options by Richard Sutton, Doina Precup, and Satinder Singh in 1999 - an option is a sub-policy with its own initiation conditions and its own termination condition, so that choosing to make coffee is a single decision that unfolds into many primitive movements.

A subgoal is the state an option aims for, and discovering useful subgoals automatically remains one of the hardest open problems in the field.

Matthew Botvinick, Yael Niv, and Andrew Barto argued in Cognition in 2009 that this framework fits the neural evidence for hierarchically organised behaviour, and proposed a role for dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and dorsal striatum in representing options and for a pseudo-reward prediction error at subgoal completion.

Supporting evidence exists - notably reports of prediction-error-like signals at subgoal achievement - but the neural evidence for hierarchical reinforcement learning is thinner and less quantitative than the evidence for the flat version, and that gap should be stated plainly.


28.3 Attractor and network models

Attractor models take a different starting point from the previous two sections.

Instead of asking what problem the brain solves, they ask what a large recurrently connected network of neurons can do dynamically, and then ask which cognitive functions those dynamics could support.

An attractor is a pattern of network activity that the network settles into and stays in - the system's dynamics pull nearby states towards it, which is why the word attractor is used.

The appeal is that attractors give you stability out of noisy components, which is what memory and decision-making both require.


28.3.1 Hopfield networks and content-addressable memory

John Hopfield's 1982 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences described a network of simple binary units with symmetric connections, and showed that its dynamics always descend an energy function, so the network must settle into one of a finite set of stable patterns.

If you set the connection weights using a Hebbian rule - strengthening connections between units that are on together, after Donald Hebb's 1949 proposal - those stable patterns can be memories you deliberately stored.

The result is content-addressable memory, meaning you retrieve a whole memory by supplying any sufficient fragment of it, exactly as a snatch of melody recovers a whole song, and quite unlike a computer's memory, which requires you to know the address.

Hopfield borrowed the mathematics from spin glasses in condensed matter physics, and the storage capacity of the standard network is limited to roughly 0.14 patterns per unit before memories interfere destructively.

The model is biologically unrealistic in obvious ways - symmetric connections, no distinction between excitatory and inhibitory cells - but it established that memory could be a collective property of a network rather than a property of any single cell, and Hopfield shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for this line of work.


28.3.2 Continuous attractors for space, head direction, and analogue memory

A Hopfield network stores isolated patterns; a continuous attractor stores a continuous family of them, forming a line, a ring, or a sheet of stable states rather than a set of separate points.

This is the natural way to hold an analogue quantity in memory - a direction, a position, an eye position, a remembered angle - because the network can sit anywhere along the continuum and stay there.

The classic instance is the head direction system, modelled as a ring attractor in which local excitation and broad inhibition maintain a single bump of activity whose position on the ring represents the animal's current heading, and which is shifted around the ring by angular velocity signals so that the heading estimate updates as the animal turns.

The strongest confirmation came from the fruit fly: Sung Soo Kim, Vivek Jayaraman and colleagues, in Science in 2017, imaged the E-PG or compass neurons of the Drosophila central complex, which are physically arranged in a ring, and directly observed a single activity bump that persisted in darkness and tracked the fly's turns.

That is an unusually direct confirmation of a theoretical prediction made decades earlier by modellers including Kechen Zhang in 1996.

An honest caveat: theory says ring attractors need finely tuned connectivity, and connectome reconstructions of the fly circuit show real asymmetries, so how the biological network achieves robustness despite imperfect wiring is an active research question as of 2026.


28.3.3 Winner-take-all and decision by competition

If you connect several populations of neurons so that each excites itself and inhibits the others, then a small initial advantage grows, and one population ends up active while the rest are silenced - this is winner-take-all competition.

Xiao-Jing Wang's spiking network model, published in Neuron in 2002, showed that such a circuit, built from biophysically realistic neurons with slow NMDA-receptor-mediated excitation, reproduces the ramping activity recorded in monkey lateral intraparietal cortex during perceptual decisions, and reproduces the relationship between accuracy and reaction time.

Kong-Fatt Wong and Wang reduced this to a two-variable system in 2006, and that reduced system turns out to approximate the drift diffusion model, a much older and simpler account in which noisy evidence accumulates until it hits a threshold.

The connection matters because it links a behavioural-level description that fits reaction time data beautifully to a circuit-level mechanism that could implement it, which is precisely the kind of bridge computational neuroscience is supposed to build.

The competition is not merely metaphorical: the models predict, and experiments have found, that changes of mind occur when the losing population briefly recovers.


28.3.4 Balanced networks and the origin of variability

Cortical neurons fire irregularly, with interspike intervals nearly as variable as a random Poisson process, and for a long time this looked like noise to be averaged away.

Carl van Vreeswijk and Haim Sompolinsky, in Science in 1996, offered a different explanation: in a large sparsely connected network with strong synapses, excitation and inhibition automatically balance each other, so that each neuron's net input hovers near threshold and its firing is driven by moment-to-moment fluctuations rather than by a steady drive.

The consequence is that irregular firing is not a defect but the natural operating regime of a recurrent cortical network, and the resulting dynamics are chaotic even when the external input is perfectly constant.

The balanced state also confers a useful property: the network responds rapidly and linearly to changes in input, because it is always poised near threshold rather than saturated.

Later refinements, notably the stabilised supralinear network of Yashar Ahmadian, Daniel Rubin, and Kenneth Miller from 2013, extended the account to explain nonlinear phenomena such as surround suppression, where a stimulus outside a neuron's receptive field reduces its response.


28.4 Normative and rational analysis

Normative analysis asks what an optimal system would do, and then compares behaviour to that benchmark.

It is the strategy that David Marr, in his 1982 book Vision, called the computational level - the level that specifies what is being computed and why, as distinct from the algorithm used and the hardware that runs it.

This section covers the main normative traditions and then, deliberately, the reason none of them is sufficient on its own.


28.4.1 Ideal observer and ideal actor analysis

An ideal observer is a mathematical construct that performs a perceptual task as well as the available information allows, given the physics of the stimulus and the known noise sources.

Its value is as a yardstick: comparing human performance to the ideal observer converts a raw performance number into a meaningful efficiency, telling you what fraction of the available information the organism actually uses.

Horace Barlow used this logic in the 1950s to argue that human observers detecting dim flashes operate remarkably close to the physical limit set by photon noise, which was a striking result because it left little room for inefficiency in the early visual pathway.

An ideal actor extends the same logic to action, asking what movement or choice would be optimal given the task and the organism's own motor noise, a programme pursued by Konrad Kording, Daniel Wolpert, and others in motor control.

The general finding is that people are often close to optimal in narrow, well-practised, low-level tasks and markedly further from optimal in high-level reasoning, which is the puzzle the next sub-section addresses.


28.4.2 Resource rationality and bounded optimality

Herbert Simon's bounded rationality, from the 1950s, made the point that real agents have limited time, memory, and computation, so full optimality is not merely unachieved but unachievable.
