Resource-rational analysis, developed by Thomas Griffiths, Falk Lieder, and Noah Goodman from 2012 and set out at length by Lieder and Griffiths in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2019, makes this quantitative: it asks what strategy would be optimal for an agent with a specified computational budget, and treats the cost of thinking as part of the objective.

The payoff is that behaviours which look like errors under classical rationality can look sensible under resource rationality - a heuristic that is slightly less accurate but far cheaper may be the right choice, and even the number of items a person commits to memory can be predicted from the cost of forgetting and the capacity available.

The framework also reframes cognitive biases: rather than defects, many become the predictable consequence of good approximation algorithms run with too few samples.

The main criticism, pressed by commentators including Eric Mandelbaum and Chaz Firestone, is that the approach risks unfalsifiability of its own, because a sufficiently flexible choice of resource cost can rationalise almost any observed behaviour after the fact - the constraint has to be specified independently of the data it explains, and that is not always done.


28.4.3 Efficient coding and redundancy reduction

Efficient coding is the proposal that sensory systems are designed to represent the natural world using as few resources as possible, given that natural signals are enormously redundant.

Fred Attneave in 1954 and Horace Barlow in 1961 independently framed this in terms of Claude Shannon's information theory, arguing that the early visual system removes predictable structure so that what is transmitted carries maximal information per spike.

The framework makes concrete, testable predictions and several have held up: centre-surround receptive fields in the retina are close to what an efficient code for natural images with correlated neighbouring pixels would require, and Bruno Olshausen and David Field showed in Nature in 1996 that imposing a sparseness constraint on a code for natural image patches produces filters resembling the oriented, localised receptive fields of primary visual cortex.

Efficient coding also predicts adaptation, because a code tuned to the current statistics of the environment must change when those statistics change, and sensory adaptation is one of the most robust phenomena in all of perception.

It is a rare normative theory with a strong track record of predicting features of neural response properties in advance rather than explaining them afterwards.


28.4.4 Why a normative account is not yet a mechanism

Showing that behaviour matches an optimal solution tells you what the system achieves; it does not tell you how, and it does not even establish that the system computes the optimal solution rather than stumbling onto a shortcut that happens to agree with it on the tested cases.

This is the core limitation of the entire normative programme, and it applies equally to Bayesian perception, reinforcement learning, and efficient coding.

There is a further and subtler problem: optimality claims depend on assumptions about the agent's cost function, its prior, and its constraints, and those are usually fitted rather than measured, so a failed prediction can always be absorbed by adjusting one of them.

Jonathan Bowers and Colin Davis pressed a version of this objection against Bayesian psychology in Psychological Bulletin in 2012, arguing that Bayesian models are often too flexible to be genuinely tested, and defenders replied that the same flexibility charge applies to any modelling framework and that constraints can be fixed independently.

The practical resolution most working researchers adopt is Marr's own: use the computational level to state the problem clearly, then insist on an algorithmic and implementational account, and treat a normative fit as a hypothesis to be mechanistically cashed out rather than as an explanation already delivered.


28.5 Symbolic, hybrid, and cognitive-architecture approaches

The frameworks so far are continuous and statistical.

But human thought also has properties that look discrete and structured: we combine concepts systematically, we follow rules, and we understand novel sentences we have never encountered.

This section covers the tradition that takes those properties as the primary data, and the attempts to reconcile them with neural implementation.


28.5.1 Production systems and the architecture tradition

A production system represents knowledge as condition-action rules, called productions, of the form if such-and-such is the case then do such-and-such, together with a working memory holding the current situation and a mechanism for choosing which rule to fire when several match.

Allen Newell and Herbert Simon developed this idea from the 1970s, and Newell's 1990 book Unified Theories of Cognition argued forcefully that psychology needed complete architectures rather than isolated models of individual tasks.

Two architectures dominate: Soar, from Newell, Paul Rosenbloom, and John Laird, aimed primarily at general intelligent agents, and ACT-R, from John Anderson at Carnegie Mellon, aimed primarily at fitting human behavioural data.

ACT-R is notable for having been given a partial brain mapping - its modules for retrieval, goals, visual processing and motor output have been associated with specific regions, and the architecture has been used to predict functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a technique that measures blood flow changes as an indirect index of neural activity) time courses, as in Anderson's work from the mid-2000s onward.

The tradition's strength is that it forces theorists to specify a complete working system; its weakness is that the many free parameters make strong falsification difficult, and its relationship to actual neural circuitry remains loose.


28.5.2 Vector symbolic architectures and hyperdimensional computing

Vector symbolic architectures (VSA), also called hyperdimensional computing, try to get symbolic structure out of vectors, which is what neurons plausibly have.

The trick relies on a mathematical fact about high-dimensional spaces: if you pick two random vectors in, say, ten thousand dimensions, they will almost certainly be nearly orthogonal, so a space of that size holds an effectively unlimited supply of distinguishable items.

Three operations do the work: binding, which ties a role to a filler using something like element-wise multiplication or Tony Plate's circular convolution from his 1995 holographic reduced representations; superposition, which adds vectors to form a set; and permutation, which shifts a vector's elements to encode order.

The crucial property is that binding produces a vector dissimilar to both inputs but invertible, so red bound to circle can be stored alongside blue bound to square and later unbound to recover which colour went with which shape.

Pentti Kanerva, Ross Gayler, and Dmitri Rachkovskij developed the framework alongside Plate from the late 1980s, and it has had a revival because the operations are cheap, noise-tolerant, and well suited to low-power hardware.

Whether the brain uses anything of this kind is unresolved; the architectures are best regarded at present as an existence proof that distributed vectors can support structured representation, not as a demonstrated neural mechanism.


28.5.3 Neural syntax and compositional binding

Compositionality is the property that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by its parts and how they are combined, which is why you can understand the dog bit the man and the man bit the dog as different despite identical words.

Paul Smolensky's tensor product representations, from 1990, provided the first influential proposal for doing this in a neural network by taking the outer product of a role vector and a filler vector, and the framework has recently been shown by Tom McCoy, Tal Linzen, and Smolensky in 2019 to describe, approximately, what some trained recurrent networks discover on their own.

On the empirical side, Steven Frankland and Joshua Greene reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2015 that patterns in a small region of left mid-superior temporal cortex distinguished who did what to whom - the same noun could be decoded differently depending on whether it was the agent or the patient of the verb - which is direct evidence for role-specific neural coding.

Frankland and Greene reviewed the broader question in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2020, arguing that tensor-like mechanisms are a viable account of compositionality in neural systems.

The evidence is suggestive rather than decisive, and the field has not settled whether the brain uses a genuine binding operation or achieves the same behavioural effects through learned, less systematic means.


28.5.4 The binding problem and its candidate solutions

The binding problem is the question of how the brain keeps features that belong to the same object together, given that colour, shape, and motion are processed in partly separate populations - if you see a red circle and a blue square, what stops the red from attaching to the square?

Christoph von der Malsburg proposed in 1981 that temporal correlation could do it, and Wolf Singer, Charles Gray, and colleagues developed this into binding by synchrony: neurons responding to features of the same object fire in synchrony, typically in the gamma range around forty cycles per second, and that shared timing tags them as belonging together.

The proposal is elegant and generated a great deal of research, including reports of stimulus-dependent synchronisation in cat visual cortex from the late 1980s.

It has also drawn sustained criticism: Michael Shadlen and Anthony Movshon, in a much-cited Neuron paper in 1999 titled Synchrony Unbound, argued that the theoretical case is weaker than it appears and that the empirical correlations are consistent with synchrony being a by-product of recurrent connectivity rather than a functional code.

Competing accounts include attention as the binding mechanism, following Anne Treisman's feature integration theory of 1980, which holds that spatial attention serially selects locations and glues features found there; hierarchical convergence, in which cells higher in the visual system simply have receptive fields tuned to conjunctions; and the vector-binding schemes of the two preceding sub-sections.

As of 2026, no candidate commands consensus, and Jerome Feldman's 2013 analysis is worth taking seriously in arguing that there are several distinct binding problems rather than one, which may be part of why a single solution has been so elusive.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognition can be described in at least five mathematical languages, and each captures something real: Bayesian inference explains why perception weights cues by reliability, reinforcement learning explains what dopamine neurons are signalling, attractor dynamics explain how noisy networks hold stable memories and reach decisions, normative analysis explains why sensory codes have the form they do, and the symbolic tradition explains why thought is compositional.

The strongest results in the chapter are those where a theory made a specific prediction that was later confirmed in neural data - the temporal difference account of dopamine, the ring attractor observed directly in the fly compass, sparse coding predicting cortical receptive fields, and distributional reinforcement learning predicting asymmetric dopamine neurons.

The weakest points are where a framework's flexibility outruns its testability, which is the live charge against the free energy principle, against loosely constrained Bayesian and resource-rational models, and to a degree against the architecture tradition.

A normative account tells you what a system achieves and not how it achieves it, so a good fit at Marr's computational level is a hypothesis awaiting mechanism rather than an explanation already given.

Several central questions remain genuinely open, including how the brain arbitrates between model-based and model-free control, whether cortical microcircuits implement predictive coding, and how features are bound into objects.

The right posture towards all of these frameworks is to use them as tools that generate testable process models, and to distrust any version of them that cannot say what evidence would count against it.


CHAPTER 29. THE NEURAL CODE (CORE)

A brain is a machine that turns the world into electrical activity, and then turns that activity back into behaviour.

The question of the neural code is the question of what the rules of that translation are - which features of neural activity actually carry the message, and which are merely the machinery that carries it.

This chapter works through four things: the candidate coding schemes, the problem of noise and how it limits what a code can carry, the question of what frame of reference and what format a code uses, and finally the difference between being able to read a code and being able to write one.

The reason this matters is practical as well as philosophical.

Every brain-computer interface, every attempt to restore sight or speech, and every claim that a scientist has "found the representation of X" stands or falls on whether the code has really been identified.

29.1 Coding schemes

Neurons communicate mostly by action potentials, also called spikes - brief, roughly all-or-nothing electrical pulses that travel down the axon, the neuron's output cable.

Because each spike is about the same size as every other, the message cannot be in the size of the pulse.

It must be in when spikes happen, how many happen, and which neurons produce them.

The competing coding schemes below are essentially competing answers to that question, and they are not mutually exclusive.

29.1.1 Rate, temporal, population, and phase codes

A rate code says the message is the average number of spikes in some window of time - the classic finding, going back to Edgar Adrian in the 1920s, that a more intense stimulus produces a faster firing rate.

A temporal code says the precise timing of individual spikes carries information beyond the average, so that the irregularity in a spike train is signal rather than noise; in the auditory system, for example, spikes lock to particular phases of a sound wave with sub-millisecond precision, and that timing is what allows you to localise a sound source.

A population code says the message is not in any one neuron at all but in the joint pattern across many neurons, which is how a motor cortex population can specify a reach direction that no single cell specifies.

A phase-of-firing code says the message is in when a spike falls relative to an ongoing background rhythm, such as the roughly 4 to 10 hertz theta rhythm of the hippocampus; the classic case is phase precession, described by O'Keefe and Recce in 1993, in which a place cell fires progressively earlier in each theta cycle as the animal crosses the cell's preferred location, so that the phase carries position information the firing rate alone does not.

The honest summary as of the mid-2020s is that the brain almost certainly uses several of these at once, and that rate and phase codes have been shown to coexist and to be read out together in hippocampal cell assemblies.

29.1.2 Labelled lines against combinatorial codes

A labelled line is a dedicated channel: whatever travels down it means one thing, because of where it goes rather than because of any pattern it carries.

The mammalian taste system is the standard textbook example, where evidence from Charles Zuker's and Nicholas Ryba's laboratories suggests that sweet-detecting receptor cells feed dedicated pathways such that activating them signals "sweet" no matter what caused the activation.

A combinatorial code is the opposite arrangement: no single neuron means anything on its own, and identity is carried by which combination of many broadly tuned neurons is active, which is how olfaction works in the account developed by Linda Buck and Richard Axel and their successors, where each odorant activates a distinctive subset of several hundred receptor types.

The dichotomy is less clean than it is usually taught.

Insects appear to use both - broad combinatorial coding for general odours, alongside labelled lines for a few compounds that demand a hard-wired immediate response, such as carbon dioxide or a species-specific pheromone - and reviews of the mosquito antennal lobe published through 2024 still treat the labelled line versus combinatorial question as genuinely open.

Even in taste, work such as Wu and colleagues in Nature Communications (2015) showed that the apparent breadth of tuning of taste afferents depends on stimulus concentration, so the same cell can look labelled at one intensity and broadly tuned at another.

29.1.3 Sparse, dense, and distributed regimes

Coding schemes can also be sorted by how many neurons are active at once for any given item.

At one extreme is local coding, where one item is signalled by one cell, sometimes caricatured as the grandmother cell; at the other extreme is dense coding, where a large fraction of the population participates in every item.

Sparse coding sits between the two: only a small fraction of cells is active for any item, but that fraction is more than one, and different items recruit different small subsets.

Bruno Olshausen and David Field showed in 1996 that if you simply demand that a set of filters reconstruct natural images while keeping activity sparse, the filters that emerge look like the oriented, localised receptive fields of simple cells in primary visual cortex - a striking result, because it gives an information-theoretic reason for a piece of anatomy that had been described but not explained.

Sparse regimes buy energy efficiency, high storage capacity, and easy readout; dense distributed regimes buy robustness to the loss of individual cells and graceful generalisation.

Human medial temporal lobe recordings by Rodrigo Quian Quiroga and colleagues from 2005 onward found neurons that respond to a specific person across photographs, drawings, and even the written name, which is often reported as evidence for very sparse coding, though Quian Quiroga himself has argued the data indicate sparse-but-distributed coding rather than literal grandmother cells.

29.1.4 Predictive and error codes

Predictive coding proposes something counter-intuitive: that what ascends through the cortical hierarchy is not the sensory signal itself but the residue left over after prediction, the prediction error.

Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard's 1999 model showed that a hierarchy minimising prediction error would reproduce extra-classical receptive field effects such as end-stopping, where a neuron's response to a bar of light falls off when the bar is extended beyond the classical receptive field - explained here as the surround successfully predicting the centre.

Karl Friston later embedded this in the free energy principle, which casts perception, learning, and action all as prediction-error minimisation.

The evidence is real but softer than the theory's ambition.

Reduced responses to predictable stimuli are found reliably in single-unit recordings in macaque inferotemporal cortex and in human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), but as Millidge, Seth, and Buckley argued in their 2021 review, a reduced response is also what simple adaptation and repetition suppression predict, so it does not by itself establish that an explicit inhibitory prediction signal is being subtracted.

This is an elegant theory with genuine explanatory reach and genuinely underdetermined evidence, and both halves of that sentence should be kept in mind.

29.2 Noise, correlation, and information

Present the same stimulus twice to the same neuron and you will not get the same answer.

That variability sets a ceiling on how much any downstream circuit can learn from the activity, and understanding the ceiling is as important as understanding the signal.

29.2.1 Trial-to-trial variability and its sources

The standard measure is the Fano factor, the variance of the spike count across repeated trials divided by its mean; a Fano factor of one is what a completely random Poisson process would give, and cortical neurons typically land between about 0.5 and 1.5.

The variability has at least two distinguishable sources: irregularity in spike generation within a single trial, and drift in the underlying firing rate from trial to trial caused by things like arousal, attention, and slow shifts in cortical state.

Mark Churchland and colleagues reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2010 that the arrival of a stimulus quenches variability - the Fano factor drops sharply after stimulus onset - and that this happens across all four cortical lobes and across many behaviours, suggesting it is a general property of cortex being driven rather than a quirk of one area.

The interpretation matters: much of what looks like noise is not thermal randomness at all but the signature of ongoing internal dynamics, which means it is in principle recoverable rather than irreducible.

29.2.2 Noise correlations and their effect on coded information

A noise correlation is the tendency of two neurons to be jointly above or jointly below their average firing rate on the same trial, over and above what the stimulus dictates.

They matter because if noise were independent across neurons, a downstream reader could average it away, and information would grow without limit as you added neurons.

Whether correlations help or hurt is not a single answer but depends on their geometry relative to the signal, a point made forcefully by Bruno Averbeck, Peter Latham, and Alexandre Pouget in 2006.

Correlations aligned with the direction in which the stimulus changes the population response are harmful; correlations lying in directions the stimulus does not use are harmless and can even be beneficial, and work published in PRX Life in 2025 argues that strong correlations in particular can be helpful while weak ones are the dangerous case.

29.2.3 Information-limiting correlations

Ruben Moreno-Bote, Jeffrey Beck, Ingmar Kanitscheider, Xaq Pitkow, Peter Latham, and Alexandre Pouget introduced the decisive idea in Nature Neuroscience in 2014.

They showed that only one very specific correlation structure actually caps information: differential correlations, whose strength is proportional to the product of the slopes of the neurons' tuning curves.

The reason is intuitive once stated - if the noise has exactly the same shape as the change the stimulus produces, a decoder cannot tell one from the other, and no amount of averaging over more neurons will separate them.

Kanitscheider and colleagues argued in PNAS in 2015 that such correlations arise inevitably from noise already present in the sensory input itself, which means they are not an optional design flaw but a consequence of the world being ambiguous.

They are also fiendishly hard to detect, because they are typically tiny and buried inside much larger correlations that do not limit information, and recordings of hundreds of prefrontal neurons show the tell-tale signature: information grows strongly sublinearly with population size, but becomes linear again once trials are shuffled to destroy the correlations.

29.2.4 Fisher information and decoding bounds

Fisher information is a formal measure of how much a set of observations tells you about an unknown parameter, such as the direction of a moving stimulus.

Its usefulness comes from the Cramer-Rao bound, which states that no unbiased estimator can have a mean squared error smaller than the inverse of the Fisher information - so Fisher information sets a hard floor on the error of any decoder, including the brain's own.

For a population code, it can be computed from the tuning curves and the noise covariance matrix, and linear Fisher information, the version restricted to linear decoders, is the quantity most often measured experimentally.

The bound has real limits that are easy to overlook: it is not always tight, it can diverge from the true minimum error when decoding windows are short, and it can be made to behave pathologically by constructing artificial tuning curves, as Bethge, Rotermund, and Pawelzik and later critics have pointed out.

Practical estimation is also biased when neurons are correlated and trials are finite, a problem Ingmar Kanitscheider and colleagues addressed with a bias-corrected estimator in PLOS Computational Biology in 2015.

29.3 Reference frames and formats

Knowing which neurons fire is not enough.

You also need to know what the numbers are relative to, and in what kind of quantity they are expressed - the difference between "three metres to my left" and "at the corner of the building", and between a numeral and a heap of pebbles.

29.3.1 Egocentric, allocentric, and object-centred frames

An egocentric frame codes position relative to the observer's own body or a part of it, such as retinal coordinates (relative to the eye) or hand-centred coordinates.

An allocentric frame codes position relative to the world, independent of where the observer is standing or looking.

An object-centred frame codes position relative to another object, as when you represent the handle as being on the left side of the cup regardless of your own vantage point.

The traditional division assigns allocentric coding to the hippocampus, whose place cells discovered by John O'Keefe in 1971 fire when the animal occupies a particular location in an environment, and egocentric coding to the posterior parietal cortex, which fuses sensory signals into body-relative representations.

That division has been eroding: rat posterior parietal cortex has been shown to carry mixed egocentric and world-centred signals (Wilber and colleagues, Journal of Neuroscience, 2014), hippocampal neurons have been reported to show egocentric tuning, and work published in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2025 describes bidirectional hippocampal-parietal signalling as a network mechanism for coordinating frames rather than segregating them.

29.3.2 Coordinate transformation and gain fields

Moving between frames requires arithmetic - to know where a seen object is relative to your body, you must combine its retinal position with where your eyes are pointing.

David Zipser and Richard Andersen showed in 1988 that when an artificial neural network is trained to perform exactly this transformation, its hidden units spontaneously develop the same odd property that had been observed in real parietal neurons: a visual receptive field whose shape and retinal location stay fixed but whose response amplitude is scaled up or down by eye position.

That scaling is the gain field, and it is a general-purpose computational trick rather than a curiosity.

Alexandre Pouget and Terrence Sejnowski argued in the late 1990s that a population of such gain-modulated cells forms a basis set - a collection of simple functions from which many different output coordinate frames can be constructed by simple weighted sums - so that the same intermediate representation can serve reaching, looking, and pointing without committing to any one frame.

The practical upshot is that the brain often does not convert from one frame to another so much as hold a format from which any frame can be cheaply read out.

29.3.3 Analogue magnitude formats and their signatures

Some quantities appear to be represented not as discrete symbols but as approximate analogue magnitudes, rather like a smeared position on a mental number line.

This system, usually called the approximate number system (ANS), has a diagnostic signature: discrimination obeys Weber's law, meaning that performance depends on the ratio of two quantities rather than their difference, so eight against four is easy and eight against seven is hard.

Andreas Nieder and Earl Miller found neurons in monkey prefrontal and parietal cortex tuned to specific numerosities with progressively broader tuning for larger numbers (2002 onward), and Manuela Piazza, Stanislas Dehaene, and colleagues found the corresponding ratio-dependent adaptation signature in the human intraparietal sulcus using fMRI in 2004.

The interpretation is contested in at least two places: whether the underlying scale is logarithmic or linear with proportionally growing noise, and whether the ANS is a dedicated number system at all or a by-product of general perceptual magnitude processing, with a 2025 review in Cerebral Cortex still asking whether an innate sense of number exists.

Analogue magnitude formats are not confined to number - duration, size, and brightness show similar ratio-dependent signatures, which is part of what fuels the general-magnitude sceptical view.

29.3.4 Format conversion as a cognitive operation

If the brain holds the same content in more than one format, then translating between formats is itself a cognitive act with a measurable cost.

Dehaene's triple-code model proposes exactly three numerical formats - the visual Arabic form, the verbal word form, and the analogue magnitude - each with its own neural substrate, and requires traffic between them for most real tasks.

The evidence for a conversion cost is that cross-format comparisons, such as judging whether the numeral 7 exceeds a display of five dots, are reliably slower and more error-prone than within-format comparisons.

Whether this reflects genuinely separate stores requiring translation, or a single shared magnitude code reached by different encoding routes, remains unsettled: magnetoencephalography (MEG) decoding studies have come down on both sides, with some reporting primarily format-dependent representations and others reporting a shared magnitude representation for digits and dice patterns.

Treating conversion as an operation is nonetheless a useful discipline, because it forces the question of who is doing the converting and where.

29.4 Reading and writing codes

29.4.1 The decoding-writing asymmetry

Decoding is the demonstration that some information is present in a pattern of activity, usually by training a statistical classifier to recover a stimulus or an intention from recorded spikes.

Writing is the demonstration that installing that pattern of activity produces the corresponding experience or behaviour.

The asymmetry is that decoding is much easier and proves much less.

A decoder shows only that information is correlated with activity somewhere in the recording; it does not show that any circuit in the brain actually uses that information, and it can succeed on features the brain ignores entirely, in the same way that a thermometer taped to a computer can decode what the computer is doing without any part of the computer reading the thermometer.

This is why causal manipulation, not decoding accuracy, is the currency of claims about the neural code.

29.4.2 Patterned stimulation and the induction of percepts and memories

The landmark early demonstration is C. Daniel Salzman, Kenneth Britten, and William Newsome's 1990 Nature paper, in which microstimulation of direction-selective clusters in macaque area MT biased monkeys' reports of motion direction towards the stimulated cells' preference, even when the display was actually moving the other way.

Modern two-photon holographic optogenetics has raised the resolution to individual cells: Luis Carrillo-Reid and colleagues in Cell (2019) and James Marshel and colleagues in Science (2019) showed that activating a small number of neurons in mouse primary visual cortex that were tuned to a particular orientation could drive the behaviour appropriate to seeing that orientation, in the absence of any visual stimulus.

Carrillo-Reid's work further identified pattern-completion neurons - individual cells whose activation recruits an entire ensemble - so that as few as two stimulated neurons could trigger the behaviourally relevant pattern.

On the memory side, Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez, and Susumu Tonegawa tagged the dentate gyrus cells active during one context with channelrhodopsin-2, a light-sensitive ion channel, and reactivated them while the mouse was shocked in a different context, producing fear of a place where nothing bad had happened - an implanted false memory, reported in Science in 2012 and 2013.

These are the strongest existing evidence that specific patterns are sufficient, not merely correlated.

29.4.3 Brain-computer interfaces as a test of code understanding

A brain-computer interface (BCI) is a system that reads neural activity and converts it into control of an external device, and it functions as an unforgiving engineering test of whether a code has been understood well enough to be used.

The results are impressive on the reading side.

Francis Willett and colleagues reported in Nature in 2023 a speech neuroprosthesis using intracortical microelectrode arrays that achieved a 9.1 percent word error rate on a 50-word vocabulary and 23.8 percent on a 125,000-word vocabulary in a participant with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; Edward Chang's group, with Sean Metzger and colleagues, reported comparable performance in the same issue using electrodes on the cortical surface.

By 2024, a New England Journal of Medicine report described a system that calibrates rapidly enough to be practical outside the laboratory.

The instructive part is what BCIs reveal about the limits of our understanding: they succeed largely because machine learning finds a usable statistical mapping, and because the brain adapts to the decoder as much as the decoder adapts to the brain, which means their success is only partial evidence that we know the code.

Writing information back in - restoring rich touch or vision through stimulation - remains substantially harder than reading it out, which is the decoding-writing asymmetry showing up as an engineering constraint.

29.4.4 Buzsaki's criterion: a code is understood when the reader circuit is identified

Gyorgy Buzsaki argued in his 2010 Neuron review, Neural Syntax: Cell Assemblies, Synapsembles, and Readers, that the field has been asking the wrong question.

An experimenter who decodes a variable from a population has shown what the experimenter can extract, not what the brain extracts; as Buzsaki puts it, the biological relevance of an assembly can only be judged from the perspective of explicit outputs, which means from the standpoint of the downstream circuit that actually receives it.

His proposal is that the meaningful unit is the cell assembly defined by the integration window of its reader - roughly a gamma cycle, some 10 to 30 milliseconds, matching the membrane time constant over which a downstream neuron sums its inputs - and that sequences of such assemblies within a theta cycle form something like a neural word.

The criterion that follows is stringent and clarifying: you have identified a neural code when you have identified the reader mechanism, specified its integration window, and shown that perturbing the pattern changes what the reader does.

Very few claimed codes in the literature currently meet it, and holding the criterion in mind is the best available protection against mistaking a successful classifier for a discovered representation.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Neural activity carries information through several coexisting schemes - rate, precise timing, population pattern, and phase relative to ongoing rhythms - and the labelled line versus combinatorial distinction, though useful, breaks down in the real sensory systems where it was first drawn.

Variability is not simply noise to be averaged away: only the specific geometry of differential correlations actually caps information, and Fisher information with the Cramer-Rao bound gives the formal floor on any decoder's error while carrying real caveats about tightness and estimation bias.

Codes are always expressed in some reference frame and some format, and gain fields provide a general mechanism for holding a representation from which many frames can be read out cheaply, while analogue magnitude formats betray themselves through ratio-dependent Weber-law behaviour.

Decoding a variable from recorded activity is far weaker evidence than writing that pattern in and observing the corresponding percept, which microstimulation, holographic optogenetics, and engram reactivation have now achieved in restricted cases.

The strictest standard, and the one this book adopts, is Buzsaki's: a code is understood only when the reader circuit that consumes it has been identified.


CHAPTER 30. MODELS, FALSIFIABILITY, AND THE HEALTH OF THE FIELD (CONTEXT)

This chapter steps back from particular findings and asks how cognitive neuroscience knows anything at all.

It covers what a model is for, how a model can be tested and how it can fail to be testable, and what happens when a whole field discovers that a large share of its published results do not hold up.

It then covers the reforms invented in response, and the persistent complaint that the field collects data far faster than it builds theory.

This matters because everything in the earlier chapters rests on this machinery.

A finding you read about is only as trustworthy as the design, the analysis, and the incentives that produced it, and a beginner who understands that will read the literature better than a specialist who does not.

30.1 What models are for

A model, in this field, is any explicit description of how something works that is precise enough to be worked out rather than merely asserted.

It might be a set of equations describing the flow of electrical current across a nerve cell membrane, or a computer program that plays the same gambling task a human volunteer played, or a statistical formula relating a brain measurement to an age.

The word covers very different objects, and much confusion in neuroscience comes from arguing about a model without first agreeing on what job it was built to do.

This section separates those jobs.

30.1.1 Models as data representation, as explanation, and as prediction

A model used as data representation simply compresses a messy dataset into a smaller, more readable form - for example, summarising the response of a visual cell by fitting it a curve whose peak tells you the orientation of edge the cell likes best.

A model used as explanation claims that the parts of the model correspond to real parts of the brain and that the mechanism written into the model is the mechanism actually operating, which is a far stronger claim.

A model used as prediction is judged only by whether it forecasts data it has not seen, and it may explain nothing at all - a deep neural network can predict responses in visual cortex quite well while remaining opaque about why.

Konrad Kording and colleagues, in their discussion of the role of theory and modelling in neuroscience, argue that these purposes carry different criteria for success, including explaining data, generalising outside the sample, being reproducible, being interpretable, inspiring new experiments, and being falsifiable, and that no single model is likely to score well on all of them.

The practical lesson for a reader is to ask which criterion a paper is actually meeting, because a model praised for fitting data has not thereby been shown to explain anything.

30.1.2 The realism-abstraction trade-off

The Hodgkin-Huxley model, from Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley's 1952 work on the squid giant axon, describes the nerve impulse in terms of specific ion currents crossing the membrane, and it is extraordinarily faithful to the biophysics - biophysics meaning the physical and chemical machinery of living tissue.

It is also highly non-linear and has many variables, which makes it hard to analyse mathematically and expensive to simulate in large networks.

The leaky integrate-and-fire model, at the other extreme, ignores the shape of the impulse and the ion channels entirely and treats a neuron as a bucket that fills with charge, leaks, and empties when it reaches a threshold.

That radical simplification is what makes network-scale simulation possible, and generalised integrate-and-fire models have been shown to reproduce the spike timing of detailed models and of real recorded neurons with high accuracy, which is the standing argument that the discarded detail was not always load-bearing.

The trade-off is real and unavoidable - more realistic models contain quantities that are harder to measure and slower to compute, while more abstract models risk having thrown away the very thing that mattered - and the honest position is that the right level of abstraction depends on the question, not on a general principle.

30.1.3 Model identifiability and parameter recovery

A model is identifiable if different settings of its internal knobs, called parameters, produce different predicted data, so that observing the data lets you work backwards to the knob settings.

Many attractive models are not identifiable in practice - two parameters may trade off against each other so smoothly that a wide range of combinations fits the data equally well, and the number the researcher reports is then close to arbitrary.

Robert Wilson and Anne Collins, in their 2019 eLife tutorial "Ten simple rules for the computational modeling of behavioral data", make parameter recovery a required step: generate artificial data from known parameter values, fit the model to that artificial data, and check whether the fitted values match the values you put in.

They also stress model recovery - simulate data from each candidate model, then check that your comparison procedure picks the right one - and they warn that a model identifiable in one range of parameters may be hopeless in another, so recovery has to be checked in the range your actual participants occupy.

This is unglamorous work, and it is the single most common thing missing from computational papers that later fail to replicate.

30.1.4 Model comparison, cross-validation, and out-of-sample prediction

A model with more parameters will always fit the observed data better, so raw goodness of fit cannot decide between models - it rewards overfitting, which is the modelling of noise peculiar to your sample as though it were signal.

Two families of correction exist: information criteria such as the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), which penalise complexity with a formula, and cross-validation, which repeatedly holds back part of the data, fits on the rest, and scores the model on the held-back part.

Cross-validation is generally the more honest test because it directly measures the thing you care about, namely performance on data the model has never seen, though it costs more computation and depends on splitting the data in a way that respects its structure.

Tal Yarkoni and Jacob Westfall, in a 2017 paper in Perspectives on Psychological Science, argued that psychology and allied fields have systematically preferred explanatory storytelling to out-of-sample prediction, and that borrowing the machine-learning habit of always reporting held-out performance would remove a great deal of self-deception.

Note the genuine disagreement here: AIC and BIC embody different goals, AIC aiming at best prediction and BIC at identifying the true model if it is among the candidates, and they routinely disagree, so reporting only the one that favours your preferred model is a known abuse.

30.2 The replication problem

Around 2011 onwards, psychology and then neuroscience went through a public reckoning with the discovery that many published findings could not be reproduced by independent teams.

Replication here means running the study again, ideally with a larger sample, and getting the same result; reproducibility, in the narrower sense, means getting the same numbers from the same data and code.

Both turned out to be weaker than assumed.

This section describes what was found and why.

30.2.1 Documented failures and their causes

Katherine Button, John Ioannidis, Brian Nosek and colleagues, writing in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2013 under the title "Power failure", surveyed 730 studies drawn from 49 meta-analyses and estimated the median statistical power of neuroscience studies at about 21 percent - power being the probability that a study will detect an effect that genuinely exists.

Scott Marek, Brenden Tervo-Clemmens and colleagues, in Nature in 2022, analysed public datasets totalling nearly 50,000 participants and concluded that brain-wide association studies - studies correlating a brain measure with a trait such as a cognitive score - need thousands of participants for reproducible results, while typical published studies had used a few dozen.

A related problem is measurement reliability: Maxwell Elliott, Annchen Knodt and colleagues, in Psychological Science in 2020, meta-analysed 90 experiments with 1,008 participants and found the average test-retest reliability of common task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures to be poor, with an intraclass correlation around 0.40, meaning the same person scanned twice on the same task gives quite different numbers.

Their qualification matters and is often dropped: intrinsic functional connectivity measured over longer scans is considerably more reliable, so the problem is specific to short cognitive tasks borrowed from group-level experimental designs, not to fMRI as such.

An unreliable measure cannot support a large true correlation, so small studies reporting large brain-behaviour correlations were, in retrospect, mostly reporting noise.

30.2.2 Analytic flexibility and the many-analysts findings

The Neuroimaging Analysis Replication and Prediction Study (NARPS), reported by Rotem Botvinik-Nezer and colleagues in Nature in 2020, gave one identical fMRI dataset to 70 independent analysis teams and asked all of them to test the same nine pre-specified hypotheses.

No two teams chose identical workflows, and the rate at which teams declared a hypothesis supported varied substantially - for some hypotheses, teams split close to evenly - even though the intermediate statistical maps from many teams were highly correlated.

The lesson is not that the teams were incompetent; it is that a chain of individually defensible choices about motion correction, spatial normalisation, smoothing, statistical model and multiple-comparison correction can move a borderline result across the threshold of significance in either direction.

Encouragingly, when the authors pooled information across all teams in a meta-analytic fashion, a consistent set of activated regions emerged, which suggests the underlying signal was real and the disagreement was about where to draw the line.

Researcher degrees of freedom is the standard term for this space of defensible choices, and its existence means that a single analysis, however honestly conducted, understates the uncertainty in its own conclusion.

30.2.3 Publication bias and the file drawer

Robert Rosenthal named the file drawer problem in 1979, describing the extreme case in which journals fill with the small fraction of studies that happened to reach significance by chance while the nonsignificant studies sit unpublished in researchers' file drawers.

The consequence is that the published literature is a biased sample of the research actually conducted, and any meta-analysis built from it inherits that bias, systematically overstating effects.

John Ioannidis and colleagues have developed excess significance tests, which compare how many significant results a literature contains against how many its studies had the power to produce, and applied them to bodies of work including the literature on brain volume abnormalities, finding significant results in excess of what the power of those studies could plausibly generate.

The most direct evidence of the size of the bias comes from Anne Scheel, Mitchell Schijen and Daniel Lakens, writing in 2021, who compared standard psychology papers with registered reports and found the first stated hypothesis supported in about 96 percent of standard papers but only about 44 percent of registered reports.

They and others note a caveat worth keeping - researchers may choose the registered-report format precisely when they suspect a null result - so the gap is evidence of substantial bias but not a clean measurement of it.

30.2.4 Small samples and inflated effect sizes

The counterintuitive core of the power problem is this: in an underpowered study, the only way an effect can reach statistical significance is if the noise happened to push the estimate upward, so the published estimates from small studies are systematically too large.

This is sometimes called the winner's curse, and it explains a familiar pattern in which an exciting first report of a large effect is followed by progressively smaller estimates as sample sizes grow, until the effect settles near zero.

Low power also lowers the positive predictive value of a significant result - the probability that a claimed discovery is real - because with few true effects detected and a fixed rate of false positives, false positives make up a larger share of the significant findings.

Button and colleagues in 2013 pressed an ethical point alongside the statistical one: underpowered research wastes public money, wastes participants' time, and in animal work costs lives, for results that cannot inform anything.

The remedy is not merely larger samples but better measures, since reliability sets a ceiling on the correlation any sample size can recover.

30.3 Reform practices

The reforms below were not imposed from outside; they were largely built by working scientists who had been burned.

They fall into two broad families - constraining flexibility before the data arrive, and making everything visible after they arrive - and they are complementary rather than alternatives.

None of them is free, and each has costs worth stating plainly.

30.3.1 Preregistration and registered reports

Preregistration means depositing your hypotheses, design, sample size and analysis plan in a public time-stamped archive before collecting data, so that the distinction between a prediction and an after-the-fact explanation is preserved.

A registered report goes further: the introduction and method are peer reviewed and accepted for publication before data collection, so the journal commits to publishing the result whatever it turns out to be, which removes the incentive to produce a positive finding.

The Scheel, Schijen and Lakens comparison described above is the strongest single piece of evidence that this works, and reviews by Christopher Chambers and Loukia Tzavella and others find broadly that these formats improve research quality.

The main honest criticisms are that preregistration constrains discovery of the unexpected, that vague preregistrations offer little real constraint, and that the format suits confirmatory hypothesis testing far better than exploratory or descriptive work - to which the standard reply is that exploratory work should be labelled as such rather than dressed up as confirmation.

30.3.2 Open data, open code, and open materials

Sharing the raw data, the analysis scripts, and the stimuli lets others check the numbers, reuse the sample for new questions, and discover errors that peer review cannot catch by reading a manuscript.

The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) supplied the missing piece: an agreed convention for how files and folders in a brain-imaging study are named and organised, with metadata attached, and an extension mechanism so the community can add new data types.

OpenNeuro, described by Christopher Markiewicz, Russell Poldrack and colleagues in eLife in 2021, is the main public archive built on that standard, at that point sharing over 500 datasets from more than 18,000 participants across multiple species and measurement types, and it follows the FAIR principles - findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable.

The costs are real: curating data for release takes time, human brain data carries identifiability and consent constraints, and code that runs on the author's machine often does not run anywhere else, which is why containerised analysis environments have become part of the practice.

30.3.3 Multi-site consortia and adversarial collaboration

If reliable brain-behaviour associations need thousands of participants, no single laboratory can produce them, which is the reasoning behind consortia such as the Human Connectome Project, the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, UK Biobank, and the ENIGMA consortium, which pools imaging and genetic data across many sites.

Adversarial collaboration attacks a different failure: proponents of rival theories agree in advance, with a neutral party, on an experiment and on which outcomes would count against each theory, so the result cannot be absorbed by either camp after the fact.

The COGITATE consortium's adversarial test of integrated information theory (IIT) and global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT), published in Nature in April 2025, is the flagship example: 256 participants across multiple laboratories, studied with fMRI, magnetoencephalography (MEG, which measures the magnetic fields produced by neural currents) and intracranial electroencephalography, with predictions preregistered by the theories' own proponents.

The outcome challenged both - the absence of sustained synchronisation within posterior cortex told against IIT's claim about network connectivity, while the general absence of a burst of prefrontal activity at stimulus offset, and the limited prefrontal representation of some conscious content, told against GNWT.

That neither theory was cleanly killed is itself informative, and critics have argued that both camps retained room to reinterpret the results, which is a fair caution about how much any single adversarial study can settle.

30.3.4 Specification curve and multiverse analysis

If the choice of analysis pipeline moves the answer, one response is to run all the defensible pipelines and report the whole distribution rather than picking one.

Sara Steegen, Francis Tuerlinckx, Andrew Gelman and Wolf Vanpaemel introduced multiverse analysis in 2016 for the space of defensible data-processing choices; Uri Simonsohn, Joseph Simmons and Leif Nelson formalised specification curve analysis, published in Nature Human Behaviour in 2020, in three steps - enumerate the reasonable, valid, non-redundant specifications, plot the results ordered by effect size with the choices marked underneath, and then conduct joint inference across the whole set.

Chirag Patel, Belinda Burford and John Ioannidis's vibration of effects, from 2015, is a closely related device from epidemiology that visualises how an estimate and its p-value swing across model choices.

Applied to neuroimaging, where the number of defensible pipelines is enormous, these methods make the fragility of a result visible instead of hiding it, and a finding that survives most of its multiverse is meaningfully stronger than one that survives a single pipeline.

The limits are worth stating: someone still decides which specifications are reasonable, the specifications are not independent so joint inference is statistically delicate, and a multiverse cannot rescue a study that was underpowered to begin with.

30.4 Theory as the scarce resource

The reforms above improve the reliability of individual findings.

They do not, by themselves, produce understanding, and a substantial body of opinion holds that reliability was never the field's deepest problem.

This section takes that argument seriously.

30.4.1 The complaint that the field is data-rich and theory-poor

The complaint runs like this: recording technology, imaging resolution and dataset size have grown by orders of magnitude, while the conceptual vocabulary used to interpret the results - attention, working memory, salience, prediction error - has changed comparatively little and remains loosely defined.

A parallel argument in psychology, made by Klaus Fiedler, Denny Borsboom, Iris van Rooij and others under the heading of the theory crisis, holds that the replication crisis is downstream of a theory crisis, because when the logical link between a theory and its empirical test is weak, almost any result can be claimed as support and almost any failure can be explained away.

The counter-argument, which deserves equal airing, is that description precedes theory in the history of every science, that cell atlases and connectomes are the anatomy on which later theory will stand, and that demanding grand theory prematurely produced exactly the untestable frameworks the critics complain about.

Both sides agree on one practical point: a theory stated in words alone is usually too flexible to be tested, and formalising it in mathematics or code is the minimum price of admission.

30.4.2 Would a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor, and what the question exposes

Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording, in PLOS Computational Biology in 2017, took the MOS 6502 microprocessor - the chip inside the Apple I, the Commodore 64 and the Atari video game system - and applied standard neuroscience methods to it, treating the running of Donkey Kong, Space Invaders and Pitfall as behaviours.

They had what neuroscience never has: complete ground truth, since the wiring of the 6502 is fully known, plus unlimited noiseless recordings from every transistor and the ability to lesion any one of them.

The methods behaved plausibly and produced familiar-looking results - lesion studies found transistors that were necessary for one game and not another, tuning curves and oscillations appeared, dimensionality reduction found low-dimensional structure - and yet none of it recovered the actual hierarchical organisation of the processor into adders, registers and instruction decoders.

The paper is a warning rather than a proof, and its critics correctly note that a microprocessor is not a brain, that its digital, engineered, non-redundant design may be unusually resistant to these methods, and that the authors did not apply the full modern arsenal.

The point that survives those objections is the one that matters here: unlimited data plus standard analysis does not automatically yield understanding, and what makes the difference is having a theory that tells you what to look for.

30.4.3 Criteria for a good theory in cognitive neuroscience

A usable list, assembled from the modelling and philosophy-of-science literature discussed above, would include the following.

• Precision - the theory is stated formally enough that two competent people derive the same prediction from it.

• Risky prediction - it forbids some observable outcomes, in the sense Karl Popper insisted on, so that a specific result would count as refutation.

• Scope with parsimony - it covers a range of phenomena without needing a new free parameter for each one.

• Bridging levels - it connects at least two of Marr's levels, that is, the computational level of what problem is being solved, the algorithmic level of what procedure solves it, and the implementational level of what tissue carries it out.

• Generativity - it suggests experiments nobody would have thought to run.

• Cumulativity - it can absorb a disconfirming result by being modified in a way that makes new risky predictions, rather than by adding an excuse.

The tension between scope and falsifiability is the central design problem: the broader a theory's reach, the easier it becomes to redescribe any result as consistent with it, which is precisely the charge levelled at the most ambitious frameworks in the next sub-section.

30.4.4 Standing programmes competing to be the unifying theory

Predictive processing holds that the brain is fundamentally a hypothesis-testing machine that continually predicts its sensory input and transmits only the prediction error, the mismatch between expected and actual input; it has been productive, generating specific and testable claims about perception, hallucination and the layered structure of cortex.

The free energy principle, associated above all with Karl Friston and set out in a 2010 Nature Reviews Neuroscience article titled "The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?", generalises this into a claim that any system that persists must appear to minimise a quantity called variational free energy, an upper bound on surprise, with perception, action, learning and attention all falling out as consequences.

The elegance is genuine and so is the criticism: opponents argue that a principle from which every outcome can be derived after the fact forbids nothing, that active inference restates ordinary feedback control in new vocabulary, and that the mathematical framework and the empirical brain claims are frequently conflated - defenders reply that the principle is a modelling framework, like the principle of least action in physics, and should be judged by the testable models it generates rather than tested directly.

Integrated information theory, from Giulio Tononi, proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's quantity of integrated information and locates it in a posterior hot zone; global neuronal workspace theory, from Bernard Baars, Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux, proposes that consciousness is the broadcast of information to a frontoparietal workspace - and, as noted above, the 2025 COGITATE adversarial test embarrassed specific predictions of both without eliminating either.

Alongside these sit connectionist and deep-network approaches, which explain by building systems that perform the task and then comparing their internal representations to brain data, and reinforcement learning, which is arguably the most successful case in the whole field of a formal theory whose variables were later found in the brain, in the dopamine prediction-error signal described by Wolfram Schultz, Peter Dayan and Read Montague in 1997.

The honest summary is that no programme currently commands consensus, that reinforcement learning succeeded partly because it was narrow, and that the most ambitious candidates face the sharpest questions about what would refute them.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Models serve at least three distinct purposes - compressing data, explaining mechanism, and predicting new observations - and a model that succeeds at one has not thereby succeeded at the others, which is why parameter recovery and out-of-sample testing are not optional extras.

The field's replication problem is well documented rather than alleged: median statistical power around 21 percent in the Button and colleagues 2013 survey, poor test-retest reliability of common task fMRI measures in Elliott and colleagues 2020, a requirement for thousands of participants for reproducible brain-wide associations in Marek and colleagues 2022, and substantial swings in conclusions across 70 analysis teams given identical data in the 2020 NARPS study.

Publication bias compounds all of this, and the roughly 96 percent versus 44 percent gap in hypothesis support between standard papers and registered reports gives a rough measure of its size.

The reforms - preregistration, registered reports, open data on shared standards, large consortia, adversarial collaboration, and multiverse or specification-curve reporting - address these failures directly and are now mainstream, though each carries costs and none can rescue an underpowered study.

Reliability is necessary but not sufficient: the Jonas and Kording 2017 microprocessor exercise showed that unlimited clean data plus standard analysis does not deliver understanding without theory to guide it.

The unifying frameworks now competing for that role, including predictive processing, the free energy principle, integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory, remain genuinely contested, and the 2025 COGITATE adversarial test challenged core predictions of the last two without settling between them.


PART FIVE. PERCEPTION: BUILDING THE WORLD FROM SIGNALS


CHAPTER 31. GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF PERCEPTION (CORE)

This chapter sets out the small number of principles that every sensory system in the brain appears to obey, whatever the sense.

Perception feels effortless and immediate, which is exactly why it is easy to misunderstand.

Nothing about the world arrives in your head ready-made; what arrives is a pattern of nerve impulses, and everything you experience is a construction built from that pattern plus a great deal of accumulated assumption.

The five ideas that follow - that perception is inference, that it is organised in hierarchies, that it adapts to context, that it is shaped by expectation, and that it eventually hands a discrete answer to the systems that act - recur in vision, hearing, touch, smell, and taste alike.

Getting them straight here makes the sense-by-sense chapters that follow far shorter and far clearer.


31.1 Perception as inference

The starting point of modern perceptual science is uncomfortable: the information reaching your senses is not enough, by itself, to tell you what is out there.

Perception must therefore be a form of guessing - a highly disciplined, statistically informed, largely unconscious guess, but a guess.

This section explains why the guess is necessary, how it is thought to be made, and why the places where it goes wrong are the most informative places to look.


31.1.1 The inverse problem and the poverty of the sensory signal

The retina - the sheet of light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye - records a two-dimensional array of light intensities, but the world it is sampling is three-dimensional.

That mapping cannot be undone by simple arithmetic, and the problem has a name: the inverse problem, meaning the task of recovering causes (objects, surfaces, distances, materials) from effects (the sensory image they happened to produce).

The difficulty is that infinitely many different scenes can produce exactly the same retinal image - a small nearby coin and a large distant plate can cast identical discs of light - so the image alone is formally ambiguous.

The same poverty afflicts the other senses: the pressure wave at your eardrum is a single one-dimensional squiggle that mixes every sound source in the room, and disentangling them is likewise underdetermined.

Because the data underdetermine the answer, the brain cannot compute the world; it can only infer it, and inference requires assumptions supplied from somewhere other than the current signal.


31.1.2 Helmholtzian unconscious inference and its modern form

The nineteenth-century physicist and physiologist Hermann von Helmholtz, in his Treatise on Physiological Optics (three volumes, 1856 to 1867), proposed that perception is a process of unconscious inference - conclusions drawn automatically, rapidly, and without any felt sense of reasoning.

His argument was that size and distance and shape have to be inferred from unreliable cues, and that the rules for doing so are learned from a lifetime of experience.

The modern restatement is the Bayesian brain hypothesis, named after the eighteenth-century clergyman and mathematician Thomas Bayes, whose theorem specifies how to update a belief when new evidence arrives.

In this framing the brain holds a likelihood - how probable the current sensory data would be under each candidate state of the world - and a prior - how probable each state of the world is in general - and combines them into a posterior, the belief that takes both into account; the percept is, roughly, the state with the highest posterior probability.

Influential formal treatments include Knill and Richards (1996) on vision as Bayesian inference, and Ernst and Banks (2002), who showed that people combine visual and touch estimates of object size almost exactly as a statistically optimal observer would, weighting each sense by its reliability.

It is worth being honest about the status of this framework: it describes a great deal of behaviour with striking accuracy, but demonstrating that the brain literally represents probability distributions, rather than merely behaving as if it did, remains an open and actively contested research problem.


31.1.3 Priors, illusions, and the diagnostic value of error

A prior is an assumption about how the world usually is, built into the perceptual machinery either by evolution or by experience.

A well-studied example is the light-from-above prior: because sunlight has come from overhead throughout evolutionary history, ambiguous shaded discs are seen as bumps when their upper half is bright and as dents when their lower half is bright, and simply rotating the image flips the percept.

Illusions are therefore not failures of a broken system; they are the visible fingerprints of a working system whose assumptions have been deliberately violated by an unusual stimulus.

The hollow-mask illusion is a clean case: a concave mould of a face, viewed from inside, is almost impossible to see as hollow because a strong prior insists that faces are convex, and the prior overrides genuine depth cues such as binocular disparity - the slight difference between the two eyes' images.

This is why perceptual scientists chase illusions so eagerly: an error tells you which assumption the brain was making, whereas a correct percept tells you almost nothing about how it was reached.

A related and unresolved debate concerns whether some psychiatric conditions, notably schizophrenia and autism, involve atypically weighted priors; the idea is attractive and has generated evidence in both directions, but it is not settled.


31.1.4 Perceptual constancies

A constancy is the perceptual system's ability to hold an object's apparent properties steady while the raw sensory signal changes wildly.

Lightness constancy means a sheet of white paper looks white indoors and outdoors even though it may reflect a hundred times more light in sunlight than in a dim room; the system does this partly by computing ratios of luminance between a surface and its surround rather than absolute values, and partly by estimating the illumination from cues such as specular highlights and the overall spread of brightnesses in the scene.

Colour constancy is the same trick for hue: a banana looks yellow under bluish daylight and under orange tungsten light, which requires discounting the illuminant, and although cortical area V4 has long been implicated - following the work of Semir Zeki in the 1980s - most researchers now agree that several mechanisms contribute, beginning as early as the retina, and no single account commands consensus.

Size constancy keeps a person's apparent size stable as they walk away from you, even though the image they cast shrinks in proportion to distance; single-cell recordings in monkeys have found neurons from V1 through V4 to inferotemporal cortex whose responses track perceived rather than retinal size.

Constancies are the strongest everyday evidence that you perceive inferred causes - surfaces, objects, people - and not the sensory data themselves.


31.2 Hierarchy and abstraction in sensory systems

Sensory cortex is not one processing stage but a chain of them, and the chain has a consistent logic: each stage sees a wider slice of the world than the one before, and cares about something more abstract.

This section describes that gradient, the trade-off it enforces, and the strong evidence that information does not flow only forwards along it.


31.2.1 Receptive fields and their enlargement along hierarchies

A receptive field is the patch of the sensory world - a region of the retina, a stretch of skin, a band of sound frequencies - within which a stimulus can change a given neuron's firing rate.

David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, working from the late 1950s onward and awarded the Nobel Prize in 1981, mapped these fields in cat and monkey primary visual cortex (V1) and found small fields tuned to the orientation of edges.

Moving forward through V2, V4, and into inferotemporal cortex, receptive fields grow steadily larger, until in inferotemporal cortex a single neuron may respond to a preferred object almost anywhere in the visual field.

Human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) - a method that measures blood-oxygen changes as an indirect index of neural activity - reproduces this gradient using population receptive field mapping, in which the aggregate field of each imaging voxel is estimated; ascending V1, V2, V3, and hV4, these fields enlarge systematically.

The enlargement is not merely bookkeeping: a bigger receptive field is what allows a neuron to be about an object rather than about a patch of light.


31.2.2 Tuning, invariance, and selectivity as a trade-off

Tuning means a neuron responds most strongly to one value of some stimulus property - a particular edge orientation, a particular sound frequency - and less strongly as the stimulus departs from it.

Invariance means the response survives changes that ought not to alter the object's identity: position, size, viewpoint, illumination, or in hearing, the speaker's voice.

These two goals pull against each other, and that tension is the central design problem of any sensory hierarchy.

A neuron that fires for a face at any position and size has bought invariance at the cost of telling you where the face is; a V1 neuron that reports precisely where an edge lies cannot tell you whose face it belongs to.

The standard resolution, articulated by James DiCarlo and colleagues (notably DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust, 2012), is that the hierarchy trades these gradually, so that the population as a whole retains both kinds of information while individual neurons at each level specialise.


31.2.3 Feedforward sweep, recurrence, and feedback

The first wave of activity travels forward through the visual hierarchy remarkably fast, reaching inferotemporal cortex within roughly one hundred milliseconds, and this feedforward sweep is sufficient for what DiCarlo calls core object recognition - identifying an unoccluded, uncluttered object at a glance.

But anatomy shows far more connections running backwards from higher to lower areas than forwards, so the feedforward story cannot be the whole story.

Victor Lamme and Pieter Roelfsema (2000) argued that feedforward and recurrent processing offer distinct modes of vision, with recurrence - activity looping back down and around - required for figure-ground segregation, that is, deciding which parts of an image belong to an object and which to its background.

The clearest modern evidence comes from Kohitij Kar and DiCarlo, who showed that images requiring extra processing time in the monkey ventral stream are exactly the hard, occluded, cluttered ones, and that briefly silencing ventrolateral prefrontal cortex selectively damages performance on those images while leaving easy images intact.

Visual backward masking - flashing a second image immediately after the first - interrupts the recurrent stage while sparing the feedforward sweep, and behaves as this account predicts: masking hurts recognition of occluded objects far more than unoccluded ones.

Whether recurrence is additionally necessary for conscious perception, as Lamme has argued, is a separate and genuinely disputed claim, treated in 31.4.4.


31.2.4 Timescales of integration along the hierarchy

Areas differ not only in how much space they pool over but in how much time.

Uri Hasson and colleagues (2008 onward) introduced the notion of temporal receptive windows, measured by scrambling a film or a story at different grain sizes and asking which brain areas still respond reliably.

Early sensory areas track events on a scale of tens to a few hundred milliseconds and respond identically whether the film is scrambled at the shot level or not; higher areas in the temporal and parietal lobes only respond reliably when the material is coherent over tens of seconds or minutes.

The gradient is hierarchical in the same order as the spatial one, and recent human fMRI work estimating spatiotemporal population receptive fields finds spatial and temporal integration windows enlarging together along the ventral stream.

The functional point is simple: recognising a phoneme needs a window of milliseconds, recognising a plot needs a window of minutes, and a single fixed timescale could not do both.


31.3 Adaptation, context, and expectation

A sensory neuron's response to a stimulus is never determined by that stimulus alone.

It depends on what came before it in time (adaptation), what surrounds it in space (context), and what the observer was anticipating (expectation).

These three are distinct mechanisms with distinct signatures, and much of the interesting recent work has been about telling them apart.


31.3.1 Adaptation as efficient recoding

Adaptation is the reduction and reshaping of a neuron's response when a stimulus is sustained or repeated.

Horace Barlow's efficient coding hypothesis (1961) supplies the standard rationale: neurons have a limited range of firing rates and are metabolically expensive, so the system should spend that range on the information that is actually varying, and should strip out redundancy - the predictable, repeated structure that carries no news.

Adaptation implements this by recentring the response curve on the recent average, so that after a few seconds in a dim room your visual system is once again devoting its full dynamic range to the small differences that matter there.

Mechanistically, much of this is captured by divisive normalization, a model in which a neuron's raw drive is divided by the pooled activity of its neighbours; Matteo Carandini and David Heeger (2012) argued that normalization is a canonical neural computation, appearing in vision, hearing, olfaction, and beyond.

Adaptation also produces aftereffects, such as the waterfall illusion in which a stationary rock face appears to drift upward after you have stared at falling water, and these aftereffects are useful because they reveal which stimulus dimensions the system has dedicated channels for.


31.3.2 Contextual modulation and surround effects

Most cortical neurons have, beyond the classical receptive field that can drive them, a much larger surround that cannot drive them on its own but powerfully modulates the response to what is inside.

Typically the surround suppresses: a V1 neuron responding vigorously to a bar of its preferred orientation will fall largely silent if that bar is embedded in a field of identical bars.

This makes sense under efficient coding, since a stimulus that matches its surroundings is predictable and hence carries little information, and it makes the neuron a detector of local difference rather than of local content.

The perceptual consequences are visible in simultaneous contrast, where a grey patch on a dark background looks lighter than the identical patch on a light background, and in the tilt illusion, where a vertical grating surrounded by a tilted one appears tilted the other way.

Surround effects are also the substrate of pop-out: an odd item in a uniform array is salient precisely because everything else has been suppressed by its neighbours and the odd item has not.


31.3.3 Expectation suppression and prediction error signatures
