Expectation suppression is the finding that a stimulus you expected produces a smaller neural response than the same stimulus when unexpected.

The landmark demonstration is Christopher Summerfield and colleagues (2008), who repeated or alternated faces in blocks where repetition was either the 80 percent likely outcome or the 20 percent likely one; the drop in fusiform face area response to a repeated face was larger when repetition was expected, showing that part of what had been called repetition suppression is actually about probability, not fatigue.

Predictive coding theories, developed by Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard (1999) and extended by Karl Friston, explain this by proposing that feedback connections carry predictions downward and feedforward connections carry only prediction error - the part of the signal that was not predicted - so a fully predicted stimulus generates little upward traffic.

Timing evidence supports a separation of mechanisms: in magnetoencephalography (MEG) - a method that records the magnetic fields produced by neural currents - repetition effects on auditory responses appear around 40 to 60 milliseconds while expectation effects appear later, around 100 to 200 milliseconds.

Two cautions are in order.

First, the amount of expectation suppression measured with fMRI has proved variable across laboratories, and some carefully controlled replications find it small or absent, so the effect is real but less robust than early reports implied.

Second, a reduced overall response is not by itself proof of predictive coding, since decoding analyses show that expected stimuli can be represented more sharply even while the summed response falls, and other architectures predict that too.


31.3.4 Attention and expectation distinguished

Attention and expectation are easy to confuse because both are top-down and both change sensory responses, but they are different variables and, importantly, they push in opposite directions.

Expectation is about probability - how likely a stimulus is - and typically reduces the response to the expected item.

Attention is about relevance - how much a stimulus matters for the current task - and typically increases the response to the attended item.

The cleanest demonstration that they are separable comes from work by Peter Kok, Floris de Lange and colleagues (2012), who crossed the two factors and found that attention reverses the sign of the expectation effect in early visual cortex; relatedly, Larsson and Smith (2012) reported that when attention was drawn away from the stimuli, expectation effects vanished while repetition suppression survived.

The practical lesson for reading this literature is that any study which manipulates predictability without controlling where attention goes has confounded the two, and a good deal of older work did exactly that.


31.4 From percept to category

Perception does not end in a continuous picture; it ends in a commitment - this is a b and not a p, this is my mother, the dots are moving left.

This final section follows the signal from graded sensory evidence to discrete category, to a decision that can drive action, to the changes practice makes, and finally to the awkward question of what any of it has to do with conscious experience.


31.4.1 Categorical perception

Categorical perception is the phenomenon in which a stimulus that varies smoothly along a physical dimension is heard or seen as belonging to one discrete category or another, with a sharp switch in between.

Its classic demonstration is Alvin Liberman, Katherine Harris, Howard Hoffman and Belver Griffith (1957), who synthesised a continuum of speech sounds from ba to da to ga and found two signatures: identification flipped abruptly at a boundary, and the ability to discriminate two sounds peaked at that same boundary while being poor for equally spaced pairs within a category.

The effect is strongest for stop consonants such as b, d, and g, and much weaker for vowels, which are identified more gradually and discriminated well within category.

The interpretation is genuinely disputed.

Howard Nusbaum and colleagues, and later critics such as Bob McMurray - whose 2022 review is pointedly titled to the effect that categorical perception as classically conceived should be retired - have shown with eye-tracking and reaction-time measures that listeners retain fine-grained within-category information they cannot report, so the discreteness may live in the response and decision stages rather than in perception itself.

Analogous boundary effects have been reported for colour and for facial expressions, and there the influence of learned linguistic categories on where the boundary falls is a live and long-running argument.


31.4.2 Perceptual decision as the interface with action

A perceptual decision is the act of committing to one interpretation so that behaviour can proceed, and it is the best-understood link between neural activity and choice.

The workhorse task is random dot motion, in which a fraction of dots move coherently in one direction while the rest move randomly, and the observer reports the direction; difficulty is set precisely by the coherence level.

The dominant model is the drift-diffusion model, developed for human reaction times by Roger Ratcliff (1978), in which noisy evidence is accumulated over time until it crosses one of two bounds, whereupon the corresponding choice is made; the model explains accuracy and the full shape of reaction time distributions with very few parameters, and it makes explicit the trade-off between speed and accuracy as a change in bound height.

Michael Shadlen and William Newsome, from the late 1990s, recorded from the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) of monkey parietal cortex and found neurons whose firing ramped upward at a rate proportional to motion strength and reached a stereotyped level just before the saccade that reported the choice - a direct neural analogue of the accumulating decision variable.

That interpretation has been sharpened rather than overturned by later work: Steinemann, Stine, Shadlen and colleagues (eLife, 2024) used high-density probes to observe the drift-diffusion signal in LIP populations on single trials, while other laboratories have shown that inactivating LIP can leave the behaviour largely intact, implying the accumulation is distributed across several areas rather than located solely there.


31.4.3 Perceptual learning and its locus

Perceptual learning is lasting improvement in a sensory discrimination through practice, and its most striking property is specificity: training on a fine orientation judgment at one retinal location and one orientation often transfers poorly to a different location or a different orientation.

Specificity was long read as proof that training changes the earliest, most retinotopic cortical maps, since only there is the coding location-specific enough to explain it.

Barbara Dosher and Zhong-Lin Lu challenged this with the reweighting account, most fully in their integrated reweighting theory (2013), which holds that the sensory representations stay largely stable while the connections from those representations to the decision stage are reweighted - relevant channels strengthened, irrelevant ones weakened - which reproduces specificity without requiring early cortex to change.

Evidence exists for both loci, and the honest summary is that the field has converged on a mixed answer whose proportions depend on task difficulty and training regime: hard, fine discriminations with extended training show the most early-cortex involvement, while easier tasks look more like pure reweighting.

Practically, this matters for attempts to use perceptual training clinically, in amblyopia or after cortical damage, where the value of the intervention depends entirely on how far the learning generalises beyond the trained condition.


31.4.4 Perceptual awareness and its dissociation from performance

The most awkward fact in perception is that sensory processing and conscious awareness can come apart.

Blindsight is the standard demonstration: patients with damage to primary visual cortex report seeing nothing in the affected part of the field yet can guess the location or direction of stimuli there well above chance, as documented by Lawrence Weiskrantz and colleagues from 1974 onward in the patient known as DB, an effect attributed to visual pathways that bypass V1 by way of the superior colliculus and pulvinar.

The reverse dissociation also occurs, in that people report vivid awareness of scene detail they demonstrably cannot use, as in change blindness, where a large alteration to a scene goes unnoticed across a brief interruption.

A serious methodological problem is that asking for a report engages decision, memory, and motor systems, so brain activity correlated with a report may reflect reporting rather than experiencing; Naotsugu Tsuchiya, Melanie Wilke, Stefan Frässle and Victor Lamme (2015) advocated no-report paradigms, which infer perceptual state from eye movements or pupil responses instead, and these tend to shrink the late frontal signatures - such as the P3 event-related potential component - that report-based studies had attributed to consciousness.

The theoretical dispute is unresolved and sharply drawn: local recurrence theories such as Lamme's, and integrated information theory, place awareness in posterior sensory cortex, while global neuronal workspace theory, associated with Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux, places it in the widespread frontoparietal broadcast of information.

An adversarial collaboration directly pitting integrated information theory against global workspace theory, reported by the Cogitate consortium in Nature in 2025, found results that fit neither theory cleanly - posterior areas carried conscious content well, as integrated information theory predicts, but the predicted sustained posterior synchrony was not found, while global workspace theory's predicted ignition at stimulus offset was also absent - which is a fair summary of where the field stands.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Perception is inference, not transcription, because the sensory signal always underdetermines its cause, and the assumptions that close that gap are visible in constancies when they succeed and in illusions when they are violated.

Sensory systems solve the problem hierarchically, with receptive fields, invariance, and integration timescales all growing together along the chain, and with recurrent and feedback connections doing work that the fast feedforward sweep cannot.

Responses are relative rather than absolute, adjusted by adaptation over time and by surround context over space, which the efficient coding tradition explains as the stripping out of redundancy.

Expectation reduces responses to predicted stimuli, consistent with predictive coding, but it must be kept distinct from attention, which usually enhances them, and the size and robustness of expectation suppression remain under active debate.

At the output end, graded evidence becomes a discrete commitment through an accumulation-to-bound process well described by the drift-diffusion model and visible in parietal cortex, and practice reshapes that mapping mainly by reweighting connections to the decision stage.

Finally, none of this machinery is the same thing as conscious awareness, which can be dissociated from performance in both directions and whose neural basis remains genuinely unsettled.


CHAPTER 32. VISION (CORE)

Vision feels effortless, and that feeling is the illusion the rest of this chapter is written to dismantle.

The eye does not send a picture to the brain, and the brain does not view one.

What travels up the optic nerve is a compressed, heavily edited code, and what the cortex does with that code is a long sequence of transformations that turn light into surfaces, objects, places, and actions.

This chapter follows that sequence from the photoreceptors at the back of the eye to the high-level regions that recognise a face or a street, and then asks how well our best computer models of vision match the biological original.

Vision matters here for two reasons: it is the best-understood part of the brain, and it has become the field's proving ground for what a good model of cognition even looks like.


32.1 From retina to cortex

The retina is not a passive film.

It is a piece of brain tissue pushed out into the eye during development, with several layers of neurons that begin analysing the image before a single signal leaves the eyeball.

By the time the message reaches the cortex it has already been reduced from roughly a hundred million photoreceptors to about one million optic nerve fibres, which means the retina throws most of the raw data away and keeps only what is informative.

This section traces that first leg of the journey.


32.1.1 Photoreceptors, bipolar and ganglion cells, and centre-surround organisation

Light is caught by photoreceptors - specialised cells at the back of the retina that convert photons into an electrical signal.

There are two broad kinds: rods, which are extremely sensitive and carry vision in dim light but do not distinguish colours, and cones, which need brighter light and come in three types tuned to short, medium and long wavelengths, giving us colour vision.

The photoreceptors pass their signal to bipolar cells, which pass it to retinal ganglion cells, whose long axons form the optic nerve.

The crucial trick appears at the bipolar and ganglion stage: the receptive field - the patch of the visual world that changes a given neuron's firing - is organised as a centre and an opposing surround, so an on-centre cell fires hard when light falls on the middle of its patch and is silenced when light falls on the ring around it.

Stephen Kuffler described this centre-surround arrangement in the cat retina in 1953, and it explains a great deal: a cell built this way is nearly blind to uniform illumination and responds strongly to edges and local contrast, which is exactly the information worth transmitting.

This is the retina's compression strategy, and it is why brightening the whole room does not overwhelm your vision.


32.1.2 Magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular channels

The ganglion cells are not all alike, and their differences set up parallel channels that stay partly separate all the way into cortex.

The magnocellular (M) channel arises from large parasol ganglion cells, has big receptive fields, responds fast and transiently, is highly sensitive to low contrast, and carries little colour information - it is well suited to motion and to coarse, rapid analysis.

The parvocellular (P) channel arises from small midget ganglion cells, has small receptive fields, responds slowly and in a sustained way, and carries red-green colour opponency - it is well suited to fine spatial detail and to colour.

A third and more heterogeneous set, the koniocellular (K) channel, occupies thin layers between the main ones and carries, among other things, the blue-yellow signal from small bistratified ganglion cells; a 2021 review by Paul Martin and Samuel Solomon summarises how much less settled the K story remains than the M and P story.

It is tempting to treat M as the "where" system and P as the "what" system, and textbooks often do, but the mapping is loose: both channels feed both cortical streams, and the cleanest statement is that they differ in speed, contrast sensitivity, spatial resolution and colour, not in job title.


32.1.3 The lateral geniculate nucleus as more than a relay

The optic nerve's main cortical route passes through the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a six-layered structure in the thalamus, the deep hub through which most sensory traffic reaches cortex.

Layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular, layers 3 to 6 are parvocellular, and koniocellular sheets lie beneath each of these, so the parallel channels are kept anatomically distinct.

The LGN was long taught as a simple relay, a post office that forwards mail unchanged, but the anatomy contradicts that: only about five to ten percent of the synaptic input to the LGN comes from the retina, while the majority comes from feedback out of layer 6 of primary visual cortex, from the brainstem, and from local inhibitory neurons.

Farran Briggs and W. Martin Usrey have argued that this corticogeniculate feedback sharpens the spatial receptive fields of LGN cells and boosts transmission of behaviourally relevant signals, and studies of arousal show that LGN responsiveness shifts with the animal's state.

The honest summary is that the LGN is a gate whose opening is controlled by the cortex it feeds, though exactly what computation that gating performs is still actively debated rather than resolved.


32.1.4 Retinotopy and cortical magnification

The visual world is mapped onto the cortex in an orderly way called retinotopy: neighbouring points in the visual field are represented by neighbouring points on the cortical sheet.

The map is not to scale, however.

The fovea - the tiny central pit of the retina that gives us high-acuity vision, occupying a fraction of one percent of retinal area - claims a hugely disproportionate share of primary visual cortex, on the order of a quarter to a half of it depending on how the boundary is drawn.

This distortion is called cortical magnification, and it is measured as cortical millimetres devoted to a degree of visual angle; in humans it falls steeply with eccentricity, from roughly sixteen square millimetres per square degree near the centre of gaze to a fraction of a square millimetre far out in the periphery.

Robert Duncan and Geoffrey Boynton showed in 2003, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) - a scanning method that infers neural activity from local blood oxygenation - that individual differences in cortical magnification predict individual differences in visual acuity, which ties the anatomy directly to what people can see.


32.2 Early and intermediate visual cortex

Primary visual cortex, also called V1 or striate cortex, sits at the back of the occipital lobe and is where the cortical analysis of the image begins.

From there signals fan out into a set of extrastriate areas - V2, V3, V4, middle temporal area and others - each transforming the representation further.

The general trend across these stages is from small receptive fields coding local features to large receptive fields coding configurations.


32.2.1 Simple and complex cells and orientation selectivity

In 1959 and 1962 David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, recording from cat visual cortex, found that V1 neurons largely ignore spots of light and instead respond to oriented bars and edges, each cell preferring a particular angle.

They distinguished simple cells, whose receptive fields have separate excitatory and inhibitory subregions so that the exact position of the bar matters, from complex cells, which respond to the preferred orientation anywhere within their receptive field and so show a first, small step towards position invariance.

They proposed a hierarchical wiring scheme in which a row of aligned LGN centre-surround cells builds a simple cell, and a set of offset simple cells builds a complex cell - an elegant model that won them a share of the 1981 Nobel Prize and that still frames the field.

The elegance should not be mistaken for closure: the feedforward-only account has been challenged for decades, because measured thalamic input to a cortical cell is often less orientation-biased than the cell itself, and intracortical inhibition and recurrent excitation appear to sharpen tuning substantially.

Hubel and Wiesel also found that orientation preference is arranged in columns running through the cortical depth, and that the columns rotate smoothly across the surface, a functional architecture present in carnivores and primates but strikingly absent in mice, where orientation preference is scattered like salt and pepper.


32.2.2 V2, V3, V4 and the emergence of form and colour

Area V2, the next stage after V1, is divided anatomically into a repeating pattern of stripes revealed by staining for cytochrome oxidase, a metabolic enzyme: thin stripes, thick stripes and pale stripes.

Colour-selective cells cluster in the thin stripes, with organised maps of hue; orientation and form signals dominate the pale stripes; and binocular disparity, the small difference between the two eyes' images that supports depth perception, is prominent in the thick stripes.

V2 neurons also become sensitive to features that V1 largely ignores, including illusory contours - edges we perceive where no luminance edge exists, as in the Kanizsa triangle - reported by Rüdiger von der Heydt and Esther Peterhans in 1984, and naturalistic texture statistics, shown by Jeremy Freeman, Eero Simoncelli and colleagues in 2013.

Area V4 receives its colour input largely from V2 thin stripes and its orientation input largely from pale stripes, and it contains cells tuned to hue, to curvature, and to moderately complex shape fragments.

Semir Zeki's 1970s claim that V4 is simply "the colour area" has not survived: V4 lesions impair colour constancy and shape discrimination and attention alike, and the modern view is that V4 is an intermediate form-and-colour stage rather than a dedicated colour module.

Area V3 and its neighbours remain the least agreed-upon part of this map, and researchers still disagree about how many distinct areas exist there and where their borders fall.


32.2.3 Middle temporal area and motion processing

The middle temporal area (MT, also called V5 in humans) is a small extrastriate region dominated by direction-selective neurons, each firing best when a stimulus moves one particular way.

It receives heavy magnocellular input, including a direct route from V1 layer 4B that partly bypasses the slower stages, and it is one of the clearest cases of a cortical area with a legible job.

The evidence linking MT to the experience of motion is unusually strong.

William Newsome and Robert Wurtz showed in the 1980s that MT lesions raise motion detection thresholds sharply, and in 1990 and 1992 Daniel Salzman, Kenneth Britten and Newsome went further: electrically microstimulating a cluster of MT neurons that shared a direction preference biased the monkey's reported direction of motion towards that preference.

That is about as close as neuroscience gets to writing a percept into a brain, and it is why MT is a standard reference case for arguing that a specific population code causes a specific perceptual judgement.

MT is also involved in depth from disparity and in structure from motion, and Gregory DeAngelis and colleagues have shown that microstimulation there can bias depth judgements too, which complicates any simple label of MT as the motion area and nothing else.


32.2.4 Contour integration, figure-ground, and border ownership

An edge detector alone cannot see an object, because the visual system must decide which fragments of contour belong together and which side of a contour is the object.

Contour integration is the linking of separate oriented elements into a continuous perceived line, and psychophysical work by David Field, Anthony Hayes and Robert Hess in 1993 showed that human observers detect a chain of aligned Gabor patches embedded in random ones, obeying an "association field" that favours smooth, co-circular continuations.

Figure-ground assignment is the further step of deciding which region is the object and which is the background behind it, a problem the Gestalt psychologists posed in the early twentieth century and left unsolved mechanistically.

In 2000 Hong Zhou, Howard Friedman and Rüdiger von der Heydt found the neural signature: many V2 neurons, and some in V1 and V4, respond to an identical local edge at different rates depending on which side the figure lies on, even when the figure's defining information is far outside the classical receptive field.

This border ownership signal appears within about seventy milliseconds, too fast for a slow deliberative process, and the field is split between explanations that build it from long-range horizontal connections within an area and explanations that require feedback from higher areas.


32.3 The two visual streams

Beyond the early areas the cortical visual system divides into two broad courses of processing, one running down into the temporal lobe and one running up into the parietal lobe.

The division is anatomically real and functionally important, but what it is for has been argued over for forty years, and the argument is instructive about how neuroscience settles questions.


32.3.1 The ventral what stream to inferotemporal cortex

The ventral stream runs from V1 through V2 and V4 into inferotemporal cortex (IT), the large expanse of temporal lobe cortex devoted to visual object processing.

Along this route receptive fields grow larger, preferred stimuli grow more complex, and tolerance to changes in position, size and lighting increases, so that an IT neuron may respond to a particular object shape across a wide range of viewing conditions.

Charles Gross and colleagues reported hand-selective and face-selective neurons in monkey IT in the early 1970s, a finding so unexpected that it was initially met with scepticism.

Mortimer Mishkin and Leslie Ungerleider named this the "what" pathway in 1982, on the basis of monkey lesion work in which inferotemporal damage impaired object discrimination while sparing spatial tasks.


32.3.2 The dorsal where and how stream to posterior parietal cortex

The dorsal stream runs from V1 through areas including MT into posterior parietal cortex, the region above and behind the ear that integrates vision with body position and movement.

Mishkin and Ungerleider called this the "where" pathway, because parietal lesions in monkeys impaired landmark and spatial tasks while leaving object discrimination intact.

Dorsal neurons care about location, motion, depth, and the spatial relation between an object and the observer, and many parietal areas contain neurons tuned to the shape and orientation of a graspable object specifically in the context of reaching for it.

The stream's outputs go heavily to premotor and motor regions, which is a strong clue that its representations are built for use rather than for contemplation.


32.3.3 Perception against action as the streams' functional division

In 1992 Melvyn Goodale and David Milner proposed a reinterpretation: the difference between the streams is not what information they carry but what the information is for.

On their two visual systems hypothesis the ventral stream builds conscious, enduring, object-centred percepts that support recognition and memory, while the dorsal stream computes fast, moment-to-moment, viewer-centred metrics that guide the hand and eye, largely outside awareness.

The account elegantly explains why dorsal representations are transient and metrically accurate while ventral ones are relational and durable, and it predicted that visual illusions which fool judgement might not fool grasping.

That prediction has had a rough ride: some studies find that grip aperture resists size illusions, others find it does not once the task is properly matched for attention and feedback, and the literature has not converged.

The fair summary in 2026 is that the anatomical two-stream division is not in doubt, that the perception-versus-action gloss on it remains the most influential single framework, and that many researchers now favour a version with substantial cross-talk between streams rather than two sealed systems.


32.3.4 Evidence from optic ataxia and visual form agnosia

The case for the hypothesis rested on an apparent double dissociation between two neurological conditions.

Optic ataxia, following damage to posterior parietal cortex, leaves the patient able to recognise and describe an object while unable to reach for it accurately, misdirecting the hand and shaping the grip wrongly.

Visual form agnosia, most famously in the patient known as DF, who suffered carbon monoxide poisoning that damaged the lateral occipital region of her ventral stream, is the mirror image: DF could not report or copy the orientation of a slot, yet posted a card through it with a smooth, correctly rotated movement.

Milner, Goodale and colleagues documented her over decades, and the case became one of the most cited in cognitive neuroscience.

It has also been vigorously challenged: later imaging showed that DF's lesions were not confined to the ventral stream, that she has dorsal damage and atrophy which grew over the years, and critics including Thomas Schenk have argued that her preserved grasping can be explained by the availability of certain cues rather than by an intact action system.

This does not overturn the dissociation, since optic ataxia patients are numerous and consistent, but it does mean the textbook version resting on one patient overstates the evidence.


32.4 High-level vision

High-level vision is where the transformations pay off: a representation from which identity, category and meaning can be read out easily.

The central puzzle is invariance - the same object produces wildly different images depending on distance, angle and light, while different objects can produce similar images - and the ventral stream somehow makes identity easy to extract despite this.


32.4.1 Object recognition, invariance, and the untangling account

James DiCarlo and David Cox, in a 2007 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, framed the problem geometrically.

Think of the firing rates of a population of neurons as coordinates in a very high-dimensional space; then all the images of one object under all its transformations trace out a curved surface, or manifold, in that space.

At the retina the manifolds for different objects are hopelessly intertwined, like sheets of paper crumpled together, so no simple decision boundary can separate them.

The proposal is that each stage of the ventral stream applies a modest nonlinear transformation, and that the cumulative effect by IT is to flatten and separate the manifolds so that a linear read-out - the kind of simple weighted sum a downstream neuron could compute - can identify the object.

The evidence is that linear classifiers trained on a few hundred IT neurons match human performance on rapid object recognition, whereas classifiers trained on V1-like representations do not, and this framing has since become the standard way of comparing brains and artificial networks.


32.4.2 Category-selective regions: faces, bodies, places, words, tools

Human fMRI has found patches of ventral and lateral occipitotemporal cortex that respond far more to one category than to others.

The fusiform face area (FFA), described by Nancy Kanwisher, Josh McDermott and Marvin Chun in 1997, responds roughly twice as strongly to faces as to other objects; the extrastriate body area, reported by Paul Downing and colleagues in 2001, prefers bodies and body parts; the parahippocampal place area (PPA), from Russell Epstein and Kanwisher in 1998, prefers scenes and spatial layouts.

The visual word form area (VWFA) in the left occipitotemporal sulcus responds preferentially to letter strings in a script the reader knows, and Stanislas Dehaene and Laurent Cohen have argued it is a region recycled by literacy from a prior role in shape processing, since writing is far too recent for dedicated evolution.

Regions responding preferentially to tools and manipulable objects sit near the left lateral occipitotemporal and intraparietal cortex, and are usually interpreted as linking shape to learned action.

The functional evidence goes beyond correlation: damage to the fusiform face region can produce prosopagnosia, the inability to recognise familiar faces despite intact object vision, and direct electrical stimulation of the region in a patient studied by Josef Parvizi and colleagues in 2012 caused faces to appear distorted while other objects looked normal.


32.4.3 Domain specificity against distributed coding

Whether these patches are genuine modules is one of the field's long-running disputes, and it is worth stating both positions squarely.

The domain-specificity position, associated with Kanwisher, holds that a small number of categories with deep evolutionary or developmental significance - faces, bodies, places, and by recycling, words - have dedicated machinery, and points to the reliability of the regions across individuals, to the selective deficits after damage, and to the causal stimulation results.

The distributed position, associated with James Haxby's 2001 study in Science, holds that category information is carried by the pattern of activity across a wide swathe of ventral temporal cortex, and showed that a category could still be decoded accurately after removing the voxels that responded most strongly to it.

Both claims can be true at once, and most researchers now hold a hybrid view: there is a broadly distributed code, and there are also focal peaks within it that behave more like specialised machinery than the distributed story predicts.

The remaining disagreement is about what the peaks are doing - representing a category, or representing visual features such as curvature, foveal bias and real-world size that happen to correlate with category - and that question is not settled.


32.4.4 Scene perception, gist, and spatial layout

A scene is not just a collection of objects; it is a space you could move through, and the brain treats it accordingly.

Mary Potter showed in the 1970s that people can determine whether a picture matches a verbal description at presentation rates of about eight images per second, and Simon Thorpe, Denis Fize and Catherine Marlot showed in 1996 that a brain response distinguishing animal from non-animal scenes appears about 150 milliseconds after image onset - fast enough to constrain how much recurrent processing the initial categorisation can involve.

This rapid summary impression is called gist, and Aude Oliva and Antonio Torralba's 2001 spatial envelope model showed that a scene's category and navigability can be estimated surprisingly well from coarse global statistics such as openness, roughness and expansion, without segmenting any objects at all.

Three cortical regions respond selectively to scenes: the PPA on the ventral surface, the occipital place area on the lateral surface, and the medial place area, also called retrosplenial complex, on the medial parietal surface.

Work by Epstein and colleagues suggests a rough division of labour in which the occipital place area is tied to the immediately visible local layout and possible paths, the PPA to recognising the specific place, and the medial place area to relating the current view to a broader remembered spatial framework, though the boundaries between these roles are still being worked out.


32.5 Vision as a benchmark for models

Vision is where computational modelling of the brain has been most successful and where its limits are clearest.

The story of the last decade is that networks built for engineering purposes turned out to predict neural responses better than models designed by neuroscientists, followed by a sober accounting of where the resemblance breaks down.


32.5.1 Deep convolutional networks as models of ventral stream

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is an artificial network that applies the same set of learned filters across every position of an image and stacks many such layers, an architecture directly inspired by Hubel and Wiesel's simple and complex cells by way of Kunihiko Fukushima's 1980 Neocognitron and Yann LeCun's later work.

After such networks became highly accurate at object classification in 2012, two groups - Daniel Yamins, DiCarlo and colleagues in 2014, and Seyed-Mahdi Khaligh-Razavi with Nikolaus Kriegeskorte in the same period - reported that the networks' internal layers predicted responses in monkey IT and human ventral cortex better than any previous model.

The striking detail was hierarchical correspondence: early network layers best matched V1 and V2, middle layers best matched V4, and late layers best matched IT, without anyone having built that correspondence in.

The result is genuine and repeatable, but its interpretation is contested, since the networks were optimised for categorisation performance rather than fitted to brains, which some read as evidence that the task shapes the representation and others read as a caution that many different architectures can fit neural data about equally well.


32.5.2 Brain-Score and quantitative model-brain comparison

Brain-Score, launched by Martin Schrimpf, Jonas Kubilius, DiCarlo and colleagues in 2018, is an open platform that turns "is this model brain-like?" into a number.

It scores a submitted network against a battery of benchmarks derived from neural recordings in V1, V2, V4 and IT and from human behavioural data on object recognition, and reports both component scores and an aggregate.

The value of the exercise is disciplinary as much as scientific: it makes model comparison public, replicable and hard to cherry-pick, and it exposed that classification accuracy on standard image datasets and brain similarity come apart above a certain performance level.

The limitations are widely acknowledged, including by its authors: benchmark scores depend on the recording datasets and the fitting procedure used to map model units onto neurons, and a high aggregate score does not establish that a model implements the same computations, only that it makes similar predictions on the tested images.


32.5.3 Adversarial examples and the divergence from human vision

An adversarial example is an image altered by a tiny, carefully chosen perturbation that leaves it visually unchanged to a person but causes a network to classify it confidently and wrongly, demonstrated by Christian Szegedy and colleagues in 2013 and by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014.

Human vision has no comparable failure mode at that perturbation scale, which is a direct and awkward mismatch for the claim that these networks are good models of the ventral stream.

Robert Geirhos and colleagues showed in 2019 that standard networks trained on ImageNet classify cue-conflict images - a cat shape rendered in elephant skin texture - by texture, while humans classify them by shape, and that training on stylised images shifts networks towards shape and improves their robustness.

The picture has grown more nuanced rather than simpler: adversarially trained networks are both more shape-biased and, in some benchmarks, more predictive of neural data, while newer work from 2025 argues that the original texture-bias framing overstated the case and that modern training recipes reduce the gap considerably.

There is also a partial bridge, in that Gamaleldin Elsayed, Geirhos and colleagues found that adversarial images crafted against robust networks can bias human choices under very brief presentation, suggesting the divergence is one of degree at some scales rather than absolute.


32.5.4 Recurrent processing for challenging images

Feedforward networks are, by construction, one-pass systems, whereas the visual cortex is dense with feedback and lateral connections that a strictly feedforward account leaves unexplained.

Kohitij Kar, Kubilius, Kailyn Schmidt, Elias Issa and DiCarlo, in Nature Neuroscience in 2019, identified "challenge" images that humans and monkeys classify accurately but feedforward networks fail, and found that in monkey IT the neural code sufficient to support the correct answer emerged roughly thirty milliseconds later for those images than for matched control images.

That extra time is the signature of recurrent computation: the answer is not available on the first pass and has to be resolved by further processing.

Kar and DiCarlo showed in 2021 that silencing ventrolateral prefrontal cortex selectively impaired recognition of exactly these late-solved images, implicating a top-down loop rather than only local recurrence within the temporal lobe.

Correspondingly, shallow recurrent networks such as CORnet-S, from Kubilius and colleagues, match neural data as well as much deeper feedforward networks while staying closer to the actual number of cortical stages, which is a point in favour of recurrence being a real part of the computation and not a modelling convenience.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Vision is a cascade of transformations, beginning in the retina, where centre-surround receptive fields discard uniform illumination and keep contrast, and continuing through parallel magnocellular, parvocellular and koniocellular channels into a thalamic stage that is gated by cortical feedback rather than being a passive relay.

Cortical processing starts with oriented simple and complex cells in a retinotopic map that hugely magnifies the fovea, and builds through V2, V4 and MT towards representations of colour, form, motion, contour grouping and border ownership.

The system then divides into a ventral course to inferotemporal cortex and a dorsal course to posterior parietal cortex, a division that is anatomically secure while its perception-versus-action interpretation, resting heavily on patient DF and on optic ataxia, remains genuinely contested.

High-level vision solves the invariance problem by progressively untangling object manifolds until identity can be read out linearly, and it does so in a cortex that shows both broadly distributed category information and reliable focal peaks for faces, bodies, places and words.

Finally, deep convolutional networks predict ventral stream responses well enough to serve as working models and to be scored quantitatively against brains, while adversarial examples, texture bias, and the timing evidence for recurrent processing on challenging images mark the places where the analogy demonstrably fails.


CHAPTER 33. AUDITION AND AUDITORY COGNITION (CORE)

Hearing begins with nothing more than pressure fluctuations in air - a one-dimensional wiggle arriving at each eardrum.

From that thin signal the brain reconstructs a world of separate, meaningful, located things: a voice, a footstep behind you, a violin inside an orchestra.

This chapter follows that reconstruction from the cochlea, the snail-shaped organ of the inner ear, up through the brainstem and the cortex, and then into two of the hardest problems the auditory brain solves - separating a scene into objects, and hearing music.

It matters because audition is the sense on which speech, music, and much of social life depend, and because the auditory system is the clearest case in all of neuroscience of a brain turning time into meaning.

Along the way we will be honest about what is settled and what is still argued over, because a good deal of auditory cognition is still argued over.


33.1 The auditory periphery and brainstem

Before any of this reaches the brain proper, the ear has already done a remarkable amount of the work.

The outer ear collects and filters sound, the middle ear's three tiny bones match the impedance of air to the fluid of the inner ear, and the cochlea performs a frequency analysis that the rest of the system depends on.

The brainstem then extracts timing information with a precision found nowhere else in the nervous system.

This section covers those four steps: mechanical frequency analysis, transduction into electrical signals, brainstem timing, and the brain's feedback control over its own ear.


33.1.1 Cochlear mechanics and frequency decomposition

The cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube divided lengthwise by the basilar membrane, a strip of tissue that is narrow and stiff at the base, near the middle ear, and wide and floppy at the apex, at the coil's centre.

Because of that stiffness gradient, a sound entering the cochlea sets up a travelling wave that peaks at a different place depending on frequency - high frequencies near the base, low frequencies near the apex - a finding for which Georg von Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961.

This orderly map of frequency onto place is called tonotopy (a spatial arrangement in which neighbouring positions respond to neighbouring frequencies), and it is preserved, in some form, all the way up to the cortex.

Von Békésy's passive travelling wave, measured in cadavers, is far too blunt to explain living human hearing, and the missing ingredient is the cochlear amplifier: the outer hair cells actively change length in time with the wave, sharpening and boosting the peak by roughly forty decibels, a hundredfold gain in sensitivity.

The motor behind that length change is prestin, a voltage-driven membrane protein discovered by Peter Dallos and colleagues around 2000, and mice lacking it lose both sensitivity and sharp frequency tuning.

A useful consequence for the clinic is that this active process leaks sound back out of the ear, producing otoacoustic emissions (faint sounds emitted by a healthy cochlea), which is how newborn hearing screening works without asking the baby anything.


33.1.2 Hair cells and transduction

Sitting on the basilar membrane is the organ of Corti, which carries two kinds of sensory cell: one row of inner hair cells and three rows of outer hair cells.

Each hair cell is topped by a bundle of stereocilia (stiff, graded-height rods of actin), and neighbouring rows are joined by tip links, fine filaments now known to be made of two proteins, protocadherin 15 and cadherin 23.

When the bundle is deflected, the tip links pull open mechanotransduction channels at their lower ends, letting positive ions rush in - a purely mechanical gate, which is why hearing is fast enough to follow sound rather than merely report it.

The identity of that channel was contested for decades; the current consensus, from work by Jeffrey Holt, David Corey and colleagues from 2013 onward, is that transmembrane channel-like protein 1 (TMC1) and its relative TMC2 form the pore, with partner proteins such as calcium and integrin binding protein 2 (CIB2) required for it to work.

The division of labour is stark: outer hair cells are mostly amplifiers, while the inner hair cells are the true sensors, carrying roughly ninety-five per cent of the information sent to the brain through specialised ribbon synapses built to release neurotransmitter continuously and with sub-millisecond timing.


33.1.3 Brainstem timing nuclei and binaural cues

Every auditory nerve fibre enters the cochlear nucleus in the brainstem, where the signal immediately splits into parallel streams handled by cell types with strikingly different jobs.

Two of them, the spherical and globular bushy cells, are specialised for preserving timing, and their axons form some of the largest synapses in the brain, including the calyx of Held, a hand-shaped terminal that wraps a whole target cell and can relay spikes reliably at rates approaching a thousand per second.

That machinery exists to serve sound localisation, which in the horizontal plane rests on two cues: the interaural time difference (ITD), the few hundred microseconds by which sound reaches the nearer ear first, and the interaural level difference (ILD), the loudness shadow cast by the head at high frequencies.

The medial superior olive computes ITDs by acting as a coincidence detector receiving excitation from both ears, while the lateral superior olive computes ILDs by subtracting contralateral inhibition, routed through the calyx of Held, from ipsilateral excitation.

The classical account is the Jeffress model of 1948, which posited delay lines and a labelled place map of azimuth, and it is well supported in the barn owl; whether mammals use it is genuinely disputed, with Benedikt Grothe, David McAlpine and colleagues arguing since the early 2000s that mammals instead read out a coarse two-channel comparison of overall firing rate between the hemispheres.


33.1.4 Efferent control and the olivocochlear system

Hearing is not a one-way street: the brainstem sends axons back down to the cochlea, a fact that surprises most newcomers.

The medial olivocochlear bundle originates in the superior olivary complex and synapses directly onto outer hair cells using acetylcholine, turning down the cochlear amplifier by a modest but measurable amount.

The leading functional account is antimasking: by reducing the response to a steady background, the reflex restores dynamic range for a signal embedded in it, which should help with hearing speech in noise, and this is the standard interpretation of the correlation between reflex strength and speech-in-noise performance.

A second proposed role is protection, and studies in guinea pigs, rabbits and mice have linked a weak reflex to greater risk of noise-induced hearing loss and cochlear nerve damage; the human evidence is weaker and the effect sizes in behavioural studies are small and inconsistent, so this should be treated as probable rather than proven.

The reflex is measured non-invasively by playing noise in one ear and watching otoacoustic emissions shrink in the other, though careful work has shown that part of that shrinkage comes from the middle ear muscle reflex, a separate protective mechanism in which the stapedius muscle stiffens the ossicular chain, and disentangling the two is a live methodological problem.


33.2 Auditory cortex

Sound reaches cortex by way of the inferior colliculus in the midbrain and the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, arriving in the temporal lobe already heavily processed.

Cortex is where frequency analysis becomes recognition - of a word, a melody, a voice.

This section covers how auditory cortex is laid out, how individual neurons in it are described, how its outputs divide into functional streams, and how the two human hemispheres differ.


33.2.1 Tonotopy and core, belt, and parabelt organisation

The dominant anatomical framework, developed in monkeys chiefly by Jon Kaas and Troy Hackett in the late 1990s and 2000s, divides auditory cortex into three concentric levels: a core of primary-like fields receiving dense thalamic input, a surrounding belt, and a lateral parabelt.

The connectivity is hierarchical - core projects to belt, belt to parabelt, and core does not project directly to parabelt - which gives audition an anatomical ladder comparable to the visual one.

In humans the core sits on the posteromedial part of Heschl's gyrus, the transverse ridge buried in the Sylvian fissure, with belt anterolateral to it and parabelt on the posterolateral superior temporal gyrus, as mapped by Hackett and colleagues in 2001 and confirmed by later imaging and intracranial recording.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, which measures blood-oxygen changes as a proxy for neural activity) reliably finds at least two mirror-symmetric tonotopic gradients running along Heschl's gyrus, meeting at a low-frequency border.

Two caveats are worth stating plainly: the exact number and orientation of human tonotopic fields is still disputed between laboratories, and tonotopy is a map of frequency, not of sound - a tonotopic peak tells you very little about what a listener is actually hearing.


33.2.2 Spectrotemporal receptive fields

To describe what an auditory neuron responds to, researchers usually estimate its spectrotemporal receptive field (STRF): a two-dimensional filter over frequency and recent time, showing which parts of a sound's spectrogram excite the cell and which suppress it.

The STRF is normally fitted by reverse correlation, working backwards from many responses to a rich stimulus, and it is then used to predict the response to a new sound - a genuine test, not a redescription.

The plain linear STRF is usually improved by adding a static output nonlinearity, giving the linear-nonlinear model, and even then it typically explains only a modest fraction of the response to natural sounds, because real cortical neurons adapt to context, to stimulus statistics, and to the animal's behavioural task.

This last point is important and comes from work by Shihab Shamma, Jonathan Fritz, Stephen David and colleagues: an animal's receptive fields change within minutes when the task changes, so an STRF is a snapshot of a filter, not a fixed property of a cell.

A useful reframing at the cortical level is spectrotemporal modulation, in which neurons are characterised by the rates of amplitude change over time and the scale of pattern over frequency they prefer, and speech and music occupy quite specific regions of that modulation space.


33.2.3 Dual streams for auditory what and where

In a 2000 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Josef Rauschecker and Biao Tian proposed that auditory cortex, like visual cortex, splits into two streams: an anterior ventral pathway for identifying what a sound is, and a posterior dorsal pathway for where it is.

Their evidence was that neurons in the anterior lateral belt of the monkey were selective for species-specific calls while neurons in the caudal belt were more sharply tuned for spatial location.

In humans the same broad split appears, with anterior superior temporal regions engaged by voice and word identity and posterior regions by location and by sensorimotor tasks.

The model has since been substantially revised: Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel's dual-stream model of speech, elaborated from 2000 to 2007, treats the human dorsal stream less as a "where" pathway than as an auditory-to-motor mapping route running through the sylvian parietal-temporal area to frontal speech regions, and Rauschecker himself has argued for an expanded sensorimotor role for the dorsal path.

It is fair to say the anterior-posterior functional gradient is well established while the clean "what versus where" label is not, and the streams are better thought of as heavily interconnected biases than as separate channels.


33.2.4 Human auditory cortex asymmetries

Human auditory cortex is anatomically asymmetric - the left planum temporale is typically larger, and left auditory cortex has thicker myelin and wider spacing between cortical columns, differences documented by Anne Galaburda and later by Peter Schleicher, Katrin Amunts and colleagues.

The best-known functional proposal is Robert Zatorre and Pascal Belin's, from a 2001 paper in Cerebral Cortex: the left hemisphere is tuned for fine temporal resolution and the right for fine spectral resolution, a trade-off forced by the fact that no system can resolve time and frequency arbitrarily well at once.

David Poeppel's asymmetric sampling in time hypothesis, published in 2003, makes a related claim in different terms, proposing that the left samples the signal in short windows of roughly twenty-five to fifty milliseconds and the right in long windows of roughly one hundred fifty to three hundred milliseconds.

There is real supporting evidence, including Anne-Lise Giraud's demonstration of matching intrinsic oscillatory rhythms in the two hemispheres and Sam Norman-Haignere's finding that anterior right auditory regions integrate over longer windows.

The asymmetry is nonetheless a statistical tendency rather than a rule, is often small, and does not by itself explain left-hemisphere language dominance, so it is better treated as one contributing factor than as the cause of lateralised speech.


33.3 Auditory scene analysis

Sound from every source in a room sums into a single pressure wave at each eardrum, and that sum is all the brain ever receives.

Recovering the sources from the sum is mathematically underdetermined - there are infinitely many decompositions - so perception must impose assumptions about how sound sources behave.

This section covers the rules the auditory system uses, the role of attention, what an auditory object even is, and how prediction shows up in brain responses.


33.3.1 Grouping, streaming, and the cocktail party problem

Colin Cherry coined the phrase "cocktail party problem" in 1953, asking how a listener follows one voice among many, and he introduced the dichotic shadowing task in which a listener repeats back speech in one ear while ignoring the other.

Albert Bregman's 1990 book Auditory Scene Analysis gave the field its framework, distinguishing simultaneous grouping - deciding which frequency components present at the same moment came from one source - from sequential grouping, deciding which sounds across time belong to the same ongoing stream.

Simultaneous grouping leans on cues such as common onset, harmonicity (components being whole-number multiples of a common fundamental frequency), and common fate, meaning shared changes in amplitude or frequency.

Sequential grouping is studied with the ABA- paradigm, alternating tones of two frequencies, which is heard as one galloping stream when the frequencies are close and the tempo slow, and as two parallel streams when they are far apart and fast - and crucially, it can flip perceptually while the stimulus stays fixed, a phenomenon called bistability.

Bregman also distinguished primitive grouping, which is automatic and probably innate, from schema-based grouping, which uses learned knowledge such as your familiarity with a particular voice or language, and both are needed to explain real performance.


33.3.2 Attentional selection of a speaker and its neural decoding

The most direct evidence that attention shapes the auditory representation itself came from Nima Mesgarani and Edward Chang's 2012 study in Nature, using electrocorticography (ECoG, electrodes placed directly on the cortical surface in patients being monitored for epilepsy surgery).

Listeners heard two talkers at once and attended to one; from the recorded activity in superior temporal cortex the researchers reconstructed a spectrogram, and it looked like the attended talker alone, not the acoustic mixture, with the attended talker identified at around ninety-three per cent accuracy.

The interpretation is that non-primary auditory cortex represents the perceived scene rather than the raw input, with the ignored talker substantially suppressed - though not to zero, and the suppression grows along the cortical hierarchy rather than appearing all at once.

The same logic works non-invasively, and since work by Edmund Lalor, James O'Sullivan and colleagues around 2014 it has become possible to decode which of two talkers a person is attending to from single-trial scalp electroencephalography (EEG, electrical recording from the scalp).

This has a concrete application: auditory attention decoding is being pursued as a control signal for neuro-steered hearing aids that would amplify whichever talker the wearer is attending to, and while laboratory decoding is now reliable, real-world latency and robustness remain unsolved.


33.3.3 Auditory objects and their formation

Timothy Griffiths and Jason Warren asked bluntly, in a 2004 paper in Trends in Neurosciences, "What is an auditory object?", and proposed three criteria: it corresponds to something in the world, it can be separated from the rest of the scene, and it can be recognised again on a later encounter.

That last criterion does real work, because it rules out treating any arbitrary grouping of energy as an object and ties objecthood to generalisation across instances.

The auditory case differs from the visual in a fundamental way: visual objects are separated primarily in space, whereas auditory objects overlap completely in the received signal and must be separated by their temporal structure and their spectral regularities.

Griffiths and Warren argued that object analysis proceeds hierarchically, with early separation in core auditory cortex and abstraction into recognisable, position-invariant representations further along the planum temporale and superior temporal sulcus.

The concept remains useful but contested at the edges - there is no agreement on whether a chord is one object or several, or on whether attention selects objects or features - and honest treatments in the field, including a 2013 review by Bizley and Cohen, present it as a working framework rather than a settled theory.


33.3.4 Prediction and the mismatch negativity

If you play a repeating tone and occasionally slip in a different one, the deviant elicits a negative-going brain response peaking about one hundred to two hundred milliseconds after onset, discovered by Risto Näätänen and colleagues in 1978 and named the mismatch negativity (MMN).

The MMN appears without attention - in sleeping infants, in coma patients, in listeners absorbed in a film - which made it a landmark demonstration that the auditory system builds a model of regularity automatically.

Two explanations compete.

The adaptation account holds that repeated tones simply fatigue the neurons tuned to them, so the deviant looks larger by contrast; the predictive coding account, argued by Karl Friston, Marta Garrido and others from around 2008, holds that the MMN is a genuine prediction error signal generated by a hierarchy of top-down predictions.

The strongest evidence for prediction comes from omission paradigms, where the expected sound is simply left out: there is no stimulus to adapt to, yet a response still occurs, and both human recordings and recent animal work using neurons that encode negative prediction errors have confirmed such responses.

Clinically, the MMN is reduced in schizophrenia with unusual consistency across laboratories, and is one of the more credible candidate biomarkers in psychiatry, though what exactly the reduction indexes is still argued.


33.4 Music and rhythm

Music is a strong test case for auditory cognition because it is universal across human cultures, structurally elaborate, and biologically puzzling - it has no obvious survival payoff.

It also gives clean experimental handles: pitch, harmony, and beat can each be manipulated precisely and studied separately.

This section covers tonal expectation, beat perception and its links to movement, the contested claims about musical training, and what disorders of music perception reveal.


33.4.1 Pitch, harmony, and tonal expectation

Pitch is the perceptual attribute that lets sounds be ordered from low to high, and it is not simply frequency: a complex tone whose fundamental frequency has been removed still sounds at that missing fundamental, which tells us pitch is inferred from harmonic pattern rather than read off a place map.

Neuroimaging and intracranial studies have located pitch-sensitive responses in anterolateral Heschl's gyrus and adjacent regions, with Sam Norman-Haignere and colleagues showing in 2013 that this region responds specifically to resolved harmonics rather than to periodicity in general, and a 2025 magnetoencephalography study in the Journal of Neuroscience finding pitch encoded earlier for harmonic complex tones, around eighty-five milliseconds, than for pure tones.

On top of pitch, Western listeners build tonality, a sense that certain notes belong and others do not, quantified by Carol Krumhansl and Edward Kessler's probe-tone method in the early 1980s, which produced stable hierarchies of stability for each key.

Those profiles are learned by exposure rather than given, which is why they differ across musical cultures, and much of the tonal expectation literature is honestly limited to Western-enculturated listeners.

Violating harmonic expectation produces the early right anterior negativity (ERAN), an electrical brain response peaking around one hundred fifty to two hundred eighty milliseconds over right frontal sites, described by Stefan Koelsch and colleagues, and it appears even in listeners with no formal musical training, indicating that harmonic knowledge is acquired implicitly.


33.4.2 Beat perception, entrainment, and motor coupling

A beat is a perceived regular pulse, and it is a construction: listeners feel a beat in rhythms where no sound occurs at every beat position, and they can feel the same rhythm in different metres depending on how they choose to hear it.

The dominant formal account is dynamic attending theory, developed by Mari Riess Jones and formalised with Edward Large in the late 1990s, in which internal oscillators entrain to the stimulus so that attention peaks at expected moments, making sounds at those moments easier to detect and judge.

The striking neural finding is that merely listening to a beat, with no movement at all, engages the motor system - supplementary motor area, premotor cortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum - a result from Jessica Grahn and Matthew Brett in 2007 and much replicated.

Aniruddh Patel and John Iversen's action simulation for auditory prediction hypothesis, from 2014, proposes that the motor system supplies the predictive timing signal rather than merely responding to it, and Jonathan Cannon and Patel's 2021 account adds a mechanism in which the supplementary motor area tracks progress through a beat cycle under basal ganglia disinhibition.

Whether observed brain rhythms at beat frequencies reflect true oscillator entrainment or merely a train of evoked responses is an active and unresolved dispute, with Keith Doelling, Luc Arnal and others arguing on both sides, so claims that "neural oscillations entrain to the beat" should be read as a hypothesis under test.


33.4.3 Musical training and cross-domain transfer

Musicians outperform non-musicians on many auditory tasks, including hearing speech in noise, and the question is whether training causes the advantage or whether people with better auditory systems are more likely to persist with music.

Patel's OPERA hypothesis, published in 2011 and expanded in 2014, offers a principled answer to why training could transfer, naming five required conditions: overlap of the brain networks used by music and speech, greater precision demanded by music, positive emotion, repetition, and focused attention.

The theory is elegant and specific, which is a virtue, but the evidence base is weaker than the theory deserves.

A 2022 meta-analysis by Giovanni Sala, Fernand Gobet and colleagues covering sixty-two longitudinal studies and nearly four thousand participants found only a small positive effect on auditory and linguistic measures, with signs of publication bias and with most effects shrinking in the better-controlled designs.

More pointedly, Colette McKay's 2021 systematic review of thirteen training studies in hearing-impaired listeners found that only four used a design capable of testing causation, and none of those four showed a benefit.

The fair summary as of 2026 is that correlational musician advantages are robust and real, that causal transfer from training is plausible and biologically motivated but not yet demonstrated at convincing effect sizes, and that this is a case where a beautiful theory has outrun its data.


33.4.4 Amusia and its dissociations

Congenital amusia is a lifelong difficulty with music - roughly speaking, tone deafness - in people with normal hearing, normal intelligence, and no brain injury, affecting on the order of one and a half to four per cent of the population, with the lower figure coming from a 2017 population estimate that corrected earlier, more generous screening.

Isabelle Peretz and Krista Hyde's work from the early 2000s established its core: a deficit in detecting small pitch changes and in holding pitch in memory, sufficient to make melodies hard to recognise and out-of-tune singing hard to notice.

The anatomy is informative, because the primary auditory cortex often responds normally; the anomaly lies in the right inferior frontal gyrus and the frontotemporal pathway connecting it to auditory cortex, suggesting a failure to bring accurately encoded pitch information to conscious access rather than a failure to encode it - Hyde, Peretz and colleagues reported reduced right arcuate fasciculus in amusics in 2009, though later work by Chen and colleagues in 2015 showed that this finding depends on the tractography algorithm used, which is a caution worth remembering.

The most theoretically valuable observations are the dissociations: Jessica Phillips-Silver, Peretz and colleagues described in 2011 a man they called Mathieu who had normal pitch perception but could not find or move to a musical beat, a condition they named beat deafness, and later work by Nathalie Bégel and others found beat-deaf cases whose beat perception was intact but whose error correction when the beat was perturbed failed, implicating perception-action coupling specifically.

Taken together, pitch amusia and beat deafness form a double dissociation, which is strong evidence that musical pitch and musical rhythm are handled by separable systems - a conclusion that no amount of correlational imaging could establish on its own.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Hearing is not passive reception: the cochlea actively amplifies its own input via prestin-driven outer hair cells, the brainstem extracts microsecond interaural timing through specialised nuclei and giant synapses, and the brain sends efferent fibres back down to adjust the ear itself.

Auditory cortex is organised tonotopically into a core, belt and parabelt hierarchy with anterior identity-biased and posterior space-and-sensorimotor-biased pathways, and with modest hemispheric asymmetries in temporal versus spectral resolution that are real but frequently overstated.

The central computational problem of audition is scene analysis - recovering sources from a summed waveform - and it is solved by primitive grouping cues plus learned schemas, with attention reshaping the cortical representation itself, as the reconstructed-spectrogram results of Mesgarani and Chang demonstrated.

Prediction is built into the system at a low level, evidenced most convincingly by responses to omitted sounds, where there is no stimulus for adaptation to explain away.

Music reveals the architecture through its failures: congenital amusia and beat deafness dissociate pitch from rhythm, showing separable subsystems, while the popular claim that musical training transfers broadly to speech remains theoretically attractive and empirically underpowered.


CHAPTER 34. SOMATOSENSATION, PAIN, AND INTEROCEPTION (CORE)


This chapter is about the senses that report on the body itself rather than on the world outside it.

Somatosensation (the family of senses carried by the skin, muscles, joints and internal organs) covers touch, limb position, temperature, pain, and the quiet signals from the gut, heart and lungs.

These senses matter for three reasons.

They are how you manipulate objects, they are how the body protects itself from damage, and they are, on a growing body of evidence, part of how feelings and the sense of being a self are built.

The chapter moves from the mechanics of a touch receptor in the fingertip, through the fiercely contested neuroscience of pain, to the strange experiments in which a person can be persuaded that a rubber hand is their own.

Along the way several textbook claims turn out to be less settled than they look, and the chapter says so plainly where that is the case.


34.1 Touch and proprioception

Touch is not one sense but a bundle of parallel channels, each with its own receptor, its own nerve fibre, and its own kind of message.

Proprioception (the sense of where your limbs are and how they are moving, without looking) rides alongside touch in the same nerves and up the same spinal pathway.

Together they form the substrate for everything from buttoning a shirt to knowing, in the dark, that your arm is above your head.


34.1.1 Mechanoreceptor classes and labelled lines

A mechanoreceptor is a sensory ending that converts mechanical deformation - pressure, stretch, vibration - into an electrical signal.

Glabrous (hairless) skin, such as the palm and fingertip, contains four classical types, and they differ in two ways: how deep they sit, and how quickly they stop responding to a steady stimulus.

Merkel cells sit at the boundary between epidermis and dermis, adapt slowly, and have small receptive fields; they resolve edges, points and fine spatial detail down to roughly half a millimetre, and they are the workhorses of Braille reading and texture perception.

Meissner corpuscles sit just beneath the surface, adapt rapidly, and are exquisitely sensitive to low-frequency flutter and to the microslips that tell you an object is escaping your grip.

Pacinian corpuscles lie deep in the dermis, adapt very rapidly, and respond to high-frequency vibration, which is why they let you feel the texture of a surface through the tip of a held tool.

Ruffini endings lie in the dermis, adapt slowly, and signal skin stretch, which contributes to the sense of hand shape and of the direction of an applied force.

The organising idea is the labelled line: the brain interprets activity in a given fibre according to which receptor it comes from, so that the same skin indentation delivers separate simultaneous reports about edges, slip, vibration and stretch.

A fifth and quite different channel deserves naming, because it upends the tidy picture.

C-tactile afferents, characterised in humans by Håkan Olausson, Francis McGlone and colleagues, are slow unmyelinated fibres in hairy skin that fire best to gentle stroking at about one to ten centimetres per second, close to skin temperature, and their firing rate tracks how pleasant people say the stroking feels.

They project not to the classic touch cortex but to the posterior insula, and they are the leading candidate for a dedicated "affective touch" system serving grooming and social bonding, though later work by Case and colleagues in 2023 showed that fast A-fibre input also contributes substantially to touch pleasantness, so the channel is not as cleanly segregated as first proposed.


34.1.2 Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and somatotopy

Fine touch, vibration and proprioception travel to the brain by a route called the dorsal column-medial lemniscal (DCML) pathway, and its architecture is worth learning because it explains the pattern of loss after spinal injury.

The first-order fibre enters the spinal cord and, unusually, ascends on the same side of the body all the way to the lower brainstem, travelling in the dorsal columns; fibres from the legs run medially in the gracile tract and fibres from the arms run laterally in the cuneate tract, so the body is already laid out in an orderly map inside the spinal cord.

In the medulla these fibres synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, and the second-order axons cross the midline and ascend as a flat sheet called the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus.

From there the third-order neuron projects to primary somatosensory cortex (S1) on the postcentral gyrus.

Because the crossing happens in the medulla, damage to the dorsal columns below that point causes loss of fine touch and position sense on the same side, while pain and temperature, which cross immediately in the cord, are lost on the opposite side.

The cortical map is somatotopic, meaning neighbouring body parts are represented by neighbouring cortex, and Wilder Penfield's homunculus drawings from his 1930s and 1940s stimulation studies on awake neurosurgical patients remain the most reproduced image in neuroscience.

The map is grossly distorted in proportion to innervation density rather than body size, so the lips and hand occupy vast territory and the trunk very little.

That classic picture has recently been amended.

Evan Gordon, Nico Dosenbach and colleagues, reporting in Nature in 2023 from very long-duration precision functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a method that infers neural activity from local blood oxygenation changes), found that the motor strip is not a continuous body map at all but is interrupted by three "inter-effector" regions sitting between the foot, hand and mouth areas.

These regions are thinner, are connected to each other and to the cingulo-opercular network involved in action control, arousal and pain, and the authors called them the somato-cognitive action network.

The finding was immediately contested by Muret, Makin and colleagues on methodological grounds, so treat it as an important and well-replicated observation whose interpretation is still being argued.


34.1.3 Active touch, tactile exploration, and haptic object recognition

Touch is normally something you do, not something that happens to you, and that distinction has consequences.

Haptics is the term for touch that includes self-generated movement, and blindfolded people can identify most common objects haptically within a few seconds, a performance that passive skin stimulation cannot approach.

Susan Lederman and Roberta Klatzky, in a landmark 1987 paper, showed that this is because hands run a small library of stereotyped exploratory procedures, each optimally suited to one object property.

Lateral motion across a surface extracts texture, pressure extracts hardness, static contact extracts temperature, unsupported holding extracts weight, enclosure gives a fast coarse estimate of global shape and volume, and contour following gives precise shape at a high cost in time.

Their later work established that exploration runs in stages: an initial grasp and lift yields rough values on several properties at once, and only then does the hand commit to the slow specialised procedure that resolves whichever property is diagnostic for the task.

This is a good example of perception as active inference rather than passive reception, since the hand is effectively choosing which experiment to run next.


34.1.4 Proprioception and the body schema

Proprioception depends mainly on two receptor organs buried in the musculoskeletal system.

Muscle spindles lie in parallel with the muscle fibres and signal muscle length and rate of change of length, which is the primary source of information about joint angle and limb velocity.

Golgi tendon organs lie in series at the muscle-tendon junction and signal muscle tension, which is information about force rather than position.

The molecular basis was pinned down by Seung-Hyun Woo, Ardem Patapoutian and colleagues in Nature Neuroscience in 2015, who showed that the mechanically gated ion channel PIEZO2 is the principal transducer in proprioceptors; mice lacking PIEZO2 in these neurons have severely uncoordinated movement, and rare humans with PIEZO2 loss-of-function mutations show profound proprioceptive deficits.

The body schema is the brain's continuously updated, largely unconscious model of the body's size, posture and configuration, used to plan movement; it is usually distinguished from the body image, which is the conscious perceptual and emotional representation of one's body.

The clearest evidence for what proprioception contributes comes from deafferented patients, of whom Ian Waterman is the most studied.

After an autoimmune reaction in his late teens destroyed the large sensory fibres below the neck, Waterman retained motor nerves and muscle strength but collapsed into helplessness, because a motor system with no feedback cannot control anything.

He relearned to stand, walk and manipulate objects using vision as a substitute, and he falls in the dark; work by Cardinali, Farnè and colleagues in 2016 using such a patient further showed that without proprioception the body schema loses the plasticity that normally lets a tool be absorbed into the represented body.


34.2 Pain and nociception
