Pain is where neuroscience is forced to be honest about the gap between a stimulus and an experience.

The International Association for the Study of Pain revised its definition in 2020 to "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage", and every clause of that sentence is doing work.

In particular, pain is not the same thing as nociception, which is the neural detection and transmission of damaging or potentially damaging stimuli; nociception can occur without pain, as under anaesthesia, and pain can occur without nociception, as in many chronic conditions.


34.2.1 Nociceptors, spinothalamic pathway, and dorsal horn gating

Nociceptors are free nerve endings with high thresholds, and they come in two main flavours.

Thinly myelinated A-delta fibres conduct at around five to thirty metres per second and carry the sharp, well-localised first pain that makes you snatch your hand back.

Unmyelinated C fibres conduct at roughly one metre per second and carry the dull, burning, poorly localised second pain that arrives a second later and lingers.

Both synapse in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, and the second-order neurons cross the midline within a segment or two and ascend in the anterolateral system, chiefly the spinothalamic tract, with collateral branches to the periaqueductal grey, parabrachial nucleus and reticular formation.

That immediate crossing is why a one-sided cord lesion produces loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side but loss of fine touch and proprioception on the same side.

Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall's gate control theory, published in Science in 1965, proposed that inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn act as a gate: large-diameter touch fibres excite these interneurons and so close the gate, while nociceptive fibres inhibit them and open it.

That is why rubbing a banged shin genuinely helps, and it is the rationale for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation and for spinal cord stimulators.

Several specific circuit details of the 1965 model have since been shown to be wrong, and Wall himself revised it in 1978, but the central idea that spinal transmission is modulated rather than merely relayed has survived fifty years of scrutiny and no rival framework has displaced it.

More recent work has extended gating outward: a 2023 study reported that proprioceptive parvalbumin-expressing neurons tonically suppress nociceptor activity within the dorsal root ganglion itself, implying a gate that operates even before the spinal cord.


34.2.2 Sensory-discriminative and affective-motivational dimensions

Melzack and Kenneth Casey argued in 1968 that pain has at least two separable dimensions: a sensory-discriminative one, concerning where the pain is, how intense it is and what quality it has, and an affective-motivational one, concerning how unpleasant it is and how urgently it demands action.

The anatomy is broadly consistent with this, with lateral thalamic nuclei projecting to S1 and secondary somatosensory cortex supporting the sensory dimension, and medial thalamic nuclei projecting to anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and insula supporting the affective dimension.

The most elegant demonstration is Pierre Rainville, Donald Price, Catherine Bushnell and colleagues, in Science in 1997, who used hypnotic suggestion on volunteers holding a hand in hot water to change how unpleasant the pain felt while holding its rated intensity constant.

Activity in the ACC tracked the change in unpleasantness while S1 did not; in a complementary later study, suggestions aimed at intensity moved S1 activity instead.

The clinical counterpart is the reported outcome of cingulotomy and of some frontal lesions, where patients say they can still feel the pain but that it no longer bothers them.

The dissociation is real and important, though the clean two-box model is an oversimplification, since intensity and unpleasantness are strongly correlated in ordinary circumstances and the ACC is anything but a dedicated pain-affect module.


34.2.3 The so-called pain matrix and its reinterpretation as salience

Early neuroimaging reliably found a set of regions activated by noxious stimulation - S1, secondary somatosensory cortex, insula, ACC, thalamus and prefrontal areas - and the set was christened the pain matrix, with the strong implication that it was the brain's pain-specific machinery.

That interpretation has been substantially undermined, principally by Gian Domenico Iannetti, André Mouraux, Valéry Legrain and colleagues.

Their key experiment, published by Mouraux and Iannetti in 2011, compared responses to nociceptive stimuli with responses to equally sudden and salient non-nociceptive stimuli, including loud sounds, bright flashes and non-painful touch.

Most of the "pain matrix" lit up for all of them, and multivariate analysis found little activity that was specific to nociception.

Their reinterpretation, set out in the 2011 paper "The pain matrix reloaded", is that these regions constitute a salience detection system for the body: a supramodal network that flags any stimulus urgently relevant to bodily integrity and mobilises defensive action.

Consistent with this, the correlation between pain-matrix magnitude and reported pain can be broken experimentally, which a genuine pain readout should not permit.

The debate is not fully closed, since Tor Wager and colleagues in 2013 derived a distributed fMRI pattern called the neurologic pain signature that predicts thermal pain intensity with high sensitivity and does not respond to social rejection or to warmth, suggesting some nociception-specific information does exist in the multivariate pattern even if the coarse regional map is not specific.

The practical caution is the one that matters most: there is at present no brain-imaging test that can serve as an objective pain-o-meter, and courts and clinics should not be told otherwise.


34.2.4 Placebo, expectation, and descending modulation

The nervous system does not only send pain signals up, it sends control signals down.

The descending modulatory system runs from ACC and prefrontal cortex to the periaqueductal grey (PAG) in the midbrain, then to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), then to the dorsal horn, where it can suppress or facilitate incoming nociceptive traffic; the discovery in the 1960s and 1970s that electrical stimulation of the PAG in rats produced surgical-grade analgesia established the pathway.

Jon Levine, Newton Gordon and Howard Fields showed in The Lancet in 1978 that placebo analgesia in dental postoperative pain was reversed by naloxone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors, which was the first strong evidence that a psychological manipulation was recruiting the body's own endogenous opioids.

Modern imaging has filled in the circuit: Falk Eippert, Christian Büchel and colleagues, in Neuron in 2009, showed that placebo increased coupling between rostral ACC and PAG and reduced nociceptive responses in the spinal dorsal horn itself, and that naloxone abolished both effects.

The mirror phenomenon is nocebo, in which negative expectation increases pain, mediated partly by cholecystokinin and by anxiety circuitry.

The theoretically satisfying reading is predictive: pain is a best estimate that combines incoming nociceptive evidence with prior expectation, so shifting the prior genuinely shifts the experience, and the descending system is the machinery by which the prior gets applied.

It follows that placebo effects on pain are not the patient being fooled or lying, though it is equally true that placebo has far weaker effects on objective disease processes than on symptom report.


34.3 Interoception

Interoception is the sensing of the internal state of the body: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, gut distension, bladder fullness, temperature, blood chemistry, inflammation.

It is mostly unconscious and mostly automatic, and for most of the twentieth century it was treated as plumbing rather than perception.

The last two decades have moved it to the centre of theories of emotion and selfhood, which makes it important to separate the well-established anatomy from the ambitious theory built on top of it.


34.3.1 Vagal and spinal visceral afferents

Interoceptive information reaches the brain by two largely separate routes.

The vagus nerve, the tenth cranial nerve, is roughly eighty percent afferent, meaning most of its fibres carry information up to the brain rather than commands down to the organs, and it reports on the heart, lungs, oesophagus, stomach and much of the intestine, signalling stretch, chemistry and inflammatory state.

The spinal route consists of thin A-delta and C fibres that travel with sympathetic nerves, enter the dorsal horn, and synapse in lamina I, the most superficial layer, which also receives nociceptive input.

A. D. Craig argued influentially from the late 1990s that this lamina I pathway is best understood not as a pain pathway at all but as a general homeostatic afferent system reporting the physiological condition of all body tissues, with pain as one of several such feelings alongside itch, temperature, muscle burn, hunger and thirst.

The two routes carry different emphases, with vagal input weighted toward visceral regulation and lamina I input weighted toward the felt, motivationally charged aspect, and both converge in the brainstem.


34.3.2 Nucleus of the solitary tract, parabrachial nucleus, and insula

Vagal afferents terminate in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) in the medulla, which is the first integration point for cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and taste information and the origin of many autonomic reflexes.

From the NTS, and from lamina I, information passes to the parabrachial nucleus in the pons, which distributes it to the hypothalamus and amygdala for autonomic and defensive responses and onward to the thalamus.

Thalamic relay is chiefly via the basal ventral medial nucleus for vagal-taste input and, in Craig's account, via a specialised posterior ventromedial nucleus for lamina I input, though the existence of that nucleus as a distinct human structure has been questioned by other anatomists and should be treated as contested.

The cortical destination is the insula, a lobe buried beneath the temporal and frontal lobes, and its organisation is the most-cited feature of the field: primary interoceptive representation arrives in the posterior insula, is re-represented in mid-insula, and reaches the anterior insula, where it is integrated with emotional, motivational and cognitive context.

Craig's proposal is that this posterior-to-anterior progression is a hierarchy of increasing abstraction culminating in subjective feeling states in the right anterior insula, an elegant claim that is widely cited and only partially verified, since the neat gradient is clearer in some datasets than others.


34.3.3 Interoceptive predictive processing and allostasis

The dominant modern framework, set out by Lisa Feldman Barrett and W. Kyle Simmons in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2015 as the Embodied Predictive Interoception Coding model, inverts the traditional picture.

On this account the brain is not primarily reading the body's state; agranular visceromotor cortices, including anterior insula and anterior cingulate, issue predictions about what the body's state should be, and ascending visceral signals serve mostly to correct those predictions.

Allostasis is the key concept, meaning regulation by anticipation rather than by reaction: rather than waiting for blood pressure to fall and then correcting it, the brain raises it before you stand up.

Barrett's stronger claim is that interoceptive prediction, not stimulus-driven sensation, is the basis of felt experience, and that chronic prediction error is a general mechanism linking metabolic dysregulation to depression, fatigue and chronic pain.

Kleckner, Barrett and colleagues in 2017 provided supporting evidence for a large-scale allostatic-interoceptive network in humans anchored on those same cortices.

The framework is powerful, is generating testable predictions, and is also broad enough to be difficult to falsify, so it is best described as the leading organising theory rather than an established fact.


34.3.4 Interoception in emotion, self, and decision making

William James argued in 1884 that emotion is the perception of bodily change, and interoception is the modern version of that claim, with Antonio Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis proposing that bodily signals, real or simulated, bias decisions before deliberate reasoning gets a chance.

Empirical work has largely relied on the heartbeat counting task, in which people count their own heartbeats without taking a pulse, and Hugo Critchley, Sarah Garfinkel and colleagues have reported that better performance is associated with greater right anterior insula activity and grey matter, and with stronger emotional experience.

That literature carries a serious methodological caveat: Olivier Desmedt, Olivier Luminet and colleagues showed in 2018 and later that heartbeat counting scores are dominated by systematic under-reporting and are strongly confounded with actual heart rate and with beliefs about heart rate, so many published associations may not measure interoceptive accuracy at all.

Garfinkel's own three-way distinction is now standard practice and helps: interoceptive accuracy, meaning objective performance, interoceptive sensibility, meaning self-reported attention to the body, and interoceptive awareness, meaning the correspondence between the two, dissociate from one another.

The heartbeat-evoked potential, an electroencephalographic response time-locked to the heartbeat, is the preferred physiological alternative because it does not depend on the participant's report.

Clinically, altered interoception is implicated in anxiety and panic, where bodily sensations are catastrophically over-weighted, in alexithymia, the difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, in depression, and in anorexia nervosa, where insular responses to visceral stimulation are altered even after weight restoration.

The honest summary is that the direction of causation in most of these associations is not established.


34.4 Body representation

The brain must decide, moment by moment, which parts of the world are the body.

That sounds trivial and is not, and the experiments that make it fail are among the most instructive in cognitive neuroscience.


34.4.1 Rubber hand and full-body illusions

Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen reported in Nature in 1998 that if a participant's real hand is hidden and a visible rubber hand is stroked in exact synchrony with the hidden one, most people begin to feel the touch as arising in the rubber hand and report that it feels like their own.

Two measures are standard: the questionnaire report of ownership, and proprioceptive drift, in which the participant's felt hand position shifts toward the rubber hand.

Asynchronous stroking, which breaks the temporal correlation, abolishes the effect and serves as the control condition.

Bigna Lenggenhager, Olaf Blanke and colleagues extended this to the whole body in Science in 2007, using a head-mounted display showing a video of the participant's own back being stroked from two metres behind, which produced self-location drift toward the virtual body; Henrik Ehrsson reported a related out-of-body illusion the same year.

Two cautions are warranted.

The illusion is far from universal, with a substantial minority of participants reporting little or nothing, and there is an active methodological debate, pressed by Peter Lush and colleagues since 2020, over how much of the questionnaire effect reflects phenomenological control - that is, participants generating the experience in line with the demand characteristics of the task - rather than genuine multisensory integration.

Proponents counter that objective measures such as skin conductance to threat and proprioceptive drift are harder to explain that way, and the argument is unresolved.


34.4.2 Sense of body ownership and its neural correlates

The prevailing computational account is Bayesian causal inference: the brain estimates whether visual, tactile and proprioceptive signals share a common cause, and when synchrony makes that likely it binds them and attributes the seen object to the body.

Ehrsson, Spence and Passingham, in Science in 2004, scanned people during the rubber hand illusion and found that activity in ventral premotor cortex tracked the onset and strength of felt ownership, with intraparietal sulcus activity reflecting the multisensory conflict.

These are precisely the regions containing multisensory neurons with visual receptive fields anchored to body parts, first described in macaques by Michael Graziano and Charles Gross, which gives the human imaging result a plausible cellular basis.

Later work has added the posterior parietal cortex as the site of the causal inference computation, direct electrophysiological confirmation from intracranial recordings in humans in 2019, and the insula as the region tying ownership to interoceptive and affective signals.

Ownership should be distinguished from agency, the feeling of causing an action, which depends more on comparing predicted with actual sensory consequences of movement and which dissociates from ownership in both experiment and pathology.


34.4.3 Phantom limbs and cortical reorganisation

Almost everyone who loses a limb continues to feel it, often vividly and often painfully, and Silas Weir Mitchell named the phenomenon phantom limb in the nineteenth century.

The standard explanation for three decades came from work in the early 1990s by Tim Pons, Herta Flor, Vilayanur Ramachandran and others: after deafferentation, neighbouring cortical territory invades the deprived zone, so that the face area creeps into the hand area, and the degree of this reorganisation correlated with phantom limb pain.

Ramachandran's mirror box, which uses a mirror to superimpose the reflection of the intact hand where the phantom is felt, was designed on the premise that restoring visual-motor congruence could reverse maladaptive reorganisation, and mirror therapy remains in clinical use with a genuinely mixed evidence base.

This whole account is now under sustained challenge.

Tamar Makin and colleagues have argued across a decade of work that the cortical representation of the missing hand is largely preserved rather than erased, that phantom pain is associated with stronger rather than weaker missing-hand representation, and that apparent "remapping" reflects unmasking and changed behaviour rather than territorial takeover.

The most decisive evidence is Hunter Schone, Makin and colleagues, published in Nature Neuroscience in 2025 after appearing as a preprint in 2023, who scanned three adults before amputation and for up to five years afterwards and found cortical hand and lip maps essentially unchanged.

The sample is tiny, which is unavoidable for a study of this design, but a longitudinal within-person design is exactly what the field lacked, and its result is hard to reconcile with large-scale reorganisation.

Flor and others continue to defend a role for plasticity, so the fair statement is that the strong reorganisation account is now the minority position among researchers who study it closely, while remaining the majority position in textbooks.


34.4.4 Disorders of body representation

Somatoparaphrenia, described by Josef Gerstmann in 1942, is the delusional denial of ownership of a limb, usually the left arm after a right-hemisphere stroke involving posterior insula, temporoparietal junction or their white matter connections; patients may attribute the arm to a relative or to the examiner, and the belief can be temporarily suspended by vestibular stimulation, which is a remarkable clue that ownership depends on ongoing multisensory input.

Asomatognosia is the milder relative, in which the limb is simply not felt as part of the body without the confabulated attribution.

Body integrity dysphoria, previously called body integrity identity disorder, xenomelia or apotemnophilia, and recognised in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases in 2019, is a lifelong desire for amputation of a healthy limb that the person experiences as not belonging; imaging by Gianluca Saetta, Peter Brugger and colleagues in Current Biology in 2020 found structural and functional differences in right superior parietal lobule, premotor cortex and insula, consistent with a developmental failure to incorporate the limb into the body schema rather than a psychiatric delusion or a purely sexual paraphilia.

Anorexia nervosa involves a distortion of body image rather than body schema, with patients overestimating body size, and it is increasingly framed as involving disturbed interoceptive and multisensory body processing rather than attitude alone.

Complex regional pain syndrome offers a striking bridge between pain and body representation, since patients often report the affected limb as alien or distorted, show neglect-like inattention to it, and can improve with therapies aimed at the body representation such as mirror visual feedback and graded motor imagery.

Taken together, these conditions show that ownership, position sense, size perception and pain are separately vulnerable, which is itself an argument that they are separately computed.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Somatosensation is not one channel but many parallel labelled lines, from Merkel cells resolving Braille dots to C-tactile fibres reporting the pleasantness of a caress, ascending by two anatomically distinct routes whose crossing points explain the classic dissociations seen after spinal injury.

Pain is constructed rather than transmitted: it separates into sensory and affective dimensions, it is gated at the dorsal horn and steered by a descending system from cortex through periaqueductal grey to spinal cord, and expectation genuinely changes it through endogenous opioid mechanisms.

Two once-standard claims should now be held loosely - that the imaging "pain matrix" is pain-specific, which the salience-detection evidence from Iannetti, Mouraux and Legrain undercuts, and that amputation causes large-scale cortical remapping, which the longitudinal work of Schone and Makin published in 2025 directly contradicts.

Interoception has a well-mapped anatomy running from vagal and lamina I afferents through the nucleus of the solitary tract and parabrachial nucleus to the insula, but the influential predictive-and-allostatic theory built upon it, and much of the behavioural literature measuring interoceptive accuracy by heartbeat counting, remain more provisional than their popularity suggests.

Finally, the body you feel yourself to have is an inference, revisable by half a minute of synchronous brushing on a rubber hand and breakable altogether by stroke, which means bodily self-awareness is a computation the brain performs and not a fact it is given.


CHAPTER 35. THE CHEMICAL SENSES (CORE)

Vision and hearing detect energy - light waves and pressure waves.

The chemical senses detect matter itself - actual molecules that drift into your nose or dissolve on your tongue.

This chapter covers the three chemical systems: olfaction (the sense of smell), gustation (the sense of taste), and chemesthesis (the chemical irritation sense carried by the nerves of touch and pain in the mouth and nose).

It matters for three reasons.

First, smell and taste are how the body decides what is food and what is poison, which makes them the most directly survival-linked senses you have.

Second, olfaction is anatomically strange - it is the one sense that reaches the cortex without first passing through the thalamus - and that strangeness has been used to argue about how perception works in general.

Third, the chemical senses are the hardest case for any theory of perception, because unlike light there is no simple physical axis such as wavelength along which smells can be arranged.

35.1 Olfaction

Olfaction begins high in the nasal cavity, in a patch of specialised tissue about the size of a postage stamp called the olfactory epithelium.

Airborne molecules, called odorants, dissolve in the thin layer of mucus covering this patch and bind to receptor proteins on the hair-like cilia of olfactory sensory neurons.

These neurons are unusual in two ways: they are among the very few neurons in the human body that are continuously replaced throughout life, and their axons pass directly through the perforated bone at the roof of the nose into the brain.

That short, exposed path is why a blow to the head can sever the olfactory nerve fibres and cause permanent smell loss, and it is also why the nose has been studied as a possible entry route for pathogens and for proteins involved in neurodegenerative disease.

35.1.1 Receptor diversity and the combinatorial odour code

In 1991 Linda Buck and Richard Axel, working at Columbia University, discovered that odorants are detected by a very large family of receptor proteins - a finding that won them the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

These are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a class of proteins that thread back and forth through the cell membrane seven times and, when a molecule binds on the outside, trigger a chemical cascade on the inside.

The human genome contains roughly 800 olfactory receptor gene loci, but more than half carry frame-disrupting mutations and are pseudogenes (broken copies that no longer produce a working protein), leaving something close to 400 functional receptors - still the largest gene family in the genome.

Each mature olfactory sensory neuron appears to express just one receptor type from this family, a striking arrangement known as the one-neuron-one-receptor rule, whose regulatory mechanism is still not fully understood.

The coding question was answered by Bettina Malnic, Junzo Hirono, Takaaki Sato and Linda Buck in 1999: one receptor responds to many odorants, and one odorant activates many receptors, so a smell is represented as a combination - a pattern across the receptor family rather than a dedicated line.

This is why 400 receptors can distinguish a vast number of smells, in the same way that 26 letters can spell an unlimited number of words.

35.1.2 Olfactory bulb glomeruli and lateral processing

All the sensory neurons expressing the same receptor type, scattered across the epithelium, send their axons to converge on the same one or two spherical tangles of neuropil in the olfactory bulb, called glomeruli (singular: glomerulus).

This converts a scattered chemical pattern into an orderly spatial map: a given odour lights up a characteristic constellation of glomeruli on the surface of the bulb, which is why odour responses can be imaged directly.

Inside the glomerulus, incoming axons contact the apical dendrites of the bulb's output cells, the mitral cells and tufted cells, which differ in their firing behaviour - tufted cells generally respond at higher rates and shorter latencies than mitral cells, suggesting they carry somewhat different aspects of the signal.

Two populations of inhibitory interneurons sharpen the output: periglomerular cells acting within and between glomeruli, and granule cells, which form reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses (synapses where two dendrites contact each other and signal in both directions) with the lateral dendrites of mitral and tufted cells.

The working assumption is that this inhibition performs contrast enhancement and gain control, improving the signal-to-noise ratio much as lateral inhibition does in the retina, though the precise computational role of granule cell inhibition remains an active area of disagreement rather than a settled result.

35.1.3 The thalamus-bypassing pathway to piriform cortex

For every other sense, information must pass through the thalamus - the paired relay structure at the centre of the brain - before reaching cortex.

Olfaction does not: mitral and tufted cell axons run in the lateral olfactory tract straight to a set of primary olfactory areas, chief among them the piriform cortex, a three-layered cortex on the underside of the brain near the junction of temporal and frontal lobes.

From piriform cortex the dominant route to neocortex is a direct projection to the orbitofrontal cortex, with a second, sparser, disynaptic route running via the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus, described in reviews by Donald Wilson and colleagues and by Tham, Stevenson and Miller in 2009 and 2015.

The thalamic route is not a bypassed vestige: Jay Gottfried's group showed in 2008 that paying attention to an odour strengthens coupling between mediodorsal thalamus and orbitofrontal cortex, suggesting the thalamus supports attentional selection rather than basic transmission.

Unlike the bulb, piriform cortex has no obvious spatial map: work by Kevin Franks, Sandeep Robert Datta and others found that odour identity is carried by ensembles of co-active neurons scattered across the structure with no apparent topography, because bulb-to-piriform projections are diffuse and overlapping.

This distributed, recurrently connected architecture is often compared to an associative memory network, and it is where the separate receptor features are thought to be bound into a single perceived odour object.

35.1.4 Odour, memory, and emotion: the privileged limbic access

The claim that smell has special access to memory and emotion is usually called the Proust phenomenon, after the passage in Marcel Proust's novel where the taste and smell of a madeleine dipped in tea unlocks a flood of childhood memory.

The anatomical argument is straightforward: primary olfactory areas project directly to the amygdala, a structure central to emotional evaluation, and to the entorhinal cortex, which is the main gateway into the hippocampus, the structure required for forming new episodic memories.

The behavioural evidence is real but narrower than the popular story: Rachel Herz and colleagues found that odour-cued autobiographical memories are not more accurate or more numerous than memories cued by words or pictures, but they are rated as more emotional and more vivid, and are accompanied by larger physiological responses.

Herz and colleagues also reported neuroimaging evidence in 2004 that the felt emotional intensity of an odour-cued memory correlates with amygdala activation during recall.

It is worth being careful here: the fact that olfaction skips the thalamus is frequently offered as the explanation for emotional potency, but this is an anatomical plausibility argument rather than a demonstrated causal mechanism, and the amygdala and hippocampus also receive rich input from the other senses.

35.2 Gustation

Taste proper is a narrow sense, and this surprises most people.

The tongue and palate detect only a handful of qualities; nearly everything you think of as the taste of a strawberry is actually smell.

Taste receptor cells are clustered in taste buds, onion-shaped groups of roughly fifty to a hundred cells embedded in the papillae, the visible bumps on the tongue, and also present on the soft palate, epiglottis and upper oesophagus.

The old classroom diagram of a tongue map, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back, is wrong - all qualities can be detected across the whole tongue, with only modest regional differences in sensitivity.

35.2.1 Taste qualities and receptor mechanisms

Five qualities are generally accepted: sweet, umami (the savoury taste of glutamate, named by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908), bitter, salty and sour.

Sweet and umami are detected by GPCRs of the T1R family working as pairs - T1R2 together with T1R3 for sweet, T1R1 together with T1R3 for umami - while bitter is detected by a separate family of roughly twenty-five T2R receptors, which is a sensible design given that bitterness is a general poison alarm and must cover many unrelated chemicals.

All three of these GPCR pathways converge on the same internal cascade, running through the G protein gustducin and phospholipase C to open the ion channel TRPM5, which is why deleting a single downstream component can abolish sweet, bitter and umami together.

Salty and sour work differently, through ion channels directly: the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) accounts for the sodium-specific appetitive salt response, while sour cells are identified by the marker PKD2L1 and depend on the proton channel OTOP1, characterised by Emily Liman's group in 2018.

Signalling out of the taste bud is also unusual: type II cells release adenosine triphosphate (ATP) not from vesicles but through the large-pore CALHM1/CALHM3 channel, shown by the groups of J. Kevin Foskett and Akiyuki Taruno in 2013, and that ATP activates P2X2 and P2X3 receptors on the sensory nerve fibres.

Candidate sixth qualities - fat, calcium, starch, metallic, and the water taste - continue to be proposed; fat sensing through the receptor CD36 has the strongest support, but none has yet achieved the consensus status of the five.

35.2.2 Central taste pathway to insular cortex

Taste information leaves the mouth along three cranial nerves: the facial nerve for the front two-thirds of the tongue, the glossopharyngeal nerve for the back third, and the vagus nerve for the throat and epiglottis.

All three converge on the nucleus of the solitary tract, a column of cells in the medulla, which is the first central relay and also the point at which taste signals are joined by visceral information from the gut.

Here the human pathway differs from the rodent pathway in a way that matters for reading the literature: in rodents the next stop is the parabrachial nucleus of the pons, whereas in primates including humans the projection is generally described as running directly to the thalamus, to the parvicellular part of the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPMpc).

From VPMpc, fibres run to the primary gustatory cortex in the anterior insula and adjoining frontal operculum, and from there to the orbitofrontal cortex, which is often called secondary taste cortex.

Note that the taste pathway is largely ipsilateral - the left side of the tongue reports to the left hemisphere - which is unlike vision and touch and is a useful clinical clue.

35.2.3 Labelled line against across-fibre pattern debate

This is one of the longest-running arguments in sensory neuroscience, and it is genuinely unresolved.

The labelled line view holds that each quality has a dedicated channel: a sweet cell drives a sweet fibre, and activity in that channel means sweet and nothing else.

The across-fibre pattern view, associated with Robert Erickson from 1963 onward and defended by Marion Frank and by David Smith and colleagues, holds that individual fibres are broadly tuned and the quality is carried by the relative pattern of activity across the whole population.

The strongest evidence for labelled lines comes from molecular work in Charles Zuker's and Nicholas Ryba's laboratories, notably Jayaram Chandrashekar and colleagues, who showed that expressing a bitter receptor in normally sweet-sensing cells made mice attracted to a bitter compound - the behaviour followed the cell, not the chemical.

Opponents reply that this establishes labelled lines at the receptor cell, not through the rest of the system, and point to recordings showing broadly tuned neurons in the brainstem and cortex; Barry Green and others have argued the two positions are partly a false dichotomy, since the periphery can be quality-specific while central populations still combine information.

The reasonable current summary is that the transduction layer is close to labelled, and the degree of labelling further up the pathway remains contested.

35.2.4 Taste, reward, and value coding

A taste is not just an identity, it is a verdict - sweet is good, bitter is bad - and these valences are largely present at birth, as shown by the facial reactions of newborn infants to sugar and quinine studied by Jacob Steiner from the 1970s.

Edmund Rolls and colleagues established a key division of labour in primates: neurons in the primary taste cortex of the insula respond to a taste regardless of hunger, whereas neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex stop responding to a food once the animal has been fed to satiety on it.

This effect is called sensory-specific satiety - the food you have just eaten becomes less pleasant while other foods remain appealing, which is why there is famously always room for dessert.

The interpretation is that the insula codes what the substance is, and the orbitofrontal cortex codes what it is currently worth, with subjective pleasantness ratings in human neuroimaging tracking orbitofrontal activity closely.

Value is not settled in the mouth alone: work on neuropod cells - specialised gut epithelial cells that form synapse-like contacts with vagal nerve fibres, described by Diego Bohórquez and colleagues - shows the intestine reports sugar to the brain within milliseconds, and this gut signal, independent of sweet taste, helps explain why animals learn to prefer caloric sugars over non-caloric sweeteners.

35.3 Flavour and chemosensory integration

What we colloquially call taste is really flavour, and flavour is a multisensory construct assembled from taste, smell, touch, temperature and irritation, with vision and sound contributing as well.

The clearest demonstration is the oldest one: pinch your nose while eating and a jelly bean becomes merely sweet, its identity gone.

35.3.1 Retronasal olfaction and the construction of flavour

Odorants reach the olfactory epithelium by two routes: orthonasally, drawn in through the nostrils when you sniff, and retronasally, pushed up the back of the throat from the mouth as you chew and swallow.

Paul Rozin argued in 1982 that olfaction is therefore a dual sense, because the same molecule produces a different experience depending on the route - orthonasal odours are perceived as out in the world, retronasal odours are referred to the mouth, an illusion called oral referral.

That referral is so complete that people routinely and confidently misattribute retronasal smell to their tongue, which is why patients who lose their sense of smell usually complain that they have lost their sense of taste.

Neuroimaging supports a genuine difference rather than a mere labelling habit: Dana Small and colleagues reported in 2005 that identical odorants delivered orthonasally and retronasally produce different patterns of brain activation, and a 2018 lesion study in Current Biology reported that retronasal odour perception depends on intact taste cortex while orthonasal perception does not.

35.3.2 Trigeminal chemesthesis

The third chemical sense is chemesthesis, chemical sensitivity carried not by taste or smell receptors but by the trigeminal nerve, the large cranial nerve supplying touch, temperature and pain to the face, mouth and nasal cavity.

Its receptors are members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channel family, which is why chemesthetic sensations feel thermal: capsaicin in chilli opens TRPV1, a channel that also responds to noxious heat, so chilli feels hot; menthol opens TRPM8, the cold channel, so mint feels cool; mustard oil and cinnamaldehyde open TRPA1.

The tingle of carbonated drinks is also largely trigeminal - dissolved carbon dioxide is converted to carbonic acid by carbonic anhydrase and the resulting acidification stimulates trigeminal fibres, which is why fizz is a feeling rather than a taste, though carbonation also activates sour taste cells.

Chemesthesis is not a separate track running alongside flavour; it is integrated into it, and it interacts with smell, so that trigeminal stimulation can suppress odour intensity and almost all odorants at high enough concentration recruit some trigeminal response.

35.3.3 Learned food preference and aversion

Most of what an individual likes to eat is learned, and the chemical senses contain one of psychology's most instructive learning phenomena.

John Garcia and colleagues, working in the 1950s and reporting through the 1960s, found that a rat made ill hours after tasting a novel flavour would refuse that flavour thereafter - conditioned taste aversion, often called the Garcia effect.

This broke two supposed laws of learning at once: one pairing was enough, and the delay between taste and illness could be hours rather than the seconds thought necessary, showing that learning is biologically prepared - animals are built to associate illness with what they ate rather than with what they saw or heard.

The mirror-image process, flavour-nutrient learning, builds preferences: a flavour repeatedly paired with post-ingestive calories becomes liked, which is how coffee, chilli and strong cheeses become pleasant despite unpromising first encounters.

Clinically this matters, because conditioned aversions acquired during chemotherapy can make patients reject foods that happened to be eaten before treatment, a problem sometimes managed by giving a strongly flavoured scapegoat food.

35.4 Chemical senses as a test case

Olfaction and gustation are not just additional senses to catalogue; they are a stress test for theories of perception built on vision and hearing.

Those theories usually assume that a stimulus can be described by a small number of physical dimensions, and that similar physical values produce similar percepts - assumptions that break down badly for smell.

35.4.1 High-dimensional stimulus spaces and their formalisation

The colour of a light is fixed by a spectrum reduced to three receptor responses; the pitch of a tone is fixed by frequency; but a smell is a molecule, and molecules vary along thousands of structural and physicochemical descriptors with no natural ordering.

The scale of the resulting space is itself disputed: Caroline Bushdid, Marcelo Magnasco, Leslie Vosshall and Andreas Keller argued in Science in 2014 that humans can discriminate more than one trillion olfactory stimuli, and Richard Gerkin and Jason Castro replied in eLife in 2015 that the estimation framework was fragile enough to yield almost any answer and that the formula used gives an upper rather than a lower bound.

This is a live dispute worth stating plainly: the honest position is that the number of discriminable smells is large but currently unknown.

Progress has come from treating the problem statistically rather than analytically - Kobi Snitz, Noam Sobel and colleagues built a physicochemical metric in 2013 that predicts perceptual similarity between odorant mixtures, and the DREAM Olfaction Prediction Challenge reported by Keller and colleagues in Science in 2017 showed that machine learning models trained on a large human rating set could predict some perceptual descriptors from molecular structure.

The most successful attempt so far is the principal odor map of Brian Lee and colleagues, published in Science in 2023, in which a graph neural network trained on odour labels produced a learned map whose coordinates predicted odour quality about as well as the median human panellist and generalised to intensity and similarity judgements it was never trained on.

35.4.2 Perceptual quality spaces and the failure of simple metrics

Vision has an orderly perceptual space: hues form a circle, and the colours nearby in that circle look alike.

Smell has no agreed equivalent, and attempts to define a small set of primary odours - from Carl Linnaeus in the eighteenth century through Hans Henning's 1916 odour prism to John Amoore's stereochemical theory in the 1960s - have all failed to survive systematic testing.

Simple structural metrics fail conspicuously in both directions: molecules differing only in the mirror-image arrangement of one carbon atom, such as the two forms of carvone, smell like caraway and spearmint respectively, while structurally unrelated molecules can smell almost identical.

Statistical analyses of large odour rating sets do recover some structure - a dominant pleasantness axis reported by Rafi Haddad, Noam Sobel and colleagues, plus a small number of weaker axes - but there is no agreement on how many dimensions the space has, and the learned representations of models like the principal odor map are effective without being interpretable in ordinary perceptual terms.

The general lesson is that a perceptual quality space need not be low-dimensional or metrically simple, and theories of perception that assume otherwise are generalising from the unusually tidy case of vision.

35.4.3 Olfactory loss as an early clinical marker

Because the olfactory system depends on continuous cell replacement and includes some of the earliest brain regions affected in several diseases, smell testing has become a cheap and surprisingly informative clinical probe.

Reduced smell (hyposmia) or absent smell (anosmia) is present in a large majority of people with Parkinson's disease and often appears years before the motor symptoms, consistent with the staging scheme of Heiko Braak, in which the olfactory structures and lower brainstem are affected before the substantia nigra.

Olfactory identification deficits also predict progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, which fits the early appearance of tau pathology in entorhinal cortex, the olfactory system's route into the hippocampus.

The standard measures are the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT), a forty-item scratch-and-sniff test developed by Richard Doty, and the Sniffin' Sticks battery, which assesses threshold, discrimination and identification separately.

Two cautions are essential: smell loss is common and has many causes - head injury, sinus disease, ageing, and viral infection, most prominently the sudden anosmia that became a diagnostic hallmark of COVID-19 in 2020, with persistent dysfunction in a minority of cases - so it is a sensitive but not specific marker, useful for enriching a screening population rather than for diagnosing an individual.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Smell works by combination rather than dedication: roughly 400 receptor types, each broadly tuned, produce a distributed code that is mapped onto glomeruli in the olfactory bulb and then dispersed again into non-topographic ensembles in piriform cortex, reached without a thalamic relay.

Taste is a much narrower sense of five accepted qualities with distinct molecular mechanisms, and the long argument over labelled lines against across-fibre patterns is best summarised as labelled at the receptor cell and contested thereafter, with value rather than identity emerging downstream in orbitofrontal cortex.

Most of what we call taste is retronasal smell referred to the mouth, combined with trigeminal chemesthesis and shaped by powerful one-trial learning of the kind Garcia described.

The chemical senses matter beyond themselves because they show that a stimulus space can be high-dimensional and metrically unruly, defeating the tidy assumptions that vision encouraged - the number of discriminable smells remains genuinely disputed, and the best current models are learned rather than derived.

Finally, because olfactory tissue is exposed and its central targets are early casualties in neurodegeneration, measured smell loss has become a useful early warning sign - sensitive, cheap, and too unspecific to stand alone.


CHAPTER 36. MULTISENSORY INTEGRATION AND PERCEPTUAL DECISION (CORE)


You do not have five separate perceptual worlds running side by side.

You have one, and the brain builds it by merging light, sound, touch and the rest into a single account of what is out there.

This chapter covers how that merging happens, how the brain decides which signals belong to the same event, and how a merged perception is then converted into a decision - a commitment to one interpretation rather than another.

It ends with confidence and awareness, because a perceptual system that commits to answers also needs some sense of how much to trust them.

The material matters because almost every real perceptual act is multisensory and almost every perceptual act ends in a choice, so a theory of perception that stops at single senses and single snapshots is a theory of something that never happens.


36.1 Combining the senses

Combining senses is not simply adding them.

A signal from the ear and a signal from the eye can only be usefully merged if they probably came from the same physical event, and even then they should not be merged equally, because one of them is usually more trustworthy than the other.

This section works through the neural machinery that performs the merge, the rules it appears to follow, and the illusions that expose those rules when the machinery is fooled.


36.1.1 Superior colliculus and the principles of multisensory enhancement

The superior colliculus is a layered structure on the roof of the midbrain (the middle segment of the brainstem) that orients the eyes, head and body toward events worth looking at.

Its deeper layers contain multisensory neurons - single cells that respond to more than one kind of input, for example both a flash and a click.

Working mainly in cats from the 1980s onward, Barry Stein, Alex Meredith, Mark Wallace and colleagues used single-unit recording (measuring the electrical spikes of one neuron at a time) to extract a set of rules from these cells.

The spatial rule says that two stimuli enhance each other's response when they come from roughly the same place, and can suppress each other when they do not.

The temporal rule says the same for time - inputs arriving close together enhance, inputs far apart do not.

The principle of inverse effectiveness says that the proportionally largest enhancement occurs when each stimulus on its own is weak and barely drives the neuron, which is exactly the regime where combining evidence is most useful.

Stein and colleagues also showed that this integration is not automatic hardware but depends on descending input from cortex, and that it matures with experience, so a cat raised without matched sight and sound does not develop the normal enhancement.

A practical payoff has been reported by the same group: repeatedly pairing sounds with lights in the blind field of animals and human patients with hemianopia (loss of vision on one side after damage to visual cortex) can recover some visual responsiveness on that side.


36.1.2 Cortical multisensory areas and early cross-modal effects

For decades the textbook picture was hierarchical: each sense is processed alone in its own primary cortex, and only later do the streams meet in dedicated association zones.

The classical meeting places are real enough - the superior temporal sulcus (STS), a long groove on the side of the temporal lobe that responds to both faces and voices, and the intraparietal areas, which combine vision and touch into body-centred maps of nearby space.

The hierarchical picture, though, has been substantially revised.

Anatomical tracing and human intracranial recording have found direct connections between early auditory and early visual cortex, and visual influences on responses in primary auditory cortex within the first hundred milliseconds.

The interpretation is contested: some of these effects appear to be genuine direct cross-modal input, while others are best explained as feedback from higher multisensory regions such as STS or parietal cortex arriving quickly enough to look early.

The safe summary is that multisensory influence is distributed across the whole hierarchy rather than confined to a late integration stage, but that the relative contribution of direct connections versus feedback is still an open empirical question.


36.1.3 Optimal cue combination and reliability weighting

If two senses estimate the same property, the statistically best combination is a weighted average in which each cue's weight is proportional to its reliability, reliability being the inverse of its variance (how scattered its estimates are).

Marc Ernst and Martin Banks tested this in Nature in 2002 by having people judge the height of a ridge by sight, by touch, or by both, while degrading the visual signal with added noise.

They first measured how variable each sense was alone, then used those numbers to predict, with no free parameters, both the weights people would give each sense and the precision of the combined judgement.

Human performance matched the prediction closely, including the key signature that the combined estimate is more precise than either sense alone, and that vision loses its usual dominance as soon as the visual signal is made noisy.

This maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) account - MLE being the statistical rule of choosing the estimate that makes the observed data most probable - has since been confirmed for many cue pairs, though it is not universal and children below about eight to ten years old typically do not combine optimally.

A crucial extension is Bayesian causal inference, developed by Konrad Körding, Ladan Shams and colleagues in 2007, which adds the prior question of whether the two signals came from one event at all.

That model explains why fusion is graceful rather than all-or-none: at small discrepancies the senses fuse, at large discrepancies the brain infers two separate causes and the cross-modal pull collapses, which a plain weighted average could never produce.


36.1.4 Cross-modal illusions: ventriloquism, McGurk, sound-induced flash

The ventriloquism effect is the capture of perceived sound location by a synchronous visible source, which is why a film's dialogue seems to come from the actor's mouth rather than from the speakers.

It is the reliability rule in action, since vision localises far more precisely than hearing, so vision wins the spatial weighting.

The McGurk effect, reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976, goes the other way: a voice saying "ba" dubbed onto a face mouthing "ga" is commonly heard as "da", a syllable present in neither channel.

The effect is genuine but its strength is far more variable across individuals, languages and stimulus sets than its fame suggests, and researchers now caution against treating an individual's McGurk susceptibility as a clean measure of that person's multisensory integration.

The sound-induced flash illusion, described by Ladan Shams, Yukiyasu Kamitani and Shinsuke Shimojo in 2000, is the reverse direction of influence - one brief flash accompanied by two beeps within about a hundred milliseconds is usually seen as two flashes.

That case is theoretically important because it refutes any simple claim that vision always dominates; hearing has the better temporal resolution, so on a timing judgement hearing is the cue that wins.


36.2 Time and the senses

Timing is the hardest part of the merging problem.

Light and sound travel at wildly different speeds, and the retina and the cochlea take different amounts of time to transduce their signals, so signals from one event essentially never arrive at cortex together.

The brain therefore needs tolerance for mismatch, and a way of retuning that tolerance as conditions change.


36.2.1 Temporal binding windows

The temporal binding window is the range of stimulus onset asynchronies - the gaps between the start of one signal and the start of another - across which the brain still treats two inputs as one event.

For audiovisual stimuli the window is broad, commonly a few hundred milliseconds, and it is asymmetric: vision leading sound is tolerated far more than sound leading vision, which matches the natural world, where sound always arrives late.

The window is not fixed.

It is wider in young children and narrows through adolescence, widens again in older adults, and has been reported as atypically wide in autism, schizophrenia and dyslexia, though the reliability and specificity of those clinical findings are debated.

Several groups, including Mark Wallace and colleagues, have shown that a few sessions of feedback training on simultaneity judgements can narrow the window by roughly forty percent, and that the narrowing transfers to speech perception, which argues that the window is a learned tolerance rather than a hard limit.


36.2.2 Simultaneity, order judgement, and recalibration

Two tasks probe this differently.

In a simultaneity judgement the observer says only whether two signals were together, which yields the width of the window and the point of subjective simultaneity - the actual physical offset that feels simultaneous, which for audiovisual stimuli usually has sound lagging vision.

In a temporal order judgement the observer says which came first, which is a finer measure but can be contaminated by response bias, and the two tasks do not always agree, so they are thought to tap partly separable processes.

Recalibration is the striking part.

After a few minutes of exposure to a consistent lag, the point of subjective simultaneity shifts toward that lag, so the previously delayed pairing now feels synchronous.

Rapid recalibration also occurs across a single trial, meaning the offset on the previous trial shifts the judgement on the current one, which suggests the brain is continuously re-estimating cross-modal delay rather than storing a fixed calibration.


36.2.3 Sensorimotor timing and prediction of self-generated input

When you move, you generate a flood of sensation, and the brain needs to distinguish that self-caused input from input caused by the world.

The standard account is the internal forward model: a copy of the motor command, called efference copy or corollary discharge, is sent to sensory areas and used to predict the sensory consequences of the movement, and the prediction is subtracted from the incoming signal.

Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith demonstrated this with a robotic tickling device, showing that self-produced touch feels weaker than identical externally produced touch, and that the attenuation is progressively abolished as delay or spatial rotation is introduced between the movement and the resulting touch - which is why you cannot tickle yourself.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures blood-flow changes as an indirect index of neural activity, implicated the cerebellum, a dense structure at the back of the brain, in generating that prediction.

The framework has clinical reach: reduced sensory attenuation has been proposed as a mechanism for the delusions of alien control and auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia, where self-generated events are misattributed to an external agent.

The attenuation result itself is robust, though whether it is best explained by prediction-based cancellation or by simpler shifts of attention and by comparison against learned expectations remains an active dispute.


36.3 Perceptual decision making

At some point looking must stop and answering must begin.

Perceptual decision making is the study of that conversion, and its great advantage as a research problem is that it produces two measurable numbers at once - which choice was made and how long it took - so a theory must explain both together or it explains neither.


36.3.1 Evidence accumulation and the drift diffusion model

The dominant framework says the brain samples noisy evidence over time, adds each sample to a running total, and commits as soon as the total crosses a threshold.

The drift diffusion model (DDM), formalised for psychology by Roger Ratcliff in 1978, describes this as a particle drifting between two boundaries, one per choice.

Its main parameters are the drift rate, meaning the average quality of the evidence per unit time; the boundary separation, meaning how much net evidence is demanded; the starting point, which captures prior bias toward one answer; and non-decision time, covering sensory transduction and motor execution.

From that small set the model predicts the full shape of the reaction time distribution for correct and error responses, not just the averages, and Ratcliff's addition of trial-to-trial variability in drift rate was what allowed it to reproduce the common pattern of errors being slower than correct responses.

The DDM is also normatively attractive because for two choices it is equivalent to the sequential probability ratio test, the statistical procedure that reaches any given accuracy in the shortest average time, so the brain would be doing the provably optimal thing.

The model's reach is now far wider than perception, being applied to memory, value-based choice and clinical populations, which is both its strength and a standing caution, since a flexible model that fits everything tests nothing.


36.3.2 Lateral intraparietal and premotor accumulation signals

The lateral intraparietal area (LIP) is a patch of parietal cortex whose neurons carry signals about where an eye movement is about to go.

In the random dot motion task, in which a monkey watches a cloud of dots of which some fraction move coherently and reports the direction with an eye movement, Michael Shadlen, William Newsome, Joshua Gold, Roozbeh Kiani and colleagues found LIP neurons whose firing rate climbs gradually during the viewing period.

The climb is steeper when the motion is stronger, it predicts which choice the animal will make and how long it will take, and firing reaches a roughly common level just before the movement regardless of difficulty, which is what a threshold crossing should look like.

Similar accumulation signals have been reported in frontal eye field, superior colliculus, dorsal premotor cortex and caudate, suggesting that accumulation is distributed across the sensorimotor circuit rather than housed in one area.

An important challenge came from Kenneth Latimer, Jonathan Pillow and colleagues in Science in 2015, who argued that in about three quarters of LIP neurons the single-trial spike trains are better described by an abrupt discrete step at a random time than by gradual ramping, with smooth ramps appearing only when trials are averaged.

Shadlen and Newsome disputed the dataset and the model comparison, Latimer and Pillow rebutted, and the exchange remains unresolved, so it is honest to say that the population-average ramp is well established while the single-trial dynamics underlying it are not.

Causal evidence is also mixed: inactivating LIP degrades decisions less than the recording results predict, in some studies barely at all, which points toward redundancy across the network.


36.3.3 Speed-accuracy trade-off and boundary setting

Everyone knows that hurrying costs accuracy, and the accumulation framework explains why with a single knob.

Raising the boundary separation demands more net evidence, which yields slower and more accurate decisions; lowering it yields faster and sloppier ones.

Model fits confirm that when people are instructed to emphasise speed the boundary parameter moves while the drift rate, which reflects the quality of the sensory evidence, stays roughly constant - which is the theoretically clean result, since instructions should change strategy, not eyesight.

Physiologically, speed emphasis appears to work partly by raising baseline activity in the decision circuits so that less accumulated evidence is needed to reach threshold, and human work by Birte Forstmann, Ratcliff and colleagues has linked speed emphasis to activity in pre-supplementary motor area and striatum, and to the strength of their connection.

This is a rare case where an abstract model parameter has a fairly direct biological interpretation.


36.3.4 Urgency, collapsing bounds, and alternatives to accumulation

The standard DDM assumes a fixed boundary, which implies that after long deliberation the observer still waits for the same amount of evidence - an odd policy when time is costly.

Two related alternatives address this: collapsing bounds, where the threshold falls as time passes, and the urgency gating model of Paul Cisek, David Thura and colleagues, in which a growing urgency signal multiplies the evidence rather than adding to it, and the evidence itself is leaky rather than perfectly integrated.

These make a genuinely different claim, because under urgency gating the system is largely tracking current evidence rather than accumulating its history, and Thura and Cisek reported dorsal premotor and primary motor activity consistent with that during a task where evidence changed within a trial.

The empirical verdict is mixed and honestly contested.

Reanalyses by Gaurav Hawkins, Ratcliff, Philip Smith and others found that fixed bounds fit most standard human datasets at least as well, that collapsing bounds show a clear advantage mainly under specific task demands such as deadlines or non-stationary evidence, and that the two model families are hard to tell apart because their parameters trade off badly.

The reasonable position is that the brain probably does apply time-dependent pressure to commit, that this pressure is more visible in some tasks than others, and that no single existing model has won.


36.4 Confidence and perceptual awareness

A decision system that produces answers without any grading of how good they are cannot learn efficiently, cannot know when to seek more information, and cannot know when to defer.

Confidence is that grading, and studying it leads naturally to the harder question of what makes a perception conscious at all.


36.4.1 Decision confidence as a computed quantity

In the accumulation framework, confidence is not a separate feeling bolted on afterward; it falls out of the same quantities that produce the choice.

The natural expression is the balance of evidence at the moment of commitment, combined with how long the commitment took, which is why decisions that are fast and lopsided feel certain and decisions that are slow and close feel shaky.

Roozbeh Kiani and Michael Shadlen tested this in Science in 2009 by giving monkeys an escape option on some trials - a small guaranteed reward for opting out instead of guessing.

Monkeys opted out most on the hardest trials, and were more accurate on trials where the option was available but declined, which shows the animal had graded access to the quality of its own evidence.

Critically, LIP firing rates on opt-out trials sat in the intermediate band predicted by the model, so the same neurons that formed the decision also carried the information needed to grade it.

Later work by Adam Kepecs, Zachary Mainen and colleagues found analogous confidence correlates in rodent orbitofrontal cortex, indicating that this is not a primate speciality.


36.4.2 Metacognitive sensitivity and its measures

Metacognition means cognition about cognition, and metacognitive sensitivity means the degree to which a person's confidence ratings actually track whether they were right.

Measuring it is harder than it sounds, because raw confidence is contaminated by two nuisances: overall task performance, since it is easier to know you are right when the task is easy, and response bias, since some people simply prefer high numbers.

Brian Maniscalco and Hakwan Lau solved much of this in 2012 with meta-d prime, defined as the first-order sensitivity that an ideal observer would need in order to produce the confidence pattern actually observed, expressed in the same units as first-order performance.

The ratio of meta-d prime to d prime, called the M-ratio or metacognitive efficiency, then gives a bias-free score in which one means confidence exploits all available information, below one means information is being thrown away, and above one is anomalous and usually signals a violated assumption.

Stephen Fleming and colleagues used such measures to show that metacognitive ability varies widely between people, that it is dissociable from task performance, and that it correlates with grey matter volume and connectivity in anterior prefrontal cortex, with lesion and stimulation studies giving converging but not unanimous support.

Later work by Fleming, Lau and others also indicates that metacognitive efficiency is partly domain-specific, so being well calibrated about perception does not guarantee being well calibrated about memory.


36.4.3 Blindsight and unconscious perception

Blindsight is the condition in which damage to primary visual cortex (V1) produces a region of clinical blindness in which the patient nonetheless performs above chance on forced-choice tests, while denying any visual experience.

Lawrence Weiskrantz and colleagues established the phenomenon from the 1970s onward, most famously with patients DB and GY, who could guess the location, orientation, motion direction and sometimes the emotional expression of stimuli they insisted they could not see.

The presumed anatomical basis is the set of pathways that bypass V1, particularly the route from the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to motion area MT, and diffusion imaging work has found that patients with V1 damage who show blindsight tend to have those connections intact while those without it do not.

The interpretation is genuinely contested.

The strong reading is that blindsight demonstrates perception without consciousness, and it has been used as a foundation stone by higher-order theories of consciousness.

The sceptical reading, argued in detail by Ian Phillips and others, is that patients may retain weak but genuine conscious experience which they decline to report because the experience does not resemble normal seeing and because forced-choice instructions and report criteria differ between the tasks that show sensitivity and the tasks that assess awareness.

Also relevant is that some patients show measurable islands of spared V1 tissue, so a residual-cortex explanation cannot be excluded case by case, and the field's current position is best described as unsettled rather than resolved in either direction.


36.4.4 Bistable perception as a probe of awareness

Bistable stimuli hold the physical input constant while the percept flips, which is exactly the experimental leverage consciousness research needs, because any brain activity that flips with the percept cannot be explained by the stimulus.

Binocular rivalry is the classic case: present a face to one eye and a house to the other and the observer sees them alternate every few seconds rather than seeing a blend.

Nikos Logothetis and colleagues recorded from monkeys during rivalry and found that only a minority of neurons in early visual cortex followed the reported percept, whereas in inferotemporal cortex the great majority did, implying that the competition is resolved progressively up the hierarchy rather than at one site.

A serious confound then surfaced: if observers press a button to report each flip, activity in frontal and parietal cortex may reflect the reporting, the monitoring and the motor act rather than the experience.

No-report paradigms, developed by Naotsugu Tsuchiya, Christof Koch, Melanie Wilke and colleagues, infer the percept instead from optokinetic eye movements or pupil size, and typically find frontal activation much reduced while the posterior activity survives.

This has become a central battleground between the two leading theories of consciousness, since global workspace accounts assign prefrontal cortex a constitutive role while integrated information and recurrent processing accounts locate the content posteriorly.

The adversarial collaboration organised by the Cogitate consortium, first circulated as a preprint in 2023 and published in Nature in 2025, tested both theories on preregistered predictions and produced results that challenged specific predictions of each and vindicated neither, which is the appropriate state of play to report.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The brain merges the senses according to intelligible rules: enhancement when signals coincide in space and time, largest proportional gain when signals are individually weak, weighting by reliability, and a prior inference about whether the signals share a cause at all - with cross-modal illusions such as ventriloquism, McGurk and the sound-induced flash being those rules misfiring rather than the system breaking.

Timing is handled by a tolerant and continuously recalibrated binding window, and self-generated sensation is separately predicted and attenuated by forward models built from efference copy.

Perception ends in commitment, and the accumulation-to-bound framework, formalised by Ratcliff and given a neural correlate in parietal and premotor ramping signals, explains choices and reaction times together and gives the speed-accuracy trade-off a concrete parameter.

That framework is well supported at the population level but faces two live challenges: whether single-trial dynamics ramp or step, and whether bounds are fixed or subject to urgency, neither of which is settled.

Confidence emerges from the same accumulation quantities and can be measured cleanly with meta-d prime, but the deeper question of what makes a percept conscious remains open, with blindsight and no-report bistable perception both admitting more than one honest reading.


PART SIX. ATTENTION: THE ALLOCATION OF LIMITED RESOURCES


CHAPTER 37. THE FORMS OF SELECTION (CORE)

At every waking moment the senses deliver far more information than the brain can fully analyse, and so the brain must choose.

Attention is the name we give to that choosing - the set of mechanisms that decide which parts of the incoming flood get deep processing, and which get only a cursory glance or none at all.

This chapter lays out the basic vocabulary of attention research: the kinds of attention psychologists distinguish, the classic arguments about where in the processing stream selection happens, the ways attention is organised in time as well as space, and the hard limits that make attention necessary in the first place.

It matters because almost every later topic in cognition - memory encoding, decision making, conscious awareness, the clinical disorders of neglect and distractibility - is built on top of these mechanisms.

The aim is not to memorise a list of terms but to see why each distinction was invented, what experiment forced it, and where the field still disagrees.


37.1 Taxonomies of attention

Researchers have carved attention up in several different ways, and the divisions cut across each other rather than nesting neatly.

One set of divisions concerns what the person is being asked to do - focus on one thing, juggle several, or keep watch over a long stretch of time.

Another set concerns what kind of thing is being selected - a place, a property, or a whole object.

A third concerns what drives the selection - the world grabbing you, or you deciding.

A fourth concerns whether the eyes move or stay still.

Keeping these axes separate is the first real skill in this literature, because a single experiment usually sits at the intersection of several of them.


37.1.1 Selective, divided, and sustained attention

Selective attention is the case where one stream is prioritised and the rest are suppressed, as when you follow one voice at a noisy party - the situation Colin Cherry named the cocktail party problem in 1953.

Divided attention is the case where two or more streams must be handled at once, and the reliable finding is that performance on each degrades relative to doing it alone, which is the everyday evidence that some resource is genuinely limited.

Sustained attention, also called vigilance (the ability to maintain readiness to detect rare signals over a long period), was first studied systematically by Norman Mackworth during the Second World War, using a clock with a jumping hand to model the radar operator's task.

Mackworth found the vigilance decrement - detection accuracy falls measurably within the first half hour on watch - and Raja Parasuraman and D. R. Davies proposed in 1977 a vigilance taxonomy predicting that the size and speed of that decline depend on the task's event rate, its memory demands, and whether the observer must compare a signal against a remembered standard.

Modern work ties the decrement to the rise of task-unrelated thought, or mind wandering, as much as to any simple depletion of a fuel-like resource, and a 2025 Frontiers in Cognition review marking seventy-five years of the phenomenon reports that no single explanation has yet won the field.


37.1.2 Spatial, feature-based, and object-based selection

Spatial selection means prioritising a region of the visual field, and it is the most studied form because it is the easiest to manipulate: cue a location, and targets there are detected faster.

Feature-based selection means prioritising a property, such as the colour red or upward motion, and its signature is that the benefit is global - Stefan Treue and Julio Martinez-Trujillo showed in monkey area MT (the middle temporal area, a motion-sensitive region) in 1999 that attending to a direction of motion at one location enhances neurons tuned to that direction across the whole visual field, including at unattended places.

Object-based selection means that once attention lands on part of an object, it tends to spread to the rest of that object, even to parts no closer in space.

The demonstration is the double-rectangle cueing task of Robert Egly, Jon Driver, and Robert Rafal in 1994: two long rectangles, a cue at one end, and targets that are equally far from the cue are detected faster when they fall inside the cued rectangle than inside the other one.

These three forms are not rivals; the current consensus is that space, feature, and object constraints interact to organise a scene, and that the object effect may itself partly reflect feature spreading within the object's boundaries.


37.1.3 Exogenous and endogenous control

Exogenous attention is stimulus-driven and reflexive - a sudden flash, a looming shape, or an abrupt onset in the periphery pulls attention to itself whether you want it to or not.

Endogenous attention is goal-driven and voluntary - you decide, on the basis of an instruction or a plan, to attend to the left side of the screen or to listen for your own name.

The two behave differently in time: exogenous capture rises within roughly a hundred milliseconds and then decays, often reversing into inhibition of return (a slowing of responses back to a recently attended location, described by Michael Posner and Yoav Cohen in 1984), while endogenous orienting builds more slowly over several hundred milliseconds and can be held indefinitely.

They also appear to lean on partly different circuitry: Maurizio Corbetta and Gordon Shulman argued in 2002 for a dorsal frontoparietal network, including the intraparietal sulcus and frontal eye fields, that carries voluntary goals, and a more right-lateralised ventral network, including the temporoparietal junction, that interrupts with salient or unexpected events.

The clean two-network story has been challenged - the networks overlap heavily and the ventral system responds to task relevance and not merely to physical salience - so it is best read as a useful organising claim rather than a settled anatomy.


37.1.4 Overt and covert orienting
