Overt orienting means moving the sensory apparatus itself, most obviously by making a saccade (a rapid ballistic eye movement) so that the region of interest falls on the fovea, the high-resolution centre of the retina.

Covert orienting means prioritising a location without moving the eyes at all, and Posner's demonstration in the late 1970s that a peripheral or central cue speeds detection at the cued location while fixation is held is the founding experiment of modern attention research.

The two are tightly linked: the premotor theory of attention, put forward by Giacomo Rizzolatti and colleagues in 1987, holds that covert attention just is the preparation of an eye movement that is not executed, and shifting attention and preparing a saccade do recruit largely overlapping frontal and parietal regions.

The strong version of that identity is disputed, however, because covert attention can be directed to a location while a saccade is being prepared elsewhere, and multivariate analyses of frontoparietal activity can decode whether the eyes actually moved, which implies the two are not encoded identically.


37.2 Classical theoretical debates

Much of twentieth-century attention research was organised around one question: how far does unattended information get before it is discarded?

The answers hardened into camps, and the camps generated the experiments.

The eventual resolution was less a victory for either side than a reframing, in which the question of where selection happens gave way to the question of what determines where it happens, and then to a neural account in which selection is not a gate at all but the outcome of competition.


37.2.1 Early against late selection

Donald Broadbent's filter model of 1958 was the first explicit answer: a filter early in processing lets one channel through on the basis of physical properties alone - which ear, what pitch, what location - and the rejected channel is never analysed for meaning.

The evidence against a hard early filter came from the unattended ear, where listeners in dichotic listening tasks (different messages played to each ear) sometimes noticed their own name, a finding usually credited to Neville Moray in 1959.

Anne Treisman's attenuation model of 1964 kept the filter but softened it: the unattended channel is turned down rather than switched off, and words with low thresholds, such as one's own name, can still get through to a recognition stage.

J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch argued in 1963 for late selection - everything is analysed for meaning, and selection happens only afterwards, at the point of response or memory.

No decisive experiment settled this, and that stalemate is itself the important historical fact, because it pushed the field toward theories in which the locus of selection is not fixed.


37.2.2 Load theory and the flexibility of the locus

Nilli Lavie's load theory, developed from the mid-1990s, proposed that both camps were right under different conditions.

Perception, on this account, has a fixed capacity that is used involuntarily: if the relevant task has low perceptual load, spare capacity spills over onto irrelevant distractors and they are processed, which looks like late selection; if the task has high perceptual load, capacity is exhausted by the relevant items and distractors get no processing at all, which looks like early selection.

Load theory makes the counterintuitive and well-replicated prediction that making a task harder perceptually can reduce distraction, and it also predicts the opposite for working memory load, where occupying the memory system impairs the control needed to keep distractors out.

Related work found that under high perceptual load only about a tenth of observers noticed an unexpected shape, against more than half under low load, tying the theory directly to failures of awareness.

The theory is genuinely contested: critics including Yehoshua Tsal and Hanna Benoni have argued that perceptual load is defined circularly, that it is confounded with the spatial spread of attention, and that some studies find distractor interference at both high and low load, with an attentional zoom account offering a rival explanation of the same data.


37.2.3 Attention as a spotlight, zoom lens, or gradient

The spotlight metaphor, associated with Posner, treats attention as a beam of fixed size that moves across the visual field and enhances whatever falls inside it.

Charles Eriksen and James St. James replaced this in 1986 with the zoom lens, in which a fixed pool of resource can be concentrated on a small region for high benefit or spread over a large one for a diluted benefit, predicting an inverse relation between the size of the attended region and the size of the processing advantage.

Behavioural and neuroimaging work supports the zoom lens: functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a method that images blood-oxygen changes as a proxy for neural activity) shows that activity in retinotopically mapped early visual cortex tracks the cued region's size before the stimulus even appears, and accuracy falls as the region widens.

Gradient accounts go further and deny any sharp boundary, holding that enhancement falls off smoothly with distance from the focus, and there is evidence that attention can be split between two non-contiguous locations, which no simple single-beam metaphor accommodates.

All three should be treated as descriptions of behaviour rather than as claims about a literal mechanism, since none of them specifies what the beam is made of.


37.2.4 Biased competition as the integrating framework

Robert Desimone and John Duncan's biased competition account of 1995 dispensed with the beam entirely.

Its claim is that objects in a scene automatically compete for representation, because neurons in visual areas such as V4 and inferotemporal cortex have large receptive fields (the region of space a neuron responds to) that contain several objects at once, and those objects mutually suppress each other's neural responses.

The signature finding, from single-neuron recordings in monkeys by Desimone, Jeffrey Moran, Sabine Kastner and colleagues, is that when two stimuli sit in one receptive field the neuron's response is intermediate between the responses to each alone - and that attending to the preferred one pulls the response back up toward the level it would have shown had that stimulus been presented by itself.

Attention on this view is not an extra process added to perception but a bias applied to a competition that was happening anyway, and the bias can come from top-down goals, from stimulus salience, or from recent experience.

The framework absorbs the earlier debates gracefully - spatial, feature-based and object-based effects are all just different sources of bias, and the early-versus-late question dissolves because competition occurs at every level of the hierarchy at once.


37.3 Attention in time

Attention is usually taught as a spatial phenomenon, but the same selective logic applies to moments.

Knowing when something will happen is as useful as knowing where, and the brain exploits temporal structure aggressively.

More radically, a body of recent work argues that attention is not a steady searchlight at all but something that pulses, sampling the world several times a second.


37.3.1 Temporal orienting and rhythmic expectation

Temporal orienting is the use of cues or regularities to prepare for a particular moment, and Anna Christina Nobre and colleagues showed from the late 1990s that a symbolic cue predicting when a target will appear speeds responses much as a spatial cue speeds them for where.

Even without an explicit cue, the variable foreperiod effect appears: as time passes without the target, its conditional probability of appearing now rises - the hazard function - and reaction times shorten accordingly.

Mari Riess Jones's dynamic attending theory, from 1976 onward, proposes that attention is an internal oscillation that can entrain (align its phase) to an external rhythm, so that peaks of attentional readiness coincide with expected event times.

Neural entrainment gives this a mechanism: low-frequency cortical activity aligns to a rhythmic stream, and targets arriving at the expected phase are processed with higher neural gain, as reported by Nobre's group and others in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2019.

A caution is warranted: some apparent entrainment effects can be produced by the stimulus-evoked response itself rather than by a true internal oscillator, and distinguishing the two remains methodologically hard.


37.3.2 The attentional blink and psychological refractory period

The attentional blink, reported by Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell in 1992, appears when items stream past at about ten per second and the observer must report two targets: if the second target follows the first by roughly two hundred to five hundred milliseconds, it is often missed entirely, while at shorter and longer lags it is reported normally.

The psychological refractory period, characterised by Harold Pashler in the 1980s and 1990s, is the speeded-response analogue: give two tasks in quick succession and the response to the second is delayed in proportion to how soon it followed the first.

Pashler's central bottleneck model explains this by dividing each task into perceptual, central response-selection, and motor stages, with the first and last able to run in parallel across tasks but the central stage able to handle only one task at a time.

Whether the two phenomena share a mechanism is disputed: Marois, Dehaene and colleagues reported in 2011 evidence for a shared cortical bottleneck in frontal and parietal regions, and cross-modal designs can elicit both effects within one paradigm, while other work argues that configural and featural processing can continue during the blink and so no single central bottleneck can be responsible.


37.3.3 Rhythmic sampling and discrete attention

The discrete sampling hypothesis holds that attention does not enhance a location continuously but visits it in pulses locked to ongoing brain rhythms.

Ian Fiebelkorn, Sabine Kastner and colleagues, and independently Rufin VanRullen and collaborators, have shown that when a location is cued and attention is held there, detection performance nonetheless oscillates at roughly four to eight cycles per second, the theta band.

Fiebelkorn and Kastner's rhythmic theory of attention, set out in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2019, proposes that each theta cycle alternates between a sampling state, in which sensory processing at the attended location is enhanced, and a shifting state, in which the system is disengaged and biased toward moving attention or the eyes elsewhere - which would make the rhythm a built-in solution to the trade-off between exploiting one location and exploring others.

VanRullen distinguishes two rhythms, an alpha rhythm near ten cycles per second governing sensory excitability and a theta rhythm near seven governing attentional selection.

The claim is contested on statistical grounds - Brookshire argued in 2022 that many behavioural oscillation findings do not survive rigorous correction for multiple comparisons - and defenders reply that the electrophysiological and single-neuron evidence stands independently of the behavioural time courses.


37.3.4 Temporal receptive windows

A temporal receptive window is the stretch of past input that can influence a region's current response, the time analogue of a spatial receptive field.

Uri Hasson, Eunice Yang, Ignacio Vallines, David Heeger and Nava Rubin established the concept in 2008 by showing observers films that were intact, reversed, or scrambled into pieces of different lengths, and asking which brain regions still responded reliably.

Early visual areas such as primary visual cortex and the motion area MT+ responded reliably whatever the temporal scrambling, because they care only about the last fraction of a second, whereas regions higher in the hierarchy - the superior temporal sulcus, precuneus, and temporoparietal junction - lost their reliability once the ordering over tens of seconds was destroyed.

Later work using narrated stories mapped this as a topographic gradient with windows of roughly four, twelve, and thirty-six seconds at successive levels.

The relevance to attention is that selection must operate at whatever timescale a region integrates over, so what counts as one attended event differs radically between early sensory cortex and association cortex.


37.4 The limits of attention

Attention exists because capacity is finite, and the most instructive experiments are the ones that make the finitude visible.

The failures are not rare pathologies but ordinary features of healthy perception, which is why they are so unsettling to encounter.


37.4.1 Inattentional blindness and change blindness

Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a fully visible, unexpected object because attention is committed elsewhere, documented at length by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock in 1998 and made famous by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris in 1999, whose observers counted basketball passes and about half of them failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk through the middle of the display.

Change blindness is the related failure to detect a large alteration to a scene when the change coincides with a disruption such as a blank frame, an eye movement, or a cut in a film - Ronald Rensink, Kevin O'Regan and James Clark's flicker paradigm of 1997 is the standard demonstration.

The two are distinct: inattentional blindness concerns missing something present, change blindness concerns missing a difference between two views, and change blindness requires a comparison against memory.

Together they support the claim that we represent in detail only what attention has touched, and that the vivid impression of a complete visual world is partly a construction.

The strong reading - that unattended items are not represented at all - is disputed, since indirect measures sometimes show effects of stimuli the observer denies seeing.


37.4.2 Capacity limits and their candidate causes

Estimates converge on a very small number of items that can be held in the focus of attention at once, with Nelson Cowan's 2001 review arguing for about four chunks in adults, close to independent estimates for visual selective attention.

There is a live theoretical dispute about what produces this number.

Slot models hold that there is a small fixed set of discrete storage places, each holding one item at fixed resolution; resource models hold that a continuous pool is divided among however many items are attended, so that precision degrades smoothly rather than items dropping out.

A third line, exemplified by work grounding these concepts in neural dynamics, argues that both are descriptions of an underlying competitive network in which mutual inhibition between item representations sets the limit, which would make the slot-versus-resource question a modelling choice rather than a fact about the brain.

Divisive normalisation - the well-documented operation in which a neuron's response is divided by the summed activity of its neighbours - offers a concrete implementation of that competition and has been used by John Reynolds and David Heeger in their 2009 normalisation model of attention to predict when attention multiplies a neuron's gain and when it instead sharpens its tuning.


37.4.3 Dual-task interference and central bottlenecks

When two tasks must be done at once, performance falls, and the theoretical question is whether this reflects a structural bottleneck that can process only one thing at a time or a graded resource that can be shared unevenly.

Pashler's bottleneck account locates the constraint specifically at response selection - deciding which action goes with which stimulus - and predicts the characteristic pattern in which lengthening the first task's central stage delays the second response one for one.

Rival capacity-sharing models, developed by Eric Ruthruff, James Johnston, Rico Fischer and others, hold that central processing can be shared between tasks, with the apparent bottleneck emerging from a strategic choice to prioritise one task rather than from a hard structural limit.

Practice matters to the debate: with extensive training the psychological refractory period effect can shrink dramatically and in some reports nearly vanish, which is easier for capacity-sharing than for a fixed structural bottleneck, though defenders reply that training may simply shorten the bottleneck stage rather than remove it.

The practical upshot is unambiguous even where the theory is not - concurrent tasks that both require decisions interfere severely, which is the basis of the evidence on driving while conversing.


37.4.4 Attention against awareness as separable constructs

For most of the twentieth century attention and consciousness were treated as effectively the same thing, on the reasoning that you are aware of what you attend to and unaware of what you do not.

Christof Koch and Naotsugu Tsuchiya argued in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2007 for a double dissociation: observers can be conscious of the gist of a scene or of an isolated object with little or no top-down attention, and can direct attention to stimuli rendered invisible by masking or binocular rivalry, so that attention influences processing without producing awareness.

They added the sharper prediction that attention and awareness can have opposite effects on the same measure, and later work by Tsuchiya, Maier and others has continued to report evidence for separable neural signatures.

The claim is contested: a substantial camp, including Dehaene, Cohen, and Prinz, holds that the dissociation runs only one way - attention without awareness is possible, but awareness without at least some attention is not - and reads the gist and iconic-memory findings as involving diffuse attention rather than none.

The disagreement is not merely verbal, because global workspace theories of consciousness make attention the gateway to awareness while integrated information and recurrent-processing theories do not, so the experiments bear directly on which theory of consciousness survives.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Attention is not one thing but a family of selection mechanisms, distinguished by what they select - place, feature, or object - by what drives them, endogenous goals or exogenous salience, and by whether the eyes move.

The historical debate over early against late selection was not won outright by either camp; load theory reframed it as a question of when capacity runs out, and biased competition reframed it again by making selection the outcome of ongoing competition among neural representations rather than the action of a gate.

Attention operates in time as well as space, through temporal orienting to expected moments, through bottlenecks such as the attentional blink and the psychological refractory period, and possibly through theta-rhythmic sampling, though the strength of the behavioural evidence for rhythmic sampling remains disputed.

The limits are real and demonstrable - inattentional blindness, change blindness, a focus of roughly four items, and severe dual-task interference - even where their causes are still argued over in terms of slots, resources, or competitive neural dynamics.

Finally, attention and awareness are probably separable, but how far is the single most contested question in this area, and it is entangled with the choice among competing theories of consciousness.


CHAPTER 38. MECHANISMS AND NETWORKS OF ATTENTION (CORE)

The brain receives far more information than it can fully process, so it must choose.

This chapter is about how that choosing is physically done - what changes in a single nerve cell when you attend to something, what changes in the rhythms of whole populations of cells, which brain regions issue the instruction to attend, and how the brain builds an internal map ranking what deserves attention next.

The material matters because attention is not a vague mental effort but a set of measurable operations, and those operations are the ones that fail in conditions ranging from stroke-induced neglect to attention deficit disorders.

We will move from the smallest scale to the largest: single-cell gain, population rhythms, large-scale networks, and finally the priority map that ties them together.

Throughout, note the distinction between a source of attention (a region that issues the control signal) and a site of attention (a region whose activity is modulated by that signal).


38.1 Neural signatures of selection

A signature of selection is a measurable change in neural activity that appears when a stimulus is attended and disappears when it is not, with the physical stimulus held constant.

This experimental logic - hold the image on the screen identical, change only where the animal or person is instructed to attend - is what makes attention research tractable.

The signatures below were mostly discovered by recording from single neurons in the visual cortex of macaque monkeys trained to attend covertly, meaning attending to a location without moving the eyes there.

Each signature is a different answer to the question of what "paying attention" actually does to a cell.


38.1.1 Gain modulation of sensory responses

Gain means the strength of a neuron's response to its preferred stimulus, roughly its volume knob.

McAdams and Maunsell (1999), recording in visual area V4 - a mid-level region of the monkey visual cortex that responds to shape and colour - found that attending to a stimulus inside a neuron's receptive field raised its firing rate by a median of about twenty-six percent, while leaving the neuron's orientation tuning curve the same shape.

That is multiplicative gain: the whole response profile is scaled up, so the cell fires more without changing what it is selective for - the volume goes up but the station does not change.

A complication is that attention sometimes looks instead like contrast gain, in which the neuron behaves as though the attended stimulus were physically brighter or higher in contrast, shifting its contrast response curve leftward rather than upward.

Reynolds and Heeger (2009) resolved much of this dispute with the normalization model of attention, which proposes that neurons divide their own drive by the pooled activity of neighbouring neurons; depending on the relative size of the attentional focus and the stimulus, the very same mechanism produces response gain in some conditions and contrast gain in others.

The normalization account is now the standard framework, though its parameters are estimated rather than measured directly, and its universality is still argued.


38.1.2 Receptive field shifts and shrinkage

A receptive field is the patch of the visual world in which a stimulus will make a given neuron respond.

Textbooks once treated receptive fields as fixed properties of a cell, but attention deforms them.

Womelsdorf, Anton-Erxleben, Pieper and Treue (2006, 2008), recording in the middle temporal area (MT), a motion-sensitive region of monkey visual cortex, showed that the centre of a receptive field shifts toward the attended location and that the field also shrinks around the attended stimulus.

The functional interpretation is that shrinking the field around the attended item reduces the extent to which nearby distractors contribute to the cell's response, effectively giving the attended stimulus a private line to the neuron.

There is a live disagreement about how important this is: a neural network modelling study by Lindsay, Rigotti and colleagues in eLife (2022) argued that plain gain changes, not receptive field reshaping, are what actually improve task performance, so the shifts may be a consequence of gain rather than an independent mechanism.


38.1.3 Reduction of noise correlations and improved population coding

Neurons are noisy; the same stimulus presented twice produces different spike counts.

A noise correlation is the tendency of two neurons to have their trial-to-trial fluctuations rise and fall together, and it matters because correlated noise cannot be averaged away by pooling across cells, so it puts a ceiling on how much information a population carries.

Cohen and Maunsell (2009), recording simultaneously from many V4 neurons, found that attention reduced these correlations, and their analysis suggested the correlation reduction contributed more to improved behavioural performance than the firing rate increase did.

Mitchell, Sundberg and Reynolds (2009) reported convergent results in the same year.

The strong claim - that decorrelation is the primary mechanism of attention - has since been qualified: Rabinowitz, Goris, Cohen and Simoncelli (2015) argued that much of the apparent decorrelation reflects attention stabilising a shared fluctuating gain signal across the population rather than a change in pairwise coupling as such.

The safe summary is that attention improves the population code, and that both rate increases and reduced shared variability contribute.


38.1.4 Baseline shifts and preparatory activity

Attention acts before anything appears.

Luck, Chelazzi, Hillyard and Desimone (1997) found that when a monkey was cued to attend covertly to a location, neurons in areas V2 and V4 whose receptive fields covered that location raised their spontaneous firing by roughly thirty to forty percent while the screen was still blank; Reynolds, Chelazzi and Desimone (1999) reported similar preparatory increases.

Kastner and colleagues (1999) showed the human counterpart using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that measures blood flow changes as an indirect index of neural activity: merely directing attention to an empty location raised the baseline signal in the corresponding part of visual cortex before any stimulus was shown.

These baseline shifts are the neural form of readiness, and they matter theoretically because they cannot be explained as a by-product of processing a stimulus - there is no stimulus yet.

Driver and Frith (2000), writing in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, pointed out the awkward implication that the visual cortex can be active in a spatially specific way without any corresponding conscious percept.


38.2 Oscillatory mechanisms

Populations of neurons do not fire steadily; their combined activity waxes and wanes in rhythms of characteristic frequency, measurable with electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical rhythms from the scalp, and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which records the associated magnetic fields.

Frequency bands are named by convention: alpha is roughly eight to thirteen cycles per second (hertz, Hz), theta is roughly four to eight hertz, beta roughly fifteen to thirty hertz, and gamma roughly thirty to ninety hertz.

The oscillatory account of attention holds that these rhythms are not epiphenomena but the mechanism by which cortex decides which signals get through.

It is an elegant family of theories with substantial evidence and substantial dispute, and this section will flag both.


38.2.1 Alpha lateralisation and functional inhibition

When you covertly attend to your left, alpha power drops over the right posterior scalp - the hemisphere that processes the left visual field - and rises over the left, a pattern called alpha lateralisation, first clearly demonstrated by Worden and colleagues (2000) and extended by Thut and colleagues (2006).

Jensen and Mazaheri (2010) built this into the gating-by-inhibition framework: alpha represents pulsed inhibition, in which each cycle of the rhythm briefly suppresses processing, so high alpha over a cortical region means that region is being functionally silenced, and information is thereby routed to the regions where alpha is low.

The framework is attractive because it makes selection a matter of blocking the irrelevant rather than only boosting the relevant.

It is contested, however: Foster and Awh (2019) argued that increased alpha ipsilateral to the target may be a by-product of target selection rather than active distractor suppression, while van Diepen, Foxe and Mazaheri (2019) and Wang and colleagues (2019) reported alpha modulations that track anticipated distractor locations independently of target location.

Whether alpha causes suppression or merely accompanies it remains open, and the best current evidence comes from causal methods such as rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which delivers magnetic pulses through the skull to perturb cortical activity.


38.2.2 Gamma synchronisation and selective routing

Fries proposed communication through coherence (CTC), the idea that two neuronal groups exchange information effectively only when their rhythms are aligned, so that spikes from the sender arrive during the receiver's window of high excitability.

On this account attention works by synchronising the sending population that carries the attended stimulus with its target area, leaving the unattended population's messages arriving at the wrong phase and therefore ignored.

Bosman, Fries and colleagues (2012) provided the key evidence: recording from monkey V1 and V4 with two stimuli present, they found that gamma-band influence from V1 to V4 was carried almost exclusively by the rhythm induced by the attended stimulus.

Later work established a division of labour by frequency - Bastos, Fries and colleagues (2015) and Michalareas and colleagues (2016) showed that gamma predominantly carries feedforward influence from lower to higher areas, while alpha and beta carry feedback in the opposite direction.

Critics note that gamma is not always present, varies with stimulus properties, and may in some cases reflect rather than implement effective connectivity; a 2025 review by Fries and colleagues on brain rhythms in cognition treats these as open controversies rather than settled points.


38.2.3 Theta-rhythmic sampling of attended locations

Attention is often described as a spotlight held steadily on a location, but a body of work suggests it flickers.

Landau and Fries (2012) and Fiebelkorn, Saalmann and Kastner (2013) showed that after a single attention-resetting cue, detection performance for a target waxes and wanes over time at roughly four to eight hertz, and that when two objects are monitored the two sample in alternation.

Fiebelkorn and Kastner (2019) proposed a rhythmic theory of attention in which theta rhythms in the frontoparietal attention network organise activity into alternating states, one favouring sampling at the current location and the other favouring the possibility of switching elsewhere, which would make periodic disengagement a design feature rather than a lapse.

The behavioural evidence has been seriously challenged: Brookshire (2022), in Nature Human Behaviour, showed by simulation that the standard analyses generate false positives when the data contain aperiodic temporal structure, and found no reliable behavioural rhythms in published datasets once that was controlled.

Fiebelkorn and others replied that the neural evidence from direct recordings stands independently of the behavioural analyses, and subsequent work has proposed more sensitive variants of Brookshire's method; the topic should be presented to learners as genuinely unresolved.


38.2.4 Pulvinar and thalamic contributions to cortical coordination

The thalamus is a central relay structure, and the pulvinar is its largest nucleus, extensively interconnected with visual and parietal cortex.

The classical view treated the thalamus as a passive relay, but Saalmann, Pinsk, Wang, Li and Kastner (2012), recording simultaneously from pulvinar, V4 and area TEO in monkeys performing an attention task, found that the pulvinar synchronised activity between the two cortical areas according to where attention was allocated, with effects prominent in the alpha band.

Because the pulvinar has few direct sensory inputs but massive reciprocal cortical connections, it is well placed to act as a coordinator of cortico-cortical communication rather than a conduit for sensory data.

Human evidence is thinner because the pulvinar is small and deep, though patients with pulvinar lesions show attentional deficits, and high-field fMRI is beginning to resolve thalamic nuclei.

The wider claim - that the thalamus regulates which cortical conversations happen - is now taken seriously across systems neuroscience.


38.3 Attentional control networks

Beyond individual regions, attention depends on distributed networks, meaning sets of areas whose activity is correlated and which are recruited together by particular task demands.

Much of what we know comes from human neuroimaging, supplemented by lesion studies and by causal perturbation in monkeys.

The key organising insight of the last quarter century is that voluntary orienting and involuntary reorienting rely on partly separate systems.


38.3.1 The dorsal frontoparietal network and top-down control

Corbetta and Shulman (2002), in a highly influential review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, identified a dorsal attention network (DAN) comprising the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) - a groove in the parietal lobe - and the frontal eye fields (FEF), a region of frontal cortex that controls gaze.

This network is engaged by cues telling you where or what to attend, and it is active during the interval between cue and target, consistent with it generating the top-down signal rather than merely reacting to stimuli.

Top-down here means driven by current goals and expectations rather than by the stimulus itself.

The dorsal network is bilateral and largely symmetric, and its activity biases sensory cortex, producing the baseline shifts and gain changes described in section 38.1.


38.3.2 The ventral attention network and reorienting

The ventral attention network (VAN) comprises the temporoparietal junction (TPJ), where the temporal and parietal lobes meet, and ventral frontal cortex, and in humans it is strongly right-lateralised.

Corbetta and Shulman characterised it as responding to behaviourally relevant but unexpected events - a target appearing where it was not cued - and described the TPJ as a circuit breaker that interrupts the dorsal network's current focus and triggers reorienting.

Supporting the anatomy, damage to right TPJ and neighbouring regions is associated with hemispatial neglect, a condition in which patients fail to attend to the side of space opposite the lesion.

The circuit-breaker metaphor has been questioned: Geng and Vossel (2013) argued that TPJ activity is better described as contextual updating, the general process of revising an internal model of the current situation, which also explains why the same region activates in tasks with no spatial reorienting at all, including reasoning about other people's beliefs.

Recent repetitive TMS work, including Parisi and colleagues (2026), supports the contextual-updating interpretation, though the two accounts overlap rather than strictly compete.


38.3.3 Frontal eye fields, intraparietal sulcus, and superior colliculus as source regions

These three structures are the leading candidates for sources of attentional control signals, and the evidence for each is causal rather than merely correlational.

Moore and Armstrong (2003) applied electrical microstimulation to the monkey FEF at currents below the threshold for triggering an eye movement, and found that responses in V4 to stimuli at the corresponding location were enhanced, exactly as voluntary attention enhances them - a direct demonstration that FEF can be a source and V4 a site.

Cavanaugh and Wurtz (2004) and Müller, Philiastides and Newsome (2005) showed that subthreshold microstimulation of the superior colliculus (SC), a midbrain structure that also controls eye movements, improves visual performance at the corresponding location without moving the eyes.

Lovejoy and Krauzlis (2010) went further by reversibly inactivating the SC with a drug and finding severe deficits in covert selection, and later comparisons suggest SC inactivation impairs attention more profoundly than FEF inactivation.

The lateral intraparietal area (LIP), within the IPS, contributes the parietal component; the striking common theme is that the structures that move the eyes are also the structures that move attention, which is the anatomical basis of the premotor theory of attention.


38.3.4 The salience network and the switching account

Seeley, Menon and colleagues (2007) described a salience network centred on the anterior insula, a region folded within the lateral sulcus, and the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, engaged by stimuli that are personally or physically significant regardless of sensory modality.

Menon and Uddin (2010) proposed that this network detects salient events and then switches control between the central executive network, which supports effortful goal-directed processing, and the default mode network, which is more active during rest and internally directed thought - the triple network model.

Goulden and colleagues (2014) supported the switching claim using dynamic causal modelling, a statistical method for inferring directed influence between regions from imaging data.

Two cautions are warranted for a beginner: the salience network overlaps substantially with the ventral attention network, and the labels come from different research traditions rather than from a demonstrated anatomical distinction; and the anterior insula is engaged by so many tasks that attributing a single function to it risks circularity.


38.4 Priority maps

If attention must choose one location out of many, something in the brain must represent how much each location is worth attending to.

A map, in this technical sense, is a set of neurons arranged so that their positions correspond to positions in space, so that a bump of activity in the map means "here".

Priority map theory is arguably the most successful integrative idea in attention research, because it gives a common currency in which very different influences can be compared.

This section develops the concept, its candidate implementations, and the influences that feed it.


38.4.1 The concept of a priority or saliency map

Koch and Ullman (1985) proposed a saliency map: a single topographic representation combining feature contrasts such as brightness, colour and motion into one measure of how much each location stands out, with attention going to the current peak and then being inhibited so the next peak can be selected.

Itti and Koch (1998, 2001) implemented this computationally, producing models that predict where human observers look in natural images reasonably well.

The term priority map is the modern refinement: salience means bottom-up conspicuousness, that is, standing out because of the physical stimulus, whereas priority combines salience with goal relevance and other factors, so priority rather than salience is what actually determines selection.

Bisley and Mirpour (2019) give the current statement of the concept, emphasising that the peak of the priority map can be read out by the attention system to select a location and by the oculomotor system to aim a saccade, which explains the tight coupling between looking and attending.


38.4.2 Candidate substrates in parietal, frontal, and collicular structures

The best-studied candidate is the lateral intraparietal area (LIP): Bisley and Goldberg, in a long series of studies from 2003 onward, showed that LIP activity tracks both the abrupt onset of a salient distractor and the location of the behaviourally relevant target, and that the peak of LIP activity predicts where attention is deployed.

Falkner, Krishna and Goldberg (2010) showed that surround suppression - activity at one location suppressing activity at nearby locations - sharpens the LIP map, which is what a winner-take-all selection process requires.

The frontal eye fields carry a similar representation with a stronger goal-related component, and the intermediate layers of the superior colliculus carry one biased toward the eventual saccade target.

White, Berg, Kan, Marino, Itti and Munoz (2017) reported the surprising result that superficial superior colliculus neurons encode saliency earlier and more robustly than V1 neurons during free viewing of natural video, which is notable because V1 is a major input to the colliculus.

The reasonable conclusion is that there is no single priority map but a set of interconnected maps in LIP, FEF and SC that constrain one another.


38.4.3 Value-driven and history-driven attentional capture

Anderson, Laurent and Yantis (2011) trained participants to associate particular colours with monetary reward, then ran a search task in which those colours were entirely irrelevant and never rewarded; the previously rewarded colours still captured attention and slowed responses.

This is value-driven attentional capture, and it is important because it fits neither of the traditional categories: the colour is not physically salient, and attending to it is contrary to the participant's goals.

Selection history is the broader category, covering any effect of what you have selected before, including priming from the previous trial and statistical learning of where distractors tend to appear.

Awh, Belopolsky and Theeuwes (2012), in a paper pointedly subtitled a failed theoretical dichotomy, argued that the classic split between bottom-up and top-down control cannot accommodate these findings and should be replaced by a three-way scheme.

A caution: effect sizes in value-driven capture experiments are modest and some replications have been mixed, with a 2025 systematic review of fifty-two experiments concluding the effect is real but strongly task-dependent.


38.4.4 Integrating bottom-up salience, top-down goals, and selection history

The integrated priority map is the synthesis: physical salience, current goals, and selection history are each computed by partly separate processes and then summed into one map, whose peak determines what is selected next.

The scheme's virtue is that it explains why an irrelevant but previously rewarded object, a physically conspicuous flash, and a deliberately sought target can all win selection - they compete in the same currency, so any one can be strongest on a given trial.

It also predicts interactions rather than strict priorities, which is what is generally observed: a highly salient distractor captures attention less when the search goal is sharply specified, and more when it is not.

The framework's main weakness is that it is a description at the computational level rather than a mechanism - it does not by itself say how the three contributions are weighted, or where the weighting is set - and connecting it to the single-cell mechanisms of section 38.1 and the rhythms of section 38.2 is the principal unfinished business of the field.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Attention is implemented in sensory cortex as measurable changes in single neurons - multiplicative gain, receptive fields that shift and shrink toward the attended item, reduced shared variability across the population, and raised baseline firing before any stimulus appears - with divisive normalization the leading unifying account.

At the population scale, attention is accompanied by rhythmic changes: alpha lateralisation that plausibly implements functional inhibition of unattended regions, gamma synchronisation that plausibly routes attended signals between areas, and theta-rhythmic sampling; each of these is well documented as a correlation and each remains genuinely disputed as a mechanism.

Control is exerted by a dorsal frontoparietal network for voluntary orienting and a right-lateralised ventral network for reorienting, with the frontal eye fields, intraparietal sulcus and superior colliculus established as causal sources by microstimulation and inactivation, not merely as correlated sites.

The priority map is the field's integrative idea: a topographic representation in LIP, FEF and SC whose peak selects the next location, and into which physical salience, current goals and selection history all feed.

The most important open problem is the joining of these levels - explaining the network and map findings in terms of the cellular and oscillatory mechanisms that must produce them.


CHAPTER 39. AROUSAL, VIGILANCE, AND EFFORT (CORE)

This chapter is about the fuel supply of thinking rather than the machinery of thinking.

Before a brain can select one thing over another, it has to be awake, alert, and willing to spend something to stay that way.

We will look at arousal - the brain's overall level of activation - and at the small brainstem nuclei that set it, at vigilance - the ability to keep watching for a rare event over a long stretch of time - and at effort, which is the price the brain seems to charge itself for controlled thought.

This matters because most real failures of attention in ordinary life are not failures of knowing what to attend to.

They are failures of staying aroused, staying on watch, or staying willing to pay.

The chapter closes by asking whether attention is a single thing at all, and concludes, honestly, that it probably is not.


39.1 Arousal and its regulation

Arousal is the brain's global readiness setting - how activated and responsive the whole system is, from deep sleep at one end to panic at the other.

It is not a thought, and it is not a decision.

It is a background condition that changes how every other process behaves, in much the same way that the volume knob on an amplifier changes every note without changing the tune.

Arousal is set largely from below, by a handful of small clusters of neurons in the brainstem and basal forebrain that send thin, enormously branched fibres up into almost the entire cortex.

Because those fibres reach nearly everywhere, a few thousand cells can change the operating state of billions.


39.1.1 Ascending arousal systems and cortical state

The ascending arousal system is a collection of small nuclei near the top of the brainstem and in the basal forebrain that release neuromodulators - chemicals that do not carry a specific message so much as change how the cells receiving them respond to every other message.

The main players are the locus coeruleus (Latin for "blue spot", a tiny bilateral nucleus in the pons that is the brain's sole source of cortical noradrenaline, also called norepinephrine), the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that supply acetylcholine, the raphe nuclei that supply serotonin, the dopaminergic midbrain, and histamine and orexin cells in the hypothalamus.

Their joint effect is on what is called cortical state - whether the cortex is sitting in slow, synchronised, large-amplitude waves, as in deep sleep and drowsiness, or in fast, desynchronised, low-amplitude activity, as in alert waking.

A rough and widely repeated division holds that the noradrenaline system tracks global arousal and readiness to switch behaviour, while the acetylcholine system is more tied to focused attention and to sharpening sensory processing, though the two are heavily intertwined and no serious researcher treats the split as clean.

An important correction to the older textbook picture came from Fuller, Saper and colleagues, who reassessed the classical "reticular activating system" account and showed that arousal is not produced by one diffuse reticular core but by several chemically distinct, partly redundant pathways - which is why damage to any single one rarely abolishes wakefulness.


39.1.2 Pupil diameter as an index of arousal and gain

The pupil, the black opening in the middle of the iris, changes size for two reasons: light, and arousal.

If you hold the light constant, the remaining moment-to-moment changes in pupil size track how aroused and engaged the person or animal is, which makes pupillometry - the measurement of pupil size over time - an unusually cheap, non-invasive window onto brain state.

Work by Reimer and colleagues in mice and by Joshi, Li, Kalwani and Gold in monkeys, both published around 2014 and 2016, showed that pupil dilation is closely coupled to desynchronised cortical activity and to firing in the locus coeruleus, with locus coeruleus spikes typically preceding dilation by a few hundred milliseconds.

Pupil size is therefore often used as a proxy for neural gain - gain being the steepness of a neuron's input-output relation, so that high gain means small differences in input produce large differences in output.

The proxy has real limits, and the field says so: Megemont, McBurney-Lin and Yang published a paper in eLife in 2022 titled, bluntly, that pupil diameter is not an accurate real-time readout of locus coeruleus activity, and imaging work by Pfeffer and colleagues in 2022 showed pupil size also tracks the cholinergic basal forebrain, the colliculi, and other nuclei.

The safe statement is that pupil size is a good index of general arousal and a rough, partial index of locus coeruleus activity specifically.


39.1.3 Tonic and phasic locus coeruleus modes

Locus coeruleus neurons fire in two distinguishable ways.

Tonic firing is a slow, steady background rate; phasic firing is a brief burst locked to a meaningful event, such as the target stimulus in a task.

Aston-Jones and Cohen, in an influential 2005 review in the Annual Review of Neuroscience, proposed the adaptive gain theory: at moderate tonic rates, the system produces strong phasic bursts to task-relevant events, which sharpens performance on the task at hand - a state they called exploitation.

At high tonic rates, phasic bursting disappears, the animal becomes distractible and restless, and behaviour shifts toward sampling alternatives - exploration.

The proposed control signal comes from the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortices, which project directly to the locus coeruleus and are thought to monitor whether the current task is still worth doing.

The theory is elegant and has organised two decades of work; it is also still only partly confirmed causally, since selectively driving one mode and not the other in a behaving animal is technically hard, and several groups now argue the locus coeruleus is more modular in its projections than the original "global broadcast" picture assumed.


39.1.4 The inverted-U relation between arousal and performance

The best-known claim in this whole area is that performance improves with arousal up to a point and then declines - an upside-down U shape when performance is plotted against arousal.

It is usually credited to Yerkes and Dodson in 1908, who trained mice on a brightness discrimination using electric shock of varying strength.

The credit is largely misplaced.

Diamond and colleagues in 2007, and a 2024 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences revisiting the curve, point out that Yerkes and Dodson used few animals, never measured physiological arousal, manipulated shock intensity rather than arousal as such, and drew a conclusion restricted to task difficulty; the smooth inverted-U of modern textbooks was projected onto their figure by researchers in the 1950s who substituted "motivation" and "performance" for the original axes.

The honest position is that the inverted-U is a useful summary of a large family of real findings - too little arousal and you are drowsy, too much and you are scattered - but it is not a single measured function with known parameters, and its shape depends on task, skill level, and which arousal measure you use.

The adaptive gain theory of the previous sub-section is attractive partly because it offers a mechanism that would generate an inverted-U, with the peak sitting at the tonic firing rate that best supports phasic bursting.


39.2 Vigilance and sustained attention

Vigilance is the ability to keep watching for a rare, faint, unpredictable signal over a long unbroken period.

It became a research topic for a very practical reason: during the Second World War, British radar operators were missing submarine contacts after only about half an hour on watch, and the Royal Air Force asked psychologists why.

Sustained attention is the broader term for maintaining performance over time, and it turns out to be one of the most fragile capacities the brain has.


39.2.1 The vigilance decrement and its explanations

Norman Mackworth, working on that radar problem in the 1940s, built the Mackworth Clock Test: a pointer stepping regularly around a blank clock face, occasionally making a double step, which the observer had to report.

Detection fell measurably within the first twenty to thirty minutes and kept falling across a two-hour watch, a pattern now called the vigilance decrement.

Two families of explanation compete.

Resource depletion theory, associated with Joel Warm, Raja Parasuraman and William Dember, holds that watching consumes a limited pool of attentional resource that is not replenished fast enough, and points to evidence that vigilance is subjectively stressful and metabolically demanding.

Mindlessness theory, associated with Robertson and with Ariga and Lleras, holds the opposite: the task is monotonous and under-arousing, attention drifts to more interesting internal content, and the decrement is boredom rather than exhaustion.

The critical test is what happens when you make the task harder - resource theory predicts a steeper decrement, mindlessness predicts a shallower one - and the weight of evidence, including work testing the related resource-control account, favours the resource side, though a hybrid position in which understimulation makes disengagement easier is now common.


39.2.2 Mind wandering during sustained tasks

Mind wandering is the occurrence of thought that is unrelated to the task in hand and not deliberately summoned.

It is measured by experience sampling, which simply means interrupting people at random moments and asking what they were just thinking about, and by that measure it occupies a startling fraction of waking life - estimates in the range of a third to a half, depending on the population and method.

Christoff and colleagues, in a 2009 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, combined experience sampling with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and found that reported mind wandering was accompanied by activity in the default mode network - a set of midline and lateral parietal regions more active at rest than during demanding tasks - and, less expectedly, by activity in executive control regions too.

Esterman and colleagues developed the gradual-onset continuous performance task (gradCPT), in which images fade in and out rather than appearing abruptly, precisely so that fluctuations in attention would show up as fluctuations in response-time variability, and used it to describe alternating "in the zone" and "out of the zone" states.

An important complication comes from Kucyi and colleagues, who reported in 2016 that spontaneous default mode network activity predicts behavioural variability even when self-reported mind wandering is statistically controlled - which suggests default mode activity is not simply the signature of a wandering mind.


39.2.3 Local sleep in the waking brain

One of the most striking findings in this area is that sleep is not all-or-none across the brain.

Vyazovskiy, Olcese, Hanlon, Nir, Cirelli and Tononi reported in Nature in 2011 that in sleep-deprived but fully awake, behaving rats, small groups of cortical neurons briefly went "offline" - falling silent for a few hundred milliseconds in the way they do during slow-wave sleep - while the animal continued moving and the overall electroencephalogram (EEG, the recording of electrical activity from the scalp or skull surface) still looked awake.

These off-periods occurred in one cortical area and not another, became more frequent the longer the animal had been awake, and, crucially, predicted behavioural errors on a reaching task when they happened in the relevant motor region.

The finding gives the vigilance decrement and the effects of sleep loss a concrete physical form: performance does not degrade because a global "alertness" quantity falls smoothly, but because patches of cortex intermittently drop out.

Similar local slow-wave intrusions have since been reported in humans using intracranial recordings and in high-density EEG, and the concept has been extended to explain lapses under sleep restriction.

It remains debated how far normal, well-rested lapses of attention share this mechanism, as opposed to being a separate phenomenon that only resembles it.


39.2.4 Individual differences in attentional stability

People differ enormously and reliably in how steadily they can hold performance, and the most sensitive measure of this is not average speed or accuracy but intraindividual variability - the trial-to-trial scatter in one person's response times.

High variability, and especially the presence of occasional very slow responses, is one of the most robust behavioural markers of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), confirmed in a meta-analysis by Kofler and colleagues in 2013 covering more than three hundred studies.

The variability is not constant across conditions: it shrinks with stimulant medication and, in many studies though not all, with faster event rates and with motivating incentives, which argues that it reflects a fluctuating state rather than a fixed deficit.

Neurally, variability has been linked to dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex, and mechanistically to noradrenergic and dopaminergic signalling, but the causal chain is not established and competing accounts, including the local-sleep account above, remain live.


39.3 Effort and its costs

Everyone knows that hard thinking feels like something, and that we avoid it when we can.

Turning that intuition into science means answering three questions: what exactly is being spent, how would we measure it, and why should the brain charge for it at all.

The answers over the last fifteen years have shifted from a simple fuel metaphor to an economic one.


39.3.1 Mental effort as a construct and its measurement

Mental effort is best defined not as a substance but as the intensity of controlled processing recruited above what the task would get automatically.

It is measured three ways, and they do not always agree.

Subjective report uses scales such as the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), a standard questionnaire that asks about mental demand, frustration and so on.

Physiological measures use pupil dilation, which grows reliably with memory load - a finding traced to Kahneman and Beatty in 1966 - and cardiac and cortical indices.

Behavioural-economic measures put effort on a price tag: Kool and colleagues' demand selection task in 2010 showed that people freely choose the easier of two equally rewarded options, and Westbrook, Kool and Braver's cognitive effort discounting paradigm (COGED) in 2013 asks how much money a person will give up to avoid a three-back working memory task in favour of a two-back, holding time constant so that impatience cannot explain the result.

That last control matters, and so does a practical finding reported since: COGED shows good test-retest reliability while the demand selection task often does not, which is a caution against treating "effort avoidance" as one well-measured trait.


39.3.2 Expected value of control and cost-benefit accounts

The dominant modern framework treats control as something the brain buys rather than something it runs out of.

Shenhav, Botvinick and Cohen proposed the expected value of control (EVC) theory in Neuron in 2013: the brain estimates, for each possible allocation of control, the payoff it would produce, the amount of control required, and the intrinsic cost of that control, and allocates control where the net value is highest.

They assign this computation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, a region on the medial wall of the frontal lobe long known to respond to conflict, errors and difficulty, arguing that all of those responses are better read as inputs to a value calculation than as separate functions.

The framework's real explanatory achievement is that it makes effort avoidance rational rather than a defect - if control carries cost, declining to use it when the payoff is small is correct behaviour.

Its weakness is that the cost term is postulated rather than derived, and rival proposals give it different content: an opportunity cost of occupying limited control circuitry, per Kurzban and colleagues in 2013, or a signal protecting the system from committing to unrewarding tasks.


39.3.3 Fatigue, glutamate accumulation, and metabolic accounts

The oldest account of mental fatigue said the brain runs out of fuel, usually glucose, and it does not survive scrutiny: the whole brain uses roughly twenty per cent of the body's energy at rest, and hard thinking raises that total only marginally, far too little to explain how tired an afternoon of concentration makes you.

A more specific metabolic proposal came from Wiehler, Branzoli, Adanyeguh, Mochel and Pessiglione, published in Current Biology in 2022.

They had thirty-nine participants perform either high-demand or low-demand cognitive work across a six-hour day while measuring brain chemistry with magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a non-invasive method that reads concentrations of specific molecules.

The high-demand group ended the day with elevated glutamate - the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter - in the lateral prefrontal cortex, and showed more impulsive, short-horizon economic choices, consistent with the idea that clearing accumulated glutamate is costly and that the fatigue signal exists to force a pause.

This is one study with a modest sample and it should be treated as a promising lead rather than a settled mechanism; the field has not yet produced a strong independent replication, and it sits alongside, not obviously above, the opportunity-cost and value-based accounts.


39.3.4 Motivation, incentives, and the modulation of control

If effort is priced, then anything that changes the perceived benefit should change how much is spent, and it does.

Offering money, or making a task personally consequential, reliably improves sustained attention, reduces response-time variability, and shrinks the vigilance decrement, at least temporarily.

The neurochemistry points at dopamine acting in the striatum, the deep forebrain structure central to reward learning and action selection.

Westbrook, van den Bosch, Määttä, Hofmans, Papadopetraki, Cools and Frank, in Science in 2020, gave participants methylphenidate (a drug that blocks reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline), sulpiride (a dopamine D2 receptor blocker), or placebo, and found that drug effects on willingness to work depended on each person's baseline striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, measured with positron emission tomography.

Modelling of their choice and eye-gaze data suggested dopamine works by amplifying attention to the benefits of working relative to its costs, rather than by reducing the cost itself - a small distinction that matters, because it says motivation changes what the decision looks at, not how much the work hurts.

The baseline-dependence also explains why stimulants help some people's concentration a great deal and others hardly at all.


39.4 Attention as a system-level phenomenon

Having spent the chapter on arousal, vigilance and effort, it is worth stepping back and asking what "attention" names.

The answer that the field is converging on is uncomfortable for textbooks: attention is not a component you could point to, but a description of what happens when limited neural machinery is forced to prioritise.


39.4.1 Attention as an emergent property of competitive dynamics rather than a faculty

Desimone and Duncan set out the biased competition account in the Annual Review of Neuroscience in 1995.

The core idea is that when two stimuli fall inside the receptive field of a single neuron - the patch of the world that neuron responds to - their representations compete, and the neuron's response is a compromise rather than the sum.

Signals from elsewhere, whether bottom-up from stimulus salience or top-down from the observer's goals held in prefrontal and parietal cortex, bias that competition so that one stimulus wins and the neuron responds as if the other were absent.

Nothing in this picture is an attention module: attention is the name we give to the outcome of the biasing, in the same way that "traffic flow" is the name for what many independently driven cars produce, not an extra thing on the road.

This reframing is important because it explains why attention effects appear at nearly every level of the visual system, growing in size from primary visual cortex forward - competition is everywhere resources are scarce.


39.4.2 Interaction with working memory and with long-term memory

Attention and working memory - the ability to hold a small amount of information available for a few seconds - are so entangled that some researchers treat them as the same mechanism seen from two sides.

Awh and Jonides, in work from the late 1990s and 2000s, showed that holding a location in mind produces enhanced activity in the visual cortex representing that location, and that a distracting task at that location damages memory for it: spatial rehearsal appears to be covert attention aimed inward.

The relationship runs the other way too, since what is held in working memory automatically biases what captures attention in the world, which is why you find your car keys faster when you have just pictured them.

Long-term memory enters as the source of expectations: knowing that traffic lights sit above eye level, or that a kitchen contains a kettle, guides the eyes before any bottom-up signal does.

A 2025 study in Nature Communications by Nobre and colleagues argued that selecting an item within working memory and selecting one from long-term memory rely on dissociable mechanisms rather than one shared spotlight, which cautions against collapsing all three into a single construct.


39.4.3 Why attention resists a single mechanistic definition

Hommel, Chapman, Cisek, Neyedli, Song and Welsh published a paper in Attention, Perception, and Psychophysics in 2019 with the deliberately provocative title "No one knows what attention is".

Their argument is that the word is used simultaneously for the thing to be explained - the fact that we process some inputs better than others - and for the explanation - a process that does the selecting - which makes many statements about attention circular.

Anderson made a related case, arguing that we reify attention, treating a summary label as though it were an entity with a location and a mechanism, and Krauzlis and colleagues have argued that much of what is credited to a cortical attention system is produced by subcortical structures such as the superior colliculus.

Not everyone accepts the eliminativist conclusion, and a reasonable defence is that "attention" remains a useful family term in the way "memory" is, provided the sub-types are specified.

The practical lesson for a learner is procedural: when you meet a claim about attention, ask which operational task it came from - a spatial cueing task, a vigil, an effort-choice task - because claims from different tasks routinely fail to transfer.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Arousal is set by a small set of chemically distinct brainstem and basal forebrain nuclei whose neuromodulators change cortical state globally, with the locus coeruleus and its noradrenaline the best-studied case, and pupil size a useful but imperfect external readout of that state.

The inverted-U relation between arousal and performance is a real family of findings but not the precise law that Yerkes and Dodson are wrongly credited with, and Aston-Jones and Cohen's tonic-versus-phasic adaptive gain theory offers a plausible mechanism for it that is still incompletely tested.

Vigilance fails within half an hour of watching, and the best current picture combines depletion of a limited resource, drift of thought toward internal content, and the physical intermittency of local sleep in cortical patches shown by Vyazovskiy and colleagues in 2011.

Mental effort is now modelled economically rather than as fuel: the expected value of control framework of Shenhav, Botvinick and Cohen makes effort avoidance rational, dopamine modulates willingness to work by amplifying benefits relative to costs, and the glutamate-accumulation account of Wiehler and Pessiglione is a promising but not yet replicated candidate for the cost itself.

Finally, attention is best understood not as a faculty but as the visible outcome of biased competition among limited neural resources, which is why the term resists a single mechanistic definition and why claims about it must always be tied back to the specific task that produced them.


PART SEVEN. LEARNING AND MEMORY: THE PERSISTENCE OF EXPERIENCE


CHAPTER 40. THE TAXONOMY OF MEMORY (CORE)

This chapter asks a deceptively simple question: is memory one thing, or many things?

The everyday word "memory" covers your recollection of last Tuesday's dinner, your knowledge that Paris is the capital of France, your ability to ride a bicycle, and your flinch at a sound that once preceded pain.

Neuroscience has spent seventy years arguing about whether those are four expressions of one machine or four different machines sharing a skull.

The answer matters practically, because it determines what you should expect when a particular piece of brain is damaged, and it matters theoretically, because a taxonomy is a claim about how the brain is built.

We will lay out the classical divisions, examine the evidence that persuaded most of the field to accept multiple memory systems, then take seriously the researchers who think the whole taxonomy is a category error.


40.1 The classical divisions

The standard textbook picture of memory is a branching tree.

The first branch is by time: how long does the trace last.

The second branch is by kind: what sort of content the trace holds, and whether you can consciously report it.

Both branchings emerged from experimental psychology in the 1960s and 1970s, before there was any brain imaging to check them against, and both have held up better than most psychological theories of that vintage.


40.1.1 Sensory, short-term, and long-term stores

Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin, in 1968, proposed what became known as the multi-store or modal model of memory, which divides memory into three stores arranged in sequence.

The sensory register holds a raw, modality-specific copy of incoming sensation - visual information stored as an image, auditory information as a sound - for roughly half a second before it decays; George Sperling's partial-report experiments of 1960 had already demonstrated that people briefly hold far more visual detail than they can report before it fades.

Attention selects a small fraction of that material and passes it into the short-term store, a limited-capacity workspace holding a handful of items for seconds unless actively rehearsed.

Rehearsal, particularly what Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart in 1972 called deep or elaborative processing (working with an item's meaning rather than its sound or shape), transfers material into the long-term store, which has no known capacity limit and can hold information for decades.

The model has been heavily revised - the short-term store is now usually described as working memory, an active manipulator rather than a passive holding tank - but a 2019 retrospective in Memory and Cognition marking its fiftieth anniversary noted that essentially all subsequent memory models are arguments with Atkinson and Shiffrin rather than replacements of them.


40.1.2 Declarative and non-declarative memory

Larry Squire's taxonomy, refined across several decades and stated compactly in a 2004 review in Neurobiology of Learning and Memory, splits long-term memory by its relationship to conscious awareness.

Declarative memory is memory whose contents you can declare - facts and events that enter awareness when retrieved, and that you can describe to another person.

Non-declarative memory is everything else: capacities and dispositions expressed through performance rather than report, where the evidence of learning is that you do something differently, not that you can say something new.

Crucially, Squire attached brain structures to the branches: declarative memory depends on the medial temporal lobe (the inner surface of the temporal lobe, including the hippocampus and surrounding cortex) together with parts of the diencephalon (deep midline structures including the thalamus), whereas the non-declarative branches depend on the basal ganglia, cerebellum, amygdala, and neocortex.

That anatomical grounding is what turned a psychological distinction into a neuroscientific claim, and it is why the taxonomy is testable rather than merely tidy.


40.1.3 Episodic and semantic memory

Endel Tulving, in a 1972 chapter in the volume Organization of Memory, divided declarative memory in two.

Episodic memory is memory for particular experiences located in subjective time and tied to the self - what you had for breakfast, where you were when you heard some piece of news - and Tulving argued it involves a distinctive kind of conscious re-experiencing he later called mental time travel.

Semantic memory is decontextualised general knowledge - that lemons are sour, that there are seven days in a week - which you possess without remembering the occasion on which you acquired it.

Tulving's own position shifted considerably over thirty years: he came to stress that the two are interdependent rather than cleanly separable, and in later work including his 2002 review he made the subjective quality of remembering, rather than the content, the defining feature of the episodic system.

The distinction remains under active argument; a 2022 review in Memory and Cognition by Renoult and colleagues explicitly revisits it and concludes that episodic and semantic memory are better treated as ends of a continuum than as two boxes, since most real remembering blends them.


40.1.4 Procedural memory, priming, conditioning, and non-associative learning

Squire's non-declarative branch has four main sub-branches, and they are genuinely different from one another.

• Procedural memory is skill and habit - riding a bicycle, touch-typing, reading mirror-reversed text - acquired gradually through practice and depending heavily on the basal ganglia (a set of subcortical nuclei involved in action selection) and the cerebellum.

• Priming is the facilitation of processing an item because you encountered it recently; having seen the word "table", you complete the fragment "tab___" as "table" faster and more often, even if you cannot recall having seen it, and priming appears to reflect changes in the neocortical regions that process the item.

• Classical conditioning, in the tradition of Ivan Pavlov, is learning that one stimulus predicts another; simple motor conditioning such as the eyeblink response depends on the cerebellum, whereas fear conditioning depends on the amygdala.

• Non-associative learning is the simplest form of all: habituation, where a repeated harmless stimulus stops producing a response, and sensitisation, where a strong stimulus makes you more responsive to everything - both studied at the level of single identified neurons by Eric Kandel in the sea slug Aplysia.

What unites these is not a shared mechanism but a shared negative property: none of them requires, or produces, conscious recollection of the learning episode.


40.2 The evidence for multiple systems

A taxonomy is only worth having if it earns its keep by predicting patterns of impairment.

The case for multiple memory systems rests on the observation that brain damage does not degrade memory uniformly, but carves it at particular joints - and that the joints it carves match the ones the psychologists had proposed.

That convergence, from human patients and from animal lesion work, is the strongest argument the systems view has.


40.2.1 Patient Henry Molaison and the medial temporal lobe

In 1953 a young man with intractable epilepsy underwent bilateral removal of his medial temporal lobes, including most of the hippocampus, at the hands of the surgeon William Scoville.

The operation controlled his seizures and destroyed his ability to form new conscious memories; he was described in the literature as H.M. for fifty-five years, and named as Henry Molaison only after his death in 2008.

Scoville and Brenda Milner's 1957 paper reporting the case is one of the most cited in neuroscience, because it showed something nobody had established: that memory formation is a separable function localised to identifiable tissue, rather than a diffuse property of the whole cortex.

Molaison's intelligence, language, personality, perception, and immediate span were essentially normal; he could hold a conversation, but a person who left the room was gone from his mind within minutes.

His memory for events well before the surgery was largely preserved, which additionally showed that the medial temporal lobe is needed to form and consolidate memories rather than to store them permanently.

Suzanne Corkin at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology studied him for decades, and it is worth noting a caution raised in later commentary, including by Corkin herself and by critics of the case: a single patient with a surgical lesion of uncertain exact extent cannot settle every question, and later magnetic resonance imaging showed his lesion was somewhat smaller than originally described.


40.2.2 Preserved skill learning in amnesia

The decisive finding was not what Molaison had lost but what he had kept.

Milner gave him a mirror-tracing task, in which one traces the outline of a star while seeing only its mirror image - a task everybody is initially bad at, and everybody improves on with practice.

Across three days of testing his error scores fell in the normal way, even though on each day he insisted he had never done the task before.

This is a dissociation within a single person and a single session of learning: the skill improved while the memory of acquiring it did not exist.

Elizabeth Warrington and Lawrence Weiskrantz extended the point in the late 1960s and early 1970s, showing that amnesic patients given fragmentary word cues produced studied words at normal rates - the phenomenon later named priming - while performing terribly on recognition tests of the same words.

Together these results made it very hard to maintain that memory is one capacity of varying strength.


40.2.3 Double dissociations across patient groups

A single dissociation can always be explained away by saying one task is simply harder than the other.

A double dissociation cannot: it requires two patient groups and two tasks, with group A impaired on task one and spared on task two, and group B showing the reverse.
