Barbara Knowlton, Jennifer Mangels, and Larry Squire reported exactly this in Science in 1996, using a probabilistic classification task known as the weather prediction task, in which participants learn by trial-and-error feedback to predict rain or sunshine from cue cards that only imperfectly predict the outcome.

Amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe damage learned the task at a normal rate while being unable to recall the training session; patients with Parkinson's disease, whose pathology centres on the basal ganglia, remembered the training session perfectly well but failed to learn the classification.

Similar impairments were found in Huntington's disease, which also damages the caudate nucleus within the basal ganglia.

The pattern is precisely what the taxonomy predicts: medial temporal lobe for declarative memory, basal ganglia for gradually acquired habit.

It should be said that the weather prediction task has since been shown to be solvable by explicit strategies in many healthy participants, so it is a less pure measure of habit learning than it was first taken to be.


40.2.4 Animal-model convergence

Human lesions are accidents of disease and surgery, never clean.

Mortimer Mishkin's 1978 work in Nature closed that gap by producing an animal model, training monkeys on the delayed non-matching to sample task, in which the animal sees an object, then after a delay must choose the new object rather than the familiar one - a task that exploits the monkey's spontaneous preference for novelty and so is learned quickly.

Monkeys given lesions designed to mimic Molaison's damage showed a severe, delay-dependent recognition impairment, while performing normally at very short delays.

Subsequent work by Stuart Zola-Morgan, Squire, and Mishkin refined the picture considerably, and by the end of the 1980s had established that much of the deficit originally attributed to the hippocampus and amygdala was in fact caused by damage to the surrounding cortex - the perirhinal and parahippocampal regions - which the early aspiration lesions had unavoidably included.

That correction is a good illustration of how the field self-corrects, and it is the reason modern accounts speak of a medial temporal lobe system with functionally distinguishable parts rather than of the hippocampus alone.

Parallel rodent work, particularly Richard Morris's water maze introduced in 1981, showed that hippocampal lesions impair place learning while sparing simpler stimulus-response learning, converging on the same divide from a third direction.


40.3 Challenges to the systems view

The systems taxonomy is the field's working consensus, and it is also under sustained and serious attack.

The critics are not fringe figures; they include some of the most productive memory researchers of the last thirty years.

Their common complaint is that the taxonomy describes patterns of results rather than explaining them, and that boxes with labels are not mechanisms.


40.3.1 Process accounts against systems accounts

The process view, associated with Henry Roediger, Teresa Blaxton, Craik, and others, holds that memory performance depends not on which system is engaged but on the match between the mental operations performed at learning and those demanded at test.

This principle, called transfer-appropriate processing and introduced by Morris, Bransford, and Franks in 1977, predicts that deep semantic study helps a meaning-based test but that shallow rhyme-based study can actually help a rhyme-based test - a result that a simple strength-of-trace account cannot produce.

Roediger and Blaxton argued that the difference between explicit tests (recall, recognition) and implicit tests (priming) is largely the difference between conceptually driven and perceptually driven processing, which can be produced within a single memory system.

Roediger, in a 1990 paper in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, went further and demanded explicit criteria for when one is entitled to postulate a separate system at all, on the grounds that the field was multiplying systems whenever it found a dissociation.

The honest summary is that process accounts explain the behavioural dissociations elegantly and explain the neuropsychological dissociations less well, since it is hard to see why a lesion should abolish conceptual processing while sparing perceptual processing if both live in the same system.


40.3.2 Eichenbaum's relational memory theory

Howard Eichenbaum proposed that what the hippocampus does is not "declarative memory" as such but relational binding: representing the arbitrary relations among the elements of an experience - this object, in that place, at this time, in that context - in a flexible network that supports inference across items never experienced together.

On this view the hippocampus is indifferent to whether the material is spatial or non-spatial, which set his account against John O'Keefe and Lynn Nadel's cognitive map theory, in which the hippocampus is specifically a spatial device.

Eichenbaum's laboratory supported the claim by recording hippocampal neurons in rats performing odour-based tasks and finding cells tuned to particular smells, to rewards, and strongly to context, rather than to place alone.

The theory reframes the taxonomy: what makes memory "declarative" is not consciousness but relational structure and the flexibility it buys, and consciousness is a by-product rather than the criterion.

This is a genuine live dispute, and recent computational work such as the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine of Whittington and colleagues in Cell in 2020 attempts to dissolve it by showing that a system generalising relational structure produces spatial map-like codes as a special case.


40.3.3 Representational accounts of the medial temporal lobe

Timothy Bussey, Lisa Saksida, Rosemary Cowell, and colleagues advanced a still more radical proposal, usually called the representational-hierarchical account.

On this view the ventral visual stream, the perirhinal cortex, and the hippocampus form a continuous hierarchy of representations, with simple features represented posteriorly and increasingly complex conjunctions of features represented anteriorly; the perirhinal cortex holds whole-object conjunctions and the hippocampus holds conjunctions of objects with contexts.

The prediction that made the account famous is that perirhinal damage should impair not only object memory but object perception, whenever the discrimination requires resolving objects that share many features - and that prediction has been confirmed in rats and monkeys, and reported in human patients with medial temporal lobe damage on simultaneous oddity discriminations where nothing needs to be remembered at all.

If correct, this means the medial temporal lobe is not a memory system in a dedicated sense; it is the top of the perceptual hierarchy, and it looks like a memory structure only because complex conjunctive representations happen to be what memory tasks stress.

The claim remains contested: Squire and colleagues have argued that apparent perceptual deficits in amnesic patients reflect uncontrolled memory demands within nominally perceptual tasks, and the empirical exchange has run for two decades without full resolution.


40.3.4 Component-process and constructive-episodic-simulation views

Morris Moscovitch's component process model treats remembering as the coordinated output of several dissociable components rather than of a system: the hippocampus performs obligatory, rapid, automatic binding of whatever attended material reaches it, while the prefrontal cortex supplies the strategic search, monitoring, and verification that make recollection goal-directed and error-checked.

This explains a familiar clinical pattern in which frontal patients remember the right material but organise, order, and source it badly - producing confabulation rather than amnesia - and it treats "episodic memory" as an achievement of several parts rather than an organ.

Daniel Schacter and Donna Addis, in 2007, added the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis: the episodic system's function is not accurate replay but the flexible recombination of stored fragments, which is what allows us to imagine specific future events we have never experienced.

The supporting evidence is that imagining the future and remembering the past activate largely the same core brain network, and that amnesic patients with hippocampal damage are impaired at imagining novel scenes as well as at recalling old ones - work reported by Demis Hassabis, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues in 2007 that Science named among that year's top breakthroughs.

The elegant part of the hypothesis is its explanation of memory error: if remembering works by recombination, then miscombination - importing a detail from the wrong episode - is not a malfunction but the price of the design.

The weaker part is that "adaptive constructiveness" is difficult to falsify, since almost any pattern of error can be described after the fact as a useful flexibility.


40.4 Organising dimensions

If the boxes are the wrong shape, what should replace them?

A growing number of researchers argue for describing memory along continuous dimensions rather than sorting it into categories, and for treating any given task as a point in that space rather than as a probe of one system.

This section sets out the three dimensions that do most of the work, and then two cautions about the criteria the classical taxonomy relies on.


40.4.1 Content, process, and timescale as orthogonal axes

The classical tree conflates three questions that are logically independent.

Content asks what is represented: a place, an object, a word, a motor sequence, an emotional value.

Process asks what operation is performed on it: encoding, binding, consolidating, retrieving, reconsolidating, or generalising across instances.

Timescale asks how long the change persists and how fast it is acquired: milliseconds of sensory persistence, seconds of active maintenance, one-shot encoding of an event, or slow incremental tuning across hundreds of trials.

Treating these as three axes rather than one hierarchy makes sense of otherwise awkward cases - semantic memory is declarative in content but slow and incremental in timescale, like a habit; fear conditioning is fast and one-shot, like an episode, but non-declarative in content.

It also predicts, correctly, that lesions should produce deficits that cut across the classical categories, which is broadly what the patient literature shows.


40.4.2 Explicitness and its confound with task demand

Squire's taxonomy is anchored on conscious awareness, which is the least directly measurable thing in the whole scheme.

David Shanks and Mark St John, in a 1994 target article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, argued that the standard evidence for unconscious learning fails two criteria: the information criterion, that the awareness test must probe the same information that drives performance, and the sensitivity criterion, that the awareness test must be as sensitive as the performance measure.

Verbal report, the usual awareness measure, is far less sensitive than a reaction-time or accuracy measure, so weak conscious knowledge can look like no conscious knowledge - which would manufacture "implicit" memory out of nothing but a measurement asymmetry.

Larry Jacoby's process dissociation procedure, introduced in 1991, was designed to address this by pitting conscious and unconscious influences against each other within the same task, on the assumption that no test is process-pure, and it remains one of the better available tools even though its independence assumptions are themselves disputed.

The upshot is a real caution rather than a refutation: explicit-implicit dissociations in healthy participants are methodologically fragile, and the strongest evidence for the distinction continues to come from patients whose deficits are too large to be explained by test sensitivity.


40.4.3 Memory as reconstruction rather than retrieval of a record

The single most important corrective to the folk picture of memory is that there is no record to retrieve.

Frederic Bartlett established this in 1932 with his War of the Ghosts studies, in which British participants repeatedly recalling a Native American folk tale progressively reshaped it toward their own cultural expectations - shortening it, dropping the parts that made no sense to them, and sharpening the parts that did - a process he explained by appeal to schemas, organised prior knowledge that fills gaps automatically.

Elizabeth Loftus made the point experimentally and consequentially: in the 1974 study with John Palmer, the verb used in a question about a filmed car crash ("smashed" versus "hit") changed both the speed estimates and, a week later, whether participants reported seeing broken glass that was never there.

The misinformation effect that followed from this work has reshaped how courts treat eyewitness testimony, and later work on false memory implantation by Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell showed that whole events can be induced.

Reconstruction fits the constructive-simulation account of section 40.3.4 rather naturally, and it also fits work on reconsolidation, in which reactivating a memory returns it briefly to a labile state during which it can be altered before being re-stored - a finding established in rodents by Karim Nader, Glenn Schafe, and Joseph LeDoux in 2000, though its scope and reliability in humans remains actively debated.

The practical lesson is that vividness and confidence are poor guides to accuracy, because reconstruction produces a coherent, confident experience regardless of whether the pieces came from the right episode.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Memory is not one capacity: the classical taxonomy divides it by timescale into sensory, short-term, and long-term stores, and divides long-term memory into declarative memory (episodic and semantic) and non-declarative memory (procedural skill, priming, conditioning, and non-associative learning), with distinct brain structures attached to each branch.

The strongest evidence is neuropsychological - Henry Molaison's preserved mirror-tracing alongside total anterograde amnesia, the double dissociation between amnesic and Parkinson's patients on probabilistic classification, and the monkey and rodent lesion models that converge on the same divisions.

But the taxonomy is a description in search of a mechanism, and serious alternatives exist: process accounts explain dissociations by the match between encoding and retrieval operations, relational and representational accounts recast the medial temporal lobe as a binder or a perceptual hierarchy rather than a memory organ, and component-process views treat remembering as an assembly of parts.

The criterion of conscious awareness that anchors the classical scheme is the hardest thing in it to measure, and the implicit-explicit distinction is more fragile in healthy participants than in patients.

Finally, remembering is reconstruction, not playback - which explains both memory's flexibility in simulating futures and its characteristic errors, and which means confidence in a memory is not evidence for its accuracy.


CHAPTER 41. WORKING MEMORY (CORE)

Working memory is the small, temporary workspace your mind uses to hold and manipulate information you are using right now.

It is what keeps a phone number alive while you cross the room to a keypad, what holds the first half of a sentence while you read the second half, and what stores the intermediate result when you multiply two numbers in your head.

This chapter explains the leading psychological models of that workspace, the brain mechanisms proposed to keep information alive over a few seconds, the control processes that decide what gets in and what gets thrown out, and the stubborn fact that its capacity is tiny.

It matters because working memory capacity is one of the strongest known predictors of reasoning ability, reading comprehension, and academic achievement - and because the field is in the middle of a genuine and unresolved argument about what, physically, a memory held for three seconds actually is.

Throughout, the abbreviation working memory (WM) is used after its first full mention.


41.1 Cognitive models

Before neuroscientists could ask which neurons hold a memory for a few seconds, psychologists had to work out what kind of thing was being held.

The models in this section are functional descriptions - they describe what the system does and how its parts divide the labour, without committing to particular brain tissue.

They disagree about whether working memory is a set of separate storage buffers, or simply the currently activated portion of long-term memory, and about whether its limit is a number of boxes or a quantity of a shared substance.

Each of these disagreements is still live in 2026, and each has generated decades of clever experiments.


41.1.1 The Baddeley and Hitch multicomponent model

In 1974, Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed replacing the older idea of a single passive short-term store with a system of cooperating components, which they called working memory.

Their argument was empirical: if short-term memory were one undivided store, then loading it with a spoken digit list should cripple an unrelated reasoning task, but in fact people can hold three digits and still reason almost normally, which suggests separate subsystems that do not compete for the same resource.

The original model had three parts - a control system called the central executive plus two subsidiary stores, one for speech-based material and one for visual and spatial material.

The model's endurance is remarkable; Hitch, Richard Allen and Baddeley published a fifty-years-on review of it in 2025 in the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, defending its core division of labour while conceding that the central executive remains the least specified part.

Its main weakness is exactly that: a component defined largely by what the other components cannot do risks being a label for our ignorance rather than an explanation.


41.1.2 Phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer, central executive

The phonological loop is the speech-based subsystem, and it has two parts - a passive store that holds sound-based traces for roughly two seconds, and an articulatory rehearsal process, essentially silent inner speech, that refreshes those traces before they fade.

Two classic findings pin this down: the word length effect, in which lists of long words are recalled far worse than lists of short words (Baddeley, Thomson and Buchanan, 1975, reported recall falling from about ninety percent for monosyllables to about fifty percent for five-syllable words), and articulatory suppression, in which forcing a person to mutter an irrelevant syllable such as "the, the, the" occupies the rehearsal process and abolishes the word length effect.

The visuospatial sketchpad is the parallel subsystem for shapes, colours, locations and mental images, and it is at least partly separable into a visual "what" component and a spatial "where" component, since a concurrent spatial tracking task disrupts spatial memory far more than it disrupts memory for object appearance.

The central executive is the attentional controller: it allocates attention between the subsystems, switches between tasks, and suppresses irrelevant responses, but it is deliberately assumed to have no storage of its own.

The episodic buffer was added by Baddeley in 2000, in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, to fix a real hole - the original model had no place to combine sound, vision and meaning into a single integrated event, and no way to explain why people can recall about sixteen words from a meaningful sentence but only about five unrelated words.

The episodic buffer is described as a limited-capacity store holding information in a multimodal code, binding material from the subsidiary systems and from long-term memory into unified episodic representations; here "binding" means tying separate features, such as a colour and a location, into one object representation.


41.1.3 Embedded-process and activated-long-term-memory accounts

Nelson Cowan's embedded-processes model, developed through the 1980s and 1990s and stated formally in 2001, denies that working memory is a set of separate boxes at all.

In his account there are three nested levels: the whole of long-term memory, a subset of it that is currently in an activated state, and within that, a narrow focus of attention holding roughly four chunks that are directly and immediately available.

The appeal is parsimony - no new storage structures are postulated, only differing states of activation of the memories you already have, which neatly explains why prior knowledge so strongly improves short-term recall.

Klaus Oberauer's related concurrent-computation model adds an intermediate "region of direct access" holding a few items, with a still narrower focus holding the single item currently being operated on.

The disagreement with Baddeley is not merely verbal: the multicomponent view predicts domain-specific interference patterns that a purely attentional account struggles to produce, while the embedded-processes view predicts a single domain-general capacity limit that the multicomponent view does not obviously require.

Most researchers now treat the two as complementary descriptions at different grains rather than as a contest with a winner, but that truce is a working assumption, not a settled result.


41.1.4 Slot models against resource models of capacity

The slot model, associated with Steven Luck and Edward Vogel's 1997 Nature study of visual short-term memory, says the system has a fixed small number of discrete slots, each holding one item at a fixed resolution; items beyond the slot count are simply not stored at all, and you guess.

The resource model, argued most forcefully by Paul Bays and Masud Husain from 2008 onward, says there is instead a continuous pool of representational precision that is divided among however many items you try to hold, so that every item is stored but each gets blurrier as the set size grows.

The evidence genuinely cuts both ways: Bays, Catalao and Husain (2009) showed precision declining smoothly with set size in a manner awkward for fixed-resolution slots, while Weiwei Zhang and Luck (2008) reported that precision stops declining beyond about three or four items, which is awkward for an infinitely divisible resource.

Hybrid proposals have followed, notably Zhang and Luck's slot-plus-averaging model, in which spare slots can redundantly encode the same item to sharpen it, and Ronald van den Berg and Wei Ji Ma's variable-precision model, in which the amount of resource assigned to each item fluctuates from trial to trial.

Formal model comparisons have not delivered a clean verdict, and the honest summary in 2026 is that variable-precision resource models currently fit the data somewhat better, while the discrete-capacity intuition survives because behaviour does look slot-like at the aggregate level.


41.2 Neural mechanisms of maintenance

The central puzzle for neuroscience is mechanical: a stimulus disappears, and several seconds later the animal or person still acts on it, so something in the brain must have carried the information across a gap in which the world provided no input.

For fifty years the standard answer was that neurons simply kept firing.

That answer is now contested, not overturned, and this section lays out the main candidates.

The key experimental setting throughout is the delayed-response task, in which a cue is shown, a blank delay follows, and only then is a response permitted.


41.2.1 Persistent delay-period activity in prefrontal and parietal cortex

In 1971, Joaquin Fuster and Garrett Alexander, and independently Kisou Kubota and Hiroaki Niki, recorded from monkey prefrontal cortex and found neurons that fired continuously throughout the delay of a delayed-response task, after the cue had gone and before the response was allowed.

Shintaro Funahashi, Charles Bruce and Patricia Goldman-Rakic sharpened this in 1989 with the oculomotor delayed-response task, showing that individual dorsolateral prefrontal neurons had "memory fields" - a given neuron fired during the delay only when the remembered target had appeared at one particular location, so the pattern of firing across the population specified where the target had been.

Crucially, when such a neuron fell silent during the delay, the monkey tended to make an error at that same location, which links the activity to the behaviour rather than merely correlating with the task.

Similar delay activity is found in posterior parietal cortex and in the frontal eye fields, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures blood-flow changes as an indirect index of neural activity, shows sustained frontoparietal signal across delays.

The strongest challenge to a simple prefrontal-storage story comes from Harrison and Tong (2009) and Serences and colleagues, who used multivariate pattern analysis - a technique that decodes what a person is holding in mind from the spatial pattern of brain activity - and found the remembered stimulus was decodable from early visual cortex, suggesting sensory areas participate in storage rather than merely feeding it forward.

This "sensory recruitment" account is itself disputed, since decodable visual signal can reflect attention or expectation as much as storage.


41.2.2 Activity-silent maintenance in synaptic weights

Gianluigi Mongillo, Omri Barak and Misha Tsodyks proposed in Science in 2008 that a memory can be held not in firing but in short-term synaptic facilitation - a brief, calcium-mediated increase in the strength of the synapses that were active during encoding, lasting about a second and refreshable by sparse bursts of activity.

On this view the memory trace is "activity-silent": it is a pattern of altered connection strengths, invisible in the average firing rate, and it becomes readable again only when the network is driven.

Mark Stokes and colleagues tested this directly by "pinging" the human brain during a delay with a task-irrelevant flash and reading the electroencephalography (EEG) response, where EEG is the recording of electrical rhythms from scalp electrodes; Wolff, Jochim, Akyurek and Stokes (2017, Nature Neuroscience) showed that the identity of the remembered item was decodable from the impulse response even when it was not decodable from ongoing delay activity.

This is elegant and economical, and it explains why delay activity often looks weak or absent for items that are being held but not currently attended.

It is not, however, a settled replacement for persistent activity: Barbosa and colleagues (2020, Nature Neuroscience) argued that persistent activity and silent synaptic traces interact, with the silent trace producing the serial biases in which the current response is pulled toward the previous trial's stimulus, and some authors have asked pointedly whether activity-silent working memory is distinguishable from ordinary short-term episodic memory retrieval.


41.2.3 Dynamic and time-varying codes across the delay

A third position holds that the population code is neither steadily persistent nor silent, but continually changing shape across the delay while still carrying the same information.

Recordings show that most prefrontal neurons are not stably tuned across the whole delay; the majority show short-lived selectivity with variable onsets and offsets, and only a minority sustain encoding throughout, a pattern Stokes and colleagues named dynamic coding.

The mathematical point is that a code can be dynamic at the level of single neurons and stable at the level of the population subspace - a fixed readout direction can still recover the item even as the individual contributors take turns, and Murray, Bernacchia, Freedman and colleagues (2017) demonstrated exactly this by finding a stable low-dimensional subspace inside otherwise time-varying prefrontal activity.

Dynamic codes have a functional advantage: they let the brain distinguish "this item, just encoded" from "this item, about to be reported", so temporal context is carried alongside content.

Recent theoretical work in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2024) frames stable and dynamic coding as endpoints of a continuum set by task demands rather than as rival facts about the cortex.


41.2.4 Bump attractors and continuous feature memory

For features that vary continuously, such as a direction or an angle, the standard model is the bump attractor, developed by Albert Compte, Nicolas Brunel, Goldman-Rakic and Xiao-Jing Wang in 2000.

The idea is that neurons are arranged conceptually in a ring by their preferred direction, with strong excitation between near neighbours and broad inhibition across the ring, so that a localised hump of activity - the bump - can sustain itself after the stimulus is removed, its position on the ring coding the remembered angle.

Because the ring is symmetric, the bump can sit anywhere with equal stability, which makes it a continuous attractor; the cost of that flexibility is that random noise makes the bump wander, so the remembered angle should drift progressively during long delays.

That is exactly what is observed: Wimmer, Nykamp, Constantinidis and Compte (2014, Nature Neuroscience) showed that trial-to-trial variability in monkey prefrontal delay activity predicted the monkey's specific behavioural error, which is the signature prediction of a diffusing bump and is very hard to explain any other way.

Adding short-term synaptic plasticity to such networks reduces diffusion within a trial while introducing attraction toward the previous trial's stimulus, which is one concrete way the persistent-activity and activity-silent accounts have been reconciled rather than pitted against each other.


41.3 Control of working memory

Storage alone is useless without control.

A workspace that admitted everything would be flooded within a second, and one that never released its contents could not be reused for the next problem.

This section covers the machinery that decides what enters, what is discarded, and what among the current contents is prioritised.

These control functions are what most closely connect working memory to what is loosely called executive function.


41.3.1 Gating: input, output, and the basal-ganglia gate

Working memory faces a stability-flexibility dilemma: contents must resist distraction, yet must be replaceable the moment they become obsolete.

The standard solution is a gate - a mechanism that normally holds representations sealed and robust, and opens only when an updating signal arrives.

Randall O'Reilly and Michael Frank's prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory model, published in 2006, proposes that the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei long known for action selection, provide that gate for thought as well as for movement.

The mechanism is disinhibition: when "Go" cells of the striatal direct pathway fire, they inhibit the substantia nigra pars reticulata, which was itself inhibiting thalamic relay to frontal cortex, so inhibiting an inhibitor releases the frontal update.

Because striatal plasticity is trained by phasic dopamine signals that report reward prediction error, the model explains how the brain could learn when to update without a homunculus deciding for it.

The model distinguishes input gating, which controls what is written into working memory, from output gating, which controls which currently held item drives behaviour - a separation supported by electroencephalographic and computational evidence from Rac-Lubashevsky and Frank (2021), and the same paper argues that motor gating uses the same canonical circuit.


41.3.2 Updating, removal, and interference resolution

Forgetting in working memory is not only decay; a great deal of it is interference, in which representations competing for the same limited codes degrade each other.

Oberauer and Lin's 2017 interference model proposes that removal is accomplished not by erasing an item but by breaking the association between the item and its context - the mental "slot" or position that pointed to it.

If that is right, removal should have two measurable consequences: reduced access to the removed item, and improved access to everything remaining, because a source of interference has gone.

Oberauer's 2018 work found the facilitation of remaining items reliably only when the instruction to forget came immediately after encoding, which suggests removal is real but slower and less complete than intuition suggests.

Proactive interference - the intrusion of earlier, no-longer-relevant material - is the residue of imperfect removal, and it is the reason a familiar item recently used in another role is unusually hard to hold, as demonstrated in the classic recent-probes task studied by John Jonides and Edward Smith, in which left inferior frontal gyrus activity tracks the resolution of that conflict.


41.3.3 Attention within working memory and the focus of attention

Attention is usually described as a filter aimed at the outside world, but the same selection can be aimed inward at the contents of memory.

Cowan's focus of attention and Oberauer's region of direct access are both attempts to formalise the observation that not all currently held items are equally available - one or a few enjoy a privileged, immediately usable status.

The empirical signature is that responses to an item currently in the focus are faster and more accurate than responses to an equally well-retained item outside it, and switching the focus from one item to another costs measurable time.

There is a live disagreement about the size of the focus: Cowan estimates about four chunks, while Oberauer and others argue for a single-item focus nested inside a wider set of directly accessible items, and the evidence depends heavily on which task is used to measure it.


41.3.4 Prioritisation, cueing, and the unattended memory item

The retro-cue paradigm, introduced by Griffin and Nobre in 2003, presents the cue telling you which item will be tested after the items have vanished, so any benefit must come from reorganising memory rather than from better perception.

Retro-cues reliably improve accuracy and precision for the cued item, and thirteen years of that literature were reviewed by Souza and Oberauer in 2016, who concluded the benefit reflects several mechanisms including protection from interference and head-start retrieval rather than one simple boost.

The theoretically important case is the uncued item, sometimes called the unattended memory item: Lewis-Peacock, Drysdale, Oberauer and Postle (2012) showed that the decodable neural signature of an unattended item drops to baseline, yet a later cue restores both the decodable pattern and accurate performance.

That result is one of the strongest arguments that maintenance can proceed without ongoing activity, and it also shows that the focus of attention and the contents of working memory are not the same thing.

A caveat worth stating plainly: how reliable the retro-cue is matters, and when uncued items are sometimes tested, participants evidently keep them in a more retrievable state, so laboratory estimates of "removal" depend on the incentives the experiment supplies.


41.4 Capacity and its consequences

The single most consequential fact about working memory is how little of it there is.

Capacity limits shape reading, arithmetic, reasoning, conversation, and the design of everything from cockpit displays to menu systems.

This section covers how the limit has been estimated, what it predicts, how expertise appears to evade it, and whether it can be trained upward.


41.4.1 The magical number and its revisions

George Miller's 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two" is among the most cited in psychology, and Miller himself treated the number partly as a rhetorical device, noting the coincidence between limits in absolute judgement and in immediate memory span.

Miller's key conceptual contribution was the chunk - a unit of meaning rather than a unit of stimulus, so that "F, B, I" is three chunks to someone who does not know the acronym and one chunk to someone who does.

Cowan's 2001 review in Behavioral and Brain Sciences argued that when rehearsal and long-term support are blocked, the real limit is closer to four chunks, and Luck and Vogel's 1997 visual estimates, ranging roughly from two to five items, agree.

The discrepancy between seven and four is therefore not a contradiction but a difference in method: seven is what you get when chunking and rehearsal are allowed to help, and four is what remains when they are prevented.

Even four is contested, since resource theorists deny there is an item limit at all and read the apparent plateau as the point where per-item precision falls below what the task can detect.


41.4.2 Individual differences and their prediction of higher cognition

Complex span tasks, such as reading span and operation span, require holding items while performing an unrelated processing task, and scores on them vary widely and stably across people.

Randall Engle, Michael Kane and Andrew Conway's programme of work established that this variation predicts fluid intelligence - the ability to reason about novel problems - strongly enough that working memory capacity accounts for a substantial share of the variance in fluid reasoning, with some estimates approaching half.

Their theoretical claim is that what complex span really measures is executive attention, the capacity to maintain a goal in the face of distraction and interference, which is why the correlation appears in tasks demanding control and largely vanishes in automatic tasks.

Supporting evidence comes from tasks such as antisaccade, in which one must look away from a suddenly appearing target; high-capacity individuals resist the reflexive look far better than low-capacity individuals.

Two cautions are in order: correlations of this kind cannot establish that capacity causes reasoning ability, since both may depend on a third factor, and Shipstead, Harrison and Engle (2016) themselves revised the account toward the view that maintenance and disengagement are separable contributors rather than a single capacity.


41.4.3 Chunking, expertise, and effective capacity expansion

Adriaan de Groot found in the 1940s that chess masters shown a real game position for a few seconds could reconstruct it almost perfectly, while weaker players could not.

William Chase and Herbert Simon's 1973 follow-up delivered the decisive control: with pieces placed at random rather than in a legal game position, the master's advantage largely disappeared, showing that the expert had not enlarged the workspace but had learned to fill each unit with more.

Their explanation was chunking - experts store tens of thousands of familiar piece configurations in long-term memory, estimated by Simon and Gilmartin at ten thousand to one hundred thousand, so a whole cluster enters working memory as one item.

Fernand Gobet and Simon later extended this with template theory, in which heavily practised chunks develop into templates with variable slots that can be filled rapidly, which better accounts for masters' ability to handle multiple boards at once.

A competing account, Anders Ericsson and Walter Kintsch's long-term working memory (1995), proposes that experts build retrieval structures in long-term memory that make it function as an extension of the workspace, and the two accounts are not fully reconciled.

The practical lesson is important and often misread: expertise does not increase capacity in chunks, it increases the informational value of each chunk, and it does so only within the trained domain.


41.4.4 Working memory training and the transfer question

If capacity predicts intelligence, the obvious hope is that training capacity would raise intelligence, and Susanne Jaeggi and colleagues' 2008 report of fluid intelligence gains from adaptive dual n-back training - a task requiring you to report whether the current item matches the one n steps back - launched a commercial industry on that hope.

The subsequent evidence has been unkind to it.

Melby-Lervåg, Redick and Hulme's 2016 meta-analysis, covering eighty-seven publications and one hundred forty-five comparisons, found reliable near transfer to other working memory tasks but no convincing evidence of far transfer to nonverbal ability, verbal ability, word decoding, reading comprehension or arithmetic when compared against treated control groups.

The methodological crux is the control condition: comparisons against a passive, do-nothing control routinely show gains that shrink to approximately zero against an active control doing something equally engaging, which points to expectancy and motivation rather than to capacity change.

A meta-analysis of n-back training specifically by Soveri and colleagues (2017) reached the same conclusion, as did a comprehensive 2019 meta-analysis in older adults.

The fair summary is that people reliably get better at the trained task and at tasks closely resembling it, that this is genuine skill learning and not nothing, and that the claim of general cognitive enhancement is not supported - though a minority of researchers continue to argue that specific training protocols and populations have not been fairly tested.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Working memory is a small, controlled workspace, and the field has two compatible descriptions of it - Baddeley and Hitch's multicomponent architecture of specialised buffers under executive control, and Cowan's and Oberauer's view of it as attention focused on activated long-term memory.

Its neural basis is genuinely unsettled: persistent delay-period firing in prefrontal and parietal cortex is real and behaviourally consequential, but activity-silent synaptic traces and dynamic, time-varying population codes account for findings that steady firing cannot, and the current best guess is that all three coexist.

Control is as important as storage, with a basal-ganglia gate plausibly deciding what is written in and read out, and removal implemented as the breaking of item-context bindings rather than as erasure.

Capacity is about four chunks when rehearsal and prior knowledge are prevented, and whether that limit is discrete slots or a divisible resource remains a live formal dispute.

Capacity predicts fluid intelligence strongly, expertise raises effective capacity by enriching chunks rather than adding them, and direct training reliably improves the trained task while failing to produce the general gains once claimed for it.


CHAPTER 42. EPISODIC MEMORY AND THE HIPPOCAMPAL FORMATION (CORE)

This chapter is about how the brain records single events and how it gets them back.

Episodic memory is memory for particular happenings that you can place in your own past - what you ate for breakfast, where you parked, the moment someone told you bad news.

It is different from knowing that Paris is the capital of France, which is a fact you hold without remembering the occasion on which you learned it.

The chapter follows an episode through its life cycle: how it is encoded, what the hippocampus does with it, how it is retrieved, what an episode actually contains, and finally what physical trace it leaves in tissue.

This matters because episodic memory is the part of memory that fails first in Alzheimer's disease, that gets manipulated in eyewitness testimony, and that has, in the last fifteen years, become the first kind of memory that neuroscientists can switch on and off in a living animal.


42.1 Encoding

Encoding is the process by which an experience that is happening now is converted into a trace that can be recovered later.

Nothing about encoding is automatic or guaranteed.

Most of what passes through your senses in a day leaves no retrievable record at all, and the interesting scientific question is what distinguishes the small fraction that sticks.


42.1.1 Levels of processing and elaborative encoding

Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, in 1972, proposed that memory strength is a by-product of how deeply you process something rather than how long you hold it in mind.

Shallow processing means analysing surface features - is this word printed in capitals, does it rhyme with "chair" - and it produces a fragile trace.

Deep or semantic processing means analysing meaning - is this word a kind of animal, does this sentence describe something plausible - and it produces a durable one.

Elaborative encoding is the specific version of deep processing in which you connect the new item to things you already know, and it reliably beats maintenance rehearsal, which is mere repetition of the item to itself.

The framework has been criticised as circular, because "depth" was originally defined by the memory it produced rather than measured independently, and Craik himself acknowledged this in later retrospective commentary; nevertheless the empirical effect - semantic study instructions produce better recall than surface study instructions - is one of the most reproducible results in the field.


42.1.2 Subsequent memory effects and encoding-related activity

The subsequent memory paradigm sorts brain activity recorded during study according to what happened on a later test: items later remembered against items later forgotten.

The difference between those two is called the difference due to memory (Dm), or the subsequent memory effect.

The method began with event-related potentials (ERPs), which are voltage changes recorded from the scalp and time-locked to a stimulus, and was carried into functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 1998 by two independent groups, Brewer and colleagues and Wagner and colleagues.

Both found the same thing: greater activity in the prefrontal cortex and in the medial temporal lobe during study predicted that an item would later be remembered.

A meta-analysis by Kim in 2011, pooling 74 fMRI studies, confirmed the prefrontal and medial temporal pattern and also identified regions where deactivation predicted later memory, notably parts of the default mode network associated with internally directed thought - a plausible signature of attention being turned outward toward the material.

Subsequent memory effects shrink with age and shrink further along the Alzheimer's disease risk spectrum, which is why the paradigm has become a candidate biomarker as well as a basic-science tool.


42.1.3 Binding of item and context

An episode is not one thing; it is a thing occurring somewhere, at some time, among other things.

Binding is the operation that ties those components into a single retrievable unit, so that recovering one component can drag the others up with it.

The binding of items and context (BIC) model, set out by Rachel Diana, Andrew Yonelinas and Charan Ranganath in 2007, assigns the labour across three neighbouring structures of the medial temporal lobe.

Perirhinal cortex handles item information - the object itself, what it is.

Parahippocampal cortex handles context - spatial layout, scene, and arguably the more abstract cognitive situation you were in.

The hippocampus receives both streams and binds item to context, producing the relational representation that makes an episode an episode rather than a list of unlinked features.

The model has been tested and partly complicated by work on the entorhinal cortex, the way station between those cortices and the hippocampus; a study by Wilson and colleagues in 2013 found both the lateral and medial entorhinal subdivisions contributing to item and to context memory rather than dividing the labour as cleanly as the model's simplest reading predicts.


42.1.4 Novelty, curiosity, and dopaminergic modulation of encoding

Encoding is not equally likely at all moments; it is gated, and one of the gates is novelty.

John Lisman and Anthony Grace proposed in 2005 a hippocampal-ventral tegmental area (VTA) loop, in which the hippocampus - having a store of what it already knows - detects that incoming information is new, and passes that novelty signal onward through the subiculum, nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum to the VTA, a midbrain nucleus that manufactures dopamine.

Dopamine is a neuromodulator, a chemical that does not itself carry the message but adjusts how strongly other messages are registered.

The VTA then releases dopamine back into the hippocampus, where it enhances long-term potentiation (the lasting strengthening of a synapse that has been repeatedly driven) and thereby improves encoding.

The loop is elegant, and it is supported by human imaging showing that the substantia nigra and VTA respond to stimulus novelty even without reward, as Bunzeck and Düzel reported in 2006.

Matthias Gruber, Bernard Gelman and Charan Ranganath extended this to curiosity in 2014: when people were in a high-curiosity state about a trivia question, they remembered the answer better, they also remembered incidental faces presented during the waiting period better, and activity in the midbrain dopaminergic regions and hippocampus tracked the effect.

A caution worth stating plainly - human fMRI cannot see dopamine, only activity in dopamine-producing regions, so the neurochemical step in the human version of this story is inferred from animal work rather than directly observed.


42.2 Hippocampal computation

The hippocampus is a curled structure buried in each temporal lobe, and it is not a warehouse.

Its subregions are wired in a way that suggests they perform distinct computations on the same incoming episode, and the theoretical framework for those computations is older and more explicit than for almost anything else in cognitive neuroscience.

The main flow is the trisynaptic circuit: entorhinal cortex to dentate gyrus, dentate gyrus to CA3, CA3 to CA1, and CA1 back out to entorhinal cortex and the wider cortex.


42.2.1 Pattern separation in the dentate gyrus

Pattern separation is the transformation of similar inputs into less similar, less overlapping output representations, so that today's parking spot does not smear into yesterday's.

The dentate gyrus is anatomically built for it: it has far more granule cells than the entorhinal cortex has input cells, and those cells fire very sparsely, so a given input recruits a small and largely distinct subset.

Human evidence came from Arne Bakker, Michael Yassa, Craig Stark and colleagues in 2008, who used high-resolution fMRI and a task with lures - objects similar but not identical to studied objects.

The dentate and CA3 region responded to a lure as though it were new, while other regions treated it as a repetition, which is the signature of separation rather than generalisation.

The fMRI evidence is limited by resolution, since dentate and CA3 are difficult to resolve separately in the living human brain, and the strongest direct evidence comes from rodent electrophysiology; Berron and colleagues in 2016 pushed toward stronger human evidence at 7 tesla.

A related literature holds that adult-born granule cells - the dentate gyrus is one of the few places where new neurons may be added in adulthood - are important for separation, but whether adult neurogenesis occurs meaningfully in adult humans is genuinely disputed, with Sorrells and colleagues in 2018 reporting essentially none and Moreno-Jiménez and colleagues in 2019 reporting abundant new neurons, using different tissue-handling methods.


42.2.2 Pattern completion in CA3 recurrent circuitry

Pattern completion is the opposite operation: given a fragment of a stored pattern, regenerate the whole thing.

CA3 is built for it because its pyramidal cells synapse heavily onto each other - a dense recurrent collateral network - which is the classic architecture of an attractor network, a system that falls into a previously stored stable state when nudged anywhere near it.

David Marr in 1971 anticipated this design, and it was formalised computationally by Edmund Rolls, Bruce McNaughton and others.

Direct evidence came from Neunuebel and Knierim in 2014, who recorded dentate and CA3 cells while conflicting spatial cues were pulled apart; the dentate output was severely disrupted, yet CA3 produced a coherent output closer to the originally stored representation than its own degraded input - completion downstream of separation, in the same animal, at the same moment.

The tension between the two operations is the crux of the design: too much separation and nothing can be recalled from a partial cue, too much completion and every similar experience collapses into one.


42.2.3 CA1 as a comparator and the entorhinal loops

CA1 receives two inputs that carry different things.

The Schaffer collaterals from CA3 arrive on the mid-dendrites and deliver the stored, completed prediction of what should be there.

The temporoammonic pathway, arriving direct from layer three of entorhinal cortex onto the distal dendrites, delivers current sensory reality without passing through the trisynaptic loop.

John Lisman and Nonna Otmakhova proposed that CA1 therefore acts as a comparator, or match/mismatch detector, signalling when prediction and reality diverge and thereby telling the system when there is something new to learn.

Chen and colleagues in 2011 tested this with high-resolution human fMRI and found CA1 activity that behaved as the model predicts, responding differentially when a learned sequence was violated.

The wider architecture is a loop rather than a line: entorhinal cortex feeds the hippocampus, CA1 and subiculum feed entorhinal cortex back, and entorhinal cortex feeds the neocortex, so that anything the hippocampus resolves is returned to the cortical regions that supplied the raw material.


42.2.4 The hippocampal indexing theory

Timothy Teyler and Pascal DiScenna proposed in 1986 that the hippocampus does not store the content of an experience at all.

Instead it stores an index - a compact pointer to the particular pattern of neocortical activity that the episode produced.

Because the hippocampus projects back to those same cortical regions, activating the index reinstates the cortical pattern, and the experience is recovered from cortex rather than from the hippocampus.

Teyler and Rudy updated the theory in 2007, connecting it to the subregional computations above: the dentate gyrus and CA3 machinery is well suited to making indices that are distinct from one another yet retrievable from a fragment.

Indexing theory is attractive because it explains why hippocampal damage can devastate the ability to recover episodes while leaving the knowledge extracted from them intact - the books are still on the shelves, but the catalogue has been burned.


42.3 Retrieval

Retrieval is not playback.

It is a cue-driven reconstruction in which a partial input reactivates a stored pattern, and the quality of what you get out depends heavily on what you put in as a cue.

This section covers how retrieval feels, what it looks like in cortex, what makes cues work, and the fact that retrieving changes the memory.


42.3.1 Recollection against familiarity and the dual-process debate

There are two ways to know you have met something before.

Recollection is recovering the episode with its detail - you remember where you met this person and what they were wearing.

Familiarity is a graded sense of priorness without any accompanying context - you know the face, and nothing else comes.

Andrew Yonelinas formalised this in 1994 as the dual-process signal detection model, in which recollection is treated as a roughly threshold-like process that either succeeds or does not, while familiarity is a continuous strength signal.

The evidence is drawn largely from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, which plot hit rate against false-alarm rate across levels of confidence; in the dual-process reading, the asymmetry of the curve indexes recollection and its curvature indexes familiarity.

This is genuinely contested.

Larry Squire, John Wixted and colleagues argued from 2007 onward that a single continuous strength signal, with hippocampus and surrounding cortex both contributing to it, can produce the same ROC shapes, and that asymmetry and curvature rise and fall together with memory strength rather than varying independently as two separate processes should.

The dual-process side answers with dissociations - frontal and hippocampal damage, and certain drug and ageing effects, hitting recollection much harder than familiarity - and the argument is not settled; a fair summary in 2026 is that most researchers accept two experientially distinct states while disagreeing about whether they require two underlying mechanisms.


42.3.2 Cortical reinstatement of encoding patterns

If indexing theory is right, retrieval should look like a partial re-run of encoding in cortex, and it does.

Jared Danker and John Anderson, reviewing the evidence in 2010, described retrieval as the reinstatement of the encoding pattern in the same content-specific cortical regions - visual cortex for a remembered picture, auditory regions for a remembered sound.

The method that made this visible is multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA), which asks whether the spatial pattern of activity across many voxels at retrieval resembles the pattern at encoding, rather than merely asking whether a region is more or less active.

Jeffrey Johnson, Kenneth Norman, Michael Rugg and colleagues showed in 2009 that reinstatement was stronger for recollection than for familiarity, tying the subjective distinction of the previous sub-section to a measurable neural one.

Gordon and colleagues in 2014 showed that cortical reinstatement statistically mediates the link between content-specific encoding activity and later recollection decisions, and Ritchey and colleagues in 2017 showed that trial-by-trial hippocampal activity at encoding predicts the fidelity of the later cortical reinstatement - the hippocampus laying down a better index yields a better cortical replay.

Reinstatement is not literal: Xiao, Wang and colleagues in 2017 documented transformed reinstatement, in which the retrieved pattern is systematically related to but not identical with the encoded one, consistent with memory being reconstructive rather than photographic.


42.3.3 Retrieval cues, context reinstatement, and the encoding specificity principle

Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson stated the encoding specificity principle in 1973: a cue is effective to the extent that the information it carries was encoded as part of the original trace.

The counterintuitive consequence is that a strong semantic associate can be a worse cue than a weak one that happened to be present at study, which they demonstrated experimentally.

Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley gave the most quoted demonstration in 1975, having divers learn word lists on land or underwater and recall them in the same or the other environment; free recall was substantially better when the environments matched.

The effect is much weaker or absent for recognition than for free recall, because a recognition test supplies the item itself as a cue and leaves little work for context to do, and this boundary condition is well replicated.

Practically, this is why mentally reinstating the context - deliberately reconstructing where you were and what was happening - is a component of the cognitive interview used in forensic settings, and why studying in the exam room helps less than it is popularly supposed to, given that recognition-heavy tests benefit least.


42.3.4 Retrieval-induced forgetting and retrieval as a learning event

Retrieval is not a neutral read; it modifies the store.

Michael Anderson, Robert Bjork and Elizabeth Bjork showed in 1994 that practising retrieval of some members of a category causes forgetting of the unpractised members of that same category, a phenomenon called retrieval-induced forgetting.

Their explanation is inhibitory: competitors that intrude during a retrieval attempt are actively suppressed, which is functional, since a memory system that could not push aside competitors would be useless, and Anderson and Spellman's later work showed the effect survives when the forgotten items are tested with independent cues, which argues against a simple blocking account.

The same act of retrieval strengthens what is retrieved.

Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke demonstrated in 2006 that testing yourself on material produces markedly better long-term retention than restudying it for the same amount of time, the testing effect, even though learners consistently predict the opposite.

The two findings are one phenomenon viewed from either side: retrieval is a learning event that strengthens its target and weakens its rivals.


42.4 The contents of episodic memory

Having covered how episodes go in and come out, this section asks what an episode actually is.

The answer turns out to constrain both the animal literature, where researchers need behavioural criteria for something they cannot ask about, and the human literature, where the boundaries of an episode turn out to be measurable in the brain.


42.4.1 What, where, and when as the defining conjunction

Tulving's definition of episodic memory required more than content; it required autonoetic consciousness, the sense of mentally travelling back and re-experiencing the event as having happened to you.

That is not testable in a bird, so Nicola Clayton and Anthony Dickinson in 1998 proposed a behavioural criterion instead: an integrated memory of what was stored, where it was stored, and how long ago.

Their scrub jays cached both perishable wax worms and non-perishable peanuts, and when recovering caches they preferred worms after a short delay but switched to peanuts after a long one, which requires holding all three components together rather than any one alone.

Clayton and colleagues carefully call this episodic-like memory, because the conjunction is demonstrated but the phenomenology is not, and a 2025 reassessment by Davies and colleagues revisited the paradigm and reaffirmed that the integrated what-where-when finding holds while the consciousness question remains out of reach.

Whether "when" in these tasks is genuine time-of-occurrence or merely trace strength - how faded the memory feels - remains a live objection, and some researchers prefer the formulation what-where-which, meaning which occasion or context.


42.4.2 Event segmentation and the boundaries of an episode

Experience arrives continuously, but memory is delivered in chunks, which means the brain must be cutting the stream somewhere.

Event segmentation theory, developed by Jeffrey Zacks and colleagues, holds that the brain maintains a running model of the current situation and posts a boundary when prediction error spikes - when what happens stops matching the model.

Christopher Baldassano and colleagues in 2017 found these boundaries directly, applying hidden Markov models (a statistical method for detecting when a system switches between stable states) to fMRI data from people watching a film, and finding a nested hierarchy of event states from short sensory segments in early cortex to minutes-long segments in the hippocampus and default mode network.

At those boundaries hippocampal activity rises sharply, and the size of that rise predicts how well the preceding segment is later remembered, which suggests the boundary is where an episode gets committed.

This explains an everyday experience with unusual precision - the doorway effect, in which walking into another room makes you forget what you came for, because crossing the threshold posted a boundary and closed the previous event model.


42.4.3 Autobiographical memory and the remote past

Autobiographical memory is episodic memory scaled up to a life, and it raises the question of whether the hippocampus is still needed for events from decades ago.

The standard consolidation model says no: the hippocampus is a temporary binding device, and over time the cortex acquires the memory independently, which predicts a temporally graded retrograde amnesia in which recent memories are lost and old ones spared.

Lynn Nadel and Morris Moscovitch's multiple trace theory, published in 1997, says yes: each act of remembering lays down a further hippocampal trace, so old episodic memories are represented by more traces, not fewer, and detailed episodic recollection stays hippocampus-dependent for life.

The theory's key prediction is a dissociation - hippocampal damage should flatten the richness of remote episodic recollection while sparing remote semantic knowledge about one's own life, and Moscovitch and colleagues have reported exactly this pattern, with the complementary pattern in semantic dementia.

This dispute is unresolved and the reason is methodological: patients rarely have damage confined to the hippocampus, and measuring the detail of a fifty-year-old memory against an unavailable ground truth is very hard.

Trace transformation theory, the current position of Moscovitch and Nadel, is a partial reconciliation: memories are not simply moved to cortex but transformed, with a gist-like semanticised version becoming cortex-dependent while any detailed, perceptually rich version remains hippocampal.


42.4.4 Memory distortion, false memory, and the constructive account

Frederic Bartlett showed in 1932, having British participants repeatedly retell an unfamiliar Native American folk tale, that recall systematically distorted the story toward their own cultural expectations, and concluded that remembering is reconstruction rather than reproduction.

The Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) paradigm makes this happen reliably in the laboratory: study a list of words all associated with an unpresented word - bed, rest, awake, tired - and participants falsely recall and confidently recognise "sleep", often with the same subjective certainty as for genuinely studied items.

Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated the applied form, showing across decades that post-event suggestion is incorporated into recollection, from the wording of a question changing speed estimates in the 1974 car-crash studies to the implantation of wholly fabricated childhood events.

Daniel Schacter's constructive account, set out in his 1999 seven sins framework and developed since, argues these errors are not defects bolted onto a good system but the cost of a good system: a memory that recombines stored elements flexibly is what allows you to imagine a future or solve a novel problem, and the same recombination occasionally assembles something that never happened.

The strongest support for this is that the same hippocampal and default-network machinery activates when people imagine future events as when they remember past ones, and that patients with hippocampal amnesia are impaired at imagining novel scenes, reported by Hassabis, Maguire and colleagues in 2007.


42.5 The engram

The engram is the physical trace - Richard Semon's term from 1904 for the enduring change left in tissue by an experience.

For most of the twentieth century it was a theoretical entity; Karl Lashley spent thirty years lesioning rat cortex looking for it and concluded in 1950 that he could not find it.

The last fifteen years changed this, because activity-dependent genetic tools made it possible to mark the specific cells active during one learning episode and then come back to them later.


42.5.1 Engram cell tagging, labelling, and reactivation

The trick rests on immediate early genes, genes such as c-fos and Arc that are switched on within minutes in a neuron that has just been strongly active, and therefore serve as a natural marker of participation.

In the c-fos-tTA system, the c-fos promoter drives a synthetic protein, the tetracycline transactivator, which in turn switches on whatever gene the experimenter has delivered by virus - but only while the animal is off a doxycycline diet.

That gives two constraints at once: the c-fos promoter picks which cells (the active ones), and the diet picks which window of time, so only cells active during a chosen hour get permanently marked.

A related tool, targeted recombination in active populations (TRAP), developed by Guenthner and colleagues in 2013, uses a drug-dependent recombinase to achieve the same time-stamped labelling with a different chemical switch.

Once labelled, the cells can be given channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive ion channel, which lets an implanted optical fibre drive exactly those cells at a later date.

Tools of this kind have limits worth naming - c-fos labelling is incomplete and somewhat biased, some labelling occurs outside the intended window, and cells that express c-fos are not necessarily all and only the cells carrying the memory.


42.5.2 Artificial induction and silencing of memories

Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez and Susumu Tonegawa's laboratory reported in Nature in 2012 that labelling the dentate gyrus cells active while a mouse learned to fear a particular box, and then shining light on those same cells while the mouse sat in a completely different and safe box, made the animal freeze.

Freezing is the standard rodent readout of fear, so this amounted to switching on a specific memory artificially, in the wrong place, with light.

The following year Ramirez, Liu and colleagues went further in Science, creating a false memory: they labelled the cells active during a safe box, then in a second box reactivated those cells at the moment the animal received a foot shock, and afterwards the mouse froze in the safe box where nothing bad had ever happened.

The complementary manipulation, inhibiting the labelled cells and thereby blocking recall of a memory the animal certainly possesses, has also been demonstrated repeatedly, which is the necessity half of the argument to set against the sufficiency half.

The correct reading is narrow but strong: these experiments show that a sparse, identifiable population of cells is both necessary and sufficient for the expression of a specific learned fear, not that the whole content of a memory sits in the dentate gyrus.


42.5.3 Engram allocation by excitability

Given millions of available neurons, which ones get recruited into a particular engram is not random.

Sheena Josselyn, working with Alcino Silva, first showed in the lateral amygdala that neurons with higher levels of the transcription factor CREB (cyclic adenosine monophosphate response element binding protein) are preferentially recruited, and that CREB acts partly by raising a neuron's intrinsic excitability - its readiness to fire.

The causal test has both directions: artificially raising CREB in a random subset of neurons biases the memory into that subset, and selectively silencing those CREB-overexpressing cells afterwards impairs recall, whereas silencing an equally sized random subset does not.

Yiu, Josselyn and colleagues extended this in 2014 by manipulating excitability directly rather than through CREB, with the same result, which rules out CREB doing this through some route unrelated to excitability.

The functional consequence is that memories encoded close together in time land in overlapping populations - Cai, Silva and colleagues showed in 2016 that this transient excitability window links memories formed within hours of each other - which is a plausible cellular basis for why events from the same afternoon come back together.


42.5.4 Engram reorganisation during systems consolidation

Takashi Kitamura, Tonegawa and colleagues reported in Science in 2017 the most detailed account yet of what happens to an engram over weeks.

Cortical engram cells in the prefrontal cortex were generated at the moment of learning, not later, receiving input from the hippocampal-entorhinal network and from the basolateral amygdala - but they were silent, meaning they carried the trace yet could not drive recall on their own.

Over the following two weeks those prefrontal cells matured into functional engram cells capable of supporting recall, while hippocampal engram cells went the other way, becoming silent - present and reactivatable by light, but no longer driving natural recall.

Amygdala engram cells, which carry the emotional valence, stayed active throughout.

This revises the standard consolidation picture in an important way: the cortical trace is not built slowly from scratch after the fact, it is laid down immediately and then slowly brought online, with the hippocampus acting as trainer rather than sole author.

The picture continues to move, and the field is currently absorbing evidence that engrams are dynamic rather than fixed, that they are distributed across many regions rather than localised, and, from work reviewed in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2025, that astrocytes - the star-shaped glial cells long treated as support staff - form ensembles of their own whose reactivation can produce recall.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Episodic memory is built, not recorded: encoding depends on depth of processing and on novelty-driven dopaminergic gating, and its success is visible in advance as prefrontal and medial temporal subsequent memory effects.

The hippocampal subregions perform complementary computations - separation in the dentate gyrus, completion in CA3, comparison in CA1 - and the hippocampus most likely stores an index to cortical patterns rather than the contents themselves, which is why retrieval takes the form of measurable cortical reinstatement.

Retrieval is cue-dependent in the specific way Tulving's encoding specificity principle predicts, and it is not passive, since the act of retrieving strengthens its target and inhibits its competitors.

An episode is defined by the conjunction of what, where and when, its boundaries are posted by prediction error and are visible as hippocampal responses at event boundaries, and its reconstructive character makes distortion an intrinsic cost of a flexible system rather than a malfunction.

Two matters remain genuinely open: whether recollection and familiarity require two mechanisms or one graded signal, and whether remote autobiographical memories ever become independent of the hippocampus.

Finally, the engram is no longer hypothetical - specific cells can be tagged, reactivated to force recall, silenced to block it, biased by excitability, and watched as they hand the memory from hippocampus to cortex over weeks.


CHAPTER 43. SEMANTIC MEMORY AND CONCEPTUAL KNOWLEDGE (CORE)

This chapter is about the part of memory that holds what you know rather than what happened to you.

Knowing that a lemon is sour, that a hammer drives nails, and that justice is a kind of fairness is semantic memory - general knowledge stripped of the time and place at which you acquired it.

Semantic memory matters because almost every other cognitive act leans on it: you cannot recognise an object, understand a sentence, plan a meal, or make an analogy without it.

We will look at how concepts are structured, where in the brain they live, how word meanings connect to bodily experience, and what happens when the system breaks down in disease.

The chapter also asks a question that has become urgent since 2020 - whether a machine trained only on text can be said to know what its words mean.

43.1 The structure of conceptual knowledge

A concept is a mental representation that groups things together and lets you treat a never-before-seen instance as a familiar kind.

The oldest theory, going back to Aristotle, was the classical view - a concept is a set of necessary and sufficient conditions, so that something is a bird if and only if it satisfies a checklist.

That view collapsed under evidence, gathered largely by Eleanor Rosch in the 1970s, that category membership is graded rather than all-or-none.

A robin strikes people as a better bird than a penguin, and they say so faster, which a checklist cannot explain.

The theories in this section are the successors to the classical view.

43.1.1 Feature-based, prototype, and exemplar accounts

Feature-based accounts describe a concept as a bundle of smaller properties - has feathers, lays eggs, flies - so that similarity between two concepts is the overlap in their features.

Prototype theory, developed by Rosch and Carolyn Mervis in the mid-1970s, says that a category is organised around a summary best example, an average of the things you have encountered, and you judge membership by resemblance to that average; this explains typicality effects and the family-resemblance structure Rosch and Mervis documented in 1975.

Exemplar theory, associated with Douglas Medin, Marguerite Schaffer and later Robert Nosofsky, denies that any average is stored at all and says you keep individual remembered instances and classify a new item by its similarity to the whole crowd of them.

Exemplar models handle some findings that defeat prototypes, such as sensitivity to how variable a category is and to correlations between features, but Gregory Murphy has argued in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review (2016) that no single exemplar theory is stated precisely enough to be the general account of concepts.

Neuroimaging suggests the argument may be miscast as either-or - Bowman and Zeithamova, working with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a method that infers neural activity from changes in blood oxygenation), reported evidence that prototype-like representations track ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus while exemplar-like representations track inferior frontal gyrus and lateral parietal cortex, implying the brain may build both at once.

43.1.2 Taxonomic and thematic organisation

Concepts relate to each other in at least two quite different ways.

A taxonomic relation is one of kind and similarity - a dog and a wolf belong together because they share shape, parts and colour.

A thematic relation is one of co-occurrence in an event or scene - a dog and a leash belong together not because they resemble one another but because they show up in the same situation.

Daniel Mirman and colleagues have proposed a dual-hub account in which the anterior temporal lobe supports taxonomic knowledge, which leans on shape and colour features, while temporoparietal cortex, particularly the supramarginal gyrus, supports thematic knowledge, which leans on action and location.

The supporting evidence includes lesion work in which anterior temporal damage biases patients toward taxonomic errors and temporoparietal damage toward thematic ones, plus fMRI meta-analyses of the same split.

The dual-hub claim is not universally accepted - proponents of a single anterior temporal hub argue the temporoparietal effects reflect control and event processing rather than a second store of meaning, and the dispute is live.

43.1.3 Category-specific deficits and what they imply

Some brain-damaged patients lose knowledge of one category while retaining others, and the pattern is startlingly specific.

Elizabeth Warrington and Tim Shallice, in a 1984 study of four patients recovering from herpes simplex encephalitis (a viral brain infection that attacks the temporal lobes), found that the patients could no longer identify living things and foods yet remained able to identify manufactured objects.
