Their sensory-functional explanation was that we tell animals apart by fine sensory detail such as shape, colour and texture, while we tell tools apart by what they are for, so damaging a sensory subsystem selectively wrecks the living-things category.

Alfonso Caramazza and Jennifer Shelton offered a rival domain-specific account in 1998, arguing that evolution built dedicated machinery for animate kinds, so the categories themselves are the units of brain organisation rather than the feature types.

A third position, developed by Karalyn Patterson, Matthew Lambon Ralph, Timothy Rogers and colleagues in a 2007 Brain paper combining semantic dementia, herpes encephalitis and a computer model, argues that no dedicated category modules are needed - because living things are crowded together in similarity space and share many features, graded damage to a single system hits them first.

The honest summary is that the phenomenon is robust and its interpretation is still contested.

43.1.4 Concepts as stable versus context-dependent constructions

The theories above mostly assume that a concept is a stable thing you retrieve, like a file.

Eiling Yee and Sharon Thompson-Schill challenged this in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review (2016) with the argument that a concept cannot be meaningfully separated from the context in which it occurs, and that what is activated for piano differs when you are talking about moving furniture rather than about music.

A stronger version of the claim, associated with Daniel Casasanto and Gary Lupyan, is that all concepts are ad hoc concepts - constructed on the fly from memory for the task at hand rather than looked up.

Later fMRI work, for example by Zhang and colleagues in Cerebral Cortex (2023), has tried to split the difference by identifying both context-free components of a concept's neural pattern and context-dependent shifts within it.

The practical upshot is that stability and flexibility are probably both real, and a good theory has to explain how a concept stays recognisably the same while its emphasis moves.

43.2 Neural organisation

Where does meaning live in the brain?

The two extreme answers - that meaning sits in one dedicated store, or that it is nothing but the sensory and motor traces spread across cortex - have each been tested to destruction, and the field has largely settled on a compromise architecture.

This section builds that architecture piece by piece, then adds the separate machinery that decides which part of your knowledge is relevant right now.

43.2.1 The anterior temporal lobe as a semantic hub

The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is the front tip of the temporal lobe, the region that includes the temporal pole just behind and above the ear.

It is the region that atrophies first in semantic dementia, and patients with that atrophy lose meaning regardless of how it is probed - they fail to name a picture, to define the spoken word, to match the object to its sound, and to use the object correctly.

That modality-blind pattern is the core argument for calling the ATL a hub rather than another sensory area, and it is supported by convergent methods: fMRI corrected for the signal dropout that plagues this region, magnetoencephalography (MEG, which records the magnetic fields produced by neural currents), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS, which uses a magnetic pulse to briefly disrupt a patch of cortex in healthy volunteers) that slows semantic judgements when applied to the ATL.

Work by Lambon Ralph, Patterson and colleagues, including a 2020 Brain study of white matter pathways in semantic dementia, points to the ventrolateral ATL as the graded centre of the hub rather than a sharply bounded module.

43.2.2 The hub-and-spoke model and modality-specific spokes

The hub-and-spoke model, set out most fully by Lambon Ralph, Jefferies, Patterson and Rogers in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017), says that conceptual knowledge requires both.

The spokes are modality-specific regions holding what a thing looks like, sounds like, how it moves, how you act on it, and its verbal label.

The hub in the ATL receives from all the spokes and learns a modality-invariant code - a compressed representation that captures deep similarity structure that no single sense could deliver, so that a whale groups with a cow rather than with a shark.

The model is implemented as a working neural network, which matters, because it lets researchers lesion the simulation and check that it produces the same graded, typicality-sensitive errors that patients produce.

Its main prediction is a dissociation - hub damage should impair meaning in every modality, spoke damage should impair only the corresponding kind of knowledge - and neuropsychological evidence broadly bears this out, with a 2012 study by Lambon Ralph and colleagues describing semantic dementia as damage to the pan-modal hub followed later by the visual spoke.

43.2.3 Distributed semantic maps across cortex

Against a hub-only picture, Alexander Huth, Jack Gallant and colleagues published a striking demonstration in Nature (2016) that word meaning is represented very broadly.

They scanned seven volunteers with fMRI while they listened to more than two hours of spoken stories from The Moth Radio Hour, then built a voxelwise encoding model mapping over ten thousand distinct words onto brain responses.

The result was a set of continuous semantic maps tiling large parts of both hemispheres, organised along interpretable dimensions such as how social or human a word is and how concrete or sensory it is, and the maps were remarkably similar from person to person.

This does not refute the hub - the ATL is poorly imaged by standard fMRI and the study was about tracking meaning during comprehension - but it does establish that semantic information is not confined to any single patch of cortex, and any complete theory must accommodate both the distributed maps and the convergence zone.

43.2.4 The semantic control network in inferior frontal and posterior temporal cortex

Knowing what a piano is and retrieving the right aspect of piano for the current sentence are different jobs.

The second job is semantic control - selectively accessing and shaping stored meaning to fit context - and Elizabeth Jefferies and colleagues have shown it depends on a separate left-lateralised network.

TMS evidence from Whitney, Kirk, Jefferies and Lambon Ralph in Cerebral Cortex (2011) showed that disrupting either left inferior frontal gyrus or left posterior middle temporal gyrus impaired demanding semantic judgements while sparing easy ones, implying a distributed control network rather than one control centre.

Meta-analysis of the imaging literature by Jackson (2021), pooling hundreds of activation peaks across 126 contrasts, recovered the same network - inferior frontal gyrus, posterior middle and inferior temporal gyrus, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.

Control is what lets you retrieve the buried meaning of a word on demand, which is why control damage produces a very different clinical picture from hub damage, as the next section describes.

43.3 Grounding and abstraction

If concepts are patterns in neurons, what makes those patterns be about anything?

This is the deepest question in the chapter and the one where philosophy, psychology and artificial intelligence meet.

43.3.1 Embodied and grounded cognition accounts of meaning

Grounded cognition, argued most influentially by Lawrence Barsalou since the late 1990s, holds that concepts are not abstract symbols but partial re-enactments of perception and action - understanding kick involves reactivating some of the machinery you use to kick.

Supporting evidence includes findings that reading action words engages motor cortex in a body-part-appropriate way, and that colour words engage visual regions.

The strong version is contested: critics note that motor activation may follow comprehension rather than constitute it, and that patients with severe motor impairment can still understand action words.

More recent statements, including a 2024 paper in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review on invariant representations in abstract concept grounding, argue that grounding comes not only from the body but from situations and stable regularities in the environment, which is why some researchers now think embodied cognition is a poorly chosen name for the position.

43.3.2 Abstract concepts and their special difficulty

Abstract concepts such as democracy, doubt or Tuesday are the hardest case for grounding, because there is nothing to see, touch or do.

They are learned later, recalled less accurately, and processed more slowly than concrete words - the concreteness effect.

Anna Borghi's Words As social Tools account proposes that abstract concepts are grounded differently rather than not at all: they draw more heavily on linguistic experience, on social interaction and inner speech, and on interoception, meaning the sense of the body's internal state.

Related work, including a 2024 study in NeuroImage on mental-state concepts, reports that abstract words engage regions involved in mentalising and in speech-related mouth movement, consistent with the social-linguistic emphasis.

There is also a case, argued in a 2018 Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B paper, for abandoning the concrete-abstract dichotomy altogether in favour of multiple graded dimensions.

43.3.3 Symbol grounding and its proposed solutions

Stevan Harnad posed the symbol grounding problem in 1990 with an analogy - trying to learn Chinese from a Chinese-only dictionary, where every symbol is defined by other symbols and nothing ever touches the world.

The standard proposed solutions are to anchor at least some symbols in sensory categories learned from experience, so that the rest can be defined on top of them, and to insist that a genuine grounding requires a system that acts in a world and suffers consequences.

Within psychology, the hub-and-spoke architecture is one concrete answer - the hub's code is not free-floating because it is learned from and constrained by the sensory and motor spokes.

The problem is not solved so much as reframed: most researchers now agree that grounding is a matter of the right kind of causal relation to the world, and disagree about which kinds count.

43.3.4 Language models as tests of distributional meaning

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict the next piece of text, and it learns word meanings from distribution alone, following the hypothesis stated by Zellig Harris in 1954 and John Firth in 1957 that a word is characterised by the company it keeps.

Emily Bender and Alexander Koller argued in 2020, with their octopus thought experiment about a creature that eavesdrops on a telegraph cable and mimics conversation without ever seeing the things discussed, that meaning cannot in principle be learned from form alone.

Dimitri Coelho Mollo and Raphaël Millière restated the issue for modern systems as the vector grounding problem, distinguishing several senses of grounding and arguing that only referential grounding is at stake; they take a more permissive view than Bender and Koller, suggesting that training with human feedback can establish a genuine referential relation.

This is a genuine open dispute, not a settled matter, and its scientific interest for us is comparative - the fact that text-only models capture a great deal of human semantic structure is evidence that distributional statistics do real work in human meaning too, while their characteristic failures on physical and spatial reasoning suggest that sensorimotor experience contributes something distinct.

43.4 Semantic dementia and other evidence

Theories of semantic memory have been shaped more by patients than by any other source, and this section covers the two clinical syndromes that anchor the field, plus the developmental evidence.

43.4.1 Progressive semantic loss and graded degradation

Semantic dementia, also described as the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia, is a neurodegenerative disease in which the anterior temporal lobes atrophy while memory for events, visual perception and everyday problem-solving remain relatively intact.

The loss is graded rather than random, and the pattern is close to a natural experiment on the structure of concepts: patients hold on to knowledge that is frequent, typical of its domain and shared across many concepts, and lose what is rare and distinctive first.

Julie Snowden, John Hodges, Karalyn Patterson and colleagues documented this progression from the 1990s onward, and Rogers and colleagues showed at the edge of semantic space that typicality and disease severity, not the modality of testing, predict when a concept collapses.

The signature error is over-regularisation - asked to draw a camel from its name, a patient draws a horse; asked to name a zebra, they say horse - which is exactly what a damaged system that retains only the typical structure of a domain would produce.

That result is important because it makes prototype-like behaviour fall out of graded damage to a distributed representation, rather than requiring a stored prototype.

43.4.2 Semantic aphasia and the control-representation dissociation

Semantic aphasia is the contrasting syndrome, seen after stroke to left inferior frontal or temporoparietal cortex, and studied intensively by Elizabeth Jefferies and Lambon Ralph.

These patients also fail semantic tests, but for a different reason - their stored knowledge is intact and their problem is retrieving the contextually appropriate part of it.

The diagnostic contrasts are clean: semantic dementia patients are consistent from test to test and are helped little by cues, whereas semantic aphasia patients are inconsistent, are strongly helped by phonemic or contextual cues, and are hurt disproportionately by distracting or unusual contexts.

Crucially, frontal and posterior lesion sites produce the same behavioural profile, which is the neuropsychological pillar of the distributed semantic control network described earlier.

Together the two syndromes give a double dissociation between the representation of meaning and control over it, which is the strongest single piece of evidence that semantic cognition has two components rather than one.

43.4.3 Development of semantic knowledge in childhood

Children build this system over years, and the order in which they build it is informative.

Jean Mandler and colleagues found that infants between roughly seven and eleven months already sort broad global domains such as animals, vehicles and furniture, and only later split finer distinctions - dogs from birds before dogs from cats - which suggests that development runs from coarse to fine.

Rosch's finding that preschoolers sort more easily at the basic level, dog rather than animal or collie, is well replicated for older children, though whether the basic level is genuinely first in infancy remains debated.

Language then accelerates everything, supplying labels that invite children to treat instances as members of a kind and giving them access to concepts they cannot see.

A computational account by Andrew Saxe, James McClelland and Surya Ganguli, developing Rogers and McClelland's earlier work, showed mathematically that a deep network learning from feature data will naturally differentiate broad categories before narrow ones - the same coarse-to-fine progression children show, and the reverse of the progression semantic dementia follows.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Semantic memory is graded rather than checklist-like, and its structure shows up in typicality effects that prototype and exemplar theories each explain part of.

The best-supported neural account is hub-and-spoke: modality-specific spokes across cortex feed a convergence hub in the ventrolateral anterior temporal lobe that learns a modality-invariant code, while a separate left frontal and posterior temporal network supplies semantic control.

The double dissociation between semantic dementia, where knowledge itself degrades in a typicality-graded way, and semantic aphasia, where knowledge is intact but inaccessible, is the strongest evidence for that two-component design.

Grounding remains genuinely unsettled - motor and sensory systems clearly participate in meaning, but their necessity is disputed, and abstract concepts appear to recruit linguistic, social and interoceptive experience instead.

Large language models are now an informative test case rather than a settled answer, showing how far distributional statistics alone can carry meaning and where they stop.

Category-specific deficits are real and replicable, but whether they reflect sensory-functional divisions, evolved category modules, or simply the crowded similarity structure of living things is still argued.


CHAPTER 44. PROCEDURAL MEMORY, HABIT, AND SKILL (CORE)

This chapter is about the kind of memory you cannot recite.

Procedural memory is knowledge expressed in performance rather than in report - the tightening of a reflex, the automatic reach for a light switch, the fingering of a scale, the eye that has learned to spot a tumour on a scan.

It matters because it is the oldest and most widely shared form of learning in the animal kingdom, because it is largely spared in the amnesias that devastate conscious recollection, and because when it goes wrong it produces some of the most stubborn disorders in psychiatry, from compulsion to addiction.

We will begin with the simplest forms of learning a nervous system can do, move through the machinery that turns a deliberate action into a habit, then look at motor skill and at the quiet learning that reshapes perception itself.

Throughout, the guiding question is the same: what changes in the brain when behaviour changes without the person deciding that it should?


44.1 Non-associative and associative conditioning

Before a brain can store a memory of an event, it must be able to change how strongly it responds to a stimulus at all.

The learning phenomena in this section are the floor of the building.

Non-associative learning means a change in response to a single stimulus, with no pairing involved.

Associative learning means the nervous system has picked up a relationship between two things - between two stimuli, or between an action and its consequence.

Both were studied first in simple preparations, and the cellular accounts we have of them are among the most complete in all of neuroscience.


44.1.1 Habituation and sensitisation

Habituation is the waning of a response to a stimulus that is repeated and turns out to be harmless - the way you stop noticing a clock ticking.

Sensitisation is the opposite: after a strong or noxious stimulus, responses to all sorts of unrelated stimuli are amplified, the way a startle after a loud bang leaves you jumpy for minutes.

The cellular account comes largely from the marine snail Aplysia californica, studied by Eric Kandel and colleagues from the 1960s onward, work recognised with a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Aplysia has a nervous system of roughly twenty thousand comparatively large neurons, which made it possible to trace a behaviour - the withdrawal of the gill when the siphon is touched - down to identified cells and identified synapses.

Short-term habituation there involves a presynaptic reduction in transmitter release from the sensory neuron, associated with depletion of the pool of synaptic vesicles ready to be released; sensitisation involves a modulatory interneuron releasing serotonin onto the sensory neuron terminal, raising intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP, a small signalling molecule) and boosting release.

Repeated training converts these short-lived changes into long-term ones by recruiting gene transcription and the growth of new synaptic connections, which is the clearest demonstration in any animal that memory can be structural.

One caution: the field has increasingly argued that postsynaptic changes - changes in the receiving neuron - were underweighted in the classic presynaptic story, so the mechanism is best described as mixed rather than purely presynaptic.


44.1.2 Classical conditioning and the Rescorla-Wagner rule

Classical, or Pavlovian, conditioning is learning that one stimulus predicts another: Ivan Pavlov's dogs learned that a bell (the conditioned stimulus, CS) preceded food (the unconditioned stimulus, US), and came to salivate to the bell.

For decades the assumption was that mere pairing in time was enough, but Leon Kamin's blocking experiments in the late 1960s destroyed that idea.

In blocking, an animal first learns that a light predicts shock; then a tone is added, so light-and-tone together predict shock; and afterwards the tone alone produces almost nothing, despite having been paired with shock many times.

Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner formalised the explanation in 1972: learning on a trial is proportional to prediction error, the difference between the outcome that occurred and the outcome that all cues present already predicted.

If the light already predicts the shock, the error is near zero when the tone is added, so the tone learns nothing - surprise, not contiguity, is the engine of learning.

The Rescorla-Wagner rule is mathematically almost identical to the delta rule used to train artificial neural networks, and its prediction-error term turned out to match the firing of midbrain dopamine neurons closely enough that it now underpins reinforcement learning accounts of the basal ganglia.

Its known limits are real and worth stating: it does not handle the timing of responses, and it struggles with phenomena such as latent inhibition, which motivated rival attention-based models from Nicholas Mackintosh and from John Pearce and Geoffrey Hall.


44.1.3 Instrumental conditioning and the law of effect

Instrumental, or operant, conditioning is learning about the consequences of one's own actions rather than about relations between external events.

Edward Thorndike established it around 1898 with puzzle boxes, in which a cat had to operate a latch to escape and reach food; escape times fell gradually across trials, with no sign of sudden insight.

From this he stated the law of effect: responses followed by satisfying consequences become more strongly connected to the situation in which they occurred, and are more likely to recur.

B. F. Skinner extended the framework in the 1930s with the operant chamber and schedules of reinforcement, showing that the pattern of reward delivery - fixed or variable, by number of responses or by time - controls the pattern of responding with great precision.

The modern refinement is that Thorndike's stimulus-response bond is only half the story: animals also encode the action-outcome relation, and which of the two controls behaviour depends on training history, which is the subject of the next section.


44.1.4 Cerebellar and amygdalar conditioning circuits

Different conditioned responses are stored in different places, and two circuits are mapped in unusual detail.

For delay eyeblink conditioning - a tone followed by a puff of air to the eye - the essential circuit is cerebellar: the tone arrives via mossy fibres through the pontine nuclei, the air puff arrives via climbing fibres from the inferior olive, the two converge on Purkinje cells and on the interpositus nucleus, and work by Richard Thompson and colleagues from the 1980s onward showed that inactivating the interpositus abolishes the learned blink while leaving the reflex blink intact.

For fear conditioning - a tone followed by a footshock - the essential circuit is amygdalar: convergence of auditory and pain information in the lateral amygdala strengthens synapses there, and the central amygdala drives freezing, blood pressure changes, and startle potentiation through brainstem and hypothalamic targets, a circuit worked out largely by Joseph LeDoux and by Michael Davis and their colleagues.

The two systems are not sealed off from one another; amygdala activity facilitates responses in the pontine input to the cerebellum and speeds acquisition of the conditioned blink, and there is an active and unsettled literature arguing that the cerebellum contributes to fear learning in its own right.

Trace conditioning, in which a gap separates the tone from the outcome, differs importantly from delay conditioning: it additionally requires the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex, and in humans it correlates with awareness of the contingency, which makes it a useful bridge between procedural and declarative memory.


44.2 Habit formation

A habit is not merely a behaviour done often.

In the technical sense used here, a habit is behaviour that has become insensitive to the current value of its outcome - it is triggered by the situation rather than pulled by the goal.

This definition is what makes habit experimentally tractable, because it yields a test.


44.2.1 Goal-directed against habitual control

Anthony Dickinson and Bernard Balleine, from the 1980s onward, argued that instrumental behaviour is supported by two systems running in parallel.

The goal-directed system encodes the action-outcome contingency together with the current desirability of the outcome, so it is flexible and can change immediately when the world changes.

The habit system encodes a stimulus-response link strengthened by past reinforcement, so it is fast and cheap to run but slow to update.

In the computational reframing offered by Nathaniel Daw, Yael Niv, and Peter Dayan in 2005, these correspond to model-based control, which searches a learned model of the world's structure, and model-free control, which caches the average value of actions; an arbitration mechanism favours whichever system is currently more reliable.

That framework is elegant and enormously influential, but it should be held loosely: the mapping of psychological habit onto computational model-free control is a theoretical proposal rather than an established identity, and several groups have argued that human tasks meant to dissociate the two do so imperfectly.


44.2.2 Devaluation tests and the transition to habit

The outcome devaluation test is the standard assay.

A rat is trained to press a lever for a food pellet; the pellet is then devalued outside the training context, either by feeding the rat to satiety on it or by pairing it with a mild illness-inducing agent so it becomes distasteful; then the lever is offered again in extinction, with no pellets delivered, so the animal must rely on memory rather than on tasting the outcome.

A goal-directed animal presses much less; a habitual animal presses on regardless, and that persistence is the operational definition of habit.

Adams showed in 1982 that the key variable is the amount of training: after moderate training rats are goal-directed, after extended training they are habitual, and interval schedules, where reward depends on time elapsed, produce habits faster than ratio schedules, where reward depends on the number of presses.

In humans the picture is less clean; devaluation effects are often small, several well-powered studies have failed to produce reliable overtraining-induced habits in the laboratory, and there is now open debate about whether standard human habit paradigms measure habit at all.


44.2.3 Dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatal contributions

The striatum, the main input structure of the basal ganglia, is divided in the rodent into a dorsomedial and a dorsolateral territory, distinguished chiefly by the cortical regions that project to them.

Henry Yin, Barbara Knowlton, and Bernard Balleine showed in the early 2000s that lesions of dorsolateral striatum leave animals permanently goal-directed - they stay sensitive to devaluation even after overtraining - whereas lesions or inactivation of dorsomedial striatum push animals into habit early.

The two regions therefore compete rather than sit in series, and over the course of training the balance of control shifts from the associative, dorsomedial loop to the sensorimotor, dorsolateral loop.

Dopamine is required for the shift, and Ann Graybiel's laboratory has shown that as a sequence becomes habitual the firing of striatal neurons develops a bracketing pattern, marking the start and end of the sequence as though it had been packaged into a single unit, a process often called chunking.

The homologous human regions are usually taken to be the caudate for the dorsomedial function and the posterior putamen for the dorsolateral function, and human imaging by Tricomi, Balleine, and O'Doherty in 2009 reported increasing posterior putamen activity with overtraining, though the anatomical correspondence across species remains an inference rather than a certainty.


44.2.4 Habit in compulsion and addiction

Barry Everitt and Trevor Robbins proposed that addiction is the pathological endpoint of the normal transition from action to habit and then to compulsion, accompanied at the neural level by a spiral of control from ventral striatum, which handles motivation and reward, to progressively more dorsal striatal territory, which handles stimulus-driven responding.

The evidence includes the finding that drug-seeking in rats becomes insensitive to devaluation and to punishment after prolonged self-administration, and that disconnecting dorsolateral striatal dopamine restores sensitivity.

A parallel argument has been made for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), where Claire Gillan, Trevor Robbins, and colleagues reported excessive habit formation on avoidance tasks in patients, suggesting that compulsions may be habits that have escaped goal-directed override rather than actions driven by obsessional beliefs.

This framework is genuinely contested.

Critics, including Marc Lewis and Hanna Pickard, argue that addicted behaviour remains sensitive to incentives - people do trade drug use for money and for valued alternatives in contingency-management studies - which is hard to square with a purely habitual account, and a 2024 review by Field and colleagues questions whether compulsion explains addiction at all.

The honest position is that the habit account captures something real about rigidity and cue-triggering, but that it is not a complete theory of addiction.


44.3 Motor skill learning

Skill is the third face of procedural memory: not a reflex modified, not an action automatised, but a movement executed better than it could be before.

The field has learned to separate several processes that older work lumped together as practice, and the separation has consequences for rehabilitation, for sport, and for how we think about expertise.


44.3.1 Adaptation, sequence learning, and de novo skill acquisition

Adaptation is the recalibration of an existing movement to a changed environment - reaching accurately while wearing prism goggles, or while a robotic arm pushes your hand sideways.

It is fast, it is largely automatic, and it decays: the aftereffect when the perturbation is removed shows the system had shifted rather than learned something new.

Sequence learning is the acquisition of an order of elements, studied with the serial reaction time task introduced by Mary Jo Nissen and Peter Bullemer in 1987, in which participants respond to a repeating sequence of targets and speed up on it without necessarily being able to state what the sequence was.

De novo skill acquisition is the third and least-studied category: learning a genuinely new mapping between what you do and what happens, such as controlling a cursor with a hand shape or learning to juggle, where there is no pre-existing movement to recalibrate.

John Krakauer and colleagues have argued forcefully, notably in a 2019 review, that adaptation has been overused as a model of skill because it is easy to measure, and that true skill involves changes in the speed-accuracy trade-off - becoming able to be both faster and more accurate - which adaptation paradigms cannot capture.


44.3.2 Error-based, reinforcement-based, and use-dependent learning

Three learning processes operate during practice and can be dissociated experimentally.

Error-based learning uses a signed, vectorial error - the direction and size of the miss - to update an internal model; it is implicit, it produces aftereffects, and it depends on the cerebellum.

Reinforcement-based learning uses only a scalar signal, success or failure, to make successful actions more likely; it is slower, but it produces memories that are strikingly durable.

Use-dependent learning is a drift toward whatever movements have simply been repeated most often, independent of whether they succeeded, and it explains part of the biasing seen after long practice.

The dissociation was made vivid by Therrien, Wolpert, and Bastian in 2016: cerebellar patients showed essentially no retention when learning was error-based, but learned substantially and retained fully when the same task was taught with binary reinforcement, provided their motor variability was in a workable range.

That result is clinically important, because it suggests reward-based training schedules for patients whose error-based machinery is damaged.


44.3.3 Cerebellar internal models and forward prediction

An internal model is a neural circuit that mimics some part of the body or world.

A forward model takes a copy of the outgoing motor command and predicts the sensory consequences it should produce; an inverse model does the reverse, computing the command needed to reach a desired state.

The forward model matters because sensory feedback is too slow to steer fast movements, so the brain must control by prediction, comparing predicted with actual feedback and correcting the difference - the sensory prediction error.

The cerebellum is the best candidate site: it receives efference copy through mossy fibres, receives error signals through climbing fibres from the inferior olive, and adjusts Purkinje cell output accordingly, a scheme anticipated in the Marr-Albus-Ito theory of cerebellar learning from the late 1960s and early 1970s.

The same predictive machinery explains why you cannot tickle yourself: predicted self-generated sensation is attenuated, and Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert, and Chris Frith showed in the late 1990s that this attenuation tracks cerebellar activity, a finding since extended into accounts of the sense of agency and of some symptoms of schizophrenia.

It should be said that long-term depression at the parallel fibre to Purkinje cell synapse, long taken to be the cellular basis of this learning, has been shown by mouse work from the 2010s not to be strictly necessary for cerebellar motor learning, so the cellular story is more redundant and more complicated than the classical theory assumed.


44.3.4 Motor memory consolidation and interference

A newly acquired motor memory is fragile for some hours before it stabilises, a process called consolidation.

Reza Shadmehr and Thomas Brashers-Krug demonstrated retrograde interference in 1996: learning force field A and then, within a short interval, force field B, wiped out the memory of A, whereas a gap of several hours between them let both survive.

Anterograde interference works the other way, with prior learning slowing subsequent learning of a conflicting mapping, and it is one reason that practice schedules matter as much as practice quantity.

The role of sleep is genuinely disputed.

Sleep-dependent gains in finger-sequence tapping were reported by Matthew Walker, Robert Stickgold, and colleagues in the early 2000s, but reanalyses attributing much of the effect to the release from within-session fatigue and to averaging artefacts - notably by Rickard and colleagues in 2008 - substantially weakened the claim, and for sensorimotor adaptation the evidence for a sleep requirement has always been thin, though recent work continues to report sleep-related stabilisation.

Primary motor cortex appears to be causally involved in consolidation, since repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS, a method of transiently disrupting cortical activity with magnetic pulses) applied over it soon after training impairs later retention, while leaving the immediate performance intact.


44.4 Priming and perceptual learning

The final section concerns the least conspicuous form of procedural memory: changes in how efficiently the brain processes a stimulus it has met before, and changes in what the perceptual system is able to discriminate at all.

These are learning without any feeling of learning.


44.4.1 Repetition suppression and its interpretations

When a stimulus is repeated, neurons that responded to it the first time typically respond less the second time, an effect visible in single-neuron recordings and as reduced blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

This repetition suppression has been used as a workhorse tool, on the reasoning that if a region shows suppression across a change in viewpoint, it must represent the object independently of viewpoint.

The interpretation is not settled, and at least four accounts compete.

The fatigue account holds that all responsive neurons reduce their firing proportionally, through synaptic depression; the sharpening account, associated with Rufin Vogels and Guy Wiggs and Alex Martin, holds that neurons coding irrelevant features drop out, leaving a sparser and more selective representation; the facilitation account holds that processing simply finishes sooner, which a slow haemodynamic measure reads as less activity; and the predictive coding account, argued by Karl Friston and by Kalanit Grill-Spector and colleagues, holds that suppression reflects reduced prediction error for an expected stimulus.

Evidence for the predictive coding view came from Summerfield and colleagues in 2008, who found repetition suppression was larger when repetitions were more probable, but the result has failed to replicate consistently across stimulus classes and monkey electrophysiology has often favoured local adaptation instead - so repetition suppression should be treated as a useful but ambiguous index of representation.


44.4.2 Perceptual priming and implicit memory

Priming is facilitated processing of a stimulus because of prior exposure to it, measured as faster or more accurate identification rather than as remembering.

Elizabeth Warrington and Lawrence Weiskrantz showed in 1968 and 1974 that densely amnesic patients, who could not recognise a studied word list, nevertheless completed word stems with studied words at above-chance rates, one of the founding demonstrations that memory is not one thing.

Daniel Schacter and Endel Tulving developed the distinction, separating perceptual priming, which is sensitive to changes in the surface form of the stimulus such as modality or font and is supported by posterior sensory cortex, from conceptual priming, which is sensitive to meaning and is supported more by left prefrontal and temporal regions.

The neural signature of priming is generally reduced activity in the regions that processed the stimulus first time - the same repetition suppression discussed above - and there is evidence that priming and recognition memory can be doubly dissociated, with occipital damage impairing visual priming while leaving recognition intact.

Priming is remarkably long-lasting: identification advantages have been reported after weeks to more than a year, despite the person having no recollection of the original exposure.


44.4.3 Statistical learning of environmental regularities

Statistical learning is the extraction of the regularities in a stream of input without instruction, feedback, or intent to learn.

Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin, and Elissa Newport showed in 1996 that eight-month-old infants exposed for two minutes to a continuous stream of synthesised syllables, with no pauses or stress cues, subsequently discriminated the recurring three-syllable units from foils - they had tracked transitional probabilities between syllables and used the dips to find word boundaries.

The finding was rapidly extended to tones, visual shapes, tactile sequences, and to species including rats and monkeys, which argues that it is a general property of nervous systems rather than a language-specific device.

The neural substrate is debated: the medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus, is now known to contribute even though the learning is implicit, which complicates the old textbook split between a hippocampal declarative system and a striatal procedural one.

There is also a live measurement problem - individual statistical learning scores are often unreliable across tasks, which has made it hard to sustain claims linking the ability to reading or language outcomes, and honest reviews say so.


44.4.4 Expertise and the reorganisation of representation

Sustained practice at a perceptual discrimination changes the brain's representation of the trained material, not just the decision made about it.

Classic examples include the enlarged cortical representation of the fingers of the left hand in string players reported by Thomas Elbert and colleagues in 1995, and the posterior hippocampal volume differences in London taxi drivers reported by Eleanor Maguire and colleagues in 2000 and confirmed longitudinally in 2011.

In vision, perceptual learning was long thought to change early cortex, because improvements were highly specific to the trained orientation, location, and eye; the reverse hierarchy theory of Merav Ahissar and Shaul Hochstein, published in 2004, reversed the emphasis, proposing that learning begins at high levels and descends to earlier levels only when finer detail is needed, which explains why easy tasks generalise and hard tasks do not.

Current evidence supports a distributed picture: some changes in early sensory areas, substantial changes in how decision areas read out sensory evidence, and reweighting of connections rather than wholesale rewiring.

The status of the fusiform face area in expertise remains a genuine dispute - Isabel Gauthier and colleagues argue it is a general region for subordinate-level expert discrimination, shown with bird and car experts and with artificial greebles, while Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues argue it is domain-specific for faces and that expertise effects there are small and inconsistent.

Expertise in the real world is in any case not only perceptual: experts bring conceptual structure and learned attention strategies, which is why a radiologist's advantage is partly in knowing where to look.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Procedural memory is a family, not a single system: non-associative changes in reflex strength, Pavlovian and instrumental associations, habits, motor skills, and perceptual tuning each have distinguishable behavioural signatures and largely distinguishable circuits.

Associative learning is driven by prediction error rather than by mere temporal pairing, a principle established by Kamin's blocking and formalised by Rescorla and Wagner in 1972, and it remains the most transferable idea in the chapter.

Instrumental behaviour is supported by competing goal-directed and habitual controllers, associated in rodents with dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum respectively, and the outcome devaluation test is what makes the distinction more than a metaphor - though the human version of the effect is weaker and more contested than the animal literature would suggest.

Motor skill decomposes into error-based, reinforcement-based, and use-dependent processes, with the cerebellum supplying forward models and sensory prediction errors, and dissociations such as Therrien and colleagues' 2016 result show these processes can be separately damaged and separately trained.

Finally, repeated exposure quietly reshapes perception through priming, statistical learning, and expertise, but the neural index most often used to study it - repetition suppression - has at least four viable interpretations and should not be read as a transparent window onto representation.


CHAPTER 45. CONSOLIDATION, REPLAY, SLEEP, AND FORGETTING (CORE)

A memory is not finished at the moment it is made.

For minutes, hours, days, and in some cases years afterwards, the brain keeps working on it - stabilising it chemically, moving it between brain regions, rehearsing it offline, editing it, and in many cases deliberately dismantling it.

This chapter follows a memory through that long afterlife.

It matters because almost everything that goes wrong with memory - the blank after a concussion, the intrusive flashback of trauma, the fog of a sleepless week, the gentle blurring of a childhood holiday into gist - happens in this afterlife rather than at the moment of learning.

It also matters because the same machinery explains something more cheerful: why sleep is not wasted time, and why forgetting is not simply failure.

45.1 Cellular consolidation

Consolidation is the process by which a fragile new memory becomes a durable one.

Neuroscientists divide it into two scales that run on different clocks.

Cellular consolidation, the subject of this section, happens inside and around individual synapses (the junctions where one neuron passes a signal to another) over minutes to hours.

Systems consolidation, the subject of the next section, happens across whole brain regions over weeks to years.

45.1.1 Protein synthesis dependence and the consolidation window

Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the durable strengthening of a synapse that follows strong or repeated activity, and it is the leading cellular model of learning.

LTP comes in two flavours: an early phase lasting an hour or two that needs only the modification of proteins already present, and a late phase lasting many hours or days that requires the neuron to manufacture new proteins.

If a drug that blocks protein synthesis, such as anisomycin, is given around the time of learning, the early phase survives but the late phase collapses, and the animal's memory fades on the same schedule.

Crucially, the same drug given a few hours later usually does nothing, which is the practical meaning of the consolidation window - a bounded period after learning during which the memory can still be derailed.

This is why a blow to the head often erases the minutes before impact while leaving yesterday intact.

45.1.2 Synaptic tagging and capture

A puzzle sits inside the protein synthesis story.

New proteins are made mainly in the cell body, yet LTP is input-specific - only the synapses that were actually active get strengthened, and a neuron may have tens of thousands of them.

Frey and Morris (1997) proposed the synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis to resolve this: activity leaves a short-lived molecular marker, a tag, at the stimulated synapse, and this tag captures the plasticity-related proteins that are shipped out generally through the cell.

Their key experiment was elegant.

A weak stimulation that would normally produce only early LTP was converted into long-lasting late LTP if a different input to the same neurons had recently received strong stimulation, because the weak input's tag captured proteins that the strong input had paid to produce.

The tag itself decays in under about three hours, which supplies a mechanism for why an otherwise trivial event can be remembered if it happened close in time to something important - a phenomenon known as behavioural tagging.

The hypothesis remains influential and was the subject of a dedicated 2024 theme issue of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, though the molecular identity of the tag itself is still not settled.

45.1.3 Transcriptional cascades and immediate early genes

For the neuron to make new proteins it must first switch on genes, and consolidation therefore reaches all the way into the nucleus.

Calcium entering the active synapse triggers signalling cascades, prominently the mitogen-activated protein kinase and extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway (MAPK/ERK), which activate a transcription factor called cyclic adenosine monophosphate response element-binding protein (CREB).

CREB in turn switches on immediate early genes (IEGs) - genes that respond to neural activity within minutes without needing new protein to be made first.

Three IEGs dominate the literature: c-fos and zif268 (also called Egr1), which are themselves transcription factors that switch on further genes, and Arc, which is an effector that goes back out to the synapse and directly regulates receptor trafficking and synaptic strength.

Blocking CREB, MAPK, or zif268 impairs the consolidation of long-term memory while leaving short-term memory intact, a dissociation that has been shown repeatedly, for example by Bozon and colleagues in recognition memory (2003).

A practical bonus is that because these genes mark recently active neurons, researchers now use them as tags to find and later reactivate the specific cells that hold a memory - the engram.

45.1.4 Modulation by arousal and emotion

Consolidation is not a fixed pipeline; its gain is turned up or down by how much the event mattered.

James McGaugh and colleagues established over several decades that emotionally arousing events release the stress hormones adrenaline and cortisol, which act on the basolateral amygdala (a nucleus deep in the temporal lobe that evaluates emotional significance), and that noradrenaline signalling there is required for the memory enhancement.

The amygdala does not store the memory itself; it projects to the hippocampus, striatum and cortex and modulates storage in those places.

Cahill and colleagues (1996) reported that amygdala activation while people watched emotionally arousing films predicted how much they recalled three weeks later.

The clean prediction, borne out in humans, is that a beta-blocker such as propranolol, which blocks noradrenaline receptors, given around an emotional event reduces the later memory advantage for the emotional material without flattening memory in general.

45.2 Systems consolidation

45.2.1 The standard model of hippocampal-to-neocortical transfer

The standard model of systems consolidation grew out of the study of patients with hippocampal damage, most famously Henry Molaison, known for decades as H.M., who after bilateral medial temporal lobe surgery in 1953 could form almost no new lasting declarative memories yet retained childhood memories.

The pattern of loss was graded in time: recent memories were hit hardest and remote ones were relatively spared, a gradient first described systematically by Ribot in the nineteenth century.

The standard model explains this by proposing that the hippocampus rapidly binds the scattered cortical fragments of an experience, then over weeks to years repeatedly reinstates them until direct cortex-to-cortex connections can support the memory alone.

On this account the hippocampus is a temporary index, and consolidated memories eventually become hippocampus-independent.

45.2.2 Multiple trace and trace transformation theories

The standard model has a persistent problem: some patients with hippocampal damage lose detailed autobiographical memories across their entire lives, with no temporal gradient at all.

Nadel and Moscovitch's multiple trace theory (1997) accounts for this by proposing that each retrieval of an episodic memory lays down a new hippocampal trace, so old, often-retrieved memories are more robust simply because they are more numerous, and that vivid episodic recollection never becomes hippocampus-independent even though the semantic gist can.

The successor account, trace transformation theory, developed by Winocur, Moscovitch and Nadel, argues that what changes with time is not location alone but the nature of the representation - a detailed, context-bound episodic trace supported by the hippocampus and a schematic, gist-like version supported by neocortex coexist and compete.

Human imaging supports a shift in mnemonic resolution, with remote gist-like memories engaging the anterior hippocampus more and the posterior hippocampus less.

This is a genuinely live dispute in the field, not a settled matter, and reviewers such as Squire on one side and Moscovitch on the other continue to read the same patient data differently.

45.2.3 Complementary learning systems and the reason for two systems

Why would evolution build two memory systems at all rather than one good one?

McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) gave the most influential answer, borrowing a failure from artificial neural networks.

Networks that learn quickly by adjusting overlapping distributed representations suffer catastrophic interference - learning something new overwrites what was learned before.

Their complementary learning systems theory proposes that the neocortex learns slowly with overlapping representations precisely so that it can extract statistical regularities across many episodes without being wrecked by any single one, while the hippocampus learns fast using sparse, highly separated representations that keep similar episodes from blurring together.

Consolidation is then the process by which the fast system tutors the slow one through repeated interleaved rehearsal, and the theory makes the falsifiable prediction, since broadly supported, that information consistent with an existing cortical schema should consolidate far faster than information that is not - as Tse and colleagues showed in rats in 2007.

45.2.4 Evidence from 2025 that consolidation reorganises hippocampal engram circuitry and degrades precision

A 2025 paper in Nature reported that systems consolidation reorganises engram circuitry inside the hippocampus itself, rather than merely handing memory over to cortex.

Tracking the synapses between CA3 engram neurons and CA1 engram neurons (CA3 and CA1 are successive stages of the hippocampal circuit) as memories aged, the authors found that these engram synapses grew denser and became increasingly clustered on CA1 dendrites, with the distance between neighbouring synapses shrinking over time.

Behaviourally, this coincided with CA1 engram neurons becoming promiscuous - firing in new contexts that merely resembled the original one, and driving behaviour there.

The interpretation is that the familiar loss of precision in old memories is not passive decay but a structural rewiring, and that its payoff is generalisation: a gist memory that can guide behaviour in new but related situations.

A companion line of work published in Current Biology in 2025 links the same transformation to adult hippocampal neurogenesis, the ongoing birth of new granule cells, which appears to help dismantle the precision of the original trace.

45.3 Replay and offline processing

45.3.1 Sharp-wave ripple replay in the hippocampus

A sharp-wave ripple (SWR) is a brief, spectacular burst of synchronised hippocampal activity - a large slow deflection with a fast oscillation of roughly 110 to 200 hertz riding on top - lasting a few tens of milliseconds.

During an SWR, the place cells that fired in sequence as an animal ran along a track fire again in the same order, but compressed roughly twenty-fold, so a ten-second run is re-run in half a second.

This is replay, first reported in sleep by Wilson and McNaughton (1994) and in compressed sequential form by Skaggs and McNaughton (1996).

The compression matters mechanically, because it squeezes the spikes into the tens-of-milliseconds window in which spike-timing-dependent plasticity can strengthen synapses.

The causal evidence is strong: Girardeau, Zugaro and colleagues (2009) and Ego-Stengel and Wilson (2010) showed that selectively disrupting ripples during sleep, without disturbing sleep otherwise, impairs spatial learning.

45.3.2 Forward, reverse, and preplay sequences

Replay is not always a simple rerun.

Foster and Wilson (2006) discovered reverse replay - sequences running backwards from the animal's current position - occurring mostly when the animal pauses at the end of a run, especially at a reward, which is exactly what a reinforcement learning algorithm would need in order to propagate value backwards along the path that earned it.

Forward replay is more common before a run, when the animal is deliberating about where to go.

More provocatively, Dragoi and Tonegawa (2011) reported preplay - sequences matching a track the animal has not yet explored, present before the experience - suggesting the hippocampus holds a pre-existing repertoire of sequences that experience assigns to places rather than building from scratch.

Preplay is contested; several groups, including Silva, Feng and Foster, have argued the effect can arise from statistical artefacts and pre-existing correlations, and the honest summary is that the phenomenon is reported but its interpretation is not agreed.

45.3.3 Ripple-spindle-slow oscillation coupling during sleep

For replay to instruct the cortex, hippocampus and cortex must be listening to each other at the right moments, and during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep three rhythms nest inside one another to arrange this.

Slow oscillations (roughly one cycle per second, generated in cortex) alternate global up-states of excitability with down-states of silence.

Sleep spindles (bursts of about 11 to 16 hertz, generated by the thalamus) ride on the up-states and appear to open cortical windows for plasticity.

Hippocampal ripples in turn cluster inside the troughs of spindles, so the memory content arrives exactly when the cortex is primed to accept it.

Helfrich, Staresina and colleagues reported in Nature Communications in 2024 that spindle-locked ripples recorded from electrodes inside the human medial temporal lobe track experimentally induced memory reactivation, and a 2024 Trends in Cognitive Sciences review by Staresina frames this hierarchical nesting as the core mechanism of sleep-dependent consolidation.

One caution is warranted: a Bayesian meta-analysis published in 2024 found the human correlation between slow-oscillation-spindle coupling and overnight memory benefit to be considerably weaker and less consistent than the enthusiasm of individual papers suggests.

45.3.4 Awake replay, planning, and the compositional recombination of experience

Replay is not confined to sleep.

Awake ripples occur during quiet rest and pauses, and Pfeiffer and Foster (2013) showed that awake replay sequences in rats sweep out toward the goal the animal is about to run to, making them look like plans rather than records.

Work by Shin, Tang and Jadhav (2019) showed that awake hippocampal replay is coordinated with prefrontal cortex during memory-guided decisions.

Most strikingly, Gupta and colleagues (2010) found replay of trajectories the animal had experienced only in pieces, and of paths never actually taken, implying the hippocampus can recombine fragments of experience into novel sequences.

That compositional capacity is one of the more attractive bridges between rodent electrophysiology and human imagination, though the leap from a rat's shortcut on a maze to a human's counterfactual daydream is an inference, not a demonstration.

45.4 Sleep and memory

45.4.1 Sleep stages and their differential contributions

Human sleep alternates between NREM sleep, including the deep slow-wave sleep (SWS) that dominates the first half of the night, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which lengthens toward morning.

The dual process hypothesis holds that SWS serves declarative memory - facts and events - while REM serves procedural, emotional and skill memory, and it was supported by early-night versus late-night experiments in which SWS-rich early sleep benefited word lists and REM-rich late sleep benefited perceptual and motor tasks.

The evidence has since become messier: several studies now tie procedural learning to NREM as well, and the clean dissociation is no longer regarded as secure.

The sequential hypothesis, associated with Giuditta and developed by Ficca and colleagues, argues instead that the two stages are complementary steps in one process - SWS selects and reactivates what is worth keeping, and REM integrates it with existing knowledge.

A 2025 paper in Communications Biology reported that a higher ratio of REM to SWS predicted greater loss of item-specific detail alongside greater gain of category-level structure, which is the sequential picture in miniature.

45.4.2 Targeted memory reactivation

Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) is the technique of pairing learning with a cue such as a sound or an odour, then quietly re-presenting that cue during sleep to bias which memories get replayed.

Rasch, Born and colleagues (2007) delivered a rose odour during learning of object locations and again during SWS, and found improved recall the next day, along with hippocampal activation in response to the odour during sleep.

Rudoy and Paller (2009) refined this by cueing individual items with their own sounds and showing that the specifically cued items were the ones that survived best - evidence that the effect is selective rather than a general arousal boost.

TMR now works as an experimental lever on consolidation, and the cueing benefit is largest when the cue lands in the up-state of a slow oscillation.

Effect sizes in healthy adults are real but modest, and attempts to sell the technique as a consumer learning-during-sleep product go well beyond what the data support.

45.4.3 Synaptic homeostasis hypothesis

Tononi and Cirelli's synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (SHY), first stated in 2003, offers a different reason for sleep.

Their claim is that waking experience produces a net increase in synaptic strength across the cortex, which is metabolically expensive and eventually saturating, and that NREM slow-wave activity globally downscales synapses in proportion, preserving the relative differences that carry information while restoring capacity - in their phrase, sleep is the price the brain pays for plasticity.

Supporting evidence includes the finding that slow-wave activity is higher after intense learning, and electron microscopy work from de Vivo and colleagues (2017) showing that cortical synapses in mice shrink by roughly 18 per cent across sleep.

SHY is contested, most vigorously by Marcos Frank, who argues that the hypothesis borrows and blurs the pre-existing concept of synaptic scaling, that the mechanism of downscaling is poorly specified, and that sleep also demonstrably strengthens some circuits.

The reasonable current position is that downscaling and consolidation are not mutually exclusive - the brain may both prune globally and strengthen selectively during the same night.

45.4.4 Sleep deprivation and cognitive cost

Sleep loss damages memory at both ends: it impairs the encoding of new material before sleep and it removes the consolidation that would have followed.

The hippocampus appears especially vulnerable; Havekes and colleagues (2016) showed that just five hours of sleep deprivation in mice caused loss of dendritic spines on CA1 neurons, a structural change that was reversible with recovery sleep.

In humans, Walker and Yoo (2007) found that a night of total sleep deprivation cut the ability to encode new pictures by roughly 40 per cent, with reduced hippocampal activation during learning.

A 2020 study found that two nights of recovery sleep restored hippocampal functional connectivity but did not fully restore episodic memory performance, which is a caution against assuming the debt can be simply repaid.

Deprivation also produces attentional lapses and slowed processing, and separating a genuine memory deficit from a general failure of attention remains a real methodological difficulty in this literature.

45.5 Reconsolidation and forgetting

45.5.1 Reactivation-induced lability and the reconsolidation window

For most of the twentieth century consolidation was assumed to be a one-way door: once shut, a memory was fixed.

Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000) reopened it, showing that if a consolidated fear memory in rats was first reactivated by presenting the conditioned tone, then followed by a protein synthesis inhibitor infused into the amygdala, the memory was lost - whereas the same drug without reactivation left it intact.

Retrieval, in other words, returns a memory to a labile state from which it must be restabilised, a process called reconsolidation, and the window is roughly the same few hours as original consolidation.

Boundary conditions matter and are well documented: memories that are very old, very strong, or reactivated without any prediction error - without something new or surprising during retrieval - often do not destabilise at all.

The finding that Hupbach and colleagues (2007) and Schiller and colleagues (2010) extended to humans, that new information delivered inside the reconsolidation window can update or overwrite the original, is the most consequential and the most replication-sensitive part of this literature.

45.5.2 Clinical exploitation in trauma and addiction

If reactivated memories are editable, then the emotional charge of a traumatic memory or a drug cue might be permanently reduced rather than merely suppressed - an appealing target for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and addiction.

Brunet and Pitman pursued this with propranolol given before a brief session in which the patient reads a personal trauma script, and open-label and small controlled trials reported substantial symptom reductions.

The larger and better-controlled trials have been less encouraging: a randomised trial reported in Neuropsychopharmacology in 2021 found symptoms fell by comparable amounts in the propranolol group and the placebo group, and Pitman's own group published three negative psychophysiological studies.

Meta-analyses find reconsolidation blockade reliable in laboratory fear conditioning but weak and inconsistent in clinical samples.

A parallel effort in addiction, including Xue and colleagues' retrieval-extinction procedure (2012), showed early promise for reducing cue-induced craving but has likewise proved hard to replicate consistently.

The fair verdict is that reconsolidation is a real biological phenomenon whose translation into treatment remains unproven.

45.5.3 Decay, interference, and retrieval failure as forgetting mechanisms

Three classical explanations for forgetting compete.

Decay says traces fade with time alone; interference says other memories compete, either retroactively when new learning obstructs old, or proactively when old learning obstructs new; retrieval failure says the trace is intact but the cue cannot reach it.

Retrieval failure has strong support from savings - Ebbinghaus showed in 1885 that apparently forgotten lists are relearned faster than fresh ones, which is impossible if nothing remains - and from context-dependent recall, where returning to the original environment restores access.

Interference has the strongest experimental pedigree, with a century of paired-associate studies behind it, and pure time-based decay is the hardest to demonstrate, since time in an awake organism is never empty of interfering events.

Retrieval-induced forgetting, described by Anderson, Bjork and Bjork (1994), shows that retrieving one item actively suppresses related competitors, and whether that reflects genuine inhibition or ordinary competition remains actively debated.

45.5.4 Active forgetting, and the adaptive value of not remembering

The most substantial recent shift is the recognition that the brain has dedicated machinery for erasing memories, not merely for failing to keep them.

Davis and Zhong's work in fruit flies identified an intrinsic forgetting pathway in which dopamine signalling activates the small GTPase Rac1 and the actin-regulating protein cofilin, which dismantles the synaptic structures holding the trace; boosting Rac1 shortens memory lifetime to under a day, while blocking it extends retention substantially, and the same pathway operates in rodent hippocampus.

Other established routes include neurogenesis-driven remodelling of hippocampal circuits, described by Akers, Frankland and colleagues in 2014 as a cause of infantile amnesia, and receptor removal at synapses.

Richards and Frankland (2017) argued the functional case directly: the goal of memory is not fidelity but the guidance of good decisions in a changing world, so forgetting outdated specifics and retaining generalisable structure is optimal rather than defective.

That argument is elegant and it fits the 2025 engram-rewiring data well, but it should be held with some care - the claim that a given instance of forgetting is adaptive rather than merely tolerated is difficult to test directly, and adaptive stories are easy to construct after the fact.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Memory stabilisation runs on two clocks: cellular consolidation over hours, requiring new protein synthesis, synaptic tags to keep it input-specific, and a transcriptional cascade through CREB and the immediate early genes; and systems consolidation over weeks to years, involving the hippocampus and neocortex.

Whether that slower process ends with the hippocampus fully released, as the standard model holds, or with an episodic trace that always needs it, as multiple trace and trace transformation theories hold, is genuinely unresolved, and 2025 evidence that consolidation rewires engram synapses inside the hippocampus and trades precision for generalisation complicates both accounts.

Replay during sharp-wave ripples is the leading candidate mechanism, and disrupting ripples causally impairs learning, with sleep providing the nested slow-oscillation, spindle and ripple structure that lets hippocampal content reach a receptive cortex.

Sleep's contribution is real and demonstrable through targeted memory reactivation and deprivation studies, though whether its core function is consolidation, synaptic downscaling, or both remains contested.

Finally, memory is editable after retrieval and actively dismantled by dedicated molecular pathways, which means forgetting should be read as part of the design rather than as its failure - while the clinical promise of exploiting reconsolidation in trauma and addiction remains, so far, unfulfilled.


CHAPTER 46. LEARNING RULES AND REWARD LEARNING IN THE BRAIN (CORE)


This chapter is about how a brain changes itself on the basis of what happens to it.

The central story is reward learning: the discovery that a small population of cells deep in the midbrain broadcasts a signal that looks remarkably like the error term used in a class of computer algorithms called reinforcement learning.

That discovery, made in the 1990s, is one of the few places where a mathematical theory invented by engineers turned out to match, almost line for line, a signal recorded from single neurons in a behaving animal.

But the chapter does not stop there.

The simple story has been complicated in productive ways - dopamine turns out to carry more than one kind of message, the brain plainly builds maps as well as habits, and a great deal of learning happens with no reward in sight at all.

By the end you should be able to say what a prediction error is, where in the brain it is computed, what it changes, and where the theory is still arguing with itself.


46.1 The dopaminergic prediction error

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter - a chemical messenger released by one neuron to influence another.

The dopamine neurons that matter for this chapter live in two small midbrain clusters, the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and they send long thin axons to the striatum and the frontal cortex.

Popular writing calls dopamine the pleasure chemical.

That is wrong, and the correction is the subject of this section: dopamine does not report how good something is, it reports how much better or worse things turned out than expected.


46.1.1 Schultz's recordings and the temporal difference correspondence

Wolfram Schultz and colleagues recorded from midbrain dopamine neurons in monkeys learning that a light or tone predicted a squirt of juice, and found a striking pattern, summarised in Schultz, Dayan and Montague (1997) in Science.

Before learning, the cells fired a burst when the unexpected juice arrived; after learning, the burst moved backwards in time to the predictive cue, and the juice itself - now fully expected - produced no burst at all.

This is exactly the behaviour of the error term in temporal difference (TD) learning, an algorithm developed by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto in which an agent updates its estimate of future reward by the difference between what it predicted and what the next moment revealed.

The quantity is called reward prediction error (RPE): the actual value of the situation minus the predicted value.

Hollerman and Schultz (1998) sharpened the correspondence by showing the signal is sensitive to timing as well as amount - deliver an expected reward earlier or later than trained, and the cells respond, because the prediction was about when as much as whether.

The match between a theory built to make machines learn and a signal recorded from a monkey's midbrain remains one of the strongest results in systems neuroscience.


46.1.2 Positive and negative prediction errors and dopamine dip coding

A prediction error must be able to go both ways: better than expected and worse than expected.

Better than expected is easy for a neuron - it fires a burst - but worse than expected runs into a hard physical limit, because a neuron cannot fire fewer than zero spikes per second.

Dopamine neurons fire at a low steady background rate, called tonic firing, of roughly a few spikes per second, and a negative error appears as a pause or dip below that baseline.

Bayer and Glimcher (2005) pointed out the resulting asymmetry: firing rate scaled cleanly with positive errors but was compressed for negative ones, raising the worry that the negative half of the signal was not properly carried.

Later work by Bayer, Lau and Glimcher and by others proposed that the duration of the pause, rather than its depth, encodes the size of the negative error, which sidesteps the floor problem.

Measurements of dopamine release in the striatum, as opposed to spikes in the midbrain, have looked more symmetric - Hart and colleagues (2014), recording release in rat nucleus accumbens, reported a signal that tracked both directions of error - so the extent of the asymmetry depends partly on what you measure.


46.1.3 Dopamine heterogeneity: novelty, salience, threat, movement

The clean prediction error story assumed dopamine neurons are more or less interchangeable.

They are not.

Menegas and colleagues (2018, Nature Neuroscience) showed that dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior tail of the striatum do not track reward value at all; they respond to novel and intense stimuli, and their activity reinforces avoidance of threatening things rather than approach to good ones.

Follow-up work from the same group (Menegas and colleagues, 2022, Neuron) tied this tail-of-striatum signal to how animals handle novel objects, and to why individual animals differ in how readily they treat the unfamiliar as dangerous.

Separately, Engelhard and colleagues (2019, Nature), imaging VTA dopamine neurons in mice navigating a virtual maze, found substantial numbers of cells tuned to the animal's own movement, position and view, not to reward.

The current consensus is roughly this: reward prediction error is a real and dominant signal in the ventral and central dopamine system, but dopamine is a family of channels defined by where the axons go, and some of those channels carry novelty, salience, threat or kinematics instead.


46.1.4 Distributional reinforcement learning signatures in dopamine neurons

Classical TD learning tracks a single number: the expected, or average, future reward.

Distributional reinforcement learning, developed in machine learning by Marc Bellemare, Will Dabney and colleagues, instead learns the whole probability distribution of possible future rewards, by running many predictors in parallel with different degrees of optimism and pessimism.

Dabney, Kurth-Nelson, Uchida and colleagues (2020, Nature) reanalysed recordings from mouse VTA dopamine neurons and reported the predicted signature: individual cells differed systematically in how strongly they amplified positive versus negative errors, and the population's set of reversal points reconstructed the actual distribution of reward sizes the mouse had experienced.

This is an elegant result and it made a genuine prediction before it was tested, which is rare.

It is not yet settled - the analysis depends on how one classifies cells and on assumptions about baseline firing, and independent replications are still accumulating - but subsequent work has extended the idea, including a 2025 Nature report from the Uchida group of a multidimensional distributional map of future reward that codes when as well as how much.


46.2 Striatal learning and action selection

If dopamine is the teaching signal, something must be taught.

The main student is the striatum, the large input structure of the basal ganglia, a set of subcortical nuclei that sit beneath the cortex and gate which actions get released.

Roughly ninety-five percent of striatal neurons are medium spiny neurons, and they receive both a massive input from cortex, carrying information about the current situation and candidate actions, and a dense dopamine input carrying the error signal.

That anatomical conjunction - cortical information and dopaminergic evaluation arriving on the same dendrite - is the physical substrate of reinforcement learning in the brain.


46.2.1 Direct and indirect pathway plasticity as go and no-go learning

Medium spiny neurons come in two flavours defined by which dopamine receptor they express.

Direct pathway cells carry the D1 receptor and project straight to the basal ganglia output nuclei, where their effect is to release, or permit, an action - the go route.

Indirect pathway cells carry the D2 receptor and reach the output nuclei by a longer route through the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, and their effect is to suppress actions - the no-go route.

Dopamine acts on the two receptors with opposite sign: a burst of dopamine excites D1 cells and inhibits D2 cells, so a positive prediction error strengthens go learning for the action just taken, while a dopamine dip disinhibits D2 cells and strengthens no-go learning.

Michael Frank's computational models of the basal ganglia, developed from 2004 onward, made this opponent scheme explicit, and optogenetic experiments - notably Kravitz and colleagues (2012), who showed that stimulating D1 cells is reinforcing and stimulating D2 cells is punishing - have supported the broad picture.

The picture is broad rather than exact: the two pathways are co-active during movement rather than strictly alternating, and several groups have argued the go and no-go labels oversimplify what are really cooperating populations.


46.2.2 Actor-critic mapping onto dorsal and ventral striatum

Reinforcement learning algorithms often split the job in two.
