A critic learns to predict how much reward a situation is worth, and generates the prediction error; an actor uses that error to adjust which action it prefers, without itself needing to represent value.

O'Doherty and colleagues (2004, Science) tested this division in humans using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that measures blood flow changes as an indirect index of neural activity.

They compared a task where choices mattered with one where rewards arrived regardless of what the person did, and found prediction error signals in the ventral striatum in both cases, but prediction error signals in the dorsal striatum only when actions mattered.

That is the pattern actor-critic predicts: ventral striatum as critic, dorsal striatum as actor.

The mapping is a useful first approximation rather than a proven anatomy, and later work has found value signals in dorsal striatum too, so the boundary is softer than the original result suggested.


46.2.3 Opponent processes and the asymmetry of learning from gains and losses

People do not weight good and bad news equally when they learn.

Across many studies, including Lefebvre and colleagues (2017, Nature Human Behaviour) and Palminteri and colleagues (2017), human learning rates are higher for outcomes better than expected than for outcomes worse than expected - an optimistic asymmetry, closely related to a confirmation bias in which people learn preferentially from evidence supporting the option they chose.

One theoretical account is opponency: dopamine handles the appetitive channel and serotonin, another neurotransmitter, handles an aversive channel that mediates behavioural inhibition in the face of punishment, a proposal associated with Peter Dayan and Quentin Huys.

There is pharmacological support - Michely and colleagues (2022, Communications Biology) found that prolonged boosting of serotonin in healthy volunteers increased learning from punishment and reduced learning from reward - but the opponency is not clean, and other studies using levodopa and citalopram have found differential rather than genuinely opposite effects.

Treat strict dopamine-versus-serotonin opponency as an attractive framework with mixed evidence rather than an established fact.


46.2.4 Dopamine manipulation in health and Parkinson disease

Parkinson disease is caused by progressive death of the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta, and it is treated with levodopa, a drug the brain converts into dopamine.

This creates a natural experiment: the same patient can be tested with dopamine restored and with it withdrawn.

Frank, Seeberger and O'Reilly (2004, Science), in a study titled By carrot or by stick, reported that patients off medication learned better from negative feedback than positive, while patients on medication showed the reverse, exactly as the D1 and D2 opponent model predicts.

This result is widely cited and widely qualified: several later studies have failed to replicate the full double dissociation, and effects depend on task, dose and disease stage.

A related and clinically serious finding is that dopamine agonist drugs can trigger impulse control disorders - pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality - in a minority of patients, which is what one would expect if the drug floors the negative learning channel so that losses stop teaching.


46.3 Model-based control and cognitive maps

Everything so far describes model-free learning: cache a value for each action, update it by prediction error, choose the highest.

It is efficient and it explains habits, but it cannot do something animals plainly do, which is work out the consequences of an action they have never taken, or immediately revalue a route when the goal moves.

That requires a model - an internal representation of how the world is arranged and what leads to what.

This section is about the evidence that brains build such models and the machinery that runs them.


46.3.1 Latent learning and the cognitive map tradition

Edward Tolman, working against the behaviourist orthodoxy of his day, argued in Cognitive maps in rats and men (1948, Psychological Review) that rats learn the layout of a maze even when nothing rewards them for it.

The demonstration was latent learning: rats allowed to wander an unrewarded maze for ten sessions looked no better than chance, but the moment food was introduced they solved the maze almost immediately, matching animals that had been rewarded all along.

The knowledge had been there, latent, waiting for a reason to be used - which is incompatible with the idea that learning is only the stamping-in of rewarded responses.

Tolman also reported shortcut experiments in a sunburst maze, taken as evidence that rats represent spatial relations rather than sequences of turns, and the discovery of hippocampal place cells by John O'Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky (1971) gave the cognitive map a physical candidate.

Honesty requires a caveat: a 2025 meta-analysis of eighty years of sunburst-maze replications found the shortcutting result poorly replicable, so the specific shortcut evidence is weaker than textbooks imply even though latent learning itself is robust.


46.3.2 Successor representation as an intermediate

Between a lookup table of cached values and a full simulator of the world sits a middle option.

The successor representation (SR), introduced by Peter Dayan in 1993, stores for each situation a prediction of which other situations you are likely to occupy in the future, discounted by how far off they are.

Because the map of expected future states is kept separate from the value of each state, an SR agent can instantly revalue a whole route when a goal's worth changes - flexibility model-free learning lacks - while avoiding the expense of simulating the world step by step.

Stachenfeld, Botvinick and Gershman (2017) argued that hippocampal place fields have exactly the shape an SR predicts, skewing backwards along frequently travelled routes and bending around barriers, and Momennejad and colleagues (2017, Nature Human Behaviour) showed human behaviour after various kinds of revaluation fits SR better than either pure alternative.

The SR's known weakness is the mirror image of its strength: because it caches the transition structure, it fails to update properly when the structure itself changes, and human participants show a partial version of that same failure.


46.3.3 Prefrontal and hippocampal contributions to model-based planning

Planning requires holding a goal, retrieving what leads to it, and evaluating imagined outcomes, and no single region does all of this.

The hippocampus supplies the relational map and, crucially, replays it: during rest and brief pauses, place cells fire out compressed sequences of trajectories, including paths to goals the animal has not yet taken.

Mattar and Daw (2018, Nature Neuroscience) gave this a normative theory - replay should prioritise the memories whose updating would most improve future choices, which predicts both forward replay before a decision, serving planning, and backward replay after a reward, serving credit assignment.

Prefrontal regions supply the goal and the evaluation: orbitofrontal cortex is repeatedly implicated in representing the current task state and the value of imagined outcomes, and damage to it produces failures of outcome-guided choice while leaving habitual responding intact.

Doll, Simon and Daw, and subsequent work, showed that model-based influence on human choice tracks activity in prefrontal cortex and hippocampus together rather than in either alone.


46.3.4 Arbitration between model-free and model-based control

If a brain has two controllers, something must decide which one drives.

Daw, Niv and Dayan (2005) proposed uncertainty-based arbitration: whichever system is currently more confident in its prediction gets control, which explains why behaviour is deliberate when a situation is new and habitual once it is over-practised.

Daw and colleagues (2011, Neuron) built the two-step task, now the standard laboratory tool, in which the first choice leads probabilistically to one of two second-stage states; a model-free learner repeats whatever was just rewarded, while a model-based learner takes account of whether the transition was the common or the rare one, and real people show a mixture of both.

Lee, Shimojo and O'Doherty (2014, Neuron) found that inferior lateral prefrontal cortex and frontopolar cortex track the reliability of each system and the comparison between them, which is what an arbitrator should look like.

Two cautions are worth stating: the two-step task's model-free and model-based indices are less clean than originally assumed, and Feher da Silva and Hare (2020) showed that instructions and task framing strongly change the apparent balance, so a person's score reflects their understanding of the task as much as their controller.


46.4 Beyond reward

Reward learning is the best-understood corner of the field, which makes it easy to mistake for the whole field.

Most of what a brain learns, it learns without any external reward at all - the statistics of faces, the sound patterns of a language, the feel of a familiar room.

This section covers the objectives, drives and mechanisms that operate outside the reward loop.


46.4.1 Unsupervised, self-supervised, and predictive learning objectives

Unsupervised learning means extracting structure from input with no labels and no reward; self-supervised learning is the modern version, in which the system manufactures its own training signal by predicting part of its input from another part - the next moment of a video, the masked part of an image.

This is attractive as a brain theory because prediction is something cortex is anatomically well suited to do, with its dense feedback connections carrying expectations downward and its feedforward connections carrying discrepancies upward, an arrangement formalised as predictive coding by Rao and Ballard (1999).

Empirically, Zhuang and colleagues (2021, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) showed that deep networks trained with purely unsupervised objectives predict responses in the ventral visual stream of primates about as well as networks trained with millions of human-supplied labels - which removes the main objection that such models needed biologically implausible supervision.

Halvagal and Zenke (2023, Nature Neuroscience) went further toward biology, deriving a local plasticity rule combining Hebbian learning - neurons that fire together wire together - with a predictive term, and showing it implements a self-supervised objective and reproduces spike-timing-dependent plasticity effects observed at real synapses.

The open question is not whether cortex does something like self-supervised prediction, which now looks likely, but which specific objective function it optimises, and there the candidates remain numerous and hard to distinguish.


46.4.2 Curiosity, information seeking, and intrinsic motivation

Animals and people pay real costs to obtain information that cannot change any outcome - a monkey will give up juice to learn early how much juice is coming.

Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka (2009, Neuron) recorded from monkey midbrain dopamine neurons and found that the same cells signalling expected juice also signalled the expected opportunity to receive advance information, as though knowing were itself a reward.

In humans, Kang and colleagues (2009) found that curiosity about a trivia answer activated striatal and midbrain regions and predicted later memory for the answer, linking curiosity to the same valuation circuitry and to encoding strength.

Bromberg-Martin, Feng, Ogasawara, White and Monosov (2024, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) reviewed the primate circuitry and distinguished several distinct drives that curiosity lumps together, including novelty seeking and the resolution of uncertainty about future events, supported by partly separate circuits including anterior cingulate cortex and the basal forebrain.

The practical upshot for learners is not sentimental: information that arrives when you were uncertain and wanted it is encoded better, which is an argument for asking a question before reading the answer.


46.4.3 Social and observational learning

Much of human learning skips personal trial and error entirely and runs on watching someone else.

Burke, Tobler, Baddeley and Schultz (2010, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) showed this uses prediction errors too, but of new kinds: an observational action prediction error, the difference between what another person did and what you expected them to do, tracked in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and an observational outcome prediction error tracked in the ventral striatum.

Suzuki and colleagues (2012, Neuron) described a complementary computation, the simulated-other reward prediction error, in which the observer runs a copy of the other person's learning process, with signals in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex tracking the simulated other's value and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex tracking the discrepancies.

The general finding is that social learning largely reuses the individual reward machinery with the referent swapped from self to other, rather than depending on a separate social module.

The mirror neuron literature is often invoked here; it is best treated as describing a mechanism for representing observed actions, not as a demonstrated mechanism for observational reinforcement learning, and that distinction is frequently blurred in popular accounts.


46.4.4 Meta-learning and learning to learn

Meta-learning means learning at two timescales: slowly acquiring the structure common to a family of problems, and then solving each new member of the family fast because the structure is already in place.

Harry Harlow demonstrated the behaviour in the 1940s with learning sets - monkeys given hundreds of two-object discrimination problems eventually solved each new one after a single trial, having learned not the answer but the rule for finding it.

Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Botvinick and colleagues (2018, Nature Neuroscience) proposed a mechanism: slow dopamine-driven synaptic learning trains the recurrent circuits of prefrontal cortex until the ongoing activity dynamics of those circuits themselves implement a fast learning algorithm, so that a network can adapt within a task even with its synaptic weights frozen.

This neatly explains why prefrontal cortex looks like it is learning on a timescale far faster than plausible synaptic change, and why dopamine lesions impair the acquisition of task structure more than moment-to-moment performance.

The theory is currently better supported by its ability to reproduce behavioural phenomena than by direct neural evidence, and distinguishing it from other accounts of prefrontal flexibility remains an active problem.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Midbrain dopamine neurons broadcast a reward prediction error - the difference between the value expected and the value obtained - and this signal corresponds closely to the error term of temporal difference learning, a result established by Schultz and colleagues in the 1990s and still the field's strongest bridge between algorithm and cell.

That signal teaches the striatum, where D1-bearing direct pathway neurons and D2-bearing indirect pathway neurons learn go and no-go tendencies with opposite sensitivity to dopamine, a scheme supported by optogenetics and by the altered learning biases of Parkinson patients on and off levodopa, though the strongest human dissociations have replicated unevenly.

The simple story has been enlarged rather than overturned: dopamine is heterogeneous by projection target, carrying novelty, threat and movement signals as well as value, and there is evidence that the population encodes a distribution of possible rewards rather than a single average.

Model-free value caching cannot explain latent learning, shortcutting, or instant revaluation, so the brain also maintains cognitive maps in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, with the successor representation as a plausible intermediate and reliability-based arbitration deciding which controller drives behaviour.

Finally, most learning is not reward learning at all - self-supervised prediction, curiosity, observation of others, and meta-learning across problem families all shape the brain, and in several of these cases the machinery turns out to be the reward machinery pointed at a different target.


PART EIGHT. LANGUAGE AND SYMBOLIC COGNITION


CHAPTER 47. SPEECH PERCEPTION AND THE AUDITORY LANGUAGE INTERFACE (CORE)

Speech is the fastest and densest signal the human brain routinely decodes.

A conversational talker produces roughly ten to fifteen speech sounds every second, and the listener converts that smear of air pressure into words, meanings and intentions with almost no conscious effort.

This chapter asks how that is possible - how the ear's raw acoustic input becomes phonemes, how the brain locks onto the rhythm of speech, how the same brain produces speech as well as hears it, and how perception and production are wired together.

It matters because speech is where the biology of hearing meets the biology of language, and because the failures of that interface show up in stroke aphasia, in developmental language disorders, and in the paralysed patients now being given back a voice by brain implants.

It also matters because the textbook picture most people carry - a speech comprehension box called Wernicke's area wired to a speech production box called Broca's area - is now widely regarded by specialists as wrong in its details, and we will look squarely at why.


47.1 From acoustics to phonemes

A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word in a given language.

The difference between "bat" and "pat" is a single phoneme, /b/ versus /p/, and yet nothing in the sound wave itself is neatly labelled "b" or "p".

The first job of the speech system is therefore a translation job: turn a continuously varying pressure wave into a discrete, reusable, category-based code.

This section covers why that translation is hard, how listeners nonetheless behave as though speech comes in clean categories, where in the brain those categories are computed, and how the system copes with the fact that every talker sounds different.


47.1.1 The lack of invariance problem in the speech signal

The lack of invariance problem is the observation that there is no fixed, constant acoustic pattern that reliably corresponds to a given phoneme.

The main culprit is coarticulation - the fact that the mouth does not produce sounds one at a time like beads on a string, but overlaps them, so that the articulation of any sound is shaped by the sounds before and after it.

The /d/ in "dee" and the /d/ in "doo" have measurably different acoustic signatures, because the tongue and lips are already preparing the following vowel while the /d/ is being released, and yet listeners hear the same consonant.

This was the central puzzle identified by the Haskins Laboratories group in the 1950s and 1960s, and it is genuinely unsolved in the strong sense: neither the motor theory of speech perception, which proposed that listeners recover the speaker's intended articulatory gestures, nor purely acoustic or knowledge-driven accounts have produced a mapping that works in all contexts.

Modern machine speech recognition sidesteps the problem rather than solving it, by learning statistical mappings over long stretches of context instead of looking for a single invariant cue.


47.1.2 Categorical perception of speech sounds

Categorical perception is the tendency to hear a smoothly varying physical dimension as a small number of discrete categories.

The classic demonstration comes from Liberman and colleagues in 1957, who synthesised a series of syllables varying in equal acoustic steps between one consonant and another, and found that listeners did not report a gradual change; they reported one consonant up to a point and then abruptly the other.

The cleanest example uses voice onset time (VOT), the interval between the release of a consonant and the start of vocal fold vibration.

An English /b/ has a VOT near zero milliseconds and a /p/ has a VOT near forty milliseconds, with the perceptual boundary sitting around twenty milliseconds - and crucially, listeners discriminate two sounds straddling that boundary far better than two sounds the same acoustic distance apart on the same side of it.

The claim has been softened in recent decades: work using continuous response measures such as mouse tracking and eye tracking shows that listeners retain graded, within-category sensitivity that forced-choice button pressing hides, so speech categorisation is now better described as sharply warped than as truly all-or-none.


47.1.3 Phonetic feature encoding in superior temporal gyrus

The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is the ridge of cortex running along the top of the temporal lobe, just below and behind the primary auditory cortex, and it is the main workshop where acoustic input becomes speech-relevant structure.

The landmark evidence comes from Mesgarani, Cheung, Johnson and Chang in 2014, who recorded directly from the cortical surface of neurosurgical patients using electrocorticography (ECoG), a grid of electrodes laid on the brain, while those patients listened to natural continuous speech.

Individual electrodes did not respond to individual phonemes; they responded to groups of phonemes sharing a phonetic feature - plosives such as /p/ and /t/ made by a full closure and release, fricatives such as /s/ and /f/ made by forcing air through a narrow gap, nasals, and vowels.

In other words the STG encodes speech in terms of manner and place of articulation features rather than storing a separate detector for every sound, which is an efficient solution to a large inventory.

Later work from the same laboratory has shown that STG sites also encode relative pitch, speech onsets after silence, and speaking rate, so the region is doing several parallel jobs, not one.


47.1.4 Speaker normalisation and talker adaptation

A child, an adult man and an adult woman saying the same vowel produce acoustically very different sounds, because vocal tract length shifts the resonant frequencies that define vowels.

Speaker normalisation is the process by which the listener discounts those talker-specific differences and recovers the intended phoneme.

Sjerps, Fox, Johnson and Chang, reporting in Nature Communications in 2019, found that human auditory cortex contains representations from which talker-specific variation has already been partly removed, so normalisation is not a late, deliberate inference but is at least partly built into early cortical coding.

There is a complementary process, talker adaptation, in which a few sentences of exposure to an unfamiliar voice or accent measurably improves comprehension of that voice, indicating that the listener is retuning category boundaries on the fly.

Researchers disagree about whether adaptation adjusts the incoming signal or shifts the stored category representations themselves, and both accounts remain live in the literature.


47.2 Temporal structure and entrainment

Speech is not just a sequence of sounds; it is a rhythm.

Stress patterns, syllables and individual speech sounds unfold at systematically different rates, and there is now substantial evidence that the brain exploits those rates by aligning its own ongoing electrical rhythms to them.

This section covers the timescales themselves, the evidence for cortical tracking of speech, the proposal that the two hemispheres divide the labour by sampling at different rates, and the vigorously contested question of how much of comprehension is prediction.


47.2.1 Syllabic, phonemic, and prosodic timescales

Speech carries information at roughly three nested timescales.

Prosody - the melody, stress and phrasing of an utterance - varies slowly, at about one to three cycles per second, which in the language of brain rhythms is the delta band.

Syllables arrive at roughly four to eight per second, in the theta band, and this rate is strikingly consistent across the world's languages.

Individual phonemes and rapid acoustic transitions, such as the formant sweeps that distinguish one consonant from another, unfold over about twenty to fifty milliseconds, corresponding to the low gamma band above thirty cycles per second.

The neat correspondence between these speech rates and the brain's own intrinsic oscillation bands is the empirical hook on which the entrainment literature hangs.


47.2.2 Cortical entrainment to the speech envelope

The speech envelope is the slow rise and fall of the overall loudness of speech over time, stripped of its fine detail; it looks like the outline of a sound waveform.

Recordings using magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures the magnetic fields produced by brain activity, and electroencephalography (EEG), which measures voltages at the scalp, show that low-frequency cortical activity follows the phase of that envelope closely, and that the strength of this tracking correlates with how intelligible the speech is.

Ghitza, Peelle, Giraud and others have argued that this tracking is functional rather than incidental: it chops the continuous stream into syllable-sized chunks that downstream machinery can then decode, with faster gamma-band activity nested inside each theta cycle to resolve phonemic detail.

The interpretation is genuinely disputed.

One camp holds that a true endogenous oscillator is being entrained and phase-reset by the speech signal; the other holds that what looks like entrainment is simply a train of ordinary evoked responses to sharp acoustic edges in the envelope, which would produce similar-looking data without any oscillator, and analyses published through the 2020s have supported this deflationary reading.


47.2.3 Asymmetric sampling in time and hemispheric division

Asymmetric sampling in time (AST) is a hypothesis put forward by David Poeppel in 2003 to explain why speech and language lean on the left hemisphere while music and voice quality lean on the right.

The proposal is that both hemispheres receive the same input but integrate it over different windows: left auditory cortex preferentially uses a short window of roughly twenty-five to fifty milliseconds, ideal for resolving rapid consonant transitions, while right auditory cortex uses a long window of roughly one hundred and fifty to three hundred milliseconds, ideal for tracking pitch, melody and syllabic and prosodic contour.

On this account lateralisation for language is not a special language fact at all but a downstream consequence of a general asymmetry in acoustic analysis.

The hypothesis is elegant and has generated a great deal of productive work, but the supporting evidence is mixed: the asymmetry is reliably found in group averages and in some stimulus designs and is weak or absent in others, and the strong claim that the two windows arise from intrinsic oscillators at different rates remains unproven.


47.2.4 Prediction and the pre-activation of upcoming input

There is broad agreement that comprehension is predictive in some sense - listeners are faster and their brain responses smaller for words that fit the context, which is the basis of the N400, a negative-going brain wave peaking around four hundred milliseconds after an unexpected word.

The contested question is whether the brain actively pre-activates the specific form and meaning of a word before it arrives.

Some studies report exactly that, including electroencephalography work using representational similarity analysis that found pre-onset neural patterns more similar for contexts predicting related words than unrelated ones, and intracranial work reporting information about an upcoming word up to two seconds before it is spoken.

Careful reanalyses published in 2024 and 2025, however, argue that these pre-onset signatures can be fully explained by the statistical dependencies between neighbouring words in natural language plus persistent encoding of words already heard, without any genuine pre-activation, and that temporal generalisation analyses show no stable overlap between pre-onset and post-onset representations.

The honest summary as of 2026 is that prediction in some weak sense is well supported, and specific lexical pre-activation during natural listening is not yet established.


47.3 Speech production

Perception is only half of the interface.

Producing speech requires coordinating roughly one hundred muscles across the lips, jaw, tongue, soft palate, larynx and respiratory system, in sequences accurate to a few tens of milliseconds.

This section covers how the motor cortex organises those articulators, how feedforward commands and sensory feedback share control, why you cannot tickle your own auditory cortex with your own voice, and how all of this is now being exploited to build speech prostheses.


47.3.1 Articulatory planning and the motor cortex speech map

The ventral sensorimotor cortex - the lower portion of the precentral and postcentral gyri, sitting just above the Sylvian fissure - contains the cortical map for the speech articulators.

Bouchard, Mesgarani, Johnson and Chang, publishing in Nature in 2013, recorded from this region while patients produced consonant-vowel syllables and found representations of lips, jaw, tongue and larynx arranged somatotopically, meaning laid out in an orderly spatial map of the body part controlled.

Two findings complicated the simple map picture.

First, the articulator representations partially overlapped at individual electrodes rather than occupying strictly separate territories, and second, the population pattern across many electrodes was organised by phonetic feature, so that the emergent cortical code looked more like the linguist's feature system than like a list of muscles.

Later work in the same region has decoded actual vocal tract movement trajectories, supporting the view that this cortex codes coordinated articulatory gestures rather than individual muscle contractions.


47.3.2 Feedback and feedforward control in speech

Speech motor control uses two modes at once.

Feedforward control issues a stored motor programme and runs it open-loop, without waiting for sensory confirmation, which is what makes fluent rapid speech possible at all - auditory feedback is simply too slow to steer each individual sound.

Feedback control monitors the auditory and somatosensory consequences of speaking and issues corrections when the outcome deviates from the target.

The best-developed formal account is the DIVA model - Directions Into Velocities of Articulators - developed by Frank Guenther and colleagues from the late 1990s onward, which assigns feedforward commands to premotor and motor cortex, auditory and somatosensory target comparison to superior temporal and supramarginal regions, and the updating of feedforward commands from feedback errors to the cerebellum.

The strongest experimental support comes from altered auditory feedback studies, in which a speaker hears their own voice played back with the pitch or a vowel formant shifted in real time; speakers compensate reflexively within about one hundred to two hundred milliseconds, and if the shift persists they gradually adapt their production, which is exactly the two-timescale behaviour the model predicts.

The framework is also used clinically to characterise stuttering, apraxia of speech and dysarthria as different failures of these control loops.


47.3.3 Efference copy and the suppression of self-generated sound

An efference copy is a duplicate of a motor command sent to sensory areas so they can anticipate the sensory consequences of the body's own action; the related term corollary discharge refers to the resulting predictive signal.

Because auditory cortex receives such a prediction before you speak, the response it makes to your own voice is markedly smaller than its response to the identical sound played back to you - an effect called speech-induced suppression, visible as a reduced N1 component of the auditory evoked response and confirmed at single-trial resolution in intracranial recordings.

The functional logic is that suppression flags self-produced sound as self-produced, freeing the system to detect the small mismatches that signal a production error.

Direct evidence for the discharge signal itself, as opposed to its consequence, was scarce until recent intracranial work, including a 2024 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reporting a corollary discharge circuit in human speech.

Clinically, this circuit is a leading candidate explanation for auditory verbal hallucinations in schizophrenia: patients show attenuated suppression of auditory cortex to self-generated sound, consistent with inner speech being misattributed to an external source, though the evidence is correlational and the account remains a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism.


47.3.4 Speech decoding neuroprostheses in paralysed patients

A speech neuroprosthesis is a brain-computer interface (BCI) that reads neural activity from speech motor cortex in a person who can no longer speak and converts it into text or synthesised voice.

Two studies published in Nature in 2023 marked the field's step change.

Willett and colleagues at Stanford, recording with penetrating microelectrode arrays from a participant with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, decoded attempted speech at sixty-two words per minute with a word error rate of 9.1 percent on a fifty-word vocabulary and 23.8 percent on a vocabulary of 125,000 words - the first large-vocabulary demonstration.

Metzger and colleagues at the University of California San Francisco, working with a participant paralysed by brainstem stroke and using a high-density surface electrode array, reached a median seventy-eight words per minute with roughly a 25 percent word error rate, and additionally drove a synthesised voice and a facial avatar.

For comparison, unimpaired conversation runs near one hundred and sixty words per minute, so these systems are approaching but not matching natural speed.

Subsequent work has pushed toward instantaneous streaming synthesis rather than sentence-by-sentence text, and toward decoders that calibrate in minutes rather than months; the outstanding obstacles are hardware longevity, signal stability over years, and the fact that results so far come from a very small number of implanted individuals.


47.4 The dual-stream architecture

The dominant contemporary framework for the speech and language interface is the dual-stream model, set out by Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel in a series of papers culminating in a 2007 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

Its central move is to say that speech sound has to be mapped onto two quite different things - onto meaning, and onto the motor commands that would reproduce it - and that these are different computational problems handled by different pathways.

This section walks through each stream, then the white matter tract that was supposed to carry the dorsal one, then the reasons the older model it replaced is no longer defensible.


47.4.1 Dorsal stream for sensorimotor mapping

The dorsal stream runs from auditory cortex backward and upward into the parietal-temporal junction and then forward to frontal motor and premotor regions.

Its job is sensorimotor integration: converting a heard sound into the articulatory commands that would produce it.

Hickok and Poeppel identify a key waypoint in the posterior Sylvian fissure at the parietal-temporal boundary, which they label area Spt, and which behaves like an auditory-motor interface - it is active both when listening to speech and when covertly rehearsing it, and it is not speech-specific, since it also responds during the imagined humming of melodies.

The dorsal stream is strongly left-lateralised, and it is the system you use to repeat a word you have never heard before, to learn new vocabulary, and to hold speech in the phonological loop of working memory.

Damage here produces conduction aphasia, in which comprehension and fluent speech are largely spared but repetition is disproportionately impaired.


47.4.2 Ventral stream for sound-to-meaning mapping

The ventral stream runs forward and downward from auditory cortex along the superior and middle temporal gyri toward the anterior temporal lobe.

Its job is recognition: mapping sound structure onto stored lexical representations and then onto meaning.

Unlike the dorsal stream, it is organised bilaterally, which explains a long-standing puzzle - unilateral left temporal damage rarely abolishes speech comprehension, because the right hemisphere ventral stream can carry much of the load.

Anterior temporal regions appear to support combinatorial processing, the assembly of word meanings into phrase meanings, while more posterior middle temporal cortex functions as a lexical interface between sound form and conceptual knowledge.

Anatomically the ventral stream is carried substantially by the extreme capsule and inferior fronto-occipital fibre systems rather than by the arcuate fasciculus.


47.4.3 The revised place of the arcuate fasciculus

The arcuate fasciculus is a curved bundle of white matter arching around the Sylvian fissure, and for over a century it was described as the cable connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area, with conduction aphasia explained as a cut cable.

Diffusion tractography, a magnetic resonance imaging method that estimates fibre pathways from the direction of water diffusion, has substantially revised this picture.

The tract's endpoints extend well beyond the classical areas, reaching posterior middle temporal gyrus behind and precentral and middle frontal gyri in front; in one tractography series the projection reached the precentral gyrus in every participant while a projection into Broca's area proper was absent in most.

Functionally, the posterior portion of the tract is associated with both production and comprehension deficits while the anterior portion is associated with production deficits alone, and the tract is now thought to serve phonological processing broadly rather than repetition specifically.

The disconnection story has also been weakened by cases of relatively preserved repetition despite severe left arcuate disruption, and by the general point that tractography reconstructs likely fibre orientations rather than directly visualising axons, so anatomical claims from it should be held with appropriate caution.


47.4.4 Why the classical Broca-Wernicke model is no longer adequate

The classical model, assembled from Broca's 1861 and Wernicke's 1874 case reports and formalised by Lichtheim and later Geschwind, holds that a posterior temporal region stores word sound images for comprehension, an inferior frontal region stores motor programmes for production, and a single tract joins them.

Pascale Tremblay and Anthony Steven Dick set out the case against it in Brain and Language in 2016 under the title "Broca and Wernicke are dead", and their survey of 159 specialists found that only about two percent regarded the classical model as the best available account, while respondents disagreed sharply even about where Wernicke's area anatomically is.

The specific failures are concrete: lesions confined to the classical Broca's area do not produce lasting Broca's aphasia, which requires much larger damage including underlying white matter and insula; comprehension deficits in Wernicke's aphasia depend on damage extending well beyond the classical territory; the model has no place for the bilateral organisation of speech comprehension, for the cerebellum, for the basal ganglia, or for the anterior temporal lobe; and it treats language as two boxes and a wire when the data show distributed, overlapping, partly domain-general networks.

The dual-stream framework is the leading replacement, but it should be understood as a coarse organising sketch rather than a finished theory - the number, boundaries and even the strict separability of the streams are still under active debate.

It is worth being clear that the classical terminology persists mainly because it is clinically convenient shorthand, not because it is thought to be true.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Speech perception begins from a signal that contains no invariant acoustic marker for any phoneme, and the brain solves this not by finding hidden invariants but by encoding phonetic features across populations of neurons in superior temporal gyrus, by warping perception toward category boundaries, and by normalising away talker differences early in cortical processing.

The brain tracks the rhythmic structure of speech at prosodic, syllabic and phonemic timescales, though whether that tracking reflects genuine oscillatory entrainment or a series of evoked responses to acoustic edges is unresolved, as is the stronger claim that listeners pre-activate specific upcoming words.

Speech production is governed by paired feedforward and feedback control loops over an articulator map in ventral sensorimotor cortex, with an efference copy suppressing auditory responses to one's own voice, and this same cortex is what current speech neuroprostheses read to restore communication at up to seventy-eight words per minute in paralysed participants.

Perception and production are joined by a left-lateralised dorsal stream for sensorimotor mapping and a bilateral ventral stream for sound-to-meaning mapping, a division that explains why repetition and comprehension can dissociate after brain injury.

The classical Broca-Wernicke model that this architecture replaces is rejected by the great majority of specialists in the field, and the dual-stream account that succeeds it should be treated as the best current sketch rather than as settled fact.


CHAPTER 48. WORDS, SYNTAX, AND MEANING (CORE)


This chapter is about how the human brain stores words, glues them together into structures, and extracts meaning from the result.

We will start small, with the single word and the storehouse that holds it, and finish large, with whole networks of cortex that appear to be dedicated to language and to almost nothing else.

Along the way we will meet two electrical brain waves that have become the workhorses of language research, an information-theory account of why some words are harder to read than others, and the recent and genuinely surprising finding that artificial language models predict brain activity rather well.

This matters because language is the most distinctive thing our species does, and because the question of whether language is the medium of thought or merely a tool for sharing thought is currently being settled - not by argument, but by data.

Throughout, I will flag where the field agrees and where it is still fighting.


48.1 The lexicon

The lexicon is the mental dictionary: the store of the words you know, together with how they sound, how they are spelled, what they mean, and how they behave grammatically.

An educated adult speaker of English commands somewhere in the range of forty thousand to sixty thousand word families, and can retrieve any one of them in a few hundred milliseconds.

That combination of enormous size and enormous speed is the central puzzle this section addresses.


48.1.1 Lexical access, frequency, and neighbourhood effects

Lexical access is the process of matching an incoming signal - a sound pattern or a string of letters - to the right entry in your mental dictionary.

The single most reliable finding in the whole field is the word frequency effect: common words such as "table" are recognised faster and more accurately than rare words such as "tureen", a difference measurable in tens of milliseconds in a lexical decision task, which is simply an experiment asking "is this string a real word, yes or no".

The second reliable finding concerns the neighbourhood, meaning the set of words that differ from the target by a single letter or a single sound - "cat" has neighbours in "bat", "cot", and "can".

Neighbourhood effects cut both ways, and the direction depends on modality: in spoken word recognition a dense phonological neighbourhood is usually inhibitory, because many similar-sounding candidates compete, whereas in visual word recognition a dense orthographic neighbourhood is often facilitatory, apparently because shared letter-to-sound regularities help.

Frequency and neighbourhood also interact, and the interaction is not uniform across the response-time distribution: analyses of the full distribution rather than the mean show density effects concentrated in low-frequency words and in the slower responses of high-frequency words, which is what you would expect if neighbours matter mainly when the target itself is weakly activated.

The picture that emerges is not a lookup table but a competition, in which many candidates are partially activated at once and the winner is the one whose evidence accumulates fastest.


48.1.2 The mental lexicon as stored form plus computed meaning

It is tempting to imagine each word as a little file card holding its form and its meaning together.

The evidence favours something looser: the form of a word - its sound shape and letter shape - looks genuinely stored, while much of its meaning looks computed on the fly from context.

Consider "bank", which is one stored form serving at least two meanings, or "run", whose dictionary entry runs to dozens of senses that no listener consults; instead, the surrounding sentence selects and shapes the sense actually delivered.

This is why modern accounts describe the lexicon as an interface rather than a warehouse: a stable, learned mapping from form to a distribution of possible meanings, with the sentence context doing the work of narrowing that distribution.

The practical consequence for neuroscience is that "where are words stored" is probably the wrong question, and "which regions carry form, which carry meaning, and how do they talk" is the right one.


48.1.3 Morphology and decomposition

Morphology is the internal structure of words - "walker" is transparently "walk" plus the agent suffix "-er", and "unhappiness" is three pieces stacked.

The key experimental tool here is masked priming, in which a prime word is flashed for perhaps 40 to 70 milliseconds and immediately covered by the target, so briefly that participants report seeing nothing yet still respond faster to related targets.

Rastle, Davis, Tyler and Marslen-Wilson, in work from 2000 and again in 2004 and 2008, found something striking: "brother" primes "broth", even though a brother is not a kind of broth, while "brothel" does not prime "broth" despite the same amount of letter overlap.

The interpretation is morpho-orthographic decomposition - very early in reading, the system strips off anything that looks like a suffix, purely on the basis of form, without checking whether the result makes sense.

Semantics catches up later and repairs the error, but the initial parse is blind, which tells us the reading system contains a fast, dumb, structure-finding stage before any meaning is consulted.

The effect is not confined to skilled adult readers of English; Fleischhauer and colleagues reported masked morphological priming in German primary school children in 2021, suggesting the mechanism comes online early in literacy.


48.1.4 Word learning across the lifespan

Between roughly eighteen months and six years a child moves from a few hundred words to well over ten thousand, at a sustained rate of something like ten new words a week during the fastest stretch.

Much of that is attributed to fast mapping, the ability to attach a new label to a new object from a single ambiguous exposure - shown a familiar cup and an unfamiliar gadget and asked for the "dax", a two-year-old reaches for the gadget by elimination.

Fast mapping was long thought to be a childhood specialisation, but adult studies using electroencephalography, which records electrical brain activity from the scalp, have found rapid neural changes after a single exposure in adults too, indicating the mechanism does not switch off.

Vocabulary growth in fact continues for decades: unlike most cognitive measures, which decline from early adulthood, vocabulary typically keeps rising into the sixties or later, and modelling work has used growth curves with early acceleration and a late plateau to capture this shape.

The honest caveat is that "vocabulary size" is notoriously sensitive to how you test it, so absolute numbers in this literature should be treated as order-of-magnitude estimates rather than measurements.


48.2 Syntax and combination

Syntax is the system that lets a finite vocabulary produce an unbounded set of sentences, by specifying how words may be combined.

The crucial property is that the combinations are hierarchical, not merely sequential: in "the man who fed the dogs left", it is the man who left, not the dogs, even though "dogs" is nearer the verb.

This section asks how the brain builds those hierarchies and where.


48.2.1 Hierarchical structure and its neural signatures

The evidence that the brain builds hierarchy rather than tracking word order comes from several directions.

Behaviourally, agreement errors track structural distance rather than word distance, which is why the sentence above resists the reading in which the dogs left.

Neurally, parametric designs that increase the depth of embedding in a sentence produce graded increases in activity in the left inferior frontal gyrus, a region on the lower front-left surface of the brain, and in the posterior superior temporal sulcus, a groove toward the back of the temporal lobe; Nelson, Dehaene and colleagues, and Matchin, Hammerly and Lau in 2017, are representative of this line.

The interpretative difficulty, which the field openly acknowledges, is that deeper embedding also costs more memory, so activity increases may index storage load rather than structure building itself.

Disentangling structure from working memory remains one of the live methodological problems in the area.


48.2.2 The role of posterior inferior frontal gyrus and posterior temporal cortex

Two regions dominate the syntax literature: the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, which overlaps with what nineteenth-century neurology called Broca's area, and the posterior temporal lobe, especially the posterior middle temporal gyrus.

They are linked by a large white matter tract, the arcuate fasciculus, a bundle of long-range fibres arcing between frontal and temporal cortex.

Matchin and Hickok, in an influential 2020 synthesis, proposed a division of labour in which posterior temporal cortex builds hierarchical lexical-syntactic structure, the anterior temporal lobe stores knowledge of entities, and the posterior inferior frontal gyrus handles linearisation and the working-memory demands of turning a hierarchy into an ordered string, which is why it is engaged more heavily in production.

Consistent with a temporal-cortex-first account, Matchin and colleagues reported in 2024 that multiple dimensions of syntactic structure are resolved earliest in posterior temporal cortex, with frontal engagement following.

Whether Broca's area is a syntax engine or a general sequencing and control resource that syntax happens to tax is still contested; Friederici's tradition leans toward the former, Matchin and Hickok toward the latter.


48.2.3 Merge, dependency, and competing linguistic formalisms

Neuroscientists must import a theory of grammar before they can look for its neural signature, and linguistics offers several incompatible ones.

Chomsky's Minimalist Program reduces syntax to a single recursive operation, Merge, which takes two elements X and Y and forms the unordered set {X, Y}, applied repeatedly to yield hierarchy.

Dependency grammar instead treats a sentence as a network of head-dependent links between words, with no invisible phrasal nodes, and construction grammar treats stored form-meaning pairings of varying size as the basic units, blurring the lexicon-syntax boundary entirely.

These are not mere notational variants for our purposes: Merge predicts brain signatures tied to abstract constituents that have no direct surface reflex, whereas dependency and construction accounts predict signatures tied to word-to-word links and to stored patterns.

Formal work, for instance Kobele's, shows Minimalist grammars can be translated into dependency structures, which means many neuroimaging results are compatible with both and cannot adjudicate between them.

The candid summary is that most current neural evidence constrains "the brain builds hierarchy" far more tightly than it constrains "the brain implements Merge specifically".


48.2.4 Neural tracking of abstract linguistic structure

The most elegant demonstration that the brain tracks structure it cannot hear comes from Ding, Melloni, Zhang, Tian and Poeppel, published in Nature Neuroscience in 2016.

They presented syllables at a fixed rate of four per second, arranged so that every two syllables formed a phrase and every four formed a sentence, with no acoustic cue whatsoever marking the phrase or sentence boundaries - the pauses and the prosody were deliberately removed.

Using magnetoencephalography, which measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by neural currents, they found cortical activity peaking not only at four hertz, the syllable rate, but also at two hertz and one hertz, the phrase and sentence rates.

Since those frequencies were not present in the sound, the brain must have been generating them internally from grammatical knowledge, and the effect appeared in both English and Mandarin listeners.

The finding has been extended to infants by Kabdebon and colleagues and is widely replicated, though sceptics argue that some of the low-frequency response could reflect the predictability structure of the stimulus rather than constituent building per se, and that debate has not fully closed.


48.3 Semantic composition

Knowing what "brown" means and what "dog" means does not tell you what "brown dog" means until something combines them.

Semantic composition is that combining operation, and this section covers where it happens and how we measure it.


48.3.1 Composition beyond single-word meaning

The cleanest experiments here strip composition down to two words.

Bemis and Pylkkänen, in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2011, compared magnetoencephalography responses to a genuine phrase such as "red boat" against a non-combinatory control such as "xkq boat" or a word list, holding the target noun constant.

They found increased activity in the left anterior temporal lobe, at the front tip of the temporal lobe, roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds after the onset of the second word - fast, and earlier than most integration accounts had assumed.

Follow-up work by Westerlund and Pylkkänen showed the effect is graded by concept specificity, appearing most clearly when a specific modifier meets a relatively general head noun, which suggests the region is doing something like feature-conjunction rather than a generic "combine" operation.

Additional composition effects have been reported in ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the left angular gyrus, but these replicate less consistently than the anterior temporal effect and should be treated as provisional.


48.3.2 The N400 as an index of semantic prediction and integration

The N400 is a negative-going deflection in the event-related potential, which is the averaged electrical response of the brain to a repeated class of stimulus, peaking around 400 milliseconds after a word appears and largest over central and parietal scalp.

It was discovered by Kutas and Hillyard in 1980, who found that "I take my coffee with cream and dog" produces a much larger N400 at the final word than "cream and sugar".

Crucially, the N400 is not an anomaly detector: its amplitude scales continuously with cloze probability, the proportion of people who would produce that word given the preceding context, so even perfectly sensible words produce larger N400s when they are less expected.

The long-running dispute, surveyed by Kutas and Federmeier in their 2011 review, is whether the N400 reflects prediction - the ease of accessing a word your brain had already partly pre-activated - or integration, the effort of merging the word into the message so far.

Evidence that shared semantic features reduce the N400 even for implausible words, and modelling work such as Rabovsky's semantic-update account and Noureddine and Kuperberg's 2024 predictive-coding model, has moved the consensus toward prediction or prediction error, but integration accounts have not been eliminated and the two are hard to separate by design alone.


48.3.3 The P600 and reanalysis or conflict

The P600 is a positive deflection peaking roughly 600 milliseconds after a word, again largest posteriorly, and it was originally tied to syntax.

Osterhout and Holcomb reported in 1992 that garden-path and outright ungrammatical sentences - "the broker persuaded to sell the stock" - elicit it, and the natural reading was that the P600 indexes reanalysis, the effort of tearing down a wrong structure and rebuilding.

That tidy story was disrupted by the semantic P600, or semantic illusion: Kolk, Hoeks, Kuperberg and others found that sentences like "the meal was devouring the child" produce a P600 with little or no N400, even though the problem there is meaning, not grammar.

Competing explanations include Kolk and Chwilla's monitoring theory, in which the system rechecks its own perceptual record when plausibility and structure conflict, and broader conflict-resolution accounts in which the P600 indexes any high-level revision or reinterpretation.

Some researchers now argue the P600 is not language-specific at all but a member of the P3 family associated with categorical decision and updating, and there is no settled resolution; a reader should treat "P600 equals syntax" as an outdated shorthand.


48.3.4 Situation models and discourse-level representation

Above the sentence sits the situation model, a term from Van Dijk and Kintsch meaning the reader's mental representation of the state of affairs the text describes, rather than of the text itself.

Zwaan, Langston and Graesser's event-indexing model of 1995 proposes that comprehenders track five dimensions simultaneously - time, space, protagonist, causation, and motivation - and that reading slows whenever an incoming clause breaks continuity on one of them, with the costs of multiple breaks adding up.

That additive prediction has held up reasonably well in behavioural work, and Zwaan's own twenty-five-year retrospective in 2025 treats the framework as durable while conceding that the mechanism of updating is still underspecified.

Neurally, situation-model work has converged on regions outside the classical language areas: the default mode network, and particularly the angular gyrus and medial prefrontal cortex, show responses tied to event boundaries and to information that persists over minutes rather than seconds.

This is important for the rest of the chapter, because it means that discourse-level meaning appears to be built partly outside the language network proper, in systems that also serve memory and event cognition.


48.4 Prediction in language

A recurring theme above is that the brain does not wait for a word before working on it.

This section makes that idea quantitative, then examines the recent and contentious use of artificial language models as brain models.


48.4.1 Surprisal, entropy, and information-theoretic accounts of processing cost

Surprisal theory, formulated by Hale in 2001 and given its modern form by Levy in 2008, states that the effort of processing a word equals its surprisal, defined as the negative logarithm of its probability given the preceding context.

A word your context makes near-certain has surprisal near zero and costs almost nothing; a word with a probability of one in a thousand has high surprisal and costs a lot.

The theory makes a sharp and testable prediction - that reading time should be a linear function of surprisal, not merely a monotonic one - and Smith and Levy showed in 2013 that this linearity holds across roughly six orders of magnitude of word probability.

Wilcox and colleagues extended the test to eleven languages in a 2023 study in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, finding surprisal a robust predictor cross-linguistically.

Entropy, the expected surprisal of the upcoming word, is a distinct quantity measuring how uncertain you are before the word arrives rather than how wrong you were after, and there is ongoing argument about whether entropy contributes independently to reading time; some studies find it does, and others find its apparent contribution absorbed by surprisal.

The information-theoretic framing is attractive because it replaces a list of separate effects - frequency, predictability, plausibility - with one currency.


48.4.2 Language models as predictors of brain response

A language model is a system trained to predict the next word in text, and the internal activation patterns it develops while reading a sentence can be used as features to predict brain activity recorded from people reading the same sentence, a technique called encoding modelling.

Schrimpf, Fedorenko, Tenenbaum and colleagues, in a 2021 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, evaluated more than forty such models against functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electrocorticography data and found that transformer models predicted responses in the language network close to the noise ceiling, meaning close to the limit set by measurement reliability itself.

Goldstein and colleagues, working with electrocorticography, which records directly from the cortical surface in patients undergoing epilepsy surgery, reported that the brain shows spontaneous pre-onset predictions and prediction-error signals of the kind these models compute.

Antonello and colleagues in 2024 showed a scaling relationship, with encoding performance improving as models grow from roughly a hundred million to tens of billions of parameters.

The finding is genuinely remarkable: a system trained only on text, with no brain data and no linguistic theory built in, turns out to be among the best available predictors of cortical responses to language.


48.4.3 The 2025 and 2026 evidence linking model features to cortical language responses

The most informative recent work has stopped asking whether models predict the brain and started asking which part of what models learn does the predicting.

AlKhamissi, Tuckute, Schrimpf and colleagues, in work presented at the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing under the title "From Language to Cognition: How LLMs Outgrow the Human Language Network", tracked thirty-four training checkpoints across eight model sizes spanning three hundred billion tokens.

Their central result is a dissociation: brain alignment rises quickly and then saturates as the model acquires formal linguistic competence, meaning knowledge of grammatical rules and structure, while functional competence - world knowledge and reasoning - keeps improving long afterwards without any corresponding gain in alignment.

That is strong converging evidence for the view developed in section 48.5, namely that the human language network encodes linguistic form rather than general cognition.

Related 2025 and 2026 work reports layer-wise correspondence between model depth and cortical processing timescales, and Nature Communications published a 2025 study finding that the temporal structure of language processing in the brain maps onto the layered hierarchy of language models; a 2026 arXiv report further finds that left-hemisphere advantage in predicting brain activity emerges specifically as formal linguistic competence develops.

Since some of this material is recent and partly preprint, individual results should be regarded as promising rather than settled.


48.4.4 What model-brain fit does and does not establish

High predictive accuracy is not a demonstration that the brain and the model compute the same way.

Three concrete worries recur in the critical literature.

First, confounding: because naturalistic stimuli are not controlled by design, model features can be correlated with low-level properties such as word length, frequency, and position in the sentence, and studies have shown that simple architectural details like positional encoding can inflate apparent alignment.

Second, the flexibility of the linking function: encoding models fit a linear map from model activations to voxels, and a sufficiently rich feature space can predict well without any representational correspondence, which is why untrained or randomly initialised networks sometimes score surprisingly well.

Third, the direction of inference: showing that a next-word predictor predicts the brain does not establish that the brain is a next-word predictor, since many architectures could produce similar representational geometry.

The constructive response, now common in the field, is to move from prediction scores to controlled comparisons and causal manipulations - lesioning model components, training on developmentally realistic data volumes as Hosseini, Fedorenko and colleagues did in 2024, and using stimuli designed to decorrelate the confounds.


48.5 The language network

The final section steps back to the level of whole networks, and to what is arguably the most consequential recent claim in the cognitive neuroscience of language.


48.5.1 Functional localisation of a language-selective network

Because the anatomy of language varies substantially between individuals, group-averaged brain maps blur real functional boundaries.

The remedy, developed by Fedorenko, Kanwisher and colleagues from 2010 onward, is the functional localiser: each participant reads meaningful sentences and, in a control condition, lists of pronounceable nonwords, and the regions responding more to sentences are defined individually within that person's own brain.

This procedure reveals a consistent left-lateralised frontotemporal network - inferior frontal regions plus large swathes of superior and middle temporal cortex, with an angular gyrus component - that responds to both words and structure.

The network is selective in a strong sense: it responds to language whether read, heard, or signed, and responds far less to arithmetic, music, working memory, or executive tasks.

The methodological point is not a technicality; precision, subject-specific mapping is what made the dissociations in the next sub-section visible at all.


48.5.2 Its dissociation from the multiple-demand network and from theory of mind

Sitting immediately adjacent to the language network in frontal and parietal cortex is the multiple-demand network, a domain-general system that ramps up whenever a task gets harder, regardless of what the task is.

Blank, Kanwisher and Fedorenko showed in 2014 that these two systems, despite being cortical neighbours, have distinguishable spontaneous fluctuation patterns, and Mineroff and colleagues in 2018 demonstrated a robust dissociation using inter-region correlations in effect size across the language, multiple-demand, and default mode networks.

Diachek and colleagues further showed that much of the frontal activity historically attributed to sentence processing was in fact task-related multiple-demand activity, appearing when participants had to make judgements and largely vanishing during ordinary passive comprehension.

A separate dissociation holds against the theory of mind network, the system supporting reasoning about other people's beliefs: Paunov, Blank and Fedorenko found in 2019 that the two networks are synchronised at rest and during comprehension yet remain functionally distinct, which matters because understanding what a speaker means often requires inferring their intentions.

So the language network is neither the brain's general-purpose difficulty system nor its mind-reading system, even though normal conversation recruits all three.


48.5.3 Language for communication against language for thought

These dissociations underpin the argument made by Fedorenko, Piantadosi and Gibson in a 2024 Nature perspective titled "Language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought".

Their case has two halves.

The first is a double dissociation: the language network is not engaged by non-linguistic reasoning tasks such as arithmetic, logic, code comprehension, or music, and conversely people who lose that network can still reason.

The second is a design argument - the properties of natural languages, including ambiguity, redundancy, and the way word order and word length are tuned to efficient transmission, look optimised for getting a message through a noisy channel rather than for supporting internal computation, since ambiguity is a virtue for a compression scheme and a defect for a reasoning medium.

The opposing tradition, running from the language-of-thought hypothesis through the strong Sapir-Whorf claims and more recent proposals that inner speech scaffolds abstract reasoning, is not dead, and critics reply that language may have shaped thought developmentally even if the adult brain no longer needs it online.

That is a real disagreement about what "primarily" means, and readers should not treat the communication view as uncontested.


48.5.4 Evidence from global aphasia and from language-deprived individuals

The strongest evidence in this argument comes from people rather than scanners.

Global aphasia is the near-total loss of language production and comprehension following extensive damage to the left perisylvian cortex, and case studies have documented such patients performing arithmetic and algebraic operations, solving logic problems, appreciating and composing music, passing false-belief tasks, and in some reported cases playing chess competently - Varley and Siegal's work on causal reasoning, Varley, Klessinger, Romanowski and Siegal's 2005 report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on preserved mathematical syntax alongside destroyed grammatical syntax, and Klessinger's case study of a severely aphasic retired professor are the standard references.

Fedorenko and Varley's 2016 review in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences collates this literature, and its force is simple: if language were the medium of thought, removing it should remove thought, and it does not.

The complementary evidence comes from language deprivation, meaning children who receive no accessible language input in early life, most commonly deaf children born to hearing parents without early access to a sign language.

Such individuals invent homesign, gestural systems with real linguistic properties including consistent ordering, yet late first-language learners of American or British Sign Language show persistent deficits in complex syntax, and Cheng, Mayberry and colleagues reported in 2019 altered white matter microstructure in the left arcuate fasciculus in this group, indicating that the network's structural development depends on timely input.

The two bodies of evidence pull in complementary directions: aphasia shows thought survives losing language in adulthood, while deprivation shows that language itself, and the cortex that supports it, needs early experience to develop normally.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Word recognition is competitive rather than a lookup, governed by frequency and by neighbourhood structure, and it begins with a fast form-based decomposition stage that strips apparent affixes before meaning is consulted.

Syntax is hierarchical, and the brain demonstrably tracks phrase and sentence structure that is nowhere present in the acoustic signal, with posterior temporal cortex resolving structure early and posterior inferior frontal cortex handling linearisation and memory load - though which linguistic formalism this implements remains open.

Semantic processing has two electrophysiological indices, the N400, best understood as graded prediction or prediction error rather than anomaly detection, and the P600, whose original syntax-only interpretation has not survived the semantic P600 findings.

Information-theoretic surprisal predicts processing cost linearly across many orders of magnitude and across many languages, and artificial language models predict cortical language responses well - but 2025 evidence indicates that alignment tracks formal linguistic competence, not reasoning, and prediction accuracy alone does not license claims of shared mechanism.

Finally, precision functional mapping reveals a language-selective network dissociable from both the multiple-demand and theory of mind systems, and evidence from global aphasia and from early language deprivation supports the view, argued forcefully but not universally accepted, that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than the medium of thought.


CHAPTER 49. READING, WRITING, AND MULTILINGUALISM (CORE)

Speech is old and reading is new.

Every healthy child learns to talk without being taught, but no child learns to read without instruction, because writing was invented roughly five thousand years ago and evolution has had no time to build a dedicated organ for it.

That gap is the puzzle at the heart of this chapter: if there is no gene for reading, what exactly is the brain doing when your eyes cross this line?

The answer, as far as the evidence takes us, is that reading borrows.

It takes circuitry evolved for recognising objects and shapes, wires it to circuitry evolved for speech, and in doing so remodels both.

This chapter follows that borrowing through four stages: the machinery of skilled reading, the process of acquiring it, what happens when it breaks down or is lost, and what changes when a single brain carries two or more languages.


49.1 Reading as cultural recycling

The starting observation is that skilled reading is fast, automatic, and remarkably consistent across people.

A competent adult identifies a printed word in roughly a fifth of a second, without effort and without the option of not doing it - you cannot look at a familiar word and see only ink.

That kind of speed and automaticity is the signature of a specialised neural circuit, not of general-purpose problem solving.

The question this section addresses is where that circuit comes from, given that it cannot have been built by natural selection for this purpose.


49.1.1 The visual word form area and its properties

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, researchers using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that tracks blood-oxygen changes as a proxy for neural activity, kept finding the same small patch of cortex lighting up when people read.

It sits in the left occipitotemporal region, on the underside of the brain in a fold called the fusiform gyrus, and Laurent Cohen and Stanislas Dehaene named it the visual word form area (VWFA).

Its properties are unusually specific: it responds more to written words and to pronounceable non-words such as "blorp" than to visually similar controls like strings of unfamiliar symbols, it responds in almost the same place in almost every literate person, and in the classic characterisation it responds to written input but not to the same words spoken aloud.

The word "prelexical" is often attached to it, meaning that it appears to handle the shape of the letter string before meaning is retrieved, acting as a recognition front end rather than a dictionary.

The exclusivity of that description is genuinely disputed.

Cathy Price and Joseph Devlin, in a paper pointedly titled "The myth of the visual word form area" and in later work developing what they call an interactive account, showed that the same patch activates during colour naming, picture naming, listening to spoken words, and Braille reading in blind people.

Their reading is that this cortex is not a word-shape module but a hub where visual, phonological, and semantic information meet, and that its apparent word specialisation reflects its strong connections to left-hemisphere language regions rather than an intrinsic love of letters.

Supporting the connectivity view, work by Zeynep Saygin, John Gabrieli and colleagues found that this region's links to perisylvian language cortex predict where it will end up, and studies of people with left-hemisphere perinatal stroke show the area can develop on the right instead.

The honest summary is that everyone agrees the region is reliably engaged by reading, and the field remains split on whether "word form area" names a specialisation or merely a location.


49.1.2 Neuronal recycling and the reuse of object-recognition circuitry

Dehaene and Cohen's answer to the reading paradox is the neuronal recycling hypothesis, set out most fully in their 2007 Neuron review "Cultural recycling of cortical maps".

The claim is that a cultural invention such as writing must find a neuronal niche, meaning a pre-existing brain system close enough to the required function and plastic enough to give up a substantial share of its resources to the new job.

For reading, that niche is the ventral visual stream, the pathway running from the primary visual cortex forward along the underside of the temporal lobe that evolved to recognise objects, faces, and shapes regardless of size, position, or lighting.

Writing systems, on this account, were shaped by the circuitry rather than the other way round: the letter shapes that survived cultural evolution are those built from line junctions the visual system already detects well, which is why the frequency of shapes like T, Y, and L junctions in scripts worldwide tracks their frequency in natural scenes.

The hypothesis makes a strong and testable prediction, namely that recycling should cost something, and there is evidence for that cost.

Dehaene and colleagues, reporting in Science in 2010 on illiterate adults, adults who became literate in adulthood, and childhood-literate adults in Portugal and Brazil, found that literacy boosted responses to written words in the left fusiform gyrus and sharpened early visual processing all the way back to primary visual cortex (V1), while responses to faces in the same territory shrank slightly and shifted rightward.

Subsequent work has been more equivocal about the size and reliability of the face cost, with Jeroen van Paridon, Falk Huettig and colleagues reporting in 2021 that the competition is weaker than the destructive-competition framing suggests, so the direction of the effect is better supported than its magnitude.


49.1.3 Orthography-to-phonology mapping and dual-route models

Getting from print to sound is not one problem but two, and the standard framework says the brain solves it two ways at once.
