The dual-route account, given its most developed computational form by Max Coltheart, Kathleen Rastle, Conrad Perry, Robyn Langdon and Johannes Ziegler in the Dual Route Cascaded (DRC) model of 2001, proposes a lexical route that looks a whole familiar word up in a stored orthographic vocabulary and retrieves its pronunciation directly, and a non-lexical route that applies grapheme-to-phoneme correspondence rules piece by piece.

A grapheme is the written unit that stands for a single speech sound, so "sh" in "ship" is one grapheme made of two letters, and a phoneme is the smallest sound unit that can change a word's identity, as /p/ and /b/ do in "pat" and "bat".

The two routes explain a simple pair of facts: you can pronounce "vurp" although you have never seen it, which needs the rule route, and you can pronounce "yacht" correctly although the rules would give you something else, which needs the lookup route.

The word "cascaded" means activation flows forward continuously as it accumulates rather than waiting for each stage to finish, which is how the model reproduces timing effects in naming latency.

The competing family of models, associated with Mark Seidenberg, James McClelland, David Plaut and colleagues, is the connectionist or triangle approach, in which a single network of weighted connections maps orthography to phonology and to semantics with no separate rule module, and regular and exception words differ only in how consistently their spelling patterns map to sound.

Both families simulate a large share of the human data, and the dispute over whether the brain contains two discrete routes or one graded system remains open.


49.1.4 Cross-script and cross-orthography comparison

Writing systems differ in how transparently spelling maps to sound, a dimension usually called orthographic depth.

Finnish, Italian, Spanish and Serbo-Croatian are shallow, meaning a letter almost always says the same thing, whereas English, French and Danish are deep, meaning the same letters behave inconsistently across words, as in "cough", "though", and "through".

The orthographic depth hypothesis predicts that readers of shallow scripts lean harder on assembling pronunciation from parts, while readers of deep scripts lean harder on whole-word lookup and on meaning, and behavioural evidence broadly supports this: children learning Finnish or Italian reach accurate decoding within a year, while English-speaking children typically need two to three.

Japanese offers an unusually clean natural experiment because a single language uses two scripts.

Kana are syllabic and almost perfectly regular, while kanji are logographic characters that map largely onto meaning, and neuropsychological and imaging evidence indicates partially different routes, with kana leaning on a dorsal occipital-to-parietal pathway and kanji on a ventral occipital-to-temporal one.

The broader neuroimaging picture is one of a shared core with local variation.

The left occipitotemporal region is engaged by reading across alphabetic, syllabic, and logographic scripts, but Chinese reading recruits the left middle frontal gyrus more heavily than alphabetic reading does, and Yang Zhang, Nan Jiang and others have shown that a reader's first writing system leaves a measurable fingerprint on how the brain handles a second one, so that Chinese-first learners of Japanese kana show frontal activation that Korean-first learners with matched proficiency do not.


49.2 Learning to read

Reading has to be installed, and installation takes years.

This section traces what has to be in place before instruction can work, what changes in the cortex as it takes hold, what literacy does back to the spoken language system, and what the neuroscience can and cannot say about how reading should be taught.

The general lesson is that the brain changes recorded in the imaging literature are consequences of learning at least as much as they are causes of it, which is a distinction the popular coverage of this field routinely blurs.


49.2.1 Phonological awareness as a precursor

Phonological awareness is the conscious ability to notice and manipulate the sound structure of speech independently of meaning, such as recognising that "cat" and "hat" rhyme, or that removing the first sound from "spin" leaves "pin".

Longitudinal studies, which follow the same children over years and so can distinguish a predictor from a correlate, consistently find that phoneme-level awareness measured before formal instruction predicts later word-reading accuracy, and that awareness at the level of whole syllables or rhymes predicts it more weakly.

The relationship is reciprocal rather than one-way: as George Hulme, Margaret Snowling and colleagues have documented, growth in reading also improves phoneme awareness, so the two skills bootstrap each other rather than one simply causing the other.

Two other predictors matter and are often underweighted.

Letter-sound knowledge is a strong independent predictor, and rapid automatised naming (RAN), the speed with which a child can name a grid of familiar colours, objects, or digits, predicts reading fluency at least as well as phonological awareness does and in some English-language studies better.

The practical upshot is that a preschooler at risk is best identified by a short battery rather than a single test.


49.2.2 Changes in cortical response with literacy acquisition

The cleanest evidence about what literacy does to cortex comes from comparing adults who never learned to read with adults who learned late, because this separates literacy from age, schooling in childhood, and general development.

In the 2010 Science study led by Dehaene, with Felipe Pegado, Lucia Braga, Régine Kolinsky, José Morais and others, the literate groups showed a strong left fusiform response to written words that the illiterate group essentially lacked, stronger early visual responses including in V1 and a particular facility with horizontally arranged stimuli, and stronger activation of spoken-language regions in the planum temporale when merely listening to speech.

Crucially, adults who became literate after childhood showed most of these changes too, which is direct evidence that the reading circuit can be installed well outside any supposed critical window.

Falk Huettig, Régine Kolinsky, Thomas Lachmann and colleagues, reviewing this literature in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2015 and afterwards, describe reading acquisition as producing a cascade of changes running from the visual periphery through to language cortex, and caution that many reported differences are modest and that sample sizes in the illiterate-adult literature are necessarily small.


49.2.3 Literacy's effects on spoken language processing

The most striking finding in this whole area is that learning to read changes how you hear.

In 1979, José Morais, Luz Cary, Jesús Alegria and Paul Bertelson published a study in Cognition, working with Portuguese adults who had never attended school and with peers who had become literate through adult programmes, asking both groups to add or delete a single consonant from a spoken item.

The illiterate adults performed poorly, particularly on non-words, while the late-literate adults performed well, which supports the conclusion that explicit awareness of phonemes does not arise spontaneously from speaking a language but is largely a by-product of learning an alphabet.

The qualification matters: illiterate adults rhyme, manipulate syllables, and discriminate similar syllables perfectly well, so what alphabetic literacy grants is conscious access to the phoneme, not the perceptual machinery underneath it.

The effect is specific to alphabetic writing, since readers of purely logographic systems show weaker phoneme awareness than alphabetic readers, and it has downstream consequences for spoken-word processing, including sharper phonological representations and faster prediction of upcoming speech.

There is an unresolved theoretical argument, pressed recently by authors including Kolinsky and Morais, about whether the phoneme is best regarded as a real prelinguistic unit that literacy reveals or as a conceptual category that alphabetic literacy largely creates.


49.2.4 Instructional method and the neuroscience evidence

The National Reading Panel in the United States reported in 2000 a meta-analysis of thirty-eight phonics studies, with Linnea Ehri and colleagues publishing the analysis in 2001, finding a mean effect of about d = 0.44 for systematic phonics instruction over control conditions, and larger effects when instruction began before first grade (d = 0.55) than after (d = 0.27).

Systematic phonics means teaching letter-sound correspondences in an explicit planned sequence, as opposed to teaching them incidentally when a word happens to cause trouble, which was the whole-language approach.

This body of work is the empirical backbone of what is now marketed as the science of reading, and it is the main reason many school systems have returned to explicit decoding instruction.

The evidence is not, however, as clean as advocacy on either side suggests.

Jeffrey Bowers argued in Educational Psychology Review in 2020 that the panel's comparisons pooled heterogeneous control conditions, many of which contained no phonics at all, so the analysis established that some phonics beats no phonics rather than that systematic phonics beats well-implemented alternatives, and the resulting exchange in that journal is worth reading in full before treating the question as closed.

The narrower neuroscience point is the one most often overstated: imaging shows that instruction changes activation in left temporoparietal and inferior frontal regions, but no brain measure to date adjudicates between competing curricula, and claims that neuroscience has proven a particular reading programme should be treated with suspicion.


49.3 Dyslexia and dysgraphia

Developmental dyslexia is a specific and persistent difficulty in accurate or fluent word reading that is not explained by low general ability, poor instruction, or sensory impairment, and it affects somewhere between five and twelve per cent of people depending on where the cut-off is drawn.

Dysgraphia is the corresponding difficulty with spelling and written production, which often co-occurs with dyslexia but can dissociate from it.

This section covers the competing causal theories, the brain findings and their variability, the different picture in adults who lose reading after brain injury, and what treatment actually achieves.


49.3.1 Phonological deficit, magnocellular, and attentional accounts

The dominant account is the phonological deficit hypothesis, associated with Isabelle Liberman, Frank Ramus, Margaret Snowling and others, which holds that dyslexia stems from imprecise or poorly accessible representations of speech sounds, so that mapping letters onto phonemes is inherently harder.

Its strength is that phonological difficulty is the most consistently observed deficit across languages and persists into adulthood even in compensated readers; its weakness is that a minority of people with clear reading difficulty show no phonological impairment at all.

The magnocellular theory, developed principally by John Stein, proposes a deficit in the fast, low-contrast, motion-sensitive magnocellular visual channel and its dorsal cortical targets, which would destabilise eye control and letter-position coding during reading.

Its status is contested: the co-occurrence of magnocellular and phonological findings in the same individuals has led many researchers, Stein included in his 2018 review, to treat the two as related rather than rival, while critics including Ramus argue the visual findings are secondary or reflect attention rather than a sensory channel.

The third family is attentional, and the best-specified version is the visual attention span hypothesis of Sylviane Valdois and colleagues, holding that some dyslexic readers can process too few visual elements simultaneously.

This account earns its place because the deficit is repeatedly found in children with intact phonology, and because white-matter network analyses have reported a double dissociation, with occipitoparietal connectivity around the left superior occipital gyrus tracking visual attention span but not phonological accuracy.

The field's centre of gravity has moved from choosing one theory to accepting multiple partly independent routes into the same behavioural outcome.


49.3.2 Neural signatures and their heterogeneity

The most reproducible imaging finding is underactivation of the left occipitotemporal cortex, including the visual word form area, during reading and reading-like tasks in dyslexic readers, and this appears in meta-analyses of both deep and shallow orthographies.

Meta-analyses using activation likelihood estimation, including work by Fabio Richlan, Martin Kronbichler and Heinz Wimmer and later cross-linguistic syntheses, additionally report reduced activity in left temporoparietal cortex around the supramarginal gyrus, altered inferior frontal activity often interpreted as compensatory, and bilateral cerebellar differences, with grey-matter reductions co-localising with the functional abnormalities.

Comparisons across writing systems find a shared core plus script-specific additions, which is usually summarised as a biological unity of dyslexia with orthography-specific overlays.

Two cautions are essential.

First, these are group averages, and the overlap between dyslexic and typical distributions is large enough that no brain measure currently diagnoses an individual.

Second, because most studies scan children who have already been failing to read for years, it is genuinely hard to separate a cause of dyslexia from a consequence of reduced reading experience, and the pre-reading longitudinal studies designed to break that ambiguity are still fewer and smaller than the field needs.


49.3.3 Acquired alexias and their dissociations

When an adult who could read loses the ability after stroke or injury, the pattern of loss is informative because it shows which components can be knocked out separately, and the resulting condition is called alexia or acquired dyslexia.

Pure alexia, also called letter-by-letter reading, follows damage to the left ventral occipitotemporal region or its inputs, and leaves speaking, listening, and often writing intact while reading collapses, producing the striking symptom of a patient who can write a sentence and then cannot read it back.

Surface dyslexia spares regular words and non-words but impairs irregular ones, so "yacht" is read as though it rhymed with "matched", which the dual-route framework interprets as loss of the lexical lookup route.

Phonological dyslexia is the mirror image, sparing familiar words while badly impairing non-words, consistent with loss of the grapheme-to-phoneme route.

Deep dyslexia adds semantic errors to that profile, so a patient reads "girl" as "child" or "listen" as "quiet", which is hard to explain without some contribution from meaning to reading aloud and is usually associated with extensive left perisylvian damage.

The parallel dissociations occur in writing, with surface and phonological dysgraphia showing the same regular/irregular and word/non-word splits, and recent lesion-network studies have begun mapping these syndromes onto specific white-matter disconnections rather than onto cortical damage alone.

These double dissociations are the strongest single line of evidence that reading is componential rather than unitary.


49.3.4 Intervention and remediation evidence

Structured, explicit, phonologically focused instruction delivered intensively in small groups is the best-supported intervention, and it works, but the effects are moderate rather than transformative.

Systematic reviews of reading intervention for elementary students with or at risk of dyslexia find average effects in the region of d = 0.3 to 0.4, with dosage - intensity and duration - among the clearest moderators, and with gains in decoding accuracy typically larger and more durable than gains in reading fluency, which remains the most treatment-resistant symptom.

Neuroimaging studies of successful remediation, beginning with Elise Temple, John Gabrieli and colleagues in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2003, report increases in left temporoparietal and left inferior frontal activity toward typical patterns after intervention.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention-related brain change by Rola Farah, Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus and colleagues found that the reported changes are real but highly variable across studies, involving left-hemisphere reading hubs, right-hemisphere homologues, and frontal and subcortical structures in different combinations, sometimes within the same participants.

Two negative findings deserve emphasis: commercial programmes based on training auditory temporal processing, on eye exercises, or on coloured overlays and tinted lenses have not held up in well-controlled trials, and the field's small samples and modest effects mean that many published treatment results are underpowered, a problem documented directly in recent methodological reviews of dyslexia treatment studies.


49.4 Bilingualism and multilingualism

More than half the world's population uses more than one language, which makes monolingualism the special case rather than the norm.

The neuroscientific questions are whether the two languages live in the same tissue, what keeps them from interfering, whether managing them confers wider cognitive benefits, and how much the age of learning matters.

The first two questions have reasonably settled answers, the third is one of the most public replication disputes in psychology, and the fourth has been reshaped by a very large dataset published in 2018.


49.4.1 Shared and separate substrates across languages

Early positron emission tomography (PET) and fMRI work in the 1990s, including studies by Karl Kim and Joy Hirsch in 1997 and by Daniela Perani, Stanislas Dehaene, Jacques Mehler and colleagues in 1996 and 1998, established the modern picture.

For highly proficient bilinguals, comprehension in both languages recruits largely the same left perisylvian network, meaning the inferior frontal gyrus, superior and middle temporal cortex, and their connections, regardless of when the second language was learned.

Where the languages diverge is under conditions of lower proficiency or later acquisition, when the weaker language recruits additional frontal and control regions, which is best read as extra effort rather than a separate language organ.

Kim and Hirsch's contribution was to show that in late learners the two languages occupied slightly separated sub-regions within Broca's area, while early learners showed overlapping tissue, and Perani's contribution was to show that proficiency accounts for more of the variance than age of acquisition does for comprehension.

More recent multivariate work, such as the Science Advances study by Xu, Wang and colleagues in 2017 using pattern analysis rather than average activation, finds that although the gross anatomy is shared, the fine-grained spatial patterns of activity differ reliably between a bilingual's two languages, so "same region" does not mean "same code".


49.4.2 Language control, switching, and inhibition

A bilingual speaking one language has the other one active in the background, which is well demonstrated by cross-language priming and by eye-tracking studies where hearing an English word draws looks toward objects whose Russian names overlap phonologically.

Something must therefore select the intended language, and David Green's inhibitory control model of 1998 proposed that the unintended language is actively suppressed rather than switched off, a proposal supported by the asymmetric switch cost, where returning to your dominant language is slower than switching into your weaker one, exactly as you would expect if the dominant one had been more heavily inhibited.

Jubin Abutalebi and Green subsequently mapped this onto a network comprising the left prefrontal cortex, the anterior cingulate cortex, the basal ganglia including the left caudate nucleus, and the inferior parietal lobule.

Within that network the anterior cingulate and presupplementary motor area are associated with monitoring for conflict, the left prefrontal and inferior frontal cortex with suppressing interference, parietal cortex with holding the current task set, and the left caudate with switching and with selecting words in the weaker language, a role supported by case reports of patients with left caudate lesions who switch languages involuntarily.

Green and Abutalebi's later adaptive control hypothesis of 2013 adds that the demands depend on the social context, so a bilingual in a community where languages are kept strictly separate faces different control demands than one in a community where dense code-switching within a sentence is normal.


49.4.3 The disputed bilingual advantage in executive function

The claim that constant language control trains domain-general executive function, and so gives bilinguals better inhibition, task switching and conflict resolution, was advanced most prominently by Ellen Bialystok and colleagues from the mid-2000s and became widely publicised.

It is now among the most seriously contested claims in cognitive psychology.

Minna Lehtonen and colleagues published a meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin in 2018 covering 152 published and unpublished studies of adults; the raw effect favoured bilinguals but was tiny, at a standardised difference of about 0.06, and after correcting for publication bias with the PET-PEESE technique the difference was no longer distinguishable from zero and was numerically slightly negative.

Kenneth Paap and colleagues, across a series of papers including a 2020 analysis of confirmation bias in the literature, report that roughly fifteen per cent of published comparisons yield a significant bilingual advantage, about what you would expect from noise plus selective reporting, and a large analysis of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study found no bilingual executive advantage in a sample of thousands of children.

The other side has not conceded, and the counterarguments are substantive rather than merely defensive: that treating bilingualism as a binary category discards the continuous variables that matter, that laboratory conflict tasks have poor reliability which mechanically depresses group differences, and that some analyses of publication bias in this literature have themselves been shown to rest on classification and exclusion decisions that inflate the apparent bias.

The defensible present position is that a broad, robust bilingual advantage on standard executive tasks is not supported, that specific effects in specific populations and contexts remain live possibilities, and that the related and separate claim about delayed onset of dementia symptoms in bilinguals rests on a different and still-mixed evidence base.


49.4.4 Age of acquisition and critical period effects

Eric Lenneberg proposed in 1967 that language must be acquired within a biologically constrained critical period ending around puberty, and Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport's 1989 study of Chinese and Korean immigrants to the United States gave the idea its most cited support, finding that grammatical judgement scores declined steadily with age of arrival up to about puberty and were scattered and generally lower thereafter.

The largest test of the idea came in 2018, when Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum and Steven Pinker analysed an online grammar test taken by about two-thirds of a million native and non-native English speakers and modelled current age, age of first exposure, and years of experience separately.

Their conclusion was that grammar-learning ability stays close to its peak until roughly 17.4 years and then declines fairly sharply, which is considerably later than the classical puberty account, though full native-like attainment still requires beginning around age ten because acquisition itself takes about thirty years to complete.

That finding has been challenged on methodological grounds, including concerns about self-selected internet samples, about whether the modelled inflection point is an artefact of the fitting procedure, and about the fact that a written grammaticality test is not a general measure of language ability.

Two things are clearer than the shape of the curve.

Phonology declines earliest and most steeply, which is why a foreign accent is the most persistent marker of late acquisition, whereas vocabulary shows little or no age limit and can grow throughout life.

And the decline is a decline in the ceiling, not a barrier: the adults in Dehaene's Portuguese and Brazilian literacy studies built a functioning reading circuit from scratch in middle age, and adults routinely reach high functional proficiency in a second language even when they never sound native.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Reading has no dedicated evolutionary machinery and instead recycles object-recognition cortex in the left ventral visual stream, yoking it to speech circuitry, with the left occipitotemporal region conventionally called the visual word form area serving as the hinge - though whether that region is truly word-specialised or simply the point where visual and language networks meet remains genuinely disputed.

Getting from print to sound involves at least two separable processes, evidenced most powerfully by the acquired alexias and dysgraphias, in which whole-word reading and letter-by-letter decoding can be destroyed independently of each other.

Literacy is not a passive add-on: it reshapes early visual cortex, and it creates the conscious awareness of phonemes that Morais and colleagues showed in 1979 does not arise from speaking a language alone.

Developmental dyslexia is reliably associated with left occipitotemporal underactivation at the group level, but it is causally heterogeneous, with phonological, magnocellular, and visual-attentional accounts each capturing part of a population that no single theory explains, and no brain measure yet diagnoses an individual.

Bilinguals run both languages through largely shared left perisylvian tissue, managed by a frontal, cingulate, and basal-ganglia control network in which the left caudate is repeatedly implicated in switching.

The popular claim that this control practice yields a general executive-function advantage does not survive correction for publication bias, and the equally popular claim that a second language must be learned before puberty overstates a real but later and gentler decline that affects accent far more than vocabulary.


CHAPTER 50. NUMBER, MAGNITUDE, SPACE, AND COGNITIVE MAPS (CORE)

This chapter is about two things that at first look unrelated - how the brain handles quantity, and how it handles space - and about the growing evidence that they are handled by overlapping machinery.

We will start with the rough, wordless sense of "how many" that human infants and many animals already possess, and follow it up to symbolic arithmetic and professional mathematics.

We will then turn to space: how the brain represents where things are relative to your body, where they are relative to each other, and how it builds a reusable internal map of an environment.

The chapter ends with the most striking result in this area, which is that the same map-building cells that track physical location also appear to track position in purely abstract spaces of ideas.

This matters because it suggests that abstract thought may not be a separate faculty bolted onto the brain, but a re-use of ancient navigation circuitry.

It also matters practically, because failures in these systems produce recognisable clinical conditions - dyscalculia, acalculia, and spatial neglect - that we will describe as we go.


50.1 The number sense

Long before anyone learns the word "seven" or the symbol 7, the brain already represents quantity.

This section covers that pre-symbolic capacity, its precise and imprecise halves, the neurons that carry it, and the disputed question of whether learned symbols get their meaning from it.


50.1.1 Approximate number system and its Weber signature

The approximate number system (ANS) is the brain's built-in, wordless estimator of quantity - it tells you roughly how many items are in a set without counting them.

Its defining property is ratio dependence, which is a form of Weber's law (the nineteenth-century psychophysical principle that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is a fixed proportion of their size, not a fixed absolute amount).

In practice this means that telling 10 dots from 20 dots is easy, telling 10 from 12 is hard, and telling 100 from 120 is exactly as hard as telling 10 from 12, because the ratio is the same in both cases.

Individual acuity is summarised by a single number called the Weber fraction, usually written w, where a larger w means fuzzier internal representations and worse discrimination.

Acuity sharpens with development: Halberda and Feigenson (2008) and related infant work report that six-month-olds need roughly a 1 to 2 ratio to tell two large sets apart, nine-month-olds manage roughly 2 to 3, and adults do far better still.

Stanislas Dehaene's 1997 book The Number Sense popularised the idea that this system is an evolved perceptual capacity rather than a cultural invention, and versions of it have been reported in monkeys, birds, and fish.

One honest caveat: a 2020 reanalysis by Testolin and colleagues in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review questioned whether numerosity estimates adhere to Weber's law as cleanly as textbook accounts imply, so the law should be read as a strong regularity rather than an exact statute.


50.1.2 Subitising and exact small-number representation

Subitising is the immediate, effortless, and exact apprehension of how many items are present when the set is very small - typically up to about four.

The behavioural signature is a sharp elbow in the data: adults enumerate one to four items almost instantly and almost without error, then reaction time and error rate climb steeply from about five onward.

The leading explanation is the parallel individuation system, also called the object tracking system, which is thought to attach a small number of mental "pointers" (Zenon Pylyshyn's FINSTs, or fingers of instantiation) to a handful of objects at once and thereby represent them as distinct individuals rather than as an estimated mass.

This is genuinely a different system from the approximate number system: it is exact but capacity-limited, whereas the ANS is unlimited in range but imprecise.

The alternative view is that subitising is not special at all, but simply the low end of one continuous estimation process where Weber's law happens to yield near-perfect performance for tiny sets, and that debate is not fully closed.

Evidence favouring two systems comes from Piazza and colleagues (2011), who found that subitising tracks visuo-spatial object individuation capacity, and from the human single-neuron work described next, which found a coding boundary near four.


50.1.3 Number neurons in parietal and prefrontal cortex

Andreas Nieder and Earl Miller, working with macaque monkeys in the early 2000s, found individual neurons that fire maximally for a particular numerosity - a "four neuron" that responds most to four items, somewhat to three and five, and little to one or eight.

These cells sit in a parieto-frontal network, principally the intraparietal sulcus and the lateral prefrontal cortex, and their tuning curves are Gaussian with a fixed width when plotted on a logarithmic scale, which is the neural counterpart of the behavioural Weber signature.

The code is a labelled-line code, meaning that quantity is signalled by which population of cells is active rather than by how fast a single population fires.

These neurons are supramodal and abstract: Nieder and colleagues (2012, PNAS) showed cells that respond to the same numerosity whether it arrives as a set of dots or a sequence of sounds, and Ramirez-Cardenas, Moskaleva and Nieder (2016) found neurons coding the empty set, numerosity zero.

The finding has been confirmed in humans: Kutter, Bostroem, Elger, Mormann and Nieder (2018, Neuron) recorded single neurons in the medial temporal lobe of epilepsy patients and found separate populations coding non-symbolic quantity (dots) and symbolic quantity (digits), with little overlap between the two formats.

A follow-up from the same group (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023) reported a change in neuronal coding regime around the number four, matching the behavioural transition from subitising to estimation and giving the two-system account a physiological anchor.


50.1.4 Symbolic number and its grounding in the approximate system

The influential claim is that learned symbols - the word "seven", the digit 7 - acquire their meaning by being mapped onto the pre-existing approximate representation, so that culture borrows an evolved perceptual system.

Supporting evidence includes the distance effect, where deciding which of two digits is larger gets slower as the digits get closer together, implying that even symbols are being converted into fuzzy analogue magnitudes.

Further support comes from the SNARC effect - the Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes - reported by Dehaene, Bossini and Giraux (1993), in which people judging whether a centrally presented digit is odd or even respond faster with the left hand to small numbers and the right hand to large numbers, as if numbers were laid out on a left-to-right mental number line.

The grounding claim is, however, genuinely contested.

Szucs and Myers (2017) and others argue that correlations between ANS acuity and mathematics achievement shrink or vanish once you control for domain-general abilities such as working memory, inhibitory control, and visual attention.

Training studies are similarly unhelpful to the strong version of the claim: Lindskog, Winman and Poom (2016) found that arithmetic training did not improve ANS acuity, and Park and Brannon's transfer effects have been hard to attribute specifically to the ANS.

A reasonable summary for 2026 is that the approximate system is real and neurally grounded, that symbolic and non-symbolic number are partly separable in the brain and partly linked, and that the symbolic system is a better predictor of school mathematics than the approximate one.


50.2 Arithmetic and mathematical cognition

Knowing roughly how many is not arithmetic.

This section covers the parietal machinery for comparing magnitudes, the split between remembering an answer and computing one, what happens when these break, and what happens at the far end of mathematical expertise.


50.2.1 Intraparietal sulcus and magnitude comparison

The intraparietal sulcus (IPS) is a groove running back-to-front along the top rear of each hemisphere's parietal lobe, and it is the most reliably reported site for numerical magnitude.

Piazza, Izard, Pinel, Le Bihan and Dehaene (2004) showed tuning curves for approximate numerosity in the human IPS using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that infers neural activity from local changes in blood oxygenation.

IPS activity is parametrically modulated by numerical distance, meaning the signal rises as two compared numbers get closer and the comparison gets harder, which is the imaging counterpart of the behavioural distance effect.

Importantly, the region is not narrowly numerical: it also responds to physical size, luminance, and duration, which supports the "generalised magnitude" view associated with Vincent Walsh's ATOM theory (A Theory Of Magnitude, 2003), that number, space, and time share a common parietal metric.

In children with developmental dyscalculia, several studies report that bilateral IPS activity is not modulated by numerical distance in the normal way, which is one of the clearer links from this region to real-world arithmetic ability.


50.2.2 Fact retrieval against procedural calculation

Adults solve 7 x 8 and 63 - 27 by different routes: the first is usually looked up from memory, the second is usually computed step by step.

The triple-code model of Dehaene (1992) and Dehaene and Cohen (1995) formalises this by proposing three representations of number - a visual Arabic form for digits, a verbal word frame for number words, and an analogue magnitude representation - and by assigning different operations to different codes.

On this account, rote multiplication tables are stored verbally and retrieved through left-hemisphere perisylvian language areas together with the left angular gyrus (a fold of parietal cortex just behind and above the ear), whereas subtraction and unfamiliar calculation lean on the quantity code in the intraparietal sulcus.

The strongest clinical support is the double dissociation reported by Dehaene and Cohen (1997) in Cortex, where one patient could still perform quantity-based approximation but had lost rote verbal facts, and another showed the reverse profile.

The model is elegant and has organised the field for three decades, but the angular gyrus part is disputed: several later imaging studies find angular gyrus activity that looks more like general task difficulty or default-mode deactivation than like arithmetic fact storage as such.


50.2.3 Dyscalculia and acalculia

Two words are needed here, and they are not synonyms.

Acalculia is an acquired loss of calculation ability following brain injury, most often to the left parietal lobe, in a person who could previously calculate.

Developmental dyscalculia is a lifelong learning difficulty with number and arithmetic that appears in childhood without any such injury, with prevalence estimates clustering around five to six percent, though reported figures range from about 1 percent to about 10 percent depending on the cut-off used.

Acalculia is a component of Gerstmann syndrome, described by Josef Gerstmann in the 1920s and 1930s, which classically combines four signs - acalculia, agraphia (loss of writing), left-right disorientation, and finger agnosia (inability to identify one's own fingers) - and is associated with damage near the left angular gyrus.

The cause of developmental dyscalculia is contested: one camp argues for a core deficit in the number sense itself, and Decarli and colleagues (2023, Psychological Science) found that severely affected children were impaired on both symbolic and non-symbolic number tasks, while another camp emphasises visuo-spatial working memory, attention and inhibition, and a 2023 fMRI study by Kuhl and colleagues even failed to find atypical brain activation in dyscalculic participants.

Multiple-deficit models, which allow several partially independent causes to combine, currently fit the heterogeneity of real cases better than any single-cause account.


50.2.4 Advanced mathematics and the non-linguistic network for it

A natural guess is that higher mathematics is parasitic on language, since both involve recursive symbolic structure.

Amalric and Dehaene (2016, PNAS) tested this directly by scanning 15 professional mathematicians and 15 equally educated non-mathematicians while they judged spoken mathematical and non-mathematical statements.

Advanced mathematical reasoning - across algebra, analysis, geometry, and topology alike - activated a bilateral network of prefrontal, parietal, and inferior temporal regions, and did not activate the classical left-hemisphere language areas beyond what mere sentence comprehension required.

The same network responds when ordinary people simply think about numbers and space, which suggests mathematics is built on number and space circuitry rather than on grammar circuitry.

A follow-up by Amalric and Dehaene (2019, NeuroImage) confirmed a distinct cortical network for mathematical knowledge that was dissociable from general semantic knowledge.

The result should be read carefully: it says that high-level mathematical semantics is not housed in language cortex, not that language plays no role in learning mathematics, and the acquisition question remains open.


50.3 Spatial cognition

We now change subject from quantity to space, though the parietal lobe will keep appearing.

This section covers the two basic ways of specifying where something is, the syndrome that results when one of them fails, the manipulation of spatial images in the mind, and the strategies people use to get from A to B.


50.3.1 Egocentric and allocentric spatial frames

An egocentric frame specifies location relative to you - to the left of my hand, straight ahead of my nose, above my head - and it changes every time you move.

An allocentric frame specifies location relative to the world or to other objects - north of the church, between the two trees - and it stays put when you move.

Egocentric coding is largely a parietal and premotor affair, and it is not one frame but several nested ones anchored to the eyes, the head, the trunk, and even gravity, which is why neglect severity can shift when a patient's head is turned relative to their body.

Allocentric coding depends heavily on the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe, which is the machinery covered in section 50.4.

Everyday navigation constantly translates between the two, since a map tells you the goal is north but your legs need to know it is to your left.


50.3.2 Parietal spatial processing and neglect as its lesion signature

Hemispatial neglect is a failure to attend to or act upon one side of space, usually the left side after damage to the right parietal or parieto-temporal cortex.

It is not blindness - the visual pathways may be intact - it is a failure of spatial attention and representation, so patients may eat food from one half of the plate, shave one half of the face, or draw only one half of a clock.

The most famous demonstration that neglect afflicts internal representations, not just incoming vision, is Bisiach and Luzzatti's 1978 study in Milan, in which patients asked to imagine standing at one end of the Piazza del Duomo described only the buildings on their right, then, asked to imagine the opposite viewpoint, described the buildings they had just omitted and omitted the ones they had just described.

Neglect can be fractionated: egocentric neglect ignores one side relative to the body, while allocentric or object-centred neglect ignores the left side of each individual object no matter where that object sits, and the two forms have been associated with partly different lesion sites although they very often co-occur.

Neglect is the clearest single piece of evidence that the right hemisphere carries a disproportionate share of spatial representation in humans.


50.3.3 Mental rotation and imagery of space

Shepard and Metzler's 1971 experiment in Science asked people to judge whether two drawings of three-dimensional block figures showed the same object, and found that reaction time rose linearly with the angular difference between them.

The linearity is the key result: it implies people are performing an analogue transformation, mentally turning the object at a roughly constant rate, rather than comparing abstract descriptions.

This was a decisive blow in the 1970s imagery debate against the view, associated with Zenon Pylyshyn, that all mental representation is propositional, though Pylyshyn continued to argue that such results reflect tacit knowledge of how objects behave rather than pictures in the head.

Neuroimaging and event-related potential studies consistently implicate a frontoparietal network, especially the superior parietal lobule and intraparietal sulcus, with motor cortex involvement when the rotated object is a body part such as a hand.

Mental rotation shows one of the larger and more replicable sex differences in cognitive psychology, favouring men on the classic block-figures task, and it is also one of the spatial skills most improved by training, which complicates simple biological readings of the difference.


50.3.4 Navigation strategies: route, survey, and beacon

Spatial knowledge is traditionally divided into three kinds.

• Landmark or beacon knowledge is the simplest: head towards the visible church tower, and you will get there, without knowing anything about the layout.

• Route knowledge is a stored sequence of stimulus-response steps: left at the pub, straight past the school, right at the postbox, which works perfectly until the route is blocked.

• Survey knowledge is map-like and allocentric: it lets you take a shortcut you have never taken, or point correctly towards a goal you cannot see.

Different brain systems support these: response and route learning depends on the caudate nucleus, part of the dorsal striatum and a habit-learning structure, whereas survey or place learning depends on the hippocampus, and healthy individuals differ in which strategy they default to.

Maguire, Frackowiak and Frith (1997) found that when London taxi drivers described shortest routes across the city, the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus were more active than during a landmark-description control task.

Maguire and colleagues (2000, PNAS) then reported that London taxi drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus than controls, with volume correlating with years of driving, and a 2006 comparison against London bus drivers - who drive constantly but on fixed routes - strengthened the case that flexible survey navigation, not driving itself, is what matters.

The finding should not be overstated: Weisberg, Newcombe and Chatterjee (2019) looked for the same hippocampal volume advantage in ordinary good navigators and did not find it, so the taxi-driver effect may require extreme and prolonged demand.


50.4 The cognitive map

Edward Tolman proposed in 1948 that rats learn a "cognitive map" of a maze rather than a chain of turns, an idea that was unpopular in a behaviourist era and had no known neural basis.

Half a century of single-cell recording has supplied that basis, and produced the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for John O'Keefe and for May-Britt and Edvard Moser.


50.4.1 Place cells in the hippocampus

O'Keefe and Dostrovsky (1971), recording from freely moving rats in Brain Research, found hippocampal neurons that fire only when the animal occupies a particular small region of the environment, called that cell's place field.

Together, a population of place cells tiles the whole environment, so the identity of the currently active cells specifies where the animal is.

Place cells are allocentric, meaning their fields are anchored to the world rather than to the animal's body or direction of gaze, and they persist in darkness, which shows they are not simply reporting the current view.

They remap when the environment changes: moving the animal to a different room produces a completely different and statistically independent assignment of cells to locations, which is how one hippocampus can store many maps.

Human place-like cells were recorded directly by Ekstrom and colleagues (2003) in epilepsy patients navigating a virtual town, confirming that this is not a rodent peculiarity.


50.4.2 Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex and their metric

Hafting, Fyhn, Molden, Moser and Moser (2005, Nature) recorded from the medial entorhinal cortex, one synapse upstream of the hippocampus, and found cells that fire not at one location but at many, arranged in a strikingly regular triangular or hexagonal lattice covering the whole enclosure.

Because the lattice has a fixed spacing and orientation regardless of where the animal is, grid cells look like a coordinate system or metric - a built-in graph paper against which distance and direction travelled can be measured.

They are thought to support path integration, which is the ability to keep a running tally of your own movement and so know your position relative to your starting point without any landmarks, the trick a desert ant uses to run straight home.

Stensola and colleagues (2012, Nature) showed the map is discretized into modules: grid cells cluster into a handful of groups, each with its own spacing, and the spacings increase geometrically by a mean ratio of about 1.42, close to the square root of two.

That modular, multi-scale arrangement is efficient - a small number of modules with incommensurate periods can specify position over a very large range without ambiguity, an argument developed formally by Wei, Prentice and Balasubramanian (2015).

Grid-like coding exists in humans too: Doeller, Barry and Burgess (2010) detected the tell-tale six-fold directional periodicity with fMRI during virtual navigation, and Jacobs and colleagues (2013, Nature Neuroscience) recorded grid-like neuronal activity directly in human patients.


50.4.3 Head-direction, border, boundary vector, object vector, and speed cells

The map is built from several complementary cell types, none of which alone would suffice.

• Head-direction cells, described by Taube, Muller and Ranck (1990), fire when the animal's head points in a particular allocentric direction, regardless of location - a neural compass.

• Border cells, reported by Solstad and colleagues (2008), fire when the animal is close to a wall or edge, and only for a particular edge.

• Boundary vector cells, proposed theoretically by Burgess and O'Keefe and then found by Lever and colleagues (2009) in the subiculum, fire at a specific distance and allocentric direction from any boundary, which explains how place fields can be anchored to the geometry of a room.

• Object vector cells, reported by Høydal, Skytøen, Andersson, Moser and Moser (2019, Nature), do the same trick for discrete objects, firing at a fixed distance and direction from any object encountered.

• Speed cells, reported by Kropff, Carmichael, Moser and Moser (2015, Nature), signal running speed with a firing rate that is largely independent of location and direction, supplying the velocity term that path integration requires.

Taken together these give the system everything a dead-reckoning navigator needs: a compass, a speedometer, a set of surveyed landmarks and walls, and a metric grid on which to integrate.

Many real cells are conjunctive, coding two or three of these variables at once, so the tidy taxonomy is a simplification rather than a strict parts list.


50.4.4 Time cells and the temporal analogue of the map

If the hippocampus mapped only space, it would be an odd structure to find at the centre of episodic memory, which is memory for events in time.

Pastalkova, Itskov, Amarasingham and Buzsáki (2008) found that when a rat runs in a wheel during the delay of a memory task - so that location and movement are held constant - hippocampal cells still fire in a reliable sequence, each cell at its own moment.

MacDonald, Lepage, Eden and Eichenbaum (2011, Neuron) named these time cells, showing that they tile an empty interval between two events, and that they "retime" when the interval is lengthened in just the way place cells remap when the room changes.

The interpretation is that the hippocampus provides a general relational scaffold, and that time cells bridge temporal gaps so that discontiguous events can be bound into a single episode.

There is a live methodological dispute over whether such firing reflects elapsed time as such or accumulated self-motion and internally generated activity, and Kraus and colleagues (2013) explicitly framed the question as time versus path integration, finding that many cells code both.

Time-cell-like sequences have since been reported outside the hippocampus, in dorsal striatum and in frontal cortex, so temporal tiling is probably a general cortical trick rather than a hippocampal speciality.


50.4.5 The generalisation of the map to non-spatial and conceptual spaces

The most consequential recent development is that these codes are not restricted to physical space.

Constantinescu, O'Reilly and Behrens (2016, Science) had people learn about cartoon birds whose neck length and leg length varied continuously, then move through that two-dimensional "bird space" mentally, and found the six-fold grid-like fMRI signature in entorhinal cortex as if participants were navigating a room.

Aronov, Nevers and Tank (2017, Nature) trained rats to manipulate a sound frequency with a joystick and found hippocampal cells that fired at particular frequencies, exactly as place cells fire at particular places, in an animal that was not moving through space at all.

Theves, Fernandez and Doeller (2019) reported hippocampal coding of distances in an abstract concept space defined by two arbitrary object features, and their 2020 follow-up argued that the hippocampus maps concept space rather than raw feature space.

The unifying proposal, associated with Behrens, Muller, Whittington and colleagues (2018), is that the hippocampal formation encodes relational structure of any kind, and that physical navigation is simply its most obvious application.

This is an elegant theory with real evidence, and it should still be held with some caution: the fMRI grid-like signal is an indirect population measure with known analysis pitfalls, and how far a two-dimensional continuous concept space resembles genuinely complex human knowledge remains an open question.


50.4.6 Successor representations and predictive maps as a unifying account

A cognitive map that told you only where you are would be of limited use; what you usually want to know is where you can get to.

The successor representation, introduced by Peter Dayan in 1993 within reinforcement learning, represents each state not by its identity but by the states you are likely to occupy next, discounted by how far in the future they are.

Stachenfeld, Botvinick and Gershman (2017, Nature Neuroscience) proposed that hippocampal place cells implement exactly this, so a place field is really a map of expected future occupancy from the current position.

The theory explains several otherwise awkward observations: place fields skew backwards along a frequently run direction, they deform around barriers rather than staying circular, and grid cells look like the principal components, or smooth eigenvectors, of that predictive map.

It also offers a computational bridge between navigation and decision-making, since a successor representation lets an agent re-evaluate goals quickly without re-planning every step, which is why the idea has been taken up in both neuroscience and machine learning.

The account is not universally accepted - competing models such as the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine of Whittington and colleagues (2020) derive similar cell types from factorised structural learning instead - but predictive-map thinking is currently the most successful attempt to state, in one formalism, what the hippocampus is actually computing.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The brain contains an evolved, wordless system for representing approximate quantity whose behavioural signature is ratio dependence and whose neural signature is numerosity-tuned neurons in the intraparietal sulcus and prefrontal cortex, alongside a separate exact system for very small sets.

Symbolic arithmetic recruits this parietal magnitude machinery together with verbal fact retrieval, a division supported by the double dissociations of acquired acalculia, though the claim that symbols derive their meaning from the approximate system is contested rather than settled.

High-level mathematics, on the evidence of Amalric and Dehaene, runs on number and space networks rather than on language cortex.

Spatial cognition rests on both egocentric and allocentric frames, and the collapse of the former after right parietal damage produces hemispatial neglect, which Bisiach and Luzzatti showed afflicts imagined scenes as well as perceived ones.

The cognitive map is now a concrete piece of neurobiology built from place cells, grid cells and their modular metric, head-direction, border, boundary vector, object vector and speed cells, and time cells.

The strongest current claim, still under active test, is that this map is not specifically spatial at all but a general engine for relational and predictive structure, which would make navigation the template for thought rather than a special case of it.


PART NINE. ACTION, CONTROL, AND DECISION


CHAPTER 51. MOTOR COGNITION AND THE PLANNING OF ACTION (CORE)


Movement looks simple from the outside and is fiendish on the inside.

To pick up a coffee cup, your nervous system must choose a goal, select one of infinitely many arm paths that would reach it, convert that path into a pattern of muscle forces, predict what the arm will feel like on the way, and correct errors faster than your senses can report them.

This chapter is about how the brain does that, and about why the doing of an action turns out to be tangled up with the thinking about actions - planning, inhibiting, sequencing, and understanding what other people are doing.

The term motor cognition names exactly this tangle: the claim that the machinery for producing movement is also used for representing possible movement, one's own and other people's.

The chapter matters because motor control is the one part of cognition where we can state the problem mathematically, test the theory against millisecond-resolution neural recordings, and watch elegant hypotheses succeed or fail in public.

It also matters clinically, because Parkinson's disease, stroke, cerebellar ataxia, and some symptoms of schizophrenia are all, at bottom, failures somewhere in this machinery.


51.1 The motor hierarchy

The nervous system does not control movement from a single place.

It controls movement through a layered arrangement, often called a hierarchy, in which lower levels handle fast, local, stereotyped business and higher levels handle slower, more abstract business such as what to do and when.

The word hierarchy is a useful simplification rather than a literal chain of command, because the levels talk back to each other constantly and some loops skip levels entirely.

The four sub-sections below walk up the ladder, from the spinal cord to the parietal lobe.


51.1.1 Spinal circuits, central pattern generators, and reflex modulation

The spinal cord is not a cable.

It contains complete circuits that can generate rhythmic, coordinated movement on their own, called central pattern generators (CPGs), which are networks of neurons capable of producing an alternating rhythm - such as the left-right alternation of walking - without any rhythmic input from the brain and without sensory feedback.

The evidence goes back to Thomas Graham Brown's experiments around 1911, in which cats with the spinal cord surgically separated from the brain still produced alternating stepping, and it was extended in the 1980s and after by Serge Rossignol, Sten Grillner, and others who showed that a spinalised cat placed on a treadmill will step and will adjust its step to the belt speed.

Evidence for a human CPG is real but weaker and still argued about, since we cannot do the decisive experiments in people; a 2002 review in Physical Therapy by Michele Basso and colleagues, and more recent modelling work such as the neuromechanical study published in the Journal of Neural Engineering in 2023, both conclude that reflexes alone cannot reproduce human walking and that something CPG-like is needed to gate reflexes into the right phase of the step.

That last point is the key one for cognition: reflexes are not fixed.

A reflex is a fast, hard-wired sensory-to-motor loop, and the same stimulus produces opposite reflex responses depending on when in the step cycle it arrives - touching the top of a cat's paw during swing lifts the leg over the obstacle, while the same touch during stance presses the leg down.

This is called reflex modulation or phase-dependent gating, and it means that even the lowest level of the hierarchy is being continuously reconfigured by the level above.


51.1.2 Primary motor cortex and the coding of movement parameters

Primary motor cortex (M1) is the strip of cortex just in front of the central sulcus whose neurons project, in primates, partly straight down to the spinal cord.

Wilder Penfield's electrical stimulation mapping in awake neurosurgical patients in the 1930s and 1940s produced the famous motor homunculus, a distorted body map with huge hand and mouth territories, and it remains broadly correct even though later work showed the map is far messier and more overlapping than the cartoon suggests.

The central scientific question was what M1 neurons actually encode, and for thirty years the field ran a genuine and unresolved argument: Edward Evarts's work in the late 1960s found cells that tracked force, whereas Apostolos Georgopoulos and colleagues in 1982 and 1986 found cells broadly tuned to the direction of reaching, such that the vector sum across the population - the population vector - pointed where the arm was going.

Neither camp was simply wrong, and later studies found M1 activity correlating with force, direction, velocity, endpoint position, joint torque, and individual muscles, often in the same neuron at different moments.

Since about 2010 the dominant response, associated with Krishna Shenoy, Mark Churchland, and colleagues, has been to argue that the question was badly posed: rather than encoding a parameter the way a thermometer encodes temperature, M1 may be better understood as a dynamical system - a machine whose activity evolves over time according to its own internal rules - that generates the time-varying command a muscle needs.

This is now the mainstream view among population-recording labs, but it is a reframing rather than a refutation, and single-neuron tuning to direction is a robust empirical fact that any account must accommodate.


51.1.3 Premotor and supplementary motor areas and their planning roles

In front of M1 lie the premotor areas, and the useful first approximation is that they specify what movement to make while M1 specifies how to make it.

Lateral premotor cortex divides into dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) and ventral premotor cortex (PMv), and both are strongly driven by external sensory cues - PMd is heavily engaged when an arbitrary stimulus tells you which of several reaches to make, and PMv is engaged by the shape and graspability of objects.

On the medial wall sit the supplementary motor area (SMA) and, in front of it, the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA), and these two are anatomically distinguishable rather than a single blob: work summarised by Simon Eickhoff, Katrin Amunts and colleagues in Brain Structure and Function in 2018 shows SMA has a body map and direct projections to spinal cord and M1 but essentially no prefrontal input, whereas pre-SMA has dense prefrontal connectivity and no direct spinal output.

The functional consequence is a rough division of labour: SMA is associated with internally generated and sequential and bimanual movements, while pre-SMA, as reviewed by Parashkev Nachev, Christopher Kennard and Masud Husain in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2008, is associated with switching between actions, resolving conflict between competing responses, and holding off a prepotent response.

A blunt clinical illustration is alien hand syndrome after medial frontal damage, in which a patient's hand reaches out and grasps objects the patient reports not wanting to grasp - the affordance gets through, the internal veto does not.


51.1.4 Parietal contributions to intention and affordance

The posterior parietal cortex sits behind the somatosensory cortex and converts what you see into the coordinates a movement needs.

It is subdivided by effector: the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) is associated with eye movements, the medial intraparietal area (MIP, or the parietal reach region) with reaching, and the anterior intraparietal area (AIP) with grasping and with the three-dimensional shape of an object considered as something to be gripped.

Richard Andersen and colleagues argued from monkey recordings that this activity is best described as intention - a plan to act with a particular effector - rather than mere attention, and human recordings from paralysed volunteers with implanted electrodes, reported by Andersen's group from 2015 onward, found neurons in this region that respond to merely imagined reaches and even to the intended goal before any command is issued.

The word affordance, borrowed from James Gibson's ecological psychology, names the action an object offers you: a handle affords grasping, a step affords climbing.

Paul Cisek and John Kalaska's affordance competition hypothesis, developed in a 2005 Neuron paper and a 2010 Annual Review of Neuroscience article, proposes that the parietal-frontal system specifies several available actions in parallel, as simultaneous partial plans, and that choosing is the competition between them being resolved rather than a separate decision stage feeding a separate motor stage.

That claim is genuinely important because it blurs the standard boundary between deciding and doing, and while the parallel-specification evidence is strong for reaching, whether all decisions work this way remains contested.


51.2 Internal models

An internal model is the brain's simulation of its own body and of the world it acts on.

The idea is that because nerves are slow and muscles are complicated, control by feedback alone would be too sluggish and unstable, so the brain must carry a model that lets it predict rather than merely react.

The four sub-sections below give the two main kinds of model, the signal that makes them possible, and the normative theory that ties the whole picture together.


51.2.1 Forward models and state estimation

A forward model takes the current state of the body and the motor command just issued, and predicts the next state - where the arm will be, and what it will feel like.

Its purpose is to defeat delay: sensory feedback from the hand takes on the order of 100 milliseconds to become usable, which is an eternity for a fast reach, so the controller works from a predicted present rather than a reported past.

The best estimate of where your arm actually is comes from combining the prediction with the delayed sensory evidence, weighting each by how reliable it is, a computation formally like a Kalman filter and known as state estimation; Daniel Wolpert, Zoubin Ghahramani and Michael Jordan demonstrated this pattern behaviourally in Science in 1995.

The cerebellum is the leading candidate site, argued for by R. Christopher Miall and Wolpert in Neural Networks in 1996 and supported by patient work showing that people with cerebellar damage overshoot and make jerky multi-step corrections as though they were reacting rather than predicting.

The evidence is convergent rather than conclusive, since no one has directly read out a forward model's prediction from cerebellar tissue.


51.2.2 Inverse models and the control problem

A forward model answers what will happen if I do this; an inverse model answers the harder question, what must I do to make this happen.

It is harder because the mapping is not unique - there are more joints than the task needs, so infinitely many arm configurations reach the same cup, a redundancy Nikolai Bernstein named the degrees of freedom problem in the 1930s.

It is also harder because the required command depends on the situation: lifting a full mug and an empty mug of identical appearance need different forces, so a single fixed inverse model would fail every time the world changed.

Mitsuo Kawato's response, with Wolpert, was the MOSAIC architecture (Modular Selection And Identification for Control), published in Neural Networks in 1998, which proposes many paired forward and inverse models, with each forward model's prediction accuracy deciding how much its partner controller contributes - so context selection and control are learned together.

MOSAIC is elegant and computationally well specified, and it is fair to say the direct neural evidence for discrete paired modules in the brain remains thin; it is better regarded as a productive hypothesis than an established finding.


51.2.3 Efference copy, corollary discharge, and sensory attenuation

Whenever a motor command is sent out, an internal copy is retained, called an efference copy, and the resulting internal prediction of its sensory consequences is called corollary discharge.

The classic demonstration is visual stability: when you move your eyes, the image on the retina sweeps violently, yet the world looks still, because corollary discharge tells the visual system to expect the sweep - whereas if you push your eyeball gently with a finger, no corollary discharge is generated and the world appears to jump.

This machinery predicts sensory attenuation, the finding that self-generated sensation feels weaker than identical externally generated sensation, which is why you cannot tickle yourself; Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Wolpert and Chris Frith showed in Nature Neuroscience in 1998 that a self-delivered tickle becomes ticklish again if the device introduces a delay or a spatial offset.

The related force-matching task, in which people asked to match a force applied to their finger reliably push about twice as hard, is the standard quantitative measure.

The interpretation is now actively disputed: some researchers argue attenuation reflects general predictability rather than self-generation specifically, and methodological critiques of the force-matching task published around 2022 and 2023 argue that part of the effect may come from the task's structure rather than from efference copy, so the phenomenon is solid while its explanation is unsettled.

Clinically, the leading account of first-rank symptoms in schizophrenia - hearing one's own inner speech as an external voice, or feeling one's movements are controlled by someone else - is a failure of corollary discharge, and patients do show reduced sensory attenuation, though whether this is cause or consequence is not settled.


51.2.4 Optimal feedback control as a normative theory of movement

A normative theory says what a system should do if it were solving its problem well, and then checks whether behaviour matches.

Emanuel Todorov and Michael Jordan's optimal feedback control theory, published in Nature Neuroscience in 2002, proposes that the motor system does not compute a desired trajectory in advance and then track it, but instead computes a feedback law - a rule mapping estimated state to command - that minimises a cost combining error and effort.

Its most striking prediction is the minimal intervention principle: correct a deviation only if it matters for the goal, and otherwise let it stand, because correcting costs effort and adds noise.

That predicts the odd fact that variability is not uniform - when you hold a cup with two hands, the two hands' forces vary a lot while their sum barely varies, which is exactly the pattern Gregor Schoner and Mark Latash described independently as the uncontrolled manifold.

Optimal feedback control explains trajectory shape, task-dependent noise structure, and flexible online corrections from a single principle, and it is the strongest normative account in motor neuroscience; its limits are that the cost function is usually fitted rather than derived, and that it says little about how such a controller is learned or implemented in tissue.


51.3 Preparation, initiation, and inhibition

Between deciding to move and moving there is a gap, and the gap is where much of motor cognition lives.

This section covers what the brain is doing during that gap, the famous electrical signature of it, the machinery for cancelling an action already under way, and how actions get bundled into sequences.


51.3.1 Preparatory activity and the null space account

If a monkey is told where to reach but must wait for a go cue, motor and premotor neurons change their firing during the delay, in a way that predicts the coming movement - this is preparatory activity.

The puzzle is obvious: if these are the same neurons that drive the muscles, why does the arm not move during preparation.

Matthew Kaufman, Churchland, Stephen Ryu and Shenoy answered this in Nature Neuroscience in 2014 with the output-null subspace idea, which rests on the fact that many neurons feed a smaller number of muscles, so there are combinations of neural activity - the output-null subspace, in the mathematical sense of a null space - that cancel out at the muscles and produce no movement at all.

Preparation, on this account, moves the population into a particular state within that silent subspace, and the go signal lets the system's dynamics carry the state into the output-potent subspace, where it does drive muscles.

The pay-off is that better-prepared states yield faster and more accurate movements, and Shenoy's group showed reaction time is predicted by how close the population state has come to an optimal preparatory region.

Churchland and Shenoy revisited and broadened this in a 2024 Nature Reviews Neuroscience review, arguing null-space activity is not a trick specific to reaching but a general computational strategy.


51.3.2 The readiness potential and its reinterpretation

In 1965 Hans Kornhuber and Luder Deecke recorded a slow negative drift in the electroencephalogram (EEG), a scalp recording of brain electrical activity, beginning up to a second or two before a self-initiated voluntary movement, and named it the Bereitschaftspotential or readiness potential (RP).

Benjamin Libet's experiments in 1983 asked people to report, using a fast clock, the moment they first felt the urge to move, and found the RP preceded that reported urge by several hundred milliseconds - widely taken to show the brain decides before you know you have decided, and much used in arguments against free will.

Aaron Schurger, Jacobo Sitt and Stanislas Dehaene proposed a deflationary alternative in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2012: if spontaneous neural activity fluctuates like noise and a movement is triggered when that noise crosses a threshold, then averaging backwards from movement onset will manufacture a smooth rising ramp even though nothing was ramping on any individual trial.

On this stochastic accumulator account the RP is an artefact of back-averaging plus a threshold, not a record of an early unconscious decision, and the decision happens late, near the threshold crossing, which is much closer to when people say it happened.

Schurger's 2021 Trends in Cognitive Sciences review, with Pengbo Hu and colleagues, argues the RP is best understood this way, but the matter is not closed - critics point out that accumulator models do not explain every property of the RP, and that the interpretation of Libet's clock reports is independently problematic.

The honest summary is that the RP no longer supports the strong anti-free-will conclusion it was long used for, without thereby establishing the opposite.


51.3.3 Response inhibition and the stop-signal network

The standard laboratory measure of stopping is the stop-signal task, in which people respond quickly to a go stimulus but must cancel on the minority of trials where a stop signal follows shortly after.

Gordon Logan and William Cowan's 1984 race model treats go and stop as independent racing processes, and its virtue is that it yields a number you cannot observe directly, the stop-signal reaction time (SSRT), which estimates how long stopping takes - typically around 200 milliseconds in healthy adults.

Adam Aron and colleagues identified a fronto-basal-ganglia network for this, with the right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG) and pre-SMA as the cortical nodes and the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a small structure in the basal ganglia, as the subcortical one, with the hyperdirect pathway from cortex to STN providing a route fast enough to broadly suppress motor output.

Direct human evidence arrived from patients with deep brain stimulation electrodes: work published in Neuron in 2020 by Chen, Starr and colleagues found short-latency cortical potentials evoked by subthalamic stimulation consistent with a monosynaptic inferior frontal to subthalamic connection, and found cortical stopping-related activity preceding subthalamic stopping-related activity.

Two caveats are worth stating: whether rIFG is specifically an inhibitory module or is instead detecting the behaviourally salient stop cue is still argued, and effective connectivity work indicates the slower indirect pathway through striatum and pallidum also contributes rather than the hyperdirect route acting alone.


51.3.4 Sequence representation and chunking of action

Most real actions are sequences, and the nervous system does not store them as long undifferentiated strings.

With practice, elements get bundled into chunks - groups executed as a single unit, recognisable behaviourally because the pause between chunks stays long while pauses within a chunk shrink, which is why a practised phone number comes out in bursts.

Ann Graybiel argued in Neurobiology of Learning and Memory in 1998 that the striatum, the input structure of the basal ganglia, performs this recoding, and rodent recordings show striatal neurons developing bracketing activity that marks the start and end of a learned sequence while the middle becomes relatively quiet - the signature of a unit rather than a list.

Xin Jin and Graybiel's later work, including a 2014 paper distinguishing striatal subcircuits for parsing versus concatenating sequences, refined this by separating the machinery that carves sequences into units from the machinery that glues units together.

On the cortical side, human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures blood-flow correlates of neural activity, points to a hierarchy: work by Atsushi Yokoi and Jorn Diedrichsen published in Neuron in 2019 found that premotor and parietal regions represent whole sequences or chunks while primary motor cortex represents the individual finger presses, so different levels of the same action are held in different places at the same time.


51.4 Action understanding and imitation

The last section takes motor cognition outward, to other people.

The central proposal is motor simulation: that you understand what someone else is doing partly by covertly running your own motor system as if you were doing it.

This is one of the most publicised ideas in modern neuroscience and also one of the most overclaimed, so the four sub-sections give the original finding, the critique, the human evidence, and the conceptual distinctions that the debate usually skips.


51.4.1 Mirror neurons and the original claims

In area F5 of the macaque ventral premotor cortex, Giuseppe di Pellegrino, Luciano Fadiga, Leonardo Fogassi, Vittorio Gallese and Giacomo Rizzolatti reported in 1992, and elaborated in Brain in 1996, neurons that fired both when the monkey performed a specific action such as a precision grip and when it merely watched the experimenter perform that action.
