Mirror neurons were later reported in the inferior parietal lobule as well, and some were described as goal-selective, firing for grasping regardless of which hand or which tool did the grasping.

The theoretical claim attached to them was large: that they provide direct, non-inferential understanding of others' actions by matching observation onto the observer's own motor repertoire, and by extension that they underpin imitation, empathy, language evolution, and, in the broken-mirror hypothesis, are impaired in autism.

The finding itself is real and has been replicated, including a single-neuron human study by Roy Mukamel, Itzhak Fried and colleagues in Current Biology in 2010 that found neurons with mirror properties in medial frontal and medial temporal cortex of epilepsy patients.

It is the interpretation, not the recording, that has drawn fire.


51.4.2 Critiques and the associative learning account

Gregory Hickok's 2009 paper in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, later expanded into the book The Myth of Mirror Neurons in 2014, made the sharpest case, arguing among other things that monkeys with premotor lesions can still recognise actions, that humans with severe speech production deficits can still comprehend speech, and that no experiment has shown mirror activity to be necessary for understanding rather than merely correlated with it.

Cecilia Heyes's associative account, developed with Caroline Catmur and Clare Press, offers a different origin story: mirror neurons need not be an adaptation for social cognition at all, but can arise from ordinary sensorimotor associative learning, because whenever you perform an action you usually also see it, so visual and motor representations are repeatedly paired.

That account makes testable predictions, and Catmur, Walsh and Heyes showed in Current Biology in 2007 that counter-training - having people make one finger movement while watching a different one - reverses the mirror response in humans, which is hard to reconcile with a fixed innate matching system.

The broken-mirror account of autism has fared poorly, with several failures to replicate and with the alternative view, articulated by Antonia Hamilton, that the evidence better fits differences in top-down social processing than a basic mirror deficit.

A fair current position is that mirror-property neurons exist and that motor simulation contributes something to how we process observed action, while the strong claim that mirroring constitutes action understanding is not supported.


51.4.3 Action observation networks in humans

Because we rarely record single neurons in people, human work studies a distributed action observation network instead.

The most cited mapping is the activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis by Svenja Caspers, Karl Zilles, Angela Laird and Simon Eickhoff in NeuroImage in 2010, which pooled 139 neuroimaging experiments and found a consistent bilateral network spanning ventral premotor and inferior frontal cortex, the rostral inferior parietal lobule (particularly the cytoarchitectonic area PFt) and anterior intraparietal sulcus, and occipito-temporal regions including the middle temporal complex and posterior superior temporal sulcus.

The superior temporal sulcus deserves emphasis because it is not a motor area at all - it responds to biological motion, the characteristic kinematics of a living body - which means the network combines visual analysis of movement with motor resonance rather than being purely a mirror system.

Fadiga, Fogassi, Pavesi and Rizzolatti showed in 1995 using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a method that delivers a brief magnetic pulse through the scalp to excite cortex, that watching someone grasp increases the excitability of precisely the muscles the observer would use, which is about as direct a demonstration of motor resonance in humans as the methods allow.

What none of this settles is function, since increased excitability during observation is compatible with understanding, with prediction, with preparing to imitate, or with a byproduct of associative learning.


51.4.4 Imitation, emulation, and motor simulation

These three words are often used loosely and mean different things.

Imitation, in the strict comparative sense used by Michael Tomasello, Josef Call and Andrew Whiten, is copying the demonstrator's bodily means - the specific movement - whereas emulation is reproducing only the end state by whatever means, so a child who reproduces an adult's odd flourish is imitating while a child who just gets the block on top is emulating.

The distinction matters because faithful copying of means, including apparently pointless steps, is unusually strong in humans; the overimitation experiments of Victoria Horner and Whiten in 2005 found that children copy causally irrelevant actions that chimpanzees sensibly skip, which looks inefficient but may be exactly what makes cumulative culture possible when a novice cannot tell which steps matter.

Motor simulation is a third and more internal notion: covertly running a motor plan without executing it, as in motor imagery, which shows the mental-chronometry signature that imagined movements take about as long as real ones and obey Fitts's law relating movement time to difficulty.

Automatic imitation, measured with tasks where an observed incompatible finger movement slows your own response, indexes the same tendency in a fast involuntary form, though whether it reflects a dedicated mirror mechanism or ordinary stimulus-response compatibility is exactly the point Heyes and colleagues dispute.

The safest summary is that humans clearly do simulate observed actions in motor terms, that simulation appears useful for prediction and for learning by copying, and that the leap from simulation to understanding remains an interpretation rather than a demonstrated fact.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Movement is controlled by a layered system in which spinal central pattern generators produce rhythm and gate reflexes by phase, motor and premotor cortex specify and prepare actions, and parietal cortex converts vision into candidate actions that compete for selection.

Because nerves are slow, the brain predicts rather than merely reacts, using forward models for state estimation, efference copy and corollary discharge for distinguishing self-caused from world-caused sensation, and something like optimal feedback control to correct only the errors that matter for the goal.

Preparation happens in an output-null subspace so that planning does not leak into movement, which also reframes the readiness potential - Schurger's stochastic accumulator account undercuts the classic Libet interpretation without proving its opposite.

Stopping an action recruits a fast fronto-basal-ganglia circuit through the right inferior frontal gyrus, pre-supplementary motor area and subthalamic nucleus, and practised sequences are chunked, with the striatum bracketing units and cortex representing sequence and element at different levels.

Finally, mirror-property neurons are a real finding whose original interpretation as the mechanism of action understanding is not supported; the associative learning account and Hickok's necessity critique have moved the field toward a more modest claim that motor simulation contributes to predicting and copying observed action rather than constituting comprehension of it.


CHAPTER 52. EXECUTIVE FUNCTION AND COGNITIVE CONTROL (CORE)


Most of what your brain does, it does without you.

You read the word in front of you whether or not you meant to, and you reach for the coffee cup by habit.

Cognitive control is the name for the smaller, slower, more effortful system that steps in when habit would give the wrong answer - when you must say the ink colour of a word instead of reading it, when you must stop a movement already begun, when you must hold a plan in mind across an interruption.

This chapter asks what that system is, whether it is one thing or many, how the brain notices that control is needed, and what happens to a person when the parts of the brain that supply it are damaged.

It matters because nearly every clinical condition that disrupts daily life - attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, schizophrenia, addiction, frontal stroke, dementia - shows up partly as a failure of control, and because the field's confident textbook picture has been under serious empirical attack for the last decade.

We will name the attacks as well as the picture.


52.1 Defining control

Cognitive control (also called executive function, meaning the set of processes that organise and direct other mental processes) is easier to point at than to define.

The pointing is easy: control is what you use in a novel situation, or when habit fights the goal.

The defining is hard because control is not a single organ or a single act - it is a family of operations that share the property of adjusting other operations.

This section sets out the standard working definition, the standard decomposition, and the measurement problem that has dogged the whole field.


52.1.1 Control as the biasing of processing toward goals

The most durable definition comes from Earl Miller and Jonathan Cohen, in an integrative review published in Annual Review of Neuroscience in 2001.

On their account, control is not a separate machine that does the thinking for you - it is a bias signal.

The prefrontal cortex (the front part of the frontal lobe, sitting behind the forehead) holds an active pattern of neural activity that represents the current goal and the mapping from situation to action, and that pattern sends excitatory signals down into sensory, memory, and motor systems, tipping the competition among pathways in favour of the goal-relevant one.

The metaphor they use is a railway switchman: the switchman does not push the train, he sets the points, and the train's own momentum carries it down the selected track.

This has an appealing consequence - control is cheap in the sense that it does not have to do the work, only to lean on the work - and it explains why control fails when the competing pathway is very strong, or when the goal representation decays.


52.1.2 The unity and diversity framework: inhibition, updating, shifting

In 2000, Akira Miyake, Naomi Friedman and colleagues published a latent variable analysis in Cognitive Psychology that became the single most cited model of executive function.

They gave a large group of students many different executive tasks, then used confirmatory factor analysis - a statistical method that estimates the hidden common factors behind a set of correlated measures - to ask how many distinct abilities the tasks tapped.

Three factors emerged: inhibition (suppressing a prepotent, that is habitually dominant, response), updating (refreshing and monitoring the contents of working memory, the small store of information held actively in mind), and shifting (switching flexibly between tasks or mental sets).

The crucial result was in the correlations between the three factors: they were substantially above zero, which means the three share something in common - unity - and reliably below 1.0, which means they are not the same thing - diversity.

In a later reworking, Friedman and Miyake recast the model as a "common executive function" factor plus separable updating-specific and shifting-specific factors, and in that version inhibition stops existing as a factor of its own, being entirely absorbed into the common factor.


52.1.3 Task impurity and the measurement problem

Every executive task requires non-executive machinery: to do a task-switching test you must see the stimulus, understand the instruction, and move a finger.

This is the task impurity problem - the score from any single task confounds the executive process of interest with everything else the task demands, so the impurity varies from task to task and does not cancel out.

Miyake and colleagues' response was statistical: use several tasks per construct and extract the latent factor, on the reasoning that what the tasks share is the executive process and what they do not share is the impurity.

The response is only partly adequate, because executive scores are usually difference scores - Stroop interference is the incongruent condition minus the congruent condition, for example - and difference scores subtract away most of the reliable variance, leaving noisy measures that correlate poorly with anything.

This is the reliability paradox: tasks that produce beautifully robust average effects in every group of participants can be nearly useless for measuring differences between individuals, and a great deal of the executive function literature is built on such tasks.


52.1.4 Control against automaticity

The traditional view held automaticity - processing that runs off without attention - to be an all-or-none property: a process either was automatic and immune to control, or was not.

Jonathan Cohen, Kevin Dunbar and James McClelland argued otherwise in Psychological Review in 1990, using a connectionist computer model of the Stroop task, in which naming the ink colour of a colour word is slowed when the word says a different colour.

In their model, reading and colour naming are simply pathways of differing strength - reading is stronger because of a lifetime of practice - and an attention unit supplies extra input to whichever pathway the task requires.

Automaticity, then, is a continuum set by pathway strength, and control is the ability to add enough bias to let a weak pathway win against a strong one.

The model reproduced the asymmetry of Stroop interference (words interfere with colour naming far more than colours interfere with reading), the effect of varying the delay between word and colour, and the gradual emergence of automaticity with practice - a good example of a theory earning its keep by predicting details it was not built to fit.


52.2 Conflict, error, and monitoring

If control is expensive, the brain needs a way to decide when to spend it.

That requires monitoring - some system that watches ongoing processing and signals when things are going wrong or are about to.

The candidate structure has for twenty-five years been the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a strip of cortex folded around the front of the corpus callosum, the great bundle of fibres joining the two hemispheres.

What exactly it monitors is one of the liveliest disputes in the field.


52.2.1 Conflict monitoring theory and the anterior cingulate cortex

Matthew Botvinick, Todd Braver, Cameron Carter, Deanna Barch and Jonathan Cohen proposed in Psychological Review in 2001 that the ACC does not exert control at all - it detects response conflict, the simultaneous activation of incompatible responses, and passes that signal to the lateral prefrontal cortex, which then raises control.

The elegance is that this closes a loop: conflict signals that control is insufficient, control is increased, conflict falls.

It predicts, and finds, the Gratton effect - interference on an incongruent trial is smaller when the previous trial was also incongruent, because conflict on trial n recruited control that is still in place on trial n plus 1.

Botvinick, Cohen and Carter published an update in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2004 defending the theory while conceding that its treatment of errors was the weakest point.

The theory remains influential but is no longer the consensus: apparent dissociations between error-related brain signals and subsequent behavioural adjustment are hard to accommodate, and several rival accounts now cover the same data.


52.2.2 The error-related negativity and error positivity

When a person makes a speeded error, the scalp electrical recording - the electroencephalogram (EEG), a measure of voltage changes at the scalp produced by synchronised neural activity - shows a sharp negative deflection peaking roughly 50 to 100 milliseconds after the erroneous response, largest at frontocentral electrodes.

This is the error-related negativity (ERN), and source modelling places its generator in or near the anterior cingulate.

Strikingly, the ERN appears even when the person does not know they have erred, which makes it a candidate for an automatic, pre-conscious comparison process.

A second, slower positive wave follows between roughly 200 and 400 milliseconds, the error positivity (Pe), and this one does track error awareness: it is large for consciously detected errors and small or absent for undetected ones.

Clay Holroyd and Michael Coles, in Psychological Review in 2002, gave the ERN a reinforcement-learning interpretation: the basal ganglia evaluate events as better or worse than expected, a dip in dopamine signals "worse than expected", and that dip disinhibits the anterior cingulate, producing the ERN and training the cingulate's action selection - an account that ties error monitoring to the same machinery that supports reward learning.


52.2.3 Post-error slowing and adaptive adjustment

After an error, people are typically slower on the next trial - post-error slowing.

The natural reading is adaptive: having erred, you raise your response threshold, trading speed for accuracy.

Wim Notebaert and colleagues challenged this in Cognition in 2009 with an orienting account - errors are rare, rare events capture attention, and the slowing is simply the cost of attention being pulled away from the task, not a deliberate strategy.

Their key manipulation was to make errors common and correct responses rare, whereupon post-correct slowing appeared, which the adaptive account does not predict.

The current position, argued by Claudia Danielmeier and Markus Ullsperger among others, is that both are real - distractor suppression and raised decision thresholds coexist with a genuine orienting cost, and whether the net effect helps accuracy depends on task and timing, so post-error slowing should not be used as a simple index of good control.


52.2.4 Alternative accounts: expected value of control, foraging, surprise

Three serious rivals to conflict monitoring now exist, and none has won.

Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen proposed in Neuron in 2013 that the ACC computes the expected value of control (EVC): it weighs the payoff a controlled process would bring, against the amount of control needed and the intrinsic cost of cognitive effort, and specifies both how much control to allocate and to what - conflict becomes just one input to a broader cost-benefit calculation.

Nils Kolling, Tim Behrens, Rogier Mars and Matthew Rushworth argued from a foraging perspective that dorsal ACC activity tracks the value of leaving the current option to search elsewhere, a signal about switching away rather than about conflict, though whether their data really rule out a difficulty account has been contested.

William Alexander and Joshua Brown's predicted response outcome (PRO) model treats the region as a general predictor of the outcomes of actions, with activity reflecting surprise - the discrepancy between predicted and actual outcomes - which naturally covers errors, conflict, and unexpected rewards alike.

The honest summary is that the dorsal ACC responds to conflict, errors, effort, surprise, volatility and foraging value, and the field has not yet agreed which of these is the primitive and which are consequences.


52.3 Inhibition and interference control

Stopping is the most intuitive form of control and the most studied.

But "inhibition" is used for at least three different things - cancelling a motor act, ignoring an irrelevant stimulus, and suppressing an unwanted memory or thought - and it is an open question whether these share any machinery.

This section takes the motor case first, where the neuroscience is strongest, then the attentional case, then the timing of control, then the awkward psychometric evidence.


52.3.1 Response inhibition and its frontal-basal ganglia circuit

The standard laboratory test is the stop-signal task: respond fast to a go stimulus, but on a minority of trials a stop signal follows at a variable delay and you must cancel the response.

Because the go and stop processes race, the model lets you estimate a latency you cannot directly observe - the stop-signal reaction time, typically around 200 milliseconds in healthy adults.

Adam Aron, Russell Poldrack and colleagues implicated a circuit comprising the right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG, on the lower outer surface of the right frontal lobe), the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA, on the medial surface just in front of the motor cortex), and the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a small basal ganglia structure whose excitation broadly suppresses motor output.

The proposed route is the hyperdirect pathway, a fast monosynaptic projection from frontal cortex to the STN that bypasses the striatum; Aron and Poldrack's 2006 Journal of Neuroscience work and later intracranial recordings in patients with deep brain stimulation electrodes support short-latency frontal-to-STN communication during stopping, with cortical stopping signals preceding subthalamic ones.

The interpretation of rIFG is disputed: Adam Hampshire and colleagues have argued the region is not a dedicated brake but a detector of behaviourally relevant signals, activating for stop signals because they are infrequent and important rather than because they are stop signals.


52.3.2 Distractor suppression and proactive filtering

Ignoring is not simply failing to attend - there is evidence for an active suppressive mechanism.

Nicholas Gaspelin and Steven Luck's signal suppression hypothesis holds that a salient object automatically generates a saliency signal, but that signal can be actively cancelled before it captures attention if it does not match the current task set.

The electrophysiological marker is the distractor positivity (Pd), a positive deflection at posterior electrodes contralateral to a distractor, which appears when a salient distractor is successfully ignored and whose size tracks how strongly the eyes curve away from it.

Importantly, suppression is largely learned: it depends on prior experience with the specific features or locations of the distractor, which is why a repeated distractor colour becomes easy to ignore while a novel one still grabs you.

This is filtering in the proactive sense - the system is set up in advance to reject a known class of input, rather than recovering after capture has occurred.


52.3.3 Proactive and reactive control modes

Todd Braver's dual mechanisms of control framework, set out in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2012, distinguishes two temporal modes rather than two mechanisms of different kind.

Proactive control is anticipatory and sustained: goal information is actively maintained in lateral prefrontal cortex before the critical event, biasing perception and action in advance, at the cost of continuous effort and of inflexibility if the prepared goal turns out to be wrong.

Reactive control is transient and stimulus-driven: the goal is retrieved only when a conflict or a cue demands it, which is cheap but late.

The framework's value is that it reframes many apparent control deficits as shifts in mode - older adults, and people with schizophrenia, often show a relative shift from proactive to reactive control rather than a global loss of ability.

The large multi-site Dual Mechanisms of Cognitive Control project has since made the framework testable at scale, with mixed results that support the temporal distinction more clearly than they support clean individual-difference measurement of it.


52.3.4 Whether inhibition is a unitary construct at all

The most damaging recent evidence is psychometric.

Alodie Rey-Mermet, Miriam Gade and Klaus Oberauer, in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition in 2018, gave a large sample eleven inhibition tasks across two age groups and asked whether a common inhibition factor could be recovered.

Individual task measures were reliable, yet they correlated only weakly with one another, and no coherent latent inhibition factor emerged even after correcting statistically for measurement error - hence their title, "Should we stop thinking about inhibition?".

This converges with Friedman and Miyake's own later conclusion that inhibition has no variance of its own once a common executive factor is extracted, and with arguments that difference-score measures are structurally incapable of supporting individual-differences research.

Two readings remain live: either inhibition is not a real unitary ability and the word names a heterogeneous collection of task-specific processes, or it is real but our tasks are too impure and too unreliable to reveal it.

The distinction matters practically, because inhibition scores are routinely used in clinical and developmental research as if they measured one thing.


52.4 The prefrontal cortex

The prefrontal cortex is the structure most associated with control, and it is not one region but a mosaic of areas with different connections, different cell architecture, and different failure modes.

This section covers its subdivisions, the leading theory of what its neurons represent, what happens when it is damaged, and how it compares across species.


52.4.1 Functional subdivisions: dorsolateral, ventrolateral, frontopolar, orbital, medial

Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, on the upper outer surface, is most associated with maintaining and manipulating information in working memory and with abstract rule use.

Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, below it, is associated with selecting and retrieving information from memory and, on the right, with the stopping circuit described earlier.

Frontopolar cortex, at the very front tip, is associated with holding a pending goal while doing something else - keeping the second errand in mind while executing the first.

Orbitofrontal cortex, on the underside above the eye sockets, represents the current value of outcomes and supports flexible revision of those values when contingencies change; medial prefrontal cortex, on the inner surface, is bound up with self-referential processing, social inference, and the monitoring functions discussed in section 52.2.

Etienne Koechlin and David Badre have separately proposed a rostrocaudal gradient across the lateral surface: posterior regions control concrete, immediate stimulus-response mappings, and progressively more anterior regions control progressively more abstract and temporally extended contingencies - an appealing organising principle with real supporting evidence, though the strict nested-hierarchy version is contested, since anterior lesions do not always spare more posterior levels as the theory requires.


52.4.2 Guided activation theory and the representation of rules

Miller and Cohen's guided activation theory (2001) states the mechanism concretely: prefrontal neurons sustain activity that represents a rule or goal, and that sustained activity biases the competition in posterior systems, so behaviour follows the rule without the prefrontal cortex performing the perception or the movement itself.

The theory's boldest prediction is that prefrontal neurons should code abstract rules as such, independently of the stimuli and responses the rules apply to.

Jonathan Wallis, Kathleen Anderson and Earl Miller tested this in Nature in 2001, training monkeys on match and non-match rules and recording single neurons: many prefrontal cells fired according to which rule was in force, regardless of which picture was being judged or which action followed.

Rule coding was found more often, and earlier, in prefrontal cortex than in the parietal or premotor regions recorded for comparison, which is what a biasing-source account requires.

More recent work complicates the picture by showing that rule information is distributed - it appears in premotor and parietal cortex and in the striatum too - so the prefrontal cortex looks less like the sole holder of rules and more like the region where they are held most abstractly and most persistently.


52.4.3 Prefrontal patient syndromes and their dissociations

Phineas Gage, the Vermont railway foreman whose left frontal lobe was destroyed by a tamping iron in 1848, survived with intelligence and language intact but with a reported transformation of character and reliability - Hanna Damasio and colleagues reconstructed the probable lesion from his skull in Science in 1994, placing the damage in ventromedial prefrontal cortex, though how much of the personality account is reliable historical record and how much later embellishment is genuinely doubtful.

The modern equivalent is patient EVR, described by Paul Eslinger and Antonio Damasio in Neurology in 1985: after removal of a large orbitofrontal tumour he scored normally or superbly on intelligence tests and on standard executive tests, yet lost his job and his marriage through catastrophic real-life decision making.

That dissociation - normal test performance with disastrous life performance - motivated Tim Shallice and Paul Burgess's 1991 Brain study, in which frontal patients with high intelligence quotients and clean neuropsychological profiles were sent to a shopping street with a set of errands and rules, and failed by breaking rules, missing tasks, and getting stuck on single items.

A different lesion profile produces utilization behaviour, described by François Lhermitte, in which a patient presented with a comb or a glass will use it, correctly and unbidden, because the object's affordance drives action in the absence of a superordinate goal - control has been removed and automaticity is running unchecked.

The general lesson of frontal neuropsychology is that dissociations are the rule: dorsolateral damage tends to impair planning and working memory, orbital and ventromedial damage tends to impair value-based and social decision making with intact reasoning, and no single "frontal lobe test" detects both.


52.4.4 Prefrontal cortex in comparative perspective

Prefrontal cortex is usually divided by cell architecture into agranular areas, which lack a distinct layer four of small granule cells, and granular areas, which have one.

The agranular medial and orbital regions are old, present in early mammals; granular prefrontal cortex is essentially a primate development, with successive additions in early primates and again in the simian lineage, which is why comparisons with rodent "prefrontal cortex" must be made carefully - the rat has homologues of the agranular regions, but no granular dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the primate sense.

Whether human prefrontal cortex is disproportionately large is a live dispute.

Katerina Semendeferi and colleagues reported that the frontal lobe occupies about the same fraction of cortex in humans as in great apes, implying no special human enlargement.

Robert Barton and Chris Venditti, and separately work by Pascal Gabi and colleagues, supported a broadly proportionate view, while Rob Passingham and Jeroen Smaers argued that when prefrontal cortex is scaled against primary sensory and motor areas rather than against the whole brain, human prefrontal cortex does deviate from the primate trend, and a 2017 Current Biology analysis by Smaers, Gómez-Robles, Parks and Sherwood reported exceptional prefrontal expansion in great apes and humans.

Much of the disagreement is methodological - which structure you take as the baseline, whether you measure grey matter or white matter, and whether you use gross lobes or cytoarchitectonically defined areas - so the safest statement is that human prefrontal white matter and connectivity look disproportionate even where grey matter volume may not.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognitive control is best understood not as a homunculus that decides, but as a biasing signal: prefrontal cortex sustains a representation of the goal and tips competitions elsewhere in the brain in its favour, which makes automaticity a matter of pathway strength rather than an all-or-none category.

The standard decomposition into inhibition, updating and shifting - unified yet separable - remains the field's organising framework, but its inhibition component has largely dissolved under psychometric scrutiny, and task impurity plus difference-score unreliability undermine much of the individual-differences literature built on it.

Monitoring signals from the anterior cingulate, indexed by the error-related negativity and the conflict effects that inspired Botvinick and colleagues' 2001 theory, are real and robust, but the field has not settled whether the underlying quantity is conflict, expected value of control, foraging value, or surprise.

Stopping has the clearest neural implementation of any control operation - a fast frontal to subthalamic hyperdirect route - yet even there the role of the right inferior frontal gyrus as a dedicated brake is contested.

Frontal patients show that intact intelligence and intact laboratory executive scores are compatible with total practical failure, which is the strongest argument that our tests measure something narrower than the ability we care about.


CHAPTER 53. GOALS, HIERARCHY, AND COGNITIVE FLEXIBILITY (CORE)


Almost nothing a person does all day is a single act.

Making coffee, writing an email, or driving to a friend's house are all nested structures: a goal at the top, sub-goals underneath, and at the very bottom the individual finger movements and glances that actually touch the world.

This chapter is about how the brain builds and holds that structure, how it swaps one configuration of the mind for another when the situation changes, and how it strikes the balance between holding on to a goal and letting go of it.

The word for the holding on is stability, the word for the letting go is flexibility, and the tension between them is one of the deepest problems in the neuroscience of cognition.

It matters because failures at this level are not small.

A person who cannot maintain a goal drifts; a person who cannot abandon one perseverates; and both patterns show up in frontal lobe injury, in schizophrenia, in obsessive compulsive disorder, and in ordinary fatigue.


53.1 Hierarchical control

Cognitive control is the family of processes that lets behaviour be guided by internal goals rather than by whatever stimulus happens to be loudest.

Hierarchical control is the observation that these goals are layered - a general intention sits above a specific rule, which sits above a specific action.

The central empirical claim of this section is that the frontal lobe is not a uniform blob of "executive function" but is organised along its front-to-back length, with different positions handling different layers of that hierarchy.


53.1.1 The rostro-caudal gradient of abstraction in frontal cortex

Rostral means toward the front of the head and caudal means toward the back, so the rostro-caudal axis of the frontal lobe runs from just in front of the motor strip forward to the frontal pole behind the eyebrows.

The gradient proposal, developed most influentially by David Badre and Mark D'Esposito in a series of studies from 2007 onward, is that as you move rostrally along the lateral prefrontal cortex (the outer side surface of the front of the brain, abbreviated PFC), the representations being used to control behaviour become more abstract.

Caudal regions near the premotor cortex are engaged when a single stimulus maps onto a single response; middle regions are engaged when which response is correct depends on a context; and rostral regions are engaged when the context itself must be selected by a still higher rule.

Badre and D'Esposito supported this with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a method that infers neural activity from local changes in blood oxygenation, and crucially also with lesion evidence: patients with damage further forward failed at the higher levels while performing the lower levels normally, whereas damage further back impaired the low levels too.

The claim is genuinely contested.

Badre and D'Esposito themselves asked in a 2009 Nature Reviews Neuroscience article whether the axis is truly hierarchical, and critics have argued that the apparent gradient could reflect task difficulty, the number of items held in mind, or simply different task content rather than nested levels of control; a large coordinate-based meta-analysis published in eLife in 2022 found gradient-like functional organisation but not a clean, single, strictly ordered ladder.


53.1.2 Dorsocaudal concrete action representation against ventrorostral abstract representation

The frontal lobe also has a dorsal-ventral axis, where dorsal means toward the top of the head and ventral toward the underside near the temples.

Combining the two axes gives a diagonal: a dorsocaudal corner sitting near the motor system, and a ventrorostral corner sitting near the frontal pole and the orbital surface.

The dorsocaudal end preferentially codes concrete, perceptible, action-ready information - which finger, which direction, which visible cue.

The ventrorostral end preferentially codes abstract information - what kind of task this is, what the overarching aim is, what the cue means rather than what it looks like.

Evidence for parallel dorsal and ventral rostro-caudal streams, rather than one line, was reported by Blumenfeld, Nomura, Gratton and D'Esposito using resting-state connectivity, and the diagonal framing is now the more common way to state the gradient.


53.1.3 Policy abstraction, contextual abstraction, and temporal abstraction

In a 2018 Trends in Cognitive Sciences review, Badre and Derek Nee argued that the word "abstraction" has been doing three different jobs in this literature, and that separating them clears up a lot of confusion.

Policy abstraction is the depth of the decision tree connecting contexts to actions: a first-order policy is stimulus to response, a second-order policy says which stimulus-response mapping to use, a third-order policy says which of those selectors to use.

Contextual abstraction is about generality of the controlling representation in the present moment - controlling behaviour by an internally maintained context rather than by the visible stimulus, which Badre and Nee locate in mid-lateral PFC.

Temporal abstraction is about span: holding a representation that stays relevant across intervening subtasks and delays, so that you can be interrupted by three other things and still come back to what you were doing.

Their conclusion is deliberately deflationary about the neat ladder picture: the lateral PFC looks like a set of specialised, meaningfully organised units rather than one clean linear gradient, and different tasks emphasise different kinds of abstraction.


53.1.4 The gradual transformation of coding dimensionality along lateral prefrontal cortex

Dimensionality here is a measure of how many independent directions a population of neurons uses to represent things.

Low-dimensional codes lump many situations into similar patterns and therefore generalise well but express less detail; high-dimensional codes separate situations finely and therefore support flexible, arbitrary readouts but generalise poorly.

Badre and colleagues proposed in 2021 that the frontal hierarchy is fundamentally a trade-off between generalisability and expressivity along this dimension.

A subsequent study, published in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2025 after appearing as a 2024 preprint, tested this directly and found that control-related coding is gradually transformed along the dorsocaudal-to-ventrorostral axis, with the most generic low-dimensional representations dorsocaudally and the most specific high-dimensional representations ventrorostrally.

This is an appealing reframing because it replaces a vague word, abstraction, with something measurable, and because it explains why the gradient is gradual rather than a set of discrete steps.


53.2 Task sets and their reconfiguration

If hierarchy describes the architecture, task sets describe what is loaded into it at any given moment.

This section is about the experimental workhorse of the field, the task-switching paradigm, and about what its costs and its neural signatures reveal.


53.2.1 The task set as a configured mapping from stimulus to response

A task set is the temporarily installed configuration that determines what you do with what you see: which feature of the stimulus to attend to, which rule to apply, and which responses the fingers are prepared to make.

The same physical stimulus supports many task sets, which is the point.

Shown the digit 3 printed in red, you can report the parity (odd), the magnitude (less than five), or the colour, and each of those is a different mapping from the identical input to a different output.

Task sets are the reason the brain needs control at all: because inputs do not determine outputs, something internal has to decide the mapping, and that something has to be maintained against competition.


53.2.2 Switch costs, residual costs, and task-set inertia

In a task-switching experiment, people alternate between two simple tasks, and performance on trials where the task just changed is reliably slower and more error-prone than on trials where it repeated; that difference is the switch cost.

Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell in 1995 showed that giving people advance warning and time to prepare shrinks the cost substantially as the interval grows from roughly 150 to 600 milliseconds, but that a stubborn remainder survives no matter how much preparation time you give - the residual switch cost.

Rogers and Monsell read the residual cost as evidence that some component of reconfiguration simply cannot be completed until the stimulus actually arrives.

Alan Allport and colleagues, notably Allport, Styles and Hsieh in 1994 and Allport and Wylie in 2000, read it the opposite way: nothing needs to be reconfigured in advance at all, and the cost is task-set inertia, the lingering activation of the previous task set and the lingering suppression of the current one, decaying only slowly.

This is a real and long-running dispute, and the modern consensus is not that one side won but that both mechanisms operate; multiple-component models are now the norm, and work such as Nieuwenhuis and Monsell's test of the failure-to-engage account added a third idea, that on some proportion of trials people simply fail to prepare at all, so the average residual cost is partly a mixture artefact.


53.2.3 Hierarchical reconfiguration: context reconfiguration against subordinate rule updating

If task sets are themselves hierarchical, then switching is not one operation but several, differing in which level changes.

Changing the higher-level context (which whole game you are playing) should be a different event from updating a subordinate rule while the context stays fixed.

Recent work using multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI data, which reads out the distributed activity pattern rather than the average signal in a region, reports exactly this dissociation: subordinate rule updating shows up in distributed sensory and frontoparietal networks and is strongly modulated by the perceptual input, whereas context reconfiguration engages lateral middle frontal cortex and is comparatively insulated from interference from lower levels.

Earlier neuroimaging of hierarchical rule switching had already found that switches at higher levels of the rule hierarchy recruited more rostral frontal cortex than switches at lower levels.

The practical upshot is that "switch cost" is not one number; it depends on how high in the hierarchy the change occurred, and higher changes generally cost more because they force reconfiguration of everything below them.


53.2.4 The geometry and dynamics of task-tailored representations, and how practice reshapes them

Neural population geometry treats the activity of many neurons as a point in a high-dimensional space and asks about the shape of the cloud of points across conditions.

Two shapes matter here: compositional geometry, in which task features are coded on separate, reusable axes that can be recombined, and conjunctive geometry, in which the specific combination of features has its own dedicated pattern.

Compositional codes generalise to new combinations; conjunctive codes are faster and less confusable but must be learned combination by combination.

A 2025 Nature Communications study found that learning a new cognitive task involves a dynamic shift from compositional toward conjunctive representations, and that it was specifically the strengthening of the highest-level conjunctive codes, not the lower-order ones, that tracked the power-law speed-up in performance.

A companion line of work published in Cerebral Cortex in 2025 showed that practice reshapes both the geometry and the timing of these task-tailored representations, with conjunctive states stabilising earlier in the trial and aligning across sessions, and that this realignment correlated with the shrinking of switch costs.

That is a satisfying closure of the loop: the behavioural cost described in 53.2.2 has a measurable representational cause, and practice reduces the cost by changing the shape of the code.


53.3 Goals, plans, and subgoals

A task set is what you are doing now.

A goal is what you are doing all this for, and a plan is the structure connecting the two.

This section covers how goals survive delay, how the brain assigns credit to steps that are not themselves rewarding, how deep people actually think ahead, and how intentions get retrieved at the right moment.


53.3.1 Goal representation and maintenance across delays

The classic finding, from single-neuron recordings in monkeys going back to Joaquin Fuster in the 1970s and Patricia Goldman-Rakic in the 1980s and 1990s, is that prefrontal neurons keep firing throughout a delay when information has to be held, and this persistent activity was long taken to be the physical form of a maintained goal.

That account has been seriously challenged.

Mark Stokes argued in a 2015 Trends in Cognitive Sciences review for activity-silent working memory: information can be held in rapid, temporary changes in synaptic strength, leaving no elevated firing to record, and be read back out when the network is pinged.

The debate is live rather than resolved.

Recent work supports a mixed picture in which the population as a whole carries information continuously even though individual neurons fire in sparse, asynchronous bursts, so what looks silent at the single-neuron level need not be silent at the population level, and both synaptic traces and spiking appear to contribute.

For goals specifically, the useful summary is that maintenance is not a single steady spotlight but a dynamic code that changes form across a delay while preserving what it is about.


53.3.2 Hierarchical reinforcement learning, options, and pseudo-reward

Reinforcement learning is the framework in which an agent learns by comparing what it got to what it expected, the difference being the reward prediction error, which in the brain is carried prominently by phasic dopamine signalling to the striatum (a deep forebrain structure central to action selection and learning).

Ordinary or "flat" reinforcement learning has a credit assignment problem for long tasks: if reward arrives only at the very end, the early steps take a very long time to be reinforced.

Hierarchical reinforcement learning solves this by introducing options, which are temporally extended sub-policies with their own termination conditions - roughly, named subroutines such as "go to the kitchen" - and by giving each option its own internal target, the subgoal.

Reaching a subgoal delivers a pseudo-reward, an internally generated stand-in for real reward, and deviations from expected subgoal progress produce pseudo-reward prediction errors that reinforce the steps leading to the subgoal before any real reward exists.

Matthew Botvinick, Yael Niv and Andrew Barto set out the framework for neuroscience in 2009, and José Ribas-Fernandes and colleagues reported a neural signature of it in Neuron in 2011, finding error signals tied to subgoal distance rather than to final reward; Carlos Diuk and colleagues extended this in 2013, and later work has localised such pseudo-reward prediction errors to ventral striatum.

The honest caveat is that hierarchical reinforcement learning only pays off when the subgoals are good ones, so the harder and less settled question is where useful subgoals come from in the first place.


53.3.3 Planning depth, tree search, and its neural correlates

Planning by tree search means mentally rolling out possible action sequences, branching at each choice point, and evaluating the leaves.

Depth is how many steps ahead you go before you stop and guess, and the striking behavioural fact is that human depth is shallow and variable - typically a small number of steps, and it shrinks under time pressure, cognitive load, and uncertainty.

In the two-step task introduced by Nathaniel Daw and colleagues, which separates model-based choice (using an internal model of the world's structure) from model-free choice (using cached values), model-based behaviour is the behavioural marker that a tree is being searched at all.

The hippocampus, a medial temporal structure best known for episodic memory and spatial mapping, is implicated causally: Kevin Miller, Matthew Botvinick and Carlos Brody reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2017 that muscimol inactivation of dorsal hippocampus in rats selectively reduced model-based planning, and hippocampal replay - the compressed re-running of place cell sequences - is the leading candidate mechanism for the rollouts themselves.

On the frontal side, damage to ventromedial prefrontal cortex reduces planning depth, and a 2025 Journal of Neuroscience lesion study attempted to disentangle which component processes of complex planning those patients actually lose.

Human fMRI of forward planning has linked medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampal activity to search difficulty, and hippocampal theta oscillations track sequential dependencies during spatial planning, though the mapping from these signals to specific search steps remains loose.


53.3.4 Prospective memory and intention retrieval

Prospective memory is remembering to do something later - to pass on a message when you next see a colleague, to take a tablet at eight o'clock - while you are busy doing something else.

It is a distinctive problem because nothing external prompts you at the moment of formation, and the cue, when it comes, must be recognised as a cue while your attention is on an unrelated ongoing task.

Paul Burgess and colleagues showed that lesions to rostral prefrontal cortex, corresponding roughly to Brodmann area 10 at the frontal pole, impair prospective memory even when ordinary episodic memory is intact, which is strong evidence that this is a separate function rather than a memory deficit in disguise.

Burgess's gateway hypothesis, stated in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2007, proposes that area 10 biases attention between stimulus-oriented processing (attending to what is in front of you) and stimulus-independent processing (attending to internally generated or maintained representations such as a pending intention), which is precisely the switch prospective memory demands.

Consistent with this, Burgess and colleagues found in 2003 that holding an intention was accompanied by activity changes in area 10 during the delay itself, before any cue appeared, and later work in Cerebral Cortex in 2012 tied lateral rostral prefrontal activity to whether the intention was in the focus of attention.


53.4 Flexibility and stability

Everything above assumes the brain can both hold a configuration and replace it.

Those two demands pull in opposite directions, and this section is about the mechanisms that arbitrate between them, the classic clinical test that exposes failures, and how much people differ.


53.4.1 The flexibility-stability dilemma and dopaminergic gating accounts

The dilemma is simple to state: a system that updates its goal whenever something new arrives is distractible, and a system that never updates is rigid, so neither pure setting is viable and something must decide when to update.

The dominant computational answer is gating, an idea developed by Randall O'Reilly, Michael Frank, Todd Braver and colleagues in the prefrontal-basal ganglia working memory model: prefrontal cortex holds the contents, and the basal ganglia act as a gate that opens to let new contents in and otherwise stays shut so that the current contents are protected.

Dopamine is the proposed signal that operates the gate, and the model assigns opposing roles to the two main receptor families, with striatal D1-mediated "go" pathways favouring updating and D2-mediated "no-go" pathways favouring maintenance.

There is a further and partly separate claim, associated particularly with Roshan Cools, that prefrontal and striatal dopamine have opposite effects on the balance: higher prefrontal dopamine, acting mainly through D1 receptors, promotes stability and distractor resistance, while higher striatal dopamine promotes flexibility and updating.

Cools has also emphasised that dopamine effects follow an inverted-U shape, so the same drug improves people who start low and impairs people who start high, which is why pharmacological findings in this area look contradictory until baseline is taken into account; her 2019 Neuron review "Chemistry of the Adaptive Mind" is the standard statement, and a 2013 review by Stan Floresco argued the inverted-U is better replaced by a family of different dose-response functions for different task components.


53.4.2 Cognitive set, perseveration, and the Wisconsin card sorting task

A cognitive set is a currently adopted way of construing a situation, and perseveration is continuing to apply it after it has stopped working.

The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) makes this visible: the participant sorts cards by an unstated rule - colour, shape, or number - learning it only from feedback, and after a run of correct sorts the examiner silently changes the rule.

The diagnostic measure is the perseverative error, sorting again by the now-obsolete rule, and Brenda Milner's 1963 study at the Montreal Neurological Institute reported that patients with dorsolateral frontal lesions achieved fewer categories and made many more perseverative errors than patients with lesions elsewhere.

The test's specificity has since been heavily qualified.

Nyhus and Barceló's 2009 critical update concluded that the WCST taxes many distinct processes at once - working memory, feedback processing, attentional set shifting, response inhibition - so a high perseverative score does not localise damage, and most assessment guidelines now warn explicitly against reading WCST scores as evidence of frontal lesion; a 2018 model-based lesion mapping study in Nature Communications tried to decompose the test into component processes with separable lesion correlates rather than treating the score as unitary.


53.4.3 Learning to be flexible: schema, structure learning, latent causes

Flexibility is not only a matter of dropping the old set; it is also a matter of having the right candidate sets ready, and that is a learning problem.

Structure learning is the inference of what kind of world you are in - which variables matter, which rules cluster together - as opposed to learning the value of one specific action.

Latent cause inference, developed for reinforcement learning by Samuel Gershman and colleagues, treats the problem as segmentation: the learner infers unobserved causes generating the observations, and when the statistics change enough it posits a new latent cause rather than overwriting the old one, which is why extinguished fear can return and why context reinstates old habits.

Anne Collins and Michael Frank applied a Bayesian nonparametric approach - a model that allows the number of clusters to grow as evidence demands rather than fixing it in advance - to task sets, showing that people spontaneously cluster stimulus-response rules into reusable sets and then transfer whole clusters to new situations.

This reframes flexibility attractively: a switch is cheap when the brain already holds the right cluster and merely selects it, and expensive when a new structure must be built, and recent work links neural replay to latent cause inference and to fast one-shot generalisation after reversals.

The framework is elegant and computationally well specified; the weaker part is the neural evidence, which is still thinner than the modelling.


53.4.4 Individual and clinical variation in flexibility

People differ substantially and stably in switch costs and set-shifting, and the differences are not simply "more or less intelligence".

Rigidity is a transdiagnostic feature: reduced set shifting and impaired probabilistic reversal learning are documented in obsessive compulsive disorder and in anorexia nervosa, where the two conditions share a strikingly similar inflexible neuropsychological profile and where longer illness duration predicts slower switching; pronounced flexibility deficits are also core to schizophrenia, and altered flexibility appears across autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

A 2025 transdiagnostic coordinate-based meta-analysis found that altered activity during set-shifting and reversal tasks across disorders falls in frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, and default-mode networks rather than in a single disorder-specific region.

Normal ageing shifts the balance too, generally toward larger switch costs and greater difficulty overriding a well-practised set, consistent with age-related decline in dopaminergic function.

Two cautions belong here.

First, greater flexibility is not straightforwardly better - the same trait that lets you drop a stale rule quickly makes you more vulnerable to distraction, which is the whole point of the dilemma in 53.4.1.

Second, genetic accounts of these individual differences, including much-cited work on the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) gene that regulates prefrontal dopamine breakdown, have a mixed replication record, and single-gene explanations of flexibility should be treated as unsettled.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Behaviour is hierarchically organised, and the lateral prefrontal cortex is organised to match, with concrete action-linked control dorsocaudally and abstract, temporally extended control ventrorostrally, though whether this constitutes a strict hierarchy remains disputed and is better described today in terms of a graded trade-off between generalisable low-dimensional and expressive high-dimensional codes.

Task sets are configurable stimulus-to-response mappings, and the costs of switching them reflect both incomplete advance reconfiguration and the inertia of the set you are leaving, with the cost scaling by how high in the hierarchy the change occurs.

Goals persist across delays through a dynamic code that is neither purely persistent firing nor purely activity-silent, and long tasks are made learnable by hierarchical reinforcement learning, in which subgoals generate pseudo-reward prediction errors in the striatum.

Planning in humans is real but shallow, depends causally on the hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and intentions held for later depend on rostral prefrontal area 10 mediating between outward and inward attention.

Flexibility and stability are traded against each other by a dopaminergic gating mechanism whose effects follow an inverted-U, so that both the perseveration of the frontal patient on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and the distractibility of the over-flexible mind are failures of the same balance.


CHAPTER 54. DECISION MAKING AND VALUE (CORE)


Every waking hour you choose - which sandwich, which route, which job offer, whether to wait for the bus or start walking.

This chapter asks how a lump of tissue turns apples and oranges and salaries and delays into something it can compare, and then commits to one of them.

We will start with how the brain builds value, move to the machinery that turns values into a choice, then add the three great complications - risk, time, and effort - and finish with the hardest case of all, which is deciding when the thing you are deciding about is another person.

This matters because the same circuits show up, damaged or miscalibrated, in addiction, in depression, in impulse control disorders, and in ordinary bad financial decisions.

It also matters because the field that studies it, neuroeconomics, has been one of the most ambitious and most criticised marriages of two disciplines in modern science, and it is worth understanding both the ambition and the criticism.


54.1 Value construction

Before you can choose, you need something to choose between - not the objects themselves, but internal quantities that stand for how good each object is for you right now.

This section is about where those quantities come from and where in the brain they seem to live.


54.1.1 Common currency and the comparison problem

The comparison problem is simple to state - to decide between an apple and a song, the brain must place both on a single scale, because you cannot subtract a song from an apple.

The proposed solution is a common currency, meaning a single internal quantity, often called subjective value or utility (utility is the economist's word for how much a thing is worth to a particular person, which is not the same as its price), into which very different goods are converted.

The evidence for a common currency is that many different rewards - juice, money, attractive faces, charitable donations - drive activity in an overlapping set of brain regions, and drive it in proportion to how much the individual person says they want them.

The idea is elegant, and it is well supported at the level of correlation, but it is worth being honest about the gap - showing that one region's activity scales with value across many goods does not by itself prove that the region is where the comparison happens, only that the information is present there.

Subjective value is also not fixed - it depends on your current state, which is why the same sandwich is worth a great deal at one o'clock and almost nothing at two.


54.1.2 Orbitofrontal cortex and economic value coding

The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is the part of the frontal lobe that sits just above your eye sockets, and it is the single structure most associated with valuing goods.

The landmark result is Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, published in Nature in 2006, who recorded from single OFC neurons while monkeys chose between different juices offered in different quantities, and found neurons whose firing tracked the value the monkey placed on an offer - combining both what the juice was and how much of it there was into one number.

Crucially, those signals were about the good, not about the movement - the same neuron responded similarly whether the monkey signalled its choice with a leftward or rightward eye movement, which is why this is called good-based rather than action-based valuation.

Follow-up work from the same laboratory showed two further properties - the value signal is largely invariant to changes of menu, meaning a juice's coded value does not depend much on what else is on offer that day (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008), and it is range-adapting, meaning the neurons rescale their firing to the range of values currently in play (Padoa-Schioppa, 2009), which is how a limited firing rate covers both penny stakes and life-changing ones.

There is a live disagreement about what OFC is fundamentally for - Wilson, Takahashi, Schoenbaum and Niv argued in Neuron in 2014 that OFC is better understood as a cognitive map of task space, meaning a representation of which situation or state you are currently in, especially when that state is hidden and must be inferred, with value being one thing you can read off such a map rather than its core job.

Schuck and colleagues (Neuron, 2016) supported the state-space view in humans using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a method that tracks blood flow as an indirect index of neural activity.

Both positions have strong data behind them, and the sensible current reading is that OFC carries both value and state information, with the argument being about which is primary.


54.1.3 Ventromedial prefrontal cortex and subjective value

The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) is the medial, lower portion of the frontal lobe, adjacent to and partly overlapping with OFC, and in human imaging it is the workhorse of value research.

Bartra, McGuire and Kable published a coordinate-based meta-analysis in NeuroImage in 2013 - a statistical pooling of the reported activation locations from many separate fMRI studies - and found that vmPFC and the ventral striatum (a subcortical reward structure) showed reliable positive correlates of subjective value across a very wide range of tasks and reward types.

The same analysis made a useful distinction - regions such as the anterior insula tracked something closer to salience or arousal, meaning how much a stimulus grabs you regardless of whether it is good or bad, rather than signed value.

Lesion evidence strengthens the case beyond correlation - patients with damage to ventromedial frontal cortex show altered weighting of the attributes that feed into a valuation, and are impaired at evaluating the whole of a multi-attribute object rather than its parts.

A caution worth carrying - vmPFC overlaps heavily with the default mode network, the set of regions more active at rest than during demanding tasks, so some apparent value signals may partly reflect that overlap.


54.1.4 Attribute integration, attention, and value construction during choice

Value is not looked up in a table; it is constructed on the spot by combining attributes - a snack's taste, its healthiness, its price, its convenience.

Hare, Camerer and Rangel showed this vividly in Science in 2009, scanning dieters deciding whether to eat particular foods - vmPFC activity tracked the value driving the choice in everyone, but in people who failed at self-control that value reflected taste alone, while in successful self-controllers it reflected both taste and health.

When self-control was exercised, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), a lateral region associated with maintaining goals in mind, became more active and its activity related to vmPFC activity - suggesting self-control works by changing which attributes get into the value computation, not by vetoing a value signal after the fact.

Attention is the other great constructor - which attribute you happen to be looking at when the decision is forming has a measurable effect on the value assigned, which is the bridge to the next section.

The practical implication is uncomfortable and well replicated - the order and manner in which options are presented to you shapes the values you form, so preferences are partly built by the situation rather than merely revealed by it.


54.2 Choice mechanisms

Having values is not the same as making a choice.

This section covers the process that takes value signals and produces a commitment at a particular moment in time, which is why response times matter as much as choices.


54.2.1 Sequential sampling and the drift diffusion account of preferential choice

A sequential sampling model says the brain does not compare options in one instant, but accumulates noisy evidence over time until the accumulated total crosses a threshold, at which point it commits.

The drift diffusion model (DDM) is the best-known member of this family - it has a drift rate, meaning the average speed at which evidence favours one option, and a boundary, meaning how much evidence you demand before deciding.

Originally developed for perceptual decisions, where there is a correct answer, the DDM was extended to preferential choice, where there is not - here the drift rate is set by the difference in subjective value between the options.

This single move explains a great deal at once - choices between similarly valued options are both slower and less consistent, because a small value difference means a slow drift and more opportunity for noise to win.

It also explains the speed-accuracy trade-off in preference - raising the boundary makes you slower and more likely to pick the item you rated higher.


54.2.2 Attentional drift diffusion and gaze-driven choice

Krajbich, Armel and Rangel, in Nature Neuroscience in 2010, tracked where people looked while choosing between snack foods and found that gaze and choice are tightly coupled - the item looked at last, and the item looked at longer, was much more likely to be chosen.

Their attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM) captures this with one change - the value of whichever item you are not currently looking at is multiplied by a discount factor less than one, so evidence drifts toward whatever is being fixated.

Krajbich and Rangel extended the model to three-option choice in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2011, where it again predicted the fixation-choice relationship quantitatively.

The important causal question is direction - does looking cause liking, or does liking cause looking?

Experiments that control fixation externally, by forcing when each item is visible, find that manipulated gaze does shift choice, so the effect is not purely that you look at what you already prefer - though both directions of influence are almost certainly at work, and the size of the causal component is still debated.


54.2.3 Divisive normalisation and context effects

Divisive normalisation is a computation found throughout sensory cortex, in which a neuron's response to its preferred input is divided by the summed activity of neighbouring neurons - it is how the visual system keeps working across enormous ranges of light intensity.

Louie, Grattan and Glimcher showed in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2011 that neurons in the monkey lateral intraparietal area encode reward value in exactly this divisively normalised way, so a target's coded value depends on the values of the other targets present.

Louie, Khaw and Glimcher argued in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2013 that this makes context-dependence a structural consequence of efficient neural coding rather than a psychological quirk - if your value code is normalised by what else is around, your preferences must be context-dependent.

The theory is genuinely elegant, and it has a strong mechanistic pedigree, but the behavioural predictions are contested - Gluth and colleagues reported in Nature Human Behaviour in 2020 that a widely cited distractor effect failed to replicate in preregistered experiments and attributed the pattern to value-based attention instead, and Webb, Glimcher and Louie replied defending the normalisation account.

Present this to yourself as unsettled - the neural computation is well documented, the claim that it explains specific behavioural anomalies is not.


54.2.4 Multi-alternative choice and violations of rationality

Standard rational choice theory assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA), meaning that adding a third option you would never pick should not change your ranking of the first two.

People and animals violate this routinely, and three violations are classic - the decoy or asymmetric dominance effect, where adding an option clearly worse than A but not clearly worse than B raises A's share; the similarity effect, where a new option steals share mainly from the option it resembles; and the compromise effect, where the middle option gains simply by being in the middle.

These are not laboratory curiosities - they are the working tools of menu design and product pricing.

Two families of explanation compete - normalisation accounts, which locate the cause in how value is encoded, and attentional or sampling accounts, which locate it in how the options are looked at and compared during deliberation.

The honest summary is that the phenomena are robust, and the mechanism is not yet resolved.


54.3 Risk, uncertainty, and time

Real choices rarely offer certain, immediate outcomes.

This section covers the three discounts the brain applies - for the chance of not getting it, for not knowing the chance, and for having to wait.


54.3.1 Risk, ambiguity, and their separable neural correlates

Economists distinguish risk, meaning the odds are known, as with a fair coin, from ambiguity, meaning the odds themselves are unknown, as with an urn of unknown composition.

Hsu, Bhatt, Adolphs, Tranel and Camerer, in Science in 2005, found that ambiguity was associated with greater activity in the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex and lower activity in the striatum, relative to risk.

Their most persuasive evidence was not the imaging but the lesion data - patients with orbitofrontal damage were relatively insensitive to the level of both ambiguity and risk in their choices, which is causal evidence that these regions matter rather than merely co-occur.

Later work, including Levy, Snell, Nelson, Rustichini and Glimcher in the Journal of Neurophysiology in 2010, showed that despite these differences, a common valuation region can encode the subjective value of both risky and ambiguous prospects on one scale - so the two kinds of uncertainty are computed partly separately but converted into a shared currency.

Most people are both risk averse and, separately and more strongly, ambiguity averse, and the two attitudes vary fairly independently across individuals.


54.3.2 Prospect theory and reference dependence

Prospect theory, introduced by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979, replaced the idea that we value final wealth with the idea that we value changes relative to a reference point - usually the status quo.

It has three central claims - outcomes are coded as gains or losses against that reference point; the value function is steeper for losses than gains, which is loss aversion; and probabilities are subjectively distorted, with small probabilities overweighted and large ones underweighted, which is why people buy both lottery tickets and insurance.

Tom, Fox, Trepel and Poldrack, in Science in 2007, reported neural loss aversion - activity in ventral striatum and vmPFC fell more steeply as potential losses grew than it rose as equivalent gains grew, and the steepness of that asymmetry across individuals correlated with their behavioural loss aversion.

De Martino, Camerer and Adolphs, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010, studied two rare patients with focal amygdala damage and found their monetary loss aversion was eliminated, which is strong causal evidence for an amygdala contribution.

Loss aversion is nonetheless one of the more contested effects in the field - the size of the asymmetry depends heavily on how the task is framed and on the participant's emotional regulation strategy, and Sokol-Hessner and Rutledge have argued (2019) that it should be understood as a flexible, context-sensitive parameter rather than a fixed personal constant.


54.3.3 Delay discounting and intertemporal choice

Delay discounting is the reduction in an outcome's subjective value simply because it arrives later, and it is usually well described by a hyperbolic function, in which value falls very steeply over short delays and then flattens out.

Hyperbolic discounting predicts preference reversal - you prefer one hundred pounds in a year to ninety pounds in eleven months, yet prefer ninety pounds today to one hundred pounds in a month - which is the formal signature of what we colloquially call weakness of will.

McClure, Laibson, Loewenstein and Cohen, in Science in 2004, proposed a two-system account, often written as beta-delta - a limbic beta system placing extra weight on immediately available rewards, and a more cortical delta system valuing rewards at all delays.

Kable and Glimcher, in Nature Neuroscience in 2007, challenged this with a unitary account - they found that activity in ventral striatum, medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex tracked each individual's own discounted subjective value for both immediate and delayed rewards, with no need for a separate impulsive system.

This dispute is not fully closed, but the unitary valuation account has become the more widely adopted default, partly because it fits individual differences without extra machinery.

Discounting rates are steeper in people with substance use disorders, and steep discounting predicts a range of real outcomes, though whether it is a cause, a consequence, or a shared vulnerability remains genuinely open.


54.3.4 Patience, serotonin, and self-control

Serotonin is a neuromodulator - a chemical messenger that adjusts the gain and character of processing across wide swathes of brain - produced mainly by neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus of the brainstem.

Miyazaki and colleagues, in Current Biology in 2014, used optogenetics - a technique in which light-sensitive proteins are inserted into specific neurons so they can be switched on with light - to activate dorsal raphe serotonin neurons in mice, and found that this prolonged the animals' willingness to wait for a delayed reward without itself being rewarding.

Their later work (Nature Communications, 2018) refined the picture - the patience-promoting effect depends on the animal's belief that a reward is likely to come, so serotonin supports persistence in the face of uncertainty rather than blind waiting, and a 2020 Science Advances paper showed that serotonergic projections to orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex contribute differently.

In humans, acute tryptophan depletion - a dietary manipulation that temporarily lowers the supply of serotonin's precursor - increases premature, impulsive responding, which converges with the animal work.

Note carefully what serotonin does and does not seem to do here - the strongest evidence is for waiting impulsivity, meaning failure to withhold a premature action, and the evidence that serotonin sets your discount rate in a straightforward economic sense is much weaker.

The popular framing of serotonin as simply the patience chemical is an oversimplification of a modulator that also participates in aversive processing, mood and behavioural inhibition.


54.4 Foraging, exploration, and effort

Not every decision is a choice between simultaneously presented options.

Often the real question is when to stop what you are doing, whether to try something unknown, and whether the effort is worth it - the problems evolution actually shaped brains to solve.


54.4.1 Patch leaving and the marginal value theorem

Foraging theory reframes decision as a stay-or-go problem - a bird in a berry bush is not choosing between bushes, it is deciding when this one has been depleted enough to justify the travel time to the next.

The marginal value theorem, formalised by Eric Charnov in 1976, gives the optimal rule - leave when the current patch's rate of return falls to the average rate available in the environment as a whole, accounting for travel time.
