The rule makes a sharp and testable prediction - longer travel times between patches should make animals stay longer in each patch, and they broadly do.

Hayden, Pearson and Platt, in Nature Neuroscience in 2011, recorded from monkey dorsal anterior cingulate cortex during a patch-leaving task and found neurons whose firing rose during each successive decision to stay and reached a threshold at the moment of leaving - and longer travel times raised that threshold, exactly as the theorem requires.

Comparable continuous decision-variable signals have since been reported in rat anterior cingulate cortex (Journal of Neuroscience, 2022), and the framework has been extended to treat foraging as an evidence-accumulation process, linking it back to the sequential sampling models of section 54.2.


54.4.2 Explore-exploit trade-off and directed against random exploration

The explore-exploit trade-off is the tension between taking the option you know is decent and sampling an option you know little about, which might be better.

Daw, O'Doherty, Dayan, Seymour and Dolan, in Nature in 2006, scanned people playing a four-armed bandit task - a game of repeatedly choosing among options with drifting, unknown payoffs - and found frontopolar cortex, the most anterior part of the frontal lobe, more active on exploratory than exploitative choices.

Wilson and colleagues later separated two distinct exploration strategies using the horizon task, in which participants know in advance how many choices remain - directed exploration, a deliberate bonus given to uncertain options because information is useful when there is time to use it, and random exploration, simply behaving more noisily.

Zajkowski, Kossut and Wilson, in eLife in 2017, used transcranial magnetic stimulation - a method that transiently disrupts activity in a targeted cortical patch using magnetic pulses - over right frontopolar cortex and selectively reduced directed exploration while leaving random exploration intact, which is causal evidence that the two strategies rest on at least partly separable systems.

A practical consequence is that a person can appear equally exploratory in two situations for entirely different computational reasons, which matters when interpreting exploration deficits in psychiatric conditions.


54.4.3 Effort discounting and the cost of action

Effort discounting means that an outcome is worth less if you must work harder for it, and it applies to both physical effort, such as squeezing a handgrip, and cognitive effort, such as sustained concentration.

John Salamone's work over several decades established that dopamine in the nucleus accumbens is central to effort-based decision making rather than to pleasure as such - rats with accumbens dopamine depleted still like sucrose and will eat freely available food, but they stop being willing to climb a barrier or press a lever many times to get the better reward.

This reframing matters clinically, because it maps far better onto the motivational flatness seen in depression and in Parkinson's disease than a simple loss-of-pleasure account does.

In humans, effort costs are represented in a network including anterior cingulate cortex and ventral striatum, and effort discounting is typically steeper and differently shaped from delay discounting, meaning the two costs are computed separately rather than converted into one another.

Cognitive effort behaves like a genuine cost in the same currency - people will forgo money to avoid a harder task, which is the empirical basis for treating mental exertion as economically real rather than merely unpleasant.


54.4.4 Anterior cingulate cortex in foraging and control allocation

The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is a strip of medial frontal cortex wrapping over the corpus callosum, and it has been assigned an unusually long list of jobs - conflict monitoring, error detection, pain, effort, foraging, and reward tracking.

Shenhav, Botvinick and Cohen, in Neuron in 2013, proposed the expected value of control (EVC) theory as a unification - ACC computes whether a given allocation of cognitive control is worth it, by weighing the payoff a controlled process would bring against the amount of control required and the effort cost of supplying it.

EVC is attractive precisely because it derives the region's diverse correlates - conflict, error, effort, reward rate - from one quantity, since all of them are inputs to the question of how much control to deploy.

There is a pointed disagreement about the foraging findings - Kolling and colleagues (2012) argued that human dorsal ACC signals the value of switching away from the current course of action, while Shenhav, Straccia, Cohen and Botvinick countered in Nature Neuroscience in 2014 that the same activity reflects choice difficulty rather than foraging value, since harder choices and switch-worthy situations are confounded in the usual designs.

The exchange is a good illustration of a recurring hazard in this literature - two very different theories can predict the same activation pattern unless the experiment is designed specifically to separate them.


54.5 Social and strategic decision

The hardest decisions involve other agents, because the value of your action depends on what they do, and what they do depends on what they think you will do.


54.5.1 Game-theoretic paradigms and their neural correlates

Game theory supplies small, precisely specified interactions that make social decisions measurable - the ultimatum game, in which one player proposes a split of a sum and the other can accept or reject for both, and the trust game, in which an investor sends money that is multiplied and the trustee decides how much to return.

Standard economic reasoning says a responder in the ultimatum game should accept any positive offer, since something beats nothing, yet people reliably reject offers below roughly a fifth to a quarter of the pot.

Sanfey, Rilling, Aronson, Nystrom and Cohen, in Science in 2003, scanned responders and found that unfair offers produced stronger activity in anterior insula, anterior cingulate cortex and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and that anterior insula activity across trials and individuals tracked the likelihood of rejection.

The insula finding was influential because it linked rejection to a region associated with visceral, aversive states, supporting the reading that rejecting an unfair offer is driven by something like felt indignation rather than by cool strategic calculation.

The interpretive caution is important - inferring disgust or anger from insula activity is a reverse inference, meaning reasoning backwards from a brain region to a mental state, and the insula is active in many conditions that have nothing to do with unfairness.


54.5.2 Trust, reciprocity, and punishment

King-Casas and colleagues, in Science in 2005, had pairs of people play repeated trust games while both were scanned, and identified a signal in the trustee's caudate nucleus reflecting the intention to trust - critically, this signal shifted earlier in time as the relationship developed, moving from reacting to the partner's generosity to anticipating it, which is what building a reputation looks like in neural terms.

De Quervain and colleagues, in Science in 2004, used positron emission tomography, an imaging method using injected radioactive tracers, to study altruistic punishment - paying a personal cost to punish someone who defected - and found dorsal striatum activation when punishment was effective, with the magnitude relating to how much people were willing to pay.

That result gave rise to the widely repeated claim that punishment feels rewarding, which is plausible and consistent with the data, but rests on the same reverse-inference logic and should be held loosely.

The oxytocin story is a cautionary tale worth learning from - an influential 2005 report that intranasal oxytocin increased trusting behaviour was followed by well-powered failures to replicate, and by meta-analyses finding the effect to be small or absent.

The current consensus is that oxytocin does not straightforwardly function as a trust hormone, and the episode is a useful reminder of how quickly a single striking neuroeconomic result can outrun its evidential base.


54.5.3 Learning about others as a model-based problem

Learning about another person can be done cheaply or expensively - model-free learning simply updates how good each action has turned out to be, while model-based learning maintains an internal model of the other agent and simulates what they will do.

Hampton, Bossaerts and O'Doherty, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2008, had people play a competitive inspection game and found that activity in medial prefrontal cortex and superior temporal sulcus tracked signals from a sophisticated model, in which the participant represents the influence of their own actions on the opponent's beliefs, and not from a simple reinforcement learning model.

Behrens, Hunt, Woolrich and Rushworth, in Nature in 2008, showed that value learned from one's own experience and value learned from another's advice are computed in partly separate circuits - the former involving ventral striatum and the latter involving regions of the mentalizing network, including the temporoparietal junction - and then combined in vmPFC.

Suzuki and colleagues, in Neuron in 2012, added the simulation half of the story, identifying signals in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex corresponding to simulated prediction errors, meaning errors in the model of what the other person expected, held separately from the participant's own prediction errors.

The overall picture is convergent and reasonably robust - social learning recruits the same reinforcement-learning arithmetic as non-social learning, but adds dedicated machinery for representing that the other agent has their own beliefs.


54.5.4 Neuroeconomics as a discipline and its critiques

Neuroeconomics is the attempt to ground economic models of choice in measured brain activity, drawing on economics, psychology and neuroscience together, and it has grown rapidly since roughly 2000.

The sharpest critique came from within economics - Faruk Gul and Wolfgang Pesendorfer's essay The Case for Mindless Economics argued that economics is a theory of choice data, that its concepts such as utility are defined by observed choices and not by internal states, and that findings about the brain therefore cannot refute an economic model even in principle.

Defenders reply that if you want to predict behaviour outside the range of your data, or to explain when models break, mechanism matters, and that this is exactly what neural data supplies.

A second, more technical critique concerns reverse inference - concluding that a psychological process occurred because a region associated with it was active - which is logically invalid whenever the region participates in more than one process, and virtually every region does.

A third concerns statistical practice - small samples, flexible analysis pipelines, and inflated effect sizes, problems that neuroeconomics shares with much of cognitive neuroscience and which the wider replication reckoning of the 2010s and 2020s has forced the field to confront through preregistration, larger samples and open data.

The fair verdict is that the strongest neuroeconomic results are those with converging causal evidence - lesion, stimulation or optogenetic - behind the correlational imaging, and the weakest are single striking fMRI findings interpreted through reverse inference.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Choice requires a common currency, and a valuation network centred on orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, together with the ventral striatum, carries signals proportional to subjective value across goods as different as juice, money and other people's welfare - although whether orbitofrontal cortex primarily codes value or primarily codes task state remains actively disputed.

Values are constructed rather than retrieved, built from attributes under the influence of attention and goals, which is why gaze predicts choice and why self-control looks like a change in which attributes are counted rather than a veto imposed after the fact.

Choices themselves are produced by noisy evidence accumulation over time, which is why response times, error rates and fixation patterns are all data about the same underlying process.

Risk, ambiguity, delay and effort are each discounted by partly separable mechanisms before being converted into the shared currency, and foraging, exploration and control allocation frame decision as a question of when to switch rather than what to pick, with anterior cingulate cortex the leading candidate for computing that question.

Social decisions reuse the same reinforcement-learning arithmetic while adding machinery for modelling another agent's beliefs.

Finally, the field's most durable claims are those supported by causal manipulation as well as imaging, and its cautionary tales - the oxytocin trust literature above all - show how easily reverse inference and small samples can manufacture a result that does not survive.


CHAPTER 55. REASONING, PROBLEM SOLVING, AND ABSTRACTION (CORE)


This chapter is about the part of thinking that feels most like thinking - working out what follows from what, finding a way through a problem that has no obvious route, and pulling a general lesson out of a particular experience.

Reasoning is the process of moving from things you already believe to a new belief.

Problem solving is the process of getting from a starting state to a goal state when the path is not handed to you.

Abstraction is the process of throwing away the surface details of an experience and keeping the structure, so that the structure can be reused somewhere else entirely.

These three matter because they are where human cognition is at its most impressive and, at the same time, where it is most reliably wrong in ways that can be measured in a laboratory.

They are also the sharpest current test of whether artificial systems think the way people do, and the honest answer as of 2026 is that the question is still open.


55.1 Forms of reasoning

There is no single mental operation called reasoning.

There are several distinct ways of getting from premises to conclusions, and they differ in how much risk they carry.

Some forms guarantee their conclusions, some merely make them likely, and some are frank guesses that happen to be the best guess available.

The brain does not appear to have one dedicated reasoning organ either, though certain frontal and parietal regions turn up again and again across reasoning tasks.


55.1.1 Deductive, inductive, and abductive inference

Deduction is inference where the conclusion is guaranteed by the premises - if all birds have feathers, and a robin is a bird, then a robin has feathers, and there is no way for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.

Induction is inference from observed cases to a general rule or an unobserved case - you have seen many swans and they were white, so you expect the next one to be white, which is a good bet rather than a guarantee.

Abduction, a term introduced by the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce in the late nineteenth century, is inference to the best explanation - the grass is wet, and rain overnight is the most plausible story that accounts for it, so you provisionally accept rain.

Neuroimaging work using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that tracks blood flow as a proxy for neural activity, has repeatedly found that deductive tasks lean more on the left inferior frontal gyrus - a region on the lower front-left of the cortex closely tied to language and to rehearsing material in working memory - while inductive tasks lean more on the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region on the upper outer surface of the frontal lobe associated with holding and manipulating information.

That dissociation is real but it is partial, not clean: the two task types overlap heavily in a frontoparietal network spanning frontal and parietal cortex, and Goel and colleagues have long cautioned that reading backwards from an activation blob to a cognitive theory - so-called forward inference - is a weak form of argument.

The safest current statement is that deduction and induction recruit overlapping frontoparietal machinery with differences of emphasis, and that abduction has been studied far less with brain imaging than the other two.


55.1.2 Analogical reasoning and relational mapping

An analogy asserts that two situations share a structure even though their surface contents are unrelated, as in "brain is to thought as stomach is to digestion".

The hard computational work in an analogy is relational mapping - lining up the roles in one situation with the roles in the other, and doing it on the basis of relations rather than surface similarity.

Christoff, Bunge, Wendelken, Wharton and their colleagues showed in a series of studies from the early 2000s onward that this specifically requires the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (RLPFC), the very front tip of the frontal lobe, roughly Brodmann area 10, where Brodmann areas are a numbered map of the cortex drawn up by Korbinian Brodmann in 1909 on the basis of cell structure.

The critical variable is relational integration - the number of relations you must hold in mind and combine at once - and RLPFC activity rises with it while other frontal regions track simpler demands.

Bunge and colleagues have argued for a hierarchy in prefrontal cortex, with more posterior regions handling single relations and the rostrolateral tip handling relations between relations.

The region appears to be domain-general, engaging for verbal analogies, visuospatial analogies, and matrix puzzles alike, which is one reason it is treated as a candidate seat of abstract thought rather than of any one content type.


55.1.3 Causal reasoning and intervention

Causal reasoning is working out what makes what happen, which is different from merely noticing that two things co-occur.

The formal advance behind modern work here is the causal graph, developed by Judea Pearl and by Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines in the 1990s, in which variables are nodes and arrows represent causal influence, and in which acting on the world - Pearl's do operator - is mathematically distinct from passively observing it.

Intervening breaks the incoming arrows to the variable you touch, which is exactly why an experiment tells you more than an observation: if you set the switch yourself, you know nothing upstream caused its position.

Alison Gopnik, Laura Schulz, David Sobel, Clark Glymour and colleagues argued in a 2004 Psychological Review paper and in later work that young children behave as if they possess this machinery, learning causal structure from patterns of evidence and from their own interventions, and by around age four inferring hidden causes and unobserved variables.

Lagnado and Sloman showed in adults that self-generated interventions produce more accurate causal structure learning than observing an identical stream of data generated by someone else, which is a striking result because the information content is matched.

What is disputed is the interpretation: whether children genuinely run something like Bayesian causal inference, or whether simpler associative and heuristic mechanisms plus a strong prior toward agency mimic it well enough to pass these tests.


55.1.4 Probabilistic reasoning and base-rate use

A base rate is how common something is in the population before you look at any individual evidence, and base-rate neglect is the well documented tendency to underweight it.

The standard demonstration is a medical test: a disease affects one person in a thousand, the test catches essentially every real case but has a five per cent false positive rate, and most people - including many clinicians - guess that a positive result means around a ninety-five per cent chance of disease, when the correct answer is close to two per cent because the far larger healthy group generates far more false positives than the tiny sick group generates true ones.

Gerd Gigerenzer and Ulrich Hoffrage showed in 1995 that simply restating the same problem in natural frequencies - ten people out of a thousand have it, nine of those test positive, and about fifty of the remaining nine hundred and ninety also test positive - raises correct performance dramatically, in their classic data from roughly sixteen per cent to roughly forty-six per cent.

Why this works is contested: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage attributed it to evolved computational machinery tuned to counts rather than percentages, while Steven Sloman, David Over and others argued for the nested-sets hypothesis, that the frequency format simply makes the set-within-set structure of the problem visually obvious and any format doing so would work as well.

It is also worth being honest that natural frequencies are a large improvement rather than a cure - a 2018 study by Weber, Binder and Krauss found that only about twenty-four per cent solved such problems even when given in frequencies, with many people converting the frequencies back into probabilities and then failing.

More recent work, including Schulz and colleagues in 2022, argues that base-rate neglect is not confined to word problems but shows up in learned-from-experience tasks too, which weakens the view that it is purely an artefact of how questions are worded.


55.2 Heuristics and biases

A heuristic is a shortcut - a rule that gets a usable answer cheaply without doing the full computation.

The central argument of the last fifty years of judgement research is about what those shortcuts mean.

One camp reads them as the source of systematic error, the other reads them as intelligent adaptations to a world where the full computation is impossible, and a third camp is now trying to state the conditions under which each reading is right.


55.2.1 The heuristics and biases programme

Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman launched the programme with a 1974 paper in Science, "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases", which proposed that people judge probability using a small set of substitutions.

Representativeness means judging how likely something is by how much it resembles a stereotype, which produces the conjunction fallacy - people rate "Linda is a bank teller and a feminist" as more probable than "Linda is a bank teller", which is logically impossible because a conjunction cannot be more probable than one of its parts.

Availability means judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind, which is why people overestimate deaths from dramatic causes like shark attacks and underestimate quiet ones like stroke.

Anchoring means being dragged toward whatever number you were exposed to first, even a transparently irrelevant one.

The programme's status in 2026 is mixed: the core effects, especially anchoring and framing, have generally survived replication scrutiny better than many social psychology findings, but several downstream applications - ego depletion and some priming-based extensions - have replicated poorly, and the field is more careful now about effect sizes than it was in Kahneman's 2011 popular synthesis.


55.2.2 Dual-process accounts and their neural evidence

Dual-process theory, associated with Jonathan Evans, Keith Stanovich and popularised by Kahneman as System 1 and System 2, holds that judgement arises from a fast, automatic, effortless process and a slow, deliberate, working-memory-dependent process.

The intuitive neural prediction is that these should map onto separable brain systems, with automatic processing in subcortical and posterior structures and deliberation in prefrontal cortex.

The evidence is weaker than the theory's popularity suggests: fMRI studies do reliably show prefrontal and cingulate engagement when people override a tempting wrong answer, but meta-analytic work has not produced two distinct activation signatures that cleanly correspond to two systems, and a great deal of what gets called System 1 is distributed across many different circuits with nothing in common except speed.

Wim De Neys has mounted the most influential internal critique, arguing from evidence that people show conflict detection - slower responses, altered confidence, autonomic arousal - even when they go on to give the intuitive wrong answer, meaning some logical sensitivity is present intuitively rather than only after deliberate correction.

De Neys and Glumicic in 2008, and De Neys in later papers, therefore proposed that the strict serial picture, where intuition proposes and deliberation optionally vetoes, should give way to a model in which multiple intuitions including logical ones compete in parallel.

This is a live disagreement, and the fair summary is that the two-process description is a useful shorthand at the behavioural level whose neural reality has not been demonstrated.


55.2.3 Ecological rationality and the defence of heuristics

Gerd Gigerenzer and the Adaptive Behavior and Cognition group at the Max Planck Institute argued that calling heuristics biases assumes the wrong benchmark.

Their concept of ecological rationality holds that a heuristic is neither good nor bad in itself - it is good if its structure matches the structure of the environment it operates in.

Their model heuristic is take-the-best, which compares two options one cue at a time in order of validity and stops at the first cue that discriminates, ignoring all remaining information; in comparative tests by Gigerenzer, Goldstein and Czerlinski it matched or beat multiple regression on real-world prediction tasks.

The statistical explanation is the bias-variance dilemma: a complex model can fit the sample it was trained on very closely but will swing wildly with new samples, whereas a simple model is systematically off but stable, and under uncertainty with limited data the stable simple model often wins on out-of-sample accuracy.

Gigerenzer pressed a stronger philosophical claim too - that many so-called fallacies rest on applying a single-case probability norm that frequentist statisticians reject - and this produced a famously sharp exchange in Psychological Review, with Kahneman and Tversky replying in 1996 that "the refutation of a caricature can be no more than a caricature of refutation".

The theory is genuinely elegant, and its bias-variance argument is mathematically solid, but critics reasonably note that identifying which heuristic a person is actually using, and predicting it in advance rather than fitting it after the fact, remains the programme's weak point.


55.2.4 Resource-rational reconciliation

Resource-rational analysis, developed by Falk Lieder and Thomas Griffiths in a 2020 Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article, attempts to dissolve the argument rather than pick a side.

Its move is to change the optimisation problem: instead of asking what answer is correct, ask what algorithm delivers the best expected value once you charge for the time, memory and computation it consumes.

Under that framing a heuristic is not a departure from rationality, it is the solution to a harder and more realistic optimisation, and the theory predicts both when people will stop computing and which shortcut they will pick.

The approach has had genuine successes - it derives anchoring-and-adjustment from a sampling process that is cut short, and it recovers overweighting of extreme outcomes from a sampler that prioritises high-impact possibilities - which turns two classic biases into predictions rather than exceptions.

The standing objection is flexibility: because the analyst chooses the cost function and the space of feasible algorithms, a sufficiently determined modeller can rationalise almost any behaviour, so the framework's value depends on those choices being independently constrained rather than fitted.


55.3 Problem solving

A problem exists when you have a goal, you are not at it, and no memorised procedure takes you there.

Research on problem solving has followed two largely separate traditions - one treating it as systematic search, the other treating it as sudden reorganisation - and the modern picture needs both.


55.3.1 Problem space search and means-ends analysis

Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, in Human Problem Solving in 1972, proposed that solving a problem is searching a problem space consisting of an initial state, a goal state, and a set of operators that transform one state into another.

Because the space of possible state sequences explodes combinatorially, no one searches it exhaustively; instead people apply heuristics that prune it.

Their central heuristic was means-ends analysis: identify the biggest difference between where you are and where you want to be, find an operator that reduces that difference, and if that operator's preconditions are not met, set up reaching those preconditions as a subgoal.

They implemented this in the General Problem Solver programme with J. C. Shaw between 1957 and 1960, and it solved symbolic logic problems, simple algebra and the Tower of Hanoi - a puzzle requiring disks to be moved between three pegs without ever placing a larger disk on a smaller one - using the same general machinery.

Newell and Simon also pioneered the method of validating this against human think-aloud protocols, comparing the programme's trace step by step with people's verbalised reasoning, which is what made the account a psychological theory rather than only an engineering result.

The framework's honest limitation is that it works best on well-defined problems where states and operators are clear, and it says much less about ill-defined problems like designing a building or writing a chapter.


55.3.2 Insight, restructuring, and the aha experience

Some problems are not solved by grinding through a space but by a sudden reinterpretation, which the Gestalt psychologists - Karl Duncker, Wolfgang Kohler, Max Wertheimer - called restructuring.

Duncker's candle problem is the canonical case: given a candle, a box of tacks and matches, people must fix the candle to a wall, and most fail because they see the box as a container rather than as a shelf, an error Duncker in 1945 named functional fixedness, the inability to see an object's non-standard use.

Mark Beeman and John Kounios, using remote-associates word puzzles where people report whether a solution arrived by insight or by deliberate work, found two objective neural correlates of self-reported insight: a burst of high-frequency gamma-band activity around 40 hertz roughly 300 milliseconds before the response, localised to the right anterior superior temporal gyrus, and, in fMRI, greater activation of that same region for insight than for non-insight solutions.

That region is plausible because it is implicated in linking distantly related concepts, as in metaphor and joke comprehension.

They also reported an alpha-band increase over right occipital cortex just before the gamma burst, interpreted as a brief gating out of visual input - effectively a blink of attention inward - and found that resting-state activity before the puzzle even appeared predicted whether a person would tend to solve by insight.

Two cautions are warranted: the insight-versus-analysis split relies on participants' own reports, and the feeling of insight is not a guarantee of correctness, since people can experience a confident aha for a wrong answer.


55.3.3 Expertise, chunking, and pattern recognition in problem solving

Adriaan de Groot found in the 1940s that chess grandmasters do not search dramatically deeper than weaker players; they simply consider better moves from the outset.

William Chase and Herbert Simon explained this in 1973 with chunking: experts have stored tens of thousands of familiar configurations of pieces in long-term memory, so a board position is perceived as a handful of meaningful units rather than dozens of separate pieces.

The decisive evidence is that the expert's memory advantage collapses when pieces are placed at random rather than in game-legal positions, showing that the advantage lies in learned structure rather than in raw memory capacity.

Fernand Gobet and Simon revised the account in 1996 to 1998 with template theory, because chunking alone could not explain how masters recall positions presented in as little as one to two seconds, or recall several boards at once; templates are larger structures with slots that can be filled rapidly with specific values.

The general principle transfers well beyond chess: in physics, Chi, Feltovich and Glaser showed in 1981 that novices sort problems by surface features such as whether an inclined plane is mentioned, whereas experts sort them by the underlying principle such as conservation of energy, which is a form of abstraction acquired through practice.

Alternative accounts exist - Ericsson and Kintsch's long-term working memory, and Linhares and Freitas's experience-recognition hypothesis - which stress conceptual rather than perceptual encoding, so the field agrees on the phenomenon while still arguing about its mechanism.


55.3.4 Frontopolar cortex and the maintenance of pending subgoals

Solving a multi-step problem requires putting one goal on hold while you pursue another, then coming back to the held goal without an external reminder.

Etienne Koechlin and colleagues, in a 1999 Nature paper and subsequent work, identified this function - which they termed cognitive branching - with the frontopolar cortex, the most anterior part of the prefrontal cortex, again roughly Brodmann area 10.

Their key contrast separated simply doing two tasks in sequence from genuinely suspending one task mid-stream and resuming it, and only the latter reliably drove frontopolar activity.

Paul Burgess and colleagues reached a convergent conclusion from lesion work: patients with damage to this region often perform normally on standard neuropsychological tests but fail badly at real-world multitasking, where you must remember to return to interrupted intentions.

Koechlin and Charron's later computational model proposes that frontopolar cortex holds the second-most-rewarding task in a pending state, driven by value signals from orbital and medial prefrontal cortex, while lateral prefrontal cortex runs the currently selected task.

Notice that this is the same territory implicated in relational integration in 55.1.2, and there is an unresolved debate about whether that reflects one underlying operation - holding and combining multiple representations - or two functions that happen to share real estate.


55.4 Abstraction and generalisation

Abstraction is what makes experience worth having.

If every situation had to be learned from scratch, learning would never pay off, so the value of a memory depends on stripping it down to a form that applies to situations not yet encountered.


55.4.1 Schemas, structure learning, and transfer

A schema is an organised body of prior knowledge about how a kind of situation is structured - what a restaurant visit involves, or how a particular maze is laid out.

Frederic Bartlett introduced the term to psychology in 1932 with his demonstration that people recalling an unfamiliar folk tale distorted it toward their own cultural expectations, showing that memory reconstructs against a schema rather than replaying a recording.

Dorothy Tse, Richard Morris and colleagues gave the idea a mechanism in a 2007 Science paper: rats that had spent weeks building a schema of where food is hidden in a particular arena could learn new food locations in a single trial, and those new memories became independent of the hippocampus - the seahorse-shaped structure critical for new episodic memories - within about forty-eight hours instead of the usual weeks.

The interpretation is that a matching schema lets neocortex absorb new information almost immediately, so consolidation, normally slow, is dramatically accelerated when the new fact slots into existing structure.

Structure learning is the broader idea, developed by Tenenbaum, Kemp, Gershman, Behrens and others, that the brain infers not just the parameters of a situation but its form - whether a domain is a tree, a ring, a line or a grid - and reuses that form when it meets a new instance.

The same machinery has a cost: a schema that does not fit produces confident, systematic errors, which is exactly what Bartlett's distorted recall demonstrates.


55.4.2 Compositionality and systematic generalisation

Compositionality means the meaning of a complex expression is determined by its parts and how they are combined, so that if you know what "jump" means and what "twice" means, you immediately know what "jump twice" means.

Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn made this the centre of a 1988 argument against connectionism, claiming that neural networks lack systematicity - the property that the ability to entertain one thought guarantees the ability to entertain its recombinations - and are therefore inadequate as models of the mind.

Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni made the challenge empirically testable in 2018 with SCAN, a small language of navigation commands where training and test sets are split so that success requires recombining known words in new ways, and standard sequence-to-sequence networks failed catastrophically despite near-perfect training accuracy.

In a 2023 Nature paper Lake and Baroni reported that a network given meta-learning for compositionality - trained across a stream of small artificial languages so that recombining is the skill being learned rather than any one language - matched or exceeded human performance on these tests.

This is genuinely important but it is contested rather than settled: papers in 2025 and 2026 argue that the meta-learning result is highly sensitive to the distribution of episodes seen during meta-training and degrades outside it, so Fodor and Pylyshyn's challenge is weakened but not closed.

For human cognition the corresponding evidence is that people generalise compositionally from a handful of examples in exactly these tasks, which is the behavioural fact any neural account has to explain.


55.4.3 Symbol-like operations in neural populations

If thought is compositional, individual neurons and populations must somehow implement operations that look like manipulating symbols and binding values to variables.

Earl Miller and colleagues provided a founding result in 2001 in Nature, recording single neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex and showing that individual cells coded an abstract rule - match versus non-match - independently of which particular pictures were shown, which is a rule detached from content.

Andreas Nieder and colleagues extended this in a 2010 PNAS paper: monkeys switching between "greater than" and "less than" rules had prefrontal neurons that coded the rule itself, and the animals generalised to set sizes never previously presented, indicating an abstract mathematical principle rather than memorised pairings.

The most prevalent signal in randomly sampled prefrontal cells in that study was the rule, not the sensory input, which is a striking statement about what prefrontal cortex is for.

Critically, this is not evidence that the brain contains literal symbols: Nicolas Rougier, Randall O'Reilly and colleagues argued in a 2005 PNAS paper titled "Rules without symbols" that a network with gated working memory and reinforcement learning develops abstract rule-like representations without any symbolic apparatus being built in.

Population-level work, including studies of variable binding through distinct neural subspaces and 2025 work by Rikhye, Halassa and colleagues showing that thalamic nuclei select abstract rules and shape prefrontal dynamics, is pushing toward mechanisms, but how variables are bound to values in biological tissue remains genuinely unsolved.


55.4.4 The gap between human and machine generalisation

Francois Chollet introduced the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) in his 2019 paper "On the Measure of Intelligence", as a benchmark of grid puzzles where each task is solved from two or three examples and each task is designed to be novel, so that memorised training data cannot help.

His argument was that intelligence should be measured as skill acquisition efficiency - how little experience you need - rather than as skill itself, because a system with unlimited training data can appear competent without generalising at all.

The empirical gap was large and public: for several years leading language models scored near zero to a few per cent on ARC while ordinary people solved most tasks, and the H-ARC dataset published in 2025, collecting attempts from over 1700 people across all 800 original tasks, gave the field a proper human baseline for the first time.

The gap has narrowed sharply since: reasoning-trained systems have made rapid progress on ARC-AGI-1, prompting the release of ARC-AGI-2 in 2025 as a harder successor, and by 2026 the strongest reported systems approach average human accuracy on the original set.

Whether that constitutes closing the gap is disputed - the same 2025 and 2026 analyses that report the scores also report qualitative differences in how the failures are distributed, with humans and machines finding different tasks hard, which suggests different underlying strategies rather than convergence.

The honest position is that the benchmark has proved a moving target and a genuinely useful one, and that the interesting question has shifted from whether machines can score well to whether they get there by abstraction or by search over an enormous hypothesis space.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Reasoning is not one operation but several - deduction, induction, abduction, causal inference and probabilistic judgement - which overlap in a frontoparietal network while differing in emphasis, and which the brain implements with no single dedicated reasoning organ.

The apparent irrationality catalogued by Tversky and Kahneman is real and replicable in its core cases, but its interpretation is contested, with Gigerenzer's ecological rationality showing that simple heuristics can beat complex models under uncertainty and Lieder and Griffiths recasting shortcuts as the optimal use of limited computation.

Problem solving works in two registers: systematic search through a problem space with means-ends analysis, as Newell and Simon described, and sudden restructuring, whose neural correlate Beeman and Kounios located in right anterior superior temporal cortex, with expertise substituting learned pattern recognition for search.

Frontopolar cortex, roughly Brodmann area 10, recurs across relational integration and the holding of pending subgoals, which may reflect one shared operation of maintaining and combining multiple representations.

Abstraction pays off because schemas accelerate learning - Tse and Morris showed one-trial learning and forty-eight-hour consolidation for schema-consistent facts - while the same schemas produce confident systematic distortion when they do not fit.

The compositionality debate begun by Fodor and Pylyshyn in 1988 remains open, and the human-machine generalisation gap measured by ARC has narrowed dramatically without settling whether machines have learned to abstract or merely to search.


PART TEN. EMOTION, MOTIVATION, AND SOCIAL COGNITION


CHAPTER 56. EMOTION (CORE)

This chapter is about what an emotion is, what the brain does when one occurs, and how we know.

Emotion is the part of mental life that is most obvious from the inside and most slippery from the outside.

Everyone knows what fear feels like, yet a century of careful work has failed to produce a single agreed definition, a single agreed brain circuit, or a single agreed measurement.

The chapter matters because emotion is not a decoration on top of thinking - it steers attention, fixes memory, and biases judgement, and because the leading theories genuinely disagree with one another in ways a learner should see plainly rather than have smoothed over.

We will move from theory, to circuits, to the interaction with cognition, to measurement, and at each step we will say where the evidence is strong and where it is contested.


56.1 Theories of emotion

A theory of emotion has to answer a specific question: what is the relationship between the situation, the body's reaction, and the feeling.

The four positions below are the historically dominant answers, and they are still, in updated form, the live options in the field today.

Note before we begin that the word affect is used throughout as a technical term meaning the raw, general pleasantness or unpleasantness plus activation of a mental state, without any particular emotion label attached to it.


56.1.1 James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, and Schachter-Singer

William James, writing in 1884, and the Danish physician Carl Lange, writing independently at about the same time, proposed what became the James-Lange theory: the emotion is the perception of the bodily change, not its cause.

On this view you do not tremble because you are afraid; you are afraid because you notice yourself trembling, and if you strip away the racing heart and the tight stomach nothing recognisable as fear is left.

Walter Cannon and his student Philip Bard attacked this in the 1920s and 1930s with the Cannon-Bard theory, arguing that the body's reactions are too slow, too similar across emotions, and too dispensable to be the source of feeling, and that instead the thalamus dispatches signals to body and cortex at roughly the same time so that feeling and bodily response are parallel effects of a common cause.

Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's 1962 two-factor theory attempted a compromise: general bodily arousal supplies the intensity of an emotion, and a cognitive appraisal of the situation supplies its identity, so that the same adrenaline surge is read as euphoria in one room and anger in another.

The honest verdict is that all three are partly right and none survives intact - Schachter and Singer's original experiment has been hard to replicate cleanly, but the modern consensus that bodily signals contribute to feeling while context and concepts determine which feeling it is, is essentially a refined two-factor position.


56.1.2 Basic emotion theory and its evidence

Basic emotion theory, associated above all with Paul Ekman and with Carroll Izard, holds that a small set of emotions - typically anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise - are biologically given, evolved packages, each with its own facial expression, physiology, and brain basis.

The flagship evidence was Ekman's 1971 fieldwork with the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, a group with almost no exposure to Western media, who nonetheless matched stories to the expected Western facial expressions at rates far above chance.

The strongest criticism is methodological: James Russell argued from the 1990s that the forced-choice format, in which a participant must pick one of six supplied labels, artificially inflates agreement, and Maria Gendron, Lisa Feldman Barrett and colleagues found that when Himba participants in Namibia were simply asked to sort photographs freely, they sorted them by behaviour and situation rather than into the six Western categories.

A large multi-author review led by Barrett in 2019, published in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, concluded that one cannot reliably infer a person's emotional state from their facial movements alone.

Defenders reply that the theory was always about coordinated response tendencies rather than obligatory facial displays, and that some cross-cultural regularity is real even if weaker than first claimed - this is a genuinely open dispute, not a settled defeat.


56.1.3 Dimensional models: valence and arousal

Dimensional models drop discrete categories altogether and describe every affective state by its position on a small number of continuous axes.

James Russell's 1980 circumplex model uses two: valence, meaning how pleasant or unpleasant the state is, and arousal, meaning how activated or sleepy it is, arranged so that states fall around the rim of a circle.

Anger and fear sit in the unpleasant, high-arousal quadrant; contentment sits in the pleasant, low-arousal quadrant; and everything shades continuously into its neighbours rather than snapping into a box.

The model's practical advantages are considerable - it is the backbone of the International Affective Picture System stimulus norms, of most wearable-sensor affect research, and of affective computing generally - and valence and arousal reliably emerge as the first two factors when people rate emotion words.

Its weakness is equally clear: two dimensions cannot distinguish anger from fear from disgust, which differ enormously in what they make a person do, so the model buys generality at the cost of resolution.


56.1.4 The theory of constructed emotion and the critique of essentialism

Lisa Feldman Barrett's theory of constructed emotion, set out in a 2017 paper in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience and in her book How Emotions Are Made, argues that the brain does not contain dedicated fear or anger circuits waiting to fire.

Instead the brain continuously predicts the causes of its own sensory and bodily signals, and an emotion is what happens when it categorises a bundle of interoceptive and situational evidence using an emotion concept it learned from its culture - interoception being the sense of the body's internal state, such as heart rate, gut, and breathing.

The critique aimed at basic emotion theory is a critique of essentialism, the assumption that a category name like anger must correspond to a single underlying essence in nature; Barrett's answer is that anger is a population of highly variable instances held together by a concept, in the way that the category vegetable is.

The theory's chief empirical support is the repeated failure of meta-analyses to find consistent, specific facial, autonomic, or neural markers for the classical categories, plus evidence that emotion vocabulary and cultural context shape what people perceive and report.

Its chief vulnerability is falsifiability - critics such as Ralph Adolphs, and the evolutionary-perspective analysis of van Heijst, Kret and Ploeger published in 2025, argue that the framework is flexible enough to absorb almost any result, and that shared mammalian defensive machinery is being underweighted.

The reader should hold both facts at once: the constructionist critique of the old evidence is strong, and the constructionist replacement is not yet decisively proven.


56.2 Circuits of affect

We now turn from what emotion is to what the brain actually does.

The honest summary of the last thirty years is that specific circuits for specific behaviours are well established, while the mapping from those circuits onto felt emotions is not.


56.2.1 Amygdala nuclei, threat learning, and their limits as a fear centre

The amygdala is an almond-shaped cluster of nuclei buried in the front of each temporal lobe, and it is not one thing: the lateral and basal nuclei, together called the basolateral complex, receive sensory input and are where associations are formed, while the central nucleus is the output station that drives bodily and behavioural reactions.

Joseph LeDoux's rat work from the 1980s onward mapped the canonical threat-learning pathway in detail: a tone paired with a mild shock strengthens synapses in the lateral amygdala, and the central nucleus then commands freezing, blood-pressure change, and stress-hormone release.

In humans, patient S.M., a woman with bilateral amygdala destruction from Urbach-Wiethe disease studied by Justin Feinstein, Ralph Adolphs, Daniel Tranel and Antonio Damasio, showed no fear of snakes, haunted houses, or threatening films.

But the same group's 2013 Nature Neuroscience report is the crucial correction: when S.M. and two amygdala-lesioned twins inhaled air containing thirty-five percent carbon dioxide, all three had full-blown panic attacks, with terror of suffocation and attempts to escape.

The amygdala is therefore necessary for learning about and reacting to external threats, and not necessary for fear as such - which is precisely why LeDoux now argues in print that calling it the fear centre is a category error, and prefers the term defensive survival circuit.


56.2.2 Ventromedial prefrontal cortex and extinction

Extinction is what happens when a cue that once predicted danger is presented repeatedly without the danger: the fearful response fades, but crucially the original memory is not erased, it is overlaid by a new, competing safety memory that is fragile and context-bound.

Mohammed Milad and Gregory Quirk showed in Nature in 2002 that neurons in the rat infralimbic cortex, a subdivision of medial prefrontal cortex, fire to the tone only on the day after extinction training, when the animal is recalling that it is safe, making their activity a marker of extinction memory rather than of extinction itself.

The human counterpart is the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, sitting behind and below the forehead, and Milad and colleagues showed in 2007 that recall of extinction activates ventromedial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus together, the hippocampus supplying the information about which context is the safe one.

This is the mechanistic backbone of exposure therapy, and it also explains the therapy's characteristic failure mode: because extinction is a new memory rather than a deletion, fear returns when the context changes, when time passes, or after a single reminder of the original threat.

Later optogenetic work, which uses light to switch genetically targeted neurons on or off with millisecond precision, has complicated the simple story - silencing infralimbic cortex during extinction training impairs later recall, but silencing it at the moment of test often does not, so its role appears to be in consolidating the safety memory more than in expressing it.


56.2.3 Insula, interoception, and feeling

The insula is a slab of cortex hidden inside the lateral sulcus, the deep fold between the temporal and frontal lobes, and it is the primary destination for signals about the body's internal condition.

Arthur D. Craig's influential proposal, developed across papers from 2002 and summarised in a 2009 Nature Reviews Neuroscience article, is that a map of bodily state arrives at the posterior insula and is progressively re-represented forward, so that by the anterior insula it has been integrated with context, motivation, and social information to yield a felt moment of subjective awareness.

Hugo Critchley and colleagues supplied a key piece of supporting evidence in 2004, showing that activity in right anterior insula tracked how accurately individuals could count their own heartbeats, and that this accuracy predicted their reported emotional intensity.

Consistent with the account, the anterior insula shows up in imaging of essentially every emotion, of empathy for others' pain, and of uncertainty and risk.

The strong version of Craig's claim, that the anterior insula is where feelings are made, is contested: the region is also active during ordinary attention and effortful task control, so its ubiquity may reflect a general role in salience and prediction rather than a dedicated seat of feeling, and patients with insular damage are impaired but not devoid of emotion.


56.2.4 Periaqueductal grey and defensive survival circuits

The periaqueductal grey is a column of grey matter wrapped around the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain, and it is the ancient machinery that actually executes defensive behaviour.

Its subdivisions are functionally distinct in a way that is worth learning as a concrete example of how the brain packages behaviour: the ventrolateral column produces freezing and the shutdown, hypoactive response to inescapable threat, while the dorsal and dorsolateral columns produce flight, fight, and a surge of blood pressure.

The central nucleus of the amygdala reaches the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey through an inhibitory relay, and freezing is produced by disinhibition, meaning that the output neurons are released from a brake rather than being directly driven.

Work by Tiago Branco, Cornelius Gross and colleagues, including a 2016 Nature review of midbrain defensive circuits, showed that these circuits can be driven directly, bypassing the amygdala - and eLife-published research on foraging rats found periaqueductal grey stimulation driving amygdala activity, which is the reverse of the textbook hierarchy.

This is the anatomical grounding for LeDoux's survival-circuit framework: the brain contains conserved, sub-cortical systems for defence, feeding, thermoregulation and reproduction, and these operate whether or not any conscious feeling accompanies them.


56.3 Emotion and cognition interacting

Emotion and cognition are not separate systems that occasionally collide.

The evidence in this section shows emotional significance reaching into perception, memory, and judgement at almost every stage, and shows cognition reaching back to change emotion in return.


56.3.1 Emotional modulation of attention and perception

Emotionally significant stimuli capture attention involuntarily and hold it, and the cost of that capture is measurable.

The clearest demonstration is emotion-induced blindness, described by Steven Most and colleagues: when pictures flash by in a rapid stream, an emotionally arousing image makes the viewer miss a target appearing a few hundred milliseconds later, even when they are trying hard to ignore the emotional picture and know it is irrelevant.

The related emotional attentional blink shows the same competition, and Adam Anderson and Elizabeth Phelps reported in Nature in 2001 that patients with amygdala damage lose the normal advantage that emotional words enjoy in these rapid streams.

There is an important qualification, however: when the competing task loads perception heavily enough, both amygdala responses and the electrical brain responses to emotional stimuli shrink, so emotional capture is powerful but not fully automatic and not immune to attention.

The functional reading is straightforward - a system that lets a snake outcompete a shopping list for processing resources is a system that keeps its owner alive, at the price of occasional blindness to everything else.


56.3.2 Emotional memory enhancement and the amygdala-hippocampus interaction

People remember emotionally arousing events better and for longer than neutral ones, and the mechanism is now unusually well specified.

James McGaugh and Larry Cahill's account is that arousal triggers release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, that noradrenaline acts on beta-adrenergic receptors in the basolateral amygdala, and that the amygdala then modulates consolidation - the slow process by which a fresh, fragile memory is stabilised - in the hippocampus and elsewhere, rather than storing the memory itself.

The decisive test is pharmacological: Cahill and colleagues showed in 1994 that propranolol, a drug that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, abolishes the memory advantage for an emotional story while leaving memory for a matched neutral story untouched.

Imaging by Strange and Dolan, published in PNAS in 2004, showed the same drug abolishing the enhanced amygdala and hippocampal responses that normally accompany emotional encoding.

Later work extended the effect to retrieval, finding that propranolol given at the time of remembering reduces the emotional memory advantage and that the reduction persists a day later when the drug is gone, which is one line of evidence behind the still-controversial proposal to use the drug to blunt traumatic memories.


56.3.3 Mood, affective bias, and judgement

Mood differs from emotion in being longer, milder, and typically not about any particular object, and it colours judgement in ways people rarely notice.

Norbert Schwarz and Gerald Clore's 1983 affect-as-information experiment is the classic case: participants telephoned on sunny days reported higher life satisfaction than those called on rainy days, but the effect vanished when the caller first mentioned the weather, because attributing the mood to the sky removed its apparent relevance to the question.

The interpretive point is subtle and important - the mood is not merely making happy memories easier to retrieve, it is being read, mistakenly, as evidence about the thing being judged.

In clinical terms this is the engine of affective bias in depression, where negative mood produces mood-congruent recall, pessimistic estimates of risk, and a tendency to interpret ambiguous faces and sentences as hostile or as rejecting, which in turn sustains the mood.

Mood also changes processing style rather than just content, with negative mood tending to promote narrow, detail-focused, systematic thinking and positive mood promoting broader, more heuristic and creative processing, although the size and reliability of these style effects has been debated.


56.3.4 Emotion regulation: reappraisal, suppression, distraction

James Gross's process model organises regulation strategies by the point in the emotion sequence at which they intervene, which is the model's main contribution.

Reappraisal is antecedent-focused: you change the meaning of the situation before the emotion is fully formed, telling yourself the crying woman in the photograph is at a wedding rather than a funeral, and it reliably lowers reported negative feeling and, in the imaging work of Kevin Ochsner and Gross from 2002 onward, raises activity in lateral and medial prefrontal cortex while lowering amygdala activity.

Expressive suppression is response-focused: you let the emotion arrive and then hide the outward signs, and it is the strategy with the worst profile - it reduces the visible expression while leaving or increasing the felt emotion and the physiological arousal, and it impairs memory for the situation and reduces rapport with the people present.

Distraction works by loading working memory with something else so that the emotional stimulus is never fully processed, and it is more effective than reappraisal for very intense stimuli but does not build any lasting change in how the situation is understood.

A caution about the neural evidence is warranted: Buhle and colleagues' 2014 meta-analysis of reappraisal studies found the prefrontal increases reliable but the amygdala decreases less consistent than the standard summary implies, and multivariate work has found that suppression recruits insular and fronto-temporo-cerebellar patterns quite unlike the reappraisal network, so the strategies are not variations on one control mechanism.


56.4 Measuring emotion

Every claim in this chapter rests on a measurement, and the measurements are weaker than the claims usually admit.

This section is about that gap.


56.4.1 Subjective report and its limits

Asking a person how they feel remains the only direct access anyone has to emotional experience, and it should not be dismissed - it is the criterion against which every other measure is validated.

Its limits are nonetheless serious: retrospective reports are reconstructions shaped by current mood and by beliefs about what the episode should have been like, and Daniel Kahneman's peak-end work showed that remembered pain tracks the worst moment and the final moment while largely ignoring duration.

Demand characteristics, meaning the participant's guess about what the experiment wants, push ratings toward the expected result, and vocabulary differs across individuals and cultures so that the same word does not denote the same state for everyone.

Alexithymia, a trait involving difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, illustrates the deepest problem, and recent factor-analytic work has found that the most-used questionnaire's difficulty-identifying-feelings scale loads heavily on general distress, so even the instrument for measuring poor introspection depends on introspection.

Experience sampling, which pings people at random moments to report the state they are in right now, substantially reduces recall bias and is now the preferred method, at the cost of participant burden and of the risk that being asked repeatedly changes what is being measured.


56.4.2 Peripheral physiology and its low specificity

Peripheral physiology means the measurable activity of the body outside the brain: heart rate, skin conductance, which is the rise in electrical conductivity of the skin when sweat glands activate, blood pressure, pupil size, respiration, and facial muscle activity recorded by electromyography.

These measures are objective, continuous, and hard to fake, which is why they are used everywhere from laboratory studies to consumer wearables.

Their fatal weakness for emotion research is specificity: skin conductance is essentially a pure index of arousal and cannot tell fear from excitement from anger, and heart rate rises for many emotions and for climbing stairs.

Erika Siegel, Barrett and colleagues published a meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin in 2018 covering over two hundred studies and found no consistent, specific autonomic signature for any of the classical emotion categories, with within-category variability as large as between-category differences.

Others, including Sylvia Kreibig in a 2010 review and Behnke and colleagues in a 2022 meta-analysis of positive emotions, argue that specificity does appear when finer emotion subtypes and better-controlled inductions are used, so the fairest statement is that peripheral physiology carries real but coarse information, and that inferring a named emotion from it is not defensible.


56.4.3 Multivariate neural signatures of affective states

Traditional functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) analysis asks whether one region is more active in one condition than another, which is why it kept finding the amygdala in fear studies and yet could not predict fear in an individual.

Multivariate pattern analysis inverts the question: it uses machine learning to find a distributed pattern across many thousands of locations that predicts the state, and it is far more sensitive because information can be carried by the pattern even where no single region shifts its average.

Luke Chang, Tor Wager and colleagues published the Picture-Induced Negative Emotion Signature in PLOS Biology in 2015, a pattern that predicted the intensity of negative feeling in new individuals with around ninety-three percent accuracy in cross-validation and, importantly, did not respond to physical pain, showing it was not a generic salience or arousal detector.

Philip Kragel and Kevin LaBar reported in 2015 that patterns for several emotion categories were separable from one another and from patterns for arousal alone, which is a genuine empirical challenge to the strong constructionist claim that there is nothing category-specific to find.

Two cautions apply: the signatures span cortical and subcortical systems rather than localising to any classical emotion region, which supports the distributed picture; and a signature trained on one induction method, such as aversive photographs, often transfers poorly to another, such as recalled autobiographical events, so what has been decoded may be the paradigm as much as the emotion.


56.4.4 Animal models and the conscious feeling problem

Almost everything known about the mechanism of threat learning comes from rodents, because only in animals can circuits be lesioned, recorded, and optogenetically controlled.

The problem is that a rat can be observed to freeze but cannot be asked what it feels, and freezing is a behaviour, not a feeling.

Jaak Panksepp argued from decades of work on subcortical circuits that the affective states themselves are ancient and shared, that stimulating the same midbrain systems produces the same defensive and appetitive behaviour and the same reported feelings in humans, and that denying feelings to other mammals is unwarranted anthropodenial.

LeDoux, with Richard Brown in a 2017 PNAS paper, took the opposing higher-order position: the survival circuits are indeed conserved, but the conscious feeling of fear requires a cortical, higher-order representation of one's own state in relation to a self, so what the rat has is a defensive response and not fear.

The practical consequence is real rather than philosophical - if the two are separable, then a drug that reduces freezing in a rat may leave human anxious feeling untouched, which is one plausible reason why anxiolytic drug development has repeatedly failed to translate from animal screens to the clinic, and this debate remains unresolved.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Emotion has no single agreed definition, and the four historical theories - James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, two-factor, and basic emotion theory - have each been partly vindicated and partly refuted, with dimensional and constructionist accounts now the main live alternatives.

The circuits are real and well mapped at the level of behaviour, but the amygdala is a threat-learning and threat-response structure rather than a fear centre, as patient S.M.'s intact panic under carbon dioxide demonstrates, and the periaqueductal grey executes defence with or without cortical involvement.

Emotion is woven into cognition rather than separate from it: it captures attention at a measurable cost, it enhances memory through a noradrenergic amygdala mechanism that propranolol can block, and it biases judgement by being misread as information about whatever is being judged.

Regulation strategies are not interchangeable, with reappraisal changing the felt emotion and suppression only hiding it while worsening the physiology and the memory.

Every measurement is limited - self-report is reconstructive, peripheral physiology has too little specificity to name an emotion, multivariate neural signatures are promising but paradigm-bound, and animal work cannot settle whether a feeling accompanies the circuit.

The reader should leave with the discipline's central tension clearly in view: the mechanisms of emotional response are increasingly well understood, while the nature of emotional experience remains genuinely open.


CHAPTER 57. MOTIVATION, REWARD, AND HOMEOSTASIS (CORE)


This chapter is about why brains do anything at all.

Perception and memory tell an animal what is out there and what happened before, but motivation is the machinery that turns that knowledge into movement toward some things and away from others.

We will take apart the word reward into separate components that can be pulled apart in the laboratory, look at the bodily drives - hunger, thirst, temperature - that set the price of everything else, follow stress as it reshapes thinking on timescales from seconds to years, and end with addiction, which is best understood as this whole system running off its rails.

The material matters because almost every psychiatric condition that costs people their lives involves a fault somewhere in this circuitry, and because the folk idea that we simply do what feels good turns out to be, in a precise and testable way, wrong.


57.1 Reward and its components

Reward is not one thing.

In everyday speech the word bundles together at least three separable processes: the pleasure something gives, the pull it exerts on behaviour, and the learning it produces about what predicts what.

Over roughly forty years, work in rodents and humans has shown that these three can be surgically and pharmacologically separated, which means the brain does not contain a single reward centre so much as a set of interacting subsystems that usually agree and occasionally do not.

This section lays out those components, and the fourth quantity that any honest account of motivation must include - effort, the cost side of the ledger.


57.1.1 Wanting and liking as dissociable processes

Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson, working at the University of Michigan from the late 1980s onward, proposed that reward decomposes into liking (the hedonic impact, the actual pleasure of a stimulus), wanting (the motivational pull that makes an animal work for it), and learning (the associations formed along the way).

Their measurement tool for liking was the taste reactivity test, in which sweet solutions placed in the mouth produce a stereotyped pattern of tongue protrusions in rats and human infants alike, while bitter solutions produce gapes - a readout of hedonic reaction that does not depend on the animal choosing anything.

The critical finding is that these two can be pulled apart: rats whose dopamine (a neurotransmitter, a chemical messenger between neurons, made in the midbrain and released into the striatum) has been almost entirely depleted will starve in front of food they still show normal liking reactions to, while animals with genetically elevated dopamine work harder for food without liking it any more.

Berridge summarised the case in an influential 2007 review in Psychopharmacology, arguing against the then-standard view that dopamine is the brain's pleasure chemical.

The current consensus is that mesolimbic dopamine - the projection from the ventral tegmental area of the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens in the ventral striatum - is largely a wanting system, and that pleasure itself is generated elsewhere.

This is not universally accepted in its strong form; a large body of work following Wolfram Schultz treats midbrain dopamine primarily as a reward prediction error signal for learning, and the field continues to argue about how much of dopamine's role is motivational versus instructional.


57.1.2 Hedonic hotspots and opioid signalling

If dopamine does not generate pleasure, something must.

Berridge's laboratory mapped the brain systematically with microinjections and found that liking reactions to sucrose are amplified only from a handful of very small sites, roughly a cubic millimetre each in the rat, which they called hedonic hotspots.

The two best characterised are in the rostrodorsal quadrant of the medial shell of the nucleus accumbens and in the caudolateral half of the ventral pallidum, and Susana Peciña and Berridge, with Kyle Smith, showed in a 2007 Journal of Neuroscience paper that these two hotspots need each other - blocking one prevents the other from enhancing liking, so they behave as a single circuit.

The chemistry involved is opioid: stimulation of the mu-opioid receptor, the same receptor morphine acts on, roughly doubles hedonic reactions, and a 2014 study from the same group found that delta and kappa opioid stimulation of the accumbens hotspot does much the same.

Further hotspots have since been reported in a rostromedial part of the orbitofrontal cortex, a far posterior zone of the insula, and the parabrachial nucleus of the brainstem, and preprint work in 2025 extended the map to the olfactory tubercle.

The striking asymmetry is that pleasure is generated by a scattered set of tiny, chemically specific islands, while wanting is generated by a large and robust system - which may be part of why pleasure is fragile and craving is not.


57.1.3 Incentive salience and cue-triggered motivation

Incentive salience is the technical term for the property a cue acquires when it has been paired with reward: the cue stops being merely informative and becomes attractive in itself, grabbing attention and triggering approach.

The cleanest laboratory demonstration is Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT), in which an animal trained separately to press a lever for food and to associate a tone with food will press harder when the tone plays, even though the tone was never paired with the lever - pure cue-triggered wanting, with no new learning and no reward delivered.

PIT is abolished by inactivating the ventral tegmental area and attenuated by blocking dopamine receptors in the nucleus accumbens, which ties the effect firmly to the mesolimbic system.

A second and revealing phenomenon is sign-tracking: given a lever that predicts food, some rats approach and nibble the lever itself rather than the food cup, treating the predictor as if it were the reward, while others (goal-trackers) go straight to the cup.

Sign-trackers, studied extensively by Shelly Flagel, Robinson and colleagues, attribute more incentive salience to cues, depend on accumbens core dopamine to do so, and are more vulnerable to cue-induced relapse - a laboratory model of why a person can be undone by walking past a particular bar.

The basolateral and central amygdala help decide which cue, at which moment, gets the motivational charge.


57.1.4 Reward and effort as coupled quantities

No account of motivation works without the cost side, because a reward that requires climbing a wall is not the same offer as the same reward on a plate.

John Salamone's laboratory built the standard test, a T-maze in which the arm holding four food pellets is blocked by a barrier the rat must climb while the other arm holds two pellets on an open path.

Normal rats climb; rats with dopamine depleted from the nucleus accumbens switch to the small easy reward, yet if the barrier is removed they still prefer the large one and they still eat with normal relish.

That double result is one of the strongest single arguments that accumbens dopamine encodes willingness to expend effort rather than pleasure - Salamone and Mercè Correa set out the argument at length in a 2012 Neuron review.

The anterior cingulate cortex, a region of medial frontal cortex, is the other pillar: lesions and inactivations there also push animals toward the low-effort option, and human neuroimaging consistently finds anterior cingulate activity scaling with both physical and cognitive effort costs.

Clinically this matters, because apathy and anhedonia in depression, schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease often look less like an inability to enjoy and more like an unwillingness to pay - a shift in the exchange rate between effort and reward.


57.2 Homeostatic and allostatic drives

Motivation does not float free of the body.

The value of a glass of water is set by how dehydrated you are, and the brain contains dedicated cell populations that measure bodily variables and convert deviations into urgent behavioural states.

This section moves from the classical homeostatic picture - detect an error, correct it - to the more recent and more demanding claim that regulation is fundamentally predictive, anticipating needs rather than reacting to them.


57.2.1 Hunger, thirst, thermoregulation, and their neural controllers

Hunger is governed largely by two opposed populations in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, a structure at the base of the brain sitting just above the pituitary gland.

Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons fire when the body is in caloric deficit, and switching them on artificially - with optogenetics, which uses light-sensitive proteins to control neurons, or with chemogenetics, which uses engineered receptors and a drug - makes a well-fed mouse eat voraciously within seconds; proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons do the opposite, and their activation suppresses feeding even in a fasted animal.
