Both populations read circulating signals of energy state, notably leptin from fat tissue and ghrelin from the stomach, and a 2024 Nature Metabolism study by Yang and colleagues characterised how their reciprocal activity coordinates feeding with metabolic rate.

Thirst is handled by the lamina terminalis, a strip of tissue at the front wall of the third ventricle comprising the subfornical organ, the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, and the median preoptic nucleus; the first two lie outside the blood-brain barrier and can therefore sample blood osmolality directly, which is why they can detect dehydration in real time.

Work by Yuki Oka, Charles Zuker and others showed that stimulating subfornical organ thirst neurons makes a fully hydrated mouse drink, and - importantly - that these neurons are switched off within seconds of drinking, long before any water is absorbed, meaning the brain uses swallowing itself as a fast predictive signal.

Thermoregulation runs through the preoptic area of the hypothalamus, which integrates skin and core temperature signals and drives shivering, sweating, vasoconstriction and, crucially, the behavioural responses of seeking shade or putting on a coat.

The common architecture is worth noting: a specialised sensor population, a fast anticipatory shut-off, and an output that recruits behaviour as well as physiology.


57.2.2 Drive states as modulators of perception and decision

A drive state does not just add an urge on top of unchanged perception; it changes how the world looks.

Edmund Rolls demonstrated in monkeys and later in humans that orbitofrontal cortex neurons responding to the sight, smell, taste and texture of food reduce their response as the animal is fed to satiety, and do so selectively for the food just eaten - the neural signature of sensory-specific satiety, the everyday fact that you have no more appetite for the main course but plenty for dessert.

This selectivity is measurable in humans: after eating a meal matching one of two food odours, participants shift their choices toward low intensities of that odour while continuing to choose high intensities of the other, an effect tracked by orbitofrontal activity.

The older term for this is alliesthesia, coined by Michel Cabanac in 1971 - the observation that the pleasantness of an identical stimulus, such as a sugar solution or a warm bath, depends on internal state.

A 2018 eLife study by Sias and colleagues found that attenuating orbitofrontal cortex prevented rodents from updating the value of a food after a change in hunger, which suggests the orbitofrontal cortex is not simply reporting current pleasantness but computing what a reward will now be worth.

The practical lesson is that value is a state-dependent construction, not a stable tag attached to objects.


57.2.3 Allostasis and predictive regulation

Homeostasis, Walter Cannon's term from 1926, describes regulation as error correction around a fixed set point, like a thermostat.

Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer proposed allostasis in 1988 as an alternative: the body's parameters are not held constant but are varied in advance to meet anticipated demand, so that heart rate rises before exertion and cortisol rises before waking.

Sterling's 2020 book and his 2012 Physiology and Behavior paper argue that this predictive strategy is far more efficient, because correcting an error after the fact is metabolically expensive while pre-empting it is cheap, and that the brain is therefore best thought of as an organ for regulating the body rather than for representing the world.

The framework has a dark side that has proved clinically useful: Bruce McEwen's concept of allostatic load, the cumulative wear on organs and brain from a regulatory system kept chronically mobilised, which links social adversity to measurable physiological damage.

It is fair to record that allostasis remains partly a reframing rather than a rival set of equations - critics note that it is often used descriptively and that predictive homeostasis was already implicit in older physiology - but the emphasis on anticipation has demonstrably changed how the field models drive.


57.2.4 Interoceptive inference and motivated behaviour

Interoception is the sensing of the body's internal state - heartbeat, breath, gut distension, blood chemistry - as distinct from exteroception, the sensing of the outside world.

Anil Seth's interoceptive inference proposal, from around 2012, and Lisa Feldman Barrett and Karen Quigley's related work, treat interoception as predictive: the anterior insula, a cortical region folded deep inside the lateral sulcus, issues predictions about expected bodily signals, compares them with what actually arrives, and treats the mismatch as a prediction error.

On this account a feeling such as hunger, breathlessness or anxiety is not a raw sensation but the brain's best inference about the state of the body, and motivated action is one of the ways the error gets resolved - you can update the model, or you can move the body until the prediction comes true, which is what active inference calls acting on the world to fulfil an expectation.

The affective colouring of these states appears to depend on connections between anterior insula and the amygdala, ventral tegmental area and ventral striatum, which is the bridge back to the reward machinery of section 57.1.

Barrett and colleagues' 2022 work in Network Neuroscience places allostatic and interoceptive processing at the top of the cortical hierarchy rather than at its periphery, and Paul Fletcher and Sarah Garfinkel among others have applied the framework to depression, anxiety and eating disorders.

The theory is elegant and generative, and its supporting evidence is at present largely correlational; strong causal tests of the specific claim that insular activity is a prediction signal rather than a sensory one are still thin.


57.3 Stress and cognition

Stress is the name for the coordinated response to a demand that threatens, or is predicted to threaten, the body's regulatory balance.

It is not intrinsically bad - the response evolved because it works - but its effects on cognition are strongly dose-dependent and time-dependent, helping on some tasks at some intensities and devastating on others.

This section follows the hormonal machinery, then the acute effects, then what happens when the system never switches off, and finally what distinguishes the people in whom it does less damage.


57.3.1 The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a three-stage hormonal cascade.

Parvocellular neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), often together with vasopressin, into a small private blood supply called the hypophyseal portal circulation that runs directly to the anterior pituitary gland.

CRH makes pituitary corticotroph cells release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into the general bloodstream, and ACTH reaches the cortex of the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys, and triggers release of the glucocorticoid hormone cortisol (corticosterone in rodents).

Cortisol mobilises glucose, suppresses non-urgent functions such as digestion, reproduction and immune activity, and acts on the brain.

The system shuts itself off by negative feedback: cortisol binds mineralocorticoid receptors and glucocorticoid receptors in the hippocampus, hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing further CRH and ACTH release, partly through slow genomic effects on gene transcription and partly through much faster non-genomic actions.

Two properties matter for later sections - the axis is normally pulsatile, releasing cortisol in roughly hourly bursts with a large peak near waking, and the hippocampus is a major feedback site, so damage there both results from and worsens excess cortisol.

Running in parallel and much faster is the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary response, which releases adrenaline and noradrenaline within seconds, well before cortisol arrives.


57.3.2 Acute stress effects on memory and control

Acute stress does not uniformly impair memory; it shifts which memory system is in charge and which phase is helped.

Encoding and consolidation of emotionally arousing material are typically enhanced by post-learning glucocorticoids acting together with noradrenaline in the basolateral amygdala, an effect established by James McGaugh and Benno Roozendaal - which is why people remember the details of an emergency vividly.

Retrieval, by contrast, is reliably impaired by acute cortisol elevation, a finding from Oliver Wolf, Lars Schwabe and others, and this dissociation explains the common experience of a blank mind in an examination followed by perfect recall an hour later.

Stress also shifts control from flexible, goal-directed, hippocampal and prefrontal strategies toward rigid, habitual, dorsal-striatal ones; Schwabe and Wolf demonstrated this experimentally in humans in 2009, and it is thought to be adaptive under threat and costly afterwards.

Amy Arnsten's work, summarised in a 2009 Nature Reviews Neuroscience paper, showed that even mild uncontrollable stress rapidly weakens prefrontal cortex function through catecholamine signalling cascades, degrading working memory and cognitive flexibility while amygdala-driven responses strengthen.

The picture is a controlled handover: under acute stress the brain trades deliberation for speed and habit.


57.3.3 Chronic stress, structural change, and cognitive cost

When the stress response fails to terminate, the changes become structural.

Bruce McEwen, Ana Magariños and colleagues showed from the early 1990s that weeks of restraint or social stress cause apical dendrites of hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons to retract and debranch, reducing the surface available for synaptic contact, and that in rodents this remodelling is substantially reversible when the stress ends.

John Morrison and Conor Liston reported the parallel finding in medial prefrontal cortex, where dendritic retraction is circuit-specific - the projections to some targets shrink while others are spared - and correlates with impaired attentional shifting.

The amygdala moves the other way: Sumantra Chattarji's group found chronic stress causes dendritic growth and increased spine density in the basolateral amygdala, a structural asymmetry that fits the behavioural profile of degraded control and heightened threat reactivity.

In humans the evidence is more indirect - smaller hippocampal volumes are associated with post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression, but the direction of causation is genuinely disputed, and the twin study by Mark Gilbertson and colleagues in 2002 found that smaller hippocampal volume was present in unexposed identical twins of trauma survivors, implying it can be a pre-existing risk factor rather than only a consequence.

Chronic glucocorticoid exposure also suppresses adult hippocampal neurogenesis in rodents, though the extent and functional significance of adult neurogenesis in humans remains one of the field's live controversies.


57.3.4 Resilience and its correlates

Most people exposed to severe stress do not develop a stress-related disorder, and resilience is now studied as an active process rather than the mere absence of vulnerability.

Steven Southwick and Dennis Charney's work identified a set of biological markers that track who copes: a higher ratio of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), an adrenal steroid that opposes several cortisol actions, to cortisol, and a stronger neuropeptide Y response relative to noradrenaline, both predicted better performance in soldiers undergoing survival training.

At the circuit level, Eric Nestler and Ming-Hu Han's laboratory produced a striking result in mice: resilience to social defeat is not passive but involves an active homeostatic increase in potassium channel currents in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons that stabilises their firing, reported in Cell in 2007 and 2014 - a rare demonstration that resilience has its own positive mechanism.

Nestler and colleagues reviewed the field in Neuron in 2024, emphasising controllability, social support and prefrontal regulation of amygdala reactivity as convergent themes across species.

The candid caveat is that most human resilience markers are correlational and modest in effect size, and that resilience is not a fixed trait of a person but varies with the stressor, the domain and the moment.


57.4 Addiction as a disorder of motivation

Addiction is where every mechanism in this chapter appears at once, distorted.

The reason it belongs in a chapter on motivation rather than one on pleasure is empirical: people with severe addictions routinely report that the drug has stopped being enjoyable long before they can stop taking it.

There are three major theoretical accounts - sensitised wanting, runaway habit, and failed control - and they are better read as complementary descriptions of different stages than as rivals.


57.4.1 Incentive sensitisation theory

Robinson and Berridge published the incentive-sensitisation theory in 1993, and it remains the most direct application of the wanting/liking split.

The claim has three parts: repeated drug exposure produces long-lasting neuroadaptations in the mesolimbic dopamine system that make it hypersensitive, or sensitised, to drugs and drug cues; that system mediates wanting rather than liking; and therefore drug wanting grows enormous while drug liking does not, and may fall.

This accounts for the defining clinical paradox of craving without pleasure, and for the fact that relapse is so often triggered by cues years into abstinence - sensitisation in animals persists for months to a lifetime, far longer than withdrawal.

It also predicts, correctly, that tolerance and sensitisation coexist, since they concern different processes.

Robinson and Berridge published a thirty-years-on assessment in the Annual Review of Psychology in 2025, defending the core claims while acknowledging that direct evidence for mesolimbic sensitisation in humans is harder to obtain than in rats, and that human positron emission tomography studies have often found blunted rather than enhanced striatal dopamine responses in chronic users - a genuine tension the theory addresses by distinguishing baseline dopamine tone from cue-triggered reactivity.


57.4.2 Habit and compulsion accounts

Barry Everitt and Trevor Robbins offered a different emphasis in 2005 and updated it in 2016 in the Annual Review of Psychology: addiction is a progressive loss of behavioural flexibility as drug seeking migrates from goal-directed action to habit to compulsion.

The neural claim is anatomical and specific - control shifts from prefrontal cortex and ventral striatum, which support actions performed for their expected outcome, to dorsal striatum, and within the dorsal striatum from the dorsomedial region toward the dorsolateral region as behaviour becomes automatic, via spiralling connections through the midbrain dopamine cells.

The behavioural signature is that a habit becomes insensitive to outcome devaluation: an animal will keep responding for a drug that has been paired with illness, whereas a goal-directed animal stops.

Compulsion is the further step of persisting despite punishment, which Everitt's group showed emerges only in a minority of rats after prolonged cocaine self-administration - a useful match to the human fact that most users do not become addicted.

The habit account explains automaticity and outcome-insensitivity well; it explains the subjective intensity of craving less well, which is roughly the complementary strength and weakness of incentive sensitisation.

It is also worth flagging that the habit framework has faced replication pressure, with several groups reporting that outcome-devaluation insensitivity in humans is weaker and less reliable than the animal literature suggested.


57.4.3 Prefrontal control failure and craving

Rita Goldstein and Nora Volkow proposed the impaired response inhibition and salience attribution (iRISA) model in 2002, updated in 2011 and again in a 2025 Annual Review of Psychology paper.

Its two limbs are that drug-related cues acquire excessive salience and value while non-drug reinforcers such as food, money and social contact lose value, and that inhibitory control weakens - a combination that leaves a strong pull with a weak brake.

The imaging evidence points to reduced grey matter and reduced task-related activity in anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus in chronic users, alongside heightened responses in orbitofrontal and striatal regions to drug cues.

Volkow's positron emission tomography work also documented reduced striatal dopamine D2 receptor availability across several substances, correlating with reduced prefrontal metabolism, though whether this is cause or consequence is not settled - primate work by Michael Nader suggesting that low D2 availability precedes and predicts cocaine self-administration argues for at least a partly pre-existing vulnerability.

A key clinical implication is that insight itself can be affected, since some of the same prefrontal regions support awareness of one's own state.


57.4.4 Behavioural addictions and the boundary of the concept

If addiction is a disorder of motivational circuitry rather than of a chemical, then behaviours with no drug in them ought in principle to qualify - and the diagnostic manuals have moved, cautiously, in that direction.

The fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), published in 2013, reclassified pathological gambling as gambling disorder and placed it alongside the substance use disorders, the first non-substance condition to be treated as an addiction, while listing internet gaming disorder only as a condition for further study.

The eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), adopted in 2019 and in force from 2022, went further and recognised both gambling disorder and gaming disorder as disorders due to addictive behaviours, gaming disorder requiring impaired control, increasing priority given to gaming, and continuation despite negative consequences, with significant impairment.

Gaming disorder's inclusion was publicly contested, with one group of researchers arguing the evidence base was thin and the risk of pathologising a common hobby real, and another arguing that clinicians needed a diagnosis for patients already presenting with the problem; that debate is not closed.

Food addiction, usually measured with Ashley Gearhardt's Yale Food Addiction Scale, is not a diagnosis in either manual, and the argument turns on whether the addictive agent would be a nutrient, a highly processed food formulation, or the eating behaviour itself - with critics pointing out that binge eating disorder may already account for the clinical phenomena.

Proposed additions such as compulsive sexual behaviour, buying-shopping disorder and social-media use disorder currently lack the neuroimaging and longitudinal evidence that supported gambling, and the honest position is that the concept's boundary is being set by an unfinished negotiation between mechanistic similarity, clinical need, and the risk of medicalising ordinary life.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Reward is not a single quantity: liking, wanting, learning and effort cost are separable, they depend on partly different chemistry and anatomy, and dopamine belongs mainly to wanting and effort rather than to pleasure, which is generated by tiny opioid-sensitive hotspots.

Motivation is anchored in the body by dedicated hypothalamic and circumventricular sensors for hunger, thirst and temperature, and the value of any reward is recomputed against the current internal state rather than fixed to the object.

The best current framing of that regulation is predictive - allostasis and interoceptive inference - which is theoretically powerful but still short of decisive causal evidence.

Stress, through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the faster noradrenergic response, systematically trades deliberation for habit, enhancing emotional consolidation while impairing retrieval and prefrontal control, and when chronic it remodels hippocampus and prefrontal cortex downward while enlarging the amygdala.

Resilience is an active biological process with its own mechanisms, not merely the absence of damage.

Addiction is best read as this whole system distorted - sensitised cue-triggered wanting, behaviour migrating from goal to habit to compulsion in the dorsal striatum, and weakened prefrontal control - and the same logic is what makes gambling, and arguably gaming, defensible as addictions without a drug.


CHAPTER 58. SOCIAL COGNITION (CORE)

Human beings are, before almost anything else, readers of other human beings.

This chapter is about the machinery that makes that reading possible - how the brain picks a person out of a visual scene, works out where that person is looking, guesses what they believe, feels a shadow of what they feel, and keeps all of that separate from its own point of view.

Social cognition is the umbrella term for these processes: the perceiving, interpreting, and storing of information about other people and about oneself as a social being.

It matters because social cognition is not a decorative add-on to thinking.

It is implicated in autism, in schizophrenia, in psychopathy, in dementia, and in the everyday ordinary business of getting through a day without offending anybody.

It also happens to be the corner of neuroscience with the most replication trouble and the worst sampling problems, so this chapter will spend as much time on what is shaky as on what is solid.


58.1 Perceiving persons

Before you can wonder what somebody is thinking, you have to notice that there is a somebody there.

The brain treats persons as a special category of visual and auditory object, with dedicated cortical territory for faces, for moving bodies, for gaze direction, and for voices.

This section works through those four channels.

A recurring theme is that "dedicated" does not necessarily mean "innate and exclusive" - almost every claim of a person-specific brain region has a rival explanation in terms of general expertise.


58.1.1 Face perception and the fusiform face area debate

In 1997 Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues reported a patch of cortex on the underside of the temporal lobe, in a fold called the fusiform gyrus, that responded roughly twice as strongly to faces as to other objects; they named it the fusiform face area (FFA).

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the method used, measures blood flow changes as a proxy for neural activity, so it tells you where activity clusters rather than what individual neurons compute.

The dispute that followed is one of the cleanest in cognitive neuroscience: Kanwisher argued for domain specificity, meaning the FFA is built for faces as a category, while Isabel Gauthier argued for the expertise hypothesis, meaning the FFA serves fine-grained individuation of any category you have become an expert in, and Gauthier's group duly showed FFA responses correlating with expertise in bird experts and car experts.

Both camps have accumulated evidence - Kanwisher's group reported a roughly threefold face advantage that expertise accounts struggle to explain, while expertise effects keep reappearing in independent labs - and the honest summary in 2026 is that the region is strongly face-biased but that nobody has decisively shown it is face-exclusive.

Two clinical facts anchor the debate: people with prosopagnosia (an inability to recognise faces, either from birth or after injury) can often still recognise objects perfectly well, and Doris Tsao and Winrich Freiwald's work in macaque monkeys found discrete "face patches" whose individual neurons fire selectively to faces, which is the kind of cellular-level evidence fMRI cannot deliver in humans.

The lesson worth carrying forward is methodological: an area that lights up for a category is not thereby proved to be for that category.


58.1.2 Biological motion and the superior temporal sulcus

In 1973 the Swedish psychologist Gunnar Johansson attached small lights to a person's major joints and filmed them moving in the dark.

Viewers who see a still frame report a meaningless scatter of dots; viewers who see the dots move immediately report a walking person, and can often report the walker's sex, mood, and whether they are carrying something heavy.

These point-light displays are the standard laboratory probe for biological motion, meaning the characteristic movement pattern of a living animal.

Neuroimaging consistently localises the response to the posterior part of the superior temporal sulcus (STS), the long groove running back along the side of the temporal lobe, with the right hemisphere generally dominant; Emily Grossman and Randolph Blake's work in the early 2000s was central in pinning this down.

Causal evidence comes from transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique that uses a magnetic pulse to briefly disrupt a patch of cortex - disrupting the right posterior STS impairs recognition of emotion from point-light bodies, which shows the region is doing work rather than merely watching.

Reduced right posterior STS response to point-light motion has been proposed as a candidate biomarker for autism spectrum disorder, though it is not yet reliable enough at the individual level for diagnostic use, and that limitation should be stated plainly.


58.1.3 Gaze following and joint attention

Where another person is looking is one of the most information-dense signals available, because gaze is a decent proxy for attention and attention is a decent proxy for intention.

Humans are unusual among primates in having a white sclera surrounding a dark iris, which makes gaze direction unusually legible at a distance - the so-called cooperative eye hypothesis, an elegant idea with suggestive but not conclusive comparative support.

Gaze following becomes joint attention when two people knowingly attend to the same thing and each registers that the other is attending too; developmental psychologists distinguish responding to joint attention, where the infant follows a pointing or looking adult, from initiating joint attention, where the infant recruits the adult's attention, typically emerging between about nine and fifteen months.

Peter Thier's group identified a gaze-following patch in posterior temporal cortex, near but distinct from the face patches, suggesting gaze direction is computed by machinery separate from face identity.

Imaging in infants using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), a wearable optical method that measures blood oxygenation through the scalp and tolerates a wriggling baby far better than fMRI, has implicated the superior temporal sulcus and temporoparietal region along with prefrontal cortex, with dorsomedial prefrontal cortex more involved when the infant initiates rather than merely follows.

Early joint attention predicts later language ability, which is one of the sturdier findings in developmental social neuroscience.


58.1.4 Voice and person identity

You can recognise a friend on the telephone within a syllable, which means the brain extracts identity from voice as well as from face.

Pascal Belin and colleagues described the temporal voice areas (TVAs) in 2000: patches along the upper bank of the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus that respond more to human vocal sounds than to matched non-vocal sounds, present bilaterally and often called voice patches by analogy with the face patches.

Voice identity recognition can fail selectively in phonagnosia, the inability to recognise familiar voices, which comes in an apperceptive form, where voices cannot be discriminated at all, and an associative form, where discrimination is intact but access to the stored identity is lost - the same apperceptive-versus-associative split described for face recognition.

Developmental phonagnosia, present from birth in people with otherwise normal hearing, was documented by Katharina von Kriegstein's group and shows that voice identity is a dissociable ability rather than a by-product of general hearing.

There is also evidence that recognising a familiar person's voice recruits face-sensitive regions such as the fusiform face area, which suggests person identity is stored in a way that crosses sensory channels rather than living separately in each.


58.2 Mentalising

Mentalising, also called theory of mind, is the attribution of unobservable mental states - beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge - to other people and to oneself.

The word "theory" is doing real work in that phrase: because mental states cannot be seen, they must be inferred, in the way an unobservable entity is inferred in a scientific theory.

This section covers the classic behavioural test, the brain network, the contested distinction between fast automatic and slow deliberate mentalising, and how the ability develops across cultures.


58.2.1 Theory of mind and false-belief tasks

The canonical test is the false-belief task, designed by Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner in 1983 and popularised in the Sally-Anne version by Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie, and Uta Frith in 1985.

Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves; Anne moves it to a box; Sally returns, and the child is asked where Sally will look.

Answering "the basket" requires representing Sally's belief as separate from reality, which is why the task is diagnostic; most typically developing children switch from "the box" to "the basket" somewhere around age four.

Baron-Cohen and colleagues found that children with autism failed the task at rates far above children with Down syndrome matched for mental age, which launched the influential mindblindness account of autism.

That account has since been substantially qualified: many autistic people pass false-belief tasks, task performance is confounded with language ability and executive function, and the double empathy problem proposed by Damian Milton in 2012 - the argument that the mutual misunderstanding runs in both directions between autistic and non-autistic people - has gained considerable traction.

The strong deficit framing is no longer the field's consensus.


58.2.2 The mentalising network: temporoparietal junction, medial prefrontal cortex, precuneus

When people read stories requiring belief attribution, a reliable set of regions activates more than for closely matched control stories: the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) bilaterally but especially on the right, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) running up the inner surface of the frontal lobe, the precuneus and posterior cingulate on the inner surface of the parietal lobe, the superior temporal sulcus, and the temporal poles.

Rebecca Saxe and Nancy Kanwisher's work from 2003 onward made the right TPJ the centrepiece, arguing it is remarkably selective for belief attribution as opposed to other social or emotional content.

That selectivity is disputed.

Jean Decety and Claus Lamm, and separately Jason Mitchell, argued that the same territory supports reorienting of attention to unexpected stimuli in entirely non-social tasks, and a well-known 2008 Cerebral Cortex paper by Mitchell was titled to that effect - activity in right TPJ is not selective for theory of mind.

The compromise position, supported by higher-resolution imaging that subdivides the region, is that adjacent but distinguishable sub-regions of TPJ handle attentional reorienting and belief attribution, with the more posterior and dorsal portion the more mentalising-specific.

It is worth noting that this network overlaps heavily with the default mode network, the set of regions more active at rest than during demanding external tasks, which has invited the speculation that the resting brain's baseline activity is substantially social - an appealing idea with only correlational support.


58.2.3 Implicit and explicit mentalising

If explicit false-belief reasoning arrives at four, why do infants under two look longer at scenes that violate an actor's false belief, as Kristine Onishi and Renée Baillargeon reported in 2005?

The two-systems answer, developed by Ian Apperly and Stephen Butterfill in 2009, proposes an early-developing, fast, automatic, but representationally limited system for tracking what others register, alongside a later-developing, slow, flexible, effortful system for full belief attribution.

This is where the chapter must be blunt about a crisis.

Several headline implicit mentalising effects, including the reaction-time paradigm of Ágnes Kovács and colleagues from 2010 and various anticipatory-looking tasks, have failed to replicate in large, well-powered, multi-laboratory attempts - notably work by David Kulke and Hannes Rakoczy from 2018 and by Kaltefleiter and colleagues in 2022, which found evidence for goal-based prediction but only mixed evidence for false-belief-based prediction.

Critics including Jonathan Phillips and colleagues have argued that many implicit findings admit low-level explanations such as attention capture by the last-seen location.

Explicit false-belief performance in preschoolers is robust and replicates; the implicit infant literature is genuinely unsettled, and anybody who tells you otherwise is overselling.


58.2.4 Development of theory of mind and its cross-cultural profile

Henry Wellman and David Liu's 2004 theory-of-mind scale broke the ability into five ordered steps - understanding that people have diverse desires, then diverse beliefs, then that knowledge depends on perceptual access, then false belief, then hidden emotion - and found American children mastering them in that order.

The interesting result is what happens elsewhere.

Wellman, Fuxi Fang, Liqi Zhu and colleagues found in 2006 that children in Beijing reliably passed knowledge access before diverse beliefs, reversing two of the American steps, and later work found the same reversed ordering in Iranian children.

The proposed explanation is cultural emphasis: societies that stress acquiring knowledge from more knowledgeable adults, and that discourage open disagreement, may make knowledge access salient earlier and diversity of opinion salient later.

A 2024 meta-analysis of theory-of-mind scale sequences across cultural contexts confirmed that the overall rate of mastery is broadly similar while the ordering of the middle steps varies, which is a useful shape of result: the destination is shared, the route is cultural.

Caregiver mental state talk - how much parents narrate thoughts, wants, and knowledge - predicts theory-of-mind performance in every population where it has been measured, which points at input rather than maturation alone.


58.3 Empathy and shared representation

Empathy is the capacity to share and understand another's emotional state while knowing that the state belongs to the other person.

That final clause is not decoration; without self-other distinction you have contagion or distress, not empathy.

This section separates the components, examines the influential claim that we simulate others' pain using our own pain machinery, and looks at what regulates and what distorts the whole system.


58.3.1 Affective empathy, cognitive empathy, and compassion

Affective empathy is feeling something appropriate to what another feels; cognitive empathy is understanding what another feels without necessarily feeling it; compassion is a warm, other-oriented concern coupled with a motivation to help.

These come apart in real people.

Psychopathy is characterised by relatively intact cognitive empathy alongside blunted affective empathy - the ability to read you without being moved by you - whereas some autistic profiles show the opposite pattern, strong affective resonance with difficulty inferring the mental state that caused it.

Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki's training studies are the sharpest demonstration that these are separable at the neural level: empathy training increased negative affect and activity in anterior insula and anterior midcingulate cortex, while subsequent compassion training increased positive affect and shifted activity to medial orbitofrontal cortex, subgenual anterior cingulate cortex, and ventral striatum, regions associated with reward and affiliation.

The practical implication - that burnout in carers may reflect empathic distress rather than too much compassion, and that compassion can be trained as a coping strategy - is attractive and moderately well supported, though sample sizes in this literature remain modest.


58.3.2 Shared neural representation of pain and its critiques

The founding observation, from Tania Singer and colleagues in 2004, was that watching a loved one receive a painful shock activated anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex in much the same places as receiving the shock oneself, while the sensory pain regions were not recruited.

This became the shared representation or neural resonance account: we understand your pain by partially instantiating it.

The critique is now substantial and comes in two forms.

First, activation overlap in a coarse fMRI map does not establish that the same neural code is being used, so researchers turned to multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), which asks whether a fine-grained pattern trained on one experience predicts another - and Anjali Krishnan, Tor Wager and colleagues reported in eLife in 2016 that somatic and vicarious pain are represented by dissociable multivariate patterns, with the Neurologic Pain Signature for felt pain failing to track vicarious pain.

Second, even where shared patterns are found, they may not be pain-specific: studies have shown the overlapping anterior insula patterns also represent disgust and unfairness, which points to a general code for aversive, arousing experience rather than a pain simulator.

The current honest position is that watching pain reliably engages the salience network including anterior insula and anterior cingulate, that some genuinely shared representation may exist in mid-insula, and that the strong claim of literally re-experiencing another's pain is not established.


58.3.3 Emotional contagion and its regulation

Emotional contagion is the automatic catching of another's emotional state, and its most studied vehicle is facial mimicry, the involuntary tendency to make small versions of the expressions you see, measurable with electromyography (EMG), which records tiny electrical signals from muscle.

The classical account, associated with Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson, runs mimicry to afferent feedback to felt emotion.

The evidence has complicated that story: a 2025 activation-likelihood-estimation meta-analysis, which is a statistical method for pooling coordinates across imaging studies, concluded that facial mimicry and emotional contagion do not share a single neural system, with mimicry recruiting motor and face-processing cortex while contagion tracked angular and supramarginal gyri, and behavioural work often finds no correlation between how much a person mimics and how much they report feeling.

Contagion is regulated rather than fixed.

It is amplified by liking, similarity, and eye contact, damped by competing goals and by explicit reappraisal, and modulated by the orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus in concert with anterior cingulate, insula, and amygdala.

Contagion is also the developmental ancestor of empathy - newborns cry when other newborns cry - but it is not empathy, because nothing in it involves knowing whose feeling it is.


58.3.4 Group membership effects on empathy

Empathy is not distributed evenly, and the biases are large enough to matter morally.

Xiaojing Xu, Xiangyu Zuo and Shihui Han reported in 2009 that anterior cingulate responses to seeing a needle penetrate a face were reduced when the face belonged to a different racial group than the viewer, in both Chinese and Caucasian participants - a symmetric ingroup bias rather than a one-directional prejudice.

Crucially, the bias tracks group membership rather than appearance as such: minimal group manipulations, in which participants are assigned to arbitrary teams by coin flip minutes before scanning, produce comparable modulation, which argues against any account rooted in perceptual unfamiliarity alone.

The effect is behaviourally consequential, predicting costly helping, and in the extreme it inverts: Mina Cikara and colleagues have documented schadenfreude responses, with ventral striatum activity to the misfortunes of rival group members.

The consoling part of the finding is that if arbitrary group boundaries can create the gap in minutes, group boundaries are also the lever for closing it.


58.4 Self and other

Social cognition is not only outward-facing.

Representing yourself, keeping that representation distinct from your representation of others, and monitoring how others evaluate you are all parts of the same system, and they share cortical real estate.


58.4.1 Self-referential processing and cortical midline structures

Ask someone whether an adjective describes them, rather than whether it describes a public figure or is printed in capitals, and two things happen: they remember the word far better afterwards, the self-reference effect described by T. B. Rogers and colleagues in 1977, and a particular set of regions activates.

Georg Northoff and colleagues' 2006 meta-analysis of imaging studies pooled the evidence and identified the cortical midline structures (CMS): ventral and dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus.

The striking part of Northoff's result was domain generality - the same midline regions came up whether the self-relevant material was verbal, spatial, emotional, or facial, which suggests they code self-relatedness itself rather than any particular content.

Later work by Dylan Wagner, Jason Mitchell and colleagues found a spatial gradient in medial prefrontal cortex, with ventral portions more engaged by judgements about oneself and by similar others, and dorsal portions more engaged by judgements about dissimilar others - so self and other are not separate boxes but ends of a continuum.

Excessive and negatively valenced self-referential processing in these midline regions is one of the more reliable neural correlates of rumination in major depression, which gives the finding clinical bite.


58.4.2 Self-other distinction and its failures

If understanding others involves simulating them, the system needs a mechanism for keeping the simulation labelled, and the right temporoparietal junction and right supramarginal gyrus appear to provide it.

Giorgia Silani, Claus Lamm and colleagues demonstrated this with the emotional egocentricity bias: when you feel pleasant and must judge someone else's unpleasant experience, your judgement drifts toward your own state, and right supramarginal gyrus activity is highest precisely on the trials where that drift must be resisted.

The causal test was decisive - inhibitory one-hertz repetitive TMS delivered to right supramarginal gyrus increased egocentric bias relative to control stimulation, published in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2013.

Self-other distinction fails in other ways too: children show larger egocentricity bias than adults, consistent with immature right supramarginal gyrus and its connections to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; the rubber hand illusion shows how easily body ownership can be reassigned; and delusions of control and thought insertion in schizophrenia have been interpreted as breakdowns of the mechanism that tags self-generated actions and thoughts as one's own.

The general moral is that the boundary between self and other is an active computation, not a given, and it can be pushed.


58.4.3 Social evaluation, reputation, and social reward

Being well thought of feels good in a literal, measurable, neural sense.

Keise Izuma, Daisuke Saito and Norihiro Sadato showed in Neuron in 2008 that acquiring a good reputation - learning that strangers had rated you positively - activated the striatum, the deep forebrain structure central to reward learning, in the same territory activated by winning money, which gave rise to the common neural currency hypothesis.

That overlap has been supported by later multivariate work showing a shared striatal code for social and monetary reward, though sceptics point out that the striatum responds to almost anything valued and that overlap alone does not prove a common code.

Social pain fits the same pattern from the other direction: Naomi Eisenberger's Cyberball studies, in which participants are excluded from a virtual ball game, found dorsal anterior cingulate and anterior insula responses resembling those to physical pain, though this too has been challenged on the grounds that dorsal anterior cingulate responds to conflict and salience generally.

What is not in dispute is behavioural: reputation concern changes conduct, and people give more to charity and cheat less when they believe they are observed, even by a picture of eyes.


58.4.4 Loneliness, social isolation, and cognitive consequence

Loneliness is the subjective experience of having fewer or poorer social connections than one wants, and it is distinct from objective social isolation - you can be lonely in a crowd and content alone, and the two predict outcomes partly independently.

John Cacioppo, who founded much of this field, argued that loneliness is an aversive signal evolved to motivate reconnection, in the same way that hunger motivates eating, but that when chronic it becomes self-perpetuating by biasing attention and interpretation toward social threat.

The physiological account involves prolonged activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the hormonal stress pathway ending in cortisol release, together with disturbed sleep, raised inflammatory gene expression, and impaired attentional control.

The epidemiology is now strong: a 2024 meta-analysis published in Nature Mental Health, pooling longitudinal data from more than 600,000 individuals, found loneliness associated with a hazard ratio of about 1.31 for all-cause dementia, 1.39 for Alzheimer's disease, and 1.74 for vascular dementia, with effects surviving adjustment for depression.

Causal direction is the standing caveat, since early dementia can cause withdrawal as easily as withdrawal can hasten dementia, but the finding holds in studies with long follow-up periods designed to reduce that reverse-causation worry, and social isolation now appears on the Lancet Commission's list of modifiable dementia risk factors.


58.5 Two-person and group neuroscience

Almost everything above was measured in one person lying alone in a scanner looking at pictures of people.

The complaint that this misses the thing it studies - that social cognition is interactive, not spectatorial - has driven a shift toward measuring two or more brains at once, and toward asking what happens at the level of groups and cultures.

This section covers that shift and is candid about how much of it is still promissory.


58.5.1 Hyperscanning and inter-brain coupling

Hyperscanning means recording from two or more brains simultaneously while the people interact, using electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical activity from scalp electrodes, or fNIRS, or two linked fMRI scanners.

The standard finding is inter-brain synchrony: correlated activity between partners that rises during cooperation, teaching, conversation, and eye contact, and that often predicts task success better than either brain alone.

The standing objection is the epiphenomenon problem - two people doing the same thing at the same time, seeing the same stimuli and moving in the same rhythm, will show correlated brain activity for boring reasons, without anything specifically social happening between them.

The field's response has been the pseudo-pair control, in which real pairs are compared against artificially recombined pairs of people who never interacted, and the demonstration that coupling is not fully explained by motor synchrony; a 2024 perspective in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience surveyed these advances and concluded that causal inference from inter-brain coupling to behaviour remains the unsolved problem.

A 2026 systematic review of fMRI hyperscanning reported that analytic methods still lack agreed standards, which is a fair summary: the phenomenon is real, its interpretation is not settled.


58.5.2 Communication as alignment of models

Greg Stephens, Lauren Silbert and Uri Hasson's 2010 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences is the cleanest demonstration in this area.

They scanned a speaker telling an unrehearsed story, then scanned listeners hearing the recording, and used the speaker's brain activity to model each listener's.

Activity in the listener's brain tracked the speaker's with a delay across temporal, parietal, and prefrontal cortex; the coupling vanished when the story was told in Russian to English-speaking listeners who could not understand it; and in some regions the listener's activity anticipated rather than lagged the speaker's, with the size of that anticipatory coupling predicting how much of the story the listener actually understood.

The theoretical framing, associated with Martin Pickering and Simon Garrod's interactive alignment account and with predictive processing more generally, is that successful communication is the convergence of two people's internal models, and that prediction is what makes conversation fast enough to work.

The caution is that neural coupling is a correlate of comprehension, and the study's own logic - no comprehension, no coupling - does not by itself tell you whether coupling causes understanding or merely reflects it.


58.5.3 Collective behaviour and social networks

Above the pair sits the group, and the tools here come as much from network science as from neuroscience.

Carolyn Parkinson, Adam Kleinbaum and Thalia Wheatley reported in Nature Communications in 2018 that friends within a real graduate cohort had strikingly similar brain responses while watching the same videos, and that neural similarity declined with each step of social distance, so that friends resembled each other more than friends-of-friends, who in turn resembled each other more than people three steps apart.

Their 2025 follow-up in Nature Human Behaviour addressed the obvious chicken-and-egg question by scanning people before they became friends and finding that neural similarity predicted which strangers would later become friends, which pushes the interpretation toward similarity attracting rather than merely accumulating - though shared background remains a plausible common cause.

Related work has shown that people accurately encode the structure of their own social networks, with the brain distinguishing social distance and centrality, and that the medial temporal lobe represents social relationships using something like the spatial-mapping machinery it uses for physical environments - an elegant idea from work by Rita Tavares, Daniela Schiller and colleagues that is suggestive rather than fully established.

Sitting behind all of this is Robin Dunbar's social brain hypothesis, that primate neocortex size tracks typical group size, an influential idea whose specific numerical predictions have been repeatedly criticised on statistical grounds.


58.5.4 Cultural neuroscience and the sampling problem in the field

Cultural neuroscience asks whether the brain processes that support social cognition differ across cultural contexts, and the best-known findings concern the self: Ying Zhu, Shihui Han and colleagues reported in 2007 that Chinese participants engaged ventral medial prefrontal cortex when judging traits of their mother as well as of themselves, whereas Western participants engaged it for self only, consistent with a more interdependent self-construal.

Such findings are typically modest in effect size and have not all replicated cleanly, so they should be held loosely.

The larger issue is the sampling problem named by Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan in 2010: research participants are overwhelmingly Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic (WEIRD), a group supplying something like eighty percent of participants while representing roughly twelve percent of humanity, and around ninety percent of neuroimaging research originates in Western countries.

This bites hardest in exactly this chapter's subject matter, because social norms, emotion concepts, gaze conventions, and beliefs about mind are among the most culturally variable things psychologists measure - the theory-of-mind sequence reversal in Chinese and Iranian children in section 58.2.4 is a concrete instance.

The problem is not only who is scanned but who designs the studies, since the questions asked and the stimuli chosen reflect the researchers' own cultural assumptions.

Anyone reading social neuroscience should treat "the brain does X" claims as shorthand for "the brains of a few hundred university students in a handful of wealthy countries did X", until shown otherwise.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The brain has person-biased machinery - fusiform face area for faces, posterior superior temporal sulcus for biological motion and gaze, temporal voice areas for voices - but in every case the claim of category-exclusivity is contested by expertise and domain-general accounts, and the fusiform face area debate between Kanwisher and Gauthier remains genuinely unresolved.

Mentalising recruits a reliable network centred on the temporoparietal junction, medial prefrontal cortex, and precuneus, and explicit false-belief reasoning around age four is robust, while the infant implicit mentalising literature has suffered serious replication failures and should not be treated as settled.

Empathy decomposes into affective, cognitive, and compassionate components that dissociate in training studies and in clinical populations, but the strong shared-representation claim about pain has been undercut by multivariate evidence that felt and vicarious pain use dissociable codes.

Self and other are not separate systems but ends of a gradient in cortical midline structures, and the boundary between them is an active computation that right supramarginal gyrus maintains and that transcranial magnetic stimulation can disrupt.

Loneliness is now a well-evidenced longitudinal risk factor for dementia, with a 2024 meta-analysis of over 600,000 people putting the all-cause hazard ratio near 1.31.

Two-person and cultural neuroscience are the field's most important growth areas and its least consolidated, with inter-brain coupling still short of causal interpretation and the WEIRD sampling problem limiting how far any of these conclusions can be generalised to the species.


CHAPTER 59. MORAL COGNITION, NORMS, AND CULTURE (CORE)

This chapter asks how a brain arrives at the judgement that something is wrong.

It covers the laboratory tasks used to study moral judgement, the emotions that accompany moral life, the social norms that groups build and enforce, and the cultural machinery that installs those norms in individual minds.

It also covers what happens when this science walks into a courtroom and is asked to say who is responsible for what.

The topic matters because moral judgement is not a decorative add-on to cognition - it is one of the main jobs the human social brain does, and it is the job on which law, punishment, and cooperation rest.

A warning runs through the whole chapter: this is a field with elegant theories and, in several places, thinner evidence than the theories deserve.


59.1 Moral judgement

Moral judgement is the process by which a person decides that an act is permissible, forbidden, praiseworthy, or blameworthy.

Researchers study it mostly by giving people short scenarios and recording their verdicts, their reaction times, and sometimes their brain activity while they decide.

This section works through the standard scenarios, the leading theory built on them, the role of intention, and the emotions that come along for the ride.


59.1.1 Dilemma paradigms and their limitations

The best-known tool in the field is the trolley problem, a thought experiment in which a runaway tram will kill five people unless the participant diverts it onto a track where it kills one, or in a harsher version pushes a large bystander off a footbridge to stop it.

Most people say diverting is acceptable but pushing is not, even though the arithmetic of lives is identical, and that gap is the puzzle the whole literature tries to explain.

These are called sacrificial dilemmas, meaning cases that pit the total welfare of a group against a rule forbidding the deliberate harming of an individual.

The paradigm has been sharply criticised: Bauman and colleagues argued in 2014 that sacrificial dilemmas lack external validity, which is the extent to which a laboratory result generalises to real life, because nobody encounters runaway trolleys and many participants find the scenarios amusing rather than grave.

There is also a cross-cultural problem - Sorokowski and colleagues, reporting in 2020 in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review, adapted the dilemma into an ecologically plausible falling-tree version and found that Yali horticulturalists in Papua were markedly less willing than Western participants to sacrifice one to save five, which suggests the supposedly rational utilitarian response is partly a cultural habit.

The honest position is that trolley studies are a useful probe of how people weigh harm against outcome, and a poor model of actual moral life.


59.1.2 Dual-process accounts of moral judgement and their critiques

The dominant theory, developed by Joshua Greene and colleagues from 2001 onward, is the dual-process account: it proposes that fast, automatic, emotionally driven responses push people toward deontological verdicts (deontology being the position that some acts are wrong regardless of consequences), while slow, effortful, controlled reasoning pushes toward utilitarian verdicts (utilitarianism being the position that the right act is the one producing the best overall outcome).

Greene tied the emotional route to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a region on the underside of the frontal lobe that attaches affective value to options, and the controlled route to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region on the outer surface involved in working memory and cognitive control.

Lesion evidence supports part of this: Koenigs, Young, Adolphs, Tranel, Cushman, Hauser, and Damasio reported in Nature in 2007 that six patients with bilateral ventromedial prefrontal damage gave abnormally utilitarian answers to the emotionally charged dilemmas, as though the emotional veto had been removed.

But the theory has taken heavy fire.

Kahane and colleagues in 2012 failed to replicate the predicted link between dorsolateral prefrontal activity and utilitarian answers, and argued that Greene's design confounded utilitarian content with counterintuitiveness, so the "reasoning" areas may simply track how odd an answer feels rather than how utilitarian it is; Paxton, Greene, and colleagues replied in 2014, and the exchange is not settled.

Kahane and Everett have separately argued that laboratory "utilitarians" are not impartial benevolent reasoners at all, since the same participants who endorse pushing the man tend to score higher on psychopathy and lower on genuine concern for the distant needy - which suggests the paradigm measures reduced aversion to harm rather than commitment to the greater good.

A further critique, restated in a 2025 review, is that the theory quietly assumes a modular brain in which emotion and reason are separable systems, an assumption most contemporary neuroscience does not grant.


59.1.3 Intention, outcome, and causal role in blame

Blame is not a function of damage alone; it depends on what the actor believed, what the actor intended, and how directly the actor caused the harm.

Young, Cushman, Hauser, and Saxe showed in a 2007 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that the right temporoparietal junction, a patch of cortex where the temporal and parietal lobes meet that is reliably engaged when people reason about others' beliefs, responds to the interaction of belief and outcome - it is what allows an accident to be excused and an attempted poisoning to be condemned even when nobody is hurt.

The causal claim was tested directly: Young and colleagues in 2010 used transcranial magnetic stimulation, a technique that briefly disrupts activity in a targeted cortical patch using a magnetic pulse, over the right temporoparietal junction and found that participants then relied less on the actor's beliefs and more on the outcome, judging failed attempts to harm as more permissible.

Later work using transcranial direct current stimulation, a weak-current method, pushed judgements in the opposite direction by enhancing the weight of intention.

Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex produces a complementary deficit: Young and colleagues reported in Neuron in 2010 that such patients under-condemn failed attempts to harm, judging by the harmless outcome rather than the malignant intent.

Causal role matters too - people blame an agent more when the harm flows directly from bodily force than when it is a side effect of an action aimed elsewhere, a contrast that some researchers call the personal-impersonal distinction and others regard as a matter of causal directness rather than emotion.


59.1.4 Moral emotions: guilt, shame, disgust, indignation

Moral emotions are feelings whose objects are the rightness or wrongness of conduct, one's own or someone else's.

Guilt targets the act and motivates repair; shame targets the self and motivates hiding; indignation, sometimes called moral anger, targets another's violation; and moral disgust responds to conduct felt to be degrading or contaminating.

Neuroimaging meta-analyses, including a 2023 voxel-based synthesis by Bastin and colleagues and its successors, find that guilt, shame, and embarrassment all engage the left anterior insula, a deep cortical region that represents bodily and emotional states, while shame and embarrassment additionally recruit the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, a region linked to social pain, and guilt more specifically recruits the left temporoparietal junction, consistent with guilt requiring a model of the person you harmed.

Moll and colleagues, in a 2005 functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study, separated indignation from ordinary disgust, finding that indignation additionally engaged the right inferior frontal gyrus and amygdala.

The claim that disgust causes moral condemnation has not held up well - Landy and Goodwin's 2015 meta-analysis of fifty experiments found only a tiny amplification effect that vanished entirely once publication bias was corrected for, and the associated cleanliness-priming results have repeatedly failed to replicate.

So the safe statement is that moral judgements are accompanied by, and correlated with, distinct emotional signatures, while the stronger claim that incidental emotions manufacture moral verdicts is currently unsupported.


59.2 Norms and social learning

A norm is a shared expectation about how people in a group ought to behave, backed by the expectation that violators will be criticised or punished.

Norms are what let strangers cooperate at scale, and this section covers how children acquire them, how group opinion reshapes individual valuation, how fairness is enforced, and what computations cooperation requires.


59.2.1 Norm acquisition and enforcement

Children do not merely learn rules, they police them.

Rakoczy, Warneken, and Tomasello showed in 2008 that three-year-olds who had seen a novel game demonstrated once would protest when a puppet then did it "the wrong way", using normative language such as "no, it doesn't go like that" - the child generalises from a single demonstration to a rule binding on everyone.

Schmidt, Rakoczy, and Tomasello reported in Cognition in 2012 that this enforcement is selective in a revealing way: three-year-olds protested moral violations such as harm regardless of whether the violator was an ingroup or outgroup member, but enforced arbitrary game conventions only against ingroup members, as if conventions were understood from the start as "how we do things".

Costly enforcement arrives later: McAuliffe, Jordan, and Warneken found in 2014 that children from around age six will give up a reward of their own to punish an unfair third party, which is the developmental signature of genuine third-party punishment rather than mere complaint.

The general picture, summarised in a 2022 Annual Review of Developmental Psychology treatment by Schmidt and Tomasello, is that norm psychology appears early, is inferred from very sparse evidence, and includes an enforcement motive from the outset.


59.2.2 Conformity and social influence on valuation

Conformity is the adjustment of one's own judgement toward the judgement of a group.

Klucharev, Hytönen, Rijpkema, Smidts, and Fernández reported in Neuron in 2009 that when participants learned their rating of a face differed from the group's, activity rose in the rostral cingulate zone and fell in the ventral striatum, a subcortical reward structure - a pattern resembling the reward prediction error signal, meaning the mismatch between expected and received reward that drives reinforcement learning.

Crucially the size of that signal predicted how much the participant later shifted their own rating, which suggests that social disagreement is processed as a kind of error to be corrected.

The interpretation was strengthened when Klucharev and colleagues in 2011 downregulated the posterior medial frontal cortex with transcranial magnetic stimulation and reduced conforming behaviour.

The story has since been qualified: a 2020 study by Zhang and Gläscher and related multivariate pattern analyses failed to find that conformity and reward learning share the same neural code, so the reinforcement-learning framing may be a useful analogy rather than a literal identity.

There is a further open question about whether the striatal shift reflects a genuine change in what a person values or merely a change in what they report.


59.2.3 Fairness, inequity aversion, and altruistic punishment

The ultimatum game is a two-player task in which a proposer divides a sum and a responder either accepts, in which case both are paid, or rejects, in which case neither is.

A purely self-interested responder should accept any positive offer, yet across many societies responders routinely reject offers below roughly twenty to thirty percent, paying to punish unfairness.

Fehr and Schmidt's 1999 inequity aversion model explains this by giving people a distaste for unequal outcomes, weighted more heavily when the inequality disfavours them, and Fehr and Gächter's 2002 Nature paper on altruistic punishment showed that in public-goods games the option to pay to punish free riders sustains cooperation that otherwise collapses.

Henrich and colleagues' fifteen-society study, published in 2001 and extended in 2005 and 2010, found that offers and rejection thresholds vary substantially with the market integration and cooperative institutions of the society, which undercuts any claim that a single fairness intuition is hardwired.

Terminology is contested - many researchers now prefer "costly punishment" to "altruistic punishment", since the punisher's motive may be personal anger rather than the good of the group, and Marsh and colleagues in 2016 found that real-world extreme altruists, namely non-directed kidney donors, were not unusually prone to rejecting unfair offers.


59.2.4 Cooperation and its computational bases

Cooperation across repeated interactions can be sustained by direct reciprocity, meaning I help you because you may help me later, or by indirect reciprocity, meaning I help you because others are watching and my reputation is at stake.

Watanabe and colleagues reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2014 that these run on partly different machinery: reputation-based indirect reciprocity engaged the precuneus, a midline parietal region associated with self-referential thought, whereas pay-it-forward giving engaged the anterior insula, a region tied to affective empathy, while both drew on the striatal reward system.

Formally, cooperation is now modelled as learning about other agents - the learner maintains a belief about a partner's cooperativeness and updates it with a social prediction error, the difference between the partner's expected and actual generosity, which is the same computational shape as reward learning applied to persons.

Hill and colleagues, in a 2022 Nature Communications study, mapped the continuous trade-off between cooperating and competing onto distinct value computations rather than a switch between two modes.

The strategic point, made by evolutionary modellers including Nowak and Sigmund, is that indirect reciprocity is computationally expensive - it requires tracking reputations and, in the more stable strategies, a theory of mind capable of judging whether a refusal to help was itself justified.


59.3 Culture and cognition

Culture is the body of socially transmitted information that shapes what people attend to, value, and know how to do.

This section covers documented cultural differences in basic cognition, the mechanism by which culture accumulates, the way cultural skills colonise existing brain circuits, and the sampling problem that makes all of this harder to assess than it looks.


59.3.1 Cultural variation in perception, attention, and self-construal

Markus and Kitayama argued in 1991 that cultures differ in self-construal, meaning the way people characteristically understand the self - as an independent entity bounded by its own attributes, or as interdependent, defined through relationships and roles.

Masuda and Nisbett's 2001 study is the canonical perceptual result: Japanese and American participants viewed underwater scenes, and Japanese participants reported more contextual and relational information and were more disrupted when a familiar focal fish appeared against a new background, while Americans reported focal objects first.

Related work by Miyamoto, Nisbett, and Masuda in 2006 suggested the physical environment itself feeds back into these habits, since Japanese urban scenes are more visually cluttered and priming people with such scenes shifted attention toward context.

Cultural neuroscience has looked for brain correlates, with Zhu and colleagues in 2007 reporting that Chinese participants engaged medial prefrontal cortex for judgements about mother as well as self, while Western participants did so only for self.

These effects are real but should be stated carefully: they are group averages with heavy overlap, some individual studies are small, and the field has been explicit since about 2015 that within-culture variation typically exceeds between-culture variation.


59.3.2 Cumulative culture and cultural transmission

Cumulative culture is the process by which a population's practices become more effective across generations because each generation inherits improvements it could not have invented alone.

Tomasello's ratchet metaphor captures the two requirements - innovation to produce improvements, and high-fidelity social learning to keep them from slipping back.

Tennie, Call, and Tomasello proposed in 2009 the zone of latent solutions hypothesis, which holds that great apes can reinvent their behavioural repertoire individually, whereas human technologies lie outside any individual's reach and therefore must be transmitted.

The evidence base is largely transmission-chain experiments, in which each participant sees only the product of the previous participant: Caldwell and Millen demonstrated ratcheting in adults building paper aeroplanes and spaghetti towers in 2008, but Reindl and Tennie in 2018 found no comparable height increase in children's tower-building chains, and other work shows that ratcheting in children depends on the durability of the cues available.

Population size and connectedness matter as well, with Henrich's 2004 Tasmania argument holding that small isolated populations can lose technologies - a claim still debated on archaeological grounds.


59.3.3 Cultural recycling of cortical circuits, in reading and in number

Reading and arithmetic are cultural inventions only a few thousand years old, far too recent for dedicated brain circuitry to have evolved, yet they are supported by remarkably consistent brain locations.

Dehaene and Cohen's neuronal recycling hypothesis, set out in 2007, resolves this by proposing that cultural skills invade cortical circuits that evolved for something related and whose properties partially fit the new task, at a cost to the original function.

The flagship case is the visual word form area, a patch of left ventral occipitotemporal cortex that in literate people responds selectively to written words and sits at nearly the same coordinates across readers of alphabets and of Chinese characters.

Dehaene-Lambertz, Monzalvo, and Dehaene reported in PLOS Biology in 2018 that as children learn to read, word-selective voxels emerge at this site and encroach mainly on cortex weakly tuned to tools rather than on face-selective cortex, and Hannagan, Agrawal, Cohen, and Dehaene showed in 2021 that a convolutional neural network trained on objects and then on words spontaneously develops a word-selective patch, which is a strong proof of principle for recycling.

For number, the analogue is the horizontal segment of the intraparietal sulcus, a groove in the parietal lobe that codes approximate numerical magnitude in human infants and in macaque monkeys alike, and which symbolic arithmetic appears to co-opt.

The disputed part is how much recycling costs the original function - the claim that literacy competes with face processing has mixed support, with some studies finding a rightward shift of face responses in literate brains and others not.


59.3.4 The problem of unrepresentative samples in the literature

Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan argued in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2010 that the behavioural sciences draw the overwhelming majority of their participants from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies, which contain roughly twelve percent of humanity but supplied more than ninety percent of the subjects.

Their sharper point was not merely that the sample is narrow but that on many measured dimensions - visual illusions, fairness in economic games, spatial reasoning, self-concept, moral reasoning - WEIRD participants are outliers rather than a representative default.

Henrich extended the argument historically in his 2020 book The WEIRDest People in the World, proposing that the Western Church's medieval prohibitions on cousin marriage dissolved dense kin networks and thereby produced the individualistic psychology that psychology has since mistaken for human nature; that historical thesis is contested, and critics have questioned both the marriage-ban data and the causal chain.

The problem is worse in neuroimaging than in questionnaire research, because scanners are expensive and concentrated in wealthy universities, and it compounds with the replication problems already noted in this chapter.

Progress since 2010 has been real but modest - more multi-site collaborations such as the Psychological Science Accelerator, more preregistration, more explicit reporting of sample origin - and the honest summary is that a large fraction of the findings in this chapter have been tested in only a narrow slice of humanity.


59.4 Agency, responsibility, and law

Moral cognition eventually has to answer to institutions that impose real consequences.

This section covers how ordinary people think about intention and free will, what the neuroscience of voluntary action actually shows, how such evidence is used in court, and whether responsibility survives the loss of a metaphysical free will.


59.4.1 Folk concepts of intention and free will

Experimental philosophy studies what ordinary people, rather than professional philosophers, actually mean by terms such as intentional and responsible.

Knobe's 2003 finding, now called the side-effect effect or Knobe effect, is that people call a foreseen but unwanted side effect intentional when it is harmful (a chairman who knowingly harms the environment while pursuing profit) and unintentional when it is beneficial - which shows that moral evaluation feeds into the supposedly descriptive judgement of intentionality, rather than the other way round.

Malle and Knobe found in 1997 that the folk concept of intentional action bundles desire, belief, intention, and awareness, with skill as a fifth component, so that lucky success is not counted as intentional.

On free will, Nichols and Knobe reported in 2007 that people describe a deterministic universe as one in which nobody is fully responsible when asked abstractly, but assign full blame to a specific agent in that universe who commits a concrete atrocity - an inconsistency they attributed to affect intruding on the concrete case.

Whether the folk concept is fundamentally incompatibilist, meaning that free will is held to require the falsity of determinism, remains genuinely contested, with later work by Nahmias, Murray, and others finding that many apparent incompatibilist responses reflect participants misreading determinism as bypassing of the agent's own reasoning.


59.4.2 The neuroscience of volition and its legal reception

The readiness potential is a slow negative electrical shift over motor cortex, discovered by Kornhuber and Deecke in 1965, that begins several hundred milliseconds before a self-paced movement.

Libet's 1983 experiment asked participants to note the clock position at the moment they felt the urge to move, and found the readiness potential preceded that reported urge by roughly three hundred and fifty milliseconds, which Libet and many later commentators read as the brain deciding before the person does.

Schurger, Sitt, and Dehaene proposed in 2012 a deflating alternative: the readiness potential is not a decision signal at all but the shape you get when you average backwards from movements triggered by ongoing random neural fluctuations crossing a threshold, and their model made and confirmed the prediction that actions initiated from a lower baseline take longer.

Schurger and colleagues restated the case in a 2021 Trends in Cognitive Sciences review titled "What is the readiness potential?", and the accumulator interpretation is now widely though not universally accepted, with critics arguing the model does not fit all datasets.

The methodological criticisms are independent and serious - the clock-reading measure of the moment of intention is unreliable, and the task involves arbitrary flicks of the wrist rather than deliberated choices of the kind law cares about.
