The legal upshot is that the Libet literature does not show what it was widely reported to show, and, as Stephen Morse has argued repeatedly, even if it did it would concern the timing of trivial motor acts rather than the capacity for rational self-governance that criminal responsibility actually requires.


59.4.3 Neuroscientific evidence in the courtroom

Neuroscience already appears routinely in criminal proceedings, mostly not as a claim that the brain made the defendant do it but as mitigation at sentencing or as a challenge to competence.

Farahany's empirical analysis in the Journal of Law and the Biosciences in 2015 found 1,585 United States judicial opinions between 2005 and 2012 mentioning defence use of neuroscientific or behavioural genetic evidence, with about 250 such opinions in 2012 alone, and the evidence appearing in roughly five percent of murder trials and a quarter of death penalty trials that year.

Its acceptance is uneven: structural evidence of gross damage, such as a tumour or a lesion visible on a computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging scan, is treated far more favourably than functional imaging offered to show a propensity, and courts have been consistently sceptical of fMRI-based lie detection, excluding it in United States v.

Semrau in 2012.

The core objection is the group-to-individual inference problem: a statistically significant difference between group averages does not license a claim about the particular brain in the dock.

There is an unresolved empirical dispute about whether neuroimages are unduly persuasive to jurors, since McCabe and Castel reported such an effect in 2008 but subsequent work by Schweitzer, Saks, and colleagues largely failed to replicate it, and a 2019 review by Scurich and Appelbaum concluded the seductive-allure effect is weak at best.


59.4.4 Responsibility without libertarian free will

Libertarian free will, in the philosophical sense, is the doctrine that a free choice requires that the agent could have done otherwise given exactly the same prior state of the universe - a condition no deterministic or merely random physical process can supply.

Compatibilism holds that responsibility does not require this, and asks instead whether the agent had the ordinary capacities that responsibility practices presuppose: responsiveness to reasons, self-control, and the absence of coercion or gross deficit.

Dennett, in Elbow Room in 1984 and Freedom Evolves in 2003, argued that the freedom worth wanting is precisely this evolved capacity for self-control and reasons-responsiveness, and that libertarian freedom is neither available nor desirable.

Vargas's revisionism proposes that our ordinary concept may indeed be partly libertarian and partly mistaken, and that the right response is to revise the concept toward one our practices can actually justify, namely holding people responsible because doing so cultivates moral agency.

Morse's position, influential in law, is that criminal responsibility never required libertarian freedom in the first place - the legal tests concern rational capacity and control, so neuroscience is relevant only when it bears on those capacities, and the recurring "my brain made me do it" argument commits what he calls the fundamental psycholegal error of assuming that a causal explanation is an excuse.

Retributivists disagree, holding that deserved punishment does require a stronger notion of desert, and abolitionists such as Derk Pereboom accept the loss of desert and argue for a purely forward-looking quarantine-and-rehabilitation model; this is a live and unresolved dispute, not a settled matter of science.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Moral judgement is built from at least three separable ingredients - a representation of the actor's intentions and beliefs supported by the right temporoparietal junction, an affective evaluation of harm supported by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and a slower deliberative weighing - but the popular dual-process story that maps these cleanly onto deontology and utilitarianism is contested and its neural predictions have not replicated cleanly.

Blame tracks intent, not just outcome, and disrupting the belief-attribution machinery demonstrably shifts verdicts toward outcome-based judging.

Norms are acquired early, inferred from sparse evidence, and enforced by children before they are old enough to explain them, while conformity and cooperation appear to run on learning machinery of the same computational shape as reward learning, with the identity of that machinery still under dispute.

Culture is not a veneer: it accumulates through a ratchet of innovation plus faithful transmission, and it recruits existing cortex for new tasks, with reading's visual word form area as the clearest documented case.

Almost all of this evidence comes from an unrepresentative slice of humanity, so confidence should be scaled accordingly.

Finally, the neuroscience of volition does not abolish responsibility - the Libet result is now best explained as an artefact of averaging over neural noise, and the legal concepts that actually matter concern rational capacity and control rather than libertarian free will.


PART ELEVEN. CONSCIOUSNESS, SELF, AND THE INNER LIFE


CHAPTER 60. THEORIES OF CONSCIOUSNESS (CORE)

This chapter surveys the main scientific theories of consciousness and asks what each one actually claims.

Consciousness is the one thing every reader has direct acquaintance with, and the one thing neuroscience has had the hardest time explaining.

The chapter begins by sharpening the question, because most disagreement in this field is disagreement about what is being asked rather than about the data.

It then walks through global workspace theory, integrated information theory, and the main rivals, and ends with the practical business of comparing theories against evidence.

The reason this matters is not only philosophical: the same theories drive bedside tests for awareness in unresponsive patients, and increasingly they drive arguments about machines.

60.1 Framing the problem

Before any theory can be judged, the target has to be specified.

The word consciousness is used for several different things, and a theory that explains one of them is not thereby a theory of the others.

This section lays out the distinctions that the rest of the chapter depends on.

60.1.1 Phenomenal and access consciousness

The philosopher Ned Block, in an influential 1995 paper, separated two senses of the word.

Phenomenal consciousness is what an experience is like from the inside - the redness of red, the ache of an ache.

Access consciousness is the availability of information to the rest of the mind: to reasoning, to speech, to the control of action.

The distinction matters because a state could in principle be phenomenal without being accessible, which is exactly what is at stake when researchers ask whether we consciously see more than we can report.

Critics reply that we only ever have evidence about access, since every measurement ultimately runs through some behaviour, and so the phenomenal-without-access case may be untestable in principle.

60.1.2 Level, content, and state distinguished

Three questions are routinely confused.

Level of consciousness asks how conscious a person is at all - awake, drowsy, anaesthetised, comatose.

Content of consciousness asks what a person is conscious of at a given moment - a face rather than a house.

State of consciousness asks what kind of consciousness is running - ordinary waking, dreaming sleep, a psychedelic state, a hypnotic state.

These come apart: a dreamer has rich content with the eyes closed and no responsiveness, so responsiveness is not the same thing as consciousness, and the dissociation is the central clinical fact behind covert awareness in unresponsive patients.

60.1.3 The hard problem and the meta-problem

David Chalmers, in 1995, named the hard problem of consciousness: even after we explain every function the brain performs - discrimination, integration, report - it still seems an open question why any of it is accompanied by subjective experience.

He contrasted this with the easy problems, which are easy only in the sense that they are ordinary scientific problems about mechanism.

In 2018 Chalmers proposed the meta-problem of consciousness: the problem of explaining why we are so strongly disposed to think there is a hard problem in the first place.

The meta-problem is itself an easy problem, since it is a question about the causes of our judgements and reports, and that is what makes it tractable.

Keith Frankish's illusionism takes the meta-problem as the whole story - the claim is that introspection misrepresents ordinary brain states as having ineffable qualities, so what needs explaining is the misrepresentation, not the qualities.

Chalmers himself resists that conclusion, and the disagreement is live rather than settled.

60.1.4 What a neural correlate of consciousness would be, and what it would not be

Chalmers defined a neural correlate of consciousness (NCC) as a minimal neural system whose states map onto states of consciousness, such that being in a given neural state is sufficient, under normal conditions, for the corresponding conscious state.

The word minimal is doing heavy lifting: the whole brain is trivially sufficient, so a correlate is only interesting if nothing can be subtracted from it.

Jaan Aru, Talis Bachmann and colleagues argued in 2012 that most published correlates are contaminated, and they proposed a three-way split: prerequisites of consciousness (arousal, attention, the machinery that has to be running beforehand), the NCC proper, and consequences of consciousness (reporting, memory encoding, evaluation, all of which happen after the fact).

Crucially, a correlate is not an explanation - finding that a signal reliably accompanies awareness leaves open whether it causes awareness, is caused by it, or merely shares a cause with it.

60.2 Global workspace theories

The oldest of the major modern families holds that consciousness is a matter of information becoming globally available across the brain.

The metaphor is a stage, or a broadcast: many specialised processes work in parallel and unconsciously, and one of them wins access to a shared channel.

60.2.1 Baars's global workspace and the broadcast metaphor

Bernard Baars proposed global workspace theory in 1988, drawing on the blackboard architectures of early artificial intelligence.

The mind is pictured as a theatre: a vast unconscious audience of specialised processors, a narrow spotlight of attention, and a stage whose contents are broadcast to everyone.

On this account consciousness is the broadcast itself, and its function is to let otherwise isolated modules coordinate on a novel problem.

The theory explains the striking narrowness of consciousness - we can attend to only one thing at a time - as a bandwidth limit on the shared channel, and it explains why unconscious processing can be massively parallel while conscious processing is serial.

60.2.2 Dehaene and Changeux's global neuronal workspace

Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux gave Baars's metaphor a specific anatomy, in work from the late 1990s onward.

They proposed that a subset of cortical pyramidal cells with very long excitatory axons - densest in prefrontal, cingulate, and parietal cortex - form a horizontal network connecting otherwise separate processors, and that this is the physical workspace.

Their global neuronal workspace (GNW) model predicts an all-or-none transition: below a threshold, stimulus processing stays local and unconscious; above it, activity self-amplifies and spreads.

This makes conscious access a threshold phenomenon rather than a graded one, and it predicts the sharp psychometric curves seen in masking, where a stimulus is either seen or not seen with little middle ground.

Their 2020 review in the journal Neuron is the standard modern statement of the model.

60.2.3 Ignition, late amplification, and the P3b signature

Ignition is the model's name for the sudden, self-sustaining, brain-wide burst of activity that accompanies conscious access.

The proposed electrophysiological signature is the P3b, a large positive deflection in the event-related potential (ERP, the averaged electrical response of the brain to an event measured at the scalp) occurring roughly 300 to 500 milliseconds after the stimulus.

Dehaene and colleagues emphasised that the P3b appears across modalities and paradigms - visual masking, the attentional blink, the auditory oddball - whenever a stimulus is reported as seen and not when it is missed.

The signature is disputed: an earlier negativity around 200 to 300 milliseconds over posterior sites, often called the visual awareness negativity (VAN), also tracks awareness, and researchers including Mika Koivisto and Antti Revonsuo have argued that the VAN is the genuine correlate while the P3b reflects the downstream act of reporting.

That argument matters because it is precisely the prerequisites-versus-consequences worry of the previous section applied to a concrete waveform.

60.2.4 Predictions and the criticisms of prefrontal centrality

GNW predicts that prefrontal cortex is not an optional extra but part of the machinery of conscious access, and this is its most contested commitment.

Opponents, notably Christof Koch, Ned Block and Victor Lamme, point to no-report experiments in which frontal activity shrinks or disappears once the requirement to report is removed, and to patients with extensive prefrontal damage who nonetheless appear to have experience.

Defenders reply that no-report designs remove reporting but not the other cognitive work the frontal lobe does, and that prefrontal lesions are rarely complete.

The 2025 adversarial test discussed later in this chapter found long-range synchrony between early visual cortex and frontal cortex, which is friendly to GNW, but failed to find the sustained frontal maintenance of stimulus content the theory had predicted, which is not.

60.3 Integrated information theory

The second major family starts from the opposite end.

Rather than asking what the brain does when a person is conscious, integrated information theory (IIT) starts from properties of experience itself and asks what a physical system would have to be like to have them.

Giulio Tononi has developed the theory through successive versions, with IIT 4.0 published in 2023.

60.3.1 Axioms, postulates, and the derivation of phi

IIT begins with axioms: properties claimed to be self-evidently true of every experience.

In version 4.0 these are existence as a zeroth axiom, plus intrinsicality (experience exists for itself, not for an observer), information (each experience is specific, and thereby differs from others), integration (experience is unified and cannot be decomposed into independent parts), exclusion (experience is definite, with these contents and no more), and composition (experience is structured, containing distinguishable elements and relations).

Each axiom is then translated into a postulate, a requirement on the physical substrate, and the postulates are made mathematically precise.

The quantity phi, written with the Greek letter, measures how much a system's cause-effect power is irreducible to the cause-effect power of its parts - roughly, how much is lost when you cut it.

The theory's central claim is an identity rather than a correlation: consciousness is the maximally irreducible cause-effect structure, and its quantity is phi.

A well-known practical objection is that phi is computationally intractable for anything but toy systems, so what gets measured in real experiments is always a proxy.

60.3.2 Posterior hot zone and the cause-effect structure claim

Because IIT ties consciousness to a substrate's connectivity rather than to its broadcasting behaviour, it predicts that the correlate sits where the connectivity is densest and most grid-like.

Koch, Tononi, Melanie Boly and colleagues argued in 2016 and 2017 for a posterior hot zone - a temporo-parieto-occipital region of the back of the cortex - as the seat of conscious content.

Evidence offered includes intracranial recordings, and the observation that large frontal lesions can spare experience while posterior lesions abolish specific contents, such as loss of colour experience after fusiform damage.

The theory also predicts that the cerebellum, despite containing most of the brain's neurons, contributes almost nothing to experience, because its circuitry is modular and feedforward and therefore has low irreducibility - and cerebellar damage does indeed leave consciousness broadly intact, which is a genuine success for the theory.

60.3.3 Panpsychist implications and the charge of unfalsifiability

If consciousness just is integrated information, then any system with non-zero phi has some experience, however faint, including very simple physical systems.

Tononi and Koch accept this, and the position shades into panpsychism, the view that experience is widespread in nature.

It also yields awkward results: a large, appropriately wired but inert grid could in principle have higher phi than a person, and a functionally identical digital simulation of a brain would have near-zero phi, so IIT denies that a conventional computer running a perfect brain simulation would be conscious.

In September 2023, 124 researchers signed an open letter calling IIT unfalsifiable pseudoscience, prompting a substantial backlash in which critics of the letter argued that the label was inflammatory and the objections were being made politically rather than scientifically.

The fair summary is that IIT makes some genuinely testable predictions and some claims that are untestable with any foreseeable method, and that the field has not agreed on where the line falls.

60.3.4 The perturbational complexity index as an applied measure

The most successful practical descendant of IIT is the perturbational complexity index (PCI), introduced by Adenauer Casali, Marcello Massimini and colleagues in 2013.

The method is deliberately blunt: deliver a magnetic pulse to the cortex with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS, a coil that induces a brief current in tissue through the scalp) and record the echo with electroencephalography (EEG, scalp electrodes measuring electrical activity), then compress the resulting spatiotemporal pattern and use how poorly it compresses as the measure.

A response that is both widespread and varied compresses badly and yields a high index; a response that dies out locally, or that spreads as a stereotyped slow wave, compresses well and yields a low one.

PCI separated conscious from unconscious states in individual people across wakefulness, non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, and several anaesthetics, with an empirical cutoff near 0.31 established by Silvia Casarotto and colleagues in 2016.

Its importance is that it needs no behaviour at all, so it can be applied to unresponsive patients, and it has revealed high complexity in some patients who appeared behaviourally unresponsive.

The measure is a proxy for the theory's spirit rather than a computation of phi, and later work, including a 2024 study by Casarotto and colleagues, shows it can dissociate from spontaneous EEG features in minimally conscious patients.

60.4 Other major theories

Global workspace and integrated information theory dominate the headlines, but they are not the only serious contenders.

The theories below differ mainly in where they locate the crucial ingredient: in a second representation, in local feedback, in prediction, or in a model of attention.

60.4.1 Higher-order theories and prefrontal reality monitoring

Higher-order theories, associated above all with David Rosenthal, hold that a mental state is conscious when it is itself the target of a further representation - a thought about the state.

A visual state carrying information about a red patch is, on this view, unconscious until some higher-order machinery represents that one is in that state.

Hakwan Lau's perceptual reality monitoring account replaces the vague higher-order thought with a computational job: circuits in prefrontal and frontoparietal cortex evaluate whether sensory activity reflects a real external cause or is internally generated noise or imagery, and activity flagged as real is experienced as perception.

The account explains a genuine puzzle - why vivid imagery is not mistaken for seeing, and why in hallucination that discrimination fails - and it fits evidence that prefrontal manipulation changes subjective confidence and visibility while leaving objective discrimination performance intact.

The standing objection is that higher-order theories seem to allow empty higher-order states: if the second-order representation misfires, one would consciously seem to see red while no first-order red state exists, and it is unclear whether that is a feature or a fatal bug.

60.4.2 Recurrent processing theory

Victor Lamme's recurrent processing theory holds that the fast feedforward sweep through visual cortex - roughly the first 100 milliseconds - is not enough for experience, no matter how far it travels.

What is required is recurrent processing: feedback from higher visual areas back to lower ones, and horizontal interaction within an area, forming local loops.

Lamme's distinctive move is that local recurrence within visual cortex is sufficient for phenomenal consciousness, without any global broadcast, which is why the theory predicts that we phenomenally see far more than we can report.

Supporting evidence comes from masking studies, from TMS applied to visual cortex, and from anaesthesia work showing that feedforward responses survive while feedback is suppressed.

The theory is parsimonious and empirically productive, but its critics argue it identifies a prerequisite rather than the correlate proper, since recurrent processing also occurs for stimuli that never reach awareness.

60.4.3 Predictive processing and self-modelling accounts

Predictive processing holds that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine: it maintains a generative model of the causes of its sensory input and updates that model using prediction errors, the mismatches between what was expected and what arrived.

Jakob Hohwy and Anil Seth have argued that conscious contents are the brain's best current predictions rather than the raw input, which reframes perception as controlled hallucination that happens to be reined in by sensory evidence.

Seth's interoceptive extension applies the same machinery inward: the feeling of being a self, and emotion generally, is cast as prediction about the state of the body, which is why he calls the experienced self a beast machine rather than a thinking thing.

Thomas Metzinger's self-model theory of subjectivity makes the parallel claim that the self is a model the brain builds and cannot see through - the transparency of the model is what makes it feel like a self rather than like a representation.

These accounts are unusually good at explaining illusions, psychedelics, and psychiatric symptoms as failures of the balance between prediction and evidence, but they are frameworks rather than sharp theories, and critics note that predictive processing describes unconscious processing just as well as conscious processing, so on its own it does not say which predictions become experiences.

60.4.4 Attention schema theory

Michael Graziano's attention schema theory (AST) begins from the observation that the brain models the things it controls.

Just as it maintains a body schema, a simplified internal model of the body used to control movement, it maintains an attention schema: a simplified model of its own attention, used to predict and control where attention goes.

Because the model is a caricature, leaving out the underlying neurons and competition, it describes attention as a non-physical essence of awareness - and when the system introspects and reports, it reports what the model says.

AST therefore aims squarely at the meta-problem: it tries to explain why we insist we have ineffable inner experience, rather than explaining the experience itself.

Detractors say this is a change of subject and not an answer, while Graziano treats that as the point, and the theory has an unusual practical appeal in that it specifies something a machine could actually be built to have.

60.4.5 Dynamic core, temporo-spatial, and other integrative proposals

Giulio Tononi and Gerald Edelman's dynamic core hypothesis, from 1998, is the ancestor of IIT: consciousness corresponds to a shifting functional cluster of thalamocortical neurons that is simultaneously highly integrated and highly differentiated, and the cluster is defined by its dynamics rather than by anatomy.

Georg Northoff's temporo-spatial theory of consciousness shifts attention to the brain's spontaneous ongoing activity rather than its stimulus responses, proposing four mechanisms - temporo-spatial expansion, globalisation, alignment, and nestedness - by which the spatial and temporal structure of neural activity becomes the spatial and temporal structure of experience.

Its distinctive claim is a common currency: time and space are shared between neural activity and phenomenal experience, so the gap between them is narrower than it looks.

Other integrative proposals include operational architectonics, various thalamocortical and neuronal-oscillation accounts, and the electromagnetic field theories of Johnjoe McFadden and Susan Pockett, which remain a minority position with limited experimental support.

Some of these are less rival theories than differences of emphasis, and one honest summary of the field is that several theories are describing overlapping parts of the same mechanism in different vocabularies.

60.5 Comparing theories

With half a dozen theories on the table, the discipline's real problem is adjudication.

This section asks what a good theory would have to do, where the theories actually conflict, and why measurement is the bottleneck.

60.5.1 The criteria a theory must meet

A serious theory of consciousness should do at least four things.

It should explain the level of consciousness, so that it says why anaesthesia, dreamless sleep, and coma abolish experience while dreaming does not.

It should explain content, so that it says why a given neural pattern is an experience of a face rather than of a sound.

It should make risky predictions - claims that could come out false - and it should generalise beyond the healthy adult human to infants, animals, split-brain patients, and possibly machines, since a theory that only works for the case it was built on has explained nothing.

By these standards no current theory is comfortable: global workspace is stronger on access than on level, IIT is stronger on level than on the specific character of contents, and recurrent processing theory is largely a theory of vision.

60.5.2 Where the theories agree and where they genuinely diverge

The agreements are larger than the public argument suggests: nearly every theory holds that consciousness depends on the thalamocortical system, that feedback and recurrence matter, that the cerebellum contributes little, and that a great deal of sophisticated processing is unconscious.

The genuine divergences are sharp and localisable.

Is the front of the brain constitutive of experience, as global workspace says, or merely the machinery of reporting and decision, as IIT and recurrent processing theory say - this is the front-versus-back debate and it is the single most consequential open question.

Is consciousness a threshold, all-or-none ignition, or a graded property that rises continuously with integration.

And is the crucial property what a system does - its function, its broadcasting - or what it is - its intrinsic causal structure, which is why IIT can deny consciousness to a functionally perfect simulation while global workspace theory would grant it.

60.5.3 Theory-neutral measurement as a prerequisite

You cannot compare theories with instruments that presuppose one of them.

The field's response has been the adversarial collaboration: proponents of rival theories agree in advance on the experiment, the analysis, and the results that would count against their own view, so that neither can reinterpret the outcome afterwards.

The Cogitate Consortium published the first large preregistered adversarial test of global neuronal workspace theory and IIT in Nature in 2025, testing 256 participants across multiple laboratories with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, which tracks blood flow as a proxy for neural activity), magnetoencephalography (MEG, which measures the magnetic fields produced by neural currents), and intracranial EEG in patients with implanted electrodes.

Neither theory came through intact: the predicted sustained posterior synchronisation that IIT required was not found, and the sustained frontal maintenance of content that GNW predicted was not found either, though long-range visual-to-frontal communication was observed.

The value of the result is less in the verdict than in the precedent, since it demonstrated that theories can be made to commit to falsifiable predictions in advance, and further adversarial collaborations targeting higher-order and predictive processing theories are underway.

60.5.4 The problem of the report and no-report paradigms

Almost every experiment on consciousness has asked the participant to say what they saw, which contaminates the measurement: the resulting brain activity includes attention, decision, working memory, motor preparation, and the act of reporting, none of which is the experience.

No-report paradigms try to remove that contamination by inferring what the participant experienced from something other than a deliberate response - most often from the eyes, since optokinetic nystagmus and pupil size track which image dominates in binocular rivalry, the phenomenon in which two different images shown to the two eyes alternate in awareness rather than blending.

Stefan Frässle and colleagues in 2014 found that frontal activity accompanying rivalry switches shrank substantially when report was removed, with middle frontal gyrus activation disappearing entirely, and Naotsugu Tsuchiya and colleagues generalised the argument in 2015.

This is the strongest single piece of evidence against prefrontal centrality, and it is contested: Jan Brascamp and colleagues in 2015 still found frontal modulation without report, and critics including Michael Pitts and Ned Block point out that removing report does not remove post-perceptual cognition, so what is really needed and not yet achieved is a no-cognition paradigm.

There is also a cost to the method - without a report you lose the trial-by-trial ground truth about what was actually experienced, and you are trusting an indirect proxy.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Consciousness is not one question but several, and the distinctions between phenomenal and access consciousness, and between level, content, and state, determine which theory is even relevant.

Global workspace theory locates consciousness in the brain-wide broadcast of information, with ignition and prefrontal involvement as its signatures, while integrated information theory locates it in the intrinsic, irreducible cause-effect structure of a substrate, concentrated in a posterior hot zone.

Higher-order, recurrent processing, predictive processing, and attention schema theories each locate the crucial ingredient elsewhere, and several of them are better read as complementary than as strictly rival.

A neural correlate is not an explanation, and the field's central methodological problem is separating the prerequisites and consequences of consciousness - arousal, attention, decision, report - from consciousness itself.

The 2025 Cogitate adversarial collaboration left neither leading theory's core predictions intact, which is the most honest available statement of where the science stands: the front-versus-back question, the graded-versus-all-or-none question, and the function-versus-structure question are all still open.


CHAPTER 61. THE EMPIRICAL SEARCH FOR NEURAL CORRELATES (CORE)

This chapter is about a stubborn practical problem: how do you catch consciousness in a laboratory?

The strategy that has dominated the field for thirty years is to hold the physical stimulus constant while the conscious experience changes, and then ask what in the brain changed with the experience rather than with the stimulus.

The brain events that track experience under that contrast are called the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC), a phrase meaning the minimal neural activity jointly sufficient for a specific conscious experience.

We will walk through the experimental tricks that create the contrast, the candidate brain signatures that have emerged, and the large preregistered adversarial experiment reported in 2025 that put two leading theories in the same room and found neither of them intact.

This matters because it is one of the few places in science where a question that began in philosophy has been turned into a measurable, falsifiable, and genuinely disputed empirical programme.

It also matters because the same methods are now being pointed at coma patients, at isolated brain tissue, and at machines.

61.1 Paradigms

A paradigm, in this context, means a standard experimental recipe - a repeatable way of arranging stimuli and tasks so that a specific question can be asked.

The paradigms in this section all do one job: they decouple what is on the screen from what the person sees.

If a picture is physically present on every trial but consciously seen on only half of them, then any brain difference between seen and unseen trials cannot be explained by the light hitting the eye.

That logic - the contrastive method, associated with the work of David Chalmers and with Francis Crick and Christof Koch in the 1990s - is the engine of the whole field.

Each paradigm below buys that decoupling in a different way, and each buys it at a different cost.

61.1.1 Binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression

In binocular rivalry, a different image is shown to each eye - say horizontal stripes to the left eye and vertical stripes to the right - and the viewer does not see a blend.

Instead perception alternates, seconds at a time, between one image and the other, while the physical input never changes at all, which makes rivalry the classic tool for isolating experience from stimulation.

Continuous flash suppression (CFS), introduced by Naotsugu Tsuchiya and Christof Koch in 2005, sharpens the trick: a rapidly changing high-contrast pattern, flashed at roughly ten times per second into one eye, suppresses a steady image in the other eye for many seconds at a stretch.

Tsuchiya and Koch reported that CFS raised detection thresholds far more than ordinary rivalry did - by more than an order of magnitude in their measurements - which is why CFS became the workhorse for asking what an invisible image can still do inside the brain.

The honest caveat is that interocular suppression is not one thing happening at one place; measurements suggest the suppression is distributed across several stages of visual processing, so a null result under CFS does not cleanly prove that a stimulus was never processed.

61.1.2 Masking, attentional blink, and threshold stimulation

Visual masking presents a target very briefly and then follows it with a second pattern, the mask, which erases the target from awareness even though the target's light reached the retina.

The attentional blink, reported by Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell in 1992, uses rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP), a stream of items flashed at one location at roughly six to twenty items per second; when two targets appear within about half a second of one another, the second is frequently missed, as though attention had blinked.

Threshold stimulation takes the opposite approach and gives up on trickery: the stimulus is set so faint, or so brief, that the same physical stimulus is reported as seen on about half the trials and missed on the other half, and the experimenter simply sorts the trials afterwards.

The great virtue of threshold work is that seen and unseen trials are physically identical by construction; its great vice is that the difference between them includes ordinary fluctuations in attention, arousal and criterion, which are not the same thing as consciousness.

Masking and the attentional blink have been read as showing that attention is necessary but not sufficient for conscious access, though this reading is a theoretical interpretation rather than a settled fact.

61.1.3 Change and inattentional blindness

Change blindness is the failure to notice a large alteration between two views of a scene when the change is hidden by a flicker, a cut, or an eye movement, as in the flicker experiments of Ronald Rensink, Kevin O'Regan and James Clark in 1997.

Inattentional blindness is the related failure to notice a fully visible unexpected object while attention is committed to another task, most famously in Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 study in which about half of viewers counting basketball passes failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk through the middle of the display.

The two are not the same phenomenon: change blindness turns on a failure to compare across time and therefore involves memory, while inattentional blindness turns on a failure to notice at all.

For consciousness research these paradigms are valuable because the missed item is unambiguously present, large, and in plain view, which makes the failure hard to blame on the eye.

They are also cautionary, because they show that the absence of a report is weak evidence for the absence of an experience - a person may have seen the gorilla and failed to encode, retain, or think to mention it.

61.1.4 No-report paradigms and the removal of task confounds

Every paradigm above ends with a person pressing a button, and that is a problem, because pressing a button requires attention, decision, working memory, and motor preparation, none of which is consciousness.

Naotsugu Tsuchiya, Melanie Wilke, Stefan Frässle and Victor Lamme argued in 2015 that the field had drifted toward finding the neural correlates of report rather than of experience, and proposed no-report paradigms in which the experimenter infers what was seen from a physiological proxy such as eye movements or pupil size instead of asking.

Frässle and colleagues had shown in 2014 that binocular rivalry alternations could be read out from optokinetic eye movements and pupil dilation, and that when report was removed a substantial part of the frontal activation previously attributed to conscious perception disappeared.

Critics, including Michael Pitts and colleagues, have pressed two counterarguments: the report versus no-report contrast may isolate task disengagement rather than consciousness, and no-report designs may also become over-inclusive, letting unconscious processing masquerade as an NCC because nothing pins down what the participant actually experienced.

The current compromise, used by the large collaboration described later in this chapter, is not to abolish report but to make some stimuli task-relevant and others task-irrelevant within the same experiment.

61.2 Candidate signatures

Having built a contrast, the field then asks what the brain signature of consciousness looks like: where it is, when it happens, and what form it takes.

Three broad families of answer are on the table - a posterior, sensory-side answer, a frontoparietal, broadcast-side answer, and a temporal answer about feedback and synchrony - and they are not merely different emphases but rival empirical claims.

61.2.1 Posterior hot zone against frontoparietal ignition

Christof Koch, Marcello Massimini, Melanie Boly and Giulio Tononi argued in a 2016 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience that the neural correlates of consciousness sit in a posterior cortical hot zone - a temporal, parietal and occipital region toward the back of the cortex - and that frontal activity reflects reporting and monitoring rather than experience itself.

Their evidence included within-state comparisons, such as contrasting dreaming and dreamless sleep in the same sleeping brain, and no-report designs in which frontal activation drops away once the button press is removed.

The opposing position, developed by Stanislas Dehaene, Jean-Pierre Changeux and Lionel Naccache, is that a conscious percept is marked by ignition - a sudden, nonlinear, late, widely distributed surge of activity that recruits prefrontal and parietal cortex and makes information globally available to memory, language and action.

The dispute has been fought partly over lesion evidence: Boly and colleagues argued in 2017 in the Journal of Neuroscience that damage to prefrontal cortex leaves experience largely intact, and Brian Odegaard, Robert Knight and Hakwan Lau replied in the same issue that the lesion cases had been misread, at one point disagreeing about the anatomical location of the central sulcus in a cited patient image.

This is a live disagreement between named laboratories, not a settled matter, and a beginner should read confident claims on either side with that in mind.

61.2.2 Late positivity, gamma synchrony, and recurrent feedback

Three electrical signatures recur in this literature, each favoured by a different theory.

The P3b is a late positive deflection in the event-related potential - the averaged voltage change measured at the scalp that is time-locked to a stimulus - arriving roughly 300 to 500 milliseconds after onset and spread broadly over the scalp; it is the most consistent scalp marker of conscious access and is the natural prediction of global workspace ignition.

Gamma-band activity, meaning rhythmic neural fluctuation above about 30 cycles per second, together with phase synchronisation of that rhythm across distant cortical sites, has been proposed since the work of Wolf Singer and Francisco Varela in the 1990s as the mechanism that binds distributed activity into one experience.

Victor Lamme's recurrent processing theory places the signature earlier and further back: consciousness arises when feedback loops carry activity back down from higher visual areas to lower ones, which shows up at the scalp as visual awareness negativity (VAN), a negative deflection over posterior electrodes at roughly 200 milliseconds.

The empirical tension is real and unresolved - several groups, including Pitts and colleagues, have argued that the VAN survives when report demands are stripped away while the P3b does not, which would demote the P3b from a marker of experience to a marker of access and reporting.

61.2.3 Content-specific decoding of conscious percepts

A correlate that only says consciousness happened is weak; a correlate that says what was consciously seen is much stronger, and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) - training a classifier to read the stimulus identity out of the pattern of activity across many recording sites - is how the field asks that question.

Decoding turns a vague claim into a sharp one: if prefrontal cortex is where conscious content lives, then the identity of a consciously seen face should be readable from prefrontal activity, and readable better than from an unconscious control condition.

Work by Jean-Rémi King and Stanislas Dehaene using temporal generalisation, in which a classifier trained at one moment is tested at every other moment, showed that unconscious processing produces brief, sequential, non-sustained patterns while conscious processing produces a longer-lasting stable pattern.

Sandra Sanchez-Vives, Sid Kouider and others have found supramodal signatures that generalise across the senses, suggesting the late marker is not purely visual.

Decoding also imposes a discipline the older methods lacked: an area can show a large average response and still carry no decodable information about what was seen, and that dissociation has repeatedly embarrassed regions once nominated as seats of awareness.

61.2.4 Distinguishing prerequisites, substrates, and consequences of consciousness

Jaan Aru, Talis Bachmann, Wolf Singer and Lucia Melloni argued in a 2012 paper in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews that the term neural correlate lumps together three quite different things and that keeping them apart is essential.

Prerequisites are the enabling conditions that must be in place beforehand - adequate arousal from the brainstem, attention directed to the right place, a functioning thalamus - without which no experience occurs, but which are not themselves the experience.

Substrates are the NCC proper, the activity that is identical with or directly causes the specific experience.

Consequences are the downstream effects of having had the experience - working memory encoding, verbal report, decision making, the motor act of pressing the button - which follow the experience and are easily mistaken for it.

Melloni and colleagues extended the point in 2011 by noting that the same measured signal, say a late frontal potential, can be a substrate under one theory and a mere consequence under another, which is exactly why the field needed an experiment designed jointly by opposing camps.

61.3 Adversarial collaboration

An adversarial collaboration is a procedure in which the proponents of competing theories agree in advance on an experiment, on what each theory predicts, and on what result would count as a failure for their own side, and then a neutral team runs it.

The point is to remove the researcher's freedom to reinterpret an inconvenient result after the fact, and it is rare because it requires theorists to accept the risk of public defeat.

61.3.1 The Cogitate Consortium design, preregistered with proponents of both theories

The Cogitate Consortium, funded from 2019 by the Templeton World Charity Foundation and coordinated by Lucia Melloni, Michael Pitts, Liad Mudrik and colleagues, set integrated information theory (IIT), Giulio Tononi's proposal that consciousness is identical to a system's integrated information, against global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT), Stanislas Dehaene's proposal that consciousness is global broadcast of information to a frontoparietal workspace.

Proponents of both theories, working with a theory-neutral consortium, jointly wrote and preregistered the design, the divergent predictions, and the interpretation rules before any data were collected.

Participants viewed pictures from four categories - faces, objects, letters and false fonts - in three orientations and for three durations of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 seconds, and were asked to detect infrequent targets, an arrangement that made two categories task-relevant and two task-irrelevant within the same session.

That design let the consortium test predictions about where content is coded, how activity is sustained over time, and how distant regions communicate, while keeping report demands controlled rather than abolished.

61.3.2 Findings in 256 participants across functional magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalography, and intracranial recording

The results were published in Nature in 2025, reporting 256 participants across three complementary methods: functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which infers neural activity from blood oxygenation with good spatial and poor temporal resolution; magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures the magnetic fields of neural currents with millisecond timing; and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), electrodes placed inside the skull of epilepsy patients for clinical reasons, which gives both timing and precision at the cost of covering only where clinical need dictates.

The published cohorts were roughly 118 for fMRI, 100 for the combined MEG and electroencephalography arm, and 38 for iEEG, with sample sizes fixed in advance.

Both theories won something: conscious content was decodable in posterior cortex and, for category, some information was present frontally, and there was a burst of frontal activity at stimulus onset consistent with ignition.

The headline conclusion of the consortium, in Melloni's framing, was not that a winner had emerged but that each theory had been shown to be vulnerable, and the authors declined to declare either refuted.

61.3.3 The challenge to integrated information theory from absent sustained posterior synchronisation

IIT predicted that a conscious percept lasting one and a half seconds should be accompanied by sustained synchronisation within the posterior hot zone, because on IIT it is the maintained pattern of connectivity within that region that constitutes the experience.

The data did not show it: the consortium reported an absence of sustained synchronisation in posterior cortex tracking the duration and content of the percept, and this was reported as a failure of a core preregistered prediction.

Two of IIT's three preregistered predictions did find support - notably that conscious content is decodable from posterior cortex and that posterior activity is sustained for the duration of the stimulus - so the failure is specific rather than global.

IIT's proponents, Melanie Boly, Christof Koch and Giulio Tononi, filed a response in the supplementary material of the same paper arguing that the synchronisation measures used may not capture the connectivity the theory intends.

Independent commentators have pressed a sharper version of the same point - that the experiment tested locational and connectivity intuitions associated with IIT rather than any direct proxy for integrated information itself - and readers should note that this defence, whatever its merits, is also exactly the kind of post hoc rescue that adversarial collaboration was designed to discourage.

61.3.4 The challenge to global neuronal workspace theory from absent offset ignition and limited prefrontal content coding

GNWT predicted ignition twice: once when the stimulus appears and enters the workspace, and again when it disappears, because the offset of a percept is itself a conscious update that should be broadcast.

The onset ignition was broadly observed; the offset ignition was largely absent, which the authors reported as a challenge to the theory.

GNWT also predicted that prefrontal cortex should carry the specific content of experience, and here the results were partial: category information was decodable frontally, but the orientation of the face or object - a genuine dimension of the conscious percept - was not well represented in prefrontal cortex.

That combination is awkward for a theory whose central claim is that the workspace holds and broadcasts the conscious content, since a workspace that does not encode what you are seeing is not doing the job the theory assigns it.

61.3.5 What the exercise established about theory testing as a practice

The most durable result of Cogitate may be methodological rather than substantive.

It demonstrated that theorists with strong public commitments will, under the right institutional arrangements, sign in advance to conditions that could embarrass them, and that a neutral consortium can execute such a design across many laboratories and three recording methods.

It also demonstrated the limits: after publication, both camps offered reasons why the failed prediction did not touch the core of their theory, which shows that preregistration constrains but does not eliminate theoretical retreat.

The exercise unfolded against a bitter background - a 2023 open letter signed by well over a hundred researchers called IIT unfalsifiable and argued it should be labelled pseudoscience until testable, a charge many in the field considered unfair and politically loaded - and Cogitate is best understood as the field's constructive answer to that dispute.

Cogitate also released its fMRI, MEG and iEEG datasets openly, which means the strongest legacy of the project may be the data other groups can now analyse with predictions nobody had thought of in 2019.

61.4 Open empirical questions

61.4.1 Whether consciousness is graded or all-or-none

Does an experience arrive whole, like a switch flipping, or does it fade in by degrees?

Global workspace theory predicts an all-or-none transition, because ignition is a nonlinear event, and studies using digits, letters and words - the kind of stimuli that are either identified or not - tend to produce sharp psychophysical curves and all-or-none subjective judgements.

Studies using simple features such as colour or contrast, and studies using graded rating scales such as the perceptual awareness scale of Morten Overgaard and colleagues, tend to find intermediate states that participants use consistently rather than as a polite hedge.

Neural data cut the same way rather than resolving it: work reported by Fosco Bernasconi, Nathan Faivre and others, and imaging studies contrasting temporal with frontoparietal cortex, suggest activity in temporal regions scales gradually with awareness while frontoparietal activity behaves more dichotomously.

Bert Windey and Axel Cleeremans argued in 2015 that the question is ill-posed as usually stated - low-level stimuli yield graded reports and high-level ones yield dichotomous reports - so the honest current answer is that the answer depends on what is being asked about, and that no consensus exists.

61.4.2 Whether prefrontal cortex is necessary

This is the sharpest anatomical dispute in the field and it remains unresolved.

Against necessity: patients with extensive bilateral prefrontal damage, and in extreme historical cases bilateral frontal lobectomy, are reported to remain vividly conscious with personality and initiative disturbed but experience intact, an argument pressed by Boly, Koch, Tononi and by Daniel Pollen and Benjamin Kozuch.

For necessity: Odegaard, Knight and Lau argued in 2017 that the lesion cases are less clean than advertised, that lesions are rarely complete, that recovery over time can mask deficits, and that the relevant loss is in subjective experience rather than in objective task performance, which most clinical assessments never separate.

Direct electrical stimulation of prefrontal cortex in epilepsy patients, reviewed in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2021, tends not to abolish or dramatically alter conscious experience the way stimulation of posterior sensory cortex produces vivid percepts, which is a point against a content-carrying prefrontal role.

The Cogitate finding that orientation was poorly decodable from prefrontal cortex leans in the same direction, but decoding failure is weak evidence for absence, since the signal may exist below the resolution of the method.

61.4.3 Islands of awareness and disconnected consciousness

Tim Bayne, Anil Seth and Marcello Massimini asked in Trends in Neurosciences in 2020 whether there can be islands of awareness - conscious states that receive no sensory input and can produce no motor output, and are therefore causally sealed off from the world.

They considered three candidate cases: an ex cranio brain, meaning a brain removed from the body and kept alive by perfusion with oxygenated fluid, as in the pig brain work of Zvonimir Vrselja and Nenad Sestan in 2019; a hemispherotomy, in which a hemisphere is surgically disconnected but left alive in the skull to treat severe epilepsy; and cerebral organoids, small brain-like tissues grown from stem cells.

The logic that motivates the question is that people who are blind, deaf, paralysed and desensitised can still be conscious, so causal isolation from the world does not obviously abolish experience.

Because report is impossible by definition, detection would have to rely on measures that do not need behaviour, such as the perturbational complexity index of Massimini and colleagues, which stimulates the cortex with a magnetic pulse and quantifies how complex and long-lasting the resulting echo is.

The subject is speculative and the authors present it as such, but it carries direct ethical weight for organoid research and for the surgical treatment of epilepsy, which is why it has moved from thought experiment to funded programme.

61.4.4 Machine consciousness and the assessment problem

The assessment problem is that behaviour is worthless as evidence in artificial systems: a large language model trained on human text can describe an inner life fluently without that being evidence of anything, so the usual behavioural tests are already defeated.

Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, David Chalmers and a large group of coauthors proposed a way around this in 2023, published in expanded form in 2025, which they call the theory-heavy or indicator-property method.

The method takes existing neuroscientific theories - recurrent processing theory, global workspace theory, higher-order theories, predictive processing, and Michael Graziano's attention schema theory - and extracts from each a set of computational properties that a system would have to implement, then inspects the architecture of an artificial intelligence (AI) system for those properties rather than interrogating its outputs.

They derived roughly fourteen such indicators and were explicit that the approach rests on computational functionalism, the working assumption that consciousness depends on performing the right computations regardless of what the system is made of, and that this assumption is itself contested.

Their conclusion was cautious and worth stating plainly: no current AI system is a strong candidate for consciousness, but there are no obvious technical barriers to building a system that satisfies many of the indicators, and the appropriate response is calibrated credence rather than a verdict.

Critics have argued that indicators derived from theories that have not themselves survived empirical test - a point Cogitate made vivid - inherit whatever weakness those theories have, which is the honest bottom line here.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The empirical science of consciousness rests on contrastive paradigms - binocular rivalry, continuous flash suppression, masking, the attentional blink, change and inattentional blindness, and threshold stimulation - that hold the stimulus fixed while experience varies, and on no-report variants that try to strip out the confounds introduced by asking people to answer.

Candidate signatures divide into a posterior hot zone account favouring sensory cortex and early recurrent feedback, and a frontoparietal ignition account favouring a late, broadly distributed P3b, with content-specific decoding now the sharpest instrument for adjudicating between them.

Aru, Bachmann, Singer and Melloni's distinction between prerequisites, substrates and consequences is the conceptual tool that keeps the field from mistaking arousal or report for experience itself.

The Cogitate Consortium's preregistered adversarial test, published in Nature in 2025 with 256 participants across fMRI, MEG and iEEG, damaged both leading theories: integrated information theory by the absence of sustained posterior synchronisation, and global neuronal workspace theory by the absence of offset ignition and the weak prefrontal coding of orientation.

Four questions remain genuinely open and should not be reported as settled - whether awareness is graded or all-or-none, whether prefrontal cortex is necessary, whether causally isolated islands of awareness can exist, and how consciousness in a machine could be assessed at all.

The most transferable lesson is procedural: preregistered adversarial collaboration constrains motivated reinterpretation without eliminating it, and it is currently the best instrument the field has.


CHAPTER 62. STATES OF CONSCIOUSNESS (CORE)

Consciousness is not a switch with two positions.

It is better thought of as a landscape with many resting places, and this chapter walks through four of them: ordinary sleep, drug-induced anaesthesia, the disorders of consciousness that follow severe brain injury, and the altered states produced by psychedelics, meditation, hypnosis, and seizures.

Each of these states is a natural experiment - a way of taking consciousness apart and watching which pieces come away first.

The practical stakes are high, because the tools we use to judge whether a person is conscious are mostly tools that measure whether a person can respond, and those two things come apart more often than anyone expected.

By the end of the chapter you should understand why a sleeping brain is not uniformly asleep, why an unresponsive patient is not reliably unconscious, and why the field now measures the brain's response to being poked rather than simply watching it idle.


62.1 Sleep

Sleep is the state we all enter every day, and it is the best-documented alteration of consciousness in existence, because it can be induced on demand in a laboratory and measured all night with cheap electrodes.

The core discovery of twentieth-century sleep science is that sleep is not one thing.

It is a structured, repeating sequence of physiologically distinct stages, each with a different electrical signature, a different chemistry, and, as far as anyone can tell, a different job.


62.1.1 Sleep architecture and its measurement

Sleep is measured by polysomnography (PSG), which is the simultaneous overnight recording of several body signals: the electroencephalogram (EEG), which records the summed electrical activity of large populations of cortical neurons through scalp electrodes; the electrooculogram, which records eye movements; and the electromyogram, which records muscle tone.

Those three channels are enough to sort sleep into stages, and by the scoring rules of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) the night is chopped into thirty-second windows called epochs, each labelled with whichever stage occupies more than half of it.

The stages are wake, then N1, N2, and N3 - collectively non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREM) - and then rapid eye movement sleep (REM).

In a healthy adult these cycle roughly every ninety minutes, four to six times a night, with about 2 to 5 percent of the night in N1, roughly half in N2, about 15 to 20 percent in N3, and about 20 percent in REM.

The shape of the night matters as much as the totals: deep N3 is front-loaded into the first two cycles, while REM periods lengthen towards morning, which is why the dream you remember on waking is usually the last one and usually the longest.

The term sleep architecture simply means this whole arrangement - how much of each stage, in what order, with what interruptions.


62.1.2 Slow-wave sleep, rapid eye movement sleep, and their cognitive roles

Slow-wave sleep (SWS, another name for stage N3) is defined by delta waves, which are large, slow EEG oscillations below about 4 hertz produced when huge populations of cortical neurons alternate together between a firing "on" state and a silent "off" state.

The dominant account of what this achieves is active systems consolidation: memories encoded during the day by the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure buried in the temporal lobe that binds together the elements of an episode, are replayed during slow-wave sleep and gradually re-registered in the cortex for long-term storage.

Recent human work has sharpened this considerably, showing that what predicts overnight memory gain is not the raw quantity of slow-wave sleep but the precise timing between slow oscillations, sleep spindles - brief 11 to 16 hertz bursts generated by the thalamus - and hippocampal ripples, and a 2021 study by Ackermann and colleagues in the journal Sleep found no reliable within-person correlation between slow-wave sleep amount and declarative memory consolidation at all.

A competing but not strictly incompatible account is the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis of Tononi and Cirelli, which holds that waking strengthens synapses indiscriminately and that slow-wave sleep globally weakens them again to prevent saturation, with supporting evidence in 2024 that slow-wave sleep specifically drives the down-regulation of AMPA-type glutamate receptors independently of REM sleep or circadian timing.

REM sleep, with its fast desynchronised EEG, darting eyes, and near-total loss of muscle tone, is more contested: it has been linked to emotional memory processing, to the abstraction of gist from individual experiences, and to synaptic pruning, and 2024 work suggests a higher ratio of REM to slow-wave sleep predicts loss of item-level detail alongside strengthened category-level structure.

Honesty requires saying that the specific cognitive job of REM sleep remains one of the genuinely open questions in the field.


62.1.3 Local sleep and state heterogeneity

The clean stage-by-stage picture assumes the whole brain is in one state at one time, and that assumption is false.

Vyazovskiy, Tononi, Cirelli and colleagues showed in a landmark 2011 Nature paper, "Local sleep in awake rats," that in sleep-deprived but behaviourally awake and active rats, small local populations of cortical neurons go briefly silent - off periods lasting roughly 50 to 100 milliseconds - accompanied by a local slow wave, while the neighbouring cortex and the overall EEG remain awake.

Crucially, these local off periods became more frequent and more widespread as sleep pressure rose, and their occurrence predicted errors on a reaching task, which gives a concrete mechanism for the everyday experience of being awake but useless after a bad night.

The converse also holds: during nominally uniform NREM sleep, some regions can remain relatively activated, which is part of why dreaming happens at all.

The practical conclusion is that sleep and wake are not exclusive global states but graded, regionally varying properties of tissue, and related sleep-like local reactivity has since been reported in awake humans around focal brain injury (Sarasso, Rosanova and colleagues, Brain, 2020).


62.1.4 Dreaming, its content, and its neural correlates

Dreaming was long assumed to be the mental life of REM sleep, but people report dreams from NREM sleep too, which meant the older story was tracking the wrong variable.

Siclari, Baird, Perogamvros, Tononi and colleagues, in a 2017 Nature Neuroscience paper, used high-density EEG and repeatedly woke sleepers to ask whether they had been experiencing anything.

Regardless of whether the sleeper was in REM or NREM, reports of dreaming were accompanied by a local decrease of low-frequency activity in a posterior cortical hot zone spanning occipital cortex, precuneus, and posterior cingulate, while high-frequency activity there tracked specific dream contents such as faces or speech.

Monitoring that zone in real time let the researchers predict, above chance, whether a sleeper would report a dream - a striking result, and a good illustration of the local-sleep principle from the previous section.

The claim is not unchallenged: a 2019 commentary by Ruby argued that the design confounds dreaming with dream recall, since a sleeper who reports nothing may have dreamt and forgotten, so what is measured may be the correlate of memory for dreams rather than of dreaming itself.


62.2 Anaesthesia

General anaesthesia is the only routine, reversible, drug-controlled abolition of consciousness in human medicine, performed tens of millions of times a year, and that makes it an extraordinary laboratory.

It is also an unusually honest one, because anaesthetists must actually get the answer right, and the field has therefore taken very seriously the ways in which the outward signs of unconsciousness can mislead.


62.2.1 Agents, mechanisms, and common endpoints

General anaesthetics are not one class of drug with one target: they are a chemically diverse set that converges on a similar behavioural outcome by different molecular routes.

Propofol, the most widely used intravenous agent, binds the beta subunit of the GABA-A receptor - the main inhibitory receptor in the brain, which passes chloride ions and quietens neurons - and potentiates it, with secondary actions on hyperpolarisation-activated cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels and voltage-gated calcium channels.

Ketamine works almost oppositely, blocking the NMDA-type glutamate receptor, the main excitatory receptor involved in learning, and produces what is called dissociative anaesthesia, in which the patient may appear awake and yet be disconnected from the world.

Dexmedetomidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that works by borrowing the brain's own sedation machinery in the locus coeruleus and produces a state closer to natural NREM sleep.

Despite these different doors, the common endpoints look similar at the network level: suppression of thalamocortical communication, breakdown of frontoparietal connectivity, and the emergence of large slow oscillations resembling deep sleep - though ketamine is the standing exception, producing unresponsiveness with a fast, high-complexity EEG, which is exactly why a theory of consciousness cannot simply equate slow waves with oblivion.


62.2.2 Loss and recovery of consciousness as a state transition

If consciousness were a simple function of drug concentration, the concentration at which a person goes under and the concentration at which they come back would be the same.

They are not.

Across species from fruit flies to humans, more drug is required to induce unconsciousness than is present when consciousness returns - a lag known as hysteresis, meaning the state of a system depends on its history and not only on current conditions.

Kelz, Friedman and colleagues named the underlying resistance neural inertia, a conserved tendency of neural circuits to resist changing behavioural state, and showed with inhaled anaesthetics in mice that brain drug concentrations were genuinely higher at induction than at emergence, so the effect is not merely drug kinetics.

The implication for theory is important: losing and regaining consciousness are not the same journey run backwards, and emergence appears to be an active process with its own arousal circuitry rather than a passive drainage of drug, a view developed in reviews such as Kelz and colleagues' "Escape from Oblivion" (2019).


62.2.3 Connected and disconnected consciousness under anaesthesia

Anaesthesia research has forced a three-way distinction that the rest of consciousness science has borrowed.

Responsiveness is the ability to act; connectedness is having experience that tracks the external world; consciousness is having any experience at all, including a dream disconnected from the environment.

These come apart, and the tool that proved it is the isolated forearm technique, in which a tourniquet applied before the muscle relaxant keeps one arm unparalysed so the patient can squeeze the anaesthetist's hand on command even while otherwise immobile.

A meta-analysis by Linassi and colleagues (2018) found that under clinical conditions a median of about 5 percent of patients showed connected consciousness after laryngoscopy, with higher rates in younger patients and in women, and importantly most of these patients report nothing afterwards, because the drugs also block memory formation.

The reverse case is equally instructive: patients woken during propofol sedation frequently report vivid dream-like experience with no relation to the operating theatre, which is disconnected consciousness - conscious, but sealed off.


62.2.4 Intraoperative awareness and its detection

Accidental awareness during general anaesthesia (AAGA) means the patient forms an explicit, reportable memory of events during surgery, and it is the outcome patients fear most.

The 5th National Audit Project (NAP5) of the Royal College of Anaesthetists and the Association of Anaesthetists, led by Pandit and Cook and reported in 2014, collected patient self-reports across some 2.77 million UK general anaesthetics and found an incidence of roughly 1 in 19,600, rising to about 1 in 8,000 when a neuromuscular blocking drug was used and falling to about 1 in 136,000 when it was not - unsurprising, since a patient who can move usually moves.

That headline figure is method-dependent and much lower than figures obtained by actively interviewing every patient with the structured modified Brice questionnaire, which asks what the last thing remembered before sleep was, the first thing on waking, and anything in between; Brice-based studies typically report around 1 in 600 to 1 in 1,000.

Both numbers are defensible and they measure different things - spontaneous complaint versus solicited recall - and the gap between them is itself a finding about how easily brief awareness is forgotten or never volunteered.

Attempts to prevent awareness with processed-EEG depth monitors such as the bispectral index (BIS) have produced mixed results: the B-Aware trial (Myles and colleagues, 2004) found benefit over routine care, while B-Unaware (Avidan and colleagues, 2008) and BAG-RECALL (2011) found BIS no better than simply monitoring the concentration of anaesthetic gas exhaled, so the value of these monitors remains genuinely disputed.


62.3 Disorders of consciousness

When severe brain injury damages arousal or awareness machinery without killing the patient, the result is a disorder of consciousness, and here the question "is this person conscious?" stops being philosophical and becomes a clinical decision with life-and-death consequences.

This is the area where the last twenty years have overturned the most settled assumptions.


62.3.1 Coma, vegetative state, unresponsive wakefulness, minimally conscious state

The clinical categories are built on two separable ingredients: arousal, meaning wakefulness and eye opening, and awareness, meaning content of experience.

Coma is the absence of both - eyes closed, no sleep-wake cycle, no response beyond reflex - and it is typically a transient state lasting days to weeks.

The vegetative state, relabelled unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS) by Laureys and colleagues in 2010 to remove the pejorative and inaccurate connotations of "vegetative," is arousal without awareness: the eyes open, sleep-wake cycles return, reflexes and even grimacing occur, but nothing the patient does is voluntary or contingent on the world.

The minimally conscious state (MCS), defined by Giacino and colleagues in 2002, is the category for patients who show reproducible but inconsistent purposeful behaviour, such as visual pursuit of a mirror, or moving to command on some trials but not others.

Distinguishing these behaviourally requires the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R), a structured examination probing auditory, visual, motor, oromotor, communication, and arousal function, repeated on several days because a single assessment misdiagnoses a substantial minority of minimally conscious patients as unresponsive.

A theory-driven physiological measure now supplements the bedside exam: the perturbational complexity index (PCI) of Casali, Massimini and colleagues (2013) delivers a transcranial magnetic stimulation pulse to the cortex and compresses the resulting spatiotemporal EEG echo, on the reasoning that a conscious brain should respond in a way that is both differentiated and integrated and therefore hard to compress; values around 0.3 to 0.4 and above indicate capacity for consciousness, and the index reaches roughly 92 percent sensitivity for minimally conscious patients while flagging a minority of behaviourally unresponsive patients as having high complexity.


62.3.2 Covert awareness and the mental imagery command-following paradigm

The decisive experiment came from Adrian Owen and colleagues in Science in 2006.

A young woman meeting every clinical criterion for the vegetative state was placed in a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner - a machine that maps brain activity indirectly through changes in blood oxygenation - and asked to imagine playing tennis, and then to imagine walking through the rooms of her house.

Imagining tennis reliably activates the supplementary motor area, a motor-planning region; imagining spatial navigation reliably activates the parahippocampal gyrus and related spatial regions; her activations were indistinguishable in location and timing from those of healthy volunteers, and they switched on and off with the instructions.

Since following an instruction requires hearing it, understanding it, remembering it, and sustaining willed effort, this was extremely strong evidence of awareness in a patient with no behavioural sign of it whatsoever.

Monti, Owen and colleagues extended the method in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2010, testing 54 patients and finding 5 who could wilfully modulate brain activity, and in one case assigning "tennis" to yes and "navigation" to no in order to ask the patient actual questions about his own family and receive correct answers.

Cheaper EEG versions of the paradigm followed, notably Cruse, Owen and colleagues in the Lancet in 2011, which matters because EEG can be brought to the bedside of patients too unstable to scan.


62.3.3 Cognitive motor dissociation and its prevalence

The condition Owen's patient was in has a name: cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), coined by Schiff in 2015 for patients who show no behavioural command-following yet demonstrate reliable command-following on brain imaging or EEG.

The key question was how common it is, and the answer arrived in a multicentre study by Bodien, Schiff, Claassen, Owen, Laureys and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in August 2024, which assessed 353 patients across six hospitals in the United States and Europe with fMRI, EEG, or both.

Among the 241 patients with no observable response to commands, 60 - one in four - showed cognitive motor dissociation.

That number should be handled carefully, as the authors themselves stress: patients were recruited at specialist centres with advanced imaging, so the sample is not a random draw from the world's unresponsive patients, and the true global rate could be lower.

It should also be read in the right direction: a negative test does not prove absence of consciousness, since a patient may be too drowsy, too deaf, too aphasic, or too fluctuating to comply on the day of testing.


62.3.4 Prognostication, communication, and ethical stakes

If a quarter of apparently unresponsive patients may be covertly aware, then every downstream decision changes.

The 2018 practice guideline of the American Academy of Neurology (AAN), with the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine and the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, formally retired the term "permanent vegetative state" in favour of "chronic," because recovery after twelve months, while uncommon, does occur, and it warned clinicians against concluding a poor prognosis before around 28 days after injury.

The 2020 European Academy of Neurology guideline goes further in urging repeated multimodal assessment - behavioural, electrophysiological, and imaging - rather than a single verdict from a single examination.
