The ethical stakes are blunt: in many jurisdictions most deaths after severe brain injury follow a decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment, and those decisions are often made within days, which risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy in exactly the population that has not yet had time to show what it can recover.

Covert awareness also raises harder questions than it answers - whether a patient answering yes-or-no questions through a scanner has the capacity to consent, whether the absence of pain behaviour means the absence of pain, and how to weigh a communication channel that works on some days and not others - and there is no consensus yet on any of them.


62.4 Altered states

The final group is the states people seek out or suffer spontaneously, rather than states imposed by drugs in an operating theatre or damage in an intensive care unit.

They matter scientifically because they change the content and structure of experience while leaving the person awake and reportable, which makes them unusually informative.


62.4.1 Psychedelics, entropic brain accounts, and receptor mechanisms

Classic psychedelics - psilocybin from mushrooms, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and dimethyltryptamine - share one pharmacological signature: they are agonists at the serotonin 2A receptor (5-HT2A), which is densely expressed on layer 5 pyramidal neurons in higher-order association cortex, and blocking that receptor with ketanserin abolishes the subjective effects.

Carhart-Harris and colleagues proposed the entropic brain hypothesis in 2014, arguing that normal waking consciousness sits just below a critical point between order and disorder and that psychedelics push brain activity towards that critical zone, increasing the diversity and unpredictability - the entropy - of moment-to-moment brain states.

The 2019 successor model, REBUS (relaxed beliefs under psychedelics), casts this in predictive-processing terms: 5-HT2A agonism in high-level cortex reduces the precision, meaning the confidence weighting, given to the brain's prior expectations, which lets bottom-up sensory and emotional information exert unusual influence, and is offered as an account of both hallucination and therapeutic change.

Supporting evidence includes increased signal diversity under LSD and psilocybin, desegregation of normally distinct networks, and a 2022 Nature Communications study by Singleton and colleagues showing that both drugs flatten the brain's control energy landscape so that transitions between states become easier and more frequent.

The theory is elegant and the imaging effects are real, but it is worth being plain that "entropy" is operationalised in many different ways across studies, that most samples are small, and that the leap from a global statistic about signal diversity to a specific claim about belief precision is an interpretation rather than a measurement.


62.4.2 Meditation, absorption, and contemplative states

Contemplative practice offers something rare: trained subjects who can enter a specified state on cue and report on it in detail.

The most informative recent work concerns jhana, a set of deep concentrative absorption states in the Theravada Buddhist tradition, studied intensively in single expert practitioners rather than briefly in many novices - notably the 7-tesla fMRI case studies by Yang, Chowdhury, Ganesan, Brewer and colleagues published in Cerebral Cortex and NeuroImage in 2024.

These reported that deeper absorption was associated with more time in a brain state anticorrelated with the default mode network - the set of midline regions including medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex that is most active during self-referential mind-wandering - along with reduced network modularity, increased global connectivity, and involvement of insula, thalamus, and brainstem.

The recurring theme across contemplative neuroscience is quieting of the default mode network, which is also reported for psilocybin, suggesting a shared substrate for the loosening of ordinary self-representation.

The obvious methodological caveat is that a case study of one or a few adepts, however densely sampled, cannot establish generality, and expectancy in highly motivated long-term practitioners is difficult to control.


62.4.3 Hypnosis and suggestion

Hypnosis is a procedure - an induction followed by suggestions - and hypnotisability is the trait that determines whether it does anything, measured with standardised scales and remarkably stable across adult life, with roughly 10 to 15 percent of people scoring as highly hypnotisable.

Jiang, Spiegel and colleagues, in Cerebral Cortex in 2017, scanned highly hypnotisable people in and out of hypnosis and reported three changes: reduced activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, a region involved in salience and conflict monitoring; increased functional coupling between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the insula, plausibly relating to enhanced control over bodily experience; and reduced coupling between dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the medial prefrontal default-mode region, plausibly relating to the dissociation between action and the sense of authoring it.

A follow-up using magnetic resonance spectroscopy found higher GABA concentration in the anterior cingulate in more hypnotisable individuals, offering a possible neurochemical trait marker.

Hypnosis is genuinely useful clinically for pain and for some functional symptoms, but the theoretical dispute is unresolved: state theorists hold that hypnosis is a distinct altered state of consciousness, while sociocognitive theorists such as Kirsch and Lynn argue it is ordinary attention, expectancy, and role enactment with no special state required, and the imaging findings above have been claimed by both camps.


62.4.4 Seizures, auras, and dissociative states

Focal seizures are the brain altering its own state without permission, and because they begin in identifiable tissue, the experience they produce points to a location.

An aura is the subjective beginning of a seizure - a rising epigastric sensation, an intense familiarity (déjà vu) or unfamiliarity, an unaccountable fear - and is itself a focal seizure confined to a small region, most often mesial temporal structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus.

The most philosophically loaded variety is the ecstatic seizure, in which patients report bliss, perfect clarity, certainty, and dissolution of time; long attributed to temporal lobe epilepsy, converging evidence reviewed by Picard and Craig and refined by direct electrical stimulation work now places the symptomatogenic zone in the dorsal anterior insula, a region implicated in interoception, the sense of the body's internal condition.

Picard's proposed mechanism is that the state arises from a transient suppression of interoceptive prediction error - the brain briefly receives no signal that anything is unexpected, which is experienced as perfect certainty and safety.

Other ictal dissociative phenomena localise elsewhere: out-of-body experiences and autoscopy, in which one sees one's own body from outside, have been elicited by stimulating the temporoparietal junction, where vestibular, visual, and bodily signals are integrated (Blanke and colleagues, from 2002 onwards).

A clinically important complication is that dissociative or functional seizures, which resemble epileptic seizures but have no epileptic discharge, are common, frequently co-occur with genuine epilepsy, and are strongly associated with dissociative symptoms and trauma history - so an altered state that looks epileptic is not always epileptic.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Consciousness is not a single global switch: sleep occurs locally in awake brains, dreaming tracks activity in a posterior cortical hot zone rather than in REM sleep as such, and different anaesthetics reach a similar behavioural endpoint through entirely different receptors.

Responsiveness, connectedness, and consciousness are three separable things, demonstrated most cleanly by the isolated forearm technique in the operating theatre and most consequentially by cognitive motor dissociation in the intensive care unit, where the 2024 Bodien and colleagues study found covert command-following in about one in four behaviourally unresponsive patients.

Because behaviour underestimates consciousness, the field has moved towards perturbing the brain and measuring the complexity of its reply, as in the perturbational complexity index, rather than relying on either bedside examination or resting brain signals alone.

Loss and recovery of consciousness are asymmetric processes separated by hysteresis and neural inertia, which means emergence is an active accomplishment rather than a passive fading of drug.

Altered states from psychedelics, deep meditation, hypnosis, and seizures converge on a small set of substrates - default mode network disengagement, 5-HT2A-rich association cortex, and the anterior insula - though the theories built on those convergences, from the entropic brain to the state account of hypnosis, remain considerably less secure than the measurements that inspired them.


CHAPTER 63. SELF, AGENCY, AND METACOGNITION (CORE)

This chapter is about the mind turning around to look at itself.

It asks three connected questions: what makes an experience feel like mine, what makes an action feel like something I did rather than something that merely happened, and how well can a person judge the quality of their own thinking.

These are not idle questions.

They are the questions that break first in schizophrenia, in depersonalisation, and in certain kinds of brain damage, and the way they break tells us how they are built.

The chapter also matters because psychology depends on people reporting what is going on inside them, and we will look hard at how far those reports can be trusted.

By the end you should be able to say what the self is made of in neuroscientific terms, and where the pieces come apart.


63.1 The senses of self

The word self is doing several jobs at once in ordinary speech.

It can mean the bare feeling of being a subject right now, or the life story you would tell an interviewer, or the felt shape and position of your body.

Neuroscience has made progress precisely by refusing to treat these as one thing.

Each has a different developmental timeline, a different set of supporting brain regions, and a different pattern of failure.

The rest of this section takes them one at a time.


63.1.1 Minimal self: ownership and agency

The philosopher Shaun Gallagher, in an influential 2000 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, distinguished the minimal self from the narrative self.

The minimal self is the self of this moment, stripped of memory and biography - simply the fact that there is someone here having this experience.

Gallagher argued the minimal self has two separable strands: the sense of ownership, which is the feeling that this body or this experience is mine, and the sense of agency, which is the feeling that I am the one causing this action.

Ordinarily the two travel together, so it takes an unusual case to prise them apart.

If someone pushes your arm, you still own the movement - it is your arm that moved - but you do not feel agency for it, and that dissociation is the clearest evidence that the two strands are genuinely different.

In thought insertion, a symptom reported in schizophrenia, patients say a thought occurred in their mind but that they did not think it, which is ownership without agency in the mental domain.


63.1.2 Narrative and autobiographical self

The narrative self is the self extended in time: the person who did those things last year and intends those things next year.

It is built out of autobiographical memory, and it is a construction rather than a record, revised continually to keep the story coherent.

Neuroimaging consistently implicates a set of regions called the cortical midline structures - the medial prefrontal cortex on the inner surface of the frontal lobe, the anterior and posterior cingulate cortex, and the medial parietal and retrosplenial cortex - in tasks where people judge whether trait words describe them, or recall episodes from their own past.

Georg Northoff and colleagues have argued across a series of reviews from 2004 onward that these midline regions are the core substrate of self-related processing.

These regions overlap substantially with the default mode network, a set of areas that are more active when a person is resting quietly than when they are performing a demanding external task, which fits the everyday observation that an idle mind drifts toward autobiography.

A caution is warranted here: overlap is not identity, and there is ongoing debate about whether the midline regions are specifically about self or more generally about internally generated, memory-based simulation of any kind, including thinking about other people.


63.1.3 Bodily self and its multisensory basis

The feeling that your body is yours is not a fixed given; it is computed, moment by moment, from the agreement between vision, touch, and proprioception (the internal sense of where your limbs are, supplied by receptors in muscles and joints).

Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen demonstrated this in a famously simple 1998 experiment in Nature.

A participant's real hand is hidden behind a screen while a rubber hand lies in view, and the experimenter strokes both with paintbrushes at the same time.

Within about a minute most people report that the rubber hand feels like their own, and their judgement of where their real hand is drifts toward the fake one.

Henrik Ehrsson and colleagues extended the effect to the whole body using head-mounted displays, producing out-of-body-like experiences in healthy volunteers, and neuroimaging of these illusions points to the ventral premotor cortex, the intraparietal sulcus in the parietal lobe, and the cerebellum - regions that specialise in fusing signals from different senses into a single spatial map.

The lesson is that body ownership is the output of a multisensory inference, and it can be fooled whenever the inputs are made to agree in the wrong place.


63.1.4 Disorders of self: depersonalisation, alien hand, delusions of control

Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder is a condition in which people report feeling detached from their own body, emotions, or surroundings, as though watching themselves from outside or through glass.

Crucially, reality testing is intact - patients know the feeling is not literally true, which distinguishes it from psychosis.

Mauricio Sierra and Anthony David proposed that the condition reflects excessive inhibition of emotional processing, with lateral prefrontal cortex over-suppressing the insula, a region deep in the cortex that registers bodily and emotional feeling states; imaging work by Nick Medford and colleagues has found reduced insula responses to aversive images, with insula activity rising again as symptoms improve.

Alien hand syndrome is different in kind: following damage to the corpus callosum or the medial frontal cortex, one hand performs coherent, apparently purposeful actions - unbuttoning a shirt the other hand just buttoned - that the patient disowns as not willed.

Delusions of control in schizophrenia, sometimes called passivity phenomena, are different again: the patient's own movement is experienced as being made by an outside force.

Chris Frith's account, developed from the 1990s onward, is that the brain's prediction of the consequences of its own commands is faulty, so self-generated action is not tagged as self-generated and feels imposed; reduced functional coupling between frontal and posterior brain regions in schizophrenia is consistent with this, though the mechanism is not settled.

It is worth stating plainly that alien hand syndrome and schizophrenic passivity are distinct: the alien hand patient owns the limb but not the intention, whereas the passivity patient attributes the intention to an external agent.


63.2 Agency and volition

Agency is the sense of authorship over one's own actions.

It is remarkably quiet when it works - you do not normally notice that you are the author of your own reach for a cup - and unmistakable when it fails.

This section works through the leading mechanistic account, the main laboratory measure, the most famous and most contested experiment in the field, and the current synthesis.


63.2.1 Comparator models of the sense of agency

The comparator model borrows its machinery from motor control.

When the brain issues a motor command it also generates an efference copy, an internal duplicate of that command, and feeds it to a forward model - a circuit that predicts what the sensory consequences of the movement will be.

The prediction is then compared with the actual sensory feedback.

When prediction and feedback match, the movement is tagged as self-produced, the resulting sensation is attenuated - which is why you cannot tickle yourself, a point Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert, and Chris Frith made experimentally around 1998 to 2000 - and agency is felt.

When they mismatch, the action is flagged as externally caused.

The model is elegant and explains a lot, but it has serious critics: Shaun Gallagher has argued it cannot be extended to agency over thoughts without an infinite regress of intentions, and a 2019 analysis in Neuroscience of Consciousness argued that a mere prediction match is not by itself sufficient to generate a felt sense of agency.


63.2.2 Intentional binding and its interpretation

Patrick Haggard, Sam Clark, and Jeri Kalogeras reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2002 that when a voluntary action causes an outcome, the perceived time of the action shifts later and the perceived time of the outcome shifts earlier, so the two feel compressed together.

The effect does not appear, or appears much less, when the movement is involuntary, which is why it was interpreted as an implicit measure of agency - a way of getting at the sense of authorship without asking people directly.

It became one of the workhorse measures of the field, used in hundreds of studies.

But the interpretation is now openly contested.

Several groups, including Suzuki and colleagues in 2019, have argued the compression is really a general multisensory or causal binding phenomenon, occurring whenever two events are perceived as causally linked whether or not an intention is involved, and recent preprints have questioned whether the specifically intentional component exists at all.

The honest summary in 2026 is that the temporal compression is a robust finding but its status as a pure marker of agency is not.


63.2.3 Libet's experiments and the readiness potential controversy

Benjamin Libet, in a 1983 study, asked participants to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it and to report, using a fast-moving clock, the moment they became aware of the urge to move.

Scalp electrodes recorded the readiness potential, a slow negative drift in electrical activity that builds before voluntary movement and was discovered by Hans Kornhuber and Lüder Deecke in 1965.

Libet found the readiness potential began roughly 550 milliseconds before the movement, while the reported conscious urge came only about 200 milliseconds before it - so brain activity apparently preceded the conscious decision by a third of a second, and the result was widely read as evidence against free will.

That reading has been substantially undermined.

Aaron Schurger, Jacobo Sitt, and Stanislas Dehaene argued in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2012 that the readiness potential is not a preparation signal at all but an artefact of averaging: neural activity fluctuates randomly, movement is triggered when a fluctuation crosses a threshold, and averaging backward from movement onset necessarily produces an apparent slow rise that was never a decision.

On this account the gap Libet measured is the gap between noise and threshold crossing, not between an unconscious decision and its conscious shadow.

The debate is live rather than closed - the accumulator model has its own critics, and later work has probed whether the early readiness potential carries any information about the upcoming choice - but the confident 1980s claim that neuroscience had refuted free will no longer stands unqualified.


63.2.4 Volition as a graded and reconstructed attribution

The current centre of gravity in the field treats agency not as a single signal but as a judgement assembled from several cues of varying reliability.

Daniel Wegner's theory of apparent mental causation, set out in his 2002 book The Illusion of Conscious Will, holds that we infer authorship when a thought precedes an action, is consistent with it, and no other cause is apparent - which means agency can be manufactured by arranging those conditions artificially, and can be missing when they are absent even for actions we really did perform.

Matthis Synofzik, Gottfried Vosgerau, and Albert Newen proposed in 2008 a two-step account that separates a low-level, non-conceptual feeling of agency from a higher-level, explicit judgement of agency, with each fed by a weighted mixture of internal sensorimotor cues and external contextual cues.

This cue-integration framing has largely absorbed the comparator model rather than replacing it: prediction is one cue among several, weighted more heavily when it is reliable.

The practical upshot is that agency is graded, partly retrospective, and socially sensitive - which is uncomfortable for legal and moral intuitions that treat authorship as all or nothing.


63.3 Metacognition

Metacognition means cognition about cognition - knowing what you know, and knowing how well you know it.

Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens gave the field its organising picture in 1990: an object level where the actual perceiving and remembering happens, and a meta level that holds a model of the object level, linked by monitoring, which carries information upward, and control, which sends instructions downward.

The sections below cover how metacognition is measured, where in the brain it lives, whether it is one faculty or many, and what it is for.


63.3.1 Confidence, calibration, and metacognitive efficiency

The usual laboratory handle on metacognition is confidence: a participant makes a difficult judgement, then rates how sure they are.

Good metacognition means confidence tracks accuracy - high when right, low when wrong.

The obvious measure, the raw correlation between confidence and correctness, is badly confounded, because someone who finds the task easy will look metacognitively skilled simply by being right a lot.

Brian Maniscalco and Hakwan Lau solved this in 2012 using signal detection theory, a framework for separating sensitivity from response bias.

They defined meta-d prime as the level of first-order sensitivity an ideal observer would need in order to produce the confidence pattern actually observed, and then the M-ratio, meta-d prime divided by d prime, which measures how much of the available evidence the confidence judgement is actually using.

An M-ratio of one means confidence is as informative as the evidence allows; below one means information is being thrown away; above one, unusually, means confidence draws on something the binary response did not.

Stephen Fleming's hierarchical Bayesian implementation, HMeta-d, published in Neuroscience of Consciousness in 2017, made the measure workable with the small trial counts typical of patient and neuroimaging studies.


63.3.2 Anterior prefrontal cortex and metacognitive ability

Stephen Fleming, Rimona Weil, Zoltan Nagy, Ray Dolan, and Geraint Rees published a landmark result in Science in 2010: across healthy individuals matched for task performance, metacognitive accuracy on a visual task correlated with grey matter volume in the right anterior prefrontal cortex, roughly Brodmann area 10, at the very front of the brain.

Follow-up work strengthened the causal claim.

Fleming and colleagues reported in Brain in 2014 that patients with lesions to anterior prefrontal cortex showed impaired metacognition for perception while their metacognition for memory was spared, and their first-order performance was intact - a striking dissociation between doing a task and knowing how well you did it.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies, which briefly disrupt a targeted region with a magnetic pulse, have produced broadly convergent results, and a 2018 Journal of Neuroscience study by Medha Shekhar and Dobromir Rahnev distinguished the contributions of dorsolateral and anterior prefrontal cortex.

The picture is not unanimous: a 2017 study found metacognitive ability substantially preserved in some patients after anterior prefrontal resection, which suggests either redundancy in the network or that the critical tissue is more circumscribed than the label suggests.


63.3.3 Domain-general and domain-specific metacognition

Is being well calibrated about your eyesight the same skill as being well calibrated about your memory?

The evidence says partly.

Jorge Morales, Hakwan Lau, and Stephen Fleming reported in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2018 that when perceptual and memory tasks were matched for difficulty, the fine-grained multivoxel activity patterns in anterior prefrontal cortex that predicted confidence were domain-specific - the perceptual code and the memory code were different - while coarser signals predicting confidence and accuracy appeared in a broad frontal and posterior midline network common to both.

Behavioural individual-difference studies point the same way: metacognitive efficiency correlates across domains, but far from perfectly, so a shared general factor sits alongside substantial domain-specific variance.

The practical implication for a learner is that calibration training in one subject will transfer to another only in part, and should not be assumed to transfer wholesale.


63.3.4 Metacognition in learning, in control allocation, and in social communication

Metacognition earns its keep by driving decisions.

In learning, judgements of learning - a person's prediction of whether they will later recall an item - guide how long they study each item; the discrepancy reduction account, consistent with Nelson and Narens, says people spend most time on what they judge furthest from being learned, though under time pressure learners often switch to the opposite strategy and abandon the hardest items.

In cognitive control, confidence signals when to keep deliberating, when to check the work again, and when to stop - low confidence is the trigger for allocating more effort, and a person whose confidence is uninformative cannot allocate effort sensibly.

Socially, confidence is the currency of shared decision making.

Bahador Bahrami and colleagues showed in Science in 2010 that two people making a perceptual judgement together outperform the better of them individually, provided they can communicate freely and their individual abilities are not too unequal, and the data fitted a weighted confidence sharing model in which the group follows whoever is more confident.

That mechanism only works if the partners' confidence scales are calibrated to each other, which turns metacognition from a private virtue into a communicative one.


63.4 Introspection as data

Almost everything in this chapter rests on somebody saying what their experience was like.

That is a methodological problem, not an incidental one, and it deserves direct treatment rather than a footnote.

This section asks how far introspective reports can be trusted, what happens when they are demonstrably wrong, and whether they can be improved.


63.4.1 The reliability of self-report

Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson's 1977 paper in Psychological Review, Telling More Than We Can Know, is the founding document of introspective scepticism.

Reviewing a wide body of evidence, they argued that people often have no direct access to the processes that produced their own judgements, and that when asked why they did something they generate an answer from plausible lay theories about what usually causes such behaviour rather than by inspecting the actual cause.

Their evidence included cases where participants were demonstrably influenced by a factor they denied, and denied being influenced by a factor that demonstrably mattered.

The paper does not show that introspection is worthless.

The distinction that survives is between reporting the content of experience, where people are reasonably good, and reporting the causes of that experience, where they are frequently confabulating - and this distinction is what licenses the continued use of confidence ratings while distrusting explanatory why-questions.


63.4.2 Confabulation and the interpreter account from split-brain work

In patients whose corpus callosum has been cut to control severe epilepsy, information can be presented to one hemisphere alone.

Michael Gazzaniga and colleagues found that when an instruction was given only to the right hemisphere and the patient acted on it, the left hemisphere - which controls speech and had no access to the instruction - immediately produced a confident explanation that was simply invented.

Gazzaniga called the responsible left-hemisphere process the interpreter: a module whose job is to weave available evidence into a coherent story about oneself, and which does that job whether or not it has the facts.

The same phenomenon appears in intact people.

Petter Johansson, Lars Hall, Sverker Sikström, and Andreas Olsson demonstrated choice blindness in Science in 2005: participants chose the more attractive of two faces, were handed back the face they had rejected by sleight of hand, and in most cases failed to notice the switch while readily explaining why they had preferred the face they had actually turned down.

The classical split-brain picture has itself been challenged - Yair Pinto and colleagues argued in Brain in 2017 for a conscious unity with split perception model, in which one conscious agent persists despite the divided perception, while Volz and Gazzaniga countered that cross-cueing between the hemispheres explains Pinto's findings - so the interpreter concept should be held as a well-supported description of confabulation rather than as a settled anatomy of consciousness.


63.4.3 Introspective training and micro-phenomenology

If naive introspection is unreliable, the natural question is whether trained introspection is better.

Micro-phenomenology, developed by Claire Petitmengin from the 1990s onward out of her doctoral work with Francisco Varela, is an attempt to answer yes.

Its central tool is the elicitation or micro-phenomenological interview, in which an interviewer guides a person back to one specific past moment, helps them re-evoke it in sensory detail, and then asks repeatedly about the how of the experience while carefully avoiding questions about why - because why-questions are exactly the ones that invite theory-driven confabulation.

The method aims to surface fine-grained structure that people ordinarily cannot articulate, such as the sequence of felt steps preceding an intuition.

Its supporters point to reproducible structural descriptions across independent interviewees; its critics note that the interviewer's guidance is itself a source of suggestion, and that inter-rater reliability and independent validation remain thinner than the method's ambitions require.

This should be reported as a promising and disciplined approach whose validation is still in progress, not as an established solution.


63.4.4 First-person methods and neurophenomenology

Francisco Varela proposed neurophenomenology in the Journal of Consciousness Studies in 1996 as a methodological response to the hard problem of consciousness - the question of why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all.

His proposal was not to solve that problem by argument but to constrain it empirically from both sides: collect rigorous first-person descriptions, using disciplined methods including contemplative training, and use them as an active constraint on the analysis of simultaneously recorded brain data, rather than treating reports as noisy afterthoughts.

The clearest demonstrations have been studies in which trial-by-trial subjective reports of readiness or attentional state predict variability in the neural response that would otherwise look like random noise.

The programme's honest standing in 2026 is that of a productive methodological stance with a modest empirical output.

It has influenced how consciousness experiments are designed, particularly the practice of collecting graded subjective reports rather than binary ones, more than it has produced a body of findings under its own name.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The self is not one thing but several separable systems - a minimal self of ownership and agency, a narrative self built from autobiographical memory in the cortical midline structures, and a bodily self computed from multisensory agreement - and each fails in its own characteristic way, as depersonalisation, alien hand syndrome, and delusions of control each show.

The sense of agency is best understood not as a single readout of a comparator but as a graded, partly retrospective judgement that weighs sensorimotor prediction alongside contextual and social cues.

The Libet result, long treated as neuroscience's refutation of free will, has been seriously destabilised by Schurger's demonstration that the readiness potential may be an averaging artefact of random fluctuation, and intentional binding has likewise lost its status as a clean marker of intention.

Metacognition can be measured properly once first-order performance is controlled for, using meta-d prime and the M-ratio, and it depends on anterior prefrontal cortex in a way that is partly domain-general and partly domain-specific.

Introspective reports are trustworthy about the content of experience and untrustworthy about its causes, a gap made vivid by split-brain confabulation and by choice blindness in healthy people.

Because every claim in this chapter ultimately rests on someone reporting their inner life, the discipline of first-person method is not a philosophical side issue but part of the empirical machinery.


CHAPTER 64. SPONTANEOUS COGNITION, IMAGINATION, AND CREATIVITY (CORE)

Most of what your brain does, it does without being asked.

You are not always solving a problem someone handed you; a great deal of the time you are remembering, rehearsing, worrying, planning, drifting, and inventing.

This chapter is about that inner traffic - where it comes from in the brain, how researchers manage to measure something as private as a daydream, and what it is good for.

It matters because for most of the twentieth century this activity was invisible to neuroscience, treated as noise to be subtracted away, and because the same machinery that produces useful planning and creative invention also produces rumination and dread.

We will move from the brain system that hosts spontaneous thought, to the phenomenon of mind wandering, to mental simulation, and finally to creativity.


64.1 The default mode network

The default mode network (DMN) is a set of brain regions that becomes more active when a person is left alone with their thoughts and less active when they are absorbed in a demanding external task.

It was not predicted by any theory.

It was discovered by accident, in the leftovers of other experiments, and its interpretation has been argued over ever since.


64.1.1 Discovery through task-induced deactivation

In brain imaging you almost never measure activity in absolute terms; you compare a task condition against a baseline condition and look at the difference.

Gordon Shulman and colleagues, in a 1997 meta-analysis pooling nine positron emission tomography (PET) studies - PET is an imaging method that tracks a radioactive tracer to estimate blood flow or metabolism - noticed something odd in that leftover comparison.

A consistent set of regions, including the posterior cingulate cortex (a midline structure toward the back of the brain), the medial prefrontal cortex (the middle surface of the frontal lobes), and the angular gyri (parietal regions near the top and back), reliably went down during attention-demanding tasks, no matter what the task was.

This is called task-induced deactivation, and because it appeared across unrelated experiments it could not be an artefact of any one paradigm.

Marcus Raichle and colleagues, in a 2001 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America titled "A default mode of brain function", argued that these regions were not being switched on by rest but were tonically active all along, constituting a baseline or default mode of brain function that tasks interrupt.

The rhetorical move was important: it reframed rest from an absence of activity into a positive state with its own physiology.


64.1.2 Component subsystems and their functions

The DMN is not one thing, and treating it as a single blob has caused a good deal of confusion.

Jessica Andrews-Hanna and colleagues, working with Randy Buckner in the late 2000s and early 2010s, used functional connectivity - the statistical tendency of two regions' signals to rise and fall together - to fractionate it into three parts.

There is a midline core, comprising the anterior medial prefrontal cortex and the posterior cingulate cortex, which is engaged particularly by self-referential judgements, such as deciding whether an adjective describes you.

There is a dorsal medial subsystem, comprising dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, the temporoparietal junction, lateral temporal cortex, and the temporal pole, which is engaged by thinking about other minds - theory of mind, moral judgement, social reasoning.

And there is a medial temporal subsystem, comprising ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior inferior parietal lobe, retrosplenial cortex, parahippocampal cortex, and the hippocampus itself, which supports memory-based construction: recalling autobiographical episodes and building imagined scenes.

The practical consequence is that a study reporting "DMN activation" without saying which subsystem has said very little.


64.1.3 Position at the top of the principal cortical gradient

A more recent way to describe the DMN abandons the idea of a network with a boundary and describes the cortex as a continuous gradient instead.

Daniel Margulies and colleagues, in a 2016 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, applied a dimension-reduction technique to whole-brain connectivity data and extracted the single axis that explained the most variation - the principal gradient.

At one end of that axis sit the primary sensory and motor regions, the parts of cortex wired most directly to eyes, ears, skin, and muscles.

At the other end sits the default mode network, and, strikingly, the DMN is also maximally distant from primary regions in terms of physical distance measured along the folded cortical surface.

The interpretation is that the DMN is the part of cortex furthest removed from immediate sensation and action, which is exactly what a system for thought detached from the here and now would need to be.

The same gradient was recoverable in macaque monkeys, which suggests it is an old organisational principle rather than a human peculiarity.


64.1.4 From task-negative to a positive account of its function

The early label for the DMN was "task-negative", defined by what suppresses it, which is an unsatisfying way to characterise any brain system.

Two lines of work have pushed toward a positive account.

The first is that the DMN is reliably activated, not deactivated, by tasks that require internally generated or self-relevant content - remembering, imagining the future, judging other people, understanding a story.

The second is that the DMN appears to integrate information over long timescales; Yaara Yeshurun, Mai Nguyen, and Uri Hasson argued in a 2021 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience that it functions to build and maintain context and narrative models, where an individual's idiosyncratic interpretation meets a shared social framework.

There is also evidence, still contested, that the DMN can support performance on tasks that are highly practised and automatic rather than merely interfering with them.

The honest position in 2026 is that the DMN is a context-and-simulation system whose deactivation during hard external tasks is a side effect of resource competition, not its defining property.


64.2 Mind wandering and spontaneous thought

Mind wandering is the everyday experience of your attention decoupling from the task in front of you and moving to something unrelated.

It is extremely common, difficult to measure honestly, and neither simply good nor simply bad.


64.2.1 Taxonomies of spontaneous thought and their measurement

The standard measurement tool is experience sampling: interrupting a person at unpredictable moments and asking what was in their mind just then.

Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert used a smartphone version of this in a 2010 study in Science with about 2,250 participants, and found that people reported thinking about something other than what they were doing on roughly 47 percent of samples.

Researchers have since insisted that "mind wandering" is not one thing.

Kalina Christoff and colleagues, in a 2016 paper in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, proposed a dynamic framework in which thought is characterised by how strongly it is constrained, with automatic constraints (a salient stimulus pulling you) and deliberate constraints (executive control holding you) varying independently, and mind wandering occupying the weakly constrained end.

Paul Seli and colleagues argued in 2018 in Trends in Cognitive Sciences for a family-resemblances view: mind wandering has no single defining feature, only overlapping ones such as being unintentional, task-unrelated, stimulus-independent, and freely moving.

Two distinctions do a lot of work empirically - intentional versus unintentional mind wandering, and task-unrelated thought versus task-related interference - and studies that collapse them tend to produce inconsistent results.


64.2.2 Neural correlates and the executive-default interaction

Kalina Christoff, Alan Gordon, Jonathan Smallwood, Rachelle Smith, and Jonathan Schooler published the key imaging study in 2009 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, embedding experience-sampling probes inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scan - fMRI measures blood-oxygen changes as an indirect index of neural activity.

They compared brain activity in the seconds before a probe on which the participant reported being off-task against activity before an on-task report.

Default network regions were more active during mind wandering, as expected.

The surprise was that executive regions, in the dorsolateral prefrontal and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, were also recruited, and were recruited most strongly when the participant reported being unaware they had drifted.

That is an awkward result for the simple picture in which default and executive systems are antagonistic, and it suggests mind wandering is a resource-consuming constructive act rather than a lapse into idling.

Jonathan Smallwood's later work with the perceptual decoupling account frames it as attention being withdrawn from sensory input to serve an internal train of thought.


64.2.3 Costs to performance and benefits to planning

The costs are well established and easy to demonstrate.

A 2022 meta-analysis by Andrew Soemer and colleagues in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review confirmed a reliable negative association between mind wandering and reading comprehension: people who drift while reading understand and remember less, and this holds across ages and materials.

Mind wandering also predicts errors in sustained-attention tasks, and in applied settings such as driving it is associated with worse outcomes.

Against this, Benjamin Baird, Jonathan Smallwood, and Jonathan Schooler argued in a 2011 paper in Consciousness and Cognition, titled "Back to the future", that the content of mind wandering is disproportionately future-oriented and concerned with personal goals - an autobiographical planning function.

The plausible reconciliation is a trade-off account: the mind is not failing when it wanders, it is reallocating from an external task to an internal one, and whether that is a cost or a benefit depends entirely on which task mattered more.

The evidence for genuine planning benefits is weaker than the evidence for performance costs, and this asymmetry should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over.


64.2.4 Rumination as maladaptive spontaneous thought

Rumination is repetitive, passive, self-focused thought about distress and its causes, and it is a strong risk factor for depression.

Susan Nolen-Hoeksema's work from the 1990s onward established that a ruminative response style predicts the onset, severity, and duration of depressive episodes, and distinguished brooding, the maladaptive form, from reflective pondering.

J. Paul Hamilton, Ian Gotlib, and colleagues have linked rumination to the default mode network, and specifically to increased functional coupling between the subgenual prefrontal cortex - a small ventral midline region associated with negative mood - and the rest of the DMN.

Their 2015 review in Biological Psychiatry framed depressive rumination as a kind of dark matter of clinical neuroscience: obviously present, hard to see directly with standard task designs.

Meta-analyses of imaging studies broadly support DMN involvement in rumination, though effect sizes vary and it remains unresolved how much of the connectivity difference is a cause of depression and how much a consequence.

The clinical significance is that rumination is spontaneous thought with the same machinery as planning and daydreaming, but stuck in a loop that never terminates in action.


64.3 Mental simulation

Mental simulation is the running of an experience offline - an event that has not happened, or has not happened yet, or happened differently.

This section argues that simulation is not a separate faculty but memory operated in a different direction.


64.3.1 Episodic future thinking and the constructive simulation hypothesis

Episodic future thinking is imagining a specific personal event that might happen to you, with a time, a place, and detail.

Daniel Schacter and Donna Rose Addis proposed the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis in 2007, in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, holding that episodic memory is not a playback device but a store of reusable fragments, and that its central function is to allow those fragments to be recombined into simulations of possible futures.

The prediction is that damage to episodic memory should damage imagination, and that is what is found.

Demis Hassabis, Dharshan Kumaran, Seralynne Vann, and Eleanor Maguire showed in 2007, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, that patients with hippocampal amnesia asked to imagine novel scenes produced fragmented, spatially incoherent descriptions rather than integrated scenes.

Endel Tulving's earlier patient K.C., who could not recall personal past events, was likewise unable to say anything about his personal future, describing his mind as blank.

A second, elegant prediction of the hypothesis is that the flexibility that makes simulation possible is also what makes memory error-prone: the same recombination that lets you picture next Tuesday lets you misremember which of two similar evenings a remark was made in.


64.3.2 Mental imagery across modalities and aphantasia

Mental imagery is the experience of perceiving in the absence of the corresponding stimulus, and it occurs in vision, hearing, smell, touch, and movement, not vision alone.

The long-running imagery debate pitted Stephen Kosslyn, who argued images are depictive and picture-like and rely on the topographically organised early visual cortex, against Zenon Pylyshyn, who argued they are propositional and language-like with the picture-quality an epiphenomenon.

Decoding studies, which train a classifier on brain activity during perception and then test it on activity during imagery, have tipped the argument toward the depictive side by showing that imagined content can be read out of early visual cortex, though the role of that cortex is still actively debated as of 2026.

Adam Zeman and colleagues named aphantasia in 2015 for the lifelong absence of voluntary visual imagery, and hyperphantasia for imagery as vivid as seeing.

Using floor and ceiling scores on the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), estimates put extreme aphantasia near 0.7 percent of people and extreme hyperphantasia near 2.5 percent, with aphantasia associated with reported difficulty in autobiographical memory and face recognition, and elevated rates in first-degree relatives suggesting a heritable component.

Critically, people with aphantasia perform normally on many imagery-dependent tasks and retain knowledge of visual features, which means what is missing is the conscious depictive experience rather than the underlying visual computation - a finding with obvious relevance to theories of consciousness.


64.3.3 Counterfactual thinking and regret

Counterfactual thinking is simulating how an event might have turned out differently - the "if only" thought.

Regret is the emotion produced when that comparison is unfavourable to the choice you actually made, and it is distinguished from simple disappointment precisely by requiring the counterfactual comparison and your own agency.

Nathalie Camille and colleagues showed in 2004, in Science, that patients with orbitofrontal cortex damage - the orbitofrontal cortex sits above the eye sockets and integrates value information - reported disappointment normally but did not report regret and did not adjust their choices to avoid it, as though the counterfactual comparison itself were unavailable.

Giorgio Coricelli and colleagues, in 2005 in Nature Neuroscience, ran the same gambling paradigm in fMRI and found medial orbitofrontal activity scaling with both immediate and cumulative regret, while lateral orbitofrontal activity tracked immediate regret only.

Counterfactual simulation is not merely painful; it is how a system with limited experience extracts extra learning from a single outcome, by evaluating the road not taken.


64.3.4 Simulation shared with memory: the same machinery run forward

The strongest evidence that remembering and imagining are one system is anatomical overlap.

Roland Benoit and Daniel Schacter published an activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis in Neuropsychologia in 2015, pooling many studies of autobiographical memory and of episodic simulation, and found a common core network: hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex, ventromedial and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex, lateral temporal cortex, and inferior parietal cortex.

That core network is essentially the default mode network, which ties this section back to 64.1.

The overlap is not total, and the differences are informative: imagining novel events tends to recruit the hippocampus more than remembering does, consistent with construction being more effortful than retrieval.

Some researchers, following Eleanor Maguire and Demis Hassabis, argue the shared ingredient is specifically scene construction - building a coherent spatial context - rather than time travel as such, and this remains a live disagreement with the Schacter and Addis position that the shared ingredient is episodic recombination.

Either way, the load-bearing claim survives: the brain does not have a separate organ for the future.


64.4 Creativity

Creativity is usually defined by two criteria together - a product must be novel and it must be useful or appropriate in its domain.

Novelty alone is randomness, and appropriateness alone is competence.

The neuroscience of creativity is young, its measures are imperfect, and its most cited findings are stronger about idea generation in the laboratory than about eminent achievement in the world.


64.4.1 Divergent and convergent thinking

Divergent thinking is generating many possible answers from one starting point, and it is usually measured with the Alternate Uses Task, in which a person lists unusual uses for a common object such as a brick.

Responses are scored for fluency (how many), flexibility (how many categories), originality (how rare), and elaboration (how developed), and originality scored by rarity is a fragile measure because it depends on the sample.

Convergent thinking is finding the single correct answer that ties disparate elements together, and it is usually measured with the Remote Associates Test, in which three words such as cottage, Swiss, and cake must be linked by a fourth - cheese.

J. P. Guilford introduced the divergent-convergent distinction in the 1950s and it has been treated ever since as a dichotomy.

Recent work, including a 2025 paper in Thinking and Reasoning, reports that divergent and convergent scores are positively correlated and that each task recruits both processes, so the distinction is better read as a continuum than as two separate abilities.


64.4.2 Default and control network coupling in creative production

The most robust neuroimaging result in this area is that creative idea generation involves the cooperation of systems that are usually anticorrelated.

Roger Beaty, Mathias Benedek, Paul Silvia, and Daniel Schacter developed the account that the default mode network supplies candidate ideas through associative, memory-based generation, while the frontoparietal executive control network evaluates and constrains them against the task requirement, with the salience network - anchored in anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate - plausibly switching between the two.

Beaty and colleagues reported in 2015 in Scientific Reports that default and executive coupling increased during creative idea production.

The strongest version came in 2018, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, where Beaty and colleagues used connectome-based predictive modelling on 163 participants to identify a functional connectivity pattern that predicted divergent thinking ability, and then showed it generalised to held-out participants and to independent datasets.

The high-creative network was characterised by dense connections between default, executive, and salience nodes.

Two cautions are warranted: the effect sizes are moderate, and the outcome predicted is laboratory divergent thinking, not artistic or scientific eminence, although self-reported creative achievement correlated with the behavioural measure at around r equals 0.54 in that sample.


64.4.3 Incubation, insight, and unconscious processing

Graham Wallas described four stages of creative work in 1926 - preparation, incubation, illumination, verification - and the middle two have attracted the most experimental attention.

Incubation is the finding that setting a problem aside and doing something else can improve later solution rates, and meta-analyses do support a modest real effect, though whether it reflects genuine unconscious work, forgetting of misleading approaches, or simply recovery from fatigue is not settled.

Insight is the sudden, confident restructuring of a problem, the "aha" moment, and Mark Beeman and John Kounios showed in a 2004 study in PLOS Biology that solutions reported as insightful, compared with solutions reported as analytic, were accompanied by increased activity in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus.

Their electroencephalography (EEG) recordings - EEG measures electrical activity from scalp electrodes with millisecond precision - found a burst of gamma-band activity around 40 hertz at that site roughly 300 milliseconds before the person pressed the button to report the solution, preceded by an increase in alpha-band activity over right visual cortex that they interpreted as a brief gating out of visual input.

The right anterior temporal region is associated with coarse semantic coding and with getting the gist of jokes and metaphors, which fits the idea that insight depends on distant associations that are weakly activated until they suddenly cohere.

This is an elegant story, and it should be said that the sample sizes in the original work were small by current standards and that replication of the precise gamma signature has been uneven.


64.4.4 Expertise, constraint, and the myth of unconstrained creativity

The popular picture of creativity as freedom from rules survives poorly on contact with the evidence.

Robert Weisberg has argued at length that creative work is ordinary cognition - remembering, reasoning, restructuring - applied within deep domain knowledge, and that celebrated creative leaps, examined closely, turn out to be incremental extensions of what the person already knew.

The ten-year rule, developed from Herbert Simon and William Chase's work on expertise and applied to creative domains by Dean Keith Simonton, John Hayes, and others, holds that roughly a decade of intense domain preparation precedes first-rate contributions, with James Kaufman and Scott Barry Kaufman reporting in 2007 that for modern writers the interval from first publication to peak work is longer still.

Simonton's historiometric analyses of hundreds of eminent figures also suggest a curvilinear relationship with formal education, in which some training helps and a great deal of it may entrench conventional framings - a finding that is suggestive rather than causally established, given its correlational and historical data.

The practical upshot is that constraints are generative: a domain supplies the vocabulary within which novelty can be recognised as novelty at all, and the empty page is harder than the difficult brief.

Creativity is therefore best modelled as constrained search over a well-stocked knowledge base, which is precisely the default-plus-control architecture described in 64.4.2.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The default mode network was discovered as the set of regions that reliably deactivate during demanding tasks, but it is better understood positively, as a fractionated system - midline core, dorsal medial, and medial temporal subsystems - sitting at the transmodal end of the principal cortical gradient, furthest from sensation and action.

Mind wandering, measured by experience sampling, occupies roughly half of waking life, recruits default and executive systems together rather than representing mere idling, reliably costs performance on external tasks such as reading, and plausibly buys autobiographical planning in return.

Rumination is the same machinery caught in a loop, and is associated with heightened coupling between the subgenual prefrontal cortex and the default network in depression.

Remembering and imagining share a single core network, so that damage to episodic memory - as in hippocampal amnesia - impairs imagining the future, and the flexibility that enables simulation is the same flexibility that makes memory fallible.

Creativity depends not on freedom from constraint but on the cooperation of a generative default system with an evaluative control system, operating over years of accumulated domain knowledge.


PART TWELVE. CHANGE, VARIATION, AND ORIGINS


CHAPTER 65. THE DEVELOPING BRAIN (CORE)

This chapter follows the human brain from a sheet of cells in an embryo to the restless, reward-hungry organ of a teenager.

The story matters because almost every fact about adult cognition in this book has a developmental history, and that history explains why some abilities are easy to acquire early and nearly impossible to acquire late.

We will look at how neurons are made, moved, wired, and then deliberately thrown away; at the famous critical periods in which experience carves the brain; at how infant minds already arrive with structure; at what actually changes in adolescence; and at the methods that let researchers study a brain attached to a wriggling, uncooperative child.

Along the way, several popular claims turn out to be shakier than their textbook confidence suggests, and where that is true, this chapter says so.


65.1 Building the substrate

Before there is cognition, there is construction.

In roughly nine months of gestation plus the first two years after birth, the human brain assembles on the order of eighty-six billion neurons and a far larger number of connections between them.

This section walks through that construction in order: making the cells, moving them, wiring them, and then editing the result.

The editing is not a flaw in the process.

Overproduction followed by selective removal is the brain's central design strategy, and it is what allows a genome far too small to specify every connection to nonetheless produce a precisely wired organ.


65.1.1 Neural induction, proliferation, migration, and differentiation

Neural induction is the moment the embryo decides that a particular sheet of cells will become nervous system rather than skin, a decision driven by signalling molecules released from neighbouring tissue that switch off the default skin programme.

That sheet rolls into a hollow tube, the neural tube, whose front end swells into the brain and whose rear becomes the spinal cord.

Lining the inside of the tube is the ventricular zone, a proliferative layer where radial glial cells act as the embryonic neural stem cells of the cortex, dividing asymmetrically so that each division yields one self-renewing stem cell plus either a neuron or an intermediate progenitor cell that will itself divide again to make neurons.

Newborn neurons then migrate outward, and radial glial cells double as the scaffold: their long fibres stretch from the ventricle to the outer surface, and young neurons climb them like ropes.

Reviews of cortical development describe radial migration in about four stages - departure from the ventricular zone, a wandering multipolar phase in which the cell has many short processes and no clear direction, a bipolar glia-guided locomotion phase, and a final terminal translocation in which the neuron settles and grows its dendrites (the branching input structures of a neuron).

The cortex is built inside-out: the earliest-born neurons form the deepest layer and each later wave migrates past its predecessors, which is why the six-layered cortex has a birth-order signature written into its anatomy.

Not all neurons travel radially; the inhibitory interneurons that damp cortical activity are born in a separate structure, the ganglionic eminence, and migrate tangentially, sideways across the developing cortex, before turning to join their target layers.

Differentiation is the last step, in which a settled cell commits to being a particular kind of neuron with a particular transmitter, shape, and set of target regions.


65.1.2 Axon guidance, synaptogenesis, and programmed cell death

Once a neuron is in place it must send out an axon, the single long output fibre, sometimes across the entire brain, and the tip of that axon - the growth cone - navigates by reading chemical gradients.

The best-characterised guidance families are the netrins, which attract many axons toward the midline of the nervous system; the slits, which repel axons and stop them from recrossing once they have crossed; the semaphorins, mostly repulsive; and the ephrins, which are membrane-bound and shape orderly maps such as the projection from retina to midbrain.

These cues are not exclusively about steering; work reviewed by Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology describes netrins, semaphorins, and ephrins also acting on axon pruning and on whether a cell lives or dies, and studies in the spinal cord show netrin-responsive neurons both misrouted and less likely to survive when netrin is absent.

When an axon arrives, synaptogenesis begins - the assembly of synapses, the specialised junctions where one neuron chemically signals another - and it proceeds far in excess of what will be kept.

Programmed cell death, or apoptosis, then removes a large fraction of the neurons produced, commonly cited as roughly half in many populations.

The classic explanation is the neurotrophic hypothesis, grounded in Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen's identification of nerve growth factor (NGF) in the 1950s: target tissues release a limited supply of survival factor, neurons that make good connections capture enough of it to live, and the rest die.

This is competition as a construction method, and it means the final wiring diagram is partly the record of who won.


65.1.3 Activity-dependent refinement and synaptic pruning

Once synapses exist, neural activity edits them.

The rule of thumb, traceable to Donald Hebb's 1949 proposal that cells which fire together wire together, is that co-active connections are stabilised while connections whose activity is uncorrelated with their target's are weakened and removed.

The best human evidence for the sheer scale of this comes from Peter Huttenlocher, a paediatric neurologist at the University of Chicago, who counted synapses in electron micrographs of post-mortem human brains and reported in 1979 that synaptic density in cortex rises steeply after birth to a peak around one to two years of age, roughly fifty percent above adult levels, before declining.

Crucially the timing is regional: primary sensory cortex peaks and prunes early, while prefrontal cortex, the region most involved in planning and self-control, prunes late, extending through adolescence and to some degree beyond.

Pruning is not purely neuronal housekeeping - microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, physically engulf and digest weak synapses, and complement proteins borrowed from the immune system tag which synapses go.

Two cautions are worth stating plainly.

First, the human data rest on relatively small post-mortem samples, so the exact peak ages should be treated as approximate rather than precise.

Second, the widely repeated claim that magnetic resonance imaging measures of cortical thinning in teenagers are a direct picture of synaptic pruning is an inference, not an observation; increased myelination and other tissue changes contribute to the same signal, and this remains genuinely debated.


65.1.4 Myelination trajectories across childhood and adolescence

Myelin is the fatty sheath wrapped around axons by oligodendrocytes, and it speeds conduction along an axon by an order of magnitude while reducing the energy cost of each signal.

Myelination is the slowest of the developmental processes described here, and its timetable is what makes late childhood and adolescence a period of steadily improving speed and coordination between distant brain regions.

Myelin water imaging, a magnetic resonance technique that isolates the signal from water trapped between myelin layers, shows the steepest gains in the first two to three years of life, with sensory and motor tracts maturing before association tracts that link the frontal and parietal lobes.

Deoni and colleagues mapped these trajectories across infancy and early childhood and found large regional differences in both rate and endpoint.

Later work combining tractography, which reconstructs white matter pathways, with myelin water imaging has argued that myelination of major tracts continues well beyond childhood, with some evidence for a renewed increase during adolescence, though whether that late change reflects true myelin gain or increased axonal packing is not settled.

The general ordering is robust even where the details are argued over: back-to-front and sensory-before-associative, with frontal connections finishing last.


65.2 Critical and sensitive periods

A critical period is a window during which a particular experience is required for normal development and after which the same experience has little or no effect.

A sensitive period is the softer version - experience matters much more inside the window than outside it, but the system does not close entirely.

The distinction matters enormously for policy and for hope, because critical implies a door that shuts and sensitive implies a door that stiffens.

This section examines the model case, the molecular machinery that opens and closes the window, the contested human cases, and what happens when the necessary experience is withheld.


65.2.1 Ocular dominance plasticity as the model case

In the 1960s David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, working in cats and later monkeys, sewed shut one eyelid of a young animal for a period and then examined primary visual cortex.

Normally cortical neurons are dominated by input from one eye or the other in roughly balanced proportions; after early monocular deprivation the deprived eye lost almost all cortical territory to the open eye, and the animal remained functionally blind in that eye even after it was reopened.

The same deprivation applied to an adult animal produced little or no such shift, which established the existence of a bounded window and won Hubel and Wiesel a share of the 1981 Nobel Prize.

The human counterpart is amblyopia, sometimes called lazy eye, in which a childhood cataract or a persistent squint deprives one eye of clear patterned input and permanently degrades its vision unless treated early.

Ocular dominance plasticity remains the model system because the manipulation is simple, the readout is quantitative, and the timing can be shifted experimentally.

One important refinement is that the window is not opened by the calendar but by the maturation of inhibition: Takao Hensch and colleagues showed that the critical period begins when a class of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons expressing the protein parvalbumin reaches functional maturity, and that manipulating inhibition can start the period early or delay it.


65.2.2 Molecular brakes on plasticity and their manipulation

If maturation of inhibition opens the window, a set of structural and molecular brakes closes it.

The most studied brake is the perineuronal net (PNN), a dense lattice of extracellular matrix rich in chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans that condenses around parvalbumin interneurons at the end of the critical period and physically restricts new connections.

Enzymatically digesting perineuronal nets with chondroitinase reopens ocular dominance plasticity in adult animals, one of the clearest demonstrations that adult rigidity is actively maintained rather than passively lost.

A second player is Otx2, a homeoprotein made outside the visual cortex and taken up preferentially by parvalbumin cells, whose accumulation tracks their maturation; Sugiyama, Prochiantz, Hensch and colleagues reported in Cell in 2008 that Otx2 transfer into visual cortex is required to activate postnatal plasticity, and later work found that halving Otx2 delays critical period onset and that Otx2 binds and promotes the proteoglycan aggrecan, so the same molecule contributes to both onset and offset.

Other brakes include Lynx1, a protein that damps cholinergic signalling and whose removal keeps adult cortex plastic, and myelin-associated inhibitors signalling through the Nogo receptor.

The practical hope is that some of these brakes can be released pharmacologically in humans, and the epilepsy drug valproate has been reported to reopen critical-period learning of absolute pitch in adults, though that finding rests on a small sample and should be regarded as preliminary rather than established.


65.2.3 Sensitive periods for language, music, and social attachment

For a first language the evidence for a genuine sensitive period is strong, drawn from congenitally deaf children whose exposure to sign language began at different ages and who show worse ultimate grammatical mastery the later they started.

For a second language the shape of the curve was long disputed until Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum and Steven Pinker analysed an internet grammar test taken by about two thirds of a million English speakers and reported in 2018 that grammar-learning ability stays near its peak until roughly 17.4 years and then declines steadily.

That is a much later inflection than the classical claim of a window closing at puberty, and it has been criticised on methodological grounds - self-selected online samples, and inference of a learning rate from an attainment measure - so it should be read as a strong but contested result rather than a closed case.

In music, absolute pitch, the ability to name a note without a reference, is strongly associated with beginning musical training before about six or seven, with the distribution of onset ages peaking around four to six.

But the critical-period reading of absolute pitch has weakened: several studies since 2019 have shown that some adults can be trained to fast and accurate absolute pitch judgement, which fits a sensitive period with a residual capacity better than a hard window.

For social attachment, the ethological work of Konrad Lorenz on imprinting in birds and Harry Harlow's rhesus monkey isolation studies established the principle that early social contact has a privileged and partly irreversible role, and the human evidence comes largely from deprivation studies discussed next.


65.2.4 Deprivation, institutionalisation, and recovery

The strongest human evidence on sensitive periods comes from children raised in severely understimulating institutions.

The Bucharest Early Intervention Project, led by Charles Nelson, Charles Zeanah and Nathan Fox from 2000 onward, is the only randomised controlled trial of foster care as an alternative to institutional care: abandoned infants in Romanian institutions were randomly assigned to remain there or to be placed with trained foster families, with a never-institutionalised community group for comparison.

Nelson and colleagues reported in Science in 2007 that children who remained institutionalised had markedly lower cognitive scores than both other groups, that foster placement produced substantial recovery, and that the recovery was largest for children placed youngest - the signature of a sensitive period.

Follow-ups have found that many outcomes were far less affected in children who spent under about twenty-four months in institutions than in those who stayed longer, and a comprehensive multilevel analysis published in the American Journal of Psychiatry in 2023 confirmed causal effects of the intervention while making clear that recovery was incomplete across most domains.

The English and Romanian Adoptees study led by Michael Rutter, following Romanian children adopted into United Kingdom families, reached a compatible conclusion: children adopted before about six months looked much like domestic adoptees, while longer deprivation left persistent deficits and elevated psychiatric risk into adulthood.

The honest summary is that early deprivation causes lasting harm, that earlier removal helps a great deal, and that no intervention studied so far fully erases the effect.

A separate and less famous point deserves stating: randomising children out of institutions was ethically defensible only because institutional care was the local status quo and foster care was scarce, and the trial has been the subject of continuing ethical debate.


65.3 The emergence of cognition

The infant is not a blank slate onto which experience writes, nor a miniature adult waiting to grow.

Modern developmental science describes a mind that arrives with a small set of structured expectations about the world and then elaborates them enormously through learning.

This section covers what appears to be present very early, and how attention, memory, language and social understanding are built on top of it.


65.3.1 Infant core knowledge: objects, agents, number, space

Core knowledge is Elizabeth Spelke's proposal that human cognition rests on a handful of ancient, domain-specific systems that operate before and independently of language.

The classic evidence is violation-of-expectation looking time: infants look longer at events that contradict a physical expectation, such as a screen rotating through the space where a hidden block should be, and longer looking is read as surprise.

Using such methods Spelke and Renée Baillargeon argued that infants in the first year expect objects to be solid, continuous in space and time, and to move only on contact; that they distinguish agents, which move by themselves and act toward goals, from inert objects; that they track small numbers exactly and larger quantities approximately; and that they use the geometry of a space to reorient.

In her 2022 book Spelke sets out six systems - objects, places, forms, number, agents, and social beings - and treats language as the mechanism that lets their outputs be combined.

The framework is influential but not unopposed.

Critics point out that looking-time results are noisy and have had a poor record in large-scale replication attempts, that longer looking can reflect familiarity as easily as surprise, and that constructivist alternatives can derive much of the same behaviour from rapid statistical learning without positing innate systems.


65.3.2 Development of attention, memory, and executive function

Newborn attention is largely exogenous, that is, captured by the stimulus rather than directed by the infant, and the shift toward endogenous, voluntary control begins in the second half of the first year as frontal and parietal circuits mature.

Executive function is the umbrella term for the deliberate control processes - working memory, which holds and manipulates information over seconds; inhibitory control, which suppresses a prepotent response; and cognitive flexibility, which shifts between rules - and Adele Diamond's work using tasks such as the A-not-B search task and the day-night Stroop task charted their emergence in infancy and the preschool years.

The trajectory is protracted: large-sample work such as the lifespan study published in Scientific Reports in 2021 found continued improvement in working memory, inhibition and planning across adolescence into young adulthood, with declines starting surprisingly early in adult life for some components, and Nature Communications published a canonical maturation curve for executive function from adolescence to adulthood in 2023.

Memory has recently been revised in an important way.

Infantile amnesia, our inability to recall our first few years, was long attributed to an immature hippocampus that could not encode episodes at all.

In 2025 Nick Turk-Browne and colleagues reported in Science that awake infant functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) showed hippocampal activity during viewing of novel images predicting later memory-driven looking from about twelve months of age, implying that infants can encode single events and that infantile amnesia is more likely a failure of later retrieval or of storage consolidation than of encoding.
