65.3.3 Language acquisition and its neural trajectory

Speech perception is already organised at birth, with newborns showing left-lateralised responses in superior temporal and inferior frontal cortex to speech and to changes in speech sounds, as documented in the infant imaging work of Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz and colleagues.

Across the first year infants narrow from discriminating the phoneme contrasts of any language to those of their own, a perceptual narrowing described by Patricia Kuhl and by Janet Werker and Richard Tees, whose 1984 study showed English-learning infants losing discrimination of non-native Hindi contrasts between roughly six and twelve months.

A central learning mechanism is statistical learning: Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport showed in 1996 that eight-month-olds segment words from a continuous artificial speech stream using only the transitional probabilities between syllables, and later work has found newborns tracking such probabilities during sleep.

The anatomical substrate matures alongside.

The arcuate fasciculus, the dorsal white matter tract connecting temporal language areas to inferior frontal cortex, is already leftward-asymmetric and is essentially established by about two years, and infant measures of left arcuate microstructure prospectively predict phonological awareness and vocabulary at kindergarten age.

The relationship between language input and brain measures is not simple, however: at least one study found greater language exposure in infancy associated with lower, not higher, arcuate microstructural values, a reminder that these imaging indices are indirect.


65.3.4 Social cognition and theory of mind development

Theory of mind is the capacity to attribute mental states - beliefs, desires, intentions - to other people and to recognise that those states may differ from one's own and from reality.

The standard test is the false-belief task introduced by Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner in 1983, in which a character puts an object in location A, leaves, the object is moved to B, and the child must predict where the character will look; most children answer correctly from around four to five years, and younger children answer B.

Implicit versions using anticipatory looking have suggested that infants under two already track others' false beliefs, but this literature has been badly damaged by failed large-scale replications, and whether infants have genuine belief representation is now one of the most contested questions in the field.

The neural story is clearer.

Rebecca Saxe and colleagues identified a network for mental-state reasoning centred on the right temporoparietal junction, together with medial prefrontal cortex and precuneus, and showed that the right temporoparietal junction becomes progressively more selective for belief reasoning across childhood as behavioural performance improves.

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy work has extended related findings to preverbal infants and to belief-versus-desire reasoning in children, though the interpretive caution above still applies.


65.4 Adolescence

Adolescence is the interval between the biological onset of puberty and the social attainment of adult roles, and in modern societies it has lengthened at both ends.

It is characterised by a distinctive behavioural profile - more sensation-seeking, more risk-taking, far more sensitivity to peers - and by a distinctive neural profile in which subcortical reward circuitry and prefrontal control circuitry mature on different schedules.

This section presents the standard account and then the substantial evidence that complicates it.


65.4.1 Asynchronous maturation of control and reward systems

The dual systems model, also called the maturational imbalance model, was proposed in similar forms in 2008 by Laurence Steinberg's laboratory at Temple University and B. J. Casey's laboratory then at Cornell.

Its claim is that adolescent risk-taking reflects a mismatch in timing: a socioemotional or reward system centred on the ventral striatum, a subcortical structure that signals anticipated reward, becomes hypersensitive early in adolescence, while the cognitive control system centred on prefrontal cortex matures gradually and linearly and peaks later.

The gap between the two curves is the window of maximum vulnerability, and the model neatly explains why adolescents can reason about risk as well as adults in a calm interview and still behave far more riskily in an emotionally charged moment.

Steinberg's version has reward sensitivity following an inverted-U with a rise in early adolescence and decline in early adulthood; Casey's version has it rising to mid-adolescence and then plateauing.

The model is elegant and has been enormously influential, including in legal argument about juvenile culpability, and it should also be said that its support is uneven.

Critics note that findings of adolescent striatal hypersensitivity are inconsistent across tasks, that the model says little about individual differences, that it does not distinguish adaptive exploratory risk from harmful risk, and that it draws a stark two-system picture from what are in fact many overlapping, gradually changing circuits.


65.4.2 Risk taking, peer influence, and their neural correlates

The single most informative experiment here is Jason Chein, Dustin Albert, Laurence Steinberg and colleagues' 2011 study in Developmental Science.

Adolescents, young adults and adults played a simulated driving game inside a scanner, once alone and once believing that friends were watching from an adjacent room.

Peer observation roughly doubled risky driving in early adolescents around fourteen and raised it about fifty percent in older adolescents, while leaving adults unaffected.

The neural correlate was specific: only adolescents showed heightened activity in reward regions, the ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex, during peer observation, and the level of that activity predicted how much risk they subsequently took.

The interpretation is that peers do not so much impair adolescent self-control as change the value of the risky option, making the reward look bigger.

Later work has found that parental presence has the opposite effect and that peer effects are stronger for reward processing than for response inhibition, which supports the valuation account over a pure disinhibition account.


65.4.3 Puberty, hormones, and cognitive change

Puberty begins when the hypothalamus resumes pulsatile release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which drives the pituitary to release hormones that in turn cause the gonads to produce testosterone and estradiol.

These steroids act on the brain as well as the body, because receptors for them are dense in the amygdala, hippocampus and parts of prefrontal cortex, and longitudinal structural magnetic resonance imaging studies such as that by Herting and colleagues in 2014 have linked testosterone and estradiol levels to the trajectory of subcortical and cortical volume change across adolescence.

Pubertal timing - how early a person matures relative to same-age, same-sex peers - has shifted earlier over recent decades and varies widely, and it is associated with mental health outcomes, with early maturation in girls fairly consistently linked to higher risk of depression and of earlier substance use.

The link between pubertal timing and cognition is much weaker and genuinely inconsistent: some studies report early puberty with lower executive function and academic performance, others the reverse, with hints of opposite directions in boys and girls, and recent work using the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development cohort combined with Mendelian randomisation, a genetic technique for causal inference, has been used to try to separate cause from correlation.

Disentangling hormonal effects from age effects is hard because the two are heavily confounded, and the cleanest designs compare children of the same chronological age at different pubertal stages.


65.4.4 Adolescence as a second sensitive period

Delia Fuhrmann, Lisa Knoll and Sarah-Jayne Blakemore argued in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2015 that adolescence may constitute a second window of heightened plasticity, by analogy with the early sensory windows but concerning higher-level and social functions.

They nominated three candidate domains: memory, where capacity may be unusually trainable in adolescence; sensitivity to social stress; and susceptibility to drugs of abuse, where rodent work shows adolescent exposure producing lasting change that adult exposure does not.

Rodent evidence for adolescent social isolation producing persistent deficits, and for reduced fear extinction during adolescence, is consistent with a period of unusual malleability.

The proposal has an attractive symmetry with the deprivation literature - heightened plasticity means heightened opportunity and heightened vulnerability at once - but the human evidence is largely correlational and the authors themselves emphasised that adolescent sensitive periods would be marked by large individual differences.

It is best described as a productive hypothesis with suggestive animal support rather than an established fact, and no molecular brake comparable to perineuronal nets has yet been shown to gate it in humans.


65.5 Methods and evidence in developmental cognitive neuroscience

Studying the developing brain is methodologically brutal.

The participants cannot follow instructions, will not stay still, tire quickly, and cannot consent for themselves; the measurements change meaning as the head, skull and tissue composition change with age; and the questions of greatest interest are causal while most feasible designs are correlational.

This section covers the four responses the field has developed.


65.5.1 Infant electroencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and awake imaging

Electroencephalography (EEG) records electrical activity from scalp electrodes and is the most infant-friendly method available, being silent, inexpensive, tolerant of a wriggling participant, and capable of millisecond timing; its weakness is poor spatial resolution, since it cannot say with confidence where in the brain a signal arose, and high sensitivity to movement artefact.

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) shines harmless near-infrared light through the scalp and measures changes in blood oxygenation from the light that scatters back, giving a rough map of cortical activity in an awake, seated, engaged infant; its limits are shallow depth, so it cannot see subcortical structures, modest spatial specificity, and the practical awkwardness of the headgear.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) offers far better spatial resolution and can reach deep structures, but the scanner is loud, confining, and utterly intolerant of motion, and infants move constantly and cannot be instructed to hold still.

Much early infant fMRI was therefore done during natural sleep, which restricts the questions that can be asked, and the recent progress has come from awake infant scanning with heavy investment in comforting, padding, short runs and aggressive motion correction.

A 2025 report from Turk-Browne's group analysing more than 750 awake infant scanning sessions quantified how much usable data such protocols actually yield, and that kind of honest methods reporting is what makes the emerging infant fMRI literature credible.


65.5.2 Longitudinal cohorts and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development design

Cross-sectional studies compare different people of different ages and therefore confound development with cohort differences and with who happens to volunteer at each age; longitudinal studies follow the same people over time and can separate change within a person from differences between people.

The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study is the largest such effort in the United States, recruiting about 11,880 children aged nine to ten across twenty-two sites and following them with annual in-person visits for at least a decade, with structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging every two years.

Its measures span physical and mental health, substance use, culture and environment, neurocognition, geocoded environmental exposures, and whole-genome genotyping, and the data are released openly to researchers.

The three tasks scanned are the monetary incentive delay task for reward, the emotional n-back for working memory and affect, and the stop-signal task for inhibitory control, and published methods papers have documented and corrected design problems in the stop-signal implementation, an example of a large cohort's transparency working as intended.

A decade in, reviews of ABCD note both real gains, such as work by Pang and colleagues in 2025 coupling adolescent attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptom trajectories to the development of inhibitory control, and a sobering lesson: brain-behaviour correlations in such data are far smaller than the older small-sample literature implied, which is one reason samples of this size were needed at all.


65.5.3 Normative modelling of developmental brain charts

Paediatricians have used height and weight growth charts for a century, expressing an individual child's measurement as a centile against a large reference population, and normative modelling brings the same logic to the brain.

Richard Bethlehem, Jakob Seidlitz, Aaron Alexander-Bloch and colleagues published brain charts for the human lifespan in Nature in 2022, aggregating structural magnetic resonance imaging from over 100 studies and 101,457 participants from birth to a hundred years, and released them as an open interactive resource.

The charts give non-linear normative trajectories for measures such as grey matter volume, white matter volume and cortical thickness, together with rates of change, so that an individual scan can be scored as a centile rather than compared against an arbitrary control group.

That reframing matters clinically, because it converts a hard-to-interpret group difference into a per-person deviation score that can be tracked over time.

The approach is expanding: subsequent work has produced lifespan normative models for brain microstructure and, in 2026, white matter micro- and macrostructural charts.

The main caveats are that the reference population is dominated by high-income countries and by scanners and processing pipelines that differ between studies, so centiles are only as representative as the aggregate behind them.


65.5.4 Causal inference from natural experiments

Almost every interesting developmental question is causal - does poverty impair brain development, does deprivation cause deficits, does early adoption help - and almost every ethical design is observational, because the exposures cannot be assigned.

The field therefore leans on natural experiments, situations where something outside the researcher's control assigns exposure in a way that approximates randomness, and on the rare cases where randomisation is genuinely permissible.

The Bucharest Early Intervention Project described earlier is the strongest example of the latter, since foster placement was randomly assigned against a background in which institutional care was the default and foster care scarce.

Baby's First Years is a second: about a thousand low-income mothers of newborns in four United States metropolitan areas were randomised to receive an unconditional monthly cash gift of $333 or $20 for the child's first four years.

Its early report, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2022 by Sonya Troller-Renfree, Kimberly Noble and colleagues, found higher-frequency electroencephalography power in the infants of high-cash families, widely reported as evidence that reducing poverty changes brain activity.

The four-year follow-up, published in 2026, found no impact on the pre-registered primary brain-activity outcome nor on the secondary frontal gamma measure, which is an important corrective and a good illustration of why pre-registration and long follow-up matter.

Other tools in this family include Mendelian randomisation, which uses randomly inherited genetic variants as proxies for an exposure such as pubertal timing, and within-family designs that compare siblings to hold shared family background constant.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The developing brain is built by overproduction and selective removal: neurons are generated in excess and pruned by competition for neurotrophic support, synapses peak in the first two years at about fifty percent above adult density and are then edited by activity with microglial help, and myelination continues for decades with frontal connections finishing last.

Experience is not equally effective at all ages, and the ocular dominance work of Hubel and Wiesel plus the molecular work on perineuronal nets, Otx2 and Lynx1 shows that critical periods are actively opened by maturing inhibition and actively closed by identifiable brakes, some of which can be released in animals.

Human sensitive periods are real but softer than the animal model suggests, with the Bucharest and English and Romanian Adoptees studies showing that earlier removal from deprivation produces substantially better outcomes while recovery remains incomplete.

Infant cognition arrives structured - object, agent, number and space expectations, statistical learning of speech, hippocampal encoding from about twelve months - though several headline infant findings, including implicit false belief and some looking-time results, have not replicated well and should be held loosely.

Adolescence involves a genuine mismatch between early-maturing reward circuitry and late-maturing control circuitry, demonstrated most cleanly by the peer-presence driving experiments, but the dual systems model is a simplification whose evidence is uneven, and the proposal that adolescence is a second sensitive period remains a hypothesis rather than a result.

Finally, the field's credibility now rests on methods that take these difficulties seriously: awake infant imaging with honest data-retention reporting, very large longitudinal cohorts such as ABCD, lifespan normative brain charts, and randomised or quasi-randomised designs whose long follow-ups sometimes overturn their own early findings.


CHAPTER 66. THE AGEING BRAIN (CORE)

This chapter is about what happens to thinking, and to the organ that does the thinking, as a person moves from their twenties into their eighties and beyond.

Ageing is not a single process that dims everything at once.

Some abilities fall steadily from early adulthood, some hold firm into very late life, and some actually improve for decades.

The brain changes too - it loses tissue in some places, accumulates small vascular injuries, and reorganises how it recruits regions for a task - and the relationship between those brain changes and the cognitive ones is looser than most people expect.

This matters because the difference between ordinary ageing and the earliest stage of a disease is a boundary that patients, families, and clinicians have to negotiate constantly, and because a growing body of trial evidence says that a meaningful share of late-life cognitive loss is not fixed in advance.


66.1 Normal cognitive ageing

Before asking what goes wrong with age, it is worth establishing what normally happens - what the average trajectory looks like in people who never develop a diagnosable disease.

The single most important fact is that the trajectory is not one curve but several, running in different directions at once.

A person of seventy is typically slower and more distractible than they were at twenty-five, and at the same time knows far more words, facts, and procedures.


66.1.1 Fluid and crystallised abilities across the lifespan

The psychologist Raymond Cattell drew a distinction, later developed with John Horn, between fluid ability and crystallised ability.

Fluid ability (the capacity to reason about novel material on the spot, with no help from prior knowledge - solving an unfamiliar puzzle, spotting a pattern in an abstract sequence) peaks in the early twenties and declines gradually and more or less linearly thereafter.

Crystallised ability (accumulated knowledge and skill - vocabulary, general information, professional expertise) rises across most of adult life, typically plateauing somewhere around the sixties, and is often still at or near its peak in the seventies.

Timothy Salthouse's large cross-sectional studies of adult samples are the standard reference for this divergent pattern, though he has argued repeatedly that cross-sectional data exaggerate early decline and longitudinal data understate it because of practice effects, so the true curve probably lies between the two.

A useful corrective came from a 2022 report in Science Advances by Tucker-Drob and colleagues, which found that within individuals the two are not independent: people whose fluid ability declines steeply gain little or no crystallised knowledge over the same period, presumably because acquiring new knowledge itself requires fluid processing.

The popular idea that wisdom simply compensates for lost sharpness is therefore too neat - the compensation works best for the people who needed it least.


66.1.2 Processing speed, working memory, and inhibition declines

Three specific capacities carry much of the age-related loss.

Processing speed - how fast a person perceives, decides, and responds, measured by tasks as simple as substituting symbols for digits against a clock - declines from early adulthood onward, and Salthouse's processing-speed theory (developed through the 1990s) proposed that this slowing is the common cause of most other cognitive age differences, because slow operations leave earlier results to decay before later ones can use them.

Working memory - the small, temporary store that holds information while you manipulate it, such as keeping a phone number in mind while looking for a pen - also shrinks with age, and it shrinks somewhat more than speed alone would predict, which is a standing problem for the pure speed account.

Lynn Hasher and Rose Zacks proposed a rival explanation in 1988: an inhibitory deficit, meaning a reduced ability to keep irrelevant or no-longer-relevant material out of mind, so that working memory becomes cluttered rather than smaller.

The two accounts have been directly pitted against one another - Salthouse and Meinz reported in 1995 that statistically controlling for interference measures reduced age-related variance in working memory, but controlling for speed measures reduced it at least as much - and the field has not settled the question, which is best read as evidence that speed, inhibition, and capacity are entangled rather than that one is the master variable.


66.1.3 Preserved semantic knowledge and emotional function

Semantic memory - knowledge of facts, word meanings, and concepts, as opposed to memory for specific personal events - is remarkably well preserved.

Older adults typically have larger vocabularies than younger ones and score higher on tests of general information; what they show instead is slower retrieval, most familiarly the tip-of-the-tongue state, where the word is demonstrably known but temporarily inaccessible.

Emotional functioning shows something stronger than preservation.

Laura Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory holds that as perceived remaining time shortens, motivation shifts from acquiring information towards pursuing emotionally meaningful goals, which predicts that older adults will prune their social networks towards close relationships and attend to and remember positive material relatively more than negative - the so-called positivity effect.

This effect is real but conditional: it is most evident in older adults with well-preserved cognitive control, which argues that it is an actively managed regulatory strategy rather than a passive dulling of negative emotional processing, though that debate is not fully closed.


66.1.4 Heterogeneity and successful ageing

Averages hide the most interesting feature of cognitive ageing, which is that variability between individuals increases with age.

Some eighty-year-olds perform like average fifty-year-olds and some perform like people with early dementia, and the average trajectory describes neither.

Emily Rogalski and colleagues at Northwestern University defined the SuperAger - a person aged eighty or over whose episodic memory (memory for specific events) matches the average for people twenty to thirty years younger - and found that these individuals show little of the expected cortical thinning, with an unusually thick anterior cingulate cortex, a midline frontal region involved in attention and motivation.

The multisite SuperAging Research Initiative, established in 2021, is now following such people longitudinally to separate resistance (not accumulating brain pathology) from resilience (accumulating it without cognitive consequence).

A caution is in order: any criterion that selects the top performers from a cross-section will capture some people who were simply always high performers, and disentangling lifelong ability from successful maintenance requires early-life data that most studies do not have.


66.2 Structural and functional change

The brain changes measurably with age in ways that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI, a scanning technique that uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue without radiation) can track in living people.

The important point in this section is that these changes are regionally selective rather than uniform, and that their relationship to cognitive change is real but modest.


66.2.1 Grey matter, white matter, and vascular change

Grey matter (the cortical surface and subcortical nuclei, where neuronal cell bodies sit) thins with age, but not evenly - prefrontal regions, which support planning and control, show among the steepest longitudinal losses, and Naftali Raz and colleagues' repeated-scan studies established that the loss is mostly shrinkage of neurons, dendrites, and synapses rather than wholesale neuron death.

White matter (the myelinated axons that connect regions, the brain's wiring) degrades in parallel, losing microstructural integrity in ways detectable with diffusion imaging.

Superimposed on this is small-vessel disease, visible on MRI as white matter hyperintensities - bright patches on certain scan sequences that reflect damage to tissue supplied by small arteries, driven largely by hypertension and other vascular risk.

These are not benign background noise: longitudinal work shows that the rate of hyperintensity expansion tracks the rate of cortical grey matter atrophy, particularly in medial-frontal, orbitofrontal, and parietal regions, which is one reason blood pressure control appears repeatedly in dementia prevention recommendations.


66.2.2 Dedifferentiation of neural representations

Dedifferentiation means that the brain's responses to different kinds of input become less distinct with age.

The landmark demonstration is Denise Park and colleagues' 2004 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which showed that in younger adults the ventral visual cortex responds sharply and selectively to faces in one patch, places in another, and words in another, whereas in older adults these category-selective responses broaden and overlap - a face-selective region begins responding to non-faces.

Crucially, this happens in a region that shows little atrophy with age, so it is a change in functional tuning rather than a simple consequence of tissue loss.

Individual differences in this neural distinctiveness predict fluid ability in older adults, accounting in some reports for a substantial share of the variance.

One proposed mechanism is a decline in the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which sharpens neural tuning by suppressing competing responses; magnetic resonance spectroscopy work has linked lower ventral visual GABA to lower neural distinctiveness, but the evidence is correlational and the mechanism should be treated as plausible rather than demonstrated.


66.2.3 Compensation accounts: hemispheric asymmetry reduction, posterior-anterior shift, scaffolding

Older brains do not simply do less; on many tasks they activate more, and in different places, than younger brains.

Roberto Cabeza and colleagues described HAROLD (hemispheric asymmetry reduction in older adults), the finding that prefrontal activity which is strongly lateralised to one hemisphere in the young becomes bilateral in the old, and argued that this is compensatory because the older adults showing it tend to perform better.

PASA (posterior-anterior shift in ageing) describes a complementary pattern: reduced activity in occipital and occipitotemporal sensory regions coupled with increased frontal activity, as though frontal control is being recruited to shore up degraded perceptual input.

Park and Reuter-Lorenz's Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition, published in 2009 and revised in 2014, packages these observations into a general claim - that the ageing brain continuously builds supplementary, less efficient neural "scaffolds" in response to structural decline, and that the level of cognition observed is the net result of the insults and the scaffolding.

The theory is elegant and has organised a great deal of data, but the compensation interpretation is genuinely contested: extra activation can equally reflect inefficiency, reduced neural specificity, or difficulty-matched effort, and the standard for calling it compensation - that the extra activity must correlate with better, not worse, performance in the older group - is not always met.


66.2.4 Neuromodulatory decline, particularly dopaminergic

Neuromodulators are chemicals that adjust the gain and signal-to-noise of neural processing across wide territories rather than carrying specific messages, and dopamine is the best-studied one in ageing.

Positron emission tomography (PET, an imaging method using injected radioactive tracers that bind to specific molecular targets) shows that dopamine D2-like receptor availability in the striatum falls by roughly five to ten percent per decade of adult life.

This produced the influential "correlative triad" claim, associated with Lars Bäckman and colleagues, that dopamine status rather than chronological age per se explains age-related deficits in fluid cognition.

The claim has had a bumpy replication history: a careful cross-sectional reproducibility study found only partial support, with digit span the one measure for which receptor availability mediated the age effect.

Longitudinal evidence has been kinder - work published in Neurobiology of Aging in 2024 and in Cerebral Cortex in 2024 and 2025 found that individuals with larger declines in D2 receptor availability over five and ten years also showed greater working memory and cognitive decline - so the honest summary is that the link is supported for working memory and related executive measures but is not the general explanation of cognitive ageing it was once taken to be.


66.3 Reserve and resilience

Two people can have the same amount of visible brain pathology and very different cognition.

That observation, first forced on the field by autopsy studies in which people with substantial Alzheimer pathology had shown no dementia in life, is what the reserve literature exists to explain.

The section below separates the concepts, reviews what predicts good outcomes, and then asks the harder question of what actually causes them.


66.3.1 Brain reserve, cognitive reserve, and maintenance distinguished

A 2020 whitepaper led by Yaakov Stern under the auspices of the Alzheimer's Association fixed consensus definitions, and they are worth keeping straight because the terms are routinely muddled.

Brain reserve is structural: the sheer neurobiological capital a person has - brain size, neuron and synapse count - such that the same absolute amount of damage leaves more substrate intact.

Cognitive reserve is functional: the adaptability of cognitive processing, shaped by lifetime experience, that lets performance stay better than the pathology would predict, for example by using alternative strategies or networks.

Brain maintenance is different from both: it is the relative absence of change in the first place, the successful avoidance of pathology and atrophy with age, rather than coping with it - a concept pressed particularly by Lars Nyberg and colleagues.

Resilience is the umbrella term covering all of these, and the practical importance of the distinction is that reserve and maintenance predict different data patterns and imply different interventions.


66.3.2 Education, occupation, bilingualism, and lifestyle correlates

The classic proxies for cognitive reserve are years of formal education, occupational complexity, literacy, and engagement in cognitively and socially demanding leisure activity, all of which are reliably associated with later dementia onset and better cognition at a given level of pathology.

Bilingualism has been the most publicised and the most contested of these.

Ellen Bialystok and colleagues reported that dementia symptoms emerged roughly four to five years later in bilinguals than monolinguals, and several meta-analyses have supported a delay of that magnitude, but a substantial number of studies have failed to replicate it.

The critical objections are methodological rather than ideological: much of the supporting evidence is retrospective and drawn from clinic samples, bilingualism is confounded with immigration status, education, and socioeconomic position, and there is no agreement on how to quantify degree of bilingualism.

The defensible position in 2026 is that bilingualism may contribute to reserve, that the effect if real is unlikely to be as large as early clinic-based estimates, and that anyone presenting it as settled is overstating the case.


66.3.3 Physical exercise and cognitive outcomes

Physical activity is the lifestyle factor with the strongest biological rationale, since exercise raises cerebral blood flow, improves vascular health, and in animals increases brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF, a protein that supports the growth and survival of neurons) and hippocampal neurogenesis.

The best-known human trial is Kirk Erickson and colleagues' 2011 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, in which 120 older adults were randomised to a year of moderate aerobic walking or stretching controls; the walking group showed a roughly two percent increase in anterior hippocampal volume, against a decline in controls, with improved spatial memory and higher serum BDNF.

That result has been enormously influential, but it should be read alongside a less flattering literature: several subsequent randomised trials, including the Swedish PHIBRA study, found fitness gains without the expected hippocampal or cognitive benefits, and meta-analyses of aerobic exercise and episodic memory in older adults report effects that are positive but small.

The honest position is that exercise is well justified for cardiovascular, metabolic, and vascular-brain reasons, that it probably yields modest cognitive benefit, and that the specific claim of hippocampal regrowth in humans rests on a smaller and less consistent evidence base than its fame suggests.


66.3.4 Causal evidence against correlational evidence

Almost everything in the reserve literature begins as an observational correlation, and observational correlations in ageing research are unusually vulnerable.

Three specific problems recur: reverse causation, where early cognitive ability drives both educational attainment and later cognition; selection and survival bias, where the less advantaged die or drop out before the study begins, which simulation work suggests actually attenuates estimated education effects; and participation bias, since more educated people volunteer for research more readily, which is a form of collider bias that can manufacture associations.

Mendelian randomisation - a method that uses inherited genetic variants, randomly allocated at conception, as proxies for an exposure, so that confounding by lifestyle is much reduced - has been applied to this question and generally supports a protective causal effect of educational attainment on Alzheimer's disease risk.

But the more careful multivariable versions complicate the story: when general cognitive ability and education are modelled together, genetic predictors of cognitive ability still predict Alzheimer's disease while genetic predictors of education largely stop doing so, implying that much of the apparent education effect is downstream of early-life cognitive ability.

Consistent with this, a longitudinal study of American men found that after accounting for general cognitive ability at around age twenty, additional education explained little variance in late-midlife cognition.

The practical upshot is that the strongest causal evidence in this whole area comes not from these proxies but from randomised trials of the kind described in 66.4.4, and that the effect of a middle-aged person taking up a new hobby should not be assumed to equal the observed advantage of people who went to university.


66.4 The boundary with pathology

Normal ageing and early neurodegenerative disease overlap in their symptoms, and for most of the twentieth century the only way to tell them apart with certainty was at autopsy.

That has changed within the last fifteen years, and the change has been disorienting as well as clarifying, because it is now possible to identify disease in people who have no symptoms at all.


66.4.1 Subjective cognitive decline and mild cognitive impairment

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) was formalised by Ronald Petersen and colleagues and requires four things: a cognitive complaint, ideally corroborated by someone who knows the person; objective impairment on testing; broadly normal general cognitive function; and intact activities of daily living - that last criterion being what separates MCI from dementia.

Roughly five to seventeen percent of people with MCI progress to Alzheimer's dementia per year, with the amnestic subtype (where episodic memory is the main deficit) at the higher end, around ten to fifteen percent.

Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) sits one step earlier: the person reports that their thinking has worsened, but formal testing is still normal for their age and education.

SCD carries a modest elevation in risk - reported annual conversion to MCI of around six to seven percent - and the large majority of people with it do not go on to dementia, which is worth stating plainly to anyone alarmed by their own forgetfulness.

Both categories are heterogeneous by design, and a substantial minority of people diagnosed with MCI revert to normal classification on retesting, which reflects both measurement noise and reversible causes such as depression, medication, poor sleep, and thyroid disease.


66.4.2 Biomarker-defined preclinical disease

The 2024 revised criteria from the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) define Alzheimer's disease biologically, by the presence of its core biomarkers, and separate a biological staging scheme from a clinical severity scheme.

The two core markers are amyloid-beta, a protein fragment that aggregates into extracellular plaques, and tau, a protein that in disease becomes abnormally phosphorylated and forms intracellular tangles; both can be measured by PET imaging or in cerebrospinal fluid.

The major practical development has been blood-based markers, particularly phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), which tracks amyloid pathology closely enough that a fully automated plasma assay reported in Nature Medicine in 2025 performed well in primary as well as secondary care.

Preclinical Alzheimer's disease means biomarker positivity with normal cognition, and it is common - a sizeable fraction of cognitively normal people over seventy are amyloid positive.

This creates a genuine ethical and conceptual problem the field has not resolved: defining disease biologically means labelling as diseased many people who will die of something else first, and critics argue that biomarker positivity is better described as risk than as disease.


66.4.3 Distinguishing ageing from early neurodegeneration

The clinically useful distinction is one of profile, not merely of severity.

Normal ageing hits speed, working memory, and executive control hardest, with the steepest structural change in prefrontal cortex, and the resulting memory problem is mainly one of effortful retrieval - the person benefits substantially from cues and from recognition testing.

Early Alzheimer's disease instead strikes the medial temporal lobe first, especially the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, and produces a genuine encoding and consolidation failure: rapid forgetting over a delay, and little or no benefit from cueing, because the information was never properly stored.

Frank neuron loss in entorhinal cortex is relatively specific to Alzheimer's disease rather than to age, and tau in medial temporal regions is the best single predictor of episodic memory performance in older adults independent of amyloid status; work published in Nature Communications in 2019 suggested that entorhinal tau functionally isolates the hippocampus by damaging the perforant path that feeds it.

Two practical caveats: the profiles overlap enough that a single assessment is often inconclusive, so change over repeated testing is more informative than any one score; and other conditions, notably vascular cognitive impairment, dementia with Lewy bodies, and depression, produce their own profiles and must be considered rather than assumed away.


66.4.4 Prevention and modifiable risk factors

The 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention and care, chaired by Gill Livingston, estimated that around forty-five percent of dementia cases worldwide could in principle be prevented or delayed by eliminating fourteen modifiable risk factors.

Those factors are low education in early life; hearing loss, hypertension, high low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, obesity, excessive alcohol, traumatic brain injury, depression, and physical inactivity in midlife; and smoking, diabetes, social isolation, air pollution, and untreated vision loss in later life - with elevated midlife LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss the two additions made in 2024.

That forty-five percent figure is a population attributable fraction, which assumes causality and complete elimination of the exposures, so it is a ceiling on what perfect prevention could achieve rather than a forecast.

The strongest randomised evidence comes from multidomain lifestyle trials: the Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER), reported by Miia Kivipelto and colleagues in 2015, showed cognitive benefit from a combined diet, exercise, cognitive training and vascular monitoring programme, and the United States POINTER trial, reported at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 2025, randomised 2,111 at-risk older adults and found that both a structured and a self-guided version improved global cognition, with the structured arm doing better, consistently across age, sex, ethnicity and apolipoprotein E e4 genotype.

Two honest qualifications: the effect sizes in these trials are modest and measured on cognitive test scores rather than on dementia diagnoses, and computerised brain training on its own has a poor record of transferring beyond the trained task, which is why the credible programmes bundle exercise, diet, and vascular risk management rather than relying on games.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognitive ageing is not uniform decline: fluid abilities such as reasoning speed, working memory, and control fall from early adulthood, while crystallised knowledge and emotional regulation are preserved or improve, though recent within-person evidence shows the two are coupled and the compensation is imperfect.

The ageing brain thins selectively in prefrontal regions, accumulates white matter and small-vessel damage, loses the sharpness of its category representations, and loses dopaminergic modulation - but these changes explain cognitive outcomes only partially, and the extra activation older brains show is only sometimes demonstrably compensatory.

Reserve, brain reserve, and maintenance are distinct concepts with distinct predictions, and the observational evidence linking education, occupation, and bilingualism to good outcomes is substantially weakened by reverse causation, survival bias, and participation bias, with Mendelian randomisation suggesting that early-life cognitive ability does much of the work attributed to schooling.

The boundary with disease is now drawn biologically, by amyloid and tau markers including blood-based p-tau217, which detects preclinical Alzheimer's disease in people with normal cognition and raises unresolved questions about what it means to call such people diseased.

The clinical signature that separates ageing from early Alzheimer's is a retrieval problem responsive to cues in the former and a storage failure unresponsive to cues in the latter, reflecting prefrontal against medial temporal vulnerability.

Finally, the FINGER and United States POINTER trials provide the best causal evidence available that structured multidomain lifestyle intervention can measurably protect cognition in at-risk older adults, with modest effects on test scores rather than proven prevention of dementia.


CHAPTER 67. INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES AND INTELLIGENCE (CORE)

People differ from one another in how quickly they learn, how much they remember, how well they reason about unfamiliar problems, and how they behave under pressure.

This chapter asks what those differences are, how psychologists measure them, what the brain has to do with them, and where they come from.

It is one of the most technically advanced areas of psychology and also one of the most socially charged, so the chapter tries to be careful about which claims are solid, which are contested, and which have quietly failed to replicate.

The word intelligence is used here in its narrow technical sense - performance on standardised cognitive tests - not as a judgement of a person's worth.

By the end you should understand why cognitive test scores hang together, what brain imaging has and has not shown about ability, what heritability actually means, and why individual variation is now treated as a scientific target in its own right rather than an annoyance to be averaged away.


67.1 The structure of cognitive ability

Before asking where ability comes from, we have to ask what shape it has.

Is there one thing called intelligence, or many separate talents that happen to be labelled with one word?

The answer that emerged from more than a century of measurement is neither extreme, and this section explains it.


67.1.1 The positive manifold and the general factor

In 1904 Charles Spearman, an English psychologist, noticed something that has been rediscovered in essentially every dataset since: when you give people a varied battery of mental tests, every test correlates positively with every other test.

Vocabulary correlates with mental arithmetic, which correlates with spotting the next shape in a visual sequence, which correlates with remembering a string of digits backwards.

This blanket of positive correlations is called the positive manifold (manifold here just means a whole set of relationships considered together).

Spearman invented a statistical method, factor analysis (a technique for inferring hidden common causes from patterns of correlation among things you can measure), and extracted a single common dimension he named g, for general factor.

His two-factor theory held that any test score reflects g plus s, a specific factor unique to that particular task; across a broad battery the first extracted factor typically accounts for roughly 40 to 50 percent of the variance.

The crucial interpretive question - whether g is a real causal property of a brain or merely a statistical summary of many overlapping causes - is genuinely unsettled, and we return to it below.


67.1.2 Hierarchical models of ability

Later work showed that one factor is too coarse and dozens of independent talents too fine, so the field settled on a hierarchy.

John Carroll's 1993 survey re-analysed hundreds of published correlation matrices and proposed a three-stratum model: many narrow abilities at the bottom, a middle layer of broad abilities, and g at the apex.

Merged with Raymond Cattell and John Horn's work, and formalised in the 1990s largely through Kevin McGrew, this became the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory, which now underpins the design of most commercial intelligence tests.

Stratum two contains roughly ten broad abilities including fluid reasoning, comprehension-knowledge, visual processing, short-term or working memory, and processing speed; stratum one contains seventy or more narrow skills beneath them.

The hierarchy is descriptive rather than explanatory - it tells you how scores cluster, not why - and rival accounts exist.

Han van der Maas and colleagues (2006) proposed a mutualism model in which initially independent cognitive processes help each other develop over childhood, so the positive manifold emerges from development with no underlying g at all; Kristof Kovacs and Andrew Conway's process overlap theory instead attributes it to executive processes that many different tests happen to recruit in common.

These models fit the data about as well as the g model does, which is precisely why the causal status of g remains disputed.


67.1.3 Fluid and crystallised distinctions

Raymond Cattell's most durable contribution was splitting general ability in two.

Fluid intelligence (Gf) is the capacity to reason about novel material - completing an abstract matrix puzzle you have never seen before, or working out the rule governing an unfamiliar sequence - and depends little on what you have been taught.

Crystallised intelligence (Gc) is accumulated knowledge and verbal skill built up through schooling and cultural exposure - vocabulary, general information, learned procedures.

The distinction earns its keep developmentally: fluid ability tends to peak in early adulthood and decline steadily thereafter, while crystallised ability holds up or keeps rising into later life, which is why an older adult may lose speed on a puzzle yet still have the larger vocabulary.

The two are nonetheless substantially correlated, since fluid ability helps you acquire knowledge in the first place, a process Cattell called investment.


67.1.4 Measurement, bias, and the limits of testing

A test score is not a direct reading of a brain property; it is a behavioural sample, and everything depends on whether the sample means the same thing for everyone.

The technical concept here is measurement invariance - the formal requirement that a test's items relate to the underlying trait in the same way across groups.

Psychometricians distinguish construct bias, tested by comparing the measurement model across groups at successively stricter levels (configural, metric, and scalar invariance), from predictive bias, tested by the Cleary regression model, which asks whether the same score predicts the same real-world outcome in each group.

The important and often-missed logical point is that a difference in average scores between two groups is not itself evidence of bias, and equally is not itself evidence of a real trait difference; only if scalar invariance holds can a mean score gap be read as a trait gap.

Modern tests are built to screen out item-level bias and many show acceptable invariance across demographic groups, but that does not neutralise unequal test familiarity, coaching access, or motivational factors such as stereotype threat (the performance cost of worrying that you might confirm a negative stereotype about your group), which Wicherts and colleagues (2005) analysed explicitly as a potential source of measurement bias.

Stereotype threat's size and robustness are themselves contested, with several large replication attempts finding much smaller effects than the original literature suggested.


67.2 Neural correlates of ability

If cognitive ability is real and stable, it ought to leave some trace in the brain.

Finding that trace has proved much harder than early enthusiasm suggested, and this section is as much about methodological hard lessons as about results.


67.2.1 Brain size, efficiency, and their weak relations

The oldest hypothesis is the simplest: bigger brain, more ability.

Jakob Pietschnig and colleagues (2015) meta-analysed 88 studies covering about 8,000 people and found a correlation of roughly r = 0.24 between in-vivo brain volume and intelligence test scores, consistent across age, sex, and test type.

A correlation of 0.24 means brain volume accounts for about six percent of the differences between people, so the relation is real but of little practical use for any individual; the authors also flagged publication bias, noting that small and null results appear to have gone unreported disproportionately.

A 2022 multiverse re-analysis by the same broad research community showed that the estimate moves noticeably depending on defensible analytic choices, which is a warning against quoting any single number too confidently.

The neural efficiency hypothesis, associated with Richard Haier's early positron emission tomography work in the late 1980s, proposed the opposite of "more is better": brighter people showed lower cortical glucose consumption while solving problems, implying they use less brain to get the same job done.

Evidence since has been mixed, with efficiency effects appearing and disappearing depending on task difficulty and expertise, so the hypothesis is best described as partially supported and heavily qualified rather than established.


67.2.2 The parieto-frontal integration theory

Rex Jung and Richard Haier (2007), reviewing 37 neuroimaging studies of about 1,557 participants in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, proposed the parieto-frontal integration theory (P-FIT).

Rather than locating intelligence in one spot, P-FIT identifies a distributed circuit: sensory cortex in occipital and temporal regions feeds information forward to inferior and superior parietal cortex, which abstracts and integrates it; parietal cortex then interacts with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the front-of-brain region that holds and manipulates information toward a goal) to test hypotheses; anterior cingulate cortex supports response selection and inhibition.

The theory places heavy weight on the white matter tracts connecting these areas, particularly the arcuate fasciculus, because on this account ability depends on how well the regions talk to each other, not merely on how large they are.

P-FIT became one of the most cited papers in its field and remains a useful organising map, but it is a summary of where activation and structural correlations tend to fall rather than a mechanistic account of how reasoning happens.


67.2.3 Network integration, modularity, and ability

Aron Barbey's network neuroscience theory (2018, Trends in Cognitive Sciences) reframed the question in terms of whole-brain dynamics.

Two properties matter here: modularity, the degree to which the brain is organised into semi-separate clusters that mostly talk within themselves, and integration, the capacity to exchange information rapidly across those clusters.

Barbey's proposal is that g reflects the flexibility with which a brain reconfigures between network states - crystallised performance drawing on easy-to-reach states that access stored knowledge, fluid performance requiring difficult-to-reach states that support novel problem solving.

The attraction of the theory is that it explains why ability is distributed and why no single region is indispensable; the weakness is that flexibility measures derived from functional imaging are noisy and their relation to behaviour has often been modest, so the theory is more a productive research programme than a settled finding.


67.2.4 Connectome-based predictive modelling of cognition

Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) is a method rather than a theory, and it changed how the field tests claims.

The connectome here means the matrix of functional connections - how strongly the activity of each brain region correlates with each other region, measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

In CPM, developed and popularised by Emily Finn, Xilin Shen, Todd Constable, Dustin Scheinost and colleagues from around 2015, the analysis selects the connections that correlate with a behavioural score in a training set, sums them per person, fits a simple linear model, and then - crucially - predicts scores for people the model has never seen.

Finn and colleagues (2015) also showed that these connectivity patterns are individually distinctive and stable enough to identify a person across scanning sessions, a result nicknamed the connectome fingerprint.

Applied to fluid intelligence, whole-brain models have accounted for roughly a fifth of the variance in some samples, with contributing connections spread across the whole cortex rather than confined to the P-FIT regions.

The honest caveat is that out-of-sample prediction accuracy drops when models are transferred to new datasets and populations, so CPM has established that brain-wide connectivity carries real information about ability while also showing that the information is diffuse and the effects are modest.


67.3 Genetics and environment

Where do these differences come from?

This is the part of the field most often misreported, so the section spends as much effort on what the terms mean as on what the numbers are.


67.3.1 Heritability estimates and their meaning

Heritability is the proportion of the differences between people in a particular population at a particular time that can be statistically attributed to differences in their genes.

It is a property of a population, not of a person, and it says nothing about how changeable a trait is - the classic illustration being that height is highly heritable yet average height rose dramatically with better nutrition.

Twin and adoption studies place the heritability of general cognitive ability at roughly 0.5 on average, but the striking and counterintuitive finding is that it rises with age: about 0.2 to 0.4 in early childhood, climbing toward 0.6 or higher in adulthood, with some estimates reaching 0.8 by late adolescence.

Thomas Bouchard (2013) named this pattern the Wilson effect, after Ronald Wilson, who first documented it in longitudinal twin data.

Over the same span, the influence of the shared family environment shrinks toward roughly 0.1 in adulthood, which appears to mean that as people gain autonomy they increasingly select and build environments that match their own dispositions.

All of these figures come overwhelmingly from Western industrialised samples and should not be assumed to generalise.


67.3.2 Genome-wide association studies and polygenic scores

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) scans millions of individual genetic variants across very large samples to see which are statistically associated with a trait.

For cognition the answer was unambiguous: no single gene matters much; instead thousands of variants each contribute a tiny amount, which is what polygenic means.

Aysu Okbay and colleagues (2022, Nature Genetics) analysed about three million people for educational attainment and identified nearly 4,000 independent associated variants.

A polygenic score (also called a polygenic index) sums a person's variants weighted by those effects; the 2022 educational attainment score explains roughly 12 to 16 percent of the variance in years of education and up to about 9 percent of variance in measured intelligence.

Two cautions are essential.

First, prediction within families is considerably weaker than prediction across the population, which shows that a chunk of the apparent signal reflects the social environments that correlate with parents' genotypes rather than direct genetic effects on the child's brain.

Second, these scores are derived from and predict well only in samples of European genetic ancestry, and transfer poorly to other ancestries, which limits both their scientific reach and any practical use.


67.3.3 Gene-environment interplay and correlation

Nature and nurture are not two separate columns of a ledger, and two technical terms capture why.

Gene-environment correlation means genotype and environment are not independent: children with reading-inclined parents inherit both relevant genes and a house full of books (passive correlation), get responded to differently because of their own dispositions (evocative correlation), and eventually choose their own niches (active correlation) - the mechanism that best explains the Wilson effect.

Gene-environment interaction means the effect of genes depends on the environment.

The best-known claim here is the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis, that heritability of cognitive ability is higher in advantaged conditions because enriched environments let genetic potential express itself more fully.

Eric Turkheimer and colleagues (2003) supported it dramatically in 7-year-old American twins: in impoverished families roughly 60 percent of IQ variance traced to the shared environment and the genetic contribution was near zero, while in affluent families the pattern was nearly reversed.

This result is genuinely contested - it has replicated in several United States samples but repeatedly failed to appear in European samples with strong welfare provision, and some of the best-powered studies find no interaction at all - which itself suggests the effect may depend on how much a society's poorest environments actually constrain development.


67.3.4 The Flynn effect and its reversal

James Flynn documented in the 1980s that raw scores on intelligence tests rose across the twentieth century in every industrialised country studied, at roughly three points per decade, gains concentrated in the abstract-reasoning tests that were supposed to be most culture-free.

Since the genome cannot change that fast, the Flynn effect is decisive evidence that environments - nutrition, health, schooling, and increasing familiarity with abstract and formal thinking - shift population averages substantially.

From the 1990s onward several Northern European countries recorded a reversal.

Bernt Bratsberg and Ole Rogeberg (2018, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) used Norwegian military conscription records covering three decades of birth cohorts and found scores peaked around the 1975 cohort and then declined by roughly 0.2 points per year.

Their decisive move was to look within families: later-born brothers scored lower than their own earlier-born brothers, which rules out both immigration-driven compositional change and dysgenic fertility, the two genetic explanations then on offer.

The rise and the fall therefore both appear to be environmental, though exactly which environmental changes are responsible remains unknown.


67.4 Beyond general ability

Cognitive ability is only one axis on which people differ, and the remaining sections widen the frame.


67.4.1 Personality, temperament, and their neural correlates

The dominant descriptive model of personality is the Big Five: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (the tendency toward negative emotion).

Temperament refers to the earlier-appearing, more biologically anchored version of these tendencies visible in infancy, the classic example being Jerome Kagan's behavioural inhibition - roughly one in five toddlers reacts to novelty with restraint and distress, and that disposition predicts shyness and anxiety risk years later.

The search for structural brain correlates of the Big Five is a cautionary tale.

Colin DeYoung and colleagues (2010) reported volume correlates for four of the five traits in 116 adults, including extraversion with medial orbitofrontal cortex, a reward-processing region.

Subsequent attempts in much larger cohorts largely failed to replicate these specific associations, and the field now expects true brain-personality correlations to be small, on the order of r = 0.1 to 0.2, requiring samples in the thousands.

That is a revision of effect size, not a claim that personality is disembodied.


67.4.2 Cognitive styles and their disputed status

A cognitive style is a claimed characteristic manner of processing information - visual versus verbal, holistic versus analytic - as distinct from how much ability a person has.

The most popular version, learning styles, holds that instruction matched to a learner's preferred modality produces better learning; this is the meshing hypothesis.

Harold Pashler, Mark McDaniel, Doug Rohrer and Robert Bjork (2008), reviewing the literature for the Association for Psychological Science, found that although the literature is enormous, almost none of it used the crossover experimental design that could actually test meshing, and the few studies that did found no benefit.

Belief in learning styles nonetheless remains widespread among teachers, a phenomenon documented by Shaylene Nancekivell and colleagues (2020).

More carefully defined style constructs, such as Herman Witkin's field dependence-independence, do measure something reliable, but the reliable part tends to correlate with general ability rather than constituting an independent stylistic dimension - which is the core of the dispute.


67.4.3 Neurodiversity as a framing

Neurodiversity, a term originating in autistic self-advocacy in the late 1990s and generally credited to Judy Singer, holds that conditions such as autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are natural variations in human neurological development rather than simply disorders to be cured.

The framing shifts attention to person-environment fit: on this view much of the difficulty an autistic person experiences arises from environments built for a different profile, so the remedy is partly to change the environment rather than only the person.

It stands in tension with the medical model, which treats these conditions as deficits requiring diagnosis and treatment, and critics of a strong neurodiversity position note that it sits uneasily with profoundly disabling presentations involving minimal language or intellectual disability.

Recent empirical work suggests the two framings overlap more in practice than in rhetoric, with people endorsing neurodiversity still recognising genuine impairment.

For a neuroscience of individual differences the framing has a substantive implication: it argues against treating a single profile as the reference standard and everything else as deviation.


67.4.4 Individual variation as signal rather than noise

For most of its history, cognitive neuroscience averaged across participants and treated the differences between them as noise obscuring the true group effect.

That assumption has been overturned from both directions.

Scott Marek, Nico Dosenbach and colleagues (2022, Nature) pooled about 50,000 scans and showed that brain-wide association studies - correlating a brain measure with a behavioural trait across people - produce effects so small that reliable detection typically requires thousands of participants, whereas the median neuroimaging study had used about 25.

The implication is stark: a large fraction of the published brain-behaviour correlation literature is underpowered and its specific findings should not be trusted, though later work by Tamas Spisak and colleagues (2023) showed that multivariate methods, which pool information across many connections at once, yield larger and more replicable effects than single-connection tests.

The constructive response has been precision neuroimaging: scanning a small number of individuals for many hours each, which reveals that functional network layouts differ substantially and stably between people in ways group averages smear away.

Between the fingerprint results, the polygenic scores, and the deep-scanning studies, variation between people has become the object of study rather than the obstacle to it.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognitive test scores all correlate positively, and that positive manifold is well described by a hierarchy with narrow skills at the bottom and a general factor at the top - but whether g names a causal brain property or merely summarises many overlapping causes is still genuinely disputed, with mutualism and process overlap accounts fitting the data comparably well.

Brain correlates of ability are real but weak and distributed: volume correlates around r = 0.24, P-FIT and network neuroscience theory both point to integration across frontal and parietal systems rather than to any single seat of intelligence, and connectome-based prediction accounts for a meaningful but modest share of variance.

Heritability of cognitive ability rises with age toward roughly 0.6 or higher in adulthood while shared-family influence fades, a pattern best explained by people increasingly selecting environments that fit their dispositions; polygenic scores now predict a modest share of variance but predict far less within families and transfer poorly across ancestries.

The Flynn effect and its within-family reversal in Norway show that population averages move for environmental reasons on timescales far too short for genetic change.

Beyond general ability, the search for brain correlates of personality has had to revise its expected effect sizes sharply downward, the learning-styles version of cognitive style has failed its decisive test, and the neurodiversity framing challenges the habit of treating one profile as standard.

Finally, the power crisis in brain-wide association studies has turned individual variation from discarded noise into the field's central measurement problem.


CHAPTER 68. EVOLUTION AND COMPARATIVE COGNITION (CONTEXT)


The human brain did not appear from nowhere.

It is a modified version of a body plan that vertebrates have been carrying for something like five hundred million years, and almost every part of it has a counterpart in a mouse.

This chapter asks two linked questions - what changed on the road to us, and what did not change at all - and then asks a third question that keeps embarrassing the first two, namely why animals on completely separate branches of the tree of life keep arriving at similar clever behaviour by completely different anatomical routes.

It matters because nearly every claim in the rest of this book rests on an animal experiment, and an animal experiment is only as good as the argument that the animal's brain is relevantly like ours.

It also matters because the question "what makes humans special" has a long history of being answered badly, usually by picking a trait we happen to have and then defining it so that only we qualify.

By the end you should be able to read a comparative claim and ask the right sceptical questions of it.


68.1 Brain evolution

The first thing to get straight is what actually varies between species.

Brains differ in absolute size, in size relative to body, in how many neurons they pack into a given volume, in how those neurons are distributed between regions, and in how long development takes.

These are separate quantities, and for most of the twentieth century the field measured only the first two, which turns out to have been a serious limitation.


68.1.1 Encephalisation, allometry, and neuron counts

Allometry is the study of how one measurement of a body scales against another - here, how brain mass scales with body mass across species.

Brain mass rises with body mass but less than proportionally, so an elephant has a huge brain in grams and a small one relative to its bulk, and in the 1970s Harry Jerison formalised the residual from that scaling line as the encephalisation quotient (EQ), the ratio of a species' actual brain mass to the mass predicted for an animal of its body size.

EQ was attractive because it put humans comfortably at the top, but it silently assumed that all brains are built to the same recipe, so that a gram of brain means the same thing in a rat and a monkey.

Suzana Herculano-Houzel broke that assumption from about 2005 onward using the isotropic fractionator, a method in which brain tissue is dissolved into a uniform suspension of cell nuclei that can then simply be counted, giving direct neuron numbers instead of inferred ones.

The results reset the field - the human brain contains roughly eighty-six billion neurons, of which only around sixteen billion are in the cerebral cortex and about sixty-nine billion are in the cerebellum, and primate brains pack far more neurons into a given mass than rodent brains because primate neurons do not swell as the brain grows the way rodent neurons do.

On this account the human brain is not a special kind of brain at all, but exactly the brain you would expect if you scaled up a generic primate to our size, which relocates the puzzle from anatomy to how our ancestors afforded the metabolic cost - Herculano-Houzel's own proposal is cooking, though that remains an argument rather than a demonstrated fact.

Herculano-Houzel and others have since proposed replacing EQ with counts of neurons in excess of those needed to run the body, and a 2021 paper in Brain Behavior and Evolution went as far as titling itself a farewell to the encephalisation quotient, so this is a live methodological dispute rather than a settled replacement.


68.1.2 Cortical expansion and areal proliferation in primates

The neocortex is the outer sheet of the cerebral hemispheres, six cellular layers thick, and it is the structure that has expanded most dramatically in primates.

Expansion happens in development, when neural progenitor cells - the dividing cells that generate neurons - go through more rounds of division before they stop, so a modest change in the timing or geometry of cell division yields a large change in final cell number.

Work by Pasko Rakic and colleagues, including a 1998 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, showed that cell-cycle durations in monkey cortex are several times longer than in rodents yet the neurogenic period is so much more prolonged that many more total divisions occur.

A particular class of progenitor, the basal radial glial cell, is abundant in the outer subventricular zone of primates and comparatively rare in mice, and it is widely credited with the extra amplification that produces a large, folded cortex.

Expansion was not uniform across the sheet - association areas, especially in parietal and prefrontal cortex, grew disproportionately relative to primary sensory and motor areas, and the number of distinct cortical areas also rose, a process called areal proliferation.

A 2025 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences argued that even the primate visual cortex is best described as the expansion of a conserved underlying architecture rather than the invention of new principles, which is the recurring theme of this whole section.


68.1.3 Human-specific genetic and developmental changes

A small number of genes are genuinely human-specific, having arisen by duplication after our lineage split from chimpanzees, and three have strong experimental support.

ARHGAP11B arose from a partial duplication of the gene ARHGAP11A, and Wieland Huttner's group showed in Science in 2015 that expressing it in embryonic mouse cortex amplifies basal progenitors and can even induce folding of the normally smooth mouse cortex - a later paper traced its distinctive activity to a single nucleotide substitution that changed the protein's tail.

NOTCH2NL, described in two 2018 papers in Cell from the groups of David Haussler and Pierre Vanderhaeghen, exists in three functional copies only in humans and prolongs the proliferative phase of cortical progenitors by tuning Notch signalling, a conserved developmental switch that decides whether a progenitor divides again or becomes a neuron.

SRGAP2C, a human-specific duplicate of SRGAP2A, acts differently - rather than making more neurons it slows down the maturation of dendritic spines, the small protrusions where most excitatory synapses sit, so human synapses take years rather than months to settle, a delay called neoteny (the retention of juvenile characteristics into later life).

The plausible interpretation is that neoteny buys a longer window in which experience, rather than genetic programme, shapes the wiring - elegant, and supported by work such as Vanderhaeghen's 2024 report in Neuron that human synaptic neoteny requires a balance between SRGAP2 and the synaptic protein SYNGAP1, but still a long inferential chain from spine timing to human cognition.

Note also that these coding-sequence stories are probably a minority of the action - much of what differs between human and chimpanzee brains lies in regulatory deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the non-coding sequence that controls when and where genes switch on, including the fast-evolving stretches known as human accelerated regions.


68.1.4 Conserved architecture across vertebrates

Against all this novelty, the striking fact is how much is shared.

Every vertebrate brain has a forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain; every one has a pallium (the upper part of the forebrain, of which our neocortex is one version), a basal ganglia system for action selection, a hypothalamus for bodily regulation, and a cerebellum for coordination and timing.

The same transcription factors - proteins that switch genes on and off - lay out the same territories in fish, frogs, birds and mammals, which is why the field speaks of a conserved vertebrate morphotype, a best guess at the brain of the last common ancestor.

The hard case is birds, whose pallium is nuclear rather than layered and looks nothing like cortex, and whether their nidopallium corresponds to our neocortex has been argued since Harvey Karten proposed cell-type-level homology in the 1960s and 1990s.

Two large papers in Science in 2025, one using single-cell and developmental data and one using enhancer-driven cell type comparison, sharpened rather than ended the debate - inhibitory and non-neuronal cell types look clearly conserved between birds and mammals, while many excitatory pallial types appear to have diverged or arisen independently.

The honest summary is that deep conservation of ingredients coexists with substantial independent rearrangement of the recipe, and anyone who tells you the bird-mammal pallium question is closed is overstating the evidence.


68.2 Comparative cognition

Comparative cognition is the study of how different species solve problems, remember, plan and infer.
