Its central discipline is refusing to grade animals on a single ladder from dumb to smart, because each species is solving the problems its ecology sets it, with the sensory equipment it has.


68.2.1 Cognition in non-human primates

Monkeys and apes are our closest comparison and provide the strongest continuities.

Chimpanzees make and use tools in population-specific traditions - termite-fishing probes, nut-cracking hammers and anvils - documented across decades of field work beginning with Jane Goodall in the 1960s and synthesised in the influential 1999 Nature paper on chimpanzee cultures led by Andrew Whiten.

On social cognition, the long-running question is whether apes represent what others believe, and Christopher Krupenye, Fumihiro Kano and colleagues reported in Science in 2016 that chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans look in anticipation towards where an actor falsely believes an object to be, which Science named a breakthrough of that year.

That result is real but contested in interpretation - critics including Cecilia Heyes have argued that apes may track behavioural regularities and lines of sight without representing beliefs as such, and a 2017 commentary put the point in its title, apes track false beliefs but might not understand them.

Macaques also show metacognition, meaning knowledge about their own knowledge - they will decline a difficult perceptual trial for a small guaranteed reward, which is hard to explain without some internal read-out of confidence.


68.2.2 Corvid and parrot cognition and convergent evolution

Crows, ravens, jays and parrots perform at ape-like levels on many tasks despite a brain the size of a walnut and no neocortex at all.

New Caledonian crows manufacture hooked tools from twigs and pandanus leaves, and Alex Taylor, Russell Gray and colleagues showed in 2007 and after that they solve metatool problems, using one tool to obtain a second tool that then obtains the food, on the first attempt and without trial-and-error learning.

The anatomical resolution of the paradox came in two parts - Seweryn Olkowicz and colleagues showed in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2016 that songbird and parrot forebrains pack roughly twice as many neurons as a primate brain of the same mass, so the walnut contains monkey-scale neuron counts; and Andreas Nieder's group has recorded single neurons in the nidopallium caudolaterale, an associative region that behaves functionally like primate prefrontal cortex, holding information in working memory and encoding rules and even numerosity.

Because the last common ancestor of birds and mammals was a small reptile-like animal some three hundred million years ago with nothing like either structure, this is convergent evolution - similar function reached independently - and it is the single best argument that flexible cognition depends on organisational principles such as dense associative circuitry with recurrent connections, not on the specific six-layered cortical wiring diagram.


68.2.3 Cephalopod cognition and an independent solution

Octopuses, cuttlefish and squid are molluscs whose lineage parted from ours more than five hundred million years ago, which makes them the most independent test case available on this planet.

An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, roughly two thirds of them distributed in the arms rather than the central brain, so much of its motor problem-solving is delegated to peripheral circuitry - a genuinely different architecture from anything vertebrate.

Learning and memory centre on the vertical lobe, and work by Binyamin Hochner and colleagues has shown that it supports long-term potentiation, the lasting strengthening of synapses that is the standard cellular model of memory, though the octopus uses a molecular route involving nitric oxide rather than the vertebrate N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor mechanism.

A 2023 connectome of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe published in eLife found a fan-out architecture reminiscent of the insect mushroom body and vertebrate cerebellum, built from different cells - the same computational trick invented three times.

Behaviourally, Alexandra Schnell and Nicola Clayton reported in 2021 that cuttlefish can delay gratification, waiting for a preferred prey item, and Schnell's 2021 review in Biological Reviews is candid that much of the octopus literature is anecdote-rich and experiment-poor, so scepticism about the more spectacular claims is warranted.


68.2.4 Insect cognition and minimal substrates for learning and navigation

A honeybee has about a million neurons, a fly about a hundred thousand, and both do more than that budget suggests.

Bees perform path integration, continuously updating a home vector by tracking the direction and distance they have travelled so they can fly straight back to the nest from anywhere, and this computation has been localised to the central complex, a small midline structure whose ring neurons maintain a compass-like representation of heading.

The mushroom bodies are the other key structure - paired centres that receive convergent sensory input and store associations, and they are the site of classic olfactory learning in Drosophila and of visual scene memory in navigating ants and bees.

Karl von Frisch established from the 1920s that bees communicate the direction and distance of food by the waggle dance, and later work from Lars Chittka's laboratory has shown bees learning to roll balls into goals from a demonstrator and transmitting the skill to naive bees.

The 2023 complete synaptic connectome of a Drosophila larva brain, and the adult fly connectome that followed, mean insects are now the only animals where cognition can be studied against a full wiring diagram - which is why claims about the minimal substrate for learning are likely to be settled here first.


68.3 What is distinctively human

This section is where careful science most often turns into flattering storytelling, so read it with your guard up.


68.3.1 Language, recursion, and the candidates for uniqueness

Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky and Tecumseh Fitch proposed in Science in 2002 that almost everything in the language faculty is shared with other animals, and that the only uniquely human component may be recursion - the ability to embed a structure inside another structure of the same kind, as in the man who fed the cat that chased the mouse ran away.

The proposal is attractively minimal, and it converts a vague question into a testable one, which is its chief virtue.

It was immediately attacked from two directions - Ray Jackendoff and Steven Pinker argued in 2005 that language has many other special properties besides recursion, and Daniel Everett argued from 2005 that the Amazonian language Pirahã lacks syntactic embedding altogether, which if true means recursion is not even universal among humans.

The Pirahã claim remains disputed on both descriptive and theoretical grounds, and the wider criticism that recursion appears outside language, in planning hierarchies and in music, is taken seriously by many researchers.

What is not disputed is that no trained ape has ever acquired anything resembling human syntax, and that human infants acquire it without instruction, so something about language really is species-typical even if the precise something is unsettled.


68.3.2 Cumulative culture and social learning capacity

The strongest candidate for a human difference may not be an individual capacity at all but a population-level one.

Michael Tomasello's ratchet effect describes culture that accumulates - each generation faithfully copies the current best solution and occasionally improves it, so complexity builds up over centuries and no individual could reinvent a smartphone or a kayak from scratch.

Claudio Tennie, Josep Call and Tomasello argued in 2009 that chimpanzee traditions instead sit within a zone of latent solutions, meaning every observed behaviour lies within what an individual chimpanzee could in principle work out alone, so nothing genuinely accumulates.

The mechanism proposed is that humans copy the process while other apes copy the product - children even over-imitate, faithfully reproducing causally irrelevant steps in a demonstration, whereas chimpanzees sensibly skip them, and Whiten's work on child and chimpanzee culture documents this contrast directly.

The claim is contested at the edges - a 2016 Scientific Reports study argued chimpanzees can improve foraging efficiency by combining witnessed behaviours, and a 2024 paper in Nature Human Behaviour reported chimpanzees acquiring by social learning a tool skill they failed to innovate, which is closer to cumulative culture than the strict view allows.


68.3.3 Mental time travel and its comparative evidence

Mental time travel is the capacity to project yourself into a remembered past or an imagined future, and Thomas Suddendorf and Michael Corballis proposed in 1997 that it is uniquely human.

The Bischof-Köhler hypothesis sharpens the claim - only humans can act for a future need they do not currently feel, so a sated animal should never store food for tomorrow's hunger.

Nicola Clayton and Anthony Dickinson's 1998 Nature study of western scrub-jays supplied the counter-evidence, showing the birds remember what they cached, where, and how long ago, retrieving perishable worms after short delays and durable peanuts after long ones - an episodic-like memory with what, where and when components.

Later work from Clayton's laboratory with Eurasian jays, and Caroline Raby's 2007 breakfast experiments, showed jays caching in the compartment where they would be hungry tomorrow, which is difficult to reconcile with the strict Bischof-Köhler position.

Sceptics reply that behavioural criteria cannot reach the felt, self-projecting quality of human remembering, and a 2024 theme issue of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B was devoted precisely to whether episodic-like memory is episodic memory - the behaviour is established, the interpretation is not.


68.3.4 The risk of anthropocentrism in framing the question

Anthropocentrism here means taking human abilities as the yardstick and grading other species by how closely they approach it, which guarantees that we come out on top because we wrote the exam.

Frans de Waal coined the complementary term anthropodenial for the opposite error, the reflexive refusal to attribute a human-like capacity to an animal even when the evidence supports it, and argued that the traditional preference for the cognitively simplest explanation can conflict with evolutionary parsimony, which favours assuming close relatives share mechanisms rather than positing repeated independent losses.

There is also a plain methodological failure of fair testing - species are routinely tested with human-friendly stimuli and response modes, so an elephant fails a mirror test designed for a small enclosure, or a chimpanzee underperforms because the task requires attending to a human experimenter's pointing.

The history of the field is a series of uniqueness claims that fell - tool use, tool manufacture, culture, planning, numerical competence, some form of belief-tracking - which should induce humility about the ones still standing.

The productive reframing, which the field has largely adopted, is to stop asking which species is smarter and start asking what problem each cognitive system evolved to solve.


68.4 Model organisms and translation

Every technique in this book that requires opening a skull was developed in an animal, so the choice of animal is not a footnote but a determinant of what can be known.


68.4.1 Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish, mouse, rat, marmoset, macaque

Caenorhabditis elegans is a one-millimetre nematode worm with exactly 302 neurons in the hermaphrodite, and John White and Sydney Brenner's team completed its wiring diagram in 1986, making it the first animal with a full connectome - a complete map of the synaptic connections in a nervous system.

Drosophila melanogaster, the fruit fly, has roughly 100,000 neurons, an enormous genetic toolkit for switching individual cell types on and off, and since 2023 to 2024 complete synapse-level connectomes for the larval brain and the adult central brain.

Larval zebrafish are transparent and have a brain of a few hundred thousand neurons, which allows whole-brain imaging at single-cell resolution in a behaving vertebrate - something impossible in any mammal.

Mice dominate mammalian systems neuroscience because of genetic tractability, cheap husbandry and a vast toolkit of engineered lines; rats are less genetically tractable but better at complex behaviour, which is why much of the classic work on spatial memory and decision-making is rat work.

Marmosets, small New World monkeys with around 630 million neurons, breed fast, are amenable to genetic modification and have smooth cortex convenient for imaging; macaques, with far larger and gyrified brains, remain the standard for visual, oculomotor and prefrontal physiology because their cortical organisation most closely resembles ours.


68.4.2 Choosing an organism for a cognitive question

The choice is a trade-off between tractability and relevance, and there is no universally right answer.

If your question is about a molecular mechanism of synaptic plasticity, a fly or a worm may answer it faster and more completely than any mammal, because you can manipulate identified cells and know the full circuit.

If your question is about how a rule is held in mind across a delay, you need an animal with the relevant machinery, and the macaque prefrontal cortex is the closest accessible model of the human one.

Practical constraints bite hard - generation time, cost, the availability of transgenic lines, whether the animal will hold still in a scanner, and ethical review that becomes properly more demanding as the species approaches us.

A common failure is picking the tractable animal and then quietly redefining the question to fit it, which is how a literature ends up full of well-controlled experiments on a phenomenon nobody actually wanted to know about.


68.4.3 Homology and analogy in cross-species mapping

Homology means similarity inherited from a common ancestor; analogy, also called homoplasy or convergence, means similarity arrived at independently.

The distinction is load-bearing because only homology licenses the inference that a mechanism discovered in one species operates the same way in another - if bird nidopallium and mammalian prefrontal cortex are analogous rather than homologous, then a molecular result in one does not automatically transfer to the other.

Deep homology is the intermediate and increasingly important case, in which structures that look nothing alike are nonetheless built by the same ancient gene networks, as has been argued for the arthropod central complex and the vertebrate basal ganglia as action-selection systems.

Establishing homology in brains is hard because soft tissue does not fossilise, so the evidence must come from living species - relative position, developmental origin, gene expression, connectivity and cell type - and any single criterion can mislead.

The practical rule is to state which criterion you are using and to expect that a structure can be homologous as a whole while containing cell types that are not, which is exactly the situation the bird pallium debate has arrived at.


68.4.4 Cross-species alignment of tasks and of neural data

Even with a well-chosen homologous region, comparison fails unless the task and the measurement are matched.

Task alignment means giving the species genuinely equivalent problems, which usually means changing the surface of the task - a monkey reports by eye movement, a mouse by licking, a human by button press - while holding the computation constant, and it means checking that the animals are actually using the same strategy rather than a shortcut.

Neural alignment has moved from anatomical landmarks and myelin maps towards function-based methods, notably the connectivity blueprint approach of Rogier Mars and colleagues published in 2018, which describes each cortical point by its pattern of connections to conserved white matter tracts and so allows a common coordinate space across species without assuming matching landmarks.

More recent work aligns species by their responses to identical stimuli - a 2025 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences mapped macaque to human cortex using responses to the same natural scenes, and joint-embedding methods now place marmoset, macaque and human connectomes in a shared space.

These methods reliably show tight correspondence in early sensory cortex and increasing divergence in association cortex, which is both a validation of the approach and a warning that the human-specific parts are precisely where cross-species inference is weakest.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Brains differ in neuron number, packing density and developmental timing, not merely in mass, and direct counting has undermined the encephalisation quotient as a proxy for cognitive capacity - the human brain looks like a scaled-up primate brain rather than a qualitatively new kind of organ.

Human-specific duplicated genes such as ARHGAP11B, NOTCH2NL and SRGAP2C have measurable effects on progenitor amplification and on the neotenous slowing of synapse maturation, but they sit inside a vertebrate architecture that is otherwise deeply conserved.

Corvids, parrots, cephalopods and insects demonstrate that flexible cognition can be built from radically different anatomy, which shifts the explanatory burden from specific structures to organisational principles such as dense associative circuitry with recurrent loops.

Candidate human uniqueness claims - recursion, cumulative culture, mental time travel - are each real as observations about human behaviour but each disputed as absolute discontinuities, and the history of the field is one of such claims steadily eroding.

Model organism choice is a trade-off between experimental tractability and relevance to the question, and every cross-species inference depends on an explicit argument about homology versus analogy plus careful alignment of both tasks and neural measurements.

Cross-species alignment works best in early sensory cortex and worst in association cortex, which is an uncomfortable fact given that association cortex is where the distinctively human capacities are supposed to live.


PART THIRTEEN. WHEN COGNITION FAILS, AND WHAT CAN BE DONE


CHAPTER 69. CLASSICAL NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL SYNDROMES (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about what happens to the mind when a specific piece of the brain is destroyed, and about what those breakdowns taught us.

Neuropsychology is the study of the relationship between brain damage and changes in thought, language, memory, perception, and action.

For most of the last two centuries it was the only method that could say a brain region was necessary for a mental function, rather than merely busy during it.

The syndromes described here - the aphasias, the amnesias, neglect, the agnosias, the apraxias - are the classical vocabulary of that field, and they still organise how a neurologist examines a patient at the bedside.

They matter because they are the raw evidence behind almost every claim in this book about which brain region does what.

They also matter because the logic of drawing conclusions from broken brains is subtler than it first appears, and the last section of this chapter takes that logic apart.

69.1 Language disorders

Aphasia is an acquired loss or impairment of language caused by brain damage, most often a stroke in the left hemisphere.

It is not a loss of intelligence, and it is not a problem with the muscles of the mouth.

It is damage to the machinery that turns meaning into words and words back into meaning.

The classical scheme sorts aphasias by three bedside questions: is speech fluent, is comprehension preserved, and can the patient repeat what you say.

69.1.1 Broca, Wernicke, conduction, transcortical, and global aphasias

Broca's aphasia, described by Paul Broca in the 1860s, is non-fluent: speech is effortful, sparse, and stripped of grammatical glue words, while comprehension is relatively good, and the patient usually knows something is wrong.

Wernicke's aphasia, described by Carl Wernicke in 1874, is the mirror image: speech flows easily and with normal melody but is emptied of meaning and littered with wrong or invented words, comprehension is poor, and the patient is often unaware of the problem.

Conduction aphasia is defined by a striking selective failure of repetition with fluent speech and good comprehension; the Lichtheim-Geschwind model attributed this to damage to the arcuate fasciculus, a bundle of fibres joining the temporal and frontal language regions, though functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a method that images brain activity by tracking blood oxygenation) and diffusion tensor imaging (a method that traces white matter fibre bundles) have implicated grey matter at the temporoparietal junction, an area often called Spt, in many cases.

The transcortical aphasias are the odd ones out because repetition is spared: transcortical motor aphasia gives sparse effortful speech but intact repetition, and follows damage anterior and superior to Broca's area, often in the watershed territory between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries; transcortical sensory aphasia gives fluent empty speech with poor comprehension but intact repetition, and follows damage in the watershed zone around, but not inside, Wernicke's area.

Global aphasia is the loss of nearly all language functions together and follows large damage across the middle cerebral artery territory, usually taking out both classical language regions.

It should be said plainly that this classical taxonomy is a clinical convenience, not a law of nature: modern lesion mapping studies find that many patients do not fit any category cleanly, and that lesion size predicts aphasia severity about as well as lesion location predicts aphasia type.

69.1.2 Primary progressive aphasia variants

Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative condition in which language decays gradually over years while other thinking is initially spared - the opposite time course from stroke aphasia, which begins at its worst.

The consensus criteria of Gorno-Tempini and colleagues in 2011, published in Neurology, define three variants.

The semantic variant erodes word meaning itself: patients cannot name objects and, more tellingly, no longer know what the words refer to, and the damage centres on the front of the left temporal lobe.

The non-fluent or agrammatic variant produces halting, effortful, grammatically broken speech with damage centred on the left inferior frontal and insular region.

The logopenic variant produces word-finding pauses and a specific failure to repeat long sentences, with damage at the left temporoparietal junction, and is frequently caused by underlying Alzheimer pathology rather than frontotemporal degeneration.

A candid caveat: a substantial minority of patients cannot be classified into any of the three, and papers in Brain Communications in 2022 and in Neurology in 2024 have argued for unclassifiable or mixed presentations.

69.1.3 Anomia and its localising value

Anomia is the failure to retrieve a word one knows, the tip-of-the-tongue state made permanent.

It is the most common single symptom in aphasia and it is present in almost every aphasia type, which is exactly why it is the least useful sign for localisation - nearly any left perisylvian lesion can produce it.

Its diagnostic value comes not from its presence but from the pattern of errors and the point at which retrieval breaks.

If the patient cannot describe the object either, the failure is semantic and points toward the anterior and ventral temporal lobe; if the patient can describe its use, its shape, and where you buy it but cannot produce the sound of the name, the failure is lexical or phonological and points toward posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex.

Case work on Brodmann area 37, the posterior ventral temporal region, suggests it acts as an interface allowing intact semantic knowledge to reach a stored word form.

69.1.4 Recovery and the reorganisation of language

Most recovery from stroke aphasia happens in the first three to six months, and it is driven by two partly competing processes.

In the acute phase, the undamaged right hemisphere increases its activity in regions that mirror the damaged left ones.

In patients who recover well, that right-sided activity tends to subside and activity returns to surviving left-hemisphere tissue around the lesion, called perilesional cortex; persistently high right-hemisphere engagement is more often associated with poor outcome.

This has led to the maladaptive-versus-compensatory dispute, and the honest summary is that the right hemisphere is not one thing: systematic reviews of right-hemisphere language pathways report that some contribute usefully, especially to comprehension, while others predict worse naming recovery.

That dispute is live, and treatments built on it - such as inhibiting the right hemisphere with non-invasive brain stimulation - are supported by encouraging but not decisive trial evidence.

69.2 Memory disorders

Amnesia is a disproportionate loss of memory with other cognitive abilities relatively intact.

The classical amnesic patient can hold a normal conversation, has an unchanged personality and intelligence, and remembers how to ride a bicycle, but cannot tell you what happened this morning.

That profile is the single strongest piece of evidence that memory is not one faculty but several.

69.2.1 Anterograde and retrograde amnesia

Anterograde amnesia is the inability to lay down new memories after the injury; retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before it.

The two usually occur together but are dissociable, and their relative severity is informative.

Retrograde amnesia typically shows a temporal gradient, described by Théodule Ribot in 1882 and therefore called the Ribot gradient: recent memories are lost more severely than remote ones, so a patient may recall childhood vividly while the last decade is blank.

Patient Henry Molaison, known during his life as H.M., reported by William Scoville and Brenda Milner in 1957 after bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobes for epilepsy, had profound anterograde amnesia with retrograde loss covering only a few years before surgery.

The interpretation of the gradient is contested: systems-consolidation theory says memories gradually become independent of the hippocampus, while multiple-trace theory says vivid episodic memories always require the hippocampus and only the fact-like residue survives.

69.2.2 Medial temporal, diencephalic, and basal forebrain amnesias

Amnesia arises from damage at three main points along one circuit, and the three produce subtly different profiles.

Medial temporal amnesia, from damage to the hippocampus and neighbouring cortex, is the H.M. type: severe failure to encode new episodes, with rapid forgetting.

Diencephalic amnesia, from damage deep in the midline of the brain, is typified by Korsakoff syndrome, a consequence of thiamine deficiency usually associated with chronic alcohol misuse; the mammillary bodies and the medial dorsal nucleus of the thalamus are both implicated, and which of them is critical remains genuinely disputed because human lesions are rarely tidy enough to settle it.

Basal forebrain amnesia follows rupture or surgical repair of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm, which starves the septal nuclei and subcallosal region that supply the hippocampus with acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter important for encoding; this form is marked less by pure forgetting than by disordered retrieval, poor memory for source and time, and confabulation.

69.2.3 Transient global amnesia and functional amnesia

Transient global amnesia (TGA) is a dramatic, self-limiting episode in which a person, usually middle-aged or older, abruptly cannot form new memories and repeatedly asks the same orienting question, while remaining alert, articulate, and able to drive or cook.

It resolves within twenty-four hours and rarely recurs.

Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, which detects restricted water movement in tissue, often shows tiny punctate lesions one to three millimetres across in the hippocampus, best seen at forty-eight to seventy-two hours; a large series reported in Neurology in 2020 found them in roughly seventy per cent of cases, and 7 Tesla scanning finds more than lower field strengths.

These dots are supportive but not proof, because similar signals appear after prolonged seizures and in posterior circulation stroke.

Functional or dissociative amnesia is different in kind: it typically follows psychological trauma, often erases autobiographical identity while sparing new learning - the reverse of the organic pattern - and has no reliable structural lesion.

69.2.4 Confabulation and source memory failure

Confabulation is the production of false memories without any intent to deceive; the patient believes what they are saying.

The clinically important distinction is between provoked confabulation, a small gap-filling error under questioning that healthy people also make, and spontaneous confabulation, in which the patient acts on a false present reality, packing to collect children who are now adults.

Armin Schnider and Radek Ptak, working from 1999 onward, argued that the core failure is an inability to suppress memory traces that were relevant in the past but are irrelevant now, so old memories are misassigned to the present - a temporal context confusion.

Lesion work implicates ventromedial prefrontal cortex, with additional orbitofrontal damage appearing crucial for the spontaneous form, and a 2023 lesion network mapping study located spontaneous confabulation to a distributed circuit rather than a single spot.

A rival account frames the same behaviour as a source monitoring failure - an inability to tag where and when a memory came from - though source monitoring deficits also occur in patients who never confabulate, which weakens the account as a complete explanation.

69.3 Attention and spatial disorders

These are disorders in which the sensory apparatus works but the world is not attended to.

A patient with neglect has intact eyes and intact primary visual cortex, and yet half of space has stopped mattering.

Such syndromes are the strongest clinical evidence that attention is a separate system layered on top of sensation.

69.3.1 Hemispatial neglect and its varieties

Hemispatial neglect is a failure to attend or respond to stimuli on the side of space opposite a brain lesion, most commonly the left side after right hemisphere damage.

Patients eat food from only one half of the plate, shave one cheek, and draw only the right half of a clock, and many show anosognosia, meaning a lack of awareness of the deficit.

Neglect fractionates in several ways: personal neglect concerns the body itself, peripersonal neglect the space within reach, and extrapersonal neglect the space beyond it; egocentric neglect is defined relative to the body midline, whereas allocentric neglect ignores the left side of each individual object no matter where that object sits.

The anatomy is disputed and the dispute is worth naming: the classical account localises neglect to the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction, while Hans-Otto Karnath and colleagues have argued for the right superior temporal gyrus, and other work stresses white matter disconnection of frontoparietal attention networks.

Neglect is also a strong predictor of poor functional recovery after stroke, independent of motor impairment, which is why it is screened for routinely.

69.3.2 Extinction and the competition account

Extinction is a milder relative of neglect: the patient detects a single touch or light on the affected side perfectly well, but fails to report it when an identical stimulus is presented simultaneously on the other side.

Because the failure appears only under competition, it cannot be a sensory loss, and this makes extinction the cleanest natural demonstration of the biased competition theory of attention.

On that account, representations of stimuli compete for limited processing resources, and one hemisphere's damage tilts the competition so that ipsilesional stimuli - those on the same side as the lesion - reliably win.

An interhemispheric rivalry version adds that the intact hemisphere becomes disinhibited and hyperactive, which is the rationale behind attempts to treat neglect by suppressing the intact hemisphere.

More recent primate work reframes extinction as a bias in decision circuitry within posterior parietal cortex rather than in attentional allocation as such, and the two framings are not yet reconciled.

69.3.3 Balint syndrome and simultanagnosia

Balint syndrome, described by Rezsö Bálint in 1909, is the rare and devastating consequence of bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital junction, most often from watershed strokes, posterior cortical atrophy, or head injury.

It is a triad.

Simultanagnosia is the inability to see more than one object at a time, so a patient shown a complex picture reports a single item and cannot assemble the scene.

Optic ataxia is the inability to guide the hand accurately to a visually seen target, despite normal strength and normal vision.

Oculomotor apraxia, sometimes called psychic gaze paralysis, is the inability to voluntarily shift gaze to a chosen object even though the eye muscles work normally.

Together these show that locating, grasping, and binding a visual world into a coherent whole are separable operations from simply seeing.

69.3.4 Rehabilitation approaches and their evidence

Visual scanning training explicitly teaches patients to search leftward with cues and anchors; it is the most established approach and it produces measurable gains, but the gains are often narrow and may not transfer far beyond the trained task.

Prism adaptation has patients reach for targets while wearing wedge prisms that shift the visual field rightward; after removing the prisms the reaching aftereffect shifts leftward, and neglect symptoms reduce, sometimes for weeks after only a few short sessions.

Limb activation therapy, which requires movement of the neglected limb in neglected space, and neck muscle vibration and trunk rotation combined with scanning training, also have supporting evidence.

The honest state of the field is that effect sizes on standard measures such as the Behavioural Inattention Test are moderate to large in the short term, but evidence for durable, real-world functional benefit is thinner, trials are small, and a proof-of-concept study nested in a phase II randomised trial reported in 2023 found that a single prism session did not increase engagement in occupational therapy early after stroke.

69.4 Recognition and action disorders

The next family of syndromes concerns knowing what something is, and knowing how to do something.

Both look at first like sensory or motor problems and neither is.

69.4.1 Apperceptive and associative agnosias

Agnosia is a failure to recognise objects that cannot be explained by loss of vision, loss of language, or general dementia; Sigmund Freud coined the term, and Heinrich Lissauer in 1890 drew the distinction still used.

Apperceptive agnosia is a failure to build a coherent percept: the patient cannot copy a drawing or match shapes, because the shape itself never comes together.

Associative agnosia is a failure to attach meaning to an intact percept: the patient can copy the drawing faithfully, sometimes line by line over many minutes, and still not know what it is - the classic description is perception stripped of meaning.

Glyn Humphreys and Jane Riddoch, studying patient H.J.A. from the 1980s, argued for an intermediate form they called integrative agnosia, in which local features are seen but cannot be bound into a whole, which is why such patients often do better with a simple line drawing than a richly detailed one.

Patient D.F., whose ventral visual stream was damaged by carbon monoxide poisoning, could not report the orientation of a slot but could post a card through it accurately, and that dissociation became a pillar of the two visual streams theory.

69.4.2 Prosopagnosia, acquired and developmental

Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognise familiar faces despite intact vision and intact knowledge of the people themselves, who can still be identified by voice, gait, or hairstyle.

Acquired prosopagnosia follows damage to occipitotemporal cortex, particularly the right fusiform gyrus, and is usually the result of stroke, haemorrhage, or head injury.

Developmental or congenital prosopagnosia occurs without any detectable brain injury and in people who have never recognised faces well; prevalence estimates cluster around two to two and a half per cent, with a 2023 study using stricter and looser criteria suggesting figures around one in thirty-three.

An important and awkward finding is that many developmentally prosopagnosic individuals show apparently normal face-selective responses in the right fusiform face area, so the deficit is not simply an absent face module; work by Zhang, Liu and Behrmann published in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2015 found that finer-grained decoding of configural face information in that region is nonetheless impaired.

Whether prosopagnosia reflects a truly face-specific mechanism or a general deficit in fine within-category discrimination for highly practised material remains an active argument.

69.4.3 Ideomotor and ideational apraxia

Apraxia is the inability to perform learned skilled movements on command despite intact strength, sensation, coordination, and comprehension of the request.

Hugo Liepmann, working from 1900, drew the standard division.

Ideomotor apraxia is a failure to execute the movement plan: asked to show how to use a toothbrush, the patient produces clumsy, spatially and temporally wrong gestures, often using the hand itself as the object, yet may brush their teeth correctly at the sink because context supplies the action.

Ideational apraxia is a failure of the plan itself, most visible in multi-step sequences: the steps of making tea appear out of order or omitted, and it is associated with larger left temporoparietal damage, frequently alongside severe aphasia.

Both are predominantly left-hemisphere syndromes and typically affect both hands, which is itself informative - the left hemisphere appears to hold the stored representations of skilled action for the whole body.

Voxel-based lesion analyses continue to centre ideomotor apraxia on left inferior parietal cortex and its connections to premotor areas.

69.4.4 Disconnection syndromes and callosal disorders

A disconnection syndrome is a deficit caused not by damage to a processing region but by severing the fibres that carry information between two intact regions.

Joseph Dejerine described the founding case in 1892: a patient with damage to the left occipital lobe and the splenium of the corpus callosum who could write but could not read what he had just written, because visual information reaching the intact right hemisphere could no longer cross to the left-hemisphere language system - alexia without agraphia.

Norman Geschwind revived and generalised this framework in his 1965 paper Disconnexion syndromes in animals and man, which reshaped clinical neurology.

The corpus callosum is the great fibre bridge between the hemispheres, and after it is cut - as was done surgically to control severe epilepsy in the split-brain patients studied by Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga - an object placed in the left hand or flashed to the left visual field can be identified by pointing but not named, because the information never reaches the speaking hemisphere.

Alien hand syndrome, in which one hand acts with apparent purpose against the person's stated intention, is associated with damage to the midbody of the callosum, and a 2021 analysis argued the syndrome is best explained by disconnection between hand control and language dominance.

A dissenting data point deserves mention: a 2025 report in Communications Psychology described a case of near-complete callosotomy without a classical disconnection syndrome, a reminder that these effects depend on the exact extent and timing of the cut.

69.5 The logic of neuropsychology

Everything above rests on one inference: from what a damaged brain can no longer do, work out how the intact mind is organised.

That inference is powerful but it is not automatic, and this section states its terms.

69.5.1 What a dissociation licenses and what it does not

A single dissociation is a patient who is impaired on task A but normal on task B, and by itself it licenses very little, because task A may simply be harder or more resource-hungry.

A double dissociation - one patient impaired on A but not B, another impaired on B but not A - removes the difficulty explanation and is the strongest neuropsychological evidence that two processes are separable.

But separable is not the same as modular, and this is where the argument bites: David Plaut showed in 1995, and again in the Cortex forum in 2003, that damaging a connectionist network with no separate components at all can still produce a clean double dissociation, because functional specialisation emerges within a distributed system without corresponding to any structural part.

Martin Davies put the modern position well in 2010: a double dissociation supports separate modules by inference to the best explanation, not the only possible explanation.

The practical upshot is that a double dissociation is strong evidence, and evidence about function, not a proof about anatomy.

69.5.2 The single-case method and its defence

The instinct of most sciences is to average across many patients, and Alfonso Caramazza argued in 1986, in Brain and Cognition, that in this field averaging destroys the very information you need.

Brain-damaged patients differ in lesion site, lesion extent, which components are broken, and what compensatory strategies they have developed, so a group mean may describe a pattern that no individual patient shows.

On Caramazza's argument, only the single case allows valid inference about the structure of the normal system, because the theory must explain one whole coherent pattern of spared and impaired performance.

The counterargument is that single cases can be idiosyncratic and are hard to replicate, and the pragmatic settlement, argued well in a 2012 Cognitive Neuropsychology exchange, is to drink from several sources: single cases for existence proofs and theory refutation, series and group studies for prevalence and prediction.

Modern statistical tools for comparing a single patient against a control sample, and a 2022 Nature Reviews Psychology paper defending single cases as a tool for developing and testing theories, have given the method a firmer footing than it had in the 1990s.

69.5.3 Lesion network mapping as the modern successor

The oldest problem in the lesion method is that patients whose lesions barely overlap can share a symptom, which defeats simple overlap analysis.

Lesion network mapping, introduced by Aaron Boes, Michael Fox and colleagues in Brain in 2015, solves this by asking not where the lesion is but what the lesion is connected to.

Each patient's lesion is placed on a reference brain, its normal functional connectivity is looked up in resting-state fMRI data from large samples of healthy people, and the resulting networks are compared across patients.

Lesions scattered across the brain often turn out to connect to one common circuit, and the technique has since been applied to more than forty symptoms, including several - hallucinations, blindsight, pathological laughing and crying, spontaneous confabulation - that had resisted classical localisation.

Its limits are real: it uses connectivity from healthy brains rather than the patient's own, it is correlational at the network level even though the lesion is causal at the site, and it has not yet been widely validated as a tool for predicting outcome in individual patients.

69.5.4 Cognitive neuropsychology's continuing role in the imaging era

In 2004 a Nature Reviews Neuroscience article asked whether inferring function from human brain lesions was a relic of a past era in the age of fMRI, and the answer that has settled out is no, for a specific reason.

Imaging shows which regions are active during a task, which is a correlation; a lesion shows which regions the task cannot survive without, which is causal necessity.

Those are different claims, and only the second can adjudicate between theories that predict the same activation pattern.

A 2016 review in Neuron argued that lesion studies have continued through the imaging decades to arbitrate conclusions drawn from fMRI, and the field has moved toward combining them - lesion-symptom mapping and lesion network mapping on one side, imaging and non-invasive stimulation on the other.

The syndromes in this chapter are therefore not historical curiosities; they remain the causal anchor for a discipline whose dominant methods are correlational.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The classical syndromes divide along informative lines: aphasias by fluency, comprehension and repetition; amnesias by whether the failure is encoding, retrieval, or source; attentional disorders by whether space, objects, or competition is at stake; and recognition and action disorders by whether the failure is in building a percept, attaching meaning to it, or executing a plan.

Each syndrome family carries a specific theoretical payload - extinction supports biased competition, patient D.F. supports two visual streams, disconnection cases show that white matter carries function, and the amnesias show memory is several systems rather than one.

Several of the classical localisations are genuinely disputed and were presented as such: the anatomy of neglect, the critical structure in diencephalic amnesia, the role of the right hemisphere in aphasia recovery, and whether prosopagnosia reveals a face-specific mechanism.

The inferential logic matters as much as the findings: a double dissociation is strong evidence for separable processes but not proof of anatomical modules, since connectionist models without modules can produce one.

Lesion network mapping since 2015 has extended the method by localising symptoms to circuits rather than sites, and lesion evidence remains necessary precisely because it is causal where functional imaging is correlational.


CHAPTER 70. NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE AND COGNITION (CONTEXT)

Neurodegenerative disease is the slow, progressive death of particular populations of brain cells, and it is the single largest natural experiment in how the brain builds a mind.

Each disease attacks a different set of brain regions, and each therefore dismantles a different part of cognition, in a different order.

That is why these diseases matter to a book about cognition and not only to a book about medicine - they tell us which brain systems carry which mental functions, by taking them away one at a time.

This chapter walks through the major degenerative diseases that affect thinking, then steps back to ask what they have in common.

The aim is not to make you a diagnostician.

The aim is to let you read a clinical description and see the cognitive architecture showing through it.

A note before starting: degeneration means loss of structure and function over time, and a proteinopathy is a disease in which a normal protein misfolds, clumps together, and accumulates where it should not.

70.1 Alzheimer disease

Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia, which is the term for cognitive decline severe enough to interfere with everyday independent living.

It was first described by Alois Alzheimer in 1906 in a patient named Auguste Deter, and the two microscopic features he reported - plaques outside neurons and tangles inside them - are still the defining features today.

Its classic signature is early and severe difficulty forming new episodic memories, meaning memories for specific events located in a particular time and place.

That signature follows directly from where the disease starts, in and around the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex, the structures that bind an experience into a retrievable record.

70.1.1 Amyloid, tau, and the pathological cascade

Two proteins define the pathology.

Amyloid-beta is a short protein fragment cut from a larger membrane protein, and in Alzheimer disease it accumulates outside neurons as dense deposits called plaques.

Tau is a protein that normally stabilises microtubules, the internal scaffolding that neurons use as transport rails, and in Alzheimer disease it becomes abnormally phosphorylated - loaded with extra phosphate groups - detaches, and clumps inside neurons as neurofibrillary tangles.

The amyloid cascade hypothesis, proposed by John Hardy and colleagues around 1991 and 1992, holds that amyloid accumulation is the upstream trigger, which then drives tau pathology, then neuronal death, then cognitive decline.

The strongest evidence for it is genetic: every known mutation that causes early-onset inherited Alzheimer disease sits in the amyloid pathway, and people with Down syndrome, who carry an extra copy of the amyloid precursor gene, develop the pathology almost universally.

The strongest evidence against it is correlational and clinical: tau burden tracks neuronal loss, regional atrophy, and cognitive decline far more tightly than amyloid burden does, and drug trials that cleared amyloid successfully produced disappointingly modest cognitive benefit.

This is a genuinely contested area, and honest sources present it as such - a 2023 critical review in the journal Brain by Karran and De Strooper argues the cascade is best read as a slow, indirect, decades-long process rather than a simple chain, and a 2025 Neurology analysis found only about a third of people diagnosed under the 2024 Alzheimer's Association criteria actually followed the cascade's predicted ordering.

Braak and Braak, in 1991, mapped the tangle pathology's spatial progression - transentorhinal cortex first, then limbic regions, then the neocortex - and that staging scheme remains the standard anatomical description of how the disease marches through the brain.

70.1.2 The staging of cognitive decline

Alzheimer disease does not begin when symptoms begin.

Pathology accumulates for an estimated fifteen to twenty years before the first complaint, a period now called preclinical Alzheimer disease - biology present, cognition normal.

Next comes mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a term introduced by Ronald Petersen and colleagues in 1999 for measurable cognitive decline that has not yet stolen independence, and only after that comes dementia.

The 2024 revised criteria from the Alzheimer's Association workgroup, led by Clifford Jack, formalised a two-dimensional scheme: a biological stage from A to D based on amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET) burden, crossed with a clinical stage from 1 to 6 running from cognitively unimpaired through subtle impairment and MCI to increasingly severe dementia.

The two dimensions are deliberately separate because they come apart in real people - two individuals with identical pathology can sit at very different clinical stages, and the 2024 framework was built explicitly to accommodate that fact.

Redefining the disease biologically is itself controversial, since it labels people who feel entirely well as having a disease, and a number of clinicians and ethicists have objected on exactly those grounds.

70.1.3 Biomarkers: imaging, cerebrospinal fluid, and blood-based

A biomarker is a measurable signal that stands in for something you cannot observe directly - here, the pathology inside a living brain.

Three generations of them exist.

Imaging came first: amyloid PET, using tracers such as Pittsburgh Compound B introduced by Klunk and colleagues in 2004, makes plaques visible in a living person, and tau PET tracers such as flortaucipir do the same for tangles and track cognition more closely.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) measures came next, sampled by lumbar puncture, with the diagnostic pattern being low amyloid-beta 42 - because the protein is being sequestered into plaques rather than floating free - alongside raised total tau and raised phosphorylated tau.

The most consequential recent development is blood-based testing, and specifically plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), which distinguishes Alzheimer pathology from other causes with accuracy approaching that of CSF.

In May 2025 the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the first such blood test for diagnostic use, the Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 to amyloid-beta 1-42 ratio, for symptomatic adults aged fifty-five and older, and a 2025 Nature Medicine study by Palmqvist, Hansson and colleagues showed the approach performs well even in primary care, where diagnostic accuracy by clinical judgement alone is poor.

This matters practically: a cheap blood draw replacing an expensive scan or an invasive spinal tap is what makes population-scale detection conceivable at all.

70.1.4 Disease-modifying therapy and the state of the evidence

Until 2021 no treatment altered the disease itself; the available drugs, cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, modestly buffered symptoms without touching the underlying process.

Two anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies - laboratory-made immune proteins targeted at a specific molecule - have now changed that, at least in principle.

Lecanemab, in the CLARITY-AD trial reported by van Dyck and colleagues in 2022, slowed decline on the Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes scale by roughly twenty-seven percent over eighteen months; donanemab, in TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 reported by Sims and colleagues in 2023, produced a comparable slowing.

Both clear amyloid dramatically and unambiguously, which settles the question of whether the drugs hit their target, but the absolute clinical difference is small, and whether it is large enough for a patient or family to notice is disputed - some commentators call it a genuine first foothold, others argue it falls below the threshold of a clinically meaningful change.

Both carry a real safety cost in the form of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), brain swelling or microbleeding visible on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which is more frequent and more severe in carriers of the APOE4 gene variant and has caused deaths; a 2025 indirect comparison by Sabbagh and colleagues put ARIA rates roughly ten percentage points lower for lecanemab than donanemab.

The regulatory verdict has split by jurisdiction, with the European Medicines Agency initially refusing and then narrowly approving lecanemab for restricted populations, which is itself a signal of how finely balanced the benefit-risk judgement is.

70.2 Other dementias

Alzheimer disease dominates public attention, but it accounts for perhaps sixty to seventy percent of dementia, and the remainder is not a footnote.

The other syndromes are cognitively instructive precisely because they spare memory and take something else first.

70.2.1 Frontotemporal dementia and its behavioural and language variants

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) attacks the frontal and anterior temporal lobes, and it typically strikes younger than Alzheimer disease, often between forty-five and sixty-five.

The behavioural variant (bvFTD) destroys social conduct, empathy, and self-regulation while memory and spatial ability stay comparatively intact - patients become disinhibited, apathetic, rigidly ritualistic, or indifferent to others' distress, and are frequently misdiagnosed as psychiatric cases for years.

The language variants fall under primary progressive aphasia (PPA), where language degrades in isolation: the semantic variant erodes word and object meaning itself, sparing fluency, while the nonfluent or agrammatic variant breaks grammar and speech production, sparing meaning.

Underneath, the pathology is heterogeneous - roughly half of cases involve misfolded TDP-43, a protein normally involved in ribonucleic acid (RNA) handling, and roughly forty-five percent involve tau, with a small remainder involving the protein FUS - and the clinical syndrome only loosely predicts which.

The correlation that does hold reasonably well is that the semantic variant is overwhelmingly TDP-43 pathology, while the nonfluent variant is more often tau, a useful anchor but not a guarantee.

70.2.2 Dementia with Lewy bodies

Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is caused by aggregates of the protein alpha-synuclein, called Lewy bodies, distributed through the cortex as well as the brainstem.

Its cognitive profile is distinctive: attention and visuospatial function suffer disproportionately, memory is relatively preserved early, and cognition fluctuates markedly - patients can be lucid one hour and profoundly confused the next, a feature that families notice long before clinicians do.

The 2017 consensus criteria led by Ian McKeith list four core clinical features: fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder in which people physically act out dreams, and spontaneous parkinsonism.

REM sleep behaviour disorder is particularly important because it can precede dementia by more than a decade, making it one of the earliest detectable markers of synuclein disease in a living person.

Indicative biomarkers include reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the striatum on single-photon emission computed tomography (a DaTscan) and abnormal cardiac MIBG scintigraphy; the 2017 criteria allow probable DLB from either two core features or one core feature plus one indicative biomarker.

One clinical fact is worth stating plainly because it is dangerous: many DLB patients react severely to antipsychotic drugs, so a misdiagnosis can do serious harm.

70.2.3 Vascular cognitive impairment

Vascular cognitive impairment covers cognitive decline caused by damage to the brain's blood supply, ranging from a single strategically placed stroke to the diffuse, cumulative injury of cerebral small vessel disease.

Small vessel disease is now understood to be the larger contributor, showing up on MRI as white matter hyperintensities - bright patches of damaged white matter - along with small deep infarcts called lacunes and microbleeds.

Its cognitive signature is not amnesia but slowness: reduced information-processing speed and impaired executive function, the umbrella term for planning, switching, and inhibiting, sometimes described as a subcortical pattern.

The mechanism is intuitive once stated - white matter carries the long-range axonal cables between distant cortical regions, so damaging it does not delete any single function but degrades the speed and reliability of every function that requires distant regions to coordinate.

Work from the St George's SCANS study by Lawrence, Markus and colleagues found lacune count and white matter microstructural integrity independently predicted executive function, while processing speed was predicted by lacune count and overall brain atrophy.

70.2.4 Mixed pathology as the common reality

The tidy disease categories above are largely an artefact of studying selected patients in specialist clinics.

In unselected community autopsy series they mostly dissolve: Schneider, Arvanitakis, Bennett and colleagues, reporting on the Rush Memory and Aging Project in Neurology in 2007, found that most dementia in community-dwelling older people involved more than one pathology at once, typically Alzheimer changes plus infarcts, plus Lewy bodies.

Later Rush analyses and other cohorts have repeatedly confirmed this, with mixed vascular and neurodegenerative pathology present in roughly thirty to fifty percent of community dementia cases.

Two implications follow, and both are important.

First, mixed pathology explains part of why single-target drugs underperform - if you remove one of three contributing pathologies, you should expect a fraction of a benefit, which is roughly what the anti-amyloid trials delivered.

Second, it means that the pure syndromes described in textbooks, including this one, are idealisations, and that the older the patient, the less likely any single label tells the whole story.

70.3 Movement disorders with cognitive features

The basal ganglia and cerebellum were long treated as motor machinery.

The diseases in this section are the clearest demonstration that they are not - damage them and thinking changes, in specific and predictable ways.

70.3.1 Parkinson disease cognition and dopaminergic overdose effects

Parkinson disease is caused by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, a midbrain nucleus that supplies the striatum, and while it is diagnosed on motor signs, cognitive impairment is common and eventually affects a majority of patients.

The early cognitive profile is executive and attentional rather than amnestic, reflecting the dorsal striatum's role in the frontostriatal loops that support set-shifting, planning, and working memory.

The most theoretically interesting finding is the dopamine overdose effect, developed by Roshan Cools, Trevor Robbins and colleagues from around 2001 building on earlier work by Gotham and colleagues in the 1980s: because dopamine depletion is uneven, medicating enough to restore the depleted dorsal circuit floods the still-healthy ventral circuit, so the same dose that improves task-switching simultaneously impairs reversal learning, which is the ability to update behaviour when reward contingencies change.

This is a striking result because it shows the drug is not simply good or bad for cognition - it is good for the functions of the sick circuit and bad for the functions of the healthy one, which is direct evidence that dopamine's effects follow an inverted-U curve where both too little and too much impair performance.

The same mechanism plausibly contributes to the impulse control disorders - gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality - that dopamine agonist drugs induce in a minority of Parkinson patients.

70.3.2 Huntington disease and striatal cognition

Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin gene, and it is fully penetrant - if you carry the expansion, you will develop the disease, with longer repeats producing earlier onset.

Its pathology is unusually focused, destroying the medium spiny neurons of the striatum first and most severely, which makes it something close to a natural lesion study of striatal function.

The cognitive consequences are executive and procedural: impaired planning, set-shifting, and psychomotor speed, degraded recognition of emotions, particularly disgust and anger, and difficulty with skill and habit learning, all with recognition memory comparatively preserved.

The genetic test means that carriers can be studied for decades before symptoms, and prodromal cohort studies such as PREDICT-HD, reported by Jane Paulsen and colleagues, have shown measurable cognitive and motor change more than a decade before formal diagnosis - which is why the field increasingly regards the boundary between healthy and affected as a convention rather than a fact.

Enroll-HD, the large global observational platform that succeeded these studies, now supports this work at scale.

70.3.3 Progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal syndrome

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a tau disease whose classic presentation, Richardson syndrome, combines early falls from postural instability, axial rigidity, and a supranuclear gaze palsy - an inability to move the eyes voluntarily, especially downward, while reflexive eye movements survive, which localises the problem above the eye-movement nuclei rather than in them.

Its cognitive profile is heavily frontal: marked slowing of thought, impaired verbal fluency, apathy, and perseveration, meaning inappropriate repetition of a response after it has stopped being useful.

Corticobasal syndrome is the clinical picture of markedly asymmetric limb apraxia - loss of the ability to execute skilled learned movements despite intact strength and comprehension - together with rigidity, cortical sensory loss, and sometimes the alien limb phenomenon, in which a hand acts purposefully without the person feeling they willed it.

The crucial and often-missed point, emphasised in reviews such as Burrell and colleagues in 2014, is that corticobasal syndrome is a clinical description, not a pathological diagnosis: the underlying disease is corticobasal degeneration in only about half of cases, with PSP pathology and Alzheimer disease accounting for much of the rest.

Both conditions produce language impairment as well, and both overlap clinically with frontotemporal dementia, which is unsurprising given that PSP, corticobasal degeneration, and a large share of FTD are all tauopathies.

70.3.4 Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome

For most of the twentieth century the cerebellum was regarded as purely motor, coordinating movement and nothing else.

Jeremy Schmahmann and Janet Sherman overturned that in a 1998 paper in Brain describing twenty patients with cerebellar lesions who showed a consistent non-motor syndrome: impaired executive function, disturbed visuospatial cognition, language deficits including agrammatism and flattened prosody, and personality change with blunted or disinhibited affect.

Schmahmann's explanatory proposal is the dysmetria of thought hypothesis - dysmetria means mis-measured, undershooting or overshooting movement, and the claim is that the cerebellum applies the same coordinating and error-correcting computation to thought that it applies to movement, so cerebellar damage produces thought that is poorly calibrated rather than absent.

The anatomical basis is real and well established: the posterior cerebellum has reciprocal connections with prefrontal, temporal and parietal association cortices and with limbic circuitry, entirely separate from the anterior motor territory.

A dedicated bedside instrument, the Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome scale, was published by Hoche, Schmahmann and colleagues in Brain in 2018, and a 2019 meta-analysis confirmed the cognitive deficits are reliable across studies.

The syndrome is well documented; the dysmetria of thought account of why it happens is elegant, widely cited, and still substantially underdetermined by evidence - it should be read as a productive framework rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

70.4 Mechanistic themes

Four ideas recur across every disease above, and together they form the closest thing the field has to a general theory.

70.4.1 Selective vulnerability of networks

The central puzzle of neurodegeneration is selectivity: the misfolded proteins involved are expressed brain-wide, yet each disease kills a specific and reproducible subset of neurons while leaving neighbours untouched.

Layer II of the entorhinal cortex is the standard example - those neurons fill with tangles in early Alzheimer disease while cells in adjacent layers of the very same region stay normal.

Frontotemporal dementia provides a mirror-image example: Seeley and colleagues showed that von Economo neurons, a large spindle-shaped cell type found in anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex and implicated in rapid social processing, are selectively lost in behavioural variant FTD, which fits the syndrome's social symptoms exactly.

Proposed explanations include high metabolic demand, long and thinly myelinated axons, distinctive calcium handling, and cell-type-specific gene expression profiles, and modern single-cell sequencing studies are testing these directly.

No single explanation currently accounts for the pattern, and this remains one of the genuinely open problems in the field.

70.4.2 Prion-like propagation along connections

A prion is a misfolded protein that induces normally folded copies of itself to misfold, propagating a shape rather than a genetic sequence, as in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

The prion-like hypothesis proposes that tau, alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta spread by the same templating mechanism, but without the infectivity between individuals that defines true prions - a seed released from one neuron is taken up by a connected neuron and corrupts the native protein there.

The supporting evidence is substantial: injecting brain-derived tau or synuclein fibrils into mouse brain produces pathology that appears first in the injected region and then in anatomically connected regions rather than merely nearby ones, and human imaging shows tau spreading patterns that track functional connectivity better than physical proximity.

The strongest human observation came from Parkinson patients who received fetal dopamine cell grafts and, more than a decade later, showed Lewy pathology inside the transplanted young neurons, reported independently by Kordower and by Li and colleagues in 2008.

Sceptics, including Walsh and Selkoe writing in 2016, argue the experimental models use unphysiologically large fibril doses and that the human evidence remains correlational, so the terminology should stay cautious - the word propagon has been proposed instead of prion to mark the difference.

70.4.3 Network degeneration as a unifying account

If pathology travels along connections, then diseases should not damage random patches of tissue but should dismantle coherent brain networks.

Seeley, Crawford, Zhou, Miller and Greicius tested exactly this in Neuron in 2009, comparing the atrophy patterns of five neurodegenerative syndromes against five intrinsic connectivity networks mapped in healthy volunteers by resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures which regions fluctuate in synchrony at rest.

Each syndrome's atrophy pattern matched one healthy network: Alzheimer disease targeted the default mode network, behavioural variant FTD the salience network, semantic dementia an anterior temporal network, and so on.

The result is important because it reframes these diseases from a list of vulnerable regions into a single principle - a network is a unit of vulnerability, not just a unit of function.

It also connects the two preceding sub-sections: selective vulnerability might be about which network is entered first, and propagation might be the mechanism by which the rest of that network follows.

The account is strongly supported for the spatial patterns it was built to explain; what it does not yet explain is why a given network is entered first in a given person.

70.4.4 Cognitive reserve modulating expression of pathology

The final theme is the loosest coupling in the whole chapter: the relationship between how much pathology a brain contains and how impaired the person is.

The Nun Study, run by David Snowdon from 1986 with a cohort of School Sisters of Notre Dame, produced the classic demonstration - some sisters met full neuropathological criteria for Alzheimer disease at autopsy while having shown no clinical dementia in life.

Yaakov Stern's cognitive reserve framework, developed from the 1990s onward, explains this by proposing that education, occupational complexity, literacy and lifelong cognitive engagement give the brain more flexible or more efficient ways of performing a task, so more pathology can be absorbed before performance visibly fails.

A useful distinction within the framework separates brain reserve, meaning the raw hardware of more neurons and synapses, from cognitive reserve, meaning more adaptable software for using whatever hardware remains.

Reserve is not protection against the disease process, and this is frequently misunderstood: pathology accumulates at the normal rate, and once decline finally becomes visible in a high-reserve person it tends to be faster, because more damage has already accrued behind the compensation.

The construct is also methodologically contested, since education is entangled with income, health care access, and childhood nutrition, and a large 2025 Nature Medicine analysis across thirty-three countries by Lövdén, Nyberg and colleagues found education relates to the cognitive level a person reaches rather than to their rate of subsequent decline - a real but narrower effect than the popular version of the idea.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Neurodegenerative diseases dismantle cognition in disease-specific patterns because each attacks a specific set of neurons and networks, which makes them evidence about cognitive architecture and not only about medicine.

Alzheimer disease is defined biologically by amyloid and tau, is now detectable by blood test and stageable independently of symptoms, and is modestly treatable by amyloid-clearing antibodies whose clinical meaningfulness and safety are honestly disputed.

The non-Alzheimer dementias - frontotemporal, Lewy body, and vascular - matter because they take social conduct, language, attention, or processing speed first while sparing memory, and because at autopsy most older people with dementia turn out to have several pathologies at once rather than one clean disease.

Movement disorders demonstrate that basal ganglia and cerebellum are cognitive structures, most sharply in the dopamine overdose effect, where a single dose simultaneously helps the depleted circuit and harms the intact one.

Four mechanistic ideas tie the chapter together: selective neuronal vulnerability, prion-like spread of misfolded protein along connections, degeneration of coherent large-scale networks, and cognitive reserve buffering the expression of whatever pathology is present - the first well documented but unexplained, the second and fourth supported yet contested, the third the most successful unifying account currently available.


CHAPTER 71. PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS AS DISORDERS OF COGNITION (CONTEXT)

Psychiatric diagnoses were built from what patients say and what clinicians observe, not from what the brain computes.

This chapter asks what happens when we look at the same conditions - schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, addiction - through the lens of cognition, meaning the machinery of perception, memory, learning, attention, and decision.

The payoff is that symptoms which look unrelated across diagnostic labels often turn out to share a single broken computation, and computations can be measured, modelled, and sometimes repaired.

The risk is that elegant computational stories outrun the evidence, and this chapter will say plainly where that has happened.

The word cognition here is used in its broad technical sense: any information-processing operation the brain performs, whether or not the person is aware of it.


71.1 Schizophrenia and psychosis

Schizophrenia is a psychiatric condition, affecting roughly three to seven people in a thousand over a lifetime, in which a person's grip on shared reality loosens.

Psychosis is the broader term for that loosening - hallucinations (perceptions without a corresponding external cause) and delusions (fixed beliefs held despite decisive contrary evidence) - and it occurs in schizophrenia but also in bipolar disorder, severe depression, some dementias, and some drug states.

The historical picture treated hallucinations and delusions as the disease itself.

The modern picture treats them as the visible surface of a deeper and more constant disturbance in how the brain holds information online, controls its own processing, and decides what in the world is worth noticing.

71.1.1 Positive, negative, and cognitive symptom domains

Clinicians conventionally sort the symptoms of schizophrenia into three families.

Positive symptoms are experiences added to normal mental life - hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech - and the word positive here means added, not good.

Negative symptoms are capacities subtracted from normal mental life - blunted emotional expression, poverty of speech (alogia), loss of motivation (avolition), and reduced pleasure (anhedonia).

Cognitive symptoms are measurable deficits in memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function (the family of control operations that plan, switch, and inhibit), and roughly seventy to eighty percent of people with a confirmed diagnosis show them on formal testing.

This third family now has its own clinical label, cognitive impairment associated with schizophrenia (CIAS), because it behaves differently from the other two.

The practical importance of the distinction is blunt: antipsychotic drugs, which work chiefly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors, treat positive symptoms well, negative symptoms modestly, and cognitive symptoms essentially not at all.

Since cognitive symptoms predict real-world functioning - whether a person can hold a job or live independently - better than hallucinations do, this is where the unmet need sits, and a 2024 critical review in the journal Brain Sciences concluded that the best-supported treatments for CIAS are still non-pharmacological, chiefly cognitive remediation (structured drill-and-strategy training) and structured physical exercise.

71.1.2 Working memory and control deficits as core features

Working memory is the ability to hold a small amount of information active and manipulable for a few seconds, such as keeping a phone number in mind while you find a pen.

Cognitive control is the related ability to use that held information to bias what you do next, for example holding the instruction "press left when the tone is high" and applying it against a habitual pull to press right.

Both are impaired in schizophrenia, they are impaired before the first psychotic episode and in unaffected relatives, and they remain impaired between episodes when hallucinations have quietened - which is the main reason many researchers, including Deanna Barch and Cameron Carter, treat them as closer to the core of the illness than the psychotic symptoms are.

The leading neural account points at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the region on the upper outer surface of the frontal lobe that sustains information across delays.

Post-mortem work by David Lewis and colleagues found reduced expression of markers in parvalbumin-containing inhibitory interneurons - a class of fast-spiking cells that rhythmically silence nearby excitatory neurons - in that region, and because these cells generate gamma oscillations (synchronised electrical rhythms around thirty to eighty cycles per second) that appear to coordinate working memory, their impairment gives a plausible cellular explanation for the cognitive deficit.

The link is well supported but not closed: the interneuron changes are correlational in human tissue, they can be affected by illness duration and medication, and the causal demonstrations come from rodent models rather than from patients.

71.1.3 Aberrant salience and prediction-error accounts of delusion
