Salience is the property of standing out and demanding attention, and the brain normally assigns it to things that matter - a snake, a familiar name, an unexpected reward.

Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error, the difference between what was expected and what occurred, and this signal is the brain's teaching signal for what deserves attention.

Shitij Kapur's 2003 paper "Psychosis as a state of aberrant salience", building on related arguments from Andreas Heinz in 2002, proposed that in psychosis excess striatal dopamine fires independently of actual events, so ordinary things - a parked car, a stranger's glance - are stamped as urgently significant, and the delusion is the patient's reasonable attempt to explain an unreasonable feeling of significance.

The theory explains several stubborn facts at once: why antipsychotics dampen the conviction and preoccupation of a delusion before the belief itself dissolves, why amphetamine can induce paranoia, and why patients often describe a "delusional mood" of loaded meaning before any specific belief forms.

Twenty years on, a 2025 review in the American Journal of Psychiatry took stock and found the framework has been enormously generative but only partly confirmed: elevated presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity in the striatum is a robust finding, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies do show blunted or disorganised reward prediction error signals in psychosis, but the specific link between those signals and delusion severity has been inconsistent across studies, with some 2025 fMRI work finding no reliable association with delusions specifically.

The honest summary is that aberrant salience is the field's default language for delusion formation and is better supported than any rival, while remaining a framework rather than a proven mechanism.

71.1.4 Hallucination as failure of reality monitoring or over-weighted priors

Two accounts of hallucination compete, and they are not entirely incompatible.

The reality monitoring account, associated with Chris Frith and with Marcia Johnson's earlier source-monitoring work, says the problem is tagging: the brain generates inner speech and imagery constantly, and normally marks it as self-generated, so a hallucination is that tag failing and an inner voice being attributed to the outside world.

The predictive-coding account says perception is a controlled inference in which prior expectations are combined with incoming sensory evidence, each weighted by its reliability, and a hallucination occurs when the prior is weighted so heavily that it is experienced as a percept even with no supporting input.

Albert Powers, Christoph Mathys, and Philip Corlett published a striking test in Science in 2017: they Pavlovian-conditioned people to associate a checkerboard image with a faint tone, then presented the image with no tone, and voice-hearers - including both psychosis patients and non-distressed clairaudient psychics - reported hearing the absent tone far more often, with computational modelling showing this tracked an over-weighting of learned priors.

Later work by the same group found these conditioned hallucinations behave as a state marker that rises and falls with symptom severity, which is a strong point in the theory's favour.

The strong-priors account is nonetheless contested; critics have argued, for instance from the case of Charles Bonnet syndrome (vivid visual hallucinations in people losing their sight), that the framework is flexible enough to accommodate almost any result and therefore risks explaining by vagueness, and that in some conditions hallucinations follow loss of sensory input rather than an excess of prior belief.


71.2 Mood and anxiety disorders

Depression and the anxiety disorders are usually described in the language of feeling, but they are also, quite literally, disorders of information processing.

Aaron Beck's cognitive model, formulated in the 1960s, made the founding claim: mood disorders are maintained by systematic distortions in what a person attends to, remembers, and infers, and correcting those distortions relieves the mood.

Modern cognitive neuroscience has kept the structure of Beck's claim while replacing his introspective vocabulary with measurable quantities such as learning rates, effort costs, and network connectivity.

This section works through four such quantities.

71.2.1 Cognitive biases in attention, memory, and interpretation

Three biases are documented repeatedly.

Attentional bias is a tendency to dwell on threatening or negative material, measured with tasks such as the dot-probe, where a target replaces one of two briefly shown words or faces and anxious participants respond faster when it replaces the threatening one.

Memory bias is preferential recall of negative autobiographical material, and interpretation bias is the tendency to resolve ambiguity in the darker direction, so that "the meeting has been moved" is read as bad news.

The clinical hope was that these biases could be retrained directly, and cognitive bias modification (CBM) was built to do that by, for example, systematically placing the dot-probe target behind the neutral stimulus.

The results are a cautionary tale in modest effects: a 2020 systematic review and network meta-analysis in Lancet Psychiatry by Fu and colleagues found interpretation bias modification outperformed waitlist and sham for anxiety, that attention bias modification showed benefits only in sensitivity analyses, and that heterogeneity and risk of bias undermined the reliability of the whole literature, with evidence for depression insufficient to draw conclusions.

The biases themselves are real and replicable; the claim that reversing them is a treatment is not established.

71.2.2 Anhedonia, reward learning deficits, and effort

Anhedonia is the loss of pleasure or interest, and it is one of the two symptoms required for a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

Diego Pizzagalli's laboratory decomposed it into components that can be measured rather than merely reported, using the probabilistic reward task, in which one of two hard-to-distinguish stimuli is rewarded three times more often than the other and healthy people gradually and unknowingly develop a response bias toward it.

Depressed participants develop that bias weakly or not at all, and in Pizzagalli's work the size of the failure predicted anhedonia severity and even clinical outcome, which locates the deficit in reinforcement learning - the updating of behaviour from reward - rather than in the momentary experience of pleasure.

A second component is effort: deciding whether a reward is worth the work, a computation involving dopamine in the nucleus accumbens and the anterior cingulate cortex.

A 2025 study in Psychological Medicine by Ang and colleagues found that anhedonia in young people with depressive symptoms was associated with difficulty modulating effort as a function of reward value and with under-exploiting the low-effort, high-reward options, alongside reduced reward sensitivity parameters.

The useful reframing is that a depressed person often can still enjoy a reward once it arrives, but has lost the machinery that makes the reward worth reaching for and that learns from it afterwards.

71.2.3 Rumination and default-network alteration

Rumination, a term formalised by Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, is repetitive, passive, self-focused dwelling on distress and its causes, and it predicts both the onset and the persistence of depressive episodes.

The default mode network (DMN) is a set of regions - chiefly the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and angular gyrus - that becomes more active when a person is not engaged in an external task and is reliably recruited by self-referential thought.

Paul Hamilton and Ian Gotlib's 2015 paper in Biological Psychiatry proposed a specific model: increased functional connectivity between the subgenual prefrontal cortex, a small ventral region repeatedly implicated in negative affect, and the rest of the DMN produces rumination in major depression, and their meta-analytic work found that this connectivity tracks reported rumination levels.

A 2019 meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies of rumination by Zhou and colleagues broadly supported DMN involvement while showing the picture is less tidy than the single-network story implies, since rumination also engages frontoparietal control regions.

Treat this as a well-replicated association with a plausible but not demonstrated causal direction: rumination and DMN connectivity travel together, and which drives which is unresolved.

71.2.4 Threat learning, extinction failure, and anxiety

Fear conditioning is the laboratory model for how a neutral cue comes to signal danger, and extinction is the separate learning that occurs when the cue is repeatedly presented without the danger, teaching a new "safe here, now" memory that competes with the original fear memory rather than erasing it.

The circuit is well mapped: the amygdala acquires and expresses the fear, and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) - the middle underside of the frontal lobe - inhibits amygdala output to express extinction, a relationship established in rats by Gregory Quirk's group, who showed vmPFC neurons fire to the conditioned tone specifically during the delayed recall test of extinction.

Mohammed Milad, Roger Pitman, and colleagues translated this to humans and found the signature failure in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): patients condition normally and extinguish normally within a session, but cannot recall the extinction memory the next day, with hypoactivation of the vmPFC and hyperactivation of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.

Milad's group also showed that vmPFC cortical thickness correlates with the magnitude of extinction recall, tying an anatomical measure to a behavioural one.

This matters clinically because exposure therapy, the front-line psychological treatment for anxiety disorders and PTSD, is extinction learning administered deliberately, so a patient who cannot consolidate extinction is a patient in whom good exposure sessions do not stick, and relapse after treatment becomes the expected outcome rather than a surprise.


71.3 Compulsivity and impulsivity

Compulsivity is the persistence of an action despite its being useless or harmful, and impulsivity is action without adequate forethought.

They sound like opposites - one rigid, one rash - but they co-occur constantly in the clinic, and both can be described as failures in the balance between two systems of control: a goal-directed system that consults a model of the world and asks what an action will get you, and a habit system that repeats what has worked before without asking.

This section traces that balance through obsessive-compulsive disorder, through transdiagnostic measurement, through the internal structure of impulsivity, and back to addiction.

71.3.1 Obsessive-compulsive disorder and cortico-striatal loops

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) pairs obsessions, which are intrusive unwanted thoughts, with compulsions, which are repetitive acts performed to discharge the resulting distress, such as checking or washing.

The dominant neural model implicates cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loops - circuits that run from a region of cortex to the striatum (the input structure of the basal ganglia), through the globus pallidus and thalamus, and back to the same cortical region, forming a closed feedback ring.

The loop most implicated in OCD is the lateral orbitofrontal one, connecting the orbitofrontal cortex (the underside of the frontal lobe, concerned with value and with detecting that something is wrong) through the ventromedial caudate and thalamus, and the leading hypothesis is that this loop is hyperactive, producing a persistent unshakeable signal that an error remains uncorrected.

The evidence is unusually convergent: resting metabolic hyperactivity in orbitofrontal cortex and caudate is one of the older replicated findings in psychiatric imaging, it normalises with successful treatment by either serotonergic medication or behaviour therapy, and deep brain stimulation (the surgical implantation of electrodes delivering continuous current) targeted at the ventral capsule and ventral striatum, which sits within this circuitry, provides meaningful relief in a substantial minority of otherwise intractable cases.

That said, the loop model describes where the abnormality sits far better than it explains what computation has gone wrong, which is what the next sub-section addresses.

71.3.2 Model-based control deficits tracking compulsivity across diagnoses

Model-based control means choosing by consulting an internal model of how the world works and simulating consequences; model-free control means choosing by the cached value of past outcomes, which is faster and stupider.

Nathaniel Daw's two-step task separates them experimentally by making the two strategies predict different choices after a rare transition, and how a person responds after such a trial yields a number for how model-based they are.

Claire Gillan, Daw, Elizabeth Phelps and colleagues published a landmark result in eLife in 2016: rather than comparing diagnostic groups, they tested nearly two thousand people online, factor-analysed their symptom questionnaires into three dimensions, and found that reduced model-based control mapped specifically onto a factor they called "compulsive behaviour and intrusive thought", and not onto anxious-depression or social withdrawal.

This is important for two reasons.

First, it cuts across diagnostic boundaries: the deficit tracked a symptom dimension shared by OCD, eating disorders, and addiction, rather than any single DSM category, supporting the idea that compulsivity is a trait the diagnostic manual has carved up badly.

Second, the deficit is not simply an inability, since later work by Gillan and colleagues showed that financial incentives can boost model-based control across a range of symptom severity, suggesting a problem in how much the goal-directed system is deployed rather than whether it exists.

71.3.3 Impulsivity as a multidimensional construct

The single word impulsivity conceals at least three separable things, and treating them as one is a persistent source of confused findings.

Impulsive action is the failure to withhold a prepared motor response, measured by stop-signal and go/no-go tasks and depending on right inferior frontal cortex and the subthalamic nucleus.

Impulsive choice is the preference for a small reward now over a larger one later, measured by delay discounting, where the steepness of the discount curve is the individual's parameter.

Impulsive personality traits are self-reported dispositions, and the widely used UPPS-P scale separates five of them: negative urgency (acting rashly when distressed), positive urgency (acting rashly when elated), lack of premeditation, lack of perseverance, and sensation seeking.

The key empirical point is that these families correlate only weakly with one another - factor-analytic work summarised by Marcus Munafò, Jeff Stein and others repeatedly recovers largely independent factors - so a person can be highly impulsive on one and unremarkable on the rest, and a study that measures only one has not measured impulsivity.

A 2024 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences nonetheless found impulsivity, properly measured, to be a stable and predictive trait over time, so the construct is fragmented rather than empty.

71.3.4 Addiction revisited as a cognitive disorder

Addiction can be read as a disorder of the same control balance, in which drug-seeking migrates from a goal-directed action to a habit and then to a compulsion that persists despite mounting cost.

Barry Everitt and Trevor Robbins argued for a progressive shift in control from the ventral striatum, which handles the initial rewarding value, to the dorsal striatum, which handles stimulus-response habit, a shift demonstrated in rodents and supported by human imaging.

Terry Robinson and Kent Berridge's incentive-sensitization theory offers a different account: repeated drug use sensitises the mesolimbic dopamine system so that cues acquire excessive incentive salience, meaning the drug is intensely "wanted" while being progressively less "liked", which explains the widely reported dissociation in which people crave a drug they no longer enjoy.

The two accounts remain genuinely in dispute; their 2025 review in the Annual Review of Psychology, marking thirty years of the theory, explicitly argues that behaviour surviving outcome devaluation - the classic evidence for habit - can equally reflect sensitised wanting rather than automaticity, so the standard test does not cleanly separate the theories.

What both share, and what justifies calling addiction cognitive, is that the disorder is located in learning and valuation systems rather than in pleasure, and that its persistence is a property of how the brain has been taught rather than of what the drug does at the moment of use.


71.4 Computational psychiatry

Computational psychiatry is the attempt to describe psychiatric symptoms as consequences of specific, formally specified information-processing failures.

Its ambition is to replace a diagnostic system based on clusters of self-report with one based on measured mechanism, in the way that fever was eventually replaced by infection.

Its methods are borrowed: reinforcement learning models from machine learning, Bayesian inference from statistics, and biophysical circuit models from systems neuroscience.

Its record so far is a mixture of genuine conceptual advance and unmet promises, and this section covers both.

71.4.1 Computational assays and latent parameter estimation

A computational assay is a behavioural task plus a mathematical model, used together to estimate quantities that cannot be observed directly.

The logic is that a person's sequence of choices is generated by hidden variables - a learning rate governing how much a single outcome shifts expectation, an inverse temperature governing how deterministically they exploit what they have learned, a risk-aversion parameter, a lapse rate - and fitting the model to the choices recovers estimates of those latent parameters.

The appeal over conventional neuropsychological testing is precision: a task score says a person did badly, whereas a fitted model can say the person learned normally from rewards but too much from punishments, which is a different claim with different treatment implications.

Two families dominate: reinforcement learning models, which describe value updating from prediction error, and Bayesian or hierarchical filtering models such as the hierarchical Gaussian filter, which describe belief updating under uncertainty and explicitly separate what is believed from how confidently it is held.

The critical caveat, developed further in 71.4.5, is that a parameter estimate is only as meaningful as the model that generated it, and a model that fits the data does not thereby prove the brain implements it.

71.4.2 Transdiagnostic dimensions and computational factor modelling

Computational factor modelling combines two statistical moves: factor analysis of many symptom items to find continuous dimensions cutting across diagnoses, and computational modelling of behaviour to find latent cognitive parameters, then examines how the two sets relate.

Gillan and Robb Rutledge set this out as a programme in Biological Psychiatry in 2023, and its distinguishing feature is that the dimensions are derived in large unselected online samples rather than in patient groups, on the grounds that psychiatric traits are continuously distributed and that the samples needed for robust discovery and replication are only obtainable at internet scale.

The recurring three-factor solution - anxious-depression, compulsivity and intrusive thought, and social withdrawal - has now been recovered in multiple independent samples, which is more replication than most findings in this field enjoy.

The approach also inverts the usual logic of psychiatric research: instead of asking which cognitive deficit characterises a diagnosis, it asks which symptom dimension a given cognitive deficit tracks, and lets the diagnostic labels fall where they may.

The main open question is external validity, since online unselected samples exclude the most severely ill and rely on self-report rather than clinical assessment.

71.4.3 Normative modelling of individual deviation

Normative modelling borrows its logic directly from paediatric growth charts.

A large reference sample is used to estimate the expected value and spread of some brain measure - cortical thickness, regional volume, a connectivity value - as a function of age and sex, and each individual then receives a deviation score saying where they sit relative to that expectation, exactly as a child receives a height centile.

The motivation is heterogeneity: comparing a patient group mean to a control group mean assumes patients resemble each other, and Andre Marquand and colleagues, whose 2019 paper in Molecular Psychiatry framed the approach for psychiatry, showed that patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder have large individual deviations that barely overlap with one another, so the group average describes almost nobody.

Subsequent applications have extended it to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism, major depression and, in a 2025 Translational Psychiatry study, to psychosis and psychopathy, and large reference charts of brain development now exist to support it.

The clinical promise is a genuinely individual-level readout rather than a group difference, and the current limitation is that a deviation score tells you a person is unusual without telling you why, and it has not yet been shown to guide any treatment decision.

71.4.4 Predictive coding and precision-weighting frameworks for symptoms

Predictive coding proposes that the brain is continuously predicting its own sensory input, that only the error - the mismatch between prediction and input - is passed up the cortical hierarchy, and that each prediction and each error carries a weight called precision, which is the estimated reliability of that signal.

Precision is the pivotal quantity for psychiatry, because a great many symptoms can be described as precision set wrongly: over-precise priors relative to sensory evidence yield hallucination, under-precise priors with over-precise prediction errors yield the sense that everything is newly significant and yield delusion as the resulting explanation, and over-precise sensory precision has been offered by Karl Friston, Rick Adams and colleagues as an account of autistic sensory intolerance.

Adams, Stephanie Stephan, Harriet Brown, Christoph Frith and Friston set out "The computational anatomy of psychosis" in 2013, arguing that a single failure of precision could produce hallucinations, delusions, abnormal smooth-pursuit eye movements, reduced sensory attenuation (the normal damping of self-generated sensation that makes it impossible to tickle yourself), and catatonia, and there is direct supporting evidence: a 2020 Molecular Psychiatry study found that precision weighting of cortical prediction error signals benefits learning, is mediated by dopamine, and is impaired in psychosis.

The framework's great virtue is unification, since it links symptoms across sensory, motor, and belief domains to one adjustable quantity, and it maps naturally onto neuromodulators, with dopamine and acetylcholine plausibly encoding precision.

Its great vulnerability is exactly the same property: a theory in which one free parameter can be raised or lowered to produce any symptom is hard to refute, and a 2025 systematic transdiagnostic review of predictive coding in neuropsychiatric disorders found the empirical support uneven across conditions and heavily dependent on which task and model were used.

This is a case where the theory is more elegant than the evidence currently warrants, and both facts should be held at once.

71.4.5 Translation barriers: reliability, generalisability, clinical utility

Three barriers stand between computational psychiatry and the clinic, and the first is the most damaging.

Reliability: a measure that gives a different answer on a second testing cannot characterise an individual, and test-retest studies have found that reinforcement learning parameters often have poor reliability, with intraclass correlations - a statistic where one means perfect agreement across sessions and zero means none - reported from about .02 to .52 for bandit tasks and .01 to .71 for reversal learning in a 2023 Behavior Research Methods study by Schaaf and colleagues, and a 2024 review in Computational Psychiatry finding a similarly wide spread across paradigms.

The picture is not uniformly bleak, since gambling-task parameters and in particular a risk-aversion parameter linked to anxiety have shown good to excellent reliability, and poor individual reliability does not prevent detecting group differences when the group means differ enough - but it does block the individual-level prediction that was the whole point.

Generalisability: parameters are estimated within a specific task under a specific model, and there is little evidence that a learning rate measured on one task predicts the learning rate measured on another, which undermines the claim that the parameter reflects a trait of the person rather than of the task.

Clinical utility: no computational assay currently determines a diagnosis, selects a treatment, or predicts an outcome well enough to be used in routine care, and until one does, the field's contribution remains conceptual - a better vocabulary for describing what is broken - rather than practical.

The constructive reading is that these are ordinary psychometric problems, that the field has begun taking them seriously in the last five years rather than dismissing them, and that tasks designed from the outset for reliable individual estimation, rather than borrowed from group-level cognitive experiments, are the obvious remedy.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Psychiatric conditions can be productively described as disorders of cognition, and in schizophrenia the cognitive deficits in working memory and control are more constant, more predictive of real-world functioning, and more treatment-resistant than the hallucinations and delusions that define the diagnosis.

Several symptom families have candidate computational explanations that are well developed but not settled: aberrant salience and prediction error for delusion, over-weighted priors or failed reality monitoring for hallucination, impaired reward and effort learning for anhedonia, and failed extinction recall for anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Compulsivity indexed by reduced model-based control cuts cleanly across diagnostic boundaries, which is direct evidence that the diagnostic manual carves the territory imperfectly, and impulsivity is not one thing but at least three weakly correlated ones.

Computational psychiatry has delivered real conceptual advances - transdiagnostic dimensions, normative individual deviation scores, and precision-weighting accounts that unify otherwise unrelated symptoms - while so far failing the practical test, because the reliability, cross-task generalisability, and demonstrated clinical utility of its measures remain inadequate.

The correct posture toward this literature is therefore neither dismissal nor enthusiasm but attention to which specific claims have survived replication, and the chapter has tried throughout to mark that line rather than blur it.


CHAPTER 72. NEURODEVELOPMENTAL AND ACQUIRED CONDITIONS (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about the conditions that change how cognition works, either from the beginning of a life or from a single bad afternoon.

Neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and dyslexia are differences in how a brain assembles itself over childhood.

Acquired conditions such as traumatic brain injury, stroke, and epilepsy are changes imposed on a brain that had already finished assembling.

The two families are worth studying together, because both act as natural experiments that reveal how ordinary cognition is put together.

They matter for a second reason too, which is that they are common, and the people who have them are your classmates, your colleagues, and possibly you.

A warning before we begin: this is a field where elegant theories are abundant and decisive evidence is scarce, and this chapter will say so repeatedly.


72.1 Autism spectrum

Autism, formally autism spectrum disorder (ASD), is a developmental condition defined by two things: persistent differences in social communication and social interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities.

Since the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), published in 2013, unusual reactivity to sensory input has also been listed as part of the second criterion.

The word spectrum is doing real work here.

One autistic person may have no spoken language and a co-occurring intellectual disability, while another may hold a doctorate and struggle mainly with small talk and fluorescent lighting.

Any theory of autism has to explain that range, and this is exactly where most theories run into trouble.

The chapter treats autism as a description of a group of people who share a diagnostic label, not as a single disease with a single cause.

72.1.1 Social cognition accounts and their limits

The most famous cognitive account of autism is the theory of mind hypothesis, sometimes called mindblindness, proposed by Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie, and Uta Frith in 1985.

Theory of mind is the everyday ability to attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to other people, including beliefs you know to be false - the classic test asks a child where Sally will look for her marble after Anne has secretly moved it.

Baron-Cohen and colleagues found that autistic children failed this false belief task at higher rates than comparison children, and the finding was enormously influential.

The account has since been battered from several directions.

Many autistic people pass first-order and second-order false belief tasks perfectly well, sometimes by explicit reasoning rather than intuition, so the deficit is not universal.

Advanced tests such as the Strange Stories and Faux Pas tasks make heavy demands on language, memory, and executive control, so failure on them does not cleanly isolate theory of mind.

The implicit or spontaneous theory of mind paradigms that were supposed to shore up the account have replicated poorly, and a 2025 theoretical review in the American Psychological Association literature questioned both the evidential basis and the internal coherence of the hypothesis.

A different challenge comes from Damian Milton's double empathy problem, first argued in 2012, which holds that the breakdown between autistic and non-autistic people is mutual rather than one-sided.

Empirical support has accumulated: Catherine Crompton and colleagues in 2020 showed that information passed down a chain of autistic people was transmitted as accurately as down a chain of non-autistic people, while mixed chains lost more information, and Morrison and colleagues in the same year found that non-autistic people misread autistic social cues too.

This does not abolish the finding that autistic people find some social tasks hard, but it relocates part of the difficulty from inside one head to the space between two heads.

72.1.2 Predictive processing and precision accounts

Predictive processing is the idea that the brain is not a passive receiver but a prediction machine: it constantly generates expectations about incoming sensation and pays attention chiefly to prediction error, the mismatch between what it expected and what arrived.

A prior, in this framework, is the brain's accumulated expectation, and precision is the weight or confidence the brain assigns to a prior or to an error signal.

Elizabeth Pellicano and David Burr proposed in 2012 that autistic perception involves hypo-priors, meaning attenuated or weakened expectations, so the world is experienced more veridically and less smoothed by past experience - their phrase was that the world becomes too real.

This neatly explains why illusions that depend on strong expectations may be weaker in some autistic people, and why unpredictable environments are exhausting.

Sander Van de Cruys, Johan Wagemans, and colleagues replied in 2013 and elaborated in 2014 that the evidence does not support uniformly flat priors.

Their alternative is that autistic brains assign inflexibly high precision to prediction errors, so learning does occur but produces sharp, overfitted models that fail to generalise to slightly different situations.

The two proposals make different predictions and the field has not settled between them.

A comprehensive review of ten years of Bayesian theories of autism, published in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews in 2023, concluded that the framework is generative and popular but that the specific parameter claims remain underdetermined by data.

This is an elegant theory with weak discriminating evidence, and it should be presented that way.

72.1.3 Sensory differences and excitation-inhibition proposals

Sensory differences are among the most consistently reported features of autism from autistic people themselves, and they come in three flavours: hyper-reactivity, hypo-reactivity, and mixed profiles that vary by modality.

The leading biological proposal is the excitation-inhibition imbalance hypothesis, put forward by John Rubenstein and Michael Merzenich in 2003, which holds that some forms of autism arise from an increased ratio of excitation to inhibition in key circuits, degrading the signal-to-noise ratio of neural processing.

Excitation here refers mainly to signalling by glutamate, the brain's principal excitatory neurotransmitter, and inhibition mainly to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), its principal inhibitory neurotransmitter.

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), a technique that measures the concentration of specific chemicals in a defined volume of brain tissue, has been the main non-invasive tool for testing this.

The results are genuinely mixed.

Some studies link reduced GABA in motor and sensorimotor regions to sensory hyper-responsiveness, others report elevated glutamate plus glutamine correlating with sensory symptoms, and a Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative workshop in 2018 concluded that reviews of the literature find evidence for increased inhibition as well as increased excitation.

The honest summary is that excitation-inhibition balance is a useful organising framework and a poor description of a specific finding, because the direction of the imbalance appears to vary by brain region, by individual, and by measurement method.

72.1.4 Heterogeneity and the case for subtypes

If autistic people differ this much from one another, the search for one mechanism may be a category error, and the productive move may be to carve the spectrum into biologically coherent subgroups.

That is what stratification research attempts, and 2025 produced the most substantial attempt so far.

A team based at Princeton University and the Simons Foundation, publishing in Nature Genetics in 2025, analysed trait combinations in more than five thousand children from the SPARK cohort and identified four classes: Social and Behavioural Challenges, Mixed Autism with Developmental Delay, Moderate Challenges, and Broadly Affected.

Crucially, the classes differed not only behaviourally but genetically, with different balances of common, inherited, and de novo variation, and with the affected genes acting at different points in development.

Independent work using functional connectivity, the pattern of correlated activity between brain regions measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), has reported a coarser two-subtype split of lower and higher connectivity linked respectively to synaptic and immune-related biology.

These findings are new, and replication in independent cohorts is the necessary next step before anyone builds clinical practice on them.

Still, the direction of travel is clear: the field is moving from asking what causes autism to asking which autism.


72.2 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is defined by developmentally excessive inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that appear early, persist across settings, and cause real impairment.

The label describes behaviour, not a mechanism, and the mechanisms turn out to be plural.

What follows sketches the two dominant cognitive models, the pharmacology that any model has to accommodate, an under-appreciated core feature, and the surprising recent literature on how ADHD behaves across a lifetime.

72.2.1 Executive dysfunction and delay aversion accounts

Executive functions are the control processes that hold a goal in mind, suppress a prepotent response, and switch strategies - working memory, inhibition, and set-shifting are the usual trio.

The executive dysfunction account, associated most strongly with Russell Barkley's 1997 synthesis, treats ADHD as a primary failure of behavioural inhibition that cascades into the other executive functions, and locates the problem in dorsal fronto-striatal circuits, meaning loops running between the prefrontal cortex and the dorsal striatum.

The trouble is that a large minority of people meeting ADHD criteria show no executive impairment on testing.

Edmund Sonuga-Barke's dual pathway model, published in 2002 and elaborated in 2003, addressed this by adding a second, independent route: delay aversion, a motivational distaste for waiting that makes a smaller immediate reward more attractive than a larger delayed one, underpinned by ventral fronto-striatal reward circuitry.

On this view two children can arrive at the same diagnosis by different roads, one through poor inhibition and one through an aversion to delay, which is why treating ADHD as a single deficit has never worked.

Later work has pressed further: a 2010 study in the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry found that timing impairments dissociate from both inhibitory and delay-related impairments, implying at least three pathways rather than two.

None of these models comfortably explains hyperfocus, the state of intense sustained absorption that many people with ADHD report, which remains a real gap.

72.2.2 Catecholaminergic mechanisms and stimulant action

Catecholamines are a family of signalling molecules that includes dopamine and noradrenaline, also called norepinephrine, and they are the chemical currency of the prefrontal circuits implicated in ADHD.

Stimulant medications such as methylphenidate work by blocking the presynaptic transporters that normally clear dopamine and noradrenaline out of the synapse, raising the concentration of both in the prefrontal cortex and striatum several-fold.

The important nuance is that more is not simply better.

Amy Arnsten and Rebecca Dudley showed in 2005, working with rats on a prefrontal-dependent delayed alternation task, that the cognitive benefit of methylphenidate was abolished by blocking either alpha-2 adrenoceptors or dopamine D1 receptors, at doses that did nothing on their own.

The relationship between catecholamine level and prefrontal performance is an inverted U: too little and the circuit is noisy, too much and it is also impaired, which is why clinical dosing is a titration rather than a maximisation.

Note also what this does not establish - that ADHD is caused by low dopamine.

A drug that helps a symptom does not identify the cause of the symptom, just as aspirin relieving a headache does not mean the headache was an aspirin deficiency.

72.2.3 Intra-individual variability as a core feature

Intra-individual variability means inconsistency in a single person's performance from trial to trial, and it is one of the most robust findings in the entire ADHD literature, often larger and more reliable than the average slowing.

The standard analytic tool is the ex-Gaussian decomposition, which splits a distribution of reaction times into a normal component described by mu, its mean, and sigma, its spread, plus an exponential tail described by tau.

Groups with ADHD show elevated sigma and, more distinctively, elevated tau, which corresponds to occasional very slow responses - the lapses in attention that teachers and partners actually notice.

Elevated tau has been proposed as an endophenotype for ADHD, meaning a measurable intermediate trait that sits between genes and diagnosis and may be more tractable for genetic study than the diagnosis itself.

A mechanistic account is the default mode interference hypothesis of Sonuga-Barke and Francisco Xavier Castellanos, published in 2007, which proposes that the default mode network, a set of regions most active during rest and inward-directed thought, fails to be suppressed properly when a task begins, and intrudes periodically on performance.

Trial-level fMRI work reported in 2025 supports the shape of this idea, finding that the coupling between task-positive activation and default mode suppression that tracks performance in typically developing children is weaker in children with ADHD.

72.2.4 Developmental course and adult presentation

The traditional picture was simple: ADHD begins in childhood, hyperactivity subsides in adolescence, inattention lingers, and a substantial fraction of cases persist into adult life.

Prospective birth cohorts have complicated it badly.

Jessica Agnew-Blais, Terrie Moffitt, Louise Arseneault and colleagues, using the Environmental Risk (E-Risk) Longitudinal Twin Study of 2,232 twins born in England and Wales in 1994 and 1995, reported in JAMA Psychiatry in 2016 that most young adults meeting ADHD criteria had no record of childhood ADHD.

Similar late-onset patterns appeared in cohorts from New Zealand, Brazil, and in the American Multimodal Treatment of ADHD follow-up reported by Margaret Sibley and colleagues in 2018.

The interpretation is contested and should be presented as such.

One camp argues for a genuinely adult-onset form of the disorder; another argues that the late-onset cases are largely artefacts of measurement, of symptoms masked in childhood by high ability or a structured environment, or of other conditions such as anxiety and substance use mimicking ADHD.

Sibley's careful re-analysis found that many apparent adult-onset cases had subthreshold childhood symptoms or a comorbid explanation, which favours the sceptical reading without closing the question.

What is not disputed is the practical point: adult presentation is dominated by inattention, disorganisation, and emotional dysregulation rather than visible hyperactivity, and it is frequently missed.


72.3 Learning disorders

Learning disorders are specific, persistent difficulties in acquiring an academic skill that are out of keeping with a person's general ability, teaching, and effort.

They are important theoretically because reading and arithmetic are cultural inventions too recent for evolution to have built dedicated machinery, so they must be running on circuitry recycled from older functions - and that makes them fragile in informative ways.

72.3.1 Dyslexia, dyscalculia, and developmental language disorder

Developmental dyslexia is a specific difficulty with accurate and fluent word reading and spelling, and the dominant explanation is the phonological deficit hypothesis: a weakness in representing and manipulating the sound structure of language.

Phonological awareness, the ability to hear that cat is made of three sounds and to remove the first one, is the strongest single predictor of later reading, and it is characteristically weak in dyslexia.

Rival and complementary accounts propose a more basic timing problem, the temporal sampling hypothesis associated with Usha Goswami, in which the brain's rhythmic tracking of the slow amplitude envelope of speech is poorly synchronised, degrading the phonological representations that reading depends on.

Dyscalculia is the arithmetic equivalent, and Stanislas Dehaene, Laurent Cohen, Anna Wilson and colleagues have linked it to an impaired number sense, the approximate, non-symbolic magnitude system supported by the intraparietal sulcus - work by Piazza and colleagues in 2010 found ten-year-olds with dyscalculia performing at the numerical acuity of typical five-year-olds.

Developmental language disorder (DLD) is persistent difficulty acquiring spoken language itself in the absence of an obvious cause such as hearing loss, and it is far more common and far less recognised than dyslexia, affecting roughly seven percent of children by the CATALISE consensus estimates led by Dorothy Bishop and published in 2016 and 2017.

72.3.2 Comorbidity and shared risk

These conditions co-occur far more often than chance would predict, and the overlap between dyslexia and dyscalculia, and between dyslexia and ADHD, is high.

The classical single-deficit framework, one disorder with one cause, cannot accommodate this, because it predicts that separate disorders should have separate causes and therefore combine only by coincidence.

Bruce Pennington's multiple deficit model, set out in Cognition in 2006 and developed with Erik Willcutt and colleagues in a 2010 Cortex paper on reading disability and ADHD, replaces it.

On this account each disorder is the probabilistic outcome of many genetic and environmental risk factors acting on many cognitive processes, some of them domain-specific and some domain-general.

Comorbidity then falls out naturally: shared domain-general risk factors produce shared weaknesses.

The concrete example is processing speed, which twin analyses indicate is a cognitive weakness common to reading disability and ADHD and is largely explained by shared genetic influences, while phoneme awareness remains specific to reading disability and inhibitory control specific to ADHD.

72.3.3 Intervention and its neural signatures

Intensive, explicit, phonologically based instruction improves reading in most children with dyslexia, and the interesting question for this book is what changes in the brain when it does.

Elise Temple, John Gabrieli and colleagues reported in 2003 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that after a remediation programme, activity in left temporoparietal and left inferior frontal reading regions increased toward the pattern seen in typical readers, and Sally Shaywitz and colleagues reported convergent findings in 2004.

Two mechanisms are usually distinguished: normalisation, in which under-active left-hemisphere reading circuitry becomes more active, and compensation, in which other regions, often right-hemisphere or frontal, are recruited to do the job by another route.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of reading intervention studies published in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews in 2022 found the evidence for both, with the most consistent effect across studies being change in the right inferior frontal gyrus.

Two cautions are warranted.

The samples are small, the tasks differ across studies, and a change in a blood-oxygen signal is not by itself proof that the intervention worked - the reading gains are the evidence for that, and the imaging tells you about mechanism.


72.4 Acquired injury and epilepsy

An acquired condition removes something from a brain that already had it, which makes these cases the closest thing cognitive neuroscience has to a controlled lesion experiment in humans.

They also carry an ethical weight the developmental conditions do not, because in most cases someone is trying to get back a capacity they can remember having.

72.4.1 Traumatic brain injury and diffuse axonal damage

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is damage caused by an external mechanical force, and its cognitive consequences come from two rather different mechanisms.

The first is focal: bruising and haemorrhage at the impact site and at the opposite pole of the skull, classically affecting orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex because of the bony ridges those regions slide across.

The second is diffuse axonal injury (DAI), in which rotational acceleration shears long white matter axons, the insulated fibres that carry signals between distant regions.

DAI explains the characteristic cognitive profile of moderate to severe TBI, which is not usually a loss of specific knowledge but a slowing and fragmentation of everything: reduced processing speed, impaired sustained attention, poor working memory, and executive difficulty.

Disconnecting a network degrades its coordination rather than deleting its contents.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), a magnetic resonance method that infers the orientation and integrity of white matter tracts from the direction in which water diffuses, is the main tool for detecting DAI, and measures such as fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity correlate with processing speed after injury.

The important methodological caveat, made explicitly in a 2017 study of inter-subject variability in diffuse TBI, is that group-average DTI analyses can obscure the fact that each patient's pattern of axonal damage is different, which is precisely why DTI has not yet become a reliable individual-level biomarker.

72.4.2 Concussion and repeated head impact

Concussion, or mild TBI, is a transient disturbance of brain function after a blow to the head, usually without visible damage on standard clinical imaging.

Most single concussions resolve within days to weeks, and the honest position is that the greater concern is not the single event but the accumulation.

Repetitive head impacts (RHI) include diagnosed concussions and, more numerously, sub-concussive blows that produce no symptoms at all - heading a football, checking in ice hockey, ordinary line play in American football.

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neuropathological diagnosis, made only after death, defined by accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein around small blood vessels and preferentially in the depths of cortical sulci, the folds of the cortex.

A 2025 study from Boston University reported neuronal changes in young athletes exposed to repeated head trauma before any CTE symptoms were evident, and a 2025 meta-analysis found memory, language, and attention to be the most prevalent cognitive features in confirmed CTE cases.

Here it is essential to be careful about what is established and what is not.

That RHI is associated with CTE pathology is well supported; the dose-response relationship, the proportion of exposed people who develop it, and the strength of the link between the pathology and any specific living clinical syndrome are all actively disputed, partly because most autopsy series are drawn from brains donated by families who suspected a problem, which is a biased sample.

The proposed clinical syndrome, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, is a research construct with proposed criteria, not a settled diagnosis.

72.4.3 Stroke and cognitive outcome

A stroke is a sudden interruption of blood supply to part of the brain, either by blockage of a vessel, which is ischaemic stroke, or by rupture, which is haemorrhagic stroke.

Cognitive consequences are the rule rather than the exception: depending on the timing and the instruments used, between roughly two thirds and three quarters of stroke survivors show cognitive impairment.

Two syndromes illustrate why location matters so much.

Aphasia, an acquired disorder of language, follows damage to the left perisylvian language network, and at least twenty percent of all stroke survivors are left with some lasting degree of it.

Spatial neglect, a failure to attend or respond to one side of space, most often follows right hemisphere damage to parietal and temporoparietal regions, and it predicts poorer functional outcome and lower quality of life.

Recovery is real but front-loaded: roughly fifty-four percent of neglect cases resolve within the first twelve weeks and around sixty percent within the first year, which is why rehabilitation intensity in the early months is so heavily emphasised.

One clinically important finding deserves emphasis - a 2013 prospective study found that eighty-eight percent of patients with post-stroke aphasia had impairment in at least one non-linguistic cognitive domain at three months, meaning that treating aphasia purely as a language problem misses most of what is wrong.

72.4.4 Epilepsy, interictal cognition, and surgical outcomes

Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, which are episodes of excessive synchronous neuronal discharge.

The word interictal means between seizures, and the striking point is that cognition in epilepsy is often impaired between seizures, not only during them.

Part of this is attributable to interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), brief abnormal electrical events visible on electroencephalography that produce transient cognitive impairment lasting a second or so - enough to lose a word in a sentence or a step in a calculation.

A 2025 study in Epilepsy and Behavior identified IEDs as the most significant confounding factor underlying memory impairment in focal epilepsy, while noting that they have not yet shown enough sensitivity or specificity to serve as a biomarker of long-term cognitive dysfunction.

The remainder is attributable to the underlying lesion, to the medications, which have their own sedating and attentional costs, and in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy to hippocampal sclerosis, the scarring and neuronal loss of the hippocampus that both generates seizures and directly damages memory.

Surgery poses the sharpest trade-off in cognitive neurology.

Anterior temporal lobectomy renders a majority of drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy patients seizure-free - the ERSET randomised trial reported eleven of fifteen surgical patients seizure-free in the second year against none of twenty-three medically treated patients - but it removes tissue that supports memory, and verbal memory decline after left-sided resection is common.

The field's response has been to predict and minimise the cost: memory fMRI before surgery predicts verbal memory decline after anterior temporal resection, and less destructive alternatives such as magnetic resonance guided laser interstitial thermal therapy show smaller neuropsychological deficits, with reported verbal and visual memory declines around a quarter of patients rather than the higher rates of open resection, although the seizure-freedom rates are also somewhat lower.

Whether that trade is worth making is a decision for the individual patient, and it is the clearest example in this chapter of neuroscience being asked to price one cognitive good against another.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Neurodevelopmental conditions are not single diseases with single causes, and the most credible current work in both autism and ADHD is stratification: dividing a heterogeneous label into subgroups that might actually share a mechanism, as the 2025 SPARK four-class analysis attempted.

Where a mechanism has been proposed - theory of mind deficit, hypo-priors, excitation-inhibition imbalance, inhibitory dysfunction - each captures part of a population and fails on the rest, and Pennington's multiple deficit model is the general lesson: complex developmental disorders arise from many partially shared risks, which is also why comorbidity is the norm rather than the exception.

Pharmacology constrains theory without settling it, since methylphenidate's dependence on both dopamine D1 and alpha-2 adrenoceptor action and its inverted-U dose response tell us how the prefrontal cortex is tuned, not what causes ADHD.

In acquired conditions, the cognitive profile follows the geometry of the damage: diffuse axonal shearing slows and fragments processing globally, while focal stroke produces syndromes as specific as aphasia and spatial neglect.

Epilepsy shows that cognition can be degraded continuously by interictal activity between seizures, and epilepsy surgery shows that removing the source of seizures can cost memory, which is why predicting that cost beforehand has become a central task.

Throughout, the responsible position is that the theories in this chapter are considerably more confident than the evidence behind them.


CHAPTER 73. INTERVENTION, REHABILITATION, AND ENHANCEMENT (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about what can actually be done for a damaged or struggling brain, and about what is claimed but not yet shown.

It covers four families of intervention: retraining through behaviour, stimulating tissue with magnets, electrodes or sound, pushing healthy cognition higher with drugs and practice, and replacing lost function with machines.

The reason to treat these together is that they share one hard problem - it is easy to make someone better at a laboratory task, and very difficult to make their life measurably better.

Throughout, the honest position is that the engineering is racing ahead of the evidence.

Some of what follows is well established, some is promising and thin, and the chapter marks which is which.


73.1 Cognitive rehabilitation

Cognitive rehabilitation is the organised attempt to reduce the everyday consequences of brain injury on thinking - memory, attention, language, planning, and spatial awareness.

It is delivered by clinical neuropsychologists, occupational therapists, and speech and language therapists, usually after stroke, traumatic brain injury (injury to the brain from an external mechanical force), or in progressive disease.

It is not one technique but a family of them, and the family quarrels internally about whether the goal is to repair the damaged function or to route around it.


73.1.1 Restitution, compensation, and adaptation strategies

Restitution, sometimes called the restorative approach, assumes that repeated, graded exercise of an impaired function can drive the surviving tissue to take the function back up.

Compensation assumes the opposite - that the lost neural function will not return, and that the practical route is to teach the person to reach the same goal by different means, using intact abilities.

A memory-impaired person given hours of drill on word lists is receiving restitution; the same person taught to use a smartphone calendar with alarms, and taught errorless learning (practising so that mistakes are prevented rather than corrected, because damaged memory systems tend to encode the error along with the correction), is receiving compensation.

Adaptation is the third and most neglected leg - changing the environment and the expectations rather than the person, for example simplifying a kitchen, reducing background noise, or renegotiating a job description.

Reviews of memory rehabilitation, such as the survey published in Cognitive Processing in 2022, converge on the view that compensatory and holistic methods have the better evidence for everyday benefit, while purely restorative drill mostly makes people better at the drill.

Modern practice combines all three rather than choosing, and the combined, team-delivered form is what most guidelines now recommend.


73.1.2 Constraint-induced and intensive therapies

Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT), developed by Edward Taub and colleagues, rests on a specific idea: after a stroke, patients stop using the weak arm because early attempts fail, and this learned non-use then masks a recovery that the tissue could have supported.

The therapy therefore restrains the good arm, and forces massed, shaped practice with the weak one - shaping meaning that the task difficulty is raised in small steps as performance improves.

Friedemann Pulvermuller and colleagues transplanted the logic to language in 2001 as constraint-induced aphasia therapy (CIAT), forcing spoken output by blocking gesture, writing and pointing during intensive small-group language games.

Randomised trials have shown CIAT improves language function in chronic post-stroke aphasia, but a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS One in 2017 reached a deflating and important conclusion - CIAT is not clearly superior to other aphasia therapies delivered at the same intensity.

The best current reading is that massed practice is the active ingredient, and constraint itself is unproven, which matters because constraint is the uncomfortable part.


73.1.3 Aphasia and neglect rehabilitation evidence

Aphasia is loss of language after brain damage, usually to the left hemisphere; neglect is failure to attend to one side of space, usually the left, after right hemisphere damage.

For aphasia the landmark result is Caterina Breitenstein and colleagues in The Lancet in 2017, a randomised trial in routine German health care showing that at least three weeks of intensive speech and language therapy, roughly ten hours per week, produced a significant improvement in everyday verbal communication in chronic aphasia - dose, not novelty, was the finding.

The Big CACTUS trial, reported in Lancet Neurology in 2019 by Rebecca Palmer and colleagues, tested self-managed computerised word-finding therapy and found a real gain in naming personally relevant words but no improvement in conversation, which is a clean example of a treatment working at the level it trains and not above it.

For neglect, prism adaptation - wearing wedge prisms that shift the visual world sideways, so the person recalibrates their reaching - is the most studied method, and meta-analyses report a genuine short-term reduction in neglect severity, with stronger prism shifts of ten degrees or more doing more work.

The dispute is over durability and function: a randomised pilot and feasibility trial published in PLOS One in 2021 found prism and sham groups improved to statistically indistinguishable degrees, and recent critical reviews note the field has no consensus on prism strength, dose, or outcome measure.

So the honest summary is that intensive aphasia therapy has good evidence, and prism adaptation for neglect has good short-term evidence and contested long-term functional evidence.


73.1.4 Measuring meaningful outcomes rather than task gains

The recurring failure mode of rehabilitation research is to report that the trained score went up while never asking whether anything in the person's life changed.

Two technical ideas guard against this: the minimal detectable change (the smallest score shift that exceeds measurement noise) and the minimal clinically important difference (MCID, the smallest shift a patient would actually notice as worthwhile).

For the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living scale in stroke, published estimates put the MCID at roughly six points, which is a far higher bar than statistical significance in a large trial.

The World Health Organization framework of impairment, activity, and participation makes the same point structurally - a gain in impairment does not automatically become a gain in participation, and participation is what correlates with life satisfaction and depression.

The practical implication for readers is to be sceptical whenever a rehabilitation claim is reported only as a change on the therapy's own task.


73.2 Stimulation-based intervention

The second family works by putting energy into neural tissue, either through the intact skull or through implanted electrodes, to change how circuits fire.

The physics differs across methods, but the clinical logic is common: identify a circuit that is misbehaving, and push it.

This family has produced both the most solid non-drug psychiatric treatment of the last twenty years and some of the field's most overheated claims.


73.2.1 Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in depression

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) uses a rapidly changing magnetic field from a coil held against the scalp to induce a small electrical current in the cortex directly beneath it, without surgery.

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) delivered to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex received United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in 2008 for major depression that had not responded to medication, and a standard course is daily sessions over several weeks.

Theta burst stimulation (TBS) is a faster patterned variant that delivers bursts of pulses at fifty hertz in a rhythm mimicking the brain's own theta rhythm, and it compresses a session from around thirty-seven minutes to about three.

Stanford Accelerated Intelligent Neuromodulation Therapy (SAINT), reported by Nolan Williams and colleagues in 2020 and 2021, added two further ideas - individual targeting by resting-state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging, and a very high dose packed into five days - and reported remission rates in treatment-resistant depression far above conventional rTMS.

It received FDA clearance in 2022, but the caution is real: the pivotal samples were small, the blinding of a treatment with obvious scalp sensations is difficult, and the field is still asking how much of the accelerated advantage survives replication at scale.


73.2.2 Deep brain stimulation for movement and psychiatric disorders

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) implants thin electrodes into a specific deep nucleus and connects them to a pacemaker-like pulse generator in the chest.

For Parkinson's disease - a degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons causing tremor, rigidity and slowness - stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus is a mature, well-evidenced treatment, and a randomised sham-controlled trial of 137 patients reported in JAMA Neurology in 2025 showed motor gains, dyskinesia suppression, and medication reduction sustained across five years.

For psychiatry the picture is genuinely contested.

DBS for obsessive-compulsive disorder shows sustained long-term benefit in open follow-up, but recent sham-controlled trials report smaller effect sizes than the early open-label reports, which is the classic signature of expectation and selection inflating early results.

For treatment-resistant depression, Helen Mayberg's subcallosal cingulate target produced striking open-label responses and long-term follow-up out to five years showing sustained improvement, yet the industry-run randomised trials of the 2010s failed their primary endpoints; a pooled analysis of 172 implanted patients published in Brain Stimulation in 2025 supports long-term effectiveness, and the field's own explanation for the trial failures is imprecise targeting, insufficient time for individual programming, and the biological heterogeneity of depression.

Readers should hold both halves: the mechanism is plausible and the long-term data are encouraging, and the blinded trials have not yet cleanly delivered.


73.2.3 Closed-loop and responsive neurostimulation

Conventional stimulation is open loop - it runs at fixed settings regardless of what the brain is doing, like a thermostat stuck on.

Closed-loop, or responsive, systems record neural activity, detect a pathological signature, and stimulate only when needed.

The NeuroPace Responsive Neurostimulation System, approved in the United States in 2013 for medication-refractory epilepsy, continuously analyses cortical activity through a small number of channels and delivers stimulation on detecting the electrical onset of a seizure.

In February 2025 the FDA approved Medtronic's BrainSense Adaptive DBS, the first closed-loop deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease, which senses beta-band oscillations associated with rigidity and slowness and adjusts stimulation moment to moment rather than requiring manual programming.

The appeal is not only efficacy but side-effect burden and battery life, since stimulation that runs only when required is stimulation that is not causing speech or mood side effects the rest of the time.

The open question is whether the biomarkers used - beta power, for instance - are reliable enough across patients and across the day to beat a well-tuned fixed setting in the long run.


73.2.4 Focused ultrasound and emerging non-invasive deep targeting

Every non-invasive electrical or magnetic method shares a geometric curse: strength falls off with depth, and you cannot reach a deep structure without dosing everything above it.

Low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) breaks that constraint, because sound can be focused through the skull to a spot a few millimetres across, deep in the brain, at intensities that modulate neurons rather than destroy them.

The likely mechanism is mechanical - pressure waves acting on mechanosensitive ion channels in neural membranes - and it is distinct from high-intensity focused ultrasound, which is already an approved treatment that thermally ablates tissue for essential tremor.

Target engagement has now been tested directly: a trial enrolling patients already implanted with globus pallidus DBS leads used those leads to record whether ultrasound was actually reaching and changing the intended target, which is a far stronger design than inferring effect from behaviour.

A double-blind sham-controlled target-engagement study followed by an open single-arm trial of amygdala tFUS in psychiatric patients was published in Molecular Psychiatry in 2025, and early-phase trials are running in pain, epilepsy, movement disorders and depression.

This is the most interesting frontier in the chapter and also the least settled - the sample sizes are small, blinding remains hard, and no tFUS neuromodulation indication has yet cleared a large pivotal trial.


73.3 Behavioural and pharmacological enhancement

The third family is not about repair but about pushing normal cognition higher.

It attracts enormous consumer money and generates comparatively weak evidence, with one notable exception drawn from the psychology of learning.


73.3.1 Cognitive training and the transfer debate

The whole commercial brain-training industry rests on far transfer - the claim that practising a laboratory task improves cognition broadly, in untrained domains and in real life.

Near transfer, improving on tasks closely resembling the trained one, is real and uncontroversial; far transfer is the disputed claim.

Adrian Owen and colleagues, publishing in Nature in 2010, trained more than eleven thousand people online and found gains on the trained tasks with no generalisation to untrained cognitive abilities, and a 2018 study in Neuropsychologia reported converging negative evidence.

Daniel Simons and colleagues, in an exhaustive 2016 review in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, concluded there was no compelling evidence of training-induced far transfer to cognitive tests or real-life skills.

The main counterweight is the ACTIVE trial, a large randomised study in older adults which reported durable effects on the trained ability and, in the speed-of-processing arm, some longer-term real-world associations - but critics note the effects are largely ability-specific and the broader claims rest on secondary analyses.

The reasonable summary is that you get very good at what you practise, and this is precisely what makes commercial claims of general brain fitness unsupported.


73.3.2 Exercise, sleep, and nutrition as cognitive interventions

The unglamorous interventions have better evidence than the technological ones, though the effects are modest and the trials are often small.

Meta-analyses of aerobic exercise in older adults with mild cognitive impairment - a state of measurable decline that has not reached dementia - consistently show statistically significant improvement in global cognition, with a moderate effect on memory across roughly two thousand participants.

The proposed mechanisms are increased cerebral blood flow, upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (a protein supporting neuron survival and synapse formation), and preservation of hippocampal volume; the hippocampal-volume claim is well known from Kirk Erickson and colleagues in 2011 but has proved harder to replicate than the cognitive effect itself.

Sleep is the strongest theoretical case, because slow-wave sleep is when hippocampal memory traces are replayed and consolidated into cortex, yet interventional evidence is weaker than the mechanistic story suggests - the same aerobic exercise meta-analyses found no significant improvement in sleep quality in people with mild cognitive impairment.

For nutrition, combined exercise-and-diet programmes show more consistent cognitive benefit than either alone, with omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidant-rich dietary patterns as the usual ingredients, but single-nutrient supplement trials in well-nourished populations have generally disappointed.

The pattern is worth stating plainly: interventions that improve vascular and metabolic health improve cognition modestly and reliably, and pills that target cognition directly do not.


73.3.3 Stimulants and nootropics in healthy users

Modafinil, a wakefulness-promoting drug, and methylphenidate, a dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor prescribed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, are the two most-used off-label enhancers among students and professionals.

Dimitris Repantis and colleagues, in systematic reviews from 2010, found modafinil produced a moderate and statistically significant improvement in attention and vigilance, no effect on memory, and insufficient data on executive function, while methylphenidate showed no consistent enhancement in healthy people.

A careful randomised trial published in Psychopharmacology in 2021 comparing methylphenidate, modafinil, caffeine and placebo in healthy men found only scattered benefits - methylphenidate improved delayed recall at twenty-four hours and reduced subjective fatigue, caffeine helped sustained attention, and modafinil produced no significant benefit on any outcome.

Two findings recur and deserve emphasis: participants systematically overestimate how much the drug helped them, and benefits are largest in the tired, the sleep-deprived, and the low-baseline performer, which suggests restoration rather than enhancement.

There is also a real inverted-U problem, where dopaminergic drugs impair those who already have high baseline dopaminergic function, so the same dose helps one person and harms another.

Commercial nootropic supplements, as distinct from prescription stimulants, have essentially no controlled evidence of cognitive benefit in healthy adults.


73.3.4 Spaced practice, retrieval practice, and evidence-based learning

The one enhancement method in this chapter with strong, replicated, practically useful evidence comes from cognitive psychology rather than neuroscience or pharmacology.

Retrieval practice, also called the testing effect, is the finding that pulling information out of memory strengthens it far more than putting it in again by rereading; Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, in 2006, showed students who practised recall retained about sixty-one per cent of a passage after a week against about forty per cent for repeated rereading.

Meta-analytic estimates put the advantage at around a standardised effect of 0.5 to 0.6, and crucially the advantage grows as the delay between study and test lengthens, which is why rereading feels better in the moment and performs worse in the exam.

Spacing, the distribution of practice over separated occasions rather than massed in one block, is the complementary principle - Karpicke and Roediger showed in 2007 that retrieval immediately after study yields very little durable learning, while spaced retrieval yields a great deal.

John Dunlosky and colleagues, reviewing ten popular study techniques in 2013, rated only two as high utility: distributed practice and practice testing, while highlighting, rereading and summarising fared poorly.

If a reader takes one actionable item from this chapter, it should be this one, because it is free, well replicated, and consistently underused.


73.4 Neuroprosthetics and brain-computer interfaces

The fourth family does not repair the brain at all - it reads from it or writes to it, replacing the lost link between the nervous system and the world.

A brain-computer interface (BCI) records neural activity, decodes an intention from it, and drives an external device.

The field has moved in twenty years from proof of concept to devices that people use daily at home, and it now faces engineering problems of durability and adaptation rather than questions of possibility.


73.4.1 Motor prostheses and cursor and limb control

The BrainGate programme, led by Leigh Hochberg, John Donoghue and colleagues, implants one or two ninety-six-channel microelectrode arrays into the motor cortex of people with paralysis and decodes intended movement from the resulting spike patterns.

Intracortical control of a robot arm by a human was first shown in 2006, and Hochberg and colleagues reported in Nature in 2012 a participant with tetraplegia using a robotic arm to lift a bottle of coffee and drink from it, the first self-directed drink she had taken in about fifteen years.

Jennifer Collinger and Andrew Schwartz and colleagues extended this in 2013 to high-dimensional control, with a participant performing seven- and later ten-dimensional reaching and grasping.

Reliability has been the quiet obstacle, and a 2025 analysis of long-term array performance across fourteen BrainGate and BrainGate2 participants is the kind of unglamorous durability study the field needs, because signal quality on chronically implanted silicon arrays tends to decline over years as tissue responds to the foreign body.

Cursor control, less dramatic than a robot arm, remains the most practically valuable output, since a cursor grants access to every other piece of software a person uses.


73.4.2 Speech neuroprostheses and communication restoration

Speech decoding turns neural activity in speech motor cortex into text or synthesised voice, and it is the fastest-moving area in the chapter.

Francis Willett and colleagues, in Nature in 2023, decoded attempted speech in a participant with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, a progressive degeneration of motor neurons) at sixty-two words per minute from a 125,000-word vocabulary, several times faster than previous systems; Edward Chang's group, with Sean Metzger and colleagues, reported in the same issue a multimodal system producing text, synthesised speech and a facial avatar in a participant with brainstem stroke.

Nicholas Card, Maitreyee Wairagkar, Willett and colleagues then published in the New England Journal of Medicine in August 2024 a system that calibrated in a single session and reached 99.6 per cent accuracy on a fifty-word vocabulary on the first day of use, with high accuracy sustained on a large vocabulary over months of daily self-directed use at home.

Two caveats belong here: these are single-participant or few-participant results, and the decoders reconstruct attempted articulation, not thought, so the widespread public framing of mind reading is inaccurate.
