The remaining barriers are surgical risk, cost, hardware longevity, and the fact that the population who would benefit most, people late in ALS, are also the hardest to enrol and support.


73.4.3 Sensory prostheses: cochlear and visual implants

The cochlear implant is the only neuroprosthesis in routine mass use, with well over a million recipients, and it works by bypassing damaged hair cells to stimulate the auditory nerve directly through an electrode array threaded into the cochlea.

Outcomes are good but highly variable, and the variability is instructive - implanted early in childhood, within a sensitive period, most children develop spoken language, whereas long-deafened adults do less well partly because cross-modal plasticity has reassigned auditory cortex to vision.

Vision has proved far harder, because the retina and visual cortex encode a vastly higher-dimensional signal than the cochlea's tonotopic map.

The Argus II retinal prosthesis for retinitis pigmentosa restored crude light perception and helped with localisation and mobility tasks, but the device gave roughly sixty electrodes against a healthy retina's million ganglion cells, its useful lifetime was limited, and Second Sight discontinued it in 2019, stranding implanted users - an ethical failure the field now cites as a warning about commercial dependency in implanted devices.

The newer PRIMA subretinal photovoltaic implant, which is wireless and aimed at geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration rather than retinitis pigmentosa, has reported form vision in trial participants and moved toward European regulatory submission, and cortical approaches such as ORION bypass the eye entirely.

The general lesson is that a prosthesis works well when the natural code it must imitate is simple and orderly, and struggles when it is not.


73.4.4 Memory prostheses and closed-loop memory enhancement

The most ambitious idea in the chapter is a device that does not move a limb or make a sound but improves memory itself.

Theodore Berger and Dong Song at the University of Southern California, with Robert Hampson and Sam Deadwyler at Wake Forest, built a multi-input multi-output model that learns the transformation the hippocampus performs from its CA3 input to its CA1 output during successful encoding, then stimulates CA1 with the pattern that a healthy hippocampus would have produced.

In non-human primates this closed-loop ensemble stimulation improved delayed match-to-sample performance, and in human epilepsy patients already implanted with depth electrodes for clinical reasons, Hampson and colleagues reported memory improvements in the region of thirty-four to thirty-seven per cent on tested recall.

Much of this work was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) under its Restoring Active Memory programme, launched in 2013 to build implantable closed-loop devices for memory impairment after brain injury.

The honest framing is that these are small studies in a convenience population of neurosurgical patients, with short-term laboratory memory measures rather than everyday memory, and with no independent large replication.

The idea is elegant and the mechanism is specified more precisely than in most of neuromodulation, which is exactly why the weakness of the clinical evidence should be stated rather than glossed.


73.4.5 Bidirectional interfaces and the co-adaptation problem

A one-way interface reads intention and sends it out; a bidirectional interface also writes information back in, most often by intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) of somatosensory cortex to create an artificial sense of touch.

Sharlene Flesher, Robert Gaunt, Collinger and colleagues showed in Science in 2021 that adding ICMS tactile feedback to a robotic arm roughly halved the time taken to grasp and transfer objects, because without touch the user must watch every movement and confirm contact visually.

The deeper problem is co-adaptation: the decoder is learning to interpret the brain at the same time as the brain is learning to drive the decoder, and two adaptive systems chasing each other can either converge on stable skilled control or oscillate and destabilise.

This is why decoder retraining schedules matter so much in practice, and why long-term users often develop a stable neural pattern for control that no longer resembles natural movement-related activity - the brain treats the interface as a new limb with its own idiom.

Rajesh Rao and colleagues have argued for framing these systems as neural co-processors, jointly optimised units rather than a brain plus a separate algorithm, which is probably the correct conceptual home for the next decade of the field.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Cognitive rehabilitation works best when it combines restoration, compensation and environmental adaptation, and its strongest single finding is that dose matters - Breitenstein and colleagues in 2017 showed intensive speech therapy improves everyday communication in chronic aphasia, while constraint per se remains unproven and prism adaptation for neglect has solid short-term but contested long-term functional evidence.

Stimulation methods span a genuine range of evidential quality, from subthalamic deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease with five-year randomised sham-controlled support, through rTMS for depression which is approved and effective but whose accelerated protocols await large replication, to psychiatric deep brain stimulation where open-label success and blinded trial failure still coexist unresolved.

Closed-loop stimulation became clinical reality with responsive neurostimulation for epilepsy and adaptive deep brain stimulation approved in February 2025, and low-intensity focused ultrasound is the credible route to non-invasive deep targeting but has not yet cleared a pivotal trial.

In enhancement, the evidence runs opposite to the marketing: commercial brain training shows near transfer but no compelling far transfer, stimulants in healthy users produce small effects that people reliably overestimate, and the best-supported intervention is the cheapest one - spaced retrieval practice.

Neuroprosthetics have crossed from demonstration to daily use, with speech decoding reaching high accuracy on large vocabularies by 2024, while the field's unsolved problems are hardware durability, the closed-loop co-adaptation of brain and decoder, and the ethical exposure of patients who depend on a device a company may stop supporting.

The single organising lesson is that a measured gain on a trained task is not a gain in a life, and that every claim in this chapter should be read against that standard.


PART FOURTEEN. COGNITION AND MACHINES


CHAPTER 74. NEUROAI: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL AND AS A THEORY (CORE)

This chapter is about the traffic in ideas between the study of brains and the building of machines.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the engineering discipline of building systems that perform tasks we would call intelligent if a person did them.

NeuroAI is the name now given to the deliberate two-way exchange between that discipline and neuroscience - the study of nervous systems.

The chapter matters because artificial neural networks have become the most quantitatively successful models of sensory and language processing in the human brain that anyone has ever built, and because that success is easy to overstate.

We will look at how the models are compared with brains, what the comparison licenses, and what artificial systems conspicuously still cannot do.

Throughout, a jargon note: an artificial neural network is a mathematical function built from layers of simple units, each unit summing weighted inputs and passing the result through a nonlinearity, with the weights adjusted by training.


74.1 The two-way exchange

Neuroscience and AI have never been separate enterprises for long.

Ideas move in both directions, and the direction of travel changes with the decade.

The productive question is not which field owes the other more, but which specific borrowings actually paid off.


74.1.1 Neuroscience-inspired architectures: convolution, attention, replay, modularity

Convolution - applying the same small filter at every position of an image - was taken almost directly from the simple and complex cells that David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel described in cat primary visual cortex in the 1960s, and from Kunihiko Fukushima's Neocognitron of 1980, which built a layered hierarchy of position-tolerant feature detectors.

Attention, the mechanism at the heart of the transformer architecture that powers modern language models, is named after the psychological capacity to weight some inputs more heavily than others, though the engineering version is a soft weighted lookup rather than a model of any particular cortical circuit.

Replay in machine learning - storing past experiences and re-presenting them during training - was inspired by hippocampal replay, the reactivation during rest and sleep of the neural sequences that occurred during waking behaviour, and it remains one of the most effective defences against forgetting in artificial systems.

Modularity, the idea of building a system from specialised interacting parts rather than one undifferentiated network, echoes the functional specialisation of cortical areas, and is currently being revived in multi-module and agentic architectures.

It is worth noting that in three of these four cases the biological inspiration was loose: the engineers took a motif, not a mechanism.


74.1.2 Artificial networks as hypotheses about neural computation

The stronger claim in NeuroAI is not that brains inspire machines but that a trained network can serve as a scientific hypothesis about what the brain computes.

On this view a network is an image-computable model - you can feed it the very same photograph the monkey saw and read out a prediction for every recorded neuron - which is something no verbal theory of vision has ever offered.

Daniel Yamins, James DiCarlo and colleagues made this concrete in 2014, showing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that a hierarchical convolutional network optimised for object recognition predicted responses in inferior temporal cortex, the highest stage of the monkey ventral visual stream, better than any hand-designed model of the day.

The hypothesis embodied in such a model is specific and falsifiable: it says that these representations arise because the system was shaped to solve this task under these architectural constraints.

That is a genuine advance in the form of neuroscientific theory, whatever one concludes about any particular model.


74.1.3 The historical cycle of borrowing between the fields

The cycle begins with Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943, who idealised the neuron as a threshold logic unit, and with Donald Hebb in 1949, whose rule that cells firing together strengthen their connection is still the template for synaptic learning rules.

Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron of 1958 was explicitly a brain model; its limitations, publicised by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert in 1969, helped trigger the first long funding winter.

John Hopfield's 1982 network of recurrently connected units with an energy function, and the parallel distributed processing movement of the 1980s associated with David Rumelhart, James McClelland and Geoffrey Hinton, restarted the exchange; Hopfield and Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for that lineage of work.

The current phase, from roughly 2012 onward, inverts the older pattern - engineering successes achieved largely without biological guidance are now being brought back into the laboratory as models of the brain.

The lesson of the cycle is that borrowings work best when they are principled and specific, and that each generation has over-promised.


74.1.4 Where the analogy has been productive and where it has misled

It has been productive wherever the model is used to predict measured neural responses to novel stimuli, because that is a demanding test the model can fail.

It has misled wherever architectural resemblance was mistaken for mechanistic identity.

Two concrete failures are instructive: convolutional networks are fooled by adversarial examples - images altered by perturbations too small for a person to see, which flip the network's answer entirely - and Robert Geirhos and colleagues reported in 2019 that networks trained on the ImageNet photograph collection classify by texture where humans classify by shape, although a 2025 re-examination using controlled feature suppression argues the effect is better described as sensitivity to local shape and is reduced by modern training recipes, so this specific claim is now contested.

Backpropagation, the algorithm that trains essentially all of these networks by propagating error signals backwards through the layers, has no accepted biological implementation, since real synapses do not have access to the precise reverse-direction weight information the algorithm assumes.

A model can therefore predict a brain area well while learning by means the brain certainly does not use, and that gap is the central interpretive difficulty of the field.


74.2 Model-brain comparison

If a network is a hypothesis, the science lives in how you test it against measured brains.

The methods below are the standard toolkit, and each has a characteristic weakness.


74.2.1 Representational similarity between networks and brains

Representational similarity analysis (RSA), introduced by Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Marieke Mur and Peter Bandettini in 2008, sidesteps the problem that a network unit and a cortical neuron are not directly comparable.

Instead of matching units to neurons, you compute, within each system, how similar its response is to every pair of stimuli, producing a representational dissimilarity matrix - a stimulus-by-stimulus table of how differently the system treats each pair.

Two systems can then be compared by comparing their tables, which is possible even across species, imaging methods, and silicon.

The weakness is that similar representational geometry does not entail similar computation; several analyses have shown that representational similarity can dissociate from the underlying algorithm, so a match is suggestive rather than decisive.


74.2.2 Encoding-model benchmarks and leaderboards

An encoding model takes a network's internal activations for a stimulus and fits a regression that predicts the measured brain response, then is scored on stimuli held out from that fitting.

Brain-Score, launched by Martin Schrimpf, DiCarlo and colleagues in 2018, aggregates over a hundred such neural and behavioural benchmarks into public leaderboards for vision and for language, so that any submitted model receives a comparable brain-alignment score.

Benchmarks of this kind imposed a discipline the field previously lacked: claims of brain-likeness became numbers other laboratories could reproduce.

They also inherit every limitation of the underlying recordings, including the noise ceiling - the fact that repeated presentations of the same stimulus do not produce identical brain responses, so no model can score perfectly.


74.2.3 Goal-driven modelling: optimise for a task, compare the representations

The goal-driven strategy, set out by Yamins and DiCarlo in Nature Neuroscience in 2016, is to specify a behavioural goal, an architecture class and a dataset, optimise the network for the goal, and only then compare the resulting internal representations with the brain's.

The intellectual appeal is that no neural data are used in fitting the model's features, so the correspondence, if it appears, is a prediction rather than a curve fit.

The strategy has been extended beyond object recognition: Aria Wang, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris, Michael Tarr and Leila Wehbe reported in Nature Machine Intelligence in 2023 that models trained with natural language supervision on large diverse image sets predicted human high-level visual cortex better than models trained on category labels alone, suggesting the training objective matters as much as the architecture.

The caveat is that goal, architecture and data are three knobs, and a good fit does not tell you which knob was responsible.


74.2.4 The identifiability problem: many models fit equally well

Identifiability is the statistical question of whether the data can single out one model among the candidates that fit.

In NeuroAI the answer is often no: given realistic amounts of neural data and standard comparison metrics, networks with quite different architectures achieve overlapping scores.

A 2023 study by Yena Han, Tomaso Poggio and colleagues, titled "System identification of neural systems: if we got it right, would we know?", tested this directly by treating one network as a stand-in brain and asking whether standard metrics could recover its architecture; identifiability improved with depth and under idealised conditions, but scores for architecture-wide motifs such as convolution versus attention overlapped so heavily that the metrics could not distinguish them.

That result should be read carefully: it does not show the models are wrong, it shows that current comparison methods have limited power to tell rival models apart.

The practical response has been to design experiments that discriminate - novel and adversarially chosen stimuli, controlled perturbations, and in-silico predictions tested in vivo - rather than to add further benchmarks of the same kind.


74.3 Language models and the language network

Language offers the sharpest test case, because here the artificial systems were built by engineers pursuing a commercial objective, and yet turned out to predict brain responses.

The language network here means the left-lateralised frontal and temporal cortical regions that respond selectively to comprehensible language, as characterised over two decades by Evelina Fedorenko and colleagues.


74.3.1 Next-word prediction as a shared objective

Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on a single deceptively simple objective: given a stretch of text, predict the next word.

Martin Schrimpf, Idan Blank, Fedorenko and colleagues reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2021 that across dozens of models, the better a model was at next-word prediction, the better its internal activations predicted human brain responses to sentences, measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and intracranial recordings.

Because that relationship held across architectures, it was read as evidence that predictive processing is a genuine organising principle of human language comprehension, not an artefact of any one model.

A later study by Eghbal Hosseini, Fedorenko and colleagues, published in Neurobiology of Language in 2024, sharpened the point by showing that models trained on roughly one hundred million words - a developmentally realistic quantity for a child - already predicted brain data about as well as models trained on billions.

That finding cuts both ways: it supports the psychological plausibility of the objective, and it undercuts the assumption that ever-larger models are converging on the brain.


74.3.2 Model surprisal predicting neural and behavioural responses

Surprisal is the negative logarithm of the probability a model assigned to the word that actually occurred - a number that is small for expected words and large for unexpected ones.

Surprisal computed from language models predicts human reading times, the amplitude of the N400 brain potential (a negative-going electroencephalographic response peaking around four hundred milliseconds after a word, larger for semantically unexpected words), and the magnitude of fMRI responses in the language network.

The relationship is robust enough to be a workhorse method, but its scaling behaviour is disputed: several studies report that surprisal from the very largest models predicts human reading times worse than surprisal from mid-sized models, and a 2025 analysis argued that some apparent advantages of large models reflect the greater dimensionality of their activation vectors rather than better cognitive modelling.

Take surprisal as a well-validated linking quantity between models and people, and treat the claim that bigger models are more human-like as unsettled.


74.3.3 Sparse feature interpretation of brain responses to language

A dense model activation is a vector of thousands of numbers with no interpretable meaning attached to any one of them, which limits what a good brain prediction can tell you.

A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is an auxiliary network trained to re-express such a vector as a combination of a few active elements drawn from a much larger dictionary, and in interpretability research those elements often turn out to correspond to nameable features.

Recent work applies this to neuroscience, replacing dense activations with sparse autoencoder features in encoding models so that a voxel's tuning can be described in words rather than in coordinates; one such study used high-field seven-tesla fMRI in a small number of participants listening to linguistically diverse sentences, and combined sparse features with surprisal to identify voxel populations tuned to processing difficulty.

This line is promising and very new, so treat individual results as preliminary; the important shift is methodological, from predicting brain responses to stating what the prediction is about.


74.3.4 What the correspondence licenses about human language mechanisms

It licenses the claim that a system trained only to predict upcoming words develops internal representations whose similarity structure resembles the human language network's, which is a real and non-obvious constraint on theories of comprehension.

It does not license the claim that the brain implements a transformer, nor that it learns by gradient descent over trillions of tokens, nor that the model understands anything.

Fedorenko and colleagues have argued a further point that the correspondence supports: the language network is specialised for language and is largely dissociable from networks supporting reasoning, which fits the observation that models good at language are not thereby good at thinking.

The honest summary is that these models are strong predictive models of one cortical system and weak explanations of it, and the field's central open problem is converting the former into the latter.


74.4 Foundation models of brain and behaviour

A foundation model is a large model pretrained on broad data and then adapted to many downstream tasks rather than built for one.

The last three years have seen this recipe turned on neuroscience itself, with consequences that are genuinely new and not yet fully digested.


74.4.1 Multimodal foundation models predicting brain activity across vision, audition, and language

Naturalistic experiments - people watching films in the scanner - deliver visual, auditory and linguistic information at once, which single-modality models cannot handle.

TRIBE, developed at Meta and the winner of the 2025 Algonauts brain-prediction challenge, addressed this by combining video, audio and text representations in one trained model of the fMRI response.

Its successor, described in 2026, was trained on more than one thousand hours of fMRI across several hundred participants and reported severalfold improvements over conventional linear encoding models in predicting responses to new stimuli, new tasks and new individuals, and was used to map the fine-grained cortical topography of multisensory integration.

The scientific promise is that a single predictive model replaces a patchwork of task-specific mappings; the scientific risk is that predictive accuracy is being purchased with model complexity that no one can interpret.


74.4.2 Large-scale functional imaging pretraining and in-silico neuroscience

In-silico neuroscience means running experiments on a model accurate enough that its predictions are worth testing in a real animal.

The clearest demonstration came in Nature in April 2025, when Eric Wang, Andreas Tolias and a large consortium reported a foundation model trained on the responses of mouse visual cortical neurons to movies, which predicted responses of tens of thousands of neurons to entirely new stimulus types it had not been trained on.

Because the same mice were later reconstructed anatomically through electron microscopy in the MICrONS project, the model could be checked against ground truth, and the paper reported that functional properties derived from the model predicted anatomical cell type and aspects of synaptic connectivity.

That combination - a digital twin that generalises, plus a wiring diagram to validate it against - is the strongest existing case that these models are capturing something real rather than fitting noise.

The obvious limitation is scope: this is mouse visual cortex responding to passive movie viewing, not cognition.


74.4.3 Foundation models of human behaviour and cognition

Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz and colleagues published Centaur in Nature in July 2025, a large language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a dataset of trial-by-trial choices from more than sixty thousand participants making over ten million decisions across one hundred and sixty psychological experiments.

Centaur predicted the choices of held-out participants better than the domain-specific cognitive models built for each task, and generalised to modified tasks, new cover stories and unseen domains; its internal representations also became more aligned with human neural data despite never being trained on brain measurements.

The claim that this constitutes a unified model of cognition is strongly contested.

A 2026 critique in National Science Open showed that when the prompt was replaced with the instruction "please choose option A", Centaur did not comply but continued producing the dataset's typical responses, which the authors argue shows the model exploits statistical regularities in the data rather than understanding the task instructions.

The fair reading is that Centaur is an impressive predictive instrument whose status as a theory of cognition is unresolved, and that predicting behaviour and explaining it have come apart here in a particularly clean way.


74.4.4 Prefrontal-centred foundational models of intelligence

A distinct proposal argues that a foundational brain model should be built around the prefrontal cortex - the frontmost cortical region supporting working memory, planning, rule use and executive control - rather than around sensory areas where progress has been easiest.

Proponents of this view, set out in Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2026, envisage a platform constrained by measured connectivity and cell types, capturing recurrent circuit dynamics, and trained to perform many cognitive tasks at once, with intelligence measured by combined performance across them rather than by any single benchmark.

A looser engineering version of the same idea already exists: architectures that decompose planning into interacting modules named after prefrontal functions such as conflict monitoring, state evaluation and task decomposition, implemented as repeated calls to a language model.

This programme is at present more manifesto than result - the biologically constrained version has not yet produced a validated multi-task model - and it should be described as a promising direction rather than an achievement.


74.4.5 Evaluation, overfitting, and the danger of benchmark-driven science

Overfitting means learning the idiosyncrasies of a particular dataset rather than the regularity it was meant to sample, and in a field organised around leaderboards it can happen at the level of the whole community.

When hundreds of laboratories tune models against the same public benchmark, the benchmark stops being a held-out test and becomes part of the training procedure, even though no individual researcher cheated.

The problem compounds with the identifiability result of section 74.2.4: if the metrics cannot distinguish architectures reliably, a leaderboard ranking may be measuring something other than brain-likeness.

Sensible safeguards exist and are increasingly used - held-out datasets released only after submissions close, as in the Algonauts challenges, prediction of responses to stimuli synthesised to break the model, and validation against independent measurement types such as anatomy.

The general principle is that a model earns scientific credit when it makes a risky prediction about something not yet measured, not when it climbs a table.


74.5 What artificial systems still lack

The gaps below are not a list of things machines will never do.

They are the specific dimensions on which biological cognition remains ahead by large margins, which makes them the places where neuroscience still has something to offer engineering.


74.5.1 Data and energy efficiency

The adult human brain runs on roughly twenty watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, while training a frontier language model consumes energy measured in gigawatt-hours and serving it requires data centres drawing megawatts.

The data gap is at least as striking: a child hears something on the order of tens of millions of words before school age and speaks fluently, while frontier models are trained on trillions of tokens.

Part of the brain's advantage is physical - synaptic events cost on the order of ten to the minus fourteen joules, and activity is sparse and event-driven, so most neurons are silent most of the time - which is the motivation for neuromorphic hardware that computes with spikes rather than dense matrix multiplications.

Part of it is presumably algorithmic and developmental, including innate structure and an embodied curriculum, and that part is not yet understood well enough to copy.

Comparisons of this kind should be handled with care, since brain and chip are not doing identical work, but the orders of magnitude involved are too large to be an artefact of the accounting.


74.5.2 Continual learning without catastrophic forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting is the failure mode in which training a network on a new task overwrites the weights supporting an old one, so that competence at the earlier task collapses rather than degrading gently.

It is a symptom of the stability-plasticity dilemma: a system plastic enough to learn quickly is by that fact unstable enough to lose what it knows.

The leading biological account is complementary learning systems theory, proposed by James McClelland, Bruce McNaughton and Randall O'Reilly in 1995, in which the hippocampus stores individual episodes rapidly and replays them to the neocortex, which extracts generalities slowly and so is never asked to learn a new regularity in one shot.

Machine learning has borrowed the mechanism with real success - experience replay, generative replay that regenerates old data rather than storing it, and hybrid replay-plus-architecture methods surveyed comprehensively in 2025 - but no method yet matches biological continual learning, and stored-sample replay scales badly as tasks accumulate.

Note the practical consequence: today's large models are essentially trained once and then frozen, which is a very poor imitation of a brain.


74.5.3 Embodiment, interaction, and grounded learning

Embodiment is the claim that intelligence is shaped by having a body that acts in and is acted on by a world; grounding is the related claim that symbols acquire meaning through connection to sensorimotor experience, a problem posed by Stevan Harnad in 1990.

A child learns the word "heavy" by lifting things, generating its own training data through curiosity-driven action, and receives a self-structured curriculum that no static text corpus provides.

Whether this is a hard requirement is genuinely disputed: language models trained on text alone display considerable semantic competence, which some take as evidence that distributional structure suffices for much of meaning, while others regard their characteristic failures on physical reasoning as exactly what ungrounded learning predicts.

Robotics is the empirical arena where the dispute is being settled, and progress there has been markedly slower than progress in text and images.


74.5.4 Compositional generalisation and causal understanding

Compositionality is the ability to combine known parts in new arrangements - knowing "jump" and "twice" and thereby knowing "jump twice" without instruction - and Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn argued in 1988 that neural networks could not achieve it in the systematic way humans do.

Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni answered part of that challenge in Nature in 2023 with meta-learning for compositionality, training a standard network on a stream of freshly generated compositional tasks so that it learned how to compose, and reporting that it matched or exceeded human systematicity on tests where both symbolic models and ordinary networks failed.

The challenge is not closed: papers in 2025 and 2026 argue that systematic compositionality still does not emerge reliably in general-purpose models and that the Fodor-Pylyshyn objection stands in weakened form, so this should be presented as a live dispute rather than a settled win.

Causal understanding is the further step of knowing what would happen under an intervention rather than what usually co-occurs, and systems trained on passive observation have no direct access to intervention, which is one principled reason to expect the embodiment gap and the causality gap to be the same gap.


74.5.5 The open question of machine consciousness and moral status

Consciousness here means phenomenal experience - there being something it is like to be the system - which is distinct from intelligence, from self-report, and from behavioural sophistication.

The most disciplined treatment to date is the 2023 report led by Patrick Butlin and Robert Long with nineteen co-authors, which took several scientific theories of consciousness - recurrent processing theory, global workspace theory, higher-order theories, predictive processing and attention schema theory - derived roughly fourteen computational indicator properties from them, and assessed current systems against those indicators.

Their conclusion was two-sided in structure and worth stating precisely: no current AI system is a strong candidate for consciousness, but no obvious technical barrier prevents building one that satisfies the indicators.

The method is openly conditional, since it assumes computational functionalism - the view that the right computations suffice for experience - which is itself contested, and a follow-up in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2025 extended the indicator approach while acknowledging its limits.

The moral question follows the empirical one: if there is a non-trivial probability that a system has experiences, precautionary frameworks argue that this generates obligations before certainty arrives, and this is now an active area of applied ethics rather than a thought experiment.

The intellectually honest position is that we do not know, that we lack an agreed test, and that behavioural fluency is emphatically not evidence, since these systems are trained on human descriptions of inner life.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Artificial neural networks are the best quantitative predictors of sensory and language cortex that neuroscience has ever had, and this is a real achievement resting on image-computable models tested against held-out neural data, from Yamins and DiCarlo's 2014 visual work to Schrimpf and colleagues' 2021 language results.

The predictive success does not by itself establish mechanistic correspondence, because current comparison methods have limited power to distinguish rival architectures, because backpropagation has no accepted biological implementation, and because leaderboard-driven science can overfit at the level of a whole community.

Foundation models have changed the scale of the enterprise - a mouse visual cortex digital twin validated against electron-microscopy anatomy in 2025, tri-modal models predicting fMRI across hundreds of participants, and Centaur predicting behaviour across one hundred and sixty psychological tasks - while also sharpening the split between predicting cognition and explaining it, as Centaur's 2026 critique made plain.

Artificial systems remain far behind biological ones in data and energy efficiency, in learning continuously without catastrophic forgetting, in grounded embodied learning, and arguably in systematic compositionality and causal understanding, and these gaps mark where neuroscience still has something to teach engineering.

On machine consciousness the defensible position is uncertainty under an explicit and contested assumption, with no current system a strong candidate and no evident barrier to future ones.


CHAPTER 75. SIMULATION, EMULATION, AND SYNTHETIC COGNITION (CONTEXT)

There is an old idea, usually credited to the physicist Richard Feynman, that you do not really understand a thing until you can build it.

This chapter takes that idea seriously and asks what happens when neuroscientists try to build brains - in software, in personalised patient models, in dishes of living cells, and in silicon chips wired to behave like neurons.

Each of these is a different bet about what the important part of a brain is, and each bet can be wrong in an instructive way.

We will look at what the big simulation programmes actually delivered, at what a simulation has to do before it counts as an explanation rather than an expensive animation, at what living tissue in a dish can and cannot teach us, and at the hardware that copies the brain's spiking style in order to copy its remarkable thrift with energy.

The chapter is tagged as context because it is not a set of findings about how cognition works; it is a set of tools and cautions about how we test claims that we know how cognition works.

Along the way we will meet a serious ethical problem that nobody has solved: what we owe to neural tissue that learns.


75.1 Large-scale brain simulation

A simulation is a computer program whose parts are meant to stand for parts of a real system, run forward in time so that the program's behaviour can be compared with the real system's behaviour.

Large-scale brain simulation means doing this for many neurons at once - thousands, millions, in ambition billions - with enough biological detail that the model neurons have realistic shapes, realistic ion channels (the protein pores in a cell membrane that let charged particles in and out, and so generate electrical signals), and realistic connections.

The appeal is obvious.

A brain is too dense, too fast, and too fragile to be observed in full, but a simulation can be paused, rewound, and taken apart neuron by neuron.

The difficulty is equally obvious: a simulation contains only what you put into it, so it can be confidently, fluently wrong.


75.1.1 The ambitions and outcomes of large simulation programmes

The two best-known efforts came from the same laboratory in Switzerland.

The Blue Brain Project, founded in 2005 at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) under Henry Markram, aimed to rebuild cortical tissue from measured biology upward; its landmark paper, Markram and colleagues in Cell in 2015, reported a digital reconstruction of roughly 31,000 neurons and about 37 million synapses from juvenile rat somatosensory cortex, assembled from morphology, electrophysiology, and connectivity data rather than hand-tuned to produce a desired output.

The larger European Human Brain Project (HBP), launched in 2013 with about one billion euros of funding and running to September 2023, was pitched in its earliest publicity as a route to simulating a whole human brain.

That framing provoked an open letter in 2014 signed by hundreds of European neuroscientists, who argued the goals were narrow, the governance was closed, and the promise was premature; the project was restructured, its three-person executive committee replaced by a broader board, and its emphasis shifted from whole-brain simulation toward infrastructure.

Its main surviving legacy is EBRAINS, a shared research infrastructure providing atlases, data, and simulation tools, plus a series of clinical modelling efforts - a real contribution, but not the thing originally advertised.

The honest summary, offered by several retrospectives published around the project's close in 2023, is that the programmes produced valuable tools, atlases, and methods, and did not produce a simulated brain that thinks.


75.1.2 What a simulation must reproduce to count as explanatory

A simulation that matches data is not automatically an explanation, because matching can be bought with enough free parameters.

The stronger standard usually demanded has three parts: the model should reproduce phenomena it was not fitted to, it should fail in the specific ways the real system fails when equivalently damaged, and it should tell you which of its components are doing the work.

The Blue Brain reconstruction is a useful example of the first: it was built from anatomical and physiological measurements and then found to produce spontaneous transitions between synchronous and asynchronous firing states as extracellular calcium concentration was varied, a behaviour that was not among the fitting targets.

The third requirement, sometimes called mechanistic transparency, is the one most often skipped.

If you cannot say which parts of the model are load-bearing, you have replaced one incomprehensible system with a second one that merely happens to sit on your hard drive.

Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording made this point with unusual force in 2017 in PLOS Computational Biology, applying standard neuroscience analysis methods - lesions, tuning curves, connectivity analysis, dimensionality reduction - to a MOS 6502 microprocessor, a chip of only 3,510 transistors whose function is completely known.

The methods produced plausible-looking results and did not recover how the chip works, which suggests that unlimited data plus current analysis habits is not a recipe for understanding.


75.1.3 Data requirements and parameter underdetermination

Underdetermination means that the data you have do not pin down a unique answer.

In neural modelling this is not a theoretical worry but a measured fact.

Astrid Prinz, Dirk Bucher, and Eve Marder, in Nature Neuroscience in 2004, simulated more than twenty million versions of a three-cell model of the pyloric circuit of the crab stomatogastric ganglion - a small, exhaustively studied rhythm generator - and found that widely different combinations of synaptic strengths and membrane conductances produced essentially indistinguishable output.

The implication cuts two ways.

Biologically, it means real animals probably do differ enormously in their underlying parameters while behaving the same, a property often called degeneracy (different physical arrangements delivering the same function), which Marder and colleagues have since tied to robustness and to individual differences in vulnerability to drugs and temperature.

Methodologically, it means that a large simulation which reproduces recorded activity has not thereby discovered the parameters of the real brain, because a vast family of alternative parameter sets would have reproduced it equally well.

Adding more neurons does not fix this; it multiplies it.


75.1.4 Simulation as hypothesis generator rather than as proof

The defensible role for large simulation is as an instrument for generating hypotheses and for checking whether a proposed mechanism is even sufficient in principle.

If you claim that a particular pattern of inhibitory connections is enough to produce cortical oscillations, a detailed model can refute you cheaply, before anyone spends three years on an animal experiment.

That is a genuine and underrated service: simulations are good at proving that something is not sufficient, and weak at proving that something is what the brain actually does.

Read this way, the disappointment around the flagship programmes is partly a disappointment about advertising rather than about science - the tools work, the claim of imminent whole-brain emulation did not.

A simulation earns its keep when it makes a prediction that an experimenter can go and falsify, and it earns nothing when its only output is a video of activity that looks brain-like.


75.2 Digital twins and in-silico experiments

A digital twin is a model tuned to one specific individual rather than to a species average.

In silico means in computer simulation, by analogy with in vivo (in a living body) and in vitro (in glass, meaning in a dish).

The digital twin idea is modest compared with whole-brain emulation, and precisely because it is modest it has produced the clearest clinical results in this chapter.

The recipe is standard: take a person's own anatomy from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), extract the connectome - the map of which brain regions connect to which - using diffusion imaging, hang a simple mathematical model of local dynamics on each region, and tune the model until it reproduces that person's own recorded brain activity.


75.2.1 Individualised whole-brain models

The best-developed platform is The Virtual Brain, an open-source simulator developed by Viktor Jirsa, Randy McIntosh, and colleagues, which represents each brain region not as thousands of individual neurons but as a neural mass - a compact set of equations describing the average activity of a population.

This coarse choice is deliberate: at the whole-brain scale the questions are about how regions interact, and modelling every cell would add parameters without adding answers.

Personalised models of this kind have been applied to stroke, where models fitted to healthy participants have been used to predict the pattern of functional disruption in individual patients, and to Parkinson's disease and traumatic brain injury for classification and prognosis.

The general finding is that individualised models add information beyond the raw imaging - simulated connectivity can improve prediction in people the model was never fitted to - which is the beginning of a real validation standard rather than a demonstration of resemblance.


75.2.2 Virtual epileptic patient and surgical planning

The Virtual Epileptic Patient (VEP) is the flagship application.

In drug-resistant focal epilepsy, surgery can cure seizures, but only if the surgeon removes the right tissue, and identifying the epileptogenic zone - the region whose removal stops seizures - is difficult even with electrodes implanted in the brain.

The VEP builds a personalised network model, places a seizure-generating equation set (the Epileptor model, Jirsa and colleagues, 2014) at each region, and uses Bayesian inference - a statistical method that returns a probability distribution over possible answers rather than a single guess - to estimate how epileptogenic each region is, given that patient's recorded seizures.

The approach is being tested properly rather than merely published: EPINOV is a randomised, multi-centre French trial begun in 2019 across roughly a dozen epilepsy centres, targeting around 356 patients, and is the largest randomised trial ever run in epilepsy surgery.

Its point is to ask whether adding the virtual model to standard practice actually improves the proportion of patients who become seizure-free one year after surgery.

At the time of writing, results have been discussed at meetings and in publications from the group, and the field should treat the headline question - does it beat standard care - as answered only when the trial's primary outcome is reported in full.


75.2.3 In-silico perturbation as a hypothesis-testing tool

The real power of a personalised model is that you can do to it what you may not do to a patient.

You can virtually remove a region and see whether simulated seizures stop, virtually stimulate a target and see whether the network calms, or virtually cut a fibre bundle and watch the consequences propagate.

This is in-silico perturbation, and it converts a descriptive model into something that produces testable counterfactual claims - statements about what would happen if.

It has an obvious practical use in surgical planning and in choosing targets for deep brain stimulation, and an obvious scientific use in distinguishing regions that merely participate in an event from regions that cause it.

The catch is that a virtual lesion tests the model's causal structure, not the brain's; the inference to the patient is only as good as the validation behind the model.


75.2.4 Validation standards for digital twin claims

Because the phrase digital twin invites a stronger reading than the models deserve, it is worth being explicit about what counts as evidence.

Fitting a model to a person's data and then reporting that it fits is not evidence, because the fit was the objective.

Useful standards are out-of-sample prediction (does the model predict data it never saw, in the same person or in new people), prospective prediction (was the prediction registered before the outcome was known), and clinical benefit against a randomised control, which is exactly what EPINOV was designed to supply.

There is also a quieter problem: two different modelling pipelines applied to the same person's scans can yield noticeably different connectomes and hence different twins, so reproducibility across pipelines is itself a validation question.

The field's own methodological papers have flagged this, and readers should be sceptical of any twin whose performance has only ever been assessed by its authors on their own data.


75.3 Organoids and reduced biological systems

If the simulation route abstracts the biology away, the organoid route keeps the biology and throws away almost everything else.

An organoid is a small three-dimensional tissue grown in culture from stem cells, which organises itself into structures resembling a developing organ.

Brain organoids, first described in a widely cited form by Madeline Lancaster and Juergen Knoblich in 2013, are typically grown from induced pluripotent stem cells - ordinary adult cells, often from skin or blood, reprogrammed back into a stem-cell-like state, a technique for which Shinya Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize.

They are extraordinary for studying development and disease, and they are not small brains.


75.3.1 Brain organoids and assembloids

A single organoid tends to resemble one region, and the regions of a real brain are defined partly by their conversations with each other.

Assembloids, developed principally by Sergiu Pasca and colleagues at Stanford from around 2017, address this by growing two or more region-specific organoids separately and then fusing them, so that, for example, cortical and subcortical tissue can be joined and migrating interneurons observed making the journey they make in a real fetal brain.

The approach has been extended to circuits spanning cortex, spinal cord, and muscle, producing preparations in which stimulating the cortical end makes the muscle twitch.

These are the first laboratory systems in which a human multi-region circuit can be watched forming and then disrupted by a specific genetic mutation.

They remain millimetre-scale, lack a blood supply, and so tend to develop necrotic cores unless vascularised by additional tricks.


75.3.2 Cultured networks trained on tasks

A separate tradition grows neurons on a multi-electrode array - a chip studded with electrodes that both record from and stimulate the cells - and then places the culture in a feedback loop with a simulated environment.

The best-known result is DishBrain, reported by Brett Kagan and colleagues at Cortical Labs in Neuron in 2022, in which human stem-cell-derived and mouse cortical neurons were embedded in a simplified game of Pong; the ball's position was fed in as patterned stimulation, the paddle was moved by the cells' own activity, and predictable feedback for hits versus unpredictable feedback for misses served as the training signal.

The cultures improved measurably within about twenty minutes, and the authors interpreted this through the free energy principle, the idea associated with Karl Friston that a system will act to reduce the unpredictability of its sensory input.

A related biohybrid line, Brainoware, reported by Feng Guo's group at Indiana University in Nature Electronics in 2023, used a brain organoid on an electrode array as the reservoir in reservoir computing - a scheme in which a fixed, complex dynamical system transforms inputs and only a simple readout layer is trained - and applied it to speaker identification and a nonlinear prediction task.

Two cautions are worth stating plainly: the paper's use of the word sentience drew substantial criticism as overreach, and the performance figures are modest next to conventional machine learning, so the interest here is in the biology and the energy budget, not in the benchmark scores.


75.3.3 What organoids can and cannot model about cognition

Organoids are best understood as models of neural development and of cell-level disease mechanisms, and they have already earned that role - they have illuminated how the Zika virus damages the fetal cortex, how microcephaly-causing mutations disturb progenitor division, and how neurons carrying autism-linked or schizophrenia-linked variants behave differently.

What they lack is nearly everything cognition requires.

They have no body and no sensory organs, so no natural input; no thalamus routing that input and no reliable long-range white matter; no consistent laminar architecture matching a real cortex; typically no vasculature, no microglia unless deliberately added, and no immune or hormonal context.

They also stall developmentally, corresponding roughly to fetal stages rather than to a mature brain, and their organisation varies substantially from batch to batch.

A culture that learns to keep a simulated ball in play demonstrates plasticity, which is a property of neural tissue, and does not demonstrate cognition, which is a property of whole organisms with goals.


75.3.4 The moral status question raised by neural tissue that learns

Moral status means being the kind of entity whose interests we are obliged to consider.

The question here is not whether current organoids are conscious - the consensus among researchers and bioethicists is that they almost certainly are not, lacking the input, the scale, and the architecture - but that we have no agreed test that would tell us if that changed.

The concern is taken seriously enough that the United States National Academies reviewed it in 2021, and a substantial 2024 and 2025 bioethics literature has grown up around it, with proposals ranging from precautionary thresholds tied to organised electrical activity, to standardised terminology, to anticipatory governance that sets rules before the capability arrives rather than after.

A frequently made intermediate argument is that the practically urgent question is not human-like consciousness but whether an organoid might acquire the moral status we already grant laboratory animals such as mice, which would bring it under existing welfare frameworks rather than requiring new ones.

Genuine disagreement exists: some philosophers hold that sentience requires embodiment and an evolutionary or metabolic stake in one's own survival, which cultured tissue lacks; others hold that suffering could in principle be realised by any sufficiently organised neural activity, embodied or not.

The one position that is hard to defend is the assumption that the question will never arise, since the explicit aim of the organoid intelligence programme articulated by Thomas Hartung and colleagues in 2023 is to make these cultures larger, longer-lived, and better connected to inputs.


75.4 Neuromorphic and alternative substrates

Neuromorphic means brain-shaped, and in engineering it refers to hardware that borrows the brain's computational style rather than merely running brain software on ordinary computers.

The term is due to Carver Mead at Caltech in the late 1980s, who observed that transistors operated below their switching threshold behave rather like ion channels, and that the brain's efficiency might follow from physics rather than from cleverness.

The relevance to a book about cognition is twofold: such hardware is a testbed for theories about why brains compute the way they do, and it forces a sharp question about whether the substrate matters at all.


75.4.1 Spiking neuromorphic hardware

The defining feature is event-driven computation.

In a conventional processor, every element is clocked and consumes power whether or not anything interesting is happening; in a spiking neuromorphic chip, a unit consumes energy only when it emits a spike, and memory sits next to computation rather than across a bus, avoiding the constant shuttling of data that dominates the energy cost of conventional machines.

The main platforms are SpiNNaker, built by Steve Furber's group in Manchester from many small ARM processors and designed specifically to deliver spikes as messages, with SpiNNaker 2 developed with TU Dresden; Intel's Loihi, now Loihi 2, with on-chip learning rules; and IBM's TrueNorth and its 2023 successor NorthPole.

Intel's Hala Point system, announced in 2024, assembles 1,152 Loihi 2 chips into a research machine of roughly 1.15 billion neurons, comparable in neuron count to an owl.

It is worth naming what these machines have not yet done: there is no neuromorphic system that beats conventional hardware on the tasks most people care about, and adoption outside research remains limited.


75.4.2 Energy efficiency as the design driver

The motivating number is the human brain's power budget of roughly twenty watts, about the draw of a dim light bulb, for a system of some eighty-six billion neurons.

Training and running large artificial neural networks costs many orders of magnitude more, and that gap - not any philosophical commitment - is what funds neuromorphic engineering.

Reported gains are real but narrow: published comparisons claim energy reductions of one to two orders of magnitude and large latency improvements for specific workloads such as sparse, streaming, or optimisation problems, while dense matrix multiplication, the operation that dominates modern artificial intelligence, remains the domain of graphics processing units (GPUs).

Readers should treat vendor benchmark ratios with care, since the comparison chip, task, and precision are chosen by the party reporting the gain.

The scientific interest is that the brain's most distinctive features - sparse spiking, local learning, colocated memory - look increasingly like solutions to an energy problem, which is a substantive hypothesis about why cognition has the shape it does.


75.4.3 Substrate independence and its limits

Substrate independence is the claim that what matters about a mind is the pattern of computation, not the material implementing it, so that a sufficiently faithful copy in another medium would have the same mental properties.

It follows from computational functionalism, the position associated with Hilary Putnam and Jerry Fodor that mental states are defined by their functional roles, and it is the assumption underneath every proposal for whole-brain emulation or mind uploading.

It is not established, and it has come under sustained pressure recently.

Rosa Cao has argued that classic multiple-realizability arguments rested on oversimplified pictures of both computation and neurobiology; Paul Thagard has argued in Philosophy of Science that energy requirements undermine substrate independence, because the Church-Turing thesis abstracts away exactly the time, space, and energy constraints that a real mind must satisfy; and a line of work in biology argues that properties such as membrane excitability, biomolecular condensates, and dynamic cell adhesion may be part of the function rather than mere implementation detail.

The counter-argument remains strong: neurons themselves are replaceable at the molecular level over time, cochlear implants substitute for hair cells without anyone claiming the resulting hearing is fake, and no one has identified a specific biological property that provably cannot be replicated.

The honest position is that substrate independence is a working assumption of a large research programme, defended by argument rather than demonstrated by evidence, and that its truth is precisely what emulation would test.


75.4.4 Reconstruction as the strongest test of understanding

The reason all four of these enterprises belong in one chapter is that they share a logic: build it, and see whether it behaves.

Reconstruction is an unusually unforgiving test, because a verbal theory can survive vagueness and a simulation cannot - every parameter you did not know, you must nonetheless supply.

That is its virtue: attempting to build a thing reveals the size of your ignorance with a precision no review article achieves, which is why the failures in this chapter are as informative as the successes.

It is not a sufficient test on its own, for the reasons Jonas and Kording demonstrated with a microprocessor and Prinz, Bucher, and Marder demonstrated with a crab: a working replica whose workings you cannot interrogate has not explained anything, and a replica that matches the data may have matched it by an entirely different route.

The productive reading is that reconstruction is the strongest available check on sufficiency - it tells you whether your proposed ingredients could in principle do the job - and that necessity, the question of whether the brain actually does it that way, still has to be settled in the animal.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The flagship simulation programmes of the last two decades, Blue Brain and the Human Brain Project, delivered atlases, tools, and infrastructure rather than the simulated brain their early publicity promised, and the retrospective consensus after the Human Brain Project's close in 2023 is that the ambition outran the data.

Simulations are underdetermined in a way that more computing power does not cure, as Prinz, Bucher, and Marder showed in 2004 by producing indistinguishable circuit output from vastly different parameter sets, so a model that fits the data has not thereby recovered the brain's parameters.

The most convincing applications are the modest ones: personalised digital twins such as the Virtual Epileptic Patient, whose claims are being tested against standard care in the randomised EPINOV trial rather than asserted from goodness of fit.

Organoids, assembloids, and cultured networks that learn simple tasks are powerful models of neural development and plasticity and are not models of cognition, since they lack bodies, sensory input, long-range architecture, and maturity - though they raise a real and unresolved question about the moral status of learning tissue.

Neuromorphic hardware is best understood as evidence that the brain's sparse, event-driven, memory-adjacent design is a solution to an energy problem, and its underlying premise of substrate independence remains a defended assumption rather than an established fact.

Building a thing is the sharpest test of whether you understand it, but only when the built thing can be interrogated, and only when success is measured by prediction rather than by resemblance.


CHAPTER 76. THE READING AND WRITING OF MINDS (CONTEXT)

This chapter asks two blunt questions.

Can a machine read what is in your mind, and can a machine write something into it?

The honest answer to both is a heavily qualified yes, and the qualifications are where all the interesting content lives.

Laboratory systems can now turn brain scans into recognisable pictures and into sentences that carry the gist of what a person was seeing, hearing, or imagining, and stimulating electrodes can put simple shapes, touches, and in animals whole false memories into a nervous system.

At the same time, every one of those demonstrations depends on conditions - a cooperating volunteer, hours of individual calibration, a large stationary scanner, or surgery - that make the science-fiction version of mind reading unavailable today.

The chapter matters because law and commerce are moving on this technology now, before the technology is mature, and the gap between what is real and what is claimed is exactly where people get harmed.


76.1 Decoding capabilities as they stand

Decoding means going backwards.

Instead of asking what the brain does when a person sees a face, the decoder asks what the person must have been seeing given this pattern of brain activity.

The dominant method uses functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a scanner that tracks blood oxygenation as an indirect and slow proxy for neural activity, together with machine learning models trained on many hours of data from that one individual.

That last point governs everything that follows in this section.


76.1.1 Visual reconstruction from brain activity

The clearest demonstrations reconstruct pictures a person was looking at from the activity of their visual cortex, the sheet of tissue at the back of the head that receives input from the eyes.

Takagi and Nishimoto, presenting at the 2023 Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) conference, fed fMRI signals into Stable Diffusion, a latent diffusion model - an image generator that works by repeatedly denoising a compressed representation of a picture - and recovered images whose layout and content plainly matched the originals.

The trick is that the brain data does not have to generate the picture by itself; it only has to steer a generator that already knows what natural images look like.

That is a real achievement and also a caution, because a strong generative prior can supply plausible detail that was never in the brain signal at all.

These reconstructions are trained per person on tens of hours of scanning, typically using shared public datasets such as the Natural Scenes Dataset, and they degrade badly when applied to someone the model has not been trained on.


76.1.2 Continuous semantic decoding of imagined and heard language

Tang, LeBel, Jain and Huth, publishing in Nature Neuroscience in 2023, built what they called a semantic decoder, which reconstructs continuous language from fMRI without any surgery.

They used a language model to turn candidate sentences into semantic features, learned how each volunteer's cortex responds to those features, and then searched for the word sequence whose predicted brain response best matched what was actually recorded.

The output is not a transcript; it is a paraphrase that often preserves meaning while losing exact wording, and it worked for speech the person heard, speech they merely imagined, and even for silent films they watched.

Horikawa's 2025 Science Advances work, which the press called mind captioning, extended the idea to generating whole descriptive sentences about remembered video clips by iteratively editing candidate captions until their features matched the brain-decoded features.

Both results are striking, and both were obtained from a handful of volunteers who each spent many hours in a scanner.


76.1.3 Decoding of intention, attention, and affective state

Decoding is not limited to what a person perceives.

Haynes and colleagues, in a 2007 Current Biology study, read out from medial prefrontal cortex - a region on the inner surface of the frontal lobe associated with planning and self-referential thought - whether a volunteer intended to add or to subtract two numbers they had not yet been shown.

Covert attention, meaning where you are attending without moving your eyes, can be decoded from early visual areas at accuracies well above chance, on the order of seventy to eighty percent in favourable designs.

Affective state - broadly, emotional feeling - is decodable in a coarse sense, along dimensions like pleasant versus unpleasant and calm versus aroused, but decoding a specific named emotion in a single individual on a single trial remains unreliable.

An important and often ignored caveat is reverse inference: observing activity in a region does not license the conclusion that a particular mental process occurred, because most regions participate in many processes.


76.1.4 Accuracy, cooperation requirements, and current hard limits

The Tang and Huth group deliberately tested whether their decoder could be used against an unwilling person, and reported that it could not.

Subject cooperation was required both to train the decoder and to run it; volunteers who silently counted, named animals, or attended to a different story defeated it, and a decoder trained on one person produced nonsense when applied to another.

The physical constraints are just as limiting: fMRI requires a person to lie still inside a large superconducting magnet, and its blood-flow signal lags neural events by several seconds, which caps how finely anything can be resolved in time.

Portable methods such as electroencephalography (EEG), which records voltage fluctuations at the scalp, are far more convenient and far less informative, because the skull blurs the signal and the recording is easily swamped by muscle and eye movement.

The fair summary is that decoding today is a consented, calibrated, per-person laboratory measurement, not a scanner you can point at a stranger.


76.2 Writing into the brain

Reading is the easier half.

Writing means delivering patterned energy - light or current - to specific neurons in a way the rest of the brain will interpret as experience rather than as noise.

The problem is not switching neurons on; that is straightforward.

The problem is that a natural percept or memory involves a precisely structured pattern across many cells over time, and current tools are blunt by comparison.


76.2.1 Patterned optogenetic and electrical stimulation to induce percepts

Electrical stimulation of visual cortex produces phosphenes, which are spots of light seen in the absence of any light entering the eye, an effect known since Brindley and Lewin's work in 1968.

The naive hope was that many electrodes would act like pixels on a screen, and that hope has largely failed, because simultaneously stimulated phosphenes merge into an indistinct blob.

Beauchamp and colleagues, in a 2020 Cell paper, got around this by tracing shapes: they stimulated electrodes in rapid sequence, and used current steering - shifting current gradually between two electrodes to place a phosphene between them - so that blind and sighted participants perceived letters drawn out like a finger tracing on skin.

Optogenetics, the technique of making chosen neurons express a light-sensitive protein such as channelrhodopsin-2 so they can be driven by pulses of light, gives far finer control in animals, and holographic two-photon methods can now activate designated individual cortical cells and thereby bias what a mouse reports seeing.

Optogenetics requires gene delivery into the brain and so has only begun to enter human use in a very limited retinal context.


76.2.2 Memory implantation in animal models

The most famous writing experiment is Ramirez, Liu and Tonegawa's 2013 Science study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

They genetically tagged the hippocampal neurons active while a mouse explored one box - an engram, meaning the physical trace of a specific memory - then reactivated that tagged population with light while shocking the animal in a different box.

Afterwards the mouse froze in fear in the first box, where nothing bad had ever happened to it, which is as close to an implanted false memory as anyone has produced.

In humans the nearest analogue is far more modest: Hampson, Deadwyler, Berger and Song reported in 2018 in the Journal of Neural Engineering a hippocampal prosthesis in epilepsy patients that recorded the person's own neural code during successful encoding and played a modelled version back, improving recall by roughly a third in a short-term memory task.

That is facilitation of a person's own memory process, not the insertion of content, and the sample sizes were small.


76.2.3 Sensory substitution and augmentation

Sensory substitution routes information from a missing sense through an intact one, on the principle Paul Bach-y-Rita summarised as seeing with the brain, not the eyes.

His tongue display, commercialised as BrainPort, converts a head-mounted camera image into a grid of small electrical pulses on the tongue; trained blind users can locate objects and read large letters, at an acuity roughly equivalent to 20/800 vision.

The vOICe system does the same job through hearing, sweeping the image left to right and coding height as pitch and brightness as loudness.

These devices work, in the limited sense that users acquire real skill and neuroimaging shows visual cortex recruited during the task, but adoption outside research has been poor because training is demanding and the bandwidth is low.

Claims of genuine augmentation - adding a sense humans do not have, such as magnetic north through a vibrating belt - rest on a much thinner evidence base, mostly small studies without control groups.


76.2.4 The distance between animal demonstrations and human application

It is worth stating plainly why the mouse results do not transfer.

They depend on genetically modifying neurons, on implanting optical fibres through the skull, and on the experimenter knowing in advance which population encodes which memory because they tagged it during the original event.

None of those conditions can be met in a person who has not consented to brain surgery and gene delivery, and no one can tag a memory that has already formed.

Human writing therefore remains confined to coarse electrical stimulation for restoring function - deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease, cochlear implants, experimental visual and memory prostheses - and coarse stimulation cannot specify content.

The honest formulation is that we can write sensations and modulate processes, and we cannot write thoughts.


76.3 Consumer and non-clinical neurotechnology

Everything above happens under ethics review with informed consent.

The consumer market operates under none of that, sells to millions, and makes claims that outrun the laboratory considerably.


76.3.1 Wearable electroencephalography and its claims

Consumer headbands such as Muse and Emotiv place a few dry electrodes on the scalp and advertise readouts of focus, calm, stress, or meditation.

The physics is unforgiving: with few electrodes, no conductive gel, and no shielding, the recording is dominated by artefacts from blinking, jaw clenching, and head movement, and a device can appear to detect concentration while actually detecting that you stopped fidgeting.

A 2023 scoping review in PLOS One found consumer-grade EEG usable for some research purposes but highly variable across devices, and independent testing has repeatedly found proprietary attention and meditation indices to track their advertised states poorly.

Raw EEG from these devices is genuinely informative for coarse things such as sleep staging and drowsiness; the marketed mental-state metrics are the weak part.

A fair position is that the sensor is often real and the interpretation layer is usually unvalidated.


76.3.2 Workplace and educational monitoring

Fatigue-detecting caps, notably SmartCap, are in routine use by mining, trucking and aviation operators, where a drowsiness alert has an obvious safety rationale.

Reporting from 2018, including MIT Technology Review, described Chinese factories, rail operators and military units fitting workers with brainwave-sensing caps and analysing the data for signs of anxiety, anger or fatigue.

School deployments of attention-scoring headbands, most publicised in China around 2019, drew heavy criticism and were curtailed after backlash.

The core objection is not accuracy but asymmetry: an employee or a child cannot meaningfully refuse, and a noisy signal used for discipline or ranking is worse than no signal, because it carries an unearned air of objectivity.

The UNESCO Recommendation adopted in November 2025 explicitly warns against workplace use for productivity monitoring or employee profiling.


76.3.3 Marketing and neuro-branding claims

Neuromarketing sells the promise of a buy button in the brain, revealed by EEG or fMRI while consumers view advertisements.

There are modest legitimate findings - some studies report that neural responses in reward-related regions add predictive power for aggregate market outcomes beyond what surveys capture - but the commercial claims go far past that.

The recurring methodological sin is reverse inference: seeing activity near the nucleus accumbens, a region associated with anticipated reward, and announcing that consumers desire the product, when that region also responds to novelty, surprise and salience.

Much of the industry's evidence is proprietary, unpublished, and never subjected to peer review or preregistration, which makes independent evaluation impossible.

Treat any neuro-branding claim without a public, replicated method as advertising about advertising.


76.3.4 Evidentiary standards for consumer neurotechnology

The regulatory gap is straightforward: a device that treats a disease is a medical device and must show safety and effectiveness, while a device that promises wellness, focus or relaxation usually escapes that requirement entirely.

Reasonable minimum standards have been proposed repeatedly and are not exotic - publish the raw signal quality, publish the algorithm's validation against an accepted reference measure, show test-retest reliability, and report performance in the messy conditions of real use rather than a quiet laboratory.

A 2025 benchmarking study in Brain Informatics found that wearable EEG performance degrades sharply in movement-rich tasks such as driving or multitasking, which is precisely where the devices are marketed.

The asymmetry that should worry a buyer is that the marketing claim and the data claim are separable: the company can be wrong about what its numbers mean and still collect and retain your neural data.

Until a validation norm exists, the consumer's only defence is to treat unvalidated metrics as entertainment.


76.4 Governance

Law is arriving faster here than the technology is maturing, which is unusual and creates its own difficulty.

Rules written against an imagined mind-reading machine may miss the actual risk, which is the accumulation and inference-rich reuse of ordinary neural data.


76.4.1 Mental privacy and neural data protection

Neural data are distinctive in three ways: they are involuntary, in that you cannot consciously withhold your alpha rhythm; they are rich, in that a recording gathered for one purpose can later be mined for another as algorithms improve; and they are hard to anonymise, since individual response patterns are close to a fingerprint.

That last property is the strongest technical argument for treating neural data as a sensitive category rather than as ordinary personal data.
