Colorado amended its privacy act in 2024 to classify neural data as sensitive, California followed later in 2024 by extending its consumer privacy law to neural data, and Montana enacted a related protection in 2025.

These statutes mostly regulate collection, consent and sale, and they apply to consumer devices where clinical rules do not reach.

Critics point out, fairly, that the harder problem is inference from data that is not neural at all - keystroke timing, gaze, voice - which these laws do not touch.


76.4.2 Proposals for neurorights

The neurorights movement, associated with Rafael Yuste and the Morningside Group's 2017 Nature commentary, proposes recognising mental privacy, personal identity, free will, fair access to augmentation, and protection from bias as rights in their own right.

Chile went furthest, amending its constitution in 2021 to protect brain activity and neural data, and its Supreme Court applied that protection in a 2023 ruling against a consumer device company, Emotiv.

United Nations Human Rights Council Resolution 58/6, adopted in April 2025, asked for guidance on applying existing human rights law to neurotechnology, and UNESCO's General Conference adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology on 12 November 2025, the first global standard of its kind, though it is not legally binding.

There is real disagreement here, and it should not be smoothed over: a substantial group of legal scholars, including critiques published in 2025, argue that new rights are unnecessary because privacy, bodily integrity and freedom of thought already cover the ground, and that inventing rights against speculative capabilities dilutes the human rights framework.

The counterargument is that existing law is drafted around behaviour and communication, and says little about the substrate that produces them.


76.4.3 Regulation of implanted devices and post-trial obligations

Implanted research devices raise a problem that ordinary drug trials do not: the trial ends, but the hardware is still in the person's head.

Surveys of investigators, including an international study published in 2024, found near-unanimous agreement that there is an obligation to continue supporting participants who benefited, alongside frank admission that funding, expertise and manufacturer cooperation frequently do not exist.

Concrete cases make the point better than principle does.

Second Sight's Argus II retinal implant was effectively discontinued, leaving recipients with unsupported hardware and failing devices; participants in early BrainGate work were left with implants after Cyberkinetics folded; and Ian Burkhart, who regained hand control through a cortical implant, had it removed when the funded study ended.

Explantation can carry a substantial cost, reported in the low tens of thousands of dollars in some deep brain stimulation cases, and there is often no clear party responsible for paying it.

The workable remedies proposed are unglamorous and specific: escrowed maintenance funding, mandatory device-support commitments as a condition of trial approval, open device specifications so a third party can maintain hardware, and consent documents that state in advance what happens if the sponsor disappears.


76.4.4 Dual use and security considerations

Neurotechnology is inherently dual use, meaning the same device serves care and coercion depending on who holds it, a point argued by Ienca, Jotterand and Elger in Neuron in 2018.

Military investment is open rather than hidden; the United States Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) ran the Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology (N3) programme from 2018 to develop wearable bidirectional interfaces for able-bodied service members, aimed at tasks such as supervising drone swarms.

A separate and more immediate risk is brainjacking, the unauthorised control of an implanted stimulator, which is not hypothetical in the sense that implanted neurostimulators use wireless telemetry, are rarely designed with strong authentication, and cannot be patched easily once implanted.

The consequences of compromise are unlike those of a stolen password, since an attacker with control of a deep brain stimulator could alter mood, movement, or impulse control.

The UNESCO Recommendation addresses part of this by prohibiting use of neurotechnology in unlawful interrogation and in coercive behavioural conformity, and by setting cybersecurity expectations, but enforcement rests with individual states.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Decoding is real and bounded: fMRI-based systems can reconstruct images and recover the gist of heard or imagined language, as shown by Takagi and Nishimoto in 2023, Tang and Huth in 2023, and Horikawa in 2025, but every such system needs a cooperating person, hours of individual training data, and a stationary scanner, and cooperation can be withdrawn simply by thinking about something else.

Writing is cruder than reading: patterned electrical stimulation can trace shapes into visual cortex, optogenetics can implant a false context-fear memory in a mouse, and a hippocampal prosthesis can boost a person's own recall, but no method can specify the content of a human thought.

The consumer market runs far ahead of the evidence, with real sensors attached to largely unvalidated interpretations of focus, calm and desire, and with no requirement to prove either.

Governance has moved quickly - Chile's constitutional amendment in 2021, Colorado, California and Montana's neural data statutes in 2024 and 2025, United Nations Human Rights Council Resolution 58/6 in April 2025, and UNESCO's Recommendation in November 2025 - while scholars continue to disagree about whether new rights are needed or existing ones suffice.

The most concrete harms visible today are not mind reading at all: they are unvalidated metrics used to judge workers and children, neural data collected and retained without meaningful consent, implant recipients abandoned when a company or a grant ends, and implanted devices whose wireless interfaces were never designed to resist attack.


PART FIFTEEN. INTEGRATION, ETHICS, AND WHAT REMAINS UNSOLVED


CHAPTER 77. THE OPEN PROBLEMS (CORE)

This chapter is an honest inventory of what the neuroscience of cognition has not solved.

Every earlier chapter described findings that hold up reasonably well.

This one describes the holes those findings sit around, and it does not try to paper over them.

The problems are grouped into four families: problems of code and representation, problems of learning, problems of integration across levels of description, and problems concerning the subject who does the cognising.

Knowing where the field is genuinely stuck matters, because a beginner who mistakes an open question for a settled fact will misread the next twenty years of results.

Throughout, where a claim is disputed, both sides are named.


77.1 Problems of code and representation

A code is a systematic mapping between one kind of thing and another - here, between patterns of neural activity and the world, or the task, or the thought.

The chapters on vision, memory, and language all assumed such a mapping existed and could be read out.

This section asks whether that assumption is safe.

The short answer is that we can decode a great deal from brain activity without knowing what, if anything, the brain itself is reading.


77.1.1 What the neural code actually is, and whether there is one

Neurons communicate mainly with spikes, brief electrical pulses called action potentials, and the central question is what feature of those spikes carries the message.

Rate coding says the message is the number of spikes in some window, so a neuron firing at eighty spikes per second means something different from one firing at ten.

Temporal coding says the message is in the precise timing of individual spikes, including their timing relative to other neurons or to an ongoing brain rhythm - the phase precession of hippocampal place cells reported by O'Keefe and Recce in 1993 is the classic example, where a cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the theta rhythm as an animal crosses its preferred location.

The debate is live and probably badly posed: many working neurophysiologists now argue that the nervous system uses whichever code the statistics of the stimulus and the demands of the task call for, so that asking for the neural code is like asking for the human language.

There is a deeper worry that goes beyond rate versus timing, namely that the notion of a code smuggles in a reader.

A code needs a decoder, and if no downstream circuit ever performs the decoding that an experimenter performs with a machine-learning classifier, then the code we report may be a property of our analysis rather than of the brain.

This is not a fringe complaint, and it recurs in 77.3.3 as the representational-versus-dynamical dispute.


77.1.2 The binding problem in its several forms

The binding problem was posed in its modern form by Christoph von der Malsburg in 1981, and it arises because the visual cortex takes an image apart.

Separate populations of neurons respond to colour, to orientation, to motion, to depth, so when you see a red square moving left beside a green circle moving right, the brain must keep track of which colour goes with which shape and which motion.

Anne Treisman's feature integration theory, developed from 1980 onward, proposed that spatial attention does the gluing: features are registered in parallel across separate feature maps, and focused attention on a location binds whatever is there, with illusory conjunctions - seeing a red circle when a red square and a green circle were shown - as the predicted failure mode when attention is overloaded.

Von der Malsburg's rival proposal was temporal synchrony, where neurons coding features of the same object fire in near-simultaneity, and Gray and Singer's 1989 report of stimulus-dependent gamma-band synchronisation in cat visual cortex was taken as support.

Synchrony has not aged well as a general solution, partly for the logical reason Goldfarb and Treisman pressed - when several objects share some features and differ in others, a single synchrony tag cannot express the pattern - and partly because the empirical link between gamma synchrony and perceptual grouping proved inconsistent across laboratories.

Jerome Feldman's 2013 paper "The neural binding problem(s)" makes the important point that binding is not one problem but at least four: visual feature binding, binding of an object to its location and to variables in a task, binding of the many properties of a remembered episode, and the binding of experience into a unified conscious scene.

The first two look tractable and are being chipped away at.

The last one is close to the hard problem of 77.4.1 and is not obviously a neuroscience problem at all.


77.1.3 How symbols and compositional structure are implemented

Compositionality is the property by which the meaning of a whole is determined by its parts and the way they are put together, so that "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" use identical parts to different effect.

Human thought and language are compositional in this way, and the difficulty is that a population of neurons encoding a set of features has, on the face of it, no way to say which feature belongs to which role.

One family of proposals is vector symbolic architectures, also called hyperdimensional computing, in which symbols are very high-dimensional vectors and roles are attached to fillers by a mathematical binding operation such as circular convolution, with superposition by addition used to hold several bound pairs at once - Tony Plate's holographic reduced representations from 1995 and Paul Smolensky's tensor product representations from 1990 are the founding versions.

These schemes are elegant, they are provably capable of representing structure in a distributed format, and they have inspired real hardware; what they conspicuously lack is direct evidence that any cortical circuit implements the binding operation they require.

A second family holds that structure need not be implemented symbolically at all, and points to large language models, which handle a great deal of syntax without an explicit symbol table, though critics including Gary Marcus argue that their generalisation to genuinely novel combinations remains brittle.

The honest position in 2026 is that we have several workable formalisms and no confirmed neural implementation of any of them.


77.1.4 How abstraction is achieved and reused

Abstraction means representing what several different situations have in common while discarding what distinguishes them, which is what lets you apply the idea of a queue to a supermarket and to a printer.

Bernardi, Salzman and colleagues gave abstraction an operational neural definition in a 2020 paper in Cell: a variable is represented abstractly if a decoder trained on one set of task conditions still works on conditions it never saw, which requires the population activity to lie in a particular geometry where the variable is coded along a consistent direction.

They found such abstract geometry in monkey hippocampus and prefrontal cortex simultaneously with the high-dimensional, condition-specific coding that supports flexible discrimination, suggesting the brain does not choose between the two.

What remains open is how these formats arise during learning, how they are addressed and reused by other circuits, and whether abstract geometry is a cause of generalisation or merely a signature of it.

The reuse question is particularly untouched: a person who learns an abstraction in one domain can often deploy it in another within seconds, and there is no accepted circuit account of that transfer.


77.2 Problems of learning

Learning in the brain must solve problems that machine learning solves with tools the brain plainly does not have.

This section takes four of them in turn.

The common thread is that artificial systems buy their competence with quantities of data, storage, and mathematical machinery that biology cannot afford.


77.2.1 Biological credit assignment across depth and time

Credit assignment is the problem of deciding which of the many synapses involved in producing an outcome deserves the blame or the credit when the outcome is good or bad.

Artificial networks solve it with backpropagation, an algorithm that computes the exact contribution of every weight by passing an error signal backwards through the same connections used in the forward pass.

Backpropagation is biologically awkward for at least three reasons: it requires the backward pathway to use exactly the same weights as the forward pathway, which is called the weight transport problem; it requires an error signal to travel without itself disturbing the activity it is correcting; and for learning across time it requires storing the whole history of activity, which is what backpropagation through time does.

Proposed biological solutions include feedback alignment, in which Lillicrap, Cownden, Tweed and Akerman showed in 2016 that random fixed backward weights still support learning because the forward weights align themselves to them; dendritic accounts in which the apical and basal compartments of a pyramidal neuron carry the target and the prediction separately, developed by Guerguiev, Lillicrap and Richards in 2017 and by Sacramento and colleagues; equilibrium propagation from Scellier and Bengio in 2017; and eligibility-trace rules such as the e-prop rule of Bellec and colleagues in 2020, which keeps a local decaying memory at each synapse so that a later reward can be matched to earlier activity.

None of these has been confirmed as the rule the cortex actually uses, and a 2025 analysis of e-prop found that biologically plausible temporal rules do not yet match backpropagation through time in the similarity of the representations they produce to recorded neural data.

Credit assignment is therefore best described as a problem with many plausible answers and no verdict.


77.2.2 One-shot learning and rapid generalisation

A child shown one zebra recognises the next zebra, and a person told once where the fire exit is remembers it.

Standard gradient-based learning cannot do this, because a single large weight change to capture one example would overwrite everything else.

The biological answer is thought to involve the hippocampus, whose dentate gyrus performs pattern separation - making similar inputs into dissimilar internal codes so they do not collide - while area CA3's dense recurrent connectivity performs pattern completion, retrieving the whole memory from a fragment.

Work on schemas by Tse, Morris and colleagues from 2007 showed that rats with a pre-existing spatial schema could learn new flavour-place pairings in a single trial and consolidate them within forty-eight hours instead of weeks, which indicates that rapid learning depends on already having the right structure to slot the new fact into.

What is unresolved is how the fast hippocampal system and the slow cortical system negotiate, how a schema is represented well enough to accept a new item, and why one-shot learning generalises correctly rather than overfitting to the single example.


77.2.3 Continual learning without interference

Catastrophic forgetting is the failure mode in which an artificial network trained on a second task overwrites what it learned on the first, and it is the sharpest single behavioural difference between current artificial networks and animals.

The underlying tension is called the stability-plasticity dilemma: a system rigid enough to protect old knowledge is too rigid to acquire new knowledge, and a system plastic enough to learn quickly forgets quickly.

Complementary learning systems theory, formulated by McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly in 1995, is the standard biological answer: the hippocampus learns fast and specifically, the neocortex learns slowly and in overlapping distributed fashion, and replay of hippocampal activity during sleep and quiet rest interleaves old material with new so the cortex never sees a purely novel training set.

Engineering has taken this seriously, and generative replay and sleep-like replay phases do measurably reduce forgetting in artificial networks, with work through 2025 on corticohippocampal hybrid architectures reported in Nature Communications.

Nevertheless the biological story is incomplete: we do not know what selects which experiences get replayed, how synaptic consolidation and systems consolidation divide the labour, or why humans still forget a great deal despite all this machinery.

There is also a mirror-image problem now recognised in artificial systems, loss of plasticity, where a network trained continually gradually becomes unable to learn anything new at all, and whether ageing brains suffer the same thing is an open empirical question.


77.2.4 The origin of inductive biases: evolution, development, or experience

An inductive bias is a built-in assumption that lets a learner generalise from little data, such as the assumption that objects persist when hidden, or that word meanings tend to pick out whole objects rather than parts.

Anthony Zador's 2019 argument, elaborated in a 2024 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) with Shuvaev and colleagues, is the genomic bottleneck: the human genome carries on the order of a gigabyte of information while the connectome comprises something like a hundred trillion synapses, so the genome cannot specify wiring synapse by synapse and must instead encode compact rules for growing circuits.

Zador draws the moral that much animal competence is innate, laid down by evolution as a highly structured starting architecture, and that the compression forced by the bottleneck acts as a regulariser that improves generalisation.

Gary Marcus makes a compatible nativist argument for human language and core knowledge, whereas researchers in the deep learning tradition reply that a small number of generic architectural motifs plus large amounts of experience can produce the same competences without innate representations.

The disagreement is real and is not going to be settled by argument, since the empirical question - how much structure is present before experience, and in what form - requires developmental data at a resolution we do not yet have.

The safest formulation, and one both camps accept, is that the useful question is not whether a capacity is innate but how innate structure and experience interact during development.


77.3 Problems of integration

Neuroscience is not one science but a stack of them, running from ion channels to social behaviour.

The problems in this section are not about missing data but about the relations between descriptions that are each locally successful.

They are as much philosophical as experimental, which is why they resist being solved by a better microscope.


77.3.1 Bridging molecular, cellular, circuit, and systems descriptions

David Marr's 1982 framework proposed three levels at which any information-processing system should be understood: the computational level, meaning what problem is being solved and why; the algorithmic level, meaning what representations and procedures solve it; and the implementational level, meaning what physical stuff carries it out.

The framework remains the standard vocabulary, and a 2024 exchange in The Journal of Physiology between Lengyel and Pillow defended it on pragmatic grounds while conceding that the levels are not as separable as Marr implied, since implementation often constrains algorithm heavily.

The practical difficulty is that biology has more than three levels and the bridges between them are missing: we can describe a potassium channel's kinetics precisely and we can describe working memory behaviourally, and there is no continuous chain of explanation connecting the two.

Efforts such as large-scale simulation projects have attempted to build the chain by brute force, with mixed results, and the European Human Brain Project's decade of work is widely regarded as having produced valuable infrastructure without delivering the promised integrated simulation.

The open problem is whether integration will come from a genuine multiscale theory or whether the levels will remain linked only by loose correspondence.


77.3.2 Reconciling localisation with distributed and network accounts

Localisation is the idea that a particular function lives in a particular place, and it has real successes - damage to the fusiform face area impairs face recognition, damage to the hippocampus impairs the formation of new episodic memories.

Against this, Michael Anderson's neural reuse or massive redeployment hypothesis, set out in 2010, holds that because building new circuitry is metabolically expensive, evolution reuses existing circuits for new purposes, so most regions participate in many cognitive domains and no region is the seat of anything.

Degeneracy compounds the problem: structurally different circuits can produce the same function under some conditions and different functions under others, so a one-to-one map from structure to function does not exist to be found.

Lesion network mapping, developed by Michael Fox and colleagues from 2015, is a partial reconciliation, showing that lesions in scattered locations that produce the same symptom tend to fall within a common functional network, so the correct unit of localisation may be a network rather than a patch of tissue.

Anderson himself has expressed pessimism that specific neural mechanisms will generally be assignable to specific cognitive operations, and this remains a minority-but-serious position rather than a consensus.


77.3.3 Reconciling representational with dynamical descriptions

A representational account says a neuron's firing stands for something - a direction of movement, a colour, a remembered digit - and explains behaviour by what is represented.

A dynamical account says the population is a dynamical system, meaning a set of variables whose current state determines how the state changes next, and explains behaviour by the trajectory the system follows rather than by what any neuron stands for.

Motor cortex is the sharpest battleground: Churchland, Shenoy and colleagues showed in 2012 that population activity during reaching contains rotational structure that is naturally described as a dynamical system generating a movement, and Michaels, Dann and Scherberger argued in 2016 in PLOS Computational Biology that reaching activity is better explained by a dynamical system than by representational tuning to movement parameters.

The complicating result in the same line of work is that recurrent neural networks trained to produce movements develop both rotational dynamics and apparent representational tuning, which suggests the two descriptions may be different views of one thing rather than rival hypotheses.

Philosophers in the embodied and dynamicist tradition, including Anthony Chemero, press the stronger claim that representations are dispensable altogether, and most working neuroscientists do not accept that, so the dispute is partly about metaphysics and partly about which description does more explanatory work in a given experiment.


77.3.4 Reconciling normative theory with mechanistic detail

A normative theory says what a system ought to do given its goals and constraints, and neuroscience has several powerful ones: Barlow's efficient coding principle from 1961, which says sensory systems should remove redundancy from their inputs; Bayesian accounts, which say perception should combine prior expectation with sensory evidence in proportion to their reliability; and reinforcement learning accounts, which say behaviour should maximise expected future reward.

These theories are attractive because they predict behaviour from first principles without needing to know the wiring, and some have direct neural confirmation, most notably the reward prediction error signal Schultz, Dayan and Montague identified in midbrain dopamine neurons in 1997.

The complaint, put most forcefully by Jones and Love in their 2011 Behavioral and Brain Sciences paper "Bayesian Fundamentalism or Enlightenment?", is that a normative model with free parameters over the prior and the likelihood can usually be fitted to any behaviour, and that the fitting is often mistaken for explanation.

Their positive proposal, which they call Bayesian Enlightenment, is that normative models should be held to mechanistic and developmental commitments as well as behavioural fit.

The open problem is a methodological one with no agreed solution: how to state a normative theory so that it forbids something specific at the level of circuits, rather than merely accommodating whatever is found.


77.4 Problems of the subject

The last family of problems concerns the thing doing the thinking.

These are the questions most likely to be dismissed as philosophy and most likely to determine whether the rest of the enterprise makes sense.


77.4.1 The hard problem and whether it will dissolve

David Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness in 1995, distinguishing it from the easy problems: explaining discrimination, reportability, attention and control is hard in the ordinary sense, whereas explaining why any of that processing is accompanied by subjective experience appears to be a different kind of question.

Illusionists, principally Daniel Dennett and Keith Frankish, argue that the hard problem is an artefact of an introspective misrepresentation, so that what needs explaining is not phenomenal experience but our conviction that we have it, and Chalmers reframed this in 2018 as the meta-problem of consciousness - explaining why we judge there to be a hard problem - while denying that solving the meta-problem would automatically dissolve the original.

Empirical work has begun to discriminate between the leading scientific theories: the Cogitate Consortium's adversarial collaboration, published in Nature in 2025 and running for seven years across 256 participants using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG) and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), tested preregistered contrasting predictions of integrated information theory (IIT) and global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT).

Neither theory passed cleanly: conscious content was decodable from posterior cortex better than from prefrontal cortex, which embarrasses global workspace theory's emphasis on prefrontal broadcasting, while the sustained posterior synchronisation IIT predicted was not found, which embarrasses IIT.

That result is genuinely important, and it is worth being clear that it bears on the easy problems only - both theories are theories of which neural events correlate with which experiences, and neither addresses why there is experience at all.


77.4.2 The relation of cognition to emotion, body, and environment

Classical cognitive science treated cognition as computation over representations inside the head, with emotion as interference and the body as a peripheral device.

That separation has eroded from several directions: Antonio Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis, from work on patients with ventromedial prefrontal damage in the 1990s, argued that bodily emotional signals are constitutive of good decision making rather than a nuisance; Lisa Feldman Barrett's theory of constructed emotion argues that emotions are not fixed circuits but categorisations the brain builds from interoceptive signals - interoception meaning the sense of the body's internal state - plus prior conceptual knowledge; and the extended mind thesis of Clark and Chalmers, from 1998, argues that reliable external resources like a notebook can be literally part of a cognitive process.

Predictive processing frameworks, particularly Karl Friston's free energy principle, attempt to unify perception, action, emotion and physiological regulation under one quantity, which is theoretically attractive and empirically slippery, since critics point out that the principle is difficult to falsify at the level at which it is stated.

The unresolved question is not whether body and environment matter, which almost everyone now grants, but whether they are causal influences on an internal cognitive system or genuine parts of it, and that distinction has proved very hard to settle experimentally.


77.4.3 Individual variability and the meaning of an average brain

Most of what is known from neuroimaging comes from averaging across dozens of people after warping their brains into a common template, which produces an average brain that may correspond to no actual person.

Precision functional mapping, pioneered by Russell Poldrack's MyConnectome study in which one person was scanned roughly twice a week for over a year, and extended by Gordon, Laumann, Dosenbach and colleagues in their 2017 paper in Neuron, showed that with enough data per individual the network layout of a single brain is stable and reliable, and that individuals differ substantially in the topography of their networks, not merely in the strength of connections.

Some of what group averaging had reported as blurred or weak boundaries turned out to be sharp boundaries in different places in different people.

This matters practically for neurosurgery and brain stimulation targeting, and it matters theoretically because a group average can be a poor model of every member of the group, a statistical trap known as the ergodicity problem.

It also raises a question the field has not answered: when individuals differ, which differences are meaningful variation in cognitive architecture and which are noise or incidental anatomy.


77.4.4 Whether cognition is the right unit of analysis at all

The categories used to carve up mental life - attention, working memory, executive function, inhibition - were inherited from introspection and mid-twentieth-century psychology, and there is no guarantee that the brain respects them.

Russell Poldrack's 2006 critique of reverse inference made the point concretely: inferring that a subject was engaged in a particular cognitive process because a particular region lit up is not deductively valid, and it is only weakly informative unless the region is genuinely selective for that process, which most regions are not.

This motivated the cognitive ontology project, which asks whether the vocabulary of cognition should be rebuilt from the bottom up using data rather than inherited from folk psychology, and terms like executive function are the usual examples of categories suspected of being convenient labels rather than natural kinds.

A different challenge comes from the 4E tradition - embodied, embedded, enacted and extended cognition - which argues that the unit of analysis should be the brain-body-environment system engaged in an activity, with Gibsonian affordances, meaning action possibilities the environment offers an organism, treated as part of the cognitive story rather than as external stimuli.

Neither challenge has displaced the standard vocabulary, and neither has produced a replacement ontology that working experimentalists have adopted, so this remains the most fundamental and least resolved item on the list.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

The neural code is not one code, and the very idea of a code presupposes a decoder whose existence in the brain has not been demonstrated.

Binding is several problems, of which the perceptual ones look tractable and the experiential one does not, and neither attention nor synchrony has settled even the tractable ones.

Learning in biology solves credit assignment, one-shot acquisition, and continual learning without interference by means that are still unknown, with feedback alignment, dendritic error coding, eligibility traces, and complementary learning systems all plausible and none confirmed.

The levels of description from molecule to behaviour remain linked by correspondence rather than by derivation, and the disputes between localisation and network accounts, representational and dynamical accounts, and normative and mechanistic accounts are all live rather than closed.

The 2025 Cogitate adversarial collaboration weakened both leading scientific theories of consciousness without touching the hard problem, which remains outside the reach of current method.

Finally, both the average brain and the inherited vocabulary of cognitive categories are open to serious doubt, which means some of the field's apparent findings may be artefacts of how it has chosen to describe its subject.


CHAPTER 78. NEUROETHICS AND SOCIETY (CONTEXT)

Every technique described earlier in this book - the scanner, the electrode, the drug, the statistical model - is used on people, paid for by somebody, reported to somebody, and eventually acted upon by somebody.

Neuroethics is the study of that whole chain, from the consent form a volunteer signs to the courtroom where a brain scan is shown to a jury.

It is not a soft appendix to the science.

It is the part of the science that decides who is studied, who benefits, and who is harmed when a finding is wrong or is oversold.

This chapter covers four things: how research on brains is ethically conducted, how brain findings are applied in law, in enhancement, in prediction and in schools, how those findings are communicated to the public, and how unequally the whole enterprise is distributed across the world.

The recurring theme is a mismatch of scale.

Brain findings are typically small, noisy, and about groups; the decisions people want to make with them are large, consequential, and about individuals.

78.1 Research ethics

Research ethics is the set of rules and habits that protect the people, and the animals, who make neuroscience possible.

Modern rules descend from the Nuremberg Code of 1947, written after the Nazi doctors' trial, and from the Belmont Report of 1979 in the United States, which set out three principles: respect for persons, beneficence (doing good and avoiding harm), and justice (fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research).

In practice these principles are enforced by a committee, called an institutional review board (IRB) in the United States and a research ethics committee (REC) in much of Europe, which must approve a study before it starts.

Cognitive neuroscience raises the general problems of medical research plus some of its own, because scanning a brain can reveal disease nobody was looking for, and because many of the most scientifically interesting participants are the least able to consent.

78.1.1 Consent in patients, children, and impaired populations

Informed consent means a person understands what will be done, what the risks are, that participation is voluntary, and that they may stop at any time without penalty.

Capacity to consent is decision specific: a person with early Alzheimer's disease may be able to agree to a thirty minute questionnaire but not to an invasive drug trial, so capacity is assessed against the particular study rather than assumed to be present or absent overall.

Where capacity is absent, permission is given by a legally authorised representative (a person or body empowered by law to consent on someone's behalf), and ethics committees usually additionally require assent - the participant's own affirmative willingness, or at least the absence of objection, expressed in whatever way they can manage.

Children are handled the same way: a parent or guardian gives permission, the child gives assent in age appropriate language, and a child's refusal to enter a scanner is normally treated as decisive even though the child cannot legally consent.

Two pressures deserve naming.

Therapeutic misconception is the common belief among patient volunteers that a research procedure is being done for their personal benefit, when in fact a study is designed to produce generalisable knowledge and may offer them nothing.

And the very populations whose brains we most need to study - people with dementia, psychosis, severe autism, or acute brain injury - are exactly those for whom consent is hardest, so excluding them to be safe is itself an injustice, because it leaves their conditions understudied.

78.1.2 Incidental findings and their disclosure

An incidental finding is something clinically relevant that a research scan reveals but the study was not looking for - a tumour, an aneurysm, an arteriovenous malformation (a tangle of abnormally connected arteries and veins), an old silent stroke.

They are not rare.

Judy Illes and colleagues at Stanford, surveying functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) investigators in a 2004 study in Science, found that a large majority of responding laboratories had encountered such findings, and that the procedures for handling them varied wildly from laboratory to laboratory.

Population estimates put the overall prevalence somewhere between roughly three and twenty per cent depending on how strict the definition is, with the rate rising steeply with age; Vernooij and colleagues, reporting on the Rotterdam Study in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007, found asymptomatic brain infarcts in about seven per cent of older adults scanned, and aneurysms in about two per cent.

The ethical problem is that a research scan is not a clinical scan.

It is often acquired with sequences optimised for function rather than anatomy, it is usually not read by a radiologist, and a false alarm can cost a healthy volunteer months of anxiety, expensive follow-up imaging, and even insurance consequences.

The consensus that has emerged is procedural rather than doctrinal: decide the policy in advance, state it plainly in the consent form, tell participants that the scan is not a medical examination and will not detect everything, and have a defined route by which a suspicious image reaches a qualified clinician and then the participant's own doctor.

What remains genuinely contested is how far the duty extends - whether investigators are obliged to have every scan formally read, which is costly, and what to do when a participant has said in advance that they do not wish to be told.

78.1.3 Animal research ethics and the three Rs

Most of what this book says about synapses, cortical columns, place cells, and dopamine signalling comes from animals, because those measurements cannot be made in healthy humans.

The governing framework is the three Rs, set out by William Russell and Rex Burch in The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique in 1959, a project of the Universities Federation for Animal Welfare advised by a committee chaired by the immunologist Peter Medawar.

The three are replacement (use a non-animal method, such as cell culture, human volunteers, or computational simulation, wherever it will answer the question), reduction (use the smallest number of animals consistent with a statistically meaningful answer, which is as much a matter of good experimental design as of compassion), and refinement (change housing, handling, anaesthesia and endpoints so that whatever animals are used suffer as little as possible).

The three Rs are now written into law in many jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom's Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 and the European Union's Directive 2010/63/EU, and they are enforced locally by animal care and use committees.

Reduction and good statistics pull in the same direction, and this is a genuine and underappreciated point: underpowered animal studies waste animals as well as money, so the ethical and the scientific arguments coincide.

Disagreement persists at the edges, particularly over non-human primates, where the scientific case is strongest - a macaque cortex resembles ours in ways a mouse cortex does not - and the welfare cost is also highest.

78.1.4 Equitable participation and the diversity of samples

Justice, the third Belmont principle, has two faces: people should not be exploited by being disproportionately enrolled in risky research, and they should not be excluded from research whose benefits they need.

Cognitive science has historically failed the second test.

Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan argued in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2010 that the field's participants are overwhelmingly WEIRD - Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic - and that this narrow slice is routinely treated as a stand-in for the human species.

Neuroimaging is at least as skewed; analyses of the published literature find the great majority of studies come from a handful of wealthy Western countries, and within those countries samples are typically whiter, wealthier, and healthier than the surrounding population.

Some of the exclusion is quietly technical rather than deliberate.

Standard electroencephalography (EEG) caps and imaging protocols work poorly with thick or braided hair, and participants have been screened out on those grounds, a problem documented and criticised in a 2022 Nature Neuroscience article by Ricard, Parker, Dhamala and colleagues on racially exclusionary practices in neuroimaging.

Large modern cohorts such as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study in the United States and the UK Biobank imaging project improve matters by recruiting at scale and with an eye to demographics, but even UK Biobank's imaging subsample is measurably healthier and better off than the general population, so representativeness remains partial.

78.2 Applied neuroethics

Applied neuroethics asks what happens when a brain finding leaves the laboratory and meets an institution that has to make a decision - a court, a school, an employer, an insurer.

The characteristic error is a category mistake: mistaking a group-average difference for a statement about an individual.

An effect that is real and scientifically important can still be far too weak to tell you anything reliable about the one person in front of you, and most institutional decisions are about one person.

78.2.1 Neuroscience in law and the responsibility debate

Neurolaw is the use of brain evidence in legal proceedings, and it is now common; reviews of United States case law find brain evidence raised in thousands of criminal cases, most often in capital sentencing and in claims of diminished capacity rather than in determining whether the defendant committed the act.

The philosophical dispute was framed sharply by Joshua Greene and Jonathan Cohen in 2004, who argued that neuroscience will change nothing in law directly but will change everything indirectly, by eroding the intuitive picture of a freely choosing self and pushing law toward a consequentialist, treatment-and-prevention framing of punishment.

Stephen Morse has argued the opposite with equal force, calling the overreach "brain overclaim syndrome": law's concept of responsibility requires only that a person could understand the wrongfulness of an act and conform their conduct to that understanding, and showing that a brain caused a behaviour is trivially true of all behaviour and therefore excuses nothing by itself.

The empirical worry is legibility rather than logic.

A scan showing a shrunken prefrontal cortex in a defendant is consistent with poor impulse control, but the same anatomy appears in many people who never offend, so the scan cannot support the inference the courtroom wants it to support.

There is one place where the science has clearly and defensibly moved the law: evidence on protracted adolescent brain development contributed to the reasoning in United States Supreme Court decisions restricting the death penalty and mandatory life without parole for juveniles, in Roper v.

Simmons in 2005 and Miller v.

Alabama in 2012, though even there the developmental evidence supported a categorical age line rather than an individual diagnosis.

78.2.2 Cognitive enhancement, fairness, and coercion

Cognitive enhancement means using a drug or a device to push cognition above a person's normal baseline rather than to restore it after illness.

The main candidates are prescription stimulants - methylphenidate, sold as Ritalin, and amphetamine salts - and the wakefulness-promoting drug modafinil, taken by students and shift workers off-label.

A widely cited 2008 commentary in Nature by Henry Greely, Barbara Sahakian, John Harris, Ronald Kessler, Michael Gazzaniga, Philip Campbell and Martha Farah argued that enhancement should not be treated as a dirty word, and proposed a policy framework built on safety, freedom from coercion, and fair access.

The evidence for the effects is more modest than the debate suggests.

Meta-analyses generally find small average gains, concentrated in sustained attention, vigilance and motivation during boring or sleep-deprived tasks, with little reliable improvement in complex reasoning, and with some evidence that people who start out performing well gain least or even lose ground.

Three ethical worries survive that deflation.

Coercion is the sharpest: if enough surgeons or air traffic controllers or students take a drug, the choice not to take it stops being free, and the pressure is applied by competition rather than by any identifiable person who could be held responsible.

Fairness is the second, because enhancement bought privately tracks wealth, and the third is authenticity - whether an achievement means the same thing when it was chemically underwritten - which is the most philosophically interesting and the least tractable of the three.

78.2.3 Prediction, stigma, and the misuse of risk scores

A risk score is a number derived from data - genetic, imaging, or behavioural - that estimates the probability of some future outcome such as psychosis, dementia, or reoffending.

A polygenic score sums the small effects of many thousands of common genetic variants identified in a genome-wide association study (GWAS), which is a scan of the whole genome for statistical associations with a trait.

These scores predict poorly at the individual level and predict unequally across groups.

Because most GWAS samples are of European ancestry, scores transfer badly to other ancestries; for educational attainment, the variance explained drops from around ten per cent in European-ancestry Americans to under two per cent in African-ancestry Americans, and surveys of the field have found that around two thirds of polygenic scoring studies to 2017 used exclusively European-ancestry participants.

Duncan and colleagues showed in 2019 that accuracy varies even within a single ancestry group, depending on age, sex and socio-economic status, which means a score is not a stable property of a person but an artefact of the sample it was built in.

The social danger is that a probabilistic and badly calibrated number gets treated as a diagnosis, with three predictable consequences: stigma attaching to people who will never develop the condition, self-fulfilling effects when a label changes how teachers or clinicians behave, and a false appearance of objectivity that lets an institution launder a judgement it would otherwise have to defend.

The honest framing is that these scores can be genuinely useful for stratifying populations in research or trial recruitment, and are usually not fit to make a decision about one individual's schooling, employment, insurance, or liberty.

78.2.4 Neuroscience in education and the persistence of neuromyths

A neuromyth is a claim about the brain that is popular in schools and false, often a garbled descendant of a real finding.

Sanne Dekker, Nikki Lee, Paul Howard-Jones and Jelle Jolles surveyed teachers in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands in a 2012 paper in Frontiers in Psychology and found that teachers endorsed roughly half of the neuromyths put to them.

The most durable are that pupils learn best when taught in their preferred learning style, usually visual, auditory or kinaesthetic; that pupils can be classified as left-brained or right-brained; that we use only ten per cent of our brains; and that particular movement exercises improve hemispheric integration.

The learning styles myth is the important one, because it is both the most popular - large surveys of United Kingdom educators have found endorsement around three quarters - and the most clearly tested; the "meshing hypothesis", that matching teaching to a preferred style improves outcomes, has repeatedly failed controlled tests, as Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork concluded in a 2008 review, and later replications have supported.

Dekker's most uncomfortable result is that teachers with more general brain knowledge were, if anything, more likely to endorse neuromyths, which suggests that exposure to neuroscience content is not by itself a cure and may increase confidence faster than discrimination.

Paul Howard-Jones, writing in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2014, argued that the fix is not more facts but a functioning interface between the two fields, with teachers involved in interpreting findings rather than receiving them.

None of this means education has nothing to learn from cognitive science; spacing of practice, retrieval practice, and the limits of working memory are well supported and genuinely useful, and it is worth noticing that these come from cognitive psychology rather than from brain imaging.

78.3 Communication

Between a result and the public sit three filters: the paper, the press release, and the news story.

Distortion at any stage compounds, and the evidence suggests that the earliest stage matters most.

78.3.1 Overclaiming in press releases and in the literature

Petroc Sumner, Chris Chambers and colleagues at Cardiff University published a study in the BMJ in 2014 that traced 462 university press releases back to the papers they described and forward to the news coverage they generated.

Around a third of press releases exaggerated a correlation into a causal claim, about forty per cent exaggerated the practical advice that readers should follow, and around a third overstated how far animal results applied to humans.

The decisive finding was conditional: when a press release exaggerated, the news usually did too, at rates of roughly sixty to eighty-five per cent depending on the type of exaggeration, but when the release was accurate, news exaggeration fell to between ten and twenty per cent.

That locates responsibility inside the university rather than only in the newsroom, and it points at a cheap intervention, since press releases are approved by the authors and can be fixed before publication.

The problem also exists inside the literature itself, in the form of spin - abstracts that present a non-significant primary outcome favourably, titles that assert what the data merely suggest, and discussions that quietly change the outcome the study was designed to test.

78.3.2 The seductive allure of neuroscientific explanation

Deena Weisberg, Frank Keil, Joshua Goodstein, Elizabeth Rawson and Jeremy Gray reported in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience in 2008 that adding logically irrelevant neuroscience language to a psychological explanation made bad explanations seem better to novices and to students in a neuroscience class, but not to experts.

The effect has replicated a number of times, including by Fernandez-Duque and colleagues in 2015 and in a 2024 classroom and online replication in Royal Society Open Science, so the basic phenomenon is reasonably solid.

An important qualification is that the closely related claim about brain images - that a picture of a brain is uniquely persuasive - has largely failed to replicate; Hook and Farah in 2013, Michael and colleagues in 2013, and Schweitzer and colleagues in legal contexts found little or no added persuasive power from the image itself.

Fernandez-Duque and colleagues also argued that the allure is not specific to the brain at all but is a general preference for explanations that name a lower physical level, which they termed a reductive allure.

The practical lesson stands either way: the presence of neuroscientific vocabulary in an argument is not evidence about the argument, and readers should ask whether removing the brain talk would change the conclusion.

78.3.3 Responsible communication of uncertain findings

Most brain findings are uncertain, and the honest problem is how to say so without implying that nothing is known.

Neuroimaging has particular reasons for humility.

Edward Vul, Christine Harris, Piotr Winkielman and Harold Pashler argued in 2009 that many strikingly high brain-behaviour correlations in social neuroscience were inflated by selecting voxels on the same data used to compute the correlation, a circularity now usually called double dipping.

Scale problems compound this: Marek, Tervo-Clemmens, Dosenbach and colleagues showed in Nature in 2022 that reproducible brain-wide associations between imaging measures and individual behaviour typically require thousands of participants, whereas typical studies used dozens.

The tools that help are unglamorous and now widely adopted: preregistration (publicly recording hypotheses and analysis plans before seeing the data), correction for multiple comparisons across the many thousands of voxels tested, reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than only p-values, sharing data and code, and treating independent replication in a new sample as the real standard of evidence.

For communication specifically, the useful habits are to state the sample size and the population studied in the same breath as the result, to name the comparison group, to distinguish "associated with" from "causes", and to say explicitly what would have to be true for the finding to be wrong.

78.3.4 Public engagement and trust

Public engagement used to be organised around what is called the deficit model - the assumption that public scepticism is caused by ignorance and can be cured by transmitting facts.

That model has fared badly, because disagreement about science often tracks trust in institutions and perceived alignment of values rather than knowledge, and pouring in more facts does not touch either.

The alternative is dialogue and participation: consulting communities before a study rather than announcing it after, returning results to the people who provided the data, and being visible when things go wrong.

Trust is also asymmetric and slow.

It is built by boring reliability over years and lost quickly by a single episode of overclaiming, which is one reason the press release problem in 78.3.1 is more damaging than its individual instances look.

There is a specific debt in neuroscience and psychiatry, where past abuses - lobotomy performed on tens of thousands of patients, coercive institutionalisation, research conducted on prisoners and on the institutionalised without consent - are remembered by exactly the communities whose participation is now most needed.

78.4 Justice and access

The final set of questions is distributive: who gets to do neuroscience, who gets studied, and who gets the treatments that result.

These are not downstream consequences of the science.

They shape which questions are asked in the first place, and therefore what is known.

78.4.1 Global inequity in neuroscience capacity

Research capacity is concentrated in a small number of wealthy countries; by one widely cited estimate, around ninety per cent of published neuroimaging research originates in Western nations.

The clinical consequence is starker than the research one.

The World Health Organization and regional surveys find the median number of neurologists in African countries is on the order of zero to two per million people, against a suggested minimum of roughly one per hundred thousand, meaning some countries have a handful of neurologists for tens of millions of people.

Epilepsy is the standard illustration, because it is common, and treatable with inexpensive drugs.

Around eighty per cent of people with epilepsy live in low- and middle-income countries, and the treatment gap - the proportion of people with active epilepsy who are not receiving appropriate treatment - runs from a few per cent in high-income countries to figures approaching one hundred per cent in some low-income settings.

That gap is not mainly about scientific ignorance.

It is about supply chains for medication, the absence of trained staff, distance to any clinic, cost, and stigma, all of which are addressable and none of which are solved by another imaging study.

Capacity-building efforts exist - the International Brain Research Organization (IBRO) runs regional schools, the International League Against Epilepsy trains clinicians, and the World Health Organization's Intersectoral Global Action Plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders, adopted in 2022, sets targets to 2031 - but the scale of the funding remains far below the scale of the burden.

78.4.2 Access to neurotechnology and to treatment

The most effective neurotechnologies are also among the most expensive.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS), in which thin electrodes are implanted to deliver continuous electrical pulses to a target such as the subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson's disease, costs on the order of forty to fifty thousand United States dollars for device, surgery and first year of care in published economic analyses.

Even where it is funded, uptake is low and uneven; commentary on scaling implanted neurotechnology notes that only around one to two per cent of eligible patients with Parkinson's disease or essential tremor in the United States receive DBS each year, with disparities by race, income and distance from a specialist centre.

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), which read neural activity and convert it into control of a cursor, a robotic arm, or synthesised speech, are earlier in development and raise a further problem: device abandonment, where a company discontinues a product or fails, and implanted users lose function they had come to depend on, which has already happened with commercial retinal and neural implants.

Governance has begun to respond.

UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology, adopted at its General Conference in November 2025, is the first global standard in this area, framing neurotechnology within human rights and explicitly calling on states to keep it inclusive and affordable and to protect mental privacy.

A recommendation is not binding law, so its practical effect will depend on national implementation, and it is too early to say whether it will change access.

78.4.3 Representation in datasets and its downstream effects

A dataset is not a neutral record; it is a set of decisions about who was invited, who could physically participate, and who was excluded by a quality control step.

Non-representative data propagates.

Normative brain charts built mostly on one population misclassify others; polygenic scores trained on European-ancestry samples predict poorly elsewhere, as described in 78.2.3; and any machine learning model inherits the demographics of its training set while presenting its output as a general fact.

The exclusions are often invisible in the published paper, because they happen in screening and preprocessing - hair type incompatible with EEG electrodes, body size limits in scanner bores, exclusion of non-native speakers from language tasks, exclusion of participants with the medications or comorbidities that are most common in poorer populations.

The remedies are known and mostly boring: report sample demographics fully, publish exclusion counts and reasons, design hardware and protocols that accommodate the variation that actually exists, recruit through community partnerships rather than through campus advertisements, and require diverse validation samples before claiming generality.

78.4.4 Who sets the research agenda

Research priorities are set by funding agencies, by large philanthropic funders, by industry, and by the incentive structures of academic careers, and none of those constituencies is the patient.

The result is documented mismatch.

Priority-setting exercises run by the James Lind Alliance in the United Kingdom, which bring patients, carers and clinicians together to rank unanswered questions, have repeatedly found that the questions those groups care most about - how to manage daily symptoms, how to support carers, which existing treatments work best against each other - are underrepresented in what researchers actually study, which skews toward mechanism and toward new products.

Large national initiatives such as the United States BRAIN Initiative, launched in 2013, and the European Union's Human Brain Project, which ran from 2013 to 2023, illustrate the top-down alternative, and the Human Brain Project in particular drew sustained criticism from within the field over its governance and its early emphasis on large-scale simulation, leading to a formal mediation and a restructuring in 2015.

Disease burden is also a poor predictor of funding: conditions with strong advocacy organisations attract disproportionate support relative to their prevalence, while stigmatised conditions attract less.

The corrective mechanisms that exist are patient and public involvement in grant review, priority-setting partnerships of the James Lind type, and funding streams reserved for questions nominated by patients, and the evidence for their effect on what gets funded is still thin.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Ethics is internal to neuroscience rather than a commentary on it: rules about consent, incidental findings, animal use and who gets recruited determine what data exist and therefore what can be known.

The characteristic failure in applying brain science is a scale mismatch, in which a real but small group-average effect is used to make a confident claim about one individual in a courtroom, a classroom, or an insurance file, and the polygenic score and the defendant's scan are the clearest cases.

Distortion in public understanding begins inside the university, since Sumner's 2014 BMJ study showed that news exaggeration largely tracks press release exaggeration, and Weisberg's 2008 finding shows that neuroscientific vocabulary can make a bad explanation feel better to non-experts, although the related claim about the persuasive power of brain images has not held up.

Neuromyths such as learning styles persist in education despite repeated failure in controlled tests, and are not cured by giving teachers more brain facts.

The field's benefits and capacity are distributed extremely unequally, with research concentrated in a few wealthy countries, treatment gaps approaching totality for a cheaply treatable condition like epilepsy in some low-income settings, and expensive neurotechnology reaching only a small fraction even of eligible patients in rich ones.

The remedies are unglamorous and mostly procedural - preregistration, honest press releases, full reporting of exclusions, diverse recruitment, and giving patients a voice in setting priorities - and the evidence that they work is real for some and still thin for others.


CHAPTER 79. THE PRACTICE OF THE FIELD (CONTEXT)

Every earlier chapter of this book described what is known about the brain.

This chapter describes instead how that knowledge gets made, by whom, with whose money, and published where.

That sounds like background, but it is not - the shape of the institutions determines which questions get asked, which get funded, and which quietly go unstudied for thirty years.

It also matters to you as a reader, because knowing how a finding was produced is most of what you need in order to judge how much weight it can carry.

So this chapter covers four things: how the field is organised, what skills a working practitioner actually needs, how to read a paper without being fooled by it, and what to read next.

79.1 How the field is organised

Neuroscience is not a single organisation with a director.

It is a loose federation of university departments, hospital research units, government institutes, and company laboratories, held together by professional societies, journals, conferences, and funding agencies.

Understanding those four connective structures explains most of the field's behaviour, including its fashions and its blind spots.

79.1.1 Societies, journals, and conferences

A professional society is a membership organisation that runs a conference and usually publishes journals.

The largest in this field is the Society for Neuroscience (SfN), founded in 1969, whose annual meeting routinely draws on the order of 30,000 attendees and which publishes The Journal of Neuroscience (JNeurosci) and the open-access journal eNeuro.

The narrower and more relevant body for this book is the Cognitive Neuroscience Society (CNS), which holds a smaller spring meeting - its 33rd annual meeting was held in Vancouver in March 2026 - and is associated with the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.

Newer venues reflect newer alliances: the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience (CCN) conference, running since 2017, exists specifically to force neuroscientists, cognitive scientists, and machine-learning researchers into the same room.

The journals themselves form a rough prestige ladder, from the general-science outlets (Nature, Science) through the specialist flagships (Nature Neuroscience, Neuron, Nature Human Behaviour) to solid workhorse journals (JNeurosci, NeuroImage, Cerebral Cortex, eLife), and a paper's location on that ladder tells you something about how novel its authors claimed it was but rather little about whether it is true.

Conferences matter for a reason that is easy to miss: a conference poster is often two to four years ahead of the published paper, so the meeting floor is where you see what the field is about to believe.

79.1.2 Funding structures and large initiatives

Almost all basic neuroscience runs on competitive public grants, principally from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) in the United States, from the European Research Council and national research councils in Europe, and from charitable foundations such as the Wellcome Trust, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Simons Foundation, and the Allen Institute.

The standard NIH research grant runs about five years, which is a real constraint - it means a project that would take fifteen years to pay off is hard to start, and a project guaranteed to produce publishable output in three years is easy to fund.

Two very large programmes dominated the 2013 to 2023 decade.

The United States Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) Initiative, announced in 2013 and funded from fiscal year 2014, has invested more than three billion dollars across more than 1,300 projects, and its clearest successes have been in tools and cell-type censuses rather than in a single unified theory.

The European Union's Human Brain Project (HBP), launched in 2013 with roughly one billion euros over ten years and concluded in 2023, was much more contested: its original promise of simulating a human brain drew an open letter of protest signed by hundreds of European neuroscientists in 2014, it was restructured after mediation, and commentators including several in Scientific American have argued it over-promised, while its defenders point to the durable EBRAINS research infrastructure it left behind.

The honest summary is that big neuroscience has been very good at building instruments and databases and much weaker at delivering the sweeping explanatory results its press releases advertised.

Similar national programmes followed - Japan's Brain/MINDS, the China Brain Project, and others - so the funding landscape is now genuinely international.

79.1.3 Team science and multi-site consortia

Team science means research done by large distributed groups rather than by one laboratory, and it has become unavoidable in human cognitive neuroscience for a simple statistical reason: the effects being chased are small, so the samples must be large, and no single site can scan tens of thousands of people.

The Human Connectome Project (HCP), begun in 2010, scanned roughly 1,200 healthy young adults with harmonised protocols and made the data public, and its protocols became a de facto standard.

The UK Biobank imaging extension has now collected brain scans on tens of thousands of participants alongside genetic and health data, and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is following about 11,875 American children recruited at ages nine and ten across 21 sites for roughly a decade.

A different model is the Enhancing NeuroImaging Genetics through Meta-Analysis (ENIGMA) consortium, which does not collect new data but pools analyses across dozens of countries and institutions by shipping an identical analysis script to each site.

The costs of this model are real: authorship lists run to hundreds of names, individual credit becomes hard to assign, scanner differences between sites introduce systematic bias that has to be statistically corrected, and the sheer expense concentrates power in a handful of consortia.

The benefit is equally real - findings from these datasets replicate, and small-sample findings frequently do not.

79.1.4 Careers, training, and interdisciplinary skill demands

The conventional path runs undergraduate degree, doctoral degree of four to seven years, one or more postdoctoral positions of three to five years each, and then, for a minority, a faculty post.

That last step is the bottleneck: far more doctorates are awarded each year than there are permanent academic positions, so most people trained in neuroscience will build a career outside academia, in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, clinical work, data science, technology companies, science policy, or publishing.

This is not a failure of those individuals, and good training programmes now say so openly and teach transferable skills deliberately.

The skill demand has also shifted hard toward computation: postdoctoral advertisements in human neuroscience now routinely require Python, R, or MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory, a numerical computing environment) and experience with machine learning, which was not true in 2005.

Training has partly moved online to fill the gap - Neuromatch Academy, a non-profit born from the pandemic shutdown of 2020, has taught computational neuroscience to more than 13,000 students in over 130 countries using freely licensed Python materials.

79.2 Skills a practitioner needs

There is no single curriculum, because the field spans molecules to behaviour.

But there is a common core, and a beginner deciding what to study first can reasonably treat the following four sub-sections as a checklist.

79.2.1 Neuroanatomy and physiology

You cannot interpret a result about the brain without knowing what the parts are and how signals move through them.

The practical minimum is: gross anatomy of cortex, subcortical structures, and the major white-matter pathways; the resting membrane potential and the action potential; synaptic transmission and the main neurotransmitter systems; and the standard directional vocabulary (rostral, caudal, dorsal, ventral, medial, lateral) so that you can read a methods section at all.

Anatomy is memorisation-heavy and unfashionable, and it is nonetheless the skill that most protects you from over-interpreting a blob on a brain map, because knowing that a region has six known functions immediately tempers a claim that its activation demonstrates one of them.

Physiology matters equally, because the signals we measure are indirect: the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal read by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a haemodynamic proxy for neural activity, lagging it by several seconds, and knowing that fact is what stops you reading an fMRI time course as if it were a spike train.

79.2.2 Programming, signal processing, and statistics

Programming is now a literacy requirement rather than a specialism, and Python has become the field's default language, with MATLAB still common in older electrophysiology and imaging laboratories and R common where the work is statistical.

Signal processing is the mathematics of extracting structure from noisy time series: filtering, the Fourier transform (a method for decomposing a signal into the frequencies it contains), spectral estimation, and event-related averaging, all of which are what turn a raw electroencephalography (EEG) recording into an interpretable waveform.

Statistics must go beyond a first course, because neuroscience data are massively multiple-comparison problems - a typical fMRI analysis tests one hypothesis at each of a hundred thousand voxels - and the correction methods (family-wise error control, false discovery rate, cluster-based permutation testing) are where analyses most often go wrong.

Mixed-effects models are the standard tool for data with nested structure, such as many trials within each subject within each site, and misapplying them by treating trials as independent observations is one of the most common errors in the published literature.

Version control with git and adherence to data standards such as the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), a community specification for how to organise and name neuroimaging files, are the unglamorous habits that make an analysis reproducible.

79.2.3 Mathematical modelling and machine learning

A model is a precise statement of a hypothesis, precise enough that it makes numerical predictions that can be wrong.

The working repertoire includes dynamical systems (differential equations describing how neural population activity evolves), Bayesian inference models of perception and decision, reinforcement-learning models of how value and prediction error drive choice, and drift-diffusion models of how evidence accumulates to a decision threshold.

Machine learning enters twice over, and the two uses should not be confused: as an analysis tool, where a classifier is trained to decode what a person saw from their brain activity, and as a theory, where a deep neural network is proposed as a model of how the visual system itself computes.

The second use is genuinely contested - work from Yamins and DiCarlo (2014 onward) showed that deep convolutional networks trained on object recognition predict responses in monkey inferotemporal cortex better than any hand-designed model, while critics reply that predicting responses is not the same as explaining them, and that a model with a hundred million fitted parameters may fit the data without illuminating the mechanism.

Both positions are held by serious people, and a beginner should hold the question open.

79.2.4 Experimental design and scientific writing

Design is where a study's fate is decided, long before any data are analysed, and the central skill is constructing a control condition that differs from the experimental condition in exactly one respect.

The associated habits are power analysis before data collection rather than after, counterbalancing of stimulus order, randomisation, blinding where feasible, and preregistration - the public, time-stamped deposit of hypotheses and analysis plan before data are collected, which makes the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analysis checkable rather than merely asserted.

Writing is not decoration; a paper is the only durable form the work takes, and the discipline of stating a hypothesis, a method, a result, and a bounded conclusion in that order is itself a check on sloppy thinking.

The single most valuable writing habit for a beginner is to state in one plain sentence what would have counted as evidence against the claim, and if no such sentence exists, the claim is not yet scientific.

79.3 Reading the literature critically

Roughly a hundred thousand neuroscience papers appear each year, and most of them will not survive.

Critical reading is not cynicism - it is the ordinary skill of matching the size of a conclusion to the size of its evidence.

79.3.1 Identifying the actual claim and the actual evidence

Begin by separating three things that papers routinely blur: what was measured, what was found, and what is claimed.

A useful discipline is to read the methods and the figures before the abstract and the discussion, because the abstract is written to sell and the discussion is where speculation is legal.

Ask specifically: how many subjects, what exactly was the control condition, was the key statistical test planned in advance or found afterwards, and is the headline effect visible in the raw data plot or only in a summary statistic.

A frequent pattern is that a title asserts a mechanism ("region X drives behaviour Y") while the design supports only a correlation, and the word "drives" is doing work the data cannot support - only an intervention, such as lesion, stimulation, or optogenetic manipulation, licenses causal language.

79.3.2 Sample size, effect size, and inferential leaps

Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect an effect that is genuinely there, and Button, Ioannidis and colleagues, writing in Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2013, showed that the median power across the neuroscience literature was around twenty percent - meaning most studies would miss a real effect four times in five.
