The counterintuitive consequence, and the one worth internalising, is that an underpowered study that does report a significant result has probably overestimated the effect size, because only unusually large sample fluctuations clear the significance threshold in a small sample.

Marek, Dosenbach and colleagues sharpened this for human imaging in Nature in 2022, arguing that brain-wide association studies - which correlate individual differences in brain measures with traits such as cognitive ability - need thousands of participants, not dozens, for stable results.

That paper was immediately and productively contested: Spisak, Bingel and Wager replied in Nature in 2023 that multivariate methods, which use whole patterns rather than testing each brain location separately, can be replicable at considerably more moderate sample sizes, so the field's current position is that the required sample depends heavily on the analysis strategy.

Effect size deserves separate attention from statistical significance, since with a large enough sample a trivially small difference becomes significant, and the question that matters is whether the difference is big enough to care about.

79.3.3 Reverse inference and construct validity checks

Reverse inference is reasoning backwards from observed brain activity to the mental process presumed to have caused it - "the amygdala was active, therefore the subject felt fear" - and Poldrack (2006) identified it as a logical fallacy, specifically the fallacy of affirming the consequent, since the amygdala also responds to novelty, salience, and ambiguity.

Poldrack's own position was not that reverse inference is worthless but that its strength is quantifiable: it is only as good as the selectivity of the region for that process, which can be estimated with Bayes' theorem given a large enough database of prior studies, and it is generally weak because most regions do many things.

This motivated his later work on cognitive ontology - the project, embodied in the Cognitive Atlas, of building an agreed vocabulary of mental processes, on the grounds that you cannot map function onto structure while the function terms themselves are inherited from folk psychology and defined inconsistently across laboratories.

Construct validity is the related question of whether your task actually measures the thing you named it after, and the honest checks are convergent (do two different tasks meant to measure the same construct correlate?) and discriminant (does your task fail to correlate with things it should not?).

Many well-known cognitive tasks perform poorly on these checks - the reliability of individual differences measured by classic conflict tasks such as the Stroop and flanker tasks is notoriously low, a point pressed by Hedge, Powell and Sumner (2018) in what they called the reliability paradox - and this is a live problem for any study trying to relate brain measures to individual differences.

79.3.4 Distinguishing established from provisional findings

A practical triage: treat a finding as established when it has been replicated by laboratories with no stake in it, using different methods, in different species or populations, and when its size is stable across replications.

Treat it as provisional when it rests on a single study, a single laboratory, a small sample, or a novel analysis pipeline, however elegant the theory it supports.

Useful signals of durability include preregistration, publicly available data and code, a registered report format (where the design is peer-reviewed and provisionally accepted before results are known, removing the incentive to reward positive findings), and the existence of a formal meta-analysis.

Useful warning signals include a very large effect from a very small sample, a result that conveniently confirms a fashionable theory, an analysis pipeline with many undocumented choices, and press coverage that outruns the paper.

The field has been reforming itself on this front since roughly 2011 - through preregistration, data sharing mandates, and journals adopting registered reports - and the reforms are real but incomplete, so the burden of triage still falls substantially on the reader.

79.4 A curated reading path

What follows is a route, not a bibliography, and the ordering is deliberate: broad textbook first, reference works second, theory third, and the current literature last, because the current literature is unreadable without the first three.

79.4.1 Introductory textbooks and their differing emphases

Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, by Bear, Connors and Paradiso, is the gentlest genuine entry point and is strongest on cellular and systems neuroscience explained slowly, with good illustrations and no assumed mathematics.

Neuroscience, edited by Purves and colleagues, covers similar ground at a slightly higher level and is notably strong on sensory and motor systems, and older editions are freely readable through the National Center for Biotechnology Information Bookshelf.

Cognitive Neuroscience: The Biology of the Mind, by Gazzaniga, Ivry and Mangun, is the standard undergraduate text for the material of this book specifically - attention, memory, language, executive control - and is organised by cognitive function rather than by anatomy.

Cognitive Psychology and Its Implications, by Anderson, and Ward's The Student's Guide to Cognitive Neuroscience are useful correctives, since a common failing among people who enter through neuroscience is weak grounding in the behavioural psychology that gives the brain data something to explain.

79.4.2 The reference handbooks and monographs

Principles of Neural Science, edited by Kandel and colleagues and now in its sixth edition (2021), is the field's standard reference, more than 1,600 pages, not designed to be read straight through but to be consulted, and its chapters are written by leading researchers in each area.

The Cognitive Neurosciences, edited by Gazzaniga and, in the sixth edition (MIT Press, 2020), by Poeppel, Mangun and Gazzaniga, is the corresponding handbook for this book's subject matter, a multi-author survey that is deliberately re-commissioned every several years so that successive editions document how the consensus shifted.

Beyond the handbooks, a small number of single-author monographs remain worth reading whole because they argue rather than survey - among them Luria's The Working Brain (1973) for clinical reasoning, Baddeley's Working Memory for a theory developed across decades, and Damasio's Descartes' Error (1994) for the emotion-and-decision argument, the last of which should be read as a stimulating hypothesis whose central experimental support, the somatic marker interpretation of the Iowa Gambling Task, remains disputed.

79.4.3 The theoretical and computational canon

Marr's Vision (1982) is the indispensable starting point, chiefly for its opening chapter distinguishing three levels of analysis - the computational (what problem is being solved and why), the algorithmic (what representation and procedure solve it), and the implementational (how neurons realise that procedure) - a framework still used daily forty years on.

Dayan and Abbott's Theoretical Neuroscience (MIT Press, 2001) is the standard graduate textbook of the mathematical side, covering neural encoding and decoding, network models, and plasticity, and it assumes calculus and linear algebra.

Rieke, Warland, de Ruyter van Steveninck and Bialek's Spikes: Exploring the Neural Code (1997) is the classic treatment of what information a spike train carries, and Rumelhart and McClelland's Parallel Distributed Processing volumes (1986) remain the readable origin of the connectionist tradition that modern deep learning descends from.

For the learning-theoretic strand, Sutton and Barto's Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (second edition, 2018) is the clearest route into the prediction-error framework that connects the Rescorla-Wagner model of animal conditioning (1972) to the dopamine findings of Schultz, Dayan and Montague (1997).

Friston's free-energy and predictive-processing writings belong here too, with the caveat stated plainly: the framework is mathematically ambitious and widely discussed, and critics argue it is difficult to falsify because it can be fitted to almost any observation, so read it as a research programme rather than as settled result.

79.4.4 Review series and the annual literature

Once the foundations are in place, reviews are the efficient way to stay current, because a good review compresses two hundred papers into thirty pages with an argument attached.

The Annual Review of Neuroscience, published since 1978, and the Annual Review of Psychology are the deepest and most carefully edited; Nature Reviews Neuroscience is the most prominent and generally the most accessible; Trends in Cognitive Sciences and Trends in Neurosciences publish short opinionated pieces that are excellent for seeing where disagreement lies; and Current Opinion in Neurobiology is useful for very recent, narrowly scoped surveys.

A practical routine for a learner is to pick two or three reviews a month in areas you care about, read them properly, and follow only the primary papers they make you curious about, rather than attempting to track journal tables of contents.

Preprint servers - bioRxiv for biology and PsyArXiv for psychology - now carry much of the field's output months before formal publication, which is valuable for currency and requires extra caution, since a preprint has not yet been peer-reviewed.

Finally, note that reviews are written by people with positions, so reading two reviews of the same topic by authors who disagree teaches more than reading either alone.

WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

Neuroscience is organised by societies, journals, conferences, and five-year grants, and those structures shape which questions get asked as much as any intellectual consideration does.

The big-money era of the 2010s, embodied in the BRAIN Initiative and the Human Brain Project, produced excellent tools, databases, and cell-type atlases while conspicuously failing to deliver the unified understanding its announcements promised, and the field's move to large multi-site consortia such as the Human Connectome Project, UK Biobank, the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, and ENIGMA is a direct response to the discovery that small samples yield unreliable results.

The practitioner's core skills are now anatomy and physiology, programming and statistics, formal modelling, and rigorous design, with computation having become a literacy rather than a specialisation.

Critical reading reduces to three questions - what was actually measured, is the sample large enough for the effect claimed, and does the causal language exceed the design - with reverse inference, identified by Poldrack in 2006, as the specific trap of reading a mental state off a brain map.

Genuine disagreements remain live, including how large a sample brain-wide association studies really require, whether deep networks explain or merely predict neural responses, and how much the free-energy framework can be falsified, and a careful reader should hold all three open.

The reading path offered here moves from an introductory textbook, through the Kandel and Gazzaniga reference handbooks, into the theoretical canon of Marr, Dayan and Abbott, and Sutton and Barto, and only then into the annual review literature.


CHAPTER 80. THE KONNECTOME PROGRAMME: MAPPING THIS OUTLINE ONTO THE FIFTEEN LAYERS (CONTEXT)

This final chapter is not about the brain.

It is about the filing system this book lives inside, and about what that filing system is for.

The konnectome repository of the Artificial Intelligence University (AIU) holds a body of source documents called the Certified_Neuroscientist corpus, and that corpus is organised not by anatomy and not by faculty but by scale, into fifteen encapsulated layers of abstraction running from the quark to the species.

This book is organised the other way, by cognitive capacity: perception, attention, memory, language, action, emotion, consciousness.

The two organisations describe the same nervous system, so they must be reconcilable, and this chapter performs the reconciliation.

The point of doing so is practical: a reader who wants to know where a claim in this book is grounded should be able to find the exact document, and a reader who wants to know what a document in the corpus is for should be able to find the capacity it explains.


80.1 The correspondence

The corpus's central claim, stated in its framework document THE FIFTEEN LAYERS IN BRIEF, is that the human nervous and endocrine systems span more than fifteen orders of magnitude and that this span is organised into exactly fifteen layers, each with its own components, its own governing laws, and its own vocabulary.

A layer of abstraction, in the engineering sense borrowed here, is a level of description that can be understood without knowing the internals of the levels above or below it, provided the interfaces between levels are respected.

The corpus adds a strong adjacency rule: ordinarily a layer communicates only with the layer directly above and the layer directly below.

It also concedes seven documented exceptions to that rule, called Layer-Skipping Channels, in which a signal travels intact across non-adjacent layers, and it argues that the exceptions follow an economic logic - biology pays the cost of layer-by-layer relay when a message needs an address, and refuses to pay it when the message is a broadcast.

The layers run: Layer 1 subatomic, Layer 2 atomic, Layer 3 ionic and simple molecular, Layer 4 macromolecular, Layer 5 subcellular and organellar, Layer 6 cellular, Layer 7 synaptic and junctional, Layer 8 microcircuit, Layer 9 brain regions and pathways, Layer 10 neural and neuroendocrine systems, Layer 11 the whole nervous and endocrine system, Layer 12 organism and behaviour, Layer 13 dyad and small group, Layer 14 community and society, Layer 15 evolution and species.

Layer 7 is singled out in the framework as the one relation-layer, because a synapse is built from parts owned by two different cells, so its strength belongs to the relationship rather than to either cell.

The mapping that follows aligns the fifteen Parts of this book with those fifteen layers.

It is a mapping, not an identity: several Parts touch several layers, and a few layers are touched by no Part at all.


80.1.1 Parts Two and Three of this outline against Layers 1 through 8, the substrate and microcircuit layers

Part Two of this book, The Substrate, and Part Three, Methods, together cover what the corpus files as Layers 1 through 8: the physics and chemistry, the macromolecules, the organelles, the cells, the synapses, and the canonical microcircuit motifs.

The corpus documents that territory in some detail: four files on Layers 4 and 5 as the slow variables, meaning the molecular machinery in which a learned weight is physically kept over hours and years; five files on Layer 6 including a catalogue of eighty-five non-neuronal cell types; a five-volume neuron catalogue; four files on Layer 7 covering sixty-four junction types; and four files on Layer 8 covering seventy-one canonical motifs.

Layers 1 through 3 are, by contrast, thin in the corpus, and honestly so, because for most cognitive questions the quark and the sodium ion are below the level at which explanation pays.

Part Three, Methods, does not correspond to a layer at all in the strict sense - it describes how a claim about any layer is made checkable - but its content is overwhelmingly about measuring the substrate layers, which is why it is grouped here.


80.1.2 Parts Five through Ten against Layers 9 through 11, the regions, systems, and global states

Parts Five through Ten of this book cover perception, attention, learning and memory, language, action and decision, and emotion, motivation and social cognition.

These are the capacities that live at the corpus's Layers 9, 10 and 11.

Layer 9 is the layer of named anatomical structure, whose unit is the region: a discrete, anatomically bounded piece of nervous tissue, or a discrete endocrine gland, that does an identifiable job by virtue of the microcircuits it contains and the connections it makes.

Layer 10 is the layer of the distributed system - the visual system, the motor system, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which is the hormonal stress circuit running from hypothalamus to pituitary gland to adrenal cortex - and the corpus catalogues forty-four such systems in seven groups, of which twenty-five are tagged as cognitive and nineteen as non-cognitive.

Layer 11 is the whole nervous and endocrine system considered as one integrated regulatory organ, and the corpus catalogues twenty-six global states and state-machinery constructs there, including sleep, arousal and the power states, calling Layer 11 the master mode register of the architecture.

The alignment is close but not one-to-one: a chapter here on visual object recognition draws on Layer 9 for the regions, Layer 10 for the ventral stream as a system, and Layer 11 for the arousal state that gates it.


80.1.3 Parts Eleven and Twelve against Layer 12, the faculty specification

Part Eleven treats consciousness, self and the inner life, and Part Twelve treats change, variation and origins - development, individual differences, and evolution of the capacities.

Both sit at Layer 12, the organism and behaviour layer: the behaving, experiencing person.

The corpus's Layer 12 document is titled LAYER_12_FACULTY_SPECIFICATION and its stated role is to hold the acceptance tests - that is, the list of things a complete system must be able to do, stated behaviourally rather than anatomically.

That framing is useful and slightly uncomfortable: it treats consciousness as something to be specified by what it licenses the organism to do, which is exactly the move that critics of functionalism reject, and this book does not pretend the dispute is settled.


80.1.4 Parts Thirteen through Fifteen against Layers 13 through 15, the tutor protocol, knowledge environment, and design method

Parts Thirteen, Fourteen and Fifteen of this book cover clinical failure and repair, cognition and machines, and integration and ethics.

The corpus files one konnectome-facing document at each of the top three layers: LAYER_13_TUTOR_PROTOCOL for the dyad, describing the training interaction between a teacher and a learner; LAYER_14_KNOWLEDGE_ENVIRONMENT for the community, describing the corpus and tool plan that a mind is embedded in; and LAYER_15_DESIGN_METHOD for the species layer, describing the iteration discipline by which the whole thing is revised.

The correspondence here is looser than at any other point in the mapping, and it should be admitted as such.

Layer 13 in nature is the dyad and the small group; the corpus's Layer 13 document is about how one teaches an artificial system, which is a dyad but a very particular one.

Layer 15 in nature is phylogeny and population; the corpus's Layer 15 document is about design iteration, which is evolution by another mechanism.

These are analogies doing real work, not measurements, and a reader should hold them more loosely than the substrate mappings.


80.2 What this outline supplies to the corpus

The corpus was built substrate-first, from the bottom up, because that is how the layer framework is constructed and because the lower layers are the ones with hard, uncontested facts in them.

That has a cost.

A substrate-first catalogue tells you everything about the hippocampus and nothing directly about remembering.

This book supplies four things the corpus did not have.


80.2.1 A cognition-first index over a substrate-first catalogue

An index, in the library sense, is a second ordering laid over a body of material that already has a first ordering.

The corpus is ordered by scale; this book is ordered by capacity; and because every chapter here names the structures it depends on, the book functions as an index that lets a reader enter by the question rather than by the scale.

Someone who asks how a skill becomes automatic can start at the relevant Part here and be routed to the Layer 8 motif files, the Layer 9 basal ganglia entries, and the Layer 10 motor system files, without needing to know in advance that those are the places to look.

That is a modest contribution in principle and a large one in practice, because the commonest failure of a large technical corpus is not that the answer is absent but that the reader cannot find it.


80.2.2 The (COG) and (NON-COG) tagging discipline extended to processes rather than structures

The corpus already tags its entries with two codes: (COG), meaning the entry participates in cognition by performing a computation that contributes to perception as interpreted, attention, memory, decision, or learning; and (NON-COG), meaning it serves a substrate or other role such as pure relay, motor execution, autonomic and endocrine regulation, early sensory filtering, or housekeeping.

Those tags are attached to things: to cell types, to junction types, to the seventy-one motifs, to the forty-four systems, to the twenty-six global states.

This book extends the same discipline to processes, asking of each capacity whether it is genuinely a cognitive operation or a substrate service dressed up in cognitive language.

The extension is where the tagging earns its keep, because the interesting disagreements in the field are almost never about whether a structure is cognitive but about whether a process is - whether, for example, early visual filtering is perception or preprocessing, a question on which the field remains split.


80.2.3 Explicit placement of the computational and oscillatory layers that the standard textbooks omit

Standard cognitive neuroscience textbooks tend to run from methods to perception to memory to consciousness, and to leave the formal material - the mathematics of neural coding, the dynamics of oscillation - either in an appendix or out entirely.

The corpus consulted these works directly, including Gazzaniga, Ivry and Mangun with Phelps and Bassett in 2024, Poeppel, Mangun and Gazzaniga's multi-author handbook in 2020, Banich and Compton in 2023, Ward in 2025, and Kandel and colleagues in 2021 for the substrate.

This book deliberately gives Part Four to analysis and theory, drawing on the computational canon - Dayan and Abbott in 2001, Gerstner, Kistler, Naud and Paninski in 2014, Sutton and Barto's second edition in 2018, and Parr, Pezzulo and Friston in 2022 - and on Buzsaki's work on brain rhythms from 2006.

The result is that the corpus now has an explicit home for two bodies of material that were previously scattered: the coding-and-decoding mathematics, and the oscillatory dynamics by which populations coordinate in time.


80.2.4 A falsifiability checklist attached to each theoretical claim

Falsifiability, in the sense Karl Popper gave the word, is the property of a claim that some observation could in principle refute it.

A large descriptive corpus drifts towards unfalsifiable statements almost by gravity, because it is easier to say that a region is involved in a function than to say what would show that it is not.

This book attaches to each theoretical claim the question of what evidence would count against it, and where a claim is genuinely contested it names both sides rather than presenting a winner.

That discipline is the reason several sub-sections here are shorter than a reader might expect: where nothing checkable can honestly be said, the honest length is short.


80.3 What the corpus supplies to this outline

The traffic runs the other way too, and in three respects the corpus is the senior partner.

Its standing rule, stated in its own README, is that its source documents are read and never edited, and that where a summary written elsewhere disagrees with a source document, the source document wins and the summary is the thing corrected.

This book is a summary in that sense, and is subordinate to the corpus on every question of fact about the biology.


80.3.1 Layer addresses for every structure named here

A layer address is the corpus's answer to the question of where a named thing sits in the fifteen-layer scheme.

Because the corpus assigns one, every structure named in this book can be given a coordinate: the perforant path and the fornix are Layer 9 interfaces, the alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor is a Layer 4 macromolecule, lateral inhibition is a Layer 8 motif, and the HPA axis is a Layer 10 system.

This matters more than it sounds, because a great many arguments in neuroscience are layer confusions in disguise, in which one party is making a claim about a molecule and the other a claim about a system, and neither notices.

Giving each term an address makes the confusion visible immediately.


80.3.2 The inside-out framing already adopted in the Layer 9 and Layer 11 volumes

The inside-out framing, associated with Gyorgy Buzsaki and set out at length in his 2019 book The Brain from Inside Out, holds that the brain does not sit passively waiting for stimuli to be pushed into it and converted to representations, but generates activity on its own account and discovers what that activity means by acting and observing the consequences.

The outside-in alternative, which dominated the twentieth century, treats the brain as a stimulus-to-response converter.

The corpus's upper-layer volumes lean inside-out in their organisation: Layer 9 defines a region by its connectional fingerprint, which is to say by what it receives and to whom it sends rather than by which stimulus excites it, and Layer 11 is built as a register of self-generated global states such as sleep and arousal rather than as a list of responses.

Two cautions are owed the reader.

The phrase inside-out does not appear as a slogan in those volumes; the framing is visible in how they are structured rather than declared in their text.

And the inside-out position is a live argument in the field, not a consensus, so a reader should treat it as the corpus's adopted stance rather than as settled fact.


80.3.3 The manuscript-and-companion workflow for turning outline entries into text

The corpus has a repeatable production method, and it is the most transferable thing in the repository.

Each layer gets an outline, then a manuscript written from that outline, then a modes companion - a separate document enumerating the operating regimes of each entry, with its mode register, its per-mode transfer function, its transition table, and its fault regimes.

A mode register, in this usage, is simply the list of distinct states a component can be in, borrowed from the way a hardware device advertises its settings.

There is also a standing chapter template, at version three, which acts as a schema that tooling can parse, so that every chapter's interface blocks and mode registers can be read by machine as well as by a person.

That template is why the corpus is more than a pile of prose: it is a pile of prose with a parseable spine.


80.4 Next steps

The outline this book expands ends with a plain statement of its own status: it is a skeleton, not a manuscript, and every Level 4 entry is a promise that something specific can be said.

The full structure is fifteen parts, eighty chapters, three hundred and thirty-two sections, and one thousand three hundred and twenty-five sub-sections.

Four pieces of work remain.


80.4.1 Expansion of each Part into a manuscript volume

The pattern already proven at Layers 4 through 11 is outline first, manuscript second, and it should be applied Part by Part here.

Fifteen Parts implies roughly fifteen volumes, which is the same order of magnitude as the corpus's existing thirty-nine source files, so the work is large but not unbounded.

The advantage of doing it Part by Part rather than chapter by chapter is that a Part is the smallest unit with a coherent subject matter, so each volume can be checked for internal consistency before the next begins.


80.4.2 A modes companion enumerating the operating regimes of each capacity

Every existing layer volume in the corpus has a modes companion, and this one does not yet.

The work is to ask of each cognitive capacity what its distinct operating regimes are - what attention looks like in focused, divided, and vigilant modes, what memory encoding looks like under stress and under rest - and to write each as a register with named transitions between modes and named fault states.

This is the sub-section of the four most likely to generate new claims rather than merely reorganise old ones, because the field describes capacities far more often than it describes the regimes those capacities switch between.


80.4.3 Cross-reference tables between chapters here and layer entries there

The mapping made in section 80.1 is prose, and prose does not scale.

What is needed is a table with one row per Level 4 sub-section, giving the layer or layers it depends on, the specific corpus files, and the entry names within them.

Such a table is mechanical to check and mechanical to maintain, which is the point: it converts the correspondence from an argument that must be reread into a fact that can be tested.

The corpus's README already warns that a pointer is not a statement, and that a file which moves must have every pointer to it moved with it, which is precisely the discipline such a table would need.


80.4.4 A verification pass attaching primary citations to every Level 4 entry

The last and least glamorous task is to walk all one thousand three hundred and twenty-five sub-sections and attach to each a primary citation, meaning the original report of the finding rather than a textbook's summary of it.

Where no such citation exists, the entry must be marked as unverified rather than quietly left to look established.

This is the step that separates a corpus from an encyclopedia of received opinion, and it is also the step most often skipped, because it is slow and it produces no new text.

It should be treated as a precondition for calling any volume finished.


WHAT THIS CHAPTER ESTABLISHED

This book and the konnectome corpus describe the same nervous system under two different orderings - by cognitive capacity here, by scale there - and the two can be aligned Part by Part onto the fifteen layers, tightly at the substrate end and only analogically at the social and evolutionary end.

The corpus supplies layer addresses, a connectional definition of regional identity, an inside-out leaning at the upper layers, and a repeatable outline-manuscript-companion workflow with a machine-parseable chapter template.

This book supplies a cognition-first index over that catalogue, an extension of the (COG) and (NON-COG) tagging discipline from structures to processes, an explicit home for the computational and oscillatory material the standard textbooks omit, and a falsifiability requirement on every theoretical claim.

Where the two disagree on biology, the corpus's source documents win, by its own Eighth Commandment.

What remains is four pieces of work: fifteen manuscript volumes, a modes companion for the capacities, mechanical cross-reference tables, and a citation pass over all one thousand three hundred and twenty-five sub-sections.


END OF MANUSCRIPT

This manuscript writes out all fifteen parts, eighty chapters, three hundred and thirty-two sections, and one thousand three hundred and twenty-five sub-sections of the companion outline.

Every line item was researched by web search before it was written.

Where the literature is divided, the text reports the division rather than picking a winner.

Where a finding is recent and not yet replicated, the text says so.

The companion outline is THE_NEUROSCIENCE_OF_COGNITION_OUTLINE.txt, in this same folder.
